en: The Greatness of Veṅkaṭācala: Nārada’s Vision of Yajñavarāha on the Summit of Mount Sumeru. In the purifying Naimiṣa forest, the great sages headed by Śaunaka performed a twelve-year sacrificial session (sattra) for the sake of protecting the world. (1)
To them came a great-minded narrator, a disciple of Vyāsa, a sage named Ugraśravas, born of Romaharṣaṇa.
Having been duly honored by them, that Sūta, the best of Paurāṇikas, narrated that divine Purāṇa named after Skanda.
He related in detail the accounts of creation, dissolution, and the lineages, as well as the genealogical histories and the periods of the Manvantaras.
Having heard the stories concerning the powers of the sacred fords, those eminent sages spoke to Sūta, the self-controlled one, out of a desire to hear further narratives.

The sages said: O Romaharṣaṇa, omniscient one, expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas! We wish to hear the majesty of the lords of mountains upon the surface of the earth. O highly fortunate one, tell us which mountains are the most prominent?
The venerable Sūta said: Formerly, on the bank of the Jāhnavī, I asked this very same question to Vyāsa, the most excellent among the best of sages; he, my supreme teacher, spoke to me.
Vyāsa said: O Sūta, in former times, during the age of the gods, Nārada, the best of sages, went to the peak of Mount Sumeru, which was beautifully adorned with various jewels.
In the midst of that, having seen the vast and radiant divine abode of Brahmā, one sees to its northern region an excellent Pippala tree.
It was one thousand yojanas in height and twice that in width; at its base was a divine pavilion endowed with various jewels.
It was adorned with thousands of ruby pillars, and featured rows of svastikas fashioned from lapis lazuli and pearl gems.
It was strewn with the nine gems, adorned with divine archways, and filled with auspicious beasts and birds made of the nine precious jewels.
The great gate of ruby, with its seven-storied gopura, was adorned with two well-fashioned door-panels of blazing vajra.
Having entered, that great sage beheld within a divine pavilion of pearls; he then ascended its lofty structure, which featured a pedestal of lapis lazuli.
In the midst of that, he beheld a lion-throne of great splendor, lofty and incomparable, adorned with eight feet and strewn with pearls. 15.
In its center was a divine lotus, adorned with a thousand petals, white with the luster of a thousand moons, and radiant with its pericarp and filaments.
Seated in its center was one who possessed the luster of ten thousand full moons, whose form was as beautiful as Mount Kailāsa, and who had the appearance of a man.
The Supreme Person, possessing four arms and noble limbs, with the auspicious face of a boar, bearing the conch, the discus, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
The god wearing yellow garments, with eyes as long as lotus petals, with a face as gentle as the full moon, and a lotus-mouth fragrant with the scent of incense.

He was the sound of the Sāman chants, the embodiment of sacrifice, with the sacrificial ladle as his beak and the offering spoon as his nose; he resembled the ocean of milk, his face radiant with a crown.
He had the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, was resplendent with a bright sacred thread, shone with the beauty of the Kaustubha gem, and possessed broad, elevated shoulders.
It was adorned with divine ornaments made of Jāmbūnada gold and excellent jewels, shining brilliantly like an autumnal cloud encircled by garlands of lightning.
He is eternally resplendent, adorned with a footstool stepped upon by the sole of his left foot, and shining with bracelets, armlets, neck-ornaments, and earrings.
He was being served day and night by the lords of sages, such as the four-faced Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and Mārkaṇḍeya, as well as by Bhṛgu and many others.
Having approached and prostrated before the Lord of the gods, who is served by Indra and the other world-protectors, as well as by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases; || 25 ||
Having praised the Supporter of the Earth with divine portions of the Upaniṣads, Nārada stood in the presence of the God, supremely delighted.
Now follows the arrival of the Earth into the presence of Varāha: In the meantime, there arose the sound of divine drums. (27)
Then the goddess Dharaṇī arrived, accompanied by her friends, resplendent in divine garments that had the appearance of an ocean of excellent jewels.
Bowed down by the weight of breasts shaped like Mount Sumeru-Mandara, she is dark-complexioned like a fresh blade of dūrvā grass and adorned with all ornaments. || 29 ||
Accompanied by her two friends, Ilā and Piṅgalā, she then [received] from them a great heap of flowers brought upon the earth.
Having scattered [the offerings] at the feet of the glorious Lord Varāha and having prostrated before the Lord of the gods of gods, she stood with her palms joined in reverence.
Śrī Varāha, having embraced that goddess and placed her upon his lap, [spoke].
Now follows the dialogue between the Earth and the Boar: with a mind inclined toward affection, he inquired after the welfare of the Earth.

The illustrious Varāha said: "O Goddess Earth, having established you upon the comfortable head of Śeṣa, and having settled the world and the mountains that support it within you, I have come here, O Goddess; for what purpose have you come here? (34)

The Earth said: "O Lord, having lifted me from Pātāla and placed me upon the head of Ananta—which is adorned with a thousand hoods, lofty like a jeweled pedestal, and set with gems—and having made me firmly stable by arranging the mountains [therein]," (35)

O Puruṣottama, tell me of those meritorious ones who are capable of upholding you, who are identical with you, and who, O mighty-armed one, are the foremost among them and have me as their support. (36)

Now follows the description of how Śeṣācala surpasses all other mountains. Śrī Varāha said: Sumeru, Himavat, Vindhya, Mandara, Gandhamādana, Sālagrāma, Citrakūṭa, Mālyavat, and Pāriyātraka—[these are the great mountains]. || 37 ||
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Siṃhādri, and Raivata; and the great mountain named Añjana, the son of Meru, which is composed of gold. (38)
O Vasundharā, all these excellent mountains are supported by you—those which have been frequented by me, by the hosts of gods, and by the hosts of sages. (39)
Among these, O Mādhavī, I shall describe the most excellent ones according to their true nature; listen: Sālagrāma, Siṃhādri, Śaileṃdra, and Gandhamādana. (40)
O Goddess, these excellent mountains, O Vasundharā, are situated in the Himavat direction; now I shall describe the well-known mountains of the southern quarter.
Aruṇādri, Hastiśaila, Gṛdhrādri, and Ghaṭikācala—all these excellent mountains are situated near the Kṣīranadī.
To the north of Hastiśaila, at a distance of exactly five yojanas, is the most excellent river among rivers, named Suvarṇamukharī.
On its northern bank is a lake named Kamala; on its shore dwells the Lord Hari, the granter of boons to Śuka.
Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of the suffering of his devotees, is united with Balabhadra and is constantly worshipped by the pure hosts of Vaikhānasa sages.

To the north of the lake named Kamalā, in a most excellent forest adorned with yellow sandalwood trees at a distance of only half of two krośas, there is the great abode of Vāsudeva known as Śrī Veṅkaṭācala.
O Goddess, there is a lord of mountains seven yojanas wide and one yojana high, composed of gold, extensive, and possessing peaks made of jewels.

O Earth, the hosts of deities headed by Indra, the lords of sages headed by Vasiṣṭha, the Siddhas, Sādhyas, Maruts, Dānavas, Daityas, Rākṣasas, and the throngs of Apsarases headed by Rambhā, dwell here eternally.
Nāgas, Garuḍas, and likewise Kinnaras perform penance there; presided over by them, the rivers there are of auspicious appearance. O Mādhavī, various divine lakes are also present here. (49)
Now follows the description of how Svāmipuṣkariṇī excels all other holy fords (tīrthas). Listen indeed to the most excellent [accounts] of all the sacred fords.
Cakratīrtha, Daivatīrtha, and likewise Viyadgaṅgā; Kumāradhārikātīrtha and Pāpanāśana; the Tīrtha named Pāṇḍava, and likewise Svāmipuṣkariṇī. || 51 ||
They say there are these seven excellent [tirthas] on the auspicious Nārāyaṇa mountain; among these, O Goddess, the auspicious Svāmipuṣkariṇī is the most preeminent.
I dwell together with you on its western bank; on its southern bank resides Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of the Universe.

In that ocean-clad land, that lake is equal to all the holy fords beginning with the Gaṅgā; O Earth, the Lordship over all the holy fords, lakes, and rivers that exist in the three worlds has been attained by the Svāmī Sarovara.
On that divine mountain, all sacred fords (tīrthas) dwell in order to serve the meritorious Svāmipuṣkariṇī; I shall tell you their number.
Sixty-six crores of holy fords exist on this meritorious, most excellent mountain; among them, O Vasundharā, six tīrthas are preeminent.
Among the five kings of sacred fords (tīrtharāja), Tumba is great like the womb; on this best of mountains, it destroys the fear of dwelling in a womb for those who have bathed there.

Dharaṇī said: "O mighty-armed one, six sacred fords (tīrthas) have been mentioned by you on this mountain. O supporter of the earth, tell me their majesty according to the proper time and according to the prescribed rite; tell me the fruits for those men who bathe in them."
The illustrious Varāha said: "O Mādhavī, listen; I shall speak of the majesty of Nārāyaṇādri."
The gods, the sages, and the yogins such as Sanaka and others [worshipped] Añjanādri in the Kṛta age, and likewise Nārāyaṇagiri in the Tretā age.
In the Dvāpara age they call it Siṃhaśaila, and in the Kali age, the learned here proclaim this mountain, Śrī Veṅkaṭācala, to be the abode of the Supreme Self.

Even if one has gone to another continent thousands of yojanas away, whoever bows with devotion toward the Lord of Mountains (the Himalaya) while facing that direction, being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
In that regard, I shall describe to you the greatness of the six sacred fords (ṣaṭtīrtha) according to their respective times.

Now, the majesty of Kumāradhārā: Listen attentively, O blessed lady, to this which destroys all sins. When the sun is situated in Aquarius (Kubha) during the month of Māgha, on the great lunar day of the full moon— || 64 ||
O Vasundharā, queen of mountains, on the day joined with the Maghā constellation, there is a lake named Kumāradhārikā, which purifies the world.
O stainless one, there dwells Kārttikeya, the son of Pārvatī, born from fire, accompanied by the divine army, and a worshipper of Śrīnivāsa.

Listen to the fruit of merit for one who bathes there at midday: O Mother of the World, he shall obtain that same fruit as one who bathes according to the rules at all sacred sites beginning with the Gaṅgā for twelve years. (67)
Whoever gives food at that sacred site, accompanied by a sacrificial fee according to their capacity, obtains as much fruit as has been described for the ritual bath.

Now, the majesty of Tuṃba-tīrtha: O Earth, when the sun is situated in Mānasa on the full-moon day, conjoined with the asterism Uttarā-phālgunī, at the fourth and most excellent watch of the day; || 69 ||
O Goddess, that man who bathes at Tuṃba, the cave of the mountain, which is the site of all five holy fords (tīrthas), is not born again in a womb.

Now, the majesty of Ākāśagaṅgā: When the sun is situated in the sign of Aries (Agnivāha) and conjoined with the constellation Citrā, on the meritorious lunar day known as the full moon, and likewise at the time of dawn—one who bathes in the river Ākāśagaṅgā shall attain liberation.

Now, the majesty of Pāṇḍavatīrtha: When the sun is situated in Taurus (Vṛṣabha) in the month of Rādha, on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) falling on a Sunday, whether in the bright or the dark fortnight, or when it coincides with a Tuesday.
Whether during the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, when it coincides with Sunday, or is joined with the Puṣya asterism, or even with the Hasta asterism; || 73 ||
The man who bathes at this sacred ford named Pāṇḍava during the time of conjunction (saṃgava) does not encounter suffering in this world and enjoys happiness in the next.

Now, the majesty of the Pāpanāśana Tīrtha: On the seventh lunar day (saptamī), whether in the bright or the dark fortnight, when it coincides with a Sunday, or is joined with the Puṣya asterism, or even with the Hasta asterism; || 75 ||
O highly fortunate one, on that lunar day known as Pāpanāśana, he who bathes according to the prescribed rules at that sacred ford on the summit of the lord of mountains—
That best of men is liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million births. || 77 ||

Now, regarding the majesty of Devatīrtha: Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret on the great mountain named Ananta, on a peak to the northwest of my divine abode within a mountain cave—a most beautiful lake renowned as Devatīrtha. (78)
O Goddess, I shall now tell you the time for bathing at that most meritorious place.
Listen to the meritorious fruit of him who bathes on these days: on Gurupuṣya, on Vyatīpāta, and likewise on Somaśravaṇaka. || 80 ||
Whatever sins there may be here, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly, they all perish at the exceedingly purifying Devatīrtha.
Merits also increase by bathing at the divine tirthas; one attains a long life endowed with sons and grandsons, and finally, having reached heaven, one is glorified in the world of the Moon. || 82 ||
O Goddess, one who gives food on those days shall be a giver of food for as long as he lives. O Vasundharā, this most profound secret has been told to you. 83.
Vyāsa said: Then, having heard this, the goddess Earth, her mind overflowing with affection, praised the Upholder of the Earth with incomparable and pleasing words.

Now follows the praise of Varāha by Dharaṇī. Dharaṇī said: "Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O Acyuta with the face of a boar! You who resemble the Ocean of Milk, whose tusks are like thunderbolts, and who possess mighty arms! (85)
O Lord Viṣṇu, at the beginning of the kalpa, I was lifted by you from the waters of the ocean with your thousand arms; I now sustain the worlds.
Resplendent with many divine ornaments and a sacred thread, wearing garments as red as the dawn and adorned with celestial jewels.
Salutations again and again to you whose lotus-feet resemble the rising sun; O you of great strength and prowess, whose tips of the fangs have the luster of the crescent moon! 88.
His limbs were smeared with divine sandalwood paste; he wore earrings of molten gold and was adorned with golden armlets that shone with sapphires.

O you who have split open the eyes of Hiraṇyākṣa with the tips of your adamantine fangs, O you of great strength; O you whose eyes are as beautiful as white lotuses, O you who are enchanting with the sound of the Sāman chants! 90.
O you who are the ornament upon the crest of the Vedas, O soul of all, O you of beautiful prowess, O long-eyed one saluted by the four-faced Brahmā and by Śambhu! 91.
O you whose form consists of all knowledge, who transcend all sound, salutations, salutations! O infinite one whose body is bliss, the death of Death, salutations, salutations! (92)
Having praised him thus, the goddess Acalā bowed at the feet of the Lord; and as she was bowing, the God, his eyes blossoming with joy, gazed intently upon her.
Having lifted up the goddess Earth, he then embraced her with his arms; having smelled the face of Earth and placed her upon his left lap, [he gazed at her].

Now follows the arrival of the Blessed Varāha with the Earth at Śeṣācala: Having mounted Garuḍeśāna, the Lord of the Earth went to Vṛṣabhācala while being praised by the lords of sages, Nārada and others. (95)

On the western bank of Svāmipuṣkariṇī, which is honored by the world, there dwells the Boar-faced One, worshipped there by the lords of sages—by the highly fortunate Vaikhānasas, those great-souled ones who are equal to Brahmā. || 96 ||
Now follows the occasion for hearing the majesty of Veṅkaṭācala. Vyāsa said: Having seen him, Nārada formerly spoke to the sages; that very thing I heard there indeed in the assembly of sages. (97)
O Sūta, that greatness of the mountains which you asked me about has been truly related by me exactly as I heard it previously from Nārada. (98)

Now follows the declaration of the fruit of this chapter: O Sūta, whoever shall read this purifying dialogue on dharma between us, either before the gods or likewise in the presence of Brāhmaṇas; || 99 ||
For all castes who listen with devotion, he attains firm establishment, accompanied by sons and grandsons.
Whatever is desired by all those who hear it, that shall come to pass.
Sūta said: Thus the blessed Vyāsa, who is served by sages, spoke to me; exactly as it was previously heard by me from my teacher Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
"O lords of sages, everything here has been spoken by me exactly so. Having heard these words of Sūta, they became delighted in their minds. (103)

The sages said: O Sūta, you have described to us the greatness of the holy mountain Mahīndra, which dwells upon the earth among the sacred mountains; it is the destroyer of sins and the bestower of the fruit of liberation.
Then, having reached Vṛṣādri together with Dharaṇī, what did Varāha say to Dharaṇī? Tell us that, O high-minded one. (105)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of Nārada’s Attainment of the Vision of Yajñavarāha on the Summit of Mount Sumeru," in the dialogue between Dharaṇī and Varāha within the *Śrīveṅkaṭācala-māhātmya*, in the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrīskanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now follows the procedure for the worship of the Śrī Varāha mantra. The venerable Sūta said: "Listen, all you sages, to this ancient and meritorious narrative, which occurred formerly in the Vaivasvata Manvantara, during the most auspicious Kṛta Yuga."
On Mount Nārāyaṇa, Dharaṇī, surrounded by her companions, [beheld] the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign of the Earth, the Divine One dwelling there in the form of a Boar. || 2 ||
Having prostrated, he questioned him whose eyes were as long as red lotuses.
Dharaṇī said: "By what mantra are you to be propitiated so that you will be pleased? O Lord of Gods, tell me that which is always dear to you. (4)
For those who recite it, it brings about all prosperity, bestows sons and grandsons, grants the status of a universal monarch, and always fulfills the desires of those who long for them.
O Varāha, O giver of honor, tell me with affection who it was that formerly bestowed the attainment of your own state upon those of self-restraint.
The venerable Sūta said: Thus questioned by the Earth, he spoke with a face beaming with a smile of affection.
Śrī Varāha said: Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret which brings about immediate prosperity; it bestows land and sons, and must be kept hidden and never revealed.
Moreover, it should be spoken to one who is desirous of hearing, who is devoted, and whose self is disciplined.
Oṃ, salutation to the illustrious Varāha and to the upholder of the Earth; joined with the wife of fire (svāhā), this mantra should always be recited by those seeking liberation. 10.
O Goddess Dharā, this mantra bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). Saṃkarṣaṇa is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and I myself am indeed its deity.
The meter is declared to be Paṅkti, and the seed-syllable is proclaimed to be Śrī. Having received that mantra from a true guru, one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times.
One should indeed offer oblations of milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter. Now, I shall describe the meditation that bestows purity of mind. (13)
Resembling a mountain of pure crystal, with eyes like the petals of a red lotus, he has the face of a boar, is gentle, possesses four arms, and wears a crown.

O You whose garment is the ocean, [I meditate upon Him] who has the Śrīvatsa on His chest, whose lotus-hands hold the discus, the conch, and the gesture of fearlessness, and who is joined by You, seated upon His left thigh.
Wearing red and yellow garments and adorned with red ornaments, he is seated upon a lotus that rests on the form of Śeṣa, who is situated in the middle of the back of the auspicious tortoise.
Having meditated thus, one should always recite the mantra one hundred and eight times; one attains all desires and shall certainly attain liberation at the end.
"O Dharaṇī, O stainless one, that which I was asked by you has been told by me to you. Therefore, tell me, O lady of pure countenance, what is it that you have resolved? (18)

Now follows the description of the attainment of one's desired goals through the *Śrī Varāha-mantra* for Dharma and others. Śrī Sūta said: Having heard this, the Earth then questioned him once again: "O Lord, by whom was this performed in the past, and what fruit was obtained? (19)
Thus questioned, the divine Lord Śrī Varāha spoke this again: "O Goddess, formerly in the Kṛta Yuga, there was a great Manu named Dharma."
Having received this mantra from Brahmā and having chanted it on this mountain, and having seen me and obtained a boon, he attained my own abode.
O Goddess, in ancient times Indra was cast down from heaven due to the curse of Durvāsas; by worshipping me here with this [rite], he regained heaven once again.
Other sages as well, O Earth, have attained the supreme goal after chanting this; indeed, Ananta, the lord of serpents, obtained it from Kaśyapa.
Having chanted [this] in Śvetadvīpa, he indeed became the supporter of the earth; therefore, it should always be chanted here by men who desire the earth.
Śrī Sūta said: Having heard this, she was well-pleased and spoke again to the Supporter of the Earth.
Dharaṇī said: "O Lord of Devas, when will Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of the Universe, the stainless one, come to the great mountain named Veṅkaṭa accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi? (26)
"How will Janārdana remain for another kalpa? Tell me this, O you who have taken the form of a boar; I have a great curiosity. (27)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Worship of the Śrī Varāha Mantra and Other Matters," in the Dialogue between Dharaṇī and Varāha within the *Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya*, in the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now follows the description of how the Blessed One became visible to the sight of all people at the request of Agastya. Śrī Varāha said: "Behold, O fair-faced one, I shall relate to you an ancient account; listen, O Great Goddess, to this meritorious narrative together with its future events and its conclusion."

O sinless goddess, in the previous Kṛta Yuga within the Vaivasvata Manvantara, having beheld the great penance of Vāyu, Śrīnivāsa, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, came to the bank of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
In this most meritorious celestial mansion named Ānanda, situated to the south, Hari—the beloved of Śrī and the one who does what is pleasing to Vāyu—shall dwell.
From that time forward, Hṛṣīkeśa, propitiated by the commander of the army, shall dwell unseen within this celestial chariot until the end of the kalpa.
Dharaṇī said: "How will the Blessed One, who is invisible to mortals, become visible?"
"Even Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of Gods, stays at your right side; tell me, O Sovereign of the Suras, how is he worshipped by people?"
Śrī Varāha said: Having arrived here, Agastya beheld the eternal Lord; having worshipped Him for twelve years, he gratified Him again and again.
There he requested your presence, saying, "May you become visible. Thus addressed, O Earth, Hṛṣīkeśa appeared together with Śrī and Bhūmi.
The Blessed Lord said: "For your sake, I shall become visible to all embodied beings; however, O celestial sage, this celestial chariot shall never be visible."
"O Lord of Sages, I shall be visible here until the end of the kalpa; of this there is no doubt. Having heard those words, the sage was delighted and departed for his own hermitage.
Then that four-armed god became visible to men and others, seated upon this celestial chariot (vimāna) which is inconceivable even to sages, and likewise seated in the north.
Being propitiated by Skanda and constantly attended by Vāyu, thus passed a great length of time consisting of four yugas.

Now follows the description of the birth of the son of Mitravarmā, named Ākāśarāja. When the twenty-eighth [Dvāpara] had arrived at its end, O Vasundharā, and after the Bhārata war was over, during the Tiṣya age; || 13 ||
O fair-faced one, kings such as Vikramārka, as well as Śakas, Śūdras, and others, shall go to the heavenly world even without knowing me. (14)
Then there was the great chariot-warrior Mitravarmā, born of the lunar dynasty, who resided in Nārāyaṇapura within the district of Tuṇḍīra.
O lady of beautiful hips, there will arise a great emergence of supreme fortune while that lord of the earth rules the world of mortals with righteousness. (16)
The earth yielded crops without being ploughed, adorned with all kinds of grain; the entire population became free from calamity and endowed with righteousness.
His wife was the charming Pāṇḍyakanyā; to him was born a son named Viyat, who was indeed the ornament of his lineage.
His wife was named Dharaṇī, born of the Śaka lineage; having entrusted the kingdom to her, Mitravarmā, the best of kings, [departed]. 19.
He went to the holy penance grove in the vicinity of Mount Veṅkaṭa.

Now follows the account of Padmāvatī’s birth from the surface of the earth. There was once a great king named Ākāśa, a sovereign ruler of the whole world; he was devoted to the vow of monogamy, and his mind was fixed upon the earth. (21)
For the sake of the sacrifice, he purified the earth from the banks of the Āraṇī; as the surface of the earth was being ploughed with a golden ploughshare, [he found the bones].
As he was scattering handfuls of seed, a maiden was seen rising from the earth—beautiful, reclining upon a bed of lotuses, and endowed with all auspicious marks. (23)
Shining like a small image made of molten gold, the king, upon seeing it, had his eyes wide with wonder.
Taking her and saying repeatedly, "She is indeed my own daughter," he rejoiced; and then an incorporeal voice spoke to him through his ministers.
"It is true; she is indeed your daughter; raise Sulocanā. Then, with a joyful heart, the king entered his own city.
Having summoned Queen Dharaṇī, the lord of the earth said this to her: "Behold this Devadattā, who has arisen from the surface of the earth for me."
"Since we two are childless, this will certainly become our daughter," having said this, King Viyat affectionately placed [the child] into the hands of the Goddess. (28)

Now, the birth of the son named Vasudāna occurred from the wife of Ākāśarāja, who was named Dharaṇī. When she had entered the inner apartments, Dharaṇī conceived a child; and King Viyat, seeing her with her affectionate eyes, was greatly pleased. (29)
The fair-browed woman said, "That creeper of mine, which yields the fruit of peace, has borne fruit."

Then, in due time, that goddess Dharaṇī, whose eyes were like lotuses, gave birth to a son at an auspicious moment when five planets were in their positions of exaltation and the sun was situated in Aries.
On that day of his birth, celestial drums resounded, a rain of flowers fell upon the house, and a breeze of pleasant touch blew.
Highly pleased at the birth of his son, he bestowed all his possessions as a gift upon those who had announced the birth of the son, with the exception of the royal umbrella and the fly-whisk.

On the auspicious twelfth day, he performed the birth rites and other ceremonies, including the gift of ten million tawny cows and more than a hundred bulls; and he himself bestowed the name Vasudāna upon him.
Śrī Varāha said: O Goddess, the son of Ākāśa, Vasudāna, who was enchanting to the mind, grew day by day like the lord of stars [the moon] during the bright fortnight. (35)
Having been initiated and disciplined by his gurus who had reached the further shore of the Vedas, he too learned his father’s missiles and weapons along with their mantras.
He studied the science of archery (dhanurveda) in its four divisions, along with its limbs and sub-limbs; by virtue of that, his father became exceedingly powerful and invincible to his enemies.
Like the cloudless sky in summer joined with the sun, he was as difficult to endure and difficult to look upon as the midday of the month of Vaiśākha.

Now follows the arrival of Nārada near Padmāvatī, who was dwelling in the garden. Dharaṇī said: "The Lord has mentioned the name of that son of Viyat; what name did he then give to his daughter, who was not born from a womb? (1)
The illustrious Sūta said: Thus questioned, the illustrious Varāha, the Lord of the Universe, spoke again.
Śrī Varāha said: The wise Ākāśarāja, having seen her reclining upon the lotus, [was struck with wonder].
And he indeed gave the daughter of the Earth the name Padminī; and when she was endowed with youth, she was surrounded by her female companions.
And as she was dwelling in the grove resounding with the songs of parrots and cuckoos, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived there by chance.
Beholding her like the very goddess of the forest's splendor, he spoke this out of wonder: || 6 ||
Nārada said: "Who are you? Whose daughter are you, O timid one? Show me your hand. Thus addressed, she of the beautiful limbs spoke of herself to the sage: || 7 ||
"O Brahman, daughter of the King of Mountains, tell me the auspicious marks," she said; thus addressed, Nārada, the best of sages, then spoke.

Then [followed] the physical characteristics of Padmāvatī as uttered by Nārada. Nārada said: "Listen, O lady of beautiful countenance; I shall describe the characteristics to you. Your two feet, O fair-browed one, are well-settled and endowed with the petals of red lotuses."
The toes are even and reddish, endowed with red, elevated nails; both ankles are well-concealed and symmetrical, and the shanks are auspicious and hairless.
The knees are even and very smooth; the thighs are symmetrical, with the upper thighs gradually tapering; the hips are broad and fleshy, and the loins are indeed to be meditated upon.
Your navel is circular and deep, both your sides are fleshy, and your waist is charming with its three folds and adorned by a line of body hair.

Your breasts are full, firm, smooth, elevated, with deeply set nipples; your hands have the luster of red lotuses and are marked with lotus designs; they possess very slender, perfectly red fingers that are even and without gaps between the joints.
O auspicious lady, your long and tender arms are adorned with rows of nails shaped like parrot beaks, resembling flower-stalks. (14)
Your back shines like a sacrificial altar, with a straight and well-proportioned waist; O auspicious one, your neck is red and long, and your shoulders are gracefully sloped.
His face was ever serene, with a luster like that of the stainless moon; his cheeks were like mirrors of gold, radiant with earrings.
O lady of beautiful countenance, your nose has the form of a sesame flower; it is exceedingly charming, resembling the stainless moon of the eighth day.
This forehead of yours is seen, beautifully adorned with dark locks of hair; your head is perfectly rounded and endowed with smooth, long tresses. (18)
"With your face graced by a smile revealing your teeth and endowed with lips as red as the *bimba* fruit, it is my firm conviction that you are worthy of Viṣṇu. (19)
At your navel is a clockwise whorl like a whirlpool born of the Ganges; for you appear like Lakṣmī herself, arisen from the Ocean of Milk. (20)
The illustrious Varāha said: Having spoken thus and being worshipped by them, Nārada then vanished. Upon hearing this, her friends then spoke to their friend Padminī.

Then Padmāvatī went to the flower forest together with her own female companions: "Let us go to the forest for the sake of flowers; spring has arrived. There are karṇikāra trees, mango trees, campaka trees, and pāribhadraka trees. (22)
Palāśa, pāṭala, and kunda trees were in bloom, as were red aśoka trees; there were lotus ponds, sindhuvāra, mālatī, and yūthikā creepers. || 23 ||
The white water-lilies and karavīra flowers have blossomed as if from mutual emulation; let us gather these flowers in this most enchanting forest. (24)
Having spoken thus, they went to the forest accompanied by the daughter of Ākāśa, wandering here and there while gathering flowers.
They beheld a certain lordly elephant, resplendent with its two white tusks, and radiant with two streams of ichor flowing from the surface of its broad cheeks.
It was lofty, accompanied by herds of female elephants, radiant with dust, and its faces were filled with sprays of water rising from the trumpeting trunks.
Seeing this, their hearts filled with agitation, they took refuge under a great tree; in that interval, they quickly beheld an excellent horse.

Then follows Śrīnivāsa’s arrival at the Puṣpāṭavī forest for the purpose of hunting: It was as white as the spotless moon, adorned with gold, and lofty like an autumnal cloud accompanied by flickering streaks of lightning. (29)
In that [dream], however, he saw a dark man whose splendor was like that of the god of love, with eyes as long as reaching to his ears and shaped like the petals of a white lotus.
Resplendent with a dark-blue crest-cloth covered in very fine silk, and adorned with earrings shimmering with the luster of ruby gems.
He held the divine bow Śārṅga, inlaid with gold and jewels, and with his other hand he carried a golden arrow.
His waist was well-proportioned and draped with a yellow silken garment; he was resplendent with jeweled bracelets, armlets, and a girdle.
His broad chest was graced by a beautiful clockwise curl, and his shoulders were radiant with a golden sacred thread, making him truly captivating.
Having seen that deer being pursued with great speed, the women stood there indeed, filled with wonder and smiling.
Seeing him mounted upon the horse, the lordly elephant, with its head bowed, raised its trunk and trumpeting loudly, turned away and fled into the forest.
When that elephant had departed from there, he arrived on horseback near the flower-gatherer, searching for the spotted deer.
Then there was a conversation between the Blessed One and the maidens. Having come together, he, seated upon his horse, said to them: "A certain deer has arrived here; it is called an *īhāmṛga*. (38)
"Or have you seen him? Tell me, O maidens. (39)
Śrī Varāha said: Those maidens replied to him, "No one at all has been seen by us."
"For what purpose have you come to our forest, O wielder of an excellent bow? All the deer dwelling here, O leader of the Niṣādas, are not to be slain."
"Go quickly from this forest protected by King Ākāśa. Having heard these words of theirs, he dismounted from his horse. (42)
"Who are you, and who is this lotus-like maiden—so fortunate, with all her limbs beautiful and her breasts full and elevated? Tell me, and having heard it, I shall go to my own mountain home. (43)
Having heard these words of hers, the friend Padmāvatī, urged by Dharaṇyātmajā, spoke to the Niṣāda Parvatālaya.
O hero, our heroine, born from the surface of the earth, is the daughter of King Ākāśa; she is known by the name Padminī. (45)

"Tell us, O one of auspicious form: what is your name, whose son are you? What is your caste, where is your dwelling, and for what purpose have you come here? Thus questioned, he replied to them with a gentle smile upon his lotus-like face. (46)
Those who know the past declare that our lineage is the family of Divākara; its names are infinite and purify the wise.
Ascetics describe him as Kṛṣṇa both by his complexion and by his name; he whose discus brings fear to the enemies of the gods who hate the Brahmins. 48.
Upon hearing the sound of whose conch his enemies indeed fell into a swoon; and among even the immortals, there was no bow at all equal to his own bow.
They call me Vīrapati, the dweller on the Veṅkaṭa mountain; therefore, from that mountain slope, I am surrounded by my followers, the Niṣādas.
Mounted on a horse for the sake of hunting, he came to your forest; pursued by me, a certain deer fled with the speed of the wind. (51)
Not seeing him, while looking at the forest, I saw this beautiful woman; drawn by desire, I have come here to you—can she indeed be obtained by me? (52)

Having heard these words of Kṛṣṇa, they became enraged and spoke again: "Once the King of Ākāśa sees you and has bound you with fetters, he will lead you away; therefore, go quickly to your own abode. (53)
Thus threatened by them, he mounted his swift-moving horse and, accompanied by all his followers, departed most rapidly for the mountain.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Nārada’s Arrival at the Hermitage of Padmāvatī and the Hunt of Śrīnivāsa," in the dialogue between Dharaṇī and Varāha within the *Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya*, in the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now follows the attainment of delusion by Śrīnivāsa upon seeing Padmāvatī. Śrī Varāha said: Having reached the divine abode and descended from his excellent horse, he dismissed all the gods who were in the form of Kairātas, along with their followers. || 1 ||
Having said, "Rest yourselves," he ascended the jeweled stairs, passed through five inner chambers, and entered the jeweled pavilion.
Having reached that beautiful palace of pearls, Hari helplessly lay down upon a couch made of nine precious gems that swayed gently.
He recollected her alone, whose luster was like the interior of a lotus, with long eyes, a slender waist, full breasts, and a face like a lotus made beautiful by a gentle smile.
The Lord Śrīnivāsa regarded that auspicious woman, born from the lotus, as none other than the daughter of the Ocean of Milk; with his mind fixed upon her, he became infatuated.

Then follows the speech of Bakulamālikā to Śrīnivāsa, who was becoming bewildered: "Then, at the time of midday, having prepared divine and excellent food—fragrant, accompanied by side dishes, worthy of the God, and most beautiful—" (6)
Having prepared pure rice, milk-rice, rice with jaggery, and rice with mung beans, as well as five kinds of cakes, including *pūrikās* and *vaṭakas*.
To see the god, the friend Vakulamālikā went quickly, accompanied by Padmāvatī, whose eyes were like lotus petals, and Citrarekhā.
Having stationed all those excellent women at the door of the god, Bakulamālikā herself entered into his presence.
Having approached the presence of the god, he paid homage with a spirit of devotion; then, seeing the god on a gem-ornamented couch, he was rendered helpless.
Having massaged his feet, she of the pure smile spoke something to him as he meditated with his eyes closed.
"Arise, O Lord of the gods; why do you lie down, O Supreme Person? O God, supreme food has been prepared; come to eat it, O Mādhava. (12)
Why do you lie here like one afflicted, O destroyer of the suffering of all the world? O Lord, what have you seen in the forest while wandering on the hunt?
O large-eyed one, your state appears like that of a lover; what [woman] have you seen—a celestial maiden, a human woman, or a daughter of the Nāgas? (14)
Tell me, O you of inconceivable nature, about that girl who has stolen my heart.
Śrī Varāha said: Having heard those words of hers, the Lord heaved a sigh. As he was sighing, Bakulamālikā, being pleased, spoke to him again.
"O Supreme Person, who is that Manoharā of yours? Hṛṣīkeśa said to him: "I shall tell you; listen to the truth. (17)

Now, the reasons for the marriage of Padmāvatī as told by Śrīnivāsa. The Blessed Lord said: "In former times, during the meritorious Tretā Yuga, I slew Rāvaṇa; at that time, the maiden Vedavatī rendered assistance to Śrī. (18)
Lakṣmī herself appeared in the form of Sītā from the earth of Janaka; yet, when I had departed for the Pañcavaṭī forest to slay Mārīca, [she remained there].
My younger brother also followed me, urged on by Sītā; meanwhile, the lord of the Rākṣasas arrived to carry off Sītā.
The fire residing in the *agnihotra* sacrifice, having learned of Rāvaṇa’s endeavor, took Sītā and placed her within Svāhā in the netherworld (*pātāla*).
In order to destroy Rāvaṇa once again, [he brought back] that auspicious Vedavatī, who had been touched by that very same Rākṣasa in the past and had cast off her body into the fire.
Having created an image identical in form to Sītā, he indeed released it; that [image], having been carried off by Rāvaṇa, was established in Laṅkā.
After Rāvaṇa had been slain, she entered the fire once again; the Fire-god [declared], "Jānakī is my own Lakṣmī, protected by Svāhā. || 24 ||
And placing his hand upon me, he said to my friend who was with Sītā: "O Lord, this Vedavatī is a well-wisher of Sītā. (25)
For the sake of Sītā, she has been held captive by him in the city of the Rākṣasas; therefore, please her with a boon along with Śrī.
Having heard these words of Agni, the auspicious Sītā said to me: "O Lord, this Vedavatī has always been dear to me. (27)
Therefore, O Lord, choose this divine Bhāgavatī as your supreme [consort].
The Blessed Lord said: "O Goddess, it shall be so; indeed, in the twenty-eighth Kali age, let her dwell in the world of Brahmā, honored by the immortals, for that duration."
"However, later the daughter of the Earth shall become the daughter of the Sky. Thus were boons previously granted by me to Lakṣmī and to Sundarī.
Today, born from the surface of the earth in the city of Nārāyaṇa, she is a virtuous woman equal to Padmā, lotus-eyed, and one to whom a boon was granted by Padma.
Gathering flowers in the forest with her suitable companions, that charming woman was seen there by me while I was wandering on a hunt. (32)
Her form cannot be described by me even in a hundred years; yet today, my union with her shall take place, as if with Lakṣmī herself.
"Understand this as a certainty: the vital breaths shall become stable. (34)

Now follows Bakulamālikā’s journey toward the city of Viyadrāja. "O Bakulamālikā, having gone there and seen that maiden, find out whether she is indeed suitable for him in terms of her beauty, charm, and other qualities; she is faultless, large-eyed, with eyes like the lotus and the blue water-lily. (35)
Having spoken thus, Bakulā spoke again to him who had fallen into a state of delusion: "O Lord of Gods, I shall go from here to where that charming woman of yours is. (36)
"Tell me the way, O Lord of Ramā, by which I shall go toward her. Thus addressed, the Lord of Ramā spoke to her regarding the *vakula* garland.
Go from here, O illustrious lady, to where the cave of Śrī Nṛsiṃha is located; descend from this delightful king of mountains by that path.
Having reached the hermitage of Agastya and seen that worshipped Liṅga known as Agastyeśa on the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī, [he performed worship]. (39)
Then proceed along the very bank to the forest of the brahmin-sage Śuka, beholding there the Svarṇamukharī river garlanded with waves.
There, a purifying lake named Padmasaras abounded with lotuses; having bathed there, [he beheld] the best of sages performing austerities on its bank.
Having paid homage to Chāyāśuka and Kṛṣṇa together with Bala, who were being constantly propitiated by the sage Śuka, O auspicious lady, [he entered].
Balabhadra, dark as a sapphire gem, clad in pure yellow garments, and possessing a fair complexion, was about to depart on a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
And having bowed down to Balabhadra, who was reciting mantras with his two hands joined in release (mudrā), rising up, and equipped with sandals; || 44 ||
O lady of beautiful countenance, having taken a golden lotus from this lake and having crossed the Suvarṇamukharī river, [traverse] the forests and groves.
Having reached the bank of the Araṇī and rested within the forest, you will behold the city of Nārāyaṇa and be filled with wonder.
And in her grove were trees rich with flowers and laden with fruit—jackfruit, mango, śirīṣa, kunda, tinduka, and pāṭala trees.
Punnāgas, excellent nāgas, rasālas, aṅkolakas, and campakas; bakulas, āmalakas, sāl trees, tālas, hiṃtālas, and padmakas. || 48 ||
Jambu, nimba, kadamba, elā, pippalī, madhuka, arjuna, priyaṅgu, hiṅgu, kharjūra, māyūra, aśoka, and lodhra—[these trees he planted]. 49.
The Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, Badarī, Bhūrja, Kīcaka, Ciñcā, Kiṃśuka, Mandāra, Śālmali, and Bījapūraka trees.
[He saw] forests crowded with betel-nut, mango, breadfruit, and coconut trees, and filled with jasmine, Arabian jasmine, kunda, yūthikā, and ketakī flowers.
Abounding with *karavīra* and lotuses, graced by royal plantains, and teeming with peacocks, parrots, garuḍas, parrots, and cranes.
On the riverbank, she beheld most beautiful groves, dense with the humming of bees, and having seen them, she attained supreme joy.
Having gone by way of the north-eastern path to the city equal to Indra’s city, which was eternally encircled by the Gaṅgā, as if by a river of flowing water; 54.
Having gone to the city of Ākāśarāja, do there what is appropriate.
Śrī Varāha said: Having thus instructed his companion named Bakulā, the lord of the gods dismissed her; accompanied by Śrī, he lay down upon a white bed.
Having bowed to the Lord of the gods of gods, her friend Bakulamālikā mounted a red horse that resembled a guñjā berry in color.
She proceeded along the path as described, beholding various wild animals, and intoxicated elephants resembling mountains, adorned with white tusks. (58)
He saw lions, resembling white clouds, intent on seizing female elephants who were accompanied by their herds, and followed by troops of lionesses.
Tigers, bears, rhinoceroses, śarabhas, gavayas, black antelopes, jackals, hares, and priyakas as well.
He saw cranes and peacocks, wild cats, wolves, parrots, boars, and likewise sweet-voiced birds.
Beholding various forms and delighting again and again, she reached the western bank of the Araṇī river, which was crowded with trees.
Having dismounted from his ruddy horse near Agastyeśa, he beheld the Agastyeśvara Liṅga, which had been well-worshipped by Agastya.
Having bathed and drunk there, he rested upon the riverbank.

Then follows Bakulamālikā’s speech to the friends of Padmāvatī residing in the celestial garden: "Having arrived there from Rājagṛha in the presence of the god, those women saw the friends of Padmālayā. (65)
Having gone near them, she asked about the rumor.
Bakulamālikā said: "Who are you women, tell me, adorned with such wonderful ornaments and garlands? From where have you come here, O fair-faced ones, and what is your purpose?"
Having heard her words, they then spoke with a smile: "Listen attentively, O Goddess; we shall now speak."

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Śrīnivāsa’s Attainment of Infatuation upon Seeing Padmāvatī," in the *Śrīveṅkaṭācala-māhātmya*, within the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrīskanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Dharaṇī and Varāha.

Now follows the account of Padmāvatī as reported by her friend to Bakulamālikā. The women said: "We are the women residing in the inner apartments of King Ākāśa; we are the friends of the daughter of the lord of the earth, Padmālayā."
Placing the princess at their head, they had previously gone into the forest, busily engaged in gathering flowers for the sake of the princess.
Seated there at the foot of a tree, we beheld a person who was dark as a sapphire and whose chest was the abode of Indirā.
With a face graced by a gentle smile, possessing two beautiful, full, and long arms, wearing polished yellow garments, and radiant with a golden bow and arrows.
Seeing him adorned with a golden crown and necklaces, armlets, and other ornaments, his lotus-eyed friend Padmālayā gazed upon him.
"Look, look! He has the appearance of molten gold," she said. Even as we were looking, he quickly vanished from sight.
Then that friend, having fainted, was led by us to Rājagṛha.

Then, concerning Padmāvatī, Viyadrāja’s inquiry to the astrologer and so forth: Having seen his daughter unwell, the king questioned the examiner of destiny: "O best of Brahmins, O sage, tell me the results of the planetary movements for my daughter. (8)
O best of kings, the Brahmin, who was equal to Bṛhaspati, having reflected upon the planets in his own soul, declared: "All the planets are favorable for your daughter."
"But, O King, the results of planetary positions are sometimes somewhat misleading. Having reflected upon the time of the inquiry, the wise man spoke to him again: (10)
Having multiplied the shadow and examined the results of that [calculation] for the ascendant, [one finds that] the Moon is in the ascendant as its lord, and Jupiter is in a quadrant. || 11 ||
The day-bird indeed sleeps, while the night-bird has gone to the kingdom; hear, O King, the fruit of this: there will surely be well-being.
A certain supreme person has arrived for the sake of the maiden; seeing him, my daughter will faint, for she shall unite with him in yoga.
A certain maiden, sent by him alone, will come; whatever word she speaks will be for your benefit.
Therefore, O Great King, do this; I speak the truth, the absolute truth. Moreover, it bestows all goals and destroys all diseases. (15)
I shall tell you; perform today that which will bring happiness to your daughter. Have the consecration of the Agastya-liṅga performed by Brāhmaṇas.
Having been addressed thus, Daivacintaka then went home to the king. || 17 ||

Then, according to the words of the astrologer, for the purpose of worshipping the Agastya-liṅga, Ākāśarāja summoned Vedic Brahmins and, having honored them, commanded: "O twice-born ones, go to the temple. (18)
"Perform the great consecration of Śambhu preceded by mantras. Having thus instructed them, he summoned us and spoke, O auspicious lady. (19)
"O maidens, prepare the requisites for the great consecration! Thus commanded by the king himself, we went to the temple. (20)
"Tell us plainly, O blessed lady, the reason for your arrival; from where have you come, for what purpose do you belong to whom, and where indeed do you wish to go? (21)
Having mounted this divine horse, you have come as if from the world of the gods.
Śrī Varāha said: Thus questioned by them at that time, the delighted Bakulamālikā spoke these sweet words, as if gladdening the young girls.
Bakulamālikā said: "I am Bakulamālikā by name, arrived from Śrī Veṅkaṭādri; desiring to see the earth, I have mounted this horse. (24)
"Would it be possible to see the goddess there in the king's palace? Having heard her words, those princesses said: || 25 ||
"O auspicious lady, you shall indeed behold the earth together with us. Having been addressed thus by them, she then went to the king's palace.
As they were thus approaching, the Earth [spoke] to Pulindinī.

Now follows Pulindinī’s reply to the question posed by Dharaṇī: She saw her approaching on the street, adorned with guñjā berries and conch shells, having tied a suckling infant to her back with the hem of her garment.
"I speak the truth; listen to what has been, what is, and what will be," she said, calling out to her as she walked along the streets with a pure smile. (29)
Having taken a golden winnowing basket and placed pearls within it, he made three heaps measuring three *prasthas* each and set them before her.
"Speak the truth—whether concerning the future or the past. Thus did the goddess Earth stand, questioning her.
Being questioned thus, she said: "Tell me honestly, O auspicious one, what was intended by her mind; tell me what you have thought regarding the middle heap."
"Om," said Dharaṇī, the beloved of the king, to Pulindā. Dharaṇī said: "The heap has been mentioned; tell me its fruit, and I shall give you a heap of wealth. (33)
The Pulinda said: "I tell you the truth, O fair-browed one; give me food for my child. Having been addressed thus, Dharaṇī took up food in a golden vessel.
Having given it to that Pulindinī, she said, "Tell the truth. Then that beautiful woman, taking food with milk, gave it to her son. (35)
The fair-browed woman spoke the truth: "O timid one, this withering of my daughter's body has come from that man; it is because of not seeing his form. (36)
For she had fallen into a fever of longing, tormented by the arrows of the bodiless god; then that very God of gods himself arrived from Vaikuṇṭha.
On the peak of Śrī Veṅkaṭādri, on the bank of Svāmipuṣkariṇī, the Lord of Ramā, the master of illusion and supreme bliss, dwells together with Śrī.
Hari, who dwells assuming any form at will and bestows the desires of his devotees, was wandering within the forest, mounted upon his horse. (39)
O Queen, having come to the grove, he beheld your daughter; seeing her who was equal to Lakṣmī, he himself fell under the sway of desire.
The Lord will send his own friend Lalitā to her side; having approached him, she will sport happily with him for a long time, just like Rameśvarī.
"This is my truthful word; see for yourself this very day, O princess! Give food to your son," she said, and Pulindinī remained silent. (42)
Having given her abundant food once more, he dismissed her; and when that blameless Pulindī had departed, [he remained].
Rising from that courtyard, he entered the auspicious inner apartments where the maiden Padmālayā sat, surrounded by her own female companions.
Having gone near her daughter, she said to the maiden who was afflicted by desire: "Daughter, what shall I do for you? Or what object is dear to you, O auspicious one? (45)
Thus questioned by her mother, that wise woman spoke softly.

Then Padmāvatī was informed of the characteristics of the Blessed One and his devotees: "That which is pleasing to the eyes in this world, which is dear to the minds of the virtuous, which Brahmā and the other gods desire to behold, and which is all-pervading and great. (47)
The most radiant among all radiant things, the deity even among deities—he is to be attained here by the virtuous who are devoted, but never by those who are not devoted.
O Mother, my mind here is directed toward that very object; let that alone, O Mother, be sought after, for it grants all desires to those who are devoted. (49)
Śrī Varāha said: Having heard this, Dharaṇī then questioned her daughter again: "O fair-eyed one, tell me the characteristics of his devotees, by attaining which [state] that [Bhagavān] is reached."
Padmālayā said: O Mother Vasundharā, listen with a concentrated mind to the secret characteristics of devotees: they are always marked on both arms with the conch and the discus. (51)
The vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with its central space is especially for them; furthermore, others likewise wear twelve marks (puṇḍras).
On the forehead, the belly, the heart, the throat, as well as on the abdomen and the two sides, on the two elbows, the pair of arms, on the back, and on the nape of the neck. (53)
The twelve names beginning with Keśava correspond to the twelve limbs; they bear "Vāsudeva" upon their heads, saying, "Let there be salutation."
O Mother, listen as I describe their delightful observances: those devoted to the complete recitation of the Vedas perform the Vedic rites. (55)
O Goddess, those who speak the truth, who never feel malice toward others, who do not engage in the censure of others, and who do not seize the property of others; || 56 ||
Know those to be Vaiṣṇavas who never remember, look upon, or touch the wives of others, even if they are beautiful. || 57 ||
Know these indeed to be devotees who possess compassion for all beings, who are devoted to the welfare of all beings, and who always sing the praises of the Lord of Gods. 58.
Know those devotees to be Vaiṣṇavas who are content with whatever they have, who are devoted to their own wives, and who are free from passion, fear, and anger. 59.
Endowed with such qualities, even those who bear the five weapons [may be initiated] by their father, or by a preceptor, or by another learned person.
Having taken up the fire according to the procedure prescribed in his own Gṛhya-sūtra, the wise man should offer sixteen oblations with the mantra of the discus and other weapons.
Then, with the root mantra and the Puruṣasūkta, and thereafter with the excellent Jātavedas mantra, one should perform [the oblation] one hundred and eight times.

Having offered oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, the wise one should heat the discus and other [emblems] there; once they are well-heated and bearable, the preceptor should have the disciple wear them while reciting the mantra.
In his two arms, he should hold a conch and a discus; likewise, the Śārṅga bow and arrows on his head; the mace should be borne on his forehead, and the sword indeed upon his heart.
Thus, these five alone should be worn by those devoted to Viṣṇu who seek liberation; or else, the discus and conch with auspicious marks should be borne on the two arms.
Thus, those devotees who are endowed with these marks are known as Vaiṣṇavas; by them alone, when possessed of virtuous conduct, is that Brahman to be attained.
In Him alone is my delight; my mind yearns for the attainment of Him. O Mother, no desire whatsoever arises in me for anyone other than Viṣṇu.
I remember the dark-complexioned Viṣṇu; I speak of Hari, the infallible. By him alone, O Mother, I live; therefore, let the means for union with him be considered.
Śrī Varāha said: Having spoken thus to her mother, the lotus-faced woman, distressed, fell silent. Hearing that, Viṣṇu reflected: "How may he become pleased? (69)

Then follows the arrival of Bakulamālikā along with her friends at the presence of Dharaṇī. In the meantime, having worshipped Agastyeśa, the maiden arrived together with Bakulasraj to see Dharaṇī. (70)
Then, having honored the arrived brāhmaṇas with excellent food and having given them full sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) accompanied by garments and ornaments, [she spoke].
Then, having caused the benedictions to be recited for the fulfillment of his desired object, he dismissed all the Brahmins and questioned his own wives.
Having worshipped Agastyeśa, those wise women returned.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of Devotion to Viṣṇu and the Account of Padmāvatī as Reported by Her Friends to Bakulamālikā," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Dharaṇī and Varāha. || 6 ||

Then, having been informed by Bakulamālikā of the news concerning Śrīnivāsa, Dharaṇī spoke. Dharaṇī said: "Who indeed is this excellent maiden who has come into contact with you? From where has she come, and for what purpose has she arrived here? To me, she appears worthy of worship. (1)
The maidens said: "This divine lady, a goddess, has come to you for the sake of a certain purpose; she was encountered by us in the temple in the presence of Śiva. (2)
When questioned, he said: "I have indeed come only to see you; can I, O Queen, see you with ease in the royal palace? (3)
Being thus questioned, we then replied: "Please proceed together with us; however, we, the female slaves of the earth, shall go to the king's palace."
"O Vasundharā, having been addressed thus by us, she has come into your presence; let her be questioned by you as to why she has arrived. (5)
The illustrious Varāha said: Having heard these words of theirs, Vasundharā questioned her.
Dharaṇī said: "O Goddess, from where have you come, and what service may I perform for you? Tell me the truth; I shall carry out the purpose of your arrival. (7)
Bakulamālikā said: "I am Bakulamālikā by name, who has come from the Veṅkaṭa mountain."
Our Lord Nārāyaṇa resides on the glorious Veṅkaṭācala mountain; once, having mounted a horse as white as a swan and as swift as thought...
Having gone out for the sake of hunting near Mount Veṅkaṭādri, he roamed through the forests at a beautiful time, the season of flowers.
Within the forest, he beheld deer, elephants, lions, gavayas, śarabhas, ruru deer, parrots, pigeons, swans, and other birds.
There, the best of gods followed a certain king of elephants, a leader of the herd shedding rut-fluid, who was tall and accompanied by female elephants.

Then, at the word of Śrīnivāsa, King Śaṅkha performed penance at Svāmitīrtha. Having gone from forest to forest, he approached King Śaṅkha, who was performing penance on the Bṛhacchaila mountain after having installed Janārdana there. (13)
And [he saw] a most purifying and excellent lake named Śaṅkhanāgabila, where [the Lord] was being constantly worshipped with devotion along with Śrī and Bhūmi.
Having reached the shore of that lake and dismounted from his horse, he assumed the attire of a king and questioned that best of monarchs.
"O best of kings, what is being done here at the foot of this king of serpents? (16)
Śaṅkha said: I am the son of King Śveta from the Haihaya country; for the pleasure of Mahāviṣṇu, I have performed all the sacrifices here.
"O Prince, because of not seeing Mahāviṣṇu, I was despondent; at that moment, a divine voice, which destroys all suffering, spoke. (18)
"O King, I shall not be present here; listen to my words clearly: go to Nārāyaṇādri and perform penance. (19)
Then, having abandoned my country, I shall propitiate the Lord through austerity, after having installed here the inconceivable God, the Lord of Śrī.
"By the grace of Agastya, I worship [him] daily according to the prescribed rites. Having heard these words of his, the Lord spoke to him with a touch of irony: ||| 21 ||
"Go to Nārāyaṇādri; why do you remain at its foot? Having ascended by this path, [you will see him] situated on the western peak."
Having bowed to Viṣvaksena, you, from the foot of the banyan tree, went to Svāmipuṣkariṇī and bathed there on the western bank.
"O son of a king, you will see an *aśvattha* tree there and an anthill; having reached the space between those two, perform penance"—thus he urged him. (24)
"A certain white boar certainly roams in this anthill; O King, he comes into the sight of only those who possess merit. (25)
Śrī Varāha said: Having thus given these instructions, the Lord mounted his horse and went out on a hunt; wandering from forest to forest, O fair-browed one, he reached the river Araṇī.

Having dismounted from his horse, he wandered there upon the auspicious bank; a breeze, cool with lotuses and *kahlāra* lilies, having come from the edge of the forest, gently attended upon Puruṣottama, removing his fatigue.
The trees, scattering showers of flowers, attended upon him; thus did that god wander among the trees bent low under the weight of blossoms.
While searching for that king of elephants, he beheld flower-gathering maidens, beautifully dressed and radiant, like flashes of lightning amidst the clouds. (29)
In their midst, he beheld a slender woman, exceedingly captivating, equal to Lakṣmī and golden-hued; his mind became fixed upon her.
Desirous of her, that man said to those maidens, "Who is this? Being thus addressed by them, he replied, "This maiden belongs to King Viyat, who is possessed of great strength."
Having heard these words of theirs, the powerful Lord mounted his horse and quickly returned to his own beautiful abode on the mountain.
Having reached his own residence there on the bank of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī, the Lord summoned me and said, "O Bakulamālikā! (33)
O friend, having gone to Viyadrājapura and entered the inner apartments, you shall find his wife Dharaṇī and inquire after her welfare.
"Ask for his daughter Rucirā, whose abode is the lotus; having ascertained the king's consent, O beautiful woman, return quickly. (35)
"Thus commanded by destiny, O Queen, I have come to your house; now do what is appropriate here, together with the king and his ministers. (36)
Then, having resolved upon the marriage through the words of Bakulamālikā and after the girl herself had reflected, let a reply be spoken. (37)
Śrī Varāha said: Then, having heard her words, the queen became truly delighted; she summoned Ākāśarāja and approached that abode of Kamalā.
In the midst of the ministers, Queen Bakulasraj spoke these words. Having heard them, the king, being pleased, addressed the ministers along with the family priest. (39)
Ākāśarāja said: "The maiden is not born of a womb; she is divine, fortunate, and dwells in a lotus. She has been requested by the God of gods, the resident of Veṅkaṭādri. (40)
"Today my heart's desire is fulfilled; tell me, what is agreeable to you? Having heard these excellent words of the king, all the ministers [replied]. (41)
With hearts full of joy, they said to King Viyadrāja, the lord of the earth: "O Indra among kings, we have achieved our purpose; may your lineage become preeminent above all. (42)
"This incomparable daughter of yours shall sport together with Śrī; let her be given to the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the Supreme Self. (43)
This is the glorious spring; let auspicious rites be performed quickly. || 44 ||
Then, according to the words of Bṛhaspati, the determination of the auspicious moment for the marriage was made: "Having summoned Dhiṣaṇa, let the auspicious moment for the marriage be fixed. (45)
Saying "So be it," he summoned Bṛhaspati from the world of the gods; the lord of men questioned him regarding the marriage of the maiden and the groom. (46)
The king said: "The birth constellation of the maiden is remembered as Mṛgaśīrṣa, while that of the god is Śravaṇa; let the conjunction of these two be considered. (47)
Having heard this, Dhiṣaṇa said: "The star Uttaraphalgunī is esteemed by astrologers as conducive to the increase of happiness for those two. (48)
"Let their marriage be performed under the constellation Uttaraphalgunī; let it be done according to the prescribed rites during the month of Vaiśākha," he said. || 49 ||
Śrī Varāha said: Then the king, having honored Dhiṣaṇa there and dismissed him, spoke to the goddess’s messenger: "Go to the temple of the god, O auspicious one. (50)
"O lady of virtuous vows, speak auspicious words to the God of gods during the month of Vaiśākha; having performed the marriage rites, please come here. (51)
Then, having dispatched the parrot as a messenger to do what was pleasing to the Goddess along with her, she sent Vāyu, her own son, to bring Indra and the other gods.

Now follows the sequence of the decoration of the city performed by Viśvakarman and others: Having summoned Viśvakarman for the work of decorating the city, he appointed him; and he, in turn, completed it within the blink of an eye.
Indra released a rain of flowers and hosts of Apsaras danced; Kubera filled that residence with wealth, grain, and other riches.
Yama made the men on earth free from disease, while Varuṇa filled them with collections of jewels, such as pearls and the like.
Having thus prepared everything, the gods went to Vṛṣācala.

Then follows the journey of Bakulā together with Śuka to the vicinity of Śrīnivāsa. Śrī Varāha said: Then, having mounted her horse, she went accompanied by Śuka; reaching the Śrī Veṅkaṭādri mountain, she arrived near the temple. (57)
Descending from her horse, she entered the interior with the parrot; there she beheld the beautiful-eyed Lord upon his jeweled throne together with Śrī.
Having bowed down, she spoke with joy: "O Lord, the task there has indeed been accomplished; this parrot has arrived to tell me the auspicious news. (59)

Now follows the account of Padmāvatī’s marriage as reported by Śuka to Śrīnivāsa. Commanded by the Lord to speak, Śuka bowed to him and said. Śuka said: "The daughter of the Earth said to you: 'O Mādhava, accept me.'"
I utter your names and I ever remember your form; your emblems are worn upon my arms and other limbs, O Lord of Ramā. (61)
"I worship your devotees here, endowed with the five sacraments; indeed, O Madhusūdana, I perform these actions for your pleasure. (62)
"O Lord of Gods, O Mādhava, show me favor; accept me, who have always acted in this manner with the permission of my parents. (63)
Thus did the daughter of the Earth, seated upon a lotus, make her request; for Hari, having heard Śuka’s words, found them exceedingly dear to himself.

Now, regarding Padmāvatī’s wearing of the auspicious garland bestowed by Śuka: The Blessed Lord said: "I shall come with the immortals to perform the auspicious wedding. O Śuka, go and tell her this: 'Thus the Lord has spoken. (65)
Having heard the words of the god and taking the forest garland given by the god, Śuka went quickly toward the daughter of Viyadrāja.
Having offered a garland of *tulasī* fragrant with musk and having prostrated before the Goddess, Śuka spoke these auspicious words, which were like the speech of a god: (67)
Having heard that, the daughter of the earth took the garland and placed it upon her head; desiring the arrival of the god, she adorned herself with appropriate ornaments.
King Viyadrāja also, joyfully and respectfully addressing Indu, said: "O King, let various kinds of food, endowed with all flavors, be prepared. (69)
Let that supreme rice-offering (paramānna) which is fit for Viṣṇu’s sacrificial food be prepared; it is highly esteemed by the gods, the sages, and even by men.
"O Moon, rich in four kinds of fragrances and possessing nectar-like rays—having thus made these preparations, await the arrival of the Lord. (71)
In the assembly hall, the king sat with a delighted mind together with his ministers, having adorned his daughter and being accompanied by Dharaṇī.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of Śrīnivāsa’s Arrival, Kamalālayā’s Auspicious Wedding, and Other Events as Narrated by Bakulamālikā to Goddess Dharaṇī," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Dharaṇī and Varāha.

Now follows the description of the marriage-ornaments prepared by Lakṣmī and others for Śrīnivāsa. Śrī Varāha said: Then the God of gods, having summoned the beautiful Lakṣmī, said: "O auspicious one, O fair-eyed lady, tell me what must be done for the sake of the wedding."
"Command me, O friend Rame; perform this dear task. Having heard Kṛṣṇa’s words, Śrī summoned her friends and urged them.
Then, commanded by Śrī, Prīti took fragrant oil; Śruti, taking a linen garment, stood in the presence of the God.
Taking up the ornaments, Smṛti also arrived with joy; Dhṛti held up a mirror, and Śānti applied musk-paste.
Taking up yakṣakardama unguent, Hrī stood before Hari; Kīrti held a golden fillet and a crown set with jewels.
Indrāṇī held the umbrella, while Sarasvatī held a chowrie; Gaurī held the second chowrie, and Vijayā and Jayā held the two fans.
Seeing that they had arrived, Śrī then rose up quickly, took fragrant oil, and anointed the Lord from his head downwards.
Having rubbed the body of the deity with fragrant powders after performing the ritual rubbing (udvartana), he brought one hundred golden water-pitchers carried by elephants.
Taking one by one from sacred bathing places such as the celestial Gaṅgā, [water] scented with camphor and other fragrances, Ramā consecrated Hari.
Having fumigated his hair with incense, he bound those locks which had become dark; and having anointed the body of that Lord with fragrant, gold-colored [unguents], he adorned him.
Having tied a yellow silken garment around her waist, adorned with a girdle, Indirā further decorated her with ornaments such as a crown.
And she showed the jewel rings on all her fingers to Dhṛti in the presence of the god.
Having seen the mirror, the God of gods himself applied the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra); thereafter, he himself, accompanied by Lakṣmī, mounted Garuḍa.

Now follows the journey of Śrīnivāsa to the city of Viyadrāja together with Brahmā and the others: "He was served by Brahmā, Īśa, Vajrin, Varuṇa, Yama, and Yakṣeśa, as well as by the lords of sages such as Vasiṣṭha, and by yogins such as Sanaka and the rest. (14)
Accompanied by his devoted bhāgavatas, he went to the city of Nārāyaṇa; the lords of the gandharvas sang and the hosts of apsaras danced. || 15 ||
Then the celestial drums resounded in the presence of the god; and the sages, chanting hymns of auspiciousness, followed after him.

The god, accompanied by hosts of deities and his attendants headed by Viṣvaksena, joined by his female companions Bakulā and others seated in their chariots, reached the well-adorned city of Ākāśarāja.
Now begins the section on the marriage with Padmāvatī: Having seen that the Lord had arrived, the maiden, seated upon Airāvata, circumambulated the city and reached the gateway of the gate-tower.
Having beheld him, Ākāśarāja also brought the bride and groom together and stood with his kinsmen, gazing upon the god Keśava.
Viṣṇu, smiling, took the garland from his own neck with his hand and placed it upon the shoulder of Kamalā as a collection of beautiful flowers.
Taking a garland of jasmine flowers, she placed it around his neck; having done this three times, they both descended from their vehicle.
Having stayed for a moment on the throne, the daughter of the earth and Hari then entered their auspicious abode together with the hosts of gods led by Brahmā. || 22 ||

Having caused the birth of the lotus-born Brahmā to perform the marriage rites, beginning with the binding of the auspicious thread and ending with the offering of parched grain (lājā-homa), he performed the rite of presenting the sprouts.
Having understood the instruction for the vow, the lotus-born Brahmā and Hari slept; then, on the fourth day, the four-faced one completed everything.
Having taken leave of King Viyat and having placed Hari upon Garuḍa, he set out with the gods to go toward the Lord who was accompanied by his two consorts.
Having reached Mount Vṛṣabha amidst the resounding blasts of divine drums, the hosts of deities headed by Brahmā praised the Lord of the gods.
Śuka and the other hosts of sages praised Puruṣottama; then, being thus lauded, the Lord entered the jeweled pavilion.
And with Ramā and Dharaṇijā, he went there to the lion-throne. || 28 ||

Then Ākāśarāja, together with the gods such as Mahendra and others, prepared to present gifts for the sake of pleasing his daughter and Viṣṇu, including the offerings bestowed by Vidyādhararāja upon the bride and groom.
In golden cauldrons there were grains of śāli rice, numerous vessels of mung beans, and hundreds of jars of clarified butter.
Thousands of water-jars, numerous vessels of curd, and divine fruits such as mangoes, plantains, and coconuts. (31)
[He gave] wood-apples, pumpkins, and plantains, as well as jackfruits and citron fruits, along with jars filled with sugar.
Gold, jewels, and pearls; millions of silken garments; thousands upon thousands of male and female slaves; and likewise tens of millions of cows.
He gave ten thousand horses, white as swans and the moon, and more than a hundred elephants that were lofty and perpetually in rut.
He gave four thousand women from his inner apartments, who were experts in dance and song, to Viṣṇu, the dweller of Śrī; and having given all these things, the Lord stood before the god.
Then, by the grace of Śrīnivāsa, Viyadrāja obtained the boon of devotion; and having witnessed all of that, Lord Hari, together with his two consorts, [bestowed it]. (36)
Being well-pleased, Veṅkaṭeśvara said to the king, his father-in-law: "O King, O Guru, choose from me whatever boon you desire. (37)
Having heard these words of Śiva, Viyadrāja said to the Lord: "O God, may my service to you alone be thus constant and unswerving in this world. (38)
May my mind be fixed upon the lotus-feet of Your Honor, and may I possess devotion toward You. || 39 ||
The Blessed Lord said: "O Indra among kings, all that you have spoken shall come to pass. Having thus granted him the boon and honored him as was fitting, [he departed]. (40)

Then, having duly honored all the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Īśa, Hari joyfully permitted them to return to their own worlds. When they had all departed, he, united with Śrī and Bhūmijā, [proceeded]. (41)
Dwelling as before on the bank of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī, the Lord remained in his divine abode, being worshipped indeed by Guha.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Śrīnivāsa’s Journey to the City of King Viyat along with Brahmā and the Others, and His Marriage to Kamalālayā," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Dharaṇī and Varāha.

Now follows the account of the Niṣāda named Vasu. Dharaṇī said: "O beloved, by whom will you be seen on this earth during the Kali age? O God, by whom will a celestial chariot be fashioned for you upon this mountain?"
"By whom indeed will Śrīnivāsa, whose form is so auspicious, be seen? Tell me this out of affection, O Lord; I have a great curiosity to hear it. (2)
The illustrious Varāha said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall tell you what will happen in the future; on this meritorious mountain, there dwells a Niṣāda named Vasu.
There was a keeper of the Śyāmāka forest who was devoted to Puruṣottama; having cooked grains of Śyāmāka rice and sprinkled them with honey, [he offered them]. || 4 ||
Having thus offered [the oblation] to the God of gods, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, his auspicious wife Citravatī, who was likewise full of devotion, [did the same].
The young woman gave birth to an excellent son named Vīra; Vasu, together with his son and his wife who was devoted to her husband, [dwelt there].
On a certain day, having sent his son away with the command, "Protect the millet," he departed with his wife, intent upon searching for honey.
The boy quickly went into the middle of the forest with the desire to see the honey-umbrella tree; having gathered ripe *śyāmāka* grains, he placed them in the fire.
Having ground it, he offered it at the foot of the tree to the Lord of Śrī; and having consumed that food offering, the hero indeed remained there in great comfort.
In the meantime, Vasu also arrived, bringing honey; seeing that the śyāmāka grains had been eaten, he rebuked his son.
Taking up his sword, he raised his hand in haste to strike him down.

Then, as Vasu was intent on killing his son, the Blessed One spoke; at that time, Viṣṇu, staying upon that tree, seized a sword with his hand. Looking about to see by whom the sword had been taken, he beheld the tree.
Having abandoned that sword, Vasu, whose body was half-climbed upon a tree, bowed down to Keśava, who held a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and spoke.
O Lord of the gods, what is this deed that is being performed by you?
The Blessed Lord said: O Vasu, listen to my words; your son is devoted to me, and he is even dearer to me than you, which is why he has come before my very eyes.
"I shall remain here for him everywhere on the shore of your master's lake. Having heard these words of the god, Vasu became filled with joy.
At that very time, however, there arrived from the Pāṇḍya country a Śūdra who, though born as such, had been endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu since his childhood.
