Now follows Raṅgadāsa’s journey to Śrī Śeṣācala for the sake of serving Śrīnivāsa: Having reached Nārāyaṇapurī and having prostrated before Śrī Varāha, he heard there that Śrīnivāsa was residing on Veṅkaṭādri. (18)
Then he went to the Self-born One (Svayaṃbhū), who is served by the gods of gods; having reached the Suvarṇamukharī river, he bathed and ascended its bank.
And having bathed in the merit-bestowing lake named Kamalā, [he beheld] the god Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Rāma, residing on its bank.
Having paid his respects, he then proceeded toward the forest filled with herds of elephants; gradually reaching Śeṣādri, he beheld a mountain stream.
Having approached that vicinity, one finds Śiva worshipped by Kapilā; before him is the Cakratīrtha, which is unfathomable and destructive of sins.
Having bathed there, he then proceeded very slowly toward Veṅkaṭādri; while traveling on the way to worship [the Lord], he was accompanied by a Vaikhānasa.
Then Raṅgadāsa, a boy of twelve years, having bathed at Svāmipuṣkariṇī, ascended [the mountain] while filled with devotion.
It was worshipped by the Vaikhānasa sage Gopīnātha at the foot of a tree in the middle of the forest, on the bank of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
He beheld Hari, the lotus-eyed one, standing together with Śrī and Bhūmi, situated in the sky, auspicious, and possessing a yellowish-blue form.
He was attended by the conch and discus situated at his sides, as well as by the mace and sword; and with his wings spread out in the sky like a canopy over the head of the God.
And [he saw] Garuḍeśāna stationed there, as well as the Śārṅga bow and the arrow behind him.

Now, regarding the construction of the divine gardens, pavilions, and other structures made by Raṅgadāsa for the sake of Śrīnivāsa: Having thus seen Śrīnivāsa, Raṅgadāsa was filled with wonder and thought, "I shall create a garden for this Lord. (29)
Having resolved everything in his mind, the wise one dwelt at the foot of a tree, offering oblations to Viṣṇu in the form of Vaikhānasa every single day.
Gradually cutting through the formidable forest, he felled the trees standing at its edge, including the *ciñcā* tree belonging to the Lord and the *campaka* tree belonging to Ramā.
Commanded by the god, he avoided those two areas frequented by the deity and then constructed stone walls on the ground all around the god.
He indeed established flower gardens all around that very wall, containing jasmine, oleander, lotus, kunda, mandāra, and mālatī flowers.
He indeed created groves of Tulasī and Campaka trees; having dug a well there, he caused the forest to flourish with its waters.
Then, having gathered flowers from the grove, she herself fashioned various garlands; having tied them, she placed them into the hand of the worshipper. (35)
Taking them, the worshipper bound them upon his shoulder and on his head for the sake of the Lord Śrīnivāsa, together with Śrī and Bhūmi.
Thus, performing service for the Lord, the noble-minded one remained there; as he continued in this manner, seventy years passed by.
While the high-souled Raṅgadāsa was engaged in gathering flowers, || 38 ||

Then, due to witnessing the play of the Gandharvas, Raṅgadāsa forgot his service to the Lord. A certain Gandharva arrived at the garden lake to bathe, accompanied by youthful daughters of the Gandharva king. (39)
Having stationed his celestial chariot in the sky, he engaged in water-sports together with beautiful women, sporting in a lotus pond.
Beholding this, Śrī Raṅgadāsa forgot his collection of garlands; though he had conquered his senses, upon seeing her playful sport, he indeed discharged his semen. (41)
As he was looking on, having emerged from that lake, he was clothed in divine garments by his beloveds with smiles.
Having ascended the celestial chariot, he went to the abode of the Giver of Wealth; but when the king of the Gandharvas had departed, Raṅgadāsa was left bewildered.
Having cast off those garlands and bathed in the lake, he felt ashamed; then, having gathered flowers once more, he slowly went to the temple.
But the Vaikhānasa, seeing him and observing that the time for worship had passed, said: "Friend, why have you come so late, having transgressed the proper time? (45)
Nor were garlands woven by you; what, then, was done in the garden? || 46 ||
The illustrious Varāha said: When questioned in this manner, Raṅgadāsa did not speak out of shame; then Madhusūdana spoke to that ashamed Raṅgadāsa.

Then, Śrīnivāsa spoke to Raṅgadāsa, who was ashamed by the contemplation of his own true nature. The Blessed Lord said: "O Raṅgadāsa, what is the use of shame? For you have been deluded by me. You are one who has conquered desire; therefore, be steadfast, O high-minded one. (48)
Like a king of the Gandharvas, you shall become a king upon the surface of the earth; having enjoyed great pleasures there, you shall always remain devoted to me.
"And when you cause a rampart and a celestial palace to be built for me, then, filled with supreme affection, I shall grant you liberation there. (50)
Perform service right here until the liberation of the body; in this way, even for my devotees who possess desires, liberation shall come to pass.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Viṣṇu said nothing further; and having heard that, Raṅgadāsa also constructed an excellent garden.

Now follows the account of the king named Toṇḍamān: Having served [his predecessors] for over a hundred years, that one of unflagging intellect departed for heaven; he was then born into the exalted lineage of Soma, renowned as Toṇḍamān. (53)

The hero Suvīra, born from the womb of Nandinī, was himself a man of great wisdom who, from the age of five, manifested devotion to Viṣṇu; he was a vast mine of virtues such as good character, valor, and prowess.
He married Padmā, the charming daughter of the Pāṇḍya king; thereafter, the king [received] a hundred maidens from various lands who chose him in a svayaṃvara.
Having obtained permission from his father, the son, possessing the prowess of a lion, sported upon the earth like the lord of the gods while dwelling in the city of Nārāyaṇa. (56)
Having set out on a hunt near the Veṅkaṭa mountain, the hero—
Now follows King Toṇḍamān’s journey to Śrī Śeṣācala for the sake of hunting. Wandering on foot accompanied by his retinue, he beheld a leader of an elephant herd discharging streams of ichor.
Seeing him, he was struck with wonder and pursued him to seize him; having crossed the Suvarṇamukharī, he spoke to the excellent parrot.
Having paid homage and received permission, he then went from forest to forest; there he beheld the goddess Reṇukā, situated in the form of an anthill.
She grants the desires of her devoted worshippers, dwells in a divine grove, is always accompanied by her retinue, and is honored even by the gods.
Toṇḍamān also, having bowed to her, then departed facing westward. || 62 ||

Now follows the account of the five-colored parrot situated near Śrīnivāsa: Having seen the five-colored parrot and desiring to seize it, he pursued it; as the bird cried out "Śrīnivāsa!", it fled toward the mountain with even greater speed. (63)
Running along, the king also ascended the king of mountains, beholding various caves and peaks on all sides.
Searching for Śuka, he went to the Śyāmāka forest; not seeing that excellent Śuka there, he beheld the forest guardian.
As the king approached, he went out quickly to meet him; bowing down with humility and standing with his palms joined in reverence, he remained there.
Toṇḍamān, having honored him, questioned that forest-dweller: "Have you seen here any parrot of five colors who has arrived? (67)
"O forest-dweller, where has he gone while uttering the name 'Śrīnivāsa'? (68)
The forest-dweller said: O Indra among kings, that five-colored one is always dear to Śrīnivāsa; he is ever by His side, nourished by Śrī and Bhūmi.
On the bank of Svāmipuṣkariṇī, in the presence of the God, that glorious parrot always remains; indeed, he cannot be captured by anyone.
Having dwelt at his own will upon this auspicious, excellent mountain for eternity, he approaches the God at the end of each day and remains in His presence.
"O Prince, I shall go to propitiate that god; please rest at the foot of this tree until my return. (72)
Dwell at your ease together with this son of yours. || 73 ||
The king said: "I shall come with you to see the Lord Janārdana; show me the Lord of Gods who dwells on the Veṅkaṭa mountain. (74)
Having heard the king's words, he placed the śyāmāka grain mixed with honey into a cup made of mango leaves and went toward Hari along with the king.
Then, as King Toṇḍamān proceeded with Niṣāda, they traveled a very long distance; beholding a rocky plateau, they reached the auspicious Svāmipuṣkariṇī in just a moment. (76)
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rites together with the king, the leader of the Niṣādas revealed Devaśarman to that high-souled monarch.
He was situated at the base of a sacred fig tree on the bank of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī, resembling an Atasī flower in complexion, with eyes as broad as lotuses.
Having four arms and noble limbs, with a lotus-like face slightly smiling, wearing divine yellow garments, and radiant with a crown and bracelets.

He was accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, who stood at His sides and were endowed with beautiful forms; He was attended on all sides by the conch, the discus, the sword, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, and the arrow.
It was attended by other divine weapons and celestial garlands; there, Skanda worshipped that Puruṣottama at the three junctions of the day.
Then, having seen the Supreme Person with His lotus feet hidden by an anthill up to the knees, both of them bowed joyfully to the Lord at that time.
But the king, with palms joined in reverence and eyes wide with wonder, was so overcome by a surge of bliss that he was not aware of anything at all.
The Niṣāda, having offered the śyāmāka grain mixed with honey to the king and having given half of it to him, ate the remaining half himself.
Having drunk the water from the lotus pond, accompanied by that king, he went once more to the holy leaf-hut in the Śyāmaka forest.
Having stayed for one night, the lord of the earth rose in the morning and, accompanied by his own army, returned and went to his own city. || 86 ||
Then follows the speech of Reṇukā to King Toṇḍamān: Having gone again to Devīvana, he dismounted from his horse; on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, he worshipped Reṇukā. (87)
There was sacrificial food and milk-rice in great abundance, along with various attendants, accompanied by animal offerings and provided with incense and lamps. || 88 ||
Having offered a hundred jars of wine scented with jasmine and saffron, the Goddess, thus worshipped and pleased, granted a boon to the king.
A certain person possessed by a spirit spoke to the best of kings: "Listen, O King, your future kingdom shall have its thorns removed. (90)
"O King, this capital city shall be named after you alone; O Great King, you shall rule the kingdom for a long time in my presence. (91)
"And there shall be the grace of the God of gods for you, O sinless one. Having granted this boon to him, [the deity] who had possessed him returned to his natural state. || 92 ||
Then, having obtained the boon, the king went once more to the sage Śuka.

Now follows the majesty of the Lotus Lake as described by Śuka. Having saluted the sage and being honored by him, he became joyful and said: "O Sage, tell me the majesty of this lake named Kamala. (94)
Śrī Śuka said: O King, in former times, due to the curse of Durvāsas, Padmā—the beloved of the lotus-eyed one—descended from the abode of the gods together with Viṣṇu.
Having reached this lake, which abounds with golden lotuses, the great goddess Ramā performed penance for ten thousand divine years.
Then, O King, the gods, searching for Śrī who was accompanied by Viṣṇu, were united with Purandara at this lake.

Seeing her seated upon a golden lotus, united with the Lotus-eyed Lord, they were filled with joy; having bowed down to the Mother of the World who holds a lotus, Indra and the other gods, with palms joined in reverence, offered praise.

Now follows the hymn of praise to Śrī Lakṣmī composed by the gods and others. The gods said: Salutations to Śrī, the sustainer of the world; salutations again and again to the mother of Brahmā. Salutations to you, whose eyes are like lotuses; salutations again and again to her whose face is a lotus. (99)

Salutations again and again to her whose lotus-face is serene, who possesses the luster of a lotus; salutations again and again to the consort of Viṣṇu, who dwells in the forest of Bilva trees. || 100 ||
Salutations again and again to her who wears variegated silken garments and possesses broad hips; salutations again and again to her whose high breasts are full like ripe bilva fruits. || 101 ||

Her auspicious palms and soles have the luster of deep red lotus petals; she is adorned with beautiful jewels, armlets, bracelets, a girdle, and anklets; all her limbs are smeared with yakṣakardama paste, and she shines with brilliant bangles.
Adorned with various auspicious ornaments and pearl necklaces, her lotus-face shone with earrings and floral ear-ornaments.
Obeisance to you, O lotus-handed one; be gracious, O beloved of Hari! Salutations again and again to you, the Goddess of Knowledge, whose form consists of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. 104.
Be gracious, O Daughter of the Ocean; look upon us with glances of compassion, for those who are seen by you attain the status of Brahmā, Rudra, and Indra. (105)

Now follows the speech of Lakṣmī, pleased by the praises addressed to Indra and the other gods. Śrī Śuka said: Thus praised then by the gods, Ramā—who dwells upon the chest of Viṣṇu and is visible together with Viṣṇu—being gratified, spoke to the deities. (106)
Śrī said: "Having swiftly slain the enemies of the gods, you shall go to your own abodes; as for those men on earth who are without a place, having been fallen from their own positions."
Having praised me with this hymn, they shall attain my abode; those men on earth who worship me with unbroken bilva leaves [shall likewise attain it]. 108.
Those gods and men who, by means of this hymn composed by you, indeed become repositories for virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation. (109)
"O gods, whatever men on earth reach this lotus lake and perform their ablutions here after praising me, the beloved of Viṣṇu," (110)
Having obtained prosperity, long life, knowledge, and illustrious sons, and having enjoyed pleasures, those men shall in the end attain liberation.
Having thus granted the boon, the Goddess, together with the Lord Viṣṇu, mounted Garuḍeśāna and departed for the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Niṣāda named Vasu and the Greatness of the Lotus Lake," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Dharaṇī and Varāha. || 9 ||

Now follows the account of King Toṇḍamān’s acquisition of the kingdom from his father. Śrī Śuka said: "O King, this lake named Padmasaras destroys the sins of men; by its glorification, remembrance, and bathing, it bestows prosperity upon people on earth. Having bathed here as well, you too should go into the presence of your father."
Śrī Varāha said: Having heard these words of Śuka, he bathed in the Padmasaras lake.
Having bowed to him and mounted his horse, Toṇḍamān went to his own city; then, after three years, his father made him the crown prince.
And having observed his son’s capacity for inspiring affection, his valor, heroism, excellent character, and devotion toward the Brahmins, the king, together with his ministers, [acted]. (4)
Having consecrated his son according to the prescribed rites and established him in his own position, the king, having entreated his son along with his wife, departed for the forest.

Then, at Vasu’s anthill, there was the manifestation of Śrī Varāha. Having obtained sovereignty, Toṇḍamān indeed ruled his kingdom; for in the forest of Niṣāda, the Lord had assumed the form of a boar.
Having eaten the cooked śyāmāka grain, he wandered about night after night; day after day, he searched for the tracks of the boar.
Not having seen that boar during the night, he remained awake holding his bow; then he saw it wandering about, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.
Seeing that boar of auspicious form in the midst of the Śyāmāka forest, he took up his bow and let out a lion’s roar.
Hearing that sound, the boar quickly emerged from the forest and departed; the leader of the Niṣādas then pursued that boar.
Having pursued him through the remainder of the night in the forest, that leader of the Niṣādas saw him entering an anthill that shone with a luster like the moon.
Seeing him departing like the full moon toward the excellent mountain of its setting, that chief of the Niṣādas was struck with wonder and, out of anger, dug up an anthill.
This Boar of the Earth was seen to fall down in a swoon; then, seeing his father unconscious, his devoted son [acted].
He praised Lord Varāha, and Hari became pleased by that; entering his father, Madhusūdana spoke.
The Blessed Lord said: "I am Varāha, the Lord of Gods; I dwell here eternally. Having informed the king, install me here and worship me."
Having washed the anthill with the milk of black cows, and having extracted from the stone slab that had arisen there the image of Varāha situated within the earth; || 16 ||
Having had me fashioned and installed by Brahmins and Vaikhānasa ascetics, that best of kings, Toṇḍamān, should worship me with various offerings. (17)
Having spoken thus, the god abandoned him, and he indeed became restored to health; then the son of the Niṣāda, having paid homage to his father who was sitting comfortably, [departed]. (18)
He reported all the words of the god to his father exactly as they were; having heard his son’s entire auspicious speech, he was filled with wonder. (19)
Then, having been informed by Vasu of the news regarding Vārāha, the Niṣāda went quickly with his followers to tell the king, Tōṇḍamān; Vasu, the lord of the Niṣādas, arrived at the palace gate.
Having learned through the gatekeepers that the lord of the Niṣādas had arrived, the best of kings summoned that ruler of the Niṣādas to the assembly hall together with his ministers.
Having honored that Vasu along with his sons and his retinue, the king, filled with joy, questioned Vasu, who dwelt in the forest: "O forest-dweller, tell me, what is the purpose of your coming?"
Vasu said: "O King, O lord of the earth, hear of the wonder that was seen by me in the forest. (23)
O King, a certain white boar was roaming about eating śyāmāka grain at night; with bow in hand, I pursued that boar.
Chased by the wind-like force, he went and entered an anthill; O King, he was seen by me on the bank of Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
Falling unconscious from anger, I collapsed upon the ground into an unexcavated anthill. My son, having arrived and seeing me lying unconscious on the earth, [acted].
Having become pure, he praised Madhusūdana, the God of gods; then, having entered into me, the Boar spoke to his son.
"O leader of the Niṣādas, report my conduct to the king immediately; let the king wash away the anthill by sprinkling it with the milk of black cows. (28)
And a certain beautiful stone is seen situated upon an anthill, as well as myself, with the face of a boar, standing with the Earth resting upon my left lap. (29)
Having had it fashioned by an artisan and then consecrated by the lords of sages, Tondaman should worship it with the Vaikhanasa, the best of sages.
Then, having gone to Śrīnivāsa, whose two feet are covered by an anthill, one should slowly wash them with the milking of tawny and black cows.
Having washed [the area] daily from the base of the pedestal up to its top, one should construct a wall on both the north and the south sides.
Having spoken thus, the Lord released me, and I became restored to health, O King; I have come here to tell you what the God of gods intends to do.

Then, following the words of the Niṣāda and his dream, the king proceeded toward Śeṣācala by way of the cave. Śrī Varāha said: "Toṇḍamān, having heard that, became well-pleased and filled with wonder; then, having deliberated upon the task with his ministers, Puṣkara and others," (34)
Desiring to go to Vekaṭādri, he summoned all the cowherds and said: "As for the black and tawny cows, whatever ones belong to me," || 35 ||
"Bring those cows along with their calves from the vicinity of Veṅkaṭādri," thus the king commanded the cowherds; and to his ministers he said, "The journey shall take place tomorrow."
Having dismissed all his subjects, the self-controlled king entered the inner apartments; after speaking that story to his wives, he went to sleep at night.
In a dream, Śrīnivāsa also showed him the path to the cave; along the way from his own city, Hari caused sprouts to spring up.
Having seen such a dream, the king rose quickly in the morning and summoned all his ministers, the subjects, and the brahmins as well. (39)
Having described such a dream, he then saw sprouts at the gate; and when the auspicious moment arrived, Toṇḍamān mounted his horse and set forth.
Seeing the fragments of sprouts, he went slowly and joyfully toward the cave; upon seeing it, he was filled with wonder and established a city there.

Then, in accordance with the words of the Blessed One, [the king] performed the milk-consecration (kṣīrābhiṣeka) and the construction of the rampart by King Toṇḍaman. Having created a subterranean passage within the inner apartments, he also caused a wall to be built. Dwell­ing there, that lord of men, having conquered this entire earth, [ruled]. 42.
Having performed the washing with milk and other rites as instructed by the God of Gods, he set about making preparations to construct a rampart wall.
Then the king was personally commanded by the God of gods: "Protect both of these excellent trees, the tamarind and the campaka."
The tamarind tree is my abode, and the campaka tree is the dwelling place of Lakṣmī; indeed, these two should always be saluted by kings, sages, gods, and men. (45)
O best of kings, having established these two, cut down the other excellent trees; construct for me a wall alone, provided with gates and towers. (46)
But a king of your lineage, a devotee of mine named Nārāyaṇa, will have a celestial chariot (vimāna) constructed and will adorn it with gold.
The Lord of Śrī, having spoken thus to Toṇḍamāna, became silent.
Having thus heard the words of the god and having constructed the enclosure wall, he performed worship together with sages born of the Vaikhānasa lineage.
Having come daily through the subterranean passage and bowed to the Lord, that best of kings ruled his kingdom with righteousness, enjoying supreme pleasures.
Now follows the story of the Brahmin named Vīraśarman, who had come to bathe in the Gaṅgā. At that very time, there was an excellent twice-born man from the South.
Setting out from the city with his wife to bathe in the Gaṅgā, that Brāhmaṇa and his Brāhmaṇī wife then became pregnant on the way.
Seeing her pregnant and unable to follow him, he, desiring to see the king, approached the palace gate.
Informed by the doorkeeper, the king summoned that best of the twice-born; having honored him according to the prescribed rites, he inquired after the welfare of the brahmin.

The king said: "O twice-born one, what is the purpose of your coming? What shall I do for you? The brāhmaṇa said: "O best of kings, I am Vīraśarman, a descendant of Vasiṣṭha and a student of the Sāmaveda. (55)
Accompanied by his wife, he set out with devotion to bathe in the Raktagaṅgā; on the way, there was this pregnant Kauśikī, endowed with great merit.
Known by the name Lakṣmī, she is virtuous and devoted to her husband; having established her in your home, I shall complete my vow.
Therefore, O King, grant her whatever food and wages she desires; meanwhile, let the royal fortune be protected until my return.
Śrī Varāha said: Having heard his words, the king gave him rice and wealth for a period of six months and provided a residence within the inner apartments.
Having deposited her there, the Brahmin, feeling joyful, went forth to bathe in the Gaṅgā; he went to the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā at Prayāga, the most excellent sacred field.
Having bathed and then gone to Kāśī, and having stayed there for three days, that best of brahmins reached Gayā and performed the śrāddha for his ancestors.
Having gone to the city of Ayodhyā, he proceeded to Badarīvana; then, having gone to Sālagrāma, he set out toward his own country.
When two years had passed, on an auspicious day in the month of Caitra, that best of the twice-born returned slowly, arriving in the month of Mādhava.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, she returned once more to the king; however, the king, having forgotten her at that time, did not remember the brahmin woman, O monarch.
The proud Brahmin woman died in the house and indeed became withered; then the Brahmin Vīraśarman [prepared] a casket of Ganges water.
Having released a single auspicious water-pot filled with Ganges water from its binding, she presented it to the king and asked, "Is my wife well? (66)
Then, remembering that brahmin, the king said, "Please stay. Having then gone into the inner apartments, he saw her dead in the house.
Without having spoken to that Brahmin, he entered the excellent cave; having paid obeisance to Śrī Nṛsiṃha, he reached the excellent cave once again.
He went to see the supreme Śrīnivāsa, who was accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi; seeing him approaching suddenly, Earth and Rame (Lakṣmī) hid themselves.
To him who was bowing down, he said, "Why have you come, O King, at an improper time? The king, having bowed to the Lord, spoke in fear regarding the deceased Brāhmaṇī.

Now, regarding the majesty of Asthisarovara: Having heard that, even the God of gods said, "Do not fear, O King, from that best of the twice-born. He then placed him upon a palanquin, accompanied by his own women.
O Lord, on the twelfth lunar day, bathe [the deity] in this lake named Asthi, located to the east of my abode, which wards off untimely death.
Having regained her life, she shall be united with her wives and the Brāhmaṇa; go quickly, O best of kings, and do as you have been told. (73)
Having heard these words of the god, the king departed for his own city, having placed the women, including her, upon beautiful palanquins.
Placing the Brāhmaṇa at his head, the king went to see the Lord; having reached the lake of Asthikūṭa, he caused those women to bathe there.
She, whose form was skin and bone, was cast by them into the lake; having regained her life, she appeared with a fully manifested body just as before.
Having bathed in the lake and emerged with her queens, the auspicious lady joyfully approached the brahmin and her returned husband.
Having worshipped Hari, the king gave wealth to the brāhmaṇa, up to a thousand niṣkas, as well as various garments. (78)
Having heard the account of the women and the power of the Lord of Veṅkaṭa, the brāhmaṇa respectfully bid him farewell for his journey to his own country.
Having offered his blessings to the king, the twice-born man then departed for his own country. When the brahmin had gone, Śrīnivāsa spoke again to the king: || 80 ||
And day after day at midday, O King, having come and worshipped me with golden lotuses as desired, he would offer food-oblations.
"Go to the city and rule the kingdom according to your own dharma, O lord of men; whatever is desired by you, O king, shall come to pass—of this there is no doubt. (82)
"O King, you must never come at an improper time; having thus performed worship at the appointed time, go and dwell in your own city."
The king said: "O Lord of Gods, I shall do so; I will worship [you] at midday. Thus, by the command of the God, he worshipped daily with golden lotuses.
Thereafter, he once beheld a tulasī flower made of clay.

Then, having heard the account of the devotee named Bhīma, born of a potter lineage in the village of Kurvagrāma, the best of kings was filled with wonder and questioned the Lord of the God of Gods. The king said: "By whom are you worshipped with earthen lotuses equal to tulasī? (86)
Questioned by the king, the God of Gods remembered and said to the king: "A certain potter, my devotee, dwells in the village of Kurva. (87)
"O King, if one worships him in one's own home, that is accepted by me. Having heard these words of the god, the king set out to see him. (88)
Having gone to Kurvapura, he went to the house of that potter; seeing that the king had arrived, he bowed down and stood before him. (89)
The best of kings questioned that man named Bhīma as he stood there. Toṇḍamān said: "O Bhīma, O best of your lineage, tell me how you worship the Lord. (90)
Śrī Varāha said: Being questioned, even the potter replied, "I do not know at all how to perform worship. O best of kings, by whom was it said that a potter performs worship?"
Toṇḍamān said: "Indeed, my worship of you was commanded by Lord Śrīnivāsa. Having heard the king's words, he then recalled the boon granted by the Supreme Deity in the past.
Bhīma said: "When the worship has been made manifest and when the king has arrived, you shall attain liberation through that conversation with Toṇḍamān. (93)
Thus, in former times, Lord Veṅkaṭeśvara granted this boon.

Then follows the attainment of Vaikuṇṭha by the devotee named Bhīma, who resided in Kurvagrāma, together with his wife. Having spoken thus, the potter likewise, along with his wife, saw the celestial chariot arrive and beheld Lord Janārdana. (95)
Prostrating himself, that best of devotees, together with his wife, gave up his life-breaths even as the king of kings looked on, and ascended a celestial chariot.
Assuming a divine form, he went to the abode of Viṣṇu together with the goddess; having witnessed that marvel there, the king returned to his own city filled with joy.
Having consecrated your own son named Śrīnivāsa according to the prescribed rites, protect both the people and the earth with righteousness. 98.
Having thus commanded his son, the wise one performed supreme austerity; as he was performing that penance, Lord Hari appeared before his very eyes.
Now follows the attainment of the same form as the Lord by King Toṇḍamān through the grace of Śrīnivāsa: Having mounted Garuḍa, the Lord, accompanied by Ramā and Bhūmi, [departed]. (100)
The Blessed Lord said: "O best of kings, what shall I do for you, who have been gratified by your asceticism? Thus addressed by the God of gods, Tonda-mān, the king of kings, [spoke].
Filled with joy and with palms joined in reverence, he spoke with a faltering voice: "I desire to dwell in your world, which is free from old age and death. (102)
O Mādhava, grant me this very boon; this is what I desire. || 103 ||
Śrī Varāha said: Having spoken thus, he prostrated himself on the earth with his eight limbs before the presence of the God; then, casting off that body, he ascended a celestial chariot.
Being praised by the Gandharvas, he attains a form similar to that of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow—a state free from grief and delusion, and devoid of old age and death.
He reached that station of Viṣṇu, which is free from rebirth.

Now follows the declaration of the fruit resulting from hearing and reciting this majesty: "O Goddess of gods, O lady of excellent complexion, this future account has been told by me; whoever causes it to be heard or whoever hears it goes to the world of Viṣṇu. (107)

The venerable Sūta said: Whoever listens with devotion or recites this ancient, meritorious narrative—including what was spoken by the God of gods along with its future events and its sequel—[shall attain the highest goal]. (108)
Having enjoyed all desires, he shall at the end go to the abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Emperor Toṇḍamān," within the "Description of the Future" section of the *Dharaṇī-Varāha-saṃvāda* (Dialogue between the Earth and Varāha) in the *Śrī-Veṅkaṭācala-māhātmya*, in the second *Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī-skānda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Śrī Sūta said: Now follows the destruction of Kāśyapa’s great sins through bathing in Svāmipuṣkariṇī. Therefore, O best of the twice-born, I shall now duly proclaim a single auspicious and purifying narrative concerning the holy Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
Formerly, a twice-born man named Kāśyapa, having bathed in this auspicious and excellent tīrtha, was liberated from a very great sin that would have led him to hell.
The sages said: O sage, what sin indeed did this one named Kāśyapa commit, that by bathing here in this best of holy places (tīrtha), he was liberated in an instant?
O Sūta, by the power of your compassion, tell this to us who are full of faith; for those of us satiated by the nectar of your words, even thirst no longer exists.
Śrī Sūta said: I shall narrate an ancient history (itihāsa) that establishes the majesty of Śrī Svāmipuṣkariṇī; it destroys the sins of those who read it.
Now follows the account of Parīkṣit: The son of Abhimanyu was a king named Parīkṣit; he resided in Hastināpura, protecting the earth according to dharma.
Once that king, devoted to the hunt, wandered in the forest; the monarch was sixty years of age and was tormented by hunger and thirst.
While diligently searching for that one lost deer in the forest, that best of kings saw a sage absorbed in meditation and spoke to him.
"O Sage, I have just now pierced a deer in the forest with an arrow; O learned one, was it seen by you as it fled, trembling with fear? (9)
Established in meditative absorption and observing silence, he did not say anything at all; then, with the end of his bow, [he struck] the shoulder of that great sage.
Having placed the dead snake there, he went to his own city in anger. That sage indeed had a certain son named Śṛṅgin.
The best of the twice-born named Kṛśa was the friend of that Śṛṅgin; then that friend named Kṛśa spoke to his friend Śṛṅgin.
"Your father is now carrying a dead snake on his shoulder; O friend, let there be no pride in you, and do not be angry at this in vain. (13)
Śṛṅgin became enraged, desiring to cast a curse upon the king, saying: "O fool-minded one, you who placed a dead snake upon my father! || 14 ||
"Let him die within seven nights, bitten by the serpent Takṣaka! Thus did the son of the sage curse Parīkṣit, the grandson of Subhadrā.
Having heard that the king had been cursed by his son, the eminent sage named Śamīka spoke to his son Śṛṅgin.
Why have you cursed the king, the protector of all the worlds? How indeed shall we remain in a world without a ruler? (17)
Through anger, sin increases; through compassion, happiness is attained. He who dispels the anger that has arisen by means of forgiveness alone— || 18 ||
In this world and in the next, such a person enjoys ultimate happiness; for those men endowed with forgiveness attain the highest good. (19)
Then Śamīka spoke to his own disciple named Gauramukha: "O Gauramukha, go and speak to King Parīkṣit."
"O high-minded one, having received this curse spoken by my son regarding the bite of the serpent-king Takṣaka, return quickly once more to my presence."
Thus addressed by Śamīka, Gauramukha went to the king; having approached him, he spoke to the monarch regarding the son of Subhadrā, Parīkṣit.
Seeing a dead snake placed upon your father's shoulder by you, Śṛṅgin, the son of Śamīka, cursed you in a fit of rage.
On the seventh day from this, let the son of Abhimanyu be bitten by the great serpent Takṣaka and be consumed by the fire of his venom.
"O King, Śṛṅgin, the son of that sage, has thus cursed you; his father has sent me to your presence to tell you this. (25)
Having spoken thus to the king, Gauramukha departed quickly; after Gauramukha had gone, the king thereafter became devoted to grief.
Then that bull among kings constructed in the center of the Gaṅgā a vast pavilion, one-pillared, exceedingly lofty, and reaching toward the clouds.
Accompanied by those who knew the mantras of the great Gāruḍa, those who knew medicinal herbs, and physicians, he applied himself with concentrated effort to destroy the poison of Takṣaka.
Accompanied by many eminent gods, brahmin-sages, and royal sages, that king, devoted to Viṣṇu, sat in that lofty pavilion.
At that moment, the Brahmin Kāśyapa, the best of mantra-experts, set out to protect the king from the potent poison of Takṣaka.
On the seventh day, the best of Brahmins, who was poor and desirous of wealth, was [there]; in the meantime, Takṣaka also arrived, disguised in the form of a Brahmin.
Then, seeing Kāśyapa on the way, he addressed him: "O Brāhmaṇa, O great sage, tell me today, where are you going? (32)
Thus questioned, the twice-born Kāśyapa then replied to Takṣaka: "Today Takṣaka has consumed the great king Parīkṣit with the fire of his venom."
"I shall go near him to extinguish that which will burn him. Thus addressed, Takṣaka spoke again to that brahmin: || 34 ||
"I am Takṣaka, O best of the twice-born; once bitten by me, one cannot be cured even in a hundred years, nor even by ten thousand great mantras. (35)
If you now have the power to treat that which has been bitten by me, then bite down on this tree, ten yojanas in height, and bring it back to life.
"O twice-born one, it appears to me that you are indeed capable of this. Having spoken thus, Takṣaka then bit that tree.
That exceedingly tall tree was also reduced to ashes; however, a certain man had previously climbed that very tree. || 38 ||
He too was then consumed by Takṣaka’s fiery poison-arrows; neither Kāśyapa nor Takṣaka recognized that man.
Then Kāśyapa made his vow even as Takṣaka listened: "Let all these, beginning with the brahmins, behold now the power of my mantra! (40)
Having spoken thus, Kāśyapa, the best of mantra-experts, restored to life that tree which had been reduced to ashes by the fire of poison through the power of his mantras. (41)
That man was restored to life along with that tree; then Takṣaka spoke to that Kāśyapa, who was skilled in mantras.
"O twice-born one, act in such a way that the word of the Sage does not prove false; I shall give you double the wealth that the king might grant you. (43)
"I give [these to you]; turn back at once, O best of the twice-born! Having spoken thus and having given him priceless jewels, that Takṣaka—
Having perceived through his vision of knowledge that the king was short-lived, Kāśyapa turned back that Brāhmaṇa, Kāśyapa, who was skilled in mantras. (45)
Having obtained the jewel from Takṣaka, he returned silently to his own hermitage; at that very moment, Takṣaka summoned all the serpents and spoke to them.
Having approached that king while disguised as sages, quickly present the offering-fruits to Parīkṣit.
Having said "So be it," all those serpents gave fruits to the king; and Takṣaka likewise [gave] one there among some jujube fruits.
Assuming the guise of a worm, he remained there to bite the king. Then, the king [received] the gifts bestowed by all those disguised as Brāhmaṇas.
Parīkṣit, having given all the fruits to his aged ministers, || 50 ||
Out of curiosity, he took a large fruit in his hand; at that moment, the sun also entered the mountain of setting.
"Lest the word of the sage prove false," all the men there, as well as the brahmins and the kings, then said to one another. (52)
While everyone was speaking thus, a worm, deeply red, appeared within that fruit; it was seen by all, including King Parīkṣit.
"What kind of worm might this bite me today? the king said, O best of the twice-born, and he placed that fruit, along with the worm, around his neck.
At that time, Takṣaka was situated within that fruit in the form of a worm; then, quickly emerging from that fruit, he enveloped the king’s body.
When the king was enveloped by Takṣaka, those standing nearby fled out of fear; immediately thereafter, O brahmins, the king [perished] by the fiery poison of Takṣaka.
The powerful [enemy], together with the palace, was quickly reduced to ashes; then, the priests, along with the king's attendants, performed his funeral rites.
The ministers, desiring to protect the world, consecrated his son, named Janamejaya, as king in the realm.
A Brahmin named Kāśyapa, the best of sages, arrived to protect the king from Takṣaka; he was censured by all the people.
Despised by all virtuous people, he wandered through every land; he found no place of rest, whether in a village or even in a hermitage.
To whichever countries he went, he was expelled from each of those lands by the great masses of people; thus driven out, he sought refuge with Śākalya.
Having prostrated before the sage Śākalya, Kāśyapa, who was censured by the people, made this request to the high-souled Śākalya: || 62 ||
Kāśyapa said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, Śākalya, beloved of Hari! Sages, other brahmins, and my own friends are censuring me. (63)
I do not know the cause for this; why do men revile me? [Is it] the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, or likewise, sexual intercourse with the wife of a guru? (64)
"O Sage, neither theft nor the fault of association have ever been practiced by me; nor have any other sins been committed by me. (65)
Nevertheless, people, including my kinsmen and others, revile me in vain. O Śākalya, if you know of any fault committed by me, speak it.
Then, O best of the twice-born, the great sage named Śākalya, having been addressed by Kāśyapa, meditated for a moment and spoke to that Kāśyapa.
Now follow the duties declared by Śākalya. Śākalya said: "You set out to protect the great king Parīkṣit from Takṣaka, but you were stopped by Takṣaka on the halfway path. (68)
Even though he is capable of treating one afflicted by poison, disease, and the like, he who does not protect such a person in this world is called a slayer of a Brahmin.
O best of Brahmins, he who, out of anger, lust, fear, greed, envy, or even delusion, does not protect a man afflicted by the disease of poison—

Whether one is a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or one who violates the teacher’s bed, even if defiled by the fault of association with such persons, there is no atonement for him. (71)
In the scriptures, expiation is indeed prescribed even for one who sells his daughter, for one who sells horses, and likewise for an ungrateful person. (72)
If one who is capable does not protect someone afflicted by the disease of poison, no atonement is prescribed for him, even through ten thousand penances.
A person of merit should not eat in the same row as him, nor should he converse with him, nor should he ever look upon that man. (74)
Merely by conversing with him, one becomes a partaker of a great sin; yet that great king Parīkṣit was virtuous and possessed of meritorious fame. (75)
A devotee of Viṣṇu and a great yogi, he was the protector of the four castes; from the son of Vyāsa, he heard the stories of Hari with devotion. (76)
Since you did not protect that king despite the words of Takṣaka, you are being censured for that reason by the best of Brahmins and even by your kinsmen.
Although that great king Parīkṣit was but a moment’s life away, nevertheless, wise men should provide medical treatment until death occurs. (78)
Indeed, medical treatment must be administered for as long as the vital breaths remain in the throat of a man about to die; for crooked is the course of time. (79)

Thus did those who have reached the further shore of the ocean of medical science recite this verse in ancient times: "Therefore, even though one is capable of treatment, if one does not administer the medicine... (80)
"And you were censured by him because you turned back halfway; having been addressed thus by Śākalya, Kāśyapa replied. (81)
Kāśyapa said: "O you of noble vows, tell me the means for the pacification of this fault of mine, by which my kinsmen and friends may accept me. (82)
"O Śākalya, beloved of Hari, show mercy toward me. Thus addressed by Kāśyapa, Śākalya, the lord of sages, [replied].
Having meditated for a moment, he then spoke thus to Kāśyapa out of compassion.
Śākalya said: I shall tell you the means for the pacification of this sin; it must be performed by you quickly, O twice-born one—do not delay. (85)
On the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī is the abode of the Lord of Lakṣmī, known as Veṅkaṭādri, who is worshipped in all the worlds. (86)
On that meritorious Śeṣa mountain, which is saluted by gods and demons alike, and which destroys the sins of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, and so forth; (87)
And Svāmipuṣkariṇī, which removes all sins and bestows auspiciousness, is situated to the north of Śrīnivāsa.
Having gone to that Veṅkaṭa mountain and bathed in the auspicious Svāmipuṣkariṇī according to the prescribed ritual resolve (saṃkalpa), [one should worship] Hari as Lord Varāha.
Having served [the deity] on the western shore and departed for the temple of Hari, he went there according to the prescribed rite to the one who dwells upon the Golden Mountain (Meru).
To Śrīnivāsa, the supreme deity who bestows fearlessness upon his devotees, the god who bears the conch and the discus and is adorned with a garland of forest flowers. (91)
"Having seen [this], you are cleansed of sin; do not entertain doubt, O twice-born one. Thus addressed by Śākalya, Kāśyapa, the bull among sages, [acted accordingly].
Having gone to Veṅkaṭaśailendra, who is saluted by gods and demons, he bathed in the auspicious Puṣkariṇī pond according to the prescribed rules.

The brahmin Kāśyapa, a master who had reached the further shore of the ocean of medical science, became restored to health; and all his kinsmen and fellow brahmins [honored] Kāśyapa, the most excellent of brāhmaṇas.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, you are indeed worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt. Thus, O Brahmins, has the majesty of Veṅkaṭācala been recounted to you.
The man who hears this with devotion is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Cessation of Kāśyapa’s Fault," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Svāmipuṣkariṇī Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now, regarding the liberation from the *tāmisra* and other hells through bathing at Svāmipuṣkariṇī: The sages said— "O Sūta, knower of the truth of all matters, master of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, O Lord, tell us of the majesty of Śrī Svāmipuṣkariṇī. (1)
By the mere remembrance of whom, a human being on earth shall become liberated. || 2 ||
Śrī Sūta said: Those who praise Svāmitīrtha, bathe there, or speak of it do not experience the twenty-eight varieties of hell.
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava, Kumbhīpāka, Kālasūtra, and likewise Asipatravana; || 4 ||
Kṛmibhakṣa, Andhakūpa, Saṃdaṃśa, Śālmalī, as well as Lālābhakṣa, Avīci, and Sārameyādana; || 5 ||
In the same way, there was the piercing by vajra-thorns, the immersion in caustic mud, the devouring by hosts of rākṣasas, and the impalement upon a stake.
O Brahmins, there is that which is called Tirodhāna, as well as that called Sūcīmukha, and that which feeds on pus and blood, and that which is tormented by poison and fire.
O Brahmins, by bathing at Svāmitīrtha, a person does not go to this collection of twenty-eight hells.
He who steals the wealth, children, or wives of others is bound by the noose of Time by the terrifying messengers of Yama.
He is cast into the terrible Tāmisra hell for many years; however, if he bathes at the Svāmitīrtha, he is not cast into that [hell].
That lowest of men who hates his mother, his father, or the Brahmins, falls into the Kālasūtra hell, which extends for ten thousand yojanas.
O Brahmins, afflicted by hunger, he is cast down upon a copper floor that is heated from below by fire and scorched from above by the rays of the sun. (12)
If one bathes in that very lotus pond, that man who, having transgressed the path of the Vedas, wanders on an evil path, is not cast down into it.
He is cast into the terrible Asipatravana forest by the servants of Yama; however, if he bathes in the Svāmitīrtha, he is not cast there.

O twice-born ones, that man who eats cooked food such as soup and the like by breaking the order of the row, or who eats out of delusion without having performed the five sacrifices, [incurs sin]. (15)
This man is cast by the servants of Yama into the Kṛmibhojana hell, where he is devoured by hundreds of worms while himself devouring swarms of worms.
And he himself shall remain turned into a worm until his sins are exhausted; however, if he bathes in the Svāmitīrtha, he is not cast down there.
Whether it be the king himself or one of his officials, whoever should take the wealth of Brahmins out of affection or even by force, or the wealth of others as well— (18)
He is also tormented with tongs in iron fire-pits; he is cast into the terrible Saṃdaṃśa hell by the servants of Yama.
If that lowest of men, who approaches a woman who should not be approached, bathes at the Svāmitīrtha, he is nevertheless cast down into it.
O twice-born ones, if a woman should approach a man who is forbidden, they both [must enter] an iron woman and an iron man.
Embracing one another while heated, they remain there as long as the moon and sun exist; then they are cast into the terrible hell named Sūcī by the servants of Yama.
If one bathes at that Svāmitīrtha, he is not cast down there; for he who oppresses all living beings through various means and afflictions [is not purified otherwise].
He is cast into the terrible Śālmalī hell, which is full of many thorns; however, if he bathes at Svāmitīrtha, he is not cast into that [hell].
Whether a king or a king’s servant, whoever follows heretical doctrines and destroys the bridges of dharma is cast into the Vaitaraṇī river.
If he bathes at the Svāmitīrtha, he is not cast down into it—even if he is defiled by association with a *vṛṣalī* or devoid of purity and proper conduct. (26)
Having abandoned shame and abandoned the Vedas, always delighting in the conduct of beasts, he [falls] into that [womb] filled with pus, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, bile, and so forth.
He is cast into the Atibībhatsa hell by the servants of Yama; however, if he bathes in the Svāmitīrtha, he is not thrown there.
The hunter who torments wild animals with dogs or with arrows shall, in the next world, be pierced by volleys of arrows by the servants of Yama.
If he bathes at the Svāmitīrtha, however, he is not cast into the hell called Prāṇarodha by the servants of Yama.
O twice-born ones, that hypocrite who slaughters animals at a sacrifice while being devoid of the performance of prescribed rites is slain in the next world in the Vaiśasa hell.
While being dragged by the servants of Yama and cast down by the messengers of Yama, if he indeed bathes in that lotus-pond, he is not cast down there.
If one makes his own wife of equal caste drink semen, he becomes a drinker of semen in the next world and is cast into the Seminal Pit (retas-kuṇḍa).
If he indeed bathes in that lotus pond, even a robber who lies in wait on the road, a poisoner, or a burner of villages is not cast down into it.
And he who steals the goods of a merchant, O best of the twice-born, is cast for a long time into the terrible hell named Vajradaṃṣṭra in the next world.
If he bathes at the Svāmitīrtha, he is not cast into those other hells that indeed exist in the hereafter.
A person does not fail to attain those [merits] by immersing oneself in Svāmitīrtha; by bathing even once in Puṣkariṇī, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
The knowledge of the Self becomes manifest, and liberation is likewise fourfold; the intellect does not delight in sin, nor does suffering arise at all.
Whatever fruit is obtained by men through the gift of a man’s weight in gold (tulāpuruṣa-dāna), that same fruit is obtained by men from immersion in Svāmitīrtha. || 39 ||
Whatever merit indeed belongs to men by the gift of a thousand cows, that merit a mortal obtains by bathing at Svāmitīrtha.
Whatever among dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa a person desires, he attains that very thing immediately by bathing in Svāmitīrtha.
O Brahmins, whether one is tainted by a great sin (mahāpātaka) or joined with all possible sins, one becomes instantly purified by immersion in Svāmitīrtha.
Wisdom, fortune, fame, prosperity, knowledge, righteousness, detachment, and purity of mind shall accrue to men from the service of Svāmitīrtha. (43)
Ten thousand killings of Brahmins, ten thousand drinks of liquor, and ten thousand acts of approaching the wives of gurus—these are the sins of the evildoers.
Ten million acts of stealing gold and ten million instances of association with such thieves quickly go to destruction by bathing in Svāmitīrtha. (45)
O believers, there are deeds equal to the killing of a Brahmin, equal to the drinking of liquor, and those which are also equivalent to violating the wife of one's guru. (46)
All those [sins] equal to the theft of gold and equal to association with such [sinners] perish by immersing oneself in Svāmitīrtha. (47)

Now, those who lack faith in the greatness of Svāmitīrtha shall attain the great hells. One should never entertain doubt regarding these matters that have been stated; for the servants of Yama cast a heated axe upon the tip of their tongues. (48)
One who speaks all of this as mere explanatory praise (arthavāda) shall indeed go to hell; he should be known as a pig, excluded from all sacred rites. || 49 ||
"O best of the twice-born, oh, what folly! Oh, what folly! Oh, what folly, that you have not come to the holy ford named Svāmitīrtha, which destroys all sins! (50)
Because it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men through the knowledge of non-duality, and because it eternally grants desired objects as well as destroys ignorance. (51)
Even while it remains present, people abandon it and take delight elsewhere; oh, the power of delusion! It is impossible for me to describe it.
For one who has bathed at Svāmitīrtha, there is indeed no fear of Death; and those men who behold Svāmitīrtha and bathe there [attain the same].
They praise him, they extol him, they touch him, and they bow down to him; for those bulls among the twice-born do not drink the breast milk of their mothers.
Thus, O Brahmins, the majesty of Svāmitīrtha has been described to you; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men, and destroys all sins.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Holy Tīrtha Svāmipuṣkariṇī," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now follows the description of the life and character of Dharmagupta. Śrī Sūta said: O residents of the Naimiṣa forest, out of respect for you, I shall once again fully proclaim the majesty of Svāmitīrtha.
A great king named Nanda, born of the Lunar dynasty, protected this earth as far as the oceans in accordance with righteousness.
He had a son known as Dharmagupta; having placed the burden of protecting the kingdom upon his own son, that Nanda [departed]. (3)
Having conquered his senses and mastered his appetite, he entered the penance grove; for when his father had gone to the penance grove, the king named Dharmagupta [ascended the throne].
Knowing the Dharma and devoted to statesmanship, he protected the earth; he worshipped the gods, headed by Indra, with various kinds of sacrifices.
While he ruled, he bestowed wealth and many fields upon the Brahmins; all remained devoted to their own duties under that king’s governance.
At times there were no afflictions arising from thieves and the like; at other times, this Dharmagupta, having mounted an excellent horse, [roamed about].
O best of Brahmins, eager for the pleasure of the hunt, he entered the forest, whose quarters were filled with *tamāla*, *tāla*, *hintāla*, and *kurava* trees.
He wandered through that forest, terrifying with lions and tigers, its horizons resonating with the humming of swarms of intoxicated bees.
In a lake filled with water, crowded with groves of lotuses, white lilies, kumudas, and blue water-lilies, and adorned by ascetics; (10)
O Brahmins, as King Dharmagupta was wandering in that forest, night fell, its quarters shrouded in darkness.
The king also, having performed the evening twilight rites with humility, chanted the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, there in the forest.
While the prince had taken refuge in this tree out of fear of lions, tigers, and other beasts, a bear, tormented by the fear of a lion, approached his vicinity.
A certain lion roaming the forest pursued that tree; being chased by the lion, the bear climbed up the tree.
Having climbed that tree, the bear saw the lord of the world, the high-souled one of great strength and prowess, stationed upon the tree. || 15 ||
Seeing the king, this forest-dwelling bear said: "O Indra among kings, do not fear; we two shall dwell here for the night."
This great being, with a massive body and bristling with large fangs, has arrived at the foot of the tree; he is a most terrifying lion. (17)
"Enjoy half the night in sleep while you are protected by me with vigilance; thereafter, O high-minded one, protect me while I am fast asleep for the remaining half of the night. (18)
Having heard those words, Hari spoke to the bear while the son of Nanda was asleep: "This king is sleeping; let him be released by me. (19)
O best of the twice-born, the bear, who knew the dharma, said to that lion: "O king of beasts, wanderer of the forest, you do not understand dharma. (20)
Alas, for those who betray trust, there is great suffering in this world; indeed, the sin of those who harm their friends does not perish even through ten thousand sacrifices. (21)
Expiation for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin may somehow be achieved; however, the sin of those who betray trust shall not perish even in ten million lifetimes.
I do not consider Mount Meru to be a great burden upon this earth; rather, I consider this betrayal of the world's trust to be a great burden.
Thus addressed by the bear, the lion became silent. When Dharmagupta had awakened, the bear went to sleep in the tree.
Then the lion said to the king, "Give this bear to me. Thus addressed by the lion, the king, without hesitation, [took up] the sleeping [bear].
He abandoned that bear, who had placed its head upon his own lap, onto the ground; then, as it was being cast down by the king, it clung to a tree.
Due to the power of his merit, the bear did not fall from the tree to the surface of the earth; that bear, approaching the king, spoke these words in anger: || 27 ||
O King, I am born of the lineage of Bhṛgu; possessing the power to assume any form at will, I am known by the name Dhyānakāṣṭha, and I have taken on the form of a bear.
O King, why have you abandoned me, who am innocent and asleep? Because of my curse, wander the earth very swiftly as one driven mad. (29)
Having thus cursed the king, the sage then spoke to the lion: "You are not a lion; you were formerly a great yakṣa, a minister of Kubera."
Once, having reached the Himavat mountain accompanied by his bride, he joyfully engaged in sport in the vicinity of Gautama out of ignorance.
Gautama also, having gone out from his hut by chance to fetch sacrificial fuel, saw you naked and pronounced a curse.
"Since you have stood today in my hermitage naked, therefore you shall become a lion this very day; of this there is no doubt."
Thus, by the curse of Gautama, you who were formerly the Yakṣa named Bhadra, the minister of Kubera, attained the state of a lion in the past.
For Kubera is indeed virtuous in character, and his servants are likewise; therefore, for what reason do you kill me, a sage who dwells in the forest? (35)
"O lord of beasts, I indeed know all this through meditation. Having been addressed thus by Dhyānakāṣṭha, he immediately abandoned his state as a lion.
Having assumed a divine yakṣa form as the attendant of Kubera, he approached the sage, who was like a wooden post in meditation, and spoke with palms joined in reverence and bowing low.
O great sage, today I have learned everything regarding my former history; at the time of pronouncing my curse, Gautama also spoke of the end of that curse.
When you have a conversation with Dhyānakāṣṭha in the form of a bear, then, having shaken off your lion-nature, you will assume the form of a Yakṣa.
"Thus, O Brahmin, Gautama, the bull among sages, spoke to me: 'O great sage, today, because my lionhood has perished, I recognize you.'"
"Pure, named Dhyānakāṣṭha, and always assuming any form at will"—having spoken thus and bowed to him, that king of the yakṣas [departed] for Dhyānakāṣṭha.
Having ascended an excellent celestial chariot, he set out for the city of Alakā; and the ministers beheld that best of kings in the form of a madman.
They brought that best of kings to his father’s presence on the bank of the Revā and informed him of his son’s loss of mental composure. || 43 ||
Then, having learned the news concerning his son, the father Nandana indeed—

Then, by virtue of Jaimini’s words, Dharmagupta—who had bathed at Svāmitīrtha—was freed from his madness. Taking his son, he went quickly into the presence of Jaimini and reported the entire account of his son from the beginning.
"O Blessed One Jaimini, my son has fallen into madness today; O great sage, tell me the means for the destruction of this insanity. (46)
Thus questioned, Jaimini, the bull among sages, meditated for a long time; having reflected for a very long duration, he spoke to the prince.
Indeed, by the curse of Dhyānakāṣṭha, your son became insane; I shall now tell you the means for his liberation from that curse.
On the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī, on the mountain named Veṅkaṭa—which removes all sins, is meritorious, and is composed of various minerals—(49)
And there is the Svāmipuṣkariṇī, a most excellent sacred ford; it is indeed the purest among the pure and the most auspicious among the auspicious. (50)
O high-minded one, having brought your son there today, bathe him—this act which is established by the Vedas, is of great merit, and purifies even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
"His madness shall perish at that very moment; of this there is no doubt. Having been addressed thus, he bowed down to Jaimini, the bull among sages.
Nanda, taking his son with him, went to Svāmipuṣkariṇī; and there he bathed his son according to the prescribed rules.
Then, immediately upon merely bathing, the son was freed from his madness; Nanda himself also bathed in the waters of Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
Having stayed there for one day with his son, the father then served Veṅkaṭeśa, Śrīnivāsa, the ocean of compassion.
Having taken leave of his son, Nanda departed for the forest to practice asceticism; O twice-born ones, when the father had gone, the son Dharmagupta also became king.
With devotion, he bestowed much wealth upon Veṅkaṭeśa; at that time, he gave money, grain, and fields to the Brāhmaṇas. || 57 ||
Immediately thereafter, he departed for his own city together with his ministers; he ruled the kingdom, from which all thorns had been removed, according to righteousness.

O Brahmins, Dharmagupta was exceedingly righteous and inherited [this lineage] from his father and grandfather; likewise, those men who were afflicted by madness, epilepsy, or evil planetary influences—[he delivered them]. (59)
O best of Brahmins, even those who have been seized [by evil] shall be liberated by immersing themselves here in this lotus-pond; I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
He who, having abandoned Svāmipuṣkariṇī, goes to another holy place, is like a cowherd who, having abandoned the milky sap of the *snigdha* plant, begs for the milky sap of the *snuhī*.
"O twice-born ones, men who recite 'Svāmitīrtha, Svāmitīrtha, Svāmitīrtha' three times in this manner at any body of water whatsoever," (62)
All those men who bathe there shall indeed go to the abode of Brahmā. Thus, O Brahmins, has this auspicious narrative of Dharmagupta been told to you.
By the mere hearing of which, even the murder of a Brahmin is destroyed.
Now follows the account of the brahmin named Sumati. Śrī Sūta said: "O all you ascetics dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, I shall once again proclaim the majesty of Svāmitīrtha."
Formerly, a wise Brāhmaṇa who had drunk liquor due to association with a Kirātī woman was liberated from that sin after bathing in Puṣkariṇī. || 2 ||
The sages said: Whose son was this Sumati? How did he drink liquor? And how, O Sūta, best of Paurāṇikas, did he become addicted to the Kirātī?
Out of compassion, please now describe this in detail for all of them.
Śrī Sūta said: In the land known as Mahārāṣṭra, there was a certain devout Brāhmaṇa, renowned by the name Yajñadeva, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
That Yajñadeva indeed had a son named Sumati, who was compassionate, hospitable to guests, and a worshipper of Śiva and Nārāyaṇa.
Abandoning both his father and his devoted wife, he departed for the land of Utkala, becoming intent on the company of libertines.
A certain Kirāta woman, dwelling in that region, was enchanting to young men; she captivated all the possessions of the youths and seized them for a long time.
That Sumati, the lowest of Brahmins, went to her house; and that Kirāti woman took hold of Sumati, the destitute twice-born man.

Now follows the acquisition of a great sin by the twice-born Sumati through association with a Kirāta woman. Then, joined with her, Sumati—intent solely upon that union—constantly stole many goods here and there.
Having given it, he enjoyed himself for a long time in her house and ate there; with a single cup, he drank wine together with her.
Thus, sporting with her for a very long time, he, afflicted by sensual desires, did not remember his parents nor his own wife.
Once, wearing the guise of a Kirāta, he went along with some Kirātas to commit a theft at the house of a certain Brāhmaṇa.
The audacious man, sword in hand, went to steal the wealth; having slain the brahmin who was the master of that house with his sword through sheer violence.
Having taken much wealth, he went to the house of the Kirātī; as he was going, the terrifying personification of Brahman-slaughter followed after him.
Wearing blue garments, she was terrifying with her intensely red hair; roaring with a loud, boisterous laugh, she caused both heaven and earth to tremble.
Pursued by her, he wandered over the surface of the earth; thus wandering the entire world, once Sumati himself—
Terrified, that wicked kinsman of the brahmin fled toward his own village; pursued by her, he ran in fear back toward his home.
Even the sin of killing a Brahmin pursued him and went to his home along with him; Sumati sought refuge, crying out, "Father! Protect me! Protect me! (19)
Having said to him, "Do not fear," the father prepared to protect him; at that moment, this Brahmahatyā addressed her father.
Brahmahatyā said: "O Yajñadeva, best of the twice-born, do not accept him at all; he is a drinker of liquor, a thief, a slayer of a Brahmin, and a perpetrator of a most heinous sin. (21)
"He is a traitor to his mother, a traitor to his father, a sinner who has abandoned his wife, and corrupted by association with Kirātīs; therefore, release this evil-minded man! (22)
O Brahmin, if you accept this son who is a great sinner, then I shall take your wife, his wife, yourself, and this son, O twice-born one. (23)
"I shall devour your lineage; therefore, release this son. If you abandon this son, I shall release you all at once. (24)
"O high-minded one, you ought not to destroy your family for the sake of a single person. Thus addressed by her, Yajñadeva then spoke to her:
Yajñadeva said: "Affection for my son torments me; how can I abandon him? Hearing those words spoken by the twice-born, Brahmanahatyā addressed him.
Brahmahatyā said: "Since he has indeed become fallen and excluded from the system of castes and stages of life, do not feel affection for this son; even the sight of him is censurable."
Having spoken thus, while Yajñadeva looked on, that Brahmahatyā struck his son named Sumati with her palm.
He wept, repeatedly crying out "Father! Father! as he addressed his father.

Now follows the means for liberation from the sin of Brahman-slaughter as told by Durvāsas to Sumati: At that time, Ruru was the father of Sumati, and his mother and wife were also there; in the meantime, Durvāsas, who was a portion of Śaṅkara, arrived at that place.
By good fortune, the righteous yogi, the best of sages, arrived; then Yajñadeva, seeing that sage who was an incarnation of Rudra, [was filled with joy].
Having praised him and prostrated, he sought refuge for the sake of his son: "O Durvāsas, you are a great yogin, truly a direct portion of Śaṅkara."
The sight of you shall never be possible for those devoid of merit; my son was a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, and a thief. (33)
Even the personified sin of Brahmin-slaughter has come here to strike him down; may it be so that this son of mine is liberated from this great transgression. (34)
"Tell me now that means by which this terrible sin of killing a Brahmin may quickly come to an end; have compassion for my son. (35)
"O Sage, this alone is my son; I have no other offspring. If he dies, my lineage will be utterly cut off from its very root. (36)
Consequently, one would certainly not even be able to offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the ancestors; therefore, O Blessed Sage, show mercy toward us.
Thus addressed, Durvāsas, who was a portion of Śaṅkara, then spoke after meditating for a very long time upon Yajñadeva, the best of the twice-born.
Durvāsas said: "The sin committed by Yajñadeva has been brought very close to you by your son; there can be no pacification of this sin even through ten thousand penances."
Nevertheless, O twice-born one, for the sake of pacifying that sin of your son, I shall declare an expiation; listen with an undistracted mind.
On the highly meritorious Veṅkaṭādri, which destroys all sins, there exists the Svāmipuṣkariṇī, which bestows auspiciousness. (41)

Then, through bathing at Svāmipuṣkariṇī, Sumati was liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin: "If this son of yours bathes here, he shall be freed from his transgression in an instant. Having heard these words of the sage, the highly intelligent Yajñadeva—
Taking his son Sumati with him, he went to Svāmipuṣkariṇī and bathed his son Sumati, who was afflicted by the sin of killing.
A voice from the sky, sweet-toned, spoke to that brahmin: "O illustrious Yajñadeva, O observer of noble vows, by means of this bath..."
Your son has become purified; do not entertain any doubt, O twice-born one. Such is the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), which acts as an axe for the tree of sin.
Thus, O brahmins, this ancient history has been told to you; by listening to it or even by reciting it, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī Tīrtha," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Now, the majesty of Rāmakṛṣṇatīrtha. Śrī Sūta said: On the highly meritorious Veṅkaṭa mountain, which destroys all sins, listen with well-concentrated minds to the majesty of Kṛṣṇatīrtha.
Where even an ungrateful person is liberated merely by immersion; [yet] those deluded by ignorance show contempt for their fathers, mothers, and teachers. || 2 ||
And whatever other evil-minded ones there may be—those who are ungrateful and shameless—they all become purified merely by bathing in this Kṛṣṇa-tīrtha. || 3 ||
Formerly, on the mountain named Veṅkaṭa, a sage named Kṛṣṇa dwelt performing penance, meditating upon Viṣṇu with a concentrated mind.
There he fashioned an excellent sacred bathing place (tīrtha) for the purpose of ritual ablution; by bathing there even once, even a mortal who has been ungrateful is liberated.
In this regard, I shall relate an ancient history that destroys sin, by the mere hearing of which a person may attain liberation.
In former times there was a great sage named Rāmakṛṣṇa, the best of Brahmins, who was truthful, virtuous, eloquent, and endowed with compassion for all living beings.
Equal toward enemy and friend, self-controlled, ascetic, with senses conquered, he was proficient in the supreme Brahman and took sole refuge in the reality of Brahman.
Possessing such power, that sage performed most severe penance; indeed, he remained with all his limbs motionless upon the entire surface of the earth.
He did not move even a single atom from his own place, remaining there for many hundreds of years while performing austerities.
He stepped upon that anthill and indeed caused his body to be covered by it; even with his body thus overwhelmed by the anthill, Rāma-Kṛṣṇa remained a great sage.
He performed penance alone and did not notice the anthill; while that bull among sages was performing penance there, Vāsava [acted]. (12)
Having released masses of clouds, the impetuous one caused rain to fall; thus he rained continuously for seven days.
Although being drenched by that great downpour of rain, the sage indeed received that rain with his eyes closed.
Then, deafening the ears with a great thunderous roar, a massive thunderbolt fell directly upon the anthill.
While that rain-cloud was pouring down, the cold winds and other elements were difficult to endure.

Now follows the manifestation of the Lord, pleased by the penance of the great sages named Rāma and Kṛṣṇa: The summit of the anthill, struck by a thunderbolt, was shattered; then the God appeared, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace. (17)
Mounted upon the son of Vinatā, adorned with a forest garland, and gratified by the penance of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, he spoke these words.

O Rāmakṛṣṇa, treasury of austerity, you who have reached the further shore of the meaning of the Vedas and Śāstras: that best of men who bathes on the day of my manifestation [attains great merit]. (19)

O Brahmin, even with the remainder of his life, one would be unable to describe the fruit of the merit of that person who, on the great lunar day of the full moon when the sun is situated in Capricorn, [performs this act].
The time for bathing is prescribed when the moon is conjoined with the Puṣya constellation. On that day, the wise mortal who bathes at Kṛṣṇatīrtha— || 21 ||
Completely liberated from all sins, he shall obtain all his desires on the day of my manifestation, by means of the auspicious waters of the Kṛṣṇa-tīrtha.
Gods, humans, and all the guardians of the quarters of great prowess come there to bathe for the complete purification of their own sins. (23)
All these great souls, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns, indeed become purified by bathing in this Kṛṣṇatīrtha.
"By your name, this great holy place shall become famous in the world. Having said this, Śrīnivāsa vanished right there.
Such is the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), which purifies great sins, bestows purity of intellect upon men, and grants all forms of sovereignty. || 26 ||
Thus, O Brahmins, the majesty of Kṛṣṇatīrtha has been narrated to you; it bestows the world of Viṣṇu upon those who hear it and those who recite it. (27)

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Rāmakṛṣṇatīrtha," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Section of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now follows the praise of the gift of water on the auspicious Veṅkaṭādri. Śrī Sūta said: On the greatly meritorious mountain named Veṅkaṭa, one who does not give water, especially to those afflicted by thirst, shall fall into the womb of an animal.
Therefore, on the lordly mountain Veṅkaṭa, the gift of water should indeed be performed according to one's capacity; for it is the great life-sustainer for all. || 2 ||
In this very context, they cite this ancient history, the most wonderful dialogue between a brahmin and a house-lizard.

Now follows the account of Hemāṅga’s attainment of the state of a house-lizard due to his failure to give water. Formerly, in the lineage of Ikṣvāku, there was a king named Hemāṅga; he was devoted to Brahmanas, absorbed in the Supreme Spirit, a conqueror of enemies, and one who had mastered his senses.
As many as are the particles of earth, as many as are the drops of water, and as many as are the stars in the sky—so many cows does he give.

Because of the darbha grass used in his desired sacrifices, the earth is remembered as *barhiṣmatī* (possessing sacrificial grass); and because many twice-born ones were gratified with gifts of cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and other such things.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, it has been heard that no gifts were given by him; thus, he took even the single draught of water with the thought that it was easily obtained.
When it was bestowed upon Bodhita by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā—what fruit would the donor obtain of that which is priceless and attainable everywhere? (8)
Thus, the evil-minded one did not offer water with his arguments; rather, he spoke with reasoning that "merit would accrue from giving what cannot be obtained. (9)
He honored those twice-born who were deformed, poor, and distressed for lack of livelihood; he did not honor the learned Brahmins who knew the Veda and discoursed upon the Supreme Truth.
All the worlds will honor those who are renowned with appropriate offerings, as well as those who are destitute, ignorant, deformed, and those who are householders.
"What other refuge can there be for the poor? Therefore, they are the objects of my compassion. Thinking thus, he gave something of his own even to those wicked recipients. (12)
Because of that great fault, he attained the state of a cātaka bird for three births; in one birth he became a vulture, and for seven births he was a dog.
O twice-born ones, having been born later in the house of King Śrutakīrti, the lord of Mithilā, this king was a house-lizard.
That evil-minded one remained at the gate of the house and along the street for eighty-eight years, subsisting on insects.

Now, by partaking of the water from the feet of Śrutadeva, Hemāṅga attained the memory of his past lives. Once, at midday, the best of sages known as Śrutadeva arrived at the house of the lord of Videha, exhausted.
Seeing him, the lord of men rose up suddenly with joy; having honored him well with the madhuparka offering, he performed the ritual washing of his feet.
Then, at the time ordained by fate, water was quickly poured upon her head; and by those droplets being sprinkled, the house-lizard was consecrated.
Immediately, she regained the memory of her past life and became deeply distressed by her own deeds; crying out, "Save me! Save me! she called to the brahmin who had come to her house.
Hearing the cry of the animal, the Brahmin was struck with wonder: "O lizard, why do you cry out? By what karma have you come to this state? (20)
"Are you a demigod or a god, a king or the best of the twice-born? Tell me, O highly fortunate one, who are you? Today I shall deliver you."
