Thus addressed, that great lord, the king, said to Śrutadeva: "I am born of the Ikṣvāku lineage and am highly proficient in the science of weaponry."
As many as are the particles of dust upon the earth, as many as are the drops of water, and as many as are the stars in the sky—so many cows have I given.
I have performed all sacrifices, I have carried out works of public utility, I have bestowed gifts, and I have well practiced the entire range of dharma.
Nevertheless, O Lord, an evil rebirth occurred for me instead of an upward one; three times I was born as a cātaka bird, and once as a vulture.
O twice-born one, in seven previous births, I attained the state of a dog because this king bore the water used for washing my feet.
Drops [of water] were thrown far away; somehow I was sprinkled by them, and then, my sins destroyed, the memory of my former birth arose within me.
"O twice-born one, twenty-eight births as iguanas are to be experienced by me; ordained by fate, they appear before me, and I am greatly terrified by these births. (28)
"I do not perceive the cause; tell me that in detail. Thus addressed, that twice-born one said: "It has been understood by the eye of higher knowledge. (29)

Now follows the liberation of Hemāṅga from his state as a lizard through the merit of Śrutadevadatta. Listen, O King, I shall explain the cause of your miserable rebirth: you did not give water on the mountain named Veṅkaṭa.
Thinking that water was easily available and not considering its true value, he did not provide it for travelers, brahmins, and others, even during the hot season, out of ignorance. (31)
Likewise, having abandoned a worthy recipient, that which is bestowed upon an unworthy recipient is like casting away a blazing fire; it is not offered into ashes.
Having abandoned the Tulasī plant, why indeed is the Bṛhatī worshipped? Let the state of being helpless, deformed, or lame not be made a ground for such preference. (33)

Indeed, even those who are helpless, such as the lame and others, are solely objects of compassion; so too are those established in austerity, established in knowledge, and devoted to the Vedas and the scriptures.
Those who possess the form of Viṣṇu are always to be honored, and never others; even among them, those possessed of knowledge are always exceedingly dear to Viṣṇu. (35)

O King, even among the wise, Viṣṇu alone is always dear; therefore, the man of knowledge is always worthy of worship, being remembered as more worthy of worship than the [external] object of worship itself. (36)
Water was not given by you, nor were the virtuous served; therefore, O delighter of the Ikṣvākus, this miserable state has been attained by you.
I shall give you the merit earned on Veṅkaṭādri for the sake of your peace; by that, you will conquer all past, future, and present collections of karma.
Having spoken thus and touched water, he bestowed the unsurpassed merit that arises from a bath performed on a single day by a Brāhmaṇa. (39)
With all his sins destroyed by that [act], having abandoned the form of a house-lizard—a form resulting from his karma—he was immediately seen as a man. (40)

Mounted upon a divine celestial chariot and adorned with divine garlands, garments, and ornaments, he appeared within the palace of the King of Mithila while the virtuous onlookers were still watching.
Having joined his palms in reverence, circumambulated, and prostrated, the king, permitted to depart and being praised by the immortals, went to heaven.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there for ten thousand years without weariness, he himself became the great chariot-warrior Kakutstha in the lineage of Ikṣvāku.
The protector of the seven islands, devoted to Brahman, esteemed by the virtuous, equal to the lord of the gods, such was that great lord, an actual portion of Viṣṇu.
Instructed by Vasiṣṭha, the king practiced all the enchanting duties in their entirety; through that, his inauspiciousness and other evils were destroyed.
Having attained divine knowledge, he achieved union with Viṣṇu; therefore, the lord of mountains, Veṅkaṭa, is meritorious and the destroyer of sins.

And in that place, the gift of water bestows the world of Viṣṇu. Thus, O Brahmins, has the majesty of the gift of water been recounted to you on the highly meritorious Veṅkaṭādri, which destroys all sins. 47.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Gift of Water," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now follows the description of the sacred field of Śrī Veṅkaṭācala and other sites. Śrī Sūta said: I shall proclaim once again the majesty of Veṅkaṭādri; listen with great attention and well-composed minds.
Whatever sacred fords exist upon the earth and those within the cosmic egg, all of them reside on the mountain named Veṅkaṭa.
In that meritorious, supreme city dwells Puruṣottama, the auspicious God who bears the conch and the discus and wears yellow garments.
[He saw] the God of gods, whose chest was adorned with the Kaustubha gem, who bestows fearlessness upon his devotees, the large-eyed one, who is known through the Vedas, and who is eternal.
Those residing in the lands of Aṅga, Kosala, Karṇāṭa, Kāśī, and Gurjara; those born in all countries such as Cola, Kerala, Pāṇḍya, and others. || 5 ||
And every year, gods, sages, Siddhas, and yogis such as Sanaka and others come with their families for the purpose of service.
Those who perform service during the great festival of Veṅkaṭeśa in the month of Bhādrapada—all of them are sinless and most excellent.
There, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, performed the great festival of raising the flag for Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa during the month of Kanyā.
And every year, for the sake of serving him, all human beings, all gods, gandharvas, siddhas, and the highly powerful sādhyas [assemble].
At the festival of Brahmā, the best of the twice-born assemble, just as the knowledge of the Vedas is the foremost among all sciences, and the syllable Om is the foremost among mantras.
Just as the wish-fulfilling cow is to cows and as life itself is to beloved objects, so too is the lordly Veṅkaṭa mountain the most excellent among all sacred fields.
As Garuḍa is among all serpents, as Viṣṇu is among the gods, and as the Brāhmaṇa is among the social classes, so [is he] among all the remaining Nāgas. || 12 ||
Likewise, Veṅkaṭaśailendra is the most excellent among all sacred fields (kṣetras), just as the celestial wish-fulfilling tree (surataru) is among trees, and just as a wife is among friends. (13)
Just as Gaṅgā is among sacred fords (tīrthas) and the Sun is among luminous bodies, so too is the Lord of Mountains, Veṅkaṭa, the most excellent of all holy places (kṣetras). 14.
Just as the thunderbolt is among weapons, as gold is among metals, as Rudra is among the devotees of Viṣṇu, and as the Kaustubha gem is among jewels; || 15 ||
Likewise, Veṅkaṭaśailendra is the most excellent among all sacred fields; there is nothing like it in the world for increasing the pleasure of Viṣṇu.
There is no month equal to Mādhava, no age equal to Kṛta; there is no scripture equal to the Vedas, and no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā. (17)
There is no gift equal to water; there is no happiness equal to that of a wife; there is no wealth equal to agriculture; and there is no gain greater than life. (18)
There is no austerity greater than fasting, no happiness higher than giving, no dharma equal to compassion, and no light like that of the eye. (19)
There is no satisfaction equal to eating; nor is there commerce equal to agriculture. There is no friend equal to righteousness; nor is there fame equal to truth.
In whatever way one considers it, there is indeed nothing equal to the state of the Blessed One.

O lords of sages, the chanting of whose name removes all sins, the salutation of whom bestows all happiness in this world, and even the pilgrimage toward whom is worthy of worship by the gods—even such is that great Veṅkaṭaśaila, the foremost of mountains. (22)
I shall further proclaim its power: all sacred fords (tīrthas) dwell therein; thus, among all of them, that lake named Śrīsvāmin is the preeminent sacred ford.

How can I describe the majesty of this place, where on the western shore the Earth-Boar, possessing an exceedingly gentle form and benefiting all people, shines resplendent while embracing his beloved? (24)
And at Śrī Svāmipuṣkariṇī, on the southern [slope], Veṅkaṭeśvara remains for all time as the bestower of boons, his form embraced by Lakṣmī. (25)
Thus, O Brahmins, has this supreme majesty of the sacred field been told to you; he who always hears it with devotion is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Sacred Field," in the *Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya*, within the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now follows the description of the majesty of Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara. Śrī Sūta said: Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the majesty of Veṅkaṭeśvara, hearing which one is liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt.
The man who beholds the Lord Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara even once attains liberation; he shall attain union with Viṣṇu.
That merit which is acquired by men in ten years during the Kṛta Yuga is accomplished in a single year during the Tretā Yuga.
In the Dvāpara age, that fruit is obtained in five months, and in the Kali age, it is multiplied ten million times for men at every single moment.
Without doubt, for those who behold the Lord Śrīnivāsa at the divine Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara, all sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas) are indeed present. || 5 ||
All the gods, sages, and likewise the ancestors are present there, [receiving offerings] once a day, twice a day, thrice a day, or indeed at all times.
O Brahmins, those who remember Mahādeva Śrīnivāsa, the bestower of liberation, or who glorify him, are liberated from the cage of sin.
They indeed go to the supreme god Nārāyaṇa, Veṅkaṭeśa, who is worshipped by Śaṅkharāja and whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Merely by remembering him, even the torment of Yama shall not occur for those men who worship Śrīnivāsa, the Great God, even once.
Of what use are gifts, of what use are vows, of what use are austerities, and of what use are sacrifices for those who do not contemplate the supreme deity Veṅkaṭeśa for even a moment? (10)
He shall be ignorant and sinful; he is to be known as mute, deaf, dull-witted, and blind; there shall always be a vulnerability in him.
O lords of sages, when the great god Śrīnivāsa has been seen even once, what further fruit is there in Kāśī, Gayā, or even Prayāga?
Having obtained this rare human birth on this earth, those men who behold or worship Veṅkaṭeśa, the supreme deity, [attain the highest goal]. 13.
Indeed, their birth is fruitful and they have achieved their purpose, and no others, when the supreme deity Veṅkaṭeśa has been seen or even worshipped. (14)
What need is there for Śambhu, Brahmā, or even Śakra and all the immortals for those men who are endowed with devotion to the Great God Veṅkaṭeśa? (15)
Those men who are engaged in bowing to them, remembering them, and worshipping them do not behold miseries, nor do they go to the abode of Yama. || 16 ||
Thousands of killings of Brahmins and tens of thousands of drinks of liquor—all these go to total dissolution upon seeing the god Nārāyaṇa. (17)
Those who always desire enjoyments and sovereignty even in the abode of the thirty gods should joyfully bow down once to the dweller of Veṅkaṭādri.
Whatever sins have been committed throughout ten million births, all of them perish by the sight of Veṅkaṭeśvara. (19)
Whether through association, curiosity, greed, or even fear, one who remembers Veṅkaṭeśa, the Great God, shall not experience suffering either in this world or the next.
By glorifying and also worshipping the Lord of Veṅkaṭācala, one certainly attains the same form as Viṣṇu; there is no doubt in this matter.
Just as a kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes in an instant, so does the sight of Veṅkaṭeśvara destroy all sins.
The devotion to Lord Veṅkaṭeśvara is recorded as being eightfold: affection for his devotees and the satisfaction of performing worship unto him. (23)
Worshiping him oneself with devotion; bodily exertion for his sake; and likewise, a longing for his greatness and attentive respect in listening to his stories. (24)
Likewise, there is the throbbing of physical changes in one's voice and body, as well as the constant remembrance of the Lord Śrīnivāsa. (25)
Taking refuge in that very Lord who dwells on Veṅkaṭādri as one's means of livelihood—thus, even in a Mleccha, these eightfold forms of devotion may exist. (26)
He alone attains liberation, O Śaunaka and others of great luster; for it is certain that liberation comes through exclusive devotion and the knowledge of Brahman.

O Brahmins, that liberation of ascetics who have sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*) through hearing the Vedānta scriptures occurs even without knowledge arising from the study of Vedānta, as well as without the stage of life of a renunciant (*yatyāśrama*) and without dispassion (*virakti*). (28)
And for all the social classes (varṇas) as well as for those in all the stages of life (āśramas), it is simply by the sight of the Lord Vekaṭeśvara alone [that liberation is attained].
Liberation, which grants freedom from rebirth, will occur without delay for worms and insects, as well as for gods and sages whose wealth is their austerity. (30)
On the lordly Veṅkaṭa mountain, by the grace of Śrīnivāsa, [all] shall be equalized; do not harbor fear, thinking, "Many sins have been committed by me. (31)
When the Great God Śrīnivāsa, Veṅkaṭeśa, has been beheld, let no one harbor pride by thinking, "Merit has been performed by me. (32)
Neither fewer nor more shall they be; rather, all these great persons [shall go] to the most meritorious place named Veṅkaṭa, which destroys all sins.
He who beholds Śrīnivāsa, the supreme deity, with devotion, does not find an equal upon this earth even among those learned in the four Vedas.
He who worships the Lord of Gods, Veṅkaṭeśvara, with devotion, goes to the abode of Hari accompanied by ten million members of his lineage.
Indeed, there is no merit equal to or greater than that of Śrīnivāsa; he who, established in delusion, hates Him who dwells on the Veṅkaṭa mountain [commits a grave sin]. || 36 ||
By him, ten thousand killings of Brahmins—which cause one to fall into hell—have been committed; by merely conversing with him, a human being would go to hell. (37)
The Vedas are devoted to Śrīnivāsa; the sacrifices are devoted to Śrīnivāsa; everything is devoted to Śrīnivāsa; therefore, nothing else exists apart from Him.
Abandoning everything else, one should take refuge in Śrīnivāsa; for whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and bathing at sacred fords, [it is attained by this]. (39)
By serving Śrīnivāsa while meditating upon Him as the dweller of Veṅkaṭādri for two ghaṭikās, that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold.
By maintaining twenty-one generations of one's lineage, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu; [this is attained] through bathing at the Svāmipuṣkariṇī tīrtha and beholding the Lord.
If it were possible for men [to attain liberation] through the service of the waters of the Gaṅgā, what need would there be for one who never beholds Vekaṭeśa, the supreme deity? 42.
That, however, should be known as a mixture (of castes) and not born from the seed of the father; therefore, with every effort, [one should worship] Veṅkaṭeśa, the ocean of mercy. 43.
O twice-born ones, he should be beheld with great effort by those who desire the world beyond. Thus, O brahmins, has the majesty of Veṅkaṭeśa been narrated to you.
He who constantly hears this and recites it with devotion shall indeed obtain the fruit of service to Veṅkaṭanātha. || 45 ||

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Glory of Veṅkaṭeśvara," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now follows the description of the continuous residence of Brahmā and the other deities on Śrī Veṅkaṭācala. Śrī Sūta said: "Therefore, I shall now fully proclaim the majesty of Veṅkaṭācala; listen with careful attention and well-composed minds. (1)
Thousands of lakṣas and koṭis of lakes and rivers, as well as oceans of great merit, forests, and hermitages [were seen].
There were merit-bestowing places born from the soil, such as sacred Vedas and forests, as well as sages like Vasiṣṭha and others, along with Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Kiṃnaras.
The Blessed Madhusūdana was there with Lakṣmī and Dharaṇī, and the Four-faced One (Brahmā) together with Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī.
The Lord of Gods, the three-eyed destroyer of Tripura, together with Pārvatī, as well as the gods headed by Heramba and Ṣaṇmukha, led by Indra, [were present]. || 5 ||
The Ādityas and other planets, as well as the eight Vasus, O twice-born ones, the ancestors, the world-protectors, and likewise other hosts of deities; || 6 ||
They dwell day and night upon the summit of the Venkata mountain, which destroys multitudes of great sins and purifies the world.
Merely by the sight of him, men shall experience bliss of mind; for the women of the Siddhas and Cāraṇas have made their dwelling upon his head.
They worship Veṅkaṭeśa, the ocean of mercy, at all times; [even] millions of sins of killing Brahmins and millions of instances of approaching women who should not be approached [are destroyed].
Those clinging to the body perish by the winds of Mount Veṅkaṭa.

Now follows the procedure for the recollection at the time of ascending the glorious Veṅkaṭācala. One should pray to that mountain Veṅkaṭādri, the increaser of merit: "O Golden Mountain, O highly meritorious one, served by all the gods! (11)
O best of mountains, I would have trodden with my feet upon you, whom even the gods beginning with Brahmā serve with faith.
Forgive this sin of mine today out of compassion for one of sinful mind; show me Mādhava, who has made his dwelling upon your head.
Having thus prayed to Veṅkaṭādri, the best of mountains, a man should then proceed with gentle steps toward the purifying Veṅkaṭācala.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rules at the Svāmipuṣkariṇī Tīrtha on the highly meritorious Veṅkaṭādri mountain, which destroys all sins; || 15 ||
Thereafter, one should offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa), even if it is only the size of a mustard seed; or one may offer balls equal in size to a śamī leaf toward the ancestors.
Those dwelling in heaven attain liberation, and even those residing in hell go to heaven.

Now follows the majesty of the sacred ford named Pāpavināśana: Beyond that, situated above it, is a great and meritorious place, renowned throughout all the worlds as the best of all tīrthas, known by the name Pāpavināśana. (18)
O Brahmins, there exists the most meritorious and pure Veṅkaṭācala, by the mere remembrance of which one no longer undergoes residence in a womb.
Having reached that, a person should bathe to the north of Svāmitīrtha; by bathing there, men go to Vaikuṇṭha—of this there is no doubt.
The sages said: O Sūta, tell us of the majesty of the holy ford named Pāpavināśa; for you, O great sage, having been enlightened by Vyāsa, know everything.
Śrī Sūta said: O best of Brāhmaṇas, I shall relate to you this auspicious narrative concerning what occurred at the hermitage of Brahmā on the beautiful slopes of the Himavat.
That holy hermitage, the auspicious abode of Brahmā, was filled with various trees on the beautiful slopes of the Himalayas.
It was filled with many shrubs and creepers, frequented by deer and elephants, resounded with the voices of Siddhas and Cāraṇas, and was a delightful forest in full bloom.
It was crowded with many ascetics and graced by forest-dwellers, as well as by highly fortunate Brahmins who resembled the blazing sun and fire.
It was crowded with ascetics endowed with self-restraint and vows, who were initiated, devoted to sacrifice, moderate in diet, and perfected in soul.
It was surrounded by Vaidikas perfected in the study of the Vedas, and by those in the student stage, householders, forest-dwellers, and mendicants.
It was surrounded on all sides by the Vālakhilya sages, who were devoted to the conduct of their own stages of life and performed the duties prescribed for their respective castes.
Now follows the account of the Śūdra named Dṛḍhamati. O twice-born ones, formerly in that hermitage, a certain bold Śūdra named Dṛḍhamati approached the presence of a Brāhmaṇa, filled with joy. (29)
Having arrived at the hermitage and being honored by the ascetics, a Śūdra named Dṛḍhamati indeed prostrated himself with all eight limbs.
Seeing those hosts of sages, who were like gods and possessed of great majesty, performing various sacrifices, Śūdraka was filled with joy.
Then the thought occurred to him to perform unsurpassed austerity; thereupon, having approached the sage Kulapati, the ascetic, he spoke to him.
Dṛḍhamati said: "O ascetic, salutations to you! Protect me, O ocean of compassion. By your grace, I desire to perform a sacrifice; be gracious unto me. (33)
Then, regarding Dṛḍhamati, the sage known as Kulapati taught the duties of a Śūdra. Having been addressed thus by the Śūdra, the Brāhmaṇa then spoke to him.
The Kulapati said: "A Śūdra, being of low birth, cannot be initiated for a sacrifice. If such is your intention, then remain devoted to service."
Instruction should never be given to one who is devoid of [proper] birth; in giving instruction, a great fault accrues to the teacher. (36)
A wise man should not teach a Śūdra, nor should he officiate at his sacrifices; likewise, he should not instruct a Śūdra in the scriptures, such as grammar and other sciences.
One should never teach poetry, nor drama, nor even rhetoric, nor the Purāṇas, nor the Itihāsas to a Śūdra. (38)
If a Brahmin should ever teach these [mantras] to a Śūdra, the other Brahmins shall expel that Brahmin from the village inhabited by those devoted to the Veda.
One should abandon a twice-born man who instructs a Śūdra, treating him like a Caṇḍāla; and one should avoid from afar a Śūdra who is possessed of Vedic syllables.
Listen to that, may prosperity be yours, together with Brāhmaṇācchadman; for the service of the twice-born is declared by Manu and others to be the duty of a Śūdra. (41)
"For you ought not to abandon your innate duty. Thus addressed by the sage, that Śūdra then reflected.
"What should be done by me today? For my faith in the vow is supreme; I shall indeed strive today so that excellent knowledge may arise for me. (43)
Having thus resolved in his mind, the Śūdra Dṛḍhamati then went some distance from the hermitage grounds and constructed a beautiful hut.
There indeed were temples for the deities and sacred shrines, as well as flower gardens and the like, and the excavation of tanks and so forth. || 45 ||
With faith, he performed austerities for the sake of his own spiritual perfection, as well as ritual ablutions, religious observances, fasts, and so forth.
Having performed the bali offering and having offered oblations, he worshipped the deities; endowed with resolve and self-restraint, subsisting on fruit, he had his senses subdued.
He constantly honored guests who arrived according to the rules with bulbs, roots, flowers, and likewise fruits.
In this manner, indeed, a very great length of time passed for him.

Now follows the sequence of ritual performance as revealed by the brahmin named Sumati to Dṛḍhamati. Then, a twice-born man named Sumati—born of the Garga lineage, truthful, and one who had conquered his senses—went to his hermitage. (50)
Having honored the sage with welcomes and gratified him with fruits and other offerings, he spoke of meritorious stories and inquired after his well-being.
Thus, having been honored with ritual services such as water for the feet and other offerings, the Brahmin greeted him with blessings and accepted his hospitable reception.
Having taken leave of him with a joyful heart, he returned to his own hermitage; thus, day after day, the Brahmin became partial toward this Śūdra. (53)
He came to his hermitage to see that one born of a Śūdra womb; for a long time, there had been association between the twice-born man and one of Śūdra origin.

Having fallen under the power of affection, he did not disregard what was said by the Śūdra. Then, when the twice-born man had arrived, the Śūdra spoke to him, who was likewise overcome by affection. (55)
"Tell me the procedure for the offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya), for you are considered my guru. Thus addressed by the Śūdra, he instructed him in all of this.
At that time, he caused the Śūdra to perform the ancestral rites (pitr-kārya) and so forth; once those ancestral rites had been performed by him, that best of the twice-born was dismissed.

Now, Sumati experienced a miserable state due to his instruction in Vedic rites for a Śūdra. Then, after being nourished by that Śūdra womb for a long time, this twice-born man was abandoned by the hosts of Brahmins and met his death.
Led away by the servants of Vaivasvata, he was cast even into the hells for thousands of crores of kalpas and hundreds of crores of kalpas.
Having experienced the hells in succession, at their conclusion he became an immobile being; thereafter he was born as a donkey, and after that as a dung-pig.
Then he was born as a dog, and afterwards he attained the state of a crow; then, having reached the condition of a Caṇḍāla, he subsequently entered a Śūdra womb.
Afterwards, he attained the status of a Vaiśya, and immediately after that, a Kṣatriya; then, being oppressed by powerful forces, that Brāhmaṇa indeed became so once more.
In his eighth year from conception, that twice-born one was initiated by his father; while residing in his father's house, he was devoted to the practice of proper conduct.
Once, while wandering through a dense forest, he was seized by a Brahmarākṣasa; weeping, wandering, stumbling, bewildered, prattling, and laughing, he was thus possessed.
Constantly crying out "Alas! Alas!", he abandoned his Vedic ritual; seeing his son in such a state, the father was tormented by grief.
Taking up his lute out of affection, he went for refuge to Agastya, who was performing austerities before Lord Śiva on the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī.
Having bowed to the sage with devotion, the father indeed informed him of the conduct of his son.

Then, at the word of Agastya, for the sake of removing Sumati’s misfortune, he set out for Veṅkaṭādri. At that time, the Brahmin spoke to the pot-born sage, the bull among ascetics: "O Brāhmaṇa, this son of mine has been seized by a Brahma-rākṣasa."
O Brahmin, do not find happiness; protect him with a compassionate gaze! I have no other son for the sake of liberating my ancestors from their debt. (69)
"O Pot-born one, tell me the means for the destruction of his suffering; in the three worlds, there is no one equal to you in ascetic virtue. (70)
"Without you, there is no protector for my son; show compassion toward my son, O Teacher, for the virtuous are indeed compassionate by nature. (71)
Śrī Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by him, the pot-born sage (Agastya) then entered into meditation; after meditating for a very long time, he then spoke to the Brāhmaṇa.
Agastya said: "O high-minded one, in a previous birth this son of yours was a Brāhmaṇa; this learned man named Sumati indeed gave his wisdom to a Śūdra. (73)
He indeed taught all these Vedic rituals; therefore, having experienced hells for thousands of millions of kalpas, he— || 74 ||
Having been born on earth in various wombs such as those of immobile beings and the like, your son has now been born as a Brāhmaṇa through the remainder of his past karma.
"Today he has been seized here by a cruel Brahma-rākṣasa sent by Yama, due indeed to a sinful deed committed in a previous birth. (76)
I shall declare to you the means for the destruction of the Brahma-rākṣasa; listen with faith, having composed your mind in concentration. (77)
On the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī, frequented by hosts of sages, stands the purifying Veṅkaṭācala, worthy of being served by the gods. (78)
Above that is a great sacred site (tīrtha) named Pāpavināśana; it is meritorious, renowned, and the destroyer of even the most heinous sins.
That holy place is remembered as the destroyer of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, vetālas, brahmarākṣasas, and even of great diseases.
"Taking the child, go to that sacred ford situated in the midst of the mountain; being self-restrained, bathe your son at that sin-destroying tirtha."
By bathing there for three days, the Brahma-rākṣasa is destroyed; no other means for his destruction exists on earth.
Therefore, go quickly to the mountain named Veṅkaṭa; there, bathe your son in the holy ford known as Pāpavināśa.
"Do not delay here; go indeed with haste, O twice-born one! Thus addressed, that brahmin prostrated himself on the ground like a staff before Agastya.
Having been granted permission by him, that brahmin set out for Veṅkaṭācala; having gone there with his son, he reached the destroyer of sins.

Then, O best of Brahmins, having first performed the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), that father, the lord of sages, bathed his son for three days in the Pāpavināśana [tirtha] to remove his miserable state; he himself also bathed there in the Pāpavināśana.
Having arrived, he drank the water and performed his daily rites; then, his son was there released from the state of a brahmarākṣasa.
He was born free from disease, healthy, and possessing a beautiful form; enriched with all prosperity, he enjoyed manifold pleasures. || 88 ||
At the end of his life, he attained liberation through bathing at Pāpavināśana; his father also attained liberation at the end of his life by bathing there.

Now follows the removal of the attainment of miserable states for one of firm intellect who performs Vedic rites. Having been instructed by him, that Śūdra, after having experienced hells in succession and having been born in many contemptible wombs, [attained liberation]. (90)
Thereafter, he was born as a vulture on the mountain Veṅkaṭācala; once, he went to the Pāpavināśana tīrtha to drink water.
Having arrived, he drank the water and sprinkled his own body; at that very moment, possessing a divine form, he was adorned with all ornaments.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot, he departed for the abode of the immortals.
Śrī Sūta said: Such indeed is the power of this holy place (tīrtha), which destroys sins; because it destroys sins, O brahmins, it is called Pāpanāśa.

Thus, O lords of sages, has this secret been told—the majesty of that destroyer of sins—by virtue of which, through ablution, both a twice-born man and a Śūdra were instantly liberated despite their blameworthy deeds.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Pāpavināśana Tīrtha," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now follows the description of the majesty of Pāpavināśana Tīrtha. Śrī Sūta said: Once again I shall proclaim the glory of the destroyer of sins; listen with great concentration and with a heart full of devotion to the Lord.
I shall proclaim this history which destroys all sins; having heard it, one is liberated from all evils—of this there is no doubt.

Now follows the account of the poor Brahmin named Bhadramati. Formerly, there was an excellent Brahmin, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, who was poor and destitute of livelihood; that twice-born man was named Bhadramati. (3)
All the scriptures were heard by that wise brahmin; he also studied the Purāṇas and the Dharmaśāstras in their entirety.
Abhava had six wives: Kṛtā, Siṃdhuyaśovatī, Kāminī, Mālinī, and Śobhā are thus proclaimed. || 5 ||
With those wives, he had two hundred sons; all those sons and others of his were tormented by hunger.
Possessing nothing yet blessed with wisdom, the noble-minded man, seeing his beloved children and wife afflicted by hunger, lamented with his senses overwhelmed.
Fie upon a birth devoid of fortune! Fie upon a birth bereft of wealth! Fie upon a birth lacking renown! Fie upon a birth that excludes hospitality! || 8 ||
Fie upon a birth devoid of right conduct! Fie upon a birth bereft of knowledge! Fie upon a birth lacking effort! Fie upon a birth deprived of happiness! (9)
Fie on a life devoid of kinsmen! Fie on a life bereft of renown! Fie on the life of a man with many offspring who is destitute of power! 10.
Ah! Virtues, gentleness, learning, and birth in a noble family—all these do not shine for one who is submerged in the ocean of poverty. (11)
Brahmins, sons, grandsons, kinsmen, as well as brothers and all disciples—these men abandon one who is deprived of power. (12)
Having thus resolved, the wise and steadfast Brahmin Bhadramati thought: "Whether one be a Caṇḍāla or a Brahmin, it is only the fortunate person who is honored. (13)
In this world, a poor man is like a corpse, despised by people; whereas one endowed with wealth—whether he be cruel or even gentle—is highly regarded. (14)
Whether devoid of virtues or possessed of them, whether a fool or a scholar, whether cruel or virtuous, or even a man devoid of dharma—(he is honored). || 15 ||
If one is endowed with the quality of sovereignty, he is surely worthy of honor; of this there is no doubt. Alas, poverty is suffering, and even therein, hope brings extreme misery.
Men overcome by desire experience suffering instantly. || 17 ||
Those who are slaves to hope are slaves to the whole world; but for those whose servant hope is, the world serves as their slave. (18)
Even one who knows the meaning of all the scriptures appears like a fool if he is poor; for those seized by the great crocodile of destitution, there is no deliverer. (19)
Alas, what suffering! Alas, what suffering! Alas, what suffering is poverty! Even therein, an abundance of sons and wives is a source of extreme misery. (20)

Having spoken thus, Bhadramati, who had mastered the meaning of all the scriptures, remained silent, filled with great distress, while reflecting in his mind upon that Dharma which bestows supreme sovereignty. (21)
Now follows the encouragement of Bhadramati’s journey to Mount Veṅkaṭa by Kāminī: At that time, among those wives, Kāminī was devoted to her husband as a deity. (22)
His wife, endowed with virtuous qualities, replied to her husband.

The beloved woman said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, you who have reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures; O my lord, highly fortunate one, O great-minded one, listen to my words. (24)
On the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī, frequented by hosts of sages, stands the purifying Veṅkaṭācala, worthy of being served by the gods.
On that lordly Veṅkaṭa mountain, which is saluted by gods and demons, there exists a purifying, auspicious holy site that burns away all sins.
Having gone there, O illustrious and high-minded one, perform your bath with diligence at Pāpanāśa, accompanied by your wife and sons. (27)
I heard of the greatness of that sacred ford from Nārada; in my childhood, the sage recounted it in the presence of my father.
On the highly meritorious Veṅkaṭādri mountain, which destroys all sins, pacifies all miseries, and bestows all prosperity. || 29 ||
Having bathed according to the prescribed ritual at the great holy site of Pāpanāśa, he then meditated in his mind upon that dharma which bestows supreme sovereignty.
Having determined that the gift of land is the most excellent of all gifts, it leads to the next world and bestows the fruit of all desires. (31)
The gift of land is proclaimed to be the supreme among all gifts; by giving that, a man obtains whatever is most desired. (32)
Having heard these words spoken by Nārada, my father, the twice-born, became joyful in mind and then proceeded to Śeṣādri. || 33 ||
Having gone there, the illustrious one bestowed a gift of land, which bestows all prosperity, upon an excellent Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas.
Then my father, O wise one, endowed with all good fortune, having attained happiness in this world, went at the end to the city of Viṣṇu.
And you, O highly fortunate one, having gone to Veṅkaṭādri, the best of mountains, diligently perform the gift of land, which grants all desires. (36)

Now follows the praise of the gift of land as recounted by Kāminī: "O Blessed Lord, listen with a well-composed mind to the majesty of the gift of land; no one in this world is able to describe it fully. (37)
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of land; the giver of land attains supreme nirvāṇa—of this there is no doubt. (38)
By giving even a very small amount of land to a learned Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires, one attains the world of Brahmā, from which there is no return. || 39 ||
The giver of land is declared to be a giver of everything; the giver of land shall become a partaker of liberation. Furthermore, the gift of land on Vṛṣādri destroys all sins. (40)
Whether one is tainted by a great sin (mahāpātaka) or burdened by all sins, by giving a plot of land ten cubits in size, one is liberated from all evils.
He who gives land to a worthy recipient obtains the fruit of all gifts; there exists no one equal to the giver of land in the three worlds. (42)
For one who bestows auspicious land upon a twice-born man deprived of his livelihood, Śeṣa is never capable of describing the fruit of that merit.
He who gives even a small amount of land to any brahmin who is devoid of a livelihood but possesses virtuous conduct is Viṣṇu himself; there is no doubt in this matter. (44)
He by whom the earth, endowed with sugarcane, wheat, fields, betel-nut trees, and other such things, is given away—he is Viṣṇu; there is no doubt about this. (45)
By giving even a small amount of land to a poor Brahmin who maintains his family but lacks a means of livelihood, one attains union with Viṣṇu.
For a Brahmin devoted to the worship of the gods, the gift of forest land yields the same fruit as bathing for three nights in the Ganges.
Listen to the fruit that one obtains by giving a "droṇikā" measure of land to a Brahmin who is devoid of a livelihood but devoted to virtuous conduct. || 48 ||
Whatever fruit a man obtains by performing hundreds of horse-sacrifices according to the rules on the banks of the Gaṅgā, he obtains that great fruit here.
O my Lord, O Blessed One, O Master, I shall declare the merit of him who gives fertile land to a poor twice-born man. (50)
Having performed thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices on the banks of the Ganges, he shall obtain that same fruit.
The gift of land is proclaimed as a great gift, a supreme gift; it pacifies all sins and bestows the fruit of liberation. (52)
Having heard this, one endowed with faith shall obtain the fruit of the gift of land, after hearing the words of his wife accompanied by this historical narrative. (53)
Being contented, he meditated in his mind upon the one who dwells on Śeṣācala.

Then, through the gift of land to Bhadramati, Sughoṣa set his mind upon attaining a good rebirth; he then proceeded toward the unsurpassed mountain of play. Thereupon, the gentle Bhadramati, who was devoted to all dharmas, [departed].
Accompanied by his wife, he went to the city named Suśālī to see the lord of brahmins named Sughoṣa, who was endowed with all forms of prosperity.
Having gone there, the twice-born Sughoṣa, who was devoted to righteousness, requested a piece of land five cubits long; and Sughoṣa, observing that he was a householder, [granted it].

Having attained joy in his mind and having honored him, he said to him: "O one of auspicious intellect, I have achieved my purpose; my birth has become fruitful, and my lineage has become stainless, since you are indeed worthy of being accepted by me. (58)
Having spoken thus and honored him, Sughoṣa, who was devoted to the Dharma and possessed of great intelligence, gave that [lute] of five cubits in length to him.
The earth is indeed sacred to Viṣṇu; the earth is protected by Viṣṇu. By this gift of earth, may Janārdana be pleased with me. (60)
O best of Brahmins, having worshipped that lord of the twice-born with this mantra, considering him to be Viṣṇu, Sughoṣa gave him the entire earth.
O Brahmins, that wise Bhadramati gave that requested land to a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya) who was a householder and a devotee of Hari.
Sughoṣa, endowed with ten million descendants, attained the abode of Viṣṇu through the gift of land, having gone to which one does not grieve.

Then, for the purpose of making a land-gift on the banks of the Pāpanāśanā river, Bhadramati went to the lordly Veṅkaṭādri mountain, which is saluted by gods and demons; the Brahmin Bhadramati, accompanied by his sons and wife, departed for that king of mountains.
The divine and unsurpassed mountain of sport, Meruputraka, frequented by Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Śailādīs, and others, which had come from Vaikuṇṭha.
There, having bathed according to the prescribed ritual (saṃkalpa) in the pure, sanctifying, and auspicious waters of Svāmisaras, accompanied by his wife, sons, and others; || 66 ||
Having bowed there according to the prescribed rite to Śvetasūkara, the supporter of the earth, on its western bank, he proceeded to the abode of Śrīnivāsa.
There, the high-minded devotee of Viṣṇu, together with his sons and others, beheld Veṅkaṭeśvara, who is served by Brahmā and the other gods.
Having prostrated with devotion before the Lord of Gods, Śrīnivāsa, the ocean of mercy, he returned accompanied by his sons, wife, and others, his sins having been destroyed.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite and performed the proper duties such as those pertaining to dharma, the high-minded one [should give it] to some learned devotee of Viṣṇu.
With the thought that it was Viṣṇu, he bestowed that auspicious gift of land which grants liberation.
Then, through the power of the gift of land, Bhadramati had a direct vision of the Blessed One; at that moment, the Lord appeared, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Mounted upon the son of Vinatā and adorned with a forest garland, he [resides] on the bank of the Pāpanāśa by the power of the gift of land. (73)
Then the gentle Bhadramati began to offer praise.

Salutations, salutations to You, the cause of all; salutations, salutations to You, the protector of all. Salutations, salutations to You, the leader of the immortals; salutations, salutations to You, the crusher of the Daityas.

Salutations again and again to the one dear to his devotees; salutations again and again to the destroyer of sins. Salutations again and again to the annihilator of the wicked; let there be salutation to that Lord of the Universe. (76)

Homage, repeated homage to Nārāyaṇa, the dwarf who is the cause, whose prowess is immeasurable; homage be to that Puruṣottama, the bearer of the glorious Śārṅga bow, the discus, the sword, and the mace. || 77 ||

Salutations to the one who dwells in the ocean of milk; salutations be to the imperishable Lord of Lakṣmī. Salutations to the one whose immeasurable radiance surpasses that of the sun and other luminaries; salutations again and again to the one who has reached the state of merit.

Salutations again and again to the one whose eyes are the sun and the moon; salutations be to you, the bestower of the fruits of sacrifice. Salutations to the one resplendent with the limbs of sacrifice; salutations be to you, the beloved of the virtuous. || 79 ||

Salutations again and again to the cause of all causes; salutations be to you who are devoid of sound and other sense objects. Salutations to you, the bestower of desired happiness; salutations again and again to the one who delights the hearts of devotees.

Salutations, salutations to You, the cause of wonders; let there be salutations to You, the upholder of Mount Mandara. Salutations to You named Yajñavarāha; salutations to the destroyer of Hiraṇyākṣa. || 81 ||

Homage be to you who assumed the form of a dwarf; homage be to you, the ender of the kṣatriya lineage; homage be to you, the crusher of Rāvaṇa; homage be to you, the elder brother of Nanda’s son. || 82 ||

Salutations to you, O Beloved of Kamalā; salutations to you, the bestower of happiness; to you, the destroyer of the suffering of those who take refuge in you, repeated salutations again and again. (83)
Praised by the brahmin, the Lord, the Blessed One who is affectionate toward his devotees, Śrīnivāsa, the treasure-house of compassion, spoke these words out of his paternal love.
"O dear one, I am pleased; may it be well with you, O twice-born! By means of this great hymn, you shall be endowed with all enjoyments and joined by sons, grandsons, and the like. (85)
"Having attained happiness in this world, may you obtain liberation at the end of the body. Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu vanished right there.
Thus, O brahmins, the power of destroying sins has been told to you; the majesty of the gift of land on its bank has also been described. (87)

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruit of the Gift of Land at the Pāpavināśana Tīrtha," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Now follows the account of the twice-born man named Rāmānuja. Śrī Sūta said: "O all you ascetics dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, I shall proclaim the majesty of the Ākāśagaṅgā tīrtha."
Near the Ākāśagaṅgā lived one known as Rāmānuja, who had mastered the meaning of all the scriptures, was a devotee of Viṣṇu, and had conquered his senses.
Established in the doctrine of the Vaikhānasas, that righteous soul performed austerities; in the summer, he stood in the midst of five fires, devoted solely to the meditation upon Viṣṇu.
Chanting the eight-syllabled mantra and meditating on Janārdana within his heart, he remained constantly in the open air during the rainy seasons and stayed submerged in water during the winters.
Beneficent toward all beings, self-controlled, and free from all pairs of opposites, he subsisted on withered leaves for some years.
For some time he subsisted on water, and for several years he lived on air alone.

Now, on the banks of the celestial Gaṅgā, there occurred the manifestation of the Blessed One, who was pleased by the penance of Rāma’s younger brother. Then, gratified by that austerity, the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, appeared before him bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
With eyes like the petals of a blooming lotus and a splendor equal to ten million suns, he was mounted upon the joy of Vinatā, adorned with a parasol and chowries.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, and a crown, and decorated with bracelets and other ornaments, he was surrounded by his servants, Viṣvaksena, Sunanda, and others.
Accompanied by Nārada and others who played the lute, flute, drum, and other instruments, he was praised with songs; possessing great majesty, he shone in his yellow garments.
His chest was adorned with Lakṣmī, his complexion was like that of a dark blue cloud, and he was attended on both sides by great yogis such as Sanaka and others.
Enchanting the entire three worlds with his gentle smile, he honored all ten directions, making them resplendent with his own radiance.
The Lord Veṅkaṭeśa, a treasure-house of compassion who is easily attained by those devoted to Him, again manifested Himself before that great sage Rāmānuja.
Then, seeing Śrīnivāsa, the treasure-house of compassion, the god clad in yellow garments, manifest before him, the great sage attained satisfaction.
Endowed with supreme devotion, he praised the Lord of the Universe.

Now follows the praise of the Lord composed by the brahmin named Rāmānuja. Rāmānuja said: Salutations to the God of gods, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace; salutations to You, the eternal, the pure, the Lord of Veṅkaṭa. (16)

Salutations to you, the destroyer of the afflictions of your devotees, whose very nature is the sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors; salutations to you, the triple-formed one who brings about creation, preservation, and dissolution.

Salutations to the Supreme Lord, salutations to the One who transcends all bounds; let there be salutations to the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Ordainer. Salutations to the One whose eyes are the sun and the moon; salutations to the One worshipped by Viriñca and the other gods.

Salutation to Him who destroys the Daityas, who is free from the conceptual distinctions of birth and so forth, who is devoid of all defects, and who removes the fear of the entire cycle of existence. 19.

Salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇa, whose prowess is immeasurable, who is to be known through the Vedāntas, the Lord of Ramā, whose abode is on Mount Vṛṣādri, the father of the Creator (Brahmā), and the remover of the suffering of all people. || 20 ||
Salutations to you, the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow; salutations to you again and again, the dweller on Mount Veṅkaṭa.
Having thus praised Veṅkaṭeśa, Śrīnivāsa, the teacher of the world, the sage Rāmānuja, the most excellent of the best of Brahmins, remained silent.
Having heard that praise so pleasing to the ear, the Lord of Veṅkaṭācala, being thus lauded by that great-souled one, attained supreme satisfaction.
Then Śauri, having embraced the sage with his four arms, spoke with great affection: "Choose indeed a boon."
"I am pleased today by your austerity and also by your hymn of praise, O great sage; delighted by your salutation, I have come as the bestower of boons upon you. (25)

Then follows the prayer addressed to the Blessed One by the brahmin named Rāmānuja. Rāmānuja said: "O Nārāyaṇa, O Lord of Ramā, O Śrīnivāsa, O You who pervade the universe! O Janārdana, O Abode of the World, O Govinda, O Destroyer of Naraka! (26)
O crest-jewel of Veṅkaṭādri, I have achieved my life’s purpose through the sight of you; for the righteous worship you, since you are the protector of dharma. || 27 ||
I know you as the Supreme Self, whom neither Bhava nor Brahmā knows, and whom likewise the three Vedas do not know; what else could be higher than this? (28)
What the yogis do not see, and what those devoted to ritual action do not see—that Supreme Self I behold; what else could be higher than this? (29)
And by this, O Veṅkaṭeśa, Lord of the World, my purpose is fulfilled; for merely by the remembrance of Your name, even those who have committed great sins [are purified].
I behold that Janārdana, by whom men attain liberation; may there be unwavering devotion in me toward Your pair of lotus feet. (31)

Now follows the time for bathing at the holy ford of the celestial Gaṅgā as described by the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "O Rāmānuja of great intellect, let your devotion to me be firm; listen also to another word being spoken by me to you, O twice-born one. (32)
Those people who perform a ritual bath in the Gaṅgā on the full-moon day when the sun enters Aries and is conjoined with the Citrā asterism—|| 33 ||
They go to the supreme abode, from which there is no return; therefore, O twice-born one, you should dwell near the Viyadgaṅgā, O younger brother of Rāma.
At the end of this body, which has been commenced by past karma, you shall attain my own nature; what is the use of saying more here, O auspicious one, in the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā? (35)
O tiger among sages, all those people who indeed bathe [there] become the most excellent devotees of the Lord; there is no need for any doubt in this matter. (36)
Rāmānuja said: By what characteristics and by what actions are the Bhāgavatas known? Since I am filled with curiosity, I desire to hear this. (37)
Now, the characteristics of the Bhāgavatas as described by the Blessed Lord. Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa said: "O best of sages, listen to the characteristics of the Bhāgavatas. (38)
But it is not possible to describe their power even in ten million years. || 39 ||
Those who are beneficial to all living beings, free from envy and free from malice, who possess knowledge, are desireless, and are peaceful—they indeed are the best of Bhāgavatas. (40)
Those who do not cause suffering to others through action, mind, or speech, and who possess the virtue of non-possessiveness, are indeed the most excellent devotees of the Lord.
Those whose minds are characterized by goodness when listening to sacred narratives, and who are devoted to my lotus feet—they indeed are the best of Bhāgavatas. (42)

Those best of men who serve their mother and father, those who are devoted to the worship of the gods, and those men who are practitioners of that [worship], rejoice upon seeing the ritual; they indeed are the most excellent devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatottama). || 43 ||
Those who are devoted to the service of those in the [four] stages of life and of ascetics, and who do not engage in censuring others—they indeed are the most excellent Bhāgavatas. (44)
Those best of men who speak words beneficial to all, and those in the world who perceive virtues, are indeed the most excellent devotees of the Lord. (45)
Those best of men who see all beings as they do themselves, and who are equal toward enemies and friends, are indeed remembered as Bhāgavatas. || 46 ||
Those who expound the Dharmaśāstras, those who are devoted to truthful speech, and those who are intent on serving them—these indeed are the most excellent Bhāgavatas. (47)
Those who explain the Purāṇas, those who listen to them in that manner, and those who are devoted to their speaker—they indeed are the best of Bhāgavatas. (48)
Those men who constantly perform service to cows and Brahmins, and those who are devoted to pilgrimages to sacred sites, are indeed the most excellent Bhāgavatas. (49)
Those men who rejoice upon seeing the prosperity of others, and those who are devoted to the name of Hari, are indeed the most excellent of Bhāgavatas.
Those who delight in planting groves, those who protect reservoirs, and those who construct lakes and wells—they indeed are the most excellent devotees of the Lord.
Those who indeed construct reservoirs, those who build temples for the gods, and those who are devoted to the Gāyatrī—these are truly the best among the Bhāgavatas. || 52 ||
Those who, upon hearing the names of Hari, rejoice and become exceedingly delighted, their bodies bristling with horripilation—they indeed are the best of Bhāgavatas. (53)
Those men who, upon seeing a grove of Tulasī, offer their salutations, and those whose ears are marked with its wood, are indeed the most excellent of Bhāgavatas.
Those who feel satisfaction upon smelling the fragrance of tulasī, and those who uproot its very root—they indeed are the most excellent of Bhāgavatas. (55)
Those who are devoted to the conduct of their own stage of life, likewise those who honor guests, and those who expound the meaning of the Vedas—they indeed are the best of Bhāgavatas. (56)
Those who, having mastered the scriptures, proclaim them for the sake of others, and who possess virtue in all circumstances—they indeed are the most excellent devotees of the Lord. (57)
Those who are devoted to the gift of water and those who are devoted to the gift of food, and who are intent upon the Ekādaśī vow—they are indeed the best of Bhāgavatas. (58)
Those who are devoted to the gift of cows and those who are devoted to the gift of maidens, and those who perform actions for my sake—they indeed are the most excellent Bhāgavatas. (59)
Those whose minds are fixed on me, who are my devotees, who are eager for my worship, and who are intent on remembering my names—they indeed are the best of Bhāgavatas.
What is the use of saying much here? I shall tell you in brief: those who indeed engage in virtuous qualities are the most excellent devotees of the Lord.
These brāhmaṇas who are devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas) have been briefly described here; even for me, they could not be fully recounted even in hundreds of millions of years.
O illustrious Rāmānuja, O high-minded one, the characteristics of my devotees are indeed consistent with your devotion to me and your affection for me. (63)
Śrī Sūta said: Thus, O Brahmins, Śaunaka and others of great luster, has the supreme majesty of the Viyadgaṅgā Tīrtha on Vṛṣādri been narrated to you.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Ākāśagaṅgā and the Conduct of the Vow of the Brāhmaṇa Rāmānuja," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now follows the determination of the worthy recipient for a gift. The sages said: "O Blessed One, O Sūta, O omniscient one, O master of the Vedas and Vedāntas! To whom should gifts be given, and what is the nature of the proper time for giving?"
And who would accept it? You ought to tell us everything.
Śrī Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, in the field named Veṅkaṭa which bestows great merit, the Brāhmaṇa is the supreme preceptor for all the social classes (varṇas).
Gifts should be given to him; that wise man delivers [others]. A Brahmin should accept them, avoiding, however, one who is devoid of good qualities.
Of one who is impotent, of one who is childless, of one devoted to deceitful conduct, of one who hates the Vedas, and likewise of one who hates the twice-born; || 5 ||
Moreover, what is given to one who abandons their own duty, to one who is devoted to another's wife, or to one who is intent on another's wealth, becomes fruitless.
Even that which is given to a Brahmin who is a singer becomes fruitless, as does that given to one whose mind is possessed by malice, to an ungrateful person, and to a deceiver.
A gift given to a Brahmin who is devoid of knowledge becomes fruitless—even if he is constant in begging, yet remains harmful and weak. (8)
Those who sell names, as well as those who sell the Vedas, those who sell the Smṛtis, and likewise those who sell dharma; || 9 ||
A gift given to one who habitually causes suffering to others becomes fruitless; this applies to whoever is devoted to evil and is censured by those of virtuous deeds.

One should neither accept gifts from them, nor give anything to them; [gifts should be given] only to one who is devoted to virtuous deeds, who is learned in the Vedas, and who maintains the sacred fires.
Indeed, it should be given to one who is without a livelihood, to a poor man with a family, to one devoted to the worship of the gods, and to a narrator of the Purāṇas.
O Brahmins, one should give with effort, especially to those who are poor; what is the use of saying more here? Listen, O best of the twice-born! (13)
It can always be given to all Brāhmaṇas; however, if it is given to the husband of a barren woman, that man is reborn as a donkey. || 14 ||
One should never salute an atheist, one who has transgressed the bounds of propriety, one who is childless, one who is dull-witted, a wicked person, a thief, or a gambler.
One should never salute a heretic, an outcast, one who has not undergone the initiatory rites, a seller of the Vedas, an ungrateful person, or one devoted to sinful deeds.
Likewise, one should not offer salutations to someone who is performing a ritual bath, or who is carrying sacrificial fuel and flowers, or who is holding a water-pot, or who is eating. || 17 ||
One should not salute a person who is quarrelsome, fierce, spitting in the midst of people, carrying food obtained as alms, or lying down. 18.

One should never salute a barren woman, one who has flowers [during her period], an adulteress, one who has recently given birth, one who causes abortion, one who violates her vows, nor a fierce woman.
A single act of disrespect toward an assembly hall, a sacrificial chamber, or even a temple destroys one's previously accumulated merit. (20)
One should not offer salutation to one who is engaged in a *śrāddha* vow, nor to one who is worshipping the deities, nor to one who is performing a sacrifice or a libation (*tarpaṇa*). || 21 ||
He who performs a salutation but does not return the salutation is to be known as one who should not be greeted; he is exactly like a Śūdra.
Therefore, at all times, a wise and excellent Brahmin should never salute a cruel twice-born man who is the husband of a barren woman.
Now, the majesty of the Ākāśagaṅgā. Śrī Sūta said: In this regard, I shall relate the history told by Nārada to the wise sage Sanatkumāra concerning the virtuous Puṇyaśīla.
I shall speak of that, O best of sages; listen with well-composed minds. Formerly, on the banks of the Godāvarī, there was one devoted to all duties. || 25 ||
That best of the twice-born was virtuous in character, truthful, and had conquered his senses; he was compassionate toward all beings and a worshiper of the gods, the sacred fires, and the brahmins.
Pure by birth due to his past actions, devoted to the welfare of his mother and father, faithful to his guru, always courteous, devoted to Brahman, and esteemed by the virtuous; || 27 ||
Endowed with such qualities, [he was born] to the wise Puṇyaśīla. || 28 ||

Now follows the account of how Puṇyaśīla attained the state of having a donkey’s face by inviting the husband of a barren woman. A brahmin, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, arrived at his house; he was then very urgently requested by Puṇyaśīla to attend the śrāddha for his ancestors. (29)
Having indeed appointed that peaceful Brahmin, learned in the Vedas, to the ancestral Śrāddha ceremony, the righteous-souled one performed the unsurpassed annual Śrāddha.
Then, after some time, in the forest of that Puṇyaśīla, an extremely terrible deformity appeared, like the face of a donkey.
Then, becoming dejected in mind, the exceedingly righteous Puṇyaśīla, sighing repeatedly in distress, sought refuge with the yogi Agastya.
On the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī, frequented by hosts of sages, there is a supreme, divine hermitage that bestows the fruits of all desires.
There, in that hermitage, they beheld the high-souled Agastya, who desired the welfare of all the worlds and was being attended day and night by the best of sages.
Gārdabhāsya, being exceedingly distressed, paid homage to him. || 35 ||
Puṇyaśīla said: O treasure of austerity, salutations to you, Agastya, who is served by sages; O ocean of compassion, protect, protect me from this great sinner with the wretched face! 36.
"By what fault did my face become so ugly here? (37)
Out of affection for me, O illustrious one, speak, O best of sages! (38)
Agastya said: O best of brahmins, highly fortunate one, of virtuous character and great intellect, listen with undistracted mind, O twice-born, to the deformity of the face. (39)

Now follows the account of why the husband of a barren woman is unfit for invitation to a Śrāddha rite: "You have appointed a certain Brahmin—a treasure-house of virtues, one who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, a learned scholar (śrotriya), yet childless—to officiate at the Śrāddha. (40)

Because of that great fault, there is deformity upon your face: those in this world who, at the time of offerings to gods and ancestors (havya-kavya) and the like, [neglect] the husband of a barren woman, a twice-born man. (41)
O Brahmin, whether they employ them in auspicious rites or even in rites for the ancestors, those [who do so] go to the state of having the face of a donkey.
One should never invite the husband of a barren woman, who is a great sinner, nor the husband of a barren woman who is exceedingly cruel, nor indeed the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī).
O best of Brahmins, one who desires his own welfare should not invite such a person to a śrāddha, even if he is learned in the Vedas and Śāstras, of noble birth, or devoted to ritual action.
O best of the twice-born, the husband of a barren woman must by no means be excluded from śrāddha rites, nor from sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, nor from vows and austerities. (45)

O best of the twice-born, even if capable, one should exclude the husband of a barren woman from the śrāddha; however, if no other worthy recipient is available, one may invite even a mere thread-weaver.
One should invite a man who has sons and is of good conduct for the sake of the śrāddha; in his absence, O best of the twice-born, one may invite either a son or even a younger brother.

Or one should engage oneself in the Śrāddha; one should abandon the husband of a barren woman. O highly fortunate one of virtuous character, it is said that [the rite] is accomplished by raising up the arm. 48.
In no way should one who performs a śrāddha engage a twice-born man who is childless or the husband of a barren woman for the purpose of the śrāddha. (49)
That śrāddha should be known as āsura; the performer shall go to hell.

Then, by bathing in the Ākāśagaṅgā, Puṇyaśīla’s transformation will cease. What need is there for much speaking here? I shall tell you the means for the removal of that defect: on the auspicious bank of the Svarṇamukhī. (51)
The highly meritorious Veṅkaṭācala, the son of Meru, who bestows the fruits of all desires, exists there, served by hosts of gods. || 52 ||
On that lordly Veṅkaṭa mountain, which is saluted by gods and demons, there is indeed a most excellent sacred bathing place (tīrtha) known by the name Viyadgaṅgā.
"Having gone to Mount Veṅkaṭa, [bathe] in the waters of Svāmipuṣkariṇī; it pacifies all sins and increases longevity and health. (54)
Having bathed according to the prescribed ritual, O high-minded one, proceed immediately to the Gaṅgā-tīrtha and perform your ablutions there in accordance with the rules for sacred sites.
O high-minded one, by merely bathing there, the deformity of this man's face will perish at that very moment; of this there is no doubt. (56)
Thus addressed by the high-souled Agastya, Puṇyaśīla bowed to that great soul and then departed for Veṅkaṭādri.
Having gone there, the illustrious one bathed in the waters of Svāmipuṣkariṇī according to the prescribed rules, and then approached the Viyadgaṅgā.
There, by bathing, that righteous and virtuous-souled man obtained a face resembling the curve of Cupid’s bow; oh, how great is the majesty of this sacred ford!
The venerable Sūta said: Thus, O Brahmins, has been related to you that which was spoken by Nārada to the sage Sanatkumāra, O Śaunaka and others of great luster.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Ākāśagaṅgā," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 22 ||
Now, the majesty of Cakratīrtha. Śrī Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, speakers of truth, I shall now fully declare the majesty of Cakratīrtha, which destroys all sins.
Those who hear of the great merit and majesty of Cakratīrtha go to the abode of Viṣṇu, from which there is no return.
Those who are averse to the gift of food, likewise averse to the gift of water, and those who are averse to the gift of a cow—these become pure by immersing themselves here.
Therefore, Cakratīrtha is the most meritorious and unsurpassed sacred site.

Now, regarding the manner of penance performed by the twice-born named Padmanābha, Śrī Sūta said: "In ancient times, Padmanābha of the Śrīvatsa lineage, having conquered his senses, performed great penance on the bank of the Cakrapuṣkariṇī."
Endowed with compassion, abstaining from food, truthful in speech, and having conquered his senses, he views all beings as himself and is free from desire for sense objects.
Beneficent toward all beings, self-controlled, and free from all pairs of opposites, he lived for some years subsisting on withered leaves.
For some time he subsisted on water, and for several years he lived on air; in this manner, the great sage Padmanābha remained thus for twelve years.

Now follows the manifestation of the Lord, gratified by the penance performed by the twice-born named Padmanābha at Cakratīrtha. He performed a formidable penance, difficult even for the gods to accomplish. Then, the Lord, the Consort of Kamalā, was pleased by that penance.
The Bearer of the conch, discus, and mace appeared before his very eyes—He whose eyes were like the petals of a full-blown lotus and whose radiance equaled ten million suns.
Opening his eyes there, he beheld Veṅkaṭeśvara—the peaceful Śrīnivāsa, the storehouse of compassion, bearing the conch and the discus. Having seen that high-souled deity, he began to offer praise.

Now follows the hymn of praise to Śrīnivāsa composed by the twice-born Padmanābha: Salutations to the God of gods, to Veṅkaṭeśa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow; salutations to you, Śrīnivāsa, who dwells upon the mountain of Nārāyaṇa. (12)
Salutations to Vāsudeva, to Viṣṇu, the destroyer of impurities; salutations to you, Śrīnivāsa, who dwells upon the mountain of Śeṣa.
Salutations to the Lord of the three worlds, to the one whose form is the universe, to the witness; salutations to You, Śrīnivāsa, who are worshipped by Śiva, Brahmā, and the other gods. 14.
Salutations to you, the lotus-eyed one; salutations to you who recline upon the ocean of milk; salutations to you, the abode of Śrī and the destroyer of wicked Rākṣasas. || 15 ||
Salutation to the God who is dear to his devotees, the Lord of the gods. || 16 ||
Salutations to You, Śrīnivāsa, the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before You. || 17 ||
Salutations to You, Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of yogis, who is eternally known through the Vedas as Viṣṇu, and who destroys the sins of Your devotees. || 18 ||
Thus was the illustrious Śrīnivāsa, who pervades the universe, praised by the sage named Padmanābha, a resident of Cakratīrtha.
Then, having attained supreme contentment, the Lord Veṅkaṭeśa, the ocean of mercy, issued a command to Padmanābha to reside permanently at Cakratīrtha.
Puruṣottama spoke words resembling a stream of nectar to Padmanābha, the best of the twice-born, who was peaceful and devoted to dharma.
Śrīnivāsa said: "O best of the twice-born, O highly fortunate one, O worshiper of my lotus feet, dwell on the bank of Cakratīrtha, performing worship until the end of the kalpa."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu vanished on that very spot; when the divine Śrīnivāsa, the teacher of the world, had disappeared.
The high-minded one made his dwelling on the bank of Cakratīrtha; then, after some time, a certain Rākṣasa of fearsome appearance appeared.
Afflicted by hunger, the cruel one came to devour that sage named Padmanābha, who was solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Then that Rākṣasa seized the Brāhmaṇa with force; having been thus forcibly seized by him, the Vipra was one who had mastered the Vedāṅgas.
He cried out repeatedly to Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the discus, the ocean of compassion and the ultimate refuge for those in distress, saying, "Protect my side! (27)
O Veṅkaṭeśa, ocean of compassion, protector of those who have sought refuge! Save me, O tiger among men, for I have fallen into the power of the Rākṣasa.
O Beloved of Lakṣmī, O Hari, O Viṣṇu, O Vaikuṇṭha, O Garuḍadhvaja! Protect me, who am assailed by Rākṣasas, as you protected the elephant seized by the crocodile.
O Dāmodara, O Jagannātha, O crusher of the demon Hiraṇyāsura! Protect me, who am being severely oppressed by the Rākṣasa, just as you protected Prahlāda.

Now follows the dispatching of the discus by the Blessed One for the sake of slaying the Asura who was intent on killing Padmanābha. O twice-born ones, while Padmanābha was thus offering praise, the wielder of the discus, a treasure-house of compassion, perceived the fear of his devotee. (31)
He dispatched his own discus for the sake of protecting his devotee; that discus of Viṣṇu was sent by the all-powerful Viṣṇu himself.
Then he arrived with speed at the bank of the Cakrapuṣkariṇī lake, [a form] resembling infinite suns and possessing a radiance equal to infinite fires.
Then, beholding Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana—which possessed a great blaze, a great roar, and which crushes the great asuras—the Rākṣasa fled.

Then, following the slaughter of the asuras by the discus sent by the Blessed One, the Sudarśana, difficult to approach due to its garland of flames, suddenly severed the head of that fleeing rākṣasa.
Then, seeing the Rākṣasa fallen upon the ground, that best of Brahmins was filled with supreme joy and praised Sudarśana.
Padmanābha said: O Discus of Viṣṇu, salutations to you, who are consecrated for the protection of the universe; salutations to you, the ornament of the lotus-hand of Nārāyaṇa.
O you of great roar, skilled in the destruction of asuras in battles; O Sudarśana, salutations to you, the destroyer of the afflictions of your devotees. 38.
Protect me, who am agitated by fear, from every kind of defilement; O Lord Sudarśana, O All-pervading One, may you always be present at Cakratīrtha.
"Be present for the welfare of the world that longs for liberation. O lords of sages, when the Brāhmaṇa had spoken thus, that Discus of Viṣṇu [appeared].
He spoke to him, named Padmanābha, as if gladdening him out of friendship.

Then, at the request of the twice-born, [the Lord] granted boons and so forth to Cakra. Sudarśana said: "O Padmanābha, I dwell eternally in this most meritorious and unsurpassed Cakratīrtha out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. (42)
Having reflected upon the suffering you will endure at the hands of that evil-minded Rākṣasa, I [have come].
"O Brahmin, urged by Viṣṇu, I have arrived here in haste; this lowest of Rākṣasas, who was your tormentor, has been slain by me. (44)
"You have been liberated from this fear, for you are always a devotee of Hari; O twice-born one, at the Cakratīrtha, which is greatly meritorious and removes all sins. (45)

For the sake of constantly protecting the world, I shall remain present before you; O twice-born one, by virtue of my presence here, [the power] of yourself and others shall likewise [be maintained]. (46)
Henceforth, there shall be no suffering arising from spirits or rākṣasas; and because of my presence here, this place shall have the renown of "Cakratīrtha. (47)
Those who perform their ablutions here at Cakratīrtha, which bestows liberation—for them, indeed, all sons, grandsons, and descendants of their lineage [attain the same].
"Having shaken off their sins, they shall go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Having spoken thus, while Padmanābha was looking on, that discus of Viṣṇu—
While other brahmins were looking on, O twice-born ones, he suddenly entered that Cakrapuṣkariṇī, which destroys all sins.
Śrī Sūta said: O best of Brahmins, O Śaunaka and others of great luster, I have related to you in its entirety the sin-destroying majesty of Cakratīrtha.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred ford equal to Cakratīrtha; having bathed here, O Brahmins, men shall partake in liberation, without a doubt. (92)
Whoever recites this chapter or listens to it with a concentrated mind obtains the supreme fruit of performing an ablution at Cakratīrtha.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Cakratīrtha," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now begins the introductory narrative concerning the attainment and subsequent cessation of the state of a Rākṣasa by the Gandharva named Sundara. The Sages said: "O Blessed One, O Sūta, best among those versed in the Purāṇas, who was that Rākṣasa who oppressed the high-souled Brāhmaṇa, a devotee of Viṣṇu?"
Śrī Sūta said: O Brahmins, listen with respect as I relate the story of that cruel Rākṣasa, and how he was born from the power of the sages' curse. || 2 ||
Formerly, in Śrīraṅga, the temple of Viṣṇu which resembles Vaikuṇṭha, all the great-souled devotees of Viṣṇu, headed by Vasiṣṭha and Atri, resided there.
The inhabitants of the city of Śrīraṅga worshipped the Lord of Gods, Śrīraṅganātha, the bestower of fearlessness upon his devotees, for the sake of liberation.
O best of Brahmins, once there was a powerful Gandharva named Sundara, the son of Vīrabāhu, who was devoted to the company of libertines.
Accompanied by a hundred women, he played joyfully with those naked young maidens in the water, himself being without clothes.
At the sacred ford of the Kaveri, Vasiṣṭha, desiring to perform his midday rites, departed from the temple of Śrīraṅga accompanied by sages.
Then, beholding those sages, those women, overcome with fear, covered themselves with their garments; but Sundara was not so reckless.
Then Vasiṣṭha, enraged, cursed that shameless man.
Vasiṣṭha said: "O handsome Gandharva, because you did not quickly cover yourself with a garment out of shame upon seeing us, therefore go from here to the state of a Rākṣasa."
When Vasiṣṭha had spoken thus, the Rāmas then, with palms joined in reverence, prostrated before Vasiṣṭha with hearts bowed down by devotion.
In the midst of the circle of sages, they spoke thus to Vasiṣṭha.
The women said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, delight of the four-faced Brahmā! O ocean of compassion, having looked upon us, you ought not to show anger. (13)
For the husband alone is said to be the supreme ornament of women; but a woman who is deprived of her husband, O Sage, even if she has a hundred sons, [is considered destitute]. 14.
In the world they are called widows; their birth is useless. O Sage, out of respect for our husbands, please grant us your favor. (15)
"A single offense should be forgiven by sages who perceive the truth. O ocean of compassion, grant forgiveness for this Sundara, your own disciple. (16)
Śrī Sūta said: Thus entreated by the women of Sundara, that best of the twice-born, Vasiṣṭha, being pleased, spoke these words once more.

Now follows the means for Sundara, so named, to be released from his state as a Rākṣasa as told by Vasiṣṭha. Vasiṣṭha said: "O fair-browed ones, my word shall never be false; I will declare the means to you—listen with faith. (18)
The curse upon her husband will certainly last for a period of sixteen years; and at the end of those sixteen years, he who was beautiful will indeed take on the form of a Rākṣasa.
"O celestial nymphs, having gone by chance to the auspicious Veṅkaṭādri, which removes all sins, he will go to that Cakratīrtha."
The great yogi Padmanābha, the lord of sages, dwells there; that very Rākṣasa will approach that sage for the purpose of devouring him.
Then the supreme discus, dispatched by Viṣṇu for the protection of the Brāhmaṇas, will sever his head from his body; of this there is no doubt.
Then, having regained his own form and being liberated from the curse, that Sundara shall once again go to the celestial realm as your husband; there is no doubt about this.
Then, having reached the third heaven, this handsome husband of yours, wearing beautiful attire, will delight you, O beautiful women.
The venerable Sūta said: Having spoken thus to those beautiful wives of Sundara, Vasiṣṭha, who was devoted to the Lord of Śrīraṅga, quickly departed for his own hermitage.
Then the women, embracing their own handsome husband Rāma, wept, tormented by grief and submerged in the midst of an ocean of sorrow. || 26 ||
