While they were looking on in this manner, Sundara became a Rākṣasa—possessing large fangs, a massive body, and red hair and beard. || 27 ||
Seeing him, the women, agitated by fear, fled to the celestial realm (Triviṣṭapa). Then this one, in the guise of a Rākṣasa, appeared beautiful yet possessed a terrifying form.
Devouring all living beings as he wandered from country to country and forest to forest with the speed of the wind, he reached Veṅkaṭādri, the best of mountains.
Having entered [the city], that great sinner then went to Cakratīrtha; in this manner, sixteen years passed while he was wandering.
Then, O lords of sages, at the end of sixteen years, this Rākṣasa came to devour that Padmanābha who was residing at Cakratīrtha.
Attacking with the speed of the wind, he praised Janārdana; and being praised by the yogi, Viṣṇu then urged forth his discus.
Then, having arrived to protect Padmanābha who was being tormented by the Rākṣasa, Hari’s discus struck off the head of the Rākṣasa.

Now follows the attainment of his true form by the one named Sundara, preceded by his liberation from the state of a Rākṣasa: Then, having cast off this Rākṣasa body and possessing a divine form, Sundara ascended an excellent celestial chariot while being showered with flowers. (34)
Bowing down with palms joined in reverence, he paid homage to that Sudarśana and praised him with the utmost devotion using foremost words as delightful to the ear as the Vedas.
Sundara said: O Sudarśana, salutations to you, the sole ornament of Viṣṇu’s hand; salutations to you, the destroyer of demons, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns.
Through the penetration of your compassion, O Viṣṇu, wielder of the discus-weapon, I have cast off my demonic body and regained my own form; salutations be unto you!
"Grant me leave to go to the third heaven, O beloved of Viṣṇu; my wives are grieving, their minds distressed by separation. (38)
O Discus, salutations to you; grant me such a form that I may remain with my mind fixed upon you for as long as I live. 39.
O lords of sages, when Viṣṇu’s discus was thus praised with devotion by Sundara, it immediately granted its grace, saying, "So be it."
Permitted by the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), Sundara bowed to that best of Brahmins; then, permitted by him, the Gandharva went to heaven.
When Sundara had gone to heaven, the lord of sages, Padmanābha, entreated that discus: "O weapon of Viṣṇu, salutations be unto you! (42)
O wielder of the discus, destroyer of the great asuras, I bow to you; please establish your presence here in this pure and auspicious Cakratīrtha.
By your presence here, effect the destruction of the sins of all those who have bathed, and grant them eternal liberation. || 44 ||
Bestow upon it the renown as "Cakratīrtha" in this world; through your presence, it shall be the destroyer of the fear of the sages dwelling here.
From this point forward, O Noble One who wields the discus as a weapon, let there be obeisance to you; O Lord, may there be no fear from ghosts, spirits, or demons. (46)
When the wheel had been thus entreated by the yogi Padmanābha, it vanished at that sacred ford after saying, "So be it."
Śrī Sūta said: Thus, O Brahmins, the origin of the Rākṣasa has been narrated to you by me, as well as the greatness of Cakratīrtha, which removes all impurities.
Having heard which, a person on earth is liberated from all sins. || 49 ||

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Cakratīrtha," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now begins the description of the majesty of Jābāli-tīrtha. Śrī Sūta said: O all you ascetics, residents of the Naimiṣa forest, [listen] regarding the most meritorious Veṅkaṭādri, which destroys all sins!
Next, O twice-born ones, I shall describe the majesty of Jābāli-tīrtha, where one named Durācāra was liberated after bathing.
The sages said: O Sūta, O knower of the true meaning of reality, who was this person named Durācāra? And what sin, indeed, was committed by that Durācāra, O sage?
O Sage, tell us in detail how one is liberated from sin through the power of bathing at this sacred ford (tīrtha), for we are desirous of hearing this.

Now follows the account of the twice-born man named Durācāra, who dwelt on the banks of the Kāverī. Śrī Sūta said: "O sages, listen to the sin of that Durācāra and how he was liberated from that sin by bathing in Jābāli-tīrtha."
A certain brahmin named Durācāra, a sinful twice-born man who was always devoted to cruel deeds, lived on the bank of the Kāverī.
O twice-born ones, he always lived together with those who were defiled by association—namely, killers of Brahmins, drinkers of liquor, thieves, and violators of the guru’s bed.
O best of the twice-born, by the fault of association with those who commit great sins (mahāpātaka), the entire Brahminhood of this twice-born man has indeed been destroyed without remainder.
If a twice-born man should dwell respectfully for even a single day with those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin), that very moment the status of that twice-born man [is lost].
But for a Brahmin, one part indeed perishes—of this there is no doubt—by serving, touching, seeing, or lying down with [such a person] for two days.
O twice-born ones, by eating together in the same row as those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin), the second part of one's Brahminhood is destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
Within three days, one-third indeed perishes; of this there is no doubt. Within four days, the fourth part certainly goes to destruction.
Furthermore, by sharing their beds, seats, and meals with them, one becomes a sinner equal to them, having associated with those who commit great sins.
Therefore, this twice-born man named Durācāra, being devoid of brahminhood, was seized by him as if by a powerful and terrifying serpent.
Helpless and intensely tormented by that vetāla, that brahmin wandered from country to country and from forest to forest.
By the ripening of his past merits and through the power of destiny, that twice-born man reached Veṅkaṭādri, the mountain of great merit that destroys all sins.

Now, through bathing at Jñābāli-tīrtha, the wicked Vetāla was freed from his great sins and other transgressions. Pursued by the Piśāca and the Vetāla, the twice-born man went [to the site], and that Vetāla immersed him in the Mahāpātakanāśana [tīrtha]. (17)
O best of Brahmins, at Jābāli-tīrtha, he who was associated with great sinners rose up in an instant, having been liberated by a Vetāla.
O Brahmins, having risen from that purifying holy place, that twice-born man, restored to his health, reflected: "Who is this near Svarṇamukhī? (19)
"How have I come here, living on the banks of the Kāverī?"—thus troubled by such thoughts, he [reached] that supreme sacred ford of Jābāli.
Having approached and bowed down to the high-souled Jābāli, the most excellent among the lords of yogis, that man of evil conduct addressed him.
"I do not know, O Blessed One, who this brahmin on the mountain is; tell me now. For I am indeed named Durācāra, a resident of the banks of the Kāverī. (22)
"O Brahmin, please tell me how I have come here. Thus was the sage of noble vows questioned by that man of evil conduct.
Having meditated for a moment, the ocean of compassion spoke to Durācāra.

Now follows the description of the fault incurred by failing to perform the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* as described by Jābāli. Jābāli said: "Due to your association with great sinners and your wicked conduct in the past, your status as a Brāhmaṇa was lost; consequently, a *vetāla* seized you. (25)
Possessed by him, you arrived here helpless and with a bewildered mind; the Vetāla submerged you in this most purifying sacred ford.
By merely bathing here, you have been liberated from sin; those men who perform the meritorious bath at Jābāli-tīrtha [attain the same]. || 27 ||
Truly, by the mere act of bathing in this meritorious tīrtha, which is a means for accomplishing virtuous deeds, the accumulation of their five great sins shall indeed perish. (28)
The fault arising from association with those who commit great sins has gone to destruction for you; that Vetāla who seized you was formerly a Brāhmaṇa. (29)
On the anniversary of his father's death, he did not perform the ancestral śrāddha rite according to the pārvaṇa method; because of that, he was cursed by his own ancestors and became a vetāla.
He too, by the power of bathing in the waters of Jābāli-tīrtha, abandoned his state as a Vetāla and attained the world of Viṣṇu.
That man who does not perform the Śrāddha rite on the anniversary of the death of his mother or father quickly attains the state of a Vetāla and subsequently experiences hell. || 32 ||
Śrī Sūta said: Merely by bathing in this sacred ford, Durācāra, the great sinner, attained the world of Viṣṇu, which is indeed free from rebirth.
Thus has been narrated to you this meritorious account of liberation from wicked conduct; therefore, it is a most sacred pilgrimage site, auspicious and the remover of all sins.
For by merely bathing there, even one of wicked conduct is liberated; it destroys even those sins that are devoid of any means of atonement.
If a twice-born man bows down to a Linga or to Viṣṇu that has been worshipped by a Śūdra, no expiation for him has been declared by the supreme sages in the Smṛtis.
Even his sin shall perish at the sacred ford named Jābāli; however, for those who have committed the reviling of Brahmins, no expiation exists.
There is no atonement for those who betray trust, for the ungrateful, and for those who take pleasure in their brother's wife; for them, no expiation exists. (38)
Their purification will indeed come from bathing at Jābāli-tīrtha. Thus, O Brahmins, the majesty of Jābāli’s sacred site has been recounted to you. (39)
Having heard which, a man on earth is liberated from all sins. || 40 ||

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Jābāli-tīrtha," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 25 ||
Now, the majesty of the Tumburu-tīrtha. Śrī Sūta said: O Śaunaka and other sages of great luster, I shall here fully proclaim the majesty of Ghoṇatīrtha, which destroys all sins.
Bathing there for people is the fruit of penance performed in previous births, occurring on the full-moon day of the bright fortnight conjoined with the asterism Uttarā-phalgunī.
When the sun is situated in Pisces, all the holy places in the three worlds, beginning with the Gaṅgā, come from every direction to the Tumba-tīrtha in the afternoon.

The sages said: O venerable Sūta, omniscient one who has reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures, [tell us how] all the rivers [merged] into the Gaṅgā at the exceedingly purifying Ghoṇatīrtha.
For what purpose indeed do they bathe there when the sun is situated in Pisces?
Śrī Sūta said: All sinful men indeed bathe here among us with great effort; having cast off the nets of their sins, people truly depart having achieved their purpose.
"How can this web of our sins be destroyed in every respect? Having reflected thus, they diligently visited sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā and others.
Having recollected the captivating, divine speech of the high-souled Nārada, the son of Brahmā, which destroys all sins.
Having gone to the glorious Veṅkaṭa mountain, which dries up sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, he bathed there in the waters of Svāmipuṣkariṇī, the most excellent of holy fords.
Immediately thereafter, O Brahmins, at the exceedingly purifying Ghoṇatīrtha, on the full-moon day of the bright fortnight conjoined with the asterism Uttarāphalgunī.
When the sun is situated in Pisces, all sacred fords bathe [there]; who in the three worlds knows the majesty of that sacred ford? (11)
Now follows the description of the great faults of those who are averse to bathing at Ghoṇatīrtha: "Therefore, O best of the twice-born, Ghoṇatīrtha is the most meritorious of sacred sites. (12)
One who destroys a grove, one who is cruel, one who sells a maiden or a horse, and one who abandons the ritual bath after a nose-bleed—these they call a slayer of a Brahmin.
They call one who steals the property of the gods, as well as one who misappropriates what has been given, and one who abandons the Ghoṇasnāna, a slayer of a Brahmin.
The wise call him a thief who destroys tanks and embankments, who is lustful for the wives of others, and who has abandoned the ritual bath at the Ghoṇa.
The wise know that base atheist who, having said "I give" to a twice-born man, subsequently reneges on his word, as one who has drunk liquor and abandoned the ritual bath at Ghoṇa.
The wise call him a thief who hates his guru, brahmins, and people, who is devoted to self-praise, and who has abandoned the ritual bath at the nose (ghoṇasnāna). 17.

The twice-born call him a thief who eats the food of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), who eats the remnants of the food of his ancestors, and who has abandoned the ritual bath at the tip of the nose (ghoṇasnāna). 18.
The wise call him a thief who gives away the food remaining from his father, who opposes his mother and father, and who has abandoned the ritual bath at the Ghoṇa.
They call him one who violates the teacher’s bed who is devoted to union with another’s wife, who delights in sexual pleasure with his brother’s wife, and who has abandoned the ritual bath at Ghoṇa.

A Brahmin who speaks like a Caṇḍāla, who always holds darbha grass in his hand, and who has abandoned the ritual bath at the nose (ghoṇasnāna)—association with such a person is the fifth [cause of impurity]. 21.

One who eats food upon hearing the sound of a menstruating woman, a horse, or a caṇḍāla, and one who has abandoned the ritual bath after sneezing—contact with these constitutes the fifth [ground for impurity]. 22.
They say that one who causes obstacles to the rites of marriage, the investiture of the sacred thread, and so forth, and who has abandoned the ritual bath at Ghoṇa, is a slayer of animals.
The wise call him a killer of an embryo who slays one who has sought refuge, who turns his back on all sacred fords, and who abandons the ritual bath at the Ghoṇa.
They call him a destroyer of cows who has abandoned the sacrifice to the ancestors, who has deserted his wife, who is the lowest of his lineage, and who has given up bathing at Ghoṇa.
O best of the twice-born, minor sins as well as those equal to great sins take refuge in one who has abandoned the bath at Ghoṇa.

Now follows the description of how bathing at Ghoṇa removes all sins: O Brahmins, whether it be one devoted to great sins, an outcaste, the lowest of his lineage, cruel, a destroyer of his family, miserable, one who has not given gifts, or one devoid of religious rites—[all such are purified by this bath]. (27)
One who slaughters animals, one who harbors malice toward others, a slanderer, likewise a speaker of untruth, one devoted to hypocrisy, and one addicted to the wives of others. || 28 ||
Betrayal of a friend, ingratitude, the killing of an embryo—these are great sins; as are the sin of being devoted to another's wife and betraying the interests of others. (29)

One who speaks untruth, one engaged in agricultural labor, a traitor to his master, a deceiver, one possessed by greed, a patricide, and one who turns his back on all the gods—[these are excluded]. (30)

One who praises himself, who creates obstacles to the Dharma, who is deceitful, who squanders what is unfit for the purpose, and who causes dissension among those who are harmonious—(these are to be avoided). || 31 ||
It causes the destruction of trees endowed with beautiful foliage and fruit; it is treacherous toward those who trust it, and it is devoted to the slaughter of heroes. || 32 ||

One who maintains no sacred fire, one who has no son, one who employs the practice of sorcery with poisons, a sinner who harbors hatred toward his guru, and one who causes discord between husband and wife; || 33 ||
A Brahmin who exercises authority over a village or a temple, one who lives as a hired servant, and one who is devoted to cruel deeds—[these are not to be invited]. (34)
One who has naturally accumulated a flood of sins, who is devoted to a multitude of secret evils, who commits offenses out of ignorance, and who performs wicked deeds through knowledge; || 35 ||
O best of Brahmins, this enchanting Ghoṇatīrtha purifies all these [sins] through bathing, drinking, and other rites; oh, how great is the majesty of this sacred site! (36)
Now follows the account of the Gandharva named Tumburu. Śrī Sūta said: Here I shall relate an ancient history that destroys sin, pacifies all evils, and bestows the fruit of liberation. (37)
In ancient times, the highly lustrous Gārgya—a Brahmin who was an expert in all branches of knowledge, omniscient, ethical, and one who had conquered his senses—spoke as follows.
Having paid homage to the high-souled Devala with a serene mind, he said: "O illustrious one, be compassionate toward me; tell me the auspicious majesty of Ghoṇatīrtha, which removes all sins. (39)
Devala said: The Gandharva named Tumburu, having cursed his devoted wife, bathed here and worshipped Veṅkaṭeśa, the ocean of compassion. (40)
He indeed attained the world of Viṣṇu, which is free from rebirth.
Gārgya said: O sage Devala, for what reason did the Gandharva named Tumburu, who is proficient in all branches of knowledge, [abduct] his beautiful wife? || 42 ||
"By what fault did he curse his wife, who was endowed with all virtues? Tell me that, O highly fortunate one, for I have a great curiosity to hear it. (43)

Now follows the method for the ritual bath of Māgha as instructed by Tumburu to his own wife. A Gandharva named Tumburu spoke with affection to his wife: "Perform, along with me, the bath that removes impurities during the three months of Māgha. (44)
In the month of Māgha, when the sun has risen—this destroyer of all impurities—perform the smearing with cow dung on this bank for the sake of worshipping Viṣṇu.
Perform service for me, Viṣṇu, with colored powders, rows of designs, white lotuses, svastikas, and minerals, during this month that bestows auspiciousness. (46)
In this month of Māgha, prepare a lamp-wick for this Mādhava; with devotion, offer incense and fire before Hari. (47)
Having become pure, prepare the cooked offering for the high-souled Mādhava with devotion, along with circumambulations and prostrations, during the month of Māgha together with me. 48.
Perform daily worship of Viṣṇu, the God of gods; and, remaining ever vigilant, listen constantly to the Purāṇas concerning Viṣṇu.
Having bathed daily with diligence, drink the water from the feet of Hari; [call out] "Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Mukunda, Nārāyaṇa, Janārdana! (50)
Constantly chant, "O Acyuta, O Ananta, O Soul of the Universe! Having abandoned anger, envy, greed, and the like, observe your vow.

By that, liberation arises for you, as well as the eternal realm of Viṣṇu. Now, regarding his wife, here are the manner of the curse given by Tumburu and the means of its release: Having heard what was spoken by her husband in this way, that beloved of the Gandharva spoke to her husband out of anger—words that were unbearable and leading to a miserable state. (52)

O sinless one, when the cold has intensified in the month of Māgha and the sun has only slightly risen in the morning, how can one immerse oneself in this [water] while afflicted by the pain of the cold? (53)
"O husband, those duties which you have mentioned cannot be performed by me repeatedly; I will not perform my morning bath together with you. (54)
"If I die from the excessive cold, you will not be my protector. Having heard these words thus spoken, her husband, the beloved of the Gandharvas, [replied]. (55)
Then Śānta, though himself peaceful, cursed his wife for speaking unpleasantly, as well as his son who was averse to dharma and his wife for her harsh speech.
Reflecting on the principle that "one should immediately punish a king who acts unrighteously with a curse," he then cursed the virtuous woman in this manner.
On the highly meritorious Veṅkaṭādri, which destroys all sins, near the Ghoṇatīrtha, within the hollow of a Pippala tree—58.
"In that place devoid of water, O fool, you shall become nothing but a frog. Having heard these words of her husband, the beloved of the Gandharva [remained silent]. (59)
Having fallen at his feet, the virtuous woman entreated Tumburu; thereafter, her husband indeed became Tumburu once again and spoke of the end of the curse.
The highly fortunate Agastya, an ascetic who had conquered his senses, bathed in the excellent Ghoṇa-tīrtha on the great lunar day of the full moon.
Indeed, when that best of Brahmins spoke of the greatness of Ghoṇatīrtha to his disciples in the vicinity of that Aśvattha tree, || 62 ||
At that time, you were settled within the hollow of a Pippala tree, having heard the greatness of Ghoṇatīrtha, which bestows liberation.
"Having shaken off all your sins, you shall sport with me. Having been addressed thus, the devoted wife, faithful to her husband, then ceased speaking. (64)
Due to her husband's curse, she assumed the extremely terrible body of a frog on that peak of Śeṣādri, to the south of Ghoṇatīrtha.
The woman went very slowly into the hollow of a Pippala tree; ten thousand years passed for her within that hollow of the Aśvattha tree.
Then, after some time, Agastya went to the enchanting Veṅkaṭādri and, having bathed at Śrī Svāmitīrtha according to the prescribed rules, [performed his rites].
Having bowed to the Lord Varāhasvāmin to the south of the sacred ford, he went to the abode of Veṅkaṭeśa, [to see] Śrīnivāsa, the ocean of mercy.
Having bowed to the eternal God of gods, the large-eyed one who is to be known through the Vedas, the highly fortunate Agastya then proceeded to Ghoṇatīrtha.
Having bathed there in that most excellent of sacred fords, that best of yogis, together with his disciples, [taught] to his disciples out of devotion beneath the shade of a Pippala tree.
The majesty of Ghoṇatīrtha destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin; it is meritorious, bestows all auspiciousness, and grants all forms of prosperity. (71)
Thus spoke the venerable sage Agastya, the most excellent among yogins.

Now, at Ghoṇatīrtha, through the sight of Agastya, Tumburu’s wife was released from her state as a frog. Having heard this, the frog fell at the feet of that yogi, and by means of the lamp of knowledge, she realized the majesty of the sage.
"O Agastya, best among yogis, O ocean of compassion, protect me, protect me! Having assumed this enchanting form, a woman has approached me. (74)
"O Brahmin, protect me out of compassion, for I have acted in opposition to my husband's word. Having spoken thus to him, the large-eyed woman then ceased. (75)

Agastya said: "Who are you, O lady of beautiful hips—blessings be upon you—who was responsible for granting you this birth as a frog? Tell me what sin you committed in your previous life; do not delay. (76)
The woman said: "O Brahmin, I am the wife of a Gandharva named Tumburu, who is proficient in all branches of knowledge; O Agastya, you who are served by sages. (77)
"My husband is Tumburu, the best of sages, who knows all dharmas; you, being pleasing in all your ways, should always perform your duties together with me. (78)
Then, having heard that reply which was beneficial for the next world, yet unbearable, extremely fierce, and indeed leading to a miserable rebirth— (79)
And indeed, O dear one, best of sages, it was spoken by me out of wicked intent. (80)

Now follow the duties of a devoted wife as told by Agastya. Agastya said: "Your husband, whose intellect is as sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass, has cursed you in a fit of rage. Such a curse is indeed fitting for one who opposes the words of her husband. (81)
But that woman who, disregarding her husband’s reply, acts according to her own will, falls into a terrible hell as long as the moon and stars exist. (82)
Women possess no independence; the husband’s command must not be transgressed, through the merit of devotion to her husband and through service to him. 83.
Women go to the abode of Viṣṇu, and not by other virtuous vows; the husband is the mother, the husband is Viṣṇu, the husband is Brahmā, and the husband is Śiva. (84)
The wise know that for women, the husband is the guru and the husband is the sacred ford; yet, by disregarding her husband's word, a woman [deprives herself] of her other meritorious deeds. (85)
Even she who is always disciplined would not become pure even once; for a woman who is deprived of her husband has been so declared by the gurus who are most learned in the Dharma. (86)
Grateful and devoted solely to her husband's will, she, being urged by her husband, should perform that vow which bestows the fruit of dharma. (87)
She who has bathed at the sacred ford of the lotus-feet of the Lord is beloved by Hari; she has, without a doubt, bathed in all the holy fords, such as the Gaṅgā and others.
Therefore, the fault committed by you returns to you; thus, while you are experiencing its fruit here, listen to the majesty of Ghoṇatīrtha.
Liberation was attained so that his auspicious body became once again in the form of a woman; therefore, this place of the Ghoṇa-tīrtha is indeed known here as Tumbutīrtha.
A renown spread throughout the world, saying, "Oh, how great is the majesty of this sacred ford! || 91 ||

Now follows the attainment of various fruits by those who bathe at Ghoṇatīrtha. Śrī Sūta said: O Śaunaka and others of great luster, those who bathe on the full-moon day at the highly meritorious Ghoṇatīrtha, which destroys all sins, [attain the following]. 92.
The merit of their sacrificial fruit shall be equal to the fruit of ten thousand holy fords (tīrthas). This applies even to one who gives a thousand tawny cows (kapilā) day after day. || 93 ||
One obtains that same fruit by bathing at Tumburu-tīrtha as one who gives away thousands of crores of jewels day after day.
One obtains that same fruit by bathing at Ghoṇatīrtha as one would from [giving] thousands of rutting elephants and likewise ten thousand horses. 95.
Whatever fruit is declared by the sages to result from the gift of ten million maidens, that same fruit one obtains from the purifying Ghoṇatīrtha.
Whatever fruit one obtains by bestowing a thousand garments of gold at Kurukṣetra, that same fruit one attains through the majesty of Ghoṇatīrtha. || 97 ||
Whoever would sacrifice their body for the sake of a guru, for the sake of a Brahmin, or for the sake of one's master, obtains that same fruit through the majesty of Ghoṇatīrtha. || 98 ||

Whatever merit belongs to those who remove the suffering of the afflicted, who are devoted to serving sacred fords (tīrtha), and who are firm in their vow of truth—that same merit shall be obtained from Ghoṇatīrtha.
Whatever fruit belongs to those who perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha) for their ancestors on the new moon day, that very fruit one indeed attains from the purifying Ghoṇatīrtha.

Whatever fruit a man obtains by bathing in the Gaṅgā, the Narmadā, the Sarayū, and the Candrabhāgā, as well as in all other holy pilgrimage sites (tīrthas), he indeed attains that same fruit from the purifying Ghoṇatīrtha.
Therefore, the wise know Ghoṇatīrtha to be the most meritorious of sacred sites.
Whoever hears this chapter, which destroys all sins, obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and the eternal world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Tumburu-tīrtha," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now follows the description of Śrī Veṅkaṭācala as the substratum of all meritorious holy places (tīrthas). The Sages said: "O Sūta, best of Paurāṇikas, how many holy places are there indeed on the greatly meritorious Veṅkaṭādri, which destroys all calamities?"
Tell me their number, and how many among them are indeed the principal ones; O best of sages, tell me which among those are the most preeminent.
Among these, how many primarily bestow delight in the true Dharma? Which among them bestow knowledge, and which bestow devotion and dispassion? (3)
O you of noble vows, tell me which among these bestow liberation in this world.
The venerable Sūta said: O observer of noble vows, sixty-six crores of meritorious tīrthas are located here on this best of mountains; among them, one thousand and eight are the principal ones.
In this [work], there are one hundred and eight gifts that bestow delight in the True Dharma; these are the principal ones among thousands and various other [gifts].
Therein, within one hundred and eight [deities], sixty bestow devotion and dispassion.

Now follows the determination of the times for bathing in the six holy tirthas, beginning with Svāmipuṣkariṇī. There, upon the summit of Veṅkaṭācala, there are indeed six [tirthas] that bestow liberation: Svāmipuṣkariṇī and, after that, Viyadgaṅgā.
After that is Pāpavināśa, and beyond that is Pāṇḍutīrtha; then comes Kumāradhārikātīrtha, and after that is Tumbustīrtha.
O twice-born ones, when the conjunction with the Maghā constellation occurs on the full moon day of the month of Kumbha, all sacred fords (tīrthas) go to Kumāradhārī.
O best of Brahmins, he who bathes there shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice; and liberation shall also be attained there—of this there is no doubt.

O twice-born ones, the rite for the gift of food there, accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), takes place on the full-moon day of the bright fortnight conjoined with the asterism Uttarāphalgunī.
When the sun is situated in Pisces, all the holy fords from every direction come together at Tumbostīrtha during the afternoon; one who bathes there is not born again.

One should cause the investiture of the sacred girdle and the marriage ceremony to be performed by means of the giving of wealth, when the sun has entered Aries and is conjoined with the Citrā asterism.
On the full moon day, they likewise come to the celestial Gaṅgā; having bathed there, a person immediately obtains the fruit of a hundred sacrifices. || 15 ||
Gold should be given there, especially the gift of a maiden, O Brahmins, when the sun is situated in Taurus on the twelfth lunar day, the day of Hari.
Whether during the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, even when conjoined with Mars, the Gaṅgā and other rivers from the three worlds come to Pāṇḍutīrtha.
Having bathed there and given a cow as a gift, one is liberated from all obstacles on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, when it falls on a Sunday. || 18 ||
Likewise, on the twelfth lunar day conjoined with Uttarāṣāḍhā, there is the destruction of sins; or if one arrives on the twelfth day conjoined with Uttarābhādrapadā. || 19 ||
Having given a Śālagrāma stone and having bathed according to the prescribed rites, one is liberated from all sins arising from hundreds of millions of births.
In the month of Dhanus, during the bright fortnight, at dawn on the twelfth lunar day, all sacred fords (tīrthas) arrive in the waters of Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
Having bathed there, a person immediately attains liberation, of this there is no doubt; provided that merit has been earned by him in thousands of previous births.
O Brahmins, his bath shall take place, but not that of anyone else who has not disciplined himself; there, a gift should be given according to one's means and in accordance with the prescribed rule.
One should give the gift of a śāligrāma stone, and especially one should give a cow.

Now follows the description of the specific excellence of listening to the Purāṇas: Those who always listen to the story of Viṣṇu, which purifies the world, truly become devotees of Viṣṇu in this world of mortals. (25)

If one is unable to listen constantly to the discourse that purifies the world, yet listens with devotion for even a moment, half a moment, or a single instant to the excellent narrative of Viṣṇu, there is indeed no misfortune for that person.
Whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices and whatever fruit is found in all acts of giving—that fruit a man obtains from hearing a Purāṇa even once. || 27 ||
In the Kali age, especially, there is no higher dharma for men than listening to the Purāṇas; nor is there anything else that bestows liberation.
Listening to the Purāṇas and the supreme chanting of Viṣṇu’s names—both of these are the great fruits of the tree of merit for human beings. (29)
By drinking nectar with effort, one person alone may become free from old age and death; but by drinking the nectar of Viṣṇu’s stories, one makes the entire family free from old age and death.

Now follows the description of the universal venerability of the narrator of the Purāṇas: Whether he be a child, a youth, or an old man; whether poor or even unfortunate—a knower of the Purāṇas is always to be saluted and worshipped by those of virtuous soul. (31)
One should never entertain a low opinion of one who knows the Purāṇas, for the speech issuing from his mouth is a wish-fulfilling cow for all embodied beings.
For those who, having been born again and again throughout thousands of millions of existences, have become despondent, who else is a greater teacher than he who grants the state of non-return? (33)
When a twice-born reciter of the Purāṇas has ascended the seat of Vyāsa, he shall not pay obeisance to anyone until the conclusion of the discourse.
A wise person should not recount sacred stories in a place crowded with wicked people, nor in a region overrun by Śūdras and beasts of prey, nor in a gambling house. (35)
In a good village crowded with virtuous people, in a fertile field, in a temple of the gods, or on the holy bank of a river, the wise man should recount sacred stories.
Those listeners who are endowed with faith and devotion, who have no longing for other activities, who are restrained in speech, pure, and unperturbed, partake in merit. (37)
Those lowest of men who listen to the meritorious narrative without devotion have no fruit of merit; they shall experience suffering birth after birth. (38)
Those who, having honored the Purāṇa with offerings such as betel leaves and other gifts, listen to its narrative with devotion, shall become neither poor nor sinful.
When this discourse is being told, those men who go elsewhere will lose their wives and their wealth midway through their enjoyments. (40)
Those who listen to this purifying story with turbans on their heads are born as sinful children, the lowest of men. (41)
Those who listen to the purifying discourse while chewing betel-leaf indeed eat dog-dung and fall into hell.
And those hypocrites who, seated upon high thrones, listen to the discourse, shall experience inexhaustible hells and indeed become crows.
Those heroes who are seated in the vīrāsana posture and those who are established upon lion-thrones, they indeed become arjuna trees by listening to the sacred narrative.
For those who listen without bowing down indeed become poisonous trees; likewise, those who listen while lying down truly become pythons.
He who listens to the discourse of the speaker while seated on the same seat incurs a sin equal to that of violating the preceptor’s bed and shall go to hell. || 46 ||
Those mortals who revile one who knows the Purāṇas and the holy narrative that removes sin, shall indeed become dogs for a hundred births.
Those who speak with difficult rebuttals while this narrative is being recited are born as donkeys, and after that, as lizards.
Those men who never at any time listen to the meritorious narrative, having experienced terrible hells, become wild boars in the forest.
Those men who create obstacles while this narrative is being recited, having suffered in hells for ten million years, become village pigs.
Those best of men who rejoice in this narrative as it is being recited—even if they do not hear it—go to the eternal, imperishable state.
Those men who cause others to hear this meritorious ancient narrative shall dwell in the abode of Brahmā for more than a hundred crores of kalpas.
Those men who provide a seat for one who knows the Purāṇas—whether it be blankets, skins, garments, or even a couch—[attain great merit]. (53)
Having reached the heavenly world and enjoyed pleasures as they desired, and having dwelt in the worlds of Brahmā and the other gods, they attain the state that is free from all affliction.
Those who bestow a new and excellent manuscript of the Purāṇa become enjoyers of pleasures and endowed with knowledge in birth after birth. || 55 ||
Those who are joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) and those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin), by the mere hearing of the Purāṇas, they go to the supreme state.

Having heard the majesty of Veṅkaṭādri, those sages then honored Sūta, the best of Paurāṇikas, who was endowed with the grace of Vyāsa, according to the prescribed rites, and attained incomparable joy.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for Listening to the Purāṇas, Preceded by the Summary of the Greatness of All Holy Tīrthas," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now, the majesty of Kaṭāha-tīrtha. The sages said: O Sūta, knower of the truth of all matters, you who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāntas—on Śrī Veṅkaṭācala, there is a most purifying holy site named Kaṭāha.
His greatness is heard of and proclaimed throughout the three worlds; O you who are instructed by Vyāsa, please tell us about this out of your compassion.
In ancient times, the illustrious Nārada, the great ṛṣi and son of Brahmā, having seen the Naimiṣa forest, arrived there, O best of the twice-born.
Then, having worshipped that son of Brahmā according to the prescribed rule with auspicious offerings such as water for honor and water for the feet, he seated him upon a pure seat of kusha grass.
Having seated him with great devotion, all these great sages, their necks bowed in humility, prostrated and made this request: || 5 ||
"O illustrious Nārada, apart from you, there is no one among the great sages in the three worlds who can instruct us in dharma; indeed, there is none."
On the highly meritorious Veṅkaṭādri, frequented by all the gods, divine, descended from Vaikuṇṭha, and served by Siddhas and Gandharvas.
Describe today, for the forest-dwellers, the greatness of the Kaṭāha Tīrtha.
The venerable Nārada said: Listen, all you sages of great luster, Śaunaka and the rest; who in the three worlds knows the majesty of the Kaṭāha Tīrtha?
Mahādeva knows the majesty of that sacred ford (tīrtha), as well as whatever merits exist within the entire cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
O best of the twice-born, those holy places such as the Gaṅgā and others resort to the Kaṭāha-tīrtha for the complete purification of their own sins.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of other castes touch that water; he who, being of deluded intellect, does not drink it [is a fool]. (12)
For having attained the state of a Caṇḍāla, he shall fall into the Kumbhīpāka hell—whether he be a celibate student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a lordly ascetic. (13)
By serving that sacred site (tīrtha), one attains the supreme state; in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas, there is praise for that sacred site.
O Brahmins, it is described in many ways as the destroyer of the five great sins; it is most exceedingly wonderful and the sole purifier of all the worlds. (15)
Even ten thousand killings of Brahmins, ten thousand drinkings of liquor, and ten thousand instances of approaching the wife of one's guru—all these causes of sin [are destroyed]. (16)
Ten million acts of stealing gold and tens of millions of associations with such sinners quickly go to destruction by resorting to that holy place. || 17 ||
Whatever various sins there may be that are devoid of atonement, they all perish through the frequenting of this sacred ford.
This sacred ford is of great merit, having issued from the feet of the Blessed One; whoever is afflicted by leprosy or other diseases should drink this every day. (19)

Now, those who are devoid of faith in the greatness of the Kaṭāha-tīrtha attain a great hell; yet even he, being freed from disease, goes to the world of Viṣṇu. Thus spoke the Lord, the god Śaṅkara, in the Rahasyānubhava in ancient times.
He recounted the majesty of that sacred ford (tīrtha) to Pārvatī; no doubt should ever be entertained regarding these things that have been spoken. (21)
And one should never say, "This is a mere explanatory eulogy" (arthavāda); for those nihilists who would claim this to be an arthavāda, [it would be a grave error]. (22)
And the servants cast a heated axe upon the tip of the tongue; therefore, the Kaṭāha-tīrtha should be resorted to with great effort. || 23 ||
It pacifies all suffering and bestows the fruit of liberation; by drinking from it with devotion, a person shall attain all desires.
Having spoken thus, O Sūta, best of Paurāṇikas, the illustrious and highly fortunate Nārada arrived at Kāśī, the purifier of the three worlds.
The Blessed One indeed spoke in brief at Naimiṣa; now we wish to hear of the majesty of Kaṭāha.
And please tell us in great detail, O Sūta, out of your compassion. (27)

Now follows the procedure for drinking from the Kaṭāha-tīrtha. The venerable Sūta said: "O all you ascetics, residents of the Naimiṣa forest, O best of the twice-born, listen to the majesty of the Kaṭāha-tīrtha."
O Brahmins, the Kaṭāhatīrtha is renowned throughout all the worlds; it bestows all prosperity, is pure, and destroys all sins.
For this indeed destroys bad dreams, destroys great sins, pacifies great obstacles, and brings about great peace for men. (30)
One should drink the enchanting sacred water with the eight-syllable mantra alone, which destroys all the sins of men by its mere recollection.
Alternatively, one may drink water while reciting the names beginning with Keśava; or else, one may drink that auspicious water while reciting even the three names.
Or else, one should drink the water of the Kaṭāha-tīrtha with the eight-syllabled mantra of Veṅkaṭeśa; that indeed bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
That brahmin who drinks the supreme sacred water (tīrtha) without a mantra [should say]: "Quickly destroy my great sin committed in other births. (34)
Having said this, he should daily perform the bath in the Svāmipuṣkariṇī and the sight of Varāha and Śrīśa, which are the sole means for achieving the path to liberation.
The drinking at the Kaṭāha-tīrtha—these three are difficult to obtain even in the three worlds; what more need be said here? They destroy even the sin of killing a Brahmin.

Now follows the account of the twice-born man named Keśava: Formerly, a certain twice-born man named Keśava, out of delusion and evil intent, killed a man of great learning with a sword and thereby incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin. (37)
Having drunk that unsurpassed water at that great holy ford, even that great sinner named Keśava was liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
The sages said: Whose son was he named Keśava, and how did he incur such a terrifying and most cruel Brahman-murder? You ought to tell this to us. (39)
Śrī Sūta said: On the beautiful bank of the Tuṅgabhadrā, frequented by Gandharvas, there was a great agrahāra (brahmin settlement) known by the name Vedāḍhya.
In that beautiful city of the Vedas, there were Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas; they were all devoted to the science of grammar and were pioneers of the science of astrology.
They were all knowers of the Mīmāṃsā and Tarka scriptures, proponents of Vedānta, devoted to the treatises on Dharma, and always intent upon the giving of food.
All those great men in that agrahāra were indeed possessed of sons; and in that agrahāra, which was rich in the Vedas, there was one known as Padmanābha.

Now follows the sequence of how Keśava, the Brahmin addicted to courtesans, incurred the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa: His son, named Keśava, was excluded from all religious rites; having abandoned his mother, his father, and even his devoted wife, [he departed]. (44)
Always attached to courtesans, he entered the house of a prostitute; after enjoying that prostitute for two days, the twice-born man then— || 45 ||
Having placed two gold coins in his hand, she gave him leave to depart in peace; though he was now penniless, the man remained solely intent on union with that courtesan.
Having constantly stolen many goods from here and there, he took them to her; for a long time he sported with her and enjoyed himself in her house. (47)
He drank wine with her from a single cup; once, that twice-born man went out with Kirātas to seize wealth.
In the house of a certain brahmin, Keśava himself, disguised as a hunter (kairāta), appeared as a kinsman of that brahmin—bold and with a sword in his hand.
Having impetuously killed the brahmin who was the master of that house with his sword, he took much wealth and entered a prostitute’s quarters.
As he was going, the terrifying Brahmahatyā followed him—wearing blue garments, fearsome, and with intensely red hair.
Roaring with a loud laugh and making heaven and earth tremble, she pursued the brahmin, who wandered about the surface of the world.
Thus wandering over the entire earth, that evil-minded kinsman of the Brahmins returned to his own village out of fear, O Śaunaka and others of great luster.
Pursued by her, he fled in fear to his own abode; the sin of Brahman-slaughter also followed him and went with him to his home. (54)
Crying out, "Protect Janaka! Protect him!", Keśava sought refuge [with him]. Saying, "Do not fear," the father prepared to protect him. (55)
Then, while Padmanābha was intent on protecting his own son, the personified sin of Brahmin-slaughter spoke; that cruel Brahmahatyā addressed her father: (56)
Brahmahatyā said: "O Padmanābha, best of the twice-born, do not accept him! He is a drinker of liquor, a thief, a killer of a Brahmin, and a perpetrator of a heinous crime. (57)
A betrayer of his mother, a betrayer of his father, one who abandons his wife, one of wicked intellect, and one whose mind is attached to a prostitute—release this evil-souled man.
"O Brahmin, if you accept this son who is a great sinner in vain, then I shall [consume] your wife, his wife, yourself, and this son, O twice-born one. (59)
"I shall devour your lineage; therefore, release this evil-minded one! If you abandon this son, I shall release you all at once. (60)
"O high-minded one, you ought not to destroy your family for the sake of a single person. Thus addressed by her, Padmanābha then spoke to her.
Padmanābha said: "Affection for my son torments me; how can I abandon my son? Hearing that, Brahmahatyā spoke to Padmanābha. (62)
Brahmahatyā said: "This son of yours has become fallen, excluded from the castes and stages of life. Do not feel affection for this son; even the sight of him is censurable."
Having spoken thus, while Padmanābha was looking on, that Brahmahatyā struck his son named Keśava with her hand.
Crying out "Father! Father! he wept repeatedly, addressing his father; then Janaka, his mother, and the wife of that evil-minded man all wept as well. (65)

Now follows the means for liberation from the sin of killing a Brahmin as told by Bharadvāja to Padmanābha: At that time, the illustrious and great sage Bharadvāja, a yogi, arrived by good fortune, O Śaunaka and others of great luster. (66)
Then Padmanābha, having seen that great sage Bharadvāja, praised him, prostrated before him, and sought refuge for the sake of obtaining a son. (67)
O highly fortunate Bharadvāja, you are a direct portion of Viṣṇu; the sight of you will never occur for those devoid of merit.
"My son became a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, and a thief; the terrifying personification of Brahmin-slaughter came to strike down my son. (69)
May it be so that this son of mine is liberated from great sins, and that this terrible Brahmahatyā may swiftly go to its dissolution. (70)
Tell me that means today; have compassion for my son. For I have but one son, O Sage, and no other offspring exists.
"If my son dies, my lineage will be utterly severed at its root; consequently, there will certainly be no one left to offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the ancestors. (72)
"Therefore, O Blessed One, O Sage, show mercy toward us. Thus addressed, Bharadvāja—who was a direct portion of Nārāyaṇa—[replied].
Having meditated for a very long time, he spoke these words to Padmanābha.
Bharadvāja said: "O Padmanābha, a most cruel sin has been committed by your son; there can be no pacification of this sin even through ten thousand atonements."
Nevertheless, O twice-born Padmanābha, listen; for the sake of pacifying this sin of your son, I shall declare an expiation. (76)
O twice-born one, it is located two hundred yojanas to the south of the Gaṅgā and five yojanas to the west of the eastern ocean.
On the northern bank of the Suvarṇamukharī, at a distance of just one krośa, is the mountain renowned as Veṅkaṭādri, which is saluted by all the worlds.
Meruputra is of great merit and is saluted by all the gods; brought from the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, he is the great mountain of Viṣṇu’s play.
On the auspicious shore of Svarṇamukhī, he dwells, honored by hosts of gods and hosts of sages, [attended] by the swift Garuḍa.
On that lordly Veṅkaṭa mountain, Nārāyaṇa himself has appeared in person, accompanied by the goddess Lakṣmī, the goddess Bhū, and the goddess Nīlā.
That Veṅkaṭeśa himself, the direct bestower of liberation, resides there; indeed, to the north of that temple of Veṅkaṭanātha, [he dwells]. (82)
O best of Brahmins, the Kaṭāha-tīrtha exists there, bestowing auspiciousness, destroying sins such as the slaughter of a Brahmin, and granting desired objects. (83)
"O best of Brahmins, drink the enchanting sacred water (tīrtha) together with Suta. Having heard those words of Bharadvāja, which were equal to the Vedas, [Sauti replied]: || 84 ||
Then, having bowed to him with his head, he went to Mount Veṅkaṭa.

Then, by the word of Bharadvāja, Keśava was liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin through drinking the water of the Kaṭāha-tīrtha. Having gone to that Veṅkaṭa mountain, the eminent brāhmaṇa bathed according to the prescribed rules in the waters of Svāmipuṣkariṇī together with his son.
Having bowed to Varāhasvāmin, he went to the abode of Śrīnivāsa; then, having performed a circumambulation and having prostrated before the temple chariot (vimāna), [he departed].
Then Padmanābha, along with his wicked-souled son Keśava, drank that Kaṭāhatīrtha, which destroys the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
At that moment, that sin of Brahman-slaughter quickly went to its dissolution; thereafter, he went to Veṅkaṭeśa, the ocean of mercy. (89)
Then, together with his son, that best of Brahmins, Padmanābha, beheld the Lord Veṅkaṭeśa, the ocean of compassion, who had manifested himself.
Satisfied by drinking from the Kaṭāha-tīrtha, he spoke these words: || 91 ||

Then follows the speech of the Blessed Lord to Padmanābha, who was accompanied by his son liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin. The Blessed Lord said: "O Padmanābha of great intellect, you who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāntas! Having reached Mount Veṅkaṭa at the word of Bharadvāja... (92)
Having drunk from the Kaṭāha-tīrtha, you have achieved your purpose; of this there is no doubt. Your son, named Keśava, has been liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Therefore, the Kaṭāha-tīrtha should be resorted to with great effort; having drunk the unsurpassed water in that tīrtha, O highly fortunate one, [one attains the goal]. (94)
"Even sinners shall achieve their purpose; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. Having come to my world, O high-minded one, be happy."
Having spoken thus, that Lord Veṅkaṭeśa then vanished from sight.
The venerable Sūta said: Therefore, O all you ascetics, Śaunaka and the others of great luster, [listen to] the majesty of Kaṭāhatīrtha, accompanied by its ancient history.
O twice-born ones, I have related this to you exactly as I heard it correctly.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Praise of Kaṭāha Tīrtha," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 28 ||
The sages said: "The power of all the holy fords (tīrthas) here has been described by you—of the rivers, the mountains, the sacred fields, and even the lakes."
O sinless one, you have explained how the river Suvarṇamukharī was brought to this earth by Agastya at the command of Padmagarbha.
We have developed a great desire to hear about the power of that origin and the multitudes of heretical sects who rely upon it; therefore, you ought to tell us this.
Having bowed down to Śambhu, Nandīśa, the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), and Vyāsa as well, Sūta, being requested by the sages, then proceeded to speak.

Śrī Sūta said: Well asked, O highly fortunate ones! This narrative, which brings about auspiciousness and bestows the perfection arising from hearing the sacred tradition (Āmnāya), has been well inquired after by you.
Listen attentively as I relate to you this divine narrative that destroys all impurity, told by Bharadvāja to the son of Pṛthā.
Having obtained Yājñasenī from the wise Drupada, the sons of Pṛthā went to the auspicious city of Hastināpura at the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Then, honored there by Bhīṣma and the son of Ambikā (Dhṛtarāṣṭra), they lived for five years together with Duryodhana and the others.
Then, in the presence of all the elders of the lineage and of Vāsudeva, the highly illustrious Dhṛtarāṣṭra was instructed by Bhīṣma and the others.
With a heart delighted by their service, he bestowed upon the sons of Pāṇḍu half of the kingdom and that excellent city known as Khāṇḍavaprastha.
Having taken leave of the Kurus, headed by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the sons of Pāṇḍu, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa, went to that city of Khāṇḍavaprastha.
Dwelling in that city called Indraprastha, which was protected by Viśvakarman, the son of Dharma, together with his younger brothers, ruled the earth.
When Kṛṣṇa had departed for his own city at the command of Nārada, the sons of Pṛthā, who were knowers of dharma, made a vow regarding Draupadī.
Now begins the introduction to Arjuna’s pilgrimage: In due order, that Kṛṣṇā (the river) should stay respectfully for one year at each person's house, according to the established determination. 14.
Whoever should see that daughter of Pañcāla staying in another's house must perform a pilgrimage for the duration of one year.
Having thus made their vow, those sons of King Pāṇḍu spent their time without indolence, engaging in activities common to the world.
Then a Brahmin from the countryside, standing in the courtyard of the royal palace, cried out repeatedly, "My cow has been stolen by thieves! (17)
And having comforted that brahmin, Dhanañjaya entered the armory with haste in order to fetch his weapons.
There he saw the princess of Pañcāla and the son of Dharma seated together; although he was aware of his vow, he nevertheless took up his bow along with its quiver.
Having gone and slain the thieves in battle, that son of the king turned back the cow and respectfully gave it to the brahmin. || 20 ||
Then Phalguna made this request to the son of Dharma: "I must undertake a pilgrimage to the sacred fords, as I have transgressed the proper time."
Having heard the words of his younger brother, the steadfast son of Dharma, the best among those who know all duties, spoke these words with reverence.

Yudhiṣṭhira said: "If one should speak a false word for the sake of a cow or for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, or if one should perform an unrighteous act [for those ends], that is truth; that is consistent with righteousness. (23)
"O you of noble vows, tell me how this deed performed by you for the sake of a Brahmin and for the sake of a cow can result in an evil state."
By neglecting or punishing thieves in the duty of protecting the subjects, the king will surely incur the fruit of both killing a Brahmin and performing a horse sacrifice.
Even knowing his enemies to be incurable, a lord of the earth does not enjoy prosperity if the thieves who cause the ruin of his own country remain unpunished. (26)
"Indeed, whatever is for the benefit of us kings and of the multitude of worlds has been accomplished by you in this manner; therefore, there is no fault in you. (27)
Śrī Sūta said: Having heard the words of the Son of Dharma, Dhanañjaya, who is ever devoted to righteousness, joined his palms in reverence and addressed him once more. (28)
Arjuna said: "O protector of the earth, do not speak thus, for you, who know the entirety of dharma and are an embodiment of radiant righteousness, would be transgressing your own vow. (29)
Indeed, a promise once uttered by a capable man who discerns what ought and ought not to be done must never be transgressed. (30)
This is the course of those who are powerless: that, due to the words of kinsmen and elders, they abandon their duty and forsake the commitment previously declared by themselves. (31)
If, out of compassion, the Noble One should turn back from going to the holy ford, who could restrain the people from reviling me for having failed in my vow? (32)
O King, my mind too is eager with curiosity for a pilgrimage to sacred sites; furthermore, O King, the command ordained by Nārada must be remembered and carried out.
Therefore, be gracious, O Great King, regarding this endeavor to go to the sacred ford; for masters ought to honor the timing of their dependents.
Saying "So be it," Arjuna, having received the consent of his brothers, gratified his elder brother with prostrations, humility, and other such marks of respect.
Having taken leave of his brothers, Bhīmasena and the others, as was appropriate, the Pāṇḍava set forth after auspicious rites for success had been performed by the noble Brahmins.
The reciters of ancient lore, astrologers, physicians, Brahmins, attendants, artisans, heralds, and bards followed after him. (37)
By the command of Yudhiṣṭhira, the affectionate courtiers and treasury officials followed him, taking with them wealth sufficient for his enjoyment and renunciation.

Now follows Arjuna’s arrival at the Suvarṇamukharī after bathing in the holy fords (tīrthas) such as the Gaṅgā. Having first reached the river Bhāgīrathī, that prince visited Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, and Kāśī as well. (39)
Beholding the holy fords of the Jāhnavī along the path bordering its banks, he reached the southern ocean with its towering waves.
Having beheld the Mahānadī river of great merit, the renowned Puruṣottama, and Siṃhācala, he attained the fulfillment of his purpose.
Then the son of Kuntī beheld the holy river Godāvarī, whose greatness had transcended all through its power to destroy the entire multitude of sins.
Having performed his ablutions with those waters according to the prescribed rites, the son of Pāṇḍu brought forth great joy through various gifts of land and gold.
Upon seeing the river named Malāpahā, he experienced auspicious joy; thereafter, he reached the Kṛṣṇaveṇī, the best of rivers.
He beheld Śrīparvata, the fixed abode of Śiva, endowed with four gates and crowded with hosts of various sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having crossed the river Pinākinī and traveled to the place frequented by celestial sages, he beheld Veṅkaṭācala, the abode beloved by Nārāyaṇa.
Standing upon the lofty peak of this mountain, he worshipped with devotion the world’s sole leader, Hari—the renowned one—for the attainment of auspicious success. (47)

Having descended from the peak of the great mountain Veṅkaṭa, he beheld the river named Suvarṇamukharī, frequented by hosts of perfected beings and sages, which had been brought down by the sage born from a water-jar (Agastya).

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Arjuna’s Arrival on His Pilgrimage to the Tīrtha," within the Suvarṇamukharī-māhātmya of the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala-māhātmya, in the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Now follows the description of the Suvarṇamukharī. Sūta said: And as Pārtha returned after having visited all those holy places, that great river increased his joy.
In the groves upon its banks, joyful women and perfected beings (siddhas) delight, being fanned by breezes cooled by showers of spray.
She was like one with hands upraised to embrace the Ganges as it flows through the sky, with her exceedingly lofty waves reaching unto the clouds.
The grounds of the hermitages on its banks shine with smoke arising from sacrificial oblations that reach the branches of the trees, and with the bark garments [of the ascetics].
On both its banks, divine liṅgas of the Wielder of the Trident shine forth, established on all sides by the lords of sages and the foremost of the gods.
The swans, the best of birds, resting in their dwellings upon her sandy banks, do not remember their own original home, Lake Mānasa.
She who nourishes with her waters—waters that have issued from the mouths of mountain channels and which have quelled the terror of drought—the crops capable of protecting the world.
Adorned with waves like creepers rising from the breasts of the ruddy geese, her circular hips were the sandy banks shimmering with whirlpools like a navel.
Her face is like a full-blown lotus, her eyes are like a pair of darting fish, she is clothed in shimmering foam, and she is enchanting with her swan-vehicle.
Conversing with the cries of water-birds, bringing delight to the eyes, and possessing the form of an unprecedented beloved, she shines as the beloved of the ocean.
To the east of the river flowing between its banks, Dhanañjaya beheld a lofty mountain named Kālahasti.
Its lofty peaks and expanses scrape the circle of the sky, while its rocky base, rooted deep in the seven netherworlds, rises upward.

Now follows Arjuna’s attainment of the service of Kālahastīśvara and other deities situated on the banks of the Svarṇamukharī. Having bathed in that great river, Arjuna beheld upon that mountain the God worshipped by the gods, known by the name Kālahastīśa. (13)
Having worshipped Mahādeva, the companion of the daughter of the mountain king, with a mind filled with devotion, he attained the state of having achieved his life's purpose.
Then, on that great mountain, the singular abode of wonders, he wandered about with a desire to behold extraordinary sights never seen before.
He beheld the Siddhas dwelling on the mountain slopes, accompanied by their women, singing the deeds of the God of gods.
He gazed with reverence upon the gandharvas seated in the groves, attended by beautiful apsarases and intoxicated by the exhilaration of flower-liquor.
In secluded places, he beheld divine yogins devoted to the meditation on Śiva, filled with reverence and bliss.
The Pāṇḍava beheld on all sides the peaceful hermitage grounds, with their entrance areas shining with offerings of bali and nīvāra grain.
He beheld peaceful sages who had restrained their senses, some abstaining from food, some subsisting on air, some eating leaves, and some feeding on heat.
The lotus-pools, their fragrance from full-blown *saugandhika* lilies perfuming the intermediate quarters of space, spread delight before his eyes. (21)
To those who were wandering with minds intent on hunting, their bows strung; || 22 ||

Then follows Arjuna’s journey to the hermitage of Bharadvāja situated on the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī. He beheld Kirātas accompanied by their wives, who had been searching for deer; then, he wandered on the charming southern slope of the mountain.
The descendant of Kuru beheld the holy hermitage of Bharadvāja, [adorned] with plantains, coconuts, mangoes, *kola* fruits, *campaka* flowers, and sandalwood trees.
With *takkola*, *aśoka*, *hintāla*, *tāla*, *ketaki*, and *dāḍima*; with *jambū*, *kadamba*, *kataka*, *khadira*, *arjuna*, and *pāṭala* trees; (25)
With *nāga*, *punnāga*, *sarala*, *devadāru*, and *karañjaka* trees; and also with *lavaṅga*, *luṅga*, *lavalī*, *priyaṅgu*, and *tilaka*.
With *bibhītaka*, *śrīphala*, *aśvattha*, *madhūka*, *plakṣa*, and *kesara*; with *pūga*, *jambīra*, *nāraṅga*, *nimba*, *āmalaka*, and *kauśika*. (27)
It was beautified by other trees rich with fruits and flowers, and was encircled by creepers such as the vāsantī, kunda, and jāti.
On all sides, it was frequented by female bees attracted by its unprecedented fragrance, and served as a refuge for ruddy geese, cranes, curlews, swans, and kāraṇḍava ducks.
It was adorned with lakes resplendent with multitudes of *saugandhika*, *utpala*, *ambhoja*, and *kairava* lotuses, their expansive waters sweet and flowing like nectar.
Having attained sovereign splendor, it was the sole abode of curiosity, filled with lions, elephants, tigers, hyenas, and large bears.
It was crowded with other deer that acted for one another's benefit; it surpassed the Caitraratha garden and eclipsed the Nandana grove.
The collection of meanings from the divine Śiva-āgamas is unsurpassed, sublime beyond speech and mind, and the cause of supreme bliss. (33)
Where parrots with melodious voices announce the deaths of the deceased, and where the sky is darkened by the smoke from the long-burning funeral fires; (34)
It creates the illusion of untimely clouds for the peacocks, as lions, weary from their sporting, arrive there at will. (35)
The elephants cooled their limbs with the spray from their trunks; beholding that hermitage, his mind was overcome with wonder.
Restraining all his followers right there at various points, the son of Pāṇḍu praised the spiritual power of the ascetics.

Then Arjuna, having performed his service to Bharadvāja, entered that hermitage together with his friends and the best of brahmins. At the forefront, the son of Kuntī beheld [the sage] possessing the radiant splendor of a flickering fire.
Bharadvāja was surrounded by many eminent sages; his entire body was smeared with ashes, and he wore a deerskin as an upper garment.
Resplendent like Mount Kailāsa enveloped in fresh clouds, he was radiant with matted locks that hung down with the brilliance of gold.
Like an autumnal cloud filled with steady streaks of lightning, it was as if the meanings of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas had come together and merged into one.

He bore an appearance as if it were voluntarily assumed, a source of auspiciousness for divine knowledge, and was constantly attended by fortitude, forbearance, compassion, contentment, and tranquility.
Approaching slowly before his lotus feet, the son of Pṛthā stood with his unbroken spiritual luster, as if surrounded by beloved, crimson-hued women.
She performed a full prostration with eight limbs, touching the surface of the earth.

Now, the manner in which Bharadvāja offered hospitality to Arjuna: Having raised up that son of Pṛthā who had arrived, the bull among sages, his mind blossoming with great joy, gladdened him with blessings. (45)
Having honored that beloved guest according to the rules with offerings of water for the feet and other rites, he asked after his well-being as he sat upon the designated seat.
Having received this honor from the sage, the middle Pandava delighted the heart of the lord of sages with his pleasing words. (47)
Then Bharadvāja remembered his celestial cow, who milks all desires; she provided an immense variety of foods, including both solid and soft delicacies.
Having eaten and paid homage to that treasury of asceticism along with his followers, Pārtha spent the remainder of the day in the delight of conversational discourse.
Then, having performed the evening twilight devotions and offered oblations into the fire, he went to his thatched cottage accompanied by Brahmins and ministers.
Seated there, greeted with the blessings of the lord of sages and being gladdened by the cool breezes from that river, he rejoiced.

"By whom was she brought from the earth, and from which mountain does she come with such great power?"—having thus inquired about the river's majesty, his mind became intent on hearing [the answer] from the lords of sages. (52)

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of Bharadvāja’s Hermitage," within the "Praise of the Majesty of the Suvarṇamukharī River" in the "Majesty of Śrī Veṅkaṭācala," in the second Vaiṣṇava Section of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 30 ||

Now follows Arjuna’s inquiry of Bharadvāja out of a desire to hear about the power of the Suvarṇamukharī. Śrī Sūta said: Having prostrated before the lord of sages, who had performed his evening rites, who possessed a splendor like that of fire, and who was seated comfortably, the bull among the Bharatas [Arjuna] spoke. (1)
Delighted by the flood of nectar from her cool fragrance, he spoke these words, profound and full of humility: || 2 ||
Arjuna said: O bull among sages, I alone am truly blessed in this world, since you have thus honored me with such distinction, as if I were your own son. (3)
My mind, its curiosity aroused by my respect for you, seems to urge me to drink the divine nectar of your words. (4)
Why was this great river born from the mountain and by whom was it brought here? What merit is obtained there by performing acts such as bathing and giving gifts? (5)
O virtuous sage, you ought to describe the power and origin of this [mantra] to me, who am bowed before you; for it is indeed your duty to show favor to your devotees.
Having heard Arjuna’s words, Bharadvāja, the best of the twice-born and a master of speech, looked at his face and spoke these words.
Bharadvāja said: O Arjuna, O mighty-armed one, you are the purifier of the Kaurava lineage; you are especially worthy of my respect, since you are the younger brother of Dharmaputra.
Many rulers of the earth have been seen by me, O Phalguna, but none like you, who are endowed with grace, straightforwardness, compassion, generosity, fortitude, and profundity.
Lineage, learning, and wealth are indeed the causes of pride for the powerful; for noble persons such as you, they are rather the causes of humility.
O Kaurava, while abundant royal enjoyments are available, who else besides you would not fall under the sway of mental derangement? (11)
I am dependent upon you, O son of Kuntī, because of your world-surpassing virtues. What is there that I should not tell you, O you whose mind is filled with curiosity? 12.
Listen, O King, to this divine tale heard by me from the mouth of a sage, by hearing which all living beings are liberated from the terror of sin. (13)

Now follows the account of Śaṅkara’s marriage as told by Bharadvāja: Previously, the goddess Dākṣāyaṇī, having been insulted by her father, abandoned that body and became the daughter of the Snowy Mountain (Himavat). (14)
Approached by the Seven Sages, the Supporter of the Earth was entreated and prepared to give his own daughter in marriage to Mṛtyuñjaya.
The Lord of the World, whose emblem is the bull, arrived at the abode of Himavat known as Oṣadhīprastha in order to marry Sarvamaṅgalā.
At his command, all beings—both stationary and moving—gathered together to celebrate the auspiciousness of the Lord of Beings.
Crushed by that immense weight, the earth, supported from below, sank down until it reached the netherworld (pātāla).
Due to this effortless lightness, she moved swiftly to the right and then rose upward; seeing her do so, fear seized everyone. (19)
Having perceived that transformation of the earth and having seen Agastya, Maheśvara said, "Come here, O highly wise one," and spoke these words.
When all these beings had assembled there, the earth was overwhelmed by their weight and underwent a state of transformation.
Therefore, O high-minded one, you ought to bring about the restoration of that land to its original state; for without you, how could this be accomplished by anyone other than yourself? (22)
For you are born from the essence of the gods and are intent upon protecting the world; therefore, my dear child, level this earth at my command.
"When all have arrived, their minds intent on the public curiosity regarding my taking of the hand in marriage, you too must remain present. (24)
If you do not remain here, no one will be able to remove the transformation of the earth; therefore, O sinless one, you must go.
I shall manifest this form, radiant with the auspiciousness of the marriage to the Daughter of the Mountain, wherever you may be.

Then, for the purpose of leveling the earth, Agastya departed toward the southern direction from the Himalayas. Having spoken thus and embraced him, Maheśvara dismissed him; saying "So be it," that sage bowed and went toward the southern quarter. (27)
When Agastya, that tiger among sages, had crossed the Vindhya mountains and reached the southern quarter, the earth attained a state of levelness.
Having removed the transformation from the earth, the gods, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras, trembling with joy, praised the sage born from the pitcher who remained there. (29)
Having gone from there, he then beheld a certain lofty mountain standing before him, supporting the earth with its wide-spreading feet.
It was as if a mine had been created by the Self-Existent One for all great medicinal herbs and jewels, blazing with unbroken splendor.
With its lofty peaks from which [water] falls from the sky to the earth, it seems to incessantly support [the world] with noble torrents.
Having slowly ascended that mountain, Agastya, the bull among sages, set his mind upon dwelling on that delightful plateau at its summit.
On the northern bank of that lake—which was comparable to nectar, possessed the splendor of clusters of lotuses and water-lilies, and was surrounded by various trees—(he stood).
Having established an excellent hermitage on that charming portion of the earth, he duly propitiated the ancestors, the gods, the sages, and the deity of the site.
Accompanied by a multitude of sages, he dwelt there for a very long time upon that mountain frequented by gods, siddhas, gandharvas, and apsarases.
While the one born from a jar remained in the penance grove, his mental faculties entirely absorbed in asceticism, the mountain, endowed with excellent beauty, reached the peak known as Agastyaśaila.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of Śaṅkara’s Marriage and Agastya’s Departure for the Southern Quarter," within the "Praise of the Suvarṇamukharī’s Greatness" in the "Greatness of Veṅkaṭācala," in the second Vaiṣṇava Section of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Arjuna and Bharadvāja. || 31 ||

Then, for the purpose of bringing about the river, there was a voice from the ether addressed to Agastya. Bharadvāja said: Once, that best of sages, having performed his morning rites, entered the temple of the deity to propitiate Śiva.
There, the goddess of speech, whose form was invisible, was heard by that great-souled one who was endowed with wonder, resplendent with clearly articulated phonemes.
A voice from the sky spoke to Agastya, the best among those who recite prayers: "Indeed, this region, though famous, does not shine because it is devoid of a river."
Averse to both knowledge and discernment, he was like a Brahmin devoid of ritual form, like an initiation ceremony lacking its sacrificial fee, or like a night bereft of moonlight.
O best of Brahmins, this earth does not shine without rivers; out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, cause some river to flow.
This [teaching], which is characterized by the liberation from the fear arising from unfathomable sins, is beneficial for the multitudes of gods; this is what was requested by the best of sages.
This is auspicious for humanity; practice this, O observer of noble vows, which brings benefit to the gods, the best of sages, and the people of the earth.
Set in motion the great river that pacifies the mire of evil.
The illustrious Bharadvāja said: Having heard those words, the brahmin became lost in thought for a moment; having completed the worship of the deity, he sat down outside the sacrificial altar.
Then he summoned the sages who had come to that hermitage, and he related to them the words uttered by the divine voice.
Having heard that wonder, the sages were delighted in their hearts.
Having paid homage to the best of sages, the son of Mitrāvaruṇa, they spoke.

Then follows the request of the great sages to Agastya for the manifestation of the Suvarṇamukharī river. The sages said: "O ocean of compassion, your divine life-story, which is the greatest wonder among wonders and the most auspicious among auspicious things, truly shines forth. (13)
By your mere utterance of "huṃ," Nahuṣa fell from his sovereignty over the gods and attained the state of an insect; therefore, nothing is surprising. (14)
The wheel of the earth was encompassed by him, and the sky was struck by his surging waves; what indeed could be more wondrous than this, that the ocean was reduced to a mere mouthful? (15)
The Vindhya mountain set out to obstruct the path of the sun; you brought it to rest. What indeed could be greater than this? (16)
Who on earth would be able to praise your wondrous deeds? Yet, through the power of my great good fortune, you have attained this embodied form.
O Great Sage, we have become fulfilled in this triple world, for we dwell here in this hermitage-place with you as our protector. 18.
O best of the twice-born, this region is indeed far from the domain of Yama; yet, though filled with all things, it does not shine for lack of a river. (19)
"What is the use of this wasted birth without bathing in a river? In a land devoid of rivers, non-birth is better than dwelling. (20)
"The ripening of our fortunes has now arrived, since you have been commanded by the gods: 'Set the great river flowing. (21)
O sinless one, now that this great river has been brought forth in this land, when indeed shall we go there and, having performed our ablutions, achieve the fulfillment of our purpose? (22)
What is the use of much deliberation? Let a firm effort be made to bring here that best of rivers, who is worthy of the world’s homage and a refuge for all. (23)
Śrī Bharadvāja said: Having honored their heart-pleasing words, that great twice-born one made this firm resolve: "I shall bring the river here. (24)

Now follows the manner of the penance performed by Agastya for the manifestation of the Suvarṇamukharī: Having been permitted by the lords of sages and having honored them as well as the gods, he performed a special worship of the Enemy of Cities (Śiva) according to the prescribed rites. (25)
Having firmly undertaken a vow that was difficult to endure due to its many hardships, he performed great penance with effort, which was not easily attainable by others.
Standing amidst the four sacrificial fires during the terrible days of summer, his gaze fixed upon the sun, he did not succumb to fatigue.
During the days of the rainy season, although he was struck by torrential downpours as unbearable as the onset of fierce winds, he did not experience agitation in his heart.
