During the winter season, standing in waters reaching up to his neck and remaining intent on recitation and meditation, he did not undergo any change whatsoever.
Then, observing the delay in the attainment of his desired object, he once again assumed a form even more terrifying to the world, characterized by an intensified state of concentration.
Having restrained the activity of his mind, abstaining from food, and having conquered his senses, he remained like a stone at that time, with his external functions unperceived.
As he was thus performing penance, a terrifying fire with blazing light, licking the clouds, issued forth from all his limbs.
Then, all directions being covered on every side by networks of wondrous crests of flame, the masses of people, agitated by intense fear, cried out in distress.
Then, when such a terrible upheaval of the world had occurred, the gods, having paid homage to the Lotus-born One, made this petition: (34)

Then follows the arrival of the Four-faced One at Agastya’s hermitage: Having comforted them, Brahmā, attended by Siddhas and Gandharvas, appeared before the pot-born sage as he was engaged in ascetic penance. (35)
Beholding that supreme Brahmā who had arrived, the twice-born one, with his mind fixed on him, bowed down and gratified him with various hymns of praise.
Then, beholding Agastya bowed low in humility, the Lotus-born One, his face bright with grace, spoke these pure words: (37)
Brahmā said: "O sinless one, I am well-pleased with your difficult penance. O observer of noble vows, choose whatever you desire; I shall grant it all to you."
Agastya said: "O Lord, by your grace, everything has been accomplished for me. If you grant my wish, I shall ask with a mind free from hesitation. (39)
Seeing this region devoid of rivers, my mind is distressed, like an excessive recitation of the Vedas that lacks understanding of their meaning. (40)
O Lord of Gods, grant me your grace so that I may purify the vast earth and protect the great river; for this alone is my desire. (41)

Then, at the request of Agastya, the Four-faced One issued a command to Gaṅgā. Śrī Bharadvāja said: Having heard the words of Agastya and saying, "Let it be so," Brahmā remembered in his mind the river that takes refuge in the path of the gods. 42.
Then the celestial Gaṅgā, approaching before the Supreme Lord, stood there radiant with her hands joined in praise upon her crown.
To her, the sustainer of all the worlds, who had arrived according to his own command with her head bowed in humility, he spoke these words: || 44 ||
Brahmā said: "O Gaṅgā, you are to be instructed by me in a task that benefits the world; for you, too, your constant state is fixed in the protection of the world, just as it is mine."
In this land devoid of rivers, the Pot-born Sage (Agastya) endeavors to bring forth a river for the benefit of all the worlds. (46)
Therefore, descending to the earth with one portion of yourself, purify the people of the world; go to the earth by this path that has been shown to you.
When the flow has set in upon the earthly realm, the best of gods and the most excellent of sages, desiring spiritual perfection, shall constantly serve it.
"Attain preeminence among rivers; protect the people who take refuge in you. Do what is pleasing to Agastya; go, auspicious lady, as you please. (49)
Bharadvāja said: Having spoken thus, Brahmā vanished along with that river and him [the sage], being specially honored by prostrations, worship, and hymns of praise. || 50 ||

Then, in the presence of Agastya, Gaṅgā accepted the emergence of a river as her own partial incarnation. Then Gaṅgā, having displayed before the lord of sages her own form composed of divine splendor born from a portion of herself, spoke these words: (51)
Gaṅgā said: "O beloved of the sages, having reached the earth as a portion of myself and assuming the form of a river, she will fulfill your desire. (52)
Bharadvāja said: Having spoken thus, once the Siddhavāhinī had departed, the sage, being asked by her who was sent by her, "By which path should one go? replied to her.
Agastya said: "O auspicious lady, walking ahead, I shall show you the path suitable for your journey; you must follow me."
Thus addressed by that sage, O sinless one, that auspicious woman was greatly delighted and said, "I shall do whatever you desire. (55)

Then the sage, having brought her down from that king of mountains whose peaks touch the clouds—she who was the very body of the river—proceeded with a most joyful heart, showing her the path she desired.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of Suvarṇamukharī," within the "Praise of the Majesty of Śrī Suvarṇamukharī" in the "Majesty of Śrī Veṅkaṭācala," in the second Vaiṣṇava Section of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 32 ||

Now follows the praise of the Suvarṇamukharī by Śakra and the other gods. Bharadvāja said: Then the inhabitants of heaven, headed by Śakra, seated in their celestial chariots, followed that great river as it pursued Agastya.
And all those eminent sages, with palms joined in reverence, followed and worshipped that divine goddess who had manifested in nine incarnations with hymns of praise.
Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas, gathered there by the thousands, praised that river and that lord of sages with auspicious hymns.
"By good fortune, this pure water, comparable to nectar, has been found!"—thus the people of the earth rejoiced, overcome by a surge of eager longing.
Then, by the command of the lotus-born god, Vāyu spoke these words while all the gods were listening: || 5 ||

Now follows the derivation of the name Suvarṇamukharī as told by Vāyu. Vāyu said: "Like gold (suvarṇa) to the fortune of the worlds, this river was brought to the earth by Agastya, making the quarters of the sky resonant (mukharīkṛta)."
Therefore, she shall attain renown, celebrated by all the world, by the name Suvarṇamukharī, the abode of the wealth of liberation.
Among all rivers, this Suvarṇamukharī is the most distinguished and worthy of worship; such indeed are the words of Brahmā. (8)

Now follows the description of the greatness of the Suvarṇamukharī brought by Agastya. Bharadvāja said: Having heard these words spoken by Pavana, the pot-born sage (Agastya) was filled with wonder and rejoiced, his limbs bristling with joy within his heart.
Thus, this divine river, providing happiness to human beings through such arrangements as bathing and drinking, became established upon the earth.
By the command of Padmagarbha, the river flowing through the sky, known by the name Suvarṇamukharī, purifies those who take sole refuge in her.
Having gradually traversed many lordly mountains, forest regions, and numerous countries, this most excellent river was attended by great rivers born from the mountains.

For those struck by disease and those who are exceedingly afflicted, they are the sole providers of health; they ward off the manifold torments accumulated within and without, and are the causes of what is dear.

With a spray of water droplets rising from the force of the great blow of its trunk—like that of a pre-eminent elephant eager for sport in its abode—it seems to joyfully offer a tribute of flowers to the sun.

The exceedingly pure [waters], which served as the support for the *saugandhika*, lotus, and night-lotus flowers—whose fragrances perfumed the quarters of the sky and which were the sole abode of the fortune of the bees. (15)
Reddened by the vermilion powder from the partings of the hair of the celestial women eager for their playful bath, and perfumed by the fragrance of *pārijāta* flowers fallen from their tresses. (16)
She bore waters that were gathered with auspiciousness, sweet, free from mud, and exceedingly pure—waters comparable to nectar, which destroy the sins of the Son of the Lord of the Gods.
Having received her birth from Mount Agastya and been brought to earth by the one born from a jar (Agastya), she—resplendent with a multitude of celebrated holy fords—arrived at the southern ocean.
The waves of the ocean, coming forward to meet her, welcomed her with showers of spray as if scattering consecrated rice and by offering precious jewel-lamps.
Embracing her with waves as hands and welcoming her who had arrived, the lord of rivers made her dear by means of his resonant speech.
When that favorable daughter of the ocean arrived, his life increased even more through the surging wave of joy.
Having thus united that river with the ocean, Agastya, having offered praise and taken his leave, departed at will, his purpose accomplished.
Arjuna said: O Brahmin, you have described this great origin of the river; O Blessed One, I am now eager to hear of its power. (23)

Now follows the majesty of the Suvarṇamukharī as described by Bharadvāja. Bharadvāja said: "O Pāṇḍava, listen! Aho! This is the eradicator [of sins] and the sole cause of all that is auspicious. I shall recount her majesty to you."
Having attained a later birth when the karma of the wise has been exhausted, bathing in the Suvarṇamukharī shall be perfected as the cause for attaining the state of Brahman.
By remembering this Suvarṇamukharī even from a distance of hundreds of yojanas, a person is liberated from sins; there is no doubt in this matter. || 26 ||
The bone of living beings cast into the waters of the Suvarṇamukharī becomes a staircase for ascending to the world of Brahmā.
Wherever men may be, by merely remembering the Svarṇamukharī and bathing even in other waters, they obtain the supreme fruit.
Men are overwhelmed by tens of millions of sins for only so long as that auspicious bath in the Suvarṇamukharī is not obtained. (29)
For their own spiritual perfection, they remember every morning the Suvarṇamukharī river, which possesses divine, celestial, and terrestrial sacred sites (tīrthas).
Born from the Agastya mountain and flowing toward the southern ocean, the Svarṇamukharī destroys all sins by mere remembrance.
With their inner selves longing for a bath in the Suvarṇamukharī, even the gods, led by Śakra, desire only the state of being mortals.
Those who eat the food and grain nourished by the waters of the Suvarṇamukharī are not tainted by great sins arising from hundreds of improper meals. 43.
Even a mere mouthful of the water of the Suvarṇamukharī, when drunk, quickly destroys the mountain-like sins of embodied beings. 34.
Even having attained a human birth by the waters of the Suvarṇamukharī, those who do not perform an ablution—their birth is in vain. (35)
A single bath in the Suvarṇamukharī performed according to the prescribed rite on auspicious festival days is equal to ten million baths in the Gaṅgā.
Like Govinda among the gods, like the moon among the stars, like a sovereign among men, and like the Kalpa tree among the trees of the earth. (37)
Like space among the great elements, like illusion among all powers, like the Gāyatrī among mantras, and like the thunderbolt among the weapons of the gods; (38)
The Rudrādhyāya is to the Yajurveda as the principle of the Self is to the [twenty-five] principles; as Ananta is among the serpents, and as the Himālaya is among the mountains. (39)
Among fields, it is like the Potri field; among the senses, it is like the mind; and among all rivers, the Suvarṇamukharī is the most excellent. 40.
One who desires purity, security, and auspiciousness should constantly remember, pay homage to, glorify, and mentally worship the auspicious Suvarṇamukharī. 41.
I take refuge in you, O Suvarṇamukharī, who arose from the mountain of Agastya, who flows toward the southern ocean, and who destroys all sins. 42.
O Mother of the World, I wash my body, which has been scorched by great sins, with your waters; unite me with spiritual welfare. (43)
Having properly recited these two hymns, a self-controlled man, having bathed in the waters of the Suvarṇamukharī, becomes pure and rejoices. (44)
Formerly created by Brahmā and subsequently gathered together by Agastya, the excellent Suvarṇamukharī is the Mandākinī herself in embodied form.
This divine [river] of such power is to be praised by those seeking merit; it should be mentally bathed in with a mind full of devotion by those desiring auspiciousness. (46)
O Pārtha, bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts performed during lunar and solar eclipses on the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī yield immeasurable fruit.
On the occasion of a solar transit, during the auspicious solstice, or on a day of Vyatīpāta, bathing in the Suvarṇamukharī shall uplift ten million members of one's lineage.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rites in the waters of the Suvarṇamukharī on one's birth-star and on the day of one's birth, one obtains security, health, happiness, and prosperity.
Having bathed in the waters of the Suvarṇamukharī, one crosses over the evil arising from bad dreams, obstacles, malevolent spirits, and planets, as well as that born of unfavorable positions.
By giving a piece of land measuring a cow’s footprint on the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī, one obtains that fruit which results from the gift of the entire earth. || 51 ||
Having given a cow adorned with clothes and ornaments on the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī to a Brahmin according to the prescribed rites, one goes to the eternal Brahman.
On all auspicious occasions, every kind of gift should be bestowed on the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī for the attainment of fruits both in this world and the next. (53)

Recitation of mantras, fire-offerings, austerity, charity, rites for the ancestors, and worship of the gods—each of these performed on the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī becomes a hundredfold more meritorious. (54)
I shall describe to you another excellent vow to be performed on the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī every year by those seeking happiness. (55)
When the glorious sage, the son of Mitra and Varuṇa, rises, he becomes obscured by the rays of the sun during the rainy season. (56)
O descendant of Kuru, those who are disciplined and perform their ablutions in this river on that day shall dwell in the abode of the gods for an entire kalpa.
O Pārtha, those who according to the prescribed rite give that image of Agastya which has been fashioned out of gold, go to the eternal Brahman.
Arjuna said: O great sage, by what procedure is this vow to be performed? Tell me all of that in its entirety, for I, a high-souled one, desire to know it. (59)

Now follows the procedure for the gift of an image of Agastya. Bharadvāja said: Having ascertained the day of Agastya’s rising, one with a restrained mind should have an image of that great sage fashioned out of gold according to one's means. (60)
He possessed a golden, radiant luster and was enchanting with his bound matted locks; he held in his lotus-like hands a rosary and a water-pot.
Wearing soft bark garments with a deer-skin as an upper robe, gentle, beautiful with marks of sacred ash, and adorned with ornaments made of rudrākṣa beads.
Having thus assumed that form and bathed with a restrained mind, he should duly honor the preceptor with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should worship the image, which is placed upon an āḍhaka measure of śāli rice and is covered with two pieces of cloth.
He who paralyzed the Vindhya mountains, who was skillful in making the ocean a mere handful, and who was brilliantly illuminated by the splendor of all the gods, beginning with Brahmā. (65)
May the Lord Agastya, born from a water-jar and honored by gods and asuras, attain great satisfaction through this gift of mine. (66)
Having recited this mantra and offered it preceded by a stream [of water] along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one is liberated from sins and goes to the eternal Brahman. || 67 ||
One is surely liberated from the multitude of great sins and secondary sins committed in other births as well as in this birth; there is no doubt in this matter. (68)
All the gods beginning with Brahmā, the great sages beginning with Sanaka, and all beings, both moving and stationary, attain joy; of this there is no doubt. (69)
Having performed this meritorious vow of the noble sage Agastya, one should feed Brahmins according to one's capacity for the sake of his pleasure, along with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
And being unable to perform that rite, one should, endowed with devotion, satisfy the Brahmins according to one's capacity by giving gifts of gold, grain, and other such things. || 71 ||
One should not let the lunar day (tithi) pass in vain; one should observe it with diligence. Furthermore, a person must perform whatever ritual action is mandatory, however small it may be.
The river Suvarṇamukharī, the ripened fruit of the ascetic merit of the great sage Agastya, is to be praised by both gods and demons.
Thus has the origin of the great river been correctly described to you, as well as its power; now tell me what more you wish to hear.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "Praise of the Power of the Suvarṇamukharī," in the Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now follows the majesty of Agastyatīrtha and Agastyeśvara. Arjuna said: Even though I repeatedly drink the nectar of your words with the cupped hands of my ears, my mind finds no satisfaction, as it yearns to hear more.
May my persistent repetition of requests, as I long to hear your words, not cause distress to your mind, O you whose soul is filled with compassion. (2)
Now I wish to hear, O Great Sage, at which various places along this river the sacred fords (tīrthas) are effective in destroying sin.
O Sage, which of the most meritorious rivers have joined with her? By bathing where do those whose sins are destroyed no longer experience fear of Yama?
The sacred abodes of Hara, Acyuta, and the other gods, as well as whatever other holy sites exist upon her two banks.
Whatever fruit is obtained by men in those fields through auspicious deeds such as ritual bathing and giving, performed according to the prescribed rules; || 6 ||
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, all of this has been understood by me along with its narrative; great joy has arisen within me, so recount it to me in due order.
Bharadvāja said: O Pārtha, that which was asked by you shall be told in detail in due order, beginning from the preeminent Āgastya-tīrtha and describing the majesty of this multitude of sacred fords.
By the high-souled Agastya, who is of the nature of indivisible knowledge, who desires the welfare of all the worlds, and who is honored by both gods and demons; (9)
When the Earth descended from that mountain, one first bathes there in the great river and thereby attains the fulfillment of all goals.
It is called Agastyatīrtha, and it is purifying throughout the three worlds; by bathing there, even those who are great sinners shall attain purity.
People who are devoted to bathing there rejoice in heaven, having destroyed the accumulation of great sins committed over many lifetimes.
Those ascetics who, having performed their ablutions at that sacred ford and restrained their senses, offer great gifts such as cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth; || 13 ||
O Arjuna, those who are composed attain at Gaṅgādvāra the full hundredfold fruit of the gifts they have performed.
Here resides the Blessed Lord Īśa, renowned by the name Agastyeśa, who was installed by the sage Agastya, the bestower of joy upon the worlds. (15)
Those who bathe in that great river and worship that Liṅga obtain the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.

Now follows the determination of the time for bathing in the Suvarṇamukharī: When the sun, having left the sign of Sagittarius (Dhanu), enters Capricorn (Makara), that auspicious northern course (uttarāyaṇa) is proclaimed. (17)
On that day, those who, being self-controlled and composed, bathe in the river and behold Agastyeśa—the Lord of Pārvatī, worshipped by the gods—[attain their goal]. (18)
Having obtained the fruit of a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices, they rejoice in heaven, honored by the hosts of gods.
At the time of the sun's transit into Capricorn, those seeking auspiciousness must certainly behold Agastyeśa.

Now, concerning the majesty of the Devarṣipitṛ Tīrtha: O Arjuna, in the northeastern direction of that sacred site, at a distance of one krośa, there are three famous tīrthas known by the names of the Devas, the Ṛṣis, and the Pitṛs. (21)
There, the celestial sages and the ancestors, having been honored by that muni, joyfully bestowed upon him everything he desired.
Then, in his presence, the celestial sages and the ancestors said, "These three sacred fords (tīrthas) shall be praised by our names in due order."
Those who, having bathed in those three holy fords and performed the prescribed libations, are liberated from the three debts, go to the imperishable heaven.

Now follows the description of the confluence of the Veṇā and the Suvarṇamukharī: Then, within a distance of two yojanas on the northeastern land, the great river named Veṇā reached the Suvarṇamukharī. (25)
With its banks and trees felled by the impact of its surging current, the river flooded the forests with a flood of water flowing forth from its tributaries.
It was filled with flocks of ruddy geese sporting on the slopes of high sandbanks, and it resounded with the playful humming of swarms of bees, restless for the fragrance of lotuses.
Having passed beyond many exceedingly lofty mountains, the beautiful Suvarṇamukharī, resplendent with abundant waters, has reached [the sea].
Those who perform their ritual ablutions according to the rules at the confluence of the two rivers shall obtain the complete fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
Having joined with the meritorious Veṇā river, the Suvarṇamukharī flowed northward along a path difficult to traverse through the mountains.
Having traveled four yojanas along that rugged path through the midst of the mountains, that river shone forth brilliantly.
To the east of that region, within a distance of one and a half yojanas, on the beautiful northern bank of the great river flowing toward the east, [he dwelt].
There exists the famous Liṅga of the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva) named Agastyeśvara; its remembrance wards off all sins for both gods and mortals. (33)
Having bathed there in that great river, those men of restrained senses behold the Lord of Pārvatī, who was installed by Agastya.
Having cast off the accumulation of sins acquired through many previous births, they rejoice for an imperishable time in the abode of the gods.
Then, turning her face toward the north, she flowed as the Suvarṇamukharī, accompanied by a multitude of holy fords, through this region for half a yojana.

Then, at the confluence of the river named Vyāghrapadā with the Suvarṇamukharī, in that region delightful with Hintāla, Tāla, and Sāla trees, the river Suvarṇamukharī flows into the one called Vyāghrapadā.
She is skillful in warding off many evils that are difficult to restrain; she is adorned by a dense circle of groves of *vānīra* reeds along her banks. || 38 ||
It was graced by the playful immersion of the wives of Siddhas and Gandharvas, and it shone with the offering flowers cast down by the daughters of ascetics. (39)
Filled with the tumultuous cries of flocks of swans, kāraṇḍava ducks, and cranes, the eastern current, having come together, entered through a path between the mountains.
The best of men who have performed their ablutions there at the confluence of the two rivers shall obtain the full fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
Now follows the description of Śaṅkhatīrtha: There, on the bank of the river named Vyāghrapadā—which removes the impurity of the world—the sinless Śaṅkhatīrtha shines forth, destroying all sins. (42)
It was the fixed abode of the Brahman-sages, frequented by gods and Gandharvas, bestowing immeasurable bliss through its sight, bathing, drinking, and other such acts. || 43 ||
O Phālguna, there dwells the Blessed Lord Īśa named Śaṅkheśa; he was established in the form of a Liṅga by the lord of sages named Śaṅkha.
Those who, having bathed well at that sacred ford, behold the one whose vehicle is the bull, attain the merit born of ten horse-sacrifices and go to the abode of the gods.

Joined with that river named Vyāghrapadā, she then traveled across a distance of one yojana and reached the vicinity of Vṛṣabhācala, where she was attended by the lords of sages, her waters being auspicious and pure.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Various Holy Tirthas, such as Agastya-tīrtha," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.

Then follows the confluence of the Suvarṇamukharī with the river Kalyā. Bharadvāja said: There, the auspicious Suvarṇamukharī meets the holy river named Kalyā, just as the Yamunā meets the Gaṅgā. || 1 ||
Born from Mount Vṛṣabha, adorned by the king of holy fords (Tīrtharāja), she is the most excellent of rivers, auspicious, and the destroyer of the flood of impurities. || 2 ||
Its two banks were adorned by clusters of various trees and creepers; it was a pleasant abode for throngs of sages and preeminent with holy hermitages. || 3 ||

Its banks were graced by the kuśa grass and unbroken rice grains from the arghya offerings presented by the twice-born, while its waters were made turbid by the washing away of the musk-paste from the breasts of celestial nymphs.
Made fragrant by the ichor trickling from the temples of elephants, it was surrounded by hundreds of sacrificial posts erected for the extensive sacrifices of Brahmins and kings.
Satisfying all men with its flood of untroubled water, this one supreme great river alone is sufficient to wash away sin.
Who is capable of praising the greatness of those two when they are joined together, where the river named Brahmaśilā flows between them? (7)
Furthermore, O descendant of Kuru, through the ascetic power of Agastya, Gayā subsequently comes into that vicinity; those who bathe there in the waters of the two rivers attain merit.
They shall obtain the fruit of a hundred Pauṇḍarīka sacrifices; sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa go to complete destruction.
There, at the confluence of the two rivers, she who purifies those sanctified by initiation joined with the Bhavanāśinī, like the purifying Kṛṣṇaveṇī.
Now follows the description of the glorious Veṅkaṭācala situated on the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī: At that time, the Suvarṇamukharī shone, united with Kalyā. (11)
Now, half a yojana to the north of the great river shines the celebrated Veṅkaṭācala, possessing a height of one yojana.
This best of mountains is the refuge of all sacred fords (tīrthas): Añjana, Ananta, Vṛṣabha, Nīla, Kesari, and Potrin.
These groves of the mountain are Nārāyaṇa and Veṅkaṭa, so called because they were formerly taken possession of by the Slayer of Madhu in the form of a boar. 14.
This mountain on the famous Veṅkaṭācala, on the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī, is celebrated by the noble ones as Varāhakṣetra.
Acyuta dwells eternally on that mountain together with the daughter of the Lord of Oceans; while they dwell there along with Śrī, one should worship the Lord of Veṅkaṭa.
Siddhas, Gandharvas, Munis, Mānavas, and Dānavas serve Him, for their minds are fixed upon that Supreme Person, the object of devotion.
O Arjuna, the desires of those who remember the Lord of the World, the dweller on Veṅkaṭādri, are swiftly fulfilled and their calamities perish. (18)
Having cast off all defects, they go to the eternal and imperishable state.
Arjuna said: On the highly meritorious Veṅkaṭādri, how did the Lord, the Blessed One, the husband of Kamalā, who is saluted by gods and demons, manifest himself? 20.
Or for which fortunate person did he, being pleased, manifest his own wondrous form there, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation? (21)
O great sage, I desire to hear in truth the majesty of Viṣṇu, the primordial god of gods; tell that to me in detail.

Now begins the description of the majesty of the Lord residing on Śrī Veṅkaṭācala. Bharadvāja said: Listen with a concentrated mind to the greatness of the Lord of Veṅkaṭa; it cannot be fully recounted even by Brahmā in detail. (23)
"You are blessed, O subduer of enemies, my dear, that your mind has become intent on hearing the majesty of the God of gods, the slayer of Madhu, endowed as you are with devotion. (24)
O Pārtha, I am one who has performed meritorious deeds, since I shall now praise the purifying exploits of Hari, the Lord of all beings.
Formerly, on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, to the high-souled Janaka—who was intent upon the initiation for a sacrifice and possessed of pure knowledge—(he spoke).
O Pārtha, I shall relate to you this sin-destroying narrative told by Vāmadeva, which is purified by the glorification of Viṣṇu.
Nārāyaṇa is the first Lord of all beings; he consists of the universe, is the creator of the universe, has the nature of consciousness, and is stainless. || 28 ||
The Blessed One has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet; by His light this entire world, with all that is moving and unmoving, shines forth. (29)
Greater than that is splendor; greater than that is austerity; greater than that is knowledge; and there is nothing higher than yoga.
Therefore, O Pārtha, bull among men, there is no knowledge higher than this; for the Lord is eternally present within all beings. (31)
And all beings indeed dwell happily in him alone; he himself is the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and the implements such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
The fruit, the giver of the fruit, and the state to be attained through it—those who offer the consecrated animal into the kindled fire go to the destination ordained by that [sacrifice]. (33)
Having made the bond of karma their sacrificial animal, those who offer it as an oblation into the kindled fire of knowledge directed toward Him partake in union with Him.
Hari, Sadāśiva, Brahmā, Mahendra, and Paramasvarāṭ—these are proclaimed to be synonyms for that Lord of All. (35)
He who, with focused mind, contemplates this majesty of Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self, does not undergo rebirth.
The witness, consisting of consciousness and bliss, devoid of qualities and free from limiting adjuncts, though eternal, assumes various states according to his own will.
He who is the purifier of purifiers, the supreme goal of those without refuge, the deity among deities, and the highest good among all that is auspicious. (38)

He is the one who is to be awakened among those to be awakened; he is the supreme object of meditation among all that is to be meditated upon; he is the most excellent discipline among disciplines, endowed with the right method. (39)
He is the light that generates all lights, the supreme austerity among austerities, the support of all beings, and Janārdana, who is without beginning or end.
Even Brahmā and the other gods are deluded regarding his true nature; they think that the unborn one undergoes birth, and that the soul of all slays his enemies. (41)
Though independent, that Lord, whose banner is Garuḍa, acts out of dependence upon His devotees; He is the witness of all actions and the omniscient one. 42.
The sages, with concentrated minds, seek his true nature; he is Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, and likewise Pradyumna again.
The fourfold form of Him is renowned as Aniruddha; thereafter, the Praṇava is proclaimed, which is His radiant heart.
The Blessed One Vāsudeva and this mantra are the illuminators of that [reality]. || 45 ||
Whoever, being composed in mind, constantly recites this king of mantras, shall become a vessel for the supernatural powers (siddhis) through the grace of Viṣṇu’s compassion. || 46 ||

Now follows the description of the creation of beings and other acts performed by the Blessed One: How Mādhava, the warder-off of calamities, the bestower of prosperity, and the giver of enjoyment and liberation, created all beings at the very beginning of the Kalpa. (47)
I shall relate all of that; listen with a concentrated mind. As Hari was contemplating creation, there appeared a supreme form of splendor.

From the mouth of that god, who was renowned as Viriñca and had resorted to the quality of passion (rajas), Śakra was born along with Pāvaka—the lord of the three worlds and the master over the act of ripening.
And from Manas was born Candra, who is eternally cooled by compassion and is the constant protector of the waters, all medicinal herbs, and the brahmins. 50.
From his two eyes arose the sun, the illuminator of the universe, the cause of time through its regulation of cold, heat, and rain, and a treasury of splendors. (51)
From his vital breaths was born Samīra, the life-breath of this world, possessed of great strength, the sustainer of the planets, constellations, heavens, rivers, and celestial chariots.
From the navel-region of that Great-Souled One, the intermediate space (antarikṣa) arose; from his head came the sky, which is the cause of the origin of all beings.
From his two lotus feet arose the earth, the refuge of the hosts of beings; from the two ears of the Supreme Self issued forth all the directions.
By his mere remembrance, the worlds beginning with Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ were produced, as well as the worlds beginning with Rasātala, and the hosts of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and others.
From his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, O best of the Kurus, he produced in succession the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and the other castes.
The Vedic hymns, sacrifices, horses, cows, rams, sheep, and so forth—these attained their origin from him whose source is inconceivable. (57)
From the mere will of that God of gods, the entire collection of beings—both stationary and moving—came into existence, as did time in its past, future, and present forms.
Assuming the form of the submarine fire (baḍavānala), he drinks the waters of the oceans; at the time of the end of the aeon (kalpānta), he emits all that which was situated within himself.
Assuming the forms of the sun and the moon, he distributes sustenance to all beings by dispelling darkness and by setting in motion the laws of time.
Having placed the worlds within His own belly at the end of a kalpa, He who assumes the playful form of a child sleeps upon the great ocean on a banyan leaf.
Then, upon a couch formed by the body of the lord of serpents with his hoods raised—a bed well-suited for comfort—he attains the sleep of yoga, accompanied by her whose abode is the lotus.
Born from the lake of her navel, she gave birth to the lotus.
The Lord of all worlds [honored] the four-faced Creator.
For this is the divine play (līlā) of Mukunda, who acts through the application of his own will; that Lord is not understood by anyone according to his true nature.
When there is a decline of Dharma and unrighteousness increases, or when the hosts of deities suffer great affliction. (65)
When the enemies of the gods, difficult to restrain due to their arrogance, increase in power, and when great fear arises for both the earth and the people dwelling upon it; || 66 ||
Or when an unavoidable calamity, producing unbearable agony, befalls his own devotees and holy men; (67)
Then, assuming forms corresponding to those [beings] out of curiosity, he quickly casts off unrighteousness and performs what is beneficial for the world. (68)

Known as Brahmā, he creates the universe through his rājasa nature; known as Hari, established in sattva, he sustains the phenomenal world; and known as Hara, having assumed a tāmasa state, he withdraws it. There is no one who can truly know the majesty of the Slayer of Madhu.

O son of the lord of the gods, listen as I describe how that Lord of the World, having assumed the form of a boar whose every limb and joint was formed from the components of sacrifice, took up residence upon this mountain.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of Creation and Other Topics," in the section on the Greatness of Viṣṇu within the Greatness of Suvarṇamukharī, in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, in the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 35 ||

Now follows the sequence of the lifting of the earth by the Boar. Bharadvāja said: Formerly, at the end of the Creator’s night, Madhusūdana awoke and sought with intense deliberation the renewed activity of living beings.
And this reflection arose in his heart: "I believe that apart from the earth, no others are capable of supporting the multitude of living beings. (2)
By means of his meditative concentration, he beheld the earth situated in the subterranean realm (pātāla), which was exceedingly agitated by fear and enveloped by a vast expanse of water.
Then he assumed a form suited for lifting up the earth: one with the sacrificial ladle as its upper lip, fire as its tongue, and the sound of the *praṇava* as its roar.
His four legs were the four Vedas, his hooves were the various penances, his body was the sacrificial hall (prāgvaṃśa), and he was endowed with a beautiful coat of hair consisting of darbha grass.

It was perfected by the Pravargya rite, possessed a belly in the form of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, had the Sruk ladle as its snout, and its limbs and joints were distributed among all the various sacrificial implements.

It has the mass of its mane consisting of divine hymns, and likewise the head of the Supreme Brahman; it is endowed with the speed of sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors, and possesses the knees of pure sacrificial animals.
Assuming the divine form of Varāha, which is composed of all sacrifices, endowed with the power of mantras following the metrical paths such as Uktā and Atyuktā, [he stood there].
To search the earth, he entered the depths of the ocean's waters, forcibly displacing them with the masses of radiant luster arising from his fangs, which resembled the young moon.
Dispelling the dense darkness that expands at the end of the eon, he repeatedly filled the cavernous interior of the cosmic egg with sounds that overwhelmed the roar of the clouds.
Making the air resonant with deep *ghurughuru* sounds, he shattered the body [of his opponent] with the forceful planting of his hooves.
Rolling here and there upon the lord of serpents, he was carried down to the bottom of the ocean by the fierce winds of his sighs.
Reaching the very bottom of the ocean, it displayed its beauty within the depths by means of its exceedingly long trunk, which was repeatedly submerged and raised from the sea.
Agitating the waters as he went, he then passed through the interior, reaching the depths of the seven netherworlds where she remained within the water, overwhelmed by fear.
Beholding the earth trembling, he, with a joyful mind, lifted her upon the tip of his own tusk and emerged from the lord of rivers.
While being praised by the sages dwelling in Janaloka, the god lovingly bore the Earth for a moment.
O Arjuna, at the time of crossing over that ocean which was suitable for the auspicious boar-incarnation, the earth sank down.
The ocean, accompanied by a shower of spray scattered by its surging waves, attained the state of auspicious musical instruments with its deep resonant sounds.
She was sent forth with a heap of pearls that took on the grace of auspicious unbroken rice-grains; once wedded by that god, she shone resplendent, drenched in water.
With his body as if drenched with perspiration arising from intense passion, the Blessed One thus lifted the earth from the very base of the netherworld (pātāla).
He established it very firmly in the midst of the waters of the ocean; by that, when the earth was lifted up, the space between the earth and the sky became filled.
Then the water, having thus established the earth for the sake of securing its support, remained uninterrupted by the boundaries he had created.
He respectfully established the world-elephants, the king of serpents, and the tortoise as the supportive foundation for all of them as well. (23)
And the ocean of mercy joined his own power, which was unmanifest in form; then, having lifted up the earth, Hari remained in the body of a boar.
Then Sanaka and the others, the inhabitants of Janaloka, praised that Supreme Person after having propitiated him in his boar-form.
By his command, Brahmā fashioned the world just as it was before.
Arjuna said: O great sage, how does this earth remain when submerged in the waters at the end of a kalpa? What is its support beneath the seven netherworlds?
How long is this period of a kalpa, and what is its nature? (28)
Now, O Brahmin sage, describe in detail for me this entire account, beginning with the description of the events of the Kalpa and followed by the description of the incarnation as Śvetavarāha. (29)
Bharadvāja said: Sixty *vināḍikās* constitute one *nāḍikā*, and sixty of those make a day. Thirty such days, consisting of two fortnights (*pakṣa*), form a month. || 30 ||
Two months are said to be a season (*ṛtu*); by six of those, a year (*vatsara*) is formed, which takes the form of two solstices (*ayana*) and consists of cold, rainy, and hot periods. (31)
The day and night of the gods and asuras are mutually inverted; these correspond respectively to the northern and southern courses of the sun.
O Pārtha, a great yuga (mahāyuga), consisting of the four ages beginning with Kṛta, consists of human years equal to the number of zeros, sky, sky, eyes, fire, and oceans (4,320,000).
The interval between the Manvantaras consists of seventy-one yugas; now hear of the Manus born in this Kalpa known as Śvetavarāha.
Svāyambhuva was the first; after him came Svārociṣa Manu, then the one known as Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, and the one called Cākṣuṣa.
These six Manus, along with their Indras, gods, and ascetics, have passed away; O Arjuna, the seventh Manu, Vaivasvata, prevails today.
Having worshipped the hosts of deities beginning with Āditya, Vasu, and Rudra at that time, he performed a hundred horse sacrifices and, becoming resplendent, attained the status of Śakra.
"I am Viśvāmitra, Atri, Jamadagni, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, and Gautama; these indeed, O Arjuna, are the seven ṛṣis. (38)
The heroic sons of Manu, headed by Ikṣvāku and endowed with great strength, protected the earth while being constantly devoted to righteousness. || 39 ||
The five sons of Sūrya, Dakṣa, Brahmā, Dharma, and Rudra—Sāvarṇi, Rauca, Bhauma, and the others—constitute the seven future Manus.
Fourteen Manus belong to your day; that period is known as a Kalpa. At its end, there shall be a night equal to it—listen to this.
O son of Pāṇḍu, at the time of the conclusion of Brahmā’s day, a terrible drought occurs on earth lasting for a hundred years.
O Dhanañjaya, when that drought occurs upon the earth and it becomes devoid of moisture, the four classes of living beings go to their destruction.
Then the sun, endowed with rays that had the appearance of heated crests, resembling fire and vomiting forth sparks of flame, [shone]. 44.
With its villages, cities, mountains, trees, and forests destroyed, the earth would become like the back of a tortoise and resemble a red-hot iron ball. (45)
Then, great clouds born from the limbs of the Creator covered the sky, resonant with the sound of thundering roars.
White, yellow, reddish, and dark blue, they were of variegated colors and terrifying; they possessed various forms such as mountains, elephants, palaces, and trees. || 47 ||
For a period of one hundred years, they spread a great rain; by that water, the great fire produced by the sun is extinguished.
Furthermore, for a hundred years, massive clouds pour down fierce rain; by that water, the oceans overflow their shores and undergo a transformation.

The water released by the clouds at the end of the eon pervades the worlds; a great darkness envelops the realms of Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and Mahar-loka. At that time, the earth, submerged in the waters, sinks down to the very base of Pātāla.
Supported by the power of Brahman, she remained somehow unperished; then, O Arjuna, the wind was produced from the breath of Brahmā.
He drives away all those great clouds that have arisen at the end of the kalpa; thus the wind increases for the duration of a hundred years.
Time blows incessantly, having arisen with an irresistible force; yet, having abandoned that fierce wind, [the breath] remains within the lotus of Hari’s navel.
In those waters, the Lotus-born Lord enters into yogic sleep; as that Lord of the universe is absorbed in yogic sleep, the world passes away.
O Pārtha, the night was of the same duration as the day; when the night had passed, he rose up again with great speed.
By the command of Hari, he indeed creates all living beings as before; in every kalpa, Hari protects the world through appropriate forms.
In this kalpa, the Lord, sporting upon the surface of the earth in the form of a boar, assumed the white-colored body of a sacrificial horse.
Adhokṣaja reached Veṅkaṭācala, his own former fixed abode, and wandered for a long time on the banks of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
Endowed with supreme devotion, Brahmā beheld the Lotus-seated One; having worshipped him, he prayed to that creator of all beings.
"O Lord, resort to your own ancient, divine body. Having accepted his entreaty, he abandoned that form of a boar.
Having displayed his intense vigor while remaining there on that mountain, he attained his own universal form, which is to be venerated by none other.
Not even all of them were able to see it, even after a long period of time.
Arjuna said: O great sage, since Hari is thus beyond the range of sight, memory, and other such faculties, how did he attain perceptibility for human beings?
Tell us who that fortunate one among the worlds was, and which lord he propitiated, so that he might reveal this narrative here.
"O knower of all the scriptures, you who speak of the hearing of Hari’s stories which removes all sins—indeed, O best of sages, the leadership of the virtuous has now fallen upon me today. (65)

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Glorification of the Varāha Incarnation" within the "Praise of the Suvarṇamukharī," in the "Glorification of Śrī Veṅkaṭācala," in the second Vaiṣṇava Section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Now follows the account of the king named Śaṅkha. Bhāradvāja said: Listen, O Pārtha, I shall relate this wondrous tale of how that Blessed One attained manifestation upon this mountain.
There was a king named Śruta, born of the Haihaya lineage, who for a long time ruled over the auspicious earth as if it were his own subjects. (2)
His son was a lord of the earth named Śaṅkha, a treasury of virtues and an expert in all the scriptures; he protected the world.
In Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals, his devotion became unwavering, having abandoned all other refuges.
With firm resolve, he constantly meditated upon the God of gods, the Lord of the world, the infinite Puruṣottama, whose majesty is wondrous.
He performed various vows, gifts, and diverse meritorious acts, strictly for the sake of pleasing the Enemy of Madhu, who is known through the Vedas.
With him alone in mind, he performed sacrifices such as the horse sacrifice (vājimedha), whereby all the brahmins were gratified through the distribution of the prescribed sacrificial fees.
Unwearied, he performed the collection of ritual acts consisting of sacrifices and charitable works, his heart ever fixed upon Keśava, who is affectionate toward his devotees.
He remembers Govinda incessantly, mutters the name of Acyuta, the Imperishable, worships the lotus-eyed one, and glorifies the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
The king constantly listens to the sacred Vaiṣṇava narratives, which enable one to cross the ocean of saṃsāra and are recounted by those learned in the Purāṇas.
This lord of the earth honored the Brahmins for the sake of pleasing Hari alone; thus, though engaged with his whole being, he remained untiring.
He did not behold the Supreme Person, who possesses eternal sovereignty and is independent; for he had not obtained a vision of Viṣṇu, whose self consists of all sacrifices.
With his heart overcome by grief, he fell into deep reflection.
Śaṅkha said: "More than a thousand people have passed away while I committed many sins, yet I did not obtain the sight of Hṛṣīkeśa."
For the vision of Viṣṇu, the slayer of Madhu, is indeed the unbroken fruit of the darkness accumulated over many previous births.
"How indeed might the Blessed One come within the range of my eyes? Or when will that supreme benefit consisting of hearing his words be obtained? (16)

Alas! Shame on me, who have committed offenses, who am devoid of the fruitfulness of ritual action, who am far removed from the grace of Nārāyaṇa, and who am within the range of the afflictions of saṃsāra.
Bharadvāja said: While the king was thus overwhelmed with anxiety and indifferent to life, Keśava, his form invisible to all who were listening, spoke.

The Blessed Lord said: Do not fall under the sway of grief; listen, for I shall speak what is for your benefit. O King, how could I ever abandon you, a virtuous man who has taken refuge in me alone? 19.
O King, this mountain named Veṅkaṭa is renowned throughout the three worlds; even more dear to me than Vaikuṇṭha itself is my abode here.
Having gone to that best of mountains and performing penance with devotion to you, when a thousand years have passed, I shall become visible to you.
"Like Bhava himself, Agastya is prepared for my immediate vision; where indeed is Viṣṇu to be seen? Thus he spoke to the Four-faced One.
"In the month of Vṛṣabha, Hari may be seen by those of self-controlled mind; go there," the Lotus-born One said to the sage.
Thus instructed by the Lotus-born [Brahmā], the Pot-born [Agastya] will come to the great abode on Mount Añjana to perform austerities.
Dwelling upon that holy mountain, you too, being devoted to austerity, shall propitiate me and obtain my vision.

Now follows King Śaṅkha’s journey to the auspicious Veṅkaṭācala by the command of the Blessed Lord. Bharadvāja said: Thus commanded by the Blessed One, the enemy of the Dānavas, Śaṅkha experienced incomparable joy in his heart, thinking, "I am blessed. (26)
Having entrusted his son Vajra with the task of protecting the subjects, he went to Nārāyaṇagiri, longing for a vision of Govinda.
On its lofty peak, he beheld the auspicious Svāmipuṣkariṇī, filled with divine waters comparable to nectar.
It is frequented by hosts of numerous Siddhas, Gandharvas, and divine sages; it pacifies the heat of worldly existence and is the refuge of all sacred fords.
It was crowded with water-crows, cranes, curlews, swans, and kāraṇḍava ducks, and it was enchanting with white water-lilies, blue lotuses, red lotuses, and fragrant saugandhika flowers.
Having seen that divine lotus-pond and having constructed a hut on its bank, he was gratified by bathing, drinking, and other such acts, his mental state being free from conceptual construction.
Having entrusted all actions to Janārdana, the Lord of the World.

Now follows Agastya’s journey to Veṅkaṭācala for the purpose of beholding the Blessed One. Constantly intent on recitation and meditation, the sage performed most rigorous penance at that very time, by the command of Parameṣṭhin. (33)
Agastya also, surrounded by hundreds of sages, reached the eastern mountain after making an effort to circumambulate [the earth] starting from the western direction.
Beholding sacred pilgrimage sites, he wandered for a very long time upon the mountain; here and there, he saw those who were longing for a vision of Hari.
[He saw] Viriñci, Guha, Śakra, Īśa, Viṣvaksena, and the others in succession, as well as Sanaka and the other lords of yogis, and the sages headed by Nārada.
He was honored by those various Siddhas, Gandharvas, Daityas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas with respectful salutations and pleasant speech.
Beholding all those wonderful things, he wandered about, having bathed in all the sacred fords, such as Skandadhārā and others.
In each of those places he worshipped Govinda, the Lord of the worlds. Thus, O best of sages, after a thousand years had passed while he was wandering, [he returned].
Not seeing the lotus-eyed one, he became overcome with anxiety and grief.
Then, at that time, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, and the Vasus once again approached Agastya; likewise, the king named Uparicara and the Vasu came to that lord of sages. (41)
O best of sages, our life has become fruitful, since you have been seen by us like a second Nārāyaṇa. (42)
O Sage, that which we were commanded by Brahmā, the Lord of the World—to be intent upon beholding Acyuta—that is now being told to you.
In the southern region there is a mountain named Veṅkaṭa; this abode of Hari is desired even more than Śvetadvīpa.
On that mountain, Govinda, the teacher of the world, will reveal his own true form to Agastya and King Śaṅkha.
At that time, there will be a vision of the God of gods for all the deities, sages, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and for us as well.
That will come to pass before long; therefore, having cast off all impurities, go to seek Agastya on that Nārāyaṇa mountain.
Thus commanded by the Creator, we have come here by good fortune and have beheld you, O illustrious one, possessed of great splendor. (48)
Having gone together with you to the bank of Svāmipuṣkariṇī, we shall also behold that Śaṅkha, the best among the devotees of the Lord.

Now follows the description of the sight of the beautiful objects on Śrī Veṅkaṭācala as seen by Agastya and others. Bharadvāja said: Having been thus instructed by Bṛhaspati and the other sages, the pot-born sage (Agastya) cast off the web of his grief and departed quickly accompanied by them.
He beheld great trees, bent down by the weight of their fruits and flowers, whose masses of spreading branches covered the horizons with shade.
From time to time along the way, he beheld lions, elephants, tigers, boars, buffaloes, and other wild beasts.
At that time, they beheld even the mountain ridges laden with clouds, adorned here and there with gold, silver, copper, and other minerals.
Hundreds of mountain torrents were seen, their boulders uprooted by the force [of the wind], quenching the gods with showers of rising spray. (54)
A gentle breeze, wafting the fragrance of lotuses and moving across the mountain ridges, brought them great delight.
Then the songs of parrots and cuckoos were heard.
There, upon those extensive rocks, they saw the Siddhas seated here and there, singing of the majesty of Kṛṣṇa’s virtues.
Having circumambulated [the mountain], all those lords of sages, headed by Agastya, beheld the divine Svāmipuṣkariṇī with its pure waters. || 58 ||
On its bank he saw King Śaṅkha, who had established his dwelling there and remained with all actions of speech, mind, and body dedicated to Hari.
Having suddenly beheld those lords of sages who were firm in their vows, he performed the worship as prescribed, preceded by prostrations and hymns of praise.
Seated there, they all, eager to honor one another and devoted to the glorification of Govinda, attained a sense of fulfillment.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of Śaṅkha, Agastya, and Others at Śrī Veṅkaṭācala," within the Praise of the Suvarṇamukharī Māhātmya, in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, in the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 37 ||

Now follows the manifestation of the Blessed Lord, who was pleased by the penance of Agastya, Śaṅkha, and the others. Bharadvāja said: Three days passed there for those whose minds were fully absorbed in Hari, the Lord of the Universe, as they were devoted to worship and hymns of praise.
When the third day had arrived, they all slept during the night; at the end of the fourth watch, they beheld an excellent dream.
He beheld the gracious Puruṣottama, holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, who had arrived to grant a boon with a smiling gaze.
Rising up with joyful hearts, they departed from their homes and bathed according to the prescribed rites with devotion in the purifying waters of Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
Having duly performed all the rites appropriate for the beginning of the day, they returned home to worship the imperishable Lord Acyuta.
Having seen the omen indicated by the birds on the path, which brings immediate welfare, they then considered the grace of the Lord to be already within their grasp.
Then, having worshipped Janārdana, the creator of the three worlds, they praised him with various pure hymns described in the Vedas.
At the conclusion of the hymn, O son of Kuntī, the lord of sages, Agastya, together with Śaṅkha, chanted the eight-syllabled mantra of Hari.
Thus, for those whose minds were dedicated to Acyuta, the Lord of the World, a single, most wonderful radiance appeared before them.
Numbering many millions of suns, moons, and fires, they stood together in the expanse of the sky like a mass of light.
Beholding that splendor, they all, whose range of vision was filled with immeasurable wonder, meditated upon the divine Nārāyaṇa, the embodiment of supreme bliss.
Transcending the paths of speech and mind, resplendent with renowned sovereignty, he possesses a thousand eyes and is endowed with a thousand arms and feet.
Resplendent with a shimmering luster like molten gold, formidable with its fangs, difficult to behold, and vomiting forth streaks of fire.
Shining with the Kaustubha gem and bearing the Goddess Śrī upon his chest, he is inconceivable, without beginning or end, and the ultimate bestower of fear.
Illuminating the entire universe within his own all-pervading self, [the Lord was beheld by] Agastya, Śaṅkha, and all the others, whose hearts were filled with joy.
Beholding the Lord of the World, they prostrated before him again and again; at that time, the weapons of Hari began to whirl for the sake of protecting the world.
Endowed with their own splendor and power, they arrived to attend upon him: the divine discus, radiant as the sun, the mace, and the sword Nandaka.
Then Puṇḍarīka, Ugrarava, Pāñcajanya, and Śaśiprabha filled the entire universe to its full extent with their resounding blasts.
The roar of Pāñcajanya caused terror among all the asuras; having heard the sound of Pāñcajanya, which was exceedingly wonderful and terrifying, [they were struck with fear]. (19)
All the deities arrived, mounted upon their respective vehicles: Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the yogis headed by Sanaka.
The sages headed by Vasiṣṭha, the Gandharvas, Uragas, and Kinnaras; Viṣvaksena, Garuḍa, and the attendants of Viṣṇu such as Jaya and others. || 21 ||
And those who are eternal and identical in form, dwelling in Śvetadvīpa, produced a wondrous rain of flowers born from the Sumanas tree.
She fell, her entire mind delighted by its thick fragrance; the divine-eyed women danced, and the foremost of the Kinnaras sang.
Trembling with joy, the gods, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas offered hymns of praise upon seeing the lotus-eyed Lord, who is gracious and compassionate toward his devotees.
Having prostrated themselves, they gratified him with various hymns of praise using the eight-limbed obeisance.

Brahmā and the others said: Victory to you, O Viṣṇu, ocean of compassion! Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one! Victory to you, the sole bestower of boons to the world! Victory to you, the destroyer of the afflictions of devotees! 26.
Who indeed can know you, who are infinite, imperishable, peaceful, beyond the reach of speech and mind, and whose very nature consists of consciousness and bliss? (27)
They declare you to be the Person (Puruṣa), subtler than the subtle, grosser than the gross, abiding within all, beyond primordial nature (Prakṛti), and immutable.
Who indeed is able to describe you, who are the essence of the Vedānta and abide within and without all things, among embodied beings who are subject to māyā? (29)
Having seen this form of yours which inspires such great terror, we are all agitated by fear; please assume a peaceful form.
Bharadvāja said: Thus praised by Viriñca and the others, the one whose banner is Garuḍa was pleased and spoke respectfully with a voice resembling the roar of clouds: || 31 ||

Then, at the request of Brahmā and the others, the Blessed One assumed a gentle form. The Blessed One said: "Casting aside this terrifying form, I shall assume a peaceful form that brings delight; behold me, free from agitation. (32)
Having spoken thus, he vanished and in that very instant appeared again, pleasant to behold, within a celestial chariot inlaid with jewels.
With a face like the orb of the moon, peaceful, and possessing the luster of blue lotus petals, he is clothed in garments of golden hue and adorned with jewel ornaments.
Beholding the beloved of Ramā, whose four hands shone with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, they prostrated themselves again and again.
Having gratified Brahmā and the others by granting their desired objects, he spoke with humility to Agastya, the preeminent among sages, who was bowed low in reverence.
The Blessed Lord said: "O lord of sages, you have now become exhausted by the terrible vows you have performed directed toward me; I shall grant you the boons you desire—speak them."
Bharadvāja said: Having heard the words of the Lord of Śrī and having prostrated again and again, that pot-born one, his entire body covered with horripilation, spoke these words. (38)

Then, by the prayer of Agastya, the river Svarṇamukharī attained a status superior to all others, like that of the Blessed Lord. Agastya said: "Whatever oblation has been offered, whatever austerity has been performed, and whatever has been studied or heard by me—all that has become fruitful because I have been honored by you. (39)
O Lord, I am that very same righteous soul throughout the three worlds, since you have now come seeking me while I was searching for you.
O Mādhava, through your grace I have already attained all my heart's desires; even upon reflection, I see nothing further to be gained at this time.
Nevertheless, O Lord, out of impetuosity this is represented to you: grant me thus uninterrupted devotion to your lotus feet.
Understand this from me: at the request of the gods, I have bathed in the Suvarṇamukharī river, which destroys the multitude of sins.
She has arrived, drawn near to the foothills of the mountain of existence; O Lord of the World, fulfill her purpose through the workings of your grace. (44)
Those who, having bathed in the waters of the Suvarṇamukharī, behold [the Lord] residing on Veṅkaṭa, shall indeed become vessels for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Foolish men of short lifespan, fallen away from the yoga of knowledge, are unable to behold you through vows, study, or ritual acts. || 46 ||
O Teacher of the World, O God, remaining forever upon this mountain, be gracious with a favorable countenance toward all and grant the objects desired by us. (47)
The Blessed Lord said: "O Brahmin, that which has been requested by you shall indeed come to pass. Truly, incomparable devotion has been shown by you toward me in this world."
O Sage, this Suvarṇamukharī river shall be like the Jāhnavī; she shall be an object of aspiration even for the gods, bestowing the prosperity they desire.
And this Svāmipuṣkariṇī, endowed with a physical form, shall flow into that divine river which is the refuge of a multitude of holy sites.
O sage, at your request, from this day forward I shall always dwell upon this mountain named Vaikuṇṭha.

Those who, with concentrated minds, behold me on this mountain Vaikuṇṭha—their masses of sins and the mire of their transgressions having been washed away by bathing in the Suvarṇamukharī—[attain liberation]. || 52 ||
On earth, they were endowed with sons and other blessings, possessed of all sovereignty; and having died, they experienced enjoyments in the third heaven until the end of the kalpa.
They shall attain my state, which is free from rebirth and radiant with absolute bliss; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
O Sage, out of respect for your words, I shall constantly attend to all who come to see me and endow them with their desired blessings.
For those seeking sons, he grants many sons; for those seeking wealth, he grants riches; and likewise, for those desiring health, he grants the most profound pacification of disease.
For those overwhelmed by intense calamities, I shall likewise provide protection from misfortune and grant all desired enjoyments, even those that are difficult to obtain, at all times.
Whatever desires they have in view when they come together here to behold me, they all obtain those very desires; of this there is no doubt.
Wherever those best of men may dwell, if they remember me, they all obtain their desired success through my grace. (59)

Now follows the disappearance of the Blessed One after bestowing a boon upon King Śaṅkha. Bharadvāja said: Having spoken thus to that sage, the Lord looked toward King Śaṅkha and, while the foremost of the Brahmins were listening, spoke these words. (60)
The Blessed Lord said: "I am pleased with your devotion, O Śaṅkha; choose a desired boon. As a granter of boons, I shall grant it to you, who are emaciated from performing penance. (61)
Śaṅkha said: O mighty-armed one, I do not beg for anything other than service to your lotus feet; I beg for that supreme state which your devotees attain.

The Blessed Lord said: "O Śaṅkha, that which has been requested by you shall come to pass exactly so. For those who are fortunate enough to possess the yoga of service to me, what indeed is there that cannot be obtained?"
Remaining in the world of Indra for the duration of a kalpa, served by hosts of apsarases, and having enjoyed manifold pleasures, you shall thereafter come to my own realm.
Thus, O lord of the earth, Nārāyaṇa—the source of the universe and the wish-fulfilling tree for those who worship him—granted these desired boons to Śaṅkha. (65)
Then, having dismissed all those beginning with Brahmā, the lotus-eyed Lord, being praised with devotion by their mental hymns, vanished right there.

Now follows the conclusion of the majesty of the glorious Veṅkaṭācala as described by Bharadvāja. Bharadvāja said: "O Arjuna, this power of Veṅkaṭādri has been recounted to you. By hearing this purifying narrative, men are liberated from their sins. (67)
Having cast off the form of the boar at the request of Brahmā, Hari, assuming a wondrous appearance, rejoiced there while deluding the world with his illusory power (māyā).
Thereafter, being entreated by Agastya and Śaṅkha, he granted them a body that was pleasant to behold, exceedingly beautiful, tranquil, and characterized by enjoyment.
By remembering Nārāyaṇa, Veṅkaṭādri, Svāmipuṣkariṇī, and likewise this narrative, people are liberated from their sins.
There is no place whatsoever in the entire universe equal to Veṅkaṭādri; there has never been, nor will there ever be, a deity equal to Veṅkaṭeśa.
A place equal to Veṅkaṭādri has never existed, nor will it ever exist; and a lake equal to Svāmitīrtha is not to be found anywhere at all. (72)
Those who, having risen in the morning, constantly remember Veṅkaṭeśa—liberation and its glory are already in their hands; no deliberation is required in this matter. (73)
Having bathed in the Svāmipuṣkariṇī tīrtha, those who, being self-restrained, behold Hari—the soul of all—residing on Varāhācala; || 74 ||
They obtain the full fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 75 ||
Those best of men who listen to the majesty of Veṅkaṭācala shall attain both liberation and worldly enjoyment, both in this world and in the next.
The majesty of Veṅkaṭācala has been recounted to you in brief. Hereafter, O Arjuna, the power of the great river shall be told.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Manifestation of Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa and Others, Pleased by the Austerities of Agastya, Śaṅkha, and Others," within the "Praise of the Majesty of Suvarṇamukharī" in the "Majesty of Śrī Veṅkaṭācala," in the second Vaiṣṇava Section of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 38 ||

Now, regarding the manner in which Añjanā performed penance for the sake of a son, Śrī Sūta said: Formerly, Añjanā, being childless, remained distressed and established herself in asceticism. Seeing her, Mataṅga, a tiger among sages devoted to Viṣṇu, [approached].
He spoke these words to her named Añjanā, who was established in most fierce asceticism.
Mataṅga said: "Arise, O Añjanā, O Goddess! For what purpose have you been engaged in asceticism? Speak, O highly fortunate Goddess, O lady of lovely countenance; what is your task?"
Añjanā said: "O Mataṅga, tiger among sages, listen to my words. My father is a Rākṣasa named Kesarī, who is devoted to Śiva. (4)
Accompanied by Pārvatī and seated upon his bull, Śambhu performed a most difficult and formidable penance for the sake of obtaining a son.
Then the God appeared and granted him an auspicious boon.
Śambhu said: Listen, O King, I shall declare to you that which was ordained by fate; although you are childless in this birth, I nevertheless grant you something else.
Your daughter shall become renowned throughout all the worlds; her son, possessed of great intelligence, will bring you joy.
Having thus granted him the boon, Hara vanished right there; and having obtained me, my father, the brahmin, became one who had fulfilled his purpose.
Then, after some time, a brahmin named Kesari, who was a great monkey, requested her, saying, "Give her to me"; thereupon her father [responded].
He gave me to him and bestowed upon him as a dowry many thousands of lakhs of cows and a lakh of elephants, that high-minded one.
There were indeed a hundred million horses and likewise a hundred million chariots, along with many garments and jewels, and a thousand male and female slaves.
O high-minded one, he gave me a thousand women from the inner apartments, skilled in dance and song, along with garments.
O sage, O brahmin, while sporting with my husband, a great deal of time has passed; yet I am childless and sorrowful, despite having performed various vows.
And there, O best of Brahmins, in that great city of Kiṣkindhā, I performed [these rites] during the months of Māgha, Vaiśākha, and likewise Kārtika.
O Brahmin, bathing, giving gifts, vows, and likewise the Cāturmāsya vow, as well as prostration and the unsurpassed circumambulation; 16.
O great sage, the gifting of Śālagrāma stones, the giving of food, as well as the giving of lamps, the gift of cows, the gift of sesame seeds, and the gift of clothing [yield great merit]. (17)
O Sage, having given gifts of land and water, as well as flowers and other offerings, I have performed all the principal Vaiṣṇava vows with the desire for the fruit of having a virtuous son. (18)
O best of Brahmins, that vow which was proclaimed by the high-souled sages regarding the Śravaṇa and other asterisms has been performed by me for the sake of pleasing the Enemy of Madhu.
Whatever principal fruits and various other kinds were offered by me, all were given with the desire for the fruit of having a virtuous son.
"Though I have performed countless and various vows, even so, not having obtained a son, I remain sorrowful, established in ascetic penance. (21)
"O Brahmin, how will my son become world-renowned in the three realms? O best of sages, bowing before you, I make this request. (22)
Speak, O tiger among sages; I am distressed and established in ascetic penance.
Śrī Sūta said: To her who was speaking thus, Mataṅga, the best of sages, replied: "Listen to my words, O Goddess, which bestow sons and grandsons. (24)
Ten yojanas to the south of here is the place known as Ghanācala, the dwelling-place of Nṛsiṃha.
O illustrious lady, above that is the enchanting Brahmatīrtha; it is located ten yojanas to the east of that place as well.
There is a preeminent river among rivers named Suvarṇamukharī; on its very northern side is the mountain known as Vṛṣabhācala.
In front of it is the auspicious lake named Svāmipuṣkariṇī; having gone there and seen its pure water, you will attain purity of mind.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite and having bowed down to that Varāha, and having paid homage to Veṅkaṭeśa, proceed from there, O lady of excellent countenance. (29)
To the north of Svāmitīrtha, in a place filled with lions and tigers, there were auspicious mango, punnāga, jackfruit, bakula, and āmalaka trees.
O lady of beautiful countenance, [the forest was filled] with sandalwood, agallochum, nimba, palmyra, hintālaka, kiṃśuka, wood-apple, holy fig, bilva, and iṅguda trees.
With such trees of great merit and various auspicious kinds, that single sacred site known as Viyadgaṅgā shines resplendently.
O Goddess, having bathed and drunk at that Añjana-tīrtha according to the prescribed rite of formal resolve (saṃkalpa), she stood facing the auspicious holy site.
"O Goddess of beautiful countenance, perform penance directed toward Vāyu; [for you shall be worshipped] by gods, rākṣasas, brahmins, men, and the best of sages. (34)
"By means of bees, birds, missiles, and various auspicious weapons, your son shall be invincible through your ascetic power; of this there is no doubt. (35)
Śrī Sūta said: Having been addressed thus, the goddess Añjanā, bowing down to him again and again, went quickly with her husband to the mountain known as Veṅkaṭācala.
Having reached the Kāpila-tīrtha and bathed there with a pure mind, she ascended Veṅkaṭādri and went to Svāmipuṣkariṇī. || 37 ||
Having bathed and bowed to Varāha, she offered salutations to Veṅkaṭeśa, repeatedly recollecting the words of the sage Mataṅga.
Then Mañjubhāṣiṇī, daughter of Añjana, quickly went to the celestial Gaṅgā; having bathed there and drunk the auspicious water, she stood upon its bank, gazing upward toward it.
Aiming for the vital breath (prāṇavāyu), she of firm vows performed penance; first subsisting on fruits, then on water, and thereafter remaining without food.
She performed austerities for a thousand years with her gaze fixed on the tip of her nose; her auspicious friend named Vipulā attended upon her.
And at the end of a thousand years, the high-minded deity Vāyu appeared; then that high-minded one spoke to her.
O best of sages, when the sun had entered Aries on the auspicious lunar day known as Pūrṇimā, conjoined with the Citrā asterism.
"I shall grant you whatever boon you desire; choose one, O lady of virtuous vows. Hearing these words of his, the chaste Añjanā then spoke:
"O illustrious one, O god Vāyu of great intelligence, grant her a son. Having heard those words of hers, Mātariśvan then spoke.
"I shall become your son and grant you renown, O lady of auspicious countenance. Having granted her this boon, the one of great strength remained right there.
Then Brahmā and the other gods, Indra and the other guardians of the world, the high-souled ones such as Vasiṣṭha, and the yogis such as Sanaka [all arrived]. || 47 ||
Vyāsa and other eminent Brahmins, the Lord of the Universe together with Lakṣmī, as well as the wives of the sages, the wives of the gods, and likewise the wives of the ṛṣis.
Mounting their respective vehicles along with their wives, servants, sons, and others, those great-souled ones arrived to see her established in asceticism.
"Marvelous! Marvelous! cried Brahmā and all the hosts of gods; then, with Brahmā and Maheśa at their head, they stood from afar in the sky, gazing upon him. (50)

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Manner of Añjanā’s Performance of Penance and Other Details," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 39 ||

Now follows the determination of the time for bathing in the Ākāśagaṅgā as proclaimed by Vyāsa. Śrī Sūta said: Having obtained the boon, Añjanā rejoiced together with her husband; seeing Brahmā and the others arrived, her mind was filled with wonder. (1)
Then the sweet-spoken Añjanā became composed in mind along with her husband; and Vyāsa, the best among the knowers of the Vedas, was permitted by Brahmā and the other gods.
Añjanā spoke this to her in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Vyāsa said: O Añjanā, listen with a pure heart to my words, which are for the benefit of all the world, having heard the speech of the sage Mataṅga.
"However, because you have gone to Veṅkaṭa and performed extremely difficult penance, a son shall be born to you who is a hero possessing prowess over the three worlds."
Therefore, on the day of your direct vision, this is the supreme holy ford; for the Gaṅgā and other sacred sites from throughout the three worlds assemble here.
There is no sacred ford (tīrtha) equal to Veṅkaṭādri anywhere in the universe; even there, the auspicious Svāmipuṣkariṇī is indeed exceedingly meritorious.
This sacred site is even more distinguished than that; it is manifest before you today, on the day joined with the constellation Citrā, when people come here for the purpose of bathing.
When the month of Meṣa has arrived, on the auspicious day of the full moon—listen, O Goddess of noble vows, I shall tell you the fruit of those [deeds].
O fair-faced goddess, whatever fruit exists at all the holy fords such as the Gaṅgā for twelve years, that fruit certainly becomes his. || 10 ||
Listen to the increase of the fruits for those men who perform acts of charity; O Goddess of beautiful countenance, know that their fruit is as described in the respective places. (11)
Añjanā said: "O best of Brahmins, O foremost among those who know the Vedas, tell me all those deeds of charity that are to be performed on Veṅkaṭādri, the most excellent of mountains. (12)

Now follows the praise of the gifts to be offered on Śrī Veṅkaṭācala as proclaimed by Vyāsa. Vyāsa said: "The gift of food and the gift of clothing—these two are highly praised; especially so is the Śrāddha for one's father on Veṅkaṭādri, the best of mountains. (13)
O best of sages, those who give gold for the pleasure of the slayer of Madhu attain all the worlds and rejoice there.
Those who perform the gift of a Śālagrāma stone on the best of mountains attain the dissolution of their physical body and experience its direct realization. || 15 ||
He who gives the gift of a cow to a preeminent brahmin who has a family shines in the world of Viṣṇu for as many years as there are hairs on that cow. || 16 ||
O Goddess, who is capable—whether in heaven or on earth—to describe the fruit of the merit of one who gives land to a Brahmin householder? (17)
O Goddess, he who gives a maiden in marriage to a twice-born man learned in the Vedas attains the world of Viṣṇu and rejoices there together with his ancestors.
O Goddess, the merit of those who provide water-stalls filled with cool water cannot be described even by Śeṣa.
He who gives sesame seeds to a learned Brāhmaṇa who maintains a household is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
The Brahmins, the best among those who know the Vedas, praise the gift of grain; for those who perform the gift of grain, there will be many sons. (21)
He who gives to a twice-born man fragrant campaka flowers and the like, umbrellas, fans, and chowries, as well as betel-leaf, camphor, and other such items; || 22 ||
