Having enjoyed pleasures for a long time, he shall then go to the heavenly world; and having enjoyed manifold pleasures there for a thousand divine years, he shall depart.

Then, having become a sovereign emperor and enjoyed the earth there for a long time, he subsequently attained the status of a Brahmin, becoming one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedānta.
Then, through the grace of the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), one attains liberation. Thus, O Goddess, has this majesty of Veṅkaṭācala been described.
Whoever should hear this constantly, and whoever should also recite it, being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Viṣṇu. || 26 ||
This has been previously narrated by the high-souled Vyāsa himself; whoever hears it or even reads it shall become one who has fulfilled his purpose.
All those born of his lineage attain liberation; of this there is no doubt. || 28 ||

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Determination of the Time for Bathing in the Ākāśagaṅgā and the Attainment of the Boon by Añjanā," in the Śrī Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Now begins the majesty of the Puruṣottama-kṣetra. Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Jaya. (1)

The sages said: O Blessed One, knower of all scriptures and perceiver of the greatness of all sacred fords, that which was previously mentioned by you when the glorification of the holy sites was introduced—the very great field named Puruṣottama, which is supremely purifying—[that we wish to hear]. || 2 ||
There resides the Lord of Śrī, whose body is composed of wood, who through his human-like play bestows liberation upon sight and grants the fruit of all sacred fords.
Tell us that in detail: by whom was that field created? The Lord Jyotiḥprakāśa is the manifest Nārāyaṇa, the Sovereign.
How does the Supreme Person reside within that wooden image? Tell me, O best among speakers, O sage, O teacher of all the worlds. (5)
"O Brahmin, we wish to hear it, for our curiosity is great. Jaimini said: "Listen, all you sages, for that is indeed a supreme secret."
Devotion to you does not arise in those who are not Vaiṣṇavas upon hearing [of you], by whose mere glorification all darkness is dissolved.

Although this Lord of the World is omnipresent and the creator of all beings, Skanda previously declared from the lotus-like mouth of Śambhu that there are indeed other sacred fields (kṣetras) which remove all sins.
This field is the supreme body of that Great-Souled One; He Himself dwells there in embodied form, for it is indeed made famous by His own name.
In that place, even those who merely wish to stay have their sins destroyed; how much more so for those who behold Gadādhara while staying there?
Oh, that supreme sacred field extends for ten yojanas; it has emerged from the waters of the King of Tīrthas and is strewn with sand.
It shone with the great Blue Mountain situated in its center, appearing from afar like a single breast of the Earth.
Formerly, having lifted up the earth in the form of a boar and made it perfectly level on all sides, he rendered it stable by means of mountains.

Having created the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, and having established the sacred fords, rivers, oceans, and holy sites in their respective places just as before, he [established them]. 14.
Oppressed by the burden of creation, Brahmā reflected: "How might I not have to undertake this heavy task again? (15)
"How indeed can living beings, overwhelmed by the threefold afflictions, be liberated?"—such was the thought that arose in the mind of Prajāpati as he reflected thus.
"I shall praise Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, the sole cause of liberation. Brahmā said: "Salutations to you, O support of the universe, the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace. (17)
O Creator of the universe, I was born from the lotus of Your navel; O You who pervade the world, You indeed know my true nature as the Supreme Reality.
That by whose māyā the entire universe, beginning with the Mahat-tattva, was created; that from whose breath the Śabdabrahman arose and became threefold.
Having relied upon that very [source], I indeed created the worlds; other than you, there is nothing whatsoever—whether gross or subtle, long or short, and so forth.

O Blessed One, through various modifications, you alone are this entire world of moving and non-moving beings, just as gold [is present] in bracelets and other ornaments according to the division of the three qualities (guṇas).

O Lord of the world, you alone are the creator and the object to be created here; you are the nourisher and the one to be nourished. O Supreme Lord, you are the support and that which is supported, and you are the sustainer.
With his mind impelled by you, everyone performs both auspicious and inauspicious deeds; consequently, he attains a corresponding state of existence ordained by you alone. (23)

O Supreme Lord, you are the refuge, the sustainer, and the witness of this world; O Teacher of the moving and the unmoving, O embodiment of all living beings, O Compassionate One! Be gracious today, O Lord of the Universe, to me who am eternally your refuge. (24)
Jaimini said: Thus being praised by Brahmā, the one whose banner is Garuḍa—resembling a dark blue cloud and marked with the conch, discus, and other signs—[appeared]. || 25 ||
Mounted upon the lord of birds, with his lotus-like face radiant and his lower lip quivering as he desired to speak, O best of the twice-born, he appeared.
The Blessed One said: "O Brahmā, that for which you praise me does not appear possible."
Beginningless ignorance is extremely firm and difficult to sever due to the bonds of karma; while it prevails, how can birth and death be brought to an end? (28)
Nevertheless, O sinless one, if you have made this resolve here, I shall explain to you the reason by which it may indeed come to pass in due course. (29)
"I am you, and you are I, O Brahman; the entire universe consists of my essence. Wherever you are, there I am; it is not otherwise—reflect upon this. (30)
On the northern shore of the ocean and to the south of the great river, that region indeed bestows the fruit of all sacred fords upon the earth. (31)
O Brahmin, those highly intelligent men who dwell there are partakers of the fruits of meritorious deeds performed in previous births. || 32 ||
O Lotus-born One, those who possess little merit or lack devotion to me are not born here; this land extends from the Ekāmraka forest as far as the shore of the southern ocean.
O Brahmin, that Nīla mountain which shines upon the shore of the ocean is the most excellent at every step and is supremely purifying in its sequence.
This place hidden within the earth is yours as well, and it is very difficult to attain; it is unknowable even to gods and demons, being concealed by my *māyā*.
Having completely renounced all attachments, I remain there as an embodied being; having transcended both the perishable and the imperishable, I abide in the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
My field, Puruṣottama, is not overcome by creation or dissolution, O Brahmin, just as you see me with a form marked by the discus and other signs.
O Grandfather, having gone there, you shall see me in such a manner at the foot of the Kalpa-nyagrodha tree within the interior of the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri).
In the western direction, there is a famous pool named Rauhiṇa; beholding me dwelling on its bank with their physical eyes, [they shall see me]. (39)
"By that water, their sins being destroyed, they shall attain union with me. Go there, O fortunate one; having seen me, as you meditate upon me," (40)
The further greatness of that sacred field shall become manifest; it will be a supreme wonder even for you.

Hidden by my māyā within the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas, that [reality] was indeed not within the range of anyone's perception; yet, by my grace, as you now offer praise, it shall become manifest and accessible to all.

Whatever merit is declared for those of pure soul through vows, pilgrimages, sacrifices, and gifts—all that one obtains here by dwelling for a single day; indeed, by merely breathing here, one gains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Having thus instructed the brahmins regarding the ritual procedure, O sages, that Lord Puruṣottama vanished right there while he was looking on.

Thus ends the first chapter, in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini, within the *Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya*, in the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: Then Brahmā went quickly to where the Blessed One himself was staying; at the conclusion of the hymn of praise, he beheld the Lord exactly as he had previously seen him.
O best of the twice-born, upon seeing that Supreme Lord, he was thrilled with recognition and became a treasury of most wonderful knowledge.
Just as he began to offer praise with eyes blossoming with joy, a preeminent crow arrived from somewhere.
Having immersed him in that pool filled with the water of compassion, he beheld Mādhava, the ocean of mercy, possessing the luster of a blue gem.
Having cast off his crow-body and rolling repeatedly upon the ground, he stood by his side with the conch, discus, and mace in hand.
O sages, having seen that transverse path so difficult for even the lords of yogis to attain, he thought: "The creation will gradually come to an end."
A doubt arose regarding liberation for human beings in the Vedānta; however, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain here for one who is a devotee of Viṣṇu.
O best of the twice-born, the Ancient Person became manifest when he declared that by chanting his name, a person is liberated from all sins. (8)
O Brahmins, when he is beheld, what indeed is difficult to attain—liberation? Even one who departs life while meditating on Viṣṇu in his mind is liberated.
What is so wonderful about the Blessed One’s direct realization that it should lead to liberation? It is the marvelous majesty of this sacred field known as Puruṣottama.

O twice-born ones, even a crow beholds Hari directly here; this field is exceedingly difficult to attain and grants liberation even to the ignorant. Oh, what majesty this field possesses—that it bestows liberation even upon a crow! How much more so for those who are constantly endowed with peace, detachment, and knowledge? (11)
The sages said: Having seen Mādhava known as Nīla, what did the Grandfather do?
And upon seeing him, in an instant, the crow was released from its bodily bondage.
Jaimini said: While he was contemplating Mādhava after seeing that most wonderful sight, the Lord of the Ancestors became distressed by the withdrawal of his own authority.
With a dejected face and sighing, he went there with great haste; having seen Mādhava on the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri), he prostrated before him with his eight limbs.

He offered praise to the Lord of the World for his firm establishment in his own office. Yama said: "Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction. (16)
All this is strung upon you, like clusters of gems on a thread; by you the world is sustained, by you it is created, and by you it is nourished.
In the form of the moon, the sun, and so forth, you eternally illumine everything—the Lord of the Universe, the Source of the World, the Abode of the Universe, and the Teacher of the World. (18)
I bow to the witness of the universe, who is devoid of beginning and end; salutations to the ocean filled with the waters of supreme compassion.
O you whose power transcends the high, the low, and that which is beyond both, O source of the universe! || 20 ||
To the sun that dispels the heat of worldly existence, the kinsman of the distressed, who [binds] all created beings through the rope of his own qualities by means of his own māyā; || 21 ||
Salutations to the wielder of the discus, whose pure yellow garment is like the filaments of a lotus, and who wields the discus that severs the shoulders of enemies in the great battle.
Salutation to the one who lifted up the earth with his tusk, whose form is the three Vedas; salutation to the Sacrificial Boar, whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire.

Salutations to Narasiṃha, whose fierce form with bared fangs puts his enemies to flight, and by whose mere play of the side-glance alone the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe are accomplished.
For this worldly existence arises repeatedly, consisting of highs and lows; it is that very one which has the luster of a dark cloud and the form of a sapphire gem.
I bow to the treasure-house of compassion, who dwells in the cave of the Blue Mountain, who bears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and who bestows auspiciousness. (26)
Salutations to You, the enemy of Mura, who destroys the entire flood of sins of those who bow before You; salutations to You whose eyes are refined by contact with the side-glances of Kamalā.
To Him whose broad chest is captivating and resplendent with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem; by taking refuge at His pair of lotus feet, one becomes a partaker of sovereign power.

Śrī, who bestows various forms of sovereignty upon those who constantly take refuge in her, is your primordial nature (prakṛti), differentiated as both the supreme and the non-supreme, through your desire to create. (29)

I bow down to that Lakṣmī, who, though the immutable Supreme Brahman, directly created the mutable world; she who is endowed with all auspicious characteristics, marked by beautiful signs, and eternally stationed upon the chest of the Lord of Lakṣmī.
Jaimini said: Thus, having been fully propitiated by Dharmarāja, the Beloved of Śrī signaled with a glance of his eye toward Śrī, who stood at his side holding a lute in her hand.
The Goddess Lakṣmī, honored by him and the destroyer of the suffering of worldly existence, spoke playfully to Yama for the welfare of all the worlds: || 32 ||
Lakṣmī said: "That for which you praise us both in this sacred field is indeed difficult to obtain; yet we cannot abandon this field of Śrī Puruṣottama. (33)
"Even at the end of a kalpa, we two are indeed sustained by the Supreme Lord; for here, the lordship over the quarters belonging to Brahmā and the others does not exist. (34)
Here, the ripening of karma never occurs at any time, even for men or animals who dwell here while committing evil deeds. (35)
For those who are bound day and night by the fetters of sin and merit are burned intensely, like a heap of cotton in a blazing fire. (36)
For you were indeed created as Yama, the restrainer of them, fashioned here in person with a body as beautiful as a dark sapphire.
Having seen the god Nārāyaṇa, one is liberated from the bondage of karma; other than this, O Sun-born one, there is sovereignty upon the land of action.
O Yama, do not fall into despondency regarding this King of Fields, the Restrainer; for even to you, this Blessed One is the Ordainer and Great-Grandfather.
Out of curiosity, he beholds even an animal that has attained the same form as Viṣṇu; for this lotus-born one knows the ripening of the karma of all beings. (40)
Having understood the greatness of this sacred field, he praises the Lord Gadādhara: "It is fitting for living beings to come under your control; they do not remain here. (41)

"O son of Vivasvat, those who are liberated while living (jīvanmuktas) and those seeking liberation (mumukṣus) dwell here. Thus addressed by Viṣṇu in the form of a woman, Yama, humbled by both his ego and shame, spoke.
Yama said: "O Mother, that which was commanded by you previously has not been heard by me."
Stricken by ignorance, how can I know the supreme secret, whose true nature even the Vedas and the Grandfather (Brahmā) do not know? (44)
Deluded by egoism, how can I know its greatness, O Queen of the Gods, since this sacred field has been ordained as the bestower of liberation? 45.
Due to the presence of Vāsudeva, the will of the Lord is unrestrained; for while Viṣṇu is the binder elsewhere, here he bestows liberation.
"He is the creator of my realm as well as of the hells and the third heaven; if there is liberation for the deceased here, then tell me that in great detail, O Mother. (47)
Indeed, what is the configuration and measurement of that field, and what is the fruit of residing there? What holy sites (tīrthas) are located here, or what other secret is there? (48)
Tell me everything regarding whose authority this field stands, so that I may completely abandon it and move about free from fear. (49)

Thus ends the second chapter, in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini, within the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eleven thousand verses.
Śrī said: "Excellent! Your intellect has arisen, having taken refuge in the presence of Viṣṇu. O son of the Sun, I shall now relate this wonderful account of the sacred field."
O Yama, just as I was seen formerly standing upon the chest of the Blessed One, so shall I be when this world of moving and non-moving beings has dissolved at the time of universal destruction.
At that time, both this sacred field and I myself were present there; then that sage, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, possessed a lifespan of seven kalpas.
When all things mobile and immobile had perished and he was submerged in the ocean of dissolution, failing to find any place of rest, he obtained no peace anywhere.
Wandering here and there in the ocean of waters during the dissolution, he beheld a banyan tree in that sacred field which resembles Puruṣottama.
Leaping again and again near the root of the banyan tree, he heard the words of the boy from my presence, O Mārkaṇḍeya.
"Having entered [this state], abandon incomparable suffering; do not indeed grieve. Having heard those words of Citra, which were inconceivable at that time, the sage—
He attained supreme amazement and did not even consider his own suffering; for this [body] is not dissolved by waters, nor is it consumed by the fire of time.
This field is neither dried up nor moved by the Saṃvartaka and other winds; it is seen like a boat in the midst of the most terrible great ocean.
There stands this great banyan tree resembling a sacrificial post; having taken hold of it, this sacred field became known as Nyagrodha, the body of the Lord.
Indeed, even by the wind of the great dissolution, his branch did not tremble; standing beneath it, that sage reflected as follows.
When this dissolution has occurred as a single ocean and all moving and stationary beings have perished, how is this region of the earth perceived as so exceedingly stable?
"Where this excellent, tender tree is seen—'O Mārkaṇḍeya, come here again and again!'—such were his humble words. (13)
Thinking thus, "Whence is this state of being without a hermitage?", he, while leaping, beheld Nārāyaṇa with the conch, discus, and mace in his hands.
Then Vaivasvata beheld me seated upon his lotus-like lap; though he was helpless against the water and wind, he remained there composed and steady.
With a joyful inner soul, that sage prostrated himself before us with all eight limbs and recited this hymn to propitiate the God. || 16 ||

Mārkaṇḍeya said: O ocean of compassion, protect me, who am wretched and tormented on all sides, devoid of devotion to you, yet attached to the pursuit of the lotus-feet of others—though those feet are enriched with the splendors of Rudra, Indra, and Brahmā. 17.

O Ocean of Compassion, protect me, the wretched one, with Your pair of lotus feet—which are served by Brahmā and the other gods, which possess inconceivable power, and which are the essential cause for attaining the highest good. 18.

O Viṣṇu, protect me, who am utterly wretched, You in whose limbs this cosmic egg shines forth with its many millions of parts, wherein the play, sport, maintenance, and creation of the world are dissolved.

Just as a single piece of gold appears manifold through various forms such as bracelets and the like, or as the sun risen in the sky appears differently in waters disturbed by the unevenness of its receptacles, so too art Thou perceived as many, though Thou art one and devoid of qualities.

O You of boundless power, although You possess a perfectly complete radiance that leaves nothing lacking and are free from all grasping and conceptualization, You assume a body in age after age, in accordance with Your compassion for the wretched.

O Lord of the World, because my intellect was previously devoid of self-knowledge, I failed to serve Your lotus feet; therefore, O Ocean of Compassion, protect me, a wretched soul who now reaps the terrible fruit of that karma. (22)

O Great-Souled One, salutations to You, the cause of the cause, who transcend Prakṛti; Your threefold body, which sports in the dissolution, creation, and maintenance of the entire world, shines forth as the source of Mahat and the other evolutes.

Having gone everywhere, it is vast, immeasurable, ever-increasing, and expanded within you; I take refuge in that form of Brahman, which is the cause of transformation, consisting of both the individual self and the universal self. 24.
O Lord of Lakṣmī, in this most terrible single ocean, there is no place to remain due to the agitation caused by the clouds, the waters, and the winds. (25)
Save me, O Viṣṇu, Lord of the World, who am submerged in the ocean of worldly existence! O Govinda, lift me up from this by the glance of your compassionate side-long look.
Śrī said: Beholding the Brahmarṣi thus offering praise, the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa himself looked upon him with a gracious eye and spoke these words.

The Blessed Lord said: "O Mārkaṇḍeya, best of the twice-born, you have become exceedingly wretched because you did not recognize me; yet, by that very means, you have performed a difficult penance and attained longevity alone. (28)

O great sage, behold him lying in a leaf-cup, ascending from the Kalpavṛkṣa tree; he is the nature of childhood for all, the very soul of Time. Having entered his wide-open mouth, you ought to remain there.
Śrī said: Thus addressed by the Blessed One, that sage, his face filled with wonder, [spoke]. (30)
Having ascended, he beheld his child-form entering his mouth; once inside, it passed through the path of the throat into the vast belly of great extent.
There, that Brahmin beheld the fourteen worlds, as well as Brahmā and the other world-protectors, the gods, the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas.
He saw the sages and celestial rishis, as well as the surface of the earth marked by oceans, with various sacred fords, rivers, mountains, and forests.
The city of Pattana was observed, together with its villages and market towns; likewise, the seven netherworlds and thousands of Naga maidens were seen.
It was most wonderful, served by nāgas with priceless jewels, and adorned with palaces of highly precious gems and brilliantly shining vessels of nectar.
He saw Śeṣa, the sustainer of the worlds, adorned with a thousand hoods, seated in the midst of his disciples, expounding all the scriptures without exception.
Whatever object exists within the belly of the cosmic egg, created by the Supreme Lord, all of that was seen by that great sage within his own stomach.
Wandering here and there, he did not see the end of the belly; then, having emerged from it, he saw me once again.
Having prostrated before the Supreme Person, who stood there exactly as he had been perceived previously, his eyes wide with wonder, he spoke this: (39)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, O Master, what is this wonder? Amidst the obstruction of the great dissolution, a creation is being perceived here."
Your māyā is difficult to cut through; how indeed can it be understood by me?
The Blessed Lord said: O Sage, perceive this field of mine as wonderful and eternal; here neither creation nor dissolution exists, nor does the cycle of worldly existence.

Having fully awakened here to me—who am eternally of one form, known as Puruṣottama, and the bestower of liberation—one who has entered into this state never again undergoes residence in a womb, being of the nature of intense bliss. (43)

Thus commanded by the Blessed One, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, turning his back on all other holy places, said with a joyful countenance after prostrating before the Teacher of the World: "I shall make my dwelling here. (44)

Mārkaṇḍeya said: Endowed with devotion and faith, he spoke thus to Viṣṇu: "O Blessed One, show me favor in this sacred field of Puruṣottama, so that, O Puruṣottama, I may remain here and not fall under the power of death."
The Blessed One said: "O brahmin-sage, establish my presence here in this sacred field that accomplishes liberation."
I shall do this without a doubt until the dissolution of all beings; at the end of the cosmic destruction, I will establish for you an eternal sacred site (tīrtha).
"By performing penance on its bank and worshipping Śiva, who is my second body, you will certainly conquer death through my compassion. (48)
Jaimini said: Thus, in former times, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, having been granted a boon, dug a pit with the discus of Hari in the north-western corner of the banyan tree.
Having occupied the Pāvana Garta and worshipped Maheśvara, the Brahmin truly conquered death through great austerity.
This excellent pit is renowned by the very name of that sage; having bathed there and beheld Śiva, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Śrī said: This sacred field, measuring five krośas, is situated within the ocean; two krośas of it are the exceedingly pure ground on the shore of the King of Tīrthas.
Strewn with golden sands and adorned by blue mountains, that Lord Viśveśvara is Nārāyaṇa himself in person.
Having restrained the collection of sense objects and stationed himself on the shore of the ocean, the sixty-fourth lord remained there to worship the Lord of the World.
Known as Yameśvara, he is the destroyer of Yama’s restraint; by seeing and worshipping him, one obtains the fruit of ten million liṅgas. || 55 ||

Thus ends the third chapter, in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini, within the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī said: At the western boundary of the conch-shaped field, at its summit, dwells that god whose banner is the bull, the bestower of all desires. (1)
At the tip of the conch is Nīlakaṇṭha; this [place] extends for one krośa and is very difficult to attain. It is indeed the supreme, purifying field of Nārāyaṇa himself.
From the waters of the King of Rivers (the ocean) up to the very root of the banyan tree, the interior portion of Śaṅkha’s belly was indeed flooded by the waters of the sea.

Through contact with whom the ocean here attained the status of the king of holy places (tīrtharāja), and by whose coming within the range of vision this Lord became the bestower of liberation. || 4 ||
Likewise, this field [Sindhu] grants liberation through bathing after death; formerly, Rudra, out of anger, severed the fifth head of Brahmā.
Holding that head which was difficult to cast off, he wandered about the universe; when he arrived here, he finally released the skull of Brahmā.
The Kapālamocana Liṅga is situated in the second circuit; whoever should behold, worship, and bow down to Kapālamocana [shall attain liberation]. || 7 ||
He casts off the cloak of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; indeed, death on its right side brings liberation from worldly existence.
O Dharmarāja, know that my first power, which proceeds from the third cycle and is named Vimalā, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Whoever should worship this with devotion, prostrate before it, or glorify it, shall obtain all desires and find liberation in the end.
Indeed, these three—the sacred pit (kuṇḍa), the banyan tree (vaṭa), and the all-pervading Lord—reside in the region of the navel; they remain established from Kapālamocana up to Ardhāśinī.
One should know the center of the conch to be well-guarded by the wielder of the discus; it drinks half of the water increased during the great dissolution. 12.
At the beginning of creation, O Dharmarāja, this Śakti of mine is known as my half-portion (ardhāṃśinī). He who, having seen her, bows down to her, enjoys eternal pleasures. || 13 ||
From the waters of the Sindhu River up to the very root of the banyan tree, it is considered to grant liberation from death for insects, birds, and human beings.
This sacred inner altar (antarvedī) is desired even by the gods; for all those who stand here behold [the Lord] bearing the discus and the lotus. || 15 ||
Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist on earth, in the sky, and in the triple heaven, numbering three and a half crores, they indeed bestow both heaven and liberation.
Among them, this Puruṣottama is celebrated as the king of sacred fords; it is considered the bestower of *sāyujya* (union) among all fields of liberation.
Those who abide here do not grieve even over old age, birth, or death; for this pool, known as Rohiṇa, is indeed filled with the water called compassion.
It remains eternally accumulated, bestowing liberation through touch; it is here that the water established during the dissolution remains, which increases [again]. || 19 ||
Afterwards, it dissolves right here; therefore, it is known by the name Rohiṇa. For that reason, let there be no anxiety in you regarding the reversal of your own authority.
"O King of the Dead, you are not the Lord here for those who are eligible for liberation. Having thus instructed Dharmarāja, Lakṣmī [spoke] to him as he stood before her. (21)
The Mother of the worlds spoke to Brahmā with humble words: "O Grandfather, O Lord of the world, everything is indeed known to you."
Declare this field, which bestows liberation upon all living beings, as well as the pure Kāmākhyā and Kṣetrapāla, established in austerity.
This Nṛsiṃha, whose very nature is Brahman, stands manifest to the right of the Lord; having torn open the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu, he shines brilliantly, O Master.
By the sight of him, sins are destroyed without a doubt; one becomes fit for both worldly enjoyment and liberation—of this there is no need for deliberation. (25)
By giving up one's life here before it, one shall attain union with Brahman (brahmasāyujya); whatever action one performs here shall become multiplied ten million-fold.
This is the shadow of the Kalpa-tree, illuminated by the sun that is Nṛsiṃha; within it, ignorance indeed perishes through knowledge, whether consciously or unconsciously at the time of death.
O Brahmins, even without these means of liberation—which are well-known in the Vedāntas, consist of hearing and so forth, and are difficult for the deluded to attain—one may achieve release here.
In Avimukta, Maheśvara, the ocean of compassion, whispers into the ear of the seeker of liberation the knowledge known as Brahman, which is the means for awakening.
By practicing with that intellect, one shall gradually attain liberation; for, through the greatness of the teacher, his knowledge does not diminish.
O Yama, let there be no doubt in you: for those who give up their lives here, liberation from their very own form occurs at that very moment.
For those performers of ritual action whose minds are deluded and who are attached to coming and going, no trust whatsoever arises here regarding Vaivasvata.
Just as one who is thirsty abandons the sweet, cool, and perfectly pure water of the Ganges to go toward a mere puddle, so too are those of deluded mind.
Abandoning this supreme sacred field, they wander to other holy sites; satisfied by the fragrance of *palāśa* leaves and *modakas*, they obtain only the fruit born of their own exhaustion. (34)
By bathing there, the Lord is like the ocean, and by his shadow, he is like the wish-fulfilling tree; moreover, any sacred field (kṣetra) whatsoever grants liberation from death to men.
Whatever object a man places his trust in with devotion, by that very thing he shall be liberated; indeed, there is no sacred site (tīrtha) like this.
He who, having abandoned this, indeed develops a liking for another path, is surely deceived by the illusory power of Viṣṇu and is greedy for worldly gain.
There is no need for you to offer many instructions; for this Karaṭa, who has assumed the form of Viṣṇu, has been directly perceived by you.
Eight Śaktis have been proclaimed for the purpose of guarding the inner altar; formerly, I was empowered by Rudra through fierce austerity.
Then, for the sake of a wife, that Gaurī was created by me as his destined partner; she emerged from my body as the abode of all beauty.
Commanded by me then, O blessed one, do my pleasing word: protect the Antarvedī for me on all sides with your own forms.
Out of affection for me, she remains established in eight forms throughout the directions: Maṅgalā is at the foot of the banyan tree, and likewise Vimalā is in the west.
Sarvamaṅgalā is situated on the back part of Śaṅkha; likewise, Ardhāṃśinī and Lambā are situated in the direction of Kubera (the north).
Kālarātri is in the south, while Marīcikā is in the east; likewise, Caṇḍarūpā is situated behind Kālarātri in the west.
This place, protected by these Śaktis of fierce form, is indeed very difficult for a man of little merit to attain. (45)
By seeing and likewise by chanting the names of these eight Śaktis, all sins are destroyed and one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
Having observed the eightfold division of Rudrāṇī, Rudra Śaṅkara also divided himself into eight forms and worships the Supreme Lord.
Having propitiated Viṣṇu through austerity, he requested this supreme boon: "O Lord, wherever you may be, there indeed I shall dwell at my ease. (48)
O Beloved of Kamalā, there is no other cause for liberation than You; O Lord, inner controller, I am Yours—without You, how could there even be a body? 49.
Those fools who do not know you rejoice in impure sense-objects; O You who resemble the stainless sky, I have gone to You for refuge. (50)
Jaimini said: The Lord, the all-pervading one, himself established that Rudra as the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) all around, while he himself remained stationed in the center. || 51 ||
The field-protector named Kapālamocana, Yameśvara, Mārkaṇḍeya, likewise Īśāna, Bilveśa, and Nīlakaṇṭhaka. || 52 ||
At the foot of the banyan tree is Vaṭeśa, and the eight lingas of Maheśvara; by seeing, touching, and worshipping them, one is liberated.
For those who die in this field, Yama has no authority over them; therefore, accomplish elsewhere that purpose for which you have come.
Nevertheless, that Lord of the World, the Master who removes the distress of those who have sought refuge, was propitiated by Yama through devotion and surrendered His very self to him. 55.
With his Sudarśana discus, he shall dispel the illusion in this excellent field that must not be abandoned, which is covered with golden sand.
Having thus deceived Yama and sent him back to the abode of Yama, he considered it well done and then spoke to Brahmā, who stood before him.
Śrī said: "In the Satya Yuga, there will be a king named Indradyumna; he will be a devotee of Viṣṇu, a performer of all sacrifices, and an expert in the scriptures. (58)
Having come here, that best of kings will perform great devotion for the pleasure of the Blessed One by means of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
O Lord of Creatures, for the sake of bestowing grace upon them, he who has arisen from a single piece of wood shall become fourfold.
Viśvakarman shall fashion the wooden images; for you, having been propitiated by Indradyumna, shall indeed be their consecrator.
O Grandfather, there shall be the installation and the crafting of images that resemble us and our counterparts.
Having heard these words of Śrī, the four-faced Brahmā and Yama both departed for their respective cities, filled with supreme joy.
And repeatedly recollecting that greatness of the sacred field, their bodies were covered with horripilation due to both wonder and joy.
O sages, at present, he who was propitiated by Indradyumna dwells there, bearing the conch and discus, glorious, and resembling a dark blue cloud.
Dwelling within a cave of the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala), bearing a wooden body, he resides for the benefit of the world together with Bala and Subhadrā.
Accompanied by the Sudarśana discus, which was fashioned from terrible [materials], he is the ocean of compassion who destroys the suffering of those who bow before him.
Upon seeing which, one is liberated from the very firm bond of sin; the ripening of a multitude of good deeds has arrived all at once. (68)
O best of sages, behold the moonlight treasury for the three-fold afflictions; indeed, there are many divine and human incarnations of Viṣṇu. (69)
The most wonderful deeds and his majesty have been described; even the gods do not regard men as being equal to him out of their own familiarity with him. (70)
O Brahmins, even for gods, asuras, humans, gandharvas, serpents, rākṣasas, and even for animals, [there is no fear] in that Hari who is made of wood.
The mind dwells within that which has become the self of all and brings about all happiness; those who possess no other essential nature live upon its bliss. (72)
The Vedic speech of Brahman is experienced here as "āha" (it says); it tears asunder the sufferings of saṃsāra and bestows imperishable bliss. (73)
Therefore, Brahman made of wood is extolled in the Vedāntas; for a wooden image never bestows liberation anywhere.
O Brahmins, the state of being uncreated is never found in that which is created; for how could liberation, which is uncreated, arise from something created, or how could it be so terrible? (75)
Without a substratum, the divine sovereignty of Brahmā is not attained; this is the supreme secret, the unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu. (76)
That image is supramundane, yet it has been manifested as mundane; where has such an image ever been heard of or seen to speak? (77)
Then he granted that boon to Indradyumna, appearing in a wooden body—the sole refuge for the poor and the helpless, and the means of crossing the ocean of worldly existence.
To Nārāyaṇa, the source of the universe and the cause of its creation and dissolution, whose feet are eternally worshipped by all that moves and is stationary, and who is the supreme refuge; (79)
It is the liberation from all sins, the shattering of all calamities, the spreading of divine powers, and the choice of all yogis. || 80 ||
The sustenance of all living beings, the support of the worlds as well, the expression of all languages, and the chastisement of all evildoers. (81)
O sages, seek refuge in Hari, the sovereign lord who is the sole refuge for those with no other resort, the drier of all mud, and whose abode is the Blue Mountain. 82.
Though motionless and possessing a wooden body, he performs divine playful pastimes; even with very little devotion, he forgives the hundreds of offenses committed by men. (83)
O sages, here I shall relate to you the sin-destroying life-story of the Supreme Soul, who sportively assumed a wooden body.
Born in Kurukṣetra, both a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya, they became friends and went about together with affection, sharing the same food and recreation. (85)

They have fallen from their conduct; they are deluded seekers of forbidden things; they are devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*; and they are bereft of the offerings of *svadhā* and *svāhā*.
Unfit vessels for the Dharma, defiled by great sins, they delighted in consuming honey and lived together with courtesans. (87)
But concern for the world beyond did not occur to them even in their dreams; thus proceeding in this manner, they spent half of their lifespan. (88)
Once, while wandering about, the two of them went to a sacrificial enclosure, hearing from afar the captivating sound of hymns and the recitation of the scriptures.
Having observed all those various rites enjoined by the Vedas, O twice-born ones, those two formerly unrighteous men then conceived faith in the path of Dharma.
Remembering their own former births, Puṇḍarīka and Ambarīṣa censured their own wicked conduct and spoke to one another.
"How shall we cross this formidable ocean of evil deeds, acquired intentionally in this very life and now free from decay? (92)
For he does not know that scripture which [prescribes] the atonement for the terrible evil deeds accumulated by us two, which is extremely difficult to obtain. || 93 ||
Nevertheless, let us ask these Brahmins, who are most devoted to Brahman and are present here in this assembly, for they have approached us with prostrations, regarding the atonement for this matter.
Having thus resolved, they saluted the brahmins and questioned them, repeatedly making known each of their own respective sins exactly as they were.
Having heard their words, those best of the twice-born closed their eyes; looking at one another with astonished faces, they said nothing at all.
"Alas! How terrible are the deeds accumulated by these two evil-minded ones, for which the scriptures are truly not sufficient to provide a footing for expiation. (97)
"Therefore, we are not able to provide atonement for these two. Among them was a certain eminent Vaiṣṇava, the leader of the assembly. || 98 ||
Having had all his impurities destroyed by the greatness of devotion to the Blessed One, he, the best among those skilled in speech, laughed and spoke these words to them: 99.
The Vaiṣṇava said: "O twice-born one, O scion of the Kṣatriyas, if you both desire liberation from this most dreadful heap of sins, go quickly to Puruṣottama."
The best of sacred fields is that wooden structure where Puruṣottama resides—the All-pervading Lord who, out of devotion, bestowed grace upon the royal sage Indradyumna.
Having propitiated that Lord of the Universe, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, you will certainly attain, according to your own desire, either the destruction of sin or liberation.
But that [sin], which is like a forest fire to a mass of cotton consisting of terrible misdeeds, cannot be brought to destruction through asceticism even in ten million lifetimes. (103)
Upon seeing him, all evil is simultaneously destroyed; therefore, do not delay, but proceed there with haste.
In the highly meritorious region of Utkala, on the shore of the southern ocean, go for refuge to the Lord who dwells upon the peak of the Blue Mountain. 105.
"The Lord, the ocean of compassion, will grant you the fulfillment of your desires. Having been thus instructed, the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya were filled with joy. (106)
O brahmins, they both proceeded toward Puruṣottama by that very same path.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sages and Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: With weary hearts, having abandoned association with courtesans and the like, both of them, observing vows of pure diet, meditated upon Viṣṇu with their minds. (1)
After some time, they reached the abode of Hari on the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri), where they bathed in the waters of the King of Tīrthas according to the prescribed rites.
Standing at the gate of the palace and prostrating with all eight limbs, the two brahmins gazed at the Blessed One, yet they did not see him at that time.
With pale faces and overwhelmed by anxiety at not seeing the Lord, they both began a fast unto death, continuing until they beheld the Blessed One.
They were chanting the name of the Blessed One, which destroys all impurity; then, during the third watch of the night, they beheld a single light.
For three days more, those two remained steadfast in their fast; then, in the midst of the seventh night, they beheld the Blessed One.
Having heard the praises of the thirty gods, the two became possessed of divine knowledge; with the slough of their sins cast off, they beheld the God manifest before them.
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, adorned with divine ornaments, and with his lotus-feet placed upon the backs of two jeweled sandals.
[He beheld] the Lord, whose eyes were like full-blown white lotuses and whose face was serene, embracing Lakṣmī with his left arm as she stood at his left side.
Some, with jeweled canes in their hands, and some with chowries in their hands, approached her who was captivating in her splendor as she took up the rolled betel leaf.
Some, rich in youth and well-adorned, held in their own hands lamps of fragrant oil and lamps with wicks made of jewels.
Behind her, another radiant woman held a parasol made of jewels, while a censer filled with the fragrant smoke of black aguru incense was held near her face.
One woman, possessing the splendor of the goddess Pramlocā, was smiling with the beauty of her form and favoring the gods before her with playful, side-long glances from her eyes.
And with a smile, [he looked] at the Siddhas, the divine hosts of sages such as Sanaka and others, who were praising him individually with their necks bowed and palms joined in reverence.
And [he saw] Nārada and other Gandharvas, enchanting with their divine singing, who, out of compassion, were listening with playful ease and focused attention.
He causes Prahlāda and other foremost Vaiṣṇavas, who were meditating on His own form before Him, to become completely absorbed in the attraction of their minds toward His own body.
It was the self-manifestation of his own universal-form body, made manifest by the gods and others reflected in the Kaustubha gem shining upon his chest.
Standing beneath a divine rain of flowers falling higher and higher, he beheld the host of Apsarases whose splendor had vanished due to the presence of Śrī.
Beholding him, who was constantly performing various graceful bodily movements and displaying divine amorous sports, those two—the Brahmin and the Kshatriya—saw him.

O twice-born ones, in an instant they both became masters of all branches of knowledge; having circumambulated the Lord of Gods three times with palms joined in reverence, they both prostrated themselves with the eight limbs of their bodies touching the ground and praised him with great joy. || 20 ||
Puṇḍarīka said: Salutations to you, O support of the universe, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction! O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be to you, the Supreme Self, the ultimate refuge. (21)
You alone are the ultimate reality, devoid of both birth and dissolution; those with the eye of meditation perceive you as the very nature of eternal bliss.
How indeed do those of deluded hearts perceive You—the pure Consciousness alone, the Lord of the worlds, the supreme substratum, higher than the highest, and utterly stainless? (23)
Those whose minds are agitated by the desire for sensual pleasures and wealth, who are utterly miserable and exhausted on the path of coming and going, never at any time partake of happiness. (24)
O Lord, have compassion for me, who am utterly wretched, who have come to you for refuge, who am deluded, whose actions are evil, and who have fallen into the ocean of existence. (25)
O Lord, who else in the entire universe exists as a kinsman like you—one who is indifferent to his own duties and is compassionate toward the wretched and the helpless? (26)
Like a bucket on a water-wheel, one suffers the misery of wandering through high and low states; O Ocean of Compassion, protect me, your servant, incessantly! 27.
Those fools who worship you with the intent of attaining worldly security and prosperity are indeed deluded by your māyā, for you grant liberation through your divine play.
O Lord of the World, even if your name "Nārāyaṇa" is chanced upon and uttered by mere whim, it is superior to you [in its power], for it is the sole means to attain the four aims of human life.
But you, through those various individual sacrifices, bestow those respective perfections; O Lord, you alone are the refuge for those fallen into the ocean of worldly existence.
Mounted upon the ship of wisdom, with compassion as his oar, O Lord, he is intent on leading the senseless across to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra.
You alone rule when meditated upon with exclusive devotion; as for those other gods established in the scriptures who bestow liberation, [they are subordinate]. (32)
They indeed cause one to attain devotion to you, which is like a jar for crossing the ocean of suffering.

Therefore, O Blessed One, be gracious toward me; O Lord, grant me firm devotion to Your lotus feet, by which I may cross this most terrible and difficult-to-traverse ocean of existence, even while remaining free from the exhaustion born of the eightfold yoga. (393)

I have no need for these petty accumulations of dharma, wealth, and desire, which are grasped by the ignorant and yield only trivial, harmful pleasures. Command me now to immerse myself in the ocean of intense, ever-increasing bliss that arises from contemplating your two lotus feet.

Having thus praised the Lord of the Universe, the twice-born man fell at the feet of the lotus-like feet, crying out "Save me, O Kṛṣṇa! with a voice moistened by tears; then, rising again, he stood praising Him with his palms joined in reverence.
Ambarīṣa said: Be gracious, O God, the soul of all, you who possess innumerable heads and arms; O you with countless noses, eyes, hands, and feet, salutations be unto you! (37)

You have transcended the thirty-six principles; you are free from conceptual proliferation, yet the source of all proliferation. O You whose form is the universe, the abode of the fourfold world—salutations be unto You! (38)
He who is one-footed, three-footed, whose feet are the sacred fords, and whose feet are the intermediate space—he from whose feet the Gaṅgā arises and purifies the three worlds. (39)
Salutations to that Auspicious Self, whose very name, when proclaimed, purifies sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and bestows all auspiciousness.
O Lord, even by the mere glorification of Your name, all perfections are born; indeed, wise and intelligent men seek You out out of curiosity. (41)
O Lord, the water from your feet removes the heat of those who take refuge in it; grant me firm devotion toward this, for I am overwhelmed by the threefold afflictions. (42)
O Lord of the World, for me who has no other master, there is nothing else remaining to be prayed for; bowing down before you, I entreat you a thousand times. (43)
May there be firm devotion to your lotus feet—the seed of all human goals—as long as I draw breath. (44)
By means of this devotion, the Grandfather (Brahmā) fashioned this creation; Rudra withdraws everything, and Lakṣmī bestows sovereignty.

With a mind focused on nothing else, I pray for that devotion which is compassionate toward the wretched; for in this beginningless mire of ignorance, which is exceedingly firm and very difficult to cross— (46)
O Lord of the World, for one who is submerged and perishing without support, there is no other refuge than devotion to You, whose majesty is supreme. (47)
These paths, which are confounded by the Śruti, Smṛti, and other scriptures, are causes of delusion; they are unable to prevail once one's devotion to you has been taken away.
"O Lord, O All-pervading One, have compassion on me who has no other refuge. Thus he praised with joy in the presence of the lotus feet of the Lord of the World. (49)
He fell upon the ground like a staff, saying repeatedly, "Be gracious! Then all those deities, having praised and fully worshipped Keśava, [departed].
Satisfied by her playful side-glances, they departed once more for heaven; thereafter, Puṇḍarīka and Ambarīṣa opened their eyes.
Deluded by the Māyā of Viṣṇu, they did not realize that which they had seen in their dream—that divine play which they had indeed witnessed with their own physical eyes.
Once again, those two human beings beheld him seated upon a divine throne, resembling a dark blue cloud, with eyes as broad as full-blown lotuses.
With red lips and a beautiful nose, adorned with divine earrings, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and wearing a garland of forest flowers.
Broad-chested, radiant with beautiful necklaces and a priceless crown, his chest marked by the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha jewels, and adorned with divine armlets.
With long, hanging arms, ever intent on protecting the miserable and the afflicted, his waist was bound with a golden thread and adorned with a central gem.
Wearing divine yellow garments, adorned with celestial garlands and perfumes, seated upon a golden lotus throne, his entire body embraced by the Goddess Śrī.
He who removes the suffering of those who have sought refuge, a vast ocean of nectar, the wish-fulfilling tree in full bloom that grants the fruit of every desire.
They beheld Halāyudha standing at his right side, by whose great strength the Lord sustains the cosmic egg.
That Naga king Bala was adorned with seven hoods, as lofty and white as the peak of Mount Kailāsa, and radiant with earrings.
It was enriched with various forest garlands, draped in divine blue veils, and its lotus-like eyes were constantly rolling, intoxicated by the wine of Varuṇī.
With a depressed back and an elevated chest, his body coiled like a serpent, and his four arms resplendent with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
Resplendent with various ornaments, destroying the sins of those who bow before her, the auspicious Subhadrā stands between the two of them, reddish like saffron.
[He saw] Lakṣmī, the abode of all beauty, who is saluted by all the gods, residing within the lotus-heart of the Lord of Lakṣmī, yet standing apart [from him]. (64)
The Goddess, holding a choice lotus, adorned with divine attire and ornaments, who is a wish-fulfilling creeper for those who seek refuge, and the destroyer of all impurities. (65)
They beheld the supreme discus standing on the left side of Viṣṇu, the divine boat that carries across those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.
O Brahmins, having seen Viṣṇu fashioned from wood, radiant with golden carvings, and situated in four forms, those two—the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya—[beheld him]. (67)
At the time of sunrise, they considered their exhaustion to have been fruitful; recollecting that playful dream-event, they were then filled with wonder.
"This is not a wooden image; it is Brahman manifesting in person. And those two placed their faith in the words of the brahmins who were present in the assembly. (69)
Where are we, great sinners, destined for a succession of torments, and where is this manifestation of Viṣṇu, which stands pervaded by the gods? (70)
"Since we two fools possess proficiency in the eighteen branches of learning, there can be no delusion; therefore, that which conforms to our statement is true knowledge. (71)
They said that the wooden Brahman situated on the bank of the king of holy fords, shining at the root of a banyan tree—by seeing him, a living being is liberated.
That very Lord of the World, established in fourfold form, manifests in four aspects whenever he descends upon the earth. || 73 ||
Then we two shall remain in his presence, sustaining our lives, until we go elsewhere, turning our backs on petty desires. (74)
Having thus resolved, the two sages became devoted to Viṣṇu; constantly chanting the name Nārāyaṇa, they attained liberation.
Jaimini said: Thus has this secret, which destroys all sins, been told incidentally; those who hear this account of Puṇḍarīka and Ambarīṣa [shall likewise be purified]. (76)
Constantly chanting [the names], filled with supreme joy, they go to the abode of Viṣṇu; endowed with supreme delight, they too proceed to the dwelling of Viṣṇu, their sins completely shaken off.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama-kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: O best of the twice-born, in what region is that Puruṣottama-kṣetra, where Nārāyaṇa himself is manifest in the form of wood?
Jaimini said: There is a region named Utkala, renowned as supremely purifying, wherein there are many sacred fords (tīrthas) and meritorious shrines.
That region is situated on the shore of the southern ocean, where the people dwelling there are indeed exemplars of virtuous conduct.

There, the gods of the earth were perfected in conduct and Vedic study, performers of sacrifices; at the beginning of creation, they were the rituals, the Vedas, and the promulgators of the Vedic scriptures.
He is proclaimed as the treasury of the eighteen branches of knowledge; by the command of Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī dwells in every house.
Modest, disciplined, and free from mental anguish and physical disease, those Vaiṣṇava people were devoted to their fathers and mothers and were speakers of truth.
And herein there was no one who was not a devotee of Viṣṇu, nor any atheist; all there were intent on the welfare of others, neither greedy, nor deceitful, nor wicked.
The people there are long-lived, and the women regard their husbands as gods; they are of excellent character, devoted to righteousness, and adorned with modesty and virtuous conduct.
Abounding in pride of beauty and youth, adorned with every ornament, they were distinguished by conduct befitting their lineage, character, age, and behavior.
There, the Kṣatriyas were devoted to their own duties, consecrated to the protection of the subjects, exuberant in their generosity, and proficient in both weapons and the sciences.
All of them constantly perform sacrifices with rituals accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees; their intentions shine forth as they possess sacrificial posts adorned with gold.
In whose houses guests are honored with offerings exceeding their desires, and who are Vaiśyas established in the livelihoods of agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing; || 12 ||
They please the gods, their preceptors, and the twice-born with devotion and even with wealth; yet a petitioner who has gone to the door of one person should not go to another's house.
There, the Śūdras were skilled in song, poetry, the arts, and crafts; they spoke kindly, were righteous, and devoted themselves to the practices of bathing and giving charity.
Those others born of mixed castes who serve the twice-born through action, mind, speech, and wealth, remain established in their respective duties.
The seasons do not change, nor does the cloud rain out of season; there is no loss of crops, no pestilence, and hunger does not afflict the people. (16)
In this place, neither famine nor pestilence arises, nor does the destruction of the kingdom occur; there is no object whatsoever existing on earth that is not obtainable there.
Thus endowed with all virtues, it was filled with various trees and creepers, including Arjuna, Aśoka, Punnāga, Tāla, Hintāla, and Śāla trees.
With *prācīnāmalaka*, *lodhra*, *bakula*, and *nāgakeśara* flowers; with coconuts, *priyāla*, *sarala*, and *devadāru* trees. || 19 ||
With dhava, khadira, bilva, panasa, and kapittha trees; with campaka, karṇikāra, kovidāra, and pāṭala trees as well. || 20 ||
With kadamba, nimba, nicula, rasāla, and āmalaka trees, as well as with nāgaraṅgas, jambīras, nīpakas, and mātuluṅgakas.
With mandāra and pārijāta trees, with nyagrodha, aguru, and candana; with excellent kharjūra and āmrātaka, and with mucukuṇda and kiṃśuka.
It was strewn with *tiṃduka*, *saptaparṇa*, *aśvattha*, and *bibhītaka* trees, as well as various other highly enchanting trees. || 23 ||
And with *mālatī*, *kunda*, and *bāṇa* flowers, with dark-red *karavīra*s, with groves of *ketakī* thickets, and with *atimukta* and *kubjaka* flowers. || 24 ||
It was surrounded by hundreds of gardens and groves of betel-nut trees arranged in rows, along with cardamom, cloves, kaṅkola, pomegranates, and citron trees.
O best of the twice-born, this preeminent region known as Utkala is filled with various trees and creepers and surrounded by mountains and rivers.
Having reached the river Ṛṣikulyā, which flows toward the southern ocean, the region is situated between the Svarṇarekhā and the Mahānadī.

O twice-born ones, there are indeed very many sacred fields in this holy place which were previously described by me during my pilgrimage; however, this Puruṣottama, which is heaven upon earth, has now been recounted.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Land of Oḍhra," in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: O sage, in which yuga did that king Indradyumna exist? In what country was his city, and how did he reach Puruṣottama? || 1 ||
And having gone there, how did he have an image of Viṣṇu fashioned? O great sage, tell all of this in detail.
O Omniscient One, we have indeed a supreme curiosity regarding the truth as it really is.

Jaimini said: Excellent, excellent, O best of the twice-born, that you inquire about this ancient [account], which is meritorious, auspicious, the remover of all sins, and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I shall relate his life and conduct as it occurred in the Kṛta Yuga; listen, all you sages, with full attention and with senses subdued.
O Brahmins, in the Kṛta Yuga there was a great king named Indradyumna; that righteous soul belonged to the Solar dynasty and was the fifth descendant from the Creator.
Truthful, of virtuous conduct, pure, and the foremost among those of sattvic nature, he always protects his subjects with justice as if they were his own children.
He was one who took pride in the knowledge of the inner self, a hero who increased his prowess in battle, ever-exerting, always a worshiper of Brahmins, and devoted to his father.
In the eighteen branches of learning, he was like another Bṛhaspati; in sovereign power, he was like Kubera, the lord of the gods, in the accumulation of treasure.
He was handsome, fortunate, virtuous, a donor, an enjoyer, and sweet-spoken; he performed all sacrifices, was devoted to Brahman, and was true to his promise.
He was beloved by men and women like the moon on a full-moon night, yet he was as difficult to behold as the sun when bringing about the destruction of the enemy host.
A Vaiṣṇava endowed with truthfulness, who has conquered anger and subdued his senses, [obtains the merit of] the Rājasūya, the best of sacrifices, and a thousand Vājimedhas.
The most illustrious king, desiring liberation and devoted to dharma, performed sacrifices; thus, endowed with all virtues, he protected the earth. (13)
He dwelt in the city named Avantī, renowned throughout the land of Mālava, which was enriched with every kind of jewel and was like a second Amarāvatī.
Remaining there, the king, possessing unsurpassed devotion toward Viṣṇu, performed that most wonderful [devotion] with his mind, speech, and actions. (15)
Proceeding in this manner, he once arrived at the time for the worship of the Lord Śrīpati, inside the temple where the deity was being venerated.
Together with learned men, poets renowned for their pilgrimages, astrologers, and Vedic scholars, he stood with the family priest.
With great respect, he spoke thus: "Let this supreme field be discovered, where we may behold the Lord of the World in person with these very eyes. (18)
Thus addressed by the foremost of kings, the Vaiṣṇava, the family priest, looking upon the multitude of pilgrims, spoke these humble words: || 19 ||
"O you virtuous ones, intent on visiting sacred fords and experts in the lore of holy places! Surely you have heard what this lord commands. (20)
Having understood his intention, a certain eloquent man who had visited many sacred fords spoke joyfully to the king, who stood with his palms joined in reverence.
"O King, O Lord, since my childhood I have wandered over this earth visiting many holy places, those very ones which have indeed been heard of by others. (22)
In the region known as Bhārata, there is a land famous as Oḍhra, situated on the shore of the southern ocean; it is the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama.
There, the mountain named Nīlagiri is surrounded on all sides by forests; in its embrace stands a Kalpa tree extending for a krośa in every direction.
By stepping upon its shadow, one casts off the sin of killing a Brahmin. To the west of it is the famous pool known as Rauhiṇa.
It is filled with causal waters that grant liberation through mere touch; situated upon its eastern bank is a [shrine] fashioned from sapphire.
The body of Śrī Vāsudeva is the direct bestower of liberation; having bathed in that pool and beheld Puruṣottama, [one attains it]. || 27 ||
Having obtained the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices, one is liberated; there stands that best of hermitages, renowned as Śabaradīpaka.
In the western direction, it is surrounded by the dwellings of the Śabaras; from there, a path leading to a single footstep (ekapadī) extends by which one may go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
There, the Lord of the World himself, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, that treasure-house of compassion, grants liberation to living beings simply by being seen.
O King, I dwelt there for a year at Śrī Puruṣottama, observing vows as a forest-dweller for the sake of pleasing the God of gods.
O Great King, for the gods who come every night to behold the Blessed One, there is indeed a divine, superhuman fragrance.
A rain of flowers from the wish-fulfilling tree of various words of praise is obtained; yet this greatness of Viṣṇu is not manifested anywhere else.
And an ancient tradition was heard there, O Lord of the Earth: even a crow, though possessing the body of an animal, is liberated upon seeing Mādhava.
O King, one who is devoid of knowledge is not entitled to perform meritorious deeds, just as a man afflicted by thirst who has come to the Rauhiṇa pool to drink water [is not permitted]. (35)
Having abandoned his life-breaths under the power of time, he attained the same form as Viṣṇu; formerly I was a fool, but now, by his grace, I am [wise]. (36)
"Among the eighteen branches of knowledge, I am either the remainder or something else besides them; my intellect has become pure, O Viṣṇu, and I perceive nothing other than You. (37)
Since you are a devotee of Viṣṇu and always firm in your vows, I have therefore come into your presence for the purpose of instructing you.
Neither wealth nor land is being requested from you now; do not perceive this as a deception, but worship Śrīdhara who resides there. (39)
Having spoken thus, while everyone was looking on, the matted-haired ascetic then suddenly vanished; the king was filled with the utmost wonder.

Having obtained [the kingdom], his mind became agitated with the thought, "How shall this be accomplished for me? and he spoke thus to the domestic priest regarding the means to achieve that very purpose.
Indradyumna said: Having now heard this superhuman account from a superhuman being, my mind hastens toward that place where the wielder of the mace (Gadādhara) resides.
"O best of the twice-born, my dharma, artha, and kāma indeed depend upon you; through your favor, I have accomplished this triad of goals without conflict. (43)
O best of the twice-born, if you were to proceed now toward this goal, then the complete fourfold aim of life would have been attained by me at this very moment. (44)
The family priest said: "Certainly, I shall do this so that you will see Keśava—the omnipresent Lord who directly bestows liberation—with your eyes covered by armor. (45)
Thus I shall strive here so that we all, together with our companions, may dwell in that sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama.
O King, what greater success could there be for a living being than this: that you shall directly behold Mādhava, the Supreme Person who stands beyond the darkness? (47)
"My younger brother, named Vidyāpati, shall now depart with spies who are accustomed to wandering through various lands. (48)
Having gone there and beheld the Lord of the World on the mountain just as he had seen him before, he measured out a portion of ground for the site of Kaṇṭakāvāsa.
"Bringing news quickly will be for our benefit. Having heard those words of his, the king spoke again.
Indradyumna said: "Excellent, O Brahmin! Having composed yourself, this resolve has been well-considered; indeed, from the very moment I first heard this, I have made my decision. (51)
I dwell in that field in the presence of the Blessed One; therefore, let your brother go, for he will accomplish his purpose as he desires.
Having spoken thus, the king entered the inner apartments filled with joy; the priest also addressed them all in due order, exactly as was appropriate.
Having honored him by the king's command, he sent him to his own hermitage at an auspicious moment, as determined by the astrologers.
Then, having mounted a flower-chariot accompanied by trustworthy scouts who were skilled at clearing the way, he set forth after the brahmins had performed the rites for his safe journey.
Then, O brahmins, that twice-born Vidyāpati, having set out and mounted his chariot, reflected thus in his mind: || 56 ||
"Oh, my birth is fruitful and this night is auspicious for me, since I shall behold the lotus-face of the Blessed One, which destroys all sins! (57)
Through means such as hearing and so forth, striving day and night, ascetics behold that which is situated within the lotus of the heart.
Today I shall behold with my own eyes that wielder of the discus, who stands upon the peak of the blue mountain and possesses a form that removes all attachment to the physical body.
O Treasure of Śrī, having beheld that form never seen before—which cannot be established by the words of the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas—I shall cross the ocean of worldly existence. 60.

Today I shall behold face to face that immeasurable Lord of the Universe who dwells upon the mountain—the mere chanting of whose name brings about the destruction of the three-fold host of sins for those who remember him. (61)

The darkness born from the intense growth of ignorance, which has been accumulated through every step by one who has failed to follow the lotus feet of [the Lord], never departs from the self; yet it goes to destruction through [His] actions. 62.

I bow to that Primordial One, who is to be known solely through self-knowledge; whom the voice of the Vedānta describes as the subtle one dwelling in one's own cave, enveloped by the five sheaths, yet situated within the Self, and whom even that voice does not fully know.

I take refuge in the Ancient One, who wears a garland of cosmic eggs upon every hair, whose heads, feet, and eyes are thousands in number, from whose breath arises the mass of the Vedas, and who is the Lord of the entire phenomenal world.

This form, which sports in the creation, destruction, and maintenance [of the world] as a peak fashioned by illusion, is the nature of the Praṇava—devoid of its own essential nature, characterized by the superimposition of what is to be rejected, and yet determined [as such]. (65)
Even though he approached my presence by chance merely to quench the thirst of a beast, he attained liberation with a body identical to his own; I shall bring him within the range of my vision.

Oh, oh! Truly, my fortune is proclaimed by this one who has arisen through the merit accumulated over ten million births; indeed, with these eyes of flesh, I shall behold the primordial root of the universe.
Reflecting thus with a delighted inner soul, the brahmin did not perceive that he had traveled a great distance due to the speed of the chariot.
When the day had passed and many days were delayed, a land that adorned the world became visible ahead on the path.

O Brahmins, he who was known as Oḍhra, the purifier of the earth's surface, while thus beholding the forest edges and mountain fastnesses along his path, arrived at the bank of a great river at the time of sunset.
Having descended from his chariot and performed his daily rites with devotion, the brahmin worshipped the evening twilight and meditated upon Madhusūdana.
Having spent the night seated upon the back of the chariot, he hurriedly crossed the great river and completed his morning rites.
Meditating upon Govinda, he set forth seated in his chariot, beholding the path of the Blessed One along which the Vedic scholars and sacrificers travel.
Passing through villages adorned with guilds of brahmins possessing the brilliance of fire, that twice-born man proceeded as far as the Eka-amraka forest.
He beheld people bearing conchs, discs, maces, and lotuses; he recognized himself as having passed through another birth and now possessed a divine form.
Quickly descending from his chariot and prostrating with all eight limbs, his eyes filled with tears of joy, he saw nothing else at all.
O twice-born ones, while seeing Viṣṇu both mentally and externally, as the brahmin thus proceeded, meditating upon, beholding, and praising Hari; (77)
He beheld the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala), covered with forests and adorned by a banyan tree like the Kalpa-tree, scraping the sky and destroying the sins of those who behold it.
"How extraordinary! These embodied beings dwell as the very personification of Hari. Having ascended to the foothills, the twice-born one searched all around.
That brahmin, eager for the sight of Mukunda, found no path; then, having spread kusha grass upon the ground, he lay down with his speech restrained.
Upon seeing that god, he went to him alone for refuge; then he heard an unhuman voice from behind the mountain.
As they were conversing among themselves regarding the subject of devotion to the Blessed One, Vidyāpati, being delighted, followed him and indeed went along.
O twice-born ones, he beheld the site of the lamp of the sacred field, renowned as Śabaradīpaka, surrounded on all sides by the dwellings of the Śabaras. 83.
Having gone there, the brahmin entered slowly and with humility; he beheld those devotees of Viṣṇu bearing conchs, discs, and maces.
Then the brahmin, having bowed his head and standing with palms joined in reverence, there appeared a Śabara named Viśvāvasu, whose body was grey with age.
O twice-born ones, having completed the worship of Hari and being adorned with the remnants of that worship, he arrived from the midst of the mountain at that very moment.
Beholding him, the twice-born man was filled with joy and reflected: "This man has arrived from the abode of Hari, exhausted and adorned with the remains of the Lord's offerings."
"From here, I, the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas, shall obtain news of Viṣṇu that is difficult to find. While the Brahmin was thus reflecting, he was addressed by the Śabara.
The Śabara said: "O Brahmin, from where have you come to this most difficult forest? You are exceedingly exhausted by hunger and thirst; please remain here at your ease for a long time. (89)
Having offered water for the feet, a seat, and the guest-offering (arghya) to the twice-born, Viśvāvasu spoke with humble words, setting forth the matter at hand.
"O Brahmin, let your sustenance be provided by fruits or by what is ripe; whatever pleases you, that indeed shall be given to you here by me, O twice-born one. (91)
O Blessed One, my fortune is great today and my life has become fruitful; for you have arrived at my home, O Brahmin, like a second Viṣṇu in person.
To the Śabara who was speaking thus, the bull among the twice-born replied: "O best of Vaiṣṇavas, I have no need for fruits nor for cooked food."
O virtuous one, make fruitful that purpose for which you have come from afar—the purpose of King Indradyumna, a resident of the city of Avanti.
"I am the royal priest who has arrived, longing for a vision of Viṣṇu; indeed, I heard this in the presence of the king during the assembly of the heretics. (95)
Then, in connection with the topic of sacred fords and holy fields, that field was indeed presented by a certain matted-haired ascetic (jaṭila) before the king.
And that twice-born man related all of that in due order; "O virtuous one, it was for this purpose that I have been sent by the king who is indeed full of longing. (97)
"I have been sent to see Hari Nīlamādhava residing here; until I have seen him and shall report the news to the king, I too [shall remain]. (98)
O virtuous one, you are surely fasting; therefore, show that Viṣṇu to me.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: Having been addressed thus by that brahmin, the Śabara was overwhelmed with anxiety: "This Janārdana, who dwells in secret, is our very means of livelihood. (1)
"An ill fortune has befallen us, by which he might become world-renowned; if I do not show him the Brahmin, he will cast a curse upon me. (2)
"A Brāhmaṇa is to be honored by all, especially this guest; if his desire remains unfulfilled, both worlds become fruitless for me. (3)
Reflecting thus, Viśvāvasu, the preeminent Śabara, recalled an ancient popular saying from his former dwelling among the Śabaras.
When this god Āditya had vanished and Āditya was absorbed within the earth, there arose King Indradyumna, whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra.
Indeed, even one who might go to the world of Brahmā in human form, having come here with his progeny and performed a hundred horse-sacrifices, [attains this].
Having performed a sacrifice, he will install a wooden image of Viṣṇu in four forms; for this Brahmin guest, great fortune has indeed arisen.
There shall be both the disappearance and the presence of the Blessed One; therefore, I will show him this infallible sapphire gem.
"It is not the work of any human being, but was fashioned by a god. Having reflected thus in his mind again and again, the Śabara [spoke].
He spoke to the Brahmin who was meditating before him upon the imperishable Viṣṇu.
Śabara said: "Indeed, we have already heard this news before: the king Indradyumna will take up residence here."
"O Brahmin, you are indeed fortunate that you behold Nīlamādhava before your very eyes; come, let us go to the mountain plateau."
Having spoken thus, he took him by the hand and proceeded along the path into the dense forest, ascending higher and higher upon a road made treacherous by rocks.

And on a path that was difficult to traverse, overgrown with thorns, shrouded in darkness, and accessible only one person at a time, he awakened the twice-born man as he traveled along by means of his speech.
Within two muhūrtas, they reached the bank of the Rauhiṇa Kuṇḍa. Seeing it, he said to the brahmin: "O best of the twice-born, this is that very kuṇḍa."
The great holy site named Rauhiṇa is the source of all waters; having bathed here, O twice-born one, a man goes to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
In the eastern part of this place is that great banyan tree, the Shadow of the Kalpa; by entering its shade, one casts off even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O Brahmin, behold between these two, situated within a bower, the Lord of the World himself, as propounded by the Vedāntas. (18)
Having seen this, abandon the entire accumulation of various evils; henceforth, do not grieve, for you have fallen into the ocean of existence. 19.
