Jaimini said: Having bathed in the pool, that wise twice-born man, his mind filled with joy, bowed from afar to Hari with his head, mind, and speech.
And with a one-pointed mind, he praised him with a voice faltering with joy. || 21 ||

Vidyāpati said: O you who transcend both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, O all-pervading one, O higher than the highest, O ultimate reality that is the transformation of all things moving and unmoving—salutations be to you! (22)
O Lord of the Universe, you alone are to be propitiated through those rites established by the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas. (23)
O All-pervading Lord, this entire universe is brought forth from you at the time of creation; O God, this world has you as its support and is protected by you alone. (24)
At the end of the eon, everything withdrawn is contained within your belly with ample space; O Soul of All, O Inner Controller, you dwell there in bliss—salutations be to you!
Salutations to you, the God of gods; salutations to you who are the embodiment of the three Vedas. Through the forms of the moon, the sun, and other luminaries, you eternally illuminate the universe.
Salutations to Him who purifies all beings; by contact with whose lotus feet the Gaṅgā, embodying all sacred fords, sanctifies all the worlds.
Salutations to you, who sustain the world, for the sake of the transformation of the oblations—purified by mantras and duly offered into the fires—which bring life to all beings. || 28 ||
Salutations to that Self which is Brahman, who is free from all impurities and whose nature is bliss, upon a portion of whom the worlds subsist.
Salutations to You, the witness of the universe, who are stainless, whose nature is the true self, whose form is auspicious, who possess the power of *māyā*, and who are free from all attachments.
Salutations to you, who possess many feet, eyes, heads, mouths, and arms; to the all-conquering one, whose nature is that of all living beings, and who takes every form.
Salutations to you, O beloved of Kamalā; salutations to you, O one whose seat is the lotus. Salutations to you, O lotus-petal-eyed one; protect me, O Supreme Person.
Truly oppressed by disease and sorrow through wandering in this essence-less saṃsāra, I have come for refuge at your lotus feet; lift me up from this mass of worldly suffering.
Jaimini said: Having thus praised the Lord of the gods, the deity whose form is the *praṇava*, he bowed down and chanted the *praṇava* mantra before Hari.

At the conclusion of his recitation, the Śabara spoke to the twice-born man, who stood before him with a tranquil mind and palms joined in reverence, considering himself to have achieved his life's purpose.
Viśvāvasu said: "O best of the twice-born, you have achieved your purpose by seeing the Lord now. The day has come to an end; let us go home, for you are hungry and weary. (36)
"Even dwelling in the forest is not a fitting state for us who are predators; while the light of the sun still shines, let us go to our own abode. (37)
Having spoken thus and taking the brahmin by the hand, O best of the twice-born, the Śabara returned to his own hermitage with great haste.
The Brahmin, too, meditating upon the Lord of the World, the ocean of bliss, did not perceive at all the sufferings born of hunger, thirst, and fatigue. (39)
Even while traveling on a path as treacherous as stone and difficult to traverse due to heaps of thorns, he experienced no suffering, but instead felt joy through his lack of attachment to the body.
O brahmins, traveling in this manner, those two—the brāhmaṇa and the śabara—both foremost among Vaiṣṇavas, reached that abode of the śabaras at sunset.
There, the best of the Śabaras honored the Brāhmaṇa who had arrived as a guest with various kinds of foods, both hard and soft.
Then, fully satisfied by the royal services provided by the Śabara—services that were extremely rare—he attained the highest state of wonder. (43)
"This Śabara dwells in the midst of a rugged forest, subsisting on forest-dwellers; how could he have [such things] within his house? (44)
"Food and drink fit for a king are easily obtained here; this is a great marvel!"—thus did the Śabara then address the Brāhmaṇa, who was filled with wonder.
Bowing low with great humility, he spoke with affectionate words. || 46 ||
The Śabara said: "O Brahmin, are you free from fatigue? Are you devoid of hunger and thirst? For city-dwellers, what happiness can there be in the abode of forest-dwellers? (47)
The conduct of the city-dwellers was unknown, especially by the Śabaras; among those who subsisted upon the king, the chief were the royal minister and the domestic priest. 48.
The priest Indradyumna, equal to the three gods, was worthy of worship and esteemed by the scriptures; he was a sovereign monarch, a lord of men, and possessed of great majesty. (49)

"But when you are satisfied, O Brahmin, he will certainly be satisfied," said the one dwelling in the forest. Having spoken thus, that twice-born man, being even more pleased, spoke with affection and humility to the Śabara who had uttered such wonderful words. (50)
Vidyāpati said: "O virtuous one, these objects which you have brought for my service are superhuman things that have never been seen here by kings."
"How wonderful is this collection of divine objects in the dwelling of a Śabara! O virtuous one, my curiosity to learn about this grows ever greater. (52)
Śabara said: "O Brahmin, my mind does not venture to reveal this; nevertheless, O best of the twice-born, out of devotion to you as a guest, I shall speak. (53)
O twice-born one, the hosts of gods, headed by Śakra, arrive daily bringing divine offerings for the worship of the Lord of the World.
Having worshipped the Lord of the World, having praised and bowed to him with devotion, and having gratified Puruṣottama with songs, instrumental music, and dances; || 55 ||
Furthermore, these excellent gods constantly go to the third heaven with these divine objects, which are the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) of the Lord of the World.
These have been given to you, a wise man; why do you express such astonishment? By partaking of the remains of Viṣṇu’s offerings, our diseases and old age have been destroyed.
Together with our sons and kinsmen, we all dwell with a lifespan of ten thousand years; by the enjoyment of Viṣṇu’s remains (nirmālya), the entire mass of our sins is destroyed.
"O best of the twice-born, it is no wonder that one should become a vessel for liberation by this; having heard of this rare rite, the Brahmin Romaharṣaṇa—"
With eyes blurred by tears of joy, he considered himself to have achieved his life's purpose: "Oh, this Śabara-born man beholds the imperishable Lord! (60)
Day and night he enjoys that divine luxury which is the remnant of his [master’s] meal; there is no one else like him in this world, including all that is mobile and immobile upon the earth.
"What is the use of returning today to my home with my unhappy family, when this Śabara on Mount Nīla is such a devotee of Viṣṇu? (62)
"Having established friendship with him, I shall remain here in this forest," the Brahmin thought for a long time, his mind deeply attached to Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (63)
He spoke again to the Śabara: "O virtuous one, if you have favor toward me, you must form a friendship with me; this is my firm resolve. (64)
What is the use of going to serve the king for the sake of unhappiness in the next world? Rather, staying here with you and worshipping Madhusūdana, [one attains bliss]. 65.
Furthermore, I shall strive so that this bondage of the body may not occur for me again; O good friend, by my good fortune, this meeting with you has come to pass.
"By your grace, I shall cross over this difficult-to-traverse cycle of existence; they praise this as the essence within the ocean of worldly existence. (67)

Indeed, through this friendship with the devotee of Viṣṇu, which carries one to the further shore of the suffering of saṃsāra, he will once again attain direct perception [of the Lord] by dwelling together with that friend.
O friend, when I have returned, the Lord Puṇḍarīkākṣa, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, and King Indradyumna will be there.
He will dwell right here in order to propitiate the Blessed One, desiring to build a vast palace here that is dear to the Blessed One.
"I shall perform a thousand services for the worship of the Lord of the World"—this was the great vow of the lord of the earth. (71)
That was promised in his presence; being pleased, may he grant me permission for it. || 72 ||
Śabara said: "Friend, such an ancient account is indeed well-known here."
Just as you have described the meeting with Indradyumna, the lord of the earth will see nothing there but Mādhava.
Before long, the Blessed One, covered by golden sands, promised Yama that he would go into concealment.
"Through the ripening of great fortune, this [being] has been made manifest by you; he will certainly remove the obstacles near the arrival of Indradyumna. (76)
"O friend, this matter must not be spoken by you in the presence of the king; for that king, having arrived here and not seeing the Supreme Lord," 77 ||
Having observed the vow of fasting unto death (prāyopaveśa) and having seen Gadādhara in a dream, he [constructed] four wooden lingas of the Lord according to His command.
Having established it himself, he shall worship it with devotion; as long as Hari remains here, so long shall our lineage endure. (79)
Because of the grace of the Blessed One, no deliberation is required here; therefore, my friend, do not feel despondent regarding this matter, for it shall be accomplished very quickly indeed.
"It will be completed very soon; friend, sleep now in peace. Tomorrow morning, you shall see again the Lord, the All-pervading One, made of sapphire. (81)
"O friend, having bathed in the Sindhu, we shall see a suitable dwelling on its bank for the king, exactly as he desires. (82)
Having thus engaged in various other meritorious conversations with one another, they both lay down to sleep on a bed strewn with sprouts in a beautiful place.
When the night had turned to dawn, having performed their ritual bath with the water of the King of Tīrthas according to the rules and having prostrated before Mādhava, the two of them— || 84 ||
Having determined a place worthy of a king for their residence, they returned there; and having been consecrated by a friend, they did so at the command of the king.
Having mounted his chariot, that brahmin went to the city of Avantī.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: Then, when the brahmin had returned in the evening amidst a throng of gods, at the time for the worship of Mādhava, a wind blew with a fierce velocity.
And he scattered golden sands everywhere; because of that, the gods, their vision obscured, were unable to look.
Then, O Brahmins, those inhabitants of heaven fixed their gaze steadily upon Puruṣottama, the beloved of Śrī, for the duration of a muhūrta while they remained absorbed in meditation.
At the conclusion of their meditation, they saw a mound of sand instead of Mādhava; likewise, seeing the pool of Rauhiṇa, their senses became agitated with distress.
They fell into great anxiety and wept bitterly, crying out, "Alas! Alas! "What is this? Surely some ill fortune has suddenly befallen us. (5)
The Lord of Śrī, who is the delight of the eyes, is not perceived by us even for a moment; O Puruṣottama, what offense of ours has been noticed?
O Lord of the World, you have abandoned all your servants at once and are no longer seen—you for whose sake you took up this physical body.
O lotus-eyed one, why do you neglect them and abandon those who are protectorless in the forest, having forsaken us—the very manifestations of your own body?
"Why do you cause the gods to become mere remnants of a story so untimely? For all of us, who are born from your portions, are indeed worshipped by sacrificers."
O Lord of Sacrifice, for Your pleasure, we—whose bodies are composed of Your ego and whose lives depend upon Your grace—perform these acts that bestow fruits as ordained by You.
"Where shall we go now, abandoned by you and fleeing in all directions? O Mādhava, what purpose is there in our celestial abodes if we do not behold you? (11)
"Deprived by you, we shall become forest-dwellers with our purposes unfulfilled—[deprived] of you who are like the stainless moon of nectar and who surpasses all beauty. (12)
If we do not behold your face, we shall not go to the abode of the gods; having undertaken supreme austerity right here, we shall remain with our vows firmly resolved.
We shall live by the forest-dweller's way of life, wearing matted hair and bark garments, until we behold you, O lotus-eyed one. (14)
O ocean of innate compassion, you ought to protect us who are wretched—us who are helpless, whose hearts are dejected, and who have come to you alone for refuge. 15.
O Lord of the World, rescue us with the raft of your auspicious vision as we sink into the shoreless ocean of grief caused by the lack of your sight. 16.
While all those inhabitants of heaven were thus lamenting there, an incorporeal voice then manifested once again.
In this matter, O gods, you ought to exert yourselves; do not act in vain. From this day forward, the sight of the Lord will be difficult to obtain on earth. (18)
Even by bowing to him at this very spot, one shall obtain the fruit of beholding him; having gone into the presence of the Self-born One, you will certainly come to know the cause.
Having heard that, all the gods approached Brahmā to hear the account of Yama’s favor and his terrible incarnation.
Having heard this, they all went to heaven with contented minds; but that brahmin Vidyāpati, mounted upon his chariot, reflected thus: || 21 ||
My purpose has indeed been accomplished, since Nīlamādhava has been seen; let me now wander about and observe this sacred field from every side.

Having circumambulated that supreme and most meritorious field known as Śrī Puruṣottama—the unsurpassed place whose very glorification removes impurity, though never seen before—I shall depart quickly. (23)

Those who circumambulate this forest of all sins, known as Puruṣottama and adorned with the Blue Mountain, obtain a hundredfold the fruit of circumambulating the entire earth; my friend taught me of this on the shore of the ocean.
Having reflected thus, O best of the twice-born, he then wandered about, beholding the sacred field and the forest filled with various groves of trees.
Resounding with the cries of various flocks of birds and filled with the humming of warbling bees, it was unpenetrated by the rays of the sun and covered by groves of shady trees.
It was endowed with flowers of every season, adorned with creepers and shrubs, and filled with cranes warbling from the banks of various reservoirs of water.
There, the water was adorned with blooming lotuses, kahlāras, kumudas, and utpalas; not even a single creeper or plant there was devoid of flowers.
Then that best of brahmins, having circumambulated that sacred field with speed, went forth; meditating and fasting, the wise one reached Avanti at the close of day.
O brahmins, having previously been informed by messengers that one who was far away had arrived, King Indradyumna experienced supreme joy upon hearing it.
Desiring his arrival and having worshipped Janārdana, he remained there with a joyful mind together with learned brāhmaṇas. || 31 ||
In the meantime, O Brahmins, that twice-born Vidyāpati was ushered in by doorkeepers holding staffs in their hands, who preceded him.
Shown the way by the citizens who were filled with curiosity and given their approval, he [bore] the very beautiful offering-garland of Mādhava known as Nīla.

Placing his hand [upon it], he entered with haste before the king. Upon seeing him, the monarch then rose from his excellent throne and, saying, "Be gracious, O Lord of the World," approached his presence. (34)
Today my life has become fruitful through the deeds of this birth, since I behold here Mādhava, whose body is like a garland of *nirmālya*.

I bow to the garland upon the head of Mukunda, which surpasses the fragrance of the celestial tree by bestowing incomparable joy, which has blinded the swarms of bees, and which, with its scent spreading on the wind, destroys the impurities of the world.

I bow to the garland of Viṣṇu, which is the abode of flowers clinging to the radiant unguents on his body, and by contact with the dust falling from whose lotus feet Brahmā and the other gods attained supreme prosperity.
She laughs at that proud Padmā who dwells in the heart-lotus along with her husband, for she herself resides on the lap of Viṣṇu amidst blossoming, beautiful flowers. || 38 ||
Where did this radiant garland, which for a long time had pervaded every limb upon the body of the Treasure of Beauty (Śrīnidhi), obtain such greatness? (39)

Victory to you, the ornament of the peak of the Blue Mountain, the destroyer of sins! O glorious one, remover of the distress of those who bow before you, protect me, who have come to you for refuge. 40.
Speaking thus with a voice faltering with tears, the king touched the ground with his head, his body covered in a mantle of quivering horripilation.
That Brahmin Vidyāpati, having destroyed all his impurities, stood before the king with a divine body, absorbed in meditation upon Mādhava.
May the wise Lord, whose abode is on the peak of the Blue Mountain, purify your sins with his splendor that washes away the sins of all the worlds, and may he bestow his grace upon you.
This command of the Lord of Śrī has been revealed to you in the form of a garland, so that you may behold your own Self, which resides in the supreme field and directly bestows liberation.
Uttering these words, he released the garland around the king's neck; the monarch, too, rose up with the garland hanging upon his heart.
Having seen him, she considered him to be the beloved of Śrī herself, entering her very heart; placing her hands upon his head, she closed her eyes slightly.
With his face moistened by tears of joy, he praised Hari.

Indradyumna said: Victory to You, the architect of the creation, sustenance, and destruction of the entire universe; You who bear the burden of as many cosmic eggs as there are hairs on Your playful universal body! 48.
O Inner Controller of all, O Lord who removes the suffering of those who bow before you, whose lotus feet are variegated by the crowns of Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra! 49.
O Supreme Being, whose sole and constant purpose is the protection of the distressed, the helpless, and the afflicted; O ocean of the waters of sincere compassion! 50.
O Lord of the World, you who are ever-compassionate toward your devotees, protect me, who am wretched, filled with beginningless delusion, and have you alone as my refuge. 51.
Praising thus, the lord of men sat down upon his own throne, surrounded by householders, celibate students, ascetics, and forest-dwellers.
Together with twice-born sacrificers skilled in the eighteen branches of knowledge, with fish, with elderly servants, and preceded by his ministers— (53)
Having honored the Vidyāpati with great respect, having seated him on a seat before him, and having first inquired after his welfare; 54.
With attentive joy, he inquired about the greatness and the true nature of Viṣṇu, whose body is like blue sapphire, and of the sacred field of Puruṣottama.
Questioned by the Kṣatriya regarding his own experience, that Brāhmaṇa [related] everything from his entry into the island of the Bhillas up to his immersion in the lord of rivers (the ocean).
He related in detail the account of that most excellent field: the ascent of the Blue Mountain and the vision of Nīlamādhava.
He [described] the bath in the Rauhiṇa pool, the greatness of the banyan tree, the eight Śambhus beginning with Nṛsiṃha, and the established presence of the eight Śaktis.
Having traversed the field by chariot, he described its length and breadth exactly as they were and in their proper sequence.
Having heard that wonderful and incomparable account previously related by the heretics, the king, filled with confidence and a joyful heart, spoke to him again: (60)
Indradyumna said: "O Blessed One, I have previously heard from you about this most excellent sacred field, which is very difficult to attain; O best of the twice-born, describe it to me now. (61)
Vidyāpati spoke: "I shall indeed describe to you, exactly as it is, the form of Viṣṇu who has the nature of a sapphire; I shall tell you of the divine form of the Lord of the Universe. (62)
That ancient image, made of sapphire stone, which, when seen with the physical eye, becomes a vessel for liberation. (63)
I, who am daily worshipped by the gods led by Brahmā, Rudra, and Indra—this divine garland has indeed been placed upon me for worship by the celestial beings.
O King, this garland born of the Sragdharā meter does not wither, nor is it deprived of its fragrance; even after many days have passed, it remains just like this. (65)
O King, do you not see me, whose sins have been destroyed by eating the remains of divine offerings, and who possess superhuman splendor? (66)

O best of kings, for one who eats even once [a day], hunger, thirst, and the loss of strength do not cause affliction; and when something is perceived, there is no need to postulate what is unperceived. (67)
O King, both enjoyment and liberation exist there simultaneously; indeed, no suffering such as old age, disease, or grief is found there. (68)

There, the all-pervading Lord of the World is present in person, with a gracious countenance, his eyes like the petals of a blooming blue lotus, bestowing the nectar of liberation upon those who have sought refuge.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Śrī Puruṣottama," in the dialogue between the sages and Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Indradyumna said: O best of the twice-born, since you have not traveled there since birth, how could you know the divine account concerning Puruṣottama?
Vidyāpati said: Standing there, I approached the Blessed One in the evening; at that time, a cool breeze wafted with a divine fragrance.
A tumultuous sound was heard in the path of the sky; it was a noise consisting of syllables such as "Go forward! and "Advance by degrees! (3).
O lord of the earth, in the presence of Vaikuṇṭha, there occurred a gathering where the mountains were covered by a shower of falling flowers from those dwelling in heaven.
There arose the sound of lutes, flutes, drums, and cymbals, never heard before, mingled with divine singing.
There, for the pleasure of the Supreme Lord, a thousand offerings were presented by the gods—offerings never before seen by humans.
Having worshipped the God according to the prescribed rite, they honored Madhusūdana with hymns preceded by cries of "Victory," while being marked only by their hands [in the gesture of salutation].
The thirty gods departed for the abode of the thirty as they had come; once they had gone, my friend Śabara Viśvāvasu remained.
He gave me these divine offerings and foods, as well as this garland; it is priceless, unfading, and bestows the happiness of sovereignty and prosperity. (9)
It destroys misfortune, sin, and demons; it is worthy and has been brought by me. Listen to the description of that supreme field of Viṣṇu.
His unprecedented skill in craftsmanship and his enchanting form cannot indeed be described by a man born of this earth. (11)
I shall describe to you that field, characterized by both destiny and human effort, which is densely covered on all sides and has a blue mountain as its center.
It is renowned for its length and breadth as being five *krośas*, and it is situated on the shore of the King of Tīrthas, covered with golden sand.
On the peak of the mountain stands a great, lofty banyan tree, vast and enduring for an eon; it is a league in length, devoid of flowers and fruit, yet radiant with its foliage.
Indeed, when the sun moves away, its shadow does not recede; for behind it is the pool known as Rohiṇa.
Adorned with blue stones rising from the water, it was surrounded on all four sides by external crystal platforms.
It was filled with delightful waters that remove the mass of sins, situated in the middle of its eastern altar, cooled by the shade of a banyan tree.
O Lord, the deity made of sapphire, bearing the discus and mace, sits upon a golden lotus measuring eighty-one finger-breadths.
The region of his forehead surpasses the beauty of the crescent moon on the eighth day; his eyes are intent upon mocking the splendor of a pair of blooming blue lotuses.
He releases one from the threefold torment arising from the rising sun of the nectar of his face; he is beautified by the sesame flowers shining upon his two nostrils.
Although his body was composed of stone, his lower lip was moistened by a beautiful smile; and from his two cheeks, blossoming with laughter, his chin and jaw appeared radiant.
The pair of corners of the mouth (sṛkkiṇī) was naturally formed as never before; the cheeks were sunken due to laughter, and the chin and corners of the mouth were auspicious.
The Lord provided an illustration for the artisans, beginning with Viśvakarman; he was adorned by a pair of ears beautified by ornaments in the shape of crocodile mouths.
Between Jupiter and Venus, he appeared like the full moon mocking them, as onlookers beheld him with a neck that was the source of the beauty of a jeweled necklace.
He bore the appearance of one born from a right-spiraling conch-shell; he had a pair of thick, long shoulders and four arms reaching down to his knees.
The omnipresent Lord, whose chest is adorned with a pure, stainless, and magnificent necklace, bears reflected within it the divine Kaustubha jewel of the fourteen worlds.
He was charming with a line of fine body hair entering the lake of his deep navel; by means of the three folds in his waist, he brought about the transformation of his necklace into a pillar.
The two buttocks of the Lord shine like a casket containing the beauty of the entire world, adorned with a girdle of excellent jewels and a string of pearls and tiny bells.
Her pair of pillar-like shanks was adorned with a garland hanging from her hips and a yellow garment, serving as the support for the auspicious archway of liberation.
The feet of the Lord shine with knees that are rounded and well-proportioned, with ankle-ornaments reaching down to the forepart of the feet, and with bracelets richly set with jewels. (30)
Adorned with necklaces, bracelets, armlets, crowns, and other ornaments, Keśava resides within the Śabdabrahman consisting of knowledge, ego, and sovereignty.
Bearing the transformations of the discus, lotus, mace, and conch, the God who illuminates all hopes stands upon the Blue Mountain.
By seeing whom and bowing with devotion, one is liberated from the bondage of the body; Lakṣmī is on his left side, embraced by him who holds a lotus in his hand.
Intent on playing the lute, her eyes fixed upon the face of the Blessed One, she was the abode of all beauty and adorned with every ornament. (34)
I beheld those two, the parents of the world, standing as firm as mountains; they were silent, yet they looked upon me with favoring, smiling glances.
"O wise one, for the sake of showing favor to the distressed, let those two remain alive; Śeṣa stands behind them with his multitude of hoods serving as a canopy. (36)
He saw Sudarśana standing before him, bearing his own form with palms joined in reverence, while Garuḍa stood behind him.
Having thus beheld him of such wondrous form, the Lord of Śrī himself, she ran toward that very spot as if drawn there by the ropes of her heart. (38)
If virtuous deeds have been accumulated over many thousands of births and they ripen simultaneously for someone, that person indeed beholds Him.
Even by means of bathing at sacred fords, asceticism, charity, sacrifices to the gods, and vows, a mortal is not able even to behold such a Supreme Person. (40)

Those who meditate upon Viṣṇu, whose form is blue and resembles the stainless sky, abiding in Puruṣottama—they, with their bonds severed, enter the city of Viṣṇu, reaching which one does not grieve here.

Whatever various fruits of action for human beings are brought forth by the eighteen branches of knowledge—all that together amounts to but a hundredth part of the merit gained from a single vision of this Viṣṇu.

O Lord of the Earth, what more need be said here? A man may obtain all his desires as far as his intellect can reach; yet, by bowing to the Lord of the Blue Mountain, he shall obtain even more than that through the majesty of this sacred field.

He alone is the giver, he is the sacrificer with rituals, he is the speaker of truth, and he is indeed one whose nature is dharma—he who has beheld Nīlādri-nātha, the most excellent of all beings through all his virtues. (44)
O King, it was from those who are the servants of Mādhava, the Lord of the World, that I learned this majesty.
Having heard this well-known narrative, which has been handed down through tradition since the primordial creation, I have indeed come here.
"Having gone there at your command and beheld Śrī Puruṣottama, I have reported it to you, O Indra among kings; do as you wish."
Indradyumna said: "O Blessed One, having heard from the words of the trustworthy one regarding Your sin-destroying form, I have achieved my purpose through contact with Your divine remains. (48)
The sins accumulated over many births have been exhausted for me; I have now become qualified for the vision of the Lord of Śrī in this world.
With my whole being, I shall go to that kingdom of great prosperity; there indeed I will establish my residence and construct fortified cities.
With the horse sacrifice (hayamedha) rite, I shall worship for the pleasure of the Enemy of Mura; day by day, I shall honor Śrīnātha with a hundredfold offerings.
"Through vows, fasts, and observances, I shall propitiate the Teacher of the World, so that he may sprinkle me with the nectar of his speech as if I were parched with heat. (52)
The Lord, the all-pervading Nārāyaṇa himself, who is compassionate toward the wretched, was thus praised with faith and devotion by him until the Lord [was fully extolled].
Nārada, curious to behold the worlds, arrived there; seeing that approaching sage, the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas and the son of Brahmā, [he was filled with wonder].

O Brahmins, at that time the king hoped for the accomplishment of his purpose; rising suddenly, he approached him who was seated upon an excellent throne with water for the feet, the guest-offering, and water for rinsing the mouth, and bowing with palms joined in reverence, he spoke as follows.
Indradyumna said: "Today my sacrifices, my charity, my study, and my asceticism have become fruitful."
O Sage, although my purpose has been fulfilled through the grace of your arrival, the second body of Brahmā has come to my house. (57)
Nevertheless, for the sake of your grace, what command shall I carry out for you? With what purpose in mind has my abode been sanctified? (58)
Jaimini said: Having heard those words of the king, which were tender with devotion and humility, the son of Brahmā spoke to the lord of the earth with a smile. (59)
Nārada said: O Indradyumna, best of kings, the gods, the Siddhas, and the Munis, together with Brahmā, have been delighted by the pure abundance of your virtues.
Each of your individual qualities, when established separately, is sufficient for your desired abiding in the abode of Brahman. (61)
Having descended to see the man staying at Badarāśrama, your resolve was known [by me] during that moment of his meditation.
Excellent is your resolve, O King, that such an intellect has arisen in you! O Lord of the Earth, devotion arises through practice over a thousand lifetimes.
While Mādhava, the husband of the worlds, was dwelling in the cave of the Blue Mountain, the highly wise Grandfather (Brahmā), having propitiated that Lord of the Universe, [attained his goal].
He fashioned this creation and attained the station of the Grandfather (Brahmā); you are born into his lineage, and thus such devotion is fitting for you.
Devotion to Viṣṇu, which yields the fruit of the four aims of life, is not the result of minor austerity; beginningless ignorance is that which intensifies the five firmly rooted afflictions.
This single devotion to Viṣṇu arises for the sake of destroying that [suffering] in the forest of worldly existence, which is crowded at every step with the perils of misery. (67)
For men wandering in this world, which is without shelter, difficult to cross, and agitated by the winds of dualities, devotion to Viṣṇu alone bestows happiness. (68)
For those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence, devotion to Viṣṇu is remembered as the boat; by taking refuge in the one divine mother, devotion to Viṣṇu alone. (69)
The peaceful ones, with contented minds, never grieve at any time—those great souls who are thrilled by drinking the nectar of devotion to Viṣṇu.

The state of Brahman is attained with very little effort by those vessels [of merit] for the sake of liberation; yet, O King, the mass of sin for living beings is threefold and exceedingly great. (71)
In the great forest fire of devotion to Viṣṇu, he acts like a moth; so too do the holy fords such as Prayāga and the Gaṅgā, as well as ascetic penances.
The horse-sacrifice, the best of rituals; very great gifts; and thousands of vows, fasts, and observances, even though they have been earned— 73.
Even the sum of all these multiplied together by millions upon millions is not said to be equal to even a thousandth part of devotion to Viṣṇu.
Jaimini said: Having heard the greatness of devotion to Viṣṇu as proclaimed by the Brahmarṣi, the lord of the earth desired indeed to know the true nature of devotion to Viṣṇu. (75)
Then, endowed with respectful courtesy, he spoke these words again to Nārada.
Indradyumna said: O great sage, you have rightly described the majesty of devotion to Viṣṇu; however, a desire to know its true nature has long resided within my heart. (77)
O best among the Vaiṣṇavas, describe now the characteristics of devotion; for I know of no other speaker on this earth besides you.
Nārada said: "Excellent, O King! You have asked about the supreme characteristic of devotion. I shall describe it to you, who are a most worthy recipient of devotion, exactly as it is."
Indeed, this should not be spoken to one who is an unfit vessel, who is blind like a man, or whose inner self is defiled. Listen attentively, O sinless King, as it is being told by me. (80)
One should cultivate eternal devotion to Viṣṇu, both in its general and specific aspects, for the attainment of ultimate happiness and the cessation of the continuous stream of suffering. (81)

Because it rests upon the conviction that "this alone is the cause," it is called devotion (bhakti). It is threefold according to the distinction of the qualities (guṇas), while the fourth is considered to be beyond the qualities (nirguṇa).

O King, that devotion which belongs to those overcome by desire and anger, who do not perceive anything else upon seeing [the world], and whose purpose is the acquisition of gain or the practice of sorcery, is tāmasī.
Devotion performed for the sake of excessive fame, or out of rivalry with others, or incidentally for the sake of the next world, is remembered as being of the nature of passion (rājasī). || 84 ||
Having perceived that worldly states are perishable and that the otherworldly is more stable, one should not abandon the dharmas prescribed for the various stages of life as seen by the seers.
That devotion which is practiced for the sake of self-knowledge is indeed *sāttvika*; for this world is the Lord of the World, and there is no other cause whatsoever. (86)
And I am not different from that, nor does it exist apart from me; the cultivation of love, which transcends external adjuncts, is the highest excellence. (87)

Indeed, this devotion known as non-duality (advaita) is difficult to attain for the sake of liberation; through sattvic devotion one reaches the abode of Brahman, and through rajasic devotion, the world of Śakra.

Having enjoyed worldly pleasures, those characterized by tamas indeed go to the world of the ancestors; then, returning to the earthly realm (bhūrloka), they possess that very devotion in its opposite form.

One of a tamasic nature may become rajasic, and likewise one of a rajasic nature may become sattvic; but it is the sattvic person who attains liberation after cultivating the realization of non-duality.

By relying on even one [of these], one shall gradually proceed upon the path to liberation; however, for one devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu, the rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis [bear no fruit]. (91)
Atonement and the like, pilgrimage to sacred sites, ascetic practices such as the *kṛcchra* penance, noble birth, and various arts—all these are merely worldly ornaments. (92)

Physical austerity is their fruit, just as a wanton woman's [fruit] is her infidelity; even one devoid of family traditions, if he possesses firm devotion and has conquered his senses, [attains success]. || 93 ||

O best of kings, one who is praised by all the worlds is not he who merely possesses knowledge of the eighteen branches of learning; rather, it is he who is devoted, of noble birth, and likewise righteous. (94)
For devotion to Viṣṇu does not arise in a man of meager fortune; yet, having accomplished that with effort, one has fulfilled his purpose and does not falter. (95)
That by which one knows the Lord of the World is proclaimed as true knowledge (vidyā); that action by which the Blessed One is pleased is the destroyer of inauspiciousness.
He is declared a devotee of Viṣṇu, endowed with those two and firm in his vows; by the dust of whose feet the entire universe, including all that is mobile and immobile, is purified. (97)
By his own will, he has power over creation, maintenance, and destruction; how much more so, then, over the petty desires and the riches of the earth, heaven, and the like? 98.
No distinction exists between Vāsudeva and his devotee; I shall now describe the characteristics of those who are devotees of Vāsudeva.
With peaceful minds, gentle toward all, and having conquered their desires and senses, they do not wish harm to others through deed, thought, or word. (100)
Their minds are perpetually moistened with compassion; they turn their backs on theft and violence; and they are filled with joy and partiality toward virtues and the affairs of others. (1)
Pure through their conduct of the virtuous, regarding the festivals of others as their own, and free from envy, let us behold Vāsudeva dwelling within all beings.
Always compassionate toward the distressed and intensely desiring the welfare of others, they were cherished in their service to the king like his own princes.
Those who lack discernment experience a delight in sense objects that is like the fear one feels toward a black cobra; they pursue external things as if out of dread. || 4 ||
But those who worship Śaṅkara and the other gods with the thought that it is their constant duty, extend that same love toward Hari multiplied a hundred-fold.

They meditate with devotion even upon the hosts of ancestors as being of the very nature of Viṣṇu; they see nothing other than Viṣṇu, nor do they perceive Viṣṇu as existing separately from anything else.

There is neither separation nor non-separation for you who possess the nature of both the totality and the individual; O Lord of the World, "I am yours"—I am your servant, and you are mine, not separate from one another.
When the Lord Antaryāmī is established in the hearts of all, there is no one other than you who is either the one to be served or the servant. || 8 ||

Thus, with their minds focused through such meditation, constantly bowing and ever chanting the praises of Hari—whose lotus feet are worshipped by the Lotus-born Brahmā—they serve the world’s people as if they were mere blades of grass.

Ever skilled in doing good for the worlds, regarding the welfare of others as their own, and moistened with compassion even toward those who treat them with contempt—such indeed are the renowned Vaiṣṇavas, whose minds are fixed on auspiciousness. 110.

Those who possess an equal mind toward a grinding stone and another’s wealth, toward a clod of earth and a fragment [of gold], toward the wives of others and [thorny] *kūṭa-śālmali* trees, and toward friends, enemies, siblings, and their own kin—these indeed are renowned as Vaiṣṇavas. (13)

With their minds fixed on the pair of lotus feet of Hari, possessing dull intellects and equanimity toward pleasure and pain, skilled in offering worship to Hari and whose speech consists of self-prostration—such indeed are the well-known Vaiṣṇavas. 14.

Victorious are the Vaiṣṇavas, whose upper arms and midsections are marked with the tilaka in the form of the wheel, mace, lotus, and conch; they wear as armor the dust from prostrating at the feet of the Enemy of Mura. 15.

Victorious indeed are the Vaiṣṇavas, whose forms are made beautiful by the ornaments they have attained—namely, the finest tulasī leaves, garlands, and sandalwood paste drawn forth from the worship of Murajit—as if to choose liberation for themselves. 16.

With their pride and conceit dissolved and their minds purified, with their egoism forcibly destroyed and stilled, those Vaiṣṇavas—having worshipped Narahari, the beloved kinsman of the immortals—truly triumph as their sorrows are brought to an end. 17.

The auspicious conduct of those who possess constant devotion toward the Blessed One has been proclaimed as Your mark; for as soon as it enters the path of their hearing, it removes the long-accumulated impurity of men. 16.

For I never seek even wealth, nor indeed do I desire the association with the exhaustion born of the body; my only concern is to enjoy the fame of being addressed with soft and gentle words as your servant alone. 19.

Those who are not devotees of Viṣṇu—whose minds here are naturally attached to evil conduct—hate even the virtuous deeds of men; though they encounter great misfortune, they remain complacent, finding delight in worldly pleasures. 120.

Those who are intoxicated by their own nature do not, even for a moment, attend to the state of supreme bliss residing within the heart-lotus; those non-Vaiṣṇavas constantly conceal the very name of Hari with webs of false speech.

Constantly coveting the wives and wealth of others, their intellects base and their bellies filled with their own burdens, considering themselves to possess supreme greatness—these human beasts are indeed devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu. (22)

Those who are incessantly addicted to ignoble associations, who revile and harm others, who are exceedingly fierce, who are indifferent to the remembrance of the feet of Nṛsiṃha, and who are defiled by men—such wicked ones must indeed be avoided from afar. 123.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: Having thus heard from Nārada, the son of Brahmā, about the supreme devotion to the Lord, Indradyumna was exceedingly pleased and spoke to him as follows.
Indradyumna said: "O Blessed One, the company of the virtuous with the learned, which destroys the disease of worldly existence, has been taught to me; it has become mine this very moment. (2)
Since you have directly realized Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, who is higher than the highest, and have come to my abode—who else here could be more virtuous than you? (3)
O Blessed One, through your presence, my darkness has come to destruction; for it has impelled my mind to worship Nīlamādhava.
Wandering throughout all the worlds, you know the history of the cosmic egg; therefore, mounting our chariot, let us behold Nīlamādhava.

The auspicious field known as Puruṣottama is adorned; it has been told to me by many that there are sacred fords (tīrthas) therein. If I come to know them through your words, they shall become fruitful for me.
Nārada said: "Behold! I shall show you the sacred field, the deities residing within that field, the holy fords (tīrthas), the Śaktis and Śambhus, as well as the majesty of the field itself."
"By my grace, you shall soon behold the Lord of Gods directly—He who bestows Himself upon His devotee—established in four forms."
"By the mere sight of whom a mortal becomes a vessel for devotion. Having thus concluded their conversation, the two, being pleased, finished their daily duties.

Having determined a time favorable for the journey on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, on a Wednesday under the Puṣya asterism at an auspicious moment, King Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada spent the night sleeping together in one place.
Then at dawn, the excellent king Indradyumna, together with his kinsmen, caused a proclamation to be made for the sake of the kingdom.
According to our means, we shall set out with our armies toward Mount Nīla; we have resolved that we will dwell there for as long as we live. 12.
Whatever livelihood has been assigned to whom, let him live therein by that means; so too the kings, along with their harems, ministers, and retinues. (13)
With chariots, elephants, horses, treasuries, and foot soldiers. || 14 ||
Let the Brāhmaṇas who maintain the sacred fire, along with merchants carrying their goods and those who live by trade, set out from there fully prepared.
They were experts in statecraft, skilled in the royal paths, knowers of the stars, masters of dance, and proficient in the science of government.

They possess excellent intelligence regarding dance, song, and instrumental music, as well as the fourfold [sciences], and they are experts in the treatises on elephants, horses, and men, and in the supreme science of medicine. (17)
They were skilled and experienced in all eighteen branches of learning, as well as in the auxiliary sciences (upāṅgas), and were curious about the meaning of magical deceptions.
There were thieves who plundered by the hundreds, as well as others who stole from the very eyes of the owner; there were those who lived by various tales, flatterers, and bards. (19)
Those who live by the scriptures, as well as others who extract arrows, gamblers, unchaste women, courtesans, those who frequent brothels, and parasites; || 20 ||
And there were farmers, as well as keepers of cattle, sheep, goats, camels, and donkeys; fowlers, and protectors of monkeys, tigers, and leopards. || 21 ||
Snake-charmers, cowherds, Śabaras, and Mleccha tribes; || 22 ||
And others who are born in the land of Mālava and obey my command—let them all go to their dwellings on Mount Nīla, having each established their respective residences there. (23)
Having thus given his command and fixed the time for the expedition, the king met with Nārada and said this to the astrologer: || 24 ||
"O astrologer, as you have previously determined for me the auspicious moment of the year, so bring together all the necessary articles for the ceremony in their entirety. (25)
At that moment, while it was being investigated according to the opinion of the domestic priest, the astrologer, accompanied by the priest, was instructed by him.
O best of the twice-born, he brought all the auspicious articles; meanwhile, that royal sage sat upon a divine throne.
First, the auspicious consecration for the journey was performed by the Brahmins with the Śrīsūkta, the Vahnisūkta, and the hymn dedicated to the deity of the year (Abdaivata).

With the Pāvamānya hymns, the Abhisūkta, and various other auspicious-increasing mantras, [he should bathe him] separately with waters from sacred fords, medicinal herbs, and all types of fragrant substances individually.
Then the king, consecrated with water drawn in Chinese silk garments, shone with a radiant body like a smokeless fire.

Having put on white garments, having sipped water for purification, and having placed the sacred grass (pavitra) upon himself, he should worship the groups of ancestors known as the Nāndīmukhas according to the prescribed rite.
Having diligently performed the *gaṇahoma* offerings and the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations for victory, [he beheld] smokeless fire, white in color and rich with the fragrance of the sound of conchs.
He circumambulated the fire, whose flames were curling to the right, which was visibly bestowing victory upon the king who sought it.

And at the conclusion of the sacrifice to the nine planets (navagrahamakha), he was served by the pitcher of the planets (grahakuṃbha) for the destruction of the malevolence of the planets and for the increase of well-being. || 34 ||
Then, with mantras proclaimed in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra) and enjoined by the prescribed rites of the astrologers, he began the performance of the auspicious dressing and adornment.
Having donned his own armor over a garment of Chinese silk, he put on a bright turban and a crown resplendent with excellent jewels.
Upon his ears adorned with jeweled earrings, he wore a highly precious neck-ornament and a necklace embellished with a central gem.
Then that best of kings took up his armlets, bracelets, and rings; he fastened a triple-stranded golden thread around his waist, resting upon his three folds.
Then she put on a beautiful girdle, well-fashioned with various gems, adorned with golden bells and a garland of pearl arches.
She placed priceless anklets upon her feet; she beheld herself adorned in a mirror held before her face.
For the purpose of performing the investiture of auspiciousness, he sat upon a golden throne, facing the east while recollecting the god Śrīdhara, the slayer of Madhu.
Viṣṇu is the abode of auspiciousness and the cause of all prosperity; by remembering him, even many sins are destroyed.
Then the king first wore a garland of seasonal flowers, fragrant and beautifully colored, which had been consecrated by his family priest.
Then, clay, a lamp, fruit, dūrvā grass, curd, and gorocanā—all these consecrated with mantras and protected by white mustard seeds—[should be offered]. || 44 ||
Then the king beheld his own self in the sacrificial offering of the daughter of Surabhi; thereafter, that lion among kings saw himself in the consecrated mirror.
His auspicious future was proclaimed by the loud chanting of peace-mantras by the Bahvṛcas, and he was protected on the road as he traveled by the Yājuṣkas with the Pathisūkta hymn.
With auspicious words from the Purāṇas and the chanting of praises by the bards of Magadha, King Kṛtavīryadhṛti manifested his prowess.
Meditating upon the Lord who bears the Garuda-banner, accompanied by Satyabhāmā and carrying away the Pārijāta tree, the king lifted his right foot from the lotus of his heart.
Having circumambulated the sage Nārada, who stood before him, he approached the middle gate, surrounded by those holding canes in their hands.
Having been instructed in the path of the stages, with the Agnihotra sacrifice as his foremost duty, he saw brahmins stationed there to his right.
They recited auspicious hymns, wore bright white garments, scattered parched grain with flowers before the king, and proclaimed his good fortune. (51)
On her left side stood courtesans, their hands busily holding chowries; they were auspicious, adorned with bright ornaments and garments, and possessed beautiful faces with smiling lotuses.
Bowing with devotion, O best of the twice-born, he honored the Brahmins with garments, ornaments, garlands, fragrances, and unguents.
He gratified those brahmins, who were imbued with the thought that they were the Lord himself, as well as the courtesans, the bards, and the poor and the helpless. (84)
With the king's permission, the minister bestowed wealth as was appropriate: white pigeons, swans, a white horse, and a white elephant.

Beholding a full water-pot placed beneath an archway fashioned from plantain trunks, adorned with mango sprouts and white garlands of fruit, and seeing many other auspicious objects, the king had the heat of the sun warded off from his head by a white parasol. (56)
He heard many musical instruments mingled with hundreds of conchs being blown simultaneously.
Then, amidst auspicious songs and shouts of victory, the king entered the palace to behold Nṛsiṃha.
Remembering whom a mortal becomes a vessel for all auspiciousness—he beheld from afar Nṛhari seated upon a divine lion-throne.
Having prostrated with all eight limbs and gratified her with words from the Upaniṣads, [he praised] Durgā, who stands at his right side and liberates one from all miserable states.
The king paid homage at the feet of her as she looked upon him with compassion; then the priest, having removed the auspicious garland from the body of the deity, [placed it around her neck].
He fastened it around the neck and anointed it with fragrant perfume; he performed the lustration ceremony for the king and joyfully wrapped his head in a turban.
Having circumambulated those two gods once more, that best of kings placed them upon the palanquin and set forth, with the two deities held in front.
Having appeared at the outer gate, he saw a well-equipped chariot yoked with ten horses possessing the speed of the wind.
Having circumambulated him, the king sat down together with Nārada. Then there arose the sounds of ḍhakkās, mṛdaṅgas, niḥsāṇas, bherīs, paṇavas, and gomukhas.
Thousands of sweet-sounding carcarī-conch shells were blown there, as were millions of chariots belonging to the kings and their attendants.
Arranged in rows around the chariot of Indradyumna, they shone forth, equipped with various weapons and adorned with banners.
With their banners raised high, adorned with gold and silver, networks of tinkling bells, and mirrors, they were equipped with various kinds of mechanical devices and emitted deep, resonant sounds.
With the foot-soldiers, elephants, and horses swift as the wind, there was the clashing of infantry, the trumpeting of elephants, and the neighing of horses.
The sounds of musical instruments, mingled with the loud rattling of chariots, were heard by the people like the roar of the ocean at the end of an eon.
At that moment, the citizens, each equipped with their own provisions, set out on horse-drawn carts, donkeys, camels, and pack-animals.
Swaying palanquins, couches, and millions of horses were seen in rows amidst the bustle of the nation's departure.
Then, hundreds of the king's female attendants, surrounded by eunuchs and mounted on various vehicles, were escorted by officials.
Surrounded by great armies, they departed from the royal palace; and the performers of sacrifices, in multitudes, left their sacrificial fires mounted upon the wooden pins (śamyā).
Having loaded them onto carts along with their wives, they set out, as well as the loads of books and the caskets for the worship of the deities.
They caused the sacrificial fuel, the sacred grass, the kuśa blades, the vessels, and the materials gathered for the oblation to be carried by other brahmins acting as cart-drivers.
The neighboring vassals, ministers, and servants, as well as the domestic chaplain, the officiating priests, the royal subjects, and those appointed to perform services; || 77 ||
Other travelers remained with all the provisions for their journey, and those appointed over the treasury brought forth the entire collection of wealth from the storehouse. (78)
Taking their leave, the king’s attendants departed quickly; likewise, all the florists and other merchants who lived by trade also left. (79)
Taking each their own merchandise, the royal officials, the guild-leaders, and the merchant-chiefs all departed together with the inhabitants of the cities and market-towns. (80)
Engaged in the playful pursuit of their respective occupations, they all set out together at the time appointed for King Indradyumna’s expedition.
Hearing the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, and war-drums pervading the quarters of the sky, all the people living in the countryside were filled with agitation.
Honoring the king’s command upon their heads, they departed for Mount Nīla; each person went by whichever path was most direct.
By the king's command, they did not seek the main highway out of haste; rather, they traveled by the difficult path leading to the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri).
Indradyumna, the king of kings, was likewise surrounded by all the city-dwellers and by the fourfold armies, who were filled with joy. || 85 ||
In the chariot situated in the midst of a row of kings' carriages arranged in a line, the royal sage shone, his retinue equal to that of Śakra.

With his mind brightened by auspicious thoughts through the songs and offerings of parched grain and flowers performed by the women of the city as part of their auspicious rites, and graced by the splendor of those auspicious customs; || 87 ||
He set out joyfully on a chariot yoked with horses swift as the wind, amidst the cool shade provided by clouds stirred up by a favorable breeze.
On the dustless surface of the earth, where the crossroads were leveled, there were men from various regions traveling on the road who were familiar with the interior of the forest.
Following the path that had been pointed out, the king, his eyes filled with joy, repeatedly gazed upon the lands and forests situated on both sides of the road.
In the midst of the forest, he encountered Carcikā, who was adorned with a garland of skulls, standing on the path as she was dividing the territory extending beyond the boundary.
Having descended from his chariot at the command of Nārada, King Vinata prostrated before her with all eight limbs and, his consciousness filled with bliss, offered praise.
Indradyumna said: Salutations to you, O Sovereign of the Thirty Gods, who wards off all calamities, and who are extolled through the conceptualizations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others. (93)
O Primordial One, O Supreme Goddess, be gracious toward the worlds; O Śivā, without you, this universe cannot endure for even a moment.
In this eternal world, the success of all undertakings and all auspiciousness indeed result from the worship of your feet; it is not otherwise in the mortal realm. (95)
O Supreme Goddess, you are the power of Viṣṇu, the Lord of the moving and the unmoving, by which the All-pervading One creates, protects, and destroys the universe.
O Goddess, show favor to me so that I may behold with my own eyes the Lord, the teacher of the moving and the unmoving, who dwells upon the Blue Mountain.
Jaimini said: Having praised the Goddess according to the instruction of Nārada, the lord of men quickly ascended his chariot, like the sun ascending the eastern mountain at dawn. 98.
Then that king, whose mounts were exhausted, set out with speed along the bank of the great river Citrotpalā, where the forests were sparse.
He encamped his army at the place renowned as Dhātukandara, remaining there intent upon performing his daily rites until the afternoon duties were completed.
He entered the river at the landing-place with his family priest, which had previously been cleared by wise men and rendered free from poisonous thorns.
Having bathed and offered libations to the gods and the ancestors, the lord of the people then duly worshipped Viṣṇu, followed by the kings and the subjects.
The illustrious king honored him with seating, lodging, and other comforts; then, together with Nārada, he entered the inner apartments.
With a joyful mind, he partook of foods that tasted like nectar; then, when the sun had gone to the western mountain, the lord of the people [retired].
Having quickly completed the evening rites when the moon had risen, the lord of the people and his dependents sat down in the midst of the assembly hall.
There, that lord of men shone with the marks of sovereignty, like the autumnal moon with its full orb among the luminaries.
The poets composed verses upon his fame, which was as pure as nectar; and singers with melodious voices sang well-composed songs.
Then, courtesans proud of their beauty, youth, and charm danced before him with perfectly pure rhythmic movements, melodies, and gestures.
The people of Magadha praised him, whose auspicious form was transcendent, with various clusters of words consisting of prose, verse, compositions, and other diverse forms.
Then that king honored the foremost Vaiṣṇava members of the assembly with highly esteemed and most beautiful perfumes, garlands, and betel-leaf.
And there, by the king's command, he honored hundreds of kings seated comfortably with royal vessels as was appropriate for each.

Then, with great reverence, they questioned Nārada, the best of sages and beloved of the Blessed One, as he sat comfortably upon a throne worthy of a lion, desiring to hear the deeds of the Blessed One which dispel all sins.
Indradyumna said: O Blessed One, treasury of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, beloved of the Lord, you alone know the life-story of Viṣṇu through your eye of knowledge.
O Sage, if you have compassion for me, then wash with the nectar of Hari’s deeds my inner self, which is defiled by the thick mud of sin.
While such a conversation was thus intermingled between the sage and the king, the gatekeeper, a servant of the Lord of Utkala, entered before the monarch.
He said: "The king of Utkala stands at the entrance of the palace, bringing a gift and wearing his crown, desiring to behold the lotus feet of Your Majesty. (16)
O brahmins, having been thus informed by the gatekeeper, that royal sage, filled with agitation upon hearing of that ornament of the region, spoke to him.
Eager to hear news of that field of Śrī Puruṣeśa, he had the illustrious King Oḍhra enter without delay.
For he, having propitiated Viṣṇu on Mount Nīla, has become perfectly pure; by the sight of him, we shall all have our sins destroyed. (19)
Having heard those words, the gatekeeper immediately ushered the lord of the earth into the assembly hall of King Indradyumna.
The lord of Oḍhra entered quickly along with his Vaiṣṇava ministers and respectfully bowed at the pair of venerable feet of Indradyumna.
The pair [of sandals] of Indradyumna is to be reverently saluted.
Having raised him up and placed that devotee of Viṣṇu before him, the lord of kings seated him at the edge of his own throne and spoke these words with great humility.
"O King, Lord of Oḍhra, may you be well in every respect; does the Lord who dwells upon the peak of the Blue Mountain reign in victory? (23)
Is your stainless intellect fixed upon the lotus feet of the Blessed One? Does it abide with equanimity toward all beings and toward Hari? (24)
Then the Lord of Oḍhra, having heard his words, joined his palms in reverence and spoke these humble words, overflowing with joy and wonder.
"O Master, by the grace of your feet, all is well with me everywhere; for when the sun is shining, how could darkness possibly prevail? (26)
The earth, having found its protector in you—a king won over by the natural excellence of his virtues—is like Amarāvatī under the protection of Jiṣṇu.
While you rule the earth, O King, the Dharma always possesses its four feet; it is heard in the Vedas that only the practice of prohibitions exists [elsewhere].
O Lord, those qualities of kings which are collectively present in you have each reached their individual limit among other rulers. (29)
Even such sovereignty, O best of kings, is difficult for you to attain—this earth consisting of eighteen islands, resembling a single house. (130)
If Brahmā had not created you, who are so affectionate toward all living beings, how could people remain free from grief when their children and kinsmen have died? (31)
The sacred tradition declares that kings are common portions of Viṣṇu; but you are the Lord himself—what other person could be such a treasury of virtues? (32)
On the shore of the southern ocean lies Mount Nīla, shrouded by forests; no people travel there, and that deity herself resides therein.
"Now it is heard that he is covered in sand by a whirlwind; because of that, even in my kingdom there is famine, pestilence, and the like. (34)
"O best of the twice-born, when you have arrived, everything will be well with me. To the lord of Utkala who had spoken thus, the king [replied]: || 35 ||
Then, showing him respect, he dismissed him for his lodging; but seeing Nārada, he became despondent and asked, "O Sage, what is this? (36)
To him who had said, "I consider that for whose sake I have labored to be indeed fruitless," Nārada, the knower of the three periods of time, spoke.
"You should not feel astonishment at this; you are indeed fortunate, the best among Vaiṣṇavas. For the desires of Vaiṣṇavas never go unfulfilled anywhere. (38)
O King, you will surely behold Nārāyaṇa, the source of the worlds, who is free from all affliction and who assumes a terrestrial form. 39.
Indeed, for the sake of bestowing grace upon you, he shall descend to the earth; the entire world, including all things moving and stationary, has come under the control of Viṣṇu.
Even that eternal Supreme Soul is not under the control of anyone; the Lord, who is affectionate toward His devotees, is subject only to devotion.
O King, how could He—who by His Māyā keeps everything from Brahmā down to a mere insect so well concealed—be dependent on anyone other than His devotees? (42)
Devotion to the Enemy of Mura is the root of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; it alone is the means for attaining them, and without it, nothing exists.
When Viṣṇu alone, by his own māyā, appears as many, there exists no cause of happiness apart from that Supreme Self.
Even those others, such as Śiva, Durgā, and so forth, who—though veiled by their respective karmas—grant desires when worshipped, they too have Viṣṇu as their ultimate refuge.
That Blessed Lord is the inner controller (antaryāmī) residing within the hearts of even the gods; they bestow only as much fruit as He impels them to give.
O Indra among kings, you are a Vaiṣṇava and the fifth son of the Lotus-born; you have mastered the eighteen branches of knowledge and are firmly established in virtuous conduct.
Having protected the earth according to justice and especially honoring the Brahmins, you will certainly behold Vaikuṇṭha in this very field with your physical eyes. 48.
"O King, my grandfather also appointed me to this task; I shall tell you everything once we have reached that most excellent field. (49)
Now indeed only a remnant of the night remains, reaching the third watch; therefore, command the king now to depart from his own palace.
"You too, having fallen under the power of sleep, go inside the house."

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Dialogue with the Sage Jaimini," within the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya of the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, in the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Jaimini said: When the son of Brahmā had spoken thus, King Indradyumna, having heard the words of the sage with a delighted inner soul, reflected with supreme intelligence and considered his exertion to have borne fruit. || 1 ||
"Oh, what supreme fortune is mine, earned through many previous births! The Grandfather of all the worlds has exerted himself for my sake."
He made his own son, who was liberated while living, his companion; for indeed, as is the companion of men, so is their undertaking. (3)
"This is the instruction of the elders, as heard in all assemblies. Thinking thus, the king dismissed the members of his court.
Then, O twice-born ones, taking the sage by the hand, she entered the inner apartments; having honored him according to the prescribed rites, she sat with him upon a couch.
The king passed the remainder of the night conversing with one another; then, when the morning was clear, he indeed completed his daily rites.
Having worshipped the Lord of the World, he crossed the great river, his path being indicated by the ruler of the Oḍhra country who was traveling ahead.
Accompanied by his army, he set out for the sacred field of Ekāmra-vanaka; having traveled some distance, he reached the river named Gandhavahā.
Having crossed the swift-flowing river of cool waters, the powerful one [arrived] at the time of the morning worship of Koṭiliṅgeśvara.
From afar, the king heard the sound of cymbals, conchs, kāhālas, mṛdaṅgas, and murajas pervading the great forest.
Thinking thus, he was pleased with the Blessed One who dwells on Mount Nīlācala, and said to Nārada: "O great sage, from where does this sound come?"
"Has the Supreme Lord, who dwells upon the peak of the Blue Mountain, arrived? For at the time of his worship, this tumultuous sound is indeed heard. (12)
"Or perhaps some other deity resides nearby, O Sage? Thus questioned by the king, the bull among sages then replied.
O King, this field is extremely difficult to attain and is guarded by the enemy of Mura; the Blessed One is not known to be there by any men.
For you are the foremost among the fortunate; by your good fortune, the Blessed One was somehow beheld by your priest through the path of restrained senses.
"For you, O best of kings, are indeed endowed with the sixfold forces; yet you are excessively intent on this rash act, O lord of the earth, and thus I have my doubts."

The Blue Mountain extends for three yojanas; this, however, is the Ekāmraka forest, the sacred field of the Lord Gaurīpati. Not far from there, O protector of the earth, he, being terrified, came as a refugee.
Indradyumna said: How did that Lord of Gaurī become afraid, and to whom did he go for refuge?
He who in the past consumed the terrible Tripura with a single arrow—wonder has arisen within me regarding this; I desire to hear that which is difficult to obtain.
Bhava is the protector of those afraid of worldly existence and is supremely purifying; for what reason is he himself afraid of fear? Who indeed is capable of conquering him?
Nārada said: O lord of the earth, I shall relate to you here an ancient account. In former times, having brought himself under control through austerity, he married Gaurī.
The Lord Nīlalohita was a celibate student on the Himālaya mountains; however, being tormented by the arrows of Anaṅga, he abandoned his celibacy. || 22 ||
O King, he took delight with that beautiful woman who was intoxicated by her youth; in his father's kingdom, he enjoyed pleasures desired even by the gods.
Then, once as she was departing from her own residence, that virtuous woman was addressed with smiling words by her mother and the women of the household in a conciliatory manner.
"Noble lady, great penance was performed by you in the dense forest for the sake of a boon; yet, O fair-faced one, a suitor has been obtained who is of no lineage, devoid of merit, and old. (25)
Day and night you do not leave the presence of such a person; tell me, my child, what is the merit in this, or what is it that has been gained through your husband's favor?
"O blessed lady, you have obtained ornaments and clothing; you shall remain for a long time as a resident of my house, cherished with the enjoyments due to a father. (27)
We have heard that whatever maidens in the three worlds are married, they depart from their father’s house, adorned with ornaments, to their husband’s residence accompanied by their husbands. (28)
But I am a mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs from the world of the ancestors; having arrived here, O illustrious lady, I was wedded by Himādri. (29)
"O lady of tremulous eyes, I spoke thus out of jest, not out of anger. You must not speak this before my son-in-law, for he is regarded as equal to Viṣṇu. (30)
Nārada said: Having heard these words of her mother, she was deeply pained by the censure of her husband; with her lips quivering in anger, she did not utter even a single word.
Concealing Ambikā’s words, she went into the presence of her husband and spoke these harsh yet affectionate words in measured syllables.
"O Master, this is not fitting at present—that you should dwell in your father-in-law's house; for how could even the Teacher of the three worlds, who is greater than the Creator himself, do so? (33)
"Therefore, O Lord, my residence here is not pleasing to me; for are there no lands suitable for the dwelling of a lord, O Master? (34)
Thus addressed by Śivā, the Lord whose banner bears the bull then mounted his bull with her and went swiftly to the Middle Country.
Having bypassed all other holy places, [he went to] the great purifier Prayāga, on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā as it flows toward the eastern ocean.
He constructed for Gaurī a beautiful city named Vārāṇasī, measuring five krośas and adorned with excellent palaces. || 37 ||
It was provided with hundreds of watchtowers, endowed with innumerable groves, possessed of various sacred bathing places, and crowded with diverse people. || 38 ||
By the command of Dhūrjaṭi, it was fashioned by Viśvakarman as a brilliant [palace], where the sins of those who dwell there are destroyed by the purifying and cool waves of the Gaṅgā.
There, in the middle of that city, which was adorned with golden walls and watchtowers, well-constructed with jeweled pillars, and fulfilling all desires; (40)
Paśupati took delight with her, as Madhusūdana does with Śrī; that city was never forsaken by Viśvanātha. (41)
O lord of men, she was known in the past as Avimuktā, the bestower of liberation upon human beings, and was served by those who fear worldly existence.
Dwelling there at that time with her husband, Gaurī, beautifully adorned, did not even remember her mother or her father, O lord of the earth. (43)
Thus, after many yugas had passed, he went to Mount Kailāsa; there the Lord established ten million of his own liṅgas.
O King, many kings protected that city; there, in ancient times during the Dvāpara age, lived one known as the King of Kāśī. (45)
He indeed gratified the Lord Śambhu with fierce austerity—the infallible one who is the conqueror of kings led by Jarāsandha.
Having resolved, "I shall prevail in battle," the king granted him a boon; and the wielder of the Pināka bow, being gratified, bestowed it upon him.
"O subduer of enemies, you shall conquer the slayer of Kaṃsa in battle; for your sake, I shall fight with the Pramathas while mounted upon Vṛṣa."
Having obtained this boon from Śambhu, that powerful lord of men became heedless and challenged Hari, the bearer of the conch and discus, to battle.
The Lord Antaryāmī, having learned of this occurrence, dispatched his discus for the slaying of the King of Kāśī.
Then that fierce-looking discus, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns, having severed the head of the King of Kāśī, [destroyed] his army and that city.
O King, knowing the power and intent of Viṣṇu, he consumed the enraged one; seeing that great feat, Paśupati then became furious.
Surrounded by his hosts, mounted upon his bull, and bearing the Pināka bow, he rushed toward him; then, seeing that Sudarśana discus first before him—
Śambhu fashioned that Pāśupata weapon, which resembled a portentous calamity; it had been obtained by Śambhu in former times from Viṣṇu, who was gratified by his devotion.
"Remembered by you, I shall also empower your weapon with my strength; however, if you become hostile toward me, it will become lusterless."
When this terrible Pāśupata weapon had been rendered fruitless and Vārāṇasī had been burnt, the bull-bannered god was struck with fear.
He praised the Supreme Person, the beginningless source of the worlds.
Mahādeva said: O Nārāyaṇa, supreme abode, Supreme Soul, higher than the highest, whose glory is existence-consciousness-bliss, stainless one, salutations be unto you! (58)
O self-luminous one, hidden by your own māyā, who performs the acts of creating the world and its causes through the differentiation of the qualities (guṇas), salutations be to you! 59.

Neither inside nor outside, neither outside nor inside, you are far away yet you dwell nearby; you are heavy and light, stable and more minute than the minute, and more massive than the massive—salutations be to You!
O incomparable one, ten million lifetimes of the four-faced Brahmā are but half a moment for me; salutations to that Self in the form of Time, who arises from the play of Your sidelong glances.
Salutations to that Soul of the Universe, whose body transcends all measure and is enveloped by multitudes of universes contained within each and every single hair. 62.
Salutations to you, who by the measure of your own time bring about the dissolution and emergence of the Creator, and who calculate the formation of the Manvantaras and other cosmic periods.
"O Lord, I have been deluded by darkness and am ignorant of Your power; therefore, forgive my offense and protect me, who have come to You for refuge. (64)
While the destroyer of Tripura was thus offering praise, Adhokṣaja abandoned his form as the discus and manifested himself.
With a serene countenance and endowed with splendor, he holds the conch, the discus, and the mace; seated upon the throne of Garuḍa and the lotus, he is adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
Resplendent with necklaces, earrings, armlets, a crown, and other ornaments, he has Lakṣmī seated on his left lap and Satyā at his right side.
Bearing a body as beautiful as a dark rain-cloud, that ocean of compassion spoke, as if possessed by anger, to the terrified Lord of Girijā.
The Blessed Lord said: O Śambhu, how has such wickedness come about in this much time? For the sake of that worm of a king, he has presented himself to fight with me.
O Dhūrjaṭi, how many of those [beings] created by my power have not been recognized by you? Truly, your Pāśupata weapon is invincible even to the gods and asuras.
That wheel, which is the very form of my wrath and which does not spare even you, wanders through the world in contempt of me; for who indeed could it spare other than you? (71)
"Previously, you were won over by me through many austerities because of your being my body; if now you wish to sport here for a long time together with Gaurī," (72)
And if you desire that this city of Vārāṇasī endure for a long time, [then establish] the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama, renowned on earth by my name.
On the shore of the southern ocean, adorned by the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala), extending for ten yojanas as far as the Viraja-maṇḍala.
Gradually, it is a purifying field as far as the Citrotpalā river; from there onwards, the region extends as far as the southern ocean.
Step by step, the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri) is the most excellent, bestowing liberation; for there I indeed abide in four bodies, composed of sapphire.
To the north of that place is the famous forest called Ekāmra; O Destroyer of Tripura, dwell there with Pārvatī, free from fear.
"By the Self-born One himself, who created all the worlds at my command, you shall be consecrated there as the sovereign over ten million liṅgas."
And this Maṇikarṇika is a holy ford consisting of all holy fords; casting aside your egoism here, depart together with your retinue.
Nārada said: Thus addressed by Vāsudeva, Tryambaka, with his neck bowed and palms joined in reverence, spoke to Madhusūdana.
