Mahādeva said: O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Master who removes the distress of those who bow before you; O Lord of the world, the fulfillment of your command is the cause of my welfare.
O Lord, as for the arrogance I displayed out of delusion, it was solely Your grace, O Master, that caused my fickleness. (82)
O Lord of Gods, since you command my departure for Puruṣottama, I shall go to that auspicious field which bestows liberation, placing it upon my head.
"Form an intention today for the sake of showing me favor; you alone must protect my field, Puruṣottama. (84)
Furthermore, so that this field shall not undergo such destruction again, it was thus created by Mahādeva in ancient times. (85)
Worshipping the god Puruṣottama together with Bala and Śrī, [one should know that] here the Lord of Umā was personally installed by the Supreme Creator.
We shall go there and behold the Destroyer of Cities, the Lord of Girijā, who is radiant like the sun amidst a mass of dense inner darkness.
This sacred field of Śambhu is the supreme destroyer of darkness; it is the auspicious washer of passion (rajas), renowned as the stainless realm (virajamaṇḍala).

Renowned for its abundance of *sattva*, it bestows liberation and is the supreme abode of Puruṣa; as many other sacred fields as you have heard of that grant liberation, [they are all surpassed by this]. (89)
O Indra among kings, all of these indeed grant liberation here; O great king, this is the field for those whose minds are defiled by evil deeds.
The secret of the wielder of the discus does not enter the path of trust.

Jaimini said: Having heard the words of Nārada, the king, his heart filled with joy and his eyes wide with wonder, spoke to that tiger among sages: "O Brahman, you have well described to me this most purifying sacred field."
"Where that Lord of Umā resides, that protector, the Supreme Person—we must certainly go there, even though the path is winding, for this is the great means for attaining our designated goal."
Jaimini said: Then, O twice-born ones, at the time of midday, those two—the sage and the king—arrived together with their armies at the sacred field known as Ekāmravana.
Having bathed at Bindutīrtha and duly worshipped Puruṣottama situated on the bank, the king proceeded to the great temple of Koṭīśvara.
Having properly sipped that water, for the sake of pleasing him, he gave many elephants, horses, wealth, jewels, garments, and ornaments.
Established in the sattvic dharma, the king bestowed [the merit] upon the twice-born while worshipping that Liṅga Tribhuvaneśa with a great ritual bath.
Having praised, prostrated with devotion, and sung before him upon his lute, he who perceived the non-duality of Viṣṇu attained incomparable joy. (98)
With palms joined in reverence, making an effort to propitiate the God, he stood with undivided mind, meditating upon the one whose banner is the bull.
Then, O twice-born ones, the blessed Lord Tryambaka, the Supreme Ishvara, being pleased, spoke these words directly to the king in clear syllables and phrases.
Koṭiliṅgeśa said: O Great King Indradyumna, a Vaiṣṇava such as you is indeed rare on this earth; your desire shall surely be fully realized after a long time.
Having spoken thus, Śambhu vanished even as the king was looking on; he then spoke again to Nārada regarding that which had been commanded by the Self-born One.
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, perform that [sacrifice] preceded by the horse-sacrifice in that field of Śrī Puruṣottama, within the body of Viṣṇu. (3)
The Antarvedī is exceedingly meritorious and is like the very heart of Viṣṇu; for its protection, I have been established by Viṣṇu in eight forms.
O best of Brahmins, I am stationed at the tip of the conch-shaped [mountain] together with Durgā; lead this king there.
Now Hari, whose body is of sapphire, has indeed vanished; therefore, by my command, establish there the sacred field of Śrī Narasiṃha.
"Therefore, O best of kings, let him perform a horse sacrifice (vājimedha) with a thousand [offerings] in our presence; at its conclusion, that wonderful tree [will appear]."
"O best of the twice-born, show him this stainless form of Brahmā; by means of it, Viśvakarman shall fashion the four images."
Brahmā himself will come to their foundation so that he may perform horse sacrifices for Hari, whereby this man shall have his sins destroyed.
Let it remain for a thousand years; at its conclusion, he shall behold the support of the entire world, which destroys all impurities.
Having assumed a wooden body that grants liberation through the mere sight of it, neither Brahmā, nor I, nor you, O Nārada, know his conduct.

He becomes pleased solely through devotion and the performance of his commands. Nārada, too, having prostrated before Mahādeva, the teacher of the world, spoke with palms joined in reverence: "O Lord, that which was commanded by you [has been done]. (12)
Even the Grandfather (Brahmā) instructed me thus regarding its conception: "O Lord, you and the Grandfather are not distinct from the Supreme Self."
O Lord, such is the abundance of this king’s fortune that for his sake You, who are beyond the reach of the minds of even the three gods, have shown Your grace.
By association with whom even evildoers cross the ocean of worldly existence—indeed, this Blessed One, the creator of all beings, possesses inconceivable majesty. (15)

Indeed, one is not devoted to that which is beyond the scope of the intellect; for even a person of little merit, by striving for a long time through the recitation of the Vedas and other such means, attains liberation without effort through their practice. 16.
The cowherd women, who subsisted on cattle and dwelt in their homes within the forest, living as forest-dwellers, attained liberation through the enjoyment of their desires. (17)
Hating him incessantly, Śiśupāla reached the interior of the assembly hall; having pierced the heart of the Hunter (Kṛṣṇa), he attained a state that is very difficult to attain. 18.
In former times, having led him home by pulling at his garment, the hunchback enjoyed him—one whom even the celestial women, though absorbed in meditation, do not obtain.
In the past, the Lord granted liberation to a Caṇḍāla who stood at a distance, but not to a highly devoted Śrotriya who was standing nearby.
For even the Lord, the Grandfather, might deceive you with illusions; those bound by bodies endure great suffering through their ascetic penances.
Gautama and others, who were devoted to celibacy and remained for an entire kalpa, could not fathom his activities, which lie beyond the scope of such-and-such or this-or-that limitations.
Neither by great effort nor by a long period of time can the conduct of this highly intelligent one be fully determined. (23)
There are many means established in the scriptures for the liberation of the wise in this world; indeed, they perform sacrifices with these in manifold ways.
The supreme means for all is dwelling in Puruṣottama, which will certainly lead to union with the Lord, just as a good friend does.
Therefore, this is the indispensable means for reaching that deceiver, wherein Hari himself has placed his dwelling and guarded it well.
"By means of the story of Indradyumna, he shall become renowned throughout the entire world; therefore, O Lord of Gods, command that he be taken along with his army. (27)
"O Bull-bannered One, having established [the image] at the foot of the mountain and initiated it for the great sacrifice, I shall return to the vicinity of your lotus feet."
Jaimini said: Having said "So be it," Mahādeva vanished from the sage's sight in an instant, O Sage; he too, remaining upon the king's chariot, proceeded toward that most excellent sacred field.
On the second day, the king reached the site of Kapoteśa, which was endowed with length and breadth and abounded in reservoirs of water and trees.
Bilveśa was situated on the shore of the ocean at the eastern boundary; it was that place, as reported by the minister, which was suitable for the encampment of the army.
Having established them in their respective places as was appropriate, the best of kings paid homage to and worshipped Bilveśvara and Kapoteśa.

Mounting his chariot accompanied by the son of Brahmā, the wise one went into the presence of Hari, O brāhmaṇas, while mentally and verbally meditating upon and praising Viṣṇu, the dweller on the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala). || 133 ||

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama-Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini [and the sages], within the Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa, the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: O great sage, how did Kapoteśasthalī also become famous? Who was the pigeon, and who was the Lord? You ought to tell this to us.
Jaimini said: In ancient times, that Kuśasthalī was indeed unfit for the habitation of all living beings; it was strewn on all sides with sharp-edged tips of kuśa grass and thorns.
When formerly no deity other than the Blessed One was worshipped, [the place] was devoid of trees and water-reservoirs, like the abode of Piśācas. (3)
"May I too become worthy of worship in this way"—such was the rivalry that arose in Dhūrjaṭi at that time; thinking thus, he set his mind upon devotion to Viṣṇu alone.
Dwelling in a region entirely free from worldly objects and remaining without possessions, I shall undertake a most great austerity and satisfy that Hari.
What could I say to the Lord of Ramā? What praise can there be for the Master of Śāradā, the Lord of the entire universe? Or what else could possibly bring him satisfaction?
Therefore, no other external object is of use for that [purpose]; rather, one should perform the internal sacrifice with a sincere mind.
I shall worship Hari, the preceptor of all moving and non-moving beings, who bestows himself upon his devotees; by his grace, may I become worthy of worship by all.
Having thus resolved, he went to the holy Kuśasthalī, free from all dualities, to the vicinity of Nīlagotra.
Then Maheśvara performed intense penance, subsisting on air alone; though the Lord possesses eight forms, he became as minute as a pigeon.
Then the Blessed One, being pleased, bestowed upon him sovereign power, by which he became equal to himself in matters such as worship and honor.
By the power of his asceticism, that land became like Vṛndāvana, its interior graced by lakes, ponds, pools, and rivers.
Its waters were made resonant by the humming of bees intoxicated with honey, amidst various trees and creepers bearing fruits and flowers in every season.
Crowded with flocks of various birds and a refuge of happiness for all creatures, it was there that Śiva was born as one resembling a pigeon due to his ascetic penance.
By the command of Murāri, he attained the status of Kapoteśvara here; by his command, Tryambaka always dwells here with Mṛḍānī.
Those who worship Kapoteśa, praise him, or bow down to him, having shaken off all impurities, indeed go to Puruṣottama.
Henceforth, O twice-born ones, I shall proclaim the greatness of Bilveśa. Formerly, the Daityas dwelling in the netherworld pierced through the surface of the earth.
They afflict the earthly realm and likewise devour its people; for the sake of relieving the earth's burden, he has taken birth from the womb of Devakī.
When that blessed Lord was protecting the earth together with the Yādavas and the Pāṇḍavas, he then came to that place.
Having bathed in the waters of the king of holy fords and having mentally bowed from afar to that Nīlamādhava, he arrived at the gateway of the Daitya.
Having seen that terrible cave, which was inaccessible to human beings, he deluded the people with his illusory power and proclaimed the worshipfulness of Śiva. (93)
Having taken a fruit of the *bilva* tree and invoked the Three-eyed Lord there, the destroyer of the asuras worshipped the Enemy of Tripura and offered praise.

The Blessed Lord said: Salutations to you who transcend the three qualities (guṇas), who are the divider of the three qualities; salutations to you who consist of the triple Veda, who transcend the triad [of time], and who possess knowledge of the three periods of time. || 23 ||

Salutations to you, whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire; who are devoted to Brahman; who are the supreme self; who are the treasury of the eightfold sovereign powers; and who possess the eightfold nature. 24.

Salutation to that One who is beyond darkness, whose form is the destroyer of darkness and is imperishable; to Him by whom the darkness of ignorance has been severed, salutation to the Darkness-less One.
Having thus praised himself by means of his own self, that blessed Lord, through his grace, beheld a cave that was easy to enter.
By that path, the Lord, accompanied by his army, descended into Pātāla; there, he who had come to relieve the earth's burden slew the Daityas who were fierce in their strength.
Returning once more and remaining in that very place, the Blessed One worshipped the bull-bannered Lord Śiva and stationed him there to block the gateway.
The immensely wise Gadādhara, constrained by devotion, said this: "O Dhūrjaṭi, remain in the temple, blocking the exit of the asuras. (29)
"O Śambhu, who other than you is capable of destroying the strength of Karburabala? Having thus established Mahādeva, he then departed for Dvāravatī.
From that time onwards, Bilveśa attained renown upon the earth; O twice-born ones, that Bilveśa is the ancient rite of Kṣetrarāja.
Having seen that imperishable Lord of Mṛḍānī, the destroyer of sins, one attains all desires and conquers even insurmountable calamity.
The greatness of Kapota and Bilveśvara has indeed been told to you. Beyond this, O sages, what else do you wish to hear? (33)

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini and [the Lord], within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 13 ||
The sages said: O great sage, tell us this: when Nārada and the king had mounted the chariot and departed, where did they go and what did they do? || 1 ||
Jaimini said: Together with Vidyāpati, his younger brother and family priest, they approached the vicinity of Nīlakaṇṭha at the edge of the sacred field.
As this lord of the earth was traveling on the road, an ill omen occurred: his left eye and arm throbbed and twitched again and again.
Seeing that, the tiger among kings was overcome with dejection and questioned the sage, a treasury of all knowledge, regarding its cause.
My unimpeded sovereignty has been attained, and this most excellent field has been reached; indeed, this pilgrimage for the sake of beholding Mādhava is auspicious.
"O Sage, tell me truly: what misfortune might befall me today? For my left eye throbs and my arm trembles repeatedly."
Having heard that, Nārada spoke, indicating what was destined to happen and making known the auspicious words uttered by the Lotus-born One.

Nārada said: "O King, let there be no despondency in you; for auspiciousness is generally beset by obstacles. And at the end of those obstacles, O King, auspiciousness returns once more to fortunate men. (8)
It is true that you are a sovereign emperor and this body is the field of Viṣṇu; he for whose sake you have come here has now vanished from sight.

On the very day that this brahmin, the lord of knowledge, beheld him, he was covered with golden sand; then, on another day at evening time, he departed for his abode in Pātāla, being exceedingly difficult to find in the world of mortals.
Jaimini said: O best of the twice-born, having heard those terrible words, which were like a thunderbolt falling, the king fell senseless upon the surface of the earth.
Seeing him fallen in that manner, all those affectionate friends, led by the family priest, rushed forward crying out "Alas! Alas! (hāhākāra).
Having repeatedly sprinkled water as cool as camphor upon their faces, they anointed all their limbs with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.
They quickly fanned him with yak-tail whisks and palm-leaf fans; Nārada also, though agitated, maintained his yogic concentration.
Knowing that there was auspicious fortune therein, he protected the life-breaths of the king; and that king, too, regained consciousness after a long time through supreme efforts.
Rising up, O Brahmins, she fell again at the feet of Nārada: "O Sage, what grave sin did I commit in which other birth? (16)

O bull among sages, during whose ripening period there was indeed most terrible suffering, yet not even in a dream had any offense been committed against the twice-born or the cows by deed, thought, or speech? (17)
O tiger among sages, whatever action has been proclaimed as obligatory, occasional, or optional—that was never indeed abandoned by me, O King.
O great sage, I have never shown disrespect toward the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, nor toward those who rely on me or my kinsmen. (19)
O best of Vaiṣṇavas, those fifty offenses against Viṣṇu have all been diligently abandoned by you, like enraged great serpents.
What auspicious deed was performed by that younger brother of the family priest, that the Blessed Lord Nīlamādhava was seen by him with his physical eye? (21)
For what purpose was this loss of the kingdom knowingly brought about by you? Or why was this not announced at the very time of the expedition? (22)
For what reason have I caused the displacement from their positions of those learned in the Vedas? How is it that these refined lands have been abandoned by them for so long? (23)
The livelihood that was maintained for me by the subjects through the prosperity of my lineage has now been abandoned for my sake; how indeed will they survive? (24)
"I shall not sustain my life-breaths if I do not behold Hari; this is my resolve, O Brahmin—for if I am destroyed, where would the subjects be? (25)
O Sage, you who are always compassionate, instruct me regarding what is auspicious and inauspicious; now, taking my son, consecrate him in Mālava.
May he protect [the people] with justice so that these subjects do not grieve; and all those kings who have assembled here shall act according to my command. (27)
Let my sons remain steadfast in the word of the Lord of Mālava, practicing the rite of fasting unto death while meditating upon Nīlamādhava.
Established in this sacred field, I shall make the remainder of my life fruitful.
Jaimini said: Having raised up King Indradyumna as he was lamenting, the son of Brahmā consoled him with humble words and spoke as follows: || 30 ||
Nārada said: O King, you who are the foremost among the wise, a Vaiṣṇava, and an ocean of fortitude—how is it that you do not constantly perceive that prosperity is always beset by obstacles? (31)
But this is the supreme good for a person earned through hundreds of births: that one with the eye of flesh should behold the Wielder of the Mace, who possesses a physical body.
The play of Hari is unrestrained; by whom can it be comprehended? O King, even though I am liberated while living, I do not transcend His divine play.
"How much have I not been deceived, though I am a firm devotee standing in his presence? His Māyā is difficult to overcome even in hundreds of births. (34)
This illusion of his is infinite and difficult to comprehend even for the Lotus-born One, who remains eternally seated upon the navel-lotus and is ever devoted to his praise.
O King, the nature of that illusory being has thus been described; now I shall tell you its specific characteristics, for you are the best among the fortunate. (36)

All three of his forms are intent upon the thought of showing you grace. He who is the creator of all moving and unmoving beings, the Grandfather of the worlds himself, said to me: "Go quickly into the presence of Indradyumna. (37)
Desiring to behold Nīlamādhava, he is proceeding to Nīlācala; for that omnipresent Lord, having vanished from sight, was entreated by Yama.
"No grief should be felt there, for it cannot be otherwise. The King should be addressed in my name: 'I am his fifth descendant. (39)
For his sake, having propitiated the Supreme Self, the Puruṣottama, I shall lead him from Śvetadvīpa at the conclusion of the great sacrifice after a thousand years.
Let that Indradyumna now remain in the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama, performing thousands of horse-sacrifices while worshipping Viṣṇu.
At the end of that time, he will behold Viṣṇu in a wooden form with his own eyes; that incarnation of Hari shall become famous by means of him.
At that time, however, the forms of Viṣṇu must certainly be installed by me; for previously Hari existed as the Maṇi-mūrti, established in fourfold states. (43)
Having seen him, the domestic priest announced it directly in his presence: "He will descend again in a body made of divine wood, divided into four parts. (44)
Therefore, O Indra among kings, do not grieve; your desire will certainly bear fruit. There is no doubt; dwell here indeed without deceit.
Jaimini said: O Brahmins, having thus consoled the king and brought him to a state of confidence, Nārada then spoke these words once again.

Nārada said: Before the most excellent sacred field (kṣetra) shaped like a conch, there indeed stands Nīlakaṇṭha together with Durgā; let us go there, for that ground is perfectly level and suitable for the horse sacrifice.

Having constructed upon that site a magnificent hall intended to endure for a thousand years for the sake of a horse sacrifice, and having beheld the form of Nṛsiṃha residing on the Blue Mountain, he made his birth successful.
Having installed its very image—a replica to be worshipped by you and constantly honored by them—facing westward, for the sake of destroying all obstacles and for the increase of fruit. (49)

"We shall commence this most excellent sacrifice in the manner appropriate for the best of sages; for delay in this matter is not conducive to welfare—such is the word of the Grandfather (Brahmā). (50)

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 14.
Jaimini said: Then those brahmins set out joyfully toward Nīlakaṇṭha; having worshipped that Mahādeva and prostrated before Śrī Durgā, they departed. (1)
Having abandoned their excellent chariot, they proceeded on foot with their attendants, their senses fully restrained, in order to ascend Mount Nīla.
It was filled with various trees and creepers, crowded with flocks of diverse birds, obstructed on all sides by uneven rocks, and surrounded on every side.
Its boulder-like temples cause confusion by producing the illusion of wandering bees, and its hips are enveloped by the waves of the southern ocean.
It is always beyond the reach of mortal reasoning and difficult for great serpents to enter; its interior is terrifying with the trumpeting of herds of rutting elephants.
It was strewn on all sides with numerous herds of deer that had long lived among wild beasts, which were fearless and unaware of the wounds inflicted by weapons.
When they, desiring to enter, could not find a path or an opening, they then learned of the mountain's summit through their association with Nārada.
They arrived where the Lord dwells beneath a black aloe-wood tree—he who removes the fear of all calamities and possesses the form of a divine lion.
Upon seeing him, millions of men's sins of killing a Brahmin dissolve—he who has a gaping mouth, fearsome teeth, and is covered with tawny manes.
Fierce and three-eyed, he was tearing open the chest of the Daitya—who lay supine upon his own thighs—with claws as hard as thunderbolts.
The Lord has the luster of the dawn, with a shimmering tongue and a face grinning with loud laughter; his arms shine with the conch and the discus, and he is radiant with a crown and a diadem.
The quarters of the horizon were terrified by the sparks of fire leaping from his eyes, while his lotus-feet sank into the earth at its very edge due to the force of his violent strides.
Then, having seen Hari in that primordial form before Nārada, they beheld him from afar without fear and, freed from their distress, bowed down to him.
Indradyumna, too, having seen him, placed his trust in the words of Nārada; confident regarding the future task, he spoke thus to the great sage: || 14 ||
O Great Sage, I have achieved my purpose, for you are indeed the supreme treasury of knowledge; this Man-Lion is difficult to propitiate and inspires fear even at the mere sight of him. (15)
This [place] is to be well-served by those like you; for one such as I, it is worthy even from afar. By the mere sight of it, I have accomplished my purpose, with all my sins completely dissolved.
O Sage, it is solely due to your presence that we remain here without fear; for how could the Blessed One, whose form is so exceedingly fierce, be [approached] by men of little strength? (17)
He propitiates the king of the Daityas, the lord of the three worlds, while rending [his foes]; for the sapphire-blue form of that ocean of mercy indeed remains present there. (18)
O best of sages, at what place does the vision [of you] and so forth grant liberation? O lord of brahmins, show me that which is considered by me to be the giver of liberation. (19)
Thus addressed, Nārada showed him that purifying place where the Lord was stationed, covered by golden sands.
O King, behold this banyan tree, one yojana in extent and two yojanas in height, which endures until the end of the kalpa and grants liberation to men.
By the mere passing of its shadow, one is released from the shroud of sin; a man who gives up his life at its base shall attain liberation.
Even by merely seeing the sinless Nārāyaṇa in the form of a banyan tree, a mortal becomes free from sin; how much more so by worshipping and praising him! (23)
To the west of this root, O King, and to the north of Nṛsiṃha, stood the omnipresent Mādhava, who bears four forms.
To favor you alone, he will manifest again here, just as Viṣṇu, whose abode is his own, appears in Śvetadvīpa, a land of enjoyment.
In Jambūdvīpa, the land of karma, this is remembered as one's own station; because it is an extreme secret of one's own, its disclosure is not approved. (26)
O lord of the earth, one who is qualified for liberation knows this place to be a ground of distrust for men, especially for those of evil deeds. (27)
O King, even that other image of Viṣṇu which was installed by the citizens here bestows liberation; how much more so this one which is self-manifested? (28)
The concealment and disappearance of the Lord of the World occurs with excellent purpose in every age, for the sake of bestowing grace upon the virtuous.
O King, through various incarnations such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others, the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, remains concealed when the cause for manifestation has ceased.
Always established in the signless state here, this ocean of compassion is like Viṣṇu in Śvetadvīpa, though the Lord may descend elsewhere.
Even while remaining here, he manifests by his grace in Dvārakā, Kāñcī, Puṣkara, and other places, like a sprout emerging from the root of a tree.
O King, let there be no doubt in your mind that his very portions have descended as incarnations in various holy fords, lands, sacred fields, and shrines.
The Lord does not for a moment abandon his own field, as if it were his very own; however, O protector of the earth, another light shall arise originating from you.
Thus was that place pointed out by the high-souled Nārada; then Indradyumna prostrated himself upon the ground with all eight limbs.
But perceiving the God to be present, as if manifest, he offered praise. || 36 ||

Indradyumna said: O God of gods, Lord of the universe, destroyer of the afflictions of those who bow before you! Protect me, O lotus-eyed one, for I have fallen into the ocean of worldly existence. (37)
O Supreme Lord, you alone are the destroyer of the flood of suffering; for the base serve the base out of a desire for a mere fragment of happiness. (38)
Of this mass of one's own great evil, consisting of the three beginningless floods, which is constantly being replenished by birth and is difficult to eradicate; (39)
How much more so when You grant liberation directly to men through the state of devotion? Yet those fools who say that You, the ocean of mercy, are dependent upon karma—[speak thus]! (40)
"O Blessed One, they do not know that this very karma was impelled by you, such that the brahmin Ajāmila abandoned the duties prescribed for his caste and stage of life. (41)
O Lord, what sin has not been committed? Yet even he was liberated by the mere chanting of Your name; simply through remembrance, he was released from those with nooses in their hands.
O Lord of Gods, all means have been proclaimed for the sake of beholding you; for when you are seen, the doubts residing within the heart are indeed shattered. (43)
Doubtless, the destruction of both sin and merit shall immediately and certainly occur; you alone are my refuge, O Lord, so show favor to me, who am wretched. 44.
"O Lord, whatever has been determined by you regarding my remaining in the womb—by that alone shall my birth come to pass; this is the only thing I beg of you. (45)
O Lord, that form of Yours which stands here as the bestower of liberation even upon those who look askance—that alone I behold with these eyes; there is no other purpose.
Having thus praised Madhusūdana with palms joined in reverence, the king bowed again upon the surface of the earth, his eyes filled with tears.
Then, while Indradyumna was listening, a voice moving through the atmosphere, speaking with the melodious tones of the Sāman chants, resounded from the midst of the sky.
"Do not fall into anxiety, O protector of the earth; I shall come within the range of your vision. Do that which Nārada spoke as the word of Brahmā. (49)
Having heard that divine speech uttered by Nārada, he, who brings pleasure to the Blessed One, placed his faith in the horse sacrifice.
And he spoke again to Nārada with a voice faltering with joy: "O Sage, that which was commanded by you at the direction of the Four-faced One—"
Indeed, this bodiless voice issued forth at that very moment; for the Grandfather is the Lord of the World, and there is never any distinction between these two.
For you are indeed the son of the Lotus-born, and your word is the word of the Blessed One; therefore, that which brings about one's welfare must be performed with diligent effort.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sages and Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 15 ||
Jaimini said: Having seen King Sumanas full of faith regarding the great sacrifice, Nārada, the delighter of the world, spoke with supreme affection. (1)
The gods become allies in the endeavors of those who perform virtuous deeds; you yourself are an example of this, since the four-faced Brahmā is your companion.
Therefore, come; let us go right there into the presence of Nīlakaṇṭha, for the sake of the destruction of all rākṣasas and the warding off of all obstacles.
O King, I place before you Nṛsiṃha with his face turned toward the west; for that Blessed Lord, the Man-Lion, though usually invisible, is now manifest.
In his presence, however, the sacrifice shall yield an extraordinary fruit. Go quickly ahead and have a temple constructed there. || 5 ||
And having come here upon my remembrance, that son of Viśvakarman will indeed swiftly construct a temple facing westward.
O King, to the south of Nīlakaṇṭha, there stands a great sandalwood tree that has grown for a long time at a distance of a hundred bows.
"O King, there shall be a sacred field situated in his western region; may you perform a thousand horse-sacrifices before it."
"Go; I shall remain right here for five days, propitiating this divine lion, who is infinite and whose form is light."
Having established [the deity] within the image, O King, I shall lead that beautiful form—endowed with life-force, senses, and mind—from one lamp to another, as it were.
Having heard these words of Nārada, the best of kings went with speed to that place in the vicinity of the sandalwood trees.
There he saw Sughaṭaka, an expert in the science of craftsmanship, who had arrived there by the command of Nārada as the son of the divine architect.
Having assumed a human form and standing there bearing weapons and a measuring-line, he indeed beheld the king who was intent on constructing a dwelling for the gods.

With palms joined in reverence, he said: "O Lord, I am an expert in the treatises on architecture; today I shall construct for you a beautiful temple of Narasiṃha. O best of the twice-born, the king also spoke to him, smiling: [14]
Indradyumna said: "You are no ordinary craftsman; you are the author of the treatises on the arts. You have been described by Nārada himself as the highly illustrious son of Tvaṣṭṛ. (15)
"In this desolate great forest, there has been no human habitation prior to this day; we have arrived here today—what is the reason for our connection with these craftsmen? (16)
"You alone are the divine architect for Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor; you always meditate upon him and remain obedient to his command. (17)
The very sage by whom you were remembered will come here on another day, taking with him a replica image of Narasiṃha.
Therefore, quickly construct today a beautiful palace for Narasiṃha, facing westward, complete with walls and gateways. (19)
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites and engaged him in the construction, the king employed his servants who were gatherers of stone materials with abundant wealth.
On the fourth day, O Brahmins, the unsurpassed temple was completed, despite requiring a long time to construct, through the power of the divine architect.
Then, at the clear dawn, following the conclusion of his daily rites, he took up the requisites for the rite of installation along with his retinue.
While the king remained there, observing Nārada’s arrival, he heard the sounds of conchs, mṛdaṅgas, and murajas.
Songs, auspicious musical instruments, the sounds of bells and elephants, as well as loud shouts of "Victory! Victory! filled the expanse of the sky.
Having heard that, King Indradyumna and his followers—thousands of kings, Vedic scholars, Brahmins, and Vaiṣṇavas—were filled with wonder.
"These sounds are undoubtedly miraculous and supportless; as they were reflecting upon this, a wind blew from the south."
O twice-born ones, showers of flowers, fragrant and resonant with the humming of swarms of bees, appeared, moistened by the waters of the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā).
Immediately thereafter, that Nārada, the son of Brahmā, beheld her reclining upon an excellent celestial chariot brought forth by the power of her ascetic penance.
It was graced by celestial women holding jeweled chowries in their hands, and adorned with various ornaments of precious gems and jewels.
Wearing celestial garlands and garments, anointed with divine perfumes, she was beautiful, her life-breath firmly established, and fashioned by Viśvakarman.
Taking up a secondary image of Narasiṃha, which was encircled by a circle of light and endowed with joy on all sides, he stood before him.
Seeing her, everyone—the king and his followers—were filled with joy, wondering: "Has the Lord who vanished been recovered by Nārada? || 32 ||

With delighted souls, they honored and praised that sage; then, O twice-born ones, having observed the form of the Man-Lion standing nearby, they considered it to be an image of the primordial Nṛsiṃha.
Then, rising up with a joyful heart, the king circumambulated Hari and touched the earth with his head.
By the king’s command, the sage dispatched the palace, which was endowed with auspicious characteristics, along with provisions suitable for the perfection of faith. (35)

O best of the twice-born, at an auspicious moment, King Indradyumna praised the image of the God of gods, which was installed upon a jeweled altar together with Dharā and Ramā, its form absorbed in yoga. (36)
By Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas, by kings, and by the wise Nārada, with secret Upaniṣads, Smṛti-based hymns, and scriptures, they were filled with joy.

Indradyumna said: O You who possess forms that are one and many, gross and subtle, and atomic; O You who transcend space, whose sole form is the nature of space; O You whose shape is space, all-pervading, stationed in space, mounted upon space, and whose hair is space, O Lotus-born One! 38.

O Divine Lion, whose radiance is like many tens of millions of suns manifested, save me from the ocean of suffering! O you whose nature is both the object of awakening and the act of awakening, you are eternally near yet situated afar; you are neither distant nor near.

You are the object of all that is to be known, yet accessible through knowledge; though beyond illusion, You are measured by inference. You are the beginning of the whole, the creator of the whole, its witness, its protector, its destroyer, and the witness of the universe—salutations to You!

O sole cause of the destruction of suffering, who are not a cause for [further] bondage; O dispeller of the multitude of doubts born from the beginningless; O you whose form is light, whose form is knowledge, whose appearance is a mass of radiance; O cause of the manifestation of the cosmic array! 41.

O Lord, grant me forever supreme devotion to Your lotus feet, which are the root of the four goals of life; for those people who are constantly engaged in Vedic and Smārta rites remain here as wretched ones, bound in the ocean of worldly existence.

He has infinite feet, many hands and eyes, and endless ears; the multitude of the quarters is His garment. He is adorned with excellent earrings that are the lords of day and night, and a beautiful necklace fashioned from the garland of constellations.

I take refuge in you, the wondrous and divine form of Nṛsiṃha, who fulfills the desires of your devotees; for the lotus-feet of yours indeed attain full bloom through the jewels in the crown of Brahmā. 44.
I bow to him whose divine feet the wives of the lords of the gods carry upon their heads—those feet beneath the ground of which the head of one composed of the five elements rolls.

I bow to that fierce divine lion, who has destroyed the multitude of sins, a lion in the ocean of compassion for those who take refuge at his feet, and who causes the vessel of the universe to tremble by the impact of his lotus feet.

I bow to Nṛhari, the womb of the three worlds, whose mass of matted hair shatters the throngs of sins as they are dispersed by its flickering rays, and whose fierce, loud laughter drowns out the sound of the clouds.

Salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you today, O Viṣṇu! Protect me, O Lord who is compassionate toward the wretched. Having approached you, O Murāri, may this bondage of my body no longer remain within the prison of saṃsāra.
O Lord, show me such compassion that at the conclusion of a thousand horse-sacrifices, I may behold your divine form with my physical eyes. 49.
O Lord of Sacrifice, just as this thousandfold sacrifice of mine is being completed without obstacle through Your grace, so may Your presence remain with me. 50.

O Lord, millions of heaps of sins go to destruction; for those who praise You, dharma, artha, and kāma are held in the palm of their hand—this is no wonder. O Viṣṇu, those men who take refuge in You are the vessels of liberation.
Having thus praised that divine lion, the king, with a joyful mind, repeatedly touched the earth with prostrations like the falling of a staff.
Jaimini said: That sacred field of Narasiṃha was created by Brahmā in ancient times for the sake of favoring Indradyumna and for the welfare of all the worlds. (53)
O Brahmins, those who behold that Nṛsiṃha stationed together with Śambhu do not undergo the bondage of a physical body; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever they have desired in their minds, those who indeed praise the one in the form of the Divine Lion with this hymn shall obtain even more than that. (55)
The God who grants all desires bestows liberation upon him on that Jyeṣṭha-śukla-dvādaśī which is conjoined with the Svātī nakṣatra. || 56 ||
Established in that field by the great seer, the divine lion, he is seen there by those who behold him, even by the son of Brahmā himself.
They obtain the full fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices by means of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), or with milk, or with coconut water. || 58 ||
Those men who, having worshipped the Great Lion with ritual offerings including milk-rice (pāyasa), bathe him either with water or with fragrant water; || 59 ||
With garlands of hibiscus flowers and most beautiful fragrant garlands, with incense and lamps containing camphor, and with exceedingly splendid betel leaves; || 60 ||

By means of beautiful hymns, recitations of praise, and loud shouts of "Victory!", by circumambulations and prostrations, and by gifts and the satiation of Brahmins—having thus gratified that Narasimha, one shall attain the world of Brahmā.
O twice-born ones, on the fourteenth day of the month of Vaiśākha, under the constellation Svātī and on a Saturday, at the time of dusk, the first incarnation of Siṃha occurred.

Having worshipped Narasiṃha there according to the rules with a concentrated mind, the mass of sins accumulated over thousands of millions of births is consumed at that very moment, like a heap of cotton by fire. (63)
Having seen, touched, paid homage, and prostrated with devotion, and having offered praise, one is liberated from sins like a snake is freed from its slough.
For him there are no diseases, nor sorrows, nor likewise mental afflictions; he attains all his desires as well as the fruit of the horse sacrifice.

O Brahmins, whatever sacrifices, gifts, or other meritorious deeds are performed by men even once in its vicinity, they shall become multiplied millions upon millions of times through the grace of Narasiṃha. || 66 ||

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the Sage Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 16 ||
The sages said: O sage, tell us what the lord of men did once Nārasiṃha was established in that sacred field; for our curiosity regarding that is great.
Jaimini said: First, he invited all the thirty gods, beginning with Indra; thereafter, he consulted with thousands of sages and brahmins.

[He saw] those who had studied the four Vedas along with the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga) and the Pada and Krama recitations, who were skilled in the sciences of sacrifice (yajñavidyā), and firmly established in Mīmāṃsā.

Those who have completed their ritual duties according to the Kalpasūtras along with their commentaries, who are proficient in the eighteen branches of knowledge, and who are experts in the Dharma—|| 4 ||
He respectfully consulted with those who were pure in their noble conduct, of high birth, speakers of truth, and especially with the devotees of Viṣṇu.
The kings of the three worlds, the Siddhas, the seven seers, the twice-born, the virtuous Śūdras, the merchants, and the lords of the islands were all invited.
O brahmins, that assembly hall of the king measured two krośas; it was constructed of stone, lofty, and plastered with white lime.
In some places the ground consists of jewels, in some it is fashioned of gold, and in others it is made of crystal or silver, according to what is appropriate for each spot.
With lofty pillars made of jewels and draped in fine silk, it was enriched with beautiful moon-like canopies, perfumes, garlands, and chowries.
Beautiful with charming windows containing strings of pearls within, it was sprinkled with the oil of black agallochum and drenched with sandalwood water.
Strewn with flowers of every season and surrounded by groves at its borders, there were ponds with crystal staircases, adorned with lotuses and ornamental gateways.
Their interiors were filled with ruddy geese, water-fowls, swans, and cranes of sweet song, and they possessed clear, cool, fragrant, and sweet waters.
On all sides of it, O twice-born ones, there were hundreds of easy descents, beautifully arranged with shade-giving trees, shining on every side.
O best of the twice-born, the sacrificial hall of King Indradyumna was constructed by Viśvakarman exactly as that of Marutta had been.
On an auspicious day and under an auspicious constellation, having seated the members of the assembly, he beheld the king seated upon his throne as well as the sages who were also seated.
Then [he honored] the hosts of perfected Brahman-sages seated upon costly carpets, the gods seated upon golden pedestals, and the twice-born according to their respective rank.
And others were seated on excellent thrones, comfortably situated according to their respective places; and in the midst of the kings, gods, and sages was the Lord of Śacī.
He saw himself seated upon the jeweled throne, the mark of universal sovereignty, adorned with divine garlands, perfumes, garments, seats, and other such luxuries.
The king, being humble, first honored him with great opulence along with his family priest; then he likewise paid him worship as if he were a destitute person.
Even the Lord of the Three Worlds considered this a marvel; then, like Indra, he honored the perfected ones and the celestial sages.
He produced amazement even in Kuvera, who possesses supreme prosperity; thereafter, he honored the gods, each with abundant wealth appropriate to themselves.
With a perfectly composed mind, the lord of the earth duly honored the king with royal paraphernalia suitable for a monarch.
Just as those kings thought, "We have now truly obtained a kingdom inherited by succession, yet our retinue is not such as this," so it was. (23)
He further honored the Vaiṣṇavas with ritual offerings, conducting them in such a way that even those who were tranquil marveled at the arrival of these worldly objects.
Then the king, overflowing with the quality of goodness (sattva), properly honored the Brahmins, the Kṣatriyas, and the Vaiśyas, with the sages at their head.
Having honored others through his ministers, he was seen with great haste, bowing humbly with his palms joined in reverence.
The high priest Nārada addressed this lofty speech to Mahendra.
Indradyumna said: "O Lord of Gods, by your grace I desire this; be gracious to me. I shall worship the Supreme Person of Sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice."
"Grant me leave, O Lord; you are the master of sacrifices. All those who dwell in the three worlds are the executors of your commands. (29)
O Lord, remain in the midst of the assembly together with the gods for as long as it takes for a thousand sacrifices to be completed.
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to perform sacrifice, not out of a longing for your station; O Lord of Gods, O Master, you always know the mental disposition of all. (31)
The embodied Lord Mādhava, whom you previously beheld here, is this very one who was concealed by the sands during your worship.

"For the sake of his further manifestation, O Indra, at the command and word of the Four-faced One, I shall perform a thousand horse-sacrifices. When he is manifested once more, there will be prosperity for you as well."
When the king had thus made his request, the gods, headed by Mahendra, [reappeared]; and that voice which had previously been heard after their disappearance—[that] Sarasvatī—[spoke].
Remembering her as bodiless, they spoke these words with great joy: "O Indradyumna, you are truly a great soul, the most truthful person on earth. (35)
"That future deed was experienced by us even in the past; we shall be your helpers in this task that purifies the three worlds. (36)
Indeed, it was there that the Lord himself, the creator of the worlds, became intent upon his task; and it was in this very place on our earth that the Blessed One spoke to us as well.
"Entering [the womb] out of compassion for them, I shall once again manifest a wooden body; this is my firm resolve. (38)
O lord of the earth, there is no displeasure here on our part, nor on that of Indra; rather, your exertion toward what is desired by us brings us great joy.
O Indra among kings, perform the horse sacrifice—a rite repeated a thousand times—with ease, for the sake of Vaikuṇṭha, who is affectionate toward his devotees.
For the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, is difficult for us to propitiate; we too, having renounced our divinity here, have become solely devoted to him.
In this field, we shall propitiate those who are disciplined and embodied in human form; for indeed, in the world of men, a beloved deed once performed attains success.
Jaimini said: When this had been spoken by the thirty gods together with Indra, the king, his inner self deeply satisfied, worshipped the Blessed One for the purpose of commencing the sacrifice. (43)
Then, having duly performed thousands of ritual services, the king, endowed with faith, honored the hosts of ancestors.
Having seated the Brahmins, who were experts in ritual and well-adorned, within the sacrificial hall, he placed Vaikuṇṭha, together with the sacred fire, before him as his chosen deity.
Desiring an auspicious moment as calculated, when the recitation of blessings had commenced, he arrived accompanied by his wife, wearing pure and festive attire.

Having caused pure brahmins to pronounce auspicious blessings for the "day of merit" (puṇyāha) and the rite of prosperity (vṛddhikarma), he then, having gathered all the necessary materials, chose the officiating priests (ṛtvijas).

Having been chosen, they initiated that best of kings along with his wife; and after enjoying themselves, being urged by the members of the assembly, they performed the desired sacrifices for the sake of initiation.
Having brought that blazing Āhavanīya fire to the altar—was it not as if the very glory of Viṣṇu, the bringer of auspiciousness to the three worlds, were present in person? || 49 ||
Having sprinkled it well, consecrated it with mantras, and obtained the permission of the lords of the directions, they released that preeminent horse, which possessed auspicious marks on its limbs.
Then that consecrated king, restrained in speech, having taken his place upon a Raurava skin in the midst of the assembly, stood like the Conqueror of Death.
For the sake of liberating those who had been invited, he indeed commanded with his eye that precious jeweled vessels for the gods be brought by the king's order.
The minister had magnificent vessels made of pure gold for the meal of the sages and the kings.
O Brahmins, for the purpose of feeding the twice-born, new vessels were provided daily; O sages, those of the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas were auspicious ones made of silver.
O best of the twice-born, for the Śūdras' meals, vessels made of pure bell-metal were indeed used; day after day, these vessels [were cleaned] at the conclusion of the meal.
Those who have been invited to a meal at a sacrificial festival there are cast away by the people like discarded leaves. (56)
Their sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons—indeed, their entire lineage—constantly offered foods of the five flavors with great respect. (57)
Honored by the king at the command of Indradyumna, they were fed and remained there like members of a family until the conclusion of the great sacrifice.
He was the king of those people of that land and their presiding lord; he was the unifier of kings, having been entreated by Indradyumna.
But Nārada, the best of kings, was an impartial observer, ever eager to perform services for others, [and a friend] to Indra and the other lords of the gods as well as to the celestial sages.
The king himself performed the ritual duties for the completion of the sacrifice; six kinds of food and drink were prepared by the men in two ways.
There, for the meal of the gods, [the offerings] were indeed consecrated by those skilled in mantra and tantra, and by mortals proficient in the science of Nala.
For the denizens of heaven, who subsist on nectar, are indeed ignorant of hunger and thirst; yet even for them, that meal was a marvel because it was unprecedented. (63)
For mortals, it is difficult to obtain a meal in the house of Indradyumna; the distinction between Indradyumna and Indra is merely his residence among mortals.
O best of the twice-born, this was indeed most wonderful, being new every single day: the increase in honor, respect, and the quantity of food served.
In this world, the application of fragrant flowers, garlands, musk, and other ointments increases mutually through mere competition with one another.
Variegated and fine silk garments, along with cushions and seats; jeweled couches, beds, and fans with jeweled handles.
With nutmeg, cloves, and camphor, as well as betel leaves, enchanting songs, and various dances; (68)
And hundreds of Sūtas and Māgadhas, experts in training and well-acquainted with the fame of their respective lineages, were appointed by Bharata, the sage. (69)
Indeed, these and other objects, though difficult to obtain, were enjoyed with great reverence by both the gods and mortals.
On one side there were various wonderful things, and nowhere were any inferior; even for the inhabitants of Pātāla, the food was indeed superior to nectar.
For those who, having eaten it, do not desire even to go to the netherworld (pātāla)—those cities which are situated in the netherworld and illuminated by floods of jewels.
Without the light of the sun, the king granted them dwellings exactly like that, in which they perceived themselves to be in the netherworld (pātāla). || 73 ||
Seated in comfort, playing, eating, and lying down with joy—indeed, nowhere else do even the gods touch the earth in such a manner. (74)
In that city of Indradyumna, which was more enchanting than even heaven, they did not abandon the earth, being intent on their joyful play as they pleased.
For they say that happiness in heaven arises from desire; however, O Brahmins, there indeed is happiness everywhere even without desire.
Having honored them with great effort, those men consider themselves worthy of being fed with respect; they do not ask anyone for anything, so how could anyone ever turn away from them? (77)
The palaces of the sovereign kings were then equal to the private homes of the common people; at that time, it was not always the case that all such abundance existed within their own dwellings.
In that regard, whatever was beyond desire was easily obtained in great abundance; thus, when the sacrifice had proceeded with joy for the gratification of the Lord of Sacrifice, || 79 ||
The earth, whose entire wealth had been taken away by that king during the horse sacrifice, was once again beautifully adorned by a rain of gold.
Thus, as the ritual for gifts, honors, and feasts proceeded daily according to the prescribed rules for the inhabitants of the three worlds there, (81)
Regarding the horse sacrifice, people sang verses to one another: "Never before has such an array for a rite been prepared as this one, as enjoined by the scriptures. (82)
Among the royal sage Indradyumna, there has never been, nor will there ever be, such a thing as supplicants who are not givers when invited by one another. (83)
O twice-born ones, such was the prosperity of that king at that time that even for the gods there was no failure of their desires; then the sovereign of sacrifices commenced.

Endowed with great faith and fully accomplished, he became even more distinguished than his predecessor; [he was] the author of the Smṛtis, the author of the Kalpas, and likewise the composer of the Śāstras. (85)

Skilled in the performance of sacrifices and adorned with the ornaments of virtuous conduct, they proceeded in due order through the rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires and ending with the final purificatory bath.
O twice-born ones, this sacrifice was performed with the approval of the assembly for the pleasure of the king; the mantras were never deficient in accent or even in syllable. (87)
Those who indeed establish the rules are the ones who prescribe the performance of rituals; this is due to the occasion for expiation and because of the necessity of expiation.
There, for the yogin who is a practitioner of karma, there is no obstruction of karma, where the divine Seven Sages are the members of the assembly and witnesses to the sacrifice.
"Yājñavalkya and the other sages, who distinguish between virtues and faults, shall perform the rites; they have been chosen here as the officiating priests. (90)
While gathered in that assembly, those sages, in the course of their mutual conversation, spoke words of dialogue, well-composed verses, and secret Upaniṣads.
O Brahmins, [recite] the ancient verses preceded by devotion to Viṣṇu, as well as the deeds of Hari, which remove the flood of all impurities.
There, in that assembly hall, the lords of the earth gathered; they consumed the sacrificial oblation at his sacrifice while standing visibly in the midst of the fire.
O Brahmins, the gods led by Mahendra, having been away from home for a long time, did not remember Amarāvatī during that sacrifice. || 94 ||
For in ancient times, Brahmā ordained that their oblation be nectar; having consumed it, the gods became joyful, heroic, and long-lived.
Apart from the subject of performing sacrifices, they enjoy all the many other objects fashioned by Indradyumna.
There, those nāga kings who dwell in the depths of Pātāla enjoy sense-objects in the world of mortals that are even superior to those [found there]. (97)
"Indeed, they certainly do not desire your descent to the netherworld; thus has this sacrifice been set in motion, which brings joy to the three worlds. (98)
In this field of Puruṣottama belonging to King Indradyumna, for the sake of propitiating Jagadīśa, by the command of the Grandfather (Brahmā), [he established it]. || 99 ||
The lord of the earth attained the status of one short of a thousand horse-sacrifices, performed exactly according to the injunctions of the sacred rites. (100)
Then, during that thousand-fold horse sacrifice (vājimedha), the lord of the earth became a possessor of divine movement day after day. || 1 ||
In the past, on the night that occurred seven days after the Soma-pressing, during its fourth watch, he meditated upon the imperishable Viṣṇu.
In that meditation, by the power of his great fortune, the king beheld Śvetadvīpa, fashioned of crystal, as if it were before his very eyes.
He stood surrounding the Ocean of Milk on all sides, with great wish-fulfilling trees that filled the quarters of the sky with the fragrance of their blossoms.
On the fruits, shoots, and bark—both on the outside and the inside—in every respect, he was adorned with all ornaments, white and marked with the conch and the discus.
And in the midst of that was constructed an excellent pavilion made of divine jewels, featuring the forms of the enemy of Mura, which were the color of great madder.
Resplendent with a jeweled lion-throne shining like the midday sun, it was enchanting with gentle breezes and cool waves from the Ocean of Milk.
In their midst, he beheld the Lord, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace; resembling a dark blue cloud and adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
He was the abode of all loveliness and the temple of the glory of beauty; he surpassed [all others] with his body, which was adorned with divine ornaments.
There, stationed on his right side, was Ananta, the upholder of the earth, resembling ten million moons and possessing a luster like that of the Himalayan mountain.
Charming, with its hoods spread out like a canopy upon its crown, marked by a pair of jeweled earrings, and possessing a beautiful blue hood-veil.
His four arms shine with a plough, a conch, and a mace, and he is adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and rings.
Adorned with a girdle and a waist-cord, decorated with divine jewels, his form was intoxicated by divine wine; he possessed a beautiful smile and lovely eyes.

And on his right side was Lakṣmī, endowed with auspicious marks, holding a boon-granting gesture, a gesture of fearlessness, and a lotus in her hands; she was the color of saffron and possessed beautiful eyes. || 14 ||
He beheld her seated upon a lotus throne, a maiden from the ocean of loveliness, whose wondrous form was the very model for the assembly of all young women in the three worlds.
And he saw his grandfather standing before him with palms joined in reverence; and on the left side of the Lord stood the discus, composed of various jewels.
O best of the twice-born, having seen that teacher of the world being praised in his dream by Sanaka and the other lords of sages, that king was indeed filled with great joy.
Standing there in meditation, he praised with a voice faltering with joy that infinite being composed of light, whose form had never been seen before.

Indradyumna said: Salutations to you, O support of the universe; salutations be to you, O soul of the universe. O you who are beyond the three qualities of absolute liberation, O collyrium of all attributes, salutations be to you.

Salutations be to you, whose essential nature is perfectly pure and stainless knowledge; salutations to you, who are designated as the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman) and who are the very form of the universe.
Homage be to you, who destroy the suffering of those exhausted and fallen into saṃsāra; homage be to you, the breaker of the knot of the heart that is so difficult to pierce. (21)
Salutations to You, the foundational pillar for the house of the fourteen worlds; salutations to the wielder of the discus, the architect who fashioned millions of cosmic eggs.
Homage again and again to the abode of nectar within the ocean of compassion; homage to the ocean of mercy, whose sole secret purpose is the upliftment of the wretched. || 23 ||
Salutation to the light of the luminaries, such as the sun and other celestial bodies; salutation to the fire within that blazes with its own inherent radiance and consumes all sin. 24.
Salutations again and again to the purifier, the pure one, the most sacred among the sacred; salutations again and again to the greatest, the most excellent, the longest-lasting. || 25 ||
Salutations, salutations to the nearest and the farthest, to the most minute; O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be unto you, the most excellent and the most meritorious. || 26 ||
Protect me, O Lord of the World, O Friend of the distressed; salutations be unto you! Having obtained you as a comfortable boat, I have crossed the ocean of worldly existence.
O Lord of Ramā, upon seeing you, my afflictions have vanished; for those who have attained you, whose nature is consciousness and bliss, there is the complete destruction of suffering. (28)
O Lord, surely [this is] caused by the arising of supreme bliss; save me, save me, whose mind is dejected and who am submerged in the ocean of worldly existence! 29.
"When the midday sun has risen in the sky, how could there be the emergence of deep darkness? Thus, remaining absorbed in meditation, he praised and bowed down to the Lord of the Universe. (130)
At the conclusion of his meditation, he himself awoke from sleep; at the end of the dream, Indradyumna also remembered himself by means of his own self.
Having seen this most wonderful dream, the elephant among kings considered himself to have already achieved his purpose regarding the horse sacrifice.
A thousandfold success has indeed arrived through my own good fortune; for the word of a celestial sage never comes to naught at any time.
"How will my Lord himself be present here before my very eyes?"—with these thoughts, the lord of the people passed the remainder of the night in deep anxiety.
He related before Nārada exactly how he had experienced the dream; and Nārada also said, "O King, your grief has vanished. (35)
O best of kings, because he beheld the Blessed One at the time of dawn, that dream was one that yields its fruit within ten days.
"At the conclusion of the sacrifice, the Blessed One will become manifest before you here—just as Brahmā, the teacher of the moving and unmoving world, has said to you through my words. (37)
You have also seen that creator of the world in this dream; therefore, let the sacrifice be performed, but do not reveal it before others.
"O tiger among kings, this dream of Hari’s conduct is difficult to comprehend; however, such a dream arises only for one who is truly fortunate. (139)

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama-kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: Thereupon, O twice-born ones, the horse-sacrifice of the king commenced; during that sacrifice, the three worlds became like a single household.
By means of scriptures and hymns that reach the heavens, resplendent with the sequence of phonemes, and through the proper placement of words and accents, all other sounds are eclipsed. (2)
There, desired objects were indeed given without restraint to the destitute; that city became like a wish-fulfilling tree for actors, dancers, and bards.
In the midst of that, on the southern bank, near Bilveśvara, a temporary shed was constructed for the purpose of bathing at the avabhṛtha ceremony.
O twice-born ones, the servants appointed by the king approached with haste and, with palms joined in reverence, announced themselves to the monarch.
"O King, a great tree was seen on the shore of the great ocean; its top has entered into the depths of the sea, with its roots floating upon the waves."
"Of madder-red color, marked everywhere with conchs and discs, and floating—this supreme wonder was seen by us near the bathing chamber. (7)
This tree, resembling the rising sun with its radiance and perfuming the entire bank with its fragrant scent, has never been seen before.
"This tree does not appear to be an ordinary one; it is clearly perceived as a celestial tree. Surely some deity has arrived here in the guise of a tree. (9)
Having heard the words of those appointed officials, the king said to Nārada: "Tell me, for what reason do they speak of that which was seen as the best of trees?"
Nārada, smiling, spoke these words to the best of kings: "Let the final oblation be offered so that the sacrifice may be fruitful. (11)
That good fortune which you previously beheld in a dream has now arrived for you—the imperishable Viṣṇu, the universal form, who was seen in Śvetadvīpa.
Then a hair that had fallen from his body became a tree; it was the stationary partial incarnation on earth of the Supreme Lord.
The Blessed One, who is compassionate toward his devotees, assumes that very form; for that tree which is not of human origin is not a fit vessel for beholding him.

O tiger among men, O best of kings, were it not for you, [this sight] would not have become an object for the eyes of all people on earth; rather, it has become so through the power of your good fortune. 15.
O Great King, it shall be the destroyer of all impurities; having completed the concluding purificatory bath on the bank of the lord of rivers.
Having performed a very great festival and completed the auspicious rites of the marriage-thread, establish here upon the great altar the Lord of Sacrifice in the form of a tree.
Having reflected thus with joy, both the king and Nārada, well-provided with all luxuries, went to that place where the divine tree stood.

Seeing him, they were all filled with joy; considering that Brahman had appeared before them in person, those highly exalted ones, liberated while living, regarded their very birth as having achieved its purpose.
King Indradyumna also immersed himself in the ocean of nectar, having seen the Lord of the Universe in a dream, just as he was beloved by the Blessed One.
Thus that best of kings beheld that tree, which had eyes for branches and four arms; considering his own exertion to have been made fruitful, he was filled with joy. (21)
O twice-born ones, the king abandoned the grief born from the disappearance of Nīlamaṇi Mādhava; bowing to him again and again with eyes filled with tears of joy, he [departed]. || 22 ||
With the sounds of conchs, kāhālas, murajas, ḍhakkās, and paṭahas, he had the tree, which was tossed by the waves, brought ashore by the twice-born.
With the sounds of singing and musical instruments, with shouts of "Victory! by the thousands, and with handfuls of fragrant flowers falling repeatedly from the sky; || 24 ||
It was surrounded by incense burners well-fumigated with black agallochum, and fanned by beautiful courtesans intoxicated with youth.
He was being fanned on all sides by whisks with jeweled handles, and was beautifully adorned with banners made of divine silk and fine linen.
He was surrounded by throngs of royal sages and kings, as well as horses and foot soldiers; he was being saluted by the Magadhas and praised by the great seers.
It was attended by officiating priests, Brahmins, learned men, and likewise by those well-versed in the Vedas, as well as by Kshatriyas, those born of Vaishya families, and virtuous Shudras.
In the world of Bhūr, they beheld the tree of Viṣṇu being surrounded and praised with various hymns from the Śrutis, the Smṛtis, and the Purāṇas.
They led her to the divine great altar, adorned with garlands and perfumes, which was covered by an excellent and variegated canopy and surrounded on all sides without any gaps.
At the command of Indradyumna, they placed him upon the sacrificial altar; by the word of Nārada, the king honored him.
With thousands of divine offerings, that best of kings, at the conclusion of the worship, questioned Nārada, the most excellent of sages.
"What kind of images of Viṣṇu will he fashion, and who indeed will do so? Having heard that, the Guru, the sage of inconceivable majesty, spoke to him.
O King, who indeed knows the activity of that one who transcends all worlds—even for him, the creator of the universes, this matter remains within the sphere of doubt. (34)
While Nārada and the king were thus deliberating, an incorporeal voice was then heard from the sky.
In that situation, while all who were listening were filled with wonder, the Blessed One remained beyond human agency and outside the path of conceptual inquiry.
"He himself will descend upon the great altar that has been well-concealed; let it remain covered for these fifteen days."
"This carpenter who has arrived, aged and with weapon in hand—having brought him inside, let them fasten the door with great effort. (38)
Let them make loud noises outside until the event takes place; for once the sound of the event is heard, it brings about deafness and blindness. (39)
He would dwell in hell and bring about the destruction of his lineage; he should never enter within [the house] nor ever look [upon her]. (40)

If anyone other than the appointed official should look [at the king's person], there will surely be great fear for both the king and the kingdom, and blindness for the pair of eyes of that beholder. (41)
Therefore, one should not look [at the image] until its consecration is performed; for the divine [image] will itself speak at the conclusion of the rite once it has been fully completed.
Having heard that task—which brings happiness to all the worlds and must be accomplished with effort—Nārada and the others [acted] exactly as it had been spoken by Viṣṇu himself. (43)
They desired to act accordingly, and a carpenter arrived there; he then spoke to the king, "Those who were seen by you in a dream—"
"I myself shall strive with that terrible one of divine form," saying this, he vanished from the altar while assuming the form of an aged carpenter.
For the purpose of deceiving human beings, the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa appeared in person.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 18 ||
Jaimini said: Then that protector of the earth, having acted accordingly, attended to everything exactly as the goddess of speech, moving through the atmosphere, had spoken.
Thus, as day after day passed, a divine fragrance was experienced; a rain of Pārijāta flowers is difficult for mortals to obtain.
There was the sound of divine music and charming songs, as well as a rain of water from the celestial Gaṅgā, beautiful with its fine droplets.
The scent of rut from Airāvata and other elephants is unbearable for forest-dwelling elephants, yet it is experienced as a source of happiness by all living beings.
O twice-born ones, all the gods who had come for the sake of the sacrifice, their anxieties dispelled upon seeing Hari manifest, sat down in worship.
Just as Mādhava was formerly [worshipped], so too did divine marks appear upon that Viṣṇu-tree during the worship of the gods.
On the fifteenth day, the Lord himself, the Blessed One who possesses four forms as previously described by me, gradually entered into Nirvāṇa.
He appeared in such a manner as was previously described to you, seated upon a divine throne together with Balabhadra and Sudarśana.
Janārdana, whose arms shine with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, assumes the form of a serpent while bearing a mace, club, discus, and lotus.
He was radiant with a crown of seven hoods shaped like parasols and adorned with earrings; Subhadrā, with her beautiful face, held a choice lotus and the gesture of fearlessness.
This Lakṣmī, whose form is the essence of all consciousness, has manifested; for in the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, she was born from the womb of Rohiṇī.
By meditating upon the form of Balarāma, she took on the appearance of Balabhadra; for she could not bear, even for a moment, to be separated from him who descends through his divine play.
O brahmins, there is no difference here whatsoever between Kṛṣṇa and Bala; however, worldly convention exists because they were born from the same womb. 13.
"She is the sister of Baladeva"—this is the traditional account from the Purāṇas. In the form of a woman within a male form, Lakṣmī dwells everywhere.
The Lord Viṣṇu exists under male names, and Kamalālayā under female names; among gods, animals, humans, and others, there exists nothing beyond these two.
For who else but the lotus-eyed one could support the fourteen worlds upon the tip of his hood? He is Ananta, known as Bala.
This Śrī is proclaimed to be his sister, whose very nature is power; and as for the Sudarśana discus, it is always held in the hand of Viṣṇu.
That form situated at the tip of the branch, in the middle of the trunk, and that which is the fourth—thus indeed are the four forms revealed by him. (18)
When the divine form of the Blessed One had manifested in four ways for the benefit of the worlds, she who moves through the intermediate space spoke once more: ||| 19 ||
"O King, having covered these images very firmly with cloths, quickly restore each to its own color by means of painting with pigments. (20)
Viṣṇu, dark as a blue cloud; Balarāma, white as a conch or the moon; the Sudarśana discus, red; and Subhadrā, ruddy as saffron.
Though beautiful with various ornaments and distinguished by various gestures, these [women] were seen in the form of wood for the sake of causing sin.
It should be carefully concealed with the bark-fibers extracted from cloth; therefore, first [conceal it] with the very bark of this tree.
Have them firmly covered at the front by artisans skilled in their craft; and year after year they should be renovated by removing the previous repairs.
Except for this bark-ointment, which is divine and eternal, if anyone were to remove this ointment through negligence, [it would be lost]. (25)
Famine and pestilence shall afflict the kingdom, and its progeny will decline; therefore, O King, you must never look upon those who have been excluded. (26)
O Indra among kings, even for human beings, these [images] are seen as causes of fear; therefore, they should be viewed with paintings and smeared with abundant ointments.
Having beheld the most wonderful Puṇḍarīkākṣa, full of grace and charm, one is liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million kalpas.
O Indra among kings, make it beautifully adorned; you shall obtain wonderful desires. The Blessed One has manifested himself out of a desire to show you favor.
"By your grace, it shall bestow the fourfold aims of life (caturvarga) upon all living beings; on the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri), one hundred cubits to the northwest of the Kalpa tree. (30)
In that region, on a very large site to the north of Narasiṃha, he built a very firm and extensive palace, one thousand cubits in height.
Having had it constructed and consecrated, install him right there; for whoever worships Mādhava, who formerly resided on this mountain, [attains the highest goal].
Formerly, you had a friendship with a Śabara named Viśvāvasu, who was the best among the Vaiṣṇavas, along with that priest.
"O Great King, let the lineage of these two alone be employed in the task of anointing and consecrating him, as well as in future festivals. (34)
Having spoken thus, that divine Sarasvatī ceased; and having heard what was instructed by her, he was delighted in his inner soul. (39)
The best of kings untied the enclosure of the great altar; then they all beheld him seated upon the jeweled lion-throne.
Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Subhadrā, Vāsudeva, and Sudarśana—[one should fashion them] with beautiful forms according to the prescribed consecrations such as plastering and so forth.
With a face smiling with compassion, a broad and elevated chest, and a cage-like pair of long arms, he is the Lord who uplifts the wretched.
His lotus-eyes are fully blossomed, and his long lower lip is red with a smile; by the mere sight of him, he removes the accumulation of sins for those who behold him. (39)
Kṛṣṇa is seated in the lotus posture, adorned with divine ornaments, surrounded by his own splendor, and remains stainless even within a wooden body.
And he beheld Baladeva, who resembled a dark blue cloud, the destroyer of all distress, with a lotus-face graced by a boisterous laugh.
With a circle of hoods spread wide and eyes rolling from drinking wine, the king of serpents rose up, possessing a full and elevated, beautiful chest. || 42 ||
Slightly bent at the back with its body coiled, it was like the peak of Mount Kailāsa with a *kakubha* flower in full bloom at its tip.
He holds a plow, a discus, a lotus, and a mace; he wears a forest garland and is radiant with necklaces, earrings, armlets, a crown, and a diadem.
Between those two stood Lakṣmī, Subhadrā, who possesses an auspicious form.
She is the fire-drill for all the gods, the one who effects the crossing over the ocean of sins; her face is like a full-blown lotus, and she holds a choice lotus and the gesture of fearlessness.
She was the abode of beauty and charm, radiant with her ornaments, her body reddened by saffron, appearing like another Lakṣmī incarnate. (47)
