O twice-born ones, he beheld [the discus] situated on the left side of Viṣṇu, fashioned from the tip of a spoke, resembling the rising sun, possessing a sharp edge, and consisting of pure luster.
Upon seeing her, the lord of the earth was submerged in an ocean of bliss; bewildered as to what ought to be done, he was no longer master of his own body. (49)
With eyes half-closed and shedding only tears, that best of kings stood with palms joined in reverence, motionless as a pillar.
The best of sages, with a smiling face, said to that lord of the earth: "That for which you have undergone this exertion has now come to pass for you. (51)
"O tiger among kings, you alone are the fortunate one on earth; behold this Lord of the World, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals. (52)
Hari, the ocean of grace for his devotees and the treasure-trove of all knowledge, whom yogis with restrained minds constantly strive to behold.
With great attentiveness, men behold for a moment this very Janārdana, who has assumed a body made of wood.
"O King, I have appeared before you in person to bestow my favor upon you; worship this Lord of the Earth and praise this ocean of compassion. (55)
When properly praised, O King, he grants all desires that are in the mind.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue with the Sage Jaimini," within the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya, in the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: Thus enlightened by Nārada, the lord of the earth praised the Lord of the worlds with words full of compassion. (1)

Indradyumna said: O Murāri, the pair of your lotus feet was not worshipped by me in my previous births; therefore, O ocean of compassion, protect me, a wretched man who now partakes in the terrible ripening of those actions. (2)

Where is your pair of stainless lotus feet, immersed in the crowns of Brahmā, Rudra, and Indra? And where am I, a wretched pauper, covered indeed by skin over a mass of excrement, blood, flesh, urine, and bones? || 3 ||

O Lord, how can I know You, who am weary from wandering through this essence-less saṃsāra? Indeed, O God of gods, those for whom worldly existence is revealed as the manifestation of suffering truly know You. || 4 ||
O Lord, I have experienced manifold states of suffering acquired through the sins of many births; yet that slight state of happiness earned by merit is like a drop of honey mixed with bitter gall.

O Lord, that very enjoyment of sense objects which I have earned through karma for the sake of experiencing happiness becomes, in its ultimate consequence, nothing but suffering for me; indeed, there is no other person as full of suffering as I am.

O All-pervading Lord, if I, the three-eyed one, had previously worshipped another even in my mind, how then would I have obtained these manifold births, with their endless suffering to be experienced again and again? (7)

Through the states of being a master, a servant, a father, a son, a beloved, a mother, or a wealthy man; through the states of being a victim, a killer, a criminal, or a wife; and through the states of being an animal, a god, and so forth. (8)

O Murāri, whether one repeatedly or even once experiences the state of lowliness by wallowing in this courtyard of worldly existence, this indeed results in the desired fruit: being far removed from Your lotus feet. || 9 ||

This treasury and this army, filled with the wealth of the entire earth; these hundreds of women who are pleasing to the mind and endowed with youth and beauty; and this circle of kings free from all thorns—[all these are mine]. (10)

Moreover, this sovereignty is a great burden to me, who am devoid of knowledge of You like a beast; O Ocean of Compassion, always grant me the removal of this weight, for I am constantly beset by distress on that account. (11)

O Lord, through the mere remembrance of you, liberation has been granted to me, who am compassionate toward the wretched; O Master, it behoves you, out of your compassionate nature, to protect me, who have wandered here like a water-wheel. 12.

In this world, which is like a tree cast adrift by a current, there is indeed no kinsman for me other than you. My wretched mind, though possessed of affectionate bonds, must be overcome regarding worldly objects.

Day and night, may my mind never depart from your lotus feet; this alone is my prayer. May those who have attained you—the ocean perfectly full of existence, consciousness, and bliss—be the fortunate ones of thousands of births.

What do they see? They perceive only a momentary pleasure in the sensory net of Indra’s illusion, which is actually manifold suffering. Where is that bondage—indestructible by hundreds of knots of desired fragments of misery—that arises from one's own actions? (15)

Where is your lotus-foot, which is infinite, devoid of beginning or end, singular, and the bestower of bliss? And where is my attachment to the ocean of illusion, filled with the whirlpools of delusion and the pits inhabited by the crocodiles of evil karma? (16)

"O Lord, by the casting of Your playful sidelong glances, lead me today to the shore, for I have fallen without support; You who constantly strive to accomplish the desired rites for those who have taken refuge in You for the fulfillment of their own purposes. (17)

O you who are compassionate by nature, protect me, a fool who wanders about, having abandoned my own welfare and failed to reach you, the Supreme Lord, the very root—wandering excessively for the sake of trivial matters. (18)

Oṃ! O Viṣṇu, sole object of worship for the world; O Lord of the universe, known through the Vedāntas, immutable; You alone have the power to destroy the vast masses of my sins. Save me, who am most wretched and a vessel of exhaustion. (19)
O Viṣṇu, having abandoned you—the sole cause of happiness—protect me, whose mind is base; for this entire fourfold assembly of beings is fast asleep during the night of delusion created by you.
Having reached the rising of the sun of your knowledge at the end, one is awakened; I take refuge in you. You alone are the creator of all worlds, your form encircled by a thousand hoods. 21.

O Supreme among the powerful, through the function of Your various manifestations, I take refuge in You as my ruler; for by Your own power, seated upon the lotus of Your chest, O Lord, You create and swallow the worlds.

I bow at the pair of feet of that auspicious-formed one, the refuge of the world and the fire-stick for the gods; O Lord, this entire web of cosmic eggs is fashioned from the network of rays emanating from Your hands.

Having thus praised you, the Sudarśana known as the Discus, the destroyer of the Daitya host, that best of kings, being himself Sudarśana (handsome), prostrated before you with his eight limbs touching the ground. || 24 ||
Save me, O Lord of the World, who am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra; O kinsman of the helpless, out of compassion protect me, the wretched one, overwhelmed by darkness. (25)

Nārada said: Victory, victory to you, O Nārāyaṇa, whose sole purpose is to ferry beings across the shoreless ocean of worldly existence! You whose divine essence is meditated upon by the foremost of yogis such as Sanaka, Sanandana, and Sanātana; you whose entire reality of all beings is transformed through the superimposition of the play of your own *māyā*! O embodiment of the three principles (*tritattva*), bearer of the triple staff (*tridaṇḍadhara*), whose divine knowledge is sung by the *Triṇāciketa*, *Trimadhu*, and *Trisuparṇa* hymns; you who consist of the Vedic meters (*chandomaya*), whose favorite seat is Garuḍa (*suparṇa*), lover of your devotees, the singular protector of those who take refuge in you! Your true nature is veiled by the net of your own *māyā*. O universal form (*viśvarūpa*), illuminator of the universe, facing every direction, with eyes everywhere, ears everywhere, with feet, heads, and necks on all sides; you whose hands, nose, tongue, skin, hair, and body-hairs are everywhere; the soul of all worlds, the bringer of happiness to all worlds, the benefactor of all worlds, saluted by all worlds! O teacher of the three worlds, to whom all gods and demons bow—Brahmā born from millions of lotuses through your playful sport, along with Rudra, Indra, the Maruts, the Aśvins, the Sādhyas, and the hosts of Siddhas—you who are beyond the range of anyone’s knowledge! Salutations to you, salutations to you!
Jaimini said: And there were other kings who were learned in the Vedas and masters of the scriptures, as well as sages, brahmins, kṣatriyas, and wise men of the vaiśya caste. || 27 ||
They praised the lotus-eyed one, who is endowed with strength, together with Bhadrā, using ancient hymns, laudatory verses, and poetic compositions in various ways.
Then Indradyumna spoke to his sinless domestic priest regarding the materials for the worship of Vāsudeva, prepared with the ritual refinements of service.
That best of kings himself worshipped them in due order, according to the injunctions and mantras, following the instruction of Nārada.
He worshipped Balabhadra with the twelve-syllable mantra, by propitiating whom Dhruva attained the most excellent of stations.
With that great, purifying Puruṣa-sūkta, which is well-known in the three Vedas, the king worshipped Nārāyaṇa according to his ability.
Having worshipped them with devotion according to his prosperity—worshipping Bhadrā with the hymn of the Goddess, Sudarśana with the Saudarśanī hymn—the best of kings [performed the rites]. (33)
To please him, the king devotedly gave gifts to the foremost of the twice-born, including the Tulāpuruṣa gifts and other great gifts (mahādānas).
Then he gave away crores of cows that formed part of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha), as well as many other cows adorned with ornaments and accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).

O best of the twice-born, through the connection with the earth being turned up by their hooves, a pit was formed; it was indeed filled with the water of their gifts and became a sacred ford (tīrtha) of great fruit.
Having bathed there and duly satiated the ancestors and the gods, a person undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices. || 37 ||
The lake of that king Indradyumna is renowned by his name; there, a person offers funeral cakes (piṇḍas) intended for the ancestors.
Having uplifted twenty-one generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā; there is no holy place (tīrtha) superior to this, for it originated from a limb of the horse-sacrifice.
The river flowing through the three paths (the Gaṅgā) might even be equal to the lake of Indradyumna; thereafter, the king began the construction of the palace.
At an auspicious time, under a favorable constellation as directed by the rules of the astrologers, and at a propitious moment, he honored Nārada and other eminent Brahmins.
Having caused the recitation of benedictions and the success of the rite, the best of kings offered the guest-offering (arghya) while remembering the Lord of the World in his palace.
Having requested the earth for a site that would endure as long as the moon and stars, he worshipped the artisans, preceded by the Vāstuyāga sacrifice.
Thus he celebrated a great festival with abundant songs and instrumental music; he gave whatever was desired to the poor, the helpless, and the distressed.
Seeing that Hari had descended for their sake and that their sins were destroyed, he dismissed the king with great honor, as they had already achieved their purpose.
Then that best of kings gave millions of pieces of wealth to the stone-carvers, who had been gathered from many regions to work the stones.
Filled with joy, the upholder of the earth spoke this in the assembly: "Whatever has been acquired by me through human effort from the eighteen islands—" || 47 ||
All of that has been offered for the pleasure of the Lord of the World; and whatever fatigue I have incurred in the course of this victorious expedition [is likewise offered]. (48)

"May this [merit] of mine be fruitful for the sake of attaining the grace of Viṣṇu through the application of my purpose. What greater fortune could there be for me than [to have seen] Hari, the teacher of all things moving and unmoving? (49)
I shall propitiate him with the prosperity won by my two arms; for Fortune always resides in the Lotus-eyed One, and my own fortune is born from His grace.
What indeed could the God of gods, the wielder of the discus, not accomplish in her? For whoever receives the fall of his sidelong glance, upon him fortune shines in every direction.
The goddess consisting of eighteen aspects dances upon the tip of his tongue; by propitiating that Lord of the World, Brahmā attained the state of Brahmanhood.
Rudra attained the state of Maheśvara and Śakra the sovereignty over the three heavens; having worshipped him, I shall worship that eternal one who is worshipped by the worlds.
By that high-souled one, the threefold heap of sin has been conquered, by whom Kṛṣṇa has been worshipped according to the ritual with its limbs and subsidiary parts.
This body is the field (kṣetra), wherein the omnipresent Lord, accompanied by egoism, manifests, disappears, and remains eternally as its master. (55)
Having worshipped here the Teacher of the worlds in his manifest embodied form, one becomes one who has realized the goal and a recipient of the four aims of human life.
May that prosperity of the kingdom which I have acquired through great expense and exertion become fruitful only by the grace of these very lotus feet.

Having worshipped the God with all ritual offerings and with the riches plundered from the ocean-girdled earth, let the imperial expedition remain fruitful until the ripening of [his] karma is reached. || 58 ||

What collection of material objects is there, indeed, by which one who is free from sin might not bring Viṣṇu before him with all his limbs? Or what human effort is there, such as the equipment for Vāsudeva, which has not been accomplished by me? (59)

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sages and Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 20 ||
Jaimini said: As the royal sage was speaking thus, a certain twice-born man, a master of the Ṛgveda, a knower of Vedānta, and one whose nature was rooted in wisdom, joyfully uttered these words.

Oh, what a mass of fortune you possess, by which this wooden form has appeared on earth—of which the Veda declares the supreme worship to be the bestower of liberation even upon those deluded by ignorance of the Self!
Those who worship this wooden log that floats on the far shore of the ocean—a thing beyond human effort—and which is difficult to propitiate, attain liberation that is very hard to achieve.
Nārada, the direct treasury of the knowledge of Brahman, replied; for indeed, his knowledge does not come from anything other than the words of the Vedānta.
For the activity of Viṣṇu does not proceed without the Veda; whether in the creation of others or of himself, the Lord possesses the authority of the Śruti as His means of knowledge.
If it were to proceed without the Śruti, who could attain its authority? Therefore, O King, this incarnation is well-established here by the Śruti.
Know that the Puruṣa who is to be known through the Vedānta and is sung in the Sāman chants is the one who brings about the supreme good for men, and not an image.
"By the mere sight of you, our most profound and dense darkness has been pacified; indeed, there already exist the Śrutis that previously illuminated this very worship. (8)
This worship, when applied to the true goal, is indeed highly praised; oh, how the humans dwelling in Bhāratavarṣa have their impurities diminished!
Among those places where Janārdana has manifested as the bestower of liberation, this region of Coḍhra is the most excellent of all.
Abiding there, they behold the one whose form is Brahman with the eye of spiritual insight; the path of the Śruti and Smṛti is profound and crowded with ritual actions.
By whom those wandering here, agitated like a water-wheel, are led; He, who consists of consciousness, is the cause for attaining the state free from falsehood.

It bestows supreme bliss and liberation even without the means such as sacred revelation (śruti) and the like, for those of evil soul who remain in a miserable state due to their incessant coming and going.
This Viṣṇu, whose body is wood, is the giver of happiness and a true kinsman; O King, the rules prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti do not apply here. (14)
In whatever manner one might come within the range of sight of a Cāṇḍāla, it grants liberation; even if he is not a devotee, a man who follows the footsteps of others may behold him.
If one who is established in discipline, possessed of devotion, and firm of mind should worship [him], he shall indeed obtain the complete fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices. (16)
Without doubt, that man attains union with Brahman; for where is there anything abundant in suffering and exertion compared to this effortless and imperishable state? (17)
It is short-lived, yields meager fruit, and is characterized by return; where is this wooden Brahman compared to the fire that consumes heaps of sin? (18)

It bestows liberation consisting of truth, consciousness, bliss, and absolute oneness even by being seen; whereas the recitation of the Vedas and other such practices are difficult for the wicked-minded to perform.
He bestows without agitation that which is to be attained by those great souls; for in other fields, the Blessed One remains very distant from those dwelling among mortals.
The all-pervading Lord, the bestower of liberation, dwells eternally in this, his own field; therefore, O highly fortunate one, remain here with your own strength and manliness.
"You are most learned and a devotee; worship this [deity] along with its limbs and sub-limbs."
Jaimini said: Having heard those words of the twice-born, Nārada was delighted in his heart: "Well spoken by this best of the twice-born, who follows the path of the Vedas! (23)
At the beginning of creation, the collection of the Vedas arose from the breaths of Brahman; therein, this meaning of the Upanishads has now become manifest. (24)
The Blessed Lord Prajāpati, whose source is the lotus, knows this matter; and now, O protector of the earth, I have come to know it from his own mouth.
By his command, everything has been done exactly as you desired; having propitiated him, remain here, for I am going into the presence of Brahmā.
"I shall announce what has been done and make it public to the enemy of Mura; therefore, O protector of the earth, construct a palace with great wealth. (27)
But by installing Narasiṃha in a palace, you shall be liberated. || 28 ||
Jaimini said: Having heard that, the lord of the earth then replied to the sage: "O Great Sage, I wish to go with you into the presence of Brahmā. (29)
"By whose grace this Lord of the World became a guest of my eyes, having offered that temple for the purpose of consecrating the Enemy of Mura. (30)
I shall announce the festival for the installation of the temple in your presence, so that the Grandfather (Brahmā) himself may come from the world of Brahmā.
"He will perform a great festival for the Blessed One in this temple; therefore, O Sage, lead me also into the presence of Vidhi."
"O Sage, having completed the consecration of the womb in the temple, we shall remain here; afterwards we two will depart. Wait for me for some time. (33)
Then that king [summoned] all those experts in the arts and sciences, each individually for the task of fashioning the stone blocks.
O twice-born ones, he respectfully engaged them with honors, gifts, and marks of respect; day by day, the well-constructed temple grew larger.
Just as the moon is filled on all sides during the bright fortnight, so too that palace, being built up, was fully completed.
Because of its great height, the number of stones cannot be perceived in a short time; it might perhaps be possible through the process of counting them as they are joined together. (37)
But the expenditure of wealth, amounting to millions, cannot be calculated; it was as much as the number of people living according to the law in the land of Bhārata. (38)
Those kings appointed by King Indradyumna were each assigned individually, yet they remained united with one another.
They too were appointed by others, and all of them were set to work there; the great roar arising from the joy of those constantly engaged in that task was incessant.
Pervading the sky, he filled the quarters of the directions; she had been propitiated by the king’s faith, devotion, and sattvic nature.
O Brahmins, the prosperity of the lord of the earth increased along with his fame; in some places it was brilliantly radiant with various jewels set in gold. (42)
In some places, its interior parts of crystal possess a luster resembling an autumnal cloud; in other places, the wall is constructed of blue stone, as dark and dense as a black cloud.
When the temple of Viṣṇu had been thus well-constructed and made most beautiful, that best of kings performed the ritual consecration of the inner sanctum according to the prescribed rules.

In order to prevent the collapse caused by lightning strikes and other such calamities, as appropriate, one should place gems and other materials obtained from human labor within the architectural treatises.
Furthermore, he carefully deposited there a great variety of highly valuable goods, precisely those appropriate for the equipment of the palace's construction.
Then, while this temple, which increases fame and is inconceivable even in thought by kings throughout the three worlds, was being constructed, (47)
O twice-born ones, even among the gods who dwell until the end of the kalpa, such a palace is not observed; indeed, nothing like this has ever been constructed anywhere on earth.
Or thus do the Ādityas converse with one another in heaven: "Oh, how great is his wisdom, that it has reached such a high degree of maturity! (49)
With longing for the lotus feet of the Blessed One, they behold and indeed perform extraordinary deeds through faith. (50)
Who indeed were the kings on this earth who were skilled in statesmanship—those universal sovereigns who were conquerors of empires and vanquishers of all enemies? (51)
By those who have accumulated vast riches by the millions, and who have performed a thousand horse-sacrifices for the Lord of the Three Heavens; (52)
It might be possible for kings, but nothing of this kind has been performed previously; neither has a thousand horse-sacrifices ever been seen or even heard of.
Indeed, where the inhabitants of the three worlds witnessed what was performed by that ruler of the earth, they remained on this earth as sharers in the enjoyments of that king.
The assembly hall of that performer of sacrifices shines like the world of Brahmā; there, the three Vedas appear in embodied form, as does the Bull of Dharma with his four feet.

Where the gods, whose desires were fulfilled by their mere resolve and who possessed wondrous intellects, came to be, this excellent palace indeed has now come within the range of my own understanding. || 56 ||
Even that which does not enter the minds of the inhabitants of the three worlds—what could be difficult for a king to obtain when he has Nārada as his companion? (57)
And the Grandfather, the creator of the worlds and lord of all the immortals, is present; or rather, for one devoted to Viṣṇu, what he intends to do is not beyond reach.
"O twice-born one, there is no difference between Viṣṇu and his world of devotees. Then, at the edge of the palace, he spoke to Nārada, the lord of sages.
Everything was accomplished for me, which was impossible even for the gods and asuras, because I was devoted to the non-dual worship of the Lord Viṣṇu himself.
"The splendor of the Lord's body has long resided within me. Having said this, he bowed his head at the feet of Nārada.
Nārada also, having raised him up and honored that best of kings, said: "O King, in truth there is indeed no difference between you and me."
But he who has manifested as the Lord of the World himself, or through his incarnation—be sure to worship him; you are now liberated while living.
When a person’s mind is possessed of such profound devotion toward His lotus feet through exclusive bhakti, what indeed could possibly exist beyond this? (64)

O King, that which cannot be earned through pilgrimages, mantras, recitations, gifts, sacrifices accompanied by abundant fees, vows, Vedic studies, or ascetic penances— [is attained through devotion]. 65.
O Indra among kings, it was not possible for that hand, which had come by virtue of your devotion, to be otherwise; do not grieve beyond this. Salutations to you in your state of devotion.
O great lord of kings, having remained on this earth for a long time in excellence, worship the Lord of the World with ritual offerings and grand festivals.
If he desires to see the Grandfather (Brahmā) and goes into the presence of the Lord, He too will instruct him in those various pilgrimages and great festivals.
And at that time, when the temple has been consecrated by the Self-Existent One, the Blessed Lord himself will grant you a boon.
I too shall come then together with the seven seers; at that time, let us both go there to the stainless world of Brahmā.
"Who on earth, other than you, is capable of reaching the world of Brahmā? Having spoken thus to the king, Nārada ascended into the sky.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Dialogue with the Sage Jaimini," within the *Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya* of the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: Then the king spoke this to him: "O Sage, how can there be a departure without a visible means of transport? Here indeed is a flower-chariot, swift as the mind."
"Having mounted this, we two shall go; wait for just a moment until I have obtained the permission of these officials in the palace. (2)
"O best of sages, having circumambulated the Lord, I am departing. Nārada, for his part, hearing these words of the king, placed his full trust in the monarch's speech.
Taking the king by the hand and entering the great altar, he bowed repeatedly to Kṛṣṇa together with the two Rāmabhadras and requested permission to depart for the realm of Brahmā.

Indradyumna, too, having circumambulated Hari with his speech, mind, and body, and having bowed again with all eight limbs while uplifted in spirit, O Brahmins, requested with joined palms for the attainment of the world of Brahmā. || 5 ||

Both of them, the sage and the king, traveled by means of a divine vehicle; having circumambulated the sun situated in the center of the celestial sphere, they proceeded higher and higher, passing beyond the sphere of Dhruva.
Being gazed upon with joy by the Siddhas residing in Janaloka, who were bowing their heads and looking up with haste, the two conversed with one another.

O Brahmins, this life-story of the Blessed One purifies the impurities of the mind. This best of sages, liberated while living, wanders through all the worlds; even while dwelling among mortals, he remains one whose conduct is entirely unimpaired.
By the grace of devotion to Viṣṇu, the king departed quickly; for in the realm of the universe, no such thing exists that is difficult to attain.
Or else, he who is a devotee of Viṣṇu attains liberation; and those two were reverently honored by the Siddhas residing in Maharloka.
Indradyumna did not remember his own former dwelling as a king; ascending higher and higher in succession, he beheld those who were the sole recipients of happiness.
Free from duality and arising from desirelessness, he performed many acts of human effort in that very moment, solely for the pleasure of the Blessed One, upon this field of action.
He reflected upon the palace: "Will it remain intact or not when I have returned to the world of Brahmā? Or will it be overwhelmed by my enemies? (13)

Or perhaps the servants might become lax in their devotion due to greed for wealth; likewise, the guilds of artisans, having received their wages, might work slowly and not construct [the temple] quickly once I have departed for the abode of Brahmā. (14)
"As long as I have not returned after taking the four-faced Creator, this palace shall no longer remain while I am far away. (15)
Those who came here in the past have not returned to this earth again; thinking thus, my enemies—those wicked-minded ones—will now surely seize my kingdom. (16)
To the lord of the earth, who was thus reflecting with a deeply agitated mind, the Sage—the treasury of knowledge regarding the past and the future—spoke.
"O Indra among kings, what are you contemplating with such a dejected mind? For this matter regarding which we two have arrived here is certainly not a subject for anxiety. (18)
Neither mental afflictions nor physical diseases ever arise here; there is neither old age nor death—what other cause for suffering could there be? (19)
O illustrious one, you have achieved your purpose, since you yourself, in a human body, have come here to the world of Brahmā and have seen Hari face to face.
"Those who have come here do not grieve over that which is to be abandoned, namely, what is like the cycle of worldly existence. To him who was speaking thus, the king said to the lord of sages:
“O Blessed One, I grieve for the king among his own kinsmen and relatives, now that this palace for the Blessed One has been commenced by me. (22)
"O Sage, knowing that I have arrived here, your servants do not attend to me; for it is certain that the consecration of what has been commenced must be performed."
"O Lord, my mind is distressed at the thought that an obstacle might arise for him. Hearing those words of his, the sage laughed and said:
For he is indeed equal to Prajāpati, and not merely an ordinary king; no harm whatsoever has been done to him on earth by anyone, as was practiced by his ancestors.

Furthermore, what business do you have with one who has caused the destruction of creation and sustenance, now that he has gone to the world of Brahmā today under the power of your majesty and fame? (26)
He whose work the four-faced Lord Brahmā constantly assists as his companion, like the sun and the moon wandering eternally through the three worlds.
O tiger among kings, does even a suspicion of obstacles arise regarding them? O Indra among kings, here before your very eyes is he who stands at a distance from your enemies. (28)
Śakra himself, the lord of the three worlds, has come to the center of the assembly; O King, who else could this man be, especially in the temple of the Lord of the World? (29)
One might even desire to destroy him with the mind; let there be no doubt in you regarding that. O King, behold him before you, possessing a splendor equal to ten million moons.
Know this mass of splendor belonging to the abode of Brahmā to be one that produces joy on all sides, like ten million oceans of nectar.
While conversing in this manner, the two of them reached the vicinity of the world of Brahmā and heard from afar the words issuing from the mouths of the brahmin-sages.
The sound of his own recitation, with its well-formed words, clear sequence of phonemes and accents, as well as the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, Chandas, Kalpas, and Gāthās; || 33 ||
"O tiger among kings, know this to be the city of Brahmā, where words are heard distinctly and brilliantly, without being confused. (34)
For this assembly is seen where the Grandfather of the worlds, the four-faced one, is seated comfortably together with the foremost of the Brahman-sages.
Worshipped by various jīvanmuktas variegated with diverse forms of consciousness, those who have come to this place do not remain in the perilous ocean of saṃsāra. (36)
"Sat" is the name of Brahman; this supreme world of his is known as Satyaloka. Above that, there is nothing whatsoever.
O King, a little above and below this very shell of the cosmic egg is the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, where indeed the liberated souls dwell.
There indeed dwells the Lord Janārdana, the master of yogis who is directly contemplated by yogis, whose body is consciousness, and whose nature is intense bliss.
Having reached which they do not return to the path of death and worldly existence; which Brahmā always worships for his own liberation along with those liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
At the end of his allotted lifespan, he departs together with these [beings]; he is this very creator of the worlds, assuming forms such as the Fish and the Tortoise.
The protector in his fierce form and the destroyer who brings forth the worlds, speaking thus to Indradyumna, reached the abode of Brahmā.
And in an instant, he returned to the courtyard at the entrance of the assembly hall, where the guardians of the quarters, Śakra and the others, were stationed all around.
For a long time devoted to meditation, they were lords of the Manvantaras; yet, appearing like ordinary men, their entry was forbidden by the gatekeepers.
Beholding Nārada together with Indradyumna, the gatekeeper bowed with humility, his neck bent low. || 45 ||
O Lord, who delights in wandering through the fourteen worlds, without you, O Master, the assembly of your father does not shine.
Indeed, there are preeminent sages and Brahmins who are the foremost knowers of Brahman, such as Gautama and others; nevertheless, this assembly of Brahmā is not delightful.
"Like a moonlit night with many stars, she shines brightly. Thus praising her, he, filled with humility, granted her entrance.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama-Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: The royal sage Indradyumna, of great fame, a sovereign emperor and the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas, has come to see Dhātṛ through the gatekeeper. || 1 ||
"If you agree, let him go before him. Being addressed thus, Maṇikodara spoke again to Nārada.
"O Lord, that one who has come here by you is indeed not an ordinary person, since you behold there the guardians of the quarters, the ancestors, and the lords of the manvantaras. (3)
In this matter, even though this mortal abode remains, there is indeed a human effort to be made: you must go to the Lotus-born One, inform him of this, and have him grant entry.
The Lord Four-faced One, with a one-pointed mind, shall go to the door of the assembly hall along with the guardians of the quarters for the purpose of singing.
For us who are stationed at the gate, the opportunity to wait is certainly fixed; you must not direct anger toward me, for I am a servant of both you and your father.
Having been addressed thus, Nārada went to Brahmā, the lord of the worlds; having prostrated with all eight limbs, he informed him concerning the ruler of the earth.
Then, with a sidelong glance, he signaled for Indradyumna to enter; the Blessed One said nothing at all, being fully attentive to the singing.

His mind filled with curiosity for the celestial singing and music, Nārada then, perceiving the king's intention, caused Indradyumna, the best of monarchs, to enter, having been closely observed by Śakra and the other gods.
O best of the twice-born, upon seeing the Grandfather, the creator of the worlds, from afar, the king considered him to be Hari himself in wooden form.

The king proceeded very slowly, bowing with palms joined in reverence; praising, prostrating, and falling down as he walked, his gait faltering with awe. At the command of Nārada, the king halted at a short distance.
Then, O best of the twice-born, the four-faced one remained for a moment listening to the meritorious deeds of the Lord of the Daughter of the Ocean being sung.
Fanned on both sides by Sāvitrī and Śāradā, the Self-born One was being praised by the Vedas, who bore pure bodies.
Calculating the succession of ages through units such as *kalās*, *kāṣṭhās*, and *nimeṣas*, he is subject neither to old age, birth, nor death, nor to the transformation of form and other qualities.

In whom indeed there are neither mental afflictions nor physical diseases among those belonging to the worlds, and wherein there are no intermediate Manvantaras, nor the revolutions of the Yugas and so forth.
He for whom the end of the kalpas and other such things do not exist is the manifest Supreme Lord; at the conclusion of the Gītā, He spoke to that king as if smiling.
O great being Indradyumna, you are truly dear to the Blessed One; this world called Satya, which is difficult for others to attain, is known to you.
For here, sages whose impurities are destroyed and who are devoted to austerity remain, desiring to attain this state, until the dissolution of all beings.
Indeed, He is the substratum of all the diverse qualities, such as consciousness, belonging to the living beings created within the fourteen worlds. (19)

Although he already knew that task, the Grandfather, honoring that best of kings, spoke to Indradyumna with supreme delight: 20. "Even though he was aware of that duty, the Grandfather, showing respect to that most excellent of monarchs, addressed Indradyumna with great joy."
"Tell me what is in your heart: for what purpose have you come here? When I am seen, is there anything desired that is difficult to attain, even immortality? (21)
Indradyumna said: O Blessed One, O Inner Controller, how could there be anything unknown to You? Nevertheless, O Lord, this question of mine is surely an act of Your compassion toward me. (22)
"Having placed your command upon my head, it was spoken by your son: 'A thousand sacrifices were performed by me, and at their conclusion, I assumed a wooden body. (23)
The Blessed One, the Lord of the past, the future, and the present, manifested himself, beholding all by virtue of the perfection of your grace.
O Lord, such is that lotus-eyed one through whom you have come to this world; if the temple for him has been commenced by me there, then [let it be completed] by you yourself.
O Lord, O Creator of the World, if you go and install the God who is the Master of the Universe, then your grace toward me shall become fruitful.
For this purpose, O Lord of the World, I have now come to Your realm together with Nārada to behold the pair of Your lotus feet.
Be gracious to me; please do this, for you alone are the Lord of the World. You alone are that Lord of the World, O All-pervading One; there is no difference between the two of you.
You are that which is established and the establisher; you are the object of knowledge and the knower.

Jaimini said: At the conclusion of this petition, that great sage Durvāsas prostrated himself with all eight limbs, stood with palms joined in reverence, and, bowing low with humility, spoke to the Creator, the teacher of the worlds. (30)
O All-pervading Lord, here at the entrance to the gate, the world-protectors along with the ancestors and the lords of the Manvantaras have been barred by the doorkeeper.
O Creator of the World, they have remained for a very long time like wretched folk; therefore, command them so that they may behold the lotus-feet of Your Majesty.
Having heard those words of Durvāsas, the God of gods then laughed and spoke these words: "Indeed, this is not even the proper occasion for them."
They compete with Indradyumna, yet they are merely under the sway of delusion; this king is liberated while living, his accumulation of karmic sins having been exhausted.
This fifth descendant of my lineage is a Vaiṣṇava devoted to Viṣṇu; for these men have attained their human status through their own actions for the sake of experiencing happiness. (35)
"Indeed, these deities, seeking access here, performed austerities; through my grace, they have now arrived for my worship."
"Nevertheless, permitted by you, let them come into my sight. Then, indeed, those gods entered by virtue of Durvāsas's word.
From afar, they bowed to Brahmā, while near the singers they saluted King Indradyumna as he conversed with palms joined in reverence.
The Lord of the World, speaking with respect about Indradyumna, favored those world-protectors as they bowed down with a sidelong glance.
"O King, you have truly constructed a palace for the residence of the Blessed One. However, O King, this is not the time for sovereignty, nor is it the time for your progeny."
A great deal of time has passed for you during this occasion of singing songs—indeed, seventy-one divine yugas, which constitute a Manvantara. (41)
Your lineage has also been severed; millions of kings have passed away. Only two things remain here: the Lord and this final temple. (42)
The first yuga belongs to the second Manu, Svārociṣa; however, for me dwelling here in his presence, there is neither death nor likewise old age.
Or else, there is no transformation of time due to the reversal of the seasons; therefore, O Indra among kings, go to the earth, to the temple and the deity.
Having made me your own, return with speed; or else, I shall indeed follow right after you.
O highly fortunate one, as soon as you have gone before me and prepared the abundant requisites for the journey, at that very moment I shall depart.
Having thus commanded Indradyumna, the Blessed Grandfather spoke to the gods who stood before him with their necks bowed in humility.
O twice-born ones, the Blessed Lord spoke with affectionate and profound words to those who stood with palms joined in reverence, trembling with awe, and casting their gaze upon his feet.
"For what purpose have all you dwellers of heaven come here simultaneously? Whatever task must be performed by me for you, inform me; do not delay. (49)
Jaimini said: Having heard these words of the Creator, all the thirty gods, freed from their feverish distress, joyfully replied to the blessed Grandfather.
The gods said: "O Lord, how is it that he who was formerly worshipped by us on the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri) as one made of jewels has now become hidden, assuming instead a body of wood?"
Having appeared at the conclusion of King Indradyumna’s sacrifice, I have come to your lotus-feet in order to understand the cause of this.
"Come here to propitiate us; be gracious and tell us that!"—when the gods had spoken thus, the blessed Lord whose seat is the lotus [replied].
"O gods, this secret was never previously revealed to anyone; for you have all come together after a long time and have asked about it. (54)
Thereafter, O gods, I shall tell you the supreme secret of the deities: in the former *parārdha*, there was the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama. (55)
Having assumed the form of a blue stone, Janārdana did not abandon it; for now, my second *parārdha* has arrived.
In the Śvetavārāha Kalpa, this time indeed proceeds as the morning of the first day of Manu named Svāyambhuva.
"This Lord, in the form of wood, shall indeed remain in the midst of the worlds for the duration of my lifespan, honoring me as his master. (58)
O gods, this Blessed One is my very self, and I am composed of him; between us two, there exists nothing whatsoever in this world of moving and unmoving beings.
For in the midst of the ocean of milk, indeed on the White Island (Śvetadvīpa) upon his couch, Puruṣottama lies down, honoring that yogic sleep (yoganidrā).
He is the root and the primordial source of the worlds; those which are indeed his body hairs are known as the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadrumas), marked with conchs and discs.
O gods, this tree standing in its midst is presided over by consciousness; it is the Satyapuruṣa who has arisen spontaneously from the waters of the ocean.
Janārdana, possessing a formidable body, was cultivated through the yoga of devotion over many thousands of births in order to enjoy the pleasures residing in the three worlds.
For the sake of destroying this terrible saṃsāra, I previously entreated him again and again, my mind distressed by [the cycle of] creation, dissolution, and maintenance.
For the destruction of all karma without exception and for the liberation of all worlds, he [is attained] even without the difficult practices of dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and yoga.
The Blessed One, the Supreme Person, has manifested for the sake of liberation; one should not consider His concealed form to be an ordinary field.

Whatever form that deity is seen by the means of valid cognition that apprehends the substratum (dharmin), he is indeed that very same one; for the Lord bestows the fourfold aims of life according to how one meditates upon him. (67)
Those whose masses of sins are utterly destroyed by the sight of it gradually become pure-souled men on earth, destined for liberation.
Jaimini said: Having heard these nectar-like words of the lotus-born one, those gods, delighted, reflected with their inner selves filled with joy. (69)
Having abandoned this divinity which is transient, they have come to this earth; in this most excellent field, we shall worship the God with great self-restraint.
O Grandfather, seeing the gods with faces blossoming with joy, [he saw] the Lord who had become manifest for the sake of bestowing grace upon Indradyumna.
The image of him that has come here will speak for itself; the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, will grant many boons.
"I shall go to establish the Lord in the palace of Indradyumna; you, indeed, must proceed there as well. (73)
"Let Indradyumna go ahead to gather the materials for the installation; you all, whose offices have now expired, shall be his assistants there. (74)
O gods, the first Manvantara has indeed passed; now, O best of deities, having gone there together with Indradyumna, [you shall dwell]. 75.
He is indeed the master and the maintainer of the palaces and the statues; therefore, having now gathered the necessary materials and being accompanied by his assistants, he [proceeds]. (76)
Even by virtue of remembering this connection of his lineage, the treasure-lotus (padmanidhi) shall go to the earth along with him at my command.
O twice-born ones, having seen the divine splendor of Brahmā, Indradyumna too was delighted in heart, and he restrained all his possessions for the sake of the Lord’s installation.
Endowed with great wonder, he prostrated before the Teacher of the World; then, with his head bowed, he accepted the command of the gods whose offices had been diminished.
O Brahmins, they came to the earth, authorized by the sacred ordinance.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama-kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: Having approached the Lord of the World after longing for him for a long time, he prostrated himself like a staff, his body covered with a cloak of horripilation.

Homage to the God who is the friend of Brahman, who brings welfare to cows and Brahmins, who destroys the suffering of those who bow before him, and who is the sole cause for the four aims of human life.
Oṃ, salutations to Vāsudeva, whose nature is pure knowledge, and who possesses the forms of Hiraṇyagarbha, Puruṣa, Pradhāna, and Vyakta. || 3 ||
Uttering this hymn of praise with eyes brimming with tears of joy, the king performed circumambulations again and again and bowed down repeatedly.
Then other deities who had indeed arrived there, filled with joy, bowed down to the Lord and praised him with delight, their hands joined in reverence.
The gods said: The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet. Having pervaded the earth on all sides, he transcends it by the measure of ten fingers.
That Person who is celebrated as the Supreme Brahman and the Supreme Self—that indeed is everything: the past, the present, and the future. (7)
Such is His greatness; this Lord, the Supreme Person, is even greater than that. All beings constitute one quarter of Him; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven.
From you the Vedic hymns were born, and from you the Person of Sacrifice (Yajñapuruṣa) as well; from you horses were produced, and likewise cows, rams, and so forth.
The Brāhmaṇas were born from your mouth; the Kṣatriyas were born from your arms; the Vaiśyas were born from your thighs; and likewise, the Śūdras emerged from your feet. (10)
From his mind the moon was born; from his eye, the sun; from his two ears, the wind along with the vital breaths; and from his tongue, the carrier of oblations (Agni).
From your navel arose the sky and the heavens; from your head the earth was born; and from your two feet the eight directions emerged, extending to the furthest reaches of hearing.
The seven sacrificial enclosures and the twenty-one kinds of fuel-sticks indeed come from you; for all beings, both moving and unmoving, were born from you alone. (13)
You alone are the Lord of the worlds; you alone are the protector; and you alone, O Supreme Lord, are the destroyer in your fierce form.

You alone are the sacrifice, you are the portion of the sacrifice, and you are the Lord of the sacrifice, higher than the highest. You are indeed the Supreme Brahman of Sound; you are the Brahman of Sound, the Sovereign of the Universe.

O Lord of the Universe, you are the self-sovereign (Svarāt), the universal sovereign (Samrāj), and the manifest ruler (Virāj). O Lord of the world, consisting of the universe, the world—below, above, and across—is pervaded by you alone.
The sacrificial priests who worship you attain the supreme abode; you are the food and the eater, the oblation and the priest, the act of offering and the bestower of its fruit.
O Lord, you are the enjoyer of all actions, you are the essence of all actions, the instrument for all actions, and the bestower of the fruits of all actions.
For you are indeed the impeller of karma and the bestower of the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha; who else besides you is the giver of liberation? O Hṛṣīkeśa, salutations be to you! (19)

Salutations to the Infinite One, who possesses a thousand forms; salutations to the eternal Puruṣa, who has a thousand feet, eyes, heads, thighs, and arms, who bears a thousand names, and who sustains thousands of millions of yugas. 20.
O Lord, we have fallen from our high station and have come to you for refuge; protect us, O Lotus-eyed One, and be the goal for those who have no other resort.
O Lord, you alone are the refuge for a living being fallen into saṃsāra; in your creation, there is no one like you who protects the wretched.
O Lord, you are the sole refuge for the poor and the helpless, the father of the world; O Master, you alone are the protector, the nourisher, and the averter of all calamities.
Save us, O Viṣṇu, Lord of the World; save us, O Supreme Lord! O Beloved of Kamalā, who else besides you is capable of protecting us?
Salutations to you, O Inner Controller; salutations to you, the storehouse of all splendor. || 25 ||
O best of the twice-born, praising him thus and prostrating themselves again and again, those gods, together with Indradyumna, went outside.
Having gone to the sacred field of Śrī Narasiṃha and having prostrated before Him, and having paid homage with supreme devotion and worshipped the Man-lion (Nṛkesarin), [one should proceed].
They went together with Padmanidhi to the peak of Mount Nīlācala, where there was an excellent palace, for the purpose of gathering the necessary materials.
They saw the exceedingly lofty Vindhya mountain rising up, pervading the circle of the sky, as if to obstruct the path of the sun.
It pervaded all directions, radiant with its diverse structure, and variegated by the graceful postures of those who had long since passed away.
Then that Vaiṣṇava Indradyumna reflected: "In the past, I went from here to Satyaloka for the purpose of bringing [the deity] back."
This excellent, full palace, which has not been within the range of vision for a very long time, exists indeed through the grace of the God; here, there is no human effort.
Where is the end of a Manvantara that obstructs the sun, the moon, and Indra? And yet, this temple remains; indeed, it is difficult to find its like.
For these palaces built by humans are like anthills; having a very short lifespan, they crumble away as trees grow over them. (34)
Out of a sense of compassion for me, however, he protected Hari’s abode; then he spoke these humble words to those companions: (35)

"Know that this temple of the Lord of the World has been caused to be built by me; the Blessed One himself has manifested in a body in the form of wood. Then, an incorporeal voice from the sky spoke to me: (36)
"Have a palace built, measuring one thousand cubits, upon the peak of the Blue Mountain, for the residence of the Lord of the Universe. (37)
For the rite of this installation, the Lotus-born One himself will come here together with the Siddhas, Brahmanical seers, and deities. (38)
"What is to be done here, or what provision is known, and how? To him who had spoken thus, the gods whose offices were now terminated replied: ||| 39 ||
The gods said: "We too do not know that; our preceptor is the highest authority. For now he is beyond our control, as he is intent on the welfare of heaven."
Padmanidhi said: "O Lord, by the command of Brahmā, I have come along with you. What is to be done by me here, or what object is being awaited?"
Jaimini said: While they were thus conversing, Nārada, who was previously sent by Brahmā and is learned in all the scriptures, stood before them.
O Sage, carry out all the requirements for the provisions according to the scriptures; by your command, the treasure Padmaka shall provide them.
Seeing him, the son of Brahmā, they rose up filled with joy; the best of kings honored him with the worship of the sixfold arghya offering.
Even those gods, assuming human forms, bowed down to him; Indradyumna also spoke to him regarding the matter of the ritual for the installation.
"I do not know, O best of sages, for I have been long abandoned by my domestic priest. O Brahmin, please instruct me in due order regarding whatever must be accomplished."

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 24 ||
Jaimini said: When this had been spoken, Nārada then deliberated according to the scriptures and, having drawn [the diagrams] in order upon a leaf, presented them to that king. (1)
The king, having heard that letter and reflecting upon it again and again, gave over to Padmanidhi those very things which had been written therein.
O Padmanidhi, bring it about; construct a hall made of gold, a divine abode for Brahmā and a stainless residence for the Brahmarṣis.
For the residence of Indra and the other gods, of the Siddhas dwelling among mortals, of the lords of sages, and of kings residing in Pātāla.
And likewise, he untiringly prepared for each individual house of the Naga kings dwelling in the three worlds a residence provided with seats appropriate to them.
"Quickly cause the collection of materials to be prepared; for Viśvakarman himself shall provide you with assistance."
To Indradyumna, who was speaking in this manner and other such words, the sage said: "Indeed, these various materials must be prepared separately with due intervals."
Three excellent chariots were well-constructed of gold, adorned with fine silk garments, jewel garlands, and other costly ornaments; they were sturdy and magnificent.
Let the chariot of Śrī Vāsudeva, marked with the emblem of Garuḍa’s banner, and the lotus-bannered chariot of Subhadrā, be placed at the front.
A chariot with sixteen wheels should be constructed with great care for Viṣṇu; fourteen for Balarāma, and twelve for Subhadrā.
The chariot of the Wheel-Bearer (Cakradhara) was sixteen cubits in width; that of Bala was fourteen, and that of Subhadrā was twelve.
He is the seat of the worlds, yet he himself possesses no physical form as a seat; since the destruction of the worlds would follow from his movement, he has no vehicle. (12)
Through pure knowledge, one should behold the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings as ever-present upon the palm of one's hand; for such a person, the mirror is eternally stainless.
Because he stands upon the palm (tala), that Lord is always marked by the word *tāla*; therefore, he alone is the basis for Śeṣa when he descends as Balabhadra.

Alternatively, for one who possesses the plough (Śiri), the plough itself should be made the supreme banner; therefore, the banner should be made perfectly pure, and thus the palm-tree banner is prescribed.
O King, this god must not be installed on an unstable chariot; whether in a palace, a pavilion, or even in a city, [an installation] there would be fruitless.
Therefore, the consecration of Hari’s chariot must first be performed; let its materials be prepared, for that ceremony is to be carried out by me.
"O King, having received this command from my father, I shall return quickly. Having heard those words of his, three chariots were prepared.

In a single day, Viśvakarman constructed, with materials provided from the treasures, a palace that was well-constructed, with excellent wheels, fine pillars, very spacious, and adorned with beautiful archways.
It possessed beautiful flags and fine banners, was variegated and captivating with various designs, and was adorned with couples in diverse postures, small figurines, and bracelets.

Seeing it fashioned from half-gold, resembling the chariot of the Sun himself, possessing a resonance as deep as a thundercloud, endowed with the qualities of a magnet, and yoked to a hundred white-hued horses with the speed of the wind; (21)
It was installed by Nārada according to the prescriptions of the scriptures, at an auspicious planetary conjunction, a favorable moment, and on a propitious lunar day as indicated by astrology.
The sages said: "O venerable Jaimini, speak; for you are indeed considered by us to be omniscient."
By what ritual procedure indeed is this chariot of Hari to be consecrated? Tell us correctly so that we may understand the full details of the rite.
Jaimini said: I shall tell you that procedure as it was established by the high-souled Nārada, exactly as it was seen by me in the past. (25)
Having constructed a very beautiful hall in the north-eastern direction of the chariot, and having built a pavilion in its center, one should prepare a perfectly pure altar there.
O twice-born ones, on the night preceding the day of installation, one should prepare a square pit measuring four cubits [on each side] and one cubit in height, located auspiciously to the north.

Then, at an auspicious moment, having had the benediction recited, one should perform the rite of sowing the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), after offering oblations (bali) according to the rules to the thirty-two deities.
Then, at dawn, one should draw a mandala in the center of the altar—either a lotus or a svastika—and place a water-pot (kumbha) there. || 29 ||
The wise man should fill its interior with the decoction of the five trees, as well as sacred waters such as those of the Gaṅgā, along with sprouts and earth.

Having filled [the vessel] with all kinds of perfumes, the five jewels, and the collection of all medicinal herbs according to the prescribed rite, the pure preceptor, facing the east, [should proceed].

While recollecting Viṣṇu, one should afterwards fill [the vessel] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); its neck should be wrapped with fine silk and adorned with garlands and beautiful fragrances.
Adorned with fruits and sprouts and accompanied by performed auspicious rites, one should there worship the Lord of Gods, the flawless Narasiṃha.
Having invoked Hari into that [liṅga] for the sake of his grace, he prayed with the king of mantras according to the prescribed rites, as well as with internal offerings.

O twice-born ones, one should worship according to the rules with various external offerings; likewise, at the northwest of that jar, [one should offer] sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and cooked rice.

The preceptor should perform one thousand and eight oblations according to the prescribed rite; he should then cause the remnants of those offerings to fall into the middle of the water-pot at the conclusion.
Having made the chariot very beautiful with banners, perfumes, and garlands, one should sprinkle its entire body with water scented with sandalwood.
One should fumigate with black aloe-wood while sounding conch shells and kāhāla trumpets; having thus established the Wind-god upon the banner of that Nṛsiṃha.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with red garlands, perfumes, and flower-wreaths, one should then pray to Suparṇa while reciting this mantra.

I bow to that stainless, golden-hued Suparṇa, the lord of birds who is composed of the Vedas; he who, though a mere body, is the cause of all life and the very form of the banner on Hari’s vehicle—merely by contemplating him, the wombs of the multitude of serpent-wives immediately fall; his mouth is stained with the mire of blood from the essence of serpents crushed by his leaping, fierce, and massive beak.

Accompanied by the chanting of the Veda, the sounding of conchs, and the extensive playing of various musical instruments, one should place him upon the top of the chariot while reciting beautiful hymns.
Above that, while causing the chariot to be bathed on all sides by that pitcher, one should sprinkle it together with Brahmā while reciting the King of Mantras three times.

Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmā priest; one should also give a fee to the preceptor (ācārya), whatever by which that teacher is satisfied.
At the conclusion, one should feed the Brahmins with milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter; one should perform the rite for Balabhadra with the twelve-syllable mantra.
The mantra for the plow-bannered deity (Lāṅgaladhvaja) should be "lāṃgalaṃ ca paviravat. Alternatively, the root-mantra is also proclaimed to consist of twelve syllables.
The chariot of Bhadrā should likewise be consecrated with the Lakṣmīsūkta; you, O Murāri, have emerged from the navel-lake assuming the form of the series of cosmic eggs.
Having recited this mantra: "Be firm as the seat of the Four-faced One and the abode of Śrī," one should raise the lotus-banner.
This is the specific distinction regarding the oblation for the three [deities] individually: each one should be offered separately with five [oblations] each. || 48 ||
Having thus established the chariots, one should duly give gold, a cow, clothing, grain, and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the deity with devotion.
When that well-adorned chariot had been thus prepared, they placed the god upon it according to the prescribed rites, preceded by the chanting of the Veda.
Accompanied by shouts of "Victory! and auspicious sounds, preceded by various musical instruments, with the waving of chowries, incense, and showers of flowers.
He was led toward the chariot by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, either by well-characterized horses, or by tamed oxen. || 52 ||
She should indeed be escorted by men who are devotees of Viṣṇu with vigilance, after all the people have been gratified with various kinds of foods, edibles, and ointments. (53)
O twice-born ones, upon the chariot, with the offering-mantra for the gods, [one should say]: "O gods, may the Ādityas and the Vasus likewise accept this offering! (54)
The Maruts, the Aśvins, the Rudras, the Suparṇas, the Pannagas, the Grahas, the Asuras, the Yātudhānas, and the deities stationed upon their chariots. || 55 ||
May the guardians of the quarters, the protectors of the worlds, and those who are the obstructors and Vināyakas, as well as the divine great sages, grant welfare to the world.
May these proceed without obstacle; may there be no adversaries; and may the Daityas and the hosts of spirits likewise be gentle and satisfied. (57)
Then the Lord is led to level ground while reciting the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī mantra, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and the Pavitra hymn.

With the Vāmadevya hymns, the purificatory mantras, the Mānastokya verses, and the Rathantara chants, he then raised the sound of musical instruments accompanied by the proclamation of "Auspicious Day" (Puṇyāha).
Then the chariot should be led very slowly out of affection for the wielder of the discus; O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the portents that occur regarding that chariot.

If the pole breaks, there is danger to the twice-born; if the axle breaks, there is the destruction of the kṣatriyas; if the balance-beam breaks, there is the ruin of the vaiśyas; and from the breaking of the yoke-pin, there shall be fear for the śūdras.
If the yoke breaks, there will be drought; if the pedestal breaks, there is danger for the subjects; and if the wheel of the chariot breaks, one should know that an enemy army is approaching.
O Brahmins, if the banner falls, another king will certainly arise; however, if the image is broken, one should predict the death of the king. (63)
O Brahmins, when the chariot was overturned, and when such initial portents and other inauspicious omens had arisen, there occurred the destruction of all the people of the land.
One should perform the *balikarma* again, as well as the *śāntihoma*; furthermore, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and indeed give them food.

And in the north-eastern direction of the chariot, one should prepare the sacrificial fire; one should perform the oblation with fuel-sticks and clarified butter mixed with honey, using [wood] from both the roots and the tips.
O best of the twice-born, having been initiated with the King of Mantras using twigs of the *pālāśa* tree, [one should offer] to Soma, to Agni, to the subjects, and likewise to Prajāpati.
Then, to the planets, to Brahmā, and finally to the guardians of the directions; wherever there were defects in the chariot, there the initiated one [should offer oblations].

One should offer oblations with the consecration mantra; thus there shall be excellence in every respect. Together with Brāhmaṇas, one should perform the recitation of the peace-mantra (śāntivācana) at the conclusion of the homa.

May there be well-being for the Brahmins; may there be constant well-being for the king; may there be well-being for the cows and for the subjects; and may there indeed be peace for the entire world. (70)
May there be constant well-being for bipeds, and may there be peace for quadrupeds. May there be welfare for all creatures, and likewise may there be welfare for ourselves. (71)
May there be peace for the Lord, and likewise auspiciousness for Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; may there be peace, may there be auspiciousness in every way, and may there be well-being for us.
O Lord, you alone are indeed the creator and the nourisher of the world; O Lord of gods, protect your subjects and grant peace, O Master of the universe. (73)
O King, having recognized that the planets are malignant for the person who has become the cause of the journey, one should perform the pacification of the planets (grahaśānti).
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 25 ||
Jaimini said: O gods, having been brought near the temple at an auspicious moment, you were established according to the prescribed rite upon level ground free from portents.
Then, at the command of Indradyumna, a very great hall, fashioned with the colors of jewels, was constructed by Viśvakarman.
In the assembly worship, there were ritual objects and sacrificial offerings, fuel-sticks and *kuśa* grass, various kinds of food, as well as diverse forms of song and dance. (3)
O brahmins, the prosperity that formerly existed on earth during the Sāmrājya age became even greater than that during the Pratiṣṭhā age.
At that time, there was a ruler of the earth named Gāla on the surface of the ground; he too, having fashioned here an image made of stone called Mādhava, [installed it].
Having established [the image] here in this palace, he worshipped it with miraculous power; and that best of kings, having constructed a smaller palace, [worshipped it there as well].
Having respectfully extracted it from there, he established it in that place; then the king, having heard of this deed of his from the mouth of a messenger, [acted accordingly].
Gāla, accompanied by his army, arrived at that Nīla mountain in a state of great wrath, having seen the preparations for the consecration—a sight difficult even for mortals to obtain even in a dream.
His mind filled with wonder, King Gāla stood there, wondering: "What is this? Who is causing such an event as this? (9)
Having diligently recognized that divine King Indradyumna—who had come from the world of Brahmā as the builder of the temple of the gods—he [perceived him].
Together with the gods, he was established as the one who performs the necessary preparations, accompanied by the preceptor Padmanidhi and by Nārada.
Having heard that Brahmā, the supreme among gods, was coming for the sake of the installation, and having heard the entire account of that divine occurrence, the king [acted]. (12)
He considered himself to have achieved his purpose in that most wonderful kingdom, thinking: "A deed more conducive to welfare than this has never occurred, nor will it ever occur. (13)
Therefore, staying near him, having understood the sequence of his ritual actions and the prescribed rules, and having also learned of the festivals, I shall perform them every year. (14)
Due to an accumulation of misfortune, I did not recognize for all this time that Janārdana was actually present here in the form of this wooden image.
"Since I have not served him, my very birth has been rendered fruitless; therefore, let me bow down before this Indradyumna, the teacher of the world."
Having approached and taken refuge in that most excellent of great devotees who had come here from the world of Brahmā, and having directly beheld the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa; || 17 ||
"Once it is established in the temple, I shall certainly attain liberation; having installed Vaikuṇṭha, he will indeed enshrine it within me. (18)
Having indeed gone to the world of Brahmā, why does he remain on earth, having assigned his duties and gathered the treasury for his lord? (19)
Accompanied by Brahmā, he will certainly go back to that abode; having deliberated with his ministers, Gāla, the devotee of Viṣṇu, did likewise.
Modestly, he joyfully approached Indradyumna; having gone there and seen him from a distance, he first prostrated himself before him.
With palms joined in reverence, King Gāla, looking up at him with trepidation from the crown of his head, slowly approached his presence.
"O Lord, you are the king of kings; though a mortal, you have gone to the world of Brahmā. What can I praise? I am but a worm among men, while you are a sovereign liberated in this very life."
O Lord, having failed to understand your greatness and consulting repeatedly with his ministers, he came here to fight; yet, upon seeing your great prowess, he has been subdued.
"O Lord, having seen this superhuman and marvelous state of the Lord of Śacī, it is certain that he has indeed come from the world of Brahmā. (25)
For such indeed is this great deed that the Great Treasure has become an executor of my command; O Best of Gods, direct your mind toward grace toward me. (26)
The gods dwelling in the three worlds are subject to his command. || 27 ||
Jaimini said: To Gāla, that elephant among kings, who was thus making his representation, he spoke these words with a smile: "O King, why do you speak so much? (28)
You too are a devotee of Hari and a sovereign lord of the earth; for this sovereignty over the land that exists on earth is indeed common to all kings. (29)
For now you alone are the sovereign on this earth; all activities of mortals, and even of the gods, are dependent upon the king. (30)
A king was created by Brahmā from portions of the eight guardians of the directions; indeed, a king devoted to the protection of his subjects is not one who has performed little merit.
O tiger among kings, by traveling upon this excellent path, one attains both fame and merit; you, moreover, are especially a devotee of Viṣṇu.
He who installs an image of Hari in a temple according to the prescribed rite does not undergo the bondage of a physical body, but goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
O King, you yourself have installed this wooden image of Mādhava, endowed with auspicious marks, which bestows liberation directly.
"Your task has been accomplished without obstacle; it took me an entire Manvantara. Or rather, there may be doubt in this matter for me, for even the Four-faced One is not independent. (35)
O best of kings, since this [image] was requested for the purpose of installation, how could anyone else install it? It is the temple of the Lord who has manifested visibly as wood. (36)
If Vidhātṛ, by his presence here, shall show favor, then, having established this Janārdana in his fourfold form, [one should proceed].
Having entrusted you [with this task], I shall depart; you alone shall perform the daily offerings, the processions, and the festivals for the Lord of the World. (38)
Whatever the Lord himself or the Great-Grandfather (Brahmā) might teach, those very things a king who is a protector of dharma should diligently carry out. || 39 ||
Then King Gāla, having heard that thought himself and realizing, "This was commanded by Indradyumna," attained supreme joy. (40)
Gāla himself stood near him like a servant ready to obey; this Indradyumna quickly performed whatever he commanded. (41)
Thus, having accumulated the necessary provisions, the lord Indradyumna, seated upon his throne and surrounded by the gods, shone like Śakra himself.
Then there were heard auspicious sounds arising from divine drums, as well as the resonances of mṛdaṅgas, flutes, lutes, cymbals, and trumpets.
In the sky, there were many trumpeting sounds from elephants such as Airāvata, along with shouts of victory from all sides mingled with showers of flowers. (44)

Sprays of water from the celestial Gaṅgā mixed with Mandāra flowers, as well as the scents of divine garlands, ointments, and incense pervading all directions, and the sounds of networks of tiny bells belonging to the gods traveling in their celestial chariots [were heard]. (45)
Then, O twice-born ones, a mass of splendor appeared upon the earth, filling the space between heaven and earth and obscuring the eyes. 46.
Gazed upon from the front by the subjects with their garlands of eyes uplifted, he then gradually beheld the preeminent celestial chariot of Prajāpati.
He was being carried on all sides on the shoulders of hundreds of golden swans, while the guardians of the quarters attended upon him in front with chowries held busily in their hands.
With the waters of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā sprinkled as fly-whisks on all sides, and with both the Moon and the Sun as parasols at his two flanks; 49.
While the hem of his garment was being gently shaken by the movement of the wind, he was being praised with secret hymns by the Brahman-sages, Gautama and the others.
Standing in their midst, the Lord of Creatures, praised by Indradyumna and others, was beheld by the hosts of gods who extolled him with shouts of "Victory! (Jaya).
He was danced before by courtesans such as Rambhā with trepidation, while being sung to by singers such as Hāhā and Hūhū.
He was respectfully entertained with the lute by hosts of perfected Vidyādharas, and worshipped from afar by ascetics with their palms joined in reverence.
Sāvitrī and Śāradā attained satisfaction through his various compositions; who else is capable of pleasing them? (54)
His body was drenched by the waters of the Jāhnavī and Yamunā; and there were the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and other twice-born ones led by Nārada.
Carrying canes in their hands and showing great humility as they beheld the divine stairs, there was a great throng of gods proceeding through the heavens.
Not a single god was counted, nor could it be discerned by which path each of those inhabitants of heaven was proceeding as they rushed forward in a frantic scramble for precedence.
Due to the extreme pressure of that [battle], their dismounts became unseated; he who is the creator, the protector, and the destroyer of the worlds, and who is identical with the universe. (58)
How could the majesty of these gods not manifest directly there? Upon seeing him, the king bowed down in awe and with devotion, his palms joined in reverence. (59)
Accompanied by those gods and by Gālarāja, headed by Nārada, he went toward the earth and prostrated himself with his eight limbs touching the ground.
Rising with supreme devotion and a joyful inner soul, he felt his entire body covered in horripilation, considering himself to have achieved his life's purpose.
Beholding the pure Grandfather (Brahmā) before the Lord of the World, the king, with palms joined in reverence, immersed himself in an ocean of bliss.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the Sage Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: Then, from the intermediate space, a ladder fashioned of jewels and gold descended, reaching down to the footstool of the lotus-born Brahmā as he sat within his celestial chariot.
Its base indeed touched the earth for the descent of the Creator; it was four vyāmas wide and provided with a series of broad steps.
Between the chariot and the palace, like a radiant rainbow, he suddenly appeared, watched with wonder by the people.
Then, O twice-born ones, the Gandharva kings, holding jeweled canes in their hands, pointed out the way, saying, "O Lord, this is the path; please come."
Having placed his hands in the hands of Durvāsas and Nārada, he then descended by means of stairs, purifying the world with his gaze.
Smiling upon seeing the chariots, the well-adorned palace, and the hall extending to the ends of the quarters, which was beautified by jeweled pillars; || 6 ||
Causing wonder even to Śakra, that divine seer-king descended from his celestial chariot, which was equipped with every kind of provision.
Being praised on all sides by those with palms joined in reverence and crowns upon their heads, the Grandfather bestows his grace upon whichever direction he gazes with a sidelong glance.
There, crores of people joined their palms together and held them over their heads; seeing Indradyumna prostrating at his lotus feet, the Lord of Creatures [spoke].
Pointing with his finger toward the gods, the ancestors, the brahmin-sages, and the ascetics, he spoke with humble words, his lips parted by a smile.
Likewise, the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, other Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases—all gathered together in one place, simultaneously overflowing with joy—(11).
Behold, O Indradyumna, your fortune which subjugates all the worlds; once, for your sake, they all assembled together, placing me at their head.
