Having spoken thus, the Grandfather (Brahmā) quickly departed from there toward the chariot of Nārāyaṇa, after prostrating before the Lord of the World and circumambulating him three times.
Immersed in an ocean of bliss, his body covered in horripilation, he himself then praised his own self directly with a voice faltering with emotion.
Brahmā said: Salutations to you, salutations to me; salutations again and again to you and to me. I am you, you are I; all this world, both moving and unmoving, is so.
The entire universe, beginning with the Mahat, is the play of Your Māyā; O Soul of the Universe, it is superimposed upon You and transformed by You alone. (16)
This entire appearance, which arises from ignorance of reality, would dissolve upon knowing You, just like the perception of a snake in a rope.
This world-appearance is indeed indescribable, due to its distinction from both existence and non-existence; it is non-dual and self-luminous—salutations be to You! (18)
All the bliss of sense objects subsists upon a portion of you, whose nature is innate bliss, by which living beings continue to live.
Free from conceptual proliferation, formless, changeless, and without support; possessing the greatness of the gross, the subtle, and the infinite, yet devoid of grossness and subtlety. || 20 ||
O you who transcend the qualities, the substratum of qualities, whose self consists of the three qualities—salutations be to you! || 21 ||
Deluded by Your māyā, I am intent solely upon creation; even now I find no peace. O Inner Controller, salutations be unto You! (22)
Born from the lotus of your navel, I remain there eternally offering praise; I am not able to transcend your Māyā—what other lord could do so? (23)
Just as I was fashioned within this cosmic egg for the work of creation, so too have millions of Brahmas been produced in accordance with the natural order within the universe.
O Lord, even among the Viriñcis numbering three and a half crores, not even one knows in truth as I do while standing before you.
Salutations to You of inconceivable majesty; salutations again and again to You whose form is consciousness. Salutations to the God above all gods; salutations to You, the God of gods. (26)
Salutations to you whose nature is both divine and non-divine, salutations to you of divine form; salutations to you who are devoid of old age and death, yet possess the form of death. || 27 ||

Salutations again and again to the one whose nature is like a blazing fire, who is the death even of Death; to the one who grants protection from death to those who have sought refuge, whose form is innate bliss, who is fond of devotion, and who is both the mother and the father of the worlds.

Salutations to you, who are ever-striving for the destruction of the suffering of those who bow before you; salutations, repeated salutations to you, an ocean whose very nature is compassion for the wretched. (29)
Salutations to you who are the supreme, whose form is the supreme, and who are the further shore; salutations to you whose nature is the shoreless shore and whose form is Brahman. || 30 ||
Salutations to you, whose essential nature is the ultimate truth, who are the supreme cause, who are pervaded by the lineage [of teachers], and who are devoted to the highest reality.

Salutations to the one who destroys the suffering of those who bow before him, the sole light of his own self, by whom it was previously requested that he descend to relieve the burden of creation upon himself.
Therefore, O Lord of the World, act so that I may partake of the form of innate bliss; when you are pleased, O Lord, what is there that remains difficult for me to attain? (33)

O ocean of mercy, I have been made distinct by you alone through the differentiation of your various divine sports, while I was confined within the prison-house of the world, shrouded by the darkness of ignorance. (34)
Wandering about, one does not find the door leading to liberation except through you. || 35 ||

Salutations, salutations to you, the sole object of worship for the world, whose lotus feet are honored by gods and demons; salutations, salutations to you, the unique moon who removes all suffering; salutations, salutations to you, who are dense with bliss and perfect awakening.

Homage, homage to you, O wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), who bestows desires difficult to attain even after eons have passed; whose wings are ever firmly bound for the sake of uplifting the multitude of sufferings of those who bow down to you as their sole refuge in distress. 37.
Be gracious, O Lord of the worlds, for those submerged in the ocean of suffering; protect us, O Mine of Compassion, with the playful casting of a sidelong glance. (38)
Having thus praised Śrī Jagannātha, that Grandfather (Brahmā), who embodies the meaning of the Vedas, went to see Sīrin, the upholder of the earth, who had descended [to earth].
Having prostrated with supreme devotion, he joyfully praised Balin: "O Lord of gods, the sky is your head; O Master, the waters are your body."
Your feet are the earth, your mouth is fire, your breaths are the wind, your mind is indeed the lord of herbs (the moon), and your two eyes are the sun.
O Lord, whose arms are like the quarters of the sky, salutations to you, the mirror of knowledge; salutations to the wielder of the plow, who is the foundational pillar for the fourteen worlds.
Salutations to the one who destroys the flood of sins for those who have taken refuge at his lotus feet; salutations to him whose infinite mouths, eyes, ears, feet, faces, and arms [pervade all].
Homage to Him who is like the sun to the mass of darkness at the rootless great root, who consists of the three Vedas, who destroys the threefold defects, and who has manifested in three descents.
Salutation to you who possess the form of a hooded serpent with a crest-jewel, the upholder of the circle of the earth; salutation to you, Kālāgnirudra, the Great Rudra. || 45 ||
Salutations to you who sleep amidst the coils of the serpent-king, which serve as your couch and canopy, while the three worlds have grown together as one within the waters of the great ocean.
O Blessed One, you alone are Śeṣa, adorned with a thousand hoods, supporting the entire material universe under the guise of the multitude of jewels upon your hoods.
O All-pervading Lord, you alone are the protector, creator, and sustainer of all; you are the devourer and the eternal upholder, and we, beginning with me, exist solely for your sake.
This god Nārāyaṇa is celebrated in the Vedāntas; O Blessed One, he is not different from you, yet through the cause [of manifestation], you assume the state of difference.
You are the bed and he is indeed the one who lies upon it; you are the covering and he is the one who covers. He who is Viṣṇu is indeed Rāma, and he who is Rāma is Kṛṣṇa himself.

"There is no difference between you two; be gracious, O You who pervade the universe! Having thus concluded his hymn of praise and having prostrated before the Supreme Lord, the powerful one [spoke]. (51)
To behold the sovereign lady of the worlds, he went to the chariot of Subhadrā, saying: "Victory to you, O Goddess! O Mother of the World! Be gracious, O Supreme Sovereign! (52)
You are the agent of cause and effect; salutations to you, the all-powerful one, who always resides within the hearts of all as the very nature of both knowledge and delusion.
O auspicious one, bestower of liberation and isolation, I bow to you, the source of the gods; O Goddess, you are the illusory power of Viṣṇu, deluding all that is moving and unmoving. 54.
Seated upon the lotus-throne of the heart, you follow the nature of Viṣṇu; you alone are Lakṣmī, Gaurī, Śacī, and likewise Kātyāyanī.
Whatever object exists anywhere, whether real or unreal, you are the power within that entire universe; who, then, is capable of praising you? || 56 ||
Victory to you, O Bhadrā! O Subhadrā, you who bestow auspiciousness upon all! You whose very nature consists of both the auspicious and the inauspicious—O Bhadrakālī, salutations be unto you!
O Goddess, you are the mother of the worlds, and Nārāyaṇa is indeed their father; you are everything in female form, while the Lord of the World is in male form.

Indeed, there is no difference between you two, nor is there anything else; for you are truly the Supreme. Just as we have been appointed by you, so too have we been directed by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu.
O Supreme Goddess, we who always carry out your instructions wander [through the world]; you alone are livelihood, activity, supreme hunger, and sleep. (60)
You are hope and you are the fulfillment of hope; you are the one who fulfills all desires. O Goddess, you alone are the cause of liberation, and indeed, you are the cause of bondage in this world.
O eternal bestower of all knowledge, you who are like a wish-fulfilling creeper for your devotees; protect me, who am bowed at your lotus feet, with the glances of your compassionate side-long looks.
Having thus praised her of auspicious form, he [beheld] Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana discus, which had assumed a fourth body and was stationed upon the chariot near him.
Having bowed with supreme devotion, he uttered this hymn of praise: "O Sudarśana, of great radiance, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns! (64)
Salutations to you, who show the path to Vaikuṇṭha to those blinded by the darkness of ignorance; salutations to the eternally radiant abode of the Vaiṣṇava light. 65.
"I bow down to that form of Viṣṇu whose prowess is irresistible. Having bowed and praised the gods, he turned back from his chariots.
Having been instructed in the path by Indradyumna and Nārada, he then ascended the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala), eager to behold the temple.
Then, O twice-born ones, having gone near the palace together with the deities, he beheld a beautiful hall that was exactly as his heart desired.
In their midst, he established the gods, serpents, and kings, as well as Brahman-sages, yogis, Brahmins, Vaiṣṇavas, and ascetics.
When the excellent divine throne was offered by the king, the Lord, the omnipresent one, himself sat down upon it along with the footstool.
By the command of his grandfather, the prosperous king requested the great sage Bhāradvāja to perform rites for pacification and nourishment.
Those deities who are intended for the ritual of offerings and worship during the consecration, as well as those in the fire-oblations, indeed assume the form of meditative visualization.
By the command of the Lotus-born One, they took their positions in the four directions, well-honored with perfumes, flowers, garlands, ornaments, and decorations.
Then the ritual proceeded, performed by the wise son of Bharadvāja, in the direct presence of the God of gods and all the inhabitants of heaven.
The king joyfully performed worship for those dwelling in the three worlds, having first worshipped the Creator of the universe along with all his limbs and subordinate parts.
Then all the inhabitants of the three worlds, having been honored by him, beheld the imperishable Brahmā himself standing in their midst.

Through the grace of Indradyumna, they attained the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), beholding the Lord of the World in person, possessed of a magnificent form and identical with Brahman.
Having established the body of the Blessed One as a most beautiful temple, Bharadvāja raised up a great banner.
Then, for the sake of the installation of Jīva, he requested his grandfather; thereupon Brahmā himself arose, having performed the rites for auspiciousness.
Accompanied by sages such as Nārada and others, by learned brahmins, by kings and kṣatriyas, and by nāgas along with supreme ṛṣis.
While the Gandharvas sang divine songs in melodious tones with melodies appropriate for auspicious occasions, and while the Apsarases danced; (81)
And while the Śākuna hymns were being recited by the twice-born, there arose the sounds of conchs, kāhālas, mṛdaṅgas, kettledrums, and other instruments, as well as lutes.
Then, as the sound grew intense, they all went up onto the chariot and, having proceeded, lowered him from the vehicle onto the path of the stairs.
Attentive, established in meditative absorption, their selves restrained through devotion, they placed their hands upon their sides, their arms, their heads, and their feet.
Slowly and gracefully, they led the healthy Nārāyaṇa from bed to bed upon soft mattresses until he reached the vicinity of the palace.
And as continuous showers of rain fell one after another from above: "Victory to you, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the World! Victory to you, destroyer of all sins! (86)

Victory to you, whose body is made of playful wood; victory to you, the bestower of the fruits of desire! Victory to you, who playfully deliver those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence; victory to you, the imperishable one! 87.
Victory to you, O ocean of compassion! Victory to you, who take refuge in the wretched! Victory, O Acyuta! Victory, O Ananta! Victory, O Īśāna! Salutations be unto you!
Being praised with these hymns by Brahmā, the Self-born, Nārada, filled with joy, offered praise while playing his lute.
Then, with a pair of jeweled parasols being held over his head from behind, he was perfumed with divine incense by Śaśin and Bhāsvat out of devotion.
Indeed, on both sides, rows of fly-whisk bearers stood, busily engaged in gracefully waving them, adorned with the beauty of youth. (91)
And thus, all of them together, filled with curiosity, led Sudarśana, Subhadrā, and Balabhadra [to their destination].
Then, having placed [the deity] for consecration upon a jeweled pillar at the gate of the palace, or within a pavilion, facing a circular mirror; 93.

O best of the twice-born, for the sake of gathering the world together, the blessed Grandfather (Brahmā) performed the consecration of Śrī and Puruṣa with jeweled jars filled with water collected from sacred fords, accompanied by the two Sūktas dedicated to them.

Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the gods who were adorned and graced with perfumes and garlands, the Blessed One himself, the creator of the world, placed them upon a beautiful jeweled lion-throne according to the sacred mantras.
Brahmā said: O support of the entire universe, established in all worlds, you who pervade everything with perfect stability, remain firmly fixed within this temple.
O Protector, when you are established, we all are established; by your command may I be established, and may everything be fulfilled through your grace. (97)
Having established the Lord of the World and touched His heart-lotus, he recited the thousand-fold king of mantras in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
O Brahmins, the consecration was performed on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, in conjunction with the Puṣya asterism, on an auspicious Thursday.
That day is exceedingly meritorious and destroys all sins; bathing, giving gifts, austerity, and burnt offerings—all these yield inexhaustible results.
On that day, those men who behold Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā with hearts imbued with devotion will undoubtedly become partakers of liberation. (101)
When the eighth day of the bright fortnight in Vaiśākha is joined with Jupiter and the Puṣya asterism, worshipping Viṣṇu on that day destroys the sins of ten million births.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 27.
Jaimini said: Then, by the power of the mantra, that Blessed Lord, the Man-lion of wondrous appearance, was beheld by all, including Indradyumna and the others.
Licking the entire world on all sides with his blazing tongue, he appeared like the risen Kālāgnirudra swallowing everything.
Pervading the cavity between heaven and earth with his intensely burning splendor, the omnipresent Lord possesses many eyes, faces, necks, hands, feet, and ears.
The God consists of every marvel and is solely a treasury of splendor; terrified by fear and deeply agitated, they were not even able to praise the Lord.
Beholding his father in such a state, Nārada then asked: "O Blessed One, how is it that he shines forth in this manner?"
Nārada said: "Far from descending for the sake of grace, this [being] is instead a source of fear; everyone has now become even more steadfast in their fear, suspecting the dissolution of the world."
O Lord of the worlds, you alone know the divine play of the Blessed One.
Having heard those words of Nārada, the lotus-born Brahmā, with a smiling face, spoke these curious words for the benefit of everyone.
Brahmā said: Having seen the Lord of the World incarnated, assuming a wooden body, [he spoke].
Fools who do not know the truth will indeed despise him who is the very embodiment of Brahman, thinking, "Let them recognize his greatness. || 10 ||
He was consecrated by that king of mantras belonging to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), by whom he had been consecrated in the past when he tore asunder the great Asura.
Having attained such a form, which is very difficult to behold and inspires fear, this is the supreme pinnacle of the embodiment of Viṣṇu, whose splendor is immeasurable.
Having worshipped her, they attain that state from which return is difficult to obtain; facing Nṛsiṃha, he spoke this hymn with great joy.

Homage be to you, the peerless lion among the best of gods; homage be to you, the peerless lion who subdues the elephants of the flood of sins. Homage be to you, the lion who reaches the further shore of the ocean of suffering; homage be to you, the divine lion composed of splendor. 14.

Homage be to you, O Lion of all diverse forms; homage be to you, O Lion liberated from the afflictions. Homage be to you, O Man-Lion of divine body; homage be to you, O Supreme Hero, the peerless Lion. 15.

Salutations to you, O lion who tears asunder the Daityas; salutations to you, O lion among the gods, supreme among deities. Salutations to you, O sole lion in the forest of Vedānta; salutations to you, O sole lion in the cave of the yogins. 16.
Homage be to you, O lion among bulls, the sole lion; homage be to you, the lion upon the peak of the Blue Mountain.
Jaimini said: Having thus praised that divine lion, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) drew a lion-yantra and placed Indradyumna upon it.
Having initiated him into the King of Mantras directly proclaimed by Atharvan, they call it the Vaiṣṇava Nirvāṇa, which those devoted to the Upaniṣads [attain]. (19)
There, the four Vedas themselves are eternally established; having studied that great mantra in ancient times, Svāyambhuva Manu [attained his goal].
The Blessed One brought forth creation from this Four-faced One; for whomsoever [practices it], the powers such as *aṇimā* shall be its incidental fruit.
This single great mantra is indeed the cause for attaining the four aims of human life; how much more so, then, for minor desires? (22)
This single great mantra bestows the fruit of all sacrifices; it bestows the merit of all sacred fords and the fruit of all gifts and vows. || 23 ||
Just as this [king] is a forest fire to the cotton-heap of the flood of all sins, so indeed is this King of Mantras a divine deity in the form of a lion.
Indeed, by practicing this, ascetics abandon the disease of worldly existence; for merely by its grasping, the planets, epilepsy, and demons [are overcome]. (25)
Dakinis, spirits, vetālas, piśācas, serpents, and planetary deities flee from afar; they are not even able to look upon him.
Then, having received the king of mantras from the four-faced one, Indradyumna [meditated upon] Nṛsiṃha, whose body was radiant and whose chest was inhabited by Lakṣmī.
Holding a discus and a Pināka bow, with eyes like the moon, sun, and fire, his two lotus-like hands extended down to his knees and his nose prominent.
Upon a seat formed by a yogic cloth, there is a lotus with thirty-two petals; in its center, consisting of the syllables of the mantra, the pericarp shines with the Praṇava.
Seated comfortably, laughing aloud, gazing at his glorious lotus-face, with his lotus-like countenance adorned by a mane of hair, and his form radiant with divine jewels.
Having spread out a thousand hoods, he saw behind the Lord Balabhadra, who held a plow and a goad, assuming the form of an umbrella.
Seeing such a Supreme Person, the king rejoiced; his mind filled with wonder, he questioned the Lotus-Seated One.
"O Blessed One, this conduct of the Slayer of Madhu is indeed marvelous. O Creator of the World, how could it be possible for us to understand it? (33)
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, the Lord himself assumed such a form made of wood; while seated upon the chariot, he entered within the temple.
Then that voice, hidden within the sky, spoke to me previously: "You shall become a fourfold form through a tree that is not of human origin. (35)
Now this one alone is seen, well-established; tell me truly, O Lord, is it illusion or is it reality? (36)
"O Creator of Existence, if you consider me a fit vessel for hearing [this],"—having heard this, he then replied to that best of kings who was filled with doubt.
Brahmā said: O King, this primordial form of the Blessed One in the likeness of Narasiṃha has been manifested for you by Nārāyaṇa through my grace.
O tiger among kings, let there not arise in you the notion that this is a wooden image; rather, this is the very form of the Supreme Brahman. (39)
Because it shatters all sufferings and bestows indivisible bliss by its very nature, this wooden block is indeed designated as the Supreme Brahman.
Thus, according to the four Vedas, the wooden deity is the creator of the worlds; therefore, he also created himself.
The Word-Brahman and the Supreme Brahman—no difference between these two is admitted; for at the time of dissolution this is indeed one, but at the time of creation, differentiation proceeds.
O King, for word and meaning are mutually dependent upon one another; indeed, a word exists through the absence of its referent, and a referent is cognized through the absence of its word. (43)

Therefore, the four Vedas are both meanings and words; for meanings and words are of such a nature. The wielder of the plow (Balarāma) has the form of the Ṛgveda, and the man-lion (Nṛsiṃha) is the Sāmaveda.
This auspicious lady is the embodiment of the Yajurveda, and the Atharvaveda is known as the Discus; thus the Veda is fourfold in its division, yet it is a single mass due to its non-difference.
Therefore, let there be no doubt in you: the one omnipresent Lord exists in manifold ways through this principle, even in his other incarnations.

O King, both difference and non-difference regarding the Lord of the World have been thus explained to you; therefore, perform your practice with devotion in whatever way brings satisfaction to your mind. (47)
For this Lord consists of all forms and consists of all mantras; in whatever manner and by whomever he is propitiated, he bestows the fruit accordingly.
O King, just as pure gold, when fashioned according to one's desire, receives various names in this world and brings satisfaction accordingly; || 49 ||
Thus, O King, the Blessed One manifested here with such majesty; for whatever one's degree of faith, one's accomplishment shall be of that same measure.
With purified action, mind, and speech, and with a pure inner self, propitiate Govinda here, who has assumed this wooden body.
For the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life according to your desire, worship this Viṣṇu with this king of mantras.
There is no mantra higher than this, neither has there been one in the past, nor will there ever be one in the future; Viṣṇu becomes pleased at that very moment when worshipped with this.
The Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, even grants his own city; what need then has he for sacrifices, pilgrimages, vows, gifts, or austerities? (54)
O King, I shall tell you the truth regarding him who indeed worships Viṣṇu in the form of wood situated on the Blue Mountain; having heard this, take it to heart. (55)
Having seen the Brahman, which is nectar in the guise of wood, situated at the foot of a banyan tree on the bank of this ocean by the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala), one shall be liberated without a doubt.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 28 ||
Jaimini said: Having spoken thus to that tiger among kings for the sake of maintaining the world, the lotus-seated Brahmā withdrew the form of the lion into his own heart.
Formerly, that form of Viṣṇu which was of the nature of light was manifested; in the past, four forms were seen at the time of descending from the chariot.
They all saw those very same [deities] once again seated upon their lion-thrones; he then worshipped Balabhadra with the sixteen-syllable mantra.

Having worshipped this flawless Nārāyaṇa with the Puruṣasūkta, the Discus with the Devīsūkta, and with the twelve-syllabled mantra, he presented them for the sake of bestowing grace upon the king. || 4 ||

Brahmā said: O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, bestower of grace upon devotees, a thousand births of Indradyumna, who was practicing devotion unto you, have passed away; at their conclusion, he beheld you.
For the sight of you, O Blessed One, is the cause of attaining union with you; even though this [man] desires to worship you through the yoga of devotion.
Therefore, command me so that I may worship you with the yoga of devotion, through [the observance of] place, time, and vows, as well as various other services.
O Lord of the World, this king, thirsting for the nectar-like essence of your command flowing from the lotus of your face, gazes upon you without blinking.
Jaimini said: Thus addressed by the lotus-born Brahmā himself, the Lord, though possessing a wooden body, laughed and spoke with a profound voice.

The illustrious Pratima said: "O Indradyumna, I am pleased with you because of your devotion and your selfless actions (niṣkāma-karma). Such prosperity has never been bestowed upon anyone other than you."
"I grant you a boon, O King: may your devotion to me remain steadfast, since you have constructed this temple for me, having renounced millions of riches. (11)
O Indra among kings, even upon its destruction, I shall not abandon this place; for even in another age, whoever else shall cause a temple to be built here [shall receive my favor]. (12)
That fame is surely yours alone; it is out of affection for you that I remain there. Truly, truly, again truly—I tell you nothing but the truth.
Even upon the destruction of the palace, I shall never abandon that place; with this wooden body, I shall remain here for a supreme aeon (parārdha).
This second [period] of the lotus-born Brahmā lasts until the completion of the second Caturyuga of this Svāyambhuva Manu.
In the first month of Kṛta-yuga, Jyeṣṭha, the conclusion of the sacrifice occurred on the tenth day; and on that very auspicious day of birth, I descended [to earth] in the month of Jyeṣṭha.
O Great King, one should perform my ceremonial bath upon that image according to the procedure for the great ablution (mahāsnāna), together with perfumes and abundant prosperity.
I shall destroy the evil accumulated over ten million births, as well as the fruit of all sacred fords, sacrifices, and likewise the fruit of all acts of charity. (18)
O Indra among kings, even as they behold it, one obtains such fruit; for to the north of the Nyagrodha tree, there is indeed a well containing all sacred fords (tīrthas).
"Having first prepared a place for bathing and covered it slightly with earth, I descended afterwards; uncovering that, reveal it. (20)
On the fourteenth day, having offered the sacrificial oblation (bali) according to the prescribed rite to the Protector Kṣetrapāla and to the Guardians of the Quarters, he is to be consecrated.
To the sounds of conchs, gongs, and drums, and to melodious chants, the twice-born should draw water from there using golden jars.
Having bathed me, along with Brahmā, Rāma, and Subhadrā, at the time of dawn on the full moon day of Jyeṣṭha, one shall attain my world.
O best of kings, that man who beholds me while I am being bathed shall not again incur the bondage of a physical body.
Having caused a firm platform to be constructed in the northeastern direction, adorned and beautified with a canopy, and sprinkled with sandalwood water; || 25 ||
There, after having me bathed by the two Rāmabhadras, he would lead me back again.
Whoever beholds me with devotion as I am proceeding facing southward, certainly obtains whatever he desires in his mind.
Then, O King, having established me for fifteen days, one should never look upon me as either deformed or beautiful.
Having performed this Jyeṣṭha-bath, one is liberated from all sins. || 29 ||
O Lord of the Earth, you should perform the great festival known as Guṇḍicā, by the mere glorification of which a person is liberated from sin.
The fifth day of the month of Māgha, the eighth day, and the bright fortnight of Caitra—these times are indeed auspicious for the great festival known as Guṇḍicā.

Especially on the second day of the month of Āṣāḍha, when it is conjoined with the Puṣya asterism, or even in the absence of that asterism, the rite should always be performed on that lunar day for my pleasure.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, conjoined with the Puṣya asterism, having placed Rāma upon the chariot along with me and Bhadrā— 33.
Having gratified many twice-born brahmins for the purpose of commencing a great festival, [he went] to the pavilion named Guṇḍicā, where I was born in the past.
Then there arose a great sacrificial altar for a thousand horse-sacrifices; no place on earth exists that is more meritorious than this. (35)
Since you have offered oblations here for five hundred years for my pleasure, there is no place on earth more pleasing to me than this.
Just as this Nīlaśikhara now, by means of your palace and in accordance with your four-faced nature, brings me great joy. (37)
Likewise, in the field of Nṛsiṃha, there is the great altar of your sacrifice; it is my place of origin and my eternal abode, which brings me joy. (35)
I have resided there for a long time, and my affection for it is supreme; this very Brahmā, my own self, has been established by him within that palace.
Indeed, out of regard for her and through devotion to you, I remain here perpetually; therefore, I have come here and shall stay for nine days.
In that place, O Great King, there is a lake consisting of all sacred fords (tīrthas); on its bank I shall remain for seven days, desiring to show you favor.
Seeing me stationed there, mortals go to my abode. There are thirty-five million sacred fords (tīrthas) in the three worlds. || 42 ||
All those [merits] go to you because of my presence in that lake; having bathed there according to the rules and having beheld me with a spirit of devotion, [they attain their goal]. (43)
Indeed, they shall never again experience the suffering within a mother's womb; then, on the ninth day, he arrived facing the southern direction.
Those who perceive the path as having the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha), having attained enjoyments equal to those of Indra and having experienced them, they enter into me at the end.
My rising, my sleeping, my turning over on my side, the covering of my path, and the great festival of the Puṣya-bath; || 46 ||
O King, one should perform a festival on the swing for me on the full moon day of Phālguna; those who behold me worshipped on the swing while facing the south [shall attain merit]. (47)
One is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt. || 48 ||
Having worshipped these two, beheld me, and prostrated before me, one shall obtain for each of them the fruit of eight thousand horse-sacrifices.

On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform the fulfillment of ritual actions; on the fourteenth day of the month of Caitra, one should worship me with *damanaka* flowers. For those people who do so during the bright fortnight, there shall be the destruction of all sins.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, known as Akṣaya, one should smear me with most beautiful fragrant unguents.
Those who would perform eternal festivals for my pleasure—each of these is proclaimed to bestow the fourfold aims of human life.
Jaimini said: O twice-born ones, having thus granted the boon to that Indradyumna, the Blessed Lord, his face like a smiling lotus, spoke to Brahmā.
O Four-faced One, everything has been accomplished by me for your pleasure; for your will is indeed my own will, and there is certainly no difference between us.
This incarnation has been undertaken by me as the very fruition of that which you previously requested of me in my form as Mādhava.
Having seen me here and having worshipped me, one is liberated by casting off the vital breaths; furthermore, all shall gradually attain union (sāyujya) with you.
Whatever a mortal expresses with speech while serving me here, that he certainly attains; and by association here, even a king attains it. (57)
"Go now to Satyaloka; let the deities go to Tridiva. Until the end of your full lifespan, I shall certainly remain here. (58)
Then all those excellent Brahman-sages and gods, filled with joy, bowed their heads to the God and departed for their own abodes.
And at that time, the Lord of the World, assuming the form of an image, remained silent, bringing joy to all people.
Indradyumna, too, being righteous-souled, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and firm in his vows, followed the Lotus-born One and then turned back at his command.
"Carry out all the pilgrimages commanded by the Blessed One; for when this Lord of the World is satisfied, the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings is indeed satisfied."

Having placed this command of the Lotus-born Brahmā upon his head, the illustrious lord of the earth, together with Nārada and the abundant treasure, performed the entire festival, beginning with the ritual bath of the eldest brother.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the second section, the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: O sage, tell us how the Lord of Śrī performed his birth-bath according to the prescribed rite, and describe to us all his other festivals as well, in accordance with the rules.
O best of sages, everything was previously told to you by Nārada; for that sage, the son of Brahmā, knows Brahman on the further shore of darkness.
O Sage, tell all that in its true essence, for our curiosity is great; oh, how great is the fortune of King Indradyumna, O Sage! (3)
While he was engaged in that work, this great and most wonderful thing occurred: indeed, neither had such a wooden image been heard of nor seen before.
As if with a living body, one should personally grant entrance like a human being, while repeatedly recollecting the sin-destroying deeds of the Blessed One.
The life-story of that king is difficult for mortals to obtain; O Blessed One, O Great Sage, there is no satiety for us as we listen.
In that same sequence, all these pilgrimages destroy every sin; it is certain that by the mere sight of them, one dwells in Vaikuṇṭha.
Since Madhusūdana himself is the speaker of the greatness of this pilgrimage, O highly fortunate one, please tell us that out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.

Jaimini said: O sages, listen now as I describe the Jyeṣṭha-bath; having resolved upon the vow on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should remain restrained in speech.

Having risen at dawn, a man should go to Mārkaṇḍeya-vaṭa and, being self-restrained, perform the rite according to the procedure for the five sacred bathing places (pañcatīrtha) after sipping water (ācamana).
Having bowed down before Śaṅkara with palms joined in reverence, one should offer a prayer in his presence.
O you of exceedingly sharp fangs and massive body, resembling the fire at the end of an eon; salutations to you, Bhairava, you should grant me your permission.

Then, O twice-born ones, having entered the sacred bathing place (tīrtha), one who bathes should duly bathe with the five Vedic Varuṇa hymns and the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta recited three times, and finally with this mantra: ||| 13 ||
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, and the remover of all sins; O Lord of Gods, I perform this bath; may my transgression perish.
Save me, who am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, seized by sin, and devoid of consciousness; O Destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, O Enemy of Tripura, salutations be unto you! 15.
Having thus bathed and gone outside, wearing clean garments and marked with the *puṇḍra*, he should offer libations to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors according to the prescribed rule.
O Brahmins, having entered the temple of Śaṅkara and touched the bull between its testicles with this mantra, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.

You are Dharma, you are the four-footed sacrifice, you are he whose horns are gold and whose body is the Triple Veda; O Lord of Rays, you are the horse-form; I bow to You, the wielder of the trident. 18.
Then, one should worship the Bull-vehicled Lord with the Aghora mantra; moreover, one should touch the supreme liṅga with the five Brahma-ṛks.
One should touch the linga with the thumb and the śakti with the fist; having worshipped according to the rules and praised the God who is the enemy of the cities (Śiva), [one should proceed].
Having bathed at Mārkaṇḍeya-vaṭa and beheld the god Śaṅkara, one obtains the unsurpassed fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
A person obtains the full fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices; finally, having attained residence in the same world as Śiva (sālokya), he subsequently gains knowledge.
And in due course, by the grace of the Lord of the World, he attains liberation; thereafter, observing silence, he should go to the god Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all ailment.
To the south of that stands the supreme banyan tree, which is the form of Viṣṇu; by the mere sight of it, the accumulation of sins of even the most wicked is destroyed.
Upon seeing him, one should bow from afar while meditating upon Puruṣottama; then one should perform a circumambulation while reciting this mantra: || 25 ||
O immortal one, you are eternally the great abode of Viṣṇu; O banyan tree, you who are the form of Viṣṇu, remove my sin; salutations be unto you! (26)
Salutation be to you whose form is unmanifest, who abide through the great dissolution; salutation to you, the sole refuge of the worlds and the wish-fulfilling tree. || 27 ||
By praising and reciting [mantras] with devotion to Janārdana at its base, one is liberated from the sins accumulated over hundreds of millions of births. (28)
By even stepping upon its shadow, a man becomes free from sin; thereafter, he should bow down to Suparṇa, who is in the form of a bird, before Hari.

Standing with palms joined in reverence out of devotion for Viṣṇu, he joyfully addressed him: "O embodiment of the Vedas, O abode of the universe, O form of the chariot, O you whose body consists of the threefold Veda! (30)

"Obeisance to you, whose form is sacrifice and who pervades the universe; salutations to you who are being pleased. Having thus praised Garuḍa, one is liberated from the sins accumulated over many births. (31)
Restraining his speech, mind, and actions, he should proceed while reflecting thus; having entered the temple of the deity, he should circumambulate it three times.
One should worship with the king of mantras, or with the Puruṣasūkta, or with the twelve-syllable mantra, or whichever one inspires devotion.
Therefore, all members of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes have the right to perform worship; for others, [the merit arises] from seeing them with devotion and from chanting their names.
One should worship the Supreme Lord according to the rite of the five offerings; then, with palms joined in reverence, one should recite this hymn of praise.
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, deliverer from the ocean of worldly existence, you who always bestow grace upon your devotees; protect me, who am prostrate at your feet. 36.
Victory to you, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the universe! Victory to you, destroyer of all sins! Victory to you, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the entire world; salutations be unto you!
Victory to you, Lord of millions of universes, whose breath is the Veda; O Supreme Self, support of the entire world, salutations be unto you! 38.

Victory to you, who dispel the suffering of the multitudes of gods led by Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra; victory to you, the abode of the entire universe! O Inner Controller, let there be salutation unto you. (39)
Victory to you, O ocean of unfeigned compassion, O you who are affectionate toward the distressed! O sole refuge for the poor and helpless, O witness of the universe, homage be to you! 40.

In the waters of the ocean of saṃsāra, which are difficult to cross due to the whirlpool of delusion, hard to traverse because of the multitude of the six waves, and terrible with the crocodiles of evil deeds; || 41 ||
In that which is without support, without foundation, devoid of essence, and frothy with suffering, [the world] is bound by the qualities of your illusion and falls from there, powerless.
O Lord of Gods, O best of deities, O manifester of supreme grace, uplift me with your compassionate side-long glances as I am submerged therein. (43)
O Lord of the World, you alone are the kinsman of those who fear worldly existence; hunger and thirst belong to the vital breath, while [the desire for] objects of enjoyment belongs to the mind. (44)
Sorrow and delusion, the decay of the body, death, and physical existence—all these belong to your creation; there is no one like you who is the protector of the distressed. (45)

O All-pervading Lord, you have descended among the worlds with the intent of showing favor to them; O Protector, for you whose every desire is fulfilled, what other motive could there be for being on earth? (46)
O Lord of the World, having attained your lotus feet, no anxiety remains; for your lotus feet are the sole means for achieving the four goals of human existence.
From the sight of it, all the desires of all people are fulfilled; thereafter, one should worship Śeṣa, who has a plow as his banner, with the appropriate mantra.

Having become one-pointed in mind, one should propitiate [the deity] by bowing down, using either the twelve-syllable mantra, the name [of the deity], or beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ). || 49 ||
Victory to Rāma, the eternally delightful one, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss! Salutations to the one of stainless form, who is free from the mire of ignorance. || 50 ||
O You who are free from the fatigue of bearing the burden of the entire world, You always wield the plough for the purpose of uprooting the threefold afflictions.
O Lord with blossoming lotus-eyes, you alone are the master capable of washing away all supreme impurities for the sake of protecting those who have surrendered in distress.

O ocean of serene compassion, O friend of the distressed, salutations be unto you, by whom the earth is supported upon the tip of the hood of the serpent whose body consists of the moving and the unmoving.
Lift me up from this shoreless ocean of existence so difficult to cross; O Supreme Lord of the highest and the lowest, salutations be unto You! (54)
Having thus praised the Naga king Bala, the wielder of the mace, one should worship Bhadralocanā, the primordial cause of the worlds.
Having praised that Jaya, O brahmins, one should prostrate and propitiate her: "Victory to you, O Goddess, O Great Goddess! Be gracious, O savior from worldly existence! (56)
Victory to you, O source of contentment for those who have taken refuge in the fire-drill of happiness; you are the effect of those whose nature is to act, and the cause of all causes. 97.
I bow to you, the foremost among those who uphold the *dhāraṇās*, who reside upon the chest of Viṣṇu and who constitute half the body of Śambhu.
I bow to the beloved of the world, who dwells within the lotus-face of the Lotus-born One, and who is the supreme soul of the acts of creation, preservation, destruction, and so forth. (59)
You alone are the incomparable power; without you, even He is not the Lord. You are the mother of all the worlds, the illusory power of Viṣṇu, the ascetic one.
I bow to that Subhadrā, who is auspicious in form and the primordial source; thereafter, one should pray to Puruṣottama for the sake of bathing in the ocean. 61.
Salutations to you, O Blessed Viṣṇu, who pervades the world of moving and unmoving beings! O Lord, may my bath in the ocean reach completion without obstacle.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the worlds, wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace! O God, grant me permission to attend upon your sacred ford.
Then, with a concentrated mind, he should proceed in silence while meditating on Viṣṇu, the lord of rivers, having obtained permission from Ugrasena who was standing on the path.
O Ugrasena, O mighty-armed one, powerful and of fierce prowess, having obtained a boon from the well-pleased [god], you have established yourself upon the shore of the ocean.
O bestower of the fully perfected fruit of bathing in the king of sacred fords, I shall perform a bath in the Indus; you should grant me your permission.
Then, O best of the twice-born, one should go thereafter to Svargadvāra, by which way the gods arrive at this sacred field of Puruṣottama.
I bow to you two who reside there on the path of the descent from heaven, coming day after day to behold the Lord of the World upon the earth. 68.
"May these two excellent witnesses, born from the waters of the ocean and endowed with all virtues, lead me as well upward by virtue of the deeds of the righteous. (69)
I pass between you two through the open gate of heaven; having made this request, one should then proceed to the presence of the King of Tīrthas.
Having seen it from afar, one is certainly liberated from great sin; having washed one's hands and feet and sipped water, one should sit upon a pure seat.
Sitting down and facing the east, he should draw a mandala before him—quadrangular, with four doors and four svastikas in the corners.
In the center of that, one should draw a beautiful eight-petaled lotus; then, one should place the eight-syllable mantra upon the two hands and the body.
The wise have declared that the placement (nyāsa) of the six limbs is performed with six syllables; thereafter, the remaining two [syllables] are to be placed upon the belly and the back.

Again, [one should place them] on the two feet, the two calves, the two thighs, the two buttocks, and the two sides; then on the navel, the back, the pair of arms, the heart, the throat, and the two armpits. (75)
One should place the syllables of the mantra in sequence upon the lips, the ears, the eyes, the cheeks, as well as the nostrils, the eyebrows, the forehead, and the head. (76)

Having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) with all [the mantras], one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with a concentrated mind; one should then perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), twenty-five times each, using the root mantra.
One should bind on this divine armor, which removes all sins: "May Govinda protect me in the east; may the lotus-eyed one protect me in the south. (78)
May Pradyumna protect [me] in the west, and likewise Hṛṣīkeśa in the north; may Narasiṃha be in the southeast, and Madhusūdana in the southwest. (79)
May Śrīdhara protect [me] in the northwest, and Gadādhara in the northeast; may Trivikrama protect above, and he who bears the form of the Boar protect below.
May the Lord who bears the conch, discus, and mace protect me everywhere; may Nārāyaṇa, whose banner is Garuḍa, protect my mind and consciousness.
May Janārdana, whose nature consists of the three qualities, protect my intellect and ego; may he, the slayer of the hosts of Daityas, always protect my senses.
Having thus bound on the armor, a man becomes free from sin; so too does a person by means of the sixteen modes of worship mentally conceived.
Having worshipped Puruṣottama according to the prescribed rule, O twice-born ones, they invoked the healthy God of gods into that mandala.

Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, augmented by offerings as far as his ability permits, he should contemplate himself as being within the presence of the King of Holy Places, the God of Gods.
Thus, with palms joined in reverence, one should utter this mantra: "O Sudarśana, salutations to you, who possess a radiance equal to ten million suns. (86)
"O Brahmins, having thus prayed near the waters of the King of Tīrthas: 'Show the path to Viṣṇu, who is blinded by the darkness of ignorance. (87)
Having descended to the ground on his knees, he should bow down, permeated by devotion: "O King of Tīrthas, salutations to you, Viṣṇu in the form of water. (88)
For the sustenance of living beings and for the sake of supreme liberation. || 89 ||

Agni and Ilā are your womb within the body; you are the placer of seed, the navel of Viṣṇu, the immortal. Having entered into you, I approach your form, which has no other cause and is replete with bliss. 90.
Reciting this mantra, O Brahmins, one should enter into the midst of the water, invoking the King of Holy Places (Tīrtharāja) while meditating upon the Lord of the Worlds.
Therefore, one should worship the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa), who stands ready to bestow the fruit of the performed ablution, with the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta accompanied by [the hymn to] Nārāyaṇa.
One should perform the six ancillary rites, beginning with the invocation, during the consecration by reciting the Pañcavāruṇaka mantra three times each.
The invocation has been explained previously; now the presence is being described: it is the conceptualization of the deity's presence for the sake of the performer obtaining his desired fruit. (94)
For the sake of internal purity, one should sip water consecrated with mantras after drinking; for the sake of purifying the external limbs, one should sprinkle oneself with water and kuśa grass.

For the sake of internal and external purification, one should sprinkle three handfuls of water consecrated by mantra upon the head; however, there is no recitation [of the mantra] while submerged within the water of the ocean.
Three times he bathed, contemplating the destroyer of sins, as his own committed evils—even those performed over ten million lifetimes—were washed away in that water.
Having risen and sipped water according to the rule, one should pray while reciting the mantra: "You are Agni, O Lord of the worlds, the depositor of seed and the kindler of desire. (98)
O Lord of Waters, you are the primary source of all beings and living creatures, the imperishable master; indeed, you are the fire-drill for the nectar of immortality and the womb of the gods.
O King of Tīrthas, take away all my sin; salutations be unto you! Whatever evil was previously accumulated throughout thousands of millions of births—[take that away]. (100)
"May that [sin] go to complete dissolution; grant me eternal Brahman. Then, having bathed, emerged from the bank, and sipped water while restraining his speech, || 101 ||
One should wear two white garments and, with devotion, apply bright marks (puṇḍraka) as well as tilakas in the form of a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.

O Brahmins, reflecting upon the gods and the ancestors according to the prescribed rule with the thought that they are the Blessed Lord, one should satisfy them according to the ritual injunctions, with a perfectly composed mind.
Then, having drawn the mandala as before, facing north, one should worship with devotion using the root mantra and these mantras.

O best of the twice-born, having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa—four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, accompanied by Dharā and Ramā, or alone—and being satisfied by the internal sacrifice, one should then invoke him externally.
Come, O Supreme Bliss, you who pervade the universe and consist of the universe; for the sake of bestowing grace, O Lord of Gods, be present within this mandala.
This entire world, both moving and unmoving, is established herein; O Lord, you yourself abide within it—I prepare this seat for you.
Since the Gaṅgā purifies the world when her waters are washed by Dharma in the form of Brahmā at his lotus feet, I offer you this water for washing the feet.

Day after day, Brahmā and the other gods worship Your lotus feet with the rays emanating from the crest-jewels fashioned from priceless gems. To You, the priceless abode of the universe, I offer this water for honor (arghya). || 9 ||
To him who, in the form of Agastya, indeed drank the king of holy waters (the ocean), I offer this well-perfumed water for sipping (ācamanīyaka). || 110 ||
I offer this madhuparka, which, having attained contact with honey, drew forth that which was in the form of water, for the purpose of drawing away all sins without exception.
I bathe with water that Lord who, having assumed the form of a boar, lifted up this earth submerged in the ocean of cosmic dissolution.
To that Universal Form, of whom millions of cosmic eggs constitute the veil, he gave two auspicious garments for the covering of all.
I offer this sacred thread to that Lord of Sacrifice, without whom even a sacrifice performed would certainly be as if unperformed. (14)
Since ornaments truly shine only by attaining contact with his limbs, I shall offer these ornaments to him who is the ornament of the entire universe.
Since the Malaya trees, endowed with fragrant juices, [shed their scent] through contact with the breezes that touch his limbs, [he offered] that fragrant unguent to him.
To him, by the mere thought of whom joy arises for those whose sins have been destroyed, I offer this fragrant garland of *sumanas* flowers.
To him who, having firmly grasped that [mind], abandons the scorching of the fire of existence—to him I offer this supreme, fragrant incense. (18)
To him whose shining illuminates this entire world by his own splendor—to that one who is the light of lamps, I offer this lamp. (19)
He who devours the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, and he who sustains it—therefore, for his nourishment, one should offer food with this [mantra].
Since even the celestial beauties were enchanted by the natural fragrance of the color upon his lips, they offered him that most excellent betel.
I bow to that Teacher of the World, an ocean of compassion, who destroys the wandering within the courtyard of worldly existence by means of circumambulation.
These mantras have indeed been taught with their respective ritual services (upacāras). Having invoked [the deity], one should contemplate the God as situated outside of oneself.
Having offered a jeweled lion-throne, one should contemplate him seated there; one should offer water for the feet (pādya) with śyāmāka grains and lotuses at his two lotus-feet.
Consecrated with dūrvā grass and parājitā plants by means of the root mantra, [the water] should be placed in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even a conch shell.
Having prepared the *arghya* according to the rules with water, sandalwood, flowers, barley, *dūrvā* grass, tips of *kuśa* grass, fruits, white mustard seeds, and sesame seeds; || 26 ||

One should sprinkle the tips of *dūrvā* and *kuśa* grass upon the head of the deity in front of him; the remainder should be cast upon the ground. This is declared to be the procedure for the *argha* offering.
One should offer water consecrated with nutmeg, *kaṅkola*, and cloves for the purpose of sipping (*ācamana*), and then present the *madhuparka*.

Cow’s curd mixed with honey and clarified butter, placed in a clean bronze vessel and covered with another similar vessel, well-prepared and accompanied by fruit—this is said to be the water for the ritual bath.
Two auspicious garments made of fine silk or cotton should be given according to one's ability; one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth. (130)
One should place ornaments such as necklaces, armlets, crowns, and neck-chains upon the limbs of the deity, according to one's capacity and in their proper positions.
O Brahmins, one should offer to Hari an upper garment (upavīta) made of silk thread, or alternatively of cotton, consecrated with fragrant sandalwood paste.
Anointment with camphor, sandalwood, musk, and saffron.
And with a garland of Tulasī leaves, along with jasmine, lotus, and campaka flowers, as well as aśoka, chura, punnāga, nāgakesara, and kesara blossoms. || 34 ||
One should offer other fragrant flowers as a garland, or a wreath, or even loose blossoms upon the head of the God.

That garland should reach down to the forepart of the feet, while the floral wreath (mālya) should be measured to the neck or the thighs; one should place a cluster of flowers (garbhaka) amidst the hair and scatter a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) upon the head.

One should offer a fragrant incense made of guggulu, aguru, uśīra, white sugar, clarified butter, honey, and sandalwood; and one should offer an auspicious lamp with cow’s ghee, using a wick containing camphor or with sesame oil.
The food was made of unbroken, well-sorted rice grains, thoroughly cooked, fragrant, and well-perfumed with clarified butter.
It was accompanied by the milk of a tawny cow, cooked plantains, and sugar; it was mixed with various side dishes, served with condiments, and provided with cakes.
The food offering for the God of gods should consist of various fruits, be heart-pleasing, fragrant, delicious, and fresh; it is not recommended if it is less than one *prastha* in quantity.

One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) after the incense, the lamp, the food offering (naivedya), the bath, the respectful oblation (argha), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), the garment, and the sacred thread (yajñopavīta). || 41 ||

In other cases, it is merely consecrated water, which is figurative. At the conclusion of the food offering (naivedya), one should give water for sipping (ācamana) and water for rubbing the hands (karaghṛṣṭika).
Then, O Brahmins, one should offer fragrant sandalwood and betel-leaf, combined with camphor, cloves, cardamom, nutmeg, and areca nut.
Having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times with undistracted mind, and having offered praise and performed circumambulation, one should pray to Puruṣottama.
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, you are the originator of all sacred fords; O Lord, you consist of all sacred fords and you consist of all the gods.
"O Lord, may this bath which has been performed by me in the King of Tīrthas through your grace indeed be fruitful; be the bestower of the fruits as they have been described. (46)
O Lord, you are the King of the Ocean and undoubtedly take the form of water; save me who am submerged in the abode of sin; salutations be unto you! (47)
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, the flawless Nārāyaṇa, one who has performed his bath in the King of Tīrthas obtains the fruit of all tīrthas.

Whatever merit is said to belong to those who perform ritual actions through the gift of ten million cows, the performance of ten million sacrifices, the feeding of ten million Brahmins, and through millions of great gifts—that very merit is indeed obtained by this [act]. (49)

Meditation, charity, austerity, recitation of mantras, ancestral rites, and the worship of the gods—all these, when performed at Siṃdhurāja, shall become multiplied by millions upon millions of times. (150)
"Will there be someone in our family who will bathe in the Sindhu and offer water with sesame seeds to the gods and the ancestors? (51)
All evils cry out and all great sins become bewildered; indeed, all undesirable things flee from one who is intent on bathing in the Sindhu.
Sin committed at another sacred site is destroyed on the shore of the Sindhu; sin committed on the shore of the Sindhu is destroyed by bathing in the Sindhu. || 53 ||
Upon merely seeing one who is constantly devoted to bathing in the Sindhu, the servants of Yama flee in the ten directions, just as deer do upon seeing a lion. || 54 ||
Yama too, seeing him, prostrated and worshipped him; he was then unable to stand before that performer of meritorious deeds. || 55 ||
The deities constantly desire: "May we attain human birth; having become perfectly pure in body, may we obtain a bath in the ocean. (56)
Even a heap of sinful karma as vast as Mount Meru or Mandara shall be consumed by bathing in the ocean, just as a pile of cotton is consumed by fire.
At the time of bathing, one should always remember the god Nārāyaṇa within the waters; especially so in this ocean, which is the very embodiment of Viṣṇu himself.

Whether one is a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a killer of a cow, or a perpetrator of any of the five great sins—all of them attain purification through bathing in the Sindhu; of this there is no doubt. (59)
A bath in the Sindhu is superior even to the gift of ten million tawny cows; by bathing in the Sindhu but once, one may uplift ten million members of one's lineage.
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and in all shrines, one obtains that entire fruit from bathing in the Sindhu; of this there is no doubt.
He who desires that his birth, life, or even his learning be fruitful, should go to the ocean and offer libations to the ancestors as well as to the gods.
The four Vedas, along with their six auxiliary limbs and the methods of *pada* and *krama*, are easily obtained; likewise, various kinds of gifts are easily obtained in Kurukṣetra. (63)
Cāndrāyaṇa fasts, Kṛcchra penances, and austerities are easily accessible; likewise, sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, are easily attainable.

With the waters of the Indus and its tributaries, the libation for the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa) is difficult to obtain; yet by the mere act of libation and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) for a month, [the goal is attained]. 65.

Indeed, all the ancestors, satisfied by the libations at the Sindhutīrtha and well-satiated by the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) of the śrāddha, ascend celestial chariots radiant as the sun and proceed swiftly to the eternal world of Brahmā. || 66 ||

Having worshipped the Lord of the World at the beginning and at the end according to the prescribed rite, and having bathed himself in the king of holy waters (the ocean), a man shall become a vessel for liberation.
Then, having performed the ritual dismissal of the sacred sites (tīrtha-visarga), the person of pure mind, having bowed to Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Subhadrā, should contemplate their form.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: Then, considering himself to have accomplished his purpose, he should proceed from there toward the Indradyumna lake, which was produced as a subsidiary part of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
On whose bank dwells Hari in the form of Narasiṃha, one should pray to Narasiṃha and bathe there according to the prescribed rite.
O Narasiṃha, salutations to you, in whose most excellent field that best of kings performed a thousand horse-sacrifices.
"O Lord, by your grace, Indradyumna has come to bathe in this lake born from the remnants of his sacrifice; please grant me permission. (4)

Then, having gone to the bank of the sacred ford and performed the rites of purification and sipping water (ācamana), one should join the palms in reverence (añjali) and, making a request, recite this mantra: || 5 ||
The surface of the earth was trampled by the hooves of ten million cows belonging to the horse-sacrifice; all things were purified by the waters taken up from the foam of their urine.
"I have come to bathe in your holy waters, which contain all sacred fords; through this bath, release me from the sin arising from thousands of previous births. (7)
Then, having entered within, O twice-born ones, one should bathe with the five Vāruṇa mantras and, while submerged in the water, should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.
O Tīrtha born from a limb of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, destroyer of all sins! May the sin accumulated over ten million births be destroyed by bathing in you.
O twice-born ones, having recited this mantra three times, one should bathe three times in that water; one should then meditate upon Hari in the form of Narasimha with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
Since the waters are called *nārāḥ* because they are the offspring of Nara, and since they were his first abode (*ayana*), one should therefore meditate upon Hari within the waters.
A person should duly offer libations to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors; thereafter, one should go to Narasiṃha, who stands facing the west.
Having seen Śambhu as a perfected being (siddha) or as an image, or Hari facing westward, one is liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million births.
One should worship that Man-Lion with an Atharvaṇa mantra; for in ancient times, this king of mantras was established by Nārada.
O twice-born ones, this mantra alone was worshipped by Indradyumna for a long time in the form of Narasiṃha; there is no other mantra equal to it.
By the mere utterance of which the Lion becomes pleased—even this wooden body was consecrated by Brahmā with this [mantra]. (16)
One should worship the Man-Lion with the previously mentioned offerings, using red hibiscus flowers and other fragrant blossoms.
One should smear the man-lion with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor; [one should offer] milk-rice mixed with sugar and cow's ghee.
He offered sweetmeats cooked in ghee mixed with pieces of camphor, as well as saṃyāva cakes, ghee-filled pastries, and various kinds of fruits. (19)
One should offer rice cooked with sugar and curd; having seen, touched, bowed to, and worshipped the Man-lion (Narasimha). (20)

A person indeed attains their respective desired goals; there is no doubt in this matter—whether it be the state of a god, the lordship of the immortals, or the state of a Gandharva, O twice-born ones. (21)
Whether it be lordship, mastery, or even universal sovereignty, whatever one desires in the mind, that one undoubtedly attains.
O twice-born ones, the procedure for the Pañcatīrthī has been told to you who asked; having performed this for five days, it is again composed of the five elements.
A mortal observer of vows, devoted to Viṣṇu, should not enter his body again at dawn on the full moon day in the waters of the king of holy fords (Prayāga).

Having bathed according to the previously mentioned rite, with pure food and controlled senses, a man should subsist on the vow of eating only one meal a day for the sake of [the deity's] pleasure, O best of the twice-born, for as long as those five days may last. (25)
Then, having entered the palace and beheld Puruṣottama Rāma seated upon the couch along with Subhadrā, one is liberated from the shrouds of sin.
Whoever beholds Hari on the full moon day of Jyeṣṭha being bathed with fragrant water drawn from a well that embodies all sacred fords (tīrthas).
No connection with sin shall prevail within his soul. O sages, listen further as I describe the procedure for the performer of the pilgrimage. 28.
On the fourteenth day, having caused a very beautiful and firm bed to be made—constructed of grass and wood, plastered with abundant white lime, and auspicious—(one should proceed).

Alternatively, O best of the twice-born, one should have a stone [image] made that will endure for a long time for the purpose of bathing the God of gods; one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth.
It was filled with various groves of trees, cooled by the southern breeze, and adorned upon the grassy banks of the surging waves of the ocean.
One should indeed prepare a canopy with sparse openings for the gods to behold, adorned with a magnificent, highly precious, and elevated awning.
They come together with Brahmā to bathe the Lord of the World, having taken water from the celestial Gaṅgā adorned with *pārijāta* flowers.
And the Brahman-sages and the thirty gods, together with Brahmā, bathed the Lord seated upon the dais here, at the command of the Supreme Creator.
He is to be honored by the inhabitants of the three heavens with shouts of victory and hymns of praise; therefore, a dais should be constructed, adorned with garlands and chowries.
It was adorned with archways made of yellow silk and various garlands of jewels, and it was sprinkled with the luster of fragrant incense and sweet-smelling sandalwood.
Having thus established the couch, O twice-born ones, they should draw water from a well and fill golden jars to its south.
One should consecrate it in the hall according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures. || 38 ||
One should fill those [vessels] with well-perfumed water while reciting the Pāvamānī verses; this rite is prescribed for the middle of the night on the fourteenth day.
O Hali, let the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—honored and respected by the king—lead Hari forward, proceeding very slowly. || 40 ||
Being fanned incessantly with yak-tail whisks and palm-leaf fans, one should not let that [image]—which has been anointed with pure unguents as in former times—be separated from the limbs of Viṣṇu.
Just as one's limbs become well-nourished day by day through the application of fragrant ointments, so too should effort be applied; for one whose limbs are emaciated does not achieve nourishment.
They should lead [the image] without negligence, honoring the Blessed One; for if, through negligence, there should be a fall of the Enemy of Mura, [it would bring disaster].
Whether it be for Bala, Subhadrā, the king, or the kingdom, it causes fear; even for those who cause downfall, there is loss and great suffering for their progeny. 44.
The residence of those evil-minded ones shall certainly be in hell; how could this wooden image have remained deluded for so long? (45)
Those who remain distrustful toward him and are hostile to the Blessed One fall into hell, excluded from all meritorious deeds.
In the religious duties of the deluded, the nihilists, the ungrateful, and those who have destroyed their own souls, arguments for lack of faith arise. (47)
For as long as something remains unseen by someone, it is indeed fashioned by him; at the end of that period, his palaces, images, and so forth perish.
Nor was this tree created by anyone, yet it has grown large and surely grants boons; therefore, it is certainly not considered a mere image. (49)
Even when the previous Manvantaras and other ages have passed away, [the merit] increases for both people and the gods in this created image. (50)
O Brahmins, such were the devotees of all the rulers of the earth; and indeed, during the Svārociṣa interval, that ocean of mercy manifested himself.
In the twenty-seventh cycle of four yugas during the Vaivasvata Manvantara, both Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna arrived at the conclusion of the Dvāpara age.
Having remained there for three days while observing their vow, they worshipped Madhusūdana with devotion, praised him, and returned once more to Dvārakā.
No one knows his true nature while he has assumed a human body; these incarnations of Viṣṇu proceed age after age.
O Brahmins, by establishing the Dharma, they merge again into their own state; and this was previously declared by Brahmā to them one with another.
The Lord Viṣṇu, assuming the form of wood, shall remain as the granter of boons until the end of a parārdha, perpetually meditated upon with pure sattva.
To whatever extent one's faith extends, to that same extent is one's accomplishment; a man who is firm-minded and devoted, yet has allowed his faith to become negligent [does not attain it]. (57)
From this, one obtains a very difficult-to-attain fruit in accordance with one's effort; previously, I told you all about the liberation of Ambarīṣa.
Therefore, having established firm devotion toward that Lord of the World, who is the very nature of the Supreme Self, dwell here in Puruṣottama. (59)
Therefore, this excellent seat of Śrī Kṛṣṇa should be approached with devotion; indeed, Subhadrā and Balabhadra should be served like kings.
While the parasols were being held aloft and fanned with chowries, the quarters of the sky resounded deeply with the incense of black aloe-wood.

When the palace was filled with various kinds of musical instruments, while the threefold symphony of song, dance, and instrumental music proceeded excellently, and it was illuminated by rows of lamps; (62)
Then, while all were in darkness during the great festival, the body of the Lord of Śrī was covered out of fear of negligence.
As the fine, smooth, and silken garments were being carried far away, the Teacher of the Worlds turned his face upward due to the speed of their movement.
The gods, their eyes turning [in alarm] and fearing his ascent during the day, cried out, "Be victorious, Rāma! Kṛṣṇa! Be victorious, Bhadra! (65)
Thus, at midnight, during the ceremonial consecration of his seniority by birth, the Blessed One was led gracefully to the couch by the Brahmins and others.
The cry of "I first! was heard among the gods in heaven, as were the celestial drums mingled with shouts of victory. (67)
Then, together with the image facing him, he should cover all the limbs of the one situated on the couch—except for the face—with fine cloths.

Having worshipped [the deity] with the previously mentioned services (upacāras), even without the offering of food (naivedya), and with the consecrated jars (adhivāsita-kuṃbha) accompanied by the chanting of propitiatory sounds (śāntighoṣa); || 69 ||
One should bathe the preeminent gods with the *samudajyeṣṭha* mantra, for the sake of bringing about a sense of fulfillment in those who perform the consecration as they witness it.
Those men who are stationed there and behold him being bathed shall never again undergo the bathing within the waters of the womb.
Those who, filled with joy and their minds yearning for the festival, behold the Lord’s Jyeṣṭha-bath, do not sink into the ocean of worldly existence.
The beginningless accumulation of sins committed by men through both conscious and unconscious acts perishes in that very instant for those who witness the ritual bathing of Hari.
"Truth, truth, and again truth I speak, O best of the twice-born: it is the pacifier of all afflictions and the destroyer of every impurity. (74)

If one performs the ceremonial bathing of the Lord of Śrī on the full moon day of Jyeṣṭha with devotion, or even gazes upon Him, whatever sins there may be that necessitate expiation—indeed, all such transgressions [are purified].
All those [sins] perish for those who behold the ceremonial bathing of Hari; indeed, there is no other rite superior to this for liberation without effort.
Whatever bathing, charity, austerity, ancestral rites (śrāddha), recitation (japa), sacrifice, and other such acts are observed by one on the birthday of the elder [brother] of Hari; || 77 ||
Rituals performed for ten million births, even if multiplied by ten million times, do not equal the merit of bathing at or beholding Lord Hari. (78)
O Brahmins, he who with devotion witnesses even once in a year the ritual bathing of Viṣṇu does not grieve in this world, which is the liberator from saṃsāra. (79)
By him were performed meritorious sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees given out of faith; great gifts were bestowed, and tens of millions of twice-born brahmins were fed. (80)
Indeed, millions of ancestral rites (śrāddhas) were performed at Gayaśīrṣa and other such sites; and during auspicious times and at sacred fords, austerities were practiced.
O Brahmins, he who beholds the bathing ceremony of Hari has effectively bathed millions of times at Ardhodaya and other such conjunctions, and at millions of sacred fords (tīrthas).
"Truth, truth, and again truth I speak, O best of the twice-born: there is no action more conducive to welfare than this, which stands upon the path revealed by the scriptures. (83)
Indeed, whoever beholds Puruṣottama being bathed while situated upon the couch obtains merit a hundred times greater than the act of bathing itself; of this there is no doubt. (84)
He who beholds the Lord of the World seated upon the couch, wet from his bath, with a heart moistened by intense bliss, incurs no sin whatsoever. (85)
Whatever merit has been declared for the acts of bathing [the image] and beholding it, one obtains that very fruit by seeing Acyuta seated upon the platform.
O twice-born ones, the Lord of the World is indeed one, yet he is situated there in three forms; even the bathing of or beholding any one of them bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"Be victorious, O Rāmabhadra! Be victorious, O Bhadra!"—he who should thus speak, or joyfully utter, "Victory to Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the World! Be victorious! [attains the fruit]. (88)

O best of the twice-born, at the time of bathing, he indeed attains liberation; this applies to those who have performed the preliminary rites such as the consecration (adhivāsa) for the act of bathing there.
Endowed with faith, he should give separate sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) to them, as well as sweet food, garments, and ornaments to the Brāhmaṇas.
Endowed with faith, one should give gifts and satisfy the poor and the helpless; those who have come to witness the bath are certainly liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 91 ||
The king should indeed honor those [deities] according to his capacity for the pleasure of Hari; seated upon an auspicious throne, he should bathe with the water remaining from the ritual ablution.
Whether it be a woman or even a man, I shall tell you the merit thereof: one who is afflicted by a chronic disease will become well, and he shall indeed conquer untimely death.

A woman who is childless, or whose children have died, or who is barren, shall obtain a son; one who is unfortunate among all people shall become fortunate, and one who is destitute shall become wealthy.
A pregnant woman obtains a son who is long-lived and possessed of excellent qualities; this is said to be the fruit arising from bathing at all the sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā. || 95 ||
The righteous-souled one certainly obtains the merit born from seeing and bathing [there]. || 96 ||
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the second section (Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: Hereafter, I shall describe the vision of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, wherein the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice is obtained at every step.
Then one should worship with various kinds of divine foods, such as edibles and drinks, as well as with perfumes and garlands, according to one's capacity and with the prescribed ritual offerings.
[He worshipped] Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Subhadrā with songs, dances, and so forth, as well as with various spectacles presented with faith. || 3 ||
Having honored the best of the twice-born with garments, sandalwood paste, garlands, and other offerings, as well as these venerable brāhmaṇas who are great devotees of the Lord; || 4 ||
