Then, having performed a great festival as was done previously for the bringing of Hari, he should lead those lords of the thirty gods facing toward the south.
At that time, whatever mortal beholds Hari walking with his face turned toward the south, accompanied by Subhadrā, is no ordinary human being.

The gods, having come for the purpose of bathing, bathed the Teacher of the World; they remained even in the sky, crowded together for that duration of time, to behold Hari as he departed toward the southern direction, his face turned southward, the destroyer of worldly existence.
He was walking facing the south in order to behold all those religious rites that exist within the treatises of Dharma.
He who beholds Murāri after He has bathed and as He proceeds facing the south obtains the entire merit born from witnessing His bathing.

Having performed the lustration ceremony for the Lord of Gods together with Rāma and Bhadrā, and having then caused him to enter the interior of the temple, one should by no means look upon him again.
This, however, has already been explained by me in detail previously, O twice-born ones.
The sages said: O Blessed One, best among the knowers, please tell us that which you have declared: the certain fruit one obtains by performing the ritual bath on the day of Jyeṣṭhā.
Jaimini said: "Indeed, I shall tell you that Jyeṣṭha-pañcaka vow; nothing superior to this has been proclaimed by the sages who have reached the further shore of the scriptures."
This is the most excellent of all vows declared in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas; it was proclaimed first by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord. (14)
Because it is the eldest among the chief vows, it is known as the Jyeṣṭha-pañcaka; the ocean is the bestower of the fruit of the eldest, and the Lord is the giver of the fruit of the eldest. || 15 ||
The merit obtained from beholding [the deity] for an entire year is gained by means of the Mañcaka alone; indeed, whatever is obtainable through the Mañcaka, one may obtain that on Mahājyaiṣṭhī.
O Brahmins, whatever fruit was previously described by me as arising from bathing and beholding [the deity], one obtains all of that during Mahājyaiṣṭhī; of this there is no doubt. (17)
The sages said: "O Brahmin, describe the Mahājyaiṣṭhī, wherein bathing yields great fruit; for a great curiosity has indeed arisen within us regarding that."

Jaimini said: When the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha occurs, and the Moon and Jupiter are situated in a single degree of the constellation Śakra (Pūrvaphalgunī) on a Thursday; || 19 ||
On this auspicious conjunction, Mahājyaiṣṭhī, which destroys all sins, there are indeed all sacred fields, all holy fords, and likewise the seven oceans.
Sacrifices, collections of great gifts, austerities, the eighteen branches of knowledge, and various vows; || 21 ||
Rites for pacification and nourishment, as well as Sāṃkhya and Yoga—all these together proceed to the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama.
Divided into groups, they each went toward one of the sacred sites, thinking, "To which fortunate person shall we go for the sight of the eldest brother's ritual bath? (23)
On the day of Mahājyaiṣṭhī, we shall enter into a state of mutual "I-ness"; there, through great yoga, they go to the supreme field of the Blessed One.

The Mahājyaiṣṭhī is a day of great merit that increases the pleasure of the Blessed One. By worshipping the Lord of Gods, the Master of the World, who is an ocean of compassion, on that day, and by beholding Him as He is being bathed, one is liberated from the treasury of sins.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim that vow known as Jyeṣṭhapañcaka; I shall tell you exactly what is to be obtained through this vow.
On the tenth day, having bathed in the morning according to the prescribed rule, one should observe the vow and choose there an Ācārya who is a Vaiṣṇava and a bull among the twice-born.
In this manner, one should undertake this pure resolve, the supreme vow.
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Savior from the ocean of worldly existence! O Keśava, from this day forth, until that lunar day of Jyaiṣṭhī, I shall observe this vow for your pleasure.
The daily performance of ablutions at all sacred fords, the observance of vows and the eating of food [accordingly], and the worship of even one of your five forms—[these constitute the path]. (30)
O Lord, by your grace, may this vow be completed three times a day for one day; and may it be fruitful for you, O Master. (31)
Then, having bathed in the five sacred fords and returned home, he should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
In the middle of that, he should place a water-pot filled with water from sacred fords (tīrtha), provided with sandalwood and fruits; upon its mouth, a copper vessel.
With a cloth wound around its neck and a vessel filled with unbroken grains [of rice], one should place therein a golden image of the god Madhusūdana.
With beautiful limbs and features, peaceful, and the Lord endowed with glory in his left [hand].
And on the right [shoulder], one should visualize the powerful Lord Garuḍa, touching him from behind, holding a conch and a discus, and seated upon a lotus throne.
O twice-born ones, the preceptor or even [the disciple] should worship him with ritual offerings; he should devoutly cause a garland of blue lotuses to be presented to the God.
Having thus performed worship on the tenth day, which destroys ten crores of sins, one should pray with palms joined in reverence while reciting this mantra: || 38 ||
O Madhusūdana, Lord of Gods, salutations to you, O beloved of Mādhavī! O ocean of compassion, protect me who have fallen into the ocean of worldly existence. 39.

On the eleventh day, one should worship Nārāyaṇa, who has four arms, holds the conch, discus, and mace, and is seated upon a lotus; [an image] fashioned from five niṣkas, or even half of that, with a garland of lotuses.
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa), sugar, plantains, and various kinds of food offerings as naivedya; having presented these, one should joyfully offer prayers.
O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be unto you, the one who carries us across the ocean of worldly existence; protect me, O lotus-eyed one, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge. 42.
When worshipped, the Lord destroys the unsurpassed heap of sins committed through the eleven sense organs, which have been accumulated throughout beginningless existence.
On the twelfth day, one should worship Yajñavārāha, fashioned from gold, with applications of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, and with a garland of campaka flowers.
Having offered various kinds of excellent cakes along with foods to be chewed and eaten, as well as fruits, one should pray to the God while reciting this hymn of praise. (45)

You upheld the earth when it was submerged in the ocean of dissolution; why are you not able to uplift me, who have fallen at your lotus feet? Therefore, O Govinda, lift me up, for I am submerged in an ocean of grief.

Indeed, for as many years as there are twelve months, whatever great or small sins have been committed by men in previous births during those years, the Lord destroys them when He is worshipped on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī). 47.

On the thirteenth day, however, one should worship Pradyumna, who holds a conch, a discus, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, is seated upon a lotus, and is fashioned with four gold neck-ornaments.
A person should worship with devotion using the ritual services as prescribed, offering a garland of Aśoka and Pāṭalī flowers that is full of the moon and brilliantly radiant. (49)
Having offered the sacrificial food (naivedya), cooked rice, and beautiful ripe fruits, one should, being pure and with palms joined in reverence, offer salutations and make this prayer.
O Lord Pradyumna, fulfiller of desires, you who assume forms at will; may all desires bear fruit, O Kāmapāla, salutations be unto you! 51.
On the fourteenth day, one should worship Narahari in the form of gold, who is delighted by Lakṣmī residing upon his chest and is radiant with his mane.
The god with his mouth wide open and a loud laugh, seated upon a lotus and a yogic belt, possessing extremely sharp claws, is the warder-off of all calamities.
One should worship the deity, who is fashioned from four gold *niṣkas* and possesses auspicious marks, with offerings and great devotion as before. (54)
Having offered a garland of hibiscus flowers and likewise a wreath of jasmine blossoms, and having prostrated at his feet with handfuls of flowers, he performed a circumambulation.
Just as you tore apart Hiraṇyakaśipu out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, so too, being worshipped, destroy this multitude of evils.

Having thus prayed to Nṛhari and prostrated like a staff upon the ground, the observer of the vow, having thus completed that five-day rite, should cause five lamps to be offered both by day and by night.
Five pairs of garments, five umbrellas, and likewise five pairs of sandals, as well as five water-pots accompanied by sacrificial threads and filled with fruits.
At the conclusion of the meal, one should give to the twice-born with a mind full of faith.
At night, one should please Vāsudeva with songs of vigilance and the like, as well as with various offerings and the recitation of Purāṇas.
Having bathed at dawn on the full moon day, one should go into the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having worshipped Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Subhadrā according to the prescribed rites, and having performed their ceremonial bathing or witnessed it as enjoined by the scriptures; 62.
Having bathed again in the ocean and returned home, he should go to that place where those images of Viṣṇu are situated in jars and worshipped with mantras.
Having established the fire to the west of them according to the prescribed rite, the domestic priest should perform the fire-ritual with their respective mantras.

One should utter the name preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava), ending in the dative case, and followed by "namaḥ. However, for the rite of fire-offering (homa), the root mantra of the deities ends with "svāhā."
One should offer oblations of charu, clarified butter, and palāśa wood-sacrificial fuel, one hundred times each, individually for each deity.
Immediately after that, one should offer a hundred flowers; then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Brahmā.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, consisting of gold and a cow with golden horns, silver hooves, and equipped with various utensils.
One should offer gifts of highly precious garments by which the Guru is pleased, and one should present images equipped with all necessary implements.
One should feed the Brahmins with milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with ghee and sugar; this is declared to be the excellent vow known as Jyeṣṭhapañcaka. || 70 ||
O Brahmins, by performing with devotion the bathing and the viewing [of the deity], a person obtains the entire fruit thereof; of this there is no doubt. (71)
That Ekādaśī which falls in the middle [of the fortnight] is proclaimed as Nirjala (waterless). Those who, endowed with devotion, worship that single day according to the prescribed rules— || 72 ||
All the Ekādaśīs performed throughout one's entire life are undoubtedly fulfilled by performing this king of vows; having observed it, one obtains the fruit of all vows.
Whatever desires he may strive for, he obtains them all without a doubt. || 74 ||

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Jyeṣṭhapañcaka Vow," in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: Hereafter I shall describe the great festival of the Mahāvedī, by which even one blinded by the darkness of ignorance may attain the radiant state. || 1 ||
In the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the third lunar day is the destroyer of sins; it is self-manifested when conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism.
Having made his resolve regarding that [task], the pure king should respectfully choose one or three preceptors, as well as a carpenter whose work has been proven.

He should choose [the site] for the forest sacrifice with garments, ornaments, and other such items; then, having gone to the forest together with a carpenter, he should select a place crowded with excellent trees.
Having established the fire in its center, the knower of mantras, using the king of mantras, should offer one hundred and eight oblations mixed with the residue of the clarified butter.

One should sprinkle clarified butter at the base of each of the trees; then, having offered the bali-oblation to the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), as well as to the Kṣetrapālas and their attendants.
One should offer a hundred oblations of milk-rice to the Lord of the Forest (Vanaspati). Thereafter, taking an axe, one should [approach] the roots of the trees in the various directions.

While reciting the mantra at the places where the clarified butter (ājya) is being consecrated, the preceptor should cut off small portions [of the sacrificial grass], while meditating upon the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
While the sounds of musical instruments resound and auspicious songs are being sung, the preceptor, having directed the carpenter there, should return to his own home.
Alternatively, one should consecrate the timbers obtained for the construction of the chariot with the prescribed ritual procedure using the prepared fire.
One should set out the chariot after having fashioned it with sixteen spokes and sixteen wheels made of strong iron, during the great festival of the King of Vighnas.
One should construct a chariot for Viṣṇu that has strong axles and a strong pole, and is surrounded by various mechanical galleries and figurines.
It was adorned with many various and diverse pieces of sugarcane, endowed with four archways, possessing four gates, and exceedingly beautiful. || 13 ||
Abounding in various wonders, adorned with golden bands, twenty-two cubits in height, and decorated with banners. || 14 ||
One should fashion a Garuda-banner made of red sandalwood, with a long nose and a stout body, adorned with two earrings.
With a serpent grasped by the tip of its beak, adorned with all ornaments, it appeared as if it had risen up, spreading its two wings in the sky as if about to fly away.
One should adorn his entire body by covering it with gold, thereby destroying the pride of strength of the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas.
One should construct a well-adorned chariot as the seat for Hari; one should likewise construct a chariot for Balarāma with fourteen chariot-components.
One should construct the excellent chariot of Subhadrā with twelve wheels; one should make the plow-bannered chariot of Sīrin consist of seven leaves.
One should fashion a lotus-banner for the Goddess out of lotus-wood; having constructed the chariots, the king should perform the consecration as previously described.
One should place trust in Brāhmaṇas according to the mantras and according to the scriptures; for Brāhmaṇas are remembered as the moving bodies of the Lord of the Universe. (21)
Thus, indeed, the triad of wheels for the triad of deities was well-constructed on the auspicious day of Viṣṇu during the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha.
O twice-born ones, having performed the consecration according to the prosperous rite as before, it must be guarded there so that no impure person may ascend it. (23)
Whether it be a bird, a human, or even a cat, a mongoose, or the like—if [the corpse] is placed to the north of the chariots within three days from that time—[the following occurs]. || 24 ||

One should perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) in a pavilion or as part of a festival; furthermore, when extraordinary portents occur, one should perform the propitiatory rite (śānti) previously described.
The road should be well-prepared so that it may reach the great altar; one should create circles on both sides of the path using shrubs and various fruits.
With clusters of *sumana* flowers, garlands, fine linen garments, and yak-tail fans, it shone there like a forest grove in full bloom.
The ground should indeed be made level, free of mud, easy to traverse, stainless, fragrant, and cleared of heaps [of refuse] from afar. (28)
Immediately following were incense burners that filled the quarters with fragrance, a sprinkling of sandalwood water, and likewise a multitude of mechanical devices.
Indeed, many seasonal flowers were brought for the sake of the flower rain, as well as many leading actors, dancers, and singers.
There were courtesans, full of pride in their youth and adorned with beauty and ornaments, as well as mṛdaṅgas, paṇavas, bherīs, ḍhakkās, and other such instruments.
There were many variegated banners of various kinds, and there were many flags there fashioned from gold and silver.
There were various kinds of Vaijayantī banners, as well as ground-vehicles, elephants, and horses, all well-armored and beautifully adorned.
Having thus gathered the necessary provisions and being pure in his vows, the protector of the earth, endowed with joy and supreme devotion, should perform a great festival. (34)
On the second day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, conjoined with the Puṣya asterism, one should worship the Lord at the time of dawn.
Together with Brāhmaṇas, Vaiṣṇavas, ascetics, and those practicing austerities, he should, with palms joined in reverence, petition the God of gods for the sake of the procession.
O Lord, O Master, just as you previously knew King Indradyumna, so may you now be victorious on your chariot toward the Guṇḍicā pavilion.
May the ten directions be purified by the glance from the corner of your eye; may all things, both mobile and immobile, attain the state of supreme liberation.
"Indeed, this incarnation has been undertaken out of a desire to favor the world; therefore, O Blessed One, come with affection and set Your foot upon the earth. (39)
Then one should scatter camphor powder and flowers; on the way, the twice-born recite the Śākuna Sūktas.
Some recited auspicious verses, some cried out "Victory! Victory!", and some indeed chanted loudly the mantra "jitaṃ te" (victory to you).
And the chief bards and panegyrists joyfully sang his holy fame, while on both sides there was a row of fly-whisks with golden handles.
They sportively swayed [the vessels], beautiful with jingling bracelets, which were perfumed by the excellent incense of black aguru cast into golden bowls.

Fragrantizing all directions as well as the courtyard of the sky, the sweet sounds of cymbals, drums, flutes, lutes, and other instruments resounded most melodiously during Govinda’s victory procession.
When this occasion had thus begun, the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas led Kṛṣṇa, preceded by Rāma, as well as Bhadrā.
Rows of parasols were gathered together, along with pearl garlands and Chinese-style arches; jeweled banners with golden staffs stood on both sides of the Enemy of Mura.
The king, the four castes, and other common people—whether lowly or great—appeared there indeed as equals at that time. || 47 ||
Making those gods—who were at times tranquil—dwell upon cotton-filled mattresses with graceful steps and movements, they followed after the chariot.
Having reached the great festival and amidst the clamor of songs, they placed the Lord of the Universe in their hand and circumambulated Him on the excellent chariot.
One should place Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Subhadrā in the middle of the chariot, within a pavilion resplendent with a beautiful moon-shaped canopy.
It was adorned with garlands of small bells and flowered chowries, its interior filled with the incense of black agallochum.
Then, having settled those best of gods upon couches, one should devoutly adorn them with various garments, ornaments, and garlands.
One should worship with those abundant offerings, permeated by devotion; for no other festival of Viṣṇu is observed that is superior to this.
Wherein the Lord of the Three Worlds himself, honoring that former command, would travel year after year out of curiosity by means of his chariot.
Those who behold him with joy and devotion as he proceeds on his chariot during the great festival of Mahāvedī shall dwell in the abode of Hari.
"Truth, truth, and again truth do I promise, O best of the twice-born: there is no festival sanctioned by the scriptures that is more auspicious than this one dedicated to Viṣṇu. (56)
Just as this Rathavihāra is a great festival of the Mahāvedī, where the gods from heaven arrive and those who are qualified proceed to the celestial realm.
What can I say of the greatness of that festival of the enemy of Mura, by the mere chanting of which the sin arising from a hundred births is destroyed? (58)
[He saw] that Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) proceeding to the great altar (mahāvedī) while seated in his chariot, along with Balabhadra and Subhadrā, who have manifested through ten million births.
Having seen it, one destroys sin; there is no need for deliberation on this point. By stepping upon the shadow of the chariot, even the killing of a Brahmin is removed.
One whose body is touched by its dust shall destroy the threefold accumulation of sins and obtain the fruit born of bathing in the celestial Gaṅgā.
Due to the falling of a thick shower of rain, the path of the chariot became muddy; yet, by the divine vision of Kṛṣṇa, it was cleared of all impurities.
In that regard, those supreme Vaiṣṇavas who indeed perform prostrations shall abandon the beginningless mire of worldly existence and attain liberation. || 63 ||
One undoubtedly obtains the fruit of giving ten million cows, ten thousand maidens, and a thousand horse-sacrifices. (64)
Even those who follow Kṛṣṇa out of curiosity for the procession are indeed constantly followed by the gods, headed by Śakra.
For those who behold the chariot moving along—the eternal Brahman made of wood—the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice is proclaimed for them at every step.
The expounders of the Vedas praise the bestower of liberation with the Vedas, or with hymns from the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth, or even with those composed by themselves.
Those who are indeed free from impurity praise the lotus-eyed Lord; having established themselves in the Vaiṣṇava yoga, they rejoice with Nārada and others.
Those who offer praise with shouts of "Victory! before Vāsudeva truly conquer various sins; of this there is no doubt. (69)

Even one who is ignorant of the laya and tāla rhythms and devoid of sweetness in song, if that best of men performs dance or sings, he undoubtedly attains liberation through association with the highest Vaiṣṇavas. || 70 ||
He who goes along with him while reciting his names obtains the same fruit as one who follows him in attendance; of this there is no doubt.

"Victory to Kṛṣṇa! Victory to Kṛṣṇa! Victory to Kṛṣṇa!"—he who, filled with devotion, utters these words as Kṛṣṇa proceeds toward the city of Guṇḍicā, shall never again experience the suffering of dwelling within a mother's womb. (72)
He who stands at the front of the chariot and fans Puruṣottama with chowries, fans, clusters of flowers, and blue garments; || 73 ||
Fanned by Apsarases and graced by Gandharvas, he sat upon the throne of Mahendra while the gods followed behind him.
He enjoys incomparable pleasures until the dissolution of all beings; and at the end of that, having reached the world of Brahmā, he shall attain liberation.
Those who indeed shower flowers before Kṛṣṇa shall surely attain all the desires residing in their minds.
Those who circumambulate the chariot while reciting the thousand meritorious names—the gods themselves, with their necks bowed in reverence, shall perform a circumambulation for them. (77)
They dwell in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, possessing prowess equal to that of Viṣṇu.
At that time, which was of great merit and frequented by gods, sages, and ancestors, the one Brahman became threefold, following its own Māyā.
[He performed] the great festival of the altar in the form of wood itself.
Wherever the Lord of the World goes mounted upon his chariot out of curiosity, at that time one should observe a great festival there upon the earth.
Even the gods, led by Indra, having abandoned their pride at that festival, formed two rows on either side.
They perform a great procession with various divine retinues.
The foremost among them there was even the god Prapitāmaha, the Supreme Lord who is the creator of the fourteen worlds.

He too, having returned from the world of Brahmā, praised the Lord of the World as He proceeded in the chariot during the great festival with hymns consisting of the Vedas, bowing down at every step to the eternal Blessed One.
Although there is no difference between Kṛṣṇa and the Ocean-born (Viṣṇu), nevertheless, this is the greatness of the great festival, wherein everyone is a follower.
There is nothing in this world superior to this great festival of the Mahāvedi; it is a yoga that removes all sins and bestows the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites.
Whatever gift a man gives there, dedicated to Kṛṣṇa, its fruit is inexhaustible; it is equal to the merit of giving Mount Meru as a gift.
Whatever action one performs before that God of gods as he proceeds toward the temple of Guṇḍicā, that very act one enjoys as inexhaustible.
Indeed, various offerings, including both hard and soft foods, which people present to the God or to a twice-born for His pleasure, yield inexhaustible merit and grant all desires. (90)
Those who indeed precede Hari, beholding his lotus-face at every step and bowing down while drenched in mud and dust; || 91 ||
Having cast off the impenetrable armor of sin accumulated over ten million births, they attain the fruit of liberation in an instant and go to the auspicious abode of Viṣṇu.
They attain the fruit of all sacrifices, holy fords, and acts of charity; there is no festival more meritorious than this state of devotion to the Blessed One.
Thus the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Subhadrā and Rāma, proceeded seated in his excellent chariot, illuminating the four quarters.
The glorious one, compassionate and mindful of his devotees, destroyed the sins of all embodied beings with a wind that issued from his majestic limbs. 95.
Indeed, for the sake of inspiring faith even in those who are ignorant and devoid of trust, this Lord—who is the natural bestower of liberation—commences the journey.
As Janārdana proceeded along the road at midday, while the sun scorched his forehead with its heat, he was accompanied by the splendor of both gods and mortals.
Exhausted and covered by that dust, the people stood there withering away; therefore, for the sake of cooling the heat, one should perform an ablution with mirrors.
With the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and cool waters scented with flowers and camphor, and with whisks and cool fans moistened with water; || 99 ||
One should fan the lotus-eyed Lord (Viṣṇu), as well as Subhadrā and Rāma, with cool, delightful drinks and various preparations of sugar-candy.
With dates, coconuts, and various types of plantain fruits, as well as with dairy products, jackfruits, and palmyra fruits. || 1 ||
With sugarcane and various kinds of sweet, heart-pleasing fruits, with scented cool waters, and with ripe betel leaves; || 2 ||
One should worship Puruṣottama with camphor, cloves, and other such offerings.
At that time, O best of the twice-born, those people who behold Janārdana and worship Him according to their ability do not experience the exhaustion born of worldly existence.
O best of the twice-born, they attain residence in the world of Brahmā.
Those bulls among men who perform three, four, or even seven circumambulations of the three deities stationed upon the three chariots; || 6 ||

Having performed ten prostrations, they stood before him with palms joined in reverence; those very hymns with which Brahmā, the lotus-born, had formerly praised them while they were stationed upon their chariot.
They praised the Lord of Gods; those men who thus praise the Supreme Lord, O twice-born ones, certainly go to the world of Brahmā. (8)
Then, in the afternoon, one should slowly lead the Lord of Gods, fanned by the southern breeze, accompanied by songs and the sounding of flutes, lutes, and other instruments.
With the recitations of praise by bards, with the sweet sounds of lutes, with incessant showers of flowers, and likewise with the waving of chowries; || 110 ||
While the Lord of Gods was thus proceeding, the sun set; thousands upon thousands of lamps were ignited.
And by the light of its radiance, the remainder of the path is traversed; likewise, [the journey is completed] for them by descending from their chariots and ascending into the pavilions.
There was a very great crush of people there out of curiosity, wishing to see [the Lord]; one should cause the God to dwell in the charming pavilion named Guṇḍicā. || 113 ||
In that place, graced by a beautiful moonlight and adorned with lovely garlands and chowries, there were pillars made of jewels and its interior was furnished with golden altars.
It was encircled by a rampart wall, radiant with a coating of white plaster, provided with excellent stairs, and adorned with four gates. || 115 ||
There, upon the great altar of the great sacrifice, which encompassed the entire cosmic egg of the three worlds, the manifestation of Maheśa in the form of a wooden body occurred.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Guṇḍicā Pilgrimage," in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: To the south of the Aśvamedhāṅga lake and of Nṛsiṃha, the Blessed One was seated there, as if descending once again. || 1 ||
Then he, possessing a divine form difficult to be perceived even by gods and demons, shone forth with offerings of worship and various kinds of food, both solid and soft.
Having worshipped the Lord of the World, one should gratify Him with songs and dances, with various offerings of flowers, and with fragrant unguents.
One should gratify the Lord of the worlds with incense made from black aloe-wood, with lamps fed by fragrant oil, and with numerous offerings.
In former times, Janārdana himself commanded this boon to the king: "Janārdana shall remain on the bank of that Bindu-tīrtha for seven days. || 5 ||
O Indra among kings, I shall remain on the bank of your sacred ford every year; and while I am present there, all other sacred fords shall likewise abide.

Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite at that sacred ford, which purifies with its flood of holy waters, those who behold [the Lord] stationed in the Guṇḍicā pavilion for seven days; || 7 ||
And may they attain union with me, Rāma, and Subhadrā; then, in that place of great merit which destroys all sins, || 8 ||

Having bathed and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods according to the rules without sloth, [at that place] which yields the singular fruit of all holy fords and is auspicious, bringing delight to Viṣṇu.
Having worshipped and bowed to that Narasiṃha situated at the edge, the man should go to the great altar (mahāvedī) and perform the rites of purification and sipping water (ācamana).
O Brahmins, a man or woman who for seven days worships as before or bows down with devotion is no longer an ordinary human being. || 11 ||
By the command of the Enemy of Mura, one attains union with Viṣṇu; seeing Him during the day is meritorious, while at night it becomes tenfold more so.
Whatever action is performed in the presence of the Lord of the Universe—whether it be very small or even vast—it shall become multiplied by millions upon millions.
O twice-born ones, whoever should give the Tulāpuruṣa gifts and the great gifts (mahādānas), when even one such gift is bestowed, it is as if everything has been given.
All gifts are equal to Mount Meru, and all brahmins are equal to Vyāsa; yet when Kṛṣṇa has gone to Mahāvedī, this yoga is indeed difficult to attain. (15)
The yogas beginning with Ardhodaya described by Skanda do not equal even a sixteenth part of the yoga known as Mahāvedya.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the supreme rite for the ancestors, the fruit of which cannot be obtained on earth even through lifelong śrāddhas performed at Gayā. (17)
Whether they dwell in heaven or in hell, or have entered the wombs of animals, as well as those belonging to the human race—all my fathers and grandfathers—(18).
O excellent sages, listen as I declare to you that ritual procedure which even a hundred world-renowned men desire to have performed by their sons.
Maghā is indeed the lunar mansion of the ancestors; it is supremely pleasing to the Pitṛs. A Śrāddha performed there with joy by sons brings them great satisfaction. (20)
The fifth lunar day is excellent, bringing about prosperity for ancestral rites; if there is a conjunction of both, it is a most meritorious lunar day.
In that place, which consists of all sacred fords (tīrthas) and is in the presence of the Enemy of Mura, the ancestors are uplifted by their sons when a śrāddha is performed.
If one should perform a śrāddha with faith for Nīlakaṇṭha and Nṛsiṃha in a most pure place, during that most rare conjunction, [it will be most meritorious]. (23)
Having delivered a hundred men, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā; the Kutapa period is praiseworthy, when the sun has grown dim. (24)

Or, being unable [to perform the full rite], one who is pure should give gold dedicated to the ancestors; having properly satiated them with sesame seeds, he brings about the highest ancestral satisfaction.
Alternatively, one should feed the Brahmins or give the value of the food; or one may provide a thousand meals to a single person endowed with virtuous qualities.
In this yoga, however, no discrimination between virtues and vices is prescribed; for when that most difficult yoga is attained, all twice-born ones become equal to sages.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the constellation presided over by the Pitṛs, there is the arrival at the Great Altar (Mahāvedī) of the Lord of the World.
If these three should be present at the Indradyumna lake, yoga is said to possess four feet, bestowing inexhaustible merit upon the ancestors.
Having performed a śrāddha here, one does not fail in the rites for the ancestors; listen, O Brahmins, to another matter which I shall tell you by way of this context.
Whoever performs a śrāddha dedicated to the ancestors on the new moon day of Nabhasya, or on any of the four Yugādis, obtains the merit arising from a part of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Indeed, the fruit of this is equal to that of a thousand Gayā-śrāddhas performed with faith; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Charity, fire-offerings, and even the chanting of mantras remove all sins for those seven days during which he dwells here in the pavilion on the dark fortnight.
That which is superior to one thing is more excellent than that; therefore, on the third day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should perform the morning bath.
In the region on the banks of the Indradyumna, in the supreme sacred field of Nṛsiṃha, a man should undertake this vow after making a formal resolve according to the prescribed rules.
This observance called Vanajāgaraṇa increases the pleasure of the Blessed One, pacifies all sins, and bestows the fruit of all religious vows. (36)
For seven days he should observe silence, performing the ritual of bathing three times a day; filled with devotion, he should worship the God at the three junctions of the day within the water-pot.
Then, the observer of the vow should light a lamp with cow-ghee or sesame oil before Hari day and night, and he should protect it with great care.
Day after day he should dwell in silence, and night after night he should remain awake; the observer of the vow should mutter the Bhāgavata mantra during the intervals between his daily duties.
Devoted to fasting, the observer of the vow should pass seven days; then, having risen on the morning of the eighth day, he should perform the consecration ceremony during that day.
Having bathed in that very best of sacred fords and returned home once more, one should place a water-pot in the east within a Sarvatobhadra mandala.
Having invoked Hṛṣīkeśa there, one should worship him with ritual offerings; and to his west, upon an altar consecrated according to the rules.

Having established the sacred fire according to the procedure prescribed for domestic rites, surrounded by Brāhmaṇas, he should perform the fire-ritual with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge.
One should offer oblations into the fire a thousand times, or a hundred times for each [verse]; this is remembered as the procedure for the oblation with that Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī.
Having consumed [the remnants], he should give a cow, clothing, and gold as a sacrificial fee; and at the conclusion, he should feed the Brahmins for the pleasure of the Witness of the Universe.
O twice-born ones, by performing this king of vows according to this procedure, whoever desires whatever objects of desire attains the four aims of life.
Or a woman endowed with faith may perform the great festival of the altar; she too obtains that same fruit as one who performs this supreme vow.
O best of the twice-born, filled with joy, I have told you what kind of fruit accrues to the performer of the pilgrimage and what fruit accrues to the performer of the vow. 48.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the dialogue between the sage Jaimini, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 34 ||
Jaimini said: Hereafter, I shall proclaim the procedure for protecting the chariot from terrible spirits, ghosts, and the like, as well as from dreadful and wondrous portents.
The sages do not obstruct those who follow the path of their own conviction; one should worship daily the gods, beginning with Kṛṣṇa, as they are stationed upon the banner.
With perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), garlands, and unsurpassed offerings, as well as with songs, dances, and the like, and by the presentation of incense and lamps. || 3 ||
One should daily offer a bali-oblation to the guardians of the directions with milk-rice (pāyasa), and one should also present an excellent bali-oblation to the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.

One should indeed guard those chariots, which are fit for mounting, with great effort, so that no man, nor any domestic animal, and especially no bird—none whose dwelling is unseemly—may ascend them. || 5 ||
On the eighth day, having again positioned the chariots facing the south, one should adorn them with garments, garlands, banners, chowries, and other ornaments.
On the ninth day, one should cause the deities to dwell within them; in the morning, this is most prosperous.
This pilgrimage toward the south is very difficult for Viṣṇu to attain; indeed, it must be undertaken with great effort by those endowed with devotion and faith.
Just as the former [festival] was, so too is this one; both are bestowers of liberation. The departure and the entry of the Lord are considered to be a single festival.
Those who know the ancient lore declare this pilgrimage to consist of nine days; this pilgrimage, which has three constituent parts, is considered complete by those who have performed it.
For them, the great festival of the Mahāvedī was perfectly fulfilled with its fruit.
Those who behold the powerful Kṛṣṇa coming from the Guṇḍicā pavilion, seated upon his chariot, facing south, and accompanied by Balabhadra and Bhadrā, become partakers of liberation.
Whatever fruit those who see Rāma and others stationed on their chariot while facing north obtain, such a fruit as that they would obtain by seeing them facing south. (13)
Whoever should see one walking on foot or traveling by chariot facing the south, his birth becomes successful; for him, there is the merit of a horse sacrifice at every step.

With hymns of praise, prostrations, and showers of flowers, with various offerings of dance, and with fans, umbrellas, and chowries, he should attend upon [the deity] before the chariot with many kinds of presents.
Those who behold Hṛṣīkeśa, Subhadrā, and the one armed with the plow (Balarāma) as they arrive at Nīlācala, seated upon their chariot and facing the south; || 16 ||
Those high-souled ones who go to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, Hari—the wish-fulfilling tree for men that grants liberation merely by being seen—go there. (17)
They saw Janārdana wandering on his chariot along the bank of the Sindhu river, casting compassionate glances at the men who stood bowed before him.
On the Blue Mountain (Nīlabhūdhar), they saw Hari proceeding toward the south, heading for the palace that is a treasury of all holy places and a wish-fulfilling tree for all acts of charity.
Those men who praise, bow down, and have faith shall certainly not return here again, but remain fixed in the world of Brahmā.
O sages, this great festival of Mahāvedī has been described to you; by the mere glorification of it, a man becomes pure.
That man who, having risen early in the morning, constantly recites this or even hears it with a focused mind, shall go to the world of Śakra.
Or, having placed an image of Hari in a chariot, whatever man performs this procession with a disposition of faith and devotion, [attains the supreme goal]. || 23 ||
He too, by the grace of Viṣṇu, having obtained the fruit born of the Guṇḍicā festival, goes to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha; there is no doubt about this.
Behold, O Brahmins, that whatever wealth or devotion accompanied by faith one possesses, to that same extent this great pilgrimage belongs to whoever desires to perform it. (25)
This is the supreme purifier, a secret proclaimed by the Creator; having performed it or even merely seen it, a man does not come to grief.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: Hereafter I shall describe the supreme festival of the Lord’s sleep; taking the full moon of Āṣāḍha as the starting point, Hari’s sleep occurs when the sun is in Cancer.
O twice-born ones, the four months of the rainy season until the full moon of Kārttika is the most meritorious time for the worship of Hari.
Whatever fruit is said to result from residing for many ages in Kāśī while established in restraints and vows, one should know that the same fruit is obtained at the sacred site of Śrī Puruṣottama.
By spending even a single day of the Cāturmāsya period in the presence of Hari, one attains the merit of those who dwell there for all four months of the rainy season.
In this field of merit, in the presence of the Lord of the World, with a pure inner self, one obtains the manifest fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Having bathed in the holy waters of the Indus and beheld Śrī Puruṣottama, one who observes the Cāturmāsya vow does not grieve from any cause whatsoever.
Dwelling during the four months of the rainy season in the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama and having a direct vision of the Lord—these two are the means to liberation.
Therefore, having completely renounced all rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis, a person should strive to dwell in the meritorious field of Śrī Puruṣottama.
During the four months of the rainy season, the Lord, the Teacher of the World, sleeps upon the couch of the serpent's coils and does not maintain his presence in all the sacred fields.

Here the Blessed Lord dwells in person, just as he does in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha; throughout all twelve months, he remains here in embodied form, bestowing liberation when beheld with the eyes, especially during the Cāturmāsya period.
Indeed, the fruit that one obtains by beholding Viṣṇu day after day while residing for eight months is obtained from a single day of the Cāturmāsya.

By residing for four months in the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama, the Lord bestows upon one the fruit arising from residing in all sacred fields, day by day, through dwelling in that field for a year.
Even one who is addicted to every sin, fallen from all proper conduct, and excluded from all dharma may dwell in Puruṣottama.
If a man who has committed sins performs even one Cāturmāsya vow, he abandons all his sins and becomes stainless both internally and externally.
By the grace of Narasiṃha, one shall go to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha. || 15 ||
Therefore, a person should dwell at Puruṣottama during the four months of the rainy season, which are sanctified by Viṣṇu’s own sleep, with all one's being.
Whether he performs other [rites] or does not perform them, he attains the fulfillment of his birth. || 17 ||
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should perform the great festival of the Lord's sleep; there, one should construct a pavilion and an excellent chamber for the bed.
In front of the deity, having spread out a bed upon a jeweled couch, provided with a pillow and a soft Chinese upper coverlet; (19)
It was auspicious, strewn with camphor dust, graced by the light of a beautiful moon, enclosed on all sides, free from gaps, and sprinkled with sandalwood paste. || 20 ||

Having constructed a single sleeping chamber that was level, smooth, pleasant, and adorned with various designs, he performed three meditative postures (pratimās) at midnight through the gateway of the virtuous.
One should fashion [the vessel] out of gold, silver, brass, or stone, according to one's faith; each subsequent material is more highly recommended than the preceding one.
Having placed those [offerings] exactly as they are at the feet of the three deities, one should worship the gods and cast the remnants upon them.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should contemplate their oneness with Kṛṣṇa and the others: "Come, come, O Blessed Lord, God, the sole life of all the worlds! (24)
"May the four months for the sake of sleep [be granted] for the increase of all auspiciousness"—having thus prayed to the lords of the gods, he took from their bodies those three garlands.

Having placed [the image] upon the substitute images (pratyarcās), one should lead it to the door of the bedchamber with auspicious hymns and songs of praise, and let it rest there for three ghaṭikās.

One should bathe them individually with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) in quantities exceeding one hundred palas each, and anoint them with fragrant sandalwood paste, along with garments, ornaments, and other such items.

Having worshipped according to the rule, one should recite the mantra with palms joined in reverence: "O you who are worshipful to the world, O Lord of the world, O you whose supreme aim is the protection of the world! (28)
O Lord, for the welfare of the worlds, having slept during the four months of the rainy season, you pacified all calamities while being honored by Śakra.
"Come, come to the bedchamber; sleep here at ease, O Lord!"—having thus entreated the Lord of Gods, one should lay down Puruṣottama.
One should firmly secure the door of Viṣṇu’s bedchamber; having put the Lord of the World to sleep, one obtains supreme happiness. || 31 ||
While Janārdana is asleep during the four months of the rainy season, one should indeed pass those four months with various vows and observances.
A devoted man shall certainly dwell in the world of Viṣṇu for an eon; O sages, listen as I speak of the rules and vows.
A devoted man should avoid beds such as couches and low stools; he should not approach his wife outside the fertile period, nor should he consume honey or rice cooked with meat for an entire month.
One should not eat paṭola, radish, or eggplant; one should avoid from afar that which is unfit for consumption, such as lentils and white mustard. (35)
One should abandon black gram, horse-gram, and fast-growing grains; and from the month of Śrāvaṇa onwards, one should successively avoid vegetables, curd, milk, and beans.

Having abandoned leather sandals that protect the feet from the king (the sun), one should not wear them; if one should spend the four months of the rainy season without observing a vow, one should become a practitioner of a vow during the month of Kārttika for the sake of pacifying that sin.
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, to Hari, to Keśava; salutations again and again. Salutations be to Nārasiṃha, to Viṣṇu, the conqueror of sin.
One should employ it in the evening, at dawn, at midday, and at the conclusion of ritual activities. || 39 ||
All his terrible sins accumulated over many births are indeed consumed by it, just as fire burns a heap of cotton.

Whether eating once a day, eating at restricted intervals, or subsisting on the remains of Viṣṇu’s offerings—whoever does so from the full moon of Āṣāḍha until the full moon of Kārtika, or even eats only at night—their reward in heaven is but meager. (41)
One should avoid oil massage, sleeping during the day, and speaking falsehoods on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, or at the time of the sun's entry into Cancer.
Or, on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, a person observing the vow should devoutly undertake the religious restriction after worshipping Madhusūdana, the God who removes all sins.
Having resolved upon the vows, worship, recitation, and so forth in its presence, the practitioner, with palms joined in reverence, should pray to Supreme Bliss.
O Lord, by Your grace the Cāturmāsya vow has been undertaken; O Keśava, through Your favor may it reach fulfillment without obstacle. (45)
O Adhokṣaja, if my departure to the next world should occur while this vow is incomplete, may it become complete through your grace.
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods, the observer of the vow, with his mind dedicated to Viṣṇu, should pass the four months while remaining established in the previously mentioned observances.
At the end of every month, one should perform the breaking of the fast for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa.
Having worshipped the Lord of the Universe, one should feed the Brahmins with sweet foods; however, if one is incapable, one may complete this excellent vow on the full moon day of Kārttika.

Having worshipped the Lord of the World within that [fire], one should then offer libations; then, with devotion to Viṣṇu, one should honor the foremost of the twice-born with sweet milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should indeed give gold and clothing according to one's ability; however, if one is incapable, one should perform the previously mentioned vow during the month of Kārttika.
And likewise, the various vows of Viṣṇu, such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
He who, having drunk milk or again subsisted on a diet of vegetables, enjoys abundant pleasures here and thereafter attains supreme Nirvāṇa.
If one should be unable even for that, then for the pleasure of the God of gods, the observer of the vow should subsist on forest fare during the excellent Bhīṣmapañcaka.

This vow has been fully described as that which brings pleasure to the Blessed One; it pacifies all sins and grants access to the world of Viṣṇu. It bestows wealth, fame, and long life, and accomplishes all desires. (55)
O sages, this secret has been told to you; now hear another. There are these vows and many other vows as well.
Know for certain that for those devoid of devotion to the Blessed One, the fruit of great sacrifices and the supreme fruit of sacred pilgrimage sites are indeed rendered fruitless. (57)
Whatever fruit belongs to gifts, to austerities, and to those actions characterized by goodness (sattva), one enjoys that entire fruit through singular devotion to Viṣṇu.
Those high-souled ones who behold this supreme festival of the lying-in do not sleep again in a mother’s womb, and they cause the festival to be celebrated.
Having made a vow for this observance at the conclusion of the festival in his presence, and having completed it to its full extent, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: Hereafter I shall describe the most excellent Dakṣiṇāyana; those twenty *kalās* which are considered to exist in the time prior to the *saṃkrānti*.
O twice-born ones, this is the auspicious time for the performance of meritorious deeds; on that occasion, one should bathe the Lord with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) as was done at his birth.
One should smear her entire body with aguru, camphor, and sandalwood, and adorn her with fragrant garlands, ornaments, beautiful garments, and lamps.
One should worship the Supreme Lord with various offerings of food; one should place a tall camphor-flame near the face of Hari.

Then she should perform the lustration ceremony with sprouts of dūrvā grass, unbroken grains of rice, and the waving of lights; accompanied by auspicious songs, dances, and the like, the woman should utter the cry of "hulu-hula."
Whoever should behold Puruṣottama when he has been worshipped or is being worshipped, Janārdana shall bestow upon him merit a hundred times greater than that of the worship itself.
During that southern solstice, those who worship the Lord of Śrī, having abandoned all sins, go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Whether the pilgrimage is very short or very long, every journey to Hari bestows liberation; for on each and every day, the Lord, when seen, certainly grants liberation.
O Brahmins, these pilgrimages have been described by the compassionate Viṣṇu for the sake of inspiring faith in the foolish; they indeed remove the sins of the wicked.
Those lowest of men who believe that merit is produced by physical exertion—here, for the Lord of Lakṣmī’s meal, the kitchen must be prepared. (10)
Having established the Vaiṣṇava fire and offered the excellent sacrificial oblation (caru), one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite for the purpose of preparing food for the Blessed Lord.
Being pure, one should offer oblations into the pure fire for Brahmā, the Lord of the Site, the Lord of Creatures, as well as for Viṣṇu, the Maker of the Universe.
The preceptor appointed by the king, devoted to the performance of rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, [should worship] Dvārapāla and Pracaṇḍa, and Kṣetrapāla in the northeast.
And in the south, one should likewise offer to Virūpa, the lord of birds, and to Durgā and Sarasvatī in the southwest.
The bali offering is prescribed for Mahālakṣmī and Maheṃdra in the eastern direction; likewise, it is for Viṣṇu’s attendants and for the Lord of Beasts (Paśupati).
One should offer the bali-oblation to Nārada in the north, then to Agni in the southwest, and to the Witness of the Universe in the northwest.
Then, for the ritual offering (balikarma), one should offer water at the beginning and the end to each of the five forms of the breaths and to the Creator of the Universe in the center.
Having offered the oblation (bali) into that fire, one should prepare the excellent cooked offering (caru) for the purpose of worshipping the Blessed One during the three junctions of the day.

O King, in this world, a king belonging to the three higher castes should not offer as oblations items such as food and edibles that have been prepared for the *caru* sacrifice unless they are properly consecrated with fire.
Whether they be noble and pure, or Śūdras and those who serve other castes—this worldly conduct itself certainly ripens prosperity for them all. (20)
The embodied Nārāyaṇa constantly eats that which has been cooked by her; for that food offering is indeed nectar, which destroys sins through its placement upon the head.
By eating it, there is the destruction of great evils such as the drinking of intoxicants; by smelling it, mental sin is destroyed; and likewise, by seeing it, the sin born of sight is destroyed.

By tasting it, one removes the sin committed through eating and that which arises from hearing; by touching it, one likewise removes the sin not committed through eating and that born of false speech. (23)
By anointing the body with it, one will surely burn away physical sin; of this there is no doubt.

For he who employs that which has been offered to Hari—the great purifier—in rites for the ancestors and the gods, his ancestors and the deities are satisfied; they likewise go to the realm of Madhusūdana.
"O twice-born ones, there exists no object more pure than this for offerings to the gods and ancestors; having assumed human form, the dwellers of heaven consume it. (26)
In that regard, there was great pride on the part of the Discus-wielding God of gods; O Great King, in former times during the Tretā Yuga, there was a great king named Śveta.
Even while established in his vows, he practiced great devotion toward Puruṣottama, according to the extent of the offerings prepared by Indradyumna.
With joy, he daily prepared various kinds of foods and delicacies with the six flavors, well-prepared for the Lord of Śrī.
And various garlands, fragrant ointments, and many divine songs, instrumental music, and dances. || 30 ||
On various occasions, there were many royal services performed for Hari, involving great expenditure of wealth and effort, which manifested his state of devotion. (31)
Various kinds of diverse enjoyments, as described in the various Vaiṣṇava scriptures, were provided by that king, who was like a sun to the lotuses of the learned.
At the time of morning worship, he went to see Hari; on a certain day, the king beheld Him being worshipped.
Having bowed down to the God of gods with joyful palms joined in reverence, that best of kings stood near the gate of the palace.
Having personally seen the unsurpassed offerings he had prepared and the thousands of gifts arranged before Hari, [he rejoiced].
Supported by meditation, he reflected in his mind: "Will Hari perhaps accept the enjoyments fashioned by men?"
He whom even the gods are unable to worship with divine offerings during the ritual of adoration, those of firm vows worship him with mental oblations.
"A sacrifice performed with a corrupted heart certainly brings no joy to Him. Reflecting thus, the king [beheld] the Lord seated upon a divine throne.
He was enjoying a meal rich in food and drink, served with great splendor, adorned with divine garlands and celestial fragrant silken garments. (39)
Filling the abode of the gods with the tinkling of her priceless jeweled anklets, she respectfully offered various flavors using a golden ladle.
Seeing him surrounded by those who resembled the Blessed One while partaking of the meal, he considered himself to have achieved his purpose, marveling at that wonder.
With his eyes opened, he beheld once again what he had seen before; from that time forth, this king attained supreme bliss.
Having offered his food and undertaken his vow, he performed very great penance for the destruction of untimely death and for the liberation from death within his own kingdom.
Constantly chanting the king of mantras, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree for those who take refuge in it, he beheld Nṛhari, the remover of sins, at the end of a hundred years.
Seated upon a lotus in a yogic posture, with Śrī resting upon his left side, his entire body adorned with divine ornaments, and his form as pure as crystal.

Being praised by the thirty gods and the Siddhas and Muktas, he—his face radiant with a smile—fell to the surface of the earth, bewildered by both wonder and fear, speaking with a voice faltering with joy: "Be gracious, O Lord! (46)
Seeing him emaciated by asceticism and bowing before him, that lion among men, who is affectionate toward his devotees, desired to speak to the stainless lord of the earth.

The Blessed Lord said: "Arise, my child! Know that I, the Lord, am pleased with your devotion. Since I am pleased, there is no boon that cannot be obtained; therefore, let a boon be requested by you."
Having heard these words of the Blessed One, the king then rose up; with palms joined in reverence and bowing low, he spoke with devotion to Janārdana.
Śveta said: O Lord, if your grace has been bestowed upon me, which is so very difficult to obtain, then, having attained your own form (sārūpya), I shall remain in your presence.
"As long as I remain in the state of kingship, let no person in my kingdom ever die prematurely; if they die at the appointed time, may they attain liberation. (51)
Having heard that, the Blessed One spoke to the supreme Śvetarāja.
"O Śveta, may your desire be fulfilled; stay at my right side, and after enjoying your own highly prosperous kingdom for a thousand years," || 53 ||
"By partaking of my remains (nirmālya), the accumulation of your sins will be entirely exhausted; with your inner self rendered perfectly pure, you shall attain union (sāyujya) with me. || 54 ||
Between the Vaṭa and the Sāgara, in this most difficult-to-attain place of liberation, [is the site] of my first incarnation as Viṣṇu in the form of a fish.
Dwell here indeed in person, for you possess a body as pure as crystal; you shall attain renown in the world of mortals by the name Śvetamādhava.
Those humans, or even animals or insects, who shall give up their lives in the space between you two will certainly attain liberation.
Where even the immortals desire death, how much more so mortal men? Such is that lake in your northern direction which destroys all sins.
Having bathed there and sipped water on its southern bank, one who has been purified by the gaze of both [parents] is liberated upon giving up his life-breaths.
This field is equal on all sides, bestowing liberation wherever one may be; it is declared to be the foremost place for those of deluded mind to place their trust.
But those people in your kingdom who eat my remains (nirmālya), their death shall never occur prematurely.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: O Brahmins, having thus granted that boon to Śvetarāja in former times, Hari, who was stationed within the temple, vanished from sight.
She who is the glory of all the worlds, the cause of their creation, maintenance, and destruction, the incomparable power of Viṣṇu, is the one who performs the serving of food.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa eats well-cooked food that is like nectar; indeed, partaking of His remains causes the destruction of all sins.
There is no merit on the surface of the earth equal to that; yet, it does not become defiled by contact with those who perform sinful actions.

By virtue of being in the presence of Padmā, all of them are considered pure; for even the remains of offerings (nirmālya) that have reached the abode of Viṣṇu are so regarded, even by those who are fallen and the like.
If they touch it, it does not become defiled; as Viṣṇu is, so too is that [place]. This applies to those observing vows, widows, and all those belonging to the various castes and stages of life.
By consuming that, those initiated for sacrifice and maintainers of the sacred fire are purified—whether they be poor or wretched, householders or even lords.
Whether they be natives of their own country or foreigners, all who have gathered there should not harbor pride regarding the consumption of the remnants of Viṣṇu's offerings.
Whether out of devotion, greed, curiosity, or for the sake of appeasing hunger, that which is eaten to the full extent of one's capacity indeed purifies one from all sins.
It pacifies all diseases, increases sons and grandsons, removes poverty, and is the most excellent, auspicious bestower of knowledge, longevity, and prosperity. || 10 ||
Therein lies the great partiality of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor; those fools who consider themselves wise revile that nectar.
Himself wielding the rod of punishment over them, he does not tolerate offenders; for those upon whom that rod falls here, their downfall is indeed certain.

Brahmā, Nārada, Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, as well as Sanatkumāra, Atri, Bharadvāja, and Kaśyapa. || 71 ||
Durvāsas, Agastya, and Mahādeva after him—these are indeed renowned Vaiṣṇavas, for they are forms of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt. (72)

By honoring these Brahmins, Viṣṇu is pleased at that very moment; having performed the consumption of the remnants at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should give the teacher’s sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
With devotion, for the pleasure of Vāsudeva, one should feed the best of the twice-born, offering a cow adorned with gold, as well as clothing and grain.
Then one should offer Dāmodara together with all the ritual services.

Oṃ! O Dāmodara, Lord of the World! Indeed, the entire universe is composed of you; all this has you as its support. You are Dharma, the creator of all beings. By your grace, may the vow I have performed be perfectly fulfilled for me. (76)
Dāmodara is the giver and the recipient, O bull-bannered one; the Lord of the World is being given away—may the Teacher of the Universe be pleased with me.
Reciting this mantra, one should give the "best of gods" (the image) to the preceptor; having completed [the rite], one should worship with devotion, praise him, and seek his favor. (78)
When the teacher is fully satisfied, Mādhava becomes satisfied; therefore, one should indeed give various articles to the Brahmins.
Then, having duly established this Cāturmāsya vow according to the injunctions, one should indeed eat together with one's beloved, learned, and own kinsmen.
Endowed with the fruits as described, one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu; there is no vow superior to this among the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas. (81)
O twice-born ones, there is no other vow like it that brings such pleasure to Viṣṇu, by the mere performance of which a man becomes one who has accomplished all his duties.
Not even by thousands of sesame vessels, nor by tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of cows, nor even by a hundred black antelope skins and ten thousand maidens [is such merit attained]. (83)
The fruit that one obtains by giving a gift after performing this supreme vow is likewise the fruit of bathing in three and a half crores of sacred fords.
O Brahmins, a man obtains whatever fruit he desires.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Cāturmāsya Vow," in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 39 ||

Jaimini said: Having performed the Prāvaraṇa festival on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, and having beheld [the deity] with devotion, a person shall attain the world of Viṣṇu. || 1 ||
I shall now describe its procedure; listen, O sages! On the fifth night, the knower of the ritual should perform the preliminary consecration of the garment.
In the pavilion before the deity, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus; one should worship the guardians of the directions in their respective quarters, as well as Kṣetrapāla and Gaṇādhipa.
One should worship Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa outside in the four directions; having placed the vessel in the center, one should sprinkle it with water from a cloth.
With the mantra beginning "dyutānastva," one should cover twenty-one types of garments that have been well-perfumed with incense.
In the midst of that, one should place the mantra while reciting the Vaiṣṇava mantra, having carefully covered it with another cloth.
Having touched [the object], one should recite this mantra while remembering Puruṣottama: "He who is the coverer of the worlds by his splendor, Viṣṇu, the imperishable. (7)
Because he dwells within it, you shall have the nature of clothing; O Lord of the World, dwell in the dwelling [of this garment]. And Indraghoṣa should provide protection for him on all sides.
One should worship with perfumes and flowers, and then worship the deity; one should apply all ointments and pass the night with dance and song.
Then, at the time of sunrise, near the morning twilight, he should again worship the God with great concentration, just as before.
Then, O twice-born ones, one should bring out that honored collection of garments, rich with cotton, silk, and linen, and likewise covered.
With umbrellas, banners, and flags, with the waving of chowries, as well as with songs, instrumental music, dances, and the scattering of flowers.

Having circumambulated the temple three times, he should then cause the deity to be circumambulated three times; then, having uncovered that which was covered, he should consecrate it with the rites of inspection and so forth.
O twice-born ones, one should wrap the gods with seven garments each, covering all their limbs except for the face, using cloths suitable for warding off the cold.
Then, having offered betel-leaf and likewise a camphor-wick, and having worshipped with dūrvā grass and unbroken grains (akṣata), one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the Lord.
Those who, at the arrival of winter, clothe the Man-Lion with fine garments, or those who behold Him thus clothed—for them there is no covering of delusion.
They never encounter the fear arising from the winds of the dualities or from cold, because of this festival of the upper garment of Viṣṇu, the God of gods. || 17 ||
Those who behold [the deity] with devotion shall indeed attain all desires; one should cause gifts to be bestowed upon Brahmins, dedicating them to the Blessed One.

One should respectfully offer a garment for protection against the cold to one's gurus, to other deities, and likewise to the poor and the helpless, with supreme joy; the Blessed One, being pleased, grants him an unsurpassed boon. (19)

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Prāvaraṇa Festival," in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Jaimini said: I shall describe the festival of the Puṣya-bath as it was told by Brahmā in the past; when the full moon day (paurṇamāsī) occurs in conjunction with the Puṣya asterism, [that is the time]. || 1 ||
Likewise, in the month of Pauṣa, one should perform the festival of Hari’s Puṣya-bath; on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), one should perform the rite of sowing seeds (Aṅkurārpaṇa) in the northeast.
Then, one should perform [worship] daily before the image in the temple of Hari, and every night one should offer an oblation accompanied by dance, song, and offerings.
On the night of the fourteenth day, however, there is the consecration (adhivāsana) of eighty-one auspicious jars made of gold.
One should place twenty-one vessels filled with cow's ghee and have a Sarvatobhadra mandala prepared in front of Hari.
In the center of that, one should place a large, auspicious mirror as a support; at night, one should perform a vigil with elaborate songs, dances, and other festivities.
O twice-born ones, at dawn he should perform the fire-rite dedicated to that deity, using fuel-sticks of the Palāśa tree, as well as sacrificial porridge and clarified butter.
One should offer one thousand oblations each to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva with their respective mantras, and at the conclusion of that, to Puruṣottama.
One should worship the reflection in the mirror with those ritual offerings; thereafter, one should consecrate those jars with the Puruṣasūkta.
With that very unbroken stream, one should bathe Puruṣottama; thereafter, one should bathe the gods with the Pāvamānīya hymns and the Śrīsūkta.
Thereafter, one should bathe [the deity] with jars of clarified butter while reciting the Gāyatrī; then, one should worship with fragrant water using the Vaiṣṇavī mantra and the Śrīsūkta.
Then, with a thousandfold stream, one should discard the *nirmālya* from the God; one should then anoint the body of the God with fragrances and sandalwood paste upon His form.
One should arrange the ornaments according to their proper places and for the sake of beauty; immediately thereafter, one should adorn [the image] with fragrant flowers and garlands.
One should place the eight weapons of the Lord, beginning with the discus, in front; then, having raised a jeweled parasol, one should worship Puruṣottama.
Furthermore, O brahmins, he was endowed with prosperity and provided with abundant offerings, while conch shells were being blown, emitting smooth and deep sounds.
While the beautiful courtesans were busily waving chowries, and amidst the auspicious songs, dances, and the recitations of praises by the bards; (16)
While the twice-born repeatedly uttered cries of "Victory!", he worshipped Keśava with three handfuls of dūrvā grass and unbroken rice grains.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the Lord of the World with lamps containing ghee and cloth-wicks, using extremely pure golden vessels and wicks infused with camphor.
One should very slowly present to each of them, near their mouth, beautifully prepared and lovely betel-leaf placed in a golden vessel.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the teacher and likewise honor the Brāhmaṇas.
Those who, filled with joy, behold the meritorious festival of the Puṣya-bath, shall have all their desires fulfilled and go indeed to the abode of Viṣṇu.
One fallen from his kingdom shall regain his kingdom and obtain universal sovereignty; one who is childless, or whose children have died, shall obtain a long-lived son.
The auspicious Puṣya-bath, which destroys poverty and bestows spiritual luster, has been described to you; now listen to [the ritual for] the northern transit of the sun.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Puṣya Consecration," in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: O best of the twice-born, when the sun enters the zodiac sign of Capricorn, desiring to go toward the northern quarter, that is the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa).
And for half of its transit, up until twenty *kalās* have passed, it is the most meritorious time, beloved by the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born. || 2 ||
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite in the waters of the Ṛtārtha-rāja, a person should worship Nārāyaṇa and bow down to the Kalpavṛkṣa tree.
Having entered the temple and performed three circumambulations of it, he worshipped the Lord Śrī Puruṣottama with the King of Mantras.
Likewise, one should worship Bala and Subhadrā with their own respective mantras; having beheld the Lord during the northern course of the sun, one is liberated from the bondage of the body.
I shall describe its procedure, a great purifier; listen! On the day preceding the transit (saṃkrānti), one should take fresh, well-ground śāli rice.

And having placed it in the eastern part of the palace, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), wrapping it in a new cloth and [adorning it] with dūrvā grass, mustard seeds, and flowers.
Having worshipped him, one should indeed recite the mantra: "May Kṛṣṇa protect you. Then, when that very night of the Lord of the World has passed— || 8 ||

Having brought the image back into the presence [of the main deity], one should contemplate it with a mind focused on their identity; then, being composed, one should worship it with the remaining offerings.
Then, one should place the remains of offerings, garments, and garlands upon her; thereafter, with great magnificence, one should circumambulate that image three times before the gods.
Having placed the Lord Trivikrama—the pervader who strides across the three worlds—upon a palanquin, one should bring him to the gate of the palace by means of three steps.
One should cause that temple to revolve, imitating that divine play; at the end of three [revolutions], it should again be slowly and steadily placed upon the pedestal with great prosperity.
In the midst of the darkness obstructed by hundreds of lamps, with umbrellas, banners, and flags, and with dances, instrumental music, and songs; || 13 ||
For those great-souled ones whose sins have been utterly destroyed by the sight of him, there is no mark upon their bodies, nor does the wandering through the nine limbs of the body occur thereafter.
Those who then follow him as he proceeds on that great journey to Trivikrama obtain, indeed, the fruit of the horse-sacrifice at every step.
O twice-born ones, by seeing the first circumambulation one is liberated from the five great sins; by the second circumambulation one would be freed from the minor defilements.
Having seen the third circumambulation, one is certainly purified from the sins that cause loss of caste; thereafter, one is released from the sins of minor offenses (upapātaka). || 17 ||
Again at dawn, one should smear the Lord of Gods with fragrant sandalwood paste, and having adorned him according to the prescribed rite with garments, ornaments, and garlands; (18)

One should worship him with ritual offerings according to one's capacity and prosperity; having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the Lord of Gods, [one should offer] consecrated grains of rice.
In vessels made of gold, [he placed offerings] mixed with curd, sugar-candy, and ghee, along with pieces of coconut and leaves of ginger.

Having circumambulated the temple three times, he should lead [the offerings] into the presence of the deity; he should place them in front in rows, accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
O Lord of the world, you are the life of all beings and their progenitor; indeed, these rice plants consist of your essence and have been produced by you alone, O Lord.
O Supreme Lord, you who have assumed a suitable form for the sake of favoring the world, please accept these offerings made out of affection for you. (23)
When you are pleased, the entire world shall prosper through these: the utterances of Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭ for the dwellers of heaven.

They shall become sources of nourishment, and by them alone shall the world be nourished. O Lord of the World, protect the entire universe, including all that is mobile and immobile, for it is composed of you. 25.
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods, one should offer a cluster of rice stalks, as well as foods and edibles made from that same [rice], and fragrant jars of curd.
One should offer food mixed with pieces of camphor and powdered black pepper, and worship the Brahmins with devotion as they stand before the God of gods.
One should devoutly offer them rice and other grains with the thought that they are the Lord himself. O brahmins, in a former kalpa, Kaśyapa performed this great festival.
Having fashioned that creation, he performed it for the pleasure of the Blessed One; and those who behold this festival created by Kaśyapa, || 29 ||
Those twice-born ones, always fulfilled by all their desires, do not grieve; having dwelt together with the gods, they shall attain liberation at the end of the kalpa.
O sages, one should perform the consecration of the kitchen and the consecration of the fire here as well, and perform the Vaiśvadeva rite day after day.
In the fire consecrated by the rite of installation, the goddess Ramā, possessing a divine form yet remaining concealed, daily prepares the cooked food for the enjoyment of the Blessed One.
