In this most meritorious festival of the Supreme Self, acts such as the gift of one's weight in gold (tulāpuruṣadāna) and others shall yield millions upon millions of times their merit.
Bathing, giving gifts, austerity, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors—all these indeed attain imperishability during a festival and during the northern course of the sun.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Transit of the Sun into Capricorn," in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: In the month of Phālguna, one should perform the excellent festival of the swing (dolārohaṇa), wherein Govinda sports indeed for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds.
One should have a secondary image (pratyarcā) made of the God of gods, known by the name Govinda; one should erect it in front of the temple on a lofty pedestal consisting of sixteen pillars.
A square pavilion with four doors, provided with an altar, beautiful with moon-like canopies, and adorned with garlands, chowries, and banners. || 3 ||
On the altar, one should prepare an auspicious seat made of *śrīparṇī* wood; then one should perform the *phalgūtsava* festival for five days or three days.
On the fourteenth day of the month of Phālguna, at the beginning of the night, O Brahmins, one should perform the fire festival to the east of the swing-pavilion.
That which is blessed by Govinda is proclaimed as the constituent part of the pilgrimage; having performed the selection of the preceptor, one should produce fire by means of friction.
Having prepared the ground according to the rules and having caused a very high and perfectly level heap of grass to be made, one should then cast the fire there.

Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the oblation according to the Kūṣmāṇḍa ritual; then, having worshipped Govinda, one should cause that Lord to be circumambulated.
One should protect that fire with great effort until the pilgrimage is completed; then, on the morning watch of the fourteenth day, [one should worship] the auspicious image of Govinda.
Having perfumed it, one should worship Puruṣottama in front of Hari; with the remnants of the ritual offerings, one should also worship the secondary image (pratyarcā).
Then, O best of the twice-born, having removed his garment and garland, the practitioner of mantra should place them upon the image while contemplating the supreme light.
Then that image truly becomes Puruṣottama himself; one should indeed carry it to the pavilion for the bath by means of a jeweled palanquin.
There, amidst the sounds of various musical instruments preceded by the blare of conchs, with shouts of victory, hymns of praise, and showers of flowers; (13)
Then one should celebrate a great festival with umbrellas, banners, flags, chowries, fans, and lamps arranged without any gaps.
Then the gods, led by the Grandfather (Brahmā), arrive together with hosts of sages to witness the great festival of Govinda.

Having consecrated [the image] upon the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana), one should worship it with ritual offerings; then, one should perform its ceremonial bath according to the procedure for the great ablution (mahāsnāna).

With the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), or with all of them together, or with any one of them, at the conclusion of the bath, one should perform the consecration with scented water while reciting the Śrīsūkta.

Having sprinkled [the deity] with water, one should adorn the God with garments, ornaments, and garlands; then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and completed the worship, one should circumambulate the temple.

Then, one should lead the deity seven times to the swing-pavilion on a well-prepared road adorned with banners, arches, and other ornaments; thereafter, one should cause him to circumambulate that pavilion seven times from below.
Furthermore, there are seven [circumambulations] in the upper region, and indeed seven on the pillar-altar; at the conclusion of the procession, one should circumambulate twenty-one times.
This sport of the Blessed One was proclaimed by the mouth of the Grandfather (Brahmā), and it was indeed previously performed by the royal sage Indradyumna.
Within the delightful interior of Vṛndāvana, which was fashioned by trees bending low with fruits and flowers and resounding with the humming of intoxicated bees; (22)
Sweet with the warbling of cuckoos, crowded with flocks of various birds, and perfumed by various excellent incenses arranged in manifold splendors. (23)
In the midst of the quarters, made fragrant by the scent of groves of blossoming ketakī flowers, it was adorned with mallikā, aśoka, punnāga, and campaka trees.
In a pavilion constructed within that forest, featuring beautiful archways, adorned with garlands, garments, and chowries, and graced with splendor; || 25 ||
One should seat the Lord in the midst of a jeweled palanquin, adorned with a crown of excellent gems and a chest beautified by a necklace of pearls.
His ears were illuminated by earrings fashioned from priceless gems; he was adorned with divine ornaments, beautiful and placed in their proper positions according to what was most graceful.
He was seated in the center of a full-blown lotus, accompanied by Śrī, the mother of the universe.
Holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, wearing a garland of forest flowers, he was most gracious, possessed of a beautiful nose, and radiant with a broad chest.
He was praised with shouts of "Victory! by the gods, Brahmā and others, standing in the sky before him with their heads bowed and palms joined in devotion.
By Gandharvas and Apsarases, by Kinnaras, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas, and by the celestial singers headed by Hāhā and Hūhū, [he was honored] with great haste. || 31 ||
He was being joyfully honored by thousands of lotus-eyes belonging to those performing dance, song, and instrumental music, who vied with one another for precedence.
Scattering the powder produced from fragrant sandalwood in all directions, one should then seat Govinda and worship him with ritual offerings.
He was situated in the midst of a multitude of cowherd women at the foot of a kadamba tree, sporting within the forest with amorous gestures, laughter, and playful charms.
Having meditated upon the Lord of the Universe, who is being carried on a swing by the playful movements of the cowherd girls and cowherds, one should scatter fragrant powders.
With camphor, red, yellow, and white [substances] on all sides in every direction, with divine garments, divine garlands, divine perfumes, and excellent incenses; || 36 ||
Honored with the waving of chowries, songs, and hymns of praise, one should slowly and gently rock the deity seated upon the swing seven times.
At that time, for those who behold Kṛṣṇa, there is no doubt regarding their liberation; the destruction of the five great sins, such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, shall occur. (38)
In this manner, one should rock the Lord three times; he is the remover of all sins, the bestower of grace upon men through devotion, and the sole cause of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (39)
His playful activity, whether artificial or innate, destroys the multitude of sins and brings about the cessation of root-ignorance.
Beholding it for a second time, one removes minor sins such as the killing of a cow; beholding it for a third time, one removes all sins without exception—of this there is no doubt. (41)
Having seen the Lord thus swaying, one is liberated from all sins; one is released from afflictions arising from the self, from other beings, and from the divine powers.
Having caused this pilgrimage to be performed, one becomes a sovereign wheel-turning monarch; a Brāhmaṇa, moreover, will certainly be born as a knower of the four Vedas and possessed of wisdom. (43)

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Ascending of the Swing," in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: In this regard, I shall describe to you the supreme annual vow (vrata), which begins on the first day of the year, specifically on the full moon day of Phālguna.
One should worship month by month those twelve very forms of Hari, the beginningless God, which are renowned by names such as Viṣṇu and others.
One should worship each one of these forms daily throughout all twelve months with flowers and likewise with twelve fruits.
Aśoka, Mallikā, Pāṭala, Kadambaka, Karavīra, Jātī flower, Mālatī, and Śatapatraka. || 4 ||
One should joyfully offer these flowers to Hari in their proper sequence: the blue lotus, the vāsantī, the kunda, and likewise the punnāga.
The pomegranate, the coconut, the mango, and likewise the jackfruit; the date, the "king of grasses" (sugarcane), and likewise the Prācīnāmalaka.
One should indeed offer these fruits in succession: the *śrīphala*, the *nāgaraṅga*, the *kramuka*, the *karamaṅgaka*, and the *jātīphala*.
Having offered foods to be chewed, swallowed, sucked, and licked, as well as sweet items, and having provided seats and other services, he praised the Teacher of the World.
O all-pervading Lord of the world, O Master of the past, the future, and the present; protect me, O lotus-eyed Viṣṇu, from the ocean of saṃsāra.
In the past, O Madhusūdana, you slew Madhu in the fierce waters of the single vast ocean where there was no support; for the sake of protecting the universe, protect me! 10.
O Trivikrama, salutations to you who, having taken three strides and destroyed the great army of the Daityas, protected the three worlds.
Having assumed the form of a dwarf containing within him the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and having bewildered [the world] with that wondrous form—to that master of illusion, obeisance! (12)
Salutations to You, Śrīdhara, who eternally maintains prosperity within Your heart and bestows that very prosperity upon Your devotees. (13)
O Hṛṣīkeśa, obeisance be to You, the presiding lord of all the senses, who is eternally the master and the sole cause of happiness for Your devotees.
O Padmanābha, salutations to you, whose lotus-navel is the eternal seat of the Creator, from which this entire world of moving and non-moving beings has arisen.
O Dāmodara, salutations to You, by Whom this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is bound by the three qualities (guṇas), yet You Yourself were bound by a rope by a cowherd girl! 16.
O Keśava, Lord, you who have slain the demon Keśin, who caused the destruction of the three worlds and are the master of all happiness, protect me! 17.
The Creator, the primordial cause of the worlds, brought forth all beings; O Viṣṇu of inconceivable majesty, Nārāyaṇa, salutations be unto you! 18.
Salutations again and again to Mādhava, whose primordial *māyā* has indeed deluded the entire universe, and who is the very essence of all dharmas. || 19 ||
You are attainable through knowledge by the wise, and you grant refuge to those who have no other resort; O Govinda, may my vow be fulfilled through your grace. (20)
At the conclusion of the worship every month, with palms joined in reverence, one should pray to Janārdana with supreme devotion at the end of the ritual service using these mantras.
Having thus observed the vow known as the Mūrtipañjara for one year, one should perform the rite of installation (pratiṣṭhā) for the sake of attaining the perfection of the complete fruit.
Twelve images of Viṣṇu fashioned from gold, made according to one's capacity, should be installed within all twelve jars.
In those [vessels] covered with mango-leaf lids, each distinct and individually, wrapped in white cloths and filled with water, fragrant scents, and sprouts; || 24 ||
Those pitchers should be placed in the eight directions and the four cardinal directions within the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala, and the deities (mūrtis) should be worshipped within them.
O twice-born ones, at the outset, the bathing of all [the deities] was performed with the twelve-syllable mantra, with the various ritual offerings (upacāras), and with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Likewise, with songs, instrumental music, dance, and other such offerings, as well as by honoring the Brāhmaṇas with twelve pairs of garments, an umbrella, and a pair of sandals.
With fans, water-pots, and couches together with stools; likewise with perfumes, garlands, excellent betel-leaves, signet rings, and earrings. || 28 ||
Lamps should be lit with clarified butter, twelve by twelve in succession; having thus passed the three watches of the night, the fire-ritual is indeed performed at dawn.

Then, for each deity, there should be three hundred oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice; thereafter, one thousand and eight oblations of sesame seeds should be offered with the Vyāhṛtis.
Having performed the consumption of the remnants at the conclusion of the Homa, one should give the teacher’s sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); twelve tawny cows, adorned with ornaments, should be given.
Then, one should feed one hundred and forty-four Brahmins; thereafter, that assembly of deities, along with the water-pot, the canopy, and the fly-whisks—
One should present this to the preceptor along with all ritual offerings; having performed this king of vows, one shall attain all desires. || 33 ||
Whatever twelve processions of Viṣṇu beginning with the Guṇḍicā are proclaimed, the merit arising from the sight of them is obtained through this vow.
By the grace of the God of gods, one attains the station of Indra, universal sovereignty as a universal emperor (cakravartin), and the eightfold supernatural powers (aṣṭaiśvarya). || 35 ||
Nārada performed this most meritorious vow; having observed it for twelve years, the sage became liberated while yet alive.
And other Vaiṣṇavas indeed performed this vow many times in the past; there is nothing superior to this for bringing about the pleasure of the Blessed Lord. (37)
"Righteous, conducive to fame and long life, promoting the status of a Brahmin and increasing the lineage—this supreme vow you all, being self-restrained, are also performing. (38)

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Jyeṣṭhapañcaka Vow," in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: O sage, we have indeed heard this meritorious vow, the "Cage of Embodiments" (Mūrtipañjara), which generates inner joy and is exceedingly great in its majesty. (1)
Twelve sacred pilgrimages have been described by you as dear to the Blessed One; among them, two remain for us—please tell us about them, O Great Sage.
Jaimini said: I shall fully describe the springtime festival known as the Damanabhañjikā procession, by the performance and witnessing of which Puruṣottama is pleased.
O Brahmins, as was previously mentioned, one should fetch on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra that grass known as damanaka, together with its roots.
In the center of that, one should fashion a very beautiful mandala known as the lotus; within it, one should place the consecrated image of the deity.
One should worship them according to the prescribed rites along with Śrī and Satyabhāmā; this rite for the God of gods should be performed at midnight.
Long ago, even at midnight, the Lord shattered the demon Damanāsura; having crushed him, he attained supreme joy and [took] that grass arising from his limbs.
On that very thirteenth day, one should visualize the Daitya as a blade of grass; then, with palms joined in reverence, one should utter these words: || 8 ||
In former times, you slew the Daitya Damana, who was a thorn to the three worlds; he is the very one who has thus transformed and stands here before you.
O Mādhava, that same joy which you felt at his birth should likewise remain with you now in the breaking of Damana.
Having spoken thus, one should cause a blade of grass to be placed in the hand of the deity; then, one should pass the remainder of the night with dancing, singing, and other such activities.
Then, O best of the twice-born, when the sun has risen, one should lead the god, preceded by Tṛṇapura, into the presence of the Lord of the World.
Then, one should worship the Lord of the World with ritual offerings as before; having slain Hiraṇyakaśipu, [one should offer] the garland of entrails produced from his body.
O Blessed One, just as you were pleased when [the previous offering] was placed upon your neck, so too have I offered this *damana* grass upon your body for your delight.

Having uttered this, one should offer auspicious fragrant grass upon the head of Hari. Then, having joyfully beheld the lotus-face of Hari which bestows delight, one whose worldly suffering has been utterly exhausted attains unsurpassed happiness.
Having taken that branch and placed it upon his head, he shall wipe away the impurities from the head of Viṣṇu; liberated from all sins, he will certainly dwell in the city of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Breaking the Damanaka Branch," in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Jaimini said: Hereafter, I shall describe the pilgrimage that bestows imperishable liberation, even for the dull-witted whose minds are bound by latent impressions, and without great effort. (1)
In the dark fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, during the middle of the night on the second lunar day, one should prepare a square pavilion smeared with lime and provided with an altar.
Then, with well-washed garments, one should prepare a space equal to a curtain, provided with excellent stairs and adorned with a beautiful canopy.
In the midst of that, one should certainly and properly place an excellent and auspicious seat; upon that, covered with a cloth, one should place a golden vessel.
To his west, a pure Brāhmaṇa, sitting comfortably, should take twenty-five [parts] of sandalwood in another vessel.
One should take more than one pala of well-ground black resin (kṛṣṇasneha), half as much agallochum (aguru), half as much saffron (kuṅkuma), and half as much silhaka.
The proportions of musk and camphor should be equal to the measure of sihlaka; having ground everything together, one should do so with water derived from the pāṭala flower.
Then one should give two palas of the finest aguru oil; having mixed them together into one, one should place them in the previously mentioned vessel.
Having covered it with *ketakī* leaves, one should wrap it with Chinese silk (*cīnavāsas*). One should protect the fragrance with the *Soma-mantra* and the *Garuḍa-mudrā*.
In this manner, one should cause it to be placed within that pavilion after having performed the consecration (adhivāsa); then, at the time of dawn, one should bring it into the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
Having paraded [the image] through the city with conchs, chowries, umbrellas, and other [regalia] up to the abode of the gods, and having placed it before the deity, one should worship Puruṣottama.
Then, having opened the cloth, one should gaze with divine vision; having sprinkled it with the king of mantras, one should perform the rites of striking and so forth.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), one should anoint all the limbs of the Lord of Śrī very slowly with a gentle touch, reciting the Śrīsūkta.
Then the Vaiṣṇavas glorify that Hari with shouts of victory, while the learned praise him indeed with various hymns and Upaniṣads.
With flutes, lutes, and other instruments, with numerous dances, songs, and instrumental performances, and with fans, chowries, umbrellas, and various other offerings; || 15 ||
On the third lunar day and subsequent days, one should anoint the Lord of the World to bring him satisfaction; by the mere thought of whom the afflictions of embodied beings are destroyed. (16)
O twice-born ones, through his very sight he then destroys the suffering of men; for the majesty of Viṣṇu is always inconceivable, being neither "like this" nor "like that."
Then, with fine garments, garlands, various kinds of food and drink, and diverse, heart-pleasing, auspicious substances derived from cow products and prepared with care; || 18 ||
Then one should worship the God with well-prepared betel leaves; for at that time, those men who behold Kṛṣṇa with devotion [attain the highest state]. (19)
There is no returning for them again, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas; having attained the true nature of Viṣṇu, they indeed dwell in the world of Viṣṇu.
Long ago in the Kali age, O Brahmins, there was a patriarch named Dakṣa; he beheld human beings who were utterly wretched due to the torments of the spiritual and other realms.
Having gone there, filled with compassion, he indeed performed the consecration according to the rules as previously described by me, O twice-born ones; that very rite was performed first.
Having smeared his limbs with sandalwood paste on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mādhava, he joyfully sang this hymn of praise to Jagannātha.
Dakṣa said: O God of gods, Lord of the universe, stainless with innate bliss, O Supreme Lord, save us who are submerged in the ocean of worldly existence! 24.
With a mind of compassion and with an auspicious glance, you have indeed refreshed these human beings who are tormented by various kinds of miseries, using your nectar-like presence. (25)
O Kṛṣṇa, satisfy my parched desires; salutations be unto You, my sin! O Lord of the worlds, You have descended to uplift those who are utterly deluded by the impurities of the Kali age. 26.
This is the descent [of the Lord] into this cave within the Blue Mountain, for the sake of those great sins that have grown deep over a long time and are difficult to abandon.

O Lord who shows compassion to the wretched and the helpless, you alone are the master capable of burning away this heap [of sins]; for even in the great conjunction of beholding you, which is devoid of the eight limbs beginning with *yama*, [the fruit is attained]. (28)
Those whose minds have arisen [intent] upon the sole means of accomplishing the fourfold aims do not grieve in the terrifying forest of existence, which is so difficult to cross. (29)
O Lord of Gods, self-knowledge does not grant liberation independently of karma; yet this teaching of yours, O Protector, would liberate even without karma. (30)
Victory to you, O Kṛṣṇa! Victory, O Īśāna! Victory, O Imperishable One! Victory, O Immutable One! Be gracious and favor us—us who are wretched, deluded, and senseless.
Having thus offered praise, he fell prostrate like a staff at the lotus-feet [of the Lord], crying out, "Be gracious, O Lord! Be gracious, O Lord! Be gracious, O Lord! (32)
Then the Blessed One spoke to Prajāpati in a melodious voice: "Arise, my child; that boon which was requested by you has been granted to you, though it is difficult to obtain."
"Through my grace, that which you desire shall come to pass; of this there is no doubt. It is known to you that the favor of me is difficult for those of little merit to obtain. (34)
"You are born from my own body and have made a request of me; therefore, having gratified you with a festival for me, I shall grant it to you. (35)
Those who joyfully behold this inexhaustible procession with devotion shall obtain at that time whatever they desire in their minds. || 36 ||
Just as the application of sandalwood paste removes heat, so too, O Dakṣa, is this festival for me the destroyer of the threefold affliction.
For with your mind impelled by me, you have indeed performed this festival; this was certainly conceived in my mind for the sake of uplifting the distressed. (38)
"O Prajāpati, I shall surely grant you everything you desire; these twelve great processions, beginning with Guṇḍicā, are indeed purifying. (39)
Each one individually bestows liberation; all together they increase virtue, desire, and wealth. || 40 ||
Whoever gazes upon even one of these with devotion, having crossed the ocean of worldly existence by means of that single act, shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Jaimini said: Having thus addressed the Lord of Creatures, the Blessed One vanished from sight.
Dakṣa Prajāpati, being full of faith, stayed on the mountain for a year by his command and witnessed great festivals.
Having become an omniscient Brahmin in the excellent lineage of Kauśika, he established the worlds in the great sacrifices according to the prescribed rules.

These expedients have indeed been proclaimed for the sake of inspiring confidence in those of small intellect; and this very one is the Teacher of the World, the manifest form of the Supreme Brahman, who was propitiated by the Lord of the Gods for the purpose of bestowing grace upon the worlds.
In whatever manner he comes within the range of vision, he certainly bestows liberation; he grants all desires to women—of this there is no doubt. (46)

The Blessed One Madhusūdana, true to his vow, dwells there; by seeing him, one crosses over the sorrow born from the ocean of worldly existence. What need is there for vows, what for austerities or gifts, and likewise what for hardships or sacrifices? (47)
What is the use of the eightfold yoga, or what is the use of the supreme Sāṃkhya?

Having bathed in the waters of the king of holy fords (the ocean) at the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama, one who beholds with the eye of flesh the wooden Brahman dwelling at the abode at the foot of the banyan tree is liberated from the bondage of the body.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: O Blessed One, knower of all scriptures, we have heard this most wonderful account of the Lord’s majesty in the form of his pilgrimage, which destroys all sins.
Just as the God who grants all desires is worshipped by those seeking their heart's wishes, so too does he bestow prosperity upon those who worship him for prosperity; please tell us how this is so.
Jaimini said: All manifestations in this world, both moving and unmoving, belong to Viṣṇu; he alone is the Supreme Lord, the source of prosperity and prosperity itself. (3)
In whatever manner a man conducts himself, in that very way he is born; his greatness is such that it cannot be measured.
In whatever manner one worships Him, in that very manner shall one obtain the fruit; indeed, that wooden [idol] is the single path for the four goals beginning with dharma.
O best of the twice-born, the path of Dharma is dense and crowded with many injunctions; thus, no one at all is capable of ascertaining its true essence.
For wealth and desire always have their roots in that [dharma] in such a gross manner; the Blessed One, without effort, brings about the increase of these three.
For the Blessed One Viṣṇu is Dharma, and this world has Dharma as its root; Janārdana is the lord of both Dharma and the world.
He in whom devotion to that [scripture] consisting of the goals of human life is firmly established, his soul satisfied in all desires, neither grieves nor longs for anything.
Hari, who bestows sovereignty over the three worlds, is indeed worshipped in the form of Śakra; when meditated upon in the form of Dhātṛ, he causes the increase of one's lineage.
In the form of Sanatkumāra, he bestows long life; when meditated upon in the form of Pṛthu, he indeed grants the perfection of one's livelihood.
When worshipped as Vācaspati, he bestows the fruit of pilgrimage sites such as the Gaṅgā; when meditated upon in his radiant form, he dispels the inner darkness.
The Moon, when worshipped, bestows incomparable good fortune; he who knows the truth of the eighteen branches of learning should meditate upon him as the Lord of Speech.
This eternal one is the bestower of the fruits of sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice; he is composed of the universe, contemplated in the form of the Lord of Sacrifice.
When meditated upon in the form of Kubera, he bestows incomparable prosperity. || 15 ||
Thus, that ocean of compassion, dwelling on that Blue Mountain (Nīlācala), assumed a body in the guise of wood for the sake of favoring the poor and the helpless.
Go there, O brahmins, and dwell with full concentration; take refuge in the pair of lotus feet of the Lord of Śrī.
If you desire enjoyments of this world and the next that are eternal, and ultimately liberation and absolute isolation (kaivalya) as you wish, then attain them there. 18.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: At the conclusion of the consecration of the temple, Hari commanded Indradyumna regarding the boons he had granted, as well as the twelve processions.
Having heard everything from you, what did that lord of the earth do—though he was established as a devotee of Viṣṇu, possessed of great intelligence? (2)
Jaimini said: Having obtained boons directly from the Lord of the World, who is the very embodiment of Brahman, that bull among men considered himself to have accomplished all his life's purposes.
Having indeed performed those pilgrimages according to the command—which bestow merit and liberation—and having worshipped the Teacher of the World in many ways with numerous offerings, || 4 ||
Having duly commanded Gālarāja with the King’s order, he spoke these sweet words, which were consistent with righteousness and justice: || 5 ||
Indradyumna said: O King, you are deeply learned and have attained steadfastness in dharma; you possess devotion toward the Blessed One through action, mind, and speech.
For the Blessed One does not indeed instruct for the sake of teaching a single person; he is the teacher of the moving and the unmoving, and the entire universe has become his disciple.
The Lord of the World has descended with the aim of bestowing grace upon me; for the sake of uplifting those of distressed minds, he shall remain here for a long time.
Endowed with devotion and faith, carry out this command; O protector of the earth, do not understand this through the conventional treatment of images.
It was directly perceived by you how the three worlds were born and descended to the earth upon the entry of this Lord of the Universe into the interior of the palace.
All the thirty gods, beginning with the Grandfather (Brahmā), arrived simultaneously; we all became as if our consciousness were lost due to his universal form. || 11 ||
For he, who consists of all that is moving and unmoving, has directly assumed the form of wood; know this Kalpa tree, which grants all desires, to have descended to the earth.

For by worshipping Him, one indeed obtains the fruit according to one's desire; yet, though striving in many ways, ascetics truly do not know Him who is established beyond darkness, whose nature is some indescribable light.
For ascetics devoted to dharma, pure, with vital energy drawn upward, and endowed with exclusive devotion—there is but one path for such yogis.
Just as one attains supreme bliss by plunging into a cool, deep reservoir of water during the summer heat, so too does one find it in this ocean of compassion.
The threefold suffering is abandoned when the Supreme Person has arrived.
Neither mother, nor father, nor friend, nor wife, nor son is such a benefactor to those who are distressed and have come for refuge as this [king] is. (17)
Therefore, attend upon him who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; cause those processions to proceed in full prosperity with the citizens and the subjects.
O best of kings, the common path of dharma for monarchs was established by a predecessor and is maintained by his successor. (19)
O Indra among kings, worship Nṛsiṃha with offerings of great power; adore him at the three junctions of the day and attain supreme liberation.
They say that guarding what has been done by another is superior to one's own deed; for he who protects what was given by another, that is indeed superior to what was given by oneself. (21)
Jaimini said: Then Śveta, that best of kings, with palms joined in reverence, received those words upon his head like a garland endowed with excellent qualities.
The royal sage Indradyumna, having propitiated Puruṣottama, departed for the world of Brahmā together with Śrī.
Thus has been narrated to you this meritorious and supreme majesty of the sacred field, as well as the greatness of Brahmadāruṇa who dwells there eternally.
O best of the twice-born, whoever hears this being recited with devotion shall obtain the complete fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
The merit gained from proclaiming the majesty of Viṣṇu is ten million times greater than that yoga which is proclaimed by Skanda as the Ardhodaya.
Whoever listens to this every morning shall become the donor of a hundred tawny cows; he shall obtain the fruit of consecration with the waters of the Gaṅgā and the Puṣkara lakes.
It is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, meritorious, and increases one's progeny; it grants attainment of the heavenly realm and removes all sins. || 28 ||
This secret has been declared, which is well-guarded in the Purāṇas; it must never be spoken to anyone other than Vaiṣṇavas. (29)

It must always be concealed from those who are afflicted by fallacious reasoning, those whose hearing of the scriptures is poorly studied, the atheists, the hypocrites, those who constantly point out the faults of others, the non-Vaiṣṇavas, and those whose lives are in vain. (30)
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Puruṣottama Kṣetra," in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: O venerable Jaimini, you who have reached the further shore of all the Vedas and Vedāṅgas; by your grace, [we have heard] the majesty of the Lord of the Universe.
[He described] the pilgrimage to that very Kṣetrarāja and all its various processions, as well as the fruit of consuming the remnants of the Lord's meal and other such acts. || 2 ||
Indeed, [I shall tell] the exceedingly rare account of King Indradyumna, as well as the manifestation of Nīlamādhava in the form of the wooden Brahman.
We have heard that which has flowed from the lotus of your mouth according to the prescribed rule; now, O best among speakers, we desire to hear more from you.
O Brahmin, we are all filled with joy; all that fruit which has been described for the listening to the Purāṇas in detail, that very fruit [is ours]. || 5 ||
What is its ritual procedure, and by what means would it be complete with all its constituent parts? If you have compassion for us, you ought to explain this correctly.
Jaimini said: "Excellent, excellent, O best of sages, that you have asked with such supreme joy! In this matter, an incomparable delight has arisen within me, causing my hair to stand on end."
I shall explain all of that to you; listen with full attention. At the commencement of hearing a Purāṇa, one should act according to one's own means.

First, having formally resolved according to the rules, one should select a Brāhmaṇa born of a pure lineage, whose limbs are unimpaired, who is tranquil, a follower of his own Vedic school, and his own family priest.

One should choose a person who knows the true meaning of all the scriptures and is adorned with most beautiful ornaments, garments, sandalwood paste, garlands, and so forth, for the purpose of hearing the recitation.
Then, having joined his palms in reverence, he should pray to the twice-born: "You are Viṣṇu; you are indeed Viṣṇu; there is never any difference between you."
"May it be free from obstacles for me through your grace; be gracious. Then he seated the chosen Brāhmaṇa upon an auspicious and highly valuable throne.
Having perfumed it, one should place a garland around his neck and anoint his head with sandalwood paste mixed with flowers. || 13 ||
Because at that time, the Brahmin was considered equal to Vyāsa, it was by that very Brahmin [that it was written] in the book which is the form of Viṣṇu.
One should perform the worship of Vyāsa with sandalwood, agallochum, and flowers, as well as with various beautiful services and offerings such as foods to be chewed and eaten.
With devotion, the ritual of offering a seat and so forth should be performed day after day. Now I shall speak thus; let the characteristics of a listener be heard.
And likewise, O twice-born ones, for the sake of providing lodging for those who follow the crowd, he himself arranged seats as was appropriate. (17)
Indeed, he should remain on a beautiful seat with an eager mind; or else, he may dwell upon the earth in a consecrated region together with all [others].
Seated before Vyāsa on a seat that was not too high, having performed his ablutions and being filled with joy, he wore two white garments.
Having sipped water for purification (ācamana), with his body marked by the tilaka of the conch, discus, and other symbols, he should meditate upon Viṣṇu in his mind and cultivate intense faith.
In the Purāṇas, in the Brāhmaṇas, in the Veda, in the performance of mantras, at sacred fords, and in the words of the elderly, faith is what yields fruit. || 21 ||
Therefore, O best of sages, one should with great effort avoid all conversation with heretics and the like, as well as idle talk, for these are causes that destroy merit.
At the time of listening to the Purāṇas, one should abandon all worldly thoughts; by this method, O Brāhmaṇas, one should listen daily with joy.
Then, when the recitation was completed, they repeatedly [applauded] with clapping of hands and so forth, [invoking him] by such names as "Victory to Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the World, Hara," and so on.
One should expand [the sound] so that it is heard as if in space; in this manner, one should perform this daily for the pleasure of the Enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu). 25.

Then, at the conclusion of the book, being intent on pleasing Viṣṇu, he should especially honor with supreme devotion a brāhmaṇa equal to Vyāsa, O twice-born ones, with garments, garlands, sandalwood paste, and ornaments. (26)

One should indeed give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's own capacity and in accordance with the prescribed rule; now hear what each person should give and how they should give it from me.
Kings should give elephants adorned with ornaments and possessing auspicious marks; likewise, Kṣatriyas [should do so], for they are indeed considered equal to kings. || 28 ||
The Brāhmaṇas [offered] books, caskets for the worship of Viṣṇu, gold, silver, grain, and clothing, out of their own devotion. (29)
And he gave Vaiśyas, richly adorned with jewels, as well as those born in the land of Sindh; and cows endowed with auspicious marks, accompanied by their calves and yielding milk.
Furthermore, those devoted to dharma would renounce gold and other such things; even Śūdras, their minds filled with supreme joy, would give them away. (31)
And garments, gold, grain, jewels, and cows—along with various ornaments—and cows that yield abundant milk, those with calves, and those pregnant for the first time. (32)

In this manner, O Brahmins, one should indeed give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) by which the preceptor is satisfied; according to one's own capacity, one should not practice deceit regarding the wealth.
Rites for pacification and nourishment, as well as vows, marriage, and other such ceremonies, and likewise the hearing of the Purāṇas, which is the means for accomplishing liberation.
Sacrifices and the like, charity, and various kinds of vows—if these are devoid of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), then they become fruitless. || 35 ||
The Asuras seize the very fruit of that action, just as the beauty of women is lost when devoid of affection for their husbands.
O twice-born ones, for archers who have turned their backs and fled from battle, there is indeed wickedness, just as there is in horses that run away without being spurred.
Just as scholarship among those learned in all the scriptures is like being mute, so too is any ritual act devoid of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) fruitless.
Since the multitude of misdeeds is destroyed by giving, it is therefore called "dakṣiṇā" (the purifier), as is sung by the Brahmins who know the scriptures. (39)
Then one should indeed feed the Brahmins with offerings prepared according to one's capacity, combined with camphor, sugar-candy, ghee, and milk-rice (pāyasa).

One should cause them to be given various kinds of food, drink, and other offerings—sixfold in variety, delicious, and like nectar—as well as gold, clothing, and so forth, according to one's ability. (41)

All this has been told to you regarding the hearing of the Purāṇas, along with the complete ritual procedure including its limbs and sub-limbs, by which this [act] becomes truly fruitful. Now, O best of sages, what else do you wish to know?
The sages said: "Oh, what great fortune is ours, that we ourselves have obtained the very fruit of listening to the Purāṇas, which destroys the multitude of our sins! (43)
We have heard the ritual procedure, along with its limbs and sub-limbs, from the lotus of your mouth; we are blessed, we are meritorious, and we are freed from the fever of worldly existence.
"Now, O Sage, this sacrificial fee is indeed given to you by my own power; for the attainment of its fruit, please accept it with a gracious mind. (45)

Having spoken thus, those sages who possess nothing prepared sacrificial fuel, kuśa grass, flowers, fruits, unbroken grains, and other offerings for him; then, being well-liberated, the sages departed for that most excellent sacred field, filled with great joy. || 46 ||

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Dialogue with the Sage Jaimini," in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śaunaka said: O Sūta, O Sūta, highly fortunate one, best among those who know all dharmas, knower of the true meaning of all scriptures, firmly established in the Purāṇas! (1)
Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, is the imperishable Lord Viṣṇu; you are his beloved disciple, and there is no one who knows more than you.
When the terrible Kali age has arrived, which is excluded from all righteous dharma, people will indeed be performers of evil deeds and devoid of all dharma.

They will have short lifespans, and their vitality, strength, heroism, austerity, and religious practices will be meager; all will be devoted to unrighteousness and devoid of the Vedas and the Śāstras.
How can the upliftment of these few people—who are devoid of pilgrimage, austerity, charity, and devotion to Hari—be achieved with little effort? (5)

It is the most excellent of holy places (tīrthas) and likewise the most excellent of sacred fields (kṣetras). For those seeking liberation, where is success to be found, or where is the assembly of sages? (6)

Where is it that austerity and mantras grant success with little effort? Where does the glorious Lord of the lords of the worlds dwell—he who is the abode of grace and compassion for devoted and affectionate followers? (7)
All of this and more has as its sole purpose the welfare of others; speak it for the prosperity of the worlds, O you who are skilled in showing favor.

Sūta said: Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! You are devoted to the welfare of others, and the impurities of your mind have been washed away by your intense attachment to devotion for Hari.
Then the son of Devakī ascends the lotus of my heart; for, O brahmin-sage, by association with you, the company of the virtuous has become attainable to me, though it is otherwise difficult to find.

It removes the accumulation of evil deeds and extends the supreme goal for those who pride themselves on their bodies; yet, in this world, meeting with the virtuous is difficult to attain for those whose minds are not self-controlled, even through the power of great merit. (11)

It removes the bondage of the heart for those afflicted by the noose of karma; it bestows the supreme state upon those who possess but little speech. The company of the virtuous is difficult to find in the three worlds, yet it is the cause of rest for humans exhausted by the cycle of birth, death, and action. (12)

Sūta said: O virtuous one, this question was formerly asked by Skanda on the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, while the sages were listening from all sides, in the presence of the Lord of Girijā, for the sake of securing the ultimate welfare of the righteous.
Skanda said: O Blessed One, creator, destroyer, father, and preceptor of all worlds, you have resolved to perform penance for the welfare of all living beings.
Now that the Kali age has arrived, which is devoid of the Vedas and the Śāstras, where does the glorious Lord, the Master of the Sātvatas, reside? (15)

Which fields are meritorious, and likewise which sacred fords and rivers? By what means is the Lord Madhusūdana directly attained? O Father, O Blessed One, please tell me out of compassion, for I am full of faith. (16)
Śrī Mahādeva said: O Six-faced One, there are many holy fords (tīrthas) and sacred fields (kṣetras) that are solely devoted to the dwelling of Hari for those seeking the supreme goal.
Some [rites] are for the fulfillment of desires, while others grant liberation; they indeed bestow benefits both in this world and the next, and bestow abundant merit.
The Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Revā, Tapatī, Yamunā river, the meritorious Kṣiprā, Sarasvatī, Gautamī, and likewise the Kauśikī. || 19 ||
The Kāverī, the Tāmraparṇī, the Candrabhāgā born from Mount Mahendra, the Citrotpalā, the Vetravatī, and the merit-bestowing Sarayū. || 20 ||
The Carmaṇvatī, the Śatadrū, the Payasvinī born from Atri, the Gaṇḍikā, the Bāhudā—all these are holy, as are the Sindhu and the Sarasvatī. || 21 ||
When these are served repeatedly, they bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation: Ayodhyā, Dvārakā, Kāśī, Mathurā, and likewise Avantikā.

Kurukṣetra, Rāmatīrtha, Kāñcī, and Puruṣottama; Puṣkara, the sacred field of Dardura, and Vārāha created by Brahmā; and the highly meritorious field named Badarī, which accomplishes all goals. || 23 ||
Having duly beheld Ayodhyā, the city that is the sole means to liberation, those who are completely freed from all sins go to the abode of Hari.

Having performed worship, dance, and chanting preceded by various services to Viṣṇu, they abandoned their homes; through constant meditation on Hari, they overcame the power of death acquired through worldly life. || 25 ||
Having bathed at Svargadvāra and beheld the abode of Rāma while pure, I see no further duty remaining for that man, since he has thereby accomplished all that was to be done. (26)
In Dvārakā, Hari himself never leaves his own abode; even today, that mansion is beheld by certain meritorious persons.
O Six-faced One, for a man who has bathed in the Gomatī and beheld the lotus-face of Kṛṣṇa, liberation arises as the ultimate remainder, even without the practice of Sāṃkhya.
In the five-krośa region between the rivers Asī and Varuṇā, the fruit is great; even the gods desire death there—what need to mention other people? (29)
Having bathed in Maṇikarṇikā, Jñānavāpī, Viṣṇupādodaka, and the Pañcanada pool, one shall not again become a drinker from a mother’s breast.
O Six-faced One, even by seeing Viśveśa in Kāśī incidentally, liberation—freed from birth and death—is produced for men. (31)

What is the use of saying more here? Nowhere else is there a place equal to this field. O Six-faced One, one who is devoted to austerity and fasting in Mathurā, having reached that birthplace, is liberated from all sins. (32)
Having bathed according to the prescribed rites at Viśrāntitīrtha and offered water with sesame seeds, one delivers one's ancestors from hell and proceeds to the world of Viṣṇu.
If a person should commit a sin there through negligence, upon reaching the holy bath at Viśrānti, he is reduced to ashes at that very moment.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rites in the Śiprā at Avantī during the month of Mādhava, men do not experience the state of a Piśāca even for hundreds of future births.
Having bathed at Koṭitīrtha and fed the best of the twice-born, and having beheld Hara Mahākāla, a man is liberated from all sins.
This is a field of liberation, the direct and sole means for attaining my world; through giving here, poverty is destroyed both in this world and the next.
Having given gold according to his ability at Rāmatīrtha in Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse, that man who acts according to the prescribed rule shall become a partaker of liberation.
Those men who, having fallen under the sway of greed, accept gifts there, shall indeed not regain their male state even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Having seen Hari in Harikṣetra and having bathed in the Pādodaka water, a person is liberated from all sins and rejoices together with Hari.

Oh, various flocks of birds dwell here, and groups of sages who subsist on fruits, roots, and leaves; indeed, the munis here have subdued the power of their senses through the practice of breath control.

In Viṣṇukāñcī Hari is manifest, and in Śivakāñcī Śiva himself resides. Through devotion to both as non-different, liberation rests in the palm of one's hand; from generating a sense of difference among men, a wretched state arises.
Having beheld the Lord of the World even once and bathed in the Mārkaṇḍeya lake, one shall not become a sucker of a mother’s breast again, even without [further] knowledge or yoga.
Having bathed in the ocean on the day of Rohiṇī, as well as in the Indradyumna lake, and having eaten the food offered to Viṣṇu, one attains residence in Vaikuṇṭha.
A field ten yojanas in extent situated upon Śaṅkha—even insects that dwell there attain the state of having four arms; of this there is no doubt. (45)
Having bathed at Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika, having performed the Śrāddha ceremony with ritual fees, and having devoutly fed the twice-born, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having bathed once in that lake and beheld the sacrificial post with a concentrated mind, the best of the twice-born becomes completely liberated from all sins. (47)
The fruit that is obtained through sixty thousand years of yoga practice is attained by one who, being pure, bathes according to the rules at Saukara and worships Hari.
The sin committed over seven lifetimes is destroyed at that very moment; it is the king of holy places, of great merit, and frequented by all sacred sites. (49)

For all sentient beings who possess desire, their wished-for goals shall be accomplished through their actions. Having bathed in the Veṇī, become pure, and beheld Mādhava, one shall enjoy the pleasures of the meritorious and, in the end, attain the state of Mādhava.
A man who bathes in the Triveṇī during the month of Māgha, being filled with devotion, obtains that same merit from the glorification of Badarī.
The Daśāśvamedhika Tīrtha bestows the fruit of ten sacrifices; it has been described in brief, my son—what more do you wish to hear? (52)

Skanda said: The sacred field of Hari known as Badarī is difficult to attain within the three worlds. Merely by remembering this field, men who have committed great sins are instantly freed from their taints and become partakers of liberation upon death.
A pilgrimage to Badarī, even if merely conceived in the mind, becomes equal to the most rigorous austerity performed at any other sacred site.
There are many sacred fords (tīrthas) in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld; yet a sacred ford equal to Badarī has never existed, nor will it ever exist.
Whatever fruit is obtained from thousands of horse-sacrifices and from subsisting on air, that same fruit is attained in a mere moment at Viśālā, the other sacred field.
In the Kṛta age, she is said to bestow liberation; in the Tretā age, she grants the perfection of yoga; in the Dvāpara age, she is called Viśālā; and in the Kali age, she is Badarikāśrama.
The gross and subtle bodies are the dwelling places of the individual soul (jīva); because she destroys them through knowledge, she is called Viśālā. 58.
For that Badarī tree from which nectar flows through its connection [to the deity] is called Badarī by the wise, where there is a gathering of sages.
One may abandon all sacred fords at every time and in every age, but Lord Viṣṇu never forsakes Badarī.
O Guha, by bathing in all the sacred fords (tīrthas) and through austerity, yoga, and meditative absorption, that fruit is fully obtained simply from the sight of Badarī.
The fruit that is obtained through sixty thousand years of yoga practice is attained by going to Badarī for a single day at Vārāṇasī.
Because it is the abode of sacred fords (tīrthas), as well as the abode of the gods and the abode of the sages (ṛṣis), it is therefore called Viśālā.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of Badarikāśrama as Superior to All Holy Places," in the dialogue between Śiva and Kārttikeya within the *Badarikāśrama-māhātmya*, in the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: How did this originate, by whom has this sacred field (kṣetra) been inhabited, and who might be its presiding lord? Tell me this in detail.
Śiva said: This [place] is established from beginningless time, just as the Vedas are the body of Hari; Hari himself is its presiding deity, and it is frequented by Nārada and others.
In ancient times, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, Brahmā prepared to violate his own daughter, who was endowed with beauty and youth.
Seeing him in such a state, out of rage I severed his head into five pieces with my sword; that skull was raised up for the purpose of killing a Brahmin.
Taking [him] by the hand, he went quickly there to visit the sacred fords (tīrthas) in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld (pātāla), preceded by the performance of austerities.
The sin of killing a Brahmin did not leave me, even though such a skull was in my hand; then I went to Vaikuṇṭha to see Hari, the Lord of Lakṣmī.
Bowing down in humility and paying homage again and again, he related his entire misfortune to that compassionate soul.
Having taken what was instructed by him, he arrived at Badarī; at that very moment, my sin of Brahman-murder approached, trembling again and again.
That skull vanished from my hand and fell away; from that time forth, I have honored that sacred field along with Pārvatī.
I remain established in austerity, bringing joy to the sages; my delight in Vārāṇasī is equal to that on the peak of Śrīśaila.

Then, on Kailāsa, she is accompanied by Śivā and possesses infinite qualities superior to those elsewhere; liberation from other places occurs through the performance of one's own duties according to the prescribed ordinances.
Merely by the sight of Badarī, liberation stands within the grasp of men; for there is the proximity of Hari’s feet, where Vaiśvānara himself resides.
There, my linga is established in the form of Kedāra; by seeing, touching, and worshipping it with a spirit of devotion, [one attains liberation]. || 13 ||
The sin committed over ten million lifetimes is reduced to ashes at that very moment; I remain in that sacred field especially for even a fraction of a moment.
Indeed, the fifteen digits (kalās) are situated here within the midst of the forms.

The auspicious yogins, who have conquered the fear of Death (Kṛtānta), who are well-attired in garments of deer-skins and elephant-hide, and who are adorned with excellent sacred ash and matted locks, worship the wearer of matted locks himself.

Satisfied by fruits, leaves, water, and air, they had overcome the exhaustion of death through the power of Śiva’s mind; dwelling upon the best of mountains, they had conquered their own minds and possessed the great exaltation of an ever-expanding, stainless intellect. (17)

With lotus-like faces possessing the delicate luster of a water-lily, having utterly conquered their enemies through the grace of Śiva, and gazing upon Śiva with their heads bowed in palms joined, they indeed worship Śiva at the onset of night. (18)

Holding rosaries in their hands, possessing peace and contentment, having performed prostrations and constant prayers to the Moon-crested Lord, they—whose very forms were the wisdom born of meditation on the lotus-feet of Śiva—thoroughly subdued the minds of all people. 19.
And for those who have died in Vārāṇasī, the liberation known as Brahman arises there for people through the worship of my Liṅga.
Having beheld the great Liṅga named Kedāra at Vahnitīrtha, resplendent near the feet of the Lord, one shall not be subject to rebirth.
Skanda said: O high-minded one, tell me how the glorious Vaiśvānara, the sole cause of all the worlds, came to reside at Badarī.
Śiva said: In ancient times, there was an assembly of sages who had sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), where the divine Gaṅgā met with the Kālindī.

There was a sacred ford named Daśāśvamedhika, renowned throughout the three worlds. There, the Lord Agni, the consumer of oblations, stood before the sages and, bowing with humility, began to inquire.

Vaiśvānara said: "Having seen you here, who possess singular vision and knowledge, you are the best among the knowers of Brahman; filled with compassion for the distressed, your hearts are tender and you are merciful. (25)
O best among the knowers of Brahman, how can there be liberation from hell for me, whose mind is stained by the sins arising from all these inauspicious marks? (26)
The lord of sages arrived before all those excellent ṛṣis; having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, he spoke these words.
Vyāsa said: There is one supreme means for your atonement of sin; for the fault known as "eating all things," take refuge in Badarī.
There dwells the Blessed One, Janārdana, the God of gods in person; Madhusūdana, who destroys the sins of both devotees and non-devotees alike. (29)
Having bathed there in the waters of the Gaṅgā and performed circumambulation of Hari, the destruction of all sins occurs by prostrating like a staff.
Then, having heard this from the mouth of Vyāsa and following the testimony of the sages, the Fire-god turned toward the north and went to Mount Gandhamādana.
Then, having reached Badarī and bathed himself in the waters of the Gaṅgā, he went to the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa; bowing down, the devoted one spoke.

Agni said: I bow to Him who is a mass of pure consciousness, the ancient and eternal Lord of the creators of the universe, the Teacher; who is manifold yet one, the sole protector of the world, whose pure intellect is the refuge of the infinite. (33)

Having approached his power consisting of illusion, I praise the Creator of the universe who employs rajas for its activity, who is the fierce cause of its maintenance through sattva, and who finally swallows it all by means of tamas.

My self is utterly deluded by ignorance regarding the Lord who is the sole form of knowledge, pervasive throughout the three worlds; because he is the refuge of knowledge, I take refuge in that omniscient Lord as the individual soul (jīva) through ignorance. (35)

I praise the one who manifests the union of bodies according to the desire of his devotees, who is joined with the yoga of bestowing the enjoyment of all enjoyments, whose Śakti is adorned with yellow silken garments, and who is praised on the eighth lunar day as consisting of the eight wonderful Śaktis.
Then the Blessed One, being pleased and praised by all while abiding within their hearts, spoke these sweet words to Pāvaka, who was seeking purification.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—for I have come as the giver of boons. O sinless one, I am pleased by this hymn and by your humility."
Agni said: "O Blessed One, everything for which I have come has been understood by you; nevertheless, I shall speak this, in order to carry out the command of the Lord. (39)
"I shall indeed become a consumer of all things; how then can there be an expiation? From this, an extreme state of fear arises within me. (40)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: By the mere sight of this sacred field, living beings have no sin; and by my grace, may there never be any sin in you.
From that time forward, the purifier, the soul of all beings, remained here in every respect, intensely present through his portion, entirely free from all defects.
Whoever, being pure, listens to this upon rising in the morning or causes it to be heard, undoubtedly obtains the fruit of having performed a bath at Agnitīrtha. || 43 ||

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Description of the Praise of the Lord Performed by Agni," in the Śrī-Badarikāśrama-Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Skānda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: O Blessed One, who are skilled in all dharmas among all beings; O Father, please tell me out of compassion the majesty of Agnitīrtha.
Śiva said: I shall briefly describe to you, out of regard for your devotion, this most secret sacred site (tīrtha) which is frequented by all other sacred sites.
O son, those who are guilty of great sins (mahāpātakin) as well as those who have committed heinous crimes (atipātakin) are purified merely by bathing, without any exertion.
That sin which does not depart even through penance until the end of life is purified by the mere act of bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha) or in the purifying fire.
Just as gold thoroughly bound with impurities becomes pure, so too does the embodied soul, having reached the sacred fire-pit (Agnitīrtha), become purified of all sins.

A man who, having performed penance in another sacred field for three years while drinking only drops of water from the tip of a blade of kusha grass, [attains that same merit] here merely by bathing.
By feeding Brāhmaṇas here with offerings according to the extent of one's wealth, poverty shall never arise in their family.
The man who, through fasting, gives up his life at Vahni-tīrtha pierces through the worlds of the Sun and others and attains the world of Viṣṇu.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains through thousands of Cāndrāyaṇa fasts and even ten million Kṛcchra penances, that is obtained from bathing at Vahnitīrtha.
O Six-faced One, it is my conviction that for those who commit the fivefold sins in this world, purification is achieved through the recitation of mantras and the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma).
Those base individuals who, under the influence of delusion, commit sin despite their knowledge, enter the womb of a Piśāca for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Whether one is without a stage of life or within a stage of life, as long as the body endures, one should not intentionally commit a sin at a sacred ford or in the sacrificial fire.

O Six-faced One, bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, the twilight rituals, and likewise the worship of the gods—each of these is said here to possess infinite merit compared to other sacred fords.
There are many sacred fords, purifying and even great; yet there has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred ford equal to Vahnitīrtha.
Neither Brahmā, nor Śiva, nor Śeṣa, nor the gods, nor the ascetics are able, nor even capable, to describe the fruit born of the Pāvaka-tīrtha.
What need have they for many sacrifices, or for gifts, observances, and restraints, for those who perform ablutions for ten days at this Pāvaka-tīrtha? (16)
The man who conquers his vital breaths at Vahni-tīrtha by means of fasting—having observed three fasts and having worshipped Janārdana—he shall become like fire itself at this Pāvaka-tīrtha. (17)
In the midst of the five rocks, there is the constant presence of Hari; right there is the Pāvaka Tīrtha, which destroys all sins.
Skanda said: How are there five stones there, and by whom were they fashioned? What is their merit and what is their fruit? You should tell me all of this in its entirety.
Śiva said: Nāradī, Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī, Gāruḍī, and likewise Mārkaṇḍeyī—these are the renowned stones that grant the fulfillment of all goals.
The blessed Nārada performed most rigorous penance upon a stone slab, subsisting only on air, for the sake of beholding Mahāviṣṇu.
For sixty thousand years, subsisting on the leaves of trees upon a stone slab, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu then assumed the form of a Brāhmaṇa there.

Out of compassion, she went before that best of sages and spoke these sweet words: "O sage, why indeed do you suffer? O you whose impurities have been worn away by austerity, tell me what it is you desire. (23)
Nārada said: Who are you, intent on showing me favor in this lonely forest? O best of the twice-born, my mind attains serenity by the sight of you.
Thus addressed by Nārada, he who bears the conch, discus, and mace, adorned with yellow garments and a shining lotus-garland, [spoke].
Janārdana, whose pure abode is Kamalā, who shines with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, was being praised by Nandana and other foremost attendants.
Afflicted by compassion, he revealed his own form to Nārada; seeing him, [Nārada] rose up suddenly, as if his very life-breath had returned to his body. || 27 ||
Having joined his palms in reverence and bowing down again and again, he, being prostrate, offered praise to the Lord of the lords of the worlds.

Nārada said: May He, the witness of all, the sovereign lord of the worlds, who assumes a body and its splendor according to the desire of His devotees, the great ocean of compassion for those who take refuge in Him, and whose divine form is purifying—may He be gracious. (29)

May he who is the embodiment of the multitude of sentient beings, whose gracious play consists of smiles and glances, be propitious for the welfare of the world and for the long-term complete satisfaction of the minds of the virtuous through his longing and other such qualities. 30.

Beautiful with the playful charm of Kandarppa’s loveliness, a festival for the senses through his clear and profound speech, a most excellent wish-fulfilling tree for those who take refuge in him—may he whose mind is moist with compassion for the wretched be gracious. (31)

May he whose mind is moistened with compassion for the wretched be gracious—He by whom those whose inner selves have been purified through the worship of his lotus feet, and whose causes of bondage have been severed by the sword of knowledge, experience the bliss of Brahman, free from all fatigue.

May He who has built a bridge across the ocean of saṃsāra, who is the cause of the processes of creation, preservation, and dissolution, whose form is assumed through the qualities (guṇas) yet whose name is beyond them, and who is the experience of the bliss of Brahman—may He be gracious. (33)

May that one Lord, the Blessed One, be gracious—he who is the cause of expansion from the subtle elements presided over by the senses, who is the most excellent among the radiant, and who, through his own *māyā*, assumes the state of the individual soul (*jīvātman*). (34)

May the one who is the foremost among those compassionate to the wretched be gracious—he by whom the Great One (Mahat) is colored by the qualities perceived through his own vision, and by whom the body composed of the five elements becomes the locus of qualities; though he is one, he is joined with manifold attributes.
Following him, the gods indeed made the ocean of calamities a mere cow's footprint and dwell in heaven free from all fear.
Salutations to Vāsudeva, and salutations to Saṃkarṣaṇa; salutations to Pradyumna and Aniruddha, the self of all beings. (37)
Today my life is blessed; today my ascetic penance has borne fruit; today my knowledge has become fruitful through the sight of you, O Janārdana. (38)
The Blessed Lord said: "O Nārada, I am pleased by this austerity and by this hymn of yours; there is no devotee of mine like you to be found in the three worlds. (39)
"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—for I stand before you as the giver of boons. Know this, O Nārada: by the sight of me, your desire shall be fully accomplished."
Nārada said: "O God, if you are the granter of boons to me, or if I am worthy of a boon, O All-pervading Lord, grant me unwavering devotion to your lotus feet."

"And you must never abandon the proximity of the Pacchila [region]; by the sight, touch, bathing, and sipping of water at my holy ford (tīrtha), one is no longer joined with physical bodies—this third boon shall be granted to me. (42)

The Blessed Lord said: "So be it; out of affection for you, I shall dwell at your sacred ford (tīrtha) for the sake of the liberation from the body of all moving and unmoving beings—of this there is no doubt. (43)
Having spoken thus, Hari himself vanished right there. The highly effulgent Nārada also, dwelling joyfully at Badarī for some days, then departed for Madhupurī.
Skanda said: Tell me the majesty of Mārkaṇḍeya-śilā; what is its merit, what is its fruit, and how did it receive such a name? (45)
Śiva said: Formerly, at the end of the Tretā Yuga, the great son of Mṛkaṇḍu, knowing his own life to be short, performed the supreme recitation (japa).
Worshipped with the twelve-syllable mantra, the imperishable Hari, knowing that [the devotee] possessed a lifespan of seven kalpas, departed from that very place into his own interior.
O Six-faced One, having heard of the exhaustion from wandering to sacred fords, Mārkaṇḍeya then obtained a vision of Nārada in Mathurā.
Honored and saluted by him, Nārada, the best of sages, recounted the greatness of Badarī, where Keśava resides.
Nārada said: "O virtuous one, why do you weary yourself with the fatigues of wandering to sacred fords? There is the great field called Badarī, where Hari is eternally present."
Having heard that one could see Hari there directly with one's own eyes, the sage, filled with wonder, went to Viśālā.
Having bathed, he sat upon a stone and recited the supreme eight-syllabled mantra; then, at the end of three nights, the Blessed Lord Janārdana became pleased.

Beholding Him, who was adorned with the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, and a forest garland, Mārkaṇḍeya rose up suddenly and, bowing down, praised Janārdana with a voice faltering with love. (53)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: In this transient cycle of existence, how is there deliverance for men through Your essential lotus feet? Save me, O Supreme Lord! (54)
O Acyuta, out of compassion, protect me—who am exhausted by the three-fold suffering, overwhelmed by manifold ignorance, and wandering in the cavern of saṃsāra. 55.
O Ocean of Compassion, save me who have experienced the intense agony arising from dwelling in the womb, as I emerge from the machinery of manifold births. (56)
With all my limbs devoured by worms and tormented by hunger and thirst within a womb filled with a garland of intestines—save me, O Madhusūdana!
Smeared with impurities and the like, motionless, exhausted, and distressed, remembering that which arises from my own karma—save me, O Madhusūdana! (58)
Incapable of speech, grasping, or breathing, and overcome by fear, I am suffering the great misery of dwelling in the womb; save me, O Madhusūdana! (59)
O Ocean of Compassion, protect me—who am afflicted by the cycle of existence with its sufferings such as old age, death, and childhood—and who perceives happiness within this ocean of misery. (60)
At times it attained the state of a worm, at times the birth of a sweat-born insect; at times it became a plant, and at times it reached the state of a human being.
O Acyuta, protect me out of compassion; you have entered into every womb, yet you are now fallen, devoid of luster, and have reached a state of helplessness. 62.
Thus praised by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya, Kṛṣṇa was pleased and said to him: "O brahmin-sage, choose a boon from me."

Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: "O Blessed One, compassionate toward the wretched, if you are pleased with me, grant me unwavering devotion in your worship and in beholding you. Your very presence upon this stone is itself the boon I seek. (64)
Sūta said: Having said, "So be it," O twice-born one, Mahāviṣṇu vanished; then Mārkaṇḍeya, being satisfied, went to his father’s hermitage.
This act of attendance is meritorious and destroys all sins; the mortal who hears it or causes others to hear it attains the supreme goal in Govinda.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Agnitīrtha, Nāradaśilā, and Mārkaṇḍeyaśilā," in the dialogue between Śiva and Kārttikeya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: "O father, tell me the majesty of the Vainateya stone; what is its merit, what is its fruit, and what would be its power?"
Śiva said: From Kaśyapa, within the womb of Vinatā, Garuḍa and Aruṇa were born, both possessed of great strength and prowess; of these two, Aruṇa is the charioteer of the Sun.
On the southern side of Badarī, at the peak of Gandhamādana, Garuḍa performed austerities with the desire to become the vehicle of Hari.

Subsisting on fruits, roots, and water, free from the pairs of opposites, and the best among those who recite prayers, he approached with one foot upon the ground and remained there reciting, free from all affliction.
For thirty thousand years he longed for the sight of Hari; then the Blessed One himself appeared, clad in yellow garments and bearing his own weapons.
He appeared like the full moon in the eastern quarter; with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, he spoke these words clearly.
Nevertheless, he did not direct his attention outward and blew his excellent conch; likewise, the high-souled Garuḍa did not turn his gaze outward.
Then, having entered the interior by way of the sequence of the vital breaths (pavana), the Blessed One appeared outside, manifesting his outward orientation.
Upon seeing the Blessed Lord Hari, Garuḍa was freed from his fear; with all his limbs covered in horripilation, he offered praise with palms joined in reverence.

Garuḍa said: Victory, victory to You, O Abode of the minds of the people of the three worlds! O Destroyer of the quality of sin! O You whose pair of lotus feet are saluted by all the gods! O Destroyer of the forest of enemies through the intense fragrance of Your lotus feet! O Radiant One! O You who have dispelled the mass of darkness from the hearts of Your own people with the multitude of rays from the tips of the crowns of all gods and asuras! O Moon-like One, who removes the entire collection of the threefold torments! O Foot, who delights in the play of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe! O You whose fame shines forth in Your threefold forms! O Sun of the world, who brings about the fullness of the world's arising! O You known as the bee upon the lotuses of the minds of Your own people! O You who shine with the knowledge of all the Vedas! O You whose mind is honored by Your own people and the sages! O You whose feet have been purified by the water [of bathing]! O Essence of the grace of the dust of the feet saluted by the minds of the gods and sages! O Lord of the worlds, salutations to You, salutations to You! 10.

Moreover: May He who is endowed with eightfold powers, who wears a forest garland, who is resplendent with yellow garments and rows of flowers, whose feet shine like beds of lotuses, and whose faculties and senses are perfectly restrained, protect me. (11)

May the Lord of the World protect me daily—he whose form shines within the lotus-heart of his devotees, whose fame arose from the destruction of wicked demons, who built the bridge, and who protects the world that has taken refuge in him. 12.

May the Great-Minded Lord protect us—he who is the moon that cools the three kinds of suffering of the stable and the moving, whose appearance is like the shining sun, and who, though one alone, assumes many forms through his power of illusion.

Having assumed a form for the sake of contemplating his devotees, and having ruled many kings during his childhood, he is the benefactor of the Vedic path in manifold ways; this is the virtuous way of the Lord. 14.

The enjoyer of sacrifice, the wearer of the heart’s bond, the universal form who stole the garment of the frail woman—may this Rāsa dance, which assumes many bodies even for the protection of the great, protect our embodied selves. 15.

May the Supreme Person, who has made His abode in all things, who is attained by men through loving devotion, who rejoices in the multitude of His servants, and whose sole compassion is for the sight of them—may He protect the universe! 16.

With the weight of the breasts of the cowherd women scratched by the tips of the claws of a jackal hanging from his neck, and having had his attire playfully arranged by young maidens—may this Śeṣa be for your peace.

May this very Daṇḍapāṇi, who dwells in the hermitage of the Great One, the chastiser of those people who have disciplined their souls according to the rules and injunctions for their welfare, and the pacifier of all suffering, be for our purification. 18.
Thus praised directly by the high-souled Garuḍa, he then summoned Gaṅgā, who flows through the three paths, for the sake of worship.
Then the five-faced one appeared visibly upon the mountain; with that water, the son of Vinatā performed the offering for his feet.

When Hari then said to Garuḍa, "Choose a boon," he replied: "By your grace, may I become your sole vehicle—glorious, endowed with strength, heroism, and prowess, and invincible to gods and daityas alike. (21)
This stone, renowned by my name, removes all sins; by the mere remembrance of it, poison and disease shall not arise for men.
Having spoken thus, the son of Vinatā then became silent; saying "Om," Viṣṇu then spoke these beneficial words.

"Go to Badarī, which is frequented by Nārada. Having performed your ablutions at the Nāradatīrtha and other sites, and having observed three days of fasting while pure, you will easily obtain my vision there. (24)
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu vanished like a flash of lightning; then Garuḍa, arriving swiftly at Badarī with joy, [proceeded]. (25)
Having reached Vahnitīrtha and taking refuge at that stone with single-minded devotion, he bathed in the Nārada-tīrthas and then undertook the practice of his vows.
Then, having beheld the presence of the Blessed One at the Nārada-tīrtha and having paid obeisance according to the prescribed rite, he departed for his city with His permission.
From that time forward, it is called "Gāruḍī" in the three worlds. || 28 ||
Skanda said: O Lord of Lords, tell me what the majesty of Vārāhī is like; what is her merit, what is her fruit, and likewise, what is her name and how is it? (29)
Śiva said: Having raised the earth from the netherworld (rasātala) and slain Hiraṇyākṣa, the enemy of the gods, in battle, he arrived at Badarī.
Mahādeva remained through the duration of the kalpa by means of yogic concentration; indeed, he established his own abode solely because of the excellence of Badarī.
The Blessed One indeed established his presence there in the form of a stone. Having gone there, a person should bathe in the pure waters of the Gaṅgā.
