Having given a gift according to one's own ability, with a tranquil mind, one should remain at the waters of the Gaṅgā for a day and night and recite [the mantra] with a one-pointed mind.
And the vision of the deity arises for that man upon the stone; what is the use of saying more here, for whatever the practitioner shall speak [shall come to pass]. (34)
That succeeds for him quickly, even if it should be very difficult to accomplish.
Skanda said: "O Lord, tell me the majesty of the Nārasiṃhī stone; by your grace, O Mahādeva, I have heard that which is difficult to obtain."
Śiva said: Having slain Hiraṇyakaśipu with the very tip of his nail as if in play, his limbs were ablaze with the fire of his wrath, resembling the fire of universal destruction.
Then, having arrived and stood at a distance, the compassionate gods praised that Blessed Lord, who had assumed a physical form through his divine play.

Then Hari, of fierce prowess, being pleased and pervading the foremost of gods and asuras with his own splendor, said: "O gods, choose from me a boon that is the sole cause of the bliss of liberation."

Then the Self-born Lord, the sovereign of the Asuras, his face adorned with a smile, spoke these words: "O Narasimha, withdraw this exceedingly fierce form of yours which strikes terror into all embodied beings."

Having thus fashioned this divine form in many ways according to the prescribed rite and having placed it upon the mountains and other locations, he said: "O gods, subduers of enemies, I am pleased; what service may I perform for you?"

Then the immortals said: "O you whose universal form agitates all things with this very appearance, we desire as our chosen boon that four-armed state which binds one to the cause of inner peace and tranquility. (42)

Then Hari, having surveyed the universe with his divine vision, went to Viśālā; seeing the world sporting in the waters of the Gaṅgā with its mind distracted, the Blessed One spoke to the gods and asuras.

Then the immortals, their fears stilled, beheld the Lord situated in the midst of the waters; having bowed and circumambulated him, they then returned in due order to their own city, their devotion firmly established.

Then all the sages, whose wealth was their asceticism, arrived bowing low under the weight of devotion; with palms joined, they praised Hari, the Man-lion of most wonderful prowess, with these words. 45.

The sages said: Salutations, salutations to you, O Lord of the worlds, Lord of the universe, source of fearlessness for all, embodiment of the universe! O ocean of compassion, O holy ford of worshipful lotus feet, O Lord of Śrī, bestow your grace upon us. (46)

You are one, yet you appear manifold through your own innate māyā, just as water in a jar is divided by its limiting adjuncts; O You who assume diverse forms according to the desires of Your devotees, be gracious, O Universal-faced One, O Creator of the Universe! 47.
Then the blessed Lord Nṛsiṃha, possessing the prowess of a lion, being pleased, spoke these charming words: "Choose a boon from me."
The sages said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the worlds, if you are pleased, then by your grace Viśālā must not be abandoned; this is the boon we desire. (49)
"So be it," they said; then all the sages departed for their own hermitages. Nṛsiṃha, too, remaining in the form of a stone, became intent on sporting in the water.
Having observed three fasts and being devoted to recitation and meditation, one beholds the very form of Nṛsiṃha in person; of this there is no doubt.
The mortal who, being pure, hears this with faith or causes it to be heard, shall be liberated from all sins and attain residence in Vaikuṇṭha.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Garuḍa-śilā, Vārāhī-śilā, and Nārasiṃhī-śilā," in the Dialogue between Śiva and Kārttikeya within the Badarikāśrama-māhātmya, in the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: For what purpose does the Blessed One dwell there with such devotion? What is the merit and what is the fruit of seeing him, touching him, and so forth?
O Father, please tell me out of compassion the fruit of consuming the food offering (naivedya) after performing a great worship, as well as the fruit of circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa).
Śiva said: In ancient times, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, for the welfare of all beings, the Blessed Lord appeared there in embodied form, established in austerity and yoga.

In the Tretā age, indeed, one who is solely intent on the practice of yoga is found among the hosts of sages; however, when the Dvāpara age has arrived, one established in knowledge is truly difficult to find.
The Blessed One became difficult to behold for both the sages and the deities; consequently, the hosts of sages and gods were unable to attain the state of the Blessed One.

Having reached the state of Svayambhū with their minds filled with wonder, those sages whose wealth is penance went there, and placing Bṛhaspati at their head, they joyfully bowed and spoke to the Lord of the World.

The gods said: Salutations to you, the refuge of all worlds, the destroyer of the distress of those seeking shelter, the provider of sustenance, filled with compassion, O Grandfather, Lord of the gods! Our calamities are to be reported to you; you are our savior and our father.
Brahmā said: For what purpose have you come, with your minds agitated by wonder, assembled together with the sages? Tell me the reason for your arrival.
The gods said: "When the Dvāpara age has arrived, the Lord of vast intellect is not seen at all in Viśālā; tell us, what is the reason for that?"
Was Viśālā abandoned by him, or did he go away of his own accord? Or was it due to some offense on our part, and how might he be propitiated? (10)

Brahmā said: "I do not know this, yet I have heard it today from your own mouths. O gods, what is the cause that the Blessed One has transcended the range of your vision? Come, let us go to the shore of the Ocean of Milk."
Having been addressed thus, those dwellers of heaven, placing Brahmā at their head, went to the shore of the Ocean of Milk, as did the sages whose wealth is penance.
Having gone there, they praised with words of variegated meaning the Lord of the World, the God of gods, Vṛṣākapi, the Sovereign of the Universe.
Brahmā said: Salutations to you, O Supreme Lord of Puruṣas, who dwell in the cave of the heart of all beings; O Vāsudeva, support of all, cause of the universe, and composed of the universe.
You alone are the cause, the lord, and the refuge of all beings; relying upon the power of *māyā*, you wander about, O uniquely beautiful one.

I bow to that Lord of the worlds, who, though one and immutable, appears as many like an actor; though all-pervading, out of compassion he becomes a bee in the lotus-heart of his devotees and bestows manifold bliss. (16)

The gods said: May the Lord Ananta, the infinite soul of all moving and unmoving beings, the ruler of the three worlds who has assumed a physical form for the sake of those people who are like trees in a forest of calamity, look upon us with his compassionate glances. (17)
I worship that Hari, by whose nectar-like essence a person, upon drinking even once, regards supreme liberation as if it were a blade of grass.
Having attained the state of a living soul due to being a reflection of ignorance, yet whose self is tranquil because of its nature as pure consciousness—may he purify the three worlds. 19.

The Gandharvas said: Those who drink even a mere drop of the water from Hari’s feet do not drink again and again the milk from their mother’s breast. When men, by chance, drink the nectar of His names and die, they go to the immortal realm; they never again descend to this world, free from all fear.
Then Hari, being thus praised, rose up visibly from the ocean and said: "Brahmā alone knows that supreme [truth], which is unperceived by others; no one else knows it."
Then Brahmā, having understood that and bowed to him, informed the inhabitants of heaven: "O gods, listen with respect."
Having seen that the world was of dull intellect, the Blessed One vanished; and having heard these words of his, all the gods went to heaven.
Then, in the form of an ascetic, I shall uplift Hari from the sacred ford named Nārada and establish him there out of a desire for the welfare of the world.
By the mere sight of whom even great sins dissolve in an instant, like deer upon seeing a lion. (25)
O Six-faced One, having conquered both merit and demerit and beheld the all-pervading Lord Hari, the Master of Badarī, they attain liberation without effort.
Most sacred fords have been abandoned by Hari due to the influence of the Kali age; yet, having reached Badarī, he remains there in person.
Having reached this age of Kali, those who desire liberation must visit Badarī, having abandoned all other sacred fords without exception.
Without knowledge or yoga, and even without the exertion of wandering to sacred pilgrimage sites, a living being attains the state of absolute liberation in a single lifetime. (29)
He by whom Hari has been worshipped throughout thousands of previous births shall go to see Badarī, where a living being does not grieve.
By uttering "Badarī, Badarī" even incidentally, that best of men kindles a lamp for the affliction of the darkness of saṃsāra. (31)
Just as the affliction of darkness does not arise through the light of a lamp, so too, having beheld Badarī, whence can there be fear of death for a person? 32.
I bow to that Lord of Badarī, by whose very sight sins weep and are rendered powerless, having beheld the path to liberation.
The earth, together with its mountains and forests, has been circumambulated ten times; likewise, at Badarī, it is as if one has performed a circumambulation of Hari at every single step.
Whatever merit is gained from a horse sacrifice and from a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices, that same merit is obtained at every step by circumambulating Hari at Badarī.
Whatever merit is gained from the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa during the four months of the rainy season, that same merit is obtained at every step by circumambulating Hari at Badarī.

That which is well-performed through the Atikṛcchra and Mahākṛcchra penances according to the Vedic rules is equal to performing a circumambulation of Hari at Badarī, where the merit is attained at every step.
O Six-faced One, by eating even a single grain of the food offered to Viṣṇu at Badarī, one purifies their sin just as fire purifies gold.
Whatever food the Blessed One partakes of with the sages such as Nārada and others, that should be eaten by all without hesitation for the sake of purifying one's being. (39)
Even the immortals, desiring to enjoy Badarī from every side by some pretext, go there devotedly to partake of Viṣṇu’s consecrated offering.
After the meal, the devotees led by Prahlāda depart for their own abodes; then they enter the realm of Hari.
Whatever sin has been committed knowingly during childhood, youth, or old age, it dissolves by eating the *naivedya* (food offerings) of Viṣṇu at Badarī.
For whatever sin a penance lasting until the end of life has been proclaimed, that is removed by eating what has been offered to Viṣṇu at Badarī.

A human being attains liberation at other sacred fords through diligent effort; however, by eating the food offering (naivedya) of Viṣṇu, a man obtains residence in the same world as the Lord (sālokya).
He who has the form of Hari in his heart, His name in his mouth, the food offering in his stomach, and the water from His feet along with the floral remains upon his head—he is Acyuta himself.
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife—all these go to destruction by eating the food offerings (naivedya) of Viṣṇu at Badarī.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred field equal to Badarī, a treasure equal to the food offering (naivedya), or a sacred field equal to that of Nārada. 47.
Badarī should be visited with great effort; one should eat what is offered there. The Lord should be beheld at Vahnitīrtha, where bathing is exceedingly difficult to attain. 48.
Whatever sacred fords, vows, and observances exist upon the earth, the water from the feet at Viśālā shall be more purifying than all of them combined. (49)
What is the use of his gifts, austerities, or the fatigue of wandering to sacred fords, if he obtains even a single drop from the water that washed Viṣṇu’s feet at Badarī?
O Six-faced One, they speak of expiatory rites only so long as the water from the feet of Viṣṇu at Badarī is not obtained.
Or for those men who desire the path of liberation without effort, they should diligently partake of the food offering (naivedya) of Viṣṇu.
Those sinful men who accept [gifts] become partakers of saṃsāra; for them, the fruit resulting from their pilgrimage is never produced.

By reviling the food offering (naivedya) of Viṣṇu, those who revile him fall into the darkness of ignorance; by consuming the food offering, there is indeed the purification of the mind—of this there is no doubt. (54)
Those who, having personally brought the food offering, feed the Brāhmaṇas—what need have they for the fruit of the Tulāpuruṣa gift? They have already achieved their life's purpose.
The merit that is obtained by making great gifts at Kurukṣetra when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu is equal to that obtained by giving even a single mouthful at Badarī. || 56 ||

Having reached the sacred field of Badarī, one should diligently offer even a single morsel of food; this is the great means there at Badarī for pleasing Hari. Even though he is dear to Viṣṇu, he becomes the beloved of Viṣṇu through providing food to ascetics.
There is no god equal to Viṣṇu, nor is there a city equal to Viśālā; there is no vessel like a mendicant, and indeed nothing equal to Ṛṣitīrtha.
Even Brahmā is unable to describe the fruit of the merit of those meritorious men who observe the Cāturmāsya vow. || 59 ||
The attainment of fruits by mendicants is proclaimed here with its distinctions; the merit arising from hearing the Vedānta is said to be tenfold. (60)
It is held that by the mere sight of Badarī, mendicants become partakers of the fruit of liberation, especially during the Cāturmāsya period.

O son, for renunciants at the site of Badarī, liberation rests in the palm of their hand without effort; even for those fools who have fallen into dullness and are hypocrites wearing saffron robes, liberation stands within the palm of their hand simply by the sight of Badarī. (62)
Whether they be wise or ignorant, whether they be renunciants or observers of fixed vows, Badarī must be visited by those who desire its fruits. (63)
Having heard this meritorious chapter, even if only incidentally, a human being is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Śiva and Kārttikeya," within the "Greatness of Badarikāśrama" section of the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, in the second part of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: O Maheśvara, O Father, please tell me out of compassion the greatness of that sacred site where your skull fell from your hand.
Śiva said: This sacred ford is extremely secret and is saluted by gods and asuras alike; even a man who has killed a Brahmin becomes pure merely by bathing there.
Five sacred fords (tīrthas) reside within the skull at Pāpamocana; bathing, austerity, and charity performed there are all held to be inexhaustible.
Having performed the piṇḍa offering according to the prescribed rites, one may deliver one's ancestors from hell; this is declared to be the Pitṛ-tīrtha, eight times superior to Gayā.
Through the libation of sesame seeds, the ancestors go to the highest heaven.
Remaining steadfast for a day and night, devoted to recitation and concentrated in mind, his great desired success arises at that very moment.
All rites for the sake of the next world performed at the Kapālamocana tīrtha are unimpeded; there is nothing superior to it for the performance of ancestral rites (pitṛkarma).
Skanda said: "O Father, where indeed is the Brahmatīrtha, what kind of fruit does it yield, and who dwells there? Please tell me. (8)
Śiva said: Once, Madhu and Kaiṭabha seized the Vedas from the lotus-mouth of Prajāpati, who was seated upon the navel-lotus of Viṣṇu, and departed.
Then, having risen from his bed, the lotus-born one, desiring to create, was unable to bring forth the world because his memory had been stolen in the absence of the Veda.
Then, having arrived at Badarī, which was protected by Hari, he bowed down and praised the eternal Blessed One.
Then, from that sacrificial pit, there emerged Hayashirsha, bearing his own weapons, clad in yellow garments, white-complexioned, four-armed, and with a most haughty gaze.

Most wonderful was he, whose eyes were manifest and harsh, who scattered the mass of clouds with his flickering rays, and who, having eclipsed the entire multitude of lights with his own splendor, appeared full of compassion, preceded by Druhiṇa (Brahmā). || 13 ||
Beholding him, even Brahmā was overwhelmed with wonder; bowing down, he offered praise with a gracious gaze.
Brahmā said: Salutations to the one whose navel is a lotus; salutations to you, the refuge of Kamalā; salutations to you, the abode of Kamalā, who wears a garland of expansive forest flowers.
Homage to the one who consists of pure consciousness, who dwells within the cave of the heart; homage to you, the Blessed One, Hṛṣīkeśa, the peaceful. || 16 ||

Salutations to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who has assumed a physical form for the sake of protecting his devotees; salutations to the Brahman, the bearer of the mace, who destroys endless afflictions. || 17 ||
Salutations to Viṣṇu, the victorious one, who has performed the task of bringing about the cessation of the various miseries of saṃsāra and who is the protector of all living beings. || 18 ||
Homage to the one whose virtuous conduct has brought all worldly existence to rest; to the one whose fame consists in the cessation and establishment of the best among gods and asuras.

Thus addressed by the Lord of the Gods, Maheśvara—who dwells in the heart and knows all the deeds of every deity—then suddenly entered between them, bound those two enemies of the gods, and indeed slew them with ease.
Then, taking his own Veda, he went into the presence of Brahmā; having given his Veda to him, he became composed after being praised.
From that time forward, that holy ford manifested by Brahmā became known as Brahmakuṇḍa, renowned throughout the three worlds.
By the mere sight of whom even people who have committed great sins are instantly freed from their transgressions and go to the world of Brahmā. || 23 ||
Those people who perform ritual bathing or likewise observe vows, having transcended the world of Brahmā, they go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Skanda said: What did the Creator do after receiving the Vedas from Janārdana? Tell me all of this and whatever else there is, out of compassion, right now.
Mahādeva said: "O dear son, even after seeing Badarikāśrama, the thought does not arise in the minds of the four Vedas to go there, even together with Brahmā."
Then, seeing Brahmā thus distressed, the Siddhas dwelling in Janaloka praised him according to the rules and, having prostrated themselves, spoke as follows: || 27 ||

The Siddhas said: "The command of the Blessed One must be carried out by all things, both stationary and moving. The Blessed One is the creator, the destroyer, the father, and the teacher of all living beings. (28)
Stability near Brahmā has been ordained by Hari himself; yet, although this cessation (nivṛtti) prevails, it remains free from affliction.
"Let one of your forms remain here in liquid form; let the second go back again to the world of Brahmā along with Brahmā. (30)
Then those Vedas, possessing hearts and having their forms divided into two, went with Brahmā to the world of Brahmā, filled with great joy.

Then the four-faced one created the three worlds according to the prescribed rules; so that within the Vedas, which exist in liquid form, the acts of bathing, giving, and austerity may not be interrupted until the dissolution of all beings.
Those men who perform three fasts with a specific fruit in mind will undoubtedly become expounders of all four Vedas. || 33 ||
And the four Vedas—namely the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan—stand in succession by the side of the Blessed One.
Those who are meritorious, pure, and have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences—such rare individuals as these hear the resonance of the Vedas even in the Kali Yuga.
The Sarasvatī rises to the north of all four Vedas; when chanted, she, in the form of water, destroys the dullness of men.
Standing in the waters of the Sarasvatī and performing recitation with a concentrated mind, his mental focus is never interrupted at any time. (37)
Even the venerable Vedavyāsa, by whose grace he became noble-minded and came to know the meaning of the Purāṇa collections—of this there is no doubt. (38)
For the welfare of all three worlds, the Lord of the universe established Speech, which bestows the power of eloquence, according to the prescribed rite. (39)
Through seeing, touching, bathing in, worshipping, praising, and bowing down to Sarasvatī, there shall never be a severance of her [lineage] in his family at any time.
For those men who recite mantras on the bank of the Sarasvatī, the accomplishment of mantras arises especially and without delay; there is no doubt in this matter. (41)
What is the use of saying more here? Speech bestows the power of eloquence; appearing in liquid form, it becomes radiant through the mere sight of men.
To the south of that place, on this side, is the famous sacred site known as Dravadhārā, where Indra performed his penance at Indrapada.
Having performed most rigorous penance and having gratified Janārdana, he attained the station of Indra, which is saluted by gods and asuras alike.
Austerity, charity, recitation, burnt offerings, vows, observances, and restraints—[all these] are said to possess infinite merit there; that sacred ford is exceedingly difficult to attain. (45)

On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight every month, O propitiation of Hari, having bathed in a sacred bathing place and approached the Sutrāmācchanda [shrine] together with his companions; || 46 ||
Having observed two fasts and having worshipped Janārdana, one is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śakra.
In that very place is Mānasodbheda, the destroyer of all sins, which is difficult for all living beings to attain; there those great sages reside.
They untie the knot of consciousness and matter everywhere; thus they are celebrated by the sages as the "Manifestation of the Mind."
"They pierce the knots of the heart, sever manifold doubts, and exhaust our karmas; thus, it became known as 'Mānasodbheda'."
If, by the power of fortune, a person should obtain even a mere drop here, he attains liberation at that very moment; what could be greater than this? || 51 ||

These hosts of sages dwell in their abodes within mountain caves, subsisting on fruits, roots, and water; they have conquered their minds and sense-objects, possess sharpened intellects, and are agitated by the fear of sin as if by the fear of the Kali age.

These sages have acquired excellent garments from the weight of hermitages containing caves and waterfalls stirred by the wind; they have subdued the invincible prowess of the senses through the practice of the three daily ablutions.
Alas, there are many means of practice that cause bodily affliction; but in this world, the means that is easily obtained is the vision of the piercing of the mind. 54.
On whichever day a meritorious person obtains this water, he gradually becomes equal to Vyāsa and even equal to Yama and the Pitṛs.
This Kāmyatīrtha brings desires under control for men; yet, through desirelessness, liberation shall be attained—this is the certainty regarding both.
If a man should perform a desire-rite out of negligence, he will certainly attain liberation after enjoying the fruit; of this there is no doubt. || 57 ||
Having enjoyed desired pleasures in the worlds such as Maharloka and others, a person returns once more to the realm of desire under the sway of craving.
The wise should strive for the attainment of the goals of human existence; it is my conviction that these are not lost here at the sacred ford of Mānasodbheda.
To the west of Mānasodbheda is the sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Vasudhārā, which captivates the minds of all and is difficult to find even in the three worlds.
Having heard from Nārada that Badarikāśrama is superior to all holy places in the three worlds, all the Vasus arrived there.
For thirty thousand years they performed most rigorous penance, subsisting on leaves and water; thereafter, they attained perfection.
Having attained joy and relief from seeing the Blessed One, their exhaustion vanished; with the lotuses of their faces blossomed by the abundance of bliss in their hearts. (63)
Having beheld the divine Nārāyaṇa and obtained a delightful boon, they attained supreme bliss and sovereignty through the happiness of devotion to Hari, and were filled with joy.
Having bathed here, drunk the water, and worshipped Janārdana, one enjoys happiness in this world and goes to the supreme state in the end.
Here, the light of the meritorious is seen from within the water; having seen which, one does not enter the dwelling of a womb again.
Those sinful ones who are born of impure fathers and whose conduct follows the ways of heretics—upon their heads, the waters of initiation rarely fall at any time.
Having remained pure for three days, having worshipped Janārdana, and having fasted with devotion to the Lord, virtuous people behold the Siddhas.
Those who are fickle there, who do not speak the truth, who are greedy, and who are intent on mockery, the property of others, the wives of others, and deceitful grasping; || 69 ||
For those whose minds are defiled—who are covered in dirt and rags, unpacified, impure, and have abandoned virtuous conduct—no fruit arises here in this world.

Those practitioners there who are peaceful, rare, and who follow the path of the prescribed rules—for them, their recitation, austerity, fire-oblation, giving, vows, and acts of worship [bear fruit]. (71)
For when performed according to one's ability, they indeed bestow inexhaustible fruits.
Whatever auspicious deeds are performed by embodied beings, they yield great results beginning with [the attainment of] Mahat, and ultimately bestow unsurpassed supreme bliss.

What fruit here is more worthy of being heard than that for which the wise, seeking rewards, go; and thereafter, those desiring what is dear to Hari, devoted to the path of heaven, become joyful? (74)

Where there are no obstructors of actions, because of fear of Hari, [those actions] are successfully accomplished; and those of good body, who are discerning and devoted to the path of action, enjoy the fruit.

Those who read this account of the sacred pilgrimage site as it has been revealed, and those who cause others to read it—adorned with a spirit of devotion—they go to the auspicious abode of Hari. (76)

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Vasudhārā Tīrtha," in the dialogue between Śiva and Kārttikeya within the *Badarikāśrama-māhātmya*, in the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śiva said: Thereupon, in the south-western quarter, five streams fall downward; know them, O Six-faced One, to be Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, Gayā, Naimiṣa, and Kurukṣetra in liquid form. (1)
Formerly, you went to the abode of Brahmā with defiled forms; corrupted by the fault of the sins of sinners, your intellects were perverted. || 2 ||
Having gone there and paid homage to Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, they all, with palms joined in reverence, spoke the reason for their arrival.
Having heard that, the Lord of the World, resorting to meditation and smiling, spoke these charming words while recollecting the hermitage of Badarī.
"Do not fear; go quickly to Hari’s Badarikāśrama, by the mere mention of which merit shall be attained immediately. (5)
Then, having bowed to the Grandfather with a surge of joy, they went with wide-open eyes to Viśālā, which possesses immeasurable splendor.
Merely by entering it, their sins were instantly dispelled; then, assuming their two-fold forms, they returned eagerly to their own abodes.
And in another form as liquid, these five remain stainless; having bathed in them according to the prescribed rite and performed his daily duties, one becomes pure.
Having obtained the fruit of each respective sacred ford (tīrtha) and having worshipped Janārdana while being devoted to five fasts, one goes at the end to the supreme state.
Having enjoyed many pleasures here, one shall attain the state of being in the same world as Hari (sālokya).
Beyond that is the supreme and pure holy site named Somakuṇḍa, where the Lord Soma, the storehouse of digits, performed his penance.
Skanda said: O best among speakers, tell me the majesty of Somakuṇḍa; by your grace, O Supreme Lord, I desire to hear it.

Śiva said: Long ago, the illustrious Soma, the son of Atri, having attained youth and repeatedly hearing from the Gandharvas about the happiness of the celestial dwellers, then approached his father to ask how that [happiness] might be obtained. 13.
Soma said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, ocean of the nectar of compassion, how is heaven—the most excellent of all things—attained by everyone? (14)
"O Lord, O Father, please tell me out of compassion what effort I must make so that I may become the master of the planets, constellations, stars, and medicinal herbs. (15)
Atri said: "O son, having propitiated Govinda through austerities, restraints, and observances, what indeed is difficult for the virtuous to attain in this world and the next? (16)
Then, having heard from Nārada about that supremely pure sacred field, he bowed to his father and departed for the northern direction toward Badarī.
Having gone there, he performed the worship of Viṣṇu with pure fruits and recited the supreme, enchanting eight-syllable mantra which is to be constantly chanted.
For eighty-eight thousand years, O Lord, he performed most supreme penance that struck fear into all the worlds.
Then the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, being pleased, approached and spoke to Soma according to the prescribed rite: "O you of noble vows, choose a boon."
Then Soma, having risen and bowed down again and again, said: "By your grace, may I become the lord of the planets, lunar mansions, stars, and medicinal herbs, as well as of all the twice-born."
Hari said: "Choose another boon from this one that is difficult for those like you to obtain. O son of Himavat, he then chose boons from them.
Then, O son, Soma, being deeply dejected, again performed great penance for thirty thousand years according to the measurement of the gods.

Then the Blessed One, his heart filled with compassion, approached him and said, "Choose a boon; may it be well with you; I stand before you as the giver of boons. Soma chose such a boon, and having heard that, Hari vanished from sight.
Thereupon, Soma, being deeply dejected, again performed great penance; he practiced that most difficult austerity for forty thousand years. (25)
Then Hari himself, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace, being pleased, spoke these charming words to Soma, the exhausted treasure-house of asceticism: || 26 ||
Arise, arise! May it be well with you; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows! I, the storehouse of asceticism, have surely been propitiated by your penance.

Soma said: "If you, O Blessed One, foremost among the givers of boons, are pleased with me, then grant me sovereignty over the planets, the lunar mansions, and the stars; likewise, O Lord of the World, over the medicinal herbs, the Brahmins, and the night. (28)

The Blessed Lord said: "O child, though what you have requested is difficult to grant, I shall nevertheless bestow it upon you; let it be so. Thereupon, all the inhabitants of heaven assembled and, with great respect, duly consecrated Soma as king.
Then, having ascended a celestial chariot adorned with white garments, the Maker of Night, being praised by the gods, departed for heaven.
From that time forward, that rare holy site became known as Somakuṇḍa; for by the mere sight of it, men indeed become free from all defects.

By touching which, even those who are censurable go to the world of Soma; where, having bathed according to the prescribed rite and having satiated the ancestors and the deities, [one attains that state].
Having performed three fasts and having worshipped Janārdana, one pierces through the world of Soma and attains the world of Viṣṇu.

For them there is no return, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. Having remained for three nights and worshipped Janārdana, while especially performing the recitation (japa), the perfection of the mantra is produced.
Whatever sin has been committed by men through action, mind, or speech—all that goes to destruction here simply by the sight of the Soma-kunda. (35)
Beyond that is the supreme Dvādaśāditya-tīrtha, which removes all sins; having performed a severe penance there once more, Kāśyapa attained the state of the Sun.

Rare in the three worlds and the sole cause for the perfection of austerity, a man who bathes according to the rules on Sundays, on the seventh lunar day, or during the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), is purified from the sins committed throughout seven lifetimes by that very act of bathing.
Having performed the Pārāka penance according to the rules, Janārdana is to be worshipped; having enjoyed happiness in the world of the Sun, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
But one who is overcome by a great disease, having bathed and drunk the water and become pure, shall be freed from disease before long; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. (39)
This supreme ford has four streams and is enchanting to the eye; Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa abide here in liquid form.
By the command of Hari himself, in this Vaiṣṇava field, the goals of human existence have become liquefied as the cause of liberation for all beings.
Those who worship these [deities] arranged in sequence—residing in the directions beginning with the East, possessing form as if they were embodiments of Dharma—will indeed always possess serenity.

These four, who are somehow gathered in one field and are unattainable even by the gods, behold [the Lord] after swiftly attaining their final birth, owing to the mass of merit accumulated in previous lives. (43)

Those wicked people who associate with the wicked, and for whom forgiveness, uprightness, life, and victory are of no primary importance, serve as playthings for village women; they do not perceive the goals of human existence before long.
In that very way, they soon perceive those goals of human endeavor which have the knowledge of reality as their sole cause.
O Six-faced One, here the gods beginning with Brahmā and the sages whose wealth is austerity come together on the auspicious festival day, purified, to bathe.

Beyond that is the holy ford named Satyapada, enchanting to all; this sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is triangular in shape and destroys all impurities. On the eleventh lunar day, Hari himself comes there to purify it.
After that, all the ṛṣis and sages whose wealth is their austerity come according to the prescribed rites to bathe in the pool named Satyapada.
There, at midday on the day of Hari, few rare individuals devoted to the vow of truth hear the singing of the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Upon the mere sight of this holy ford, even great sins flee in fear, like deer upon seeing a lion. (50)
Having performed his bath according to the injunctions prescribed in his own Vedic branch, the wise man attains Satyaloka and from there reaches the state of ultimate liberation.
Having remained pure for a day and night and having fasted, and having worshipped Janārdana according to his ability, he becomes a recipient of liberation while still alive.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, established in the triangle and composed in mind, perform penance daily to please the source of all the worlds.
The sacred ford (tīrtha), adorned with a triangle and known by the name Satyapadapradam, should be visited with great effort by those desiring liberation from all sins.
Even Brahmā is unable to describe the greatness of those who perform recitation, austerity, hymns to Hari, worship, praise, and salutation. (55)
Then [he reached] the hermitage of Nara-Nārāyaṇa named Ativimala; there, two kinds of supremely pure water are seen.

It is certain that through both [means] there arises joy for both; having bathed there with effort and having worshipped Janārdana, one is liberated from all sins at that very moment—of this there is no doubt. (57)
Then, on the peak that is the abode of Nārāyaṇa, there shall be a pure and holy sacred site (tīrtha) of stainless form, which brings about the manifestation of Urvaśī. || 58 ||
Skanda said: O Father, how did the manifestation of that Urvaśī occur upon the peak? What is the merit there, and what is the fruit? Tell me, for my curiosity is great. (59)
Śiva said: O Six-faced One, Mūrti was the wife of Dharma; from her were born Nara and Nārāyaṇa, who were indeed the Lord himself in person.
Having received the command of their parents, they both set their minds upon performing penance; in those two mountains, they stood like the very embodiments of asceticism.
Seeing them, Śakra was struck with wonder and dispatched Manmatha along with his attendants to Mount Gandhamādana so that their asceticism might be destroyed.
Having displayed his prowess according to the prescribed rites and having recognized the manifestation of Nārāyaṇa’s strength, the Lord of the World, perceiving their dejected minds, spoke to them.
Hari said: "For what purpose have you come? Please accept hospitality."
Having spoken thus, and having given them fruits and roots as well as Urvaśī, she vanished right before their eyes, creating an obstacle for them.
Having gone to heaven while she was terrified, they told Śakra of Hari’s power; and Śakra, having obtained Urvaśī, became filled with singular joy.
From that time forth, that sacred ford became famous by the separate name of Urvaśī, where the Blessed One himself dwells, consisting of ascetic power.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite and fasted for two nights, and having worshipped Hari there, a man shall become Nārāyaṇa.
O son, having reached Urvaśīkuṇḍa, a man attains the world of Urvaśī by the mere act of bathing, according to his desire.
The Blessed One, the very embodiment of austerity, always remained there in the vicinity of Urvaśī-kuṇḍa, contemplating the welfare of all living beings.

Even the wind carries above it the fragrance obtained solely from the lotus feet of the Lord of Śrī; through contact with which, the ripening of the burden of sins does not occur upon the laps of those afflicted by the impurities of the Kali age.

Through association with whom, the weary one—dwelling alone in the mountain caves and serving only Acyuta—attained joy; now, bearing the pair of feet of the Lord of Śrī, he approaches from all sides toward the great wind of austerity that brings about tranquility.

A worm, though full of its own filth, mocks the gods when it has subdued its wicked impulses and become free from desire; wherever it may dwell, by casting off the offering of flowers defiled by its own contact, it shall attain that supreme state.

Where the minds of sages, devoted solely to Your planted lotus feet, perceive no external objects; and where You Yourself, O Lord of the Cowherds, bestow Your own abode upon those people who have approached You through the proper succession.
There are many sacred sites on the mountain inhabited by Nārāyaṇa that swiftly remove all sins; I know them, but other people do not.
In this terrible cave of saṃsāra where the self is obscured, a man who reaches Urvaśīkuṇḍa shall dwell there for one day.
On the southern side of Urvaśī, the weapons of the Lord of the World are present; by the sight of them, one shall not suffer from the fear of weapons. (77)
Whoever hears this with devotion, or causes it to be heard while composed in mind, being liberated from all sins, attains the same world as Hari.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Pañcadhārā and Other Tīrthas," in the dialogue between Śiva and Kārttikeya within the *Badarikāśrama-māhātmya*, in the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śiva said: To the south of Brahmakuṇḍa is the great Narāvāsagiri, where Meru, the beauty of the world, was established by the Blessed One. || 1 ||
Skanda said: "O Father, how was Mount Meru established by the Blessed One in the presence of men? I have a great curiosity; please tell me if it pleases you. (2)
Mahādeva said: When the Blessed One’s residence in Viśālā was established, the gods, great seers, Siddhas, along with the Vidyādharas and Cāraṇas [gathered there]. || 3 ||
Leaving behind the peaks of Mount Meru, they were eager for a vision of the Blessed One; the joy of beholding the Blessed One surpassed even their celestial abode. || 4 ||
Then, O Six-faced One, for the sake of their happiness, the Blessed Lord, who increases the joy of all, playfully produced peaks of Mount Meru with a single hand and established them there.
Then, having beheld the mountain made of gold, they all became serene and praised the flawless Nārāyaṇa.

The gods said: To him who, for our happiness and for rest from worldly existence, assumed playful forms and brought the golden mountain here; to him, the conqueror of hundreds of harassers of the gods, the sole partisan of the thirty deities, whose glory is fierce austerity—to him we offer salutation.

Whatever that best among the knowers of the one [Brahman] performs out of compassion—He who is like a mass of fire to the mountain of cotton that is the suffering of the wretched—may He be pleased with that very act of His, which has never been performed by any person whatsoever.

May he—who, like a compassionate father, bestows perfect instruction upon us of lofty intellects, being himself full of his own attainment; who is an ocean of nectar filled with the casting of glances expert in protecting the three worlds—ward off our calamities. (9)

The sages said: We bow eternally to You, the perpetual and eternal One, upon whom this entire universe is superposed as a single toy for the play of the unborn, all-pervading Lord, appearing as real; and whose form is ever-resorted to even by the multitude of suns.

The Siddhas said: "It is our firm conviction that by the mere fragment of whose grace even great beings attain perfection, while others who dwell in worldly existence cross the terrible ocean of saṃsāra without delay. (11)

The Vidyādharas said: O All-pervading Lord, you who possess a multitude of excellent qualities, whose form is auspiciousness, O Supreme Ruler, cause of the lineage of honor! For those intoxicated by the taste of the nectar from your lotus feet, it is not at all surprising that they have attained their life's purpose. (12)
Then the Blessed One became pleased with those inhabitants of heaven; being told, "Choose a boon," they spoke to that foremost of granter of boons: (13)
The Lord of Ramā, the God of gods himself, is well-pleased with you; Badarī must never be abandoned by you, nor ever Mount Meru.
May those people who behold the peak of Meru, partakers of merit, indeed find their residence upon Meru through your grace. (15)
"Having enjoyed pleasures there for a long time, may there be absorption into you at the end. Having spoken thus, "So be it," Hari vanished on that very spot.
From that time forward, they all dwelt upon the peaks of Mount Meru, being protected again and again in the presence of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Sometimes the sages, whose wealth is their asceticism, remained in heaven, and sometimes they stayed in the midst of Mount Meru, free from fear and free from agitation.
The Blessed One also remained right there in human form, bearing a bow and arrows, glorious and like fire through his asceticism; established in penance, he brought joy to the multitude of sages.
Beyond that is the supreme sacred site (tīrtha) saluted by the guardians of the world (lokapālas), where Hari himself established the guardians of the world.
Skanda said: "O Father, O high-minded one, how were the world-protectors (lokapālas) established there by the Blessed One? Great is my curiosity; please tell me."
Śiva said: Once, Hari, residing here in the midst of Mount Meru, prepared to observe the conduct of the gods and the foremost sages.
Seeing him, the inhabitants of heaven rose up suddenly, paid homage, and all said with humility: "Be gracious, O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord! (23)
Having rested for a moment and duly observed that sparse terrain, they conversed with one another, reflecting upon the presence of sages and gods there.
Then, laughing, the Blessed One Madhusūdana spoke, having summoned the guardians of the world: "Those such as you must not remain here."
For indeed, sages, ascetics, and perfected beings dwell here together with their wives; this assembly hall for those such as yourselves was established by me just as in former times.
Then, having gone quickly to that beautiful and excellent mountain, Hari summoned the world-protectors and established them there, O Guha.
Right there, having struck the fire with a mountain-staff out of a desire for water, he created for them a most beautiful pleasure-pool.
Where the gods wander at their own will accompanied by their wives, and the Gandharvas sing and express their approval for the inhabitants of heaven.
There, the days pass for embodied beings as if they were mere moments, due to their delight in forests delightful with the fragrance of flowers. (30)
The Blessed One also bestows bliss upon them right there; he himself comes for their immersion on the twelfth lunar day and on the full moon day.

After that, O Guha, all the ṛṣis and sages whose wealth is penance, having bathed there according to the prescribed rite at midday, behold with their own eyes the supreme, unattached light within the water.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to result from bathing in all the sacred fords (tīrthas), that fruit is obtained in that very instant simply by beholding the Daṇḍapuṣkariṇī.
Where the rites performed for specific desires bear fruit for the wise, and where the offering of funeral cakes yields eightfold the merit compared to Gayā.
O Six-faced One, every act of sacrifice, charity, austerity, and ritual performed on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha is said to be inexhaustible.

Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite, one becomes one who has fulfilled all duties; for this [place] within the Badarī-tīrtha is guarded by the best of the gods. It must not be spoken of anywhere; it has been told to you by me out of affection for you.

What need is there for much to be said here? Those of abundant merit behold this renowned place, protected by the gods alone. This secret is never even incidentally conceived in the minds of others; it is meditated upon day after day only by the gods. (37)

For those who have indeed performed their entire ritual duty toward the Blessed One according to the sequence of the rules for the practice of Vedic study, they behold Daṇḍoda—the excellent sacred ford difficult to find in the three worlds; it is not otherwise, for it has been clearly perceived.
There is no holy ford superior to Daṇḍodaka, no immortal equal to Viṣṇu, and there has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred field equal to Viśālā.
Those who desire to dwell eternally by the side of the Blessed One should, with great effort, cultivate and expand their discernment. (40)
Skanda said: "O you who abide in the state of truth, what holy places (tīrthas) are there here that depend upon the Gaṅgā? Tell me briefly those many places that bring about spiritual welfare."
Mahādeva said: Where the Gaṅgā meets [the Yamunā] in the vicinity of Mānasodbheda, that pure and meritorious tīrtha is greater than Prayāga. || 42 ||
The fruit that would result from subsisting on air for thirty thousand years is obtained by men merely by bathing at the confluence of the Gaṅgā.
To the south of Saṅgama, the Dharmakṣetra is celebrated, where the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa were born in bodily form and through sacred revelation.
That sacred field is the most supreme of all purifiers in the mortal world; there alone does the Blessed Lord Dharma abide in his fourfold form.
Whatever sacrifice, austerity, or gift is performed by men there, there is no exhaustion of that merit even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Then, in the southern quarter, there is the place named Urvaśī-saṅgama, which removes all sins from embodied beings merely by their bathing there.
Then follows the Kūrmoddhāra, which is the direct and sole means for devotion to Hari; by merely bathing there, the purification of the inner being of all creatures arises.
Beyond that is Brahmāvarta, which is the direct cause for attaining the world of Brahmā; by the mere sight of this sacred site, the destruction of all sins occurs. (49)
"There are many sacred fords (tīrthas) here that are difficult for embodied beings to reach; yet, out of regard for you, my child, this has been told to you in brief. (50)
Whoever should constantly hear this, or cause it to be heard with a concentrated mind, being liberated from all sins, attains the abode of Viṣṇu.
The king attains victory; he who desires a son obtains a son; he who desires a daughter obtains a daughter; and the maiden finds a virtuous husband.
One who desires wealth obtains wealth, which is the sole means for fulfilling all desires. || 53 ||
The man who listens with devotion and a concentrated mind for even a single month will undoubtedly attain his desired goal, however difficult it may be to obtain. (54)
In whosever homes this greatness [of the scripture] resides, there shall never be terrible fear of mental or physical ailments, nor poverty, nor strife. (55)
Neither untimely death nor [fear of] serpents and the like, nor even misfortune occurs; likewise, there is no affliction from evil dreams or malevolent planets, nor fear of a foreign kingdom. (56)
It should be recited with great effort during war and the commencement of a military expedition, and with diligence during marriage, dispute, and any auspicious rite. (57)
Whether it be a complete chapter, or merely a section, or even half of that, for the wise, there shall be the accomplishment of all undertakings; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (58)
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory! (Jaya).
The sages said: O Sūta, you have narrated to us the meritorious majesty of Āśvina; we now desire to hear further concerning the glory of Kārtika.
In the Kali age, what destination can there be without effort for those men of defiled minds and evil deeds who are submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra? (3)
"O Lord, tell me this truth: what is that dharma which is superior to all dharmas and brings about liberation, and which grants liberation to men even in this world?"
Sūta said: That which I was asked by you, the sage Nārada, the son of Brahmā, asked of Brahmā, the teacher of the world. || 5 ||
In that very same manner, Satyabhāmā, eager to hear it, questioned Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Universe, regarding the majesty of Kārttika itself.
And that which was spoken by the Vālakhilya sages in the assembly of seers, in the form of a dialogue between Śrī Sūrya and Aruṇa, is exceedingly captivating.
On Mount Kailāsa, Śaṅkara himself described the majesty of Kārttika before Ṣaṇmukha, accompanied by various ancient narratives.
O best of Brahmins, the greatness of Kārttika was previously told by Nārada to Pṛthu after he had heard it from the mouth of Brahmā.
Once, the yogi Nārada arrived at Satyaloka and, with great humility, questioned the Grandfather of all the worlds.
Śrī Nārada said: O Brahman, what fire consumes the abundant fuel of terrible sin, both dry and moist? You ought to tell me that.
O Lord of Gods, there is certainly nothing within the three worlds, nor even within the cosmic egg, that remains unknown to you in your threefold form. 12.
"O Grandfather, tell me specifically of those holy places (tīrthas) which belong to that month—the best of months and the most excellent among the gods. (13)
Brahmā said: Among months, Kārttika is the most excellent; among gods, Madhusūdana; and the holy place named Nārāyaṇa—this triad is indeed difficult to attain in the Kali age.
Nārada said: "O Blessed One, I am your servant and your devotee, O beloved of Hari! Tell me the duties of the Vaiṣṇavas; you are omniscient, O Grandfather. (15)
O Lord, you should first tell me the greatness of the month of Kārttika, as well as the greatness of offering lamps and the observances for those who practice vows.

O Lord, [tell me] the majesty of Gopīcandana and likewise that of Tulasī, as well as the majesty of Dhātrī and the procedure for bathing and other rites; when the commencement of the vow should be performed, and likewise the procedure for its formal conclusion (udyāpana).
You ought to explain every single duty pertaining to Viṣṇu, by which, through your grace, I may attain the state that is free from all affliction.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of his son, Brahmā, filled with joy, remembered Rādhā and Dāmodara and spoke to his offspring.
Brahmā said: "Well asked by you, my son, for the sake of uplifting the world! I shall describe the majesty of Kārtika; of this there is no doubt."
All the holy fords on one side, and all sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees on the other, are not worth even a sixteenth part of the month of Kārttika.
O son, dwelling on one side in Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, or the Himalayas, and on the other side the month of Kārttika—this latter is considered superior to all merit.
On one side are all gifts, including gold equal to Mount Meru; on the other side, O child, is Kārttika, which is always dear to Keśava.
Whatever merit is performed with Viṣṇu in mind during Kārttika, I see no exhaustion of it; this has been told to you by me, O Nārada. (24)
Having attained this human state, which is difficult to obtain and serves as a staircase to heaven, one should so discipline oneself that one does not fall from it again.

O best among the upholders of dharma, he who, having attained this human birth so difficult to obtain, does not practice the dharma as proclaimed for the month of Kārttika, is a slayer of his mother and father. (26)
Indeed, the month of Kārttika is the most excellent among all months; it is the supreme merit among merits and the purifier among purifiers. (27)
O Sage, in this month the thirty-three gods are present; here, bathing, gifts, meals, and vows [are efficacious]. (28)
O Nārada, they bestow sesame-cows, gold, silver, land, garments, and gifts of cows with their whole being.
The gods accept those gifts offered according to the prescribed rites; O best of Brahmins, whatever has been given and likewise whatever austerity has been performed [is accepted by them].
That has been declared by the powerful Viṣṇu to yield inexhaustible fruit; indeed, liberation from sins is highly commended in the month of Kārtika.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, one should give with effort during the month of Kārtika; whatever is given by men in Kārtika dedicated to Viṣṇu [is of great merit].
For that gift of food, O best of Brahmins, especially attains imperishability, just as [the flow of] rivers and mountains, O Nārada. (33)
O brahmin-sage, the depletion of the oceans never occurs; yet, O sage, whatever gift is given during the month of Kārttika [is inexhaustible].
O Brahmin, there is no exhaustion of merit for him; his sin goes away in a thousand ways—he who, upon seeing that Kārttika has arrived, avoids the food of others.
Day after day, one effortlessly obtains the fruit of the *atikṛcchra* penance; there is no month equal to Kārttika, and no age equal to the Kṛta Yuga. (36)
There is no scripture equal to the Veda, no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā; there is no gift equal to food, and no happiness equal to that found with a wife. (37)
Wealth acquired through righteous means is difficult for givers to find; likewise, for those subject to the laws of mortality, it is difficult to offer such wealth at a sacred pilgrimage site.
O tiger among sages, in the month of Kārttika, one who fears sin must perform the worship of the Śāligrāma stone and the remembrance of Vāsudeva. (39)
He who passes such a month of Kārttika without performing any religious rites undoubtedly incurs the exhaustion of previously accumulated merit. (40)
Nārada said: O Grandfather, tell me how one who is incapable [of the full observance] should perform the excellent Kārttika vow, so that he may obtain its fruit. (41)
Brahmā said: When a mortal is unable [to perform it himself], he should then observe the vow in this manner: having given wealth to another, he should have that person perform the Kārttika vow.
Therefore, O best of divine sages, one should undertake merit preceded by the resolve to give; even if one is unable to give material wealth, [one should still do so]. (43)
Then he should perform the drinking of water from a sacred ford; and that mortal who is unable even for that should always joyfully [perform it] for Hari.
And one should perform recollection by name according to the prescribed rules; then, by that means, the fruit arising from the Kārtika vow remains unbroken.
One should perform the vigil for Hari in the temple of either Viṣṇu or Śiva; in the absence of a temple for Śiva or Viṣṇu, one may do so even in the temples of all other deities.
Whether situated in a difficult forest or fallen into calamity, one should perform [the rite] at the foot of an Aśvattha tree or even in groves of Tulasī.
By singing compositions bearing the name of Viṣṇu in the presence of Viṣṇu, a person obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
The man who plays musical instruments shall also obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice; the dancer shall attain the fruit arising from bathing in all the sacred fords.
A man who provides the materials for these [rites] shall obtain all this merit; even by merely hearing or seeing them, one shall attain a sixth part of the fruit.
Even when a man has fallen into calamity and cannot obtain water anywhere, or when he is afflicted by disease, he should perform purification even with the name of Viṣṇu.
He who, while established in the vow, is unable to perform the rite of completion (udyāpana), should afterwards feed Brāhmaṇas for the sake of fulfilling the vow.
If one is unable to offer a lamp oneself, one should light another's lamp, or one should diligently protect it from wind and other dangers.

In the absence of the worship of Śrī Viṣṇu, one should perform the worship of Tulasī and Dhātrī; if even these are unavailable, the observer of the vow should worship Brāhmaṇas or cows; and in their absence as well, he should chant the names of Viṣṇu within his mind.
Nārada said: O Brahmin, speak specifically of the religious duties (dharmas) pertaining to the month of Kārttika.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Praise of the Kārtika Vow," in the *Kārtikamāsa-māhātmya* of the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Brahmā said: Now, O Nārada, I shall describe the religious duties of the month of Kārttika. Upon seeing that Kārttika has arrived, he who avoids the food of others— || 1 ||

He indeed attains liberation; there is no need for deliberation on this point. Among all dharmas, the worship of the guru is considered supreme. O best of sages, through service to the guru, one obtains everything.
When the Guru is pleased, all the gods, including Indra, shall be pleased; when the Guru is angry, all the gods, including Indra, shall be angry.
When the month of Kārttika has arrived, having performed many religious rites, || 4 ||
Without having performed service to one's guru, one finds only hells.
Whatever has been instructed by the teacher, that he should perform.
O Brahmin, once commanded by the Guru, one must not transgress his word; even if suffering and the like are encountered, one should go to the Guru for refuge.
Whether in the state of being a mother or a father, the wise person should remember only the guru; for that which is not obtained from the guru is indeed not obtainable anywhere else.

By the grace of the guru, one certainly attains everything; of this there is no doubt. Medhāvin, Kapila, and Sumati, who possessed great ascetic power, attained immortality through their perfect service to their guru, Gautama.
Therefore, with every effort, one devoted to Viṣṇu should perform service to the guru during the month of Kārttika; thereby, one shall attain liberation.
That best of the twice-born who imparts the Vaiṣṇava dharma to men indeed obtains the merit of gifting the earth together with its oceans.
O observer of noble vows, they will give with their whole being sesame-cow gifts, gold, silver, land, garments, and gifts of cows.
Of all gifts whatsoever, the gift of a daughter in marriage is preeminent.
A thousand cows and a hundred oxen are equal [in merit].
A vehicle is equal to ten oxen, and a horse is equal to ten vehicles; the gift of an elephant excels a thousand gifts of horses. (13)
The gift of gold is equal to thousands of gifts of elephants; and the gift of knowledge is equal to thousands of gifts of gold. || 14 ||
The gift of land excels the gift of knowledge by ten millionfold; the gift of a cow excels a thousand gifts of land. || 15 ||
The gift of food is indeed superior to thousands of gifts of cows; for this world is said to be supported by food, therefore one should give it in the month of Kārtika.
By merely avoiding the food of others, a person obtains the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa vow; day by day, he attains the fruit of the Atikṛcchra penance.
In the month of Kārtika, one should avoid meat, especially fermented preparations; by eating meat even once, one attains the womb of a Rākṣasa.

But for those who have been consuming [forbidden] foods, if a vow of restraint is observed during Kārttika, they will certainly attain the state of Viṣṇu’s own form, the station that bestows liberation. || 19 ||
O child, the fruit that one obtains by giving the earth to Brahmins during an eclipse of the sun or moon, that same fruit belongs to one who sleeps upon the ground.
He provided a meal for the brahmin couple, honored them with ointments, and gave them blankets, jewels, and various kinds of garments.
Cushions should also be given along with coverlets; O observer of noble vows, give sandals and a parasol in the month of Kārttika.

One who sleeps on the ground during the month of Kārttika destroys the sins accumulated over an entire age; and he who performs a vigil at the break of dawn in the month of Kārttika [attains the same].
O celestial sage, one obtains the fruit of donating a thousand cows by bathing in the river in front of Dāmodara, as well as by listening to the stories of Viṣṇu and beholding the Vaiṣṇavas. (24)
If one does not [worship] during the month of Kārttika, his merit for ten years shall be taken away; therefore, the wise man should remember Puṣkara through action, mind, and speech.
O tiger among sages, [the merit] in Kārtika becomes a hundred thousand times ten millionfold; likewise, Prayāga in the month of Māgha and Puṣkara in Kārtika [yield the same]. (26)
In the month of Mādhava, Avantī destroys the sins accumulated over an entire Yuga; blessed are those men in this world, especially in the Kali age. (27)
Those men who constantly perform the worship of Hari for the sake of His pleasure undoubtedly deliver their ancestors from hell. || 28 ||
When the bathing of Viṣṇu with milk and other substances is performed for the sake of the ancestors, they attain heaven for ten million kalpas and dwell there together with the gods.
O best of Brahmins, those by whom the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa has not been worshipped in the month of Kārtika shall not have Kamalā (Lakṣmī) in their home for ten million lifetimes.
Alas! They are robbed and ruined, fallen into the abyss of the Kali age—those by whom Hari was not worshipped with devotion using dark and white lotuses.

Whoever worships the Lord of Gods, the husband of Kamalā, with a single lotus, effects the destruction of the sins of ten thousand years. By means of the practice of worshipping at Puṣkara, Śveta indeed attained liberation.
The Lord of Gods, when bowed to and worshipped with even a single lotus, forgives thousands of offenses as well as seven hundred.
O best of sages, he who worships Hari with a hundred thousand Tulasī leaves during the month of Kārtika obtains the fruit of a pearl for every single leaf.

The man who carries Tulasī, brought forth from Kṛṣṇa, upon his face, head, and body, and who rubs his limbs with the remains of Kṛṣṇa’s offerings (nirmālya), becomes liberated from all diseases as well as from sins. || 35 ||
Water from the conch, devotion to Hari, the water from his feet, sandalwood paste, and the remains of incense—these remove even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O best of Brahmins, in the month of Kārttika, being devoted to the morning bath, one should give gifts of food to the Brahmins according to one's capacity.
Of all gifts, the gift of food is preeminent; for by food the world is born, and by food alone it prospers. (38)
For they know that food is indeed the supreme life-force of all beings; the giver of food is a giver of everything in this world and becomes the performer of all sacrifices and other rites. (39)
O Brahmin, what need has he for bathing at sacred fords, or even for pilgrimages to deities? Everything is accomplished through the gift of food; of this there is no doubt.
In former times, the twice-born Satyaketu, by means of the simple gift of food alone, attained the fruit of all merit and reached liberation, which is very difficult to obtain. (41)
One who is steadfast in the Kārttika vow should perform the excellent gift of a cow; by the gift of a cow, the vow reaches completion—of this there is no doubt. (42)

O Nārada, there is no gift in this world superior to the gift of a cow, which enables one to cross the ocean of saṃsāra; indeed, there is no one in this world as truly auspicious as the Brāhmaṇa Suśarman.
O best of Brahmins, even if one gives various gifts in the month of Kārtika, if he is devoid of the remembrance of Hari, they never purify him at all.
The greatness of remembering the Name cannot be described by me, just as Puṣkara formerly liberated those dwelling in hell. (45)
"Govinda, Govinda! Hare, Murāri! Govinda, Govinda! Mukunda, Kṛṣṇa! Govinda, Govinda! O Discus-wielder! Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! || 46 ||
That mortal who, endowed with faith and devotion, daily recites even half a verse or a single quarter-verse from the Bhāgavata during the month of Kārtika, [attains the supreme goal]. (47)

The birth of those men has passed in vain who have not heard the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, who have not indeed worshipped the Ancient Person (Puruṣa), and who have not offered oblations into the mouths of the gods upon earth. || 48 ||
O best of Brahmins, I do not possess the power to describe the meritorious fruit of that man who recites the Gītā during the month of Kārtika.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a scripture equal to the Gītā; the Gītā alone is eternally the remover of all sins and the bestower of liberation. (50)
By the recitation of even a single chapter, even those who have committed every sin are liberated from terrible hell, just as the dull-witted Brāhmaṇa was.
O Sage, Viṣṇu has not determined the limit of the merit of one who makes a gift of a Śāligrāma stone during the month of Kārttika.
O great sage, O brahmin, listen to the fruit of the merit of that person who, having worshipped a śāligrāma, makes a gift to a śrotriya. || 53 ||
Whatever fruit may arise from the gift of the earth extending as far as the seven oceans, one obtains that same fruit by the gift of a Śāligrāma stone. (54)
Just as a Brahmin widow, by the gift of a Śāligrāma stone in the month of Kārttika, became a woman with a living husband on the fifth day of her marriage.
Therefore, in the month of Kārttika, preceded by ritual bathing and charity, the gift of a Śāligrāma stone must be performed; there is no doubt in this matter.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Kārttika Vow," in the Kārttikamāsa-māhātmya of the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, within the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Brahmā said: Listen further, O best of Brahmins, to the majesty of Kārtika; beginning from the tenth day, one should conclude it on the tenth day.
One should begin on the full moon day and complete it on the following full moon day; or, being devoted, one may begin on the day of Hari (the eleventh lunar day) of the month of Āśvina.
Having paid homage to Dāmodara, one should first make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "O Dāmodara, salutations to you, the destroyer of all sins. (3)
You ought to grant me permission to perform the vow of Kārttika; O Lord of Gods, O Puruṣottama, make it free from obstacles for the duration of this month.

Having thus prayed according to the prescribed rite, one should observe the Kārttika vow. Listen indeed to that which was spoken by Bhāskara as he spoke to Anūru, and which I have heard—namely, the cause for attaining heaven in the Kali age. || 5 ||
Sūrya said: Among the twelve months, Mārgaśīrṣa is the most bestower of merit.
Therefore, Vaiśākha on the bank of the Narmadā is declared to yield meritorious fruit; however, the month of Māgha at Prayāga is said to yield a hundred thousand times that merit.
Therefore, Kārttika is declared to yield great fruit even from water alone; on one side [are placed] all gifts, as well as vows and religious observances. (8)
On one side, the Kārttika bath was placed by Brahmā upon a scale; for those in the Kali age who possess progeny and prosperity, [the latter outweighed the former].
Know for certain that they have performed with devotion the Kārtika bath, the offering of lamps, and the cultivation of the Tulasī grove.
Sleeping on the ground, celibacy, as well as the avoidance of split pulses; the chanting of Viṣṇu’s names, truthfulness, and likewise listening to the Purāṇas. || 11 ||
Those who perform [these rites] in the month of Kārtika are indeed liberated while living; there is no duty equal to Kārtika, nor anything more meaningful than Kārtika.

There is no meritorious act equal to Kārttika, nor is there any gift for liberation superior to that given in Kārttika; it was performed by Yudhiṣṭhira for the sake of dharma, and by Dhruva for the sake of wealth.
This vow was performed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa for the sake of fulfilling desires and by Nārada for the sake of liberation; therefore, it is indeed excellent and dear to Kṛṣṇa.
Aruṇa said: O Bhāskara, the soul of all, tell me from when this vow was begun so that it may become perfectly fruitful; and which deity is to be worshipped here? (15)
Bhāskara said: "I, Viṣṇu, Śarva, the Goddess, and likewise Vighneśvara—I am one who has become fivefold, like a stage director in a drama. (16)
Know, O Lord of Birds, that all these are indeed our own divisions; therefore, [we are] with the Sauras, the Gāṇeśas, the Śāktas, the Śaivas, and the Vaiṣṇavas.
The Kārtika bath must be performed for the removal of all sins; it should be undertaken when the sun is situated in Libra for the pleasure of the Sun-god.
Starting from the full moon of Āśvina until the full moon of Kārttika, men should perform ritual bathing for the satisfaction of Śiva.
Beginning from the fortnight of the Goddess, on the fourteenth day of the Great Night (mahārātri), one should perform the ritual bath with the thought, "May the Goddess be well-pleased. (20)
Starting from the fortnight of Gaṇapati, the fourth lunar day that occurs in the month of Kārttika—on each of those days, one should perform a bath for the gratification of Gaṇapati.
Beginning from the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina until the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika is completed; Janārdana is well-pleased with him by whom this is performed.
There is no month equal to Kārttika, no city like Kāśī, no sacred ford equal to Prayāga, and no god higher than Keśava. (23)
Whether performed through incidental circumstances or by force, whether done knowingly or unknowingly, one who performs the ritual bath of the month of Kārttika shall not behold the torments of Yama.
If he lacks the capacity for bathing, one should give wealth or other resources to another; by grasping the hand of that person who has bathed, one becomes a partaker of merit. || 25 ||
Alternatively, by giving a garment to those twice-born ones who perform the Kārtika bath, one obtains the fruit arising from that bath.
Rādhādāmodara is to be worshiped, especially during the month of Kārtika. || 27 ||
In the absence of gold or silver, [one may use] even one made of copper, or one made of clay, or one produced as a painting, or one decorated with colored powders.
Those men who worship the images of Dāmodara and Rādhā beneath a Tulasī plant should be known as liberated while living; of this there is no doubt. (29)
Even a man burdened with thousands of sins becomes necessarily liberated by the Kārttika bath; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (30)
O Bird, in the absence of Tulasī, worship should be performed at the foot of a Dhātrī tree; however, the primary rite of worship must be performed within the solar disc.
All the gods are imperceptible, but this Blessed One is perceptible; all the gods are subject to time, yet the Sun is the time of time itself.
A person who is unable to propitiate Him in this manner should worship His image; however, the merit gained from worshipping a Brāhmaṇa is even greater than that from an image. (33)
A poor man may be a worthy recipient of gifts, but one who possesses knowledge is especially so; in the absence of Brahmins, beautiful black cows should be honored.
An image of Viṣṇu, whether mobile or immobile, is praised. He who offers salutation to images installed by Śūdras goes to hell along with ten ancestors and ten descendants. (35)
By the touch of one who has been worshipped by a Śūdra, one may burn one's lineage down to the seventh generation.
Therefore, one should worship that [liṅga] which was established by Brahmins after due deliberation; even more so, that which was made by the gods bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In the absence of an image, one should worship either an Aśvattha or a Vaṭa tree; for Viṣṇu exists in the form of the Aśvattha, and Śiva exists in the form of the Vaṭa.
In the month of Kārtika, the lowest of men who eats Tulasī-vegetables or betel leaf—whether unknowingly or intentionally—shall go to hell. (39)
Hari is eternally present within the discus-marked Śāligrāma stone; therefore, one should worship the Śāligrāma with every possible effort. (40)
Due to the power of Rudra’s curse, cows are intent on consuming excrement; nevertheless, they are to be worshipped, for they bestow the fruits of both worlds.
He who takes his meal from a Palāśa leaf, which has arisen as a portion of Brahmā, during the month of Kārttika, shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
The Blessed One has the form of the Aśvattha tree, and Sadāśiva has the form of the Vaṭa tree; therefore, with every effort, one should worship the Aśvattha in the month of Kārttika.
That woman who, having worshipped Rādhā-Dāmodara beneath that [tree], performs one hundred thousand circumambulations during the month of Kārtika on Saturdays, [attains the supreme goal].
One should feed a married couple who are the very embodiments of Rādhā and Dāmodara; having fed them along with their wives, one should afterwards eat while maintaining silence.
Even a barren woman obtains a son; what then need be said of others? For Viṣṇu is ever present in times of distress, just as he is with a Brāhmaṇa.
On the Bodhi tree among trees, and on the stones at Śāligrāma; therefore, the worship of Viṣṇu should indeed be performed at the foot of the Aśvattha tree.
The worship of the Aśvattha tree should be performed by touch on a Saturday; on any other day, a man becomes poor through contact with the Aśvattha.
Those men who perform ritual bathing, keeping vigil, lighting lamps, and tending the Tulasī grove during the month of Kārtika are the very embodiments of Viṣṇu.
Those men who perform the sweeping of Viṣṇu’s temple, the offering of svastikas and other auspicious signs, and the worship of Viṣṇu, are indeed liberated while living.
I shall declare the proper time for bathing and the fruit obtained at sacred fords and other such places; learn from me all those various duties pertaining to the ritual bath.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Description of the Glory of Kārtika," in the *Kārtikamāsa-māhātmya* of the second section (*Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Brahmā said: O Sage, when two nāḍīs of the night remain, one should go to a body of water, carrying tulasī mud, as well as a cloth and a water-pot.
Having arrived near the water and placed his bowl on the bank, he should perform the washing of his feet and then recite the place, time, and other relevant details.
One should remember the Gaṅgā and other rivers, as well as Viṣṇu, Śarva, and the other deities; standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should utter this mantra.
"O Janārdana, O Lord of Gods, O Dāmodara, I shall perform the morning ablution in the month of Kārtika for your pleasure, together with you. (4)

O Keśava, having performed the obligatory and occasional rites during the month of Kārtika, which destroys all sins, I shall perform my ablutions and offer the arghya; grant that this be free from obstacles.

One should cause the offering of *arghya* and other honors to be given in due order to the deities of the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and others: "O Hari, together with Rādhā, accept this *arghya* offered by me. (6)
Salutations to the one whose navel is a lotus; salutations to you who recline upon the waters. Salutations be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa; accept this water offering; salutations be to you.
O destroyer of the lords of demons, accept this arghya offered by me, who am observing vows and have bathed according to the rules during the month of Kārtika.
May the Kiranā, the Dhūtapāpā, the Puṇyatoyā Sarasvatī, the Gaṅgā, and the Yamunā—these five rivers—purify me.
A person should offer the arghya according to the prescribed rule for other rivers as well; at all sacred bathing places (tīrthas), one should perform the remembrance of the Ganges (Jāhnavī).
