No other sacred ford on the Jāhnavī should ever be remembered [as superior]; having recited these mantras, one should perform the bath for removing impurities.
Then follows the bath with clay, the bath for the ancestors, and thereafter the bath for the guru; after that, one should sprinkle one's own head with the Pāvamānī verses.
Having performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite as well as the libation (*tarpaṇa*) which is an ancillary part of the bath, one should then sprinkle water upon one's head while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*.
Then, having come outside, one should place the sacred water (tīrtha) upon the head; having drunk the sacred water three times, one should take hold of a tulasī leaf with the hand.

Then, having emerged from the water, one should press the *cāñcala* (the lower garment) outside, [saying]: "Whatever impurity of water has been defiled by me through the accumulation of bodily excretions... (15)
To avoid that fault, I shall satisfy Yakṣman; having wrung out the garment, one should perform the tilaka and other rites. (16)
Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, to the fruit arising from the Kārtika bath, as it was told in detail by the Sun to Aruṇa.
Aruṇa said: O Blessed One, tell me specifically at which holy ford (tīrtha) or sacred field (kṣetra) the fruit arising from Kārttika is obtained through the practice of ritual bathing.
Sūrya said: The Kārtika bath must be performed in water wherever possible; however, in some cases during Kārtika, the bath may be performed with warm water.
The merit from bathing in cool water is ten times greater than that; the merit gained by performing it in the water of an external well is a hundred times greater still.
The fruit resulting from the consecration of a stepped well is a thousandfold greater than that of a well; ten-thousandfold more merit than that arises from bathing in a pond.
Ten times that merit is gained from bathing in mountain springs; greater than that is the merit of bathing in a river during the month of Kārttika.
O best of birds, bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha) is said to be ten times more meritorious than [bathing] in a river; the merit is ten times greater still where there is a confluence of two rivers.
In the confluence of these three rivers, there is no end to merit: the Sindhu, the Kṛṣṇā, and the Veṇī, as well as the Yamunā and the Sarasvatī.
The Godāvarī, Vipāśā, Narmadā, Tamasā, Mahī, Kāverī, Śarayū, Śiprā, and likewise the river Carmaṇvatī. || 25 ||
The Vitastā, Vedikā, Śoṇa, Vetravatī, Aparājitā, Gaṇḍakī, Gomatī, Pūrṇā, Brahmaputrā, and the lake; 26.
The Vāgmatī, the Śatadru, and likewise Badarikāśrama—these are difficult to reach during Kārttika; now learn from me of other holy places (tīrthas). || 27 ||
Of all places, Āryāvarta is indeed merit-bestowing; Kolhāpurī is superior to that, and the pair of Kāñcīs is remembered as even more excellent than that. (28)
The abode of Anantasena, Varāhakṣetra, and then the meritorious Cakrakṣetra; and superior even to that is Muktikṣetra. (29)
Avantī is superior to that, and Badarikāśrama is superior to that; Ayodhyā is superior to that, and Gaṅgādvāra is even greater than that. (30)
Beyond that is the Kanakhala tirtha, and beyond that is the excellent Madhupuri; yet even a single month of Kartika spent in the waters of the Yamuna at Mathura [is superior]. 31.
Those by whom [the bath] was performed indeed dwell in Vaikuṇṭha for a long time; there, Rādhā and Dāmodara themselves have bathed during Kārtika.
Therefore, Madhupurī is the most excellent, and the Yamunā is especially so. || 33 ||
Then, in the excellent city of Dvārāvatī, Keśava bathes every day together with sixteen thousand women and the Yādavas.

That man by whom a tilaka of earth from Dvārakā is worn upon his head should be known as liberated while living; of this there is no doubt. The greatness of bathing at Dvārakā cannot be fully described by me. (35)
For those whose minds are dedicated to Govinda, there arises the merit-bestowing Bhāskarā; superior even to that is the Bhāgīrathī where she meets with the Vindhya.
Therefore, ten times that merit is produced here at this king of holy places.
At the end of ten thousand years in the Kali age, Viṣṇu will abandon the earth; half of that [time] will be occupied by the waters of the Gaṅgā, and half of that by the hosts of deities.
As long as the Gaṅgā remains here, so long do the sacred fords exist; they remove the sins of men from their respective locations for that very duration. (39)
When the Gaṅgā has disappeared, who indeed will take away that sin? Having reflected thus, people will go to other excellent holy places on the surface of the earth.
Therefore, O lords of sages, as long as the Jāhnavī remains, let dharma be practiced; thereafter, one should dissolve into the earth.
Having grasped this very firm samādhi until the Kṛta Yuga arrives, otherwise the wise one would be led astray by the Kali age. (42)
Kāśī is even more excellent than that, for its destruction never occurs; by taking refuge in it, even the Gaṅgā dispels all sin.

Even when Brahmā has passed away, there shall be no destruction of Kāśikā; for the sake of beholding it, even the Gaṅgā has become north-flowing. In that city is the holy site Pañcanada, renowned throughout the three worlds. (44)
When the month of Kārtika arrives, they will go to the Raurava hell; our ancestors will cry out, "Will there be [anyone] in our lineage? (45)
"May someone among the most fortunate go to the auspicious Pañcanada and perform for us the libation (tarpaṇa) that delivers one from the ocean of hell. (46)
When the month of Kārttika arrives, the Tīrtharāja and other sacred fords undoubtedly come to Pañcagaṅgā for the purpose of bathing.
But having committed even a hundred thousand sins, by bathing in the auspicious Pañcanada and worshipping Bindumādhava, they go to dissolution at that very moment.
For those who have bathed even once in the auspicious Pañcanada during the month of Kārttika, the fruit shall be ten million times greater than that obtained from bathing in all other sacred fords.
Brahmā said: He who desires to perform a ritual bath in the Kāverī during the month of Kārttika is indeed liberated from all sin by that act alone and shall attain union with Viṣṇu.
Who could describe the supreme and most excellent majesty of the Kāverī? In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history.
O Brahmin, listen with an attentive mind regarding the region of the Kāverī; on the northern bank of the Gautamī, there is [a place] born from the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu.
The Gaṅgā, who destroys the sins of the three worlds and is honored by the people, once reflected, being apprehensive about sin. (53)
"All the worlds have gathered together and are indeed casting their sins upon me; how can that sin be removed?"—thus she was then absorbed in anxious thought.
She went to Kailāsa to question Bhava, the beloved of Girijā; having seen Mahārudra there, she who was born from the foot of Hari spoke to him.
Gaṅgā said: O Mahārudra, salutations to you; I have come to question you, for indeed all the worlds, having gathered together, cast their sins upon me. (56)
O Lord of Pārvatī, I am unable to endure that sin; tell me the means by which that sin might not come upon me. (57)
Having heard these words of Gaṅgā, the Supreme Lord replied. Rudra said: "First, for the removal of sin, [the merit] from the lotus-foot of Padmanābha—" (58)
O Goddess, you have manifested; for what purpose do you perform penance? The lordship over the destruction of sins has been ordained for you by Viṣṇu.
Nevertheless, I shall tell you the means for the removal of sin: the goddess Kaveri, the daughter of Kavi, is the best among rivers. (60)
And she is the most excellent of all, for she is under the power of Hari; in her resides the capacity to strike down all sins. (61)
The man who performs a ritual bath in the Kāverī during the month of Kārttika is liberated from sin and goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
"Therefore, O Goddess, go to her; from that you shall be liberated from sin. Having been told this, she then went to the Kāverī, the remover of sins.
Merely by the touch of its water during the month of Kārttika, Gaṅgā, who had been born from the foot of Viṣṇu, shook off her sins and returned to her own abode.
Every year during the month of Kārttika, Gaṅgā, the purifier of the three worlds, comes with devotion to bathe in the sin-removing Kāverī.
Merely by the touch of its water during the month of Kārttika, Gaṅgā, who had been born from the foot of Viṣṇu, shook off her sins and returned to her own abode.
Therefore, the wise praise the ritual bath at the time of Libra (tulāsnāna) in the Kāverī; O Sage, he who performs the tulāsnāna in the Kāverī with devotion [attains great merit]. 67.
Having been instantly liberated from all evils, one then attains the supreme goal; therefore, bathing in the Kāverī during the month of Kārttika is highly recommended.
Having heard this history, one who is devoted to the Kārttika vow obtains the fruit of bathing in the Kāverī and attains the supreme goal.
A bath taken during the remainder of the night is supreme and brings satisfaction to Viṣṇu; one taken at sunrise is middling, provided the Kṛttikā constellation has not yet set.
Only at that time should the bath take place; otherwise, it is not the Kārtika bath. Women should perform the bath only after receiving permission from their husband.
Whatever act consistent with dharma is performed without consulting her husband leads to ruin; for women, there is no other dharma whatsoever apart from their husband. 72.
She who carries out the command of her husband, even if she commits a thousand sins, is truly righteous in this world; she does not become so merely through vows and the like. (73)
Even if her husband is poor, fallen, foolish, or even wretched, he is such a refuge for women that by abandoning him, she would go to hell.
O child, although there is laxity among men regarding the rite of bathing in the Kali age, nevertheless I shall describe the bath during the months of Kārttika and Māgha.
That man whose hands, feet, speech, and mind are well-restrained, and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and renown, is the one who partakes in the fruit of the sacred fords.
One who lacks faith, one whose soul is evil, an atheist, one of divided mind, and a rationalist—these five do not partake in the fruit of the sacred ford.
The Brahmin who, having risen early in the morning, always bathes at a sacred ford (tīrtha), being liberated from all sins, attains the Supreme Brahman. || 78 ||
Bathing is declared to be fourfold by the wise who know the rules of bathing; it is likewise remembered as being Vāyavya, Vāruṇa, Divya, and Brāhma. (79)

The Vāyavya bath consists of dust from a cow; the Vāruṇa bath is performed in oceans and similar waters; the Brāhma bath is that prescribed by Vedic mantras; and the Divya bath is water from clouds or the sun's rays.
Among all types of baths, the Vāruṇa bath is distinguished as the most excellent; a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya should perform the bath accompanied by mantras.

For it is likewise recorded in the tradition that for a Śūdra and for women, [the recitation] should be performed in silence; this applies to the child, the young woman, the old woman, and to men, women, and eunuchs alike.
People are liberated from all sins by bathing during the months of Kārttika and Māgha; indeed, those who have bathed in Kārttika obtain their desired fruit.
In ancient times, at the confluence of the Nandā at Puṣkara, the most excellent of holy places, Prabhañjana was liberated from his birth as a tiger.
By Nandā’s word alone, she went to that supreme [state] in the month of Kārtika. Thus has the procedure for the ritual bath been declared; what more do you wish to hear? (85)

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Kārtika Bath," in the *Kārtikamāsa-māhātmya* of the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: When should the bath be performed, and how should one conduct oneself throughout the day? O Grandfather, explain that daily ritual (āhnika) in detail.
Brahmā said: The observer of the vow should always rise when a fourth part of the night remains; having praised Viṣṇu with many hymns, he should deliberate upon the duties of the day.
In the south-western direction of the village, one should void excrement according to the prescribed rule, having placed the sacred thread on the right ear and facing northward there.
Having hidden a blade of grass upon the ground, having covered his head with a cloth, and having restrained his mouth with a garment, he remained unattached, carrying a water vessel.
If one must void urine or feces at night, one should do so facing south; then, having risen, one should indeed go near the water-pot.

One should perform purification with earth to remove the odor and the smear; it is traditionally taught that there should be one application of earth on the penis, three on the hand, and two applications on both together.
This should be understood as the purification for urine; now hear the purification for feces: five applications [of earth] are required at the anus, or seven, and likewise ten on the left hand.
Seven applications of earth should be given to both [hands], and three to the feet; this is the purification for a householder, while that for a student (brahmacārin) is twofold.
For a forest-dweller it is threefold, and for ascetics it is fourfold; this is declared to be the purification for the day, and one should perform half of it at night.
For one on the path, it shall be half of that; for women and Śūdras, half of that again. For one devoid of the acts of purification, all ritual actions are fruitless.
Then, one should untiringly perform the purification of the teeth and tongue. [This bestows] longevity, strength, fame, luster, progeny, cattle, and wealth. (11)
"O Lord of the Forest, grant us Brahman-knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence. One should take up a tooth-stick measuring twelve finger-breadths. 12.
One must not take [wood] from a milk-exuding tree, nor likewise from a cotton plant, nor from a thorny tree, nor indeed from a burnt tree. (13)
At the outset, one should perform the cleaning of the teeth with a very soft twig that has been well-impregnated with fragrance.

On the day of fasting, on the ninth and sixth lunar days, on the day of a Śrāddha, on Sundays, during an eclipse, and on the first and new moon days, one should not perform the cleaning of the teeth. When no specific rule for cleaning the teeth is prescribed, one should perform twelve mouthfuls of rinsing.

Having cleansed his teeth according to the rules and rinsed his mouth with water, he should apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on his forehead and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with water.
Having offered an "empty-space lamp" (ākāśadīpa) especially in a temple, on a riverbank, on a royal highway, or in the presence of a *tulasī* plant; 17.
Having taken the materials for worship, one should go to the temple of one’s chosen deity; then, having performed the worship, the wise person should sing and dance. 18.
Having recited the names of Viṣṇu, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for Hari; when two nāḍīs of the night remain, one should go to a body of water.
There, the observer of the Kārttika vow should perform his bath according to the prescribed rule; having wrung out his garment, he should likewise apply the sectarian mark (tilaka).

Then one should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) according to the path prescribed in one's own Sūtra; thereafter, the recitation (japa) of the Goddess should be performed until the rising of the sun.
This has been declared as the duty for the remainder of the night; now that which pertains to the day is described, by the performance of which this entire month of Kārtika becomes fruitful. (22)
Then, having recited the Thousand Names of Viṣṇu at the conclusion of the twilight prayers, one should go to the temple and begin worship once again.
One should spend one *prahara* of the day in activities such as dancing and singing; thereafter, one should properly devote half a watch (*yāmārdha*) to listening to the Purāṇas. (24)
Having performed the worship of the Purāṇa as well as the worship of Tulasī, and having completed his midday rites, he should eat food free from split pulses.
That mortal who, having performed the offering to the gods (balidāna), the sacrifice to all beings (vaiśvadeva), and the presentation to guests, then eats, indeed eats nothing but nectar. || 26 ||
Twice-born men should be fed according to one's ability every day or on festival days; one should consume sacrificial food (haviṣya) and completely avoid meat.
One should eat Tulasī with water from a sacred site (tīrtha) for the sake of purifying the mouth; one should then spend the remainder of the day in the affairs of worldly life.
In the evening, he should go again toward the temple of Viṣṇu; having performed the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), he should offer lamps there according to his ability.
Having prostrated before Viṣṇu, Hari, and performed the auspicious lustration ceremony (nīrājana), one should keep vigil during the first watch of the night while reciting hymns and other prayers.
When the first watch has passed, the wise man should sleep; he should observe the vow of celibacy, or otherwise approach his wife during her fertile period.
Desiring her, he may approach his wife without incurring any fault; thus he should act every day according to the rule until the end of the month.
Thus, he who performs this supreme vow in the month of Kārttika, being liberated from all sins, goes to the same world as Viṣṇu.

There is nothing else on this earth superior to the Kārtika vow, which is dear to Viṣṇu, for removing diseases, destroying sins, bestowing true wisdom, securing sons, wealth, and other blessings, and serving as the very foundation of liberation. (34)

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Daily Duties," in the *Kārttikamāsa-māhātmya* (The Greatness of the Month of Kārttika) within the second section, the *Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Brahmā said: Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe the great vow of Kārtika; by hearing which, you will be liberated from all sins and attain liberation.
When the month of Kārtika has arrived, one should avoid prohibited things: anointing with oil, food belonging to others, and likewise eating food that has been cooked in oil.
One should avoid fruits containing many seeds as well as split pulses during the month of Kārtika; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
The bottle-gourd, the gṛñjana, the eggplant, the fruit of the bṛhatī, food that has been kept overnight, as well as burnt rice and lentils.
Furthermore, eating twice a day, honey, food from others, eating from a bronze vessel, [eating] nails, leather, mushrooms, sour gruel, and anything foul-smelling; || 5 ||

The food of a group, the food of a courtesan, as well as that of one who performs sacrifices for a village, the food of a Śūdra, contact with a Śūdra, and likewise the food of one in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka).

One observing the Kārttika vow should avoid food offered at ancestral rites (śrāddha), food served during seasonal propitiatory ceremonies, as well as the birth-rite (jātaka) and naming ceremony (nāmaka), and likewise the fruit of the śleṣmātaka tree.

One should never cause food to be eaten from prohibited leaves. [However, one may eat] from leaves of the Madhuka, Palāśa, Kadalī, Jambū, Plakṣa, and Makūṭikā; but one should never eat from these leaves at Puṣkara.
When the month of Kārttika has arrived, he who performs the practice of eating forest-grown food goes to the supreme world of the discus-bearing Lord Viṣṇu.
O Sage, the morning bath, as well as the worship of Hari and the listening to sacred narratives, are highly recommended during the month of Kārtika.
The gift of Gopīcandana and the gift of a cow to a learned Brahmin (śrotriya) should be performed in the month of Kārtika; by that, one shall attain liberation.
One should likewise give the gift of plantain fruit, the gift of myrobalan fruit, and the gift of clothing to a twice-born man afflicted by the cold.
One should give gifts of vegetables and the like, and especially gifts of food; furthermore, a gift of a śāligrāma stone should be made to a twice-born man.
He who gives uncooked rice, ghee, and milk-rice to a reciter of the Purāṇas attains sovereignty, which is equal to the merit of feeding a hundred Brāhmaṇas.
He who worships the Beloved of Kamalā with lotuses during the month of Kārttika attains merit; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (15)
He who offers a Tulasī leaf with devotion to Viṣṇu in the month of Kārtika is liberated from the cycle of worldly existence and goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
In the month of Kārttika, one should worship the Lord whose banner is Garuḍa with ketakī flowers; when thus worshipped, [the merit lasts] for a thousand births—of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, for one who makes a gift of a conch shell as well as one marked with a discus, their sins are destroyed by the mere act of giving; of this there is no doubt. (18)
But for one who performs the recitation of the Gītā during the month of Kārtika, which is dear to Viṣṇu, even a hundred years would not suffice to describe the fruit of his merit.
He who practices the hearing of the glorious Bhāgavata, being liberated from all sins, attains supreme liberation (nirvāṇa). || 20 ||
He who observes a fast without food on the eleventh day is liberated from the sins committed in previous births; of this there is no doubt.

One obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices by partaking of the food offering (naivedya) of the Śāligrāma; however, having eaten the food offering of another deity, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
But he who sounds the bell at the time of the deity's worship attains supreme satisfaction for Hari; there is no doubt in this matter. || 23 ||
That man who avoids food given by others during the month of Kārtika for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu attains perfect delight for Dāmodara.
But he who honors with devotion a guest who is weary from the road and has arrived at his home at the proper time, effects the destruction of thousands of births. (25)
Those fools who revile the high-souled Vaiṣṇavas fall, together with their ancestors, into the hell known as Mahāraurava.
Indeed, upon seeing the brāhmaṇas who are devotees of the Lord, he does not even go forward to face them; Hari does not accept his worship for twelve years.
He who hears the censure of the Blessed One and of those devoted to Him, yet does not depart from it, is likewise not dear to Hari.
Indeed, whoever performs a circumambulation of Keśava during the month of Kārttika undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice at every step. || 29 ||
He who performs a prostration like a staff before Keśava in the month of Kārttika undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. || 30 ||
O tiger among brahmins, he who, endowed with devotion, causes food to be given to his family during the month of Kārttika, his merit is infinite.
As for the man who engages in sexual union with another's wife during the month of Kārttika, the extent of his sin cannot even be described. || 32 ||
Yama is not even able to look upon one on whose forehead the sectarian mark made with Tulasī clay is seen; how much less so his terrifying messengers? (33)
Whether it be vegetables, salt, or whatever else may be available, that should be given in the month of Kārttika for the pleasure of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
These and many other religious duties are dear to Viṣṇu during the month of Kārttika; one should perform such merit-giving acts for the satisfaction of the God according to one's ability. (35)
For the sake of joy and contentment, one should renounce one's own desired object; at the end of the month, one should give it to an excellent Brahmin for the completion of that vow.
All other vows on one side and the vow of truth on the other: therefore, with every effort, one should always speak the truth. (37)
In other religious practices, eligibility is determined by distinctions of family and caste; however, in the month of Kārttika, every person whatsoever shall be entitled to participate.
The merit of those by whom even a single morsel of food for a cow is especially given in the month of Kārttika—the Grandfather (Brahmā) is not able to describe its fruit. (39)
He who sweeps the temple of Viṣṇu in the morning during the month of Kārttika shall have a very firm dwelling arise for him in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
If one should give abundant pieces of sacred wood during the month of Kārttika, there is no destruction of that merit even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
He who applies lime and other substances to the temple of Viṣṇu in the month of Kārttika, or even draws paintings and the like there, rejoices in the presence of Viṣṇu.
The tax imposed by wicked kings upon temples or sacred fords—those people who liberate them possess eternal dharma. (43)
In the month of Kārttika, whatever Brahmin performs the recitation of the Śatarudrīya in the presence of Gabhastīśvara attains mastery over mantras.
But those mortals who, remaining in Vārāṇasī for three years, have performed the Kārtika vow together with its ancillaries and subsidiaries, being solely intent on devotion; || 45 ||
In this world, it is said that the fruit of those [deeds] becomes manifest through prosperity, progeny, fame, and a mind devoted to dharma. (46)
One should avoid onion, horn, meat, a bed, sauvīraka, as well as black mustard, intoxicants, and flattened rice.
One who observes the Kārttika vow should always avoid eating the dhātrī fruit on Sundays and visiting foreign lands, except for the purpose of pilgrimage. 48.
One observing the Kārttika vow should avoid censuring the gods, the Vedas, the twice-born, teachers, cows, those observing vows, women, kings, and great souls. (49)

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should have an oil massage performed for Naraka; on other occasions, one should avoid bathing with oil during the month of Kārttika. One should also avoid the nālikā, radish, pumpkin, and wood-apple.

One who observes the vow must never speak with a menstruating woman, an outcaste, a barbarian, a fallen person, one who neglects his vows, those who hate the twice-born, or those excluded from the Vedas. (51)

A follower of the Vaiṣṇava vow should never eat food that has been seen by these [animals], nor food seen by crows, nor food from a woman who has recently given birth, nor food cooked twice, nor burnt food.
In sequence, [he offered] the fruits of the kūṣmāṇḍa, the bṛhatī, the taruṇī, and likewise the mūlaka; as well as the śrīphala, the kaliṅga, and the fruit born of the dhātrī tree.
Coconut, bottle-gourd, patola, the fruit of bṛhatī, the leather-stalked eggplant, cavallī vegetables, and likewise that which is born from tulasī; || 54 ||

These vegetables are to be avoided in sequence starting from the first lunar day (pratipad); in this very manner, the observer of the vow should also perform the observances during the month of Māgha.
Even the four-faced Brahmā here would not be capable of describing the merit of one who observes the Kārtika vow according to the prescribed injunctions.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kārtika Vow," in the *Kārtikamāsa-māhātmya* (The Greatness of the Month of Kārtika) within the second section, the *Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: "O Blessed One, I have achieved my purpose by taking refuge at your feet. O best of gods, there remains nothing further for me to hear here."
Nevertheless, O Blessed One, there is something remaining in my heart that I must ask; for even though I have drunk the nectar of your words, no satiety arises within me. (2)
O Lord, O Four-faced One, I desire to hear from you the greatness of the gift of lamps; tell me also of him by whom one was given in the past.
Brahmā said: Having bathed in the morning and become pure, one should diligently offer a lamp; by that, sins shall perish like darkness at the rising of the sun.
Whatever sin has been committed since birth by either a woman or a man, all of that goes to destruction through the offering of lamps during Kārttika.
In this regard, I shall describe to you an ancient history (itihāsa) which destroys all sins upon hearing and bestows the fruit of offering lamps.
Long ago, O Sage, in the Draviḍa country there was a Brāhmaṇa named Buddha; his wife was wicked and devoted to immoral conduct.
Due to the fault of association with her, his lifespan was exhausted and he met his death; even though her husband had died, that wife remained particularly unrighteous in her conduct.
Indeed, she felt no shame for her conduct out of fear of public scandal; deprived of son and kinsmen, she always subsisted on food obtained through alms.
She did not eat little food nor consume leftovers; she was always intent on the cooking of others and avoided pilgrimages and such activities. || 10 ||
O twice-born one, she had not even heard that discourse. Once, a certain brāhmaṇa who was devoted to pilgrimage [arrived]. (11)
A learned man named Kutsa arrived at her house; seeing that she was devoted to improper conduct, that best of Brahman-sages, his eyes red with anger, spoke to that unchaste woman.
Kutsa said: O foolish woman, I shall speak now; give heed to my words.
O messenger, why do you nourish this body, which is the cause of suffering, filled with pus and blood, and composed of the five elements? 14.
The body certainly perishes like a bubble on the water; yet, relying upon this impermanent body, you consider it eternal within your heart. (15)
Therefore, O deluded one, abandon the delusion dwelling within you through reflection; remember the Supreme God and listen with reverence. 16.
When the month of Kārttika has arrived, perform rites such as bathing and giving gifts; likewise, offer lamps for the pleasure of Dāmodara. (17)

Likewise, one should perform the offering of a hundred thousand wicks and so forth, as well as a hundred thousand lotuses and so forth; and likewise, one should perform circumambulation of the God and prostrations.
Perform the observance and the breaking of the fast with devotion indeed during the month of Kārttika; for this vow is for widows as well as for married women. (19)
It pacifies all sins and destroys all calamities; therefore, let an excellent lamp be offered there during the month of Kārtika.
A lamp-offering in the month of Kārttika certainly brings pleasure to Hari; even one who has committed great sins is liberated through the gift of a lamp. (21)
In former times, there was a certain excellent brahmin named Harikara; that twice-born man was constantly addicted to unrighteous objects and devoted to courtesans.
He was one who caused the depletion of his father’s wealth and acted like an axe for the cutting down of his lineage; once, at a game of dice, he lost his father’s great fortune.

Having fallen [from his state] due to association with the wicked, he consequently became miserable; however, at one time, through association with the virtuous in the course of a pilgrimage, [he was transformed]. (24)
O child, that twice-born man who committed great sins arrived at Ayodhyā; having reached it in the month of Kārtika, he always resided in the house of a prosperous brahmin.
Under the pretext of gambling, he quickly offered a lamp before Lord Hari; thereafter, after some time, the brāhmaṇa died and attained liberation.
Even one who has committed a great sin (mahāpātaka) has attained fearlessness by going to Hari; therefore, you too should likewise perform the offering of lamps in the month of Kārttika.
"Likewise, perform other acts of charity as well, endowed with devotion. Having thus instructed her, the brahmin Kutsa then departed for another house.
Having heard Kutsa's words, she was filled with remorse and resolved, "I shall observe the vow in the month of Kārttika. (29)
At the time of sunrise during the month of Kārttika, she performed her ablutions in the water, offered lamps, and observed the vow for one entire month.

Then, after some time, her life having come to an end, she met with death; yet, due to the greatness of the gift of the lamp, even though she was a committer of great sins, [she attained a higher state]. || 31 ||
That woman went to the path of heaven and attained liberation in due time; therefore, O Nārada, who could describe the greatness of offering a lamp? || 32 ||

The offering of lamps during the month of Kārtika bestows the fruit of great merit; for that man who is devoted to the Kārtika vow and performs the offering of lamps and other rites, [there is great reward]. (33)
Indeed, by hearing this history of the gift of lamps, one shall attain liberation.
Who here is able to describe the greatness of the gift of a lamp? O Nārada, listen now to the greatness of rekindling another's lamp. (35)
Even one who lacks power themselves, if they can awaken another, shall also obtain [the fruit]; there is no need for deliberation on this point. (36)
Indeed, whoever gives a wick, oil, or a vessel for the sake of a lamp, or provides assistance to those giving an excellent lamp, [attains great merit]. (37)
He indeed attains liberation; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. Who indeed could describe the greatness of offering lamps during the month of Kārtika? (38)
Even if one lacks the power oneself, one may still kindle another's lamp; that other person too attains the fruit thereof—there is no need for deliberation on this point. (39)
Then, in the house of a prostitute named Indumatī, there was a mouse which attained liberation—so difficult to reach—by the light of another's lamp. (40)
Therefore, with every effort, one should kindle the lamp of another; by that, one attains liberation, just like the mouse—of this there is no doubt. || 41 ||
O Sage, such is the fruit for one who has awakened by the light of another's lamp; by whom can the majesty of actually offering a lamp be described? (42)

Nārada said: I have heard the greatness of offering lamps during the month of Kārttika, and I have also indeed heard the greatness of rekindling another's lamp. Now, I desire to hear the majesty of the sky-lamp (vyomadīpa).
Brahmā said: O son, listen with a concentrated mind to the greatness of the sky-lamp (ākāśadīpa), by the mere hearing of which the inclination toward offering lamps arises.
When the month of Kārtika has arrived, I shall describe the merit of him who, devoted to the morning bath, offers a sky-lamp.
Having become the sovereign of all worlds and endowed with every prosperity, he shall enjoy happiness in this world and, at the end, attain liberation.

Preceded by the rites of bathing and giving, a sky-lamp (ākāśadīpa) should be offered atop the temple of Hari for one month during the month of Kārtika; on the pure full moon day of Kārtika, one should formally conclude it according to the prescribed rite.
He who, according to the prescribed rite, offers a lamp in the sky during the month of Kārttika, shall not undergo rebirth even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
In this regard, I shall describe to you an ancient history, by the mere hearing of which one obtains the fruit of a lamp offered to the sky. 49.
Formerly, however, there was a hunter named Niṣṭhura, a thorn to the world, who dwelt on the banks of the Yamunā like another personified Kāla-mṛtyu (the God of Death).
Wandering in the forest, he made his livelihood by killing all the deer; wielding a bow, he constantly harassed travelers through the profession of a thief.
O Sage, in the month of Kārtika, he went quickly to a certain village for the purpose of theft; meanwhile, in that city of Vidarbha, there was a king named Sukṛti.
At the word of the Brahmin named Candraśarman, the wise man established a sky-lamp atop the temple of Hari during the month of Kārtika.
Having offered a lamp with great devotion, he listened to the discourse during the night; at that very time, however, a thief arrived there for the purpose of stealing.
Beholding the sky-lamp given by the king, he stood still for a moment; at that time, by the turn of fate, a vulture arrived with great speed.
Having arrived quickly, he took the oil vessel together with its lamp; holding it with his own mouth, he took refuge at the very top of the tree.
Having drunk oil there and established a lamp, that king of birds perched upon the top of a tree and remained for a mere moment.
At that time, by the turn of fate, a cat also climbed the tree occupied by the excellent bird in order to seize it.
He stood for a moment gazing at the lamp before his face, while Candraśarman recounted the greatness of the sky-lamp.
There, for a moment, the bird and the cat listened to King Sukṛti, due to the fault of their own restless movements.
There, a cat seized a bird that had descended from a branch; impelled by fate, they both then fell from the tree onto a rock.
There on the ground, the bird and the cat, their limbs broken and dead, were endowed with divine bodies and ascended to heaven mounted upon celestial vehicles.
Having seen all of that, the hunter, who had approached for the purpose of stealing, turned back with a wicked intent upon seeing the sage narrating the story. (63)
Addressing Candraśarman, he spoke these words: "O Candraśarman, while I had come for the purpose of thievery, I indeed beheld this."
At that time, by the turn of fate, a bird took hold of the beautiful sky-lamp offered by the virtuous king.
Having drunk the oil, he placed that beautiful vessel, containing a lamp, upon the top of a tree and remained there for a moment.
A cat also arrived there to seize the excellent bird; impelled by fate, both of them took refuge in two separate branches.
For they had listened for a moment to the story being told from your mouth, but afterwards, due to the fault of restlessness, the cat seized the bird.
They both fell from the tree and met their death in a mere instant; then, assuming divine forms, they both ascended a celestial vehicle and went to heaven.
Having seen that wonder, I have come to question you; O twice-born one, tell me who those two—the cat and the bird—were in the past. (70)
"By what karma were these two born as animals and then liberated? Hearing these words of the hunter, Candraśarman then spoke.
Listen, hunter, I shall relate their story exactly as it happened. Formerly, there was a sinful cat and likewise one born of the Śrīvatsa lineage. (72)
Known as Devaśarman, he was a thief of divine property; yet he attained the status of a performer of worship for Ahovalanṛsiṃha.
Having seized the oil, wealth, and other such items obtained at that temple, he sustains his family with those very things.
Having lived out his lifespan in this very manner, he then met his death; because of that sin, he went to Kālasūtra, Mahāraurava, and Raurava.
Having thus reached the Forest of Sword-Leaves (Asipatravana) breathless, he is then cut by the terrifying, massive-bodied messengers of Yama.
Having experienced all of those [rebirths], he became a Brahmarākṣasa; thereafter, due to his evil deeds, he was born in the womb of a dog and then became a Caṇḍāla.
Having thus undergone a hundred births on earth as a cat, he now, by divine providence, heard the greatness of the sky-lamp; freed from all sins, he went to the abode of Hari.
In former times, this vulture was a brahmin in Mithilā who had mastered the Vedas; he was a great lord renowned in the world by the name Śaryāti. (79)
He engaged in union with female slaves as well as with courtesans; due to that great transgression, he then met his death.
Having remained for four yugas in the most terrible Kumbhīpāka hell, he then attained the state of a vulture on earth due to the remainder of his karma.
Impelled by fate, a vulture arrived there for the purpose of drinking oil. || 82 ||
Having offered a sky-lamp and heard the narrative of Hari, his entire mass of sins was destroyed, and he went to the abode of Hari.
"O hunter, all this has been told; go as you please. Having heard his words, the hunter also went to his own home. (84)
O Sage, he duly performed the vow of the sky-lamp; having spent the remainder of his life in that manner, he went to the abode of Hari.
O Great King, Sunanda was also filled with wonder; he performed the month-long rite according to the prescribed rules, following the path described by Candraśarman.
Having bathed in the morning and become pure, O King, in the month of Kārttika, the king worshipped Janārdana with tender tulasī leaves.
At night, the king should indeed offer a sky-lamp with this mantra: || 88 ||

Having offered salutations to Dāmodara, the All-pervading One who assumes the universal form, I shall present this sky-lamp, so dear to Hari. O Lord of Gods, grant that it may be free from obstacles until the month is completed. (89)
"O Lord of Gods, may devotion toward you increase through this vow. With this mantra, that king indeed performed the offering of a lamp.
Furthermore, during the Brāhma-muhūrta, he indeed offered the lamp of the sky; having performed the morning worship of Viṣṇu, he performed his morning ablution.
Having performed the rite of formal relinquishment and having completed the offering of the sky-lamp, and after feeding the Brahmins, he offered the vow to Viṣṇu.
O best of sages, by the power of that merit, that king enjoyed captivating pleasures here for a hundred thousand autumns.

He enjoyed [the fruits of his merit] together with his wife, along with his excellent sons, grandsons, and kinsmen; and then, O best of the twice-born, at the end [of that life], he ascended a most beautiful celestial chariot.
O Sage, having ascended together with the women, he went upon the path to liberation; he was four-armed, clad in yellow garments, and bore the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Like Viṣṇu himself in the world of Viṣṇu, being constantly praised by the immortals, that high-minded king sported there according to his desire.
Therefore, having attained this human birth which is so difficult to obtain, one should offer the sky-lamp according to the prescribed rite during the month of Kārttika; it is dear to Hari.
O Lord of Sages, those mortals who offer a sky-lamp here in the month of Kārtika for the pleasure of Hari shall never behold the god Yama, whose face is exceedingly cruel.
Now I shall further proclaim the majesty of the Lamp of the Sky; listen to that which was spoken of old by the Vālakhilyas, O best of the twice-born. (99)
The Vālakhilyas said: "O best of sages, beginning from the month of Kārtika and proceeding through the sequence of the months starting with Kṛṣṇa, let the gift of lamps be made from the sky."
He who, at the arrival of the evening twilight during the month of Tulā, should offer a sky-lamp with sesame oil continuously for one month; || 1 ||
To the glorious Lord of Śrī, he is never separated from Śrī; the lineage of sky-lamps should be twenty cubits at most in height. || 2 ||
The medium [size] should be nine cubits, and the smallest five cubits; one should act in such a way that it is visible to people standing at a distance. || 3 ||
Likewise, the offering of lamps in caskets made of clouds and other materials is especially distinguished; a small banner (patākikā) should be made with one-ninth the length of the bamboo pole.
One should place either a handful of peacock feathers or a water-pot on top; this lamp, which pleases Viṣṇu, is the means for the liberation of the ancestors.
On the eleventh day, or from the time the sun enters Libra, one should offer a lamp to Dāmodara in the month of Nabhas (Śrāvaṇa) while the moon is in Libra, together with a swing.
I offer this lamp to you; salutations to the infinite Creator! It is like a lamp for the sky, truly the savior of one's father.
Helika had two sons; among them, one was Piśācaka, who attained liberation—so difficult to obtain—through the merit of giving lamps to the sky.
Salutation to the ancestors who have passed away; salutation to Dharma and Viṣṇu; salutation to Yama, to Rudra, and to the Lord of the Wilderness.

Those mortals who, with this mantra, offer a lamp in the sky for the sake of their ancestors—even those who have gone to hell—truly attain the highest state; thus has the gift of lamps been described by me. (110)
One should kindle it for the sake of attaining prosperity, progeny, and success, as well as for the sake of health.
In the dark fortnight of Kārttika, during the five lunar days beginning with the twelfth, the rite of Nīrājana for men is prescribed to be performed in the early part of the night.
Especially in the abodes of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, as well as in gabled chambers, shrines, assembly halls, and rivers.
Indeed, upon the walls, in the gardens and ponds, at the city gates and pleasure groves, as well as in the secluded stables and the elephant sheds.
At the time of dusk, one should offer such beautiful lamps; thus, by those who have performed the offering of lamps according to the prescribed rite during the month of Kārttika—
Those who are seen to be recipients of jewels are proclaimed for this very reason; if one is unable to give a lamp, one should instead protect another's lamp.
Who among the men standing on this earth is able to describe the fruit obtained by one who, with devotion, gives oil for the sake of a lamp to a student of the Vedas? (17)
One should offer various kinds of lamps in the presence of Viṣṇu during the month of Kārttika, when the month of Kārttika has arrived and the sky possesses a clear luster.
At night, Lakṣmī, who was born from the ocean, comes to behold the wonders of the world; wherever she sees lamps, [she remains there].
One should never take pleasure in darkness; therefore, a lamp should always be established during the month of Kārtika.
For those seeking the form of Lakṣmī, the gift of lamps is especially prescribed; particularly in a temple, on a riverbank, or on a royal highway. (21)
The glory of one who gives a lamp at a place where sleep occurs spreads in every direction; likewise for him who, seeing the home of a weak person devoid of lamps, provides a lamp. (22)
Whether he be a Brahmin or of another caste, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu [after passing through] a difficult and uneven place filled with insects and thorns.
He who offers gifts of lamps does not go to hell; he who offers a lamp according to the prescribed rite at Pañcanada during the night [attains the same].

In his lineage are born children who become the illuminators of the family; [he is honored] on the paternal side by the gift of food, and in the months of Jyeṣṭha and Āṣāḍha by the gift of water. (25)
In the month of Kārttika, that same fruit is obtained by them through the kindling of another's lamp and through the service of Vaiṣṇavas. || 26 ||
One obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices by [observing the vow] in Kārtika. Formerly, there was a twice-born man named Harikara who was always devoted to sin. (27)
Indeed, through the occasion of a gambling match, that best of brahmins offered a lamp during the month of Kārtika; by the power of that merit, he attained heaven.
In former times, O descendant of Dharma, by the gift of a lamp in the sky, the king ascended an excellent celestial chariot and went to the world of Viṣṇu.
I shall describe the merit of him who offers a camphor lamp before Viṣṇu during the month of Kārttika, especially on the Prabodhinī day. || 130 ||
Those men born in his family are dear to Hari; having sported for a very long time, they attain liberation in the end.
He whose lamp burns day and night in the house of Hari, especially on the Ekādaśī day, goes to the abode of Hari.
The hunter also, having offered a lamp at a temple of Śiva on the fourteenth day, went to the world of Śiva by means of devotion toward that supreme Liṅga. || 33 ||
A certain cowherd, having lit a lamp for the Lord who wields the Śārṅga bow on the new moon night and repeatedly crying out "Victory! Victory!", became a sovereign king.
Nārada said: Speak further, O Lotus-seated One, for I am not yet satiated; by drinking the nectar of your speech, my thirst increases all the more.

Brahmā said: Having bathed in the morning and become pure during the month of Kārtika, one who is devoted to Viṣṇu should worship the Lord Dāmodara with tender tulasī leaves; he indeed attains liberation—there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
But he who worships with gold and other materials while devoid of devotion—He does not accept his worship; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. || 3 ||
This devotion is declared to be the supreme [duty] for all castes alike; an action devoid of devotion is not a cause of what is pleasing to Viṣṇu.
If worshipped daily with devotion even with just half a leaf of Tulasī, the Lord Hari, the Supreme Sovereign, personally appears before one's eyes.
In former times, Viṣṇudāsa went swiftly to the world of Viṣṇu through devotion and the worship of Tulasī; meanwhile, the Cōla attained only a secondary status.
Listen to the majesty of Tulasī, which destroys sins and increases merit; I shall relate that which was formerly spoken by Viṣṇu to Ramā.
When the month of Kārttika has arrived, those men who worship Tulasī and Hari with devotion go to the supreme abode.
Therefore, with every effort and with great devotion, one should worship the destroyer of all afflictions using the tender leaves of the Tulasī plant.
As long as the planted Tulasī plant spreads its roots, for that many thousands of yugas one is honored in the world of Brahmā.
If one performs a bath in water joined with Tulasī leaves, being liberated from all sins, he rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu.
O great sage, by merely planting a tree in Vṛndāvana for the purpose of cultivation, one is liberated from all sin and becomes fit for absorption into Brahman.
O Brahmin, that house in which a grove of Tulasī stands becomes a sacred pilgrimage site; the servants of Yama do not go there.
Those excellent men who plant a grove of Tulasī—which removes all sins, bestows merit, and grants desires—do not behold the son of the Sun (Yama).
Whatever man wears fragrance mixed with Tulasī wood, sin shall not touch his body, nor likewise that which is being committed.
O twice-born one, wherever there may be the shade of a grove of Tulasī trees, there a Śrāddha ceremony should be performed for the sake of the satisfaction of the ancestors.
For one on whose ear or head a Tulasī leaf is seen, even Yama is unable to look upon him, much less his terrifying messengers. (17)
He who daily listens with reverence to the greatness of Tulasī, being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Brahmā. || 18 ||
In this very context, O Brahmin, they cite this ancient history concerning Tulasī, which destroys sin through its mere hearing.
Formerly, in the land of Kaśmīra, there were two Brāhmaṇas named Harimedhas and Sumedhas, who were solely devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
Endowed with compassion for all beings and knowing the true meaning of all principles, those two best of the twice-born once became intent upon a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
As they were traveling together, the two Brahmins, overwhelmed by fatigue in the wilderness, beheld a grove of Tulasī there, O subduers of enemies.
Seeing that great grove of Tulasī, Sumedhas then circumambulated it and, filled with devotion, offered his salutations. || 23 ||
Having seen this, Dharimedha spoke with supreme joy, desiring to know again and again the majesty of Tulasī and its fruit.
Harimedhā said: O Brahmin, for what reason did you offer salutation to the gods, the sacred fords, the religious observances, and the foremost of Brahmins, even though they were present? (25)
Sumedhā said: Listen, O illustrious Brahmin, to these well-spoken words; for the heat of the sun oppresses us both, so let us go to the vicinity of this banyan tree. (26)
"Taking refuge in its shade, I shall tell you according to the truth. Thus addressed by Harimedha, Sumedhas was joined with him. (27)
The knower of dharma went to a banyan tree possessed of a great hollow; having rested there, that brahmin spoke to Harimedha. (28)
Listen, O tiger among brahmins, to the supreme narrative of Tulasī, who was born in the ocean by the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Formerly, when Purandara had lost his sovereignty due to the curse of Durvāsas, Brahmā and the others, together with the gods and the asuras, churned the ocean of milk.
Airāvata, the Kalpa tree, the Moon, and Kamalā; likewise Uccaiḥśravas, the Kaustubha gem, and Hari as Dhanvantari. (31)
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, divine medicinal herbs such as the harītakī and others, which bring about the welfare of the world, were also born. (32)
Then Viṣṇu, holding with both hands the jar of nectar which bestows freedom from old age and death, beheld the supreme Sutala in his mind and immediately attained the highest bliss.
From that jar of nectar, drops of tears of bliss fell, and instantly Tulasī was born as a circular cluster.
She was endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament. || 35 ||
There, the gods, headed by Brahmā, gave to Hari the goddess Lakṣmī and Tulasī who had appeared; indeed, the Blessed Lord Hari accepted them.
Therefore, Tulasī is exceedingly dear to the Lord of the worlds. || 37 ||
She, the beloved, is worshipped by all the hosts of gods like Viṣṇu himself; Nārāyaṇa is the protector of the world, and Tulasī is his beloved.
"Therefore, O Brahmin, I have offered my salutation to her. As the high-souled Sumedhas was speaking thus, [the sage said: 39.
Then, a great celestial chariot, radiant as the sun, was seen from afar; at that moment, O Sage, the banyan tree fell down before him.
In that very same manner, two men emerged from that tree, illuminating all directions with a splendor resembling the sun. (41)
Indeed, those two paid homage to Harimedha and Sumedha; and upon seeing them, Harimedha and Sumedha were overwhelmed with fear.
Both of them, resembling gods, filled with wonder, spoke.

Harimedha and Sumedha said: "Who are you two, resembling gods, who are the source of all auspiciousness? Bearing fresh garlands of mandāra flowers, you are like immortals; you are worthy of salutation and worship by us, possessing the forms of deities. (44)
When addressed thus by the two brahmins, those two who had emerged from the tree replied: "You two alone are our father, mother, and likewise our preceptor."
"Likewise, Bandhu and the others are none other than you two; of this there is no doubt. Jyeṣṭha said: "As for me, I am from the world of the gods, known by the name Āstīka. (46)
Once, my mind attached to sensual pleasures, I went to the Nandana grove on the mountain, surrounded by hosts of Apsarases, for the sake of sport. (47)
The celestial women gazed at me as they desired; the pearl and jasmine garlands fell from those women.
Seeing that very act of the scorching Romaśa, the sage became enraged: "This is not the fault of women, for they are indeed dependent on others. (49)
"This very man of wicked conduct deserves a curse," he said; "becoming a Brahmarākṣasa, you shall wander within this banyan tree. (50)
Then, being propitiated by me, he granted a release from the curse, as well as the greatness of the Tulasī leaf and the name of Viṣṇu, O twice-born one.
"When you hear it, you shall immediately attain supreme liberation. Having been thus cursed by the sage, he remained deeply distressed for a long time.
By divine providence, through the sight of you, I have certainly attained liberation from the curse of the brahmin while dwelling here in this banyan tree; now hear the story of the second one.
This best of sages, who was formerly devoted to serving his guru, disregarded his guru’s command and became a Brahmarākṣasa.
Through your grace, I have now been liberated from the Brahmin’s curse; furthermore, the fruit of a pilgrimage to sacred fords has been accomplished here by you both. (55)
"Thus, their ever-increasing merits shall grow day by day. Having spoken thus, those two excellent sages were saluted again and again.
Having taken leave of them, those two supreme bulls among sages departed for their own abode with great joy, setting out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Praising the meritorious Tulasī, O best of sages, they both departed. Thus, O Nārada, who indeed could describe the greatness of Tulasī?
Therefore, O Nārada, in this month of Kārtika, which grants satisfaction to Hari, the worship of Tulasī must be performed; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. (59)
Thus, O best of sages, the primary vows (aṅga-vratas) have been declared; I shall now proclaim the secondary vows (upāṅgas), as taught by the Vālakhilyas.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Tulasī," in the *Kārttikamāsa-māhātmya* of the second section (*Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The Vālakhilyas said: Kṛṣṇa spoke to Dharma regarding the twelfth lunar day known as Vatsa; for the worship of Vatsa, the twelfth day should be joined with the time of Godhūli.

On the first day, the Vatsapūjā (worship of the calf) should be performed at a banyan tree. One should smear with sandalwood paste and other unguents a cow that has a calf, is of the same color, well-behaved, and prolific, and worship her with flower garlands.
On that day, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should avoid food cooked in oil, food cooked in a pot, cow’s milk, cow’s ghee, curd, and milk.
At the end of the day, for half a ghaṭikā on both sides of the half-disk of the sun, the lustration (nīrājana) should be performed, and one should observe the auspicious and inauspicious signs.
Having first prepared various lamps placed in golden vessels and the like, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with the lamps and then observe for auspicious or inauspicious signs.
Having caused [the lamps] to be offered, one should place all the lamps facing toward the Unsurpassed (Uttara); nine principal lamps are prescribed, and one may also arrange others.
If the flame is situated to the right, radiant, possessed of a crest, and steady, it is said to bestow happiness; however, if it is the opposite, it brings suffering.
In the dark fortnight of the month of Kārtika, during the five lunar days beginning with the twelfth, the rite of Nīrājana for men is prescribed to be performed in the early part of the night.

The first lamp indicates the fortnight, the second the month, the third the season here, and the fourth likewise the solstice; the fifth lamp determines the year and its auspicious or inauspicious nature.
May these lamps, born from the rays of the sun and destroyers of darkness, illuminate me at the three periods of the day and indicate what is auspicious and inauspicious.
Having consecrated it with the mantra, one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) in due order.
First the gods, then the Brahmins, the elephants and the horses—the elder, the superior, and the inferior—and the women headed by his mother. (12)

Then one should place the consecrated lamps in their respective positions. If they are dry, there will be the destruction of prosperity; if they are white, there will be a loss of food; if they are excessively red, there will be battles; and if they have black flames, there will be death. (13)
A cowherd woman named Ekāṅgī performed this very vow; within three years, she became endowed with wealth and grain.
Therefore, the worship of cows should be performed on the twelfth day of the month of Kārttika. Those men who, having heard this greatness of the cow-vow (govrata), carry it out— || 15 ||
By the power of that cow-vow, they were not separated from their cattle on earth; whatever offense against cows may have been committed, it shall be dissolved through this vow.
The Vālakhilyas said: One should observe this vow on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja, near the festival of lamps (Dīpotsava).
Having bathed in the morning on the thirteenth day and having performed the cleansing of the teeth, one should observe the vow for three nights, being fully devoted to Govinda.

At the conclusion of this vow, the Govardhana festival should likewise be performed; a [lunar day] exceeding three muhūrtas should be accepted, and penetration by the following day does not constitute a fault.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, at the onset of night, one should offer a lamp and an oblation to Yama; thus, untimely death is destroyed.
In ancient times, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, by the power of compassion, the son of Hemanaka himself was liberated from untimely death.
The messengers said: "O Yama, having shown mercy before us, tell us the means by which one might not be deprived of life during such a great festival. (22)
Yama said: He who, year after year, offers a fine lamp at the door of his house on the night of the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina; || 23 ||
"O messengers, he must be brought here by this mantra even during a festival; and when untimely death has arrived, let my command be carried out. (24)
"May Yama, together with Death, the noose, the staff, and Time (Kāla), as well as myself, be pleased by the offering of a lamp on the thirteenth lunar day. (25)
Whoever offers a lamp at the doorway with this mantra, for him no fear of misfortune or untimely death shall arise during festivals.

The Vālakhilyas said: On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, which is joined with the preceding [thirteenth] lunar day, one should diligently perform a ritual bath at the time of dawn.
If a man bathes in the Riktā [tithi] at any time other than at sunrise, the merit arising from his annual observance is surely destroyed; of this there is no doubt. (28)
Likewise, O gods, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina at sunrise, an oil massage during the latter watch of the night is especially recommended. (29)
If the fourteenth day does not exist on two days at moonrise, or if it occurs on both days, then the former [the earlier one] alone is to be accepted.
If, out of force or even by compulsion, one does not perform the oil massage on the fourteenth day because of being a person of refined character, he shall go to the Raurava hell.
On the fourteenth day of Dīpāvalī, Lakṣmī resides in the oil and Gaṅgā resides in the water; indeed, he who performs his morning bath on this day does not behold the realm of Yama.
Furthermore, one should whirl the Apāmārga, the Tumbī, and another plant, the Prapunnāḍa, during the midst of the bath for the sake of the destruction of hell.
And having recited this supreme mantra three times, thrice over.

O Apāmārga plant, together with clods of earth from a furrow and provided with thorny leaves, remove my sin as you are being whirled around again and again. One should whirl the Apāmārga and the Prapunnāḍa over the head.

Having bathed while still wearing wet clothes, one should offer a lamp to Mṛtyu and his son. The two dogs, Śyāma and Śabala, who are brothers and servants of Yama—may they both be satisfied by the offering of a lamp on the fourteenth day, O you who are born from Death.
One should perform this bath together with beloved kinsmen; having performed the libation (tarpaṇa) as an ancillary part of the bath, one should thereafter offer libations to Yama.
To Yama, the King of Dharma, to Death, to Antaka, to Vaivasvata, to Kāla, and to the Destroyer of all beings. || 38 ||
Salutations to you, O Audumbara, Dadhnya, Nīla, Parameṣṭhin, Vṛkodara, Citra, and Citragupta. || 39 ||
These fourteen mantras should each be accompanied by the word "namas"; with each one, he should offer three handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds.

It should be performed either with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītin) or over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin); for Yama possesses a dual nature, being both a deity and a progenitor.
Even one whose father is still living should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for Yama and Bhīṣma; having worshipped the deities, a lamp should be offered for Naraka.

In this very context, the procedure for bathing for one who desires prosperity is now declared by me: on the fourteenth day of the waning moon of Āśvina, on the new moon day, and on the first day of the month of Kārttika.
When he bathes, he should perform an oil-bath at moonrise on the second lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, when the moon is in conjunction with the Svāti constellation.
A human being who bathes for auspiciousness is never separated from prosperity; because of the lustration with lamps here, this is remembered as Dīpāvalī.

Even during the waning of the moon, at the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), on the day of Rāhu’s descent (pāta), or on the day of the lunar day's exhaustion (dinakṣaya), an oil massage here causes no fault; rather, performed in the morning, it serves to remove sin.
Indeed, by eating the leaf-vegetable of the māṣa plant on that day—the fourteenth lunar day known as Pretākhyā—a man is liberated from all sins.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, or on the lunar day when the moon has waned, or at the new moon and so forth, when conjoined with the Svāti constellation, then the Festival of Lights (Dīpāvali) shall take place.
One should observe this continuous festival for three days, starting from the day of Dīpotsava; thus was the great king Bali addressed by the gratified Hari.
"Ask for a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever resides in your mind. Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, Bali spoke this speech: || 50 ||
"What is there to be asked for my own sake? Everything has already been given by me. For the sake of the world, however, I shall make a request; if you are able, grant that to me as well. (51)
Today the earth was given by me to you who were in the guise of Vāmana; yet it has been traversed by you in three strides within three days.
Therefore, O Hari, let there be sovereignty on the surface of the earth for three days.
"O Earth, may this wife of yours always remain firmly established in the homes of those men who offer lamps in my kingdom. (54)
"May the darkness of the loss of fortune and progeny always fall upon the home of those in whose house this [lamp] shall fall into darkness within my kingdom. (55)
And those who offer lamps for the sake of the hell-beings on the fourteenth day—for them, all the hosts of ancestors shall no longer dwell in hell.
O Keśava, how can lamps blaze within the homes of those who, having reached the kingdom of Bali, did not observe the festival of lights?
In the kingdom of Bali, those people who cause grief and discourage others—there is no doubt that sorrow shall always fall upon their own homes. (58)

One should pray, "May the sovereignty belong to Bali on the three fourteenth days. Long ago, having requested this earth in the form of Vāmana, he made Bali a dweller of the netherworld (pātāla) and gave it to Indra as a guest-offering.
In this manner, Hari granted those three days to the Lord of the Daityas; therefore, one should by all means indeed celebrate a great festival on this occasion.
O lords of sages, the Great Night (Mahārātri) arises on the fourteenth day; therefore, its festival should be observed by those devoted to the worship of Śakti.
Having reached the kingdom of Bali, the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras, as well as medicinal herbs, Piśācas, mantras, and likewise jewels [remained there].
Everyone indeed rejoices and dances at the onset of night; their respective mantras attain success in the kingdom of Bali, without a doubt. (63)
Just as the people were greatly delighted upon attaining the kingdom of Bali, so too on that very day the people became exceedingly joyful.

When the sun is situated in Libra, at the onset of night on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the lunar fortnight, men with torches in their hands should provide a guide for the path of the ancestors.
Those hungry ghosts who reside in hell always behold the path due to their vow; there is no doubt to be entertained here by the best of sages.
In the month of Āśvina, the three lunar days beginning with the fourteenth (bhūta) have been proclaimed; for rites such as the offering of lamps, those occurring at midday should be adopted.
If these three lunar days should occur before the time of conjunction (saṃgava), they must be joined with the preceding day for rites such as the offering of lamps.
The sages said: O twice-born ones, we wish to inquire about the majesty of Kaumodinī; on that day, what food should be eaten, and whose worship should one perform? (69)
For what purpose is it performed? Who is its presiding deity? What should be given there, and specifically, what should not be given? (70)
What is designated here as "exultation," and what is proclaimed here as "sport"? O best of sages, please tell me the entire fruit of Dīpāvalī. (71)

The Vālakhilyas said: "Then, at the time of dawn, O lords of sages, you shall come; having bathed and having worshipped the gods and the ancestors with devotion, you shall then offer salutations. (72)
Having performed the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha with curd, milk, ghee, and other offerings, one should not eat there during the day, except for children and the sick.
Then, at the time of dusk, one should worship the auspicious Indirā; one should prepare a pure pavilion for Lakṣmī with various kinds of cloths.
Adorned with various flowers and variegated sprouts, one should worship Lakṣmī there and also worship the gods.
One should also worship the divine ladies with many offerings of service, and with devotion, perform the massaging of the feet for Lakṣmī and the others.
On this day, in ancient times, all the gods were liberated from the prison of Bali by Viṣṇu, and Lakṣmī was also set free.
Then the gods, together with Lakṣmī, went again to the Ocean of Milk; therefore, O lords of sages, they slept there happily for a long time.

Couches containing the essence of the Sūtras, along with excellent pillows, should be prepared and covered with cloths resembling the foam of milk, arranged according to their respective directions. (79)
Accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas, he should install those deities and Lakṣmī; Lakṣmī, freed from the fear of the Daityas, was sleeping comfortably within the interior of a lotus.

Therefore, for the sake of her satisfaction, one should perform the ritual of the "Happy Sleep" here according to the rules; on that day, [one should offer] a lotus-bed for the increase of Lakṣmī's happiness. (81)
One should build a house for her so that Lakṣmī might not depart from it anywhere; yet men do not act in this way toward Lakṣmī, who desires their peaceful sleep.
How indeed can those who are devoid of concern for wealth sleep at night? Therefore, a person should worship Lakṣmī with every possible effort. (83)
He shall indeed be liberated from poverty and become established in his own caste; [he should offer] a mixture of nutmeg, cloves, cardamom, cinnamon, and camphor. (84)
Having caused cow’s milk to be boiled and added sugar in the appropriate measure, one should prepare sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas) from it and offer them to Lakṣmī.
One should offer other four kinds of edible foods, saying, "May Śrī be pleased. Before Hari has awakened, one should first awaken Lakṣmī with women.
Whether it be a woman or a man, Lakṣmī does not abandon him for as long as a year who, at the time of awakening, awakens Lakṣmī [the goddess]. || 87 ||
Having obtained safety from the Brahmins, the enemies of the gods, fearing Viṣṇu, praised her in the Ocean of Milk once they realized that Śrī was asleep, resting upon the lotus.
You are the light—the glory of the sun, moon, fire, lightning, and the golden stars; you are the light of all lights. Salutations to You who abide as the light of lamps. 89.
That Lakṣmī who resides on earth on this auspicious day of Dīpāvalī, and that Lakṣmī who dwells in the cow-pen on the full moon of Kārttika—may she grant me boons. 90.
Then, at twilight, one should offer a lamp and likewise a firebrand; one should wave it over one's own head, which wards off all misfortunes.
Likewise, lamp-trees should be erected according to one's ability in temples and other such places, at crossroads, in cremation grounds, and by rivers, mountains, or houses. (92)
The grounds of the royal highways should be adorned with cloths and flowers at the roots of trees, in cow-pens, at crossroads, and in houses. || 93 ||
Immediately thereafter, having decorated the entire city at nightfall, he first fed the Brahmins and satisfied those who were hungry.
One should eat while adorned and graced with new garments; thereafter, at the time of afternoon, the king shall cause a proclamation to be made throughout the city.
"Today, let the kingdom of Bali and its worlds be enjoyed as you wish! Having thus commanded, "O children, play as you please," by the king— (96)
One should give them toys, and then observe the auspicious or inauspicious [omens]; whatever is in one's mind should be performed during the reign of Bali.

O lords of sages, injury to living beings, drinking liquor, sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached, theft, and betrayal of trust—these five are said to be the gates of hell in the kingdom of Bali; one should renounce them. (98)
Then, at the time of midnight, the king himself should go to the city on foot, very slowly, to behold its beauty; and having seen the joy of King Bali’s kingdom, he should return to his own home.

When midnight had thus arrived and the people’s eyes were half-closed in sleep, the women of the city, with joyful faces, drove away Alakṣmī from the courtyards of their own homes by beating winnowing baskets and drums.

If the conjunction of the new moon (darśa) occurs during the single watch (ekarajanī) of the staff (daṇḍa) on the following day, then one should abandon the previous day, and the "Happy Night" (sukharātrikā) shall take place on that subsequent day.
Those men, whether Vaiṣṇavas or non-Vaiṣṇavas, who do not celebrate the festival of King Bali’s reign—their religious merits shall be in vain; of this there is no doubt. (102)
One should keep a vigil at night by means of reciting the Purāṇas and so forth, or by gambling, or likewise by singing before Lord Hari. (103)

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Rituals for Vatsadvādaśī, Yamatrayodaśī, Narakacaturdaśī, and Dīpāvalī," in the Kārtika-māsa-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Brahmā said: On the first lunar day (pratipad), one should perform an oil massage and then the lustration rite (nīrājana); well-attired, one should spend the day with sacred discourses, songs, and acts of charity.
In ancient times, Śaṅkara created a most enchanting game of dice on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārtika, O Satyavat.
Listen now to the greatness of even the day of Bali’s kingdom according to its true essence: men and women alike should bathe with sesame oil.
If one does not perform it out of delusion, he goes to the abode of Yama; formerly, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, there was the great Bali, the lord of the Dānavas.
He gave the earth, together with his own head, to Vāmana; at that time, the Lord himself, being pleased, spoke to Bali.
"O sinless one, because you have devotedly given me this land on the first day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika, I am well-pleased with you."
"O King, I grant you a boon," he said, and then bestowed the boon: "O King, let the first lunar day of Kārtika be known by your very name. (7)
O King, whatever worship—including the ritual bathing with oil—those who perform on this day shall become inexhaustible; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
From that time onwards, this first lunar day (pratipad) has been renowned in this world; it must never, under any circumstances, be observed when overlapped by the preceding day.
One should not apply oil massage there, otherwise one would meet death; when the new moon (darśa) occurs on the first lunar day (pratipad) for the duration of even a single muhūrta.

If there be an auspicious occasion on that day, his wealth and other assets will perish; likewise, if the first lunar day (pratipad) or the new moon (darśa) should be joined with the asterism of Bala, [the same result follows].
If, out of delusion, a woman performs any act of distress upon that [image], there will certainly be widowhood for women and death for the offspring.
If it should be unpierced on the following day for even a single muhūrta, that alone is declared by the wise to be suitable for festive rites and other such activities. (13)

If even a very small portion of the [proper] lunar day does not remain on the following day, then the previous overlapping day (pūrvaviddhā) should be observed; if it is performed thus, one shall not incur any fault.
On that day, one should fashion an image within the house or in its courtyard; there, using cow dung, and one should also place curd before it.
Having placed the lamp there, one should perform the rites according to the injunctions; for those who do not perform the oil massage on that day, O bull among sages, [there is a great fault]. (16)
For them, there will certainly be no auspiciousness for as long as a year, according to whatever form one stands upon that auspicious day. (17)
That [period] shall be a rainless one for him; therefore, one should perform auspicious rites if one desires to enjoy divine and captivating pleasures that are favorable to oneself. || 18 ||
Celebrate the delightful festival of lights on the thirteenth lunar day and those following; for Śaṅkara and Bhavānī were engaged in a game of dice in sport.
In ancient times, having defeated Śambhu at dice, Gaurī sent him forth naked; for this reason, Śaṅkara remains miserable while Gaurī always abides in happiness.
Having abandoned gambling everywhere as forbidden at every step, the wise declare that for whom victory comes first, for him there is happiness for a year.
Requested by Bhavānī, Lakṣmī remained present in the form of a cow; Govardhana is to be worshipped in the morning, and one should engage in gambling at night.
At that time, the cows should be adorned and spared from being yoked to burdens or being milked.
O upholder of Govardhana, O protector of Gokula, you who raised the mountain with the arm of Viṣṇu, grant us ten million cows.
May that Lakṣmī of the world-protectors, who abides in the form of a cow and yields ghee for the sake of sacrifice, dispel my sin. (25)
May cows be before me; may cows be behind me; may cows be my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows. (26)
Thus ends the worship of Govardhana. Having satisfied the gods with sincere devotion, virtuous men with [proper] conduct, others with food and drink, and the learned with the gift of speech; || 27 ||
The inhabitants of the inner apartments were honored with garments, betel, incense, flowers, camphor, saffron, and various kinds of foods and delicacies.
