The king should satisfy the villagers with gifts of bulls, the vassal lords with wealth, and the multitudes of foot soldiers with auspicious neck-ornaments and bracelets engraved with his own name; thus the king should gratify those virtuous men individually.
Having gratified the wrestlers and men according to their merit, as well as the bulls and buffaloes fighting with their rivals, [he then proceeded].
Likewise, the king himself, mounted upon a dais, should watch the warriors and the well-adorned foot soldiers, as well as the actors, dancers, and bards.
One should cause the cattle, buffaloes, and other livestock to fight and settle them; one should draw the calves away from the cows by means of a dialogue of calls and responses.
Then, O observer of noble vows, at the time of afternoon, one binds the Mārgapālī in the eastern direction upon a pillar of a fortress or a tree.
O beloved, having caused the elephants and horses to gaze upon a divine image made of kuśa and kāśa grass adorned with many hanging ornaments, one should lead them beneath the path-guardian tree.
O best of the twice-born, one should have cows, bulls, buffaloes, and buffaloes—along with jars filled to the brim—bound as guardians of the path by those who have performed the fire-oblations.

Then, O observer of noble vows, one should perform a salutation with this mantra: "O Mārgapālī, salutations to you, the bestower of happiness upon all the world! By your grace, may my horses, elephants, and cows be well. (36)
O son, cows and great bulls, as well as kings, princes, and especially Brahmins, walk upon the surface of the path of Mārgapālī.
Having completely crossed the path-guardians, they were indeed free from disease and happy; having performed all this here during the night, [they proceeded] against Bala, the lord of the Daityas.
Then, having prepared a mandala on the ground, one should perform worship after drawing the lord of the Daityas as Bali with five-colored pigments.
He was adorned with every kind of ornament, accompanied by Vindhyāvalī, and surrounded by Kūṣmāṇḍa, Maya, Jaṃbha, Ūru, Madhu, and Dānava.
Having again fashioned the king of the Daityas in his own likeness, with a full and broad face, adorned with a crown and prominent earrings, and possessing two arms; || 41 ||
Then, being well-pleased, he should worship together with his mothers, brothers, and kinsmen in a spacious hall in the middle of the house.
With lotuses, water-lilies, flowers, kahlāras, and red lotuses; with fragrant flowers, food offerings, and oblations consisting of milk, jaggery, and milk-rice (pāyasa). || 43 ||

O King of kings, whoever—along with his ministers and his domestic priest—performs worship with offerings of liquor, meat, wine, and various foods to be licked, sucked, and eaten, while reciting this mantra, shall experience happiness for an entire year. (44)
O King Bali, son of Virocana, O Lord, O future Indra, O enemy of the gods, I bow to you; please accept this worship. (45)
Having thus performed the ritual of worship, one should then keep a vigil at night; for a moment during the night, one should engage in performances of actors, dances, and storytelling.
And the people, having established King Bali within the interior of their homes with white rice, should worship him with fruits and flowers.
O observer of noble vows, everything there should indeed be performed for the sake of the bali offering—those various acts which the sages who perceive reality declare to be inexhaustible.
Whatever gift is given here, whether it be small or great, all of it becomes inexhaustible, auspicious, and pleasing to Viṣṇu.
O Bala, may all the merit of those men who do not perform worship to you at night, as well as the dharma of the Vedic scholar, accrue to you.
And furthermore, O child, Viṣṇu himself, being pleased with Bala, gave him that which brings benefit and is a great festival for the Asuras.
Thus, for every year, during the month of Kārtika, a single day and night was given by the king of the Dānavas as if it were a mirror upon the earth.
For the king who performs this in his kingdom, whence can there be fear of disease? There shall be abundance of food, security, health, and unsurpassed prosperity for him. (53)
And all people shall be free from disease and devoid of all calamities.

Since the Kaumudī is observed in order to establish one's state of being upon the earth, O observer of noble vows, whatever state of mind—whether joy, sorrow, or otherwise—one maintains during this festival, by that very state one's entire year indeed passes away. (55)

If one weeps during the year, the year will be weeping; if one is delighted, it will be delightful; if one experiences enjoyment, the year will be enjoyable; and if one is healthy, it will be healthy. (56)
This lunar day in the month of Kārtika is declared to be sacred to Viṣṇu and to the Dānavas.

Those who perform the worship of King Bali with auspiciousness during the Festival of Lights, which generates joy for all people, bring delight to their entire year through great happiness; such families possess the wisdom that finds true pleasure in the enjoyment of giving. || 58 ||
Having thus performed the worship with offerings, one should afterwards engage in the sport of the cows.
On the day of the cattle-sport (Gavām-krīḍā), if the moon should be seen at night, King Soma destroys the cattle as well as those who worship Surabhi.

The playing with cows is prescribed when the first lunar day (pratipad) coincides with the new moon (darśa); if one should perform it when the first day is overlapped by the previous tithi, there will be the destruction of sons, wife, and wealth.

Then the cows, adorned with ornaments and honored with offerings of grass and other gifts, should be led outside the city to the accompaniment of the sounds of songs and musical instruments; having brought them back from there, one should subsequently perform the rite of *nīrājana*.
If, however, the first day is short, the woman should perform the Nīrājana rite; then, on the second day, she should perform the auspicious garland ceremony in the evening.

Having thus performed the Nīrājana rite, one is liberated from all sins. For the ritual of drawing the stick (yaṣṭikākarṣaṇa), the first lunar day (pratipad) should be joined with the preceding tithi.
One should make a very firm and new staff out of kuśa or kāśa grass; it should be carried to the gate of a temple, the gate of a king, or to a crossroads.
The princes would take hold of her from one side and those of low caste from the other, and they would pull her back and forth repeatedly according to their respective strength. (66)
An equal number [of days] should be assigned to both; all [the planets] are indeed most powerful. Here, victory belongs to those of lower birth, while for the king, victory lasts for a year.
A line should be drawn behind both [the players] over the one who draws it; he who leads [his opponent] to the end of that line shall be victorious, and not otherwise. (68)
The king should diligently establish this emblem of victory.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the First Day of the Bright Fortnight of Kārttika," in the Kārttikamāsa-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 10 ||
Nārada said: O Blessed One, filled with humility, I desire to question you; tell me that vow by which a mortal does not behold death.
Brahmā said: O best of Brahmins, if you ask about the most excellent of vows, listen to the vow known as Yamadvitīyā, which destroys death.
O Lord of Sages, on the second day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika, one should perform [this rite] according to the prescribed injunctions; it wards off all death.
O Lord of Sages, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* of the second watch, one should contemplate what is beneficial for the self in the mind and never recall what is harmful. (4)
Then one should perform the morning bath, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth. Thereafter, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents— || 5 ||
Having performed his daily rites, joyful and adorned with earrings and armlets, he went to the Udumbara tree and prepared an excellent mandala.
Having fashioned an auspicious eight-petaled lotus made of udumbara wood, [one should worship] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Sarasvatī, the giver of boons.
O best of the twice-born, one with a steady mind should worship her who is joined with a lute and a book, using sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron.
Then, for the destruction of death, [one should worship] with flowers, incense, food offerings, coconuts, fruits, and so forth, as well as a milch cow adorned with ornaments.
And one should give a cow along with its calf to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, for the sake of destroying untimely death and for crossing over the ocean of worldly existence.
"O Brahmin, I give this gentle cow to you"; with this mantra, one should give the cow to a Brahmin who is a teacher of the Veda.
If, however, such a person cannot be found, one should devotedly give a pair of sandals to a Brahmin; then, having completed the worship, one who is devoted to Puruṣottama [should proceed].
One should properly salute with devotion those who are the best among kinsmen and those advanced in age; one should also satisfy one's own relatives with various kinds of delightful fruits.
Then, O Sage, having approached the house of whichever sister may be endowed with a brother, one should offer salutations with perfect devotion.
"O fortunate and auspicious sister, I have come to your abode for the sake of my own welfare to pay homage to the lotus-feet of yours. (19)
Having spoken thus to that sister, he should salute her with the thought that she is Viṣṇu; then, having heard her brother’s excellent words, the sister— || 16 ||
O Nārada, a sister should speak these words to her brother: "O brother, today I have become blessed and auspicious through you. (17)
"O lamp of your lineage, O brother, you must dine today in my house for the sake of your own long life, on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika. (18)

Formerly, Yama was fed and honored in his own home by Yamunā; on this day, even those in hell were liberated by Yama, and though bound by the nooses of karma, they wander about according to their own will.
"O man, we have been deprived of food today; having found that sinner who did not eat in his sister-in-law's house on this Yamadvitīyā day, we are now exceedingly joyful and shall devour him. (20)
"Thus do sins such as the killing of a Brahmin cry out here; therefore, O brother, take your meal in my house during the month of Kārtika. (21)
O son, on this second day of the bright fortnight, renowned throughout the three worlds, even wise men do not eat at their own homes.
Having been addressed thus, the observer of the vow should say "So be it" and, filled with great joy, O highly fortunate one, should honor his sister with garments, ornaments, and decorations. (23)
Then, having saluted her elder sister and received her blessing, all the sisters should be gratified with gifts of clothing and ornaments. (24)
In the absence of one's own sister, however, [the guest] should go to the house of his paternal uncle’s daughter or his own father’s sister and respectfully take his meal there. (25)
O son, he who thus performs this second rite named after Yama shall be liberated from untimely death and surrounded by sons, grandsons, and other descendants. || 26 ||
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures here as well as other things according to his desire, he attains liberation in the end; otherwise, my word would not be true.
All these vows and various kinds of gifts are appropriate only for the householder; therefore, one should take recourse to the life of a householder.
Mādhava has declared that for the man who, established in the vow, listens to the narrative of Yamadvitīyā, all his sins are destroyed.
Sūta said: On the second day of the month of Kārttika, in the forenoon, one should worship Yama; having bathed on that daughter of the Sun, a man does not behold the world of Yama.
O Śaunaka, on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, Yama was formerly fed and honored in his own home by Yamunā.
On the second day, there was a great release, and the denizens of hell were satisfied; freed from their sins, they were all liberated from their bondage.
Having eaten here and being fully satisfied, they all remained there according to their own will; for them, a great festival took place, which brought happiness to the realm of Yama.
Therefore, this Yamadvitīyā is renowned throughout the three worlds; for that reason, O Brahmin, the wise should not eat in their own homes on that day.
With affection, one should eat from the hand of one's sister, which increases strength; on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, Yama is worshipped and gratified.
Salutation to that Lord who is the soul of Yama, mounted upon a buffalo-seat, bearing a staff and a mallet, and surrounded by joyful servants.

Those sisters who are well-dressed women, by whom [others] have been gratified with gifts of clothing and the like—for them there shall be neither quarrel nor fear of an enemy for the duration of a year. (37)

O sinless son, I have explained to you in its entirety, along with its secret mysteries, that which is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, and the means for accomplishing dharma, kama, and artha. 38.

On whichever lunar day the god Yamarāja was fed by Yamunā out of sisterly affection, on that very same day, whoever here eats from the palm of his sister's hand attains supreme wealth and auspicious prosperity.
Sūta said: A specific detail regarding this matter has been proclaimed by the great seers, the Vālakhilyas; I shall relate that fully, so listen, O best of sages. (40)
The Vālakhilyas said: On the second lunar day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, which is known as the day of Yama, the worship of Yama must by all means be performed during the afternoon.
In former times, Yamunā would come every day and entreat Yama, saying: "O brother, come to my house for a meal, surrounded by your attendants."
Yama speaks every day, whether today, tomorrow, or the day after; for those whose minds are distracted by their affairs, no opportunity arises. (43)
Then once, O lords of sages, he was invited by Yamunā against his will and went there on the second day of the month of Kārtika.
O bird, having dismissed the inhabitants of hell along with his hosts, the son of the Sun was entertained as a guest by Yamunā, who prepared various kinds of cooked foods.
Having been anointed by Yamunā with oils fragrant with perfumes, and having had his body rubbed with an unguent, the son of the Sun was bathed.
Then ornaments were given, as well as various garments and sandalwood; garlands were also presented, and he sat upon the couch.
Having prepared various kinds of cooked foods in a golden vessel, the goddess Yamunā, with a delighted mind, fed them to Yama.
Having eaten, Yama also honored his sister with ornaments and various garments; then he said, "O beautiful lady, choose a boon. Hearing those words of his, Yamunā spoke this speech: || 49 ||
Yamunā said: "Come to my house every year for the sake of a meal. (50)
"O Yama, today all sinners must be released from hell; grant happiness to those who this very day shall take their meal from the hand of my sister—this alone do I choose. (51)
Yama said: "But he who, having bathed in the Yamunā, has offered libations to the ancestors and the gods... (52)
He eats in his sister’s house and even honors his sister; yet, O daughter of the Sun, he never beholds my door.
In the north-eastern direction from Vīreśa, Yamatīrtha is celebrated; having bathed there according to the rules and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, [one attains the fruit].
The best of men, facing the sun, observing silence, with a concentrated mind and a steady posture, should recite these names until midday. (55)

Yama, the slayer, the Lord of Ancestors and King of Dharma, Vaivasvata, the wielder of the staff, Time (Kāla), the lord of beings, and the one who follows the deeds performed—these they recite as the ten names of Kṛtānta.
Then, having worshipped Yameśvara, one should go to the house of the sister; there, he should first be respectfully fed by her with this mantra: || 57 ||
"O brother, I am born after you; eat this auspicious food for the pleasure of King Yama, and especially for Yamunā. (58)
Then, having gratified his sister with garments, ornaments, and other gifts, he shall not behold the realm of Yama even in a dream.
And those who have been placed in prison by kings on my day must certainly be sent to their mother's house for the sake of a meal.
"Today, on this very day, I must deliver the wicked from the hells; those who today make me a prisoner shall be struck down by me in every way. (61)
If there is no younger sister, then she should go to the house of the elder sister; in her absence, she should then go to the house of the paternal aunt who has children.

In their absence, she may likewise be the daughter of her mother’s sister or her maternal uncle; or else, she may determine the order [of succession] through those related by the same womb, by the same lineage, or by marriage.
In the absence of all [these], any sister indeed should be honored; or else, in the absence of her, one should have it performed by a cow, a river, and so forth.
Even in her absence, O Goddess, one should imagine the forest as her sister; one must never eat in her own house.
"Those of wicked conduct who eat [thus] fall into hell. Having spoken thus, Dharmarāja then departed for Saṃyaminī.
Therefore, all the best of sages who perform the Kārtika vow eat from the hand of their sister; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
The Vedic revelation of the Sun declares that if one, having reached the Yamadvitīyā day, does not partake of a meal at his sister's house, the merit earned throughout the year perishes.
But that woman who feeds her brother on the lunar day sacred to him, and honors him with betel leaves, shall not attain widowhood. (69)
Surely there would never be a loss of his brother's lifespan if that second lunar day, which extends into the afternoon, were used for the brother's meal. (70)
If, due to ignorance or delusion, it was not eaten at the sister's house—whether because one was traveling abroad, lacking food, afflicted by fever, or perhaps intoxicated; || 71 ||
Having heard this narrative, one shall obtain the fruit of a meal; especially so in the month of Kārtika, while taking refuge in the shade of a dhātrī tree.
Whoever partakes of the meal shall attain Vaikuṇṭha.
Śaunaka said: The greatness of Kārttika bestows the fruit of great merit. When did the dhātrī tree originate, and how did it attain renown? (1)
Why is this [river] pure, and why is it the destroyer of sin? By whom was Āmardakī made? Tell me this in detail.

Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, I shall relate how this [vow] indeed bestows merit. On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should perform the worship of the Dhātrī tree.
The great Āmardakī tree destroys all sins; on the fourteenth day known as Vaikuṇṭha-caturdaśī, a man who goes into the shade of a Dhātrī tree [attains this].
There one should worship Hari, the Lord of Gods, together with Rādhā; then one should perform one hundred and eight circumambulations.
One should perform one hundred and eight circumambulations with each individual item—whether with gold, silver, or even *āmalaka* fruits. (6)
Having prostrated with the eight limbs of the body, one should pray to the Supreme Lord; and having taken refuge in the shade of a Dhātrī tree, one should listen to this narrative.

Thereafter, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's capacity. When the Brāhmaṇas are satisfied, Hari—the bestower of liberation—is also pleased. In this regard, I shall relate to you a narrative that yields meritorious fruit; even Brahmā is not able to fully describe the fruit of the Āmardakī.

In ancient times, when a single ocean had arisen and all moving and stationary things had perished, when the hosts of gods and asuras had vanished and the serpents and rākṣasas were utterly destroyed; (10)
There, the eternal Supreme Soul, the Lord of the lords of gods, meditated upon the supreme Brahman, which is the highest and immutable state of the Self.
Then, as he was chanting the Brahma-mantra, his breath issued forth from his mouth; and out of affection upon seeing it, tears flowed from his eyes.
Pierced by a flood of tears of love, that drop fell upon the ground; from that drop there arose the great Dhātrī tree itself.
Abounding in many branches and twigs, and weighed down by the burden of its fruit, it is proclaimed as the primordial growth of all trees. (14)
Brahmā first created him, and after that he created the progeny—the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas.
The Blessed Lord likewise created stainless human beings; those gods came to that place where Dhātrī, the beloved of Hari, was located.
Seeing her, those illustrious ones were filled with great wonder; "We do not know this tree," they thought again and again. (17)
While they were reflecting thus, an incorporeal voice spoke: "This is indeed the Āmardakī mountain, for it is a preeminent Vaiṣṇava site. (18)
Indeed, by the mere remembrance of this, one obtains the fruit born of the gift of a cow; by seeing it, the merit is twofold, and likewise, by eating it, it is threefold.
Therefore, with every effort, Āmardakī should always be served; she is declared to be the remover of all sins, belonging to Viṣṇu, and the destroyer of evil.
Viṣṇu stands at its base, and above him is the Grandfather (Brahmā); and upon its trunk is established the Lord Rudra, the Supreme Sovereign.
Savitṛ resides in the branches, and the deities in the twigs; the deities dwell in the leaves, and likewise the Maruts in the flowers.
All the lords of creatures are thus established in their respective fruits; for this Earth has indeed been described by me as being composed of all the gods. (23)

Therefore, she is to be worshipped for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. Once, the yogi Nārada stood before Brahmā; having prostrated before the Lord of the World, he, being greatly amazed, asked: || 24 ||
Śrī Nārada said: Just as a beloved grove of excellent *tulasī* is always dear to Hari, so too is a grove of *dhātrī* trees especially dear to Śrī Hari during the month of Kārtika.
Brahmā said: The worship of Hari in a Dhātrī grove and taking one's meal in the shade of Dhātrī trees—he who performs these in the month of Kārtika, his sin is destroyed. || 26 ||
When the sun is situated in Libra, all holy places, sages, gods, and sacrifices constantly take refuge in the Dhātrī tree during the month of Kārtika.
Whatever merit a human being performs under the shade of the Dhātrī tree, let that become multiplied ten millionfold; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (28)
In this very context, they cite this ancient history.
O best of the twice-born, there was a certain vaiśya in the city of Ayodhyā who, by the turn of fate, was afflicted by poverty and deprived of both sons and wife.
O Nārada, he quenched the fire of his stomach with alms; once, a Vaiśya merchant, tormented by hunger, begged from him.
O Nārada, having received some chickpeas as alms, she went to the shade of a Dhātrī tree; there, during the month of Kārtika, she ate them.
O Nārada, some chickpeas remained there; they were given by that Vaiśya to a twice-born man who was emaciated by hunger. (33)
By the power of that merit, he became a wealthy king on earth; therefore, one should always practice giving in the month of Kārttika.

O best of sages, in the Dhātrī grove for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals, he who takes refuge in the shade of the Dhātrī tree during the month of Kārttika and listens to the story of Hari is liberated from sins, just like the son of the twice-born.
Nārada said: O Brāhmaṇa, who was that son of a twice-born man, and what sin did he commit in the past? How did his liberation come about? Tell me this in detail.
Brahmā said: Formerly, there was an excellent twice-born man on the northern bank of the Kāverī.
There was one renowned as Devaśarman, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; his son was of wicked conduct, and the father spoke these beneficial words to him.
Now the month of Kārtika, which is dear to Hari, is underway; perform therein ritual bathing, charity, vows, and observances. (39)
O son, perform the worship of Hari accompanied by Tulasī flowers, as well as the offering of various lamps, prostrations, and circumambulations. (40)
Having thus heard his father's words, the wicked-souled son, filled with rage, spoke to his father while reviling him with trembling lips. (41)
The son said: "O father, I will not perform the accumulation of merit during Kārtika. Hearing these words of his son, he spoke to that son with anger. (42)
"O evil-minded one, become a mouse in a hollow of a tree in the forest. Frightened by the fear of this curse, he bowed to his father and said: || 43 ||
"O Guru, tell me how my liberation from this evil birth may come to pass. Thus entreated, the Brahmin spoke the means for his deliverance.
O son, when you hear that merit arising from the Ujjavrata which is dear to Hari, then your liberation shall come about through listening to that narrative.
Having been addressed thus by his father, he instantly became a mouse; dwelling for many thousands of years in a cave within the forest.
Once, in the month of Kārtika, Viśvāmitra, together with his disciples, having bathed in the river and worshipped Hari, took refuge in the shade of an āmalakī tree.
He recounted the greatness arising from the month of Kārttika to his disciples; at that time, a certain man of wicked conduct, a hunter wandering on a hunt, arrived there.
Having seen the hosts of sages, the slayer of living beings resolved to kill them; yet, by the mere sight of them, he then became possessed of excellent understanding.
Then, having bowed to the brahmins, he said, "What is being done here by you? Being addressed in this manner, Viśvāmitra, the lord of brahmins, spoke to him.
Viśvāmitra said: Among all months, Kārttika is declared to be the most excellent; whatever rite is performed during that month increases like the seed of a banyan tree.
Whoever performs bathing, giving gifts, worship, and the feeding of Brahmins during the month of Kārttika, that shall yield inexhaustible fruit. || 52 ||
Having heard the dharma taught by the sage, the twice-born one, upon hearing it, cast off his mouse body and then assumed a divine form. (53)
Then, having bowed to Viśvāmitra and related his own account, he was permitted by the sage and departed for heaven, seated upon a celestial chariot.
The son of Gādhi was struck with wonder, and the hunter especially so; having performed the Ūrja-vow, even the hunter went to the abode of Hari.
Therefore, with every effort during the month of Kārttika, one should take refuge in the shade of the Dhātrī tree before Keśava and engage in listening to the sacred narratives.
Even the mouse was liberated from its wretched birth by hearing the narrative of Ūrjaka; whoever hears this or causes it to be heard shall undoubtedly partake in liberation.

Taking shelter in the shade of a Dhātrī tree, one should partake of the forest meal; first performing his bath in the water situated within the forest, and having completed his daily obligatory rites, he should then worship Mādhava.
Taking refuge in the shade of the Dhātrī tree, endowed with devotion for Hari, one should listen to the divine narrative that proclaims the greatness of the month. (59)
Then, one should devoutly feed the Brahmins who are most eminent in their knowledge of the Veda; thereafter, O best of Brahmins, one should eat oneself while recollecting Hari.
O Brahmin, when the vow has been performed in this manner during Kārtika, the month dear to Hari, whatever sin is destroyed—listen with an attentive mind, my son. (61)
From eating food not offered to Hari, from looking at the sun while eating, and likewise from the sin of hearing the voice of a woman in her menses while eating; (62)

Furthermore, whatever fault may arise from the touch of another at the time of eating—whether from consuming forbidden food or from the defilement of the meal by impure substances—[is removed by this].
Likewise, O beloved of Hari, by abandoning even one who is pure during a meritorious time, all the sin committed through these [acts] is certainly destroyed.
Therefore, with every effort, one should take one's meal from the nurse.
If a Brahmin indeed wears a garland of dhātrī and likewise a garland of tulasī during the month of Kārtika, his merit shall be infinite.
A person who especially offers a garland of lamps while taking refuge in the shade of the Dhātrī tree shall obtain infinite merit.
Rādhā and Dāmodara are to be worshipped especially beneath a Tulasī plant; in the absence of a Tulasī, an auspicious worship should be performed at the foot of a Dhātrī tree.
He who has eaten even once under the shade of a Dhātrī tree during the month of Kārtika, having given a meal to a married couple, is liberated from the defects of food. (69)

He who, when the month of Kārtika is complete, worships the auspicious Āmalakī tree for the pleasure of Rādhā and Dāmodara, and after having fed a married couple, eats himself afterwards—his prosperity shall never diminish. (70)
O Sage, any devotee of Viṣṇu in this world who wears the dhātrī fruit becomes dear to the gods; what then need be said of human beings? (71)
With his limbs smeared with āmalaka fruit, endowed with āmalaka fruit, and having his food made of āmalaka fruit, a man becomes Nārāyaṇa. (72)
To him who constantly carries āmalaka fruits in the hollow of his joined palms, the divine Nārāyaṇa grants his desired boon.
A man desiring prosperity should always perform his bath with *āmalaka* fruits; Viṣṇu is especially pleased by *āmalaka* on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*).
On the ninth day, on the new moon, on the seventh day, at the sun's transit, on Sundays, and during lunar and solar eclipses, one should avoid bathing with *āmalaka* fruits.
That man who, taking refuge in the shade of the Dhātrī tree, offers a funeral cake (piṇḍa), his ancestors attain liberation through the grace of Mādhava.
O child, that man who wears the dhātrī fruit on his head, in his hand, in his mouth, on his arms, or on his neck, is truly adorned with the dhātrī fruit.
As long as the garland of *dhātrī* fruits remains rolling upon a man's neck, for that long Keśava rolls with affection upon his body. (78)
The life of that person in whose house these three—the dhātrī fruit, tulasī, and earth originating from Dvārakā—are present, is truly fruitful.
For as many days as a man wears the Dhātrī garland in the Kali age, for that many thousands of yugas shall his residence be in Vaikuṇṭha.
That man who carries a pair of garlands made of dhātrī and tulasī around his neck shall dwell in heaven for ten million kalpas.
He who, having gone into the shade of a Dhātrī tree on the twelfth day, should worship Hari, and there likewise cause the Brāhmaṇas to take their meal; || 82 ||
And he who himself partakes there of such things as soup and solid food, for him there is no return even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
One should worship Hari with the fruits and leaves of both the tulasī and the dhātrī plants. || 84 ||
Indeed, when Tulasī and Dhātrī are watered during the month of Kārtika, sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa go to destruction. || 85 ||
Just as the twice-born Dharmadatta attained liberation in former times. (86)

Nārada said: "In the month of Kārttika, she (the goddess) is to be served and always worshipped by men; yet you previously stated that she is not to be served during the Cāturmāsya. Therefore, explain everything in its entirety before me. (87)

Brahmā said: O brahmin-sage, that auspicious tenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika—beginning from that day, she (the goddess) is to be worshipped in rites for the gods and the ancestors. Starting from the tenth day, one should worship Madhusūdana with her leaves and fruits.
Those men who indeed worship [the deity] go to Vaikuṇṭha; when the Kārtika vow is completed, one should partake of a meal in the forest.
O highly fortunate one, one should partake of the forest meal on the tenth, or the twelfth, or even on the full moon day, or on the fifth.
Equipped with all necessary utensils and accompanied by the elderly and children, the wise man should enter the forest, which is beautifully adorned with dhātrī trees.
It was adorned on all sides by mango trees, bakas, aśvatthas, picumandas, kadambakas, as well as nyagrodhas and tamarind trees.
Having gone there, O one of great wisdom, one should first perform a Puṇyāha ceremony; likewise, having worshipped the Vāstupīṭha, one should have it constructed at the root of a Dhātrī tree.
O Mahāmati, having constructed an auspicious square altar (vedikā) one cubit in length, as well as a secondary altar (upavedikā) at the front of that altar; 94.

Indeed, for the purpose of seating the deity, the work with the metallic elements is sufficient; one should cause a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and pavilion (maṇḍapa) to be constructed on the western side of the altar (vedikā).
One should have the pit (kuṇḍa) made thus: joined with three girdles, provided with leaves of the Pippala tree, and one cubit in length; it should be gentle (saumya). || 96 ||

Afterwards, having bathed and performed the recitation of mantras (japa), one should perform the worship of the deity; then, having established the sacred fire, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rules.

Having diligently prepared milk-rice (pāyasa), clarified butter, jaggery, soup, fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood, and likewise a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) for the planets and the deities of the site (vāstudeva).
Dhātrī, Śānti, Kānti, Māyā, Prakṛti, Viṣṇupatnī, Mahālakṣmī, Ramā, Mā, and Kamalā. (99)
Indirā, Lokamātā, Kalyāṇī, Kamalā, as well as Sāvitrī, Jagaddhātrī, Gāyatrī, and Sudhṛti; || 100 ||
Aṃtajñā, Viśvarūpā, Sukṛpā, and Abdhisaṃbhavā—along with the principal deities—one should commence the protective fire-oblation (rakṣā-homa). || 1 ||
With the mantra "saṃsṛṣṭā" and with the mantra "ṛṣabhaṃ me," one should offer as an oblation a cake combined with jaggery and soup.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) with the root mantra, one should then perform the fire-oblation for the planets and other deities in their respective order.

O highly wise one, in the *dhātrī* oblation, however, milk-rice (*pāyasa*) is used for the protection oblation; then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice, one should perform the offering of the ritual portions (*bali*).
And the world-protectors, beginning with Indra, should be diligently worshipped for protection everywhere around the Dhātrī tree, which is provided with an altar.
One should subsequently present an offering of soup mixed with jaggery, saying: "O Goddess Dhātrī, salutations to you; accept this most excellent offering."
O bestower of all auspiciousness, mixed with jaggery and soup, grant me sons of great wisdom and grant me glory that brings forth well-being.
Grant me wisdom, intelligence, good fortune, and devotion to Viṣṇu; make me forever free from disease and always sinless.
"O Goddess, grant me luster and likewise make me wealthy"—thus one should pray to the Goddess and offer the oblation while performing circumambulation.
But those who perform circumambulation at the time of offering the oblation go to the same world as Viṣṇu, together with their ancestors.
Then, having performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should complete the remainder of the fire sacrifice.
Those who behold here with their own eyes the Lord of Ramā, who possesses a gentle smile and resides at the root of the Dhātrī tree, attain union (sāyujya) with Viṣṇu.
Then, having performed the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should worship the forest deities; thereafter, O Lotus-born One, one should offer perfumes and unbroken grains (akṣata) to the Brahmins.
Afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins and then eat together with one's kinsmen; subsequently, one should bring the household back inside along with the elderly, children, and others.
Then, the wise man should remain celibate at night and sleep upon the ground; he should do this either by joining with those residing in the village or by doing it himself.
For the sake of liberation from all sins, having thus performed this entire supreme act of eating in the forest, one should dedicate it to Kṛṣṇa.
Whatever fruit one obtains from a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred royal consecrations, that same fruit one attains by eating forest fare.
Therefore, O illustrious one, the *dhātrī* is purifying and a destroyer of sins; she is indeed the sustainer of men, and like a mother (*dhātrī*), she performs her duties. (18)

By drinking its juice one gains long life; by bathing in it, one indeed accumulates merit. Through mere baths, one destroys misfortune and attains liberation. Indeed, no obstacles arise for men through bathing in the *dhātrī* tree.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, perform the ritual bath with *dhātrī* fruit with great effort; having attained divinity, O Nārada, you shall go to the abode of Hari.
O best of sages, wherever one performs the ritual bath with the *dhātrī* fruit—whether at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) or even in one's own home—there Hari is present.
O brahmin-sage, O best of munis, he whose bones within the body are washed with a bath of dhātrī does not dwell in a womb again.
O best of Brahmins, those men whose hair has been dyed with the water of the Dhātrī tree go to Keśava, having destroyed the impurity of the Kali age.
The dhātrī fruit brings great merit, and bathing with it is remembered as most meritorious; O child, O best of sages, eating it is even more meritorious than that. (24)
Neither the Gaṅgā, nor Gayā, nor Kāśī, nor the Veṇī, nor Puṣkara is so; for on the day of Mādhava, the Dhātrī tree alone is truly meritorious.
O son, O child, the sages know that bathing with *dhātrī* fruit, the chanting of Hari’s name, the Ekādaśī fast, and the *śrāddha* rite at Gayā are all equal. (26)
The man who touches the Dhātrī tree day after day is liberated from all sins arising from mind, speech, and body. || 27 ||
O best of sages, one should not bathe with *dhātrī* fruits on the new moon day, nor on the seventh, ninth, or Sunday, nor during the sun's transit (*saṃkrānti*).
O best of sages, in whichever house the Dhātrī plant always stands, ghosts, kūṣmāṇḍa spirits, and rākṣasas do not go there. || 29 ||
He who does not wear a garland made of dhātrī fruits around his neck cannot be known as a Vaiṣṇava, even if he is devoted to Viṣṇu. (130)
A garland of *tulasī*, and especially a garland of *dhātrī* fruits, as well as a garland of lotus seeds, must not be discarded by those who desire virtue, wealth, and pleasure. (31)
For as many days as a man wears the Dhātrī garland during the Kali age, for that many thousands of yugas shall his residence be in Vaikuṇṭha.
Consisting of all the gods, the Dhātrī tree is dear to the heart of Vāsudeva; it should always be planted, served, and worshipped by men.
Thus has this entire supreme majesty of the foster-mother been recounted; it should always be heard by devotees, as it bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
Whoever eats food while taking shelter in the shade of a Dhātrī tree during the month of Kārtika, his sin arising from the consumption of impure food perishes for the duration of that year. (135)
Sūta said: After the best of celestial sages had departed, having taken leave of the Lord of Śrī, Satyabhāmā, her face blooming with joy, then spoke to Vāsudeva.
Satyabhāmā said: "I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose; my life is fruitful. What gift, vow, or austerity must have been performed by me in the past? (2)

O Lord, tell me all of this: by what means did I, born as a mortal woman, become the one who took half of your body? In another birth, what was my character, who was I, and whose daughter was I? How did I come to become your beloved? Tell me that in its entirety.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen with a focused mind, O beloved, to how you were in your previous birth.
I shall tell you all about that meritorious vow she performed. At the end of the Kṛta Yuga, there was a most excellent twice-born man in Māyāpurī.
There was one named Devaśarman, a descendant of Atri, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; that aged man had a daughter named Guṇavatī.
Being childless, he gave his daughter to his own disciple named Candra; he regarded that very man as a son, and he, being self-controlled, regarded him as a father.
Once, while the two of them had gone to the forest seeking kusha grass and sacrificial fuel, they were slain by a rākṣasa who appeared in the form of Death himself.
By the power of their respective merits, both went to the world of Viṣṇu; then Guṇavatī, hearing that both had been slain by the Rākṣasa, [was overcome with grief].
Afflicted by the grief arising from her father and husband, she lamented piteously; having quickly sold all the household utensils, she performed that work.
Then, having performed the rites for the next world for those two according to her ability, that woman who had restored the dead to life made her dwelling in that very city.
By her, two vows were perfectly observed from birth until death: the vow of Ekādaśī and the proper observance of the month of Kārtika.
Thus, Guṇavatī remained perfectly observant of her vows every year; however, on one occasion, she became ill, emaciated in body, and afflicted by fever.
O beloved, she had gone to the Gaṅgā to bathe; then, having somehow entered the water very slowly, she began to tremble, afflicted by the cold.
While she was thus overwhelmed, she saw a celestial chariot departing from the sky; then, seated upon that chariot, she went to the realm of Vaikuṇṭha.
By the merit of the Kārttika vow, she attained proximity to me; then, at the request of the gods headed by Brahmā, she [descended] to the earth. (16)
"I have come, O Gaṇas; you all have also gone with me. For all these Yādavas, O beautiful lady, are indeed my own attendants. (17)
Your father was Devaśarman, and this one named Satrājit is indeed he; he who was named Candra is Akrūra, and you are that auspicious Guṇavatī.
"By the merit of your Kārtika vow, which bestows great pleasure upon me, you previously established a grove of Tulasī plants at my gateway. (19)
Therefore, O auspicious lady, this wish-fulfilling tree has come to your courtyard; [it bears witness to] the Kārtika vow that was performed by you from birth until death.
"At no time shall you ever suffer separation from me. Satyovāca said: "How indeed is that month Kārtika the best among all months? (21)
"O Lord of the gods of gods, you are dear to me; let the reason for that be told. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O beloved, you have asked well; listen with a one-pointed mind. (22)
The dialogue between Pṛthu, the son of Vena, and the great seer Nārada; for in this very manner, having been questioned in the past by Pṛthu, Nārada spoke.
Nārada said: Formerly, there was an asura named Śaṅkha, the son of the Ocean, who seized the offices of the world-protectors, beginning with Indra.
The gods and others, stationed in the fortress of the cave on the Golden Mountain, observed him; at that time, the Daitya reflected upon the situation.
"Although the thirty gods have been deprived of their authority and conquered by me, they are still observed to be endowed with strength; what, then, should be done by me in this matter?"
"O gods, that has been understood by me; you are endowed with the power of Vedic mantras. I shall take those away from you, and then you will all indeed become devoid of strength. (27)
Thinking thus, the Daitya then, observing Viṣṇu asleep, quickly carried off the Vedas of the primordial Self-born from Satyaloka.
Those Vedas were indeed taken away by him; out of fear of him, they departed and entered the waters, accompanied by the seeds of sacrificial mantras.

While searching for them, Śaṅkha too wandered within the ocean; however, the Daitya did not see them stationed together anywhere at that time. Then Viṣṇu, praised by the gods and awakened, spoke to them.
Viṣṇu said: "O hosts of gods, I am the giver of boons [to you] through these auspicious songs, musical instruments, and other such offerings."
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Ūrja, you awakened me; therefore, this lunar day is to be honored, for it bestows upon me exceeding joy.
"All the Vedas have been carried away by Śaṅkha and remain situated within the waters; O gods, I shall bring them back after slaying the son of the Ocean."
From this day forward, let the Vedas, together with their mantras and seed-syllables, always rest within the waters every year during the month of Kārttika.
Those best of men who perform the morning bath at this time have all effectively performed the final purificatory baths (avabhṛtha) of sacrifices; of this there is no doubt. || 35 ||
"From this day forward, I too shall dwell within the waters; you as well, along with the lords of sages, should come with me. (36)

"O Indra, you must always provide protection for those observing the Kārtika vow. Having said this, Lord Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a small fish, fell from the sky into the water while Vindhyavāsinī was looking on. (37)
Having slain the demon Śaṅkha, Viṣṇu came to the Badarī forest; there, having summoned all the sages, the Lord issued this command: || 38 ||

Viṣṇu said: "Search for those Vedas that have been scattered within the waters; bring them forth quickly from the depths of the ocean. Meanwhile, I shall remain at Prayāga, accompanied by the hosts of deities. (39)
Nārada said: Then, by all those sages endowed with the power of asceticism, [it was done]. (40)
And those Vedas were extracted together with their seeds and accompanied by the sacrificial rites; whatever portion was obtained by whomsoever from them, that indeed belonged to him alone.
O King, from that time onwards, each one was born as that very same ṛṣi; then all the sages, having gathered together, went to Prayāga.
They presented the recovered Vedas to Viṣṇu along with Vidhātṛ; and having regained all the Vedas in their entirety, Brahmā was filled with joy.
Accompanied by hosts of divine sages, he performed the horse sacrifice; at the conclusion of the sacrifice, all the deities immediately made this petition: ||| 44 ||
The gods said: "O God of gods, Lord of the world, O Master, hear our petition! This is a time of joy for us; therefore, be the granter of our boon. (45)
In this place, O Lord of Ramā, by your grace, this Brahmā has recovered the lost Vedas, and we too have obtained our shares of the sacrifice.
"Indeed, may this place of ours, which increases merit on earth and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, remain forever so by your grace. (47)
This time as well is highly meritorious, purifying even those who have slain a Brahmin; may it grant inexhaustible merit for what is given. Grant us this boon in this manner. (48)
Viṣṇu said: "O gods, that which has been proposed by you is also my choice. Let it be so; however, let this first [site] be known as Brahmakṣetra, for it is easily accessible."
A king born of the solar dynasty will bring the Gaṅgā here; she shall unite with the Kālindī, the daughter of the Sun, at this place.
And may you all, beginning with Brahmā, dwell here together with me; this sacred site shall become renowned as "Tīrtharāja" (the King of Holy Places).
All sins are destroyed by the sight of the King of Tīrthas; when the sun has entered Capricorn, it destroys the sins of those who bathe there.

May this time also always bestow great meritorious fruit upon men; through baths during Māgha when the sun is in Capricorn, may there be the fruit of residence in the same world [as the deity] and other such rewards.

Nārada said: Having spoken thus to the gods, the God of gods, together with Brahmā, vanished on that very spot. All the gods, including Indra and the others, remained there in their respective portions and likewise attained invisibility.
He who worships Lord Hari at the root of a Tulasī plant during the month of Kārtika, having enjoyed all pleasures here in this world, shall go to the city of Viṣṇu in the end.
Pṛthu said: O Brahmin, regarding that vow of Ūrja which has been described by you in detail, therein you have mentioned the worship of Viṣṇu at the root of the Tulasī plant.
Therefore, I desire to ask about the greatness arising from Tulasī; how is she so exceedingly dear to that God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow?
How did she come into being, and in what place, O Nārada? Tell me this in brief, for you are considered by me to be omniscient. (3)
Nārada said: Listen attentively, O King, to the majesty arising from Tulasī; I shall relate all of that to you, including its history and ancient accounts.
In ancient times, Śakra went to Mount Kailāsa to see Śiva, surrounded by all the gods and attended by hosts of Apsaras.
When he reached the abode of Śiva, he saw there a man of terrible deeds, fearsome with fangs and a gaping mouth.
Being questioned by him thus again and again—"O sir, who are you? Where has the Lord of the World gone?"—he did not speak at that time, O King.
Then Vajrapāṇi, becoming enraged, rebuked him and spoke these words: "O you! Even though questioned by me, you did not give an answer. (8)
"Therefore, I shall slay you with my thunderbolt; who is your protector, O evil-minded one? Having thus spoken, the wielder of the thunderbolt then struck him forcefully with his vajra.
By that [act], his throat turned blue and the thunderbolt was reduced to ashes; thereafter, Rudra blazed forth with splendor as if consuming everything.
Upon seeing him, Bṛhaspati quickly joined his palms in reverence; and having prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground before Indra, he began to offer praise.
Bṛhaspati said: Salutations to the Lord of the gods, the three-eyed one with matted hair; salutations to Śarva, the destroyer of Tripura, the slayer of Andhaka. (12)
To the one who is deformed, exceedingly beautiful, and multiformed; to the source of auspiciousness; to the destroyer of sacrifices, and to the bestower of the fruits of sacrifices. || 13 ||
Salutations to Kālāntaka, to Kāla, and to the bearer of the serpent Kāla; salutations again and again to the Brahmin who struck off the head of Brahmā.
Nārada said: Thus praised then by Bṛhaspati, Śambhu spoke to him, withdrawing the flames from his eyes that were capable of burning the three worlds.
"Choose a boon, O Brahmin; I am pleased by this hymn of yours. By granting life to Indra, may you attain the fame, 'O Vajra, he who restored life'! (16)
Bṛhaspati said: "O Lord, if you are pleased, protect Indra who has come to you for refuge; let this fire born from the eye on your forehead be extinguished. (17)
Īśvara said: "How is it that the fire enters again into my forehead-eye? I shall cast it far away so that it may not afflict Indra."
Nārada said: Having spoken thus, he seized him by the hand and cast him into the salt ocean; he fell at the confluence of the Sindhu-Gaṅgā and the sea.
Then he assumed the form of a child and wept there; by the sound of him weeping, the earth trembled repeatedly.
From Svarga up to Satyaloka, all were deafened by its roar; hearing it, Brahmā went there, wondering, "What is this? (21)
At that moment, he saw the boy in the lap of the ocean; seeing that Brahmā had arrived, the ocean also joined his palms in reverence.

Having bowed his head to the child, he placed him upon his lap and said: "O Brahman, this little son of mine was born in the Sindhu-Gaṅgā; O Teacher of the World, perform today the birth-rite and the other purificatory ceremonies."
Nārada said: While the ocean was speaking thus, that boy, the son of the Ocean, [spoke].

He seized Brahmā by the beard, shaking him again and again; as he shook his beard, water flowed from his two eyes. Then, having somehow freed himself from the beard, Brahmā spoke to the Ocean: 25. He seized Brahmā by the beard, shaking him again and again; as he shook his beard, water flowed from his two eyes. Then, having somehow freed himself from the beard, Brahmā spoke to the Ocean.
Brahmā said: "Since this water of mine has been held by him with his two eyes, he shall therefore become known by the name Jalandhara."
By this very [means], this youth, who has mastered all weapons and missiles, shall become incapable of being slain by any living beings, with the exception of Rudra.
From where this has arisen, there indeed it will reach its end.
Nārada said: Having spoken thus, he summoned Śukra and consecrated him in the kingdom; then, taking leave of the lord of rivers, Brahmā vanished from sight.
Then, his eyes wide with wonder at the sight of her, Sāgara requested Vṛndā, the daughter of Kālanemi, to be his wife.

Then those Asuras, headed by Kālanemi, being greatly delighted, gave that daughter to him; and he too, having obtained her as his most excellent friend and submissive wife, ruled the earth with Śukra as his companion, being powerful.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Jalandhara," in the *Kārttikamāsamāhātmya* of the second section (*Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa*) within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: Those Daityas who were previously defeated by the gods and had taken refuge in Pātāla have now gone to the earth’s surface and dwell there without fear, having sought shelter with him.
Once, seeing Rāhu with his head severed, that king of the Daityas questioned Bhārgava there regarding the cause of that decapitation.
He related the churning of the ocean performed by the gods, as well as the seizure of the jewels and the defeat of the Daityas.
Having heard then of the destruction of his father, his eyes red with rage, he dispatched the messenger Ghasmara into the presence of Śakra.
The messenger, having gone to the celestial realm, entered the excellent Sudharmā assembly hall; with his head bowed low, he spoke these wonderful words to the Lord of the Gods. || 5 ||
Ghasmara said: "Jalandhara, the son of the Ocean and lord of all the Daitya people, has sent me as his messenger; hear what he says."
"Why have you churned my father, the ocean, with a mountain? Return all those jewels to me immediately! (7)
Having heard these words of the messenger, the lord of the thirty gods was struck with wonder; filled with fear and rage, he spoke to the fierce Ghasmara.
Indra said: Listen, O messenger, to how the ocean was formerly churned by me; likewise, the mountains, terrified by fear of me, were placed within my own belly.
In former times, other enemies of mine, the sons of Diti, were also protected by him; therefore, whatever was born from that [union] was indeed seized by me as well.
In ancient times, Śaṅkha, the son of the Ocean, likewise hated the gods; he was slain by my younger brother and entered the belly of the ocean.
"Therefore, go and tell him everything regarding the cause of the churning. Nārada said: "Thus dismissed by Indra, the messenger then went to the earth."
Then he related all those words to the Daitya; having heard them, the Daitya’s lower lip quivered with rage.
Accompanied by the army of the Daityas, he went to Triviṣṭapa to fight; then a great battle ensued, resulting in the destruction of both gods and Dānavas.
In that battle, Bhārgava restored the dead Daityas to life by means of the *mṛtajīvinī* spell and drops of water consecrated with mantras.
Likewise, Aṅgiras brought back to life even the gods in that battle, having repeatedly fetched divine medicinal herbs from Mount Droṇa.
Seeing the gods thus risen again in battle, Jalandhara, overcome by anger, spoke these words to Bhārgava: || 17 ||
Jalandhara said: "The gods have been slain by me in battle; how can they rise up again? It is renowned that your science of restoration (saṃjīvinī-vidyā) exists nowhere else."
Śukra said: "Having brought celestial herbs from Mount Droṇa, Aṅgiras is indeed reviving the gods; therefore, quickly remove that Mount Droṇa."
Nārada said: Having been addressed thus, that lord of the Daityas then took Droṇācala and quickly cast him into the ocean; he then returned once more to the great battle.
Then, seeing the gods slain, the preceptor went to the mountain Droṇa; however, there the one worshipped by the gods did not see the lord of mountains.
Having learned that Droṇa had been seized by the Daityas, Dhiṣaṇa, overwhelmed with fear and his body agitated by gasping breaths, arrived from afar and spoke.
"O gods, flee from this battle, for he is not capable of being conquered; indeed, he is born from a portion of Rudra—remember the deeds of Śakra! || 23 ||
Having heard those words, the gods, overwhelmed with fear, then fled in the ten directions while being pursued by the Daitya.
Seeing the gods routed by the Daityas, the son of the Ocean entered Amarāvatī amidst the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and cries of victory.
When the Daitya had entered the city, the gods, led by Śakra and tormented by the Daitya, reached a cave in the Golden Mountain and dwelt there.
Then, having installed Śumbha and the other chief Daityas individually in all the offices formerly held by Indra and the others, he himself returned once more to the cave of the Golden Mountain.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Victory over Jalandhara," in the *Kārttikamāsamāhātmya* of the second section, the *Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 15.
Nārada said: Seeing the Daitya approaching once more, all the gods, including Indra, trembled with fear and began to offer praise to Viṣṇu. || 1 ||

Salutations to You, the destroyer of suffering, who are ever intent upon the welfare of Your devotees through various forms such as the Fish and the Tortoise; salutations be to You, the author of the creation, preservation, and dissolution of the universe by Brahmā and others, holding the mace, conch, lotus, and discus in Your hands.

To him who is beloved by Ramā, the slayer of the Asuras, whose vehicle is the enemy of serpents (Garuḍa), who wears yellow garments, who brings to fruition sacrifices and other rites, the dispeller [of darkness], and the refuge—unto him we bow, we bow. 3.

Salutations to You, O Viṣṇu, the thunderbolt that shatters the mountain of suffering for the immortals tormented by the Daityas; we bow, we bow to You who recline upon the couch of the lord of serpents and whose two eyes are the sun and the moon. 4.
Nārada said: A person who recites this hymn named *Saṃkaṣṭanāśana* (The Destroyer of Distress) shall never be afflicted by difficulties through the grace of Hari. (5)
While the gods were thus offering praise to the enemy of the Danujas, Viṣṇu then became aware of the calamity that had befallen the deities.
Rising up suddenly, the enemy of the Daityas, filled with anger and a distressed mind, mounted Garuḍa with speed and spoke these words to Lakṣmī: || 7 ||
The Blessed Lord said: "Your brother Jalandhara has caused the slaughter of the gods; summoned by them, I shall go today with haste for battle."
Śrī said: "O Lord, O ocean of mercy, if I am always your beloved because of my devotion, then why is it that your brother must be slain by me in battle?"
The Blessed Lord said: "Because he was born from a portion of Rudra, because of the word of Brahmā, and out of affection for you, this Jalandhara is not to be slain by me."
Nārada said: Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu, mounted upon Garuḍa and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and sword, went with speed to fight where those gods were offering praise.
Then, tormented by the wind from the wings of the fierce Aruṇānuja and crushed by the whirlwind, the Daityas wandered through the sky like clouds.
Then Jalandhara, seeing the Daityas tormented by the wind, his eyes rolling with rage, rushed toward Viṣṇu.
Then a great battle took place between Viṣṇu and the lord of the Daityas, as they filled the sky with their arrows until it became devoid of any open space.
Viṣṇu cut down the Daitya’s banner, umbrella, bow, and horses with volleys of arrows, and struck him in the heart with a single shaft.
Then the Daitya, rising up with mace in hand and full of haste, struck Garuḍa on the head and cast him down to the ground.
Viṣṇu, as if laughing, cut the mace with his own sword; meanwhile, [the opponent] struck Viṣṇu firmly in the heart with a clenched fist.
Then those two of great strength fought with a wrestling match, making the earth resound with their arms, fists, and knees.
Having thus fought for a very long time, the powerful Viṣṇu, with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, spoke to the king of the Daityas.
Viṣṇu said: "Choose a boon, O Lord of Daityas; I am pleased with your prowess. I shall grant you even that which is not to be given, whatever dwells in your mind. (20)
Jalandhara said: "O Bhāvuka, if you are pleased, grant me this boon: dwell today in my house with my sister, along with your retinue."
Nārada said: Having replied, "So be it," the Blessed One, together with all the hosts of gods and accompanied by Ramā, then went to the city of Jalandhara.
Having installed the Dānavas in the offices of the gods, the mighty-armed Jalandhara returned once more to the surface of the earth.
Having brought under his own control whatever was endowed with jewels among the gods, gandharvas, and siddhas, the son of the Ocean remained there.
Having stationed the exceedingly powerful Daitya Niśumbha in the subterranean realm of Pātāla, that mighty one brought Śeṣa and the others to the surface of the earth.
Having made the gods, gandharvas, siddhas, and others—including serpents, rākṣasas, and humans—his citizens in his own city, he ruled over the three worlds.
Having thus brought the gods under his own control, Jalandhara protected his subjects according to dharma, like his own legitimate sons.
While he ruled the kingdom according to the Dharma, no one was seen who was diseased, nor indeed suffering, nor likewise oppressed, nor was anyone seen who was wretched. (28)
While the lord of the Dānavas was thus ruling the earth righteously and with a desire for perfect vision, I once came there to behold his splendor and to serve the Lord of Śrī.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Arrival of Nārada in the Assembly of Jalandhara," in the Kārtika-māsa-māhātmya of the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, within the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: O King, having honored me according to the prescribed rites, he, being exceedingly devoted, then spoke these words with a smile and full of affection.
From where have you come, O Brahman? O Lord, has anything been seen by you? For what purpose have you arrived here? Command me, O Sage.
Nārada said: O Lord of Daityas, I went to the peak of Kailāsa by chance; there I beheld Śaṅkara seated together with Umā.
In the great forest of Kalpa trees, ten thousand yojanas in extent, crowded with hundreds of wish-fulfilling cows (Kāmadhenus) and brilliantly illuminated by wish-granting gems (Cintāmaṇis).
Seeing that great marvel, I was then filled with wonder, thinking: "Could such supernatural power exist anywhere in the three worlds, or not? (5)
At that time, O Lord of Daityas, your prosperity was also remembered by me; desiring to behold it, I have come here into your presence.
Beholding this prosperity of yours, which is surely lacking the jewel of a woman, I conclude that there is no one else in the three worlds more prosperous than Śiva.
Although the apsarases, nāga maidens, and others remain under your control, they certainly cannot equal Pārvatī in beauty. (8)
Who else can be compared to her, by whom the four-faced Brahmā was formerly made to abandon his self-composure, having become submerged in the ocean of her loveliness?
For even the Enemy of Madana (Śiva), though free from passion, was formerly led astray by his own playful sport in the thicket of beauty through the form of a female fish.
Even the Creator, while fashioning [beings], looked again and again at her form; yet among all the apsarases he created, not even one was equal to her.
Therefore, that prosperity belongs to the enjoyer of the jewel among women; it is not yours, O Lord of Daityas, even though you are the sovereign of all jewels.
Having spoken thus and taken his leave, when he had departed, that king of the Daityas became afflicted by the fever of love upon hearing of her beauty.
Then, deluded by the illusory power of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇumāyā), he dispatched the son of Siṃhikā as a messenger even to the Three-eyed Lord (Tryambaka).
Rāhu went to Kailāsa, making it possess the luster of the white moon with his own body's darkness, which had the brilliance of the moon of the dark fortnight.
Having been announced to the Lord of that place by Nandin, he entered; impelled by the sign of Tryambaka’s creeper-like eyebrows, he spoke these words.
Rāhu said: O bull-bannered one, listen to the command of the Lord, the sovereign of the three worlds, who is served by gods and serpents and is the master of all jewels.
How can your auspicious wife Haimavatī belong to one who dwells perpetually in cremation grounds, who carries a burden of bones, and who is clothed only by the directions?
I am the supreme lord of jewels, and she is known as the jewel among women; therefore, she is suitable for me alone, and certainly not for you who subsist on alms.
Nārada said: While Rāhu was speaking thus, there emerged from the space between the eyebrows of the wielder of the trident (Śiva) a fierce being with a voice like a sharp thunderbolt.
With a lion’s face, a protruding tongue, blazing eyes, and great stature, with hair standing erect and a withered body, he was like another Nṛsiṃha. || 21 ||
Seeing him approaching to devour him, Rāhu, overcome with fear, fled outside with great speed, but he (the Sun) seized him.
And that Rāhu, O mighty-armed one, spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud: "O God of gods, protect me, who have come to you for refuge. (23)
"O Mahādeva, he has come here to devour me, a Brāhmaṇa. Having heard these words of the Brāhmaṇa, Mahādeva then spoke.
"Since this messenger belongs to another, he is not to be killed"; hearing "Release him!", the man released Rāhu in the sky.
Then, having released Rāhu, the man addressed Rudra. The man said: "Hunger afflicts me excessively, and I am utterly emaciated by hunger. (26)
"O Lord of Gods, O Master, command me: what shall I eat? The Lord said: "Quickly eat the flesh of your own hands and feet."
Nārada said: Thus commanded by Śiva, that man ate the flesh produced from his own hands and feet until he was reduced to nothing but his head.
Seeing him with only his head remaining, Śiva was then highly pleased; filled with wonder, he spoke to that man of terrible deeds.
The Lord said: "Indeed, you shall be known by the name Kīrtimukha; always remain at my gateway. Those who do not perform your worship are certainly not dear to me. (30)
Nārada said: From that time forward, Kīrtimukha has remained at the door of the Lord; for those who do not first worship him here, their worship [of the Lord] shall be in vain.
He who was released by Rāhu remained on that very same barbarian land; therefore, he became famous on earth as "Barbarodbhūta" (Born of the Barbarians). || 32 ||
Then Rāhu, perceiving himself as having been born once again in this world, approached Jalandhara and related all that had transpired.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Messenger's Words," within the Legend of Jalandhara, in the Glorification of the Month of Kārttika, in the Vaiṣṇava Section of the Second Part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 17.
Nārada said: Having heard that, Jalandhara, his body agitated with anger, quickly went forth surrounded by tens of millions of Daityas.
As he was proceeding, Śukra came before him within the range of his vision; then Rāhu, having stumbled with force, fell to the ground along with his crown.
Then, filled with hundreds of his celestial chariots surrounded by the Daitya armies, the sky shone as if covered by clouds during the rainy season.
Then, seeing his exertion, the gods, led by Śakra, went unobserved and made their request to the wielder of the trident.
The gods said: "O Lord, O All-pervading One, how is it that you do not know of this calamity of the gods? Therefore, for our protection, slay the son of the Ocean."
Nārada said: Having heard these words of the god, the bull-bannered Lord laughed and, summoning Mahāviṣṇu, spoke these words.
Īśvara said: O Viṣṇu, why was Jalandhara not slain by you in battle? Furthermore, you went to his abode, abandoning your own Vaikuṇṭha.
Viṣṇu said: "Because you were born from a portion of me, and because you are the brother of Śrī, I have not slain him in battle; you must slay this Dānava."

Īśvara said: "This one of great splendor cannot be slain by me with these weapons and missiles, nor by the gods. Let each of you give a portion of your own energy to me for the purpose of creating a weapon."
Nārada said: Then the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, offered their own splendors; seeing that they had attained unity, the Lord released his own great light.
With that [splendor], Mahādeva created the supreme weapon named Sudarśana, a discus most terrifying with its garlands of flames. || 11 ||
Then Hari fashioned the thunderbolt from the remainder; at that moment, Jalandhara was seen upon the grounds of the slopes of Kailāsa.
Surrounded by tens of millions of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, all the gods, having observed him, departed as they had come. (13)
And by the command of Śiva, all the hosts, led by Nandin, Bhava’s face, and Senānī, assembled with great haste for battle.
The hosts, intoxicated by battle, descended with speed from Kailāsa; then a battle took place on the ground in the valley of Kailāsa.
It was crowded with the terrible weapons and missiles of the Daityas, lords of the Pramathas, and filled with the sounds of a multitude of kettledrums, clay drums, and conchs that gladden heroes.
Resounding with the sounds of elephants, horses, and chariots, the earth trembled; [it was further shaken] by a torrent of spears, javelins, arrows, maces, darts, and battle-axes.
The sky, filled and as if covered with meteors, shone brilliantly; the earth, strewn with slain chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry, likewise shone.
It was covered as if by fragments of the head of Acala struck by the thunderbolt, and likewise by the multitudes of Daityas struck down by the Pramathas, and the Gaṇas struck down by the Daityas.
At that time, the earth became impassable, thick with the mire of fat, blood, and flesh; then Bhārgava restored to life the multitudes of Daityas slain by the Pramathas.

Furthermore, in that battle, by the power of the *mṛtasaṃjīvinī* [life-restoring] spell, he [Śukra] was seen again and again; seeing him, all the Gaṇas became agitated and filled with fear, and they reported all of Śukra’s actions to the God of Gods.
Then, from the mouth of Rudra, there arose an exceedingly terrifying Kṛtyā, with shanks as tall as palm trees, mouths like caves, and breasts that crushed the trees.
Having reached the battlefield and devouring the great asuras, she seized Bhārgava by his private parts and vanished into the sky.
Seeing the army of the Daityas held in check by the descendant of Bhṛgu, the Gaṇas, their faces unfaded with joy and intoxicated by battle, then struck them down.

Then the army of the Daityas, tormented by the fear of the Gaṇas, broke apart like a mass of straw scattered when struck by the force of the wind. Seeing the army broken through fear of the Gaṇas, Niśumbha, Śumbha—the two generals—and the heroic Kālanemi, filled with indignation, advanced.
Those three of great strength warded off the army of the hosts, discharging showers of arrows like clouds during the rainy season. || 27 ||
Then those volleys of the Daityas' arrows, like swarms of locusts, blocked the sky and all the directions, causing the army of the Gaṇas to tremble.
The hosts, pierced by hundreds of arrows and raining down showers of blood, appeared like *kiṃśuka* trees in spring; nothing could be distinguished.
Then those hosts—already fallen, being felled, shattered, and mangled—all abandoned the battlefield and turned their backs in retreat.
Then, beholding their own army broken, Śailādi, Lambodara, and Kārttikeya—those indignant ones—hurriedly and forcefully repelled the foremost of the Daityas.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Defeat of Rudra's Army," in the Legend of Jalandhara, within the Greatness of the Month of Kārttika, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: Having seen those lords of the Gaṇas—Nandin, Gajavaktra, and Ṣaṇmukha—the Dānavas rushed forward out of indignation for the sake of single combat.
Kālanemi rushed impetuously at Nandin, Śumbha at Lambodara, and the armored Niśumbha at Ṣaṇmukha.
Niśumbha forcefully pierced Kārttikeya’s peacock in the heart with five arrows; it fell down, rendered unconscious.
Then, as soon as the enraged Śaktidhara seized his spear, Niśumbha with great speed struck him down with his own spear.
Nandīśvara struck Kālanemi with volleys of arrows; he cut down his horses with seven, his banner with three, and his charioteer with three more.
But Kālanemi, filled with rage, cut Nandin’s bow; casting that aside, the powerful one struck him in the chest with his trident.
With his heart pierced by the spear, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed, he [Śailādi] seized a mountain peak and cast it down as well.
Then Śumbha and Gaṇeśa, whose vehicles were a chariot and a mouse respectively, fought on and pierced each other with volleys of arrows.
Then Gaṇeśa pierced Śumbha in the heart with a feathered shaft and, with three arrows, felled the charioteer to the ground.
Then Śumbha, becoming exceedingly enraged, pierced the lord of the Gaṇas with sixty arrows and the mouse with three, and roared with a voice like a thundercloud.
The mouse, its body pierced by arrows and suffering intense pain, moved about; and Lambodara fell down and became a foot-soldier, O King.
Then Lambodara, having struck Śumbha in the heart with his axe, felled him to the ground and once again mounted the mouse.
Both Kālanemi and Niśumbha, out of anger, simultaneously struck Lambodara with arrows, like two great elephants being prodded with goads.
Seeing him being thus oppressed, the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra then rushed forward with speed, accompanied by ten million spirits (bhūta).
The Kūṣmāṇḍas, Bhairavas, Vetālas, and hosts of Yoginīs, as well as throngs of Piśācas and Yoginīs and various Gaṇas, followed after him. || 15 ||
Then, with shouts of "kila-kilā," deep-sounding lion-roars, and the beating of kettledrums, cymbals, and clay drums, the earth trembled.
Then the spirits rushed forward and devoured the Dānavas; they leaped up, fell down, and danced upon the field of battle.
Nandi and Kārttikeya, having regained their composure, quickly struck down the Daityas in battle with continuous volleys of arrows.
Then, with the Daityas cut to pieces, shattered, slain, fallen, and devoured, that army became agitated and dejected in countenance.
Then, seeing the army utterly shattered, the powerful son of the Ocean advanced against the hosts in a chariot adorned with a great banner.
Then, from both armies, there arose the thundering of elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, along with lion-like roars.
By the volleys of Jalandhara’s arrows, which were like masses of mist, the space between heaven and earth became completely obscured.
Having pierced Gaṇeśa with five arrows, Śailādi with nine, and Vīrabhadra with twenty, he roared with a voice like a thundercloud.
Then Kārttikeya swiftly pierced the Daitya with his spear; though pierced by the spear, he fought on with his mind somewhat agitated.
Then Jalandhara, his eyes overcome with rage, struck Kartikeya with a mace, and he fell upon the surface of the earth.
In that very same manner, he violently threw Nandin to the ground; thereupon, the Lord of the Gaṇas, enraged, struck the mace with his axe.
Vīrabhadra pierced the Dānava in the heart with three arrows; with seven more, he cut down his horses, banner, bow, and parasol.
Then the lord of the Daityas, exceedingly enraged, raised a terrible spear and struck down Gaṇeśa; he then mounted another chariot.
Then, filled with rage, he rushed impetuously toward Vīrabhadra; thereafter, those two, resplendent like the sun, fought with one another.
Vīrabhadra, moreover, struck down his horses with arrows; the lord of the Daityas cut off his bow and, armed with an iron club, leapt forward.
That Daitya, approaching Vīrabhadra with haste, struck him on the head with an iron club; and that hero, his head split open, fell to the ground vomiting blood.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Fall of Vīrabhadra," in the Legend of Jalandhara, within the *Kārttikamāsamāhātmya* of the second section, the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 19.
Nārada said: Seeing Vīrabhadra fallen, the hosts of Rudra fled from the battle out of fear, crying out to Maheśvara. || 1 ||
Then, hearing the clamor of the hosts, the moon-crested Lord mounted his bull and approached the battle as if laughing.
Beholding Rudra approaching, the Gaṇas once again turned back from the battle and struck the Daityas with showers of arrows, accompanied by lion-like roars.
And upon seeing him, all the Daityas fled in terror, just as sins flee out of fear upon seeing one who observes the Kārttika vow.
Then Jalandhara, seeing those Daityas turned back from the battle, rushed toward Caṇḍīśa in rage, discharging arrows by the thousands.
Śumbha, Niśumbha, Aśvamukha, Kālanemi, Balāhaka, Khaḍgaroman, Pracaṇḍa, Ghasmara, and others went to Śiva.
Seeing the host of Gaṇas shrouded in the darkness of arrows, Śiva cut through that web of shafts and covered the sky with his own arrows.
Then he afflicted the Daityas with storms of arrows and, with floods of fierce volleys of shafts, cast them down to the surface of the earth.
Then he severed Khaḍgaroman’s head from his body with an axe, and he split Balāhaka’s head in two with a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga).
Having bound the gluttonous Daitya with a noose, he struck him down upon the earth; some were slain by the bull, while others were felled by arrows.
The asuras were unable to remain there, like elephants tormented by a lion; then Jalandhara, his soul overcome with rage, rushed impetuously toward Rudra.
He challenged him in battle with a roar like a fierce thunderbolt. Jalandhara said: "Fight with me; what is the use of these [other gods] being slain by you?"
