"O wearer of matted locks, show whatever strength you possess! Having said this, he struck the bull-bannered god with seventy arrows.
Laughing, as it were, he cut down those arrows that reached him with sharp shafts; then, with spears, he severed the horses, the banner, the umbrella, and the bow.
With his bow broken and deprived of his chariot, he, full of speed, raised a mace and rushed toward Śiva; at that moment, Śiva cut the mace in two with his arrows.
Nevertheless, raising his fist, he advanced with the intent to kill Rudra; meanwhile, he was driven back a distance of one krośa by Śiva with volleys of arrows.
Then the Daitya Jalandhara, perceiving Rudra to be superior in strength, unleashed a wondrous Gandharva illusion intended to delude Rudra.
Then the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases sang and danced, while others played instruments such as cymbals, flutes, and drums.
Beholding that great marvel, Rudra was so bewildered by the sound that he did not even perceive the weapons falling from his hands.
Seeing Rudra become one-pointed in meditation, the Daitya Jalandhara, afflicted by lust, went quickly to where Gaurī was staying.
In battle, having stationed the two named Śumbha and Niśumbha, he—possessing ten staff-like arms, five faces, three eyes, and wearing matted locks—was endowed with great strength.
Jalandhara became mounted upon a great bull; then, seeing Rudra approaching, the beloved of Bhava [Pārvatī]—
From the midst of her companions, she approached and came within the range of his vision; then the lord of the Danujas beheld Pārvatī, whose limbs were exquisitely beautiful.
At that moment, he released his own prowess and his limbs became paralyzed; then Gaurī, perceiving him to be a Dānava, was overwhelmed with fear.
Then she vanished and went swiftly to Lake Uttaramānasa; not seeing her there, the Daitya, in an instant, [saw her] like a flash of lightning.
He went swiftly once more to the battle where the bull-bannered god was; at that time, Pārvatī also remembered Viṣṇu in her mind out of fear.
Just then, she saw that god seated nearby. Pārvatī said: "O Viṣṇu, the Daitya Jalandhara has performed a most extraordinary feat. (27)
Is that conduct of that evil-minded one not known to you? Viṣṇu said: "The path has been shown by him alone; we too shall follow it. (28)
"Otherwise, he would not have been slain, for he was well-protected by his devotion to his wife. Nārada said: Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu went back to the city of Jālandhara.
Then Rudra, followed by the Gandharvas, stood in the battle; seeing that his illusory power had vanished, he then understood.
Then Bhava, his mind filled with wonder, again went out to battle against Jalandhara in a rage; and that Daitya, seeing Śiva returned once more, covered him with a shower of arrows in the fray.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between Śiva and Jalandhara," in the Jalandhara Episode of the *Kārttikamāsamāhātmya*, within the second section (*Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: Viṣṇu, having gone to Jalandhara, the capital city of that Daitya, set his mind upon breaking the chastity of Vṛndā.
Then, in the midst of her dream, Queen Vṛndārakā beheld her husband mounted upon a buffalo, smeared with oil, and naked.
Adorned with black flowers, frequented by hosts of flesh-eaters, shaven-headed, having come from the southern direction, he was then enveloped in darkness.
Her own city, along with herself, had suddenly sunk into the ocean; then that young woman awoke, reflecting upon that dream.
She beheld the risen sun, which was repeatedly spotted and lusterless; perceiving this as an ill omen, she wept, overwhelmed by fear.
Finding no peace anywhere on the grounds of the city gates or the watchtowers, she then went to the city garden accompanied by two female companions.
Even there, that young woman, wandering in fear, found no happiness anywhere; having gone from forest to forest, she was not even aware of herself at that time.
Then, as she was wandering, that young woman beheld two exceedingly terrifying Rākṣasas with lion-like faces, who were fearsome with their fangs and mouths.
Seeing them, she became exceedingly distraught and intent on flight; then she beheld a peaceful ascetic with his disciples, who was observing a vow of silence.
Then, out of fear, she wrapped her creeper-like arms around his neck and said, "O Sage, protect me; I have come to you for refuge. (10)
Then, seeing her agitated and pursued by the Rākṣasa, the Sage, with a roar of "Hum," angrily turned those two terrible beings away.
Seeing them terrified by the sound of the "huṃ" and turned away in flight, Vṛndā prostrated herself on the ground like a staff and spoke these words.
Vṛndā said: "O ocean of mercy, I have been protected by you from this terrible fear; I wish to say something, so please listen to it out of compassion. (13)
"O Lord, my husband Jalandhara has gone to fight Rudra; tell me, O observer of noble vows, how he fares there in battle."
Nārada said: Having heard those words, the sage looked upward with compassion; at that moment, two monkeys arrived, bowed down, and stood before him.

Then, commanded by the sign of her creeper-like eyebrows, they went into the sky; returning in half a moment, they stood before him in prostration, having arrived with the head and the trunk, each holding a hand.
Seeing the headless trunk and the two hands of the Son of the Ocean, she fell to the ground in a swoon, distressed by the calamity that had befallen her husband.
Then, having been sprinkled with water from the sage’s water-pot and comforted by him, she, distressed, placed her forehead against her husband’s forehead and wept.
Vṛndā said: O Lord, you who formerly delighted me with pleasant conversation, why do you not speak today to me, your beloved, though I am innocent?
How has he who, together with Viṣṇu, conquered the gods along with the Gandharvas—that conqueror of the three worlds—been slain today by an ascetic?
Nārada said: Having thus wept, Vṛndā then spoke these words to that sage. Vṛndā said: O ocean of mercy, O best of sages, restore my beloved to life! (21)
"O Sage, in my opinion, you alone are capable of restoring him to life. Nārada said: Having heard those words, the sage spoke while smiling. (22)
The sage said: "He cannot be brought back to life, for he was slain in battle by Rudra; nevertheless, filled with compassion for you, I shall restore him to life. (23)
Nārada said: Having spoken thus, the brahmin vanished; meanwhile, the son of the Ocean embraced Vṛndā and, with a joyful heart, kissed her face.
Then Vṛndā too, seeing her husband, became joyful in heart; staying in the midst of that forest, she took delight with him for many days.
Once, at the conclusion of their amorous play, having beheld Viṣṇu as that very same person, Vṛndā, filled with anger, rebuked him and spoke these words.
Vṛndā said: "Fie upon your character, O Hari, you who approach another's wife! You have been fully recognized by me as a false ascetic concealed by illusion. (27)
Those two gatekeepers of your own whom you showed me through your illusory power—they themselves shall become Rākṣasas and carry off your wife. (28)
And you too, afflicted by grief for your wife, wander in the forest with the monkey as your companion; this lord of serpents has come to you to be your disciple. (29)
Having spoken thus, Vṛndā then entered the fire, even though she was being restrained by Viṣṇu, whose mind was deeply attached to her.
Then Hari, repeatedly remembering her, accompanied by Vṛndā and covered in dust and ashes, remained right there; though being exhorted by hosts of gods and Siddhas, he did not attain peace.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Vṛndā’s Entry into the Fire," within the Legend of Jalandhara, in the *Kārttikamāsa-māhātmya* of the second section, the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: Then Jalandhara, beholding Rudra of wondrous valor, created Gaurī by means of his illusory power (māyā), as if to delude the Three-eyed Lord.
And Śiva beheld Pārvatī, bound upon the chariot and weeping, while being struck by Niśumbha and his other foremost followers.
Seeing Gaurī in such a state, Śiva too became distressed in mind; forgetting his own prowess, he stood silent with his face cast downwards. || 3 ||
Then Jalandhara swiftly pierced Rudra with three arrows, striking him in the head, the chest, and the belly, right up to the feathers at their shafts.
Then, awakened by Viṣṇu, he realized that it was an illusion; he assumed a fierce form, becoming exceedingly terrifying with garlands of flames.
Seeing his exceedingly fierce form, the great asuras were unable to stand before him; they fled in the ten directions.
Then Rudra pronounced a curse upon Śumbha and Niśumbha: "Having fled from my battle, you two shall be slain by Gaurī."
Again, Jalandhara impetuously rained down sharp arrows; at that time, the vast surface of the earth was completely shrouded by the darkness of those shafts.
Even as Rudra swiftly cut down his multitude of arrows, the powerful one quickly struck the bull with an iron club.
By that blow, the bull turned away from the field of battle; though being dragged by Rudra, he did not remain on the battlegrounds.
Thereupon, Rudra, assuming a fierce form, became exceedingly enraged and hurled with great speed the Sudarśana discus, which possessed the brilliance of the sun.
Scorching heaven and earth with its speed, it fell upon the surface of the earth; it severed from the body that head, which possessed large and wide eyes.
His body fell from the chariot, making the surface of the earth resound; and the vital energy (tejas) emerged from his body and merged into Rudra.
The splendor arising from the body of Vṛndā dissolved into Gaurī; then the gods, headed by Brahmā, their eyes blossoming with joy.
Having bowed their heads to Rudra, the gods reported the deeds of Viṣṇu. The gods said: "O Mahādeva, the gods have been protected by you from the fear born of the enemy. (15)
Something else has arisen there; what shall we do? Viṣṇu stands bewildered and infatuated by the beauty of Vṛndā. (16)
Īśvara said: "Go, O gods, for refuge to Viṣṇu in order to dispel this delusion; seek the protection of Māyā in her form as Mohinī, and she will accomplish your task. (17)
Nārada said: Having spoken thus, the Lord then vanished along with the hosts of all beings; and the gods praised Mūlaprakṛti, who is affectionate toward her devotees.

The gods said: We bow to that Mūlaprakṛti, from whom arise the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas which cause creation, maintenance, and destruction; and by whose will this universe expands through existence and non-existence.
We bow to that Supreme Nature who, manifesting in twenty-three divisions, presides over the entire world; whose forms and actions even the three gods, though they be conscious, do not fully know. 20.

We ever bow down to that Mūlaprakṛti, who is affectionate toward her devotees, for those men who are constantly endowed with devotion to her never encounter poverty, fear, delusion, defeat, or the like. (21)
Nārada said: He who recites this hymn at the three junctions of the day with a one-pointed mind will never be touched by poverty, delusion, or suffering. (22)
Praising him in this manner, those gods beheld the sky there occupied by a circle of splendor, with its quarters pervaded by flames.
From the midst of that, they all heard the voice of Bhāratī moving through the sky. Śakti said: "I alone, divided threefold, abide by means of the three qualities (guṇas). (24)
Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Svarā—these exist through the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas; go there, O gods, for she will accomplish your task.
Nārada said: O King, as they were listening to those words, that great light vanished at that time, while the eyes of the gods remained wide with wonder.
Then all those gods, urged by his words, went there and, intent on devotion, bowed down to Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Svarā.
Then, O protector of the earth, seeing those gods prostrate before them, those who are compassionate toward their devotees gave seeds to them and spoke these words.
The goddesses said: "Sow these seeds where Viṣṇu resides; from that, your task will attain success. (29)

Nārada said: Then the hosts of gods and Siddhas, being delighted, took up seeds and scattered them upon that spot on the surface of the earth where Viṣṇu, deprived of happiness, was constantly staying, accompanied by Vṛndā.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Liberation of Jalandhara," in the *Kārtika-māsa-māhātmya* of the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) within the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: From those seeds sown there, O best of kings, three forest trees arose: the Dhātrī, the Mālatī, and the Tulasī.
The dhātrī is known as arising from Dhātṛ; the mālatī is known as arising from Mā; and tulasī arises from Gaurī; they possess the qualities of tamas, sattva, and rajas respectively.
O King, seeing the two trees in the form of women, Viṣṇu, who was captivated by the extraordinary beauty of Vṛndā’s form, then rose up in agitation.
Having seen him, she entreated him out of delusion, her mind being attached by desire; and Tulasī and Dhātrī also gazed upon him with passion.
And because the seed that was formerly offered by Lakṣmī was indeed accompanied by envy, the woman born from it became devoted to envy toward him. || 5 ||
Therefore, she acquired the contemptible name "Barbarī"; moreover, because of her passion for him, the Dhātrī and Tulasī plants were always pleasing to him.
Then, his suffering forgotten, Viṣṇu, being saluted by all the gods, went joyfully to Vaikuṇṭha together with those two.
Therefore, for the concluding rite (udyāpana) of Kārttika, the worship of Viṣṇu is prescribed; for it is traditionally held that such worship at the base of the Tulasī plant bestows delight upon Him.
O King, that house in which a grove of Tulasī stands is indeed like a sacred pilgrimage site; the servants of Yama do not enter it.
Those excellent men who plant a grove of tulasī—which constantly removes all sins and grants all desires—do not behold the son of the Sun (Yama).
Beholding the Narmadā, bathing in the Gaṅgā, and contact with a grove of Tulasī—these three are remembered as being equal.
By planting, protecting, sprinkling, seeing, and touching it, Tulasī destroys the sins of men accumulated through speech, mind, and body.
He who performs the worship of Hari and Hara with Tulasī blossoms does not enter the chamber of the womb; he becomes a partaker of liberation, of this there is no doubt. (13)
The holy places beginning with Puṣkara, the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, and the gods beginning with Vāsudeva all reside within a Tulasī leaf.
He who gives up his life while holding a Tulasī blossom cannot be seen even by Yama, regardless of whether he is burdened with hundreds of sins.
O best of kings, that man who wears sandalwood paste made from Tulasī wood attains union with Viṣṇu; this is the truth, the absolute truth. || 16 ||
O King, sin does not touch that body, even while it is being committed here, wherever there may be the shade of a grove of Tulasī.
In that place, a śrāddha ceremony should be performed; what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible when offered with emblic myrobalan fruits mixed with tulasī leaves. (18)
The merit of bathing in the Gaṅgā is said to accrue to that man who bathes with these waters; likewise, a man should perform the worship of the deity with dhātrī leaves and fruits.
One shall obtain the fruit of worshipping with floods of gold, jewels, and pearls; for in Kārtika, all sacred fords, sages, gods, and sacrifices are present.
When the sun is situated in Libra, they remain constantly resorting to the dhātrī tree; [one should offer] a tulasī leaf on the twelfth day, and a dhātrī leaf in the month of Kārtika.

That man who plucks [the leaves] shall go to most censurable hells; even the four-faced Lord Brahmā would not be capable of describing the greatness of the Dhātrī and Tulasī, just as he is incapable of describing the greatness of the Lord who wields the Śārṅga bow.

He who hears with devotion the account of the origin of Dhātrī and Tulasī, or causes others to hear it, is cleansed of all sins and goes to heaven together with his ancestors, seated upon the foremost celestial chariots.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Dhātrī and Tulasī Trees," in the Kārtika-māsa-māhātmya of the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, within the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pṛthu said: "O you who have observed the *ūrja* vow, please speak again of that great fruit which has been proclaimed; by whom was this auspicious majesty practiced?"
Nārada said: Formerly, in the region of the Sahya mountain, in the city of Karavīra, there was a certain Brāhmaṇa, a knower of dharma, renowned by the name Dharmadatta.
He was one who performed the vows of Viṣṇu and was always properly devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu; once, during the month of Kārttika, he [prepared] for the vigil in honor of Hari.
When a quarter of the night remained, he went to the temple of Hari; as he was departing, he took up the articles for the worship of Hari.
By him was seen a demoness of terrifying appearance as she arrived; seeing her, he was then terrified with fear, his limbs trembling.

Out of fear, she struck her with all the implements of worship and with water; yet, by remembering the name of Hari and using water mixed with *tulasī*, as soon as that [water] touched her, her sin indeed went to its dissolution.
Then, having recollected her own condition born from the ripening of the karma of her previous birth, she prostrated herself like a staff before the brahmin and spoke.
Kalahā said: "O Brahmin, I have reached this state through the ripening of my past karma; how then shall I attain the highest goal once again? (8)
Nārada said: Having seen her properly prostrated and recounting her own deed, the brahmin, being exceedingly amazed, then spoke these words. (9)
Dharmadatta said: By what ripening of karma have you come to such a state? From where do you come, who are you, and what is your character? Tell me all of that.
Kalahā said: O Brahmin, in the city of Saurāṣṭra there was a twice-born man named Bhikṣu; I was formerly his wife, known as Kalahā, and exceedingly cruel. (11)
Never, even at my husband's word, have I performed a virtuous deed; nor have I offered him sweet food, despite being one whose nature was to obey her husband's commands.
When my husband, his mind constantly distressed by me who was ever fond of quarreling, set his heart upon marrying another woman; (13)
Then, O twice-born one, having taken poison, I gave up my life; thereupon, the servants of Yama bound me as I was being bound and led me away.
And Yama, having seen me at that time, questioned Citragupta.
Yama said: "O Citragupta, examine what deed has been performed by her; let her receive the fruit of that action, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious. (16)
Kala said: Then Citragupta, rebuking me, spoke these words. Citragupta said: "Not even the slightest meritorious deed has been performed by her."
While eating this delicious food, she did not offer any to her husband; therefore, let her remain in the womb of a bat, feeding upon her own excrement. (18)
"Even then, out of hatred for her husband, she was constantly quarrelsome; therefore, O Hari, let her remain in the womb of a sow that eats excrement. (19)
Since she always eats from cooking pots and eats here and there alone, she has therefore become a cat that devours its own offspring.
Indeed, she has even committed suicide for the sake of her husband; therefore, let this most censurable woman remain alone, even within the body of a ghost.
Therefore, this woman must be led to the region of Maru by the soldiers; then, remaining within a corpse of a deceased being, she shall stay there for a long time.
And this performer of inauspicious deeds shall experience three births in the higher realms.

Kalahā said: "For five hundred years, I have indeed remained in the body of a ghost, afflicted by hunger and thirst. Having entered the body of a merchant, I came to the southern land, to the confluence of the Kṛṣṇā and Veṇī rivers."
Just as I reached that shore, I was forcibly dragged far away from his body by the hosts of Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Then, O best of the twice-born, you were seen by me while I was emaciated by hunger; indeed, my sins had been removed through contact with the water from the *tulasī* leaves held in your hand.
O best of Brahmins, perform that task by which I may attain liberation from this triple birth, beginning with my current state as a ghost-body.

Having reflected thus upon Kalahā’s words, the foremost of the twice-born—filled with fear, wonder, and grief at the ripening of that karma, his mental state moved by compassion upon seeing her exhaustion—meditated for a long time and spoke these words out of sorrow.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the History of Dharmadatta," in the *Kārttikamāsamāhātmya* of the second section, the *Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa*, within the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 24.
Dharmadatta said: Sins are dissolved through gifts, vows, and other rites at sacred fords; however, you, who reside in the body of a *preta*, have no entitlement to them.
My mind is distressed by this sight of your exhaustion; indeed, it finds no peace until I have rescued you from your suffering.
Therefore, by means of half the merit of this Kārtika vow which I have observed throughout my life, may you attain a virtuous state.
Nārada said: Having spoken thus, as Dharmadatta was about to consecrate her with water mixed with *tulasī* while causing her to hear the twelve-syllable mantra, [the following occurred].
At that moment, liberated from her state as a preta, she became like a blazing crest of fire, assuming a divine form endowed with beauty like that of Indirā.
Then she prostrated herself on the ground like a staff before that twice-born man, and spoke these words with a voice faltering with joy.
Kalahā said: "O best of the twice-born, by your grace I have been liberated from hell; you have truly become a boat for me as I was sinking in the ocean of sin. (7)
Nārada said: While she was speaking thus, O Brahmin, she beheld a radiant celestial chariot descending from the sky, yoked with attendants who bore the form of Viṣṇu.
Then, attended by hosts of Apsaras, she was helped down from that foremost of celestial chariots by the two gatekeepers, Puṇyaśīla and Suśīla.
Then Dharmadatta beheld that celestial chariot with wonder; seeing those two in the form of Viṣṇu, he fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff.
Then Puṇyaśīla and Suśīla, having raised up that bowed twice-born man, greeted him and spoke these words consistent with dharma.

The two Gaṇas said: "Excellent, excellent, O best of the twice-born! For you are always devoted to Viṣṇu, compassionate toward the distressed, all-knowing, and solely intent upon the vows of Viṣṇu. (12)
This auspicious Kārtika-vow which you have observed since childhood—by giving half of its merit to me, its religious fruit has become doubled. (13)
The sin produced over hundreds of previous births has gone to destruction; indeed, whatever sin she possessed born of her past actions has vanished through these very baths.
O virtuous one, having ascended this celestial chariot by means of the vigil for Hari and other such rites, she is being led to Vaikuṇṭha, endowed with manifold enjoyments.

O ocean of mercy, through the merits arising from the gift of lamps, she has attained a form resembling your own splendor; and by the worship of tulasī and the auspicious Kārtika vows offered by you, she has come into the presence of Viṣṇu.
At the end of this existence, you too shall go with your two wives to the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, into the presence of Viṣṇu, and attain a form identical to his.
They are blessed, they have accomplished their purpose, and their birth is fruitful—those by whom Viṣṇu has been worshipped with devotion, just as you have done, O Dharmadatta.
What does Viṣṇu, when properly propitiated, not bestow upon embodied beings—he by whom, in ancient times, Auttānapādi was established in the position of Dhruva?
By the mere remembrance of whose name embodied beings attain a good destination. || 20 ||
For this lord of serpents, who was formerly seized by a crocodile, was liberated by the mere remembrance of [the Lord's] name; having come into his presence, he became known by the name Jaya.
"Since Viṣṇu has been worshipped by you, you shall attain his presence for many thousands of years, indeed accompanied by two wives."
Then, when your merit has been exhausted and you descend to the earth, you will become a king renowned as one born of the Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśa). || 23 ||
There was one named Daśaratha, accompanied by two wives, and also by this third one, who shares half of your merit.
Even there, Viṣṇu will manifest his presence upon the earth; having assumed the form of your son, he will perform the work of the immortals.
Compared to this vow of yours at birth, which brings such satisfaction to Viṣṇu, neither sacrifices, nor gifts, nor sacred fords are indeed superior.

"You are blessed, O foremost of Brahmins, since you have performed this vow which brings satisfaction to the Teacher of the World; for by the merit of its half-portion, this [attainment] of the same world as Murāri is being brought about by us with success. (27)

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Liberation of Kalahā," within the *Dharmadatta-Opākhyāna* (The Story of Dharmadatta) of the *Kārttikamāsa-Māhātmya* (The Greatness of the Month of Kārttika), in the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: Having heard those words, Dharmadatta was filled with wonder; prostrating himself on the ground like a staff, he spoke these words. (1)
Dharmadatta said: "All people indeed propitiate Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the distress of his devotees, through sacrifices, gifts, vows, pilgrimages, and austerities according to the prescribed rules."
There is something that brings pleasure to Viṣṇu and causes His presence; by performing it, all those [other rites] indeed become as if already accomplished.
The two Gaṇas said: "Well asked by you, O Brahmin! Listen with a one-pointed mind to this meritorious narrative, including its history, as it occurred in the past."
In ancient times, there was a sovereign emperor named Cola in the city of Kāñcī; it is after his very name that those lands became renowned as the Colas.
While he ruled, there was not a single man on earth who was poor, suffering, evil-minded, or afflicted by disease.
Both banks of the Tāmraparṇī river belonging to that performer of exalted sacrifices were richly adorned with golden sacrificial posts and resembled the Caitraratha grove.
O twice-born one, once that king went to Anantaśayana, where the Lord of the worlds was reclining in yogic sleep.
There, the king, having duly worshipped the Lord Śrīramaṇa with divine gems, pearls, and beautiful golden flowers, [proceeded].
Having prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground and sat there, he indeed beheld a Brahmin approaching in the presence of the deity.
There he saw a twice-born man named Viṣṇudāsa, a resident of his own city, holding water and Tulasī in his hand for the purpose of worshipping the gods.
Having arrived there, that brahmin-sage worshipped the God of gods, bathing Him with the Viṣṇu-sūkta and with the blossoms and leaves of the tulasī plant.
Seeing that his previous worship with jewels had been eclipsed by the worship of Tulasī, the king became enraged and spoke this: || 13 ||
Cola said: "O Viṣṇudāsa, how is it that this worship of mine here, rich in splendor with rubies and gold, has been covered over by Tulasī leaves? (14)
"You do not know devotion to Viṣṇu; in my opinion, you are a wretch, you who indeed conceal this most splendid worship! (15)
Having heard those words, that best of brahmins, filled with anger and disregarding the king's dignity, then spoke these words.
Viṣṇudāsa said: "O King, you do not know devotion; you are arrogant because of your royal splendor. Tell me, how much of Viṣṇu’s vow have you previously performed? (17)
The two attendants said: Having heard those words of the brāhmaṇa, that best of kings laughed and then spoke these words with pride to the twice-born Viṣṇudāsa.
The king said: "O Brahmin, if you speak thus, being excessively proud of your devotion to Viṣṇu, how great can your devotion to Viṣṇu be, when you are poor and destitute? (19)
O Brahmin, neither sacrifices, gifts, and the like have ever been performed by you for the gratification of Viṣṇu, nor has a temple ever been built by you anywhere before.
"Even for one such as you, this pride persists despite your devotion; therefore, let all these twice-born ones hear my words today. (21)
"This dispute shall proceed until there is a direct manifestation of Viṣṇu; then let everyone behold it, and they will understand the devotion of us both. (22)
The two Gaṇas said: Having spoken thus, the king then departed for his own royal palace; having appointed Mudgala as the preceptor (ācārya), he commenced a Vaiṣṇava sacrificial session (satra).
It was frequented by hosts of sages, abounding in food and abundant in sacrificial fees; it was that prosperous Brahmakṛta which had previously existed in the field of Gayā.
Viṣṇudāsa also remained right there in the temple as a practitioner of vows, constantly performing the prescribed observances that bring satisfaction to Viṣṇu.
The vow of Māgha and Kārttika, the proper cultivation of a Tulasī grove, and the recitation of the twelve-syllable mantra of Hari on the Ekādaśī day.
With the sixteen types of ritual services and auspicious offerings such as dance and song, he performed the daily worship of Viṣṇu; thus he observed these vows.
Constantly remembering Viṣṇu even while walking on earth or sleeping, he, possessing equal vision, beheld Viṣṇu abiding in all beings.
For the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu, he constantly observed special observances during the months of Māgha and Kārttika, as well as the ritual for their formal conclusion.

Thus, as the two of them—the Lord of Cola and Viṣṇudāsa—were propitiating the Lord of Śrī, a very great length of time passed while they remained established in their vows, with all their senses and actions dedicated to Him.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Dispute between the Cola King and the Brāhmaṇa Viṣṇudāsa," in the Kārtika-māsa-māhātmya of the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, within the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: Once, O twice-born one, after Viṣṇudāsa had performed his daily rites, he prepared some cooked food; meanwhile, someone carried it away unobserved. || 1 ||
Not seeing him, that twice-born man did not cook again at that time, out of fear of breaking his vow regarding the evening worship.
On the second day, having cooked again, as soon as he went to offer the oblation to Viṣṇu, someone else stole it once more. || 3 ||
O King, in this manner, for seven days, no one at all took away his cooked food; then, filled with wonder, he reflected thus in his mind: ||| 4 ||
"Aha! Who comes daily and carries away my cooked food? My place as one who has renounced his field must by no means be abandoned by me. (5)
Furthermore, if I were to cook again here and eat it, how could my evening worship possibly be neglected? (6)
Even if one has prepared food in this manner, it must not be eaten by me; for nothing at all is consumed by Vaiṣṇavas without first being offered to Hari.
Having fasted for seven days, I remain here established in my vow; today I shall properly perform the preservation of the cooked food here.
Having thus prepared the cooked food, he remained right there unobserved; meanwhile, he saw a Caṇḍāla standing there intent on taking away the cooked food.
Beholding him emaciated by hunger, with a dejected face and reduced to nothing but skin and bone, that foremost of the twice-born became filled with compassion in his heart.
Seeing the Brahmin carrying food, he said, "Stop, stop! Why do you eat that dry food? O sir, take this ghee!"
And seeing that foremost of Brahmins approaching and speaking thus, he ran toward him with speed out of fear and fell down, unconscious.
Seeing the Caṇḍāla terrified and unconscious, that foremost of the twice-born approached with haste and, out of compassion, fanned him with the ends of his own garment.
Then Viṣṇudāsa beheld that very person who had arisen, the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Seeing him, that best of the twice-born was so overwhelmed by sattvic emotions that he was then unable even to offer praise or prostration.
Then Śakra and the other gods arrived at that very spot; the Gandharvas and Apsaras also sang and danced with joy.
At that time, that place became crowded with hundreds of celestial chariots, thronged by hundreds of divine sages, and filled with the resounding noise of songs and musical instruments.
Then Viṣṇu, having embraced his devotee who was firm in his virtuous vows, granted him his own form and led him to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
The consecrated King Cola beheld Viṣṇudāsa as he was traveling toward the presence of Viṣṇu, seated within an excellent celestial chariot.
Seeing Viṣṇudāsa departing for the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, he quickly summoned his own guru, Mudgala, and spoke these words.
Cola said: "That brahmin, in emulation of whom I performed sacrifices, gifts, and other such acts—he, assuming the form of Viṣṇu, is going to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha. (21)
"By me, having been initiated, this Vaiṣṇava sacrifice was properly performed; you offered oblations into the fire, and the Brahmins were made fully satisfied with gifts and other offerings. (22)
"Even now, that Lord certainly does not become gracious toward me; yet, through the devotion of Viṣṇudāsa alone, Hari granted him a direct vision. (23)
Therefore, Viṣṇu is not pleased by gifts or sacrifices alone; devotion alone is the supreme means for the vision of the All-pervading Lord. (24)
The two Gaṇas said: Having spoken thus, they consecrated their own nephew upon the royal throne; for he had been initiated into sacrifice since childhood and thus attained the state of being sonless.
Therefore, even today in that region, only nephews are born who always share in the portion of the kingdom and abide by the boundaries established by him.
Then, having approached the sacrificial enclosure and standing before the sacrificial pit, he quickly and loudly proclaimed three times, thereby awakening Viṣṇu.
"O Viṣṇu, grant me firm devotion through my mind, speech, body, and actions. Having spoken thus, he fell into the fire while everyone was looking on.
Then Mudgala, out of anger, tore out his own topknot; consequently, even today, those of his lineage are known as the Mudgalas, the "Topknot-less. (29)
At that moment, Viṣṇu, who is affectionate toward his devotees, appeared from the sacrificial fire-pit; Acyuta embraced him and caused him to ascend a preeminent celestial chariot.
Embracing him and granting him a state of identity with Himself, the Lord of Gods, surrounded by the deities, went to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha together with him.

Nārada said: He who was Viṣṇudāsa is indeed Puṇyaśīla, and he who was King Cola is named Suśīla; both of these, possessing forms equal to his own, were made by that beloved of Ramā to stand as his gatekeepers.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Liberation of Colaviṣṇudāsa," in the Kārttikamāsa-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Dharmadatta said: I have heard that Jaya and Vijaya were the two gatekeepers of Viṣṇu; what indeed did they perform in the past, such that they now bear those forms? (1)
The two Gaṇas said: O twice-born one, in ancient times, two sons were born to Kardama by the very sight of Devahūtī, the daughter of Tṛṇabindu.
The elder was named Jaya and the younger Vijaya; later, Kapila, a knower of the yoga-dharma, was born of that same [wife]. (3)
Both Jaya and Vijaya were always devoted to Viṣṇu; with their entire collection of senses fixed upon Him, they became virtuous in character.
Both of them were constant performers of the eight-syllable mantra and observers of the Viṣṇu-vow; Viṣṇu always granted them his direct manifestation during their daily worship.
Once, invited by Marutta for the sacrificial rite, those two, who were skilled in sacrifice and honored by hosts of celestial sages, went there.
There, Jayanta became the Brahmā priest and Vijaya became the Yājaka; then they both performed the entire sacrificial rite in its full perfection.
Having performed the avabhṛtha bath, Marutta gave them much wealth; taking that wealth, the two of them departed toward their own hermitage.
Then those two sages, dividing that wealth for the purpose of performing separate sacrifices to Viṣṇu for the sake of his satisfaction, vied with one another.
Thereupon Jaya said, "Let the share be divided equally," but Vijaya replied, "This is not so; whatever has been acquired by whomsoever belongs to him."
Then Jaya, out of anger, cursed Vijaya, whose mind was greedy, saying to him: "Since you have seized this and do not give it back, therefore become a crocodile! (11)
Having heard that curse, Vijaya also cursed him: "Since you, deluded by pride, have cursed me, therefore go to the state of an elephant."
Having seen the omnipresent Lord Viṣṇu during his daily worship, the two of them related those events and entreated the Lord of Ramā for the removal of their curses.
Jayavijayā said: "O Lord, O Ocean of Mercy, how shall we two, your devotees, come to be born from the wombs of a crocodile and an elephant? Let that curse be revoked. (14)
The Blessed Lord said: "The word of my two devotees shall never become untrue; even by me it can never be made otherwise."
Indeed, in the past, I manifested within a pillar at the word of Prahlāda; likewise, by the speech of Ambarīṣa, I truly came forth myself from his womb.
"Therefore, having yourselves experienced these two curses you brought upon yourselves, you shall attain my eternal abode," saying this, Hari vanished.
The two Gaṇas said: Then those two became a crocodile and an elephant on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī; yet, remembering their former births, even in that womb they remained steadfast in the vow of Viṣṇu.
Once, that elephant went to the Gaṇḍakī river to bathe during the month of Kārtika; at that moment, a crocodile seized him, as he was remembering the cause of his curse.
Seized by the crocodile, that elephant then remembered the Lord of Śrī; at that moment, Viṣṇu appeared, bearing the discus, the conch, and the mace.
Then, having hurled his discus, the Lord rescued both the crocodile and the elephant; bestowing upon them his own form, he led them to Vaikuṇṭha.
From that time forward, that place has been remembered as Harikṣetra, for even the stones there were marked by the friction of the wheels.
Both of them, O twice-born one, are renowned in the world as Jaya and Vijaya; they are the gatekeepers who were indeed asked about by you, and they are eternally dear to Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O knower of dharma, you too, who are ever established in the vow of Viṣṇu and have abandoned envy and hypocrisy, should become one who looks upon all with equanimity.
Always bathe at dawn during the months of Libra, Capricorn, and Aries; remain steadfast in the vow of Ekādaśī and be a protector of the Tulasī grove. || 25 ||
Always honor the Brahmins, the cows, and the Vaiṣṇavas; do not eat masūra lentils, fermented gruel, or eggplants.
"In this same way, O Dharmadatta, at the end of your body's life, you too shall attain that supreme abode of Viṣṇu through devotion to Him alone, just as we have."
For as long as one is born from this vow which causes the satisfaction of Viṣṇu, neither sacrifices, nor gifts, nor sacred pilgrimage sites are indeed superior to it.

"You are blessed, O foremost of Brahmins, since you have performed this vow that brings satisfaction to the Teacher of the World; for we are being led to the same world as Murāri, having obtained half of the fruit of his merit. (29)
Nārada said: Having thus instructed Dharmadatta, those two, traveling in their celestial chariot, went together with Kalahā to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
For that Dharmadatta, having gained conviction and remained steadfast in that vow, at the end of his body's life, went to the abode of that Lord accompanied by his two wives.
The man who hears this ancient history or causes others to hear it attains, through the grace of the Teacher of the World, an intellect that brings about the presence of Hari.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of Dharmadatta’s Attainment of Liberation," in the Kārtika-māsa-māhātmya of the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, within the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O beloved, having heard those words, Pṛthu, his mind filled with wonder, duly honored Nārada and then bid him farewell.
Formerly, in the city of Avantī, there was a certain Brahmin named Dhaneśvara; he had fallen away from the duties of a Brāhmaṇa, being a man of sinful deeds and very wicked intellect.
Once, while traveling from country to country for the purpose of buying and selling, that lord of wealth arrived at the city of Māhiṣmatī.
Because it was formerly established by Mahiṣa, it is called Māhiṣmatī; there the Narmadā, the destroyer of sins, shines as she flows along its ramparts.
Seeing there the men who had come from various countries to observe the Kārtika vow, he dwelt for one month while carrying on his trade.
Wandering constantly along the banks of the Narmadā for the purpose of selling [the goods], he saw Brāhmaṇas engaged in bathing, silent recitation, and the worship of the gods.
Some were reciting the Purāṇas, while others were devoted to listening to them; some were intent on dancing, singing, and instrumental music, and others were absorbed in hearing the glories of Viṣṇu.

Some were intent on the concluding rite of completion, some were devoted to the night vigil, some were engaged in the worship of Brahmins and cows, and likewise some were devoted to the offering of lamps.
Overcome with curiosity, the Lord of Wealth wandered here and there constantly, beholding [the deity] through seeing, touching, and speaking.
Likewise, he obtained the hearing of the name of Viṣṇu and other [devotions] from the Vaiṣṇavas; thus the twice-born one remained for a month on the bank of that Narmadā.
Then, bitten by a black serpent, he fell down overwhelmed; thereafter, the servants of Yama bound him, who had abandoned his body.
By the command of Yama, they cast that lord of wealth into the Kumbhīpāka hell; yet as soon as he was thrown there, it became cool.
Just as the fire in the Kumbhīpāka hell had become cool from the previous throwing of Prahlāda, Yama, having seen that wonder, summoned him and questioned him.
Just then, Nārada arrived there and spoke in haste. Nārada said: "O son of Aruṇa, this man is certainly not worthy of experiencing the hells."
Because at the end of his life there arose a deed that removes one from hell—he who would perform the acts of seeing, touching, or speaking with those of meritorious deeds. (15)
Then that man certainly obtains a sixth part of their merit; for Dhaneśvara had indeed formed a friendship and association with them. (16)
Those who observe the Kārttika vow for the entire month shall partake in a portion of their merit.
Therefore, this one who dwells in the womb of a yakṣa indeed possesses merit against his will, for he has beheld all the hells that display the experience of sin. (18)

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Having spoken thus, when Nārada had departed, that son of Sūrya—his own virtuous deeds awakened by hearing those words—again led that brāhmaṇa with his servant, intending to show him all those various hells.
Then, having led Dhaneśvara to the hells, the attendant of the departed (Pretapa), acting as an executor of Yama’s commands, spoke while intending to show him all of them.
Pretapa said: "O Lord of Wealth, behold these terrible hells of great terror; in these, evildoers are constantly cooked by the servants of Yama. (21)

A sin committed unintentionally is declared to be "dry," while one committed intentionally is called "moist. Through these categories of moist and dry sins, [the transmigrating beings] are established in two types of states.

Those sins which exist in eighty-four distinct varieties—namely the miscellaneous (prakīrṇaka), those unworthy of sitting in the row (apāṅkteya), and likewise those that cause defilement (malinīkaraṇa)—[are all destroyed].
Likewise, that which causes loss of caste, that termed a minor offense (upapātaka), the heinous sin (atipāpa), and the great sin (mahāpāpa)—sin is thus remembered as being of seven kinds. (24)
Because you had contact with those who observed the Kārttika vow, you shall be cooked in these seven hells in successive order.
"Indeed, by the accumulation of that merit, these hells have been removed. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "Having thus shown him the hells, the Lord of the Dead then led him away. (26)
He indeed became a Yakṣa there in the world of the Yakṣas, the realm of Dhaneśvara; he is this very one, renowned as Dhanayakṣa, a follower of Dhanada.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus to Satyabhāmā, who was exceedingly dear to him, Vāsudeva went to his mother’s house to perform the evening twilight rites.

Brahmā said: Indeed, such is the power of this Kārttika month, for it bestows liberation and grants worldly enjoyment; even by the mere sight of one observing this vow, the many sins accumulated over lifetimes go away, leading to liberation.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Birth as the Yakṣa Dhaneśvara," in the Kārtika-māsa-māhātmya of the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, within the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: This greatness of Kārtika that you have described is indeed wonderful; how could this [greatness] have been achieved by one who lacks the capacity to perform it himself? (1)
Brahmā said: One does not possess the power to act by one's own capacity; the fruit is obtained through a means. By giving wealth to a Brāhmaṇa, one may obtain the highest fruit.
One may have [the work] performed by a disciple, a group of servants, women, or even a trusted person; by taking the fruit from even such a person, a man becomes a sharer in the merit. || 3 ||
Nārada said: "Even merits that have not been given are sometimes obtained by someone somewhere. I wish to hear this; curiosity has arisen within me. (4)
Brahmā said: "O twice-born one, listen with a focused mind; I shall tell you the means by which one obtains merits and even sins, even though they have not been given."
Whatever has been done by one person, whether good or evil, that results for him arises for the whole kingdom in the Tretā age, but in the preceding [age] it occurs only in the city.

In the Dvāpara age, however, [the fruit arises] in the midst of the lineage; but in the Kali age, the agent alone [experiences it]. Whatever action was performed through ignorance in childhood, its fruit is experienced in a dream.
Whatever [sin] was committed during youth or childhood out of ignorance, its fruit shall manifest; however, the fruit of actions performed with full knowledge lasts until the end of one's life.
By associating with a sinner for six months, a man becomes a sinner; by associating with either sinners or the righteous for ten months, he likewise becomes so.
From eating in the same row as another, one is tainted by a twentieth part of that person's merit and demerit; from sitting on the same seat with two people, one is tainted by a thousandth part.
He who eats the food of another indeed consumes that person's sin; through the recitation of prayers and other rites, sixteen parts of the sin resulting from contact with a sinner are destroyed.
From praising another, from giving commands, from eating from the same vessel, and from sharing a bed or a garment, one shares a sixth part of the other's merit and demerit. (12)
A man takes all [the merit and demerit] of his wife and of his legitimate son; he takes half from his disciple and likewise a fourth part of both sin and merit. (13)
A woman who obeys her husband's command takes away half of her husband's merit; by eating what has been cooked with her own hands, she removes a tenth part of his sin.
He who gives a year’s worth of food incurs half the sin [of the recipient], while the man who consumes that year’s worth of food enjoys half of the merit [of the donor]. (15)
The patron of the sacrifice surely experiences one-sixth of the priest’s sin or merit, while the priest experiences one-tenth of that [the patron’s]. (16)
The one who exerts effort, the one who consents, the one who provides the means, and the supervisor share one-sixth of the merit and demerit, while the witness receives one-tenth.
Whatever work is performed by his hand, he shall take a sixth part of the merit from it, except for food, provided it is not done for the sake of a hired servant or a pupil.
Through social interaction, as well as through constant conversation and the like out of affection, one obtains a tenth part of the merits and sins [of others]; of this there is no doubt. (19)
By virtue of his association with merit, that lowest of the twice-born, Ekadanta, having beheld various hells, attained heaven at that very moment.
Nārada said: "O Grandfather, why is it that some people do not perform such a Kārtika vow, which involves little effort yet yields great fruit? (21)
Brahmā said: For the sake of increasing his own creation, the Creator indeed produced both dharma and adharma. Those who practice dharma alone attain an auspicious state.
Those men who practice unrighteousness go to a downward state; heaven is the fruit of meritorious deeds, while hell is the opposite of that.
Two alone were created by the Ordainer as the guardians of those two: Śatakratu and Yama; and they both act in accordance with merit and sin. (24)
The violation of the guru’s bed and others are known on earth as the sons of Desire; the killing of one's father and others are the sons of Anger; now hear of the sons of Greed. (25)
These leaders of hell, beginning with the seizer of Brahmins' property, were created by Yama; when men are pervaded by them, they do not perform [righteous deeds].
Indeed, those who have been liberated by such means perform religious duties such as vows and the like.
Faith and intelligence are always present on earth as destroyers [of obstacles]; yet a person pervaded by those two [qualities] engages in the hearing and other [devotional acts] of Śrī Viṣṇu. (28)
The one of very dull intellect does not perform that by which he indeed goes to blind darkness; I shall tell you what was said by Kṛṣṇa to Satyabhāmā. (29)
Through teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or even eating in the same row, a man receives a fourth part of the merits and sins [of others] behind their backs.
From sharing a single seat, a single vehicle, or through the contact of bodies during breathing, one will certainly partake in a sixth portion of the merits and sins [of the other]. (31)
Through touching, speaking with, or even praising another, a human being constantly receives a tenth part of that person's merits and sins. (32)
Through seeing and hearing [another], and likewise through mental contemplation, a person shall obtain a hundredth part of that other's merits and sins.
He who utters censure, slander, or reproach against another incurs the sin committed thereby and gives away his own merit. (34)
If a man performs service for one who is performing meritorious deeds—whether he be a wife, a servant, a disciple, or any other person whatsoever—[he too gains merit]. (35)
And even if no material gift corresponding to his service is given, he too shall partake in the fruit of that merit in accordance with the nature of his service. (36)
Whoever bypasses the serving of food arranged in a single row shall receive a sixth part of the merit of that which was bypassed.
Whoever performs his bath, twilight prayers, and other rites while touching or conversing with him, shall certainly give a sixth part of the merit of that action to him. (38)
If a man, under the pretext of teaching the Dharma, asks for another's wealth, the giver of that wealth shall obtain the fruit arising from that meritorious deed. (39)
He who performs a meritorious deed after stealing another's property—the agent of the action incurs the sin therein, while the fruit thereof belongs to the owner of the wealth. (40)
If a man dies without having discharged his debt to another, the creditor takes away that man's merit in proportion to that debt. (41)

The provider of counsel, the one who gives consent, the one who provides the necessary implements, and the one who supplies the strength—each of these shall receive a sixth part of the merit and the demerit. (42)
A king shall take a sixth part of the merits and sins from his subjects; likewise, a teacher from his pupil, a husband from his wife, and a father from his son. (43)
A woman shall obtain half of even her husband’s merit; constantly devoted to his will, she remains a source of satisfaction to him. (44)
When one performs meritorious acts such as giving through the hand of another, the agent shall receive a sixth part of the merit, except in the case of a hired laborer or a son.
The provider of livelihood shall set aside a sixth part of the merit for the enjoyer of that livelihood—whether for himself or for another—if he does not cause [the latter] to perform service.

For in this way, merits and sins accumulated by others constantly come to one even without being given; however, in the Kali age, this rule must not be applied, for the doer alone is indeed the enjoyer of his own merit and sin.

In the Kali age, firm knowledge does not exist; in the Kali age, virtuous action is performed out of pride; in the Kali age, yoga accompanied by hypocrisy surely perishes—of this there is no doubt. (48)
Formerly devoted to asceticism yet hypocritical, Satī, through the power of her purity, attained the supreme state by witnessing the worship of her parents and by serving her husband with vigor.
Nārada said: O Blessed One, I desire to hear of the most excellent of vows; [tell me] the procedure for the month-long fast and its appropriate fruit.
Brahmā said: "Excellent, O sinless Nārada! I shall explain everything that you have asked. O best among the wise, listen with devotion as I speak. (51)
Just as Viṣṇu is among the gods, as the sun is among those that give heat, as Meru is among the peaked mountains, and as Vainateya is among birds; || 52 ||
Likewise, fasting for a month is the most excellent of all vows; indeed, whatever merit exists in all vows and in all sacred pilgrimage sites [is obtained thereby]. (53)
One does not obtain that merit which arises from all forms of giving and from sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, which is obtained by fasting for a month.
Then, having obtained the permission of the guru, one should perform a month-long fast; thereafter, having performed the Atikṛcchra, the Pārāka, and the Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
O Sage, having ascertained the strength or weakness of one's body, a forest-dweller, an ascetic, or even a widow, may perform the month-long fast.
Then, having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one should perform the month-long fast with the permission of the preceptor and the Brahmins.
One should undertake this vow for thirty days; with devotion, one should worship Hari three times a day in the abode of Acyuta.
One should worship the one whose banner is Garuḍa with offerings of food, incense, lamps, and various kinds of flowers, through mind, deed, and speech.
A man devoted to his own duty, a virtuous wife who has conquered her senses, or a chaste widow, should worship Vāsudeva. (60)

The tasting of objects such as the sight of forms, fragrances, and so forth has been fully described; one should avoid dwelling upon any other [sensations] and the complete release of morsels of food. (61)
One observing a vow should avoid anointing the limbs, anointing the head, betel-leaf, and the application of unguents; he should avoid all these and whatever else has been forbidden.
One established in a vow should not touch anyone engaged in improper acts, nor should one speak with them; a householder observing a vow should do so while staying in a temple.
Having observed the month-long fast according to the prescribed rule, a man should thus complete this vow for exactly thirty days, neither more nor less. (64)
Then, on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), one should worship the meritorious Lord who has Garuḍa as His banner, after having fed the best of the twice-born with gifts of clothing and other offerings.
One should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), prostrate, and ask for their forgiveness; having asked the Brahmins for forgiveness, one should dismiss them after honoring and worshipping them.
Thus, at the end of the month-long fast, having invited thirteen Brahmins, he should perform the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice while fasting on the Ekādaśī day.
Then, preceded by a salutation, one should feed the Brahmins, and give them betel, pairs of garments, food, and coverings.
Having given yoga-bands, threads, and a bed with its furnishings to the foremost of the twice-born, and having honored them, he should dismiss them.
The procedure for the month-long fast has been duly proclaimed; hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for the lunar days beginning with the ninth.
Listen to that which was proclaimed by the Vālakhilyas to the sages, O Nārada. (71)

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Month-long Fasting Vow (Māsopavāsa-vrata), preceded by the Account of the Attainment of the Fruits of Merit and Sin Bestowed," in the Kārtika-māsa-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 30 ||

The Vālakhilyas said: The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika was when the Dvāpara Yuga began. It should be observed, according to the sequence, as falling within the forenoon for the giving of gifts and the afternoon for fasting.
Here, a Daitya named Kūṣmāṇḍaka was slain by Viṣṇu; from his body hairs arose the creepers produced from the Kūṣmāṇḍa.
Therefore, by the gift of a pumpkin (kūṣmāṇḍa), one certainly obtains the fruit; on this very ninth day, a man should perform the festival of Kṛṣṇa.
By performing the marriage ceremony of Tulasī according to the ritual prescribed in one's own Vedic branch, the fruit of giving away a daughter in marriage is attained; of this there is no doubt.
Having reached the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, one who has conquered his senses should fashion an auspicious golden image of Hari together with Tulasī.
The observer of the vow should worship there with devotion according to the rules for three days; thus, by the prescribed method, he should perform the marriage rite.

In this very context, the three-night period should be accepted in accordance with the ninth day and so forth; the ninth day, when it extends across midday and is pierced by the preceding [eighth] day, is to be accepted.
He who protects and maintains both the Dhātrī and Aśvattha trees together, his merit shall not perish even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Formerly, on the eleventh day of the lunar fortnight, Kanaka’s daughter Kiśorikā devoutly performed the evening rite for the marriage of Tulasī.
By that [act], Sulocanā was liberated from the blemish of widowhood; therefore, the rite of marriage with a Tulasi plant should be performed every evening.
This must certainly be performed every year by the Vaiṣṇavas; I shall now proclaim its ritual procedure so that the rite may be complete with all its constituent parts.
One should fashion an auspicious image of Viṣṇu made of gold weighing one pala; or one may prepare it according to one's capacity, weighing half of that, or half of that again.
Having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the rite of infusing life) for both Tulasī and the form of Viṣṇu, one should then awaken the Lord with the hymns and other recitations previously mentioned.
One should worship with the sixteen services accompanied by the recitation of the Puruṣasūkta; then, having recollected the place and time, one should worship Gaṇeśa there.

Then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and performed the *nāndīśrāddha* rite, one should bring forth the image of Viṣṇu amidst the sounds of Vedic recitations, musical instruments, and the like.
She should be placed near the Tulasī plant, concealed by cloths, [with the thought]: "Come, O Blessed Lord, O God Keśava; I shall worship you. (16)
"I shall give you Tulasī; be the granter of all desires. He should offer the arghya, the pādya, and the seat (viṣṭara) three times.
Then, having recited "ācamanīyam" three times, he should cause it to be offered; thereafter, curd, ghee, and milk, placed within a vessel made of bell-metal.
"O Vāsudeva, accept this madhuparka; salutations to you! Having performed all the rites, including the application of turmeric paste and the anointing with oil," (19)
At the time of *godhūli*, Tulasī and Keśava should be worshipped again; they should be placed separately facing one another, and one should recite auspicious verses.

When the sun is just beginning to be visible, one should utter the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), having stated one's own lineage (gotra) and ancestral sages (pravara), as well as the three ancestors and so forth.
O Lord, who are without beginning, middle, or end, and the protector of the three worlds, accept this Tulasī according to the marriage rite.
Born from the seed of Pārvatī, residing in the ashes of Vṛndā, without beginning, middle, or end—I give to you this beloved one. (23)
"Like a daughter, she was raised by me with constant care and service; O sir, I give this Tulasi, dear to you, to you—please accept her. (24)
Having thus offered the *tulasī*, he should thereafter worship those two; then, preceded by the wedding festival, he should perform a night vigil.
Then, at the time of dawn, one should worship Tulasī and Viṣṇu after performing the ritual installation of the fire with the twelve-syllable mantra.

One should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with milk-rice, clarified butter, honey, and sesame seeds; then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, one should subsequently offer the *pūrṇāhuti*. Having duly honored the preceptor, one should complete the remainder of the fire-sacrifice.
Whatever vow has been undertaken for the four months of the rainy season, one should fulfill it accordingly after having declared it to the twice-born, as well as any other [vow]. || 28 ||
"O Lord, O Master Janārdana, this vow has been performed by me for your pleasure; by your grace, may whatever was deficient reach completion. (29)
If a man performs the breaking of the fast during the fourth quarter of the Revatī asterism conjoined with the twelfth lunar day, he brings his vow to fruitlessness.

Then, whatever items have been avoided during the Cāturmāsya or the autumn season, one should offer those to the Brāhmaṇas; thereafter, one may eat all that which was renounced while remaining established in the vow.
The meal should be eaten here together with the husband and wife, as well as with the twice-born brahmins.
Then, having eaten those fallen leaves of Tulasī that remain after the meal, one is himself liberated from sins.
By eating a stalk of sugarcane, as well as an emblic myrobalan fruit and a jujube fruit at the end of a meal, one's impurity from that meal is destroyed.
If any man has not eaten even one of these three, he should be known as *ucchiṣṭa* (impure) for a year; there is no doubt about this.
Then, having worshipped again in the evening with beautiful stalks of sugarcane, as well as Tulasī and Vāsudeva, one becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.

Then, having performed the ritual dismissal and offered the inheritance to Hari, one should say: "O Lord, O Master, go to Vaikuṇṭha accompanied by Tulasī; accepting the worship performed by me, be forever satisfied. (37)
Go, go, O best of gods, to your own abode, O Supreme Lord; go to where Brahmā and the other gods are, O Janārdana.

Having thus bid farewell to the Lord of Gods, one should cause all [the icons], beginning with the primary image (mūrti), to be presented to the preceptor; by doing so, the person becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.

He who performs the marriage ceremony with Tulasī every year, being full of devotion, will certainly become endowed with wealth and grain; he shall obtain great fame both in this world and in the next. (40)

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Marriage of Kūṣmāṇḍa and Tulasī on the Ninth Day," in the *Kārtika-māsa-māhātmya* of the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

The Vālakhilyas said: The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika was when the Dvāpara Yuga began. It should be understood that, according to the sequence of giving gifts and observing fasts, the day should be taken as extending into both the forenoon and the afternoon.
Here, a Daitya named Kūṣmāṇḍaka was slain by Viṣṇu; from his body hairs were produced the creepers that originate from the kūṣmāṇḍa.
Therefore, by the gift of a pumpkin (kūṣmāṇḍa), one certainly attains the fruit; on this very ninth day, a man should perform the festival of Kṛṣṇa.
By performing the marriage ceremony of Tulasī according to the ritual prescribed in one's own Vedic branch, the fruit of giving a maiden in marriage is attained; of this there is no doubt.
Having reached the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, one who has conquered his senses should fashion an auspicious golden image of Hari together with Tulasī.
The observer of the vow should worship there with devotion according to the prescribed rules for three days; thus, in accordance with the stated injunctions, he should perform the marriage rite.

In this very context, the three-night period should be observed starting from the ninth day; the ninth day, when it extends through midday and is joined by the preceding [eighth] day, is to be accepted.
He who protects and maintains both the Dhātrī and Aśvattha trees together does not lose his merit even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Formerly, on the eleventh day, a young girl named Kiśorikā, the daughter of Kanaka, performed with devotion the evening rite for the marriage of Tulasī.
By that [act], Sulocanā was liberated from the blemish of widowhood; therefore, the rite arising from the marriage of Tulasi should be performed every evening.
This must certainly be performed every year by the Vaiṣṇavas; I shall now declare its ritual procedure so that the rite may be complete in all its constituent parts.
One should fashion an auspicious image of Viṣṇu made of gold weighing one pala; or, according to one's capacity, one may prepare it weighing half of that, or even half of that again.

Having performed the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) for both Tulasī and the form of Viṣṇu, one should then awaken the Lord with the hymns and other recitations previously mentioned.
One should worship with the sixteen services and the hymns of Puruṣasūkta; then, having recollected the place and time, one should worship Gaṇeśa there.

Then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should perform the Nāndī-śrāddha; with the sounds of Vedic recitations, musical instruments, and the like, one should bring forth the image of Viṣṇu.
She should be placed near the Tulasī plant, concealed by cloths, [saying]: "Come, O Blessed Lord, O God Keśava; I shall worship you. (16)
"I shall give you the Tulasī; be the granter of all desires. He should offer the Arghya three times, as well as the Pādya and the Viṣṭara.
Then, having recited "Ācamanīyam" three times, one should cause it to be offered; thereafter, curd, ghee, and milk, placed within a vessel made of bell-metal.
"O Vāsudeva, accept this madhuparka; salutations unto you! Having performed all the tasks, including the application of turmeric paste and the anointing with oil," || 19 ||
At the time of *godhūli*, Tulasī and Keśava should again be worshipped; they should be placed separately facing one another, and one should recite auspicious verses.
When the sun is just visible, one should utter the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), having stated one's own lineage (gotra) and ancestral lineages (pravara), as well as the three ancestors and so forth.
O Lord, protector of the three worlds, who are without beginning, middle, or end, accept this Tulasī according to the rites of marriage.
I give to you your beloved, born from the seed of Pārvatī, who resides within the ashes of Vṛndā, and who is without beginning, middle, or end.
"Like a daughter, she has been raised by me with constant care and service; O sir, I give this Tulasī, who is dear to you, to you—please accept her. (24)
Having thus offered the Tulasī, he should thereafter worship those two; at night, he should perform a vigil preceded by the festivities of a wedding.
Then, at the time of dawn, one should worship Tulasī and Viṣṇu after performing the consecration of the fire with the twelve-syllable mantra.

One should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with milk-rice, clarified butter, honey, and sesame seeds; then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, one should subsequently offer the *pūrṇāhuti*. Having duly honored the preceptor (*ācārya*), one should complete the remainder of the fire-sacrifice (*homa*).
Whatever vow has been undertaken for the four months of the rainy season, one should fulfill it accordingly after having explained it to the twice-born, as well as any other [vow]. || 28 ||
"O Lord, O Master Janārdana, this vow has been performed by me for your pleasure; by your grace, may whatever was deficient therein attain completion. (29)
If a person breaks their fast during the fourth quarter of the Revatī asterism when it is conjoined with the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), they shall bring their vow to fruitlessness.

Then, whatever articles have been avoided during the Cāturmāsya or the autumn season, one should offer them to the Brāhmaṇas; thereafter, one may eat all those things that were renounced while established in the vow.
The meal should be eaten here together with the husband and wife, as well as with the twice-born brahmins.
Then, having eaten those fallen leaves of Tulasī that remain after the meal, one is himself liberated from sins.
By eating a stalk of sugarcane, as well as the fruit of the dhātrī and the kola fruit at the end of a meal, one's impurity from that meal is destroyed.
If one has not eaten even one of each of these three, that man should be known as "impure" (ucchiṣṭa) for the duration of a year; there is no doubt about this.
Then, having again performed worship in the evening with beautiful stalks of sugarcane, as well as to Tulasī and Vāsudeva, one becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.

Then, having performed the rite of dismissal and offered the final gifts to Hari, one should say: "O Lord, O Master, go to Vaikuṇṭha accompanied by Tulasī; accepting the worship performed by me, be forever satisfied."
Go, go, O best of gods, to your own abode, O Supreme Lord; go, O Janārdana, to where Brahmā and the other gods reside.

Having thus dismissed the Lord of Devas, one should cause all [the icons], beginning with the primary image (mūrti), to be given to the preceptor; by doing so, the person becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.

He who performs the marriage ceremony with Tulasī every year, being full of devotion, will certainly be endowed with wealth and grain; he shall obtain vast fame both in this world and in the next. (40)

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Marriage of Tulasī on the Kūṣmāṇḍa-Navamī," in the Kārtika-māsa-māhātmya of the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, within the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The Vālakhilyas said: Having bathed properly during the bright fortnight of Kārttika and being fully restrained by his vows, one should undertake the five-day vow on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī).

While the high-souled Bhīṣma lay upon his bed of arrows, he then expounded the duties of kings, the duties of liberation, and the duties of charity; these were heard at that time by the heirs of Pāṇḍu and by Kṛṣṇa as well.
Then, with a delighted mind, Vāsudeva spoke: "O Bhīṣma, you are most blessed; the dharmas have been proclaimed by you."
On the eleventh day of the month of Kārtika, water was requested by you; Arjuna then brought the water of the Gaṅgā with the speed of an arrow.
Your limbs are satisfied; therefore, from this day forward until the end of the full moon, may all the worlds gratify you with the offering of arghya.
Therefore, with every effort, you should perform this vow known as Bhīṣmapañcaka, which brings me complete satisfaction.
Having performed the vow of Kārttika, if one does not perform the Bhīṣmapañcaka, his entire Kārttika vow shall become fruitless.
If a man is unable and lacks the capacity during the month of Kārttika, he shall obtain the fruit of Kārttika by performing the Bhīṣmapañcaka.
To the one of true vows, the pure, the son of Gaṅgā, the great-souled Bhīṣma, who has been a celibate since birth—to him I offer this water of honor (arghya).
With this mantra, using the left hand, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for all castes.
Because it is an ancillary part of the vow, the Pāpapūruṣa [effigy] must be offered on the full moon day; the Bhīṣmapañcaka must be performed in every way by one who is childless.
He who, together with his wife, observes the Bhīṣmapañcaka vow for the sake of a son, shall obtain a son within the year after offering the Pāpapuruṣa.
Therefore, the Pañcaka of Bhīṣma must certainly be performed; I have described the Pañcaka of Bhīṣma as that which brings pleasure to Viṣṇu.
Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, to the specific details regarding Bhīṣmapañcaka, which was formerly explained in full detail by Rudra to Kārttikeya.
Īśvara said: O best among those who observe vows, I shall proclaim this highly meritorious vow, since it was from Bhīṣma that this five-day vow was obtained.
From the presence of Vāsudeva, the Bhīṣmapañcaka was spoken by him; who, other than Keśava, is capable of describing the virtues of this vow?
Now listen to the ancient dharma of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, which was practiced by Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Garga, and others during the Kṛta Yuga and other ages. (17)
In the Tretā Yuga and other ages, it was practiced by Ambarīṣa through enjoyments and other means, while by Brahmins it was practiced through celibacy, recitation, fire-offerings, and ritual acts.
This is likewise for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas who are devoted to truth and purity; it is difficult for those devoid of truth and impossible for those of childish minds. (19)
"O best of Brahmins, they say that what Bhīṣma does is difficult and cannot be accomplished by ordinary men; therefore, because he performs it, everything becomes accomplished. (20)
This vow is of great merit and is the destroyer of great sins; therefore, the Bhīṣmapañcaka should be performed by men with diligent effort. (21)
Having bathed according to the proper ritual procedure during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should undertake the five-day vow on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī).
Having bathed especially in the morning and likewise at midday, the observer of the vow should apply cow dung while in a river or at the waters of a mountain spring.
Having bathed, observed silence, and put on washed garments, a man of firm vows should properly satisfy the ancestors in due order with barley, rice, and sesame seeds.
One should diligently offer water libations and the respectful *arghya* offering to Bhīṣma; worship of Bhīṣma must be performed, and one should zealously bestow gifts.
Having diligently offered the five jewels especially to a Brahmin, one should also always worship the Lord Vāsudeva together with Lakṣmī.
Having worshipped the Pañcaka, one is satisfied for ten million births. || 27 ||
Whatever a mortal gives, even if it consists of the five elements, he obtains the entire fruit of the vows performed throughout the year.
Having performed the offering of water and likewise the presentation of the *arghya*, the man who acts with this mantra shall become a partaker of liberation. (29)
Water is offered for Bhīṣma, who belongs to the Vaiyāghrapāda lineage, whose ancestral sages (pravaras) are the Sāṅkṛtyas, who is childless, and whose armor was Bhīṣmavarmā.
For the sake of the descent of the Vasus, and for the son of Śantanu, I offer this water of honor (arghya) to Bhīṣma, who has observed celibacy since birth.
This is the mantra for the arghya offering. Whoever completes the five-day rite according to this procedure obtains merit equal to that of a horse sacrifice; of this there is no doubt. || 32 ||
For five days, one must also diligently observe the prescribed restraints; for in this matter, O lady of excellent complexion, nothing can be accomplished without such restraint.
Hari bestowed [the boon] upon Bhīṣma, who was deprived of the northern solstice; being well-pleased, he granted him a pure lagna even though it was devoid of the northern solstice.
Then one should worship Lord Hari, the remover of all sins; immediately thereafter, the Bhīṣmapañcaka vow must be performed with diligence.
One should bathe [the deity] with devotion using water, honey, milk, and ghee, as well as with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and water scented with sandalwood.
One should smear Keśava, whose banner is Garuḍa, with fragrant sandalwood, saffron, and camphor mixed with uśīra.
One should worship with beautiful flowers accompanied by perfumes and incense; the devoted one should offer guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter to Kṛṣṇa.
One should offer a lamp for five days, both by day and by night; one should present the divine food of the God of gods, which is supreme rice-pudding (paramānna).
Having thus worshipped the God, and having recollected Him and bowed down, one should mutter the mantra "Oṃ namo vāsudevāya" one hundred and eight times.
And one should perform oblations with sesame, rice, barley, and other grains smeared with clarified butter, using the six-syllable mantra accompanied by the utterance of "svāhā."
Having performed the evening twilight devotion (saṃdhyā), having prostrated before the one whose banner is Garuḍa, and having recited the mantra as before, he should always sleep upon the ground.
