This entire procedure should be performed for five days; however, there is a specific distinction in this vow—listen now to that which is not otherwise deficient.
On the first day, the observer of the vow should worship the feet of Hari with lotuses; on the second day, he should worship the region of the knees with bilva leaves.
Then, with his mind fixed on Him, he should worship the head of the wielder of the discus with *mālatī* flowers out of devotion to the God of gods on the full moon day of Kārttika.
Having briefly worshipped that Hṛṣīkeśa on the eleventh day, and having properly consumed cow-dung on the eleventh day, one should observe the fast.
On the twelfth day, the observer of the vow should consume cow urine with the recitation of mantras upon the ground; on the thirteenth day, milk; and likewise on the fourteenth day, curd.

Having consumed [the medicine] for the sake of bodily purification and having fasted for four days, on the fifth day he should bathe, worship Keśava according to the rules, feed the Brāhmaṇas with devotion, and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Having abandoned an evil mind, the wise man, through the practice of celibacy, should renounce liquor, meat, and sexual intercourse, which is the cause of sin. 49.
A man devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa with vegetables and the food of sages should thereafter eat at night, preceded by the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Thus, having performed it correctly, one shall obtain the fruit as described. || 51 ||
He who is a drinker of intoxicants and drinks them from birth until the end of life—by performing this Bhīṣma-vrata, he attains the supreme state. || 52 ||
Women should perform that which increases dharma at the command of their husbands; and widows should perform it for the sake of greatly increasing the happiness of liberation. 53.

In ancient times in Ayodhyā, there was a certain king named Atithi; having performed this very difficult vow at the word of Vasiṣṭha, he enjoyed all pleasures here on earth and in the end went to the city of Viṣṇu.

In this manner, one intent on the vow should constantly perform the five-day rite known as Bhīṣmapañcaka, according to the rule of fasting, or by consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), or by subsisting on milk, roots, fruits, or sacrificial food (haviṣya).
When the full moon day arrives, having performed worship as before, one should devoutly feed the Brāhmaṇas and give a cow along with its calf.

That which is celebrated on earth as the Bhīṣmapañcaka, lasting from the eleventh to the fifteenth [lunar day], is declared to be for one who abstains from eating; Viṣṇu bestows auspicious fruit upon that person who observes the prohibition of food during this vow. (57)

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Bhīṣmapañcaka Vow," in the Kārttikamāsa-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: O Brahmin, it is heard that for all vows there is a concluding rite (udyāpana); in the absence of this concluding rite, one shall never obtain the fruit [of the vow].
A wise person should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) for the sake of attaining the fruit of the vow performed; otherwise, even the most excellent vow that was undertaken becomes fruitless.
O Lord, even if this most excellent of vows is performed during the month of Kārtika, one shall not obtain the fruit prescribed for the vow in the absence of its formal conclusion (udyāpana).
Therefore, O Lord, tell me—the best of disciples, who have sought refuge in you and follow your path—the procedure for the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the month of Kārttika.

Brahmā said: Now I shall describe the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the month of Kārttika, which destroys all sins; listen to that, together with its ritual procedure, in brief and with great devotion. || 5 ||

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Ūrja, the observer of the vow should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) for the sake of completing the vow and as a means to please Viṣṇu.
Above the Tulasī plant, one should construct an auspicious pavilion, adorned with plantain pillars and variegated with various precious minerals.
A beautiful garland of lamps should be arranged there in the four directions; the four gates should be adorned with fine archways and decorated with flowers and chowries.
And at the doors, one should worship the door-keepers individually, made of clay: Jaya and Vijaya, as well as Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍaka.
Nanda, Sunanda, Kumuda, and Kumudākṣaka—one should worship these at the four gates, endowed with devotion. (10)
In the vicinity of the base of the Tulasī plant, one should properly decorate a mandala known as Sarvatobhadra, richly adorned with four colors.
Above that, one should place a jar filled with precious gems; there, one should worship the God who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
One should worship [the deity] clad in yellow silk garments and endowed with splendor; furthermore, the observer of the vow should worship Indra and the other world-protectors within the pavilion.
On that day, one should fast with devotion, being tranquil and with a mind bowed in reverence; at night, one should keep a vigil with auspicious songs, instrumental music, and other such offerings.
Those who sing with devotion during the vigil for the Wielder of the Discus (Cakrapāṇi) are liberated from the accumulation of sins produced over hundreds of previous births. || 15 ||
Then, on the full moon day, he should invite thirty excellent brahmins along with their wives, or else a single brahmin.
Then, having performed the morning bath as well as the worship of the deity, he should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and establish the sacred fire there.
With the mantra "ato devā," one should offer sesame seeds and milk-rice (pāyasa) for the sake of pleasing the God of gods and each of the deities individually. (18)
Then, having completed the remainder of the *homa* and having honored the Brahmins with devotion, a man should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins according to his capacity. (19)
Then, the observer of the vow should worship a tawny cow there according to the prescribed rite; likewise, he should give that cow, together with her calf, to a Brahmin who maintains a household.
Having honored the guru, the instructor of the vow, along with his wife, with garments, ornaments, and decorations, he should ask those brahmins for forgiveness.
"O Lord of Gods, by your grace, may he be forever pleased with me; and whatever sin has been committed by me throughout seven births, may it be destroyed through this vow. (22)
May all that [evil] go to destruction, may my lineage be stable, may my desires bear fruit, and may there be devotion to Hari. (23)
"May there be association with the virtuous in birth after birth for me. Having thus asked for forgiveness from those brahmins and having propitiated them, he should dismiss them. (24)
O best of sages, one should give that image of the Guru, together with its garment; thereafter, the devoted person, joined by friends and the Guru, should eat himself.
He awakens on the twelfth day; on the thirteenth, he is joined by the gods; and on the fourteenth, he is seen and worshipped. Therefore, he is to be honored here on that lunar day.
One should worship the Lord of the gods made of gold with the permission of the guru; for on this full moon day, there shall be the great festival procession of Puṣkara.
Since Viṣṇu assumed the form of a fish after granting boons, whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, or chanted on that day shall yield inexhaustible fruit. (28)
O Nārada, this is indeed the rite to be performed in the month of Kārtika; for that man who duly observes the vow of Kārtika in this manner, [attains the supreme goal]. (29)
Whatever fruit one obtains by performing the vow in the month of Kārtika, those who do so are blessed, they are always worthy of honor, and their success is indeed fruitful.
Those who are devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu and observe vows during the month of Kārtika—the sins residing within their bodies dissolve at that very moment.
"Where shall we go today, O Lady, since this man has performed the Ūrjavrata?"—thus do all the sins cry out here again and again. (32)
Therefore, there exists nothing equal to the month of Kārttika; it is said to be like fire for the burning away of all sins. (33)
The man who, endowed with faith, either listens to or causes others to hear this greatness of the *ūrjodyāpana* shall attain union (*sāyujya*) with Viṣṇu.

Nārada said: How may one who is unable to perform the conclusion of the vow during the month of Kārttika attain perfection? How is a living being liberated from the ocean of worldly existence, which is full of suffering? (35)
Brahmā said: A pure man who listens to the greatness of Kārttika with self-restraint shall obtain the fruit of the concluding rite (udyāpana) and dwell in the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Conclusion of the Vow," in the *Kārttikamāsa-māhātmya* (The Greatness of the Month of Kārttika) within the second section, the *Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*, of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Brahmā said: I shall tell you the majesty of the fourteenth lunar day known as Vaikuṇṭha-caturdaśī; listen to that which was previously proclaimed by the Vālakhilyas in brief.
The Vālakhilyas said: On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha arrived at Vārāṇasī from Vaikuṇṭha during the Kṛta Yuga.
When one-fourth of the night remained, he bathed at Maṇikarṇikā, took a thousand golden lotuses, and then departed.
With exceeding devotion, having performed the Vaiśveśvarī worship, he then worshipped Śiva together with Śivā using lotuses.
Having first performed the rite a thousand times under a single name, he thereafter began his worship; Śiva observed his devotion to him.
One lotus was seized by Hara, having hidden it from the midst of the lotuses; thereafter, Viṣṇu offered worship, but there remained only one lotus less.
He looked here and there, but nowhere was a lotus to be found; "Is this a delusion regarding the lotuses, or is it a delusion regarding my own names? (7)
Having reflected for a moment, that Hari said, "There was no confusion regarding my name; however, a confusion arose concerning Padma. Thus he reflected again and again.
"I have made the resolve for a thousand lotuses for the purpose of worship; O Mahādeva, how can I worship you with one fewer lotus? (9)
"If I go to bring him, there will be a breaking of my seat; what should be done after this? Thus, Hari was then agitated with anxiety.
O lords of sages, one form arose in his heart; O lords of sages, they call me "Puṇḍarīkākṣa" (the Lotus-eyed One). || 11 ||
"My eye is like a lotus; I shall offer it for the sake of the lotus," having thus resolved in his mind, he gave up his index finger.
Having plucked that [eye] from the middle of his eye, Mahādeva was worshipped; thereupon Maheśvara, being pleased, spoke these words.

Mahādeva said: "There is no devotee of mine equal to you in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile. The sovereignty of the three worlds is granted to you; become the protector of the world."
"Choose another boon, may you be blessed, whatever is desired by your mind; I shall certainly grant it—there is no need for hesitation in this matter. (15)
But those men who, having taken recourse to devotion to me, hate Janārdana, are haters of me; O Viṣṇu, they shall certainly go to hell.
Viṣṇu said: "O Maheśvara, the protection of the three worlds has been commanded to me; yet how am I to slay the Daityas, who are difficult to subdue and possess great strength? (17)
Śiva said: "O Lord Viṣṇu, accept this Sudarśana discus, the destroyer of great daityas, which has been offered by me to you. (18)
"O Blessed One, perform the slaughter of all the Daityas with this. Having thus given the discus to Hari, he then spoke these words. (19)
Śiva said: In the year known as Hemalamba, in the glorious month of Kārttika, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, at the time of sunrise—|| 20 ||
On the day of Mahādeva, during the Brāhma-muhūrta, having bathed at Maṇikarṇikā, he worshipped the Vaiśveśvara Liṅga, which had come from Vaikuṇṭha.
Therefore, my beloved shall become renowned in all the worlds as the fourteenth lunar day named Vaikuṇṭha, [honored] with thousands of lotuses.
"I grant you another boon; listen to my words, O Viṣṇu: worship must be performed for you by all castes during the early hours of the night. (23)
One should observe the fast during the day and perform your worship in the evening; thereafter, my worship must be performed, otherwise it shall be fruitless. (24)
For the worship of Hari, the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) that extends throughout the night is to be accepted; one should perform the worship of Śiva at the time of dawn.
Those men by whom Viṣṇu was first worshipped with thousands of lotuses, and Śiva was worshipped afterwards, are indeed liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Having bathed in the Pañcanada in the evening, one should worship Bindumādhava; or, having bathed in Viṣṇukāñcī, one should worship Anantasena.
Then, having bathed at Rudrakāñcī, one should worship Praṇaveśa; first, having bathed at Vahnitīrtha, one should thereafter worship Nārāyaṇa.
Then, having bathed at Retodaka, one should worship Kedāreśa; first having bathed in the Sūryaputrī, one should worship Veṇīmādhava.
Then, having bathed in the Jāhnavī, one should worship Saṅgameśa; all forms of prosperity shall be under his control—this truth has been spoken by me, O Viṣṇu.
Having thus granted him boons, Śiva vanished; therefore, both Hari and Hara should be worshipped with every effort.
In the Kali age, Viṣṇu abandons the earth for ten thousand years; half of that time [is spent by] the waters of the Gaṅgā, and half of that [by] the village deities.
On the full moon day of the month of Kārttika, one should perform the Tripura festival; a lamp must certainly be offered in the temple of Śiva during the evening.
A lord of the Daityas named Tripura performed austerities at Prayāga; Brahmā, being well-pleased by his penance, granted him a supreme boon.
"Death shall not come to you from gods, asuras, or humans. Having thus obtained this boon, the Daitya [entered] that which was fashioned by Viśvakarman.
When he, having ascended that celestial chariot called Tripura, began to oppress the three worlds, Hara was then praised by the gods.
The slayer of enemies destroyed Tripura with a single arrow; on the full moon day of Kārttika, all the gods offered him praise.
On that day, lamps were offered by all the gods to Hara; indeed, lamps should be offered in every way for the satisfaction of Hara.
Twenty-seven hundred wicks together constitute a lamp; one who offers a lamp on the full moon day is liberated from all sins. (39)
On the full moon day, at twilight, the festival of Tripura should be performed; one should offer lamps in the temple with this mantra.
May insects, moths, mosquitoes, trees, and whatever living beings move in water or on land, upon seeing this lamp, never again be subject to birth; and may even outcastes always become Brahmins. (41)

Therefore, a great festival should be held for Tripurā on the full moon day; and he who should behold the Lord on the Kārttika full moon when it is conjoined with the Kṛttikā nakṣatra [attains the highest goal]. (42)

By performing the rite of releasing a bull here, one shall become a Brahmin for seven births, wealthy and a master of the Vedas; furthermore, by eating only at night, one shall go to the city of Śiva.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Vaikuṇṭha-Caturdaśī and Tripurī-Pūrṇimā Vows," in the Kārtika-Māsa-Māhātmya of the Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa, within the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 35 ||
Brahmā said: O best of Brahmins, those three auspicious lunar days at the end of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārtika, ending with the full moon, bring forth blessings.
The designation "Antipuṣkariṇī" brings about the destruction of all sins for one who indeed performs a complete ritual bath during the month of Kārttika.
On these lunar days, one obtains the full fruit from bathing; for on the thirteenth day, all the Vedas go there and indeed purify living beings.
On the fourteenth day, the gods together with their sacrifices indeed purify living beings; on the full moon day, the excellent holy places are established by Viṣṇu.
Indeed, those who bathe with warm water during the three days beginning with the full moon of Kārttika purify even all beings, including those who have slain a Brāhmaṇa or drunk liquor.
One who is unable to observe the vow for the entire month goes to the Raurava hell for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras; such a person should perform it during these three days.
Having obtained the full fruit of that, the man who indeed honors the gods, the ancestors, Viṣṇu, and his guru rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu.
If a householder does not truly perform his ablutions and other rites for three days while feeding his family, he will certainly go to hell.
Having delivered all his ancestors, he goes to the supreme state; so too does he who performs the recitation of the Gītā during the final three days.
He who recites the Thousand Names for three days undoubtedly attains the fruit of performing horse-sacrifices day after day. (10)
He is never stained by sins anywhere, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water; some men attain divinity, while others attain the state of a siddha.
Who on earth or in heaven is capable of describing the fruit of the merit of one who indeed listens to the Bhāgavata scripture for three days? (12)
By some, the state of Brahman is attained through three days of practice; or liberation is achieved through the knowledge of Brahman, or by dying at Prayāga.
Alternatively, by practicing for three days in the month of Kārttika, he who performs the worship of Hari during those three days in Kārttika— || 14 ||
O best of Brahmins, there is no returning for him even after hundreds of millions of kalpas, during the final three days of every month in the month of Kārttika.
O sinless one, even there, a particular excellence of merit exists on the full moon day; having risen at dawn, one should perform purification, bathing, and other such rites.
Having completed all his duties, one who is devoted to Viṣṇu should perform the worship of Viṣṇu on the full moon day of Kārttika, either in a garden or even at home.
There one should construct a pavilion adorned with plantain pillars, draped with mango sprouts, and beautifully decorated with stalks of sugarcane.
Having well-adorned [the deity] with variegated garments, one should worship the God there; one should worship Hari with mango sprouts, flowers, fruits, and other offerings.
A pure man, observing the rules of restraint, should listen to the greatness of Ūrja in its entirety, or even a single chapter, or even a single verse.
Or one should listen to this meritorious story for even a single moment day after day; however, if a person should be unable to listen every single day, [he should listen at least once]. (21)
Or if one should listen to it during a meritorious month or on a meritorious lunar day, by the power of that merit, a person shall be liberated from sin.
One who knows the Purāṇas, who is pure, skillful, tranquil, free from envy, virtuous, compassionate, eloquent, and wise, should narrate the meritorious story. (23)
When one who recites the Purāṇas has ascended the seat of Vyāsa, he shall not bow down to anyone until the completion of the discourse.
A wise person should not recount sacred stories in a place crowded with wicked people, nor in a region overrun by Śūdras who are like beasts of prey, nor in a gambling house. (25)
Those who are endowed with faith and devotion, who have no longing for other activities, who are restrained in speech, pure, and skillful—such listeners partake in merit. (26)
Those lowest of men who listen to this meritorious narrative without devotion have no fruit of merit; they shall experience suffering birth after birth. (27)
And at the end of the month, one devoted to worship should honor the Paurāṇika with perfumes, garlands, garments, ornaments, and wealth.
And those who listen to the story with devotion are neither poor nor sinful. (29)
When this narrative is being recited, those men who depart for elsewhere will find their wives and their wealth destroyed midway through their enjoyments.
A man seated upon a high seat should not bow down; likewise, he may become a poisonous tree or a python in the forest while sleeping. (31)
Those men who create obstacles while this narrative is being recited, having suffered in hells for ten million years, become village pigs.
Those people who cause others to hear this auspicious ancient narrative shall remain in the abode of Brahmā for more than a hundred crores of kalpas.
Those men who give a seat for the sake of one who knows the Purāṇas—whether it be a woolen blanket, a deerskin, a garment, a couch, or even a wooden plank—[attain great merit].
Those men who provide garments for wearing and offer ornaments and the like shall dwell in the abode of Brahmā.

When the reciter is fully satisfied, all the deities become satisfied. Therefore, a person endowed with devotion and faith should gratify him with devotion; for him, the fruit of merit becomes complete—of this there is no doubt. (36)
Whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices and whatever fruit is found in all acts of giving—that fruit a man obtains by listening to a Purāṇa even once.

In the Kali age, especially, there is no higher dharma for men than listening to the Purāṇas, nor is there any other path to liberation; indeed, there is nothing superior to the hearing of the Purāṇas and the chanting of the names of Viṣṇu.
Whoever should hear or even cause others to hear this greatness of Ūrja shall obtain the fruit of going to Badarī, the king of sacred fords. || 39 ||
It removes all diseases, destroys all sins, and is auspicious. || 40 ||
And having heard this in a single word, one who is indeed devoted to approaching those who should not be approached shall liberate both the seller of his daughter and his sister. (41)
Having heard this greatness, whoever honors the reciter with cows, land, gold, and garments is indeed equal to Viṣṇu. (42)

One who desires merit should give a manuscript of the Dharmaśāstra, the Purāṇas, or the Vedic sciences and so forth, specifically to a reciter. For those who bestow the knowledge of the Purāṇas enjoy infinite rewards. || 43 ||
Whoever recites this with devotion, or having heard it, retains it in mind, is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. || 44 ||
This must not be told to anyone who lacks faith or is of evil mind.

Having failed to honor the teacher—who proclaims the Dharma—with the foremost understanding and single-minded devotion, one who nevertheless enjoys pleasures will thereafter experience suffering in the hells and in other future births.
Therefore, one should worship with devotion the Guru who awakens one to the ultimate reality. O sinless one, I have told you but a mere fraction of this greatness.
Indeed, it cannot be told in its entirety even in hundreds of years; for in the past, on the peak of Kailāsa, Śiva spoke it to Pārvatī. (48)
Even after speaking of the greatness of Kārttika for as long as a hundred years, he did not reach its end; being unable to continue, he desisted.

One desiring a son, one desiring wealth, and one desiring a kingdom shall obtain their respective fruits; what need is there for much speaking on this matter? One desiring liberation shall attain liberation. (50)
Sūta said: Thus addressed by Brahmā, Nārada, overflowing with love, bowed down again and again and departed as a wandering sage at his own will.
This was also spoken by Śaṅkara to his son out of a desire for his welfare; having heard those words of his father, the six-faced one was filled with joy.
Kṛṣṇa recounted the majesty of Kārttika to Satyabhāmā; delighted by this, Satyā then performed the vow.
Having heard this supreme majesty from the Vālakhilya sages, the ṛṣis became devoted to the vow of the month of Kārttika; therefore, Kārttika is exceedingly dear to them.
Having studied all the scriptures, this auspicious treatise—which brings pleasure to Viṣṇu—is like the extracted essence of milk; there is no scripture equal to it.
Vyāsa said: Having thus spoken to all those sages, Sūta, the most excellent knower of dharma, then became silent; and they, in turn, then performed worship for him.
Then those supreme ṛṣis, having returned to their own hermitages, were filled with joy and performed the auspicious vow exactly as they had been instructed by Sūta.
Those who indeed perform the Kārttika vow according to this method, being liberated from all sins, go to the abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Hearing the Purāṇas, Preceded by the Narration of the Greatness of the Last Three Days Known as Puṣkariṇī," in the Kārtika-māsa-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: I bow to Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, who brings joy to the world, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, Mādhava, who is affectionate toward his devotees. || 1 ||
Then, having paid homage to the God of gods, the Lord of Ramā, who was seated comfortably on Śvetadvīpa, the four-faced one questioned his father.
Brahmā said: O Hṛṣīkeśa, sustainer of the world, whose hearing and chanting are meritorious; O Lord of gods, omniscient one, Lord of all, please speak on that which has been asked.
"Among months, I am Mārgaśīrṣa," you said previously. I wish to know the greatness of that month according to its true essence. || 4 ||
Who is the deity there, what is the gift, how is the bath performed, and what is the ritual procedure? What should be done by men there, and what should be eaten, O Lord of Ramā? (5)
O Acyuta, please tell me everything regarding what should be said—such as worship, meditation, mantras, and so forth—and whatever ritual action is performed therein.

The Blessed Lord said: Well asked by you, O Brahmin, who brings benefit to all the worlds! By performing which [act], all [other] rites such as sacrifices (iṣṭa) and charitable works (pūrta) become accomplished.
O son, whatever merit is found in all sacrifices and whatever fruit is found in all sacred fords—that fruit one attains when [this rite] is performed in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
O son, the fruit that a man obtains through gifts such as the tulāpuruṣa and others is indeed attained by listening to this greatness.
Neither by sacrifices, Vedic study, charity, and the like, nor by bathing in all the sacred fords, nor by renunciation and yoga, did I become subject to the control of men. (10)

Through bathing, giving, worship, meditation, silence, recitation, and so forth, one becomes submissive [to the deity] in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa as it is not in other months; thus has the secret been declared. (11)
The month of Mārgaśīrṣa was concealed by others through various means such as religious duties (dharma), for the gods dwelling in heaven considered it to be the cause of my attainment.
Whoever among those of meritorious deeds are devoted to me, for them the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, which removes my [worldly] intoxication, must certainly be observed.
Those men who do not observe the Mārgaśīrṣa [vow] on the field of battle at Bhārata are to be known as embodiments of sin, deluded by the Kali age. || 14 ||
O dear one, whatever fruit a man obtains during all eight months, that same fruit is attained in the month of Māgha when the sun is situated in Capricorn.
A hundredfold more merit than that of Māgha is obtained in the month of Vaiśākha; a thousandfold more than that is obtained when the sun is situated in Libra (Tulā).
Therefore, when the sun is situated in Scorpio, the merit is ten million times greater; for this reason, the month of Mārgaśīrṣa is superior and is always dear to me.
O son, that mortal who rises at dawn and performs his bath according to the prescribed rules—to him, being pleased, I grant even my own self.
In this regard, they also cite this narrative; listen to it, my son. There was indeed a great-souled one known as Nandagopa who existed upon the earth. (19)
O sinless one, in that beautiful Gokula, there were thousands of cowherd girls whose hearts had long been attached to my form. (20)
I bestowed upon them the wisdom regarding the immersion in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa; thereafter, they performed their bath at dawn according to the prescribed rites.
Worship was performed, sacrificial food was eaten, and salutations were offered by them; O sinless one, I was pleased because of this ritual being thus accomplished.
"Indeed, a boon was granted by me, being well-pleased, to those women; therefore, men should observe the month of Mārgaśīrṣa according to the prescribed rites. (23)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Fruits of the Mārgaśīrṣa Bath Performed by the Gopīs," in the *Mārgaśīrṣa-māhātmya* within the dialogue between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, in the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Brahmā said: You have described the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, which removes pride, as being joined with a specific rite; O Lord of Gods, O Keśava, tell me everything regarding that rite.
The Blessed Lord said: Having risen at the end of the night and performed ritual ablutions according to the rules, one should respectfully bow to one's own guru and, remaining alert, remember me.
Having duly discharged urine and feces outside the village, one should, being pure and restrained in speech, recite the thousand names with devotion.
Having performed purification according to the rule, sipped water while restrained and pure, and having first cleansed his teeth, he should perform his bath according to the prescribed rite.
O high-minded one, having taken the earth from the root of a *tulasī* plant together with its leaves, and having consecrated it with the root mantra or the *gāyatrī*, || 5 ||

With his limbs anointed by the mantra itself, he should bathe in the waters while reciting the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn; bathing is prescribed to be performed with either water drawn up from a source or water left undrawn.
The wise knower of mantras should prepare the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) with this mantra; "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya" is declared to be the root mantra.

With darbha grass in hand, having sipped water according to the rule and being pure before him, the wise man, having prepared a square area measuring four cubits on all sides, should invoke Gaṅgā with these mantras: ||| 8 ||
You are born from the foot of Viṣṇu, you belong to Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu is your deity; protect us from this sin that begins at birth and ends with death.
"Three and a half crores of sacred fords," Vāyu said, "O Jāhnavī, they are all yours, existing in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space."
Your name among the gods is Nandinī and also Nalinī; you are the daughter of Dakṣa, the bird Vihagā, and Viśvagā, as is held by the yogins.
Vidyādharī, Suprasannā, as well as Lokaprasādinī, Kṣemā, Jāhnavī, Śāntā, and Śāntipradāyinī. || 12 ||
One should always recite these names of merit at the time of bathing; there, the Ganges that flows through the three paths is ever present.

Having joined the hollowed palms together with [the mantra] recited seven times, and having placed them upon the head with hands folded in reverence, one should perform the bath with earth three, four, five, or seven times, after likewise addressing it according to the prescribed rule.
O Earth, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, and trodden by Viṣṇu; O Clay, take away my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me. (15)
You were uplifted by the boar Kṛṣṇa, who possesses a hundred arms; salutations to you, O source and womb of all beings, O lady of excellent vows! 16.
Having bathed in this manner, and thereafter having sipped water according to the prescribed rule, one should rise and put on two white garments on the bank.

Having sipped water (ācamana), he should offer libations to the gods, the ancestors, and likewise to the sages; then, having wrung out his garment and sipped water again, he should be wrapped in a clean, washed cloth.

O best of the twice-born, having taken beautiful, pure clay and consecrated it with the mantra, the Vaiṣṇava should then unweariedly apply the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the forehead and other parts according to the prescribed number.
A Brāhmaṇa should always bear twelve Puṇḍras; O son, four Puṇḍras are prescribed for Kṣatriyas and two for Vaiśyas; one Puṇḍra is ordained for women and for Śūdras. (20)

O sinless one, twelve *tilaka* marks are always prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa: on the forehead, the belly, the chest, the hollow of the throat, the two sides of the abdomen, the two arms, the two ears, the back, the sacrum, and the head. (21)
A Kṣatriya should wear the marks on the forehead, the heart, and the arms; a Vaiśya on the forehead and the heart; and for Śūdras and women, on the forehead alone.
One should meditate on Keśava at the forehead, Nārāyaṇa on the abdomen, Mādhava on the chest, and Govinda on the hollow of the throat.
And Viṣṇu in the right side of the belly, Madhusūdana in the arm, Trivikrama at the root of the ear, and Vāmana on the left side.
One should place Śrīdhara on the left arm and Hṛṣīkeśa on the ear; Padmanābha should be on the back, and one should assign Dāmodara to the sacrum.
With the water used for that washing, one should place Vāsudeva upon the head; such is the rite for a Brāhmaṇa, and one should understand it to be the same for a Kṣatriya.
One should meditate on Keśava at the forehead and likewise on Mādhava at the heart; and on both arms, O dear one, one should indeed remember Madhusūdana.
The rule for the Kṣatriya has been declared; now listen to the duty of the Vaiśya. He should meditate on Keśava on his forehead and likewise on Mādhava in his heart.
A woman and a Śūdra should likewise remember Keśava on the forehead; by this method, one should apply the sectarian marks (puṇḍra) for my satisfaction.
The dark [color] is said to bring peace; likewise, the red brings subjugation. They say the yellow brings prosperity, while the auspicious white brings liberation. (30)
The single-minded and highly fortunate ones, devoted to the welfare of all the world, apply the *puṇḍra* in the shape of Hari’s foot, including the space between the toes.
Indeed, this temple of Hari is provided with a central aperture; it is lofty, gentle, straight, subtle, well-proportioned, and most enchanting.
That lowest of the twice-born who makes an upward sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) without an intervening space indeed excludes me, who reside there together with Lakṣmī.
Those lowest of the twice-born who apply an unbroken *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* have, without a doubt, placed the paw of a dog upon their foreheads.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining the same world as Hari, a Brāhmaṇa should always wear a large *puṇḍra* marked with a gap and endowed with auspiciousness. (35)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for Wearing the Tripuṇḍra," in the *Mārgaśīrṣa-māhātmya* within the dialogue between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, in the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Brahmā said: O Keśava, tell me how many kinds of *puṇḍra* marks should be made; a great curiosity has arisen in me regarding the hearing of [the rules for] these *puṇḍras*.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, my son, I shall explain; the *puṇḍra* is remembered as being of three kinds: together with the clay of the *tulasī* plant and with the sacred *gopīcandana*.

The wise should apply the *puṇḍra* mark there using yellow sandalwood paste; moreover, the devoted practitioner, having taken the clay from the root of the sacred *tulasī* of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, should wear the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* marks, for Hari is pleased by that.
Learn from me as I speak the greatness of Gopīcandana.

That man who, taking clay originating from Dvāravatī in his hand, constantly applies the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) upon the surface of his forehead, the fruit of his ritual action shall then become ten millionfold.

Even if one is devoid of ritual action, devoid of mantra, devoid of faith, or deprived of the proper time, if one applies Gopīcandana upon the forehead, one always attains the imperishable fruit of that rite.

If a twice-born man always wears a beautiful mark made of Gopīcandana on his forehead—day and night, every day, at all times—he obtains that merit which is gained at Kurujāṅgala during a solar eclipse, as well as at Prayāga in the month of Māgha; moreover, he dwells in my abode like a god.
O Four-faced One, in whatever house a person dwells who wears gopīcandana upon his forehead with devotion, there I always reside, accompanied by Śrī and having slain Kaṃsa.

Whoever would constantly wear upon their forehead the sacred earth originating from Dvāravatī—which removes the impurities of the Kali age—conjoined with my mantra, shall not behold Yama, even if burdened by sins.

O son, at the time of death, if one who has killed a cow or a child, or even a Brahmin, should have Gopīcandana on his arms, forehead, heart, and head, he shall go to my world, the realm of the Lord of Kamalā. || 10 ||
The planets do not afflict him, nor the hosts of rākṣasas, yakṣas, piśācas, uragas, or the leaders of bhūtas—O son, he on whose forehead-paṭṭa my gopī-candana remains by my power.
He on whose forehead a straight and gentle vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is seen—even if he is a Caṇḍāla, he is a pure soul and is certainly worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt.
He who performs religious rites while not having bathed, being impure and joined with sin, becomes purified at that very moment through contact with Gopīcandana.
Whether he be impure or of improper conduct, even if he should commit a great sin, a man marked with the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* shall always remain pure.

O Four-faced One, for my pleasure, for the sake of auspiciousness, or for protection, my devotee, being composed, should always wear the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*—which destroys worldly existence—during my worship and fire-offerings (*homa*) both morning and evening. (15)
If a mortal wearing the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) dies anywhere, even if he be a dog-eater (outcaste), he is honored in my world, seated upon a celestial chariot.
Whenever a mortal who wears the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) eats the food of another, I then deliver twenty generations of his family from hell.
O highly fortunate one, he who, having looked into a mirror or even in water, diligently applies the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), attains the supreme goal.
The ring finger is said to bestow peace, the middle finger becomes the granter of long life; the thumb is declared to grant nourishment, and the index finger is the giver of liberation. (19)
Whoever gives a piece of Gopīcandana to a Vaiṣṇava, by him one hundred and eight generations of his lineage are indeed delivered.
Sacrifice, charity, austerity, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors—all these become fruitless if they are devoid of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra). 21.
I do not look upon that face of men which is devoid of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark; for it is indeed like a cremation ground. (22)

One should apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and wear the symbols of the Fish, the Tortoise, and others; for the sake of Viṣṇu’s grace, one should perform that which is exceedingly dear to Mahāviṣṇu.
Furthermore, in the Kali age, whatever man takes the clay originating from my city and bears the marks marked with the Fish and the Tortoise, [he attains the fruit]. || 24 ||
"Know, O best of the gods, that I have entered his body; there is no distinction between him and me, and one who desires his own welfare must not do anything to harm him. (25)
He in whose body my signs of incarnation are seen—though he be a mortal, he is not to be known as a mere mortal; he is surely my own body.
For that embodied being, even evil arises in the form of good deeds; for in the Kali age, my weapons are seen depicted in paintings. (27)
In whomever one is marked by both of these signs—the fish-seal and the tortoise-seal—my own splendor is infused into that person's body.

One who has the conch, the lotus, the mace, the discus, the fish, and the tortoise fashioned upon one's own body constantly effects the increase of merit and the destruction of sins accumulated over hundreds of births. (29)
What can Yama do to him whose body is eternally marked by the weapons of Nārāyaṇa, even if he has committed ten million sins? (30)
Whatever fruit is said to be obtained by one dwelling for ten million births at Śaṅkhoddhāra, that fruit one obtains daily by bearing the mark of Śaṅkha on the right arm.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed at Puṣkara from the sight of the Lotus-Eyed One, that same fruit is multiplied ten-millionfold when a lotus is placed upon a conch shell. || 32 ||
In the Kali age, Gadādhara bestows daily the merit of Gayā upon that person in whose left arm a mace is seen depicted. || 33 ||
Whatever was proclaimed regarding the fruit of seeing the Liṅga at Ānandapura near Cakrasvāmī, that same fruit is obtained when the Gadā and Cakra are drawn.
What will he achieve by going to holy places such as Prayāga, if his body is already marked with my weapons by means of the Gopīcandana clay? (35)
Whenever one should see a body marked with the conch and other signs, at that very moment I am pleased and I indeed burn away his sin.
He upon whose body the conch, discus, mace, and lotus remain day after day, night and day, is of my own nature.
In the Kali age, having made oneself endowed with the weapons of Nārāyaṇa, whatever meritorious deed one performs is equal to Mount Meru; of this there is no doubt.

O son, if one performs a śrāddha with devotion while marked by the conch-weapon, then even that which is deficient in ritual procedure becomes complete, and what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
Just as fire, impelled violently by the wind, consumes wood, even so do my weapons indeed burn away all sins upon being beheld. (40)
A seal engraved with my name and endowed with the eight syllables, fashioned from gold or silver, and joined with my own weapons such as the conch and others—[41]
He who preserves [this] for the Blessed One, especially in this Kali age, should be known as equal to Prahlāda; otherwise, he is not dear to me.
He whose body bears the Nārāyaṇī mudrā and marks such as the conch, and who wears a garland made of dhātrī fruits or produced from tulasī wood; 43.
That Vaiṣṇava who has the twelve-syllable mantra applied to his body and the weapons [of Viṣṇu] upon his person is indeed equal to me, O Brāhmaṇa.
O son, whatever food is eaten in the house of a Brahmin whose body is marked with the conch, that very food I eat myself along with the ancestors.
He who, upon seeing an object marked with the weapon of Kṛṣṇa, does not show it honor, loses the merit acquired over twelve years; it goes to Bāṣkaleya.
O giver of honor, if one who is marked by the weapons of Kṛṣṇa should die in a cremation ground, he attains that same destination which is proclaimed for those who die at Prayāga.
The gods, headed by Vāsava, establish their hermitages there, where his body is eternally adorned with weapons even in the Kali age.
And whatever man, marked with my weapon, performs worship for me, I always take away his thousands of offenses.
Having fashioned an image of me out of wood and clearly marked with weapons, he who brands his body with them—indeed, there is no Vaiṣṇava equal to him.
He who holds in his hand a metal seal marked with eight syllables and adorned with symbols such as the conch and lotus is worshipped by both gods and demons.
In former times, the Nārāyaṇī mudrā was held in the hand by Prahlāda, as well as by Vibhīṣaṇa, Bali, Dhruva, Śuka, Māndhātṛ, Ambarīṣa, and the twice-born sages headed by Mārkaṇḍeya.
O giver of honor, having marked your body with weapons such as the conch and other signs, and having thus propitiated me, you have obtained the great fruit you desired.
I dwell within the body of that person whose form is drawn with Gopīcandana clay and marked on the limbs with the conch, discus, lotus, and other symbols.
Having fashioned a wheel made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or even iron, the wise and discerning man should wear it; it should have twelve spokes, six angles, and be adorned with three folds.
In this manner, the wise man should have the Sudarśana disc fashioned; the conch, disc, and mace should always be worn like the sacred thread and other such emblems.
Especially by Brāhmaṇas, and particularly by Vaiṣṇavas, the sacred thread and the topknot must likewise be accompanied by the mark of the discus.
The [sacrificial] act of a Brahmin who is devoid of the mark of the discus becomes fruitless; "My body marked with the discus is pure"—such indeed is the Vedic revelation.

The wise should offer oblations to the gods (havya) and to the ancestors (kavya) to one who bears the mark of the discus. My armor, marked by the discus, is impenetrable even by gods and dānavas; [one wearing it] shall be invincible to all beings, to enemies, and even to rākṣasas.
Indeed, for anyone—whether it be a householder, a son, or another—in whose body my armor marked with the discus remains, no inauspiciousness exists.
A Brahmin should indeed bear the Sudarśana on his right arm and the conch on his left; so the knowers of the Vedas understand.
The knower of mantras, having established each one separately with its respective mantra, [should proceed].
A mace should be worn on the forehead, and likewise a bow and arrow on the head; Nandaka should be placed in the middle of the heart, and the conch and discus on the two arms.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always wear the *cakra* and the other [marks]. After wearing them, the best of the twice-born should speak as follows in that regard: || 64 ||
Whatever belongs to me as my possession—sons, friends, wife, and so forth—all of this, together with my body, is offered by me for the pleasure of Viṣṇu. (65)
Thereafter, remaining steadfast in your own duty, you shall live out your life with me, your every desire fulfilled at all times through unwavering devotion. (66)

Those lowest of men who, upon seeing one marked with the conch and the discus, utter insults—after looking at their faces, one should gaze at the sun and utter the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; only then does one become pure, and not otherwise.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Methods for Wearing Gopīcandana, the Conch, the Discus, and Other Weapons, as well as Their Respective Mudrās," in the dialogue between Brahmā and Viṣṇu within the second section, the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eleven thousand verses.
Brahmā said: O Keśava, tell me what fruit is obtained by one who has marked himself with the heated discus, who is thus initiated, and who wears garlands of lotus seeds and Tulasī? || 1 ||
The Blessed Lord said: "O twice-born one, that person who wears a garland produced from Tulasī wood—whether he be impure or of improper conduct—comes to me alone; of this there is no doubt. (2)
That man on whose body a garland made of *dhātrī* fruit or produced from *tulasī* wood is seen is indeed a devotee of the Lord (*bhāgavata*).
He who wears around his neck a garland made of Tulasī leaves, especially one offered by me, is worthy of being saluted even by the inhabitants of heaven.
A garland made of Tulasī leaves or even fashioned from Dhātrī fruits grants liberation to sinners; how much more so, then, for those who serve me?
Whoever wears this garland made of Tulasī leaves that has been offered to me obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices for every single leaf.
O child, to that man who wears a garland made from Tulasī wood, I grant daily the fruit arising from Dvārakā.
Having offered with devotion a garland made from tulasī wood to me, that man who wears it with devotion indeed has no sin whatsoever.
I am always pleased with him, for he is indeed as dear to me as my own life. That man who wears a garland made from Tulasī wood has no need for expiation, nor is there any impurity in his body.
That mortal on whose head, arms, or body there is an ornament of wood produced from Tulasī wood is dear to Me.
Adorned with garlands of Tulasī wood, one should perform meritorious acts; for the ancestors and the deities, such merit shall become ten millionfold. || 11 ||
Upon seeing a garland made of Tulasī wood, the messengers of the King of the Dead flee far away, like a leaf blown by the wind.
In whatever house there is a piece of Tulasī wood, whether dry or fresh, no sin whatsoever enters that house in the Kali age. (13)
Adorned with garlands made of Tulasi wood, he wanders upon the earth; for him there is no bad dream, no ill omen, and no fear from enemies anywhere. (14)
Those rationalists of evil intellect who do not wear the garland, being consumed by the fire of my wrath, shall not return from hell.
Therefore, a garland made of *tulasī* should be worn with great effort; likewise, one fashioned from lotus seeds, or from *dhātrī* fruits, bestows great merit when worn with devotion. (16)

Adorned with that vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), the conch, and other such signs, and holding kuśa grass in his hand while remembering me, he should perform the twilight prayers (sandhyopāsti) and other rites at the root of a tulasī plant.
Having performed the twilight prayers and other rites, the devotee should then worship me; if the Guru is present there, he should first go and bow to the Guru.

Having offered some gift as a token of respect, he should joyfully prostrate himself like a staff; then, having sipped water (ācamana) with a one-pointed mind, he should enter the pavilion of worship.

Having sat upon a beautiful seat covered with a black antelope skin and kuśa grass, and being properly seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).

Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and having conquered his senses with the mantra, he should then face north and cause the unsurpassed heart-lotus within his chest to blossom by means of the sun of higher knowledge (vijñāna).

Upon the pericarp, one should place the Sun, the Moon, and Fire; the Vaiṣṇava man should contemplate this triad within that which consists of three. Above them, he should install a pedestal composed of various jewels.

Upon that [lotus], one should place a lotus made of mantra-syllables, which is soft and very smooth, possessing a luster like the rising sun, and having eight petals representing the eight sovereign powers (aṣṭaiśvarya).
There he beheld the Lord seated, resembling ten million moons, four-armed, and bearing the great lotus, the conch, the discus, and the mace.

May I behold Him whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, who is endowed with all the auspicious marks, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha jewels, and who is clothed in yellow garments. (25)
He was endowed with various ornaments, adorned with divine decorations, his limbs anointed with divine sandalwood paste, and graced with divine flowers.
Adorned with a forest garland of tender Tulasī leaves, he was as beautiful as ten million rising suns, endowed with divine splendor.
Having thus meditated upon Śiva, whose body is closely embraced by her who is marked with all auspicious characteristics, one should, being pure and with a concentrated mind, recite the mantra. (28)
One should recite the mantra a thousand times or a hundred times, according to one's capacity; having performed the mental worship, one should thereafter proceed according to the prescribed rule.
In accordance with the traditional lineage, having placed a conch shell before me, it should be filled with sprouts of dūrvā grass, flowers, and scented water.
The preceptors, having placed a vessel for perfumes and flowers on the right, should set down a water-pot on the left side, purified with cloth and well-scented.
One should place a bell in front of me and arrange lamps in the cardinal directions; all other ritual implements (sādhana) should be placed in their respective locations.
For the sake of the arghya, pādya, ācamanīya, and madhuparka, one should indeed place four vessels before me.
O Four-faced One, one should place siddhārtha seeds, unbroken rice grains, flowers, the tips of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, sandalwood, fruit, and barley into the vessel for the arghya offering.
O son, for my satisfaction, the preceptor should place dūrvā grass, viṣṇupadī, śyāmā, and lotus as the fourth, into the vessel for the water for the feet.
O son, one should indeed place kaṅkola, cloves, and the fruit produced from the mālatī flower with faith into the vessel for the water for sipping (ācamanīya).
The worshipper should indeed offer with faith into the vessel of the madhuparka cow’s milk, curd, honey, clarified butter, and sugar-candy.

In the absence of the aforementioned types of substances, one who is skilled in the ritual rules should always perform the rite with leaves or flowers, while maintaining the mental visualization (bhāvanā) of each respective substance.

Then one should perform the placement on the hands (kara-nyāsa) and likewise the placement on the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa); one should perform either the fivefold or the sixfold placement according to the traditional injunction.
One should practice the recollection of me; one should remember oneself as equal to me. At the commencement of worship, a person should recite the auspicious hymn of the Four-faced One (Brahmā).

Then one should worship the conch Pāñcajanya, which is dear to me; O child, by worshipping it, my supreme bliss is attained. O child, during the worship of the conch, one should utter these mantras: [41]
O Pāñcajanya, you were born from the ocean in ancient times, held in the hand by Viṣṇu, and fashioned by all the gods; salutations be unto you!
By your roar, the clouds, gods, and asuras tremble; O Pāñcajanya, who possess the brilliance of ten thousand moons, salutations be unto you! 43.
The wombs of the wives of the enemies of the gods dissolve in a thousand ways by your roar; O Pāñcajanya in the netherworld, salutations be to you!
By the mere sight of Śaṅkha, sins go to dissolution; how much more so when he is touched? They vanish like snow at the rising of the sun. || 45 ||
Having bowed down and holding a conch in his hand, the Vaiṣṇava who bathes me with devotion using these mantras gains infinite merit.
Then, one should perform an oil massage with well-perfumed oil; likewise, one should perform the rubbing of the body with musk and sandalwood paste. (47)

O child, having bathed [the deity] with auspicious waters scented with fragrances and accompanied by mantras, one should then offer the arghya, followed by water for the feet (pādya) and water for sipping (ācamanīya). Thereafter, one should present the madhuparka and all the other ritual services (upacāras).
Having adorned it according to the prescribed rite with divine garments and ornaments, one should worship the pedestal with flowers and place the deity upon it.

One should offer garments, ornaments, perfumes, and so forth to me with faith; one should present various kinds of food offerings mixed with milk-rice and cakes, and with devotion, one should likewise offer betel-leaf along with camphor.
One should devoutly and properly offer fragrant flowers, as well as incense made of ten ingredients or eight ingredients, and a most beautiful lamp.
Having led her around, bowed down, and praised her with hymns of praise with devotion, and having laid her upon a couch, one should present the auspicious *arghya* offering.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Worship of Śaṅkha," in the Mārgaśīrṣa-māhātmya, within the dialogue between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, in the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Brahmā said: O Unconquered One, O Acyuta, tell me what fruit one obtains from bathing Hari with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and whatever [fruit] is obtained with water from a conch shell.
The Blessed Lord said: For those men who perform a bath with milk upon my head, it is remembered that for every single drop, they obtain the merit born of a hundred horse-sacrifices.

Milk is ten times more effective than [water], curd ten times more than that, ghee ten times more than curd, honey ten times more than ghee, and sugar is even more effective than that; however, the mantra recited over water containing fragrant flowers is praised as the most excellent of all. (3)
O tiger among gods, bathing me with cow’s milk on either the twelfth or the fifteenth day destroys even the greatest of sins.
Just as curds and other such transformations arise from milk, even so do all remaining desires arise for me from the bathing with milk.
Through bathing with milk one gains good fortune; through curd, the enjoyment of sweet food; and the man who bathes me with ghee shall go to my city.
He who causes [this] to be performed with honey and sugar in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa is born as a king in this world, having returned here from heaven.
He who performs my ritual bath with milk during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa shall obtain on this earth a kingdom filled with elephants, horses, and chariots.
O son, he who performs this supreme and most excellent bath with milk in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa conquers the Moon, Indra, Rudra, and the Maruts in the heavenly world.
The greatness of the milk-bath is radiant and increases nourishment; O my son, misfortune dissolves through this bath of milk.
O giver of honor, that person on earth who bathes me with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa shall not be an object of grief for his kinsmen.
O son, that man who bathes me with the milk of a tawny cow obtains the fruit of giving a hundred tawny cows in charity.
The preceptor who, having placed holy water from a sacred ford into a conch shell, bathes [the deity] with even a single drop during the month of Sahas (Kārttika), indeed delivers his own lineage.
The person who, having taken cow’s milk and placed it in a conch shell, bathes me with devotion, shall obtain the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 14 ||

Having placed water along with unbroken rice grains and *kuśa* grass into a conch shell, whoever bathes [the deity] during the month of Sahas (Mārgaśīrṣa) shall obtain the fruit of all sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
He who performs the ritual bath of the Blessed One with eight conch shells in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa out of devotion is the most excellent and is glorified in my world.
O my son, he who bathes me with sixteen conch shells is freed from sin and is honored in the heavenly world for a very long time.
He who bathes me with twenty-four conch shells, having resided for a long time in the world of Indra, is born as a king upon the earth.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should bathe [the deity] with exactly one hundred and eight conchfuls; such a person obtains the merit of [giving] gold within a conch to Śaṅkheśa. || 19 ||
If one who is devoted bathes me with the sound of a conch in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, his ancestors remain established in heaven for that long.
He who performs the ritual bath with a conch shell one thousand and eight times, that Gaṇa attains liberation until the dissolution of all beings.
O best of gods, he who constantly bathes me with a conch shell obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā and rejoices eternally like a deity.
O son, he who takes water in a conch shell and bathes me while saying "Namo Nārāyaṇa" is liberated from all sins.
Having placed water for washing the feet into a conch shell, he who gives it mixed with sesame seeds to high-souled Vaiṣṇavas shall obtain the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Whether it be water from a river, a lake, a pond, a well, or any other source—even that which is produced in the Ganges or brought by Śaṅkha—all such water becomes [equivalent to] Gaṅgā-water. || 25 ||
That Vaiṣṇava who, having taken the water from my feet and placed it in a conch, constantly carries it upon his head, is a sage, the best among those who practice asceticism.
"O son, by my very command, whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist in the three worlds dwell here within the conch; therefore, the conch is remembered as the most excellent. (27)
Holding a conch with water in his hand, the Vaiṣṇava who bathes [the Lord] with these mantras during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa—I become pleased with him. (28)
In the conch and other parts, the Moon is the presiding deity; in the belly, Varuṇa is the deity; on the back, Prajāpati; and at the front, Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī.
One should diligently bathe me with their excrement as the first offering; indeed, even the gods are not capable of calculating the measure of that merit.
O Lord of Gods, when a conch shell filled with flowers, water, and unbroken grains (akṣata) stands before me, duly worshipped, its prosperity is manifested in every direction.
Having filled a conch shell with ointment, one should worship me; then my supreme pleasure shall indeed last for a hundred years.
Whoever offers me an *arghya*—having placed water along with flowers, water, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) into a conch shell—his merit is indeed infinite.
He who, having himself prepared the arghya water in a conch shell, performs a circumambulation, has thereby circumambulated the earth with its seven continents.
And having whirled it above my head, that Vaiṣṇava who sprinkles the temple with the water from the conch—no inauspiciousness shall occur in his home. || 35 ||
For him who touches his head with water from the feet placed in a conch shell, there shall be no mental anxieties, no exhaustion, and no fear of hell anywhere.
Seeing the water from the conch upon their heads, the planets, Rākṣasas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Piśācas, serpents, and Dānavas flee in the ten directions.
He who bathes me with devotion amidst the loud sounds of musical instruments and the resonant chanting of auspicious songs shall indeed become liberated while living. (38)

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Worshipping Śaṅkha," in the Mārgaśīrṣa-māhātmya, within the Dialogue between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, in the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Brahmā said: O Acyuta, tell me truly, O Lord, the entire greatness of the sound of the bell as well as that of sandalwood, and whatever fruit one obtains thereby.
The Blessed Lord said: O Lord of Gods, listen to the fruit of merit for him who sounds the bell before me at the time of the rites of bathing and worship. || 2 ||
For thousands of millions of years and hundreds of millions of years, he shall dwell in my world, attended by hosts of apsarases.
Since the bell consists of all musical instruments and embodies all the gods, one should therefore cause the sound of the bell to be made with every effort.
The bell, consisting of all musical instruments, is always dear to me; by sounding it, one obtains the merit arising from hundreds of millions of sacrifices.
The sounding of the bell should always be performed, especially at the time of worship; [it grants the merit of] thousands of Manvantaras and hundreds of Manvantaras.
O son, I am constantly pleased by the sound of the bell, as well as by the sound of the kettledrum and the conch shell accompanied by the ringing of bells.
O Lord of Gods, my worship, accompanied by the mṛdaṅga drum and the conch and joined with the Praṇava, constantly bestows liberation upon men.
"O son, know me to be present wherever a bell accompanied by sound stands before me, and wherever I am worshipped by Vaiṣṇavas."
Whoever places before me a bell marked with the figure of Vainateya, or one joined with the Sudarśana, I shall remove his sin. (10)
Whoever sounds the bell at the time of my worship, his sins—even those accumulated over a hundred lifetimes—are destroyed.
At the time of my sleep, one should devoutly sound the bell; during the time of my worship, the fruit produced is multiplied ten millionfold.
O Lord of Gods, those who worship me seated upon Suparṇa, endowed with the conch, lotus, and mace, together with the discus and accompanied by Śrī; || 13 ||
What will they achieve with pilgrimages to sacred fords or by visiting deities? What is the use of sacrifices, or of vows, or of gifts, or of fasts? (14)
Those by whom my image as Nārāyaṇī, mounted upon Garuḍa, is installed, shall go to my abode for ten million kalpas in the Kali age. || 15 ||
Whoever places me before them, whether in a temple or in a house, thousands of crores of sacred fords (tīrthas) and deities reside there.

But that fortunate one who, endowed with pure intention, worships me seated upon Garuḍa on the eleventh day or likewise at night, and having performed song and dance, shall deliver his ancestors from hell. || 17 ||
Furthermore, O son, I shall speak again; listen to me regarding Ghaṇṭā.
"O son, know me to be present wherever there stands before you a bell inscribed with my name, and where the Vaiṣṇavī [image] is worshipped. (19)
But he who sounds the bell marked with the emblem of Vainateya during the offering of incense, the lustration ceremony, the ritual bath, the time of worship, or the application of unguents; || 20 ||
O child, before me every day you shall obtain the fruit of ten thousand sacrifices, ten thousand cows, and that which arises from a hundred Cāndrāyaṇa fasts.
Worship performed even outside the prescribed rules becomes fruitful for men; indeed, being pleased by the sound of the bell, I grant my own abode.
A bell marked with the sign of the enemy of serpents (the Garuda) and provided with a wheel destroys, by its very sounding, the fear of ten million births.
O Lord of Gods, seeing the bell marked with the Garuḍa, I feel joy every day, just as a poor man does upon obtaining wealth. (24)
Whoever places a beautiful discus upon the head of the bell-handle, or installs my beloved Vainateya, has established [the emblem] throughout the three worlds. || 25 ||
Whoever hears the sound of the bell and the discus at the time of death—even if burdened by ten million sins—the servants of Yama perish.
O son, all defects indeed perish by the sound of the bell; it becomes a festival for the deities, including the Rudras, and for the ancestors. (27)
In the absence of even the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa) or the discus, there is no doubt that I bestow grace upon my devotees by the sound of the bell. 28.
In whatever house there is always a bell joined with the enemy of serpents (a peacock), there is no fear of snakes, nor any arising from fire or lightning.
He in whose house there is no bell, nor a conch before me—how can he be known as a devotee of the Lord? How can he be dear to Him? (30)
O my dear son, I shall proclaim the greatness of sandalwood; by performing this, I shall undoubtedly be exceedingly pleased. (31)
It was accompanied by sandalwood and flowers, mixed with camphor and agallochum, combined with musk, and provided with nutmeg. || 32 ||
Indeed, he who constantly offers me that which is produced from Tulasī wood—endowed with Tulasī and sandalwood, and bringing me supreme happiness—[attains my favor]. (33)
That best of men dwells in heaven for infinite ages, having offered Tulasī and sandalwood with devotion to Mahāviṣṇu in the Kali age.
One who worships me with mālatī flowers shall not become a suckling again; and he who offers me sandalwood paste produced from tulasī wood [attains the same]. (35)
The sandalwood paste from the wood of the *tulasī* plant [destroys] all sins committed over hundreds of previous births for all the gods indeed. (36)
And it is especially always desired by the ancestors, just as it is for me. || 37 ||
Sandalwood from the Śrīkhaṇḍa tree and even black aloe-wood remain superior only so long as the sandalwood paste from Tulasī wood is not offered to me. (38)
The fragrance of musk and the scent of camphor remain [only as such] so long as the sandalwood paste from Tulasī wood is not offered to me. (39)
Those who offer me tulasī wood and sandalwood paste in the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa during the Kali age have achieved their life's purpose; of this there is no doubt. (40)
Indeed, he who, having become a devotee of the Lord, does not offer *tulasī* and sandalwood paste during the month of Sahas (Kārttika) is not truly a devotee of the Lord. || 41 ||
He who anoints my form with a paste of saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood during the month of Sahas (Mārgaśīrṣa) shall dwell in heaven for ten million kalpas.
One should anoint [the image] with sandalwood paste mixed with camphor and agallochum; especially musk is always my favorite. (43)
To him who indeed anoints me with sandalwood paste after placing it upon a conch shell during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, I grant satisfaction for a hundred years.
He who always serves with devotion in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa with Tulasī leaves and Āmalaka fruits shall obtain his desired fruit. || 45 ||

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Fruit of Offering Tulasī Wood and Sandalwood Paste to the Blessed Lord," within the Mārgaśīrṣa-māhātmya, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, in the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Brahmā said: O Lord of Gods, tell me the majesty arising from the various species of flowers, and by which specific flower a man obtains what fruit.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, my son, I shall proclaim the greatness arising from flowers, by which flower I am truly pleased; of this there is no doubt. (2)
Mallikā, Mālatī, Yūthikā, and Atimuktaka; Pāṭalā, Karavīra, Jayantī, and likewise Vijayā. (3)
Kubjaka, stabaka, karṇikāra, kuraṇṭaka, campaka, cātaka, kunda, bāṇa, karcūra, and mallikā. || 4 ||
The Aśoka, the Tilaka, and likewise the Aparayūthika—these varieties of flowers, my son, are recommended by me for worship.
The flower and leaf of the ketakī, as well as the bhṛṅgarāja, and the leaf and flower of the tulasī, bring me immediate delight.
The lotuses arising from the water, as well as the red and blue lotuses, and the white lotus in the month of Sahas (Mārgaśīrṣa), are indeed exceedingly dear to me.
And those very flowers, my son, are praised by me which possess the right color as well as flavor and fragrance.
In my view, even scentless flowers are considered praiseworthy, as well as other fragrant ones, provided one avoids the ketaki.
Bāṇa, Campaka, Aśoka, Karavīra, Yūthikā, Pāribhadra, Pāṭalā, Bakula, and Giriśālinī; (10)
The bilva leaf, the śamī leaf, the leaf of bhṛṅgarāja, and the leaves of tamāla and āmalakī are recommended for my worship, O son. (11)
With flowers grown in the forest or leaves produced on the mountains—fresh, without holes, sprinkled with water, and free from living creatures.
Or one may worship me with flowers grown in a garden; through the excellence of the species of flower, the merit becomes especially great. (13)

Whatever fruit a man obtains by giving ten gold pieces to a worthy recipient endowed with austerity, virtue, and good qualities, and who has mastered the Vedas—that same fruit a mortal obtains by the gift of a flower at Sahya. || 14 ||
O son, if one offers even a single *droṇa* flower to me after giving ten gold pieces, the fruit thereof is even greater.
Understand from me how there was a distinction between one flower and another. || 16 ||
A thousand *droṇa* flowers are surpassed by a single *khadira* flower; a thousand *khadira* flowers are surpassed by a single *śamī* flower. (17)
A single *bilva* flower is superior to a thousand *śamī* flowers; a single *baka* flower is superior to a thousand *bilva* flowers. (18)
The *nandyāvarta* flower is superior to a thousand *bakapuṣpa* flowers; indeed, the *karavīra* flower is superior to a thousand *nandyāvarta* flowers. (19)
The white flower of a thousand karavīra plants is supreme; the palāśa flower is superior to the white karavīra flower. (20)
A single *kuśa* flower is superior to a thousand *pālāśa* flowers; indeed, a forest garland (*vanamālā*) is superior to a thousand *kuśa* flowers. (21)
Indeed, the campaka flower excels a thousand vanamālās; and the aśoka flower is superior to a hundred campaka flowers.
A thousand *aśoka* flowers are surpassed by the supreme *śevantī* flower; a thousand *śevantī* flowers are surpassed by the supreme *kujaka* flower. (23)
For a single *mālatī* flower is superior to a thousand *kujapuṣpa* flowers; and a *sandhyā* flower excels a thousand *mālatī* flowers. (24)
Indeed, the *trisandhyā* flower is superior even to a thousand *sandhyā* flowers. || 25 ||

The white [sandalwood] of the three junctions is superior to the red [sandalwood] of the three junctions; the kunda-flower [sandalwood] is distinguished as even more excellent than the white [sandalwood] of the three junctions.
Indeed, a single jasmine flower excels a thousand kunda flowers; among all species of flowers, the jasmine flower is supreme here. (27)
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who, according to the prescribed rite, offers me a most beautiful garland made of a thousand jasmine flowers. (28)
For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas, he shall dwell eternally in my city, possessing prowess equal to my own. || 29 ||
Those flowers which are excellent for my worship, their leaves are also recommended; in their absence, their fruits as well.
By worshipping me with these leaves, flowers, and fruits, one shall obtain for each of them the merit of ten gold pieces.
To those who worship with these varieties of flowers during the month of Sahas, I grant devotion; being pleased, I do so indeed—of this there is no doubt.
"Whatever he desires—be it wealth, sons, a wife, or anything else—that I shall grant him, O Lord of Gods, being propitiated by these flowers. (33)

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruit of Placing a Garland Adorned with a Thousand Jātī Flowers upon Viṣṇu’s Neck, Preceded by the Narration of the Preeminence of the Jātī Flower," in the Mārgaśīrṣa-māhātmya of the Dialogue between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Brahmā said: O Lord, describe accurately the majesty of the glorious Tulasī, by whose mere presence your pleasure becomes even greater.
The Blessed Lord said: Jewels, golden flowers, and even those made of pearls do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of offering a *tulasī* leaf. (2)
That man who performs my worship with Tulasī blossoms shall not enter the womb again; he shall become a partaker of liberation.
O child, having placed a tulasī plant there, one should worship me with its leaves; such a person rejoices in heaven, in Śvetadvīpa, and in my abode.
If one worships me even once with the fragrant, pure, and unbroken leaves of the glorious Tulasī, Yama, having observed the sin residing within his body, shall then wipe it away.

Fie upon the youth, life, wealth, and progeny of those who have not procured a Tulasi plant for my worship on the meritorious day of Ekadashi; neither happiness is seen here nor in the hereafter for them.
Having seen my Linga worshipped with heaps of Tulasī leaves on the full moon day of the month of Sahas (Mārgaśīrṣa), one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
Whoever indeed constantly worships me, the Lord of Ramā, with Tulasī, their great sins are destroyed; how much more so, then, their minor offenses?
Withered flowers should be avoided, and stale water should be avoided; however, the Tulasī leaf is not to be avoided, nor is the water of the Ganges.
O son, flowers such as the mālatī and others may bloom only so long as my auspicious Tulasī, who is dear to me, has not been obtained.
The man who worships me even once with a bilva leaf shall partake in liberation, become free from fear, and come into my presence.
Among the bilva leaf, the śamī leaf, the jasmine leaf, and the lotus, the tulasī leaf is most dear to me, even more so than the Kaustubha gem.
The Tulasī with unbroken leaves and endowed with flower-clusters, born from the Ocean of Milk like this very Lakṣmī, is always dear to me.
Whether it be non-black or black, Tulasī is dear to me; just as whether it be white or dark, the twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī) is dear to me.
Whoever, having taken a tulasī leaf, worships me with devotion, by him all is worshipped—the entire world including gods, asuras, and humans. (15)
Countless jewels such as the Kaustubha and others may roar with pride only so long as the black Tulasī flower-cluster of Kṛṣṇa has not been obtained. (16)
The man who worships Kṛṣṇa with devotion using black Tulasī goes to the radiant realm where Viṣṇu dwells together with Śrī.
Those who offer a tulasī leaf to the monks for the purpose of my worship, as well as other devotees, go to my imperishable abode.
The man who worships me with Tulasī that is black or fair in hue, having cast off his body, attains the eternal Vaiṣṇava goal. (19)
Brahmā said: O Keśava, tell me truly the greatness of offering incense and also of the lamp, as well as the fruit that a mortal obtains thereby.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, my son, I shall declare the fruit that comes from the offering of incense, and the supreme majesty of the offering of lamps, which brings me the highest delight. (21)
By offering me agallochum along with camphor and the fragrance of divine sandalwood during the month of Sahas (Mārgaśīrṣa), one shall indeed deliver a hundred generations of one's lineage.
That Vaiṣṇava who indeed perfumes my abode with incense arising from black agallochum shall be liberated from the ocean of hell.
To whoever offers me incense made from buffalo-guggulu mixed with clarified butter and sugar, I grant his every desire.
Guggulu, when burned as incense, destroys all misfortunes; likewise, agaru bestows various kinds of desired objects.
Incense produced from aguru purifies both the body and the home; incense arising from sarjarasa destroys yakṣas and rākṣasas.
Jātipuṣpa, ela, guggulu, harītakī, kūṭa, sarjarasa, guḍa, sailācchaḍa, and nakha—these ten ingredients together are called the ten-ingredient incense (daśāṅga-dhūpa). || 27 ||

If one offers ten-ingredient incense during the month of Sahas (Jyeṣṭha), which is very dear to me, I grant even those desires that are exceedingly difficult to attain, as well as strength, nourishment, and devotion toward one's children and wife.

In this incense of mustā, there is sweetness pleasing to men, auspiciousness, and the power of subjugation through molasses; whoever, having abandoned all sins, performs the oblation before me, shall attain me. (29)
No fear exists for him—whether born of heaven, earth, or the intermediate space—for whose limb the remains of my incense have been rubbed.
