But a man who, endowed with devotion, beholds Madhupurī with faith—even a slayer of a Brahmin is purified; how much more so, then, one who has committed other sins?
As one desiring to bathe in Mathurā proceeds step by step, sins depart from the body, leaving it entirely hopeless.
They go there as a secondary result, or even by means of trade or service; merely by bathing in Madhurā, they go to heaven, their sins destroyed.
For those who even utter her name, there is always liberation; of this there is no doubt. There, it is always the Kṛta Yuga, and it is always the northern course of the sun.
O Four-faced One, whoever hears the sweetness of my temple when it is uttered by another is immediately liberated from sin. (12)
O son, even those men who dwell there for three nights—when they are touched, their joyful foot-dust purifies others.
Just as tiny sparks set a mass of grass ablaze, so does the city of Mathurā consume great sins.
Whatever accumulation of merit may arise from bathing in all the sacred fords (tīrthas), Mathurā is declared to be far superior to that in every respect within the entire region.
Whatever merit arises from the study of all four Vedas, that same merit is produced for those men who remember Mathurā.
For a sin committed elsewhere perishes upon reaching a sacred ford; however, a sin committed at sacred fords will become as indelible as adamantine cement.
Sin committed in Mathurā perishes in Mathurā; by staying there, a person attains that which is known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (18)
O Four-faced One, whatever sin has been commenced is indeed experienced over ten years elsewhere, but in Mathurā, it is experienced in ten days.
Neither in heaven, nor in the netherworld, nor in the atmosphere, nor among humans is there anything equal to Mathurā; for it is always truly dear to me.
Of all sacred places, Mathurā is the supreme and greatest; there, He performed various childhood sports together with the cowherds. (21)
Whatever fruit is obtained in the land of Bhārata for thirty thousand and thirty hundred years, that same fruit is attained by one who remembers Mathurā.
O son, whatever merit is obtained at the Sannihati when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, one obtains even more than that day after day in Mathurā.
O son, one obtains that same fruit which is gained at the king of holy sites (Prayāga) after a full thousand years by staying for one month in the city of Madhu.
O son, the fruit that is obtained at Vārāṇasī after a full thousand years is attained at Mathurā in a single day.
A man who gives land at the fields of Godāvarī, Dvārakā, and Kurukṣetra, or who performs the rites at Gayā for six months, does not equal one who stays in Mathurā for even a single day. (26)

Neither Dvārakā, nor Kāśī, nor Añcī, nor Māyā, nor the place where Gadādhara resides is equal to that holy site; for if the ancestors have been fully satiated by the waters of the Yamunā, they truly do not desire the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
Those men who treat Mathurā as if it were an ordinary city should be known as being burdened with heaps of sin. (28)
He who has not seen Mathurā but in whom the desire to see it arises—even if he dies anywhere else, his rebirth occurs in Mathurā. (29)
O Four-faced One, one might count the particles of dust on the earth even in the course of time, but there is no known number for the holy places (tīrthas) in Mathurā.
"O, build, O, build a dwelling toward the city named Mathurā! There I shall dwell eternally, surrounded by the daughters of cowherds. (31)
Furthermore, my other disciples who are submerged in saṃsāra, listen! If you desire intense bliss, take up residence in my city. (32)
Alas! Though endowed with eyes, the world does not see the Great Bliss; even while Mathurā exists, it constantly clings to the cycle of worldly existence.
Having obtained the incomparable human womb through the conjunction of fortune, their life has passed in vain if they have not beheld the city of Mathurā. 34.
Oh, the extreme weakness of my intellect! Oh, the cruel decree of fate! Oh, the power of delusion, that Mathurā is not resorted to at all! 35.
But he who, having abandoned Mathurā, sets his mind elsewhere, that fool wanders in saṃsāra, deluded by my māyā. (36)
Even having reached Mathurā, if one still directs his longing elsewhere, what knowledge can that evil-minded person possess? He is merely deluded by ignorance. (37)
Those who have been abandoned by their mother and father, those who have been forsaken by their own kinsmen, and those for whom there is no refuge anywhere—my city is their refuge.
For those overwhelmed by heaps of sin, those defeated by poverty, and those who have no refuge anywhere—my city is their refuge. (39)
The most excellent place among all that is essential, the supreme secret among all secrets—for those seeking a destination, Mathurā is the ultimate goal. (40)

That cannot be attained through those merits, nor through those gifts, nor through austerities, nor through hymns of praise; it cannot be attained through various yogas, but is attainable through my power alone.
Only for those fortunate ones who possess firm and abundant devotion toward me, and upon whom my compassion rests, shall there be a destination in Mathurā.
The same destination that belongs to the wise sage who knows Brahman and is disciplined in yoga, belongs also to the man who gives up his life-breaths in Mathurā. 43.

If cities such as Kāśī exist in the world, Mathurā alone among them is blessed; for she bestows the fourfold liberation upon men through birth, the sacred thread ceremony, religious vows, and final release.
That goal which cannot be attained even through yogic practices for hundreds of manvantaras, is attained here effortlessly by my grace.
Where there is no fear of sins, where there is indeed no fear of Yama, and where there is no dread of dwelling in a womb—who would not take refuge in that sacred field? (46)
Now hear the fruit of that merit which is found in Mathurā: those who have reached Mathurā and died in Mathurā [attain this result]. (47)
Even insects, moths, and the like are born with four arms; even those trees that fall from the bank attain the supreme goal.
Those who are mute, dull-witted, blind, or deaf, and those devoid of austerity and religious observances—even they, having died in due course of time, go to my world.
Those bitten by snakes, those killed by wild beasts, those destroyed by fire or water, and those who have met with untimely death—whosoever [die] in Mathurā go to my world.
"Truly, truly, O best of sages, I speak with an oath: there is nothing anywhere equal to Mathurā, which grants all desired objects. (61)

Who would not take refuge in that Mathurā, which bestows the three goals of life upon those who desire them, grants liberation to those seeking release, and gives devotion to those longing for devotion? (52)
Such a Madhupurī should be performed in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa; in its absence, indeed, Puṣkara should be performed according to the prescribed rules.
Know, O wise one, that the eldest pit belongs to Brahmā, the middle pit to Viṣṇu, and the youngest pit has Rudra as its presiding deity. 54.
O son, in these [waters], bathing, giving gifts, performing ancestral rites according to the rules, and offering great worship should be performed, for they bring me pleasure.
O son, that which is the full moon in the month of Sahas (Mārgaśīrṣa) is dear to me; whatever merit is performed on that day shall be pleasing to me. || 56 ||
O son, on the full moon day, the gift of a cow, the gift of food, the gift of gold, and the gift of land should be performed according to the prescribed rites.
Indeed, on the full moon day of the month of Sahas (Kārttika), one should cause the gift of a dwelling to be made; whatever is performed on that full moon shall yield inexhaustible fruit.
Indeed, a feast for the Brahmins should be prepared according to the extent of one's wealth; the festival must be performed specifically on the Pūrṇā day for the completion of the vow.
O son, just as Mathurā is dear to me during the month of Sahomāsa, so are the kings of holy places (tīrtharāja) and others not; and in its absence, Puṣkara is [dear].
The full moon day (pūrṇā) should indeed be observed by the wise at Puṣkara and Mathurā; or rather, the full moon day should be observed according to the prescribed rite wherever one may be.
He who does not perform bathing, giving, and likewise worship on the full moon day is cooked in the Raurava and other hells for sixty thousand years.
Therefore, with every effort, the wise should honor Pūrṇā when conjoined with the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, for she bestows infinite fruit.
O child, as has been told to you, the month of Mārgaśīrṣa is dear to me; listen now to the fruit of merit for that man who observes it with devotion. || 64 ||
One shall obtain that merit which is found in tens of thousands of sacred fords (tīrthas), that merit which comes from ten million vows, and that merit which is found in all sacrifices. || 65 ||
One without a son obtains a son, and one without wealth obtains wealth; likewise, a seeker of knowledge obtains knowledge, and one seeking beauty attains beauty. (66)
A Brāhmaṇa shall become endowed with spiritual luster, a Kṣatriya shall be victorious, a Vaiśya shall attain the status of a lord of treasures, and a Śūdra shall be purified from sin. (67)
O giver of honor, whatever is difficult to find and hard to attain within the three worlds, all that a mortal may obtain during the month of Sahas, of this there is no doubt. (68)
O Four-faced One, O mighty-armed one, those men who are attached to these sensual pleasures, though they may be satisfied in the end, are indeed not worthy of such desires.

For true devotion to me, which brings one under my power and is auspicious, is indeed very difficult to obtain; yet it is attained, O son, by listening to [this] during the month of Sahas (Mārgaśīrṣa). 70.
This month is pleasing to me and is always dear to me; O Four-faced One, everything is obtained from it through my grace. (71)

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Mathurā," in the *Mārgaśīrṣa-māsa-māhātmya* (The Greatness of the Month of Mārgaśīrṣa) within the dialogue between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, in the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now begins the *Śrīmadbhāgavata-māhātmya*. Vyāsa said: We perpetually offer salutations to Kṛṣṇa, whose essential nature is the mass of Śrī, Sat, Cit, and Ānanda; who showers infinite bliss; and who is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, so that we may attain the aesthetic relish (*rasa*) of devotion.
In the Naimiṣa forest, having saluted the high-minded Sūta as he sat there, the sages, who were skilled in relishing the nectar-like essence of his stories, spoke to him.
The sages said: When the king had gone to Hastināpura after consecrating his grandson Vajra in the illustrious land of Mathurā, what did those two do and how?
Sūta said: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Jaya."
O Brahmins, when King Parīkṣit, the lord of the earth, had set out upon the great road, he proceeded toward Mathurā with the desire to behold Vajranābha.
Knowing that his paternal uncle had arrived, Vajra, overflowing with affection, went out to meet him, saluted him, and then led him to his own residence.
Having embraced him, that hero, whose mind was solely fixed on Kṛṣṇa, approached the wives of Hari, such as Rohiṇī and the others, who had come to the temple, and paid them homage.
Highly honored by them, Parīkṣit, the lord of the earth, having rested and sitting comfortably, spoke to Vajranābha.
Śrī Parīkṣit said: O father, surely our fathers and grandfathers were uplifted from the flood of abundant suffering by your ancestors, and I too have been protected.
"I am unable, dear father, to repay your kindness sufficiently; therefore, I entreat you, my lord: may you be occupied with happiness in the kingdom. (10)
You should not entertain even the slightest anxiety regarding your treasury, army, and so forth, nor concerning the subduing of enemies and the like; rather, you should serve your mothers well.
"Having reported this to me, you must perform the complete abandonment of all sovereign powers. Hearing this, Vajra was exceedingly pleased and replied to him.
Śrī Vajranābha said: "O King, what you say to us is worthy of you; for I have been favored by your father through the imparting of the science of archery. (13)
Therefore, not even the slightest anxiety arises in me, who have firmly embraced the duty of a warrior; however, there is one supreme concern—let that be reflected upon.
Although I was consecrated in Mathurā, I remained in a desolate forest; where indeed have the subjects here gone, that the kingdom is so pleasing to you? (15)
Thus addressed, Viṣṇurāta quickly summoned Śāṇḍilya, the family priest of Nanda and the others, in order to dispel his thunderbolt-like doubt.
Then, leaving his hermitage, Śāṇḍilya arrived quickly; honored by Vajranābha, he sat down upon an excellent seat.
Then Viṣṇurāta quickly provided the introduction; being supremely pleased, he spoke to those two while consoling them.

Śrī Śāṇḍilya said: Listen with attentive minds to this secret concerning the land of Vraja. Because it is called "vrajana," meaning pervasion, it is termed "Vraja" due to its all-pervading nature. (19)
The Supreme Brahman, which transcends all attributes, is said to be all-pervading; it is eternal bliss, the supreme light, and the imperishable abode of the liberated.
In him, Kṛṣṇa, the son of Nanda, whose very body is eternal bliss, who delights in the Self and has attained all desires, is experienced by those permeated with love.
But Rādhikā is his very self; because he delights with her alone, he is called "one who delights in the self" (ātmārāma) by the wise who know the hidden truth. (22)

His desired objects of enjoyment, however, were the cows, the cowherds, and the cowherd girls; since all his pastimes and so forth are eternal, he is therefore one whose desires are already fulfilled.
But this secret of His is said to be beyond primordial nature (prakṛti); the play of Him who sports with prakṛti is experienced by others. (24)
In whom creation, maintenance, and dissolution occur through the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas—his play is thus twofold: the real and the conventional.
The first is real and self-evident to living beings, while the second is conventional; without the first, the second does not exist, nor does the second ever lead to the first.
But this worldly pastime of His, which is within our range of perception, includes the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, and within that, the district of Mathurā on earth. (27)
Right here is that land of Vraja, where the reality that is so well-concealed shines forth at all times for those who are filled with divine love. 28.
Once, at the end of the Dvāpara age, when those authorized for the secret pastimes were assembled here just as they are now, Hari [appeared].
Those who are desired for the purpose of entering into their own [bodies] descend together with their own [attendants]; at that time, other beings such as gods also descend from all sides.
Having fulfilled the desires of all, Hari became invisible; by him, the threefold worlds were established here as they were before, without a doubt. (31)
They are divided into two categories: the eternal ones and those who desire to attain them, such as the gods and others. Among these, the gods and others were formerly led to Dvārakā by Kṛṣṇa.
Furthermore, by the path of the mace, they were placed in their respective offices; and Kṛṣṇa, whose sole form is the bliss of love, always [protected] those who desired that state.
Having then integrated them into his own daily rites, he caused all those daily [deities] to become invisible to those who were unworthy. (34)
Because those who are engaged in worldly pastimes have no authority there, they do not come here; therefore, it is secluded on all sides.
Therefore, O Vajranābha, you should not worry; by my command, settle many villages here, and your success will be achieved.
Having bestowed names everywhere in accordance with the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa, you must cause those villages to be inhabited; this supreme earth is to be enjoyed by you abundantly.
You must establish your royal residence at Govardhana, Dīrghapura, Mathurā, Mahāvana, Nandigrāma, and Bṛhatsānu.
As you enjoy the groves by rivers, mountains, mountain torrents, pools, and other such places, your subjects will flourish in the kingdom and you yourself will be filled with joy. (39)
This ground of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda) should be served by you with great effort; by my grace, may the sacred sites of Kṛṣṇa manifest here for you.
Through the constant service of this Vajra, Uddhava will meet with you; then, together with his mother, you shall obtain this secret from him. || 41 ||
Having spoken thus, Śāṇḍilya departed while remembering Kṛṣṇa; then Viṣṇurāta and Vajra attained supreme joy.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Land of Vraja as Taught by Śāṇḍilya," in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata-Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The venerable sages said: O Sūta, after Śāṇḍilya had instructed them and returned to his own hermitage, what did those two kings do, and how? Tell us that.
Śrī Sūta said: Then, thousands of guild-leaders were summoned from Indraprastha by Viṣṇurāta and brought to the site of Mathurā.
Having recognized the Brāhmaṇas of Mathurā and the ancient Vānaras there, Svarāḍ established their status as worthy of honor.
Vajra, however, through that assistance and by the grace of Śāṇḍilya as well, [described] the places of the divine play of Govinda, the cowherds, and the gopīs in their proper sequence. (4)

Having understood this, he established them by means of designations and settled many villages through the construction of sacrificial pits, wells, and other works of public utility, as well as by the installation of images of Śiva and other deities.
And by superimposing the essential nature of Govinda, Harideva, and others upon himself, he spread his singular devotion to Kṛṣṇa throughout his kingdom and rejoiced indeed.
The subjects, however, were joyful and devoted to the chanting of Kṛṣṇa's glories; filled with supreme bliss, they praised his very reign.
Once, the wives of Kṛṣṇa, distressed by separation from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, joyfully beheld the Yamunā and, free from envy, questioned her.
The wives of Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O beautiful one, just as we are the wives of Kṛṣṇa, so too are you; yet we are afflicted by the pain of separation while you are not, O Kālindī—tell us why that is."
Having heard that, Kālindī, perceiving their mutual rivalry as wives, spoke these words with a mind supremely compassionate toward them.
Śrī Kālindī said: For Kṛṣṇa, who delights in the Self, Rādhikā is certainly his very soul; by the power of her service, separation from him shall not touch us.
All the consorts of Śrī Kṛṣṇa are merely the expansion of her very own portions; for her, there exists only eternal union through the yoga of mutual facing.
She is indeed he, and he is indeed she; under his control, she takes on the form of love for him. Through contact with the moon-like row of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s nails, she is known as Candrāvalī.
Assuming another form and being intensely eager for their service, I beheld here itself the complete absorption of Rukmiṇī and the others.
Even for you, there is no separation from Kṛṣṇa in every respect; however, because you do not know this, you have fallen into such agitation. (15)
In this very same way, in the past, during the occasion of Akrūra's departure, there was only a semblance of separation for the gopīs, which was allayed by Uddhava. (16)
If your union with him were to take place right here, then you would also obtain eternal sport with your own beloved. (17)
Śrī Sūta said: Having been addressed thus, those wives, longing for union with their own beloved through the sight of Uddhava, spoke again to the gracious lady.
The wives of Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O friend, you are blessed by your beloved, for whom there is no falling away; since your own purpose is perfectly accomplished, we have become your maidservants. (19)
But if a white [cow] can be obtained, it would accomplish all our purposes; therefore, O Kālindī, speak so that its acquisition may also come to pass. (20)
Śrī Sūta said: Thus addressed, Kālindī, recollecting Kṛṣṇacandra who possesses the form of sixteen digits, then replied to them accordingly.
While proceeding to Badarī, the ground of spiritual practice, Kṛṣṇa told his minister: "He resides there in person, causing people to grasp that very yoga."

The land of Vraja, which is the ground of the fruit [of liberation], was already given to him along with its secret doctrine; yet the fruit remains hidden here, and thus that Uddhava is now invisible.
Near Govardhana Hill, at Sakhīsthala, desiring its very dust, that Uddhava surely resides there in the form of sprouts and creepers. (24)
Hari has certainly bestowed upon him the nature of a festival for himself; therefore, staying there on the banks of the Kusuma lake with those possessing thunderbolts (the gods), [he should act]. 25.
Having gathered people from all the worlds, a festival should be commenced with lutes, flutes, and drums, and with sweet musical performances such as hymns and poetry. (26)
In that great festival which will surely be spread out, there will certainly be a glance from Uddhava; he alone shall bring about the fulfillment of your desires, like the sun bringing forth light.
Śrī Sūta said: Having heard this, they were delighted; having paid homage to the Kālindī, they returned and related it to Parīkṣit, who was near Vajra.
Having heard that, Viṣṇurāta was pleased and, accompanied by him, arrived there immediately and had all of that performed with haste.
Not far from Govardhana, in the Vṛndāvana forest at Sakhīsthala, the festival of Kṛṣṇa-saṃkīrtana commenced amidst an ocean of flowers.
In the temple of the Beloved of the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, when it was as if filled with the splendor of the *kīrtana* itself, everyone became focused on nothing else.
Then, while everyone was looking on, Uddhava emerged from a thicket of grass, shrubs, and creepers; he was dark-complexioned, wearing a garland and clad in yellow garments.
Wearing a garland of *guñjā* berries and repeatedly singing of the Beloved of the cowherd women, the festival of congregational chanting shone forth intensely upon His arrival. (33)
Just as a crystal palace or floor becomes radiant through the arrival of moonlight, so then everyone was submerged in an ocean of happiness and forgot everything else.
In an instant, their consciousness returned; seeing him in the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they worshipped Uddhava, having regained their heart's desire.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Meeting of Parīkṣit and Others with Uddhava near Mount Govardhana," in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata-Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: Then Uddhava, seeing them intent upon the glorification of Kṛṣṇa, honored them, embraced them, and spoke to Parīkṣit.
Uddhava said: O King, you are blessed; by your singular devotion to Kṛṣṇa, you are eternally fulfilled, for your mind is immersed in the festival of the congregational chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s names.
By good fortune, affection has been established toward the wives of Kṛṣṇa and Vajra; O dear one, this is worthy of you, whose bodily splendor was bestowed by Kṛṣṇa.
Among all those residing in Dvārakā, these are undoubtedly blessed—those for whom the Lord commanded Pārtha to provide a dwelling in Vraja.
The moon-like mind of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, endowed with the splendor of Rādhā’s face, always shines as it adorns His pleasure-grove with rays of light.
Kṛṣṇacandra is eternally full; his sixteen digits, which are indistinguishable from the radiance of a thousand consciousnesses, abide here as his very nature.
Thus, O Indra among kings, Vajra is the destroyer of the fear of those who have sought refuge; his place is situated at the right foot of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
In this incarnation, Yogamāyā has been intensely activated by Kṛṣṇa; by its power, through their self-forgetfulness, these [demons] are perishing—of this there is no doubt.
Without the light of Kṛṣṇa, however, there is no realization of one's own self for anyone; that light is always veiled by Māyā for living beings.
When, at the end of the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, Hari himself dispels his own māyā, then that [truth] shall become manifest.
That time has indeed passed; therefore, hear this other [account]: at another time, its manifestation shall arise from the Śrīmad Bhāgavata.
Wherever and whenever the scripture of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata is recited or even heard by the devotees of the Lord, there Śrī Kṛṣṇa is certainly present. (12)
Wherever there is even a single verse or half a verse of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, there the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa shines resplendent with the cowherd girls.
Those who, having obtained a human birth in Bhārata, have not heard the Bhāgavata while remaining subject to sin, have indeed committed suicide. (14)
By those who have constantly served the scripture of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the lineage of their fathers, mothers, and wives has been successfully delivered. (15)
From the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, there shall arise for Brahmins the light of knowledge, for kings victory over enemies, and for Vaiśyas as well as Śūdras wealth and health. (16)
It fulfills all the desires of women and others as well; therefore, what fortunate person would not constantly serve the Bhāgavata?
One who has attained perfection through many births obtains the Śrīmad Bhāgavata; therein arises the illumination that brings forth devotion to the Lord. 18.
In the past, Bṛhaspati gave me the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, which was obtained through the grace of Sāṃkhyāyana; by that means, I have become the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
And he has told a narrative; O Viṣṇurāta, learn it, wherein the tradition of hearing the Bhāgavata is also made known. (20)

Śrī Bṛhaspati said: When Kṛṣṇa, assuming the form of the Māyā-puruṣa, looked [upon the world], there appeared Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, through the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas respectively. (21)
Then three Puruṣas arose, and he assigned them their respective offices in due order: for creation, for preservation, and for dissolution.
Brahmā, having arisen from the navel-lotus, addressed him. Śrī Brahmā said: "O Nārāyaṇa, O Primordial Person, O Supreme Self, salutations be unto you. (23)
"I have been appointed by you to the task of creation; may the sinful quality of rajas not afflict me while I am mindful of you, O Lord, through your grace. (24)
The illustrious Bṛhaspati said: O Brahman, when the Blessed Lord had previously instructed him in the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, he said, "Serve this for the sake of your own perfection."
Brahmā, being supremely pleased by that [prayer], performed the seven-day rite for seven days in order to shatter the seven enclosures and attain Kṛṣṇa incessantly.
Having attained his heart's desire through the service of the Śrī Bhāgavata Saptāha, he, together with the Saptāha, perpetually expands creation again and again.
Viṣṇu also entreated the Supreme Person for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose, since even he had been appointed by Him for the protection of living beings.

The illustrious Viṣṇu said: "O Lord, I shall protect the subjects as is appropriate, through both the path of worldly engagement and the path of renunciation, by means of the application of action and knowledge. (29)
Whenever, in the course of time, there shall be a decline of the Dharma, I will indeed establish the Dharma through my incarnations at those very times.

To those who seek worldly enjoyments, I shall certainly grant the fruits of sacrifices and other rites; likewise, to those dispassionate ones who seek liberation, I shall grant the fivefold liberation.
How shall I protect even those who do not desire liberation? Tell me, how shall I protect both myself and my royal fortune?
Therefore, that primordial Puruṣa also instructed him on the Śrīmad Bhāgavata and said: "Recite this for the attainment of all your goals."
Then Viṣṇu, with a gracious soul, became capable of protecting the supreme truth through his splendor, month after month, as he remembered the Bhāgavata.
When Viṣṇu himself is the speaker and Lakṣmī is intent upon listening, then the hearing of the Bhāgavata occurs again and again within a single month.
When Lakṣmī herself speaks and Viṣṇu is intent on listening, the savoring of that nectar for two months is exceedingly beautiful.
Viṣṇu remains established in his office while Lakṣmī’s mind is free from anxiety; therefore, her enjoyment of the Bhāgavata shines forth most abundantly.
Then Rudra, who had previously been appointed to the office of destruction, also petitioned that Male Deity in order to increase his own power. (38)
Śrī Rudra said: "O God of gods, O my Lord, my powers exist for the constant, the occasional, as well as for the elemental dissolution."
But in the case of a final destruction, I possess no power; this is a source of great sorrow for me, and for that reason I entreat you. (40)
Śrī Bṛhaspati said: Nārāyaṇa gave the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam to him as well; and by its constant service, he conquered the quality of darkness (tamas).
By him the Bhāgavata narrative was served for the duration of one year; consequently, at the time of ultimate dissolution, Sadāśiva attained Śakti through him.
Uddhava said: O Guru, having heard this narrative regarding the majesty of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata and having obtained the Bhāgavata, I rejoiced after bowing down to him.
Then, adopting the Vaiṣṇava method, I have thoroughly cultivated the relish for the Śrīmad Bhāgavata within the span of a single month.
By that alone I became the beloved friend of Kṛṣṇa; then, I was appointed by Kṛṣṇa to the group of his own beloved women in Vraja.
While the gopīs were afflicted by the pain of separation, the message of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata was personally delivered through my mouth by Him who eternally sports [in Vṛndāvana]. (46)
Having obtained that according to my understanding, they were freed from separation; yet I did not know its secret, though its wonder was beheld.
When Brahmā and the other gods had departed after praying to Kṛṣṇa for residence in heaven, Kṛṣṇa himself bestowed that secret upon me in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam.
In front of the root of the Aśvattha tree, he established that firm [devotion] in me; because of that, having gone to Badarī, I dwell here among the creepers of Vraja.
Therefore, I always remain here in this Nārada-kuṇḍa by my own will; for the manifestation of Kṛṣṇa to devotees arises from the Śrīmad Bhāgavata.
Therefore, for the sake of their purpose, I shall proclaim the Śrīmad Bhāgavata; in this matter, you yourself shall act as my assistant. (51)
The illustrious Sūta said: Having heard that, Viṣṇurāta bowed down to Uddhava and spoke. Śrī Parīkṣit said: "O servant of Hari, you must perform the recitation of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam. (52)
"I am to be commanded as to what must be done, and likewise, I shall be your helper in this matter. Śrī Sūta said: Having heard these words, Uddhava, with a joyful mind, spoke. (53)
Uddhava said: "Once Śrī Kṛṣṇa has departed from the earth, the powerful Kali will create great obstacles whenever a virtuous undertaking is about to take place. (54)
Therefore, go forth on a conquest of the quarters and carry out the suppression of Kali; as for me, however, having adopted the Vaiṣṇava way of life, I shall do so within a mere month.
Having spread the savor of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata with your assistance, I shall lead these [souls] to the eternal abode of the Enemy of Madhu.
Śrī Sūta said: Having heard those words, the king was both delighted and anxious with thought; he then made known his own intention to Uddhava.
Śrī Parīkṣit said: "O father, abiding by your word, I shall indeed suppress Kali; but how will the attainment of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata come about for me? (58)
"But I, who have sought refuge at the soles of your feet, am worthy of your favor. Śrī Sūta said: Having heard these words, Uddhava spoke to him once again.
Uddhava said: O King, you should not entertain any anxiety whatsoever; for you alone possess the primary qualification for the scripture of the Blessed Lord.
Until this time, men devoted to ritual action have for the most part not even heard news of the Bhāgavata.
By your grace, many men on the field of battle in Bhārata will attain eternal happiness upon obtaining the Śrīmad Bhāgavata. || 62 ||
The venerable sage Śrī Śuka, who is the very embodiment of the Delight of Nanda, will undoubtedly cause you to hear the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam.
By that means, O King, you shall eternally attain the abode of the Lord of Vraja; thereafter, the circulation of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata shall take place upon the earth.
"Therefore, O Indra among kings, go and perform the subduing of Kali. Śrī Sūta said: Having been addressed thus, the king circumambulated him and departed for the conquest of the quarters.
Vajra, however, having appointed Pratibāhu as the lord of his own kingdom, remained right there together with the Mothers, his heart intent upon the Lord of the Bhāgavatas.
Then, for one month in Vṛndāvana near Govardhana, the tasting of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata was initiated by Uddhava.
While that was being savored, the pastimes of Hari, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, as well as Kṛṣṇa himself, shone forth everywhere. (68)
Then everyone beheld themselves situated within him; Vajra, however, saw himself at the lotus-like foot of Kṛṣṇa on the right side.
Released from the separation from Kṛṣṇa, her own self shone upon that ground; and those mothers of his likewise [shone] while Kṛṣṇa illuminated the night of the Rāsa dance.
Beholding themselves in the moon in the form of the radiance of its digits, they were filled with wonder; freed from the disease of separation from their beloved, they returned to their own abode.
And all those others who were there entered into another eternal pastime; they immediately became invisible to the people of the mundane world.
In the groves of Govardhana, among the cows, and in Vṛndāvana and other places, they rejoice eternally with Kṛṣṇa and are seen by those intent on divine love.
Śrī Sūta said: Whoever hears or even recites this account of attaining the Blessed One, for that person indeed the attainment of the Blessed One and the destruction of suffering arise. (74)

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata," within the dialogue between Parīkṣit and Uddhava, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The venerable sages said: Well done, O Sūta! Live long; may you live long as you thus instruct us. We have heard from your mouth the unprecedented majesty of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata.
O Sūta, now tell me the nature and the means of proof of that [Brahman], as well as the injunction for its hearing; and likewise, tell me the characteristics of its speaker and of the listener.
Śrī Sūta said: Now, the glorious Bhāgavata and the glorious Bhagavān always possess one and the same essential nature, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Know that to be indeed the Bhāgavata which is the speech of those devotees attached to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, wherein His sweetness is fully revealed. (4)
Know that the Bhāgavata is that speech which is devoted to the fourfold limbs of knowledge, discernment, and devotion, and which is capable of crushing illusion.
Who indeed knows the measure of that infinite one whose nature is the Imperishable? That direction [of his location] was shown by Hari to Brahmā in four verses.
O Brahmins, it is precisely those [beings] such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others who, by virtue of plunging into that infinity, are capable of bringing about one's own desired ends. (7)
And for the benefit of humans whose intellects are of limited scope and so forth, that dialogue between Parīkṣit and Śuka which was proclaimed by Vyāsa [is here presented]. (8)
This work known as the Bhāgavata, consisting of eighteen thousand verses, is the supreme refuge for those seized by the crocodile of the Kali age.
Now, the listeners who take refuge in the glorious narrations of Viṣṇu are examined; listeners are considered to be of two kinds: the superior and the inferior. (10)

The peacock, the *cātaka* bird, the swan, the parrot, fish, and so forth are proclaimed as superior; whereas the wolf, the *bhūruṇḍa* bird, the bull, the camel, and so forth are declared to be inferior. (11)
But he who, through total indifference to everything else, is devoted to the study of the scriptures of Kṛṣṇa, is like a cātaka bird that has lost the water from a cloud. || 12 ||
A listener who extracts the essence from various things heard is like a swan; just as a swan takes the pure milk from water that has become one with it.
Śuka spoke well and with moderation, gladdening Vyāsa and his listeners; for Śuka, being so well-instructed, spoke just as he would to his teacher and those standing by his side.
Never making a sound while tasting the flavor, the listener becomes as attentive as a fish in the ocean of milk. (15)

He who cries out in a discordant way to those connoisseurs and listeners is indeed a wolf; like a wolf in the forest that attacks deer, he assails those who are absorbed in the aesthetic flavor of the flute’s sound.
One who merely instructs others but does not practice himself after having heard the teaching is like the bird called Bhūruṇḍa on the peak of the Himalayas. || 17 ||

One whose intellect is blinded by the distinction between the essential and the non-essential grasps at everything he hears, just as a bull consumes both sweet grapes and dregs without making any distinction. 18.
That camel which would take pleasure in the opposite while emitting a sweet sound, would rather graze on neem, abandoning even a mango tree laden with fruit. (19)
There are also many other distinctions between the two, such as the bee and the donkey, which are to be understood through their respective behaviors arising from their respective natures. (20)

He who, having stood before [the teacher] and bowed according to the rules, desiring to hear the pastimes of Hari while abandoning all other talk—being highly proficient, humble, with palms joined in reverence, a disciple full of trust, intent on reflection, devoted to inquiry, pure, and always dear to the people of Kṛṣṇa—is indeed declared by the teachers to be a true listener. (21)

He whose mind is like that of the Blessed One, who is free from expectations, compassionate toward the wretched, skillful in awakening others in many ways, and a speaker honored by the sages; || 22 ||
Now, O Brahmins, hear the procedure for the service of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata on the land of Bhārata, by which there shall be a continuous succession of happiness.
The service of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam is to be known as fourfold: rājasic, sāttvic, tāmasic, and likewise devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). || 24 ||
That which is performed for seven days like a sacrifice—with exertion, haste, and joy—is rājasa; it is characterized by many offerings and the like, and is outwardly splendid.
Whether for a month or even for a season, the hearing [of this] is endowed with sweetness; it is sattvic, effortless, and increases all forms of bliss. (26)
That which is performed for a year with dullness and lacking faith, yet accompanied by both forgetfulness and remembrance, is the tamasic practice; and that too bestows happiness.
Having abandoned the rigid adherence to rules regarding years, months, and days, service performed at all times through pure loving devotion is considered to be beyond the gunas (nirguṇa). 28.

Even in the account concerning Pārīkṣita, that [state] is proclaimed as being devoid of qualities; therein is the narrative of seven days, corresponding to the number of days remaining in his lifespan.
Otherwise, whether it be threefold or even devoid of qualities, the service of hearing the Lord’s teachings should be performed according to one's desire and in whatever manner possible.
For those who are intensely longing for the taste of exclusive devotion to the pastimes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and who have no desire even for liberation, the Bhāgavata is their wealth.
Even those who are weary of the torments of saṃsāra and desire liberation—for them, this medicine for existence should be practiced with effort in the Kali age.
And for those who delight in sense objects and long for worldly pleasures, their accomplishment now in the Kali age comes only through the path of ritual action.
Because of the absence of the wealth of capability and discernment, it is extremely difficult to attain; therefore, even by them, the narrative of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata should be cultivated.
The narrative of the Bhāgavata bestows wealth, sons, wives, vehicles and the like, fame, homes, freedom from rivalry, and sovereignty.
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures here in this world that are desired by the mind, those who associate with the Śrīmad Bhāgavata go at the end to the abode of Śrī Hari.
One should serve those who speak of the Bhāgavata and those who delight in hearing it, both with one's body and with one's wealth. (37)
By virtue of his grace, he too shall engage in the service of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata; for everything other than Śrī Kṛṣṇa is designated as "wealth. (38)
The listener and the speaker are considered to be of two types: one who seeks Kṛṣṇa and one who seeks wealth. When the listener is like the speaker, happiness increases therein. (39)
But when both are reversed, there is a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa) and a failure of the fruit; however, for those who seek Kṛṣṇa, success occurs even with delay. (40)
For one who seeks wealth, success comes through the fulfillment of ritual injunctions; but for one who seeks Kṛṣṇa—even if devoid of merit—pure love alone is the supreme injunction. (41)
Indeed, one who possesses desire must personally perform this rite until its completion; having bathed, performed the daily obligatory duties, and sipped the water from the feet of Hari. (42)
Having worshipped both the book and the teacher with ritual offerings, one should joyfully either recite or listen to the Śrīmad Bhāgavata.
One should observe silence during the meal, eating either milk or sacrificial food (haviṣya); one should maintain celibacy, sleep on the ground, and avoid anger, greed, and the like. (44)

At the conclusion of the discourse, one should perform recitation daily; at the completion, one should observe a vigil. Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should satisfy them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās). || 45 ||
Having given garments, ornaments, and other gifts to the preceptor, one should also present a cow; when this rite has been performed in this manner, one obtains the desired fruit.
Wives, homes, sons, kingdom, wealth, and whatever else is desired—none of these shine here; rather, the pursuit of desire is a mere mockery. (47)
The scripture Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, which eternally brings about the attainment of Kṛṣṇa and bestows the fruit of the bliss of divine love, was spoken by a parrot in the Kali age.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Śrīmad Bhāgavata-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now begins the glorification of the greatness of the month of Vaiśākha: Having bowed down to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Jaya. (1)
Sūta said: Once again, the king questioned Nārada regarding the meritorious greatness of Mādhava, concerning Brahmā, the supreme lord, who was born from the limbs [of the Lord]. || 1 ||
Ambarīṣa said: O Brahman, I have previously heard from you the true majesty of all the months, exactly as it was spoken by you at that time.
"Vaiśākha is certainly the most excellent month among all these months; therefore, [I shall describe] the greatness of Mādhava in detail. (3)
O Brahman, I have a great curiosity to hear how he became dear to Viṣṇu, and what are the duties dear to Viṣṇu in the month beloved by Mādhava?
In that regard, what duties dear to Viṣṇu must be performed by him? What is the gift, what is its fruit, and with whom as the object should one practice these?
"With which substances should this Mādhava be worshipped at the arrival of the month of Mādhava? O Nārada, explain this in detail to me, who am full of faith. (6)
Śrī Nārada said: Formerly, when questioned by me, Brahmā explained the ancient duties pertaining to the months—those which were previously proclaimed to Śrī by the Supreme Soul.
Then the months were distinguished as Kārttika and Māgha; among them, Mādhava established Vaiśākha as the best of months.
Like a mother to all living beings, he is the eternal bestower of what is desired; through gifts, sacrifices, vows, and ritual ablutions, he is the destroyer of all sins.

He is the essence of the performance of dharma-sacrifices, the essence of austerity, and is worshipped by the gods; he is like the Vedic knowledge among all sciences, and like the syllable Om among mantras.
Among trees he was like the celestial wish-fulfilling tree, among cows like the cow of plenty; among all serpents he was like Śeṣa, and among birds like Garuḍa.
Just as Viṣṇu is among the gods, as the Brāhmaṇa is among the social classes, as life itself is among dear things, and as a wife is among friends; || 12 ||
Just as the Gaṅgā is among rivers, as the sun is among luminous bodies, as the discus is among weapons, and as gold is among metals; || 13 ||
Just as Rudra is among the Vaiṣṇavas, and as the Kaustubha is among jewels, so too is Vaiśākha the most excellent among the months that are causes of dharma.
In this world, there is nothing equal to this for securing the pleasure of Viṣṇu: namely, being intent on the Vaiśākha bath during the month of Meṣa (Aries) before the rising of the sun.
The Blessed Lord, accompanied by Lakṣmī, takes great delight in that [tree], just as the gratification of living beings arises solely through food. (16)
In the same way, Viṣṇu is undoubtedly pleased by the Vaiśākha bath; seeing people devoted to the Vaiśākha bath, he rejoices.
By that alone, he is liberated from sins and honored in the world of Viṣṇu; having bathed once when the sun is situated in Aries, and having performed his morning rites at dawn.
Freed from great sins, he shall attain union with Viṣṇu, even if he performs only a single step for the purpose of bathing during the month of Vaiśākha.
He undoubtedly obtains the fruit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices; or else, even one with a deceitful mind may merely form a mental resolve.
He too shall undoubtedly obtain the merit of a hundred sacrifices, who goes for the distance of a bow’s length to bathe when the sun has entered Aries.

Freed from all bonds, he shall attain union (sāyujya) with Viṣṇu. Whatever holy places exist in the three worlds and those situated within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), [all are attained by him]. || 22 ||
O Indra among kings, all those sins exist within even a small amount of external water; as long as they remain there, the recorded sins roar under the command of Yama.

O King, as long as a living being does not perform a bath in the water during the month of Vaiśākha, all the deities of the sacred fords and other holy sites [remain dissatisfied] throughout that month of Vaiśākha.
O King, she is always present there, having taken refuge in the water outside, from the time of sunrise until six ghaṭikās have passed.

O King of kings, they remain there by the command of Viṣṇu out of a desire for the welfare of men; however, after bestowing a most terrible curse upon those men who do not come [to bathe], they return to their own abode. Therefore, one should perform the ritual bath.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Vaiśākha Bath, Preceded by the Praise of the Month of Vaiśākha," in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa, within the *Vaiśākhamāsamāhātmya* of the second *Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa*, in the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: There is no month equal to Mādhava, no age equal to Kṛta, no scripture equal to the Vedas, and no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā. (1)
There is no gift equal to water; there is no happiness equal to that of a wife; there is no wealth equal to agriculture; and there is no gain greater than life. (2)
There is no austerity equal to fasting, no happiness higher than giving, no dharma equal to compassion, and no light equal to the eye. (3)
There is no satisfaction equal to eating; nor is there trade equal to agriculture. There is no friend equal to righteousness; nor is there fame equal to truth. (4)
The wise know that there is no source of prosperity equal to health, no protector superior to Keśava, and nothing in the world as purifying as Mādhava.
The month of Mādhava is always most excellent and dear to the one who lies upon Śeṣa; he who passes this month, so beloved by Mādhava, without observing a vow, [is lost].
Excluded from all dharmas, he quickly goes to the womb of an animal—he among mortals who have reached Mādhava without observing the vows.
O best of the upholders of dharma, for those who have made no restriction regarding the consumption of available foods during the month of Mādhava, their sacrifices and charitable works are in vain.
One certainly attains union with Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt. Although there are many other vows and various religious observances here in this world, [this is the foremost].
Those acts which cause physical exhaustion and lead to rebirth—by merely bathing in Vaiśākha, one is not born again on this earth. (10)
Whatever merit is found in all acts of giving and whatever fruit is obtained at all sacred fords—that fruit one attains by the gift of water during the month of Mādhava.
One who desires prosperity and is unable to give water should always provide instruction to others; this is more beneficial than all other forms of giving.
On one side all gifts, and on the other side the gift of water; when placed upon a scale, the gift of water was previously declared superior. (13)
Indeed, that mortal who provides a water-station for travelers on the road, having delivered ten million members of his lineage, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
O best of kings, there is no doubt that the gift of a water-shed (prapā) brings supreme delight to the gods, the ancestors, and the sages; this is the truth. (15)
By providing water for drinking, those who are exhausted by the fatigue of the journey are satisfied; by that act, the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others—are also gratified.
O King, in the month of Vaiśākha, one should offer water to those who desire water, an umbrella to those desiring shade, and a fan to those desiring a fan. (17)
To a Brāhmaṇa who has a family, when the month of Mādhava has arrived, the gift of water, an umbrella, and a fan is especially distinguished.
And by not giving a water-pot, one is born on earth as a cātaka bird. || 19 ||
O King of kings, he who gives cool water to a high-souled person afflicted by thirst shall obtain the merit of ten thousand Rājasūya sacrifices by that act alone.
Whoever fans with a fan a Brahmin afflicted by the heat and fatigue of the summer, becomes free from sin by that act alone and shall become the lord of birds.
O King, he who does not give a fan to a twice-born man in the month of Vaiśākha encounters only hells, beset by hundreds of wind-related diseases.
He who, even with a cloth, fans an excellent twice-born man weary on the road, is thereby liberated and shall attain union with Viṣṇu.
He who, with a pure mind, gives even a palm-leaf fan, having shaken off all sins, goes to the world of Brahmā. (24)
A person who does not offer a fan—which instantly removes fatigue and is meritorious—will experience the torments of hell and be born on earth as a miserable wretch. (25)
O Lord of Men, for the sake of pacifying internal and other forms of suffering, one who dwells [in this world] should diligently offer an umbrella during the month of Vaiśākha. (26)
That man who provides no shelter during the month of Vaiśākha, which is dear to Mādhava, is born on earth as a most cruel, shadowless Piśāca.
He who gives divine sandals in the month of Mādhava, which are dear to Mādhava, goes to the world of Viṣṇu, having set aside the messengers of Yama.
He who gives footwear during the month of Vaiśākha at the arrival of Mādhava shall have neither a world of hell nor any worldly afflictions.
He who gives a pair of sandals to a Brahmin who asks for them shall undoubtedly become a king on earth for ten million births.
He who constructs a shelter for the destitute on the road to relieve their fatigue—even Brahmā is unable to describe the fruit of his merit. (31)
If one feeds a Brāhmaṇa guest who has arrived at midday, even Brahmā could not determine the limit of the merit resulting from that act. 32.
O lord of men, the gift of food provides immediate nourishment for human beings; therefore, no gift equal to food is found in the worlds. (33)
Even Brahmā is unable to describe the fruit of the merit belonging to him who offers hospitality to a Brahmin exhausted by the journey.
Wives, children, home, and the like, as well as clothing, ornaments, and finery—these are unbearable for a man who does not eat, but they are certainly bearable for one who has eaten. (35)
Therefore, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to food; for by whomsoever it was not given in the month of Vaiśākha to a Brahmin weary on his journey. (36)
That person becomes a piśāca on earth and eats nothing but his own flesh; therefore, food should be given to a twice-born man according to one's means.
O protector of the earth, the giver of food causes one to forget even his mother, father, and other kin; therefore, those who dwell in the three worlds praise food.
Mothers and fathers are merely the causes of birth; however, the wise declare in this world that he who provides food is the true father. (39)
O conqueror of enemies, all holy fords, all deities, and all dharmas abide in the giver of food. (40)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of Gifts," in the *Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya* (The Greatness of the Month of Vaiśākha), within the *Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa* (The Section on Viṣṇu), in the *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa.
Nārada said: "O best of the twice-born, that mortal who indeed gives a couch to a distinguished brahmin—upon which he may lie at ease and comfortably, attended by cool breezes—" (1)
For when the body has become a means for accomplishing the Dharma, one attains freedom from disease; having given that [body], one casts off all suffering and becomes free from defilement.
In the month of Vaiśākha, for those twice-born who are exhausted and tormented by the heat, one attains the unbroken state that is difficult even for yogins to reach.
O lord of men, having given a divine couch that removes fatigue, one never suffers in this world from birth, death, old age, and the like.
Having taken [the water], wherever the Brahmin lies down, established in his livelihood, all the sin—whether committed knowingly or unknowingly—is transferred to him as he sits. || 5 ||
O Indra among kings, he goes to dissolution like camphor in fire; that man certainly attains the liberation of Brahman upon his bed. || 6 ||
Whoever should give a bedding in the month of Vaiśākha, which is dear to those who delight in bathing, shall indeed be endowed with all enjoyments in that very same birth.
Surely he continues with his lineage unassailed by diseases and other afflictions; he attains long life, supreme health, fame, and fortitude.
Within his family, for a hundred generations, no one shall be born who is unrighteous; having enjoyed all pleasures, he will then pass away.
Having shaken off all evil, he attains the Brahman-nirvāṇa. He who gives a pillow to a learned Brāhmaṇa, the best of the twice-born— || 10 ||
Without whom men can never find peaceful sleep anywhere, he becomes the refuge of all and enjoys sovereignty upon the earth. (11)
Furthermore, O Indra among kings, he is born happy, wealthy, and devoted to dharma for seven lifetimes, becoming victorious in every respect.
Afterwards, joined by seven generations of his lineage, he is fit for becoming one with Brahman; this applies even to one who gives a mat made of grass or some other kind of mat. (13)
There Viṣṇu himself lies, where the Supreme Lord resides; just as wool placed within water is never dissolved by the water.
Likewise, a living being moving through saṃsāra is not bound by it; like one who is attached to his seat or bed but remains happy everywhere because he possesses a mat, so too is the yogin. 15.
Whoever should give a mat or a blanket for the purpose of a bed in a place of refuge, by that alone one shall be liberated; there is no need for deliberation on this point. (16)
Through sleep, suffering is diminished; through sleep, fatigue is diminished. That sleep of one resting upon a mat certainly brings about happiness. (17)
O King, he who gives a woolen blanket in the month of Vaiśākha at the arrival of Mādhava lives for a hundred years, freed from both untimely death and death by the appointed time.
One should give very fine clothing to an eminent brahmin who is emaciated by the heat; such a person attains a full lifespan and the supreme goal in the hereafter. || 19 ||
Therefore, by giving divine camphor, which removes all suffering, to a twice-born man, one attains liberation and finds the cessation of misery. || 20 ||
And he who gives flowers and saffron to a twice-born man shall become a sovereign king who brings all the world under his control.
Having enjoyed the pleasures of sons, grandsons, and others, one may attain liberation; sandalwood instantly removes the torment residing in the skin and bones.
Having given that which is scented with water—whether it be a reed-mat, a wooden seat, or a mat of kusha grass—one who is liberated from the threefold suffering shall attain liberation. (23)
O Indra among kings, he who possesses the assistance of the gods shall attain the destruction of sins and the destruction of suffering through all his enjoyments, and thereby reach final liberation.
One who knows the duties of Vaiśākha should offer yellow orpiment and musk; being liberated from the threefold affliction, he attains supreme nirvāṇa. || 25 ||
He who offers betel leaf with camphor when the Sun is in Aries, having enjoyed the happiness of a sovereign ruler, attains supreme liberation.
The man who gives a *śatapatrī* and a *yūthī* in the month of Meṣa becomes a sovereign ruler of the whole earth and subsequently attains liberation. || 27 ||
Whoever offers a ketakī or even a mallikā flower at the arrival of the month of Mādhava attains liberation, by the command of the Subduer of Madhu.
O King, listen now to the fruit of the merit of him who gives fragrant betel nut (pūgīphala) and a coconut fruit to a twice-born man. || 29 ||
For seven births he shall be a Brahmin, wealthy and a master of the Vedas; thereafter, accompanied by seven generations of his lineage, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
O King, I am not able to describe the fruit of the merit of one who, having constructed a rest pavilion, gives it to a twice-born man. (31)
He who quickly causes a pavilion with beautiful shade to be constructed, strewn with sand and provided with a water-shed, shall indeed become a lord of the world. || 32 ||
He who constructs a road, a garden, a pond, a well, or even a pavilion is a righteous soul; what need has he for sons to achieve his purpose? (33)
A well, a pond, a garden, a pavilion, a water-shed, the practice of the true Dharma, and a son—these are said to be the sevenfold lineage.
In the absence of even one of these, human beings do not ascend higher. [These are: listening to the true scriptures, pilgrimage to sacred fords, and association with virtuous people. (35)
The gift of water, the gift of food, the planting of the Aśvattha tree, and likewise a son—these seven are known as the "excessive gifts" by those who possess supreme knowledge. (36)
One who lacks a lineage does not attain the worlds, even after performing hundreds of righteous deeds; therefore, one should seek a lineage, for through lineages one may proceed to the highest state.
Neither for cattle, nor for birds, nor for wild animals, nor even for trees, does happiness reach the upper worlds; what then can be said of human beings? (38)
Offering excellent betel, combined with areca nuts, betel leaves, camphor, and agallochum. (39)
One is liberated from all bodily sins; of this there is no doubt. The giver of betel-leaf certainly attains fame, fortitude, and prosperity. (40)

A sick person, having given it, shall become free from disease; one who is already healthy shall attain liberation. He who gives buttermilk, which destroys the heat of fever, in the month of Vaiśākha— || 41 ||
One who possesses knowledge and wealth is born upon this earth; of this there is no doubt. There is no gift comparable to buttermilk during the hot seasons. 42.
Therefore, buttermilk mixed with the juice of citron and seasoned with excellent salt should be given to a twice-born man exhausted by the journey. (43)

He who, having given that which destroys thirst and aversion to food, may attain liberation; and he who, for the sake of cooling the heat, should give curd and sugar-candy in the month of Vaiśākha— [44]
O protector of the earth, I am unable to describe the fruit of the merit of one who would offer divine rice grains to her who is beloved by Madhusūdana. (45)

He shall obtain a full lifespan and receive the fruit of all sacrifices; he who gives cow-derived ghee—the very form of splendor—to a twice-born man, having attained the fruit of the horse-sacrifice, rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu.
In the month of Vaiśākha, when the sun is in Aries, one who offers rice mixed with jaggery shall certainly dwell in Śvetadvīpa, liberated from all sins.
And whoever gives a stalk of sugarcane to a Brāhmaṇa in the evening for the sake of allaying the heat of the day, his merit is infinite. || 48 ||
By giving a cooling drink in the evening during the month of Vaiśākha for the sake of relieving fatigue, one is liberated from all sins and attains union with Viṣṇu.
One should give a fruitful beverage to a twice-born man in the evening during the month of Meṣa; by that, the ancestors undoubtedly partake of the drinking of nectar (sudhā).
In the month of Vaiśākha, one who offers a refreshing drink mixed with well-ripened mango fruits will certainly see all their sins destroyed. (51)
Whoever should give a jar full of beverages on the new moon day of Caitra has, without a doubt, performed a hundred Śrāddhas at Gayā. || 52 ||

On the new moon day of Caitra, a person who gives a water-pot filled with refreshing drinks, combined with musk, camphor, jasmine, and uśīra grass, dedicated to the ancestors, shall become the possessor of ninety-six [villages].

Nārada said: Anointing with oil, sleeping during the day, eating from a bell-metal vessel, sleeping on a bedstead, bathing at home, and the consumption of forbidden food—[these are to be avoided]. || 1 ||

In the month of Vaiśākha, one established in the vow should avoid these eight things: eating twice a day and eating at night. Furthermore, he who, being firm in his vow, eats from a lotus leaf in Vaiśākha [attains great merit].

He, liberated from sin, goes to the world of Viṣṇu. In the month of Vaiśākha, at midday, one should perform the washing of the feet of twice-born men learned in the Vedas; that is the vow known as Suvratottama.
He who, having seated upon a pleasant seat a twice-born man exhausted by the journey who has come to his own home at midday, and having performed the washing of his feet; || 5 ||
Having placed those waters upon one's head, all bonds are shattered; one certainly becomes as if bathed in all the holy fords, such as the Gaṅgā and others.
If one passes the month of Vaiśākha without bathing or eating at improper times, he will enter the womb of a she-donkey and subsequently become a mule.
Even a man who is firm-limbed, free from disease, and otherwise healthy, may enter the womb of a Cāṇḍāla woman if he bathes at home during the month of Vaiśākha.
O King of kings, he who does not perform an external bath in the month of Vaiśākha when the sun is situated in Aries shall go through a hundred births as a dog.
He by whom Vaiśākha is passed without bathing and without giving shall surely become a Piśāca; therefore, one should depart from non-Vaiśākha.
He who, with a greedy mind, does not give water and food in the month of Vaiśākha, will undoubtedly obtain neither the destruction of sin nor the destruction of suffering. || 11 ||
He who, devoted to Viṣṇu, performs a ritual bath in a river during the month of Vaiśākha, is liberated from the sins accumulated over three lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
One should perform a bath in a river flowing into the ocean at dawn when the sun has risen; one is liberated from the sins accumulated over seven lifetimes at that very moment. (13)
The person who performs a bath at dawn in the seven Gaṅgās is liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million births; of this there is no doubt.
The Jāhnavī, Vṛddhagaṅgā, Kālindī, Sarasvatī, Kāverī, Narmadā, and Veṇī are proclaimed as the seven Gaṅgās. || 15 ||
Whoever performs the morning bath during Vaiśākha in natural pools (devakhāta) is liberated from the sins committed since birth; of this there is no doubt. || 16 ||
O Great King, when the month of Vaiśākha has arrived, whoever performs an immersion in ponds in the morning effects the destruction of great sins. (17)

It is certain that all rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, reside even in the waters outside [the body] that are as small as a cow’s footprint; knowing this, one obtains a fruit superior to all sacred fords (tīrtha). || 18 ||

O King, just as milk is superior to its essence (the watery portion), curd is superior to milk, and ghee is superior to curd, so too is the month of Ūrja (Kārttika) superior [to all other months]. || 19 ||
Māgha is superior to Kārtika, and Vaiśākha is indeed superior to Māgha; dharma performed in that month increases like the seed of a banyan tree.
Whether a man be wealthy or extremely poor, or even one who is dependent on others, he should give to the twice-born whatever object he obtains.
Roots, tubers, fruits, vegetables, salt, molasses, jujube, leaves, water, and buttermilk—these lead to infinite [merit].
One never obtains what has not been given, even by Brahmā and the other gods of the three worlds.

For one who is devoid of giving becomes destitute; and due to this lack of possessions, he commits evil deeds. From evil, he inevitably goes to hell. Therefore, one who desires happiness must give at that time. (24)

Just as a house, though endowed with all virtues, is unattractive if it lacks furnishings, so too all religious duties performed throughout the months go in vain if they are devoid of Vaiśākha. || 25 ||

Just as a maiden, though endowed with all auspicious marks, is indeed not one whose husband will live [if she lacks the specific mark], so too, O King, even a ritual performed with all its parts and limbs is known to be in vain if it is devoid of Vaiśākha.

Just as virtues are in vain when devoid of compassion, so too are ritual acts without the Vaiśākha dharma; just as a vegetable dish, though endowed with every excellence, does not please the palate when lacking salt. (27)

Likewise, merit devoid of Vaiśākha is not to be cultivated by the virtuous, nor is it a cause for attaining fruit; just as a beautiful woman, though adorned with ornaments, does not shine if she is lacking a garment, so too the collection of rites, even when well-performed by men, does not shine if it is devoid of that month of Madhu.
Therefore, by every possible effort, dharma must indeed be practiced by any living being whatsoever during the month of Vaiśākha; this is the certain conclusion. || 29 ||
Aiming for Madhusūdana, when the sun is situated in Aries, one should bathe in the morning and worship Viṣṇu; otherwise, one shall go to hell.
A certain king named Mahīratha, though attached to sensual desires, conquered his senses and went personally to Vaikuṇṭha by means of the practice of bathing in the month of Vaiśākha.
The month of Vaiśākha is fruitful, having Madhusūdana as its presiding deity; it yields greater fruit than pilgrimages to sacred sites, austerities, sacrifices, gifts, and burnt offerings.
The prayer mantra: "O Madhusūdana, Lord of Gods, while the sun is in Aries during the month of Vaiśākha, I shall perform my morning bath; O Mādhava, grant that it be free from obstacles. (33)

The Arghya Mantras: In the month of Vaiśākha, when the sun is in Aries, one devoted to the morning bath [should say]: "I shall offer this water of honor (arghya) to you; accept it, O Madhusūdana. (34)
O all rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, and all sacred fords and lakes, accept this arghya offered by me; be fully propitious.
O Ṛṣabha, punisher of sinners, you are Yama, the one who looks upon all with equanimity; accept this water offering given by me, and grant me the fruit as it has been described.
Having thus offered the arghya, one should thereafter perform the ritual bath; then, having put on two garments and performed all the rites in their entirety, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped Madhusūdana with flowers produced in the month of Mādhava, and having heard the divine narrative of Viṣṇu that extols this very month; || 38 ||
Freed from the sins accumulated over ten million births, one shall attain liberation.
He is never wearied on earth, nor in heaven, nor in the netherworld; he is never again born in a womb anywhere, nor does he ever become a suckling infant once more.
He who eats from bell-metal in Vaiśākha, who has not heard sacred stories, who does not bathe, and who does not give gifts, goes only to the hells. (41)
The sin of a thousand killings of Brahmins might somehow be pacified; however, that sin of one who has not bathed in Vaiśākha never departs.
With one's own body acting with independence in the water, and with one's own tongue, one should utter the two syllables "Ha-ri. (43)
If that lowest of men does not perform the morning bath in Vaiśākha, he has reached death even while living; of this there is no doubt. (44)
If a foolish-minded person does not worship Madhusūdana with any means whatsoever during the month of Mādhava, he shall attain the womb of a sow.

He who worships Madhusūdana with tulasī leaves during the month of Vaiśākha shall become a sovereign emperor and enjoy pleasures for ten million births; thereafter, accompanied by ten million kinsmen, he shall attain union with Viṣṇu.

One should serve Viṣṇu through various paths of devotion and religious observances; with a mind focused on no other, one should constantly meditate upon Him, whether as possessing attributes (saguṇa) or as devoid of attributes (nirguṇa).

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Duties of Vaiśākha," in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa within the *Vaiśākhamāsamāhātmya*, in the second section (*Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ambarīṣa said: Vaiśākha is superior to all religious duties and even to the duties of austerity; how did it become greater than all other months and even greater than acts of charity? (1)
Nārada said: O highly wise one, I shall tell you that; listen and be single-minded. At the end of the kalpa, Viṣṇu, the king of gods and the great lord, lies upon Śeṣa.
This multitude of worlds residing within his belly lies in the ocean of dissolution; for though manifold, it has attained oneness through the powers of his yogic illusion.
Then, at the end of a moment, awakened by the Vedas, that ocean of compassion provided protection for the multitudes of living beings within his womb.
He set his mind upon creating the world in order to bring about the attainment of the fruits of various karmas; from his navel there arose a golden lotus, the refuge of the universe.
He brought forth Brahmā, known as the Vairāja Puruṣa; in him, the Blessed One created the fourteen worlds.

[He saw] many diverse multitudes of living beings with various dispositions and latent tendencies, as well as the three qualities, primordial nature, the worldly boundaries, and their presiding lords.
He established the divisions of the social classes and stages of life, as well as the formulation of dharma, together with the four Vedas, the Tantras, and likewise the Smṛtis.
In ancient times, the Great Lord Maheśvara, whose very nature is his own command, appointed the sages as promoters of the teachings for the protection of Dharma through the Purāṇas and Itihāsas.

All the subjects, having faith in the dharmas set in motion by them—which arose from the distinctions of caste and stage of life—performed those duties appropriate to themselves that grant satisfaction to Viṣṇu.
But as they were proceeding to visit their own hermitages, the Lord, though imperishable and dwelling within their hearts, appeared visibly for the sake of testing them and to inspire awe.
"In this [age], people indeed perform virtuous deeds that are never deficient. Thinking thus, the wise Lord reflected upon what that time might be.
The rainy season was created by me because these subjects were perishing; therein, being afflicted by mud and other impediments, they could not perform their religious duties in full.
"Upon seeing them, there would be only anger; I would feel no satisfaction toward them. Let those looked upon by me not suffer; therefore, I shall look at them. (14)
Even in autumn, fulfillment does not arise from cultivation; some are attached to ripe fruits, while others are afflicted by rains. (15)
Seeing some who are afflicted by the cold, anger alone arises in me; and as I behold this deficiency, no satisfaction is born within me. (16)
They do not wish to be awakened when winter arrives at dawn; for when the sun rises in the morning, I become angry upon seeing them still unarisen. (17)
Likewise, even in the cold season, these creatures are distressed at dawn; for they are truly and constantly unable to obtain ripe fruits.
Furthermore, those who, afflicted by the cold, think "I shall bathe in the morning," would suffer a lapse in their religious duties and would never achieve spiritual fulfillment. (19)
Thinking, "This is not the time for contemplation," the Lord, agitated by such anxiety, considered the spring season to be the warder-off of all calamities.
For bathing, giving gifts, as well as sacrifice, ritual action, and even enjoyment, this season is indeed favorable for the performance of various religious duties.
Objects of wealth are certainly obtainable by embodied beings without effort; indeed, the satisfaction of embodied beings arises from whatever object may be at hand. (22)

With leaves, flowers, fruits, and other vegetables, as well as with pleasant words, garlands, betel, sandalwood paste, and so forth, and by washing his feet and other such services; || 26 ||

Viṣṇu, together with the gods, the lords of sages, and the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, showed it to Ramā.

Having waited together with men who have performed their rites of hospitality, she there grants the desired heart's wishes to those virtuous men.

Even there, the Lord will endure whatever lapse of ritual occurs among the mobile-souled ascetics during their stay in Māseya and other places.
Just as when the subjects and people of the countryside see a king who has arrived in their land, they attend upon him with great honors such as humility and the like; || 35 ||

Then the king will perceive that his revenue and so forth, though previously deficient, has become complete; and if it should even increase further, he will certainly grant what is desired, being well-pleased. (36)

To those men who offer worship, she grants their desired wishes; likewise, to those who do not, she completely takes away their wealth and other possessions.
This is indeed the time for the examination of Mahāviṣṇu, the protector of Dharma, the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow; therefore, this month is truly the most excellent.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Preeminence of Vaiśākha," in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa, within the *Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya* of the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: O Lord of the Earth, he who does not give water in the month of Vaiśākha to those distressed by thirst and exhausted by travel shall attain birth as an animal.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history, the most wonderful dialogue between a brahmin and a house lizard.
Formerly, in the lineage of Ikṣvāku, there was a king named Hemāṅga; he was devoted to Brahmanas, generous, a conqueror of enemies, and one who had mastered his senses.
As many particles of dust as there are on the earth, as many drops of water as there are, and as many stars as there are in the sky—so many cows did he give away.

By means of which the auspicious earth was made rich with sacrificial grass through performed sacrifices, and many twice-born ones were gratified with gifts of cattle, land, sesame seeds, gold, and other offerings.
Therefore, it has been heard that no gifts were given by him; thus, O King, he took even water alone with the thought that it was easily obtained.
What fruit would the giver obtain of that which was bestowed by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, upon Bodhi—a gift that is priceless and attainable from all sides? || 7 ||
Out of evil intent and through sophistical arguments, he did not give water to the twice-born; yet his statement, "There would be merit in giving what is difficult to obtain," was well-reasoned.

He honored those twice-born who were deformed, poor, and distressed for want of livelihood; yet he did not honor those Brahmins who were learned in the Vedas, knowers of reality, and exponents of the Absolute.
All people will honor those who are renowned with highly valuable offerings, as well as those twice-born who are destitute, ignorant, or physically impaired.
"What indeed is the refuge for the poor? Therefore, they are the objects of my compassion. Thinking thus, the man of wicked intellect gave something himself to those unworthy recipients. (11)
Due to that great fault, he experienced the state of a cātaka bird for three births; in one birth he was a vulture, and for seven births he became a dog.
