And at the gate of the house and the main street, there dwells a female insect-eater; by that evil-minded one, [the king] has been kept confined for eighty-seven years.
Once, at midday, the best of sages, renowned as Śrutadeva and well-versed in the Vedas, arrived at the house of the lord of Videha.
Seeing him, the lord of men rose up suddenly with joy; having honored him with the madhuparka offering and other rites, he performed the washing of his feet.
Then, at the time ordained by fate, the house-lizard was sprinkled with water being swiftly carried upon its head and with the droplets splashed from it.
Immediately regaining her memory and distressed by the recollection of her past deeds, she cried out, "Save me! Save me! to the Brahmin who had come to her home.
Hearing the cry of an animal born as a beast, the Brahmin was astonished and said: "O lizard, why do you cry out? By what karma have you come to this state? (19)
"Are you a god, some Puruṣa, a king, or perhaps a twice-born brahmin? Tell me, O illustrious one, who are you? Today I shall deliver you."
Thus addressed, that king spoke to the high-minded Śrutadeva: "I am born of the Ikṣvāku lineage and am well-versed in the Vedas and the Śāstras. (21)
As many particles of dust as there are on the earth, as many drops of water as there are, and as many stars as there are in the sky—so many cows did I bestow.
All sacrifices have been performed by me, works of public utility have been carried out by me, gifts have also been given, and the King of Dharma has been propitiated. (23)
Nevertheless, an evil rebirth befell me despite my lack of upward progress; three times I was born as a cātaka bird, and once as a vulture.
"O twice-born one, in a previous birth, while I was a dog for seven lifetimes, I was sprinkled with water from the washing of the feet by this king. (25)
"By some means, drops were cast far away and I was sprinkled by them; thereby the memory of my former births arose and all my sins were destroyed. (26)
Indeed, twenty-eight future births as an iguana are seen for me, ordained by fate; I am greatly terrified by those births.
"I do not perceive any cause for this; tell me that in detail. Thus addressed, the sage spoke, having understood through the eye of higher knowledge (vijñāna).
Listen, O King, I shall explain the cause of your birth in a wretched womb: you did not give water during the month of Vaiśākha, which is dear to Mādhava. (29)
Thinking that water was easily available and concluding it to be worthless, he did not provide it for the twice-born travelers, even during the heat of the summer season, out of ignorance. (30)
Likewise, having cast away a worthy recipient, one bestows it upon an unworthy one; for one does not offer oblations into ashes after casting away a blazing fire.

Among distinguished trees, the Aśvattha has attained the state of being worthy of service; yet, having abandoned the Tulasī, is the Bṛhatī now being worshipped? 33.
The state of being helpless does not serve as a determinant for being worthy of worship; for even those who are helpless, such as the lame and others, are merely objects of compassion. (34)
Those who are established in austerity, established in knowledge, and proficient in the Vedas and scriptures—being forms of Viṣṇu, they are always to be honored, and never others. (35)

Even among those, O Brahmins, the man of knowledge is always exceedingly dear to Viṣṇu; for even among men of knowledge, O King, Viṣṇu alone is eternally beloved. Therefore, the man of knowledge is always worthy of worship, being remembered as more worthy of worship than the most worshipful.
Contempt for those of virtuous conduct brings suffering both in this world and the next; indeed, service to great men is the cause for attaining the goals of human existence.
Just as even millions of those born blind do not see things as they truly are, so too the association of tens of thousands of dull-witted people does not yield any benefit.
Holy fords are not made of water, nor are gods made of clay or stone; they purify only after a long time, whereas the virtuous purify by their mere sight.
Those who are well-instructed by them never falter anywhere due to serving the virtuous; nor do they suffer from birth, death, old age, and the like, as if they were nourished by nectar. (40)
"Water was not given by you, nor were the virtuous served; therefore, O delighter of the Ikṣvākus, this miserable state has been attained by you. (41)
"In the month of Vaiśākha, I shall bestow upon you the merit performed by me for the sake of peace, by which you, O sage, will conquer the collection of karmas—past, future, and present. (42)
Having spoken thus and touched water, he bestowed that unsurpassed merit.
When the gift was bestowed by the Brāhmaṇa and the ritual bath was performed on that same day, all his sins were destroyed; he then abandoned that house-lizard. || 44 ||
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot and adorned with divine garlands, garments, and ornaments, he [disappeared] within the house of the King of Mithilā while all living beings were looking on.
Having joined his palms in reverence, circumambulated him, and prostrated, the king, permitted to depart and being praised by the immortals, went to heaven.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there for ten thousand years without weariness, he himself became the mighty lord Kākutstha in the lineage of Ikṣvāku.
The protector of the earth consisting of seven islands, devoted to Brahman, honored by the virtuous, a friend of the Lord of the Gods, he was a great lord who was indeed a portion of Viṣṇu.
Instructed by Vasiṣṭha, however, he performed all the delightful duties prescribed for the month of Vaiśākha; by that, all his inauspiciousness was destroyed.

This [rite] bestows longevity, fame, and nourishment; it destroys the flood of great sins and is the primary cause for the goals of human life. Indeed, by means of this, Viṣṇu is pleased.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the House Gecko," in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya (The Greatness of the Month of Vaiśākha) within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa (The Section on Viṣṇu), the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa.

Nārada said: Having witnessed that marvel, the King of Mithilā, the most eminent among those who know the Dharma, sat comfortably with palms joined in reverence and, filled with wonder, spoke these words. || 1 ||
The King of Mithilā said: "This great wonder has been seen, as well as the conduct of the virtuous, by which means the king, the joy of the Ikṣvākus, became liberated. (2)
Indeed, I have a great curiosity to hear that Dharma in detail; out of compassion for me, a man of faith, O learned one, please speak of it at length. (3)
Thus questioned by the king, the high-minded Śrutadeva, having exclaimed "Excellent! Excellent!", spoke to the best of monarchs.
Śrutadeva said: O best of royal sages, your intellect is perfectly resolved, since your mind is intent upon hearing the dharmas dear to Vāsudeva.
Without the merit accumulated over many lifetimes, the mind of no embodied being whatsoever is ever inclined toward discourse on the stories of Vāsudeva.
Since such a thought has arisen in you, a young prince and sovereign of kings, I consider you to be a pure devotee of the Lord and the best among the virtuous.
Therefore, O gentle one, I shall declare to you the auspicious Bhāgavata duties, by knowing which a living being is liberated from the bondage of birth and worldly existence.
Just as purity, just as bathing, just as the twilight rites and libations, just as the fire-sacrifice and the ancestral offerings, so indeed are the virtuous observances of Vaiśākha.

Without performing the religious duties in Vaiśākha, also known as Mādhava, one shall not ascend to higher realms; indeed, no dharma equal to that of Vaiśākha exists among all the varieties of dharma.
Indeed, there are many laws that, like subjects without a king, are plundered by calamities; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 11 ||
All the religious duties enjoined for Vaiśākha are indeed easy to perform: the offering of water-pots, the gift of drinking water, and the creation of shade along the road and so forth. (12)
The gift of sandals and shoes, as well as an umbrella and a fan, and the gift of honey mixed with sesame seeds and products of the cow, removes fatigue. (13)
The construction of ponds, wells, tanks, and so forth as resting places for travelers, as well as the gift of coconuts, sugarcane, camphor, and musk; (14)
Scented unguents, a bed, a couch, and likewise the gift [of them]; as well as the delightful mango fruit and the urvāruka as an elixir (rasāyana). || 15 ||
On the day of Damana, one should offer flowers; likewise, on the evening of Sāyā, molasses-water; on the full moon day (Pūrṇā), various kinds of food; and likewise, curd-rice every day.
The constant offering of betel-leaf, the karīraka fruit on the new moon day of Caitra, and the daily morning bath before the sun has risen; (17)
The worship of Madhusūdana, as well as listening to the sacred narrative, abstaining from oil massage, and likewise eating from leaves; 18.
At intervals, he should fan those afflicted by fatigue with a fan, and he should worship Hari every day with fragrant and delicate flowers.

Day after day, one should offer curd-rice as a fruit-offering and present incense and lamps; one should also give mouthfuls of food to cows and the wives of bulls, and perform the washing of the feet of the twice-born.

The gift of jaggery and ginger, the offering of ground āmalaka fruit, hospitality toward travelers, and the gift of rice and vegetables—these virtues are indeed highly praised in the month of Vaiśākha, which is dear to Mādhava. (21)

Likewise, the offering of flowers to Viṣṇu, the worship of Hari with seasonally appropriate sprouts and other offerings, and the presentation of curd-rice as an oblation, are the causes for the destruction of the entire multitude of sins. (22)

That woman who does not worship Mādhava with flowers produced in season, whether in a temple or in her own home, never attains a son or happiness anywhere; O Great-souled One, she destroys the life of her husband or even her own.

When the month of Mādhava has arrived, accompanied by Ramā, and Viṣṇu has gone to his home for the sake of examining the people’s bridge of dharma along with the sages and the gods—at that time, the fool who does not worship him with flowers [is lost]. (24)

That deluded soul, having reached Raurava, shall thereafter enter the womb of a Rakshasa five times; water and food must always be given here, for they are the cause of life for living beings afflicted by hunger.
By giving water one is born as an animal, and by taking food one is indeed born as a piśāca; O protector of the earth, I shall relate to you that wonderful story concerning the taking of food.

On the bank of the Revā, my father was a piśāca who ate his own flesh; his limbs were exhausted by hunger and thirst, and at the foot of a shadeless śālmalī tree, he had lost consciousness due to the lack of food. (27)

For one whose throat-passage has many openings due to hunger, thirst, or past karma, even a minute fissure, with flesh settled within the middle of the throat, would cause pain reaching even unto the end of life. || 28 ||

Seeing water that was cold and turbid, resembling the Kālakūṭa poison, situated in a pond on its bank—having arrived there by the turn of fate while on the way for the sake of a pilgrimage to the Gaṅgā. || 29 ||

Seeing that wondrous sight at the foot of a silk-cotton tree—a man who, tormented by his own past deeds, was repeatedly tearing off and eating his own flesh while crying out in many ways and grieving, afflicted by hunger and thirst—[he spoke]. (30)
That evildoer rushed at me to kill me, but struck down by my splendor, he fled; and with a heart moistened by compassion, I said to him, "Do not fear, for I have granted you freedom from fear."

"Who are you, dear one? Tell me at once the cause here; I shall release you from this distress, do not despair. Thus addressed, he spoke to me, not knowing me to be his son, while I was formerly in the city named Bhūvara in the land of Ānarta.

By name I am Maitra, born of the Sāṃkṛti lineage, and devoted to austerity, learning, charity, sacrifice, and other such duties. All branches of knowledge have been studied and taught by me, and I have performed ablutions in all the sacred fords.

"O dear one, because not even a mere morsel of alms was given by me at the proper time during the month known as Vaiśākha, out of greed, I have now fallen into this wretched state of being a Piśāca; there is no other cause—this is the truth that has been spoken."
"Now there is a son of great renown in my house named Śrutadeva; you must tell him of my condition—that by not giving food in the month of Vaiśākha, he has become a piśāca. (35)

Your father was seen on the bank of the Narmadā; he had not gone upward but remained at the foot of a tree. In the month known as Vaiśākha, he consumed his own flesh and felt deep remorse for the sake of his father’s liberation.

Having bathed in the morning, having worshipped Viṣṇu, and having sincerely gratified me with water offerings, food should be given to an excellent Brāhmaṇa endowed with virtues; indeed, one who does so is liberated and goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.

"Thus it was said before you: 'Speak,' and this compassion is for my sake; there is no doubt in this matter. May there be well-being and auspiciousness for you in every way. Having heard these words of my father, I spoke. (38)

Having prostrated my body like a staff before his feet for a long time, deeply afflicted with grief, I cried out repeatedly with tearful eyes: "O Father, I am your son; I have come here by the power of fate. (39)

"Since you have fallen from your duty and are censurable to the Brahmins, there can be no liberation from suffering for your ancestors. Tell me, O best of the twice-born, by what action he may indeed be liberated; I shall certainly perform it. (40)

Then, with his inner soul entirely pleased, he said: "Having undertaken a journey, return home quickly; when the month arrives and the sun is situated in Aries, you must offer food rich in qualities to Viṣṇu."

"O high-souled one, best of the twice-born, give a gift; from that, liberation shall come for you along with your lineage. Thus instructed by his father, he performed the pilgrimage, returned to his own home, and in the month of Mādhava, he gave a gift of food at Akara.

Therefore, my father, having been liberated, approached me while mounted upon his vehicle; having greeted me with blessings, he departed for the realm of the Lord of Śrī, which is difficult to conceive, from which those who have gone do not return again. (43)

Therefore, giving has been declared in all the scriptures; this essence of dharma, most righteous, has been proclaimed to you. Tell me what else you wish to hear; having heard it, I shall tell you everything—this is the truth.

Moreover, O King, even that which is desired by the virtuous, if it is unbearable to the mind for some reason, leads to misfortune. (13)
What need is there to say that what is unpleasant is clearly a cause of suffering? In this very regard, they cite this ancient history. (14)
This great wonder, which destroys sin and causes the hair to stand on end for those who hear it: formerly, Dakṣa, the lord of progeny, underwent initiation for a sacrifice.
He went to the Silver Mountain to summon the Lord of Beings; seeing him, Śambhu did not rise, out of a desire for his very welfare.
I am the eternal teacher of all the immortals, accessible through the Chandoga Veda; indeed, these lords of the gods, beginning with Candra and Indra, are my servants who offer me tribute.
A master should not rise for his servant, nor a husband for his wife, nor a teacher for his pupil; such is the opinion of those who know the scriptures. (18)
"Nor is kinship the cause of being a guru; such is the Vedic revelation. Rather, he in whom strength, knowledge, austerity, and tranquility abound [is the guru]. (19)
If that master [behaves thus] toward others, they become base and fall into servitude; yet masters and the like rise up again if they treat servants and the like with respect.
Their lifespan, wealth, fame, and progeny perish instantly; therefore, I shall not rise, for this father-in-law of mine is dear to me.
Thus, seeking his welfare, the Lord did not move from His seat; but seeing Mṛḍa not having risen, the Prajāpati became enraged.
In the presence of the Lord of Girijā, he did not praise him in many ways, saying: "Oh, the pride! Oh, the pride of this indigent man who has not disciplined his soul! (23)

The poor man, afflicted by the cold, wears as his sacred raiment the skin of an elephant; his home is a cremation ground, and indeed, a serpent is his ornament. (26)
Neither fortitude nor knowledge avails when one has fled from that wolf; for he is constantly beset by evil beings such as ghosts, spirits, and demons.
His lineage is not heard of anywhere, nor is he esteemed by the virtuous; he was previously deceived in vain by the evil-minded Nārada.
"Since I have been awakened by you, I give this virtuous maiden to you; let her, who follows a separate dharma, dwell happily in your house. (29)
"He is not to be praised by us, nor even my son in any way, just as a potter’s jar has fallen under the control of a caṇḍāla. (30)
Thus Dakṣa, his mind utterly deluded, did not summon Umā or that Mṛḍa; having rebuked him in many ways, he went home in silence.
Then, having gone to the sacrificial enclosure together with the officiating priests and sages, he performed the sacrifice according to the prescribed rites, while indeed censuring the Great Lord.
Excluding Brahmā and Viṣṇu, all the gods assembled together—the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kinnaras. || 33 ||

Though being restrained by Rudra, she was fickle due to her feminine nature; and even though answered back, she remained determined that she must go once more. (35)
O woman of excellent complexion, he constantly reviles me in the midst of the assembly; having heard that which is unbearable, you will surely abandon your body. (36)
"Even that which is unbearable must be endured by me, who desires a home; O Goddess, you do not behave at all in the manner that I have acted. (37)
"Therefore, do not go to the hall; surely no auspiciousness will come to pass. Thus admonished, the goddess again succumbed to her fickleness. (38)
Satī departed from her home alone, traveling on foot; seeing her, the bull silently bore the goddess upon his back.
Then, hosts of spirits by the millions followed the virtuous lady; having reached the sacrificial enclosure, she first went to the hall of the wives.
Seeing her silent, she emerged from there out of distress; then, remembering her husband’s words, she went to the northern altar-ground (uttaravedikā). || 41 ||

Such are these great-souled ones; is fate adverse to them? (45)

But that [arm], protected by the sage’s mantra, could not be severed by its power; however, Hara, having learned of this, came in person and cut off the arm of the evil-minded one.

It was destroyed in an instant for that great-souled one; thereupon, the great chariot-warrior Hemakānta was filled with wonder.

Reflecting upon his own deeds, the king then remained silent; O King, through the power of that gift of an umbrella, the remembrance of Viṣṇu arose within him.

Having thus instructed the best of kings with the words, "By Viṣṇu himself it was commanded," [he said], "Establish Hemakānta in your father's lineage and then return to me again. (72)
Thus commanded by the Blessed One, the mighty Viṣvaksena approached Hemakānta and warded off the messengers of Yama.
He touched the limbs of the lord of the earth with his most auspicious hand; through the touch of one devoted to the Blessed One, the king’s disease was destroyed in an instant.
Then Viṣvaksena went to his city along with him; seeing him, the great lord Kuśaketu was filled with wonder.
He bowed his head with devotion and prostrated like a staff upon the ground; he then caused the attendant of the Supreme Soul to enter his home.
Having praised him with various hymns, he honored him with magnificent offerings; then, with a pleased mind, the mighty Viṣvaksena spoke to him.
Having heard what was previously spoken by Viṣṇu concerning Hemakānta, Kuśaketu installed his son upon the throne.
Permitted by Viṣvaksena, he entered the forest together with his wife; having taken leave of and honored Hemakānta, Viṣvaksena departed.
The wise and high-minded King Hemakānta then went to the presence of Viṣṇu in Śvetadvīpa; thereafter, he performed the auspicious rites prescribed for the month of Vaiśākha.
Devoted to Brahman, established on the path of righteousness, peaceful, self-controlled, and having conquered his senses, he performed every year those religious duties that bring pleasure to Viṣṇu.
Compassionate toward all beings, initiated into all sacrifices, he flourished with every prosperity and was surrounded by sons, grandsons, and other kin.
Having enjoyed all pleasures, he attained the world of Viṣṇu.

I do not see any duties equal to those of Vaiśākha, which are easy to perform, causes of great merit, resembling a fire for the fuel of sin, easily accessible, and the cause of all human goals from dharma up to liberation. (84)

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pacification of Sins such as Brahman-slaughter for Hemakānta through the Praise of the Gift of an Umbrella," in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya, within the Nārada-Ambarīṣa-saṃvāda, in the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 10 ||

The King of Mithilā said: The religious duties of Vaiśākha are easily accessible, they bestow a mass of merit, they are pleasing to Viṣṇu, and they are the immediate causes for attaining the goals of human existence.
Why are those eternal duties enjoined by the Vedas not renowned in the world, while rajasic and tamasic dharmas are so extensively celebrated? (2)
Some praise the month of Māgha, while others have proclaimed the Cāturmāsya vows; these are difficult to perform, require great effort, and entail the expenditure of much wealth. || 3 ||
They describe the characteristics of Vyatīpāta and other such [yogas] here at great length; explain this distinction in detail for me, who am desirous of hearing it.
Śrutadeva said: Listen, O King, I shall explain how these [virtues] are not well-known, and how the other dharmas have attained fame upon the earth. (5)
On this earth, there are many people of rajasic and tamasic nature who are lustful; they desire worldly enjoyments and the prosperity of sons, grandsons, and so forth.

A man exerts great effort [in worldly affairs] but does not worship for liberation; people with petty hopes and many undertakings worship for the sake of desires.
By him indeed, the qualities of passion (rājasa) and even those of darkness (tāmasa) have been made famous; however, these sattvic qualities which bring pleasure to Hari have not been proclaimed.
These dharmas are indeed desireless and bestow rewards both in this world and the next; yet foolish people, deluded by the illusory power of the Divine, do not understand them. 10.
Just as every desire is fully accomplished when sovereignty is attained, so too that very place, having been reached for the sake of delusion, is lost through that same sovereignty.
And I shall directly declare the reason for the concealment on the surface of the earth of those sattvic men here who perform the duties prescribed for Vaiśākha. (12)
In ancient times, there was a sovereign ruler in Kāśī, an ornament of the Ikṣvāku dynasty, renowned as Kīrtimān, the son of Nṛga, and possessed of great fame.
That best of kings, who had conquered his senses and subdued his anger and was devoted to Brahman, once while engaged in hunting arrived at the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
As he was traveling on the road during the harsh heat of the month of Vaiśākha, he saw the disciples of that great-souled one being made to work again and again.
In some places they construct water-stalls and even pavilions with shade; having cleared away the crumbling banks, they create pure ponds.
In some places they fanned those seated under trees with fans; in some places they gave sugarcane stalks, in some places perfumes, and in some places fruit.
At midday they give gifts of parasols, and in the evening, drinks; sometimes they offer betel-leaf and an application of camphor to the eyes.
Some were in a forest of beautiful shade, some in well-swept courtyards, and some were truly spreading out beneficial sand.
O King, as they were making a swing suspended from the branch of a tree, he asked, "Who are you? and they replied, "We are the Vāsiṣṭhas. (20)
"What is this? he asked. Dharmas enjoined for Vaiśākha replied: "These are being performed by us directly as the means for attaining the goals of human life. (21)
"And by the command of Vasiṣṭha," they said to the best of kings, "what is the fruit for men who perform this, and who is pleased? (22)
"Explain this to me in detail, exactly as you have heard it. Thus questioned by the king, they replied to the lord of the earth.
"For those who perform virtuous deeds on the path solely by following the command of their guru, we have no authority here; ask your guru what is appropriate. (24)
"That man of great renown surely knows these dharmas according to their true nature"—having been thus answered by the disciples of Vasiṣṭha, he departed quickly.
Seeing the king approaching his holy hermitage, which was enriched by knowledge and yoga, Vasiṣṭha became delighted in his heart.

He performed the rites of hospitality according to tradition for that great-souled one and his followers. Once he was well-seated and the guest-rites were completed, the pleased king questioned that preceptor.
The king said: "A great wonder was seen on the road, a meritorious deed performed by your disciples. When I questioned them about it, they did not speak of the auspicious act being done. (28)
We have no leisure here for praising this dharma; rather, we must perform the rites that have been enjoined by our preceptor. (29)
"Go to the Guru," they said; thus addressed, I have come into your presence, my mind distracted by hunting, exhausted, and seeking hospitality. (30)
This meritorious path was indeed seen by you and caused to be constructed by your disciples; therefore, O Lord of Sages, there arose in me a desire to hear about these dharmas. (31)
Since you, as the primordial source, indeed practice these dharmas from the beginning, [speak of them] to this disciple who is prostrate and desirous of hearing those dharmas.
"O bull among sages, speak to me, who am full of faith, in detail. Thus was the highly illustrious one questioned by the king born of Ikṣvāku's lineage. (33)
Having been properly questioned by him now, he attained satisfaction in his mind: "Aha! Your Majesty's intellect is resolute today, and well-trained. (34)
Since your mind has become entirely devoted to the stories of Viṣṇu and to the practice of His dharma as well, your merit has borne fruit.
Having thus addressed the king, he, filled with joy, said to him: "Listen, O King, I shall explain that which I have now been asked by you. (36)
Merely by hearing which one is liberated from all sins; even if one abandons all dharmas and conducts oneself with a mind attached to sense objects, [one is freed]. (37)

He who is devoted to the Vaiśākha bath is dear to the Enemy of Madhu; he by whom the month of Vaiśākha is not honored after performing the religious duties along with their ancillaries is not so. (38)
For one by whom Vaiśākha is spent without bathing, giving gifts, and performing worship—those meritorious acts—Hari remains exceedingly far away. (39)
By that very deed he is a Caṇḍāla; no deliberation is required here regarding this. For by him Hari has been propitiated through the great dharmas prescribed for Vaiśākha.
Being pleased by those [offerings], the Lord of the World—the husband of Lakṣmī and the destroyer of the entire multitude of sins—grants whatever is desired. || 41 ||
Viṣṇu is pleased by subtle spiritual practices rather than by arduous efforts or even by wealth; when worshipped with devotion, he grants one's heart's desire.
Therefore, O King, devotion to the enemy of Madhu must always be practiced; for even when worshipped with water alone, Hari, the Lord of the World, destroys all suffering.
Just as one afflicted by thirst quickly attains satisfaction through water, so too even a small gift yields great merit, while a large gift may yield little. (44)
The smallness or greatness of an action is not the cause of its being small or large; rather, it is the nature of the action itself, for the course of karma is profound.
These duties prescribed for Vaiśākha, even when performed with very little effort, bring great destruction to expenses and are auspicious, causing delight to Viṣṇu. (46)
Therefore, O protector of the earth, you too should perform those rites prescribed for Vaiśākha; and cause all the people of your kingdom to perform these auspicious practices.
O King, that lowest of men who does not perform the religious duties prescribed for Vaiśākha, even though he has been instructed in many ways, is to be punished by you. 48.
Having thus thoroughly established the necessity [of this practice] through the authoritative scriptures, he subsequently proclaimed in their entirety the duties prescribed for the month of Vaiśākha.
Having heard all those dharmas and having worshipped his guru with devotion, that king returned home and practiced all the dharmas.
O King, being devoted to Keśava, the stainless god of gods, that lord of the earth saw no one other than Padmanābha, the Lord of Devas.
Having sounded the drum and proclaimed throughout his own kingdom by means of his soldiers: "Any mortal over eight years of age who does not complete eighty [years] shall indeed [be punished]. (52)
"Any person whatsoever who does not bathe at dawn while the sun is situated in Aries shall certainly be punished by me, executed, and banished from the realm. (53)
Whether it be a father, a son, a wife, or even a friend—if they are devoid of the duties of Vaiśākha, they must be restrained by me like a thief. (54)

Having bathed in the auspicious waters in the morning, you should give gifts to the foremost of Brahmins; O sinless ones, perform your duties such as the construction of water-stations (prapās) according to your ability.
He settled a Brahmin who expounded the Dharma in every village, and he appointed him as the authority over five villages.
For the sake of punishment against those who have abandoned dharma, he was served by ten horsemen; thus he proceeded everywhere by the command of the sovereign of the whole earth. (57)
This tree of Dharma has flourished and spread extensively throughout all lands; whatever men meet their death within the realm of the king [attain merit through it]. (58)
And even through negligence, O best of kings, they go to the abode of Hari; indeed, the world of Viṣṇu is certainly attained swiftly by human beings. (59)
Even if one bathes but once at dawn when the sun has entered Meṣa, even under some pretext, being liberated from all sins, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
By bathing once during the month of Vaiśākha, one does not encounter the Dharma of Yama; at that time, O King, the son of the Sun (Yama) went to his own record-office.
At that time, Citragupta became exhausted from the work of writing, for the records of past sins arising from evil deeds had been wiped away.
As people established in their own duties departed for the world of Viṣṇu in an instant, all the hells became empty, being utterly devoid of sinful living beings.
By the power of Vaiśākha, even the path with broken vehicles became passable; all people, their forms rendered pure, go to the abode of Hari.
All the worlds of the gods likewise became empty; when the triple heaven had become empty and the hells were also empty— (65)
Nārada, having approached Dharmarāja, spoke these words: "O King, the sound of wailing is no longer heard, as it was previously heard in hell. (66)
Likewise, no record is made of their evil deeds; Citragupta stands here like a sage, observing a vow of silence.
"O Indra among kings, tell me the reason why men of sinful deeds, whose deceit and hypocrisy have increased, do not go to your palace. (68)
When these words had been spoken by the high-souled Nārada, King Vaivasvata, filled with a certain dejection, spoke.
O Nārada, this king who currently resides upon the earth is exceedingly devoted to Hṛṣīkeśa, the Ancient Supreme Person.
He awakens [the people] to the duties of Vaiśākha with the sound of a drum; for a mortal who is more than eight years old, but less than eighty, [should do so]. (71)
"Indeed, whoever has not performed the Vaiśākha rites is to be punished by me, without a doubt; for out of fear of that, all people never transgress. (72)
By that very deed, O Nārada, people go to the abode of Viṣṇu; through the observance of Vaiśākha, they shall go to the temple of Hari.
"O best of sages, by that king the path has now been destroyed for me; indeed, the hells and even the worlds of the dwellers of heaven have been made empty. (74)

Thus I have become like a piece of wood; nothing is within my range. Yet, having fought him today, I shall by all means slay that one of great strength.

Having spoken thus and taken leave of the twice-born one, he, accompanied by his followers, proceeded to the earth; that Kāla, mounted upon a buffalo and raising a terrifying staff, [departed]. (80)
Then, he was surrounded by his exceedingly fierce attendants—Death, Disease, Old Age, and others—and by fifty crores of Yama’s messengers.
He quickly besieged the entire city of that royal sage and blew a most terrible conch shell that struck fear into all the worlds.
Having heard that and recognizing him as Yama, the son of Vivasvat, that royal sage prepared all his resources and departed from the city in a rage.
There, a terrifying battle took place between them, causing the hair to stand on end, involving Mṛtyu, Kāla, as well as Roga, Yama, and Dūtapati.
Having conquered him in an instant, the royal sage, out of wrath, put [his enemies] to flight; then King Yama himself, enraged, approached him in fury.
He fought with many arrows and let out a lion’s roar; the king, moreover, cut his bow as well with three shafts. (86)
Then Yama, taking up his sword and shield, came to slay him; but seeing him, the king, filled with rage, again cut off that sword and shield.

And he deeply embedded an arrow, shining like a black serpent, into [Yama’s] forehead. Struck by that, Yama became enraged and then took up his staff; having consecrated the staff with the Brahma-weapon (Brahmāstra), he discharged it at him.
Then a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the people who were watching; at that time, Viṣṇu dispatched his belly for the protection of his devotee.

Then, desiring to kill Yama, he launched a most wonderful discus with a thousand spokes; thereupon, the god’s devotee, becoming terrified, quickly stepped aside.
O thousand-spoked one, salutations be unto you, the ornament of Viṣṇu’s hand; you were formerly held by Hari for the protection of all the worlds.
Today I entreat you to protect Yama, who is a devotee of Viṣṇu and possesses great strength.
For you alone, and no other, are the time of destruction for men who offend the gods; therefore, protect this Yama and show mercy, O Lord of the World.
O Great King, while the gods looked on from the sky, the discus, having been thus praised by the king, left Yama and returned once more to the presence of the king.
Then Yama, deeply despondent, went to the abode of Brahmā; there he beheld him seated, surrounded by beings both embodied and unembodied.
The eternal refuge, the seed of the universe, the grandfather of all the worlds, he was being worshipped by the gods, the world-protectors, and the lords of the directions.
By means of the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other texts; by the gods established in embodied forms; and by the oceans, rivers, and lakes in their personified states. || 98 ||
Likewise, with all embodied beings, with trees such as the aśvattha and others without exception, with ponds, wells, and tanks, and with mountains possessing physical forms; || 99 ||
By means of days and nights, as well as fortnights, months, and years; and by means of kalās, kāṣṭhās, nimeṣas, seasons, solstices, and yugas.

Among them, Saturn entered like a bashful bride; looking down at the surface of the earth, he displayed a withered face.

"Why has this guest arrived? Is all well with the inhabitants of heaven? And what is this extraordinary marvel? This cloth has been completely cleansed. (107)
The scribe, overcome by great dejection, had never once wiped that cloth, being fearful of violating his religious duty. (108)

O Lotus-seated One, as long as you are my protector, I see nothing as fruitless.
Having spoken thus, O best of kings, he became motionless; then a tumultuous roar arose within the assembly hall.

Then, having ascertained the opinion of the assembled worlds, that Veda-born one restrained the wind from their speech.
Having warded off the people, the noble-minded Lokasūtra slowly raised Mārtaṇḍi with his two arms, which were as thick as śāla trees, while fanning him with the wind.
He seated that agitated man, who was dependent on others, upon a throne; and once he was seated, the son of Vyoma addressed this to the son of the Sun.
"By whom have you been overcome? By whom have you been driven from your place? O Lord, by whom has this cloth—the painting-cloth belonging to you—been wiped clean? (118)

"Tell me everything without omission: from what cause have you come? O dear one, he who is the lord of all is your creator and mine as well; why, moreover, does this suffering dwell within your heart regarding Mārtaṇḍa?"
Thus addressed by the Wind-god, the son of the Sun spoke these truthful words; looking at the face of the son of Kuśaketu, he uttered this most piteous speech with a faltering voice. (120)

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Victory of Kīrtimān," in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya, within the second section (Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa. || 11 ||
Yama said: "Listen to my words, O Lord; I have been humiliated by you, O Grandfather. I consider the violation of my authority to be worse than death. (1)
O Lotus-seated One, a steward does not indeed perform his duty; he who consumes the wealth of his master shall become a wood-worm.
O Lord of the Earth, that wise man who, out of greed, consumes wealth [belonging to others] goes to the womb of an animal or to hell for three hundred kalpas.
O Lotus-born One, that man who, being devoid of desire, does not carry out his appointed duty, shall experience terrible hells and thereafter become a crow.
But he who, intent on his own affairs, neglects the business of his master, shall become a sinful-souled rat in that house for three hundred kalpas.
A man who, having been an appointed official (niyogin), remains constantly in his own home though capable of performing his duties, is born as a cat.
Therefore, O Lord, by your command, I shall govern the subjects with righteousness: rewarding the doer of merit with merit, and the sinner with sinful retribution.
O Lord, having investigated thoroughly with the sages who are well-versed in the Dharmaśāstras, you have inflicted upon me this torment for my conduct at the beginning of the kalpa.
Indeed, I would not be able to carry out such a command; for your command has been set aside on earth by King Kīrtimān.
Out of fear of him, O Lord of the World, someone exists somewhere protecting the earth, which has the ocean for its garment, together with the dharma of Vaiśākha.
Having abandoned all dharmas, having abandoned the worship of ancestors, and having abandoned the service of the sacred fire as well as virtuous rites such as pilgrimages; || 11 ||
Having abandoned both Yoga and Sāṃkhya, having abandoned the restraint of breath, and having abandoned fire-offerings and Vedic recitation, they committed manifold sins. (12)
Having performed the virtuous rites of Vaiśākha, men indeed go to the world of Viṣṇu together with their fathers and likewise with their grandfathers.
Their deceased fathers, as well as the fathers of those ancestors, and likewise their maternal grandfathers and their progenitors and so forth, all go there. (14)
And their leaders were the ancestors of my mothers; yet this suffering, O Lord, is once again the splitting of my head. (15)
"O Lord, having wiped away my writing, my beloved's ancestors depart; for he who was born from the seed of my ancestors and was held in the womb of my nurse. (16)
Whatever action has been performed by one person is experienced by that very same person; for he alone among those in the family knows all that was done, having cast aside [all else]. (17)
O Lord, O Father, you are fully capable of delivering both sides; indeed, all those born from the womb belong to your beloved as well.
O Lord of the World, O Viṣṇu, they all go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu; indeed, O God, I have no need for such a command.
Devoted to the Vaiśākha-dharma, he shall leave me and go to Hari; having uplifted twenty-one generations of his family and cast off all sin, he will become exceedingly radiant.
Having abandoned my path, he indeed proceeds to the abode of Hari; O God, a human being does not attain such a destination through sacrificial rites.
Neither by all the sacred fords, nor by gifts and the like, nor by austerities, nor by vows, nor even by being endowed with all dharmas, does one attain that goal. (22)

Neither by falling at Prayāga, nor by falling in the midst of battle, nor by falling from the Bhṛgu cliff, nor even by dying in Kāśī, do all people attain that goal which is reached by one who is devoted to Vaiśākha.

Having bathed in the morning, performed worship of the gods, heard the narrative known as the Māsa-māhātmya, and practiced the appropriate Vaiṣṇava duties, he indeed becomes the sole lord of the world of Viṣṇu.
"O Lotus-seated One, I consider the world of Viṣṇu, the Lord of the universe, to be immeasurable; for it cannot be filled from all sides even by millions of floods. (25)
In this world, through the entire abode of Mādhava, they behold the Grandfather (Brahmā)—whether they abide in improper conduct or proper conduct, whether they are pure or impure. (26)
"O King, by your command, people perform the Vaiśākha rites; for he who was our great enemy is especially so for you. (27)
O Lord of the worlds, that king must be subdued by you, for he has abandoned all dharmas simply by performing the Vaiśākha bath once.
Unconditioned beings go to Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Hari; yet we have shown neglect toward him who takes sole refuge at the feet of Liṅgu. (29)
"A king shall lead the entire world; of this there is no doubt. Indeed, this 'cloth of punishment' (daṇḍapaṭa) is today offered by you with your own feet. (30)
Incomparable sovereignty over the world was attained by that king; what indeed is the use of a son being born who only causes distress to his mother?
He who does not strike down his enemy is like the sun in the month of Jyeṣṭha; for a young woman is born in vain if she has only wicked sons.
Her fame does not flash forth like lightning from a cloud, if she does not rescue her father from sin by means of knowledge or by strength.
That disease born from the mother's womb is produced upon the earth when a son becomes opposed to virtue, wealth, and pleasure. (34)
For he is called a slayer of his mother by the virtuous; that son is the lowest of men. And his mother was the king’s wife, renowned in the world for her noble deeds. (35)

In this world, she alone is a true mother of heroes, and he is truly a hero—of this there is no doubt—since through her, one who possesses such fame was born for the sake of wiping away the stain upon Malla.
"O Lord of the World, this has never been undertaken by any kṣatriya; indeed, the wiping of a cloth [for the feet] has not been heard of in the ancient scriptures. (37)
Therefore, O Lord of the lords of the world, I do not know that king who is devoted to Hari, other than him who, sounding his resonant drum, is destroying my path to my home. (38)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sufferings of Yama," in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya, within the second section (Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa. || 12 ||

Even a single prostration made to Govinda is equal to the final purificatory bath of a hundred horse-sacrifices; the performer of a sacrifice returns to birth, but a prostration to Hari leads not to rebirth.
What need has he for Kurukṣetra, and likewise what need for the Sarasvatī, on the tip of whose tongue the two syllables "Ha-ri" reside? (4)
If a Brāhmaṇa, while eating with a dog-cooker woman, especially one who is menstruating, should remember Viṣṇu at the time of death, he attains that supreme state.
Having abandoned the accumulation of sin born from eating what is forbidden to eat, one attains union with Viṣṇu, because mindfulness is dear to Viṣṇu.
Thus, O Yama, the month named Vaiśākha is indeed dear to Viṣṇu; by merely hearing of its religious merit, one is liberated from all sins.
What need is there to say that he who is intent upon its performance attains [the goal], for it is in this that the Supreme Person is celebrated and by which He is pleased? (8)
How is it that he, who is devoted to its performance, does not go to a state of rebirth? He is our Lord of the worlds, the progenitor, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
In the month of Mādhava, let him perform these desired duties; Viṣṇu, with a gracious soul, will always stand by his side as his helper.
O son of Sūrya, you are not capable of instructing that king; nor does any inauspiciousness ever exist for the devotees of Vāsudeva, and no fear of birth, death, old age, or disease arises for them.
To the extent that an appointed official exerts himself in the master's affairs according to his ability, by that much he becomes one who has accomplished his purpose; he does not go to hell at all.

Therefore, for one who has declared the truth, there is neither debt nor sin; when one's own duty has been performed with effort, there is no fault in the embodied being.
Therefore, you ought not to grieve over this impossible task.
Thus addressed by Brahmā, the son of Sūrya, his mind once again deeply distressed, spoke in a piteous voice with eyes clouded by falling tears.
"O Father, by the worship of your feet, everything has indeed been attained by me. O Lotus-born One, I shall not go again to carry out a command. (17)
O Lord, while this king of great prowess was ruling over the circle of the earth, they caused him alone—the sovereign—to deviate from his own duties. (17)
O compassionate one, I have accomplished my purpose, just like a son who offers the funeral cake at Gayā; therefore, please fulfill this eternal task for me.
"Free from fever, I shall then further carry out your command. Having heard what was spoken by Yama, Brahmā again became absorbed in reflection.
Brahmā spoke to him again, consoling him in many ways. Brahmā said: "The king, who is devoted to the dharma of Viṣṇu, must not be apprehended by you."
If you deceive me out of anger, we shall indeed go into the presence of Hari; having reported all this deed to him, we shall afterwards abide by what is commanded by him.
He alone is the creator of the world and the protector of dharma; he is our wielder of the rod of punishment, our teacher, our maker, and our regulator. (23)
O Bull, no rebuttal has been prescribed for us regarding what he has said; indeed, no rebuttal to the word of a king is ever seen anywhere on this earth. (24)
Having thus consoled Yama, Brahmā went with him to the Ocean of Milk and praised the Supreme Lord, who is pure consciousness alone and devoid of attributes.
Then Viṣṇu, Hari, the Supreme Person, who is one and without a second according to Sāṃkhya and Yoga, appeared when he was praised by Brahmā.
Yama and Brahmā quickly paid homage to him; then Mahāviṣṇu spoke to them in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
"Why have you two come here? What suffering has been caused by the demons? Why is the face of Yama withered, and for what reason does he stand with his neck bowed? (28)
"Tell me this, O Brahmin," he said; and thus addressed, the lotus-born one replied: "While that king, the best of your servants, rules the earth, men indeed [shall be as follows]. (29)
Those who are devoted to the Vaiśākha dharma go to the supreme, imperishable state; consequently, the city of Yama becomes empty, and because of that, he is exceedingly distressed.
He waged war with him and then took up his staff to slay him; but, defeated by your discus, he has come into my presence today.
And we are not able to inflict punishment upon your high-souled devotees; therefore, O Great Lord, we have come to you alone for refuge.
"Therefore, having punished the king, protect this Yama of your own. Thus addressed, he laughed and spoke to Brahmā and to Yama himself.
I would even renounce Lakṣmī, or my life-breaths, or my body; or even the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem, and the Vaijayantī garland.
I am not able to abandon Śvetadvīpa, Vaikuṇṭha, the Ocean of Milk, nor even Śeṣa and Garuḍa, for they are my devotees.
Having renounced all enjoyments for my sake and even sacrificed their lives, how could I bear to abandon those illustrious ones who are my very self? (36)
Therefore, I shall indeed devise a means for the pacification of your suffering; and I have granted a lifespan of ten thousand years to that king upon this earth.
O Narāntaka, eight thousand years have now passed since he was led away by him while his lifespan remained, even though he had already attained union with me.
From him there will arise a wicked-souled king named Vena; he shall plunder all these great dharmas proclaimed in the Vedas.

Thereafter, having become Pṛthu, I shall again set forth the Dharmas; then, among the people, I shall establish those proclaimed in the Vaiśākha [month].
Among a thousand, there may be one who is my devotee, whose life is dedicated to me, and who has renounced all worldly accumulation; indeed, one should proclaim these qualities to such a person.
"Indeed, let someone on this earth understand these teachings of mine; then your purpose will be accomplished, O Narāntaka, do not despair. (43)
"I shall cause you to receive your share this month of Mādhava as well, through all the noble men who are devoted to the Vaiśākha duties. (44)

Those men on earth who, day after day, do not take their own share [of offerings] while making offerings intended for you, do not deserve to suffer. (46)
Bathing, the offering of water (arghya), the water-pot, and curd-rice on the final day—in Vaiśākha, all such actions of theirs shall become fruitless.
Therefore, O King, abandon your anger toward me, who am devoted to you and entitled to a share; for whoever in this world acts as such, those men are indeed entitled to a share.

O illustrious one, by my command you must then inflict punishment; and I shall dispatch Sunanda to cause the king to pay his share.

One should perform a ritual bath every day and indeed offer the arghya water to Yama; otherwise, the entire merit of the month of Vaiśākha would become fruitless.

"One should honor that very speaker of the Dharma with one's own resources. Thus instructed by Sunanda, the king acted accordingly.

Whoever does not know these auspicious [observances] prescribed for Vaiśākha, even when the ripening of merit accumulated over many births has arrived— (66)
"One's mind should be fixed with absolute resolve upon the duties prescribed for Vaiśākha. Maithila said: "In a former Manvantara, there was indeed a wicked-souled king named Vena. (67)
"For this king, the joy of the Ikṣvākus, is indeed a resident of Vaivasvata's realm"—thus have I heard previously, and now it is spoken by you. (68)
"This one has gone to Vaikuṇṭha; later Vena will become king. O high-minded Śrutadeva, cut asunder this doubt.

O King, as this auspicious and eternal rite was proclaimed by Mārkaṇḍeya to me in the past eon that has passed away, so has it been told to you.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Consolation of Yama’s Suffering," in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa, within the *Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya* (The Greatness of the Month of Vaiśākha) of the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrutadeva said: He who bathes in the morning during the month of Vaiśākha when the sun is situated in Aries, having worshipped Madhusūdana and heard this narrative of Hari— || 1 ||

But he who, being a fool of mind, abandons the sacred narrative while it is being recited and pursues something else, remains bound by sin; however, one who is liberated from evil goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Having reached the Raurava hell, one shall attain birth in the womb of a Piśāca; in this very context, they cite this ancient history.
It is the destroyer of sin, purifying, righteous, immediately worthy of worship, and ancient; [it was established] of old on the auspicious bank of the Godāvarī at the sacred site of Brahmeśvara.

The two disciples of Durvāsas were supreme ascetics (paramahaṃsas) solely devoted to Brahman; they were always established in the knowledge of the Upaniṣads and remained free from all worldly expectations.
"Eating only as much as is obtained by begging, both of them were meritorious dwellers in the cave; devoted to truth and devoted to austerity, they were thus renowned throughout the three worlds. (6)
Between those two, O King, is the one devoted to truth who is always intent on the stories of Viṣṇu, even in the absence of listeners as well as expounders.

Having abandoned sacred fords and temples that are situated too far away, as well as numerous ritual acts that are contrary to the narrative.
He hears divine stories and indeed tells them himself to listeners; O Lord of Men, without such stories, he knows nothing else worthy of being served.
And the speaker explains it in his own home while afflicted by diseases and other ailments; meanwhile, the sage, intent on bathing in a well, listens to the very discourse.

From that, there arises purification of the mind, and one attains detachment toward Viṣṇu; yet devotion to Viṣṇu is born, as well as affection for the virtuous. (14)
The stainless Brahman, devoid of qualities, is immediately realized within the heart; indeed, for a man lacking knowledge, ritual action becomes fruitless. (15)
And their conduct was manifold, just like that of the Andhakas and Darpaka; likewise, many actions were performed by those whose souls were filled with grief.

They exist indeed for the purification of the mind; through the purification of the mind, one attains sacred learning (śruti). Having attained sacred learning, one acquires knowledge, and having known, one becomes fit for meditation.
In that place where there is no discourse on Viṣṇu and no virtuous people, hearing, meditation, and reflection—though enjoined by the Vedas—are of little avail in many ways. (18)

Where there is no discourse on Viṣṇu, one who dies there shall go to darkness; likewise, in that village where there is no Vaiṣṇava sanctuary or even a black antelope (kṛṣṇamṛga).
Where there is no discourse concerning Viṣṇu, nor any virtuous people who take refuge in Him, a man who dies there will quickly go to a hundred births as a dog.
Having reflected upon the knowledge of the Upaniṣads and reached this certainty, the sage remained constantly devoted to the stories of Viṣṇu and dedicated to the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
He never considers anything superior to hearing [the teachings]; whereas the other is devoted to asceticism, devoted to ritual action, and stubbornly dogmatic. (23)
He neither explains nor listens to sacred discourse himself; abandoning the story being told, he goes off to bathe at a holy ford. (24)
O protector of the earth, even when a conversation has begun at a sacred ford, [the mind] wanders far away due to the power of restlessness, out of fear of the loss of merit from ritual action. (25)
People go away for the sake of their household duties after the meeting; there, no listeners nor speakers remain by his side, being occupied with their own tasks.
But for that evil-souled one of wicked intellect, as his time of destruction drew near, the story of the Lord reached neither his tongue nor his ears anywhere. (27)
Because he was neither a listener nor a speaker, due to his dull intellect and stubbornness, the sage immediately met his death through the power of dharma after falling into the five elements.
He became a weak Piśāca named Chinnakarna, dwelling in a Śamī tree; he was without shelter, without food, and his throat, lips, and palate were parched.
Thus, as he was suffering in this manner, ten thousand divine years passed; deprived of food and exceedingly distressed, he saw no protector for himself.
Reflecting upon his own deeds, he wandered about like one intoxicated or insane; though he roamed about out of hunger, the deluded-minded man found no peace.
For one who has perfected the self, the wind touching the body is like a fire; likewise, water is like the fire of cosmic destruction, and fruits, flowers, and the like are poison.
This industrious man of dejected mind found no happiness anywhere; while he was thus occupied in that desolate forest, (33)
In a field devoid of discourse, his own abode being bereft of holy men, Satyaniṣṭha then, by the power of destiny, arrived at the city of Paiṭhinasī.
While traveling on the road, he saw one whose ears were severed and who was in great agony; seeing him running away from him, weeping and tormented by hunger. (35)
Having said, "Do not fear," the Lord of Sages asked, "Who are you? and, "Why do you have such a state? You shall have no suffering beyond this."
Thus reassured by him, Chinnakarṇa, being extremely overwhelmed, said: "I am an ascetic devoted to penance, the supreme disciple of Durvāsas. (37)

O Sage, I am a resident of the Brahmeśvara field, devoted to ritual action yet possessed of stubbornness; out of foolishness and the fear of neglecting my duties, I acted thus, O sage of evil intellect. (38)
Even when being spoken of by the virtuous, the sacred narrative of Viṣṇu was not honored; nor was that story, which destroys the effects of karma, explained to listeners. (39)
By the ripening of that great karma, I met my death; with my ears severed, I became a Piśāca overwhelmed by suffering, known by that name. (40)
I did not see any protector whatsoever from this suffering; yet, by good fortune, having come within the range of your vision, I am now freed from sin. (41)
Today the deities are pleased with me, as are my gurus and those who are virtuous; and Hari has become gracious toward me, since I have obtained his vision.
He fell at his feet upon the ground, crying out, "Save me! Save me! Then, the illustrious one, who was devoted to truth, was overcome with compassion.
The lord of sages raised him up with his two most auspicious arms; then, having sipped water for purification, he bestowed upon him unsurpassed merit.
By the power of that merit born from listening for even a moment to the greatness of the month of Vaiśākha, all his inauspiciousness was instantly destroyed.
Released from his piśāca body, he assumed a divine form; having ascended a celestial chariot, he bowed down to that great sage.
Having taken his leave and circumambulated him, he departed for the supreme abode of Viṣṇu; thereafter, the wise Satyaniṣṭha went to the city of Paiṭhinasī.

Reflecting thus again and again upon the greatness of hearing [this account], Śrutadeva said: "Wherever the meritorious and auspicious story of Viṣṇu, which removes the impurities of the world, is found... (48)
Therein are all sacred fords and various holy sites where the auspicious and meritorious river of Viṣṇu’s narratives flows.
For the inhabitants of that region, liberation is held in the palm of their hand; of this there is no doubt. || 50 ||

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Liberation by the Piśāca," within the "Praise of Narratives" section of the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa, in the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrutadeva said: O protector of the earth, listen further to the sin-destroying majesty of the month of Vaiśākha, which is so dear to the enemy of Madhu (Kṛṣṇa). || 1 ||
Formerly, in the land of Pañcāla, there was a king named Puruṣayaśas, the son of the wise and meritorious Bhūriyaśas. || 2 ||

O King, when his father had passed away, he remained established in the kingdom, devoted to righteousness, endowed with the qualities of heroism and generosity, and highly skilled in the science of archery.
The high-minded one ruled the entire earth according to his own dharma, yet he was beset by a great defect arising from the failure to give water in a previous birth.
O sinless one, after some time, he met with the loss of his prosperity; his horses and elephants, afflicted by a great disease, met their death.
There was an incomparable famine that deprived the land of its people; at that time, the kingdom and the treasury were like a kapittha fruit devoured by an elephant.
Knowing the king to be weak and deprived of both treasury and kingdom, they resolved in their minds: "This is the time to conquer him."
Hundreds of enemy kings arrived against that monarch; they conquered in battle that king who was the ruler of the Pāñcāla territory.
Defeated, the king then entered a mountain cave together with his wife Śikhinī and accompanied by his circle of nurses and attendants.
His path unknown to others and overwhelmed by many sufferings, he was brought to dissolution by him for fifty-three years.
The king reflected repeatedly, "What is this? For I am pure by birth through my actions and devoted to the welfare of my mother and father. (11)
Devoted to his guru, always courteous, friendly toward Brahmins, and intent on dharma; compassionate toward all beings, devoted to the gods, and having conquered his senses.
I have no brother, no son, nor any dear friends; how could there be anyone renowned for compassion or prowess to me, even though I am of noble birth? (13)
By what karma was this poverty, which brings such manifold suffering, obtained? By what has my defeat come today, and by what this dwelling in the forest? (14)
Thus, the king, his mind distressed and agitated by anxiety, remembered the two preeminent sages named Yāja and Upayājaka, who were omniscient.
Those two great-minded lords of sages, summoned by the king, arrived; seeing them, the king, the beloved of Pañcāla, rose up suddenly. (16)
Deeply distressed by his exile, devoid of royal insignia, and with his path unknown to anyone, he bowed his head with devotion.
He stood silent for a moment after falling at their feet; then, lifted up by them with both arms, his eyes were wiped as they were filled with tears.
He worshipped them according to the rules with auspicious offerings of forest produce; once those two brahmins were well-seated, he, with his neck bowed low, questioned them.
"O Brāhmaṇas, tell me the cause of the king's sorrow—he who is pure by birth through his actions and who is dear to the ancestors and the gods. (20)
For one such as I—who fears evil, is compassionate, and is devoted to my guru—whence could there be poverty, loss of treasury, or defeat by enemies? (21)
Why is it that I dwell in the forest, and why am I alone? I have no son, nor do I have a brother, nor do I have beloved friends. (22)
"Or how could there have been famine in this sinless land protected by me? O best of sages, explain this to me in detail; tell me the cause."
When they were thus addressed by that extremely distressed spirit, those two high-souled and best of sages, absorbed in meditation, replied as follows.
Yāja and Upayāja said: "Listen, O King, we shall tell you the cause of your sorrow. Formerly, O King, for ten births you were a hunter of great sin. (25)
He was cruel toward all people, always devoted to violence; he possessed not even a trace of dharma anywhere, nor did he have self-restraint or tranquility.
The tongue does not utter the names of Viṣṇu in any way whatsoever, nor does the mind remember the pair of lotus feet of Govinda. (27)
"O King, you have not bowed your head in salutation to the Supreme Self anywhere; thus, nine births have passed for you, O evil-minded one. (28)
When your tenth birth arrives on the Sahya mountain, you shall become a hunter—cruel to all people and a bringer of death to men.
Devoid of compassion, living by the sword, and ever devoted to violence; devoid of virtue, accompanied by your wife, you are a rogue who causes suffering to travelers. (30)
A man-eating Rākṣasa [ruled] over the people of the Gauḍa country; in this manner, years passed by for him as he remained ignorant of his own welfare. (31)
"Because you have killed the young offspring of deer and birds, being devoid of compassion and possessed of evil intent, you shall suffer childlessness in this birth. (32)
Because he was a betrayer of trust, his brothers were not truly brothers; because he caused suffering on the road, he was abandoned by his friends. (33)
Due to their disparagement of the virtuous, they suffered defeat at the hands of their enemies; moreover, poverty fell upon their home through the fault of never having given anything away.
Because it always causes agitation, travel abroad is difficult to endure; and because it is disliked by everyone, its suffering is exceedingly unbearable. (35)
Because you previously lived without food due to your constant cruel deeds, therefore, O high-minded one, there has been this seizure of your kingdom in this birth.
Now, I shall also declare the causes for your birth into a noble family; for when you were born in the Gauḍa country during your final birth as a hunter.
While he remained thus on that path which was devoid of compassion, intent on its own cruel activity, thick with thorns, and the end-maker of all beings; (38)
Two divine Vaiśyas, wealthy and oppressed by the heat, arrived; and there was a sage named Karṣaṇa, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. || 39 ||
Wearing matted hair and bark garments, meritorious and carrying a water-pot, he saw them and, taking up his bow, stood blocking their path. (40)
Having pursued the two Vaiśyas and cut their bodies apart, you shall kill one of them and take the entire stake from him. (41)
Furthermore, as [the enemy] prepared to strike him, he fled swiftly out of fear; casting his stake into a thicket, he ran away, terrified and desiring to save his life. (42)
The sage Karṣaṇa, fearing death at the hands of the hunter, ran swiftly in the heat of the sun, afflicted by thirst and the scorching sun.
Falling into a swoon, with sweat pouring from him and consciousness remaining as his only remnant, the Vaiśya abandoned him and fled, intent on saving his own life.
First, having seen the Brahmin fainted on the road as you were running after him, where was the wager deposited, and how far had the merchant gone? (45)
Thus questioned, he prepared to revive the exhausted twice-born man; blowing into his ears the *nāgara* root, which is the cause of recollection.
Having wiped his eyes with water from a puddle mixed with worms and mud, he fanned the face of the weary man with leaves.
Having made the sage appear as if unconscious, you spoke with a composed mind: "O sage, you should have no fear of me, the wielder of weapons, in this forest. (48)
One who possesses nothing is happy in this world; whence can there be terrible fear for you? With a worn-out, broken bowl, nothing at all shall happen to me. (49)
"Tell me this much, O learned one: where has the merchant fled? Where was the wealth cast into a thicket by him as he fled so swiftly? (50)
"Otherwise, I shall kill you if you speak falsely. Karṣaṇa said: "The wealth was deposited in a thicket; I fled from this path. (51)
Thus he spoke when questioned out of fear and a desire to save his life: "Go, O Brahmin, along the path happily, casting away all fear of me."
Not far from here, there is auspicious water in a pond; having drunk that holy water, go to the village with your fatigue dispelled.
"Right now the royal officers will arrive along the road, intent on searching for my footprints upon hearing the cry of the merchant lord. (54)
"O twice-born one, because I am afflicted by thirst, I am unable to follow you; therefore, fan yourself with this leaf, and the heat will be somewhat relieved."
Having given that Palāśa tree to him, you returned again to the forest; by the power of that merit, during the month of Vaiśākha when the heat was intense, [the following occurred].
Although you were born for the sake of your own purpose, by means of the path established for the protection of the Sage, your birth occurred in a most extensive and highly meritorious royal lineage.
If you desire happiness, sovereignty, or the abundance of wealth, grain, and so forth; or if you desire heaven, liberation, or even union with the state of Hari; (then perform this).
Practice the Vaiśākha duties, and you shall attain all happiness; for this month is named Mādhava, and the third lunar day is called Akṣaya.
Give a cow that has calved for the first time to a Brahmin who is in distress; by that, your treasury shall be replenished, and give a bed, so that there may be happiness. (60)
Bestow the gift of an umbrella, and you shall attain imperial sovereignty; perform your ablutions according to the rule, and likewise worship Mādhava.
"O King, if you desire sons whose qualities are equal to your own, then fashion a divine image and give it [to me]; by that, victory shall be yours."
O ruler of the earth, perform the gift of water for the sake of the welfare of all beings, and practice these duties prescribed for Vaiśākha correctly.
By that, all the worlds will come under your control, there is no doubt, provided you perform these duties with a mind free from desire.
In this meritorious month of Vaiśākha, for the pleasure of the Slayer of Madhu, Viṣṇu will become manifest before one whose mind is purified by your hymn of praise.
And those wise men of old knew that for those persons by whom these merit-bringing dharmas have been practiced, their worlds are indeed imperishable, as stated in the Purāṇa.
"All this has been told to you exactly as it was seen and heard," [he said], having thus addressed the king and the two brahmin priests.
Then Yāja and Upayāja departed as they had come; thereafter, the king of great prowess was enlightened by his two domestic priests.
Endowed with faith, he performed all the Vaiśākha duties exactly as they had been instructed, and likewise worshipped Madhusūdana.
Then, having attained his power and accompanied by all his kinsmen as well as the remnants of his army, he reached the city of Pañcāla.
Then, having heard of the king's entry into the city, the hostile monarchs returned once more, arrogant and defiant.
Then a battle took place between the king of the Pañcālas and the monarchs; that single great car-warrior of mighty arms conquered them all.
When the kings had fled along the roads of various lands, the valiant one personally seized the treasuries, elephants, and horses of those monarchs.
There were a *nirbuda* of horses, three *koṭis* of elephants, an *arbuda* of chariots, and likewise ten thousand long-necked [beasts]. (74)
By the greatness of the religious merit of the month of Vaiśākha, all those kings arrived at that city in an instant, bringing three hundred thousand donkeys.
The tax-payers, their resolutions shattered, were trampled underfoot; yet there was incomparable abundance of food in the territories of Pāñcāla.
By the grace of the Slayer of Madhu, his kingdom became one under a single umbrella; he also had five sons endowed with the qualities of heroism and magnanimity.
Dhṛṣṭakīrti, Dhṛṣṭaketu, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, as well as others—Vijaya and Citraketu—were like those with peacock banners.
The subjects were devoted and protected according to dharma; by the power of Vaiśākha, proof of this appeared at that very moment.
Furthermore, the lord of the city of Pañcāla performed those religious rites with a mind free from desire for the pleasure of the Slayer of Madhu.
Satisfied by this dharma, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana became manifest on the third lunar day known as Akṣayā.
Having seen him, he was struck with wonder at the Supreme Self, the infallible Nārāyaṇa, four-armed and bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
The god, wearing yellow garments and adorned with a forest garland, accompanied by Lakṣmī and his attendants, was seated upon Garuḍa. || 83 ||
Beholding that unbearable splendor, his eyes immediately closed; leaping up and falling down again, he wandered about in joy like one intoxicated or insane.
With his entire body covered in horripilation and his eyes clouded with falling tears, he, prostrate on the ground with palms joined in reverence, praised Him with supreme devotion.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Victory and the Destruction of Poverty for the Lord of the Pāñcāla Country," in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa, within the *Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya* of the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Śrutadeva said: His heart overflowing with the joy of that vision, he immediately rose and bowed his head; gazing at this God who is the soul of the universe and the sovereign of all worlds, his eyes remained fixed upon him for a long time.

Having washed his feet, he held that water which, having issued from his feet, purifies the world including the Brahmas; and he worshipped him with great splendors, using costly garments, ornaments, and unguents. || 2 ||

With offerings of garlands, incense, lamps, and the consumption of nectar, and by surrendering his skin, limbs, wealth, and self, he praised Viṣṇu—the ancient Puruṣa, Nārāyaṇa, who is beyond qualities and without a second.

I bow to the stainless one, the supreme lord of the creators of the universe, who is worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods; by whose *māyā* even the most excellent among those who know reality are deluded, [yet he remains] the sovereign lord of the creators of the universe.

The deluded are bewildered by the activities of Māyā and by the qualities (guṇas); wonderful indeed is the Lord’s sport! Though effortless, He alone creates this manifold universe through His own Self, preserves it, and finally devours it, yet He remains unattached.

Although your every desire is fulfilled for the sake of bestowing happiness upon all gods and asuras or inflicting suffering upon them, even so, at this time, you maintain your essential nature (sattva) for the protection of your own kin and the subduing of the wicked.

O Lord whose universal form is beyond all qualities, by good fortune, those of highly matured yoga have held within their hearts Your lotus feet—the abode of all sacred waters—which destroy the sins of those who bow to them; for them, the quality of darkness (tamas) serves as a bond for the Rākṣasas, while the quality of passion (rajas) [is transcended]. || 7 ||

Those whose very state of being living beings has its disposition offered up by overflowing devotion have attained Your state of liberation merely by the remembrance of Your feet; [freed] from the bondage of the serpent-noose of time called *saṃsāra*, and from the sufferings of repeated birth, old age, and so forth. (8)

I wander through the wombs like a mouse seeking food, my thirst having increased because I have forgotten Your feet. Surely I gave nothing in charity, nor did I hear Your stories, nor was I ever served by holy men.

Therefore, his supreme fortune destroyed by enemies, he entered the forest remembering the secret sin of his own preceptor; and when those two kinsmen of the distressed were remembered, they approached me out of sorrow and awakened me from my state.

Through the auspicious duties of Vaiśākha enjoined by the Vedas, which are the causes for attaining the goals of human existence such as heaven and liberation, I have performed all those meritorious rites of the month of Mādhava upon understanding them.

Therefore, supreme grace arose within me, and by that, all these prosperities have been intensified; neither fire, nor sun, nor moon and stars, nor earth, water, ether, wind, speech, or mind [could rival it].

Even those wise ones whom you consider to be abundant worldly beings take away sin after a long time when served; yet others, who have abandoned all cravings and fixed their minds upon your feet, destroy it by a moment’s service.

Salutations to the Independent One whose actions are manifold; salutations to the Supreme One who bestows constant grace. Deluded by Your māyā, I wander among the qualities in the form of wife and wealth, perceiving what is meaningless as meaningful.

While your lotus feet—which destroy the very root [of suffering], remove all sins, and are perfectly pure—exist, one is instead occupied with attachment to children, self, and wife, which are the causes of misfortune for those desiring happiness. (15)

With his thirst for worldly existence further increased, he finds neither sleep nor peace anywhere regarding that very [existence]; yet you, having attained this rare birth as a god among men—which through effort is the cause of all human goals—[should not act thus].

O Lord, with my mind utterly deluded and longing for sense objects, I do not worship Your lotus feet; yet, being firmly established in ritual actions, I perform them while giving offerings with an ever-increasing thirst for their results.

And again, with a mind wavering amidst hundreds of thoughts such as "May I exist" and "May I exist even more today," may compassion arise for the living being at that very moment, O All-pervading Lord, whose power is infinite and who possesses the universe as Your form.

For the company of great men indeed causes the ocean of worldly existence to become like a cow's footprint; O Lord, as soon as association with the virtuous occurs, then the mind is born toward You, the Supreme Lord. (19)

I truly consider the departure of the entire kingdom to be a direct favor bestowed upon me by you, noble sir, just as it was for you by the hosts of Brahmins, gods, and asuras, and even by flocks of swans whose thirst has been quenched.

From this moment, O Lord, I remember only Acyuta with devotion—his lotus feet which remove worldly existence, which are sought by the destitute, and which bestow abundant fortune; I desire nothing other than Your lotus feet.

Therefore, I do not cherish sovereignty nor a treasury of sons and the like, for this body is constantly falling away, born of passion; rather, I ever worship that lotus-foot which is to be served and meditated upon by sages.
