Be gracious, O Lord of gods, O Abode of the Universe! May my memory remain fixed upon your lotus feet, and may my attachment always abide, O Lord, in the hosts of attendants who bear the emblems of the consort, the treasury, the son, and the self.

May my mind be ever fixed upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa; may my words be employed in describing His divine stories; may these eyes of mine be for gazing upon Your form; may my ears be for His stories; and may my tongue be for that which is offered to Him. 24.

O Lord, may my nose forever be engaged in the fragrance of Your lotus feet and in the scent of the unguents and perfumes used by Your devotees; and may my two hands always be occupied with sweeping and other tasks in Your temple. 25.

O All-pervading Lord, may my feet always be intent upon visiting the sacred fields that recount Your deeds, and may my head be ever engaged in worshipping You. May I have a longing for Your sublime stories, and may my intellect be constantly occupied with meditating upon You.

May my days be spent with sages who have come to my home singing of the arising of Your holy stories; O Viṣṇu, may I never be deprived of the opportunity for discourse with You, even for a moment or half a blink of an eye.

O Viṣṇu, I do not long for the station of Brahmā, nor sovereignty over the whole earth, nor even liberation; I always desire only service at Your feet, which is sought after by Śrī, Brahmā, Śiva, and the other gods. (28)
Thus praised by the king, the lotus-eyed Viṣṇu was pleased and spoke to that lord of the earth in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Blessed Lord said: "I know you, O best of servants, to be free from desire and stainless; nevertheless, I shall grant you a boon that is difficult even for the gods to obtain."
O Lord of Men, may there be a divine lifespan of ten thousand years and all prosperities; may there be firm devotion to me, and in the end, even union with me (sāyujya).
And those on earth who praise me with the hymn composed by you—to them, being pleased, I shall grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt. (32)
This third [tithi] shall become renowned on earth by the name Akṣaya; on this day, I, being pleased with you, shall bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Those foolish men who perform acts such as ritual bathing and giving charity—whether by pretext or by their own nature—go to my imperishable abode.
And those men who perform a śrāddha ceremony on the third day of the waxing moon (Akṣayatṛtīyā) for the sake of their ancestors, that indeed leads to their infinite [merit].
And there is no lunar day on earth equal to or superior to this one in the world; even a very small act performed on this day shall yield inexhaustible fruit.
O best of kings, for one who gives a cow to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains a household, enjoyment and liberation—known as the rain of all prosperity—rests in the palm of his hand. (37)
For he who gives a bull, which destroys all sins, shall be liberated from untimely death and attain long life. (38)
For those who perform religious duties that are dear to me during the month of Vaiśākha, I remove their fear of death, old age, and birth, as well as their sins. (39)

I would indeed be satisfied by all the religious duties of the month of Vaiśākha; yet I would not be satisfied even by the religious duties of other months, for the month of Mādhava is dear to me. (40)
Even those who have abandoned all dharmas and are devoid of celibacy, if they are devoted to the month of Vaiśākha, go to my imperishable state.
That supreme abode, which is difficult to attain even through austerities, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, or sacrifices—men devoted to Vaiśākha go to that very place.
O sinless one, just as the remembrance of my feet destroys even a thousand sins, so too does this month [of Mārgaśīrṣa] destroy them, even if they are devoid of any prescribed expiation.
Instructed by his guru, you remained devoted in the forest during the month of Vaiśākha; having fully propitiated the Lord of the Universe, everything was obtained by you, O King.
Pleased by this dharma, I shall become manifest before you, after you have enjoyed pleasures according to your desire—pleasures that are very difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Having thus granted him the boon, Janārdana, the God of gods, vanished right there while everyone was looking on.
Then that excellent king became utterly amazed, his body thrilled and nourished with joy, like a monarch who has recovered lost wealth. (47)
Thereafter, with his mind fixed on Him and devoted solely to Him, he ruled the earth, constantly and perpetually instructed by great teachers.
The king considered no one else to be most dear except Vāsudeva, through whose association his wives, ministers, sons, and others became beloved. 49.
He performed all the rites prescribed for Vaiśākha again and again; by the power of that merit, he was surrounded by sons, grandsons, and other descendants.
Having enjoyed all her heart's desires, which were difficult even for the gods to attain, she finally attained union (sāyujya) with the divine Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus.
Those who hear this supreme narrative and cause others to hear it, all of them, liberated from sin, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Sāyujya by the Lord of Pañcāla," in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya, within the second section (Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa. || 16 ||
Śrutakīrti said: O giver of honor, even as I listen once more to all the duties of Vaiśākha which bestow fruits both in this world and the next, I am not yet satiated.
Wherein there is no deceitful dharma, and wherein are the auspicious stories of Viṣṇu—there is never satiety for one listening to that scripture, which is a nectar for the ears.
By good fortune, the merit accumulated in previous births has reached its culmination, since you have come to my home under the pretext of a guest. (3)
Having drunk the most wonderful nectar of speech issuing from your lotus-face, I am so satisfied that I no longer desire even the supreme status of Brahmā or liberation itself.
Therefore, speak again in detail to me of those very divine dharmas which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and which bring pleasure to Viṣṇu.
Thus addressed by the king in the past, the highly illustrious Śrutadeva, with a delighted soul, began once more to proclaim auspicious dharmas.
Śrutadeva said: Listen, O King, I shall relate the sin-destroying narrative concerning the duties of Vaiśākha, which has been meditated upon repeatedly by the sages. (7)
On the bank of the Pampā, there was a certain twice-born man of great renown named Śaṅkha; when his preceptor had gone to the Siṃha region, he went to the auspicious river Godāvarī.
Having crossed the holy Bhīmarathī river in the forest of Kaṇṭakācala—a place that was waterless, desolate, and terrible during the month of Vaiśākha—he was emaciated by his austerities.
At the time of midday, that twice-born man sat down to meditate beneath a tree; then a certain wicked hunter, deceitful and bearing a bow, appeared.
Cruel toward all beings like another Kālāntaka, he [beheld] that initiated brāhmaṇa wearing earrings, who resembled the sun.
Having seen him, the one of fierce intellect bound him and seized his earrings and other ornaments, as well as his sandals, umbrella, rosary, and water-pot.
Afterwards, having dismissed that brahmin, he of deluded intellect said, "Go! (13)
Then, on a path strewn with pebbles, scorched by the rays of the sun, parched, and harsh, he—his feet burning, his vital seed drawn up, and fasting—wandered at times over ground covered with grass.

Flying swiftly toward somewhere with satisfaction, crying out "Hā! Hā!", he went quickly; seeing the sage distressed upon the earth as the sun had reached the meridian, compassion arose within him. || 15 ||
To that hunter, who is averse to dharma and possesses a sinful mind, I indeed give this foot-protector that bestows happiness. (16)

"Whatever has been taken in the forest by the very act of theft—which is their own duty—that belongs entirely to them; such is the legal determination for hunters. Therefore, I shall give you these sandals to repeatedly dispel your suffering. (17)
"Whatever may be for my benefit, let that be mine, for I am a sinner. These two worn-out sandals remain upon my feet; I have no further use for them, therefore I shall indeed give them to you. (18)
Having thus resolved in his mind, he went quickly and gave those [fruits] to that eminent brahmin who was suffering with feet scorched by sugar-candy.
Taking his two sandals, he attained supreme peace; and having greeted the hunter with blessings, saying, "May you be happy," he departed.
Surely this man has ripened his merit by giving [this gift] during Vaiśākha; for Viṣṇu generally becomes pleased even with a hunter of evil intellect. (21)
And because of the attainment of everything, that happiness which arose for me once more—having heard those words, I was struck with wonder, thinking, "What is this? (22)
He spoke again to the Brahmin, who was most devoted to Brahman and a speaker of sacred truth: "How can that merit which was given by me to you become mine? (23)
"You praise Vaiśākha, saying that Hari will be pleased; tell me this, O Brahmin: what indeed is Vaiśākha, and who is Hari? (24)
"O ocean of compassion, what is that Dharma and what is its fruit? I wish to hear it. Hearing these words of the hunter, Śaṅkha became pleased in his mind. (25)
And praising Vaiśākha with a mind full of wonder once more, he said: "Now this deceitful hunter has given me a pair of sandals! (26)
Oh, how strange and wonderful is this disparity that has arisen in the mind of the evil-minded one! Indeed, the fruit of all dharmas is realized only in future births. (27)
The fruit of the religious duties of the month of Vaiśākha was obtained instantly, in a single moment, even by that evil-minded hunter of sinful conduct and wicked soul. || 28 ||
Ah, through the providential gift of these sandals, there has arisen a purification of being; for that which is dear to Viṣṇu is that which is stainless with the satisfaction [of the deity]. (29)
Manu and others, the foremost among those who know dharma, declare that very [observance] to be dharma; these dharmas pertaining to the month of Mādhava are exceedingly dear to Viṣṇu.
Keśava is not so pleased by all manner of gifts, austerities, and great sacrifices as he is by the religious observances belonging to the month of Mādhava.
There is no dharma like this to be found among all dharmas; let them not go to Gayā, nor to the Gaṅgā, nor to Prayāga, nor to Puṣkara.
Not Kedāra, not Kurukṣetra, not Prabhāsa nor Syamantaka; not Godā, nor Kṛṣṇā, nor Setu, nor Marudvṛdha. (33)
And the river of stories proclaiming the greatness of the Vaiśākha dharma—by bathing therein, Viṣṇu indeed immediately takes up residence within the heart. (34)
Whatever is accomplished in this month known as Mādhava with very little effort, that cannot be achieved through gifts involving great expense, nor even through religious duties or sacrifices.
"O hunter, this month is named Mādhava, which increases merit; in that month, you have given me these sandals that destroy all suffering."
Therefore, that former merit of yours has reached its fruition; the Blessed One, being pleased, will likely ordain your welfare, O hunter. (37)
"Otherwise, how could you have such auspicious wisdom? While the sage was speaking thus, the powerful one, impelled by Death, [acted].
Overwhelmed with rage, the lion rushed forth for the purpose of slaying the tiger; however, by the power of fate, he saw an elephant in his path, provided there by the Lord.
Intent on killing him, he went toward him as he stood there trampled by his foot; O King, a battle then ensued between those two, like that of a lion and an elephant in the forest.
Exhausted and desisting from the fight, they stood watching; meanwhile, that which had been said by the high-souled sage concerning the hunter was fulfilled.
By chance, they both heard [the account] which destroys all sins; through that very hearing of the greatness of the month, their hearts became pure.
Released from the curse, they were instantly liberated from their bodies and went to heaven, assuming divine forms, becoming celestial beings anointed with divine fragrances.
Mounted upon a divine celestial chariot and attended by divine women, they immediately stood before him with their heads bowed and palms joined in reverence.
The Lord of Sages, the expounder of Dharma, while on the road, addressed the hunter; seeing them both, he was struck with wonder and, standing still, asked, "Who are you two? (45)
But from what womb were you two born, or how did your death come to pass? Why, without cause, in this forest, are you intent on slaying one another? (46)
"O sinless ones, explain all of this to me correctly and in great detail. Thus addressed by that sage, they replied once more with these words.
The two sons of the sage Mataṅga were Dantila and another, Kohala; due to the fault of a curse, they were born with the names Dantila and Kohala.
"Endowed with beauty and youth, and proficient in all branches of knowledge, our father, who was skilled in the matters of dharma and worldly affairs, spoke concerning the two of us. (49)
A Brahmanical sage named Mataṅga, the most excellent knower of all dharmas, [was born] in the month of Vaiśākha, O beloved of Madhusūdana. || 50 ||
"Construct water-stalls on the road and fan the people for a moment; provide shade along the path, as well as abundant food and cool water. (51)
Perform your ablutions at dawn and likewise worship the Lord; and constantly listen to that discourse by which bondage is brought to an end. (52)
And although I was thus admonished with many words, I, the evil-minded Daṇḍin—known as Kohala—became angry and intoxicated. (53)
Enraged, their father, who was devoted to righteousness, immediately cursed them both.
One should immediately abandon a son who is averse to dharma, a wife who speaks unpleasantly, and a king who is unrighteous, unless they themselves fall [from their status]. 55.

"Those who enter into association out of courtesy or greed for wealth—all of them go to hell for as long as fourteen Indras endure. Having realized this, we two, overwhelmed by pride and anger, uttered a curse. (56)
"May this angry Daṇṭila become a lion overflowing with rage; and may the intoxicated Kohala become a rutting leader of a herd of elephants. (57)
But later, having felt remorse, we both prayed for liberation; our father, being further entreated by us, granted us freedom from the curse. (58)
Having attained this wretched birth, even after some time has passed, a meeting will occur there between you two, who are each intent on slaying the other.
At that very moment, by chance, a conversation between the hunter and Śaṅkha concerning the dharma of Vaiśākha occurred even while they were listening.
He will depart in an instant, and from that, liberation will come; once released from the curse, you two sons shall first assume your original forms.
"Only after reaching me shall you dwell; otherwise my word shall not be so. Thus cursed by their preceptor, the two evil-minded ones entered into a miserable birth.
Having by chance attained this meeting, we have both heard that auspicious and divine conversation of yours, even though you were each desirous of slaying the other. (63)
"By that, our liberation occurred instantly, in a mere moment. Having thus related everything and having bowed to the Lord of Sages, [they departed]. (64)

Having taken leave of one another and received permission, they went into the presence of their father; then, having observed that very situation, the sage, a treasure-house of compassion, spoke to the hunter.
Behold the great fruit of hearing the majesty of Vaiśākha; by merely hearing it for a moment, liberation stands within the grasp of those two.

To that bull among sages, a treasure-house of compassion, free from desire, possessed of supreme intellect, pure in essence, and the sole vessel for meritorious deeds, as he was speaking thus, the hunter—having laid down his weapons—spoke again: (67)
The hunter said: "O sage, I, a sinner of most wicked intellect, have been favored by you. For the great and virtuous are compassionate by their very nature. (1)
Where is a hunter such as I, of low birth, and where is such an intellect as this? I consider it solely to be the supreme grace bestowed upon me by you alone.
Therefore, O Holy One, I am your disciple; I am a worthy object of your compassion, O Giver of Honor! I am to be favored; I am your son. Bestow your grace upon me, O Treasure of Mercy! (3)
May this evil thought, which bestows misfortune, never arise in me again; for by associating with the virtuous anywhere, one never again experiences suffering.
Therefore, O Brahmin, awaken me with those well-spoken hymns that remove all afflictions, by which those seeking liberation shall truly cross the ocean of worldly existence.
For the virtuous who possess an even mind and likewise are endowed with compassion for all beings, there is nowhere any distinction between low and high, nor indeed any between one's own and another.
Then, having reflected with one-pointed concentration, he asks about the purification of the mind: "Whether one is possessed of all defects, or even whether one has abandoned all dharmas... (7)
And whenever he, filled with remorse, questioned his teachers, they would then truly instruct him in that knowledge which liberates one from the cycle of worldly existence.
Just as the Gaṅgā is destined to destroy the sins of human beings, so too are the virtuous known to be by nature the uprooters of dullness.
O compassionate one, kind to your devotees, do not hesitate to let me understand [this], for I am desirous of hearing, bowed before you, and pure through my association with you.
Having heard these words of the hunter, his mind once again filled with wonder, he exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! and spoke these verses on dharma.
Śaṅkha said: "O hunter, if you desire peace, perform the divine duties in the month of Vaiśākha which are pleasing to Viṣṇu and liberate one from the ocean of worldly existence."
"The fierce heat oppresses us, and there is neither shade nor water here; therefore, let us go to another place where shade exists. (13)
Having gone there, having drunk water, and having taken refuge in a pleasant shade, I shall describe to you the sin-destroying majesty of that place. (14)
"Regarding Viṣṇu and the month of Mādhava, exactly as it was seen and as it was heard"—having been addressed thus by that sage, the hunter spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Not far from here there is water in a lake, and there are indeed wood-apple trees (kapittha) there, weighed down by the burden of their fruit. (16)
"Let us go there; you will find contentment, of this there is no doubt. Having been thus instructed by the hunter, the sage went along with him.
Having gone some distance from there, he saw before him a lake crowded with cranes and kāraṇḍava ducks, and adorned with ruddy geese.
It was beautified on all sides by swans, cranes, curlews, and other birds, and it resounded with the sweet notes of kīcaka reeds as well as the humming of bees.
It was exceedingly beautiful, filled with crocodiles, tortoises, fish, and other creatures, and vast with white water-lilies, blue lotuses, kahlāras, puṇḍarīkas, and the like.
It was adorned on all sides with hundred-petaled red lotuses, made resonant by the sweet warbling of birds, and a festival for the eyes.
The bank was adorned with thickets of kīcaka reeds as well as trees—namely banyan trees, karañjas, nīpas, and likewise ciñciṇī trees.
With nimba, plakṣa, and priyāla trees, with auspicious campakas and bakulas, as well as with punnāgas, tuṃbaras, kapitthas, and āmalakas. (23)
It was beautified on all sides by *jambū* trees that had been crushed, and by wild elephants, deer, boars, buffaloes, and other such creatures.
It was adorned with hares, śallaka deer, and gavayas, as well as with rhinoceroses, mṛgas, and other animals, along with tigers, lions, and wolves.
It was beautifully adorned with wild asses, śarabhas, and marīs, as well as by monkeys leaping swiftly from branch to branch.
It was terrifying with cats, bears, and likewise with *ruru* deer; with the sounds of crickets, with shrieks, and with the whistling of hollow bamboos.
Filled with the weight of timber shattered by the force of a terrible wind, such a divine lake was revealed by the hunter himself. (28)
Greatly afflicted by thirst, that tiger among sages saw [it] after bathing in this delightful lake at the time of midday. (29)
Having put on two garments and performed the midday rites, he should then perform the worship of the deity and, being untiring, eat the fruit.
Seated comfortably, he again questioned the hunter, who was devoted to dharma, regarding the delicious wood-apple brought by the hunter, which was capable of removing his fatigue.
"What indeed should I say to you today at the outset, O you who are devoted to dharma? For dharmas are many, consisting of various paths and diverse kinds. (32)
In that regard, even the subtle rites prescribed for the month of Vaiśākha bestow great benefit; they grant fruits both in this world and the next to all living beings whatsoever. (33)
"Ask whatever you have in mind, and ask that which was [the subject] at the beginning. Thus addressed by that sage, the hunter spoke with palms joined in reverence: (34)
The hunter said: "By what karma did you come to this birth as a hunter, which is full of darkness? And by what means did you attain such an intellect or association with a great soul? (35)
"Tell me this and more, O Lord, if you consider me worthy," he said; thus addressed, the great sage named Śaṅkha spoke again.
With a voice as deep as a thundercloud and a face like a blooming lotus, Śaṅkha said: "Formerly, in the city of Śākala, you were a twice-born man who had mastered the Vedas."
There was one named Staṃba, possessed of great luster and born of the Śrīvatsa lineage; due to the fault of association with a certain courtesan who was his beloved, [he fell]. (37)
Having abandoned his daily obligatory rites, he came to the house constantly like a Śūdra; he was of empty conduct, wicked, and had utterly forsaken his religious duties.
And at that time, Kāntimatī was your wife, a Brāhmaṇa woman; she, the fair-browed one, attended upon you, that lowest of Brāhmaṇas, along with your fellow-villagers.
Washing the feet of both as she seeks to do what is pleasing to you, she lies beneath both, devoted to the words of both.
Though she was being restrained by the courtesan, she remained steadfast in her vow of devotion to her husband; indeed, while thus serving her husband along with the courtesan, [she continued].
A very long time passed while she remained sorrowful upon the earth; then, on another day, her husband [brought] a bean together with radishes.
He ate the food of a Śūdra, *nipāva* beans mixed with sesame; having consumed that unwholesome food, he vomited and was purged. (44)
From his indolence, a terrible disease called bhagaṃdara arose; being consumed by that disease day and night, he suffered greatly. (45)
As long as wealth remained in his house, the courtesan stayed with him; but having taken that wealth, she no longer dwelt in his home.
Having approached the side of another, she became terrible and utterly merciless; then he, speaking piteously and intensely tormented by the affliction of disease, [lamented]. (47)
Speaking thus while weeping, his mind agitated by pain, he said to his wife: "O Goddess, protect me, who am exceedingly cruel and attached to a courtesan."
"O beautiful and pure lady, I have done you no wrong at all. What wicked and contemptible man would not consent to his wife when she has prostrated before him? (49)
O blessed lady, O highly fortunate one, for five out of ten births he will be a eunuch, censured day and night by virtuous people.
"Having indeed insulted you, a virtuous woman, I shall surely attain a base birth; for I am consumed by the anger born of this offense against you. (51)
To her husband who was speaking thus, she replied with her palms joined in reverence: "O beloved, you should feel no dejection, nor should you feel any shame toward me. (52)
Nor is there any anger toward you on my part by which you might be consumed as you say; for indeed, sins committed in the past result in sufferings in this world. (53)
That virtuous woman or man who endures these is supreme; for whatever evil was committed by me, a sinner, in a previous birth— [54]
"While she was eating that, I felt neither pain nor any kind of despondency"; having spoken thus to her husband, that fair-browed woman protected him.
Having brought wealth from her father and her kinsmen, that woman of excellent complexion meditated upon her husband, the god who dwells in the Ocean of Milk.
Day and night, she cleansed away both feces and urine, painfully and very slowly scraping away her husband's worms with her fingernail.
That woman of excellent complexion neither slept at night nor by day; tormented by her husband's suffering, she spoke these words in her distress.
May the gods and the renowned ancestors protect my husband; may they make my husband free from disease and cleansed of all sin. (59)
"For the sake of my husband's health, I shall offer to Caṇḍikā well-prepared food consisting of blood and flesh, accompanied by buffalo meat. (60)
"I shall have sweetmeats (modaka) prepared for the high-souled Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa), and on Saturdays, I shall observe ten fasts. (61)
I shall not enjoy sweets, nor indeed shall I enjoy clarified butter; deprived of oil massage, I shall remain here—of this there is no doubt. (62)
"May this husband of mine live for a hundred autumns, free from disease. Thus did that queen speak as each day passed by. (63)
Then, at that time, a certain high-souled sage named Devala, afflicted by the heat, came to his house in the evening during the month of Vaiśākha.
Then his wife said: "A physician has indeed come to our house; by him the destruction of the disease will surely occur, so I shall offer him hospitality. (65)
Having recognized you as one averse to dharma, he was deceived by the pretext of being a physician; having performed the washing of your feet, he cast that water upon his own head.
And she gave a cooling drink to that high-souled one who was afflicted by the heat; at your command, she provided that which wards off the torment of the summer heat.
When the sun had risen in the morning, that sage departed just as he had come; then, after a short time, your assembly took place.
As Trikaṭvī was being led away, she broke her husband's finger; suddenly, the two teeth became joined together.
That very tender fragment remained in the mouth of her husband; having bitten off the finger, the husband then met his death.
On a most delightful bed, remembering that unchaste woman, your wife Kāntimatī learned that her husband had died. (71)
Having sold her bangle and obtained a great quantity of fuel, that virtuous woman then prepared a funeral pyre, placing her husband in its midst.
Embracing him with both arms and clasping his feet with her own, she pressed her face against his face and likewise her heart against his heart.

Placing her own hips against his hips, the auspicious goddess settled herself upon his body; then, the virtuous lady caused the husband’s afflicted body to be cremated along with herself as the fire blazed. (74)

Having suddenly cast off her body, she embraced her husband and went to the world of Murāri; and by this gift of water, as well as from washing the feet of Mādhava, she attained that realm accessible even to yogis.

At the time of death, having cast off your body with thoughts of a courtesan, you will be freed from all sins; yet, being addicted to violence and a constant source of distress to others, you shall indeed obtain a birth of terrible form fraught with disease.

O noble one, permission was granted by you even for the gift of a drink during the month of Mādhava; because of that, this hunter has become wise and has developed the good sense to inquire about the dharmas, which are the sole cause of all happiness. (77)

The water remaining from the washing of the sage’s feet, which removes all sins, was borne upon my head; by that merit, this union with you has occurred in this forest, through which I shall again obtain prosperity and progeny.
Thus all this has been told—whatever meritorious and sinful karma was performed in a previous birth, as seen with divine vision. (79)
I shall tell you that which is to be kept secret, about which you wish to hear; indeed, purity of mind has arisen in you—may it be well with you, O high-minded one! (80)

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Hunter’s Previous Birth," within the Legend of the Hunter, in the Dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa, in the Greatness of the Month of Vaiśākha, in the second Vaiṣṇava Section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 18 ||

The hunter said: "Auspicious Bhāgavata duties should be performed with Viṣṇu as the objective; even among those, specifically the rites dedicated to Mādhava—this was indeed stated by you previously. (1)
O Brahman, what is that Viṣṇu like, and what indeed is his characteristic? What is his measure, and by which true states of being is the all-pervading Lord to be known? || 2 ||
O Brahman, O high-minded one, tell this to me, your servant: what are the Vaiṣṇava duties, and by what means is Hari pleased?
Thus questioned by the hunter, that twice-born man spoke again, having prostrated before Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the worlds, who is free from all ailment.
Śaṅkha said: Listen, O hunter, I shall describe the stainless form of Viṣṇu, which is inconceivable even to Viriñci and other sages of purified souls. (5)
He is designated as the Lord of all, possessing full power and full qualities; yet He is devoid of [material] qualities, partless, infinite, and His very form is existence, consciousness, and bliss.

This entire universe, consisting of the moving and the non-moving, which is unlike anything else, that which has the Supreme Lord as its object of praise and refuge, and that which remains subservient to His will; || 7 ||
Now I shall describe the characteristics of Brahman, the Supreme Self: namely, creation, maintenance, and dissolution, as well as cyclic recurrence and restraint. (8)
He from whom these—illumination, bondage, liberation, and mental modification—arise, is that all-pervading Lord known as Brahmā, who is esteemed by the wise.

The wise declare him to be "Brahman manifest," and even those beginning with Brahmā as "Brahman" afterwards; they know that the word "Brahman" when applied to Brahmā and others is used with a qualifying prefix.

No others who possess but a single fraction of that power can ever attain the state of Brahman; for this [nature] of the Great Lord—from whose birth and so forth [the world arises]—is indeed to be known through the scriptures.
O high-minded one, the Śāstras, the Vedas, the Smṛtis, the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, the Pañcarātra, and the Mahābhārata are indeed of that same nature.
Mahāviṣṇu is to be known through these alone and by no other means whatsoever; and a man who does not know the Veda never truly recognizes this Viṣṇu anywhere.
The all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is to be known through the Vedas and is eternal, cannot be known by the senses, nor by inferences, nor by logical reasonings. || 14 ||
Having understood his very births, deeds, and qualities according to their own intelligence, the multitudes of living beings are liberated, even though they are always subject to his control.
In due order, the majesty of Viṣṇu becomes increasingly supreme; for within each one—whether among the gods, sages, ancestors, or mothers—resides his power.
One should first recognize the Supreme among Men through direct perception, through scripture, and likewise through inference—in terms of power, knowledge, and happiness. (17)

Therefore, one should know that the Bhūtas, endowed with knowledge and other qualities, are a hundred times greater; and one should know that the human Gandharvas are a hundred times superior to the Bhūtas.

The gods are those who possess pride in their respective principles (tattvas); from those gods who possess pride in their principles, there are more than a hundred Vidyās; and from the gods who possess pride in their principles, the seven Ṛṣis are superior.
For Agni is indeed superior to the Seven Sages; likewise, the Sun and others are superior to Agni. From the Sun comes Bṛhaspati; from Bṛhaspati, Prāṇa; and from Prāṇa, the mighty Indra.

From Indra came the goddess Girijā, and from the goddess came Śambhu, the teacher of the world; from Śambhu came the great goddess Buddhi, and from Buddhi came Prāṇa, who is superior in strength. (21)

There is nothing superior to the vital breath (prāṇa); everything is established in the vital breath. This entire universe is born from the vital breath; this world has the vital breath as its essence.
All this is woven upon the vital breath (prāṇa), for it moves by means of the vital breath alone; they call this the support of all, the Sūtra, possessing the luster of a dark blue cloud.
The existence of this vital breath depends solely upon the side-glance of Lakṣmī; that Lakṣmī, in turn, partakes only of a fraction of the grace of the God of gods.

"There is nothing whatsoever superior to Viṣṇu, nor is there anything equal to him in any way. The hunter said: "How did this life-force (prāṇa), known by the name 'Sūtra,' become superior among living beings? (25)

Or how is there a definitive conclusion regarding this? O Lord, how is there a preponderance of vital breaths? Tell me this, O Brahman: how is the All-pervading One superior to the vital breaths? (26)
Śaṅkha said: Listen, O hunter, I shall explain the definitive conclusion as you have asked it, concerning the superiority of life-force over all living beings. (27)
In former times, the eternal Lord Nārāyaṇa, Janārdana, having created the gods beginning with Brahmā during the lotus-creation, spoke this: || 28 ||
"In the universal sovereignty, I shall establish Brahmā as your lord and master; O lords of the gods, whichever deity among you is superior shall be installed in the position of crown prince. (29)
"Install him, who is rich in virtue and endowed with the qualities of heroism and magnanimity. Thus addressed by the Lord, all the gods, led by Śakra, [acted accordingly].
Thus they disputed with one another, saying, "I shall be the greatest! I shall be the greatest! And while all were thus disputing, some regarded the Sun as supreme. (31)
Some favored Śakra, some the supreme Kāma, while others remained silent; seeing no way to reach a decision, they went to Nārāyaṇa to ask him.
Having bowed down once more, all the immortals, with palms joined in reverence, spoke again: "O Mahāviṣṇu, everything has been thoroughly deliberated by us all."
"We do not know at all which god is superior among us; you alone must declare the decision, for the gods are indeed in doubt. (34)
Thus questioned by all the immortals, he laughed and spoke this: "When this [individual self] indeed departs from this body of Vairāja... (35)
Indeed, whichever deity rises up when another has entered [the body], that deity is certainly superior; it cannot be otherwise under any circumstances. (36)
Thus addressed, they all then said, "So be it. Then the lord of the gods, named Jayanta, emerged first from his foot.
Then they called him "the lame one," for his body did not fall at that time; though he was unable to move, he remained there hearing, drinking, speaking, smelling, and seeing.
Afterwards, the Prajāpati named Dakṣa emerged from his private parts; at that time they called him "Ṣaṇḍha," yet his body did not fall then. (39)
Hearing, drinking, speaking, smelling, seeing, and even moving about, Indra, the lord of all the immortals, remained behind, having emerged from his hand.
They said that this man was handless, yet his body did not fall; he remained sitting, hearing, drinking, speaking, smelling, seeing, and even moving.
The Sun, the best among the radiant, emerged from his two eyes; at that time they called him "the one-eyed" (kāṇa), yet his body did not fall then.

Hearing, drinking, speaking, smelling, seeing, and even moving about, he remained as before; yet when the two life-breaths, the Nasatyas, the universal healers, departed from him, they said of him, "He does not smell," and then his body fell.

Even while hearing, drinking, speaking, smelling, or remaining motionless, the sense of hearing has departed from the ears toward the directions; yet the body does not fall at that time. Then they call such a person deaf, but by no means dead.
Then, even while drinking, speaking, not hearing, and not moving, Varuṇa departed from the tongue; thereafter, people called him one who knows no taste, yet his body did not fall at that time.
Living, moving, eating, and likewise knowing even while lying dead, from him the pervasive Lord of Speech, Fire, emerged as speech. (46)
Then they called him mute; yet his body did not fall at that time. He remained alive, moving, eating, as well as perceiving and even breathing. (47)
Afterwards, Rudra, whose nature is the awakening of the mind, emerged; then they called this [body] inert, yet the body had not yet fallen.

"Living, moving, eating, as well as knowing and even breathing, he remains; but when the vital breath has departed, they then know him to be dead. Then the gods, their minds filled with wonder, spoke thus once again: || 49 ||
"He who shall produce a body and remain established in this manner—he indeed shall be superior among us and will become the crown prince. (50)
Having thus given their promise, they entered in due order; Jayanta entered at the feet, yet that corpse did not rise.
Dakṣa entered the secret organ, but that body did not rise; then Indra entered the hands, yet that body still did not rise.
The sun entered the eye, yet that body did not rise; the quarters of space entered the ears, yet that body did not rise. (53)
Varuṇa entered the tongue, but that body did not rise; the two Aśvins entered the nose, but that body did not rise. (54)
Agni entered the speech, yet that body did not rise; Rudra entered the mind, yet that body did not rise. (55)
Afterwards, that vital breath (prāṇa) entered, and then the body rose up; then the gods, having determined that the pervasive lord Prāṇa was superior to the gods, [honored him].
Then, because of his strength, knowledge, fortitude, detachment, and even his vital energy, they consecrated the great lord as the crown prince.

Because it is the cause of the most excellent state, they then sang that one [breath] as the *uktha*; therefore, the entire universe, consisting of all things moving and stationary, is of the nature of prāṇa.
This Lord of the worlds is complete with full and powerfully abundant portions. || 59 ||

There is nothing in the world devoid of breath; indeed, that which is deprived of breath does not flourish. Nothing here remains stable when deprived of breath, and nothing exists at all without breath. Therefore, breath has become superior to all living beings, possessing greater strength than all, and is the inner self of every living being. (60)
Indeed, no one superior or even equal to Prāṇa has been seen in the scriptures, nor has such a person ever been heard of before. || 61 ||

The vital breath (prāṇa), following after its various functions, is indeed the one God manifest in manifold ways; therefore, those devoted to the worship of prāṇa declare prāṇa to be the most excellent. It is capable of effortlessly creating, destroying, and protecting the universe.
The remaining beings—Śeṣa, Ahi, Śiva, Śakra, and others, whether sentient or insentient—none whatsoever shall overcome him except for Vāsudeva. (63)
The vital breath (prāṇa) consists of all the gods; it is all-pervasive, composed of all the gods, eternally following Vāsudeva, and likewise remains under the control of Viṣṇu.
But he neither hears nor sees anyone who is hostile toward Vāsudeva; even the gods, Rudra and the other lords of the deities, act in opposition to him.
The vital breath, which pervades all, never acts in opposition anywhere; therefore, the wise declare that the vital breath is the power of Mahāviṣṇu.
Having thus understood the majesty and the characteristics of Mahāviṣṇu, one should cast off the body-limbs (liṅga) that follow former bonds, just as a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.
Having heard the words uttered by Śaṅkha, the hunter, his mind once again serene, departed for the supreme and stainless Nārāyaṇa after casting off [his former state]. (68)
Bowing down with humility, he questioned that sage once again: "O Brahmin, [tell me] concerning this Prāṇa, the teacher of the world and possessed of great majesty. (69)
How indeed has the greatness of the Lord of All not become renowned in the world, among the gods, the sages, and the high-souled kings? (70)
"His greatness is heard of thousands of times in the world and in the Purāṇas; tell this to me, O Brāhmaṇa, for I have a great curiosity to hear it. (71)
Śaṅkha said: In ancient times, Prāṇa, desiring to worship the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all affliction, joyfully went to the bank of the Gaṅgā with the intent to perform horse-sacrifices.
Accompanied by various hosts of sages, he performed the purification of the ground with ploughs; meanwhile, one named Kaṇva, who had attained meditative absorption, remained hidden within an anthill.
Having emerged as the most excellent of all, he spoke thus out of anger; seeing Prāṇa standing before him, he cursed that great lord.
"From this day forward, O Lord of Gods, your greatness shall not attain renown in the three worlds, and especially not in the world of mortals. (75)
"They shall indeed become renowned as incarnations throughout the three worlds. When he was addressed thus by that sage, Vāyu spoke to him in anger: || 76 ||
"I have been cursed without cause; though I am innocent and patient, therefore, O mighty-armed Kaṇva, become a hater of your guru immediately. (77)
"May you have a livelihood censured by the world," so said Sadāgati. From that time forth, O great lord, this very Prāṇa has [been such] in this world. (78)
His greatness was not renowned in the world, especially in the mortal realm; however, after Kaṇva had consumed his preceptor due to a curse, he then became a disciple of Sūrya.
All this that you have just asked has now been told; O hunter, ask me whatever else is to be heard from this point on, without hesitation.
The hunter said: "Were living beings created by the Lord by the millions or even by the thousands? They are seen with diverse actions, following various eternal paths. (1)
For these, Mahāmati, do not have a single intrinsic nature; how much less so [for all things]? Ask me about all of that, and explain it to me in detail according to its true reality.

Śaṅkha said: "Indeed, the multitudes of living beings are of three kinds, characterized by the qualities of passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and darkness (tamas). Those of passionate nature perform passionate deeds, and likewise, those of dark nature perform dark deeds. (3)

These [beings], being characterized by sattva, perform sattvic actions in their respective order; however, in the course of worldly existence, there may occur an imbalance of these qualities in some cases.
By performing various kinds of actions—some high and some low—they become partakers of their fruits; in some cases there is happiness, in some cases suffering, and in some cases both.

It is solely due to the inequality of the qualities (guṇas) that these men attain their various states; these living beings, abiding in primordial nature (prakṛti), are bound by these three qualities.
The fruit of actions is the transposition of those very actions according to their qualities; these people, for the most part, return to their original nature in accordance with their qualities.

Those who abide in primordial nature (prakṛti) are natural-born and are deluded by the qualities (guṇas) and actions; they go toward a natural course of existence, for there is no deviation from primordial nature.
Those characterized by tamas are always full of suffering, their conduct being perpetually dark; they are merciless and cruel in the world, living solely for hatred.
Those beginning with the Rākṣasas and ending with the Piśācas go to the tāmasa state; those characterized by passion (rājasa) have mixed intentions and are the performers of both merit and sin.
Through merit they attain heaven, and at times through sin they undergo torment; therefore, these unfortunate ones revolve again and again.
Those who are virtuous in character, compassionate, full of faith, and free from malice—being of the nature of sattva—they abide practicing the conduct of sattva.
Those pure ones of great majesty go upwards when their qualities have ceased; therefore, for those whose karmas are distinct, their states are separate and of various kinds.
In accordance with their qualities and actions, the all-pervading Lord Viṣṇu, the Great Master, truly causes them to perform actions for the sake of attaining their own true nature.
Indeed, for Viṣṇu, whose desires are fulfilled, there is neither partiality nor cruelty; he performs creation, maintenance, and destruction with perfect equanimity. (15)
All those partake of the fruits of their actions solely through their own qualities; just as rain equally nourishes all trees planted in a grove.

For indeed, O dear one, trees that have returned to their natural state from the water of a single irrigation trench do not, in any way, incur either partiality or cruelty on the part of the planter of the grove. (17)
The hunter said: O sage, when does liberation occur for people who possess full enjoyment—is it at the time of creation, or at the time of dissolution, or even at the time of establishment? (18)
O Brahman, tell me in detail this activity of the Blessed One, concerning the time of creation, as well as that of dissolution and maintenance. (19)
Śaṅkha said: A thousand cycles of four yugas is called a day of Brahmā; his night is of equal duration, for his day and night together constitute one full day.
They say that fifteen days constitute a *pakṣa* (fortnight), and a month consists of two such [pakṣas]. They call two months a season (*ṛtu*), and three seasons an *ayana*.
If two such solstices (ayanas) were to pass for him as one hundred years do for us, they know that to be a single Brahmakalpa of this Brahmā.

For such is the duration of the period of dissolution (pralaya), according to the opinion of those who know the Vedas; dissolution is declared to be threefold: the human, occurring at the end of a Manu-period, [the elemental, and the absolute].
Indeed, at the end of the day of Brahmā, there is the second [type of dissolution], the daily one; thereafter, at the dissolution of Brahmā, they know it as the Brāhma-pralaya.
They know that the dissolution of Manu occurs in a single moment of Brahmā; indeed, when fourteen such dissolutions have passed in succession, [the next creation begins].

They say that the dissolution of the three worlds occurs daily, while their re-establishment constitutes the state of dissolution for the [other] pralayas; however, the destruction of all three worlds occurs within a Manvantara.
At that time, there would be the destruction of volitions, yet no depletion of the worlds; they would be replenished by waters alone, just as before, so again. (27)
At the end of a Manvantara, there is the rebirth of sentient beings; O hunter, at the dissolution of a day [of Brahmā], there is the destruction of everything.
Except for Satyaloka, all the worlds, together with their presiding deities, perish when the four-faced one is asleep—along with their sentient beings and their material elements. (29)
The gods who pride themselves on their realization of the principles, as well as certain sages—all of them, established in Satyaloka, remain asleep.
They remain in a state of sleep, beyond the reach of the senses, for the duration of a kalpa; then, at the end of the night, Brahmā fashioned [the world] again as it was before.
The sages, gods, ancestors, worlds, duties, and the social classes, each individually—these are indeed the ten incarnations of the divine Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus.
These, as well as many others, become [manifest] by necessity, including the deities and sages, until the end of the kalpa of the Lord of Speech (Brahmā).
Furthermore, those who have attained liberation, as well as kings, virtuous men, and those who have achieved perfection and reached the supreme state, all return once more together with Brahmā. (34)
Established in Satyaloka, they return by that very same path; having entered that mass [of light], they go again, being known by that name as established in the Vedas.
They are born into various lineages, always devoted to their respective duties; this occurs for all the Daityas as well when the Kali Yuga comes to an end.
Those whose abode is hell go to their own destination along with Kali; and those who are situated in his assembly, as well as others bearing his name, do the same.
By their own past actions, they are born as the ordainers of those various deeds. I shall now describe the time of creation, and likewise the time of liberation.
And remain with a concentrated mind toward the gods, beginning with Brahmā; for a single blink of the God of Gods is considered equal to a kalpa of Brahmā. (39)

At the conclusion of that [period], there arises the opening of the eyes of the crest-jewel of the gods; at the end of the closing of his eyes, the desire occurs to create the worlds contained within his belly. (40)

He saw within his own belly all the multitudes of living beings in their many forms—those yet to be created and those already liberated—all of whom had attained the dissolution of their limiting marks (liṅgabhaṅga).

All those who were asleep, established in the flow [of existence], and even all those who had entered into darkness, having undergone the dissolution of their subtle bodies (liṅgabhaṅga) according to the prescribed rule in the previous kalpa; || 42 ||

The sheaths of living beings, from humans up to the level of Brahmā, are both liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and destined for final liberation; they were liberated in previous kalpas as well, from Brahmā down to the level of humans.

For those established in meditation remain even while situated within the belly of Viṣṇu; at the very first moment of his opening of the eyes, the all-pervading Lord consists of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha).
Having manifested through his prior excellence and from Vāsudeva as the Vyūha, the Great Lord, having granted to Brahmā liberation known as Sāyujya, [departed]. (45)

Thereafter, the All-pervading Lord bestowed upon those great-souled ones the knowledge of reality leading to union (sāyujya), as well as similarity of form (sārūpya) for some, and proximity (sāmīpya) for others.
Having likewise granted the state of *sālokya* to others, the Lord Janārdana beheld all the worlds situated under the control of Aniruddha.
Having placed the creation under the control of Pradyumna, Hari himself set his mind upon creating; he married Māyā, Jayā, Kṛti, and Śānti.

The all-pervading Mahāviṣṇu, endowed with those [energies] beginning with Vāsudeva, which possess complete qualities and consist of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha), is himself of the nature of the fourfold manifestation. || 49 ||
Viṣṇu, whose desires are fulfilled, brought forth the world with its diverse karmic latencies; then, at the end of his opening [of the eyes], he again resorted to his yogic power (yogamāyā).

From Saṃkarṣaṇa, who abides in the cosmic manifestation (vyūha), he withdraws this entire world of moving and non-moving beings. Thus, all this work of the Great Soul has been described as it should be contemplated.

"That which is inconceivable and difficult to be discerned even by yogis such as Brahmā and others. The hunter said: "What indeed are the Bhāgavata duties, and by what means does Viṣṇu become pleased? (52)
"I desire to hear those now; speak them to us, O Sage. Śaṅkha said: "That by which there may be purification of the mind, and which is beneficial to the virtuous. (53)
Know that to be the quality of sattva which is not censured by anyone, which is declared in the Śruti and Smṛti, and which is performed without desire for reward.
But that which is not opposed to the world, they know to be the quality of sattva; for those dharmas are fourfold, according to the divisions of caste and stage of life.

They are considered to be of three kinds: obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya). When all of these, along with their respective duties, are offered to Viṣṇu, [they lead to liberation]. || 56 ||
Then indeed, those auspicious duties pertaining to the Bhāgavatas are to be known as sāttvika; those whose deity is another god and which are performed with desire are considered rājasa.
Those dharmas which have yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and the like as their deities, which are cruel toward the world, violent in nature, and censured, are remembered as tāmasa.
Those who, established in goodness, constantly perform auspicious and virtuous deeds that please Viṣṇu without desire for reward—they indeed are remembered as Bhāgavatas. (59)
Those whose minds are always fixed on Viṣṇu, whose tongues bear the name of the All-pervading Lord, and whose feet are at His heart—they indeed are remembered as Bhāgavatas.
Those who are devoted to virtuous conduct, who are benefactors to all, and who are always free from the sense of "mine"—they indeed are remembered as Bhāgavatas. || 61 ||
Those who have faith in the scriptures, in their guru, in the virtuous, and in sacred rites; those who are constant devotees of Viṣṇu—they indeed are remembered as Bhāgavatas.
For those for whom the eternal dharmas are esteemed as dear to Viṣṇu, and those dharmas proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti, they are considered eternal.
Wandering through all lands, observing all activities, and listening to all teachings—these belong to those whose minds are unattached to sense objects. (64)
The sight of these [sinners] is of no benefit to the virtuous, just as a beautiful woman is of no use to a eunuch; indeed, the minds of the good melt simply by the sight of the holy ones.
Just as a moonstone melts upon contact with the moonlight of the moon, so too, through the hearing of the true scriptures, the mind becomes free from the objects of the senses.
For the stainless form of splendor of virtuous men indeed persists, just as a sun-stone glows through contact with the light of the lotus-born Sun.
Indeed, that Bhāgavata dharma which is always dear to Viṣṇu is resorted to with faith by those people who are free from desire. 68.
By them were seen many subtle dharmas that yield fruit both in this world and the next, which please Viṣṇu and liberate one from all suffering. (69)
Having extracted the essence of dharma arising from Vaiśākha like cream from curd, the Blessed One spoke it to Ramā in the Ocean of Milk out of a desire for her welfare.
Likewise, the creation of shade along the path, the providing of water-stations, fanning with fans, and the offering of resting places. || 71 ||
The gift of an umbrella and sandals, the gift of camphor and fragrances, and the construction of step-wells, wells, and ponds when one possesses the means; 72.
In the evening, the gift of beverages, flowers, and betel-leaf destroys sin, especially the gift of cow-products.
Giving buttermilk mixed with salt to one who is weary on the road, performing an oil massage, and washing the feet of a twice-born man; || 74 ||
The gift of a mat, a woolen blanket, and a couch, as well as the gift of a cow, and the gift of sesame seeds mixed with honey, are the destruction of sin. (75)
In the evening, there is the offering of sugarcane stalks and cucumbers, as well as the bestowing of elixirs and the libations for the ancestors.

These dharmas have also been declared for the disciples during this month dear to Mādhava; having bathed at dawn upon the rising of the sun, one should listen to them as recited by a community of twice-born brahmins.
Having thus performed the daily obligatory rites, one should worship Madhusūdana and listen with a concentrated mind to the sacred narrative concerning the month of Mādhava.
One should avoid anointing with oil and eating from a vessel of bell-metal; one should also avoid consuming forbidden foods and idle chatter.
The bottle-gourd, the *gṛñjana*, garlic, sesame-cake, sour gruel, fried grains, and likewise the *ghṛtakośātakī* [must be avoided]. (80)
One should avoid upodakī, kaliṅga, and the potherb of śigru; one should also avoid niṣpāva, kulittha, and masūra.
One should avoid eggplants, *kaliṅga* fruits, and *kodrava* grains; likewise, one should avoid *taṇḍulīyaka* greens, safflower, and radishes.
A wise man should avoid underwood fruit, wood-apple, as well as śleṣmātaka fruit, in every way during this month dear to Mādhava.
Having consumed any one of these, he will certainly become a caṇḍāla; he enters a hundred animal births—of this there is no doubt to be made. (84)
In this manner, one should observe the month-long vow for the pleasure of the Slayer of Madhu; when the vow is thus completed, one should have an image of the Lord fashioned.
One should present to a Brāhmaṇa an image of Madhusūdana, accompanied by a cloth and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), which has been well-adorned with all available riches.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one should duly offer curd-rice, along with a water-pot, betel-leaf, fruit, and a monetary gift (dakṣiṇā).
"I give [this] to Dharmarāja; by this, may Yama indeed be pleased," having thus uttered the name and lineage of the father in the anti-clockwise direction (apasavya). || 88 ||
One should offer inexhaustible curd-rice for the sake of the satisfaction of the ancestors; likewise, one should offer it to the gurus and afterwards offer it to Viṣṇu.
Excellent cold water, curd-rice placed in a bell-metal vessel, along with a monetary gift (dakṣiṇā), betel-leaf, edible snacks, and fruits.
"I give this to you, O Viṣṇu, with the desire to conquer the world of Viṣṇu. Having spoken thus, he should give a cow according to his capacity to a householder.
He who performs the month-long vow in this manner, free from hypocrisy, is liberated from all sins and truly uplifts a hundred generations of his lineage.
Even as all beings look on, having pierced through the solar disc, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, which is difficult even for yogins to attain.
Thus, to that best of the twice-born, he explained all the Mādhava duties—those most beneficial ones desired by Viṣṇu and others—which had been previously requested by the hunter.

Even as they were looking on, the five-branched banyan tree suddenly fell to the ground; alas! from that tree, a certain fierce serpent with a long body who had been dwelling in a hollow, immediately abandoned his body and that sinful birth, and stood there with palms joined and head bowed.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Bhāgavata Dharmas," in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa, within the *Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya* (The Greatness of the Month of Vaiśākha), in the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrutadeva said: Then Śaṅkha, filled with wonder along with the hunter, asked him, "Who are you, and from where does this splendor of yours come? (1)
O gentle one, by what action has your mind become auspicious? How is it that you have attained liberation so suddenly? Explain this to me in detail.
Then, questioned by Śaṅkha, he fell upon the ground like a staff; bowing low with humility and joining his palms in reverence, he spoke these words.
Formerly, I was a certain Brahmin at Prayāga who spoke excessively; endowed with beauty and youth, I was intoxicated by the pride of my learning.
I am Rocana by name, the son of the sage Kusīda; I was once wealthy, possessed of many sons, and always defiled by egoism.
Sitting, lying down, sleep, sexual intercourse, tending to the eyes, worldly talk, or idleness—these were my occupations. (6)
Fearing the censure of the world, I always perform my duties with mere outward pretense and hypocrisy; I never possess true faith.
How much time has passed for me, wicked and evil-minded? Then, in this month of Vaiśākha, there was indeed a twice-born man named Jayanta.
He caused the duties pertaining to that month, which are dear to the Bhāgavatas, to be heard by the twice-born residents of that sacred field who were performers of meritorious deeds.
Thousands of women, men, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, having bathed in the morning and worshipped the imperishable Madhusūdana, [proceeded].
Having become pure and observing silence, they constantly listen to the discourse uttered by Jayanta, being devoted to the stories of Vāsudeva.
Devoted to the religious duties of Vaiśākha and free from hypocrisy and laziness, I entered that assembly out of curiosity and a desire to see.
With my head still covered by a turban, I did not even offer a prostration; moreover, I kept betel in my mouth and wore my upper garment. (13)
I engaged in the diversion of conversation by delighting them with worldly talk; indeed, through such worldly talk, the mental agitation of everyone arose.
Spreading out my bedding in one place, censuring in another, and laughing in yet another, I have thus passed the time until this story was completed.
Afterwards, by that very same fault, my life was suddenly cut short and my intellect destroyed; on the following day, I met my death through the disorder of the humors (sannipāta).
Having reached the hell Halāhala, which is filled with molten lead, and having experienced torment there for fourteen manvantaras.
Then, having been born in succession through hundreds of thousands and likewise eighty-four thousand wombs, I have now come to rest in this tree.
Ten yojanas wide and a hundred yojanas high, within its seven-yojana hollow, I am a fierce, dark, and cruel serpent.
"O brahmin-sage, having been previously afflicted by my past karma, I have lived here as a bird; ten thousand years have passed for me in this hollow without food. (20)
O Sage, having by chance heard the nectar of the story uttered from your lotus-like mouth, my two eyes have instantly destroyed all my inauspiciousness.
Having cast off my serpent birth, I am now a man wearing a divine form; with palms joined in reverence and bowing down, I have come to you for refuge at your feet.
O best of sages, I do not know in which birth you were my kinsman; I have never done anything to benefit you. Yet, how could the virtuous ever fail to be compassionate? (23)
For the virtuous, who possess equanimity of mind and are always compassionate toward all beings, helping others is their very nature; their intention is never otherwise.
Grant me your grace today, so that my mind may be fixed upon dharma, and there may never be any forgetfulness of the divine Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus.
May there always be association with great souls of virtuous conduct; for poverty alone is the supreme collyrium that blinds one with pride. (26)
Having thus praised him in many ways and bowed down again and again, he stood silently before him with palms joined in reverence and body bent low.
Lifting him up with both arms, Śaṅkha, overflowing with perfect love and freed from all fatigue, touched his limbs with his most auspicious hand.
He bestowed his grace upon that twice-born man who possessed a divine form; filled with compassion, he spoke to him directly concerning the events yet to come.
O twice-born one, by hearing the greatness of this month and also by hearing the greatness of Hari, all your bonds have been instantly destroyed.
Having transcended your stain and having gradually returned to earth, you shall become an excellent brahmin in the rugged and meritorious land of Daśārṇa.
There you will become renowned as Vedaśarman, an expert in all the Vedas; and there, your auspicious memory of past lives shall become eternal.
Thus, you, being auspicious, have abandoned all worldly desires and maintain a continuous stream of mindfulness; you perform all the religious duties prescribed for Vaiśākha, which are dear to Hari.
Free from dualities, free from longing, unattached, devoted to the Guru, with senses conquered, he will always engage in discourse concerning the stories of Viṣṇu in that birth.
Then, having attained perfection and with all bonds destroyed, you reach the supreme abode, which is difficult even for yogis to attain.
"Do not fear, my son; may it be well with you through my grace. [This has occurred] whether from laughter, or from fear, or likewise from anger, or from hatred, or even from desire. (36)
Or, by uttering the name of Viṣṇu even once out of affection—which removes all evil—even the most sinful go to the stainless abode of Viṣṇu.
O best of the twice-born, what need is there to mention those who, endowed with faith, having conquered anger and subdued their senses, depart after hearing this narrative with compassion? (38)
Some, solely through devotion and intent only on conversation about [the Lord], even if they have abandoned all religious duties, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Some worship Viṣṇu out of hatred and the like, or out of devotion; they too go to the supreme abode, just as Pūtanā did when she took away his life.
One should always associate with the great, and the discharge of speech should be based upon them; this is the rule enjoined by the Śruti for those seeking liberation. (41)

That utterance of speech, even if it is not composed as a verse in every line, is a flood that washes away the sins of the people—in which virtuous men hear, sing, and praise the names of the Infinite One, adorned with His glory.

To whom should one go for refuge, other than that Compassionate One, who—being all-pervading—does not desire arduous service, nor does He require vast impressions, nor beauty or youth; yet, when remembered even once, He goes to His own radiant abode? (43)
Go for refuge to that very Nārāyaṇa, who is free from ailment, affectionate toward his devotees, unmanifest, accessible to the mind, and a treasure-house of compassion.
O high-minded one, perform all these duties prescribed for Vaiśākha; by that, the Lord of the World will be pleased and shall bestow happiness upon you. (45)
Having spoken thus, he ceased, being greatly amazed upon seeing the hunter; then that divine person spoke again to that bull among sages.
The divine being said: "O Śaṅkha, I am blessed and I am graced by you, who are compassionate. By good fortune, my miserable birth has ended, and I am attaining the supreme goal. (47)
Having thus circumambulated him and received his permission, he departed for heaven; then at evening, O King, Śaṅkha was gratified by the hunter.
Having performed the evening twilight rites, he passed the remainder of the night with various narratives concerning kings and high-souled gods.
Having witnessed the playful incarnations with one's own eyes, and having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, having washed one's feet and restrained one's speech; || 50 ||
Meditating on the *tāraka* Brahman and having performed the proper rites such as purification, one should bathe in the month of Vaiśākha when the sun is in Aries, before the rising of the sun.
Having performed his twilight rituals and other duties, and likewise having offered libations to all, he—gladdened in spirit—summoned the hunter, sprinkled water upon his head, and gazed at him.
He bestowed the auspicious two-syllabled name "Rāma," which is superior to all the Vedas; for even a single name of Viṣṇu is considered superior to all the Vedas.
And among those infinite names, this thousand names is superior; by such a thousand names, the name of Rāma is considered equal.
Therefore, O hunter, chant that name "Rāma" incessantly; perform these duties, O hunter, until the end of your life. (55)
Then your birth shall take place in the family of the sage Valmīka; you will attain fame on earth by the name Vālmīki.
Having thus instructed the hunter, he set out toward the southern direction; the hunter, having circumambulated him and bowed down again and again, [departed].
Having followed him for some distance, weeping and afflicted by separation, he watched his course again as long as it remained within the range of his vision.
He returned with great difficulty, reflecting upon that very same [incident] in his heart; having constructed a forest along that path, he established a perfectly pure water-station (prapā).

He indeed performed these most suitable rites prescribed for the month of Vaiśākha, using wild fruits such as wood-apples (kapittha), jackfruit (panasa), rose-apples (jambū), mangoes (cūta), and others.
Providing food for those weary from the fatigue of the roads, as well as sandals, sandalwood paste, umbrellas, and even fans.
And here and there, with its shade provided by carpets of sand, it likewise removed the fatigue born of sweat from travelers.
Having bathed in the morning and chanting the mantra "Rāma" day and night, he was born as a member of the Vyādha caste, the son of Valmīka.
A certain sage named Kṛṇu performed difficult penance in that very lake, free from all external activities. || 64 ||
In the course of time, an anthill grew upon his body; therefore, they called that bull among sages "Valmīka."
O King, when Kṛṣṇa came to the mind of the sage at the conclusion of his penance and its cessation, the senses of the sage faltered as he remembered the women.
A certain actress took him up; from her was born the forest-dweller who became renowned throughout the worlds as Vālmīki, possessed of great fame.
He who indeed proclaimed throughout the world the divine story of Rāma—which severs the bonds of karma—through his own captivating compositions. (68)
Śrutadeva said: O King, behold the greatness of the month of Vaiśākha, which bestows prosperity even now; even a hunter, by giving a pair of sandals, attained the rare state of a sage. (69)
Whoever hears or even causes others to hear this supreme narrative, which destroys sins and causes the hair to stand on end, shall never again become a suckling infant.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of Vālmīki’s Birth," within the Legend of the Hunter, in the Dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa, within the Greatness of the Month of Vaiśākha, in the second Vaiṣṇava Section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 21 ||
Maithileya said: Which lunar days (tithis) in this month known as Vaiśākha are meritorious, and what specific gifts are recommended on those respective days? || 1 ||
"Tell me in detail which ones are renowned in the world. Śrutadeva said: "There are thirty meritorious lunar days (tithis) in Vaiśākha when the sun is in Aries."
The merit performed on the eleventh lunar day becomes multiplied by millions upon millions; it is equal to the merit found in all acts of giving and the fruit obtained at all sacred fords.
On the eleventh day of Vaiśākha, one who is immersed in water truly obtains the merit of bathing, giving, austerity, burnt offerings, worship of the deities, and hospitable rites.
The hearing of this very discourse bestows immediate liberation; it is for one who is afflicted by disease and the like, as well as for one oppressed by poverty. (5)

Having heard this meritorious narrative, a man becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose; for by this [narrative], these auspicious [days] have been brought forth even for one who has neither bathed nor given gifts.
He is considered a great slayer of cows, ungrateful, and a slayer of his father; he has mastery over reservoirs of water and mastery over his own body.
Mādhava is to be served with the mind, as is Time, the most excellent of qualities; and the virtuous are compassionate—who would not serve Mādhava? (8)
By the poor and the wealthy, by the lame and the blind, by eunuchs and widows, and likewise by women and men.
O King, for children, youths, the elderly, and even those afflicted by disease, the dharma pertaining to Vaiśākha is indeed exceedingly easy to accomplish.
Having reached this month, perform these auspicious duties; for who would not exert effort in this regard? What indeed could be more auspicious than that? (11)
That lowest of men who does not perform those dharmas which are exceedingly easy to practice—for him alone are the hellish worlds easily attained; of this there is no doubt. (12)
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe that most excellent lunar day (tithi) in that month, which destroys all sins, like the essence extracted from curd.

In the month of Caitra, which is highly meritorious, when the sun is situated in Aries, this [tithi] destroys sins, has the ancestors as its presiding deities, and bestows the fruit of ten million Gayās.
In this very context, an ancient and meritorious verse concerning the ancestors is heard; listen to that virtuous story, O King, while Sāvarṇi rules the earth. (15)
At the end of the thirtieth Kali Yuga, when all dharma has vanished, there will be a certain twice-born man in Ānarta known as Dharmavarṇa.
O King, having seen people devoted to sin in the Kali Yuga—during its very first quarter when they have abandoned the duties of their respective castes—the sage [acted].
Once, he went to the sacred field of Puṣkara, where high-souled sages, observing a vow of silence, were performing a sacrificial session (satrayāga).
There, the sages engaged in meritorious discourse concerning the scope of the scriptures; among them, some who were firm in their vows praised the Kali age.
O King, that merit which is accomplished in one year during the Kṛta age for the propitiation of Mādhava is accomplished in a month during the Tretā age, and in a fortnight during the Dvāpara age.
Therefore, in the Kali age, ten times the merit of remembering Viṣṇu shall arise; indeed, even a very small amount of merit in the Kali age becomes multiplied ten millionfold.
But toward one who is devoid of merit and abandoned by the duty of giving, he practices compassionate giving, having indeed uttered the name of Hari but once.
He indeed was surely one who ascends upward, as well as a giver of food during a famine; on this occasion, the sage Nārada arrived there. (23)
Holding his penis with one hand and his tongue with the other, that best of sages danced there like a madman while laughing.
Then the members of the assembly said to him, "O Nārada, what is this? The wise one, while dancing and laughing, replied to them all. (254)
"Since we have been declared here by those of purified souls who were dancing out of contentment, we have attained perfection; there is no doubt that this meritorious Kali age has arrived. (26)
That is the truth, there is no doubt: much is accomplished by even a little. Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, attains satisfaction merely through remembrance. (27)
Nevertheless, O sons, I shall declare to you two things that are certainly difficult to accomplish: the constant restraint of the penis and also of the tongue. (28)
For he alone would be Janārdana in whom duality might exist; therefore, you must not remain here upon the arrival of the Kali Yuga. (29)
Abandoning this heretical Bharata, wander at your pleasure to whatever lands your heart finds delight in. (30)
Having heard those words, the sages of celebrated vows immediately concluded their sacrificial session and departed at their pleasure.
Having heard that, Dharmavarṇa also set his mind on abandoning the earth; he took up the ascetic vow of upward-radiance, carrying a staff and a water-pot.
Having thus become a wearer of matted hair and bark garments, he went forth once more with a mind full of wonder to behold the improper conduct of the Kali age.
There he saw terrible people devoted to sinful conduct and wicked; all were heretical twice-born men, as well as Śūdras and wandering mendicants.
The wife hates her husband, and likewise the disciple hates his teacher; the servant becomes a slayer of his master, and the son is intent on the murder of his father. || 35 ||
All twice-born men have become like Śūdras, and cows have become like goats; likewise, the Vedas have become mere songs, and auspicious rites are now equal to common actions. (36)
In that place, spirits such as bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas are the deities who bestow fruits; people devoted to sin and steeped in delusion worship those very beings with faith. (37)
All were devoted to sexual indulgence, having staked their very lives for its sake; they were speakers of perjured testimony, with minds always intent on deceit. (38)
In the Kali age, there is one thing in the mind, one in speech, and one in action; for all, that knowledge which is based on reasoning is to be honored in the king’s palace. (39)
In the Kali age, even minor arts and sciences such as singing and the like, which bring pleasure to kings, attain honor; whereas the most excellent ones do not.
In the Kali age, all twice-born men learned in the Vedas shall be poor; indeed, devotion to Viṣṇu generally does not exist among men at all. (41)
In the Kali age, the field of merit will for the most part abound in heretics; Śūdras will be expounders of dharma, and ascetics will wear matted hair.
All mortals will be short-lived, and people will be devoid of compassion and deceitful; all will be mere preachers of dharma, and all will be festivals for seizing [possessions]. (43)
Devoted to vain censure and intent on malice toward everyone, they even desire their own worship when the Lord has come to their own home. (44)
In the Kali age, the brother will go to his sister and the father to his daughter; indeed, all will be devoted to Śūdra women, and all will be devoted to courtesans.
Those of wicked intent do not recognize the virtuous at all, yet they consider them to be full of great sin; out of stubbornness, they expose even a single fault in the righteous.
Indeed, the wicked proclaim the multitude of vices as virtues; yet in the Kali age, people devoid of merit seize only upon the faults.
The leech, though endowed with the quality of dharma, drinks blood and not milk; likewise, medicinal herbs are devoid of essence, and the seasons are out of their proper order. 48.
There will be famine in all kingdoms, and daughters will not give birth at the proper time; in the Kali age, men will take delight in the arts of actors and dancers.
O King, those fools who, though superior in virtue and devoted to the Vedas, Vedāntas, and sciences, look upon their servants as equals, are fallen in every respect.

Having abandoned all rites of ancestral offerings (śrāddha) and having forsaken the practices ordained by the Vedas, the names of Viṣṇu never resided upon their tongues; immersed in the aesthetic flavor of erotic passion (śṛṅgāra-rasa), they sang only those songs.
