In the Kali age, it is a wonder that among people there was nowhere to be found service to Viṣṇu, nor discourse on the scriptures, nor initiation for sacrifice, nor even a trace of inquiry; neither pilgrimages nor the duties of charity existed anywhere. 52.
Seeing them, Gharma-varṇa was also terrified and utterly amazed; seeing his lineage going to ruin because of sin, he departed for another continent.
Wandering through all the continents and indeed throughout all the worlds, that wise one once went to the realm of the ancestors, filled with curiosity.
There he saw [beings] most terrible, exhausted by their karmic deeds.
There he saw his own ancestors fallen into a blind well below—some running, some weeping, some falling, and others already fallen.
At that time, a certain mouse arrived at the base of the dūrvā grass which served as their refuge—grass from which the wretched birds hung by their beaks, fearing the cutting of the dūrvā.
By that, three parts were consumed and only one part remained; seeing that root being diminished, they were dragged down by suffering.
Looking down, they saw a blind well, terrifying with its precipitous fall, difficult to escape from, most dreadful, and acquired through their own actions; they were deeply distressed.
Seeing them at the front, which was difficult to cross and devoid of any support, he became astonished and, being compassionate, spoke these words: || 60 ||
Who are you that have fallen here, and by what difficult deed? In whose lineage were you born, and how was your powerful liberation achieved? (61)
"Tell me this, and then there will be peace for you. Thus addressed by him, the ancestors were then deeply distressed.
Preceded by Dharmaśruti, they spoke these piteous words. The ancestors said: "We belong to the Śrīvatsa lineage, yet we are bereft of progeny on this earth."
"Because we were deprived of the piṇḍa-śrāddha, we are being cooked [in hell]; moreover, due to our sins in the Kali age, our lineage has become extinct. (64)

"In our lineage there is no one to offer funeral cakes (piṇḍa) now that it has perished through sin; therefore, we wretched souls, devoid of a thread [of progeny], shall fall into the blind well. (65)
For in this lineage there is but one of great fame who maintains the color of righteousness; he, living in detachment as a solitary wanderer, has never entered the state of a householder.
"By means of that thread, we support ourselves by hanging from the stalks of durva grass; however, because it is devoid of thread, a rat gnaws at its root every day. (67)
"O gentle one, look! Since only one remains, Nala has been reduced to a mere fragment; he exists being eaten by a mouse. (68)
And when his life-span is exhausted, O dear one, a mouse will carry off what remains; thereafter we shall fall into a well of blinding darkness from which it is difficult to emerge. (69)
Therefore, you too, having gone to the earth, awaken Dharmavarṇa—the sage who has turned his back on the householder's life—by means of our words which are worthy of compassion.
"Indeed, your ancestors, having fallen into hell, were seen by me in a blind well difficult to escape, hanging by blades of dūrvā grass, and were exceedingly afflicted. (71)
O Sage, that dūrvā grass indeed has the form of a bamboo; its root is constantly being eaten day after day by a mouse named Kāla.
Through the gradual destruction of the lineage, you alone have been left remaining; thus, O Sage, three parts of the root of the dūrvā grass have perished.
Only one portion remains here because you exist upon the earth; indeed, a mouse eats a little of you as your lifespan gradually comes to an end.
If you were to fall, our own downfall would follow; even when our lineage has perished, you too would fall into the very same well of blinding darkness. (75)
Therefore, having entered the householder stage, perform the increase of progeny; by that, there will be an upward path for both us and you, without a doubt.
Many sons should be desired, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā, or performs the horse sacrifice, or releases a dark-colored bull.
If even a single person, during the month of Vaiśākha, Māgha, or Kārtika, shall perform a ritual bath, a śrāddha, or an act of charity dedicated to us; || 78 ||
By that, may there be an upward path for us and deliverance from hell; let there be at least one devotee of Viṣṇu, or at least one who observes the day of Hari.
Or even if one person alone should hear the story of Viṣṇu, which destroys all sins, for him a hundred past generations and a hundred future generations [are saved].
Even one who is shrouded in sin never sees hell anywhere; what is the use of many other sons who are devoid of compassion and righteousness? (81)
Those born in a family who do not truly worship Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa—indeed, there is no world for one who has no son; all people know this.
And even there, one endowed with compassion and such a spiritual lineage is difficult to find; having thus enlightened him with these truthful words, [he spoke]. (83)
"Set your mind upon the householder's life, for you are dispassionate and have drawn up your vital energy. Having heard the words of his ancestors, Dharmavarṇa was greatly astonished.
Bowing with palms joined in reverence, weeping and trembling, he said: "By name I am Dharmavarṇa, a member of your lineage, yet stubborn and obstinate. (85)
Having heard these words of the high-souled Nārada at the sacrificial session, [he understood that] in the Kali age, no one possesses such firmness of tongue or such firmness of secret [devotion].
Seeing those most wicked people on the earth, he became apprehensive; fearing association with the evil-minded, he wandered and lived in another continent.
Indeed, three quarters of this Kali age have already passed, and even during the final quarter, three and a half parts have elapsed; these are now the progenitors.
"I do not know the suffering you endure; my birth has passed in vain, for in the family where I was born, the debt to my parents has certainly not been repaid. (89)
Of what use is that enemy born merely as a burden upon the earth, who, once born, does not worship Viṣṇu, the ancestors, the gods, and likewise the sages? (90)
"I shall carry out your command; please instruct me as to how there may be no affliction from the Kali age on this earth, nor even from the cycle of worldly existence."
"Even the duties that ought to be performed by me as a son on this earth [must be fulfilled]," thus was he addressed by that wise descendant of his lineage, who was devoted to righteousness. (92)
O lord of the earth, with their minds somewhat consoled, they said this: "Son, behold this condition of your high-souled ancestors."
Since we are falling due to the absence of progeny, hanging by only a blade of dūrvā grass, you, having attained the state of a householder, must rescue us through progeny. 94.
Those who are devoted to the stories of Viṣṇu, those who remember Hari incessantly, and those who are intent upon righteous conduct—Kali does not indeed afflict them.
O giver of honor, Kali does not indeed afflict that person in whose house a Śāligrāma stone resides, or else the Bhārata [Purāṇa] remains in the home. (96)
Kali does not indeed afflict him who is devoted to the month of Vaiśākha, who is intent on the ritual bath of Māgha, and who is a donor of lamps in Kārtika.
He who listens every day to the divine story of the high-souled Viṣṇu—which destroys sins and bestows liberation—is indeed not afflicted by the Kali age.
In whose house the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is performed, in whose house auspicious Tulasī resides, and in whose courtyard a noble cow dwells—Kali does not indeed afflict that person. 99.
Therefore, there is no fear for us here, even in this age characterized by sin. Go quickly to the earth, my son; this month is called Mādhava.
For the benefit of all, when the sun is situated in Aries, thirty lunar days (tithis) are meritorious while the sun is in Aries. || 101 ||
The merit performed on each [of these days] becomes multiplied by ten million times ten million; even among those, the new moon day in the dark fortnight of Caitra grants liberation to men.
It is dear to the ancestors and the gods, and it bestows immediate liberation for those who indeed perform the Śrāddha ceremony on that day in honor of their ancestors.

O son, those who perform the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) along with the water-pot (sodakuṃbha) on the new moon day of the month of Madhu obtain that fruit which is imperishable; indeed, they who perform the Śrāddha on that Amāvāsyā.

A śrāddha performed by them in the sacred field of Gayā becomes ten millionfold meritorious, provided they perform the śrāddha during the new moon in the month of Madhu, even if it consists merely of vegetables.
By him, a crore of ancestral rites (śrāddhas) has undoubtedly been performed at Gayā; he has offered a water-pot filled with refreshing drinks and scented with camphor and agallochum.

He who does not give [this] on the new-moon day in the month of Madhu is a slayer of his ancestors, without a doubt; whereas he who gives a *karīraka* fruit along with water on the new-moon day in Madhu [attains merit].
And he who performs the ancestral rite (śrāddha) endowed with devotion brings prosperity to his lineage; likewise, in the world of the ancestors, this river showers down nectar.
From the gift of a water-pot, for those who give gifts such as funeral offerings (śrāddha), there flows forth a mire of food, soup, ghee, cakes, linctuses, and milk-rice.
Therefore, O high-minded one, go at once, or else when the new moon occurs, perform the *śrāddha* rite, the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), and the gift of water-jars.
For the benefit of all, take recourse to the life of a householder; being satisfied with virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and having obtained excellent progeny.
"Furthermore, you shall live as a sage and move about happily on the island. Having been thus instructed by his ancestors, the sage quickly went to the earth.
In the month of Caitra, when the sun was situated in Aries during that auspicious month, having bathed in the morning and having offered libations to the ancestors, the gods, and the sages; || 13 ||
Having likewise performed the *sodakuṃbha* śrāddha, which destroys sin, and having thereby bestowed upon the ancestors liberation free from rebirth; || 14 ||
Having obtained a virtuous progeny, he himself performed the marriage ceremony and proclaimed that lunar day in the world as the destroyer of sins.
He himself, moreover, returned joyfully and with devotion to Gandhamādana. || 16 ||
Therefore, this lunar day called Madhu-darśā is most meritorious; no lunar day equal to it has been seen or even heard of in the world.
Śrutadeva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the sin-destroying majesty of the Akṣayā Tṛtīyā occurring in the bright fortnight of the month of Mādhava.
And those who perform the morning bath there at the rising of the sun are all liberated from sin and go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

Whoever performs a libation (tarpaṇa) intended for the gods, the ancestors, and the sages, by him everything has been studied, by him every sacrifice has been performed, and by him a hundred śrāddhas have been offered.
Those men who, having worshipped Madhusūdana, listen to this narrative on the Akṣayyā Tṛtīyā day, are partakers of liberation.
Whatever auspicious gift people perform there for the pleasure of the Enemy of Madhu, that indeed bears inexhaustible fruit by the command of the Teacher of Spring.
This lunar day is highly auspicious, presided over by the gods, sages, ancestors, and deities; it bestows satisfaction upon these three when the eternal dharma is practiced.
And as for the renown of this lunar day, O tiger among kings, I shall also explain that; listen with an attentive mind.
In ancient times, there was a battle between Purandara and the powerful [Bali]; thereafter, a duel took place between the gods and the Daityas.
Having conquered the Daitya Bali who dwells in the depths of Pātāla, he returned to the earth and went to the hermitage of Utathya.
There he saw his wife, who was pregnant and moving slowly, beautifully adorned with a girdle fastened around her swaying hips.

She surpassed the intoxicated bees and cuckoos with the resonant sound of her tinkling bracelets; she was a beautiful woman of radiant and variegated garments, sweet-spoken, and possessed of a pure smile.
She was graced by breasts whose surfaces were like shimmering jars, possessing a divine face with a smiling lotus, and beautiful eyes like blue lotuses.
She was beautiful with cheeks as pale as the interior of a ketaki flower, standing at the entrance of the leaf-hut, sighing from exhaustion, and looking downcast.
Seeing her sleeping somewhere on a bed, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, became infatuated and forcibly enjoyed her while she was pregnant.
Then, while still within the womb, the fetus, distressed and fearing his own fall, covered the opening of the birth canal with his foot.
Then that semen of the enemy of Bala fell upon the very ground; the Lord Pākaśāsana became enraged at it while it was still in the womb.
And with eyes copper-red with rage, he cursed him while he was still in the womb: "O evil-minded one, become blind from birth, since you have insulted me with your foot."
Then, having covered the vaginal opening with his foot, the one named Dīrghatapas was born from the semen that had been discharged from the webbed membrane.
Afterwards, Indra departed quickly, fearing the sage’s curse; seeing Hari fleeing, all the young students laughed.
Then, becoming ashamed, he went to a beautiful cave on Mount Meru; remaining hidden there, he performed a great and difficult penance.
While the lord of the gods dwelt there, having dissolved himself within Mount Meru out of shame, the Daityas, led by Bali, learned of that news through their secret spies.
Having attacked the gods, Śambara and other powerful beings enjoyed Amarāvatī and the riches of the guardians of the quarters. || 22 ||
In that kingdom of the gods which was without a protector, the deities, led by Agni, being unaware of a guardian, were forcibly oppressed.
They questioned the god Dhiṣaṇa, the preceptor of the gods who is free from sin; they asked about the news of Indra: "Where does our lord reside? (24)
"This kingdom has been seized by the Daityas and is left without a protector for the denizens of heaven. Why does that Lord not come? O All-pervading One, a great deal of time has passed. (25)
"Let us go to that place where we seek Dhiṣaṇa and that powerful lord. Thus questioned by the gods, Dhiṣaṇa then spoke to them.
Having conquered Bali in the netherworld (rasātala), he went to the hermitage of Utathya; there, having enjoyed his wife with firm resolve, he was rebuked by that sage’s disciples.
Ashamed, however, he entered a cave of Mount Meru to go to heaven; there the powerful lord remained together with Śacī, reflecting upon his own deeds.
Having heard these words of his, the gods, led by Agni, went quickly to the cave of Meru to behold and entreat the Lord.
There, having seen the lord of the gods, the subduer of Pāka, hidden within the cave, they praised him with various hymns [recalling] his world-renowned heroic deeds.
O Indra, salutations to you; let there be homage to you, the sovereign of all the gods. We have been tormented by the Daityas, and being deprived of you, we are now severely afflicted.
"O dear one, having fallen from our positions, we wander through various lands in misery; therefore, O Lord of the Gods, come and slay our enemies, O subduer of foes! (32)
Thus praised by the gods, he then emerged from the mouth of the cave, bowing his head in shame and looking at the ground with his eyes.
He said nothing at all, his speech faltering due to grief; perceiving this, Bṛhaspati spoke to that terrifying lord of the gods.
O Lord of the Gods, let there be no fear in you; this world is subject to karma. Honor and dishonor, pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat—all these are dependent upon action.
These things come to pass in accordance with past karma; of this there is no doubt. The individual soul follows its karma, experiencing suffering as ordained by destiny through the power of time.
The wise generally do not grieve nor do they rejoice because of happiness; therefore, O Lord, this suffering has come to you as a result of your past karma (prārabdha).
"Having attained that state, O Maghavan, you ought not to grieve at all. Thus addressed by his preceptor, Maghavan spoke to the lords of the immortals.

Indra said: "O giver of honor, through the fault of associating with another's wife, my strength, heroism, stainless fame, the power of counsel, the power of the scriptures, and the power of knowledge [have been lost]. (39)
"My vigor has vanished; therefore, I dwell in silence. Having heard these words of Pākaśāsana, they were joined by their own teacher. || 40 ||
They consulted in private once more for the sake of regaining his strength; then the Guru, the best among the knowers of truth, spoke to them with compassion.
Bṛhaspati said: This month named Vaiśākha is indeed dear to the Slayer of Madhu; and all lunar days (tithis) in this month, which is beloved by Mādhava, are meritorious.
And even there, during the bright fortnight of this month, on the day called Akṣayā, whoever indeed performs acts such as bathing and giving gifts with faith— || 43 ||
Thousands of his sins are surely destroyed, there is no doubt; likewise, faultless sovereignty, strength, and fortitude arise.
Therefore, on that third lunar day, we shall perform the virtuous acts of bathing, giving gifts, and so forth, by means of Hari, the enemy of Bala, for the attainment of our welfare.
And that power of the vidyā and the two mantra-śāstras shall arise, and strength, fortitude, and fame shall likewise exist as they did before. (46)
Having reflected thus, the preceptor, being composed by the gods, had Indra perform these duties which are dear to Hari.
On that third [day] called Akṣayyā, which bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation, the strength, fortitude, and other qualities of the Lord remained as they were before.
Even the fault of associating with another's wife vanished instantly; thereafter, Śakra, his inauspiciousness destroyed, was like the moon released from the mouth of Rāhu. (49)
Then, having conquered the asuras, Hari shone in the midst of the gods like [the sun] among the deities, accompanied by the gods. (50)
And by the greatness of the third [day], he, endowed with good fortune, entered Amarāvatī along with his riches, amidst the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments. || 51 ||
Permitted by Śakra, the gods returned to their own abodes; thereafter, they received their sacrificial portions just as before.
The ancestors received their shares of the funeral cakes as before; the sages were gratified by their Vedic study, and there was defeat for the Daityas.
From that time forward, this third day known as Akṣaya became famous throughout all the worlds in this universe, bestowing satisfaction upon the gods, sages, and ancestors.
Therefore, this third lunar day, known as Akṣaya, is most meritorious; it cuts through all karma and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men. || 55 ||

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Excellence of Akṣayya-tṛtīyā," in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, within the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa. || 23 ||
Śrutadeva said: O Indra among kings, on these meritorious lunar days, the twelfth day (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha destroys the entire multitude of sins.
Of what use are gifts, of what use are austerities, and of what use are fasts and vows? Of what use are sacrifices and works of public utility for those by whom the Dvādaśī has not been observed? (2)
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving a thousand cows at the Gaṅgā during an eclipse, that same fruit one attains by bathing in the morning on the day of Hari.
Whatever food is given to a worthy recipient on the auspicious twelfth day of the bright fortnight, for every single mouthful of that offering, it shall be equivalent to feeding ten million Brahmins.
He who gives a vessel of sesame seeds mixed with honey on the twelfth lunar day, having shaken off all bonds, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, one should perform a vigil for Hari; while still alive, he shall be liberated, and all the deities shall be gratified.
Whatever fruit one obtains by bathing at sacred fords during a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse, or a solar conjunction, that same fruit one attains by bathing in the morning on the day of Hari.
On the twelfth lunar day, one should worship Viṣṇu with tender Tulasī leaves; having uplifted his entire lineage, he shall become the lord of the world of Viṣṇu.

A person, intending for Yama, the ancestors, the gurus, the gods, and Viṣṇu, [should give] on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mādhava a water-pot along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Listen now to the meritorious fruit of one who gives curd-rice: it is as if he were to perform a feeding of ten million people every single day at Prayāga. || 10 ||
Whatever merit is gained by providing delightful food of six flavors for a full year, one obtains that same fruit by following the command of Madhuśāsana.
Whoever makes a gift of a Śāligrāma stone on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha is liberated from all sins.
Whoever bathes Madhusūdana with milk on the twelfth lunar day obtains that fruit which arises from the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
On the thirteenth day, one should worship Viṣṇu with substances consisting of milk, curd, sugar, and honey for the pleasure of Madhusūdana.
One obtains that very fruit at the Gaṅgā; of this there is no doubt—[the same as] he who with devotion bathes the Lord Viṣṇu with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). || 15 ||
Having uplifted his entire family, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu—he who, for the pleasure of Hari, should offer a refreshing drink on this [day] at the time of sunset.
He who offers the elixir of *urvāruka* at the time of sunset quickly casts off his accumulated sins, just as a serpent sheds its worn-out skin. (17)
One would be liberated from the bondage of karma through this elixir of the urvāruka fruit; one should offer stalks of sugarcane, mango fruits, and grapes. (18)
There shall be no interruption in his lineage for a hundred generations, he who offers fragrant unguents on the evening of the twelfth day.
One is liberated from all external afflictions; of this there is no doubt. Whatever merit one performs on the twelfth day (Dvādaśī), O best of kings— || 20 ||
In the bright fortnight of the month of Mādhava, however, that [act] shall yield inexhaustible fruit. O protector of the earth, I shall tell you how it became renowned and by whom it was originated.
It destroys all sins for everyone and bestows all auspiciousness. Formerly, in the land of Kashmir, there was a twice-born man named Devavrata.
He had a daughter named Mālinī, who was of beautiful form; he gave her to the wise Satyaśīla, an eminent brāhmaṇa.
Having married her, the wise one went to his own country called Yavana; yet she, though endowed with beauty and youth, did not become dear to him at all.
O King, that husband always remained full of hatred toward her and stayed harsh with her; indeed, he bore no ill-will toward anyone else except her. (25)
Filled with anger and greedy for power over him, that woman asked the king: "Were there women in the past who were abandoned by their husbands? (26)
O King, they said to her, "Your husband will become submissive; we have gained confidence, for we are women who despise the abandonment by a husband. (27)
"For in the past, husbands were indeed brought under control by employing medicine; therefore, go today to the Yoginī, and she will give you auspicious medicine. (28)
"You should not entertain any doubt; the husband will become like a servant. O King, having gone to the temple of the Yoginīs, act according to their word. (29)
Though she was a woman of evil conduct, she attained incomparable faith in her; with great haste, she took refuge in a hut provided with a hundred pillars.
Extremely expansive, highly radiant, and likewise free from fatigue, the Yoginī was present there, clothed in a long garment.
Covered with long manes and endowed with radiance, she was accompanied by her attendants and gazed slowly and steadily.
With a rosary in her hand, she was praying when she was requested by her; she then gave her a mantra that brings things under control, causes agitation, and produces conviction.
Then, having bowed down, she should offer a ring made of materials, joined with diamonds and rubies, and endowed with an intensely red luster.
Joined with soft gold and possessing a luster equal to the rays of the sun, she was then delighted upon seeing that ring placed at her feet.

And she understood that the heart of her husband was born from his humiliation; then, O King, she was addressed by that female ascetic who was intent on his welfare: 36. "Then she was indeed addressed by that female ascetic, who was engaged in what was beneficial for him."
This powder, endowed with protection, brings all beings under one's control. Having applied the powder to your husband, place the protective amulet around his neck. (37)
Your husband will be submissive; he will not go to any other beautiful woman, nor will he ever speak unpleasantly even to you, though you are a woman of ill-conduct. (38)
Taking that protective powder, she returned once more to her husband's house; at nightfall, the powder mixed with milk was administered to her husband.
For she placed the protection around her neck without making any inquiry; then that husband, O best of excellent kings, swallowed the powder. (40)
From that powder, the disease of consumption arose; the husband became emaciated day by day, and terrible worms born of malignant ulcers appeared in his private parts.
O King, after only a few days, there was no longer any stability for her husband; that unchaste woman of wicked conduct lived according to her own will.
Then her husband Hatatejas, his senses agitated, spoke to her while weeping day and night: "O beautiful one, I am your slave."
"Save me, who have come to you for refuge; I do not desire another woman. O Lord of the Earth, having realized that this was known to him, she became afraid.
Desiring her husband's life rather than his ornaments, she was indeed not intent on his welfare; she went quickly to the Yoginī and reported everything to her. (45)
And she gave a second medicine for the pacification of the burning sensation; and when that medicine was given, her husband became healthy at that very moment.
The husband remains in the house under the pretext of domestic chores, while paramours born from all castes indeed reside within the home.
Not at all was the husband able to utter anything whatsoever; consequently, due to that very fault, [eruptions] broke out on all his limbs.
And there were worms that pierce the bones, resembling Yama, the Ender of Time; by them, the cutting off of the nose, the tongue, and both ears was performed.
Lameness came upon her breasts and her fingers as well; because of that, she met her death and underwent the torments of hell.
And having been burnt in a copper vessel fifteen thousand times, she was born repeatedly in the wombs of dogs a hundred times over.
With their noses cut off, their ears severed, and their heads constantly covered in worms; with their tails lopped off and their legs broken, they were beaten from house to house.
Afterwards, in the Sauvīra country, she was born as a female dog in the house of a maidservant belonging to a brahmin named Padmabandhu, overwhelmed by manifold sufferings.
With her ears cut off, her nose cut off, and her tail and feet mangled, she remains perpetually afflicted; with her head constantly filled with worms, she dwells in the womb of worms.
Thus, O King, thirty years have passed in this birth; by the power of destiny and the ripening of karma, it is now the month of Vaiśākha, with the sun situated in Aries.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, however, the son of the Sun-god, having bathed in the river and become pure, went home while still wearing his wet clothes.
Having reached the Tulasī altar, she washed her two feet; meanwhile, that bitch had fallen asleep in the lower part of the altar. (57)

Before the time of sunrise, she was drenched with the water used for washing the feet; her inauspiciousness was instantly destroyed, and in an instant, she came to possess the recollection of her former births.
Remembering the deed she had previously committed, that dog, distressed and miserable, constantly cried out to the ascetic, "O Sage, save me! again and again.
And, overwhelmed by fear, she recalled her own deed and related it to the Lord of Sages: her administration of poison to her husband as well as her own misconduct. (60)
O Brahmin, any other young woman who practices submissiveness toward her husband, yet performs religious duties in vain and behaves wickedly, is cooked in a vessel of copper.
The husband is her lord, her teacher, her master, and her supreme deity; having acted with such treachery toward him, how could that virtuous woman attain happiness? (62)
One goes to a hundred animal births and even to hundreds of millions of worm-habitations; therefore, O protector of the earth, women must always carry out the word of their husband.
"O Brahmin, if you do not rescue me today while I am before your very eyes, I shall again behold that loathsome womb accompanied by agonizing torments. (64)
Therefore, O Brahmin, deliver me, who am evil-doing and a practitioner of sin, by the gift of merit during the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha. (65)
O Brahmin, whatever merit-increasing Dvādaśī was observed by you, the merit performed on that day through bathing, giving gifts, and the offering of food—[all that has been accounted for]. (66)
O Brahmin, even for a woman of wicked conduct, liberation will come through that [place], where indeed a man who is a Brahmin has bathed in his own home. (67)

One obtains the fruit of all sacred fords; of this there is no doubt. Whatever has been performed there—whether ascetic penance, charity, burnt offerings, or the worship of the gods—[yields its full result]. (68)
That which is performed on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be known as having inexhaustible fruit; grant me all such fruit as there may be. (69)
Whatever fruit may come from fasting on the twelfth day and breaking the fast on the thirteenth, that very fruit shall truly be attained by him, and through it, liberation will occur.
Have mercy, O illustrious one, upon this wretched woman, O you who are compassionate toward the distressed! Janārdana is the lord of the helpless, the lord of the world, and your own lord. (71)
Their subjects are exactly like that; as is the king, so are the people. O destroyer of the path of Vaivasvata, protect us who are deeply afflicted by suffering! 72.
O you who are compassionate toward the distressed, [save] me, a miserable bitch dwelling at your gate; whether it be a thousand killings of Brahmins or a thousand killings of cows. (73)
O great sage, even millions of forbidden acts are surely consumed by that auspicious lunar day; whatever great merit is performed on it, having given it to me.
"O Lord, uplift me who am agitated; O Protector, uplift me who am wretched! At the end, I utter the word of salutation to you, the best of the twice-born. (75)
Having heard these words of hers, the son of the sage said to the dog: "O dog, living beings experience the results of their own actions, consisting of both pleasure and pain. (76)
Therefore, what is to be done by you, a base woman of sinful character, who has brought your husband, a twice-born man, under your control by means of protective powders and such? (77)
Whatever sin is committed against the virtuous becomes a source of suffering for oneself; whatever merit is performed for the virtuous becomes a remover of one's own suffering. (78)
Whatever is done for the sake of the wicked leads to the ruin of both; it is like milk mixed with sugar offered to the sons of Kadrū. (79)
"Thus it is seen to increase poison; likewise, it would become a source of evil," said the daughter of the sage to the dog, who was the very embodiment of suffering. (80)
Again, that talkative woman cried out with a loud voice to her father: "O Lotus-Born One, protect the female dog living at his door! (81)
"Always eating the remnants of your food, protect me," she said again and again; for those whom a high-souled householder maintains as his dependents [must be protected]. (82)
"It is the opinion of those who know the Vedas that their rescue must be performed; for they are like outcasts, crows, and dogs at all times. (83)

Householders should daily provide food as an object of compassion for those who eat their offerings; however, they should not abandon a dependent who is incapable of working, even if that person is afflicted by disease or other ailments.
"He would fall downward without a doubt; such is the opinion of those who know the Vedas. (85)

For the Creator, having made himself the sole agent of the worlds, protects all living beings; since Hari assumes the designations of wife and so forth, his command is indeed the protection of those he must nourish.

If a living being, having abandoned the protection of those whom he must support, conducts himself according to the whims of his own will with a distracted mind, he is a traitor to the gods and a destroyer of all; he goes to the worlds of the god of death.

"Because it is your duty and because of your compassion, deliver this woman of evil mind. Hearing these words of her who was afflicted by grief, the son of the house, Padmabandhu, a treasure-house of mercy, quickly emerged from the dwelling.
"What is this? he asked her; the son reported everything to him. Having heard his son's words, he, filled with wonder, spoke thus to him: || 89 ||
Padmabandhu said: "O my son, why have you uttered such words? O fair-faced one, such speech does not belong to the virtuous in this world. (90)
Sinful people who seek their own happiness become overwhelmed by suffering; behold, my son, all people indeed exist for the sake of benefiting others.
The moon, the sun, the wind, the night, fire, water, sandalwood, trees, and the virtuous—all remain intent upon benefiting others. (92)
O son, out of compassion and knowing that the Daityas were exceedingly powerful, Dadhīci gave his bones as a gift for the benefit of the gods. (93)
O highly fortunate one, in former times, King Śibi indeed gave his own flesh to a hungry hawk for the sake of a pigeon.
In former times, there was a king named Jīmūtavāhana upon the circle of the earth; by him also, his own life was given to the high-souled Garuḍa.
Therefore, a wise Brahmin should be compassionate; for when the god rains upon the pure, does he not also rain upon the impure? (96)
Why does the moon not always illuminate the houses of the Caṇḍālas? Therefore, I shall [punish] this bitch who begs again and again.
"I shall uplift her with my own merits, just as one pulls a cow sunk in the mud," said the high-minded one, rejecting his son's plea and making this vow.
"Great merit has been bestowed, arising from the day of the twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī). Go, O dog, to the abode of Hari, with all your impurities washed away. (99)
At those words, O King, she was suddenly adorned with divine ornaments; casting off her worn-out body, she assumed a beautiful, divine form.
Possessing the splendor of a hundred suns and resembling Sāvitrī herself, she departed after taking leave of that brahmin, illuminating the ten directions.
Having enjoyed great pleasures in heaven, she was later born on the surface of the earth from the gods Nara and Nārāyaṇa, known by the name Urvaśī.
By the power of the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, that excellent woman became beloved of the gods and attained the state of an Apsaras. || 3 ||

That form which is accessible to yogis, radiant as fire, most excellent, worthy of being chosen, and the very nature of ultimate reality—attaining which even the virtuous fall into delusion—that very form has been attained by the Goddess in the guise of a dog.
Thereafter, that Padmabandhu indeed proclaimed that Loveṭī, who increases merit and is dearer than life to Madhudviṭ, on that auspicious lunar day.

Exceeding ten million lunar and solar eclipses, possessing a form of merit superior to all other forms, surpassing all sacrifices combined, she was proclaimed by the twice-born throughout the three worlds.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Liberation by the Dog," in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa within the *Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya*, in the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrutadeva said: O King of kings, those three meritorious lunar days at the end of the bright fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha, ending with the full moon, are bringers of auspiciousness.
The last [three] are known as Puṣkariṇīs, which bring about the destruction of all sins; for one who is unable to perform the full ritual bath during the month of Mādhava, [these are prescribed]. (2)
On these lunar days he should bathe; he shall obtain the full fruit indeed. For on the thirteenth day, all the gods remain there and purify living beings.
Together with Viṣṇu, they reside at the mountain-tirthas of Pūrṇā; indeed, on the fourteenth day, the gods, accompanied by sacrifices, purify these very places.
Indeed, they purify all these—whether a slayer of a Brahmin or a drinker of liquor—for in ancient times, auspicious nectar was produced on the Ekādaśī day of the month of Vaiśākha.
On the twelfth day, that [nectar] was guarded by the powerful Viṣṇu; on the thirteenth day, Hari indeed caused the gods to drink the nectar (sudhā).
And on the fourteenth day, he slew the Daityas who were enemies of the gods; on the full moon day, the attainment of sovereignty over all the gods indeed took place.
Then the gods, being well-pleased and with eyes wide open with joy, granted a boon to these three lunar days.
These three lunar days of the month of Vaiśākha are indeed auspicious; they bestow the fruits of sons, grandsons, and so forth upon men, and grant the destruction of their sins.
That lowest of men who has not bathed during this entire month shall obtain the full fruit by bathing for three lunar days.
A man who fails to perform bathing, giving of gifts, and other rites even on these three lunar days, enters the womb of a Cāṇḍāla and thereafter experiences the Raurava hell.
He who bathes with warm water during the three lunar days of the month of Mādhava goes to the Raurava hell for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras.
He who does not offer curd-rice (dadhyanna) intended for the ancestors and the gods, having entered a ghostly womb (paiśācī yoni), remains there until the dissolution of all beings (ābhūtasaṃplava).
And for those who have engaged in sensual desires, once the vow of Mādhava has been performed, union with Viṣṇu is inevitably attained; there is no doubt in this matter. || 14 ||
If one who is devoted to the rules of the month-long fast should perform it for even three days, he shall obtain the full fruit thereby and rejoice in the abode of Viṣṇu.
"Truly, we shall bestow a curse upon that man who does not perform his ablutions and other rites directed toward the gods, the ancestors, Viṣṇu, and his guru. (16)
"May he be without progeny, without life-span, and without ultimate welfare"—having granted this boon in ancient times, the gods returned to their own abodes. (17)
Therefore, these three days are meritorious and destroy the flood of all sins; the last one, known as Puṣkariṇī, increases one's sons and grandsons.
Whatever fortunate woman gives cakes and milk-rice to a Brāhmaṇa even once on the full-moon day, she shall obtain a son endowed with fame.
He who recites the Gītā during the final three days obtains, day by day, the fruit of horse-sacrifices; of this there is no doubt. || 20 ||
Who on earth or in heaven is capable of describing the meritorious fruit of one who recites the Thousand Names for three days? (21)
Having bathed the god Madhusūdana with milk on the full moon day while reciting his thousand names, one indeed goes to the stainless world of Viṣṇu.
But he who worships Madhusūdana with all his riches—his worlds do not perish even at the transition of the ages and kalpas.
If the month of Vaiśākha passes for one without bathing and without giving gifts, he is considered a slayer of a Brahmin, a murderer of his guru, and likewise a destroyer of his ancestors.
By constantly reciting even half a verse or a single quarter-verse from the Bhāgavata during the month of Vaiśākha, a mortal attains the state of Brahman.
Whoever indeed listens to this scripture of the Bhāgavata for these three days is never tainted by sins, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
By some men divinity was attained, and by others even the state of a Siddha; by some the nature of Brahman was reached through three days of devoted service.
Liberation is attained indeed either through the knowledge of Brahman, or by dying at Prayāga, or else by bathing in water with self-restraint during the month of Vaiśākha.
By releasing a blue bull on the full moon day of Vaiśākha and by bathing in water, a man, liberated from all bonds, goes to the supreme state.
By giving a cow with its calf to a preeminent Brahmin who is settled with a family, one is liberated from untimely death in this world and shall go to the supreme state in the next.
He who passes the Vaiśākha full moon without performing ritual bathing and giving gifts will, after entering a hundred births as a dog, be born as a worm in excrement.
Three and a half crores of sacred fords in the three worlds, fearing the accumulation of sins, gathered together and took counsel.
People cast their own filth upon us; filled with anxiety as to how that might be removed from us, they remain thus possessed by thought. (33)
They went for refuge to Hari, the Lord of the Tīrthas, the omnipresent protector; and having praised him with many hymns, they immediately made their petition.
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, destroyer of the flood of all sins! People who are most sinful among us, having bathed here, [are cleansed] of their sins in every respect. (35)
Having abandoned their own station on earth, they go forth as bearers of Your command; O Janārdana, how then shall that sin of ours depart?
"Tell us, who seek refuge at your feet, the means for that," thus was the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, entreated by the holy fords (tīrthas).

Laughing, the Blessed Lord spoke to the holy fords with a voice as deep as a thundercloud: The Blessed Lord said: "During the bright fortnight, when the sun is in Aries, on the final three days of the month of Vaiśākha..."
O you who are as dear to me as my own life, in this meritorious place consisting of all sacred fords (tīrthas), bathe yourselves in the waters situated outside before the rising of the sun.
May you quickly become free from sin, meritorious in form, and perfectly pure; and by you who are freed from sin, let those who have not bathed for three days [be purified].
"Let that sin, cast off by you people, remain within them"—thus did Viṣṇu, whose feet are the source of all holy places (tīrthapada), grant a boon to the sacred fords.
Having taken leave of them through his yogic power, he vanished right there; and having returned to his own abodes, those sacred fords remained eternal.
Indeed, every year during the month of Vaiśākha, and likewise on the final three days, by that [observance], they cast off the flood of their sins and attain the state of great purity. (43)
But those who do not perform their ablutions during the final three days of Vaiśākha—may they become the refuge of the sins of all people. (44)
Thus do the holy fords proclaim a curse upon those who do not bathe; there is no sinner equal to him who does not bathe for three days.
Having examined the scriptures, [such a thing] has neither been seen nor indeed heard of; therefore, on the three days, one should perform bathing, giving gifts, worship, and so forth.
"Otherwise, one goes to hell for as long as fourteen Indras [reign]. Thus, O Śrutakīrti of great intelligence, all this has been declared. 47.
The greatness of the month of Vaiśākha has indeed been asked about, exactly as it was seen and heard; thus, this record of its majesty and the description of Mādhava have been narrated.
Even Brahmā himself was not able to describe it in its entirety, even in hundreds of years; formerly, on the peak of Kailāsa, Śaṅkara himself [taught it] to Pārvatī. (49)
Although he spoke for a hundred years to her as she questioned the greatness of Mādhava, he did not reach the end; being unable to continue, he desisted.
Who indeed is capable of describing the supreme majesty in its entirety, except for Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all affliction? (51)
In ancient times, all the sages, desiring the welfare of people, explained even a minute fraction of a fraction of its sin-destroying majesty.
O Lord of the Earth, its end has not been explained by anyone because of the [great] difficulty; therefore, during the month of Vaiśākha, you should perform virtuous deeds such as giving gifts.
"By that, you shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt. Having thus enlightened Janaka, the King of Mithilā, [he departed].
Then Śrutadeva, having taken leave of him, set his mind on departing; that royal sage was filled with joy, his eyes clouded with falling tears. (55)
For the sake of his own prosperity, he caused a delightful festival to be held; having circumambulated the village, he placed him upon a palanquin.
Then, accompanied by the fourfold army, he followed behind in person; and having reached the inner apartments once more, he was joined by all his riches as well.
Having honored him with garments, ornaments, cattle, land, sesame seeds, and gold, and having prostrated and circumambulated him, he stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
Then that sage Śrutadeva, possessed of great splendor and high renown, being satisfied and supremely delighted, departed for his own abode. (59)
On the thirteenth, fourteenth, and full-moon day of the month of Mādhava, one should perform bathing, giving gifts, worship, and listening to the sacred narrative.
One who is devoted to the Vaiśākha-dharma shall indeed attain liberation, just as the Brahmin Dhanaśarman and the pretas did in former times. (51)
Nārada said: O Ambarīṣa, this supreme narrative has been told to you; by hearing it, all sins are destroyed and all prosperity is bestowed.
"By that [knowledge], one attains worldly enjoyment, liberation, wisdom, and final release. Having heard these words of his, the highly illustrious Ambarīṣa—
With his inner disposition filled with joy and free from outward activity, he bowed down with his head, prostrating himself upon the ground like a staff.
He honored him again with all his possessions; having been thus honored, the venerable sage Nārada took his leave of him. (65)
The wise one departed for another world, for he could not remain in one place due to the curse; the royal sage Ambarīṣa also [performed] these auspicious rites as spoken by Nārada.

Having dissolved all phenomena (dharmas), he became merged in the supreme Brahman, which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). Sūta said: Whoever [recites] this supreme narrative, which destroys sin and increases merit... (67)
O bestowers of honor, he who hears or even reads this attains the supreme goal; and those in whose house a written manuscript of it remains [attain the same].
Liberation is indeed within their grasp; how much more so for those whose very selves consist of hearing it! 69.
The *Ayodhyāmāhātmya* begins. Victorious is Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara and the delighter of Satyavatī’s heart, from whose lotus-like mouth the world drinks the nectar of his speech. (1)
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory" (Jaya).
Vyāsa said: All the sages dwelling on the Himavat mountains, who had mastered the Vedas, were high-souled knowers of the three periods of time, and resided in the Naimiṣa forest.
Those who are devoted to the Arbuda forest, those dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, those indeed who delight in Mount Mahendra, and those who reside in the Vindhya mountains; || 4 ||
Those who delight in the Jambūvana forest, those who dwell by the Godāvarī, those who have taken refuge in Vārāṇasī, and likewise those who reside in Mathurā; || 5 ||
Those who dwell in the first stage of life and are devoted to Ujjayinī, as well as those who have taken refuge in Dvārāvatī and likewise those who resort to Badarī; || 6 ||
Those who dwell in Māyāpurī and those who reside in Kāntī—these and many other stainless sages, together with their disciples.
While the twelve-year sacrificial session of the high-souled King Rāma was being held at Kurukṣetra, that great field of merit, all those stainless sages assembled there, having been duly summoned.

All of them were pure-minded and had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; having bathed there according to the prescribed rule, they performed their rites, such as the recitation of prayers and so forth.
Placing Bhāradvāja, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, at the forefront, they seated him in turn upon various seats provided with bull-hide covers and other materials.
Seated comfortably during the intervals of the sacrificial session, they then engaged in various conversations concerning diverse sacred fords (tīrthas) with one another.
Then, at the conclusion of the conversations of those sages of purified souls, the highly intelligent Sūta, possessed of great splendor, arrived there.

The disciple of Vyāsa, a knower of the Purāṇas named Harṣaṇa, having bowed down to those sages according to the prescribed rule, sat down before them; having sat down according to the rule, he [spoke] by the word of the sages. (13)
The stainless and eminent sages, Bhāradvāja and others, questioned Sūta Romaharṣaṇa, the best of sages and disciple of Vyāsa.

The sages said: "O highly fortunate one, O great-minded one, we have heard from you all the discourses concerning various sacred fords (tīrthas), along with all the Purāṇas together with their secret doctrines."
Now we wish to hear the eternal greatness of the great city of Ayodhyā, radiant with its virtues and accompanied by its secret mysteries. (16)
Of what nature is that ever-pure Ayodhyā, the city beloved by Viṣṇu? It is proclaimed in the Veda as the foremost among cities, the bestower of liberation. (17)
What is its configuration? Who were the rulers there? Which holy places are sacred there, and what is their majesty like? (18)
O Sūta, what kind of fruit is obtained by men from serving Ayodhyā? What is its history, O Sūta, and what are its rivers and confluences? (19)
In that regard, O Sūta of superior virtues, we desire to hear from you all the merit that comes from bathing and giving gifts there, O Mahāmati. (20)
You now know all of this to be true in its proper sequence; you ought to speak of the majesty of the great city of Ayodhyā.
Sūta said: O you whose wealth is asceticism, by the grace of Vyāsa I know all the Purāṇas, along with the Itihāsas, together with their secret doctrines, according to their true essence.
Having bowed down to him, I shall proclaim before you the majesty of the great city of Ayodhyā, exactly as it is, along with its secret mysteries.

I always bow down to the son of Parāśara, the supreme person—Vedavyāsa, who possesses knowledge, who bestows vast intelligence, who is to be known through the Vedas and their auxiliary limbs, who is most excellent, tranquil, one who has subdued the objects of the senses, who is expansive with pure splendor, who is ever-humble, and the sole source from whom all that is to be known arises. 24.
Oṃ, salutations to that Blessed One, Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor, by whose grace I indeed come to know the majesty of Ayodhyā. (25)
"Listen, all you sages, with full attention along with your disciples; I shall recount the greatness and the great glory of Ayodhyā. (26)
What was uttered by Skanda was heard by Agastya from Nārada; that was previously proclaimed by Agastya to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana.
O you whose wealth is asceticism, this was obtained by me from Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana; therefore, I shall speak it to you with reverence, as you desire to hear it.
I bow to the Supreme Self, Rāma, whose eyes are like lotuses, who is dark as the flax flower, the end-maker of Rāvaṇa, and the imperishable.
That supreme and holy city of Ayodhyā is difficult for evildoers to attain; who would not serve Ayodhyā, wherein Hari himself is personally present? (30)
Having reached the bank of the Sarayū, there was a divine and most beautiful city, resembling Amarāvatī, inhabited mostly by those rich in asceticism.
Abounding in elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, it was established in supreme prosperity, with walls, broad streets, and gateways possessing the luster of gold.
It was everywhere well-provided with verandas and seats, with its fourfold divisions clearly demarcated; it possessed many-storied palaces and featured numerous walls of exquisite craftsmanship.
It was adorned with ponds of pure, beautiful water in which lotuses were in full bloom, and it was embellished with divine temples and the chanting of the Vedas.
It attained excellence through the sounds of lutes, flutes, drums, and other instruments; likewise, it was adorned with *śāla*, *tāla*, coconut, jackfruit, and *āmalaka* trees.
In the same way, it was adorned with mangoes, wood-apples, and other trees, as well as with Aśoka trees; it was endowed with various groves containing trees that bear fruit in all seasons. || 36 ||
It was adorned with *mālatī*, jasmine, *bakula*, *pāṭalī*, *nāga*, and *campaka* trees, as well as with *karavīra*, *karṇikāra*, and *ketakī* flowers.
It was adorned with nimba, jambīra, kadalī, mātuliṅga, and mahāphala trees, as well as by Nāgara people rich in the fragrance of shining sandalwood.
She was accompanied by princes endowed with a radiance equal to that of the gods, and surrounded by beautiful, excellent women like celestial nymphs. (39)
It was filled with eminent and virtuous poets, with twice-born ones equal to Bṛhaspati, and likewise with merchants and citizens who were like wish-fulfilling trees.
With horses equal to Uccaiḥśravas and with elephants like the elephants of the quarters, it was endowed with various such features and was equal to the city of Indra.
In her were born all those protectors of the earth who originated from the solar dynasty, headed by Ikṣvāku, and were entirely devoted to the protection of their subjects.
On whose bank flows the river named Sarayū, possessing holy waters, resounding with warbling bees and birds, and shining forth as it originates from Lake Mānasa.

Enveloped by the waters of the Dharma, possessing the most excellent confluence of the Ghargharā, with its banks inhabited by lords of sages, that river, exalted throughout the world, remains awake. 44.
O best of sages, the Jāhnavī issued forth from the big toe of Hari’s right foot, while the auspicious Sarayū emerged from his left big toe.
Therefore, these two most meritorious rivers are honored by the gods; merely by bathing in them, one removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Then the sage Agastya, born from a pitcher, having learned of the greatness of the holy ford (tīrtha) for the purpose of pilgrimage through the grace of Skanda, arrived at that Ayodhyā.
Having come from here and performed his journey in due order, he bathed according to the prescribed injunctions and offered libations to those ancestors.
Having worshipped all the deities according to the rule, and having paid homage to all the sacred fords (tīrthas) in accordance with the prescribed ritual, || 49 ||
Having accomplished his purpose through the sight of the greatness of the sacred ford, Agastya became filled with intense bliss; his entire body was covered with horripilation as if by a new form.
Having stayed there for three nights and having performed his journey according to the prescribed rites, that best of sages set out while praising the greatness of Ayodhyā.
Beholding him approaching, radiant with abundant joy, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa immediately asked the cause of his bliss.
Vyāsa said: O Brahmin, from where have you just now come, O best of sages? A mass of supreme bliss has arisen within you at this moment.
O Brahmin, tell me why there was such an abundance of joy for you; from your joy, a great delight has arisen in my heart as well. (54)
Agastya said: "O best of sages, O ascetic rich in penance! Having witnessed the power of Ayodhyā today, oh, what a great marvel and what a wonder has arisen within me!"
"Therefore, a flood of bliss has now arisen within me. Having heard those words of Agastya, Vyāsa spoke to that sage:
Vyāsa said: O Blessed One, tell me in truth and in detail, along with its secret mysteries, the greatness of the great city of Ayodhyā, which is preeminent in its virtues. (57)

What is the sequence for a pilgrimage to sacred sites? Which are the sacred sites? What is the prescribed rite? O great sage, best among speakers, explain all of this in detail: what is the fruit there of bathing and of giving gifts? (58)
Agastya said: "O ascetic, how most blessed is your intellect, since it is seen that your inquiry is directed toward the greatness of Ayodhyā."
The letter *a* is declared to be Brahmā, and the letter *ya* is said to be Viṣṇu; the letter *dha* is the form of Rudra, and thus the name Ayodhyā shines forth.
Because Ayodhyā cannot be overcome by any minor offenses nor by major sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, they therefore know it as Ayodhyā.
O twice-born one, this primordial city of Viṣṇu does not touch the earth; situated upon Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana disc, it bestows merit upon the ground.
O ascetic, by whom can her greatness be described, wherein the Lord Viṣṇu himself dwells in person with devotion? (63)
Starting from the thousand-streamed [river], it extends for one yojana toward the eastern direction; likewise, it extends for one yojana toward the western direction, with that as its equal limit.

With the Sarayū and Tamasā rivers as its southern and northern boundaries, this is the configuration of that sacred field; it stands as the inner chamber of Hari. O Brahmin, this city of Viṣṇu is said to be shaped like a fish.
O twice-born one, its head is at Gopratāra in the west, and it is black in color.

Indeed, the western part of that city lies between the south and the north; O highly fortunate one, in that city Viṣṇu himself, known as Hari, who has previously manifested his power, dwells preeminently.
Vyāsa said: "O Blessed One, O tiger among sages, what is the power of this Viṣṇu-Hari who has been praised by you? How did he attain such renown? Explain all of this to me in detail."

Agastya said: In ancient times, there was a preeminent Brāhmaṇa renowned as Viṣṇuśarman; he was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and was devoted to the performance of righteous deeds.

Constantly devoted to yoga and meditation, and solely intent on devotion to Viṣṇu, that best of Vaiṣṇavas, while once performing a pilgrimage, arrived at Ayodhyā, thinking, "Viṣṇu himself dwells here."
Reflecting thus in his mind, the hero prepared to perform penance; he indeed performed penance there, subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits.
In the summer, that great ascetic practiced penance standing in the midst of five fires; during the rainy season, he remained without shelter, and in the winter, he stayed in a lake.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite and likewise performed the worship of Viṣṇu, he should bring the collection of his senses under control with a purified inner self.
Having absorbed the mind into Viṣṇu and performed the restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma), the wise man, by the utterance of the syllable Om, causes the lotus of the heart to blossom.
In the midst of that, having duly fashioned the mandalas of the Sun, Moon, and Fire, one should contemplate Hari in his embodied form, eternal, in that place.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu, who wears yellow garments and holds the conch, discus, and mace, with flowers, one should fix the mind upon Him.
Meditating upon Hari in the form of Brahmā and chanting the twelve-syllabled mantra, that brāhmaṇa remained there for three years subsisting only on air.

Then that best of the twice-born, having meditated and prostrated before Hari, the Lord of the Universe and the Teacher of all moving and unmoving beings, Viṣṇuśarman thereafter praised Nārāyaṇa with unwearied devotion.
Viṣṇuśarman said: Be gracious, O Lord Viṣṇu; be gracious, O Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). Be gracious, O Lord of the gods of gods; be gracious, O lotus-eyed one.

Victory to you, O Kṛṣṇa! Victory to the inconceivable one! Victory to Viṣṇu! Victory to the imperishable one! Victory to the Lord of Sacrifice, O Protector! Victory to Viṣṇu, O Master, O All-pervading One!
Victory, O infinite remover of sins! Victory, O dispeller of the fever of rebirth! Salutations to the one whose navel is a lotus; salutations to the one who wears a garland of lotuses.
Salutations to the Lord of all, the Lord of beings; salutations to the slayer of Kaiṭabha! Salutations to the Protector of the three worlds, the Root of the universe, O Lord of the world! 82.
Salutations to the God of gods; salutations indeed to Nārāyaṇa. Salutations to Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, and salutations to the one whose weapon is the discus.
You are the mother of all worlds; you alone are the father of the universe. To those afflicted by fear, you are a well-wishing friend; you are the father and you are the grandfather.
You are the oblation, you are the exclamation Vaṣaṭ, you are the Lord, and you are the consumer of the sacrifice; you alone are the instrument, the cause, and the agent—the Supreme Lord.
O Mādhava, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, lift me up!
Be gracious, O Mandaradhara; be gracious, O Madhusūdana; be gracious, O Beloved of Kamalā; be gracious, O Lord of the World. || 87 ||
Agastya said: As that high-souled one was thus praising him with devotion of mind, Viṣṇu, the soul of the universe, appeared mounted upon Garuḍa.
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, clothed in yellow garments, the imperishable Acyuta, with a gracious soul, spoke to Viṣṇuśarman.
The Blessed Lord said: "I am pleased with you, my child, by virtue of this great austerity and by this hymn of praise, O wise one; you are now cleansed of all sin."
"Choose a boon, O best of Brahmins; I stand before you as the giver of boons. I cannot be seen by anyone, O twice-born one, unless they have performed austerities. (91)
Viṣṇuśarman said: "O Lord of Gods, I have achieved my purpose now through the sight of you; O Lord of the Universe, grant me unwavering and singular devotion to you. (92)

The Blessed Lord said: "May my devotion to Viṣṇu, which bestows liberation, remain indeed unwavering; and may the Ganges herself, who bestows liberation, remain truly unwavering right here for me. (93)
"O illustrious one, this place shall attain fame by your name. (94)
Agastya said: Having spoken thus, the Lord of the gods of gods, having excavated that spot with his discus, manifested the water of the Gaṅgā from the region of Pātāla.
With that pure water, the Blessed One, an ocean of compassion, by the power of his mercy, instantly made the surface of the earth free from dust.
From that time forth, O twice-born one, it became renowned as Cakratīrtha; it became famous throughout the three worlds, auspicious, and the destroyer of the multitude of sins.
By bathing and giving gifts there, a person shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Then the Blessed One, the infallible Viṣṇuśarman, filled with supreme compassion and affectionate toward the twice-born, spoke once more.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Brahmin, let my form remain here preceded by your name; known as Viṣṇuharī, it shall grant liberation to devotees. (100)
Agastya said: Having heard these words of Vāsudeva, the wise brahmin installed an image of the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu) preceded by his own name.
From that time forward, O lord of brahmins, he remained there as Viṣṇu Hari by name, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, clad in yellow garments, and possessing four arms.
Beginning from the tenth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika and making the full moon day the limit, the annual pilgrimage shall take place.
Having bathed at Cakratīrtha, a man is liberated from all sins; he is glorified in the heavenly world for many thousands of years.
Whoever offers funeral cakes (piṇḍas) there, intended for the ancestors, those ancestors, being satisfied, go to the world of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt. || 105 ||
Having bathed at Cakratīrtha and beheld the all-pervading Lord Viṣṇu-Hari, a person attains the destruction of all sins and is glorified in the highest heaven.
Having given gifts there according to his own capacity, that wise man, freed from all stain, shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
Moreover, at any other time, a man who has conquered his senses, by beholding the god Hari even once at that Cakratīrtha, is liberated from all sins.

Thus Hari, the ocean of all virtues, whose form is the object of meditation and who is the conscious self, remains here in his supreme form for the sake of liberation. He who, having performed ablutions at Cakratīrtha, dwells here with abundant devotion and worships Him as the embodiment of merit, shall reside in the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Viṣṇu and Hari," in the Ayodhyā-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having thus related the narrative concerning Cakratīrtha, the sage Agastya spoke again of the Lord Viṣṇu, the slayer of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Agastya said: In ancient times, Brahmā, the creator of the world, having recognized Hari as the imperishable one, himself established his residence there with the Lord who dwells in Ayodhyā.
Having arrived there, Brahmā performed the pilgrimage according to the prescribed rites and duly conducted the sacrifice, provided with various necessary materials.
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, created there a vast pool named after himself, accompanied by various deities.
It was filled with the vast waves of water, removing all impurity, and densely crowded with clusters of night-lilies, blue lotuses, white water-lilies, and white lotuses.
It was enchanting with birds such as swans, cranes, and ruddy geese; it shone with trees upon its banks and was teeming with flocks of winged creatures.
There, in that pool, all the gods bathed and were endowed with purity; they truly became free from passion and possessed stainless splendor.
Then, having suddenly witnessed that great marvel, all those gods prostrated before Brahmā and spoke with devotion, their palms joined in reverence.
The gods said: "O Blessed One, O Lotus-seated Lord, tell us in truth the entire majesty of this excavated pit, which possesses stainless luster."
"O best of gods, by bathing here the impurity of all of us has been removed; we are all struck with wonder upon seeing this great marvel of this pool. Therefore, please tell us. (10)
Brahmā said: "Let all you gods listen attentively and with wonder to the majesty of this sacred pool, which is endowed with manifold fruits."

By bathing here according to the prescribed rites, even beings who are sinful in nature, clad in beautiful garments, ascend a celestial chariot drawn by swans and dwell in the world of Brahmā until the dissolution of all beings.
In this matter, O best of sages, by means of giving and fire-offerings according to their ability, the foremost of gods shall obtain the merit of the Tulā and Aśvamedha sacrifices. (13)

"In this lake of mine, a man becomes glorious through bathing; therefore, here, according to the prescribed rite, one should perform bathing, giving of gifts, recitation of prayers, and so forth. (14)
It shall indeed be equal to all sacrifices and the destroyer of great sins; from now on, it will attain the unsurpassed renown as "Brahmakuṇḍa. (15)
"And in this pool, O best of gods, my presence shall always abide on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika."
"O gods, my annual festival shall always take place; it will bestow auspiciousness and destroy heaps of great sins. (17)
Gold indeed should always be given, as well as various garments; according to one's own capacity, the gods and the twice-born should be satisfied.
Agastya said: Having spoken thus, O ascetic, this Brahmā, the god of gods and grandfather of the worlds, vanished along with the deities after beholding the holy ford.
From that time forward, that pool became renowned as supreme on earth; it is a great pool situated to the east of Cakratīrtha.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, that Agastya, the pitcher-born mass of asceticism and best of sages, being questioned again, related the story to Vyāsa.
Agastya said: Listen to another, O illustrious one, a holy site difficult for evildoers to attain, known as Ṛṇamocana, situated on the bank of the Sarayū.
O best of sages, it is situated seven hundred bows to the northeast of Brahmakuṇḍa, within the waters of the Sarayū.
There, previously, an excellent sage named Lomaśa by name performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rites during the course of a pilgrimage.
Thereupon, he became freed from his debt and cleansed of all taint; having witnessed that great marvel, he spoke joyfully to the sages.
"Behold indeed the great virtues of this most excellent holy site! Having thus raised his arms upward, he spoke with joy, his eyes filled with tears.
Lomaśa said: This unsurpassed sacred site is known as Ṛṇamocana; by bathing there, the discharge of the debts of living beings occurs.
Whatever threefold debt humans owe—pertaining to this world and the world beyond—all of that perishes in an instant merely by bathing at this sacred ford.
This is the supreme of all holy places (tīrthas), producing immediate conviction; its fruit has been fully experienced by me here in this very life, including the discharge of my debts.

Therefore, in this matter, those endowed with faith who always desire the fruits [of their actions] should perform bathing and giving according to the prescribed rule and to the best of their ability. (30)
One should bathe and give gold, clothing, and so forth, according to one's ability. || 31 ||
Agastya said: Having thus spoken of the majesty of the holy place, Lomaśa, the best of sages and foremost of ascetics, vanished while joyfully praising the virtues of the sacred site.

O Brahmin, this which has been described is known as Ṛṇamocana; by bathing there, the debt of living beings is destroyed in that very instant. The Ṛṇamocana Tīrtha is located in the waters of the Sarayū to the east.
Two hundred bow-lengths away is the holy ford (tīrtha) known as Pāpamocana; by bathing there, a human being becomes purified of all sins at that very moment—of this there is no doubt.
O best of sages, I witnessed there that supreme majesty.
A twice-born man named Narahari, born in the land of Pañcāla, became a sinful soul through the influence of association with the wicked. (36)
Through association with sinners, he who reviled the path of the three Vedas committed various kinds of sins, including the killing of a Brahmin.
O Brahmin, once that twice-born man, who had committed great sins, came to Ayodhyā on account of his association with virtuous people during the course of a pilgrimage.
Having bathed at the Pāpamocana-tīrtha and having come into the company of the virtuous, that twice-born man’s heap of sins was destroyed, and he became sinless in an instant. (39)
O Lord of Sages, a rain of flowers fell from heaven upon his head; having ascended a divine celestial chariot, the twice-born man went to the world of Viṣṇu.
O bull among the twice-born, having witnessed that great marvel, I too performed a bath there with supreme faith, especially so.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, men should especially perform ritual bathing and give gifts there for the purification of all sins.
But at other times, when the bath has been performed, there shall be the destruction of all sins. || 43 ||
Formerly, at the confluence of the Sarayū, there exists an excellent holy site (tīrtha) measuring one hundred bows in extent, known as Pāpamocana-tīrtha.

Known as Sahasradhārā, it is the destroyer of all sins; it was there, by the command of Rāma, that the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy warriors, formerly cast off his life-breaths through yoga and attained the state of Śeṣa.
They know the measure of a bow (dhanus) to be exactly three and a half cubits; a number of four cubits is designated as a staff (daṇḍa).
Sūta said: Having thus heard those words from the pot-born sage at that time, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa questioned him again out of curiosity.
Vyāsa said: O observer of noble vows, tell me in detail the greatness of Sahasradhārā; for as I listen to the majesty of this sacred site, my mind knows no satiety.
Agastya said: O sage, listen attentively as I relate the story of the origin of the Sahasradhārā Tīrtha and its great excellence.
Formerly, Rāma, the lord of the Raghus and sovereign of men, having indeed accomplished the work of the gods, entered into a consultation with Kāla.
For whoever might come near and see us two while we are conversing— || 49 ||
"I shall quickly abandon him"—thus he made this agreement.
While he was thus conversing and Lakṣmaṇa was standing at the door, that mass of asceticism, Durvāsas, a treasury of splendors, arrived.
Having arrived, he quickly spoke with affection to Lakṣmaṇa, being distressed by hunger.
Durvāsas said: "O son of Sumitrā, go quickly and announce me before Rāma as one who seeks a favor; you ought not to act otherwise. (54)
Agastya said: Fearing the curse, that son of Sumitrā went quickly before those two and informed Rāma that Durvāsas, the son of Atri and a mass of ascetic power, had arrived seeking an audience.
Rāma also, having taken leave of Kāla and sent him outside, went forth; seeing that sage, the Lord bowed down and respectfully fed him with due honor.
Having personally and respectfully sent away Durvāsas, the best of sages, the hero then abandoned Lakṣmaṇa out of fear of breaking his vow of truth.
Then the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, being of noble mind, made the word of his elder brother come true and arrived at the bank of the Sarayū.
Having gone there and bathed, he quickly took recourse in meditation; then, having united his peaceful mind with the conscious self (cidātman), he remained established therein.

Then, having split the earth in a thousand places, Śeṣa, the best of serpents, adorned with a thousand hoods, appeared there; and Indra, the lord of the gods, also arrived from the world of the gods together with the immortals.
Then, while the gods looked on, Śakra spoke sweetly to Lakṣmaṇa, who was true to his promise and had become one with the essence of Śeṣa.
Indra said: "O Lakṣmaṇa, arise quickly and ascend to your own station! O hero, slayer of enemies, the task of the gods has been accomplished by you."
"Attain the supreme, eternal abode of Viṣṇu! Śeṣa too, with his shimmering hoods, has arrived in your form. (63)
Having split the earth in a thousand places with their circles of a thousand hoods, they emerged through the thousand fissures of the earth because they had pierced it.

"O observer of noble vows, Śeṣa has been scorched by the jewels on his thousand hoods; therefore, this auspicious great holy site situated on the bank of the Sarayū shall undoubtedly become famous as 'Sahasradhārā'. (65)

The measurement of this sacred field is twenty-five *dhanus*. By bathing, giving gifts, and performing ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) here with faith, a person whose soul is purified of all sins shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
A wise man who bathes here, having worshipped the imperishable Śeṣa and having duly honored the sacred ford (tīrtha), shall attain the world of Viṣṇu.

Therefore, one should perform the ritual bath here according to the prescribed rules; the Brahmins should especially be meditated upon as being like the serpent Śeṣa and worshipped with particular care.
Gold, food, and garments should be given by those endowed with faith; bathing, giving gifts, and the worship of Hari—all this shall attain imperishability. (69)
Therefore, this great sacred ford (tīrtha), which bestows the fruits of all desires, shall exist eternally upon the earth; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
On the fifth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should here diligently perform [the rite] dedicated to the Nāgas.
A grand festival should be held by the virtuous, preceded by the worship of Śeṣa; for when such a festival is performed there at that great holy site by men, [great merit is obtained].
Having gratified the twice-born with devotion, preceded by the worship of the serpents, all the hooded snakes, being satisfied, do not afflict human beings. (73)
Those who, with concentrated minds, perform their ablutions here during the month of Vaiśākha, shall not return to this world again, even after hundreds of millions of kalpas.

Therefore, in this month of Mādhava, men should diligently perform bathing, giving of gifts, and worship of Hari, especially of the Brāhmaṇas; for when performed here at this sacred site (tīrtha), it bestows the fruit of all desires upon human beings. || 75 ||
Whoever should give a milch cow, adorned with ornaments and accompanied by her calf, to a worthy recipient—a twice-born man—here at this excellent sacred site, dedicating it to Viṣṇu; || 76 ||
His residence shall be eternal in the everlasting world of Viṣṇu; by bathing at this sacred ford, a human being attains imperishable heaven.
In this regard, men endowed with faith should especially honor a Brahmin couple in the month of Vaiśākha with ornaments and garments. (78)
For the pleasure of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, and especially for the attainment of Lakṣmī, all the holy fords (tīrthas) situated upon the earth indeed [assemble] in the month of Vaiśākha.

And all [the holy places] shall undoubtedly assemble here; therefore, for men who bathe here especially during the month of Vaiśākha, there will be the great fruit of bathing in all the sacred fords (tīrthas).

Agastya said: Having spoken thus to Lakṣmaṇa, who had gone to the celestial realm, the lord of sages established Śeṣa—who was capable of removing the burden of the earth—in that holy place; then, placing Lakṣmaṇa upon his vehicle, he departed for heaven with reverence.
