From that time forward, that holy place attained supreme renown; the greatness of this tīrtha is remembered as being most excellent in the month of Vaiśākha.

Especially on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, or at other excellent festival times, a person should perform the special ritual bath at the Sahasradhārā Tīrtha; thus he shall attain heaven.

O best of men, that wise person who here performs ablutions and acts of charity at this sacred ford according to the prescribed rites, with devotion and according to his capacity, becomes pure in soul and, through his devotion, attains identity with the Lord of Śrī who reclines upon the serpent, enjoying abundant pleasures in this world. (84)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Brahmakuṇḍa-Sahasradhārā Tīrtha," in the Ayodhyā-Māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Having heard these words with respect from the one born from a jar (Agastya), the wise sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana spoke these sweet words.
Vyāsa said: O Blessed One, having heard this supreme and wonderful majesty of the sacred ford from you, my mind has attained the highest bliss.
"Tell me truly of another excellent holy place (tīrtha) while I listen; O you of noble vows, there is no satiety for my mind as I hear."
Agastya said: Listen, O Brahmin, I shall describe another unsurpassed holy site (tīrtha) known as Svargadvāra, which always removes all sins.
No one, O child, is capable of describing the greatness of Svargadvāra in detail; therefore, O observer of noble vows, listen to it in brief.
Starting from the Sahasradhārā in the east toward the waters of the Sarayū, the distance is said to be six hundred and thirty-six dhanus.
The width of the Gate of Heaven has been described by those experts learned in the Purāṇas: "There has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred ford equal to the Gate of Heaven."
Truth, truth, and again truth—what I have spoken is not false. There is no sacred ford (tīrtha) equal to the gateway to heaven within the entire sphere of the universe.
O observer of noble vows, having abandoned all the celestial and terrestrial holy fords, they arrive there every morning and remain, taking refuge in that place.
Therefore, one who desires for oneself the fruit of bathing in all sacred fords (tīrthas) should especially perform the morning bath here.
O twice-born one, living beings who give up their lives within the gateway of heaven go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
Behold this gateway to liberation for men, which brings about the attainment of heaven; therefore, this unsurpassed holy site is renowned as Svargadvāra (the Gateway to Heaven).
The gateway to heaven is extremely difficult to attain, even for the gods; of this there is no doubt. Whatever a human being desires therein, that he obtains. (13)

At the gateway to heaven lies supreme perfection; at the gateway to heaven lies the supreme goal. Whatever is chanted, given, offered in sacrifice, seen, whatever austerity is practiced, and whatever is performed—including meditation, study, and all acts of charity—becomes inexhaustible. (14)
Whatever sin has been accumulated previously over thousands of other births, all of that perishes for one who has entered the gateway to heaven. || 15 ||
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of mixed castes; as well as worms, Mlecchas, and others who are of mixed origin and sinful birth. || 16 ||
"Insects, ants, and whatever other beasts and birds there may be, they too have met their end through time at the gateway to heaven; listen, O twice-born one. (17)
All those birds have the Kaumodakī mace in their hands and possess the banner of Garuḍa; in that auspicious city of Viṣṇu, human beings are born as Viṣṇus.
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, even if one has gone to a heretical sect, by casting off one's life at the gateway to heaven, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
The sages, deities, Siddhas, Sādhyas, Yakṣas, and the hosts of Maruts—those who indeed established their distinction merely by means of the sacred thread (yajñopavīta).
The hosts of deities manifest their presence here at midday; therefore, people perform their midday ablutions there with great devotion.
Those who, having conquered their senses, practice fasting unto death at Svargadvāra, as well as those who observe month-long fasts, go to the supreme abode.
Those men who delight in the gift of food, who give jewels and land, and who give cows and clothing to Brahmins, go to the abode of Hari.
Where the perfected ones, the great-souled sages, and likewise the ancestors all go to heaven, it is therefore known as Svargadvāra (the Gate of Heaven). || 24 ||
Having divided his own body fourfold, Hari himself, the God of gods, Rāghava, dwells here eternally together with his brothers.
Having abandoned the world of Brahmā, the eternal four-faced Grandfather now delights here eternally together with the gods.
Śiva, whose abode is Kailāsa, was stationed right there.
Even a heap of sinful karma as large as Mount Meru or Mandara, upon reaching the gateway to heaven, is entirely brought to destruction.
That auspicious goal which belongs to those of knowledge and austerity, and that goal which belongs to those who perform sacrifices—such a goal is ordained for those who die at the Gate of Heaven.
The gateway to heaven is frequented by hosts of sages, gods, and asuras devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, as well as by ascetics seeking liberation.
Whatever fruit is obtained from residing in Kāśī for sixty thousand years, that same fruit is attained in half a moment in the city of the son of Daśaratha during the Kali age.
That same goal which belongs to those who cast off their bodies at Vārāṇasī while engaged in yoga is attained merely by bathing in the Sarayū on the day of Hari.
One who dies at Svargadvāra never beholds hell; for all those favored by Keśava attain the supreme goal.
O best of the twice-born, this place exists surpassing all those sacred fords (tīrthas) that exist indeed on the earth, in the intermediate space, and in heaven. 34.
Having attained devotion to Viṣṇu, those who are firmly resolved indeed rejoice, having withdrawn through their power the desire that was established within the sense-objects. (35)
Having applied themselves with all their power to austerity, their power is firmly established in penance; for them there is no return, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Even while being struck by hundreds of weapons, the wise man who dwells [in this state] goes to the supreme abode, having reached which he does not grieve.
He who is separated at the gate of heaven goes to the supreme goal; he should not discriminate between the northern or the southern course.
For all those who resort to the gateway of heaven, every moment is auspicious; by merely bathing there, the sins of embodied beings go to their dissolution. (39)
Whatever sins people commit on earth with their bodies, Ayodhyā is declared with reverence to be the supreme place for them. (40)
Especially on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, the annual festival of that Candrahari is remembered by the gods.
O Brahmin, at its conclusion, those engaged in the vow should diligently perform the rite of completion (udyāpana) with a thousand lamps, which yields a fruit superior to that of all sacrifices.
When that is performed, heaven shall be attained by men through the destruction of great sins.
Śrī Vyāsa said: O Blessed One, tell me in truth of the auspicious origin of that Candrahari, as well as the procedure for the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the Candra-vrata.

Agastya said: Having bowed to Viṣṇu, whose abode is Ayodhyā, the moon—the repository of nectar—eagerly came to personally witness the greatness of the sacred ford (tīrtha). Having arrived here, the moon then undertook a pilgrimage to the holy sites.
Then, having propitiated Viṣṇu through difficult penance, performed in due order according to the prescribed rites and accompanied by various wonders; || 46 ||
Having obtained his grace, he installed Hari while first uttering his own name; for that reason, he is remembered as Candrahari.
By the grace of Vāsudeva, that place became wonderful; for that is indeed the most secret abode of Vāsudeva, O observer of noble vows.
O Brahmin, in this place, which is always the sustainer of liberation for all beings, the perfected ones (siddhas) are ever established in the vow of Govinda.
Constantly assuming various outward marks, desiring the world of Viṣṇu, those liberated souls with conquered senses practice the supreme yoga.
Just as one attains spiritual merit (dharma) here, it cannot be attained anywhere else; likewise, gifts, vows, and burnt offerings—all shall attain imperishability.

The attainment of all desired fruits always arises for living beings; therefore, beings should here diligently perform, in due order, acts such as giving, the worship of Brahmins, and especially the honoring of married couples.
The merit that arises for men from beholding all the gods is equal to the fruit of all sacrifices and the merit of bathing in all sacred fords.
All that merit arises for living beings from the sight of this [place]; therefore, it is celebrated in the Purāṇas and other texts as a great field of merit (mahākṣetra).

And here, the concluding rite (udyāpana) is to be performed by men with the twice-born at their head; and before the Moon-destroyer (Śiva), it is known as the "Candrasahasra-vrata" (The Thousand-Moon Vow). || 55 ||
When two years and a half, plus five fortnights and two days have passed, one intercalary month falls during the eighth part of a day. (56)

Or, when one has reached eighty-three years of age plus four months, that man who lives for as long as a thousand moons must perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) and diligently undertake the pilgrimage.

O Brahmin, that supreme merit which is proclaimed for those who constantly perform sacrifices, that merit which belongs to speakers of truth, and that merit which belongs to the giver of gold—all that merit one obtains by living for a thousand years. (58)
Such a meritorious vow, which bestows all happiness, is described here.

Having bathed on the fourteenth day, being pure and having first performed the cleansing of the teeth, and having observed celibacy while having controlled his speech, body, and mind; and likewise having done so on the full moon day, he should perform the worship of the Moon.
First, the Mothers should be worshipped in the sequence beginning with Gaurī; then, preceded by the Vṛddhi-śrāddha, one should worship the officiating priests with devotion. (61)

With self-restraint, an image resembling the orb of the moon should be fashioned; it may be made in a number of one thousand, or half of that, or half of that again, according to one's own means, or even half of that, or half of that.
Then, either according to one's faith or by inference from one's capacity for action, or else sixteen auspicious [vessels] should be prepared with great effort. (63)
Then one should perform the worship of the Moon according to the procedure prescribed in the Āgamas; an auspicious image should be made for each [deity] out of sixteen black gram beans (māṣas).
The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with the Soma mantra according to one's means; one should perform the installation of the image while reciting the Soma mantra.
One should diligently cause the Soma-utpatti and the Soma-sūkta to be recited; thereafter, one should perform the worship of the Moon according to the procedure prescribed in the Āgamas.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the moon and the placement of its digits (kalās) upon the water in the mandala, as well as the placement of the eleven sense organs, according to the prescribed ritual.
A mandala resembling the lunar disc should be fashioned with auspicious rice grains; and in its center, a water-pot filled with cow's milk should be placed.
One should place full water-pots (kalaśas) outside the squares; and within the mandala, worship of the Moon should be performed with the names in their proper sequence.
Salutations indeed to Himāṃśu, and salutations to Soma and Candra.
Salutations always to Candra, the widower; salutations to Kumudabandhu.
Salutations indeed to Sudhāṃśu, to Soma, and to Oṣadhīśa; salutations to Abja, to Mṛgāṅka, and salutations to the treasury of the lunar digits.
Homage to the Lord of the constellations, homage to the Lord of the night; constant homage indeed to Jaivātṛka, the King of the twice-born.
Thus, the Moon should be praised in sequence with these sixteen names.

Then, being self-restrained, one should duly offer [the water] according to the ritual preceded by mantras; having taken water from a conch shell along with flowers, fruits, and sandalwood paste. (74)
Salutations to you, O Moon, who are born again and again at the end of every month; together with Rohiṇī, accept this water offering from me.
Having thus worshipped the Moon according to the prescribed rite, one should bow down. Furthermore, there should be sixteen other jars filled with milk and containing jewels.
For the sake of peace, those [images] should be given to a twice-born man along with clothing and coverings; thereafter, one should perform an ablution with milk-rice and water.
The satisfaction of the officiating priests should be ensured according to one's wealth; in particular, one should feed a Brāhmaṇa there along with his family. (78)
The Brahmin couple should be honored with effort by means of garments; thereafter, the excellent giving of abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) must be performed.

Images, beginning with cows, should be given to the twice-born; likewise, gold, silver, clothing, and especially food should be given out of joy to the twice-born for the great pleasure of Candra. (80)

The wise man should spend the remainder of the day according to the rules for the fast; on the following day, he should perform the worship of the Blessed One, eat together with his kinsmen, and release himself from the observance.

And thus he performs this supreme vow of the Thousand Moons; even a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—a man whose soul is purified by this vow shall go to the world of the Moon. (82)
O Brahmin, whatever kind of person is dear to Nārāyaṇa, by performing that very thing with self-restraint, a man shall become one who has fulfilled his purpose. || 83 ||

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Conclusion of the Thousand-Moon Vow," in the Ayodhyā-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Agastya said: To the southeast of that station of Candrahari is situated the deity named Dharmahari, the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age.

In former times, Dharma, who knew the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences and was firmly established in his own duties, arrived there with the desire to undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Having arrived there, he performed a grand procession with great devotion; and beholding the incomparable majesty of Ayodhyā, he was filled with wonder.
Raising his two arms aloft, the brahmin, filled with joy, exclaimed: "Oh, how delightful is this sacred ford! Oh, how supreme is its majesty! (4)
No other city like Ayodhyā is seen anywhere else; it never touches the earth, being perpetually supported by the discus of Viṣṇu.
How can this place, wherein Hari himself is present, be compared to anything else? Oh, indeed, all sacred fords (tīrthas) bestow the realm of Viṣṇu!
Oh, Viṣṇu! Oh, the sacred ford! Oh, the great city of Ayodhyā! Oh, the incomparable majesty! What is there remaining here that is not worthy of praise? (7)
Having spoken thus, Dharma, filled with joy, danced there many times upon beholding the greatness of Ayodhyā, especially so.
Seeing Dharma dancing in that manner, the Blessed Lord Hari himself, clad in yellow garments, appeared, moved by compassion. Having bowed down to him, Dharma then praised Hari with great reverence.
Dharma said: Salutations to Viṣṇu, who dwells in the ocean of milk; salutations to him who reclines upon the couch; salutations to the one whose divine feet were touched by Śaṅkara.
Salutations to You whose feet are worshipped with devotion, who are dear to Brahmā and the other gods; salutations again and again to Mādhava, the one of auspicious limbs and beautiful eyes. 11.

Salutations to the one whose feet are like lotuses; salutations indeed to the one with a lotus-navel. Salutations to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, whose body is touched by the waves of the ocean of milk.
Oṃ, salutations to Yoganidrā; salutations again and again to the divine Govinda, whose self is cultivated by the stars of yoga, and who has Tārkṣya as his seat. || 13 ||
Salutations again and again to the one with beautiful hair, beautiful nose, and beautiful forehead; to the wielder of the discus, who is well-attired, golden-hued, and the bearer of Śrī. || 14 ||

Salutations to you, O Subāhu; salutations to you with the beautiful shanks. Salutations to the one with excellent garments, the most divine, the possessor of perfect knowledge, the wielder of the mace.
Salutations again and again to Keśava, to the Peaceful One, and to Vāmana; salutations to you, the God who loves righteousness and is clad in yellow garments.
Agastya said: Thus praised by Dharma, the Lord of the World, the husband of Śrī, Hṛṣīkeśa of noble intellect, being pleased, spoke joyfully to Dharma. (17)
The Blessed One said: "O Dharma of noble vows, I am pleased with this hymn of yours. O knower of dharma, choose a boon, whatever is dear to your heart. (18)
The man who, unwearied, praises me with this hymn, shall obtain all desires; he shall always be honored and endowed with prosperity.
Dharma said: "O Blessed One, O God of gods, O Lord of the universe! If you are pleased, O Teacher of the world, I shall establish you here under my own name."
Agastya said: Having declared, "So be it," the omnipresent Lord Dharmahari appeared; by the mere remembrance of the omnipresent Lord Dharmahari, a man shall be liberated. (21)
Having bathed in the waters of the Sarayū with a mind agitated by pure reflection, one should behold the Lord Dharmaharin; thus, one is liberated from all sins.
In this place, charity, as well as fire-offerings, recitation of mantras, and the feeding of Brahmins—all these become inexhaustible and lead to residence in the world of Viṣṇu.
Whatever misdeed may have been committed, whether through ignorance or even knowingly, an expiation must be diligently performed for its destruction. (24)
By means of the prescribed rite of expiation, his sin is destroyed; therefore, an expiation must be performed here according to the rules. (25)

Whether through ignorance or knowledge, and likewise due to the restraint of kings and others, if there should be a cessation of obligatory rites for a man who lacks self-control, he too must here diligently perform expiation.
Here the Lord Viṣṇu himself dwells in person with devotion; therefore, his majesty cannot indeed be described by mortals. (27)
O best of the twice-born, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, his annual festival must be performed according to the prescribed rites.
Having bathed at Svargadvāra and beheld the omnipresent Lord Dharmaharin, a man—his soul purified of all sins—shall dwell eternally in the world of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, in the southern region, there is an excellent mine of gold, where Kubera rained down a shower of gold out of fear of the son of Raghu.
Vyāsa said: O Lord, knower of reality, tell me how the rain of gold occurred; and how did fear arise in Kubera regarding King Raghu? (31)
O observer of noble vows, explain all of this to me in detail; having heard the secrets of these narratives, my mind is not yet satiated.
Agastya said: Listen, O Brahmin, I shall describe the supreme origin of gold, by hearing which great wonder arises in men. (33)
In ancient times, there was the Lord of the Raghus, the enhancer of the Ikṣvāku lineage, Raghu, who ruled the earth through the noble prowess of his own arms. (34)
By that virtuous and wise king, who protected his subjects with perfect justice, his true fame was proclaimed as he scorched the host of his enemies with his majesty.
With the flood of his fame, white in its radiance, he completely anointed the ten directions; through his successive victories, he established the means for his mature sovereignty.
Having marched against various countries accompanied by his fourfold army, he brought all beings under his control and seized wealth as tribute.
Then that exceedingly powerful hero, having punished the most eminent kings who possessed superior forces, swiftly seized various kinds of jewels.
Having conquered all the directions and gathered a collection of jewels, that king returned to Ayodhyā, his auspicious capital city. (39)
Having arrived there, the descendant of Kakutstha, his mind eager for sacrifice, formed the pure resolve to perform the rites befitting his own lineage.
Having recognized the sage Vasiṣṭha, as well as Vāmadeva and Kaśyapa.
The king also summoned other eminent sages who resided at various sacred fords, through that most excellent of brahmins who was humble in conduct.

Seeing them all standing there like blazing fires, and perceiving that they had arrived, the highly illustrious Raghu, conqueror of enemy cities, himself went forth according to the prescribed custom. (43)
Then, having consoled all those best of the twice-born, Kakutstha spoke words consistent with dharma for the successful completion of the sacrifice.
Ravi said: "O sages, all of you listen to my words; I wish to perform a sacrifice, and you ought to grant me permission for it."
"O best of sages, let my sacrifice now be properly prepared; having considered this in its true essence, O lords of sages, please speak. (46)
The sages said: "O King, the sacrifice known as Viśvajit is the most excellent among sacrifices; perform it now with diligence and do not delay in vain. (47)
Agastya said: Then the king performed a sacrifice known as Viśvadigjaya, which was sweet with various ritual preparations and for which his entire wealth was given as the sacrificial fee.
Causing satisfaction and joy to the sages through various kinds of gifts, he gave away his entire possession to the twice-born with great reverence.
When all those [guests] had departed for their own homes after being honored, and when the kinsmen were satisfied and the sages had bowed down.
By means of that sacrifice performed according to the rules, the lord of men, whose conduct was auspicious, instantly shone like Indra in heaven.
In the meantime, there arrived a sage, the best among those who have restrained their senses, known as Kautsa, a disciple of the sage Viśvāmitra.
"O wise one, bring fourteen crores of gold coins quickly as a fee for the preceptor, in order to purify that lord of men."

Having been entreated with persistence by his preceptor with the words "Give me [the dakṣiṇā]," that sage Kautsa arrived in anger; he then came with great earnestness to beg from Raghu, the ornament of kings, who had already given away all his wealth as the sacrificial fee.

Perceiving that he had arrived, Raghunātha, the scorcher of foes, rose up with great respect and honored him according to the prescribed rites; for him, every act of hospitality was performed using only earthen vessels.

Beholding such an abundance of offerings for worship, the Lord of Sages was struck with wonder and, devoid of joy, turned away from the southern direction; then, being an expert in the knowledge of speech, he spoke these sweet words.
Kautsa said: "O King, may prosperity be yours; I shall now depart elsewhere. (57)

Since you have given away all your possessions as a sacrificial fee solely for the purpose of procuring wealth for your guru, I do not beg from you; therefore, due to the lack of wealth, I am going elsewhere.
Agastya said: Having been addressed thus by that sage, Raghu, the conqueror of enemy cities, reflected for a moment and spoke to him with humility and palms joined in reverence.
Raghu said: "O Blessed One, observer of the vows of a sage, stay for one day in my palace; O Blessed One, I shall strive with all my might for your sake."
Agastya said: Having spoken these most noble words to the sage, the high-minded Rāghava set out from there with the desire to conquer Kubera.
Then, as he was approaching, Kubera informed him with spoken words and made his mind gracious, providing an inexhaustible rain of gold.
Where that excellent gold mine had become a rain of gold, he showed the sage the mine that had been pointed out by him.
Raghu handed over that excellent mine to him; and the lord of sages, having quickly accepted it out of respect for his preceptor’s purpose, [departed]. (54)
He who was superior in all other virtues reported everything to the king; then Kautsa, the best among the wise, being pleased, granted boons.
Kautsa said: "O King, obtain a virtuous son endowed with the qualities of your own lineage; this mine of gold shall swiftly grant the fruits desired by your heart. (66)
May this supreme holy site, which always removes all sins, flourish here; by bathing and giving gifts here, prosperity arises for men.
The annual festival is prescribed for the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha; by my word, may men obtain the fulfillment of various desired fruits.
Agastya said: Having thus granted boons to the king, Kautsa, with a satisfied mind, set out eagerly for his own preceptor’s hermitage to attend to his own business.
Then that king, having accomplished his purpose, collected the remainder of that wealth and, having bestowed it upon the twice-born according to the prescribed rites, protected his subjects.
Thus, the greatness of the gold mine was obtained from the Lord of Sages.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Dharmahari and Svarṇakhani," in the Ayodhyā-Māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Vyāsa said: O Blessed One, tell me in truth how the sage Viśvāmitra, out of such anger, treated his own disciple Kautsa with such persistence.
At that time, you earnestly sought after an object that was difficult to obtain; if you have compassion for me, please relate all of this to me. (2)
Agastya said: Listen yourself, O twice-born one, with your senses fully attentive, to this story. Viśvāmitra, the best of sages, possessed the eye of divine knowledge. (3)
In his own hermitage, the disciplined practitioner performed difficult austerities with great self-restraint. Once, the sage Durvāsas arrived there to see him.
Having arrived, that twice-born man, overcome by hunger, spoke aloud: "O twice-born one, let pure, warm milk-rice be given quickly to me, whose mind is afflicted by hunger."
Having heard these words, Viśvāmitra quickly and with great care took the milk-rice in a vessel and, having offered it to him, then departed himself.
Seeing him rise after taking that [gift], Durvāsas, intent on discerning auspicious marks, looked at the sage and spoke these sweet words: (7)
"Wait a moment, O best of Brahmins, while I go to bathe. Stay, stay! Wait a moment! Wait! Here I come right now. (8)
Having spoken thus, Durvāsas then departed for his own hermitage.
Then Viśvāmitra, devoted to austerity, remained there for a thousand divine years with a steady mind, as immovable as Mount Sānu.
Devoted to his service was the sage Kautsa, firm in his vows, possessed of a most noble mind, and free from envy.
Having returned, that sage Durvāsas, his impurities cleansed, ate the milk-rice immediately and departed for his own hermitage.
When that best of sages had departed, Viśvāmitra, a treasury of asceticism, sent Kautsa—the foremost among the learned—back toward his home.

Having been dismissed, he said to his teacher, "Let a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) be requested. Viśvāmitra, however, said to him, "What fee will you give? Your service has been your fee; go home, O one of firm vows."
When the disciple, being persistent, spoke to the guru again and again, then the guru, becoming greatly enraged, spoke harshly to the disciple.
"O Brahmin, collect fourteen crores of gold for me as my sacrificial fee; afterwards, go back toward your home."
Having been thus addressed by his preceptor, Kautsa reflected and approached the descendant of Kakutstha, the conqueror of the quarters, and requested him for his preceptor’s fee.
Thus has that which was asked by you been told to you, O best of sages; now hear from me something else, the supreme cause of the sacred fords (tīrtha). || 18 ||
Therefore, in the southern region, there is a confluence frequented by the Siddhas, renowned on earth as the meeting point of the Tilodakī and the Sarayū.

Having bathed there, O highly fortunate one, men become free from passion. That righteous soul who, restrained in his vows, bathes there obtains the same fruit that would result from ten horse-sacrifices performed.
And he who gives gold and other gifts to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas attains an auspicious state and shines like fire. || 21 ||
Having offered food according to the prescribed rite at the world-renowned confluence of the Tilodakī and the Sarayū, one is not born again. || 22 ||
The man who, having observed a fast, gratifies the Brahmins, that person obtains the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. || 23 ||
If one who is restrained in their vows remains there for a month, eating but a single meal a day, the sins committed throughout their entire life are instantly destroyed.
On the new moon day of the dark fortnight of Nabhasya, there shall be the annual pilgrimage; it was formerly established by Rāma as another river, like a second Sindhu.
O observer of noble vows, because the water in that river always shone dark like sesame seeds for the horses born in Sindh to drink, [it was known as the Śyāmalikā]. 26.

The river known as Tilodakī is always possessed of meritorious waters; by bathing anywhere other than at its confluence in that Tilodakī, one who observes pure vows is liberated even from the sins accumulated over seven births.

Therefore, O Sage, the bath with sesame-water, which removes all sins, should be performed with great effort by living beings desiring righteousness; bathing, giving, vows, and fire-offerings—all these shall attain imperishability. (28)

Thus, having performed a pilgrimage in due order through various rites, he—whose expansion of virtues was celebrated, who had acquired merit, and whose sins were somehow cast off—worshipped Hari with a surrendered heart at every sacred ford and proceeded toward the supreme abode.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Power of Tilodarka," in the Ayodhyā-māhātmya of the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, within the second part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Agastya said: O Brahmin, situated on the western bank from that confluence is the place renowned as Sītākuṇḍa, which bestows the fruits of all desires.
O Brahmin, by bathing there, a man is liberated from all sins; indeed, that pool was fashioned by Sītā herself, and by the granting of a boon by Rāma, it was made a treasury of great fruit.
Śrī Rāma said: Listen, O Sītā, I shall proclaim the greatness of this very place on earth as it truly is; O fortunate one, out of affection for you, I shall speak of it. (3)
O lady of pure smiles, whatever bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offering, or austerity is performed here according to the prescribed rite, all of it becomes inexhaustible.
O Goddess, a bath taken there specifically on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa removes all sins for men who bathe at any time.
Thus Rāma, who is beloved by his subjects, granted a boon to Sītā; from that time forward, that sacred ford has existed everywhere upon the earth.
Known among people as Sītākuṇḍa, it is most wonderful; having bathed in that sacred ford, a man shall surely attain Rāma.

There, by bathing, giving gifts, and especially through austerity, and by worshipping Rāma and Sītā with perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, and various extensive displays of wealth, one shall be liberated; of this there is no doubt.
One should bathe during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa; thus, dwelling in a womb does not occur. Even at other times, a man who bathes goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
O Brahmin, on the beautiful western border of the land of the all-pervading Viṣṇuhari, there is a deity named Cakrahari, who bestows the fruits of all desires.
O Brahmin, the majesty of that Cakrahari cannot be described by humans, even by the steadfast and the most excellent among the wise.

Then, in the western quarter, there is the famous temple of Viṣṇu known as Harismṛti, which is meritorious and bestows the fruit of the supreme goal; by the mere sight of it, one is liberated from all sins.
By the sight of those two, the sins of embodied beings depart—whatever sins those men on earth may commit. (13)
Long ago, when a most terrible battle had arisen between the gods and the asuras, the gods were defeated in combat by the Daityas, who were intoxicated by the pride of their boons.
As those gods were fleeing, Hara, their leader, paralyzed them all and placed the lotus-seated Brahmā at their head.
[He meditated on] Viṣṇu reclining upon the ocean of milk, lying upon the couch of Śeṣa, with Lakṣmī seated at his side, her hands resting upon his lotus-feet.
His majesty of qualities was celebrated by the best of sages, such as Nārada and others, and he was incessantly praised with folded hands by Garuḍa standing before him.
The sky was marked by droplets of spray from the waves of the milk-ocean, and it shone with the brilliance of a vast necklace of shimmering stars.
Wearing yellow garments, he was imbued with an intensely smiling and blossoming expression; he bore large earrings upon his two ears, radiant with pearls.
Like a pure jewel-creeper, she was a resident of Śvetadvīpa; she wore a crown of rubies and a supreme bracelet.
It was like another instance of Mitra’s terrifying the demon Rāhu and turning him back; it bore a circle of radiance from the Kaustubha gem and was intensely crimson.
With a humble mind, he quickly sought refuge in her, praising her as if she were the supreme creative conception of the kalpa for the manifestation of the Four-faced One (Brahmā). || 22 ||
At that moment, Śambhu, having become composed, together with all the hosts of gods, offered praise to Viṣṇu, the conqueror of the enemies of the deities.
Īśvara said: Salutations to Hari, who is like the moon that removes the most intense delusion, and who bestows the bliss of the Garuḍa for crossing the ocean of worldly existence. || 24 ||

I take refuge in devotion to the Blessed One, which flows like a river through the garden of the mind, possessing the moonlight of the mind’s association and the crest-jewel of throbbing consciousness. (25)
She whose power of enthusiasm shines forth, who pervades the three worlds, who is the primordial limit of all entities and beings, is indeed Vaiṣṇavī. || 26 ||
For living beings dwelling within the joints of lotus petals shaken by the wind, as if they were about to fall, the remembrance of Hari alone provides stability.
Salutations to you, whose self is the Sun, who are garlanded with rays of consciousness, and who bring about the blossoming of the beauty within the calyx of the heart-lotus. 28.
Salutations to Him who possesses self-restraint, the eternal goal of yogis, the Supreme Lord who stands beyond both light and darkness. (29)

Salutations to the one who has consumed the oblation for the sake of the sacrifice, whose form consists of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and who is adorned by the divine assembly of sages singing the praises of Sarasvatī.

Salutations to the peaceful one, the treasury of Dharma, the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), whose nature is immortality; salutations to the one who establishes the yoga of disciples, the sole cause of individual life; salutations to the formidable one, the ordainer of Māyā, the thousand-headed.
Salutations to the one whose nature is yogic sleep, who creates the world from the lotus born at his navel; salutations to the cause of the world's existence, who exists in the form of water.
Salutations to the powerful Jīva, the Supreme Self who is the object of action and cognition; salutations to the Protector, the Life-force of all beings, the All-pervading Creator. || 33 ||
Salutation to the one who is proud, who possesses the form of a lion, who effects the destruction of the Daityas, who is valor, whose mind is infinite, and who sustains the existence of the universe.
Salutation to Rudra, the intensely formidable, the secret one, whose inconceivable abode severs the great, thick darkness of ignorance that is the cause of saṃsāra. 35.

Salutation to the peaceful one, who bestows the state of absolute liberation where all waves of agitation have subsided; salutation to the Self consisting of all things, who transcends all phenomenal states.
I bow to Viṣṇu, the elixir for the eyes, who is dark like the petal of a blue lotus, who possesses the splendor of shimmering filaments, and who bears the Kaustubha gem. 37.

Agastya said: Thus praised, the boon-granting Garuḍa-bannered Lord, with a gracious soul and filled with compassion, showered all the gods with the nectar of his glance. He spoke these sweet words to the deities who were bowed down in humility: || 38 ||

The Blessed Lord said: "O wise ones, through meditative absorption I know your entire intention—that the position [of the gods] has been overpowered by the strides of the Daityas, who are arrogant in battle. (39)
"The prowess of those weak in strength has been overcome by their powerful enemies; however, I shall now perform austerities for the sake of your strength."
Having gone to the city of Ayodhyā, I shall perform supreme penance, remaining concealed for the sake of increasing your splendor and for the pacification of the Daityas. (41)
"O sirs, you too, with pure minds, should perform intense penance; O gods, go quickly to Ayodhyā for the destruction of the Daityas. (42)
Agastya said: Having spoken thus to the gods, the Lord whose vehicle is Garuḍa vanished; he quickly arrived at Ayodhyā and performed supreme penance.
O learned one, because he remained hidden for the sake of increasing the splendor of the gods, that deity attained renown by the name Guptahari. || 44 ||
Because the discus named Sudarśana fell from the palm of his hand before Hari’s arrival, he is remembered as Cakrahari.
By the mere sight of those two, one is liberated from all sins; by that power, Hara [is known], and the gods possess formidable splendor.
Having conquered all the Daityas in battles and regained their own positions, they then shone with immense joy while afflicting the Asuras.
Then, having all quickly assembled with Bṛhaspati at their head, all the gods, eager to behold Hari, whose lotus feet are honored by the garlands upon their crowns, arrived in Ayodhyā.

Having arrived there and heard his various qualities with great reverence, they then worshipped him with meritorious dispositions, bowed with palms joined in prayer, and remained fixed in meditation, contemplating Hari with one-pointed minds.
Beholding them arrived and bowing down with devotion at his feet, Janārdana, the yellow-robed soul of the universe, being pleased, spoke: (50)

The Blessed Lord said: "O gods, it is by good fortune that you have all gathered here after a long time. O deities, what desire of yours shall I fulfill now? Tell me quickly; why do you delay? Be fearless."
The gods said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the lords of gods, O Master of the universe, by you everything has now been accomplished; indeed, every task has been fully achieved."
Nevertheless, O Lord, O All-pervading One, you must always and eternally remain right here for our protection, having brought your senses under control. (53)
In this very way, one should always act for the destruction of the enemy faction. || 54 ||

The Blessed Lord said: "I shall do exactly this: I will bring about the destruction of your enemies, O Asuras, and I will always increase the splendor of those who are illustrious. Furthermore, this story shall attain the highest renown in the world forever."
This god, renowned throughout the world by the name Guptahari, shall attain fame for my supreme and most secret abode.
In this place, he who is the best among living beings and performs worship, sacrifice, recitation, and so forth with supreme devotion, attains the highest goal. (57)
Whoever here, having conquered the senses, makes a gift according to their ability, attains incomparable heaven and never grieves. (58)
In this matter, for my pleasure, cows accompanied by their calves should be diligently offered according to the prescribed rites by living beings who desire merit. (59)
With golden horns and silver hooves, covered with two pieces of cloth, provided with a bronze milking vessel, and possessing a copper-colored back, she was endowed with many excellent qualities.
With a jewel-tail, yielding milk, and adorned with ornaments of bells; she is worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and being well-pleased, she grants nectar-like offspring.
To a twice-born man who is learned in the Vedas, virtuous, pure-souled, devoted to Viṣṇu, wise, and delighting in compassion.
A cow should be given to a true Brāhmaṇa; thus one enjoys happiness everywhere. It should not be given to one who is merely a twice-born, for such a gift would cause the donor to fall.
For my pleasure, this should be given here with a pure inner self.
For those who, intent on devotion to me, bathe here for the sake of purification, their ascent to heaven is eternal and liberation rests in the palm of their hand.
Likewise, on the seat (pīṭha) of Cakrahari, men should diligently perform supreme gifts for my pleasure, as well as recitations, fire-sacrifices, and other rites. (66)
O most excellent ones, you too should perform the pilgrimage according to the prescribed rite at this auspicious confluence near this secret abode of Hara.
On its western side, extending for three yojanas from Gopratāra and other points, the Sarayū river joins the Ghargharā, which flows with surging waves of water.
Having bathed here according to the prescribed rite, one should diligently behold the deity named Guptahari, who bestows the fulfillment of all desires and aims. (69)

Agastya said: Having spoken thus, the infallible Lord, clad in yellow garments, vanished. The gods also, having diligently performed the departure according to the prescribed rites, remained forever in Ayodhyā, utterly enchanted by the virtues of Hari. (70)
From that time forward, O best of Brahmins, that place became renowned upon the earth; and especially on the full moon day of Kārttika, there shall be an annual festival.

There, preceded by a bath at the confluence of the Vibhu-gupta-hrada, and having bathed in this sacred ford (tīrtha) of Gopratāra situated at the junction of the Sarayū and Ghargharā rivers, one should worship this Lord who bestows the fruits of all desires. (72)
Likewise, the festival of Cakrahari should be celebrated with great effort by men on the seventh lunar day (Hari-tithi) during the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Thus, he who undertakes this pilgrimage rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu.
The venerable Sūta said: When the pitcher-born sage had thus spoken and ceased, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa spoke again, filled with wonder.
Vyāsa said: O Brahmin, rich in asceticism, you have told me this most wonderful tale, by which my mind has been filled with amazement.
Tell me in detail of your most wonderful majesty.
Listen, O best of Brahmins, to the most wonderful greatness of Saṅgama; I shall relate it to you exactly as I heard it in its entirety from Lord Skanda. (78)

O Brahmin, ten thousand crores and ten hundred crores of holy fords (tīrthas) always reside at the confluence of the Gharghara waters with the Sarayū river; this has been learned by me from Skanda. (79)
The presence of the deities, the gods, the Siddhas, and likewise the Yogins, as well as that of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, is ever-present there. (80)
Having bathed with a concentrated mind in the waters of that confluence, and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, he should give gifts according to his capacity.
O Brahmin, listen now with a focused mind as I describe to you the fruit that one who is pure obtains by offering oblations with the Vaiṣṇava mantra. (82)
It is equal to a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices performed at Kurukṣetra, that great field, when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu.
May there arise that merit which comes from the gift of gold day after day. || 84 ||
On the new moon day, on the full moon day, on both the twelfth days, during the solstices, and at the vyatīpāta yoga, bathing indeed bestows the world of Viṣṇu.
A man might stand on one foot for a thousand yugas; yet, he who bathes according to the rules at Saṅgama on the full moon day of Pauṣa attains a result that is no different from that.
That man who hangs with his head downwards for ten thousand ages at the confluence of those pure-souled ones who have bathed in the holy waters— || 87 ||
That prosperity which belongs to men cannot be attained even by hundreds of sacrifices.
In the month of Pauṣa, bathing especially bestows abundant fruit.

Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or one of mixed caste, whoever performs the bath with devotion especially in the month of Pauṣa, goes to the abode of Brahmā, from which there is no return.
O Brahmin, listen also to the fruit obtained by him who, in the month of Pauṣa, offers an excellent lamp enriched with ghee according to the rules and with faith. (91)
Whatever sin may have been accumulated over various births, whether it be small or great, all of that perishes quickly, just like salt placed in water.
The meritorious man who gives a lamp constantly attains longevity, health, sovereignty, progeny, and supreme happiness as his perpetual reward.
But that wise person who, being self-restrained and observant of vows, keeps a vigil here on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Pauṣa, shall go to the abode of Hari.
Keeping a vigil at night and having offered lamps everywhere, the Brahmin, self-restrained and pure in his vows, should perform the fire-oblation (homa).

A devotee of Viṣṇu, performing the worship of Viṣṇu and listening to the stories of Hari, should keep the night awake with songs, instrumental music, and dances that please Viṣṇu, as well as through meritorious discourses. (96)
Then, at the clear dawn, having bathed according to the rules with devotion, one should worship Viṣṇu and the Brahmins, and give gold and other gifts according to one's capacity.
The wise man who, endowed with faith, gives gold, food, and garments at the confluence according to the prescribed rite, attains the supreme goal.
Year after year, however, a vigil should be observed by those devoted to merit.

Hari is to be worshipped and the twice-born are to be properly gratified by men according to their capacity; by that, there is supreme satisfaction for Viṣṇu, and sins become fruitless, just as serpents become devoid of venom at the sight of Tārkṣya. || 100 ||
Having bathed there, one goes to heaven; having bathed here, one becomes happy. || 101 ||
Whatever living beings there may be in the three worlds, they all attain supreme satisfaction when satiated with the waters produced from the confluence.
For all beings here whose minds are afflicted by suffering and who are seeking a refuge, there is no destination equal to a gathering together. (103)
By performing a ritual bath at the confluence, a person delivers seven generations of descendants, seven generations of ancestors, and himself—all these beings.
In this world, they are equal to those born blind and likewise to the lame; for they do not come together here to bathe at the confluence of the Sarayū and the Ghaṅghara.
Just as the Brāhmaṇa is among the social classes, so is the confluence among sacred fords; indeed, a man who stands at the confluence of the Sarayū and Ghargharā is always established in Viṣṇu.
By bathing here, by giving gifts according to one's ability, and by performing oblations according to the prescribed rules, a man who has conquered his senses shall attain heaven.
Whether it be a man or a woman, whoever performs the ritual bath according to the rules, will indeed dwell in the heavenly realm; of this there is no doubt. (108)
Just as fire would burn everything, whether dry or moist, so too do all sins become reduced to ashes by immersion in contact with that [water]. || 109 ||
On one side are all the sacred fords (tīrthas) with their various ritual fruits; yet the confluence arising from the union of the Sarayū and Ghargharā rivers would be superior. (110)
Whatever fruit is recorded in the Śruti for bathing at all sacred fords (tīrthas), such a fruit shall fully accrue to men from bathing at this confluence.
O sinless one, there exists another sacred ford named Gopratāra in the very vicinity of the confluence, which destroys even the most heinous sins.
By bathing and giving gifts there, a man never grieves; there has been no sacred ford equal to Gopratāra, nor will there ever be one.
O learned one, just as Maṇikarṇikā exists in Vārāṇasī, so too, O Brahmin, is the abode of Mahākāla in Ujjayinī. (114)
O Brahmin, just as Cakravāpī is remembered as the most excellent of sacred sites in Naimiṣa, so too in Ayodhyā is the great site named Gopratāra.
O learned one, it was there that, by the command of Rāma, the people of the city of Sāketa attained incomparable heaven after immersing themselves in the supreme waters. 116.
Vyāsa said: O learned one, O observer of noble vows, tell me how the people of the city of Sāketa attained heaven, and how Rāghava did so. (117)
Agastya said: O sage, listen attentively to this story in great detail, concerning how that Rāma and the citizens went to heaven.
Formerly, having unweariedly accomplished the work of the gods, Rāma, whose intellect was heroic, set his mind upon going to heaven along with his two brothers.
Then, having learned [of the situation] through their scout, the monkeys—who can assume any form at will—along with the bears, cow-tailed macaques, and rakshasas, sprang up in great numbers.
The sons of the gods and Gandharvas, as well as the sons of the sages, all these monkeys, having learned of Rāma’s passing, assembled together.
Having followed after Rāma, all those leaders of the monkey troops said: "O sinless King, we have arrived here in order to follow you. (122)
O Rāma, O bull among men, if you were to go away without us, O King, we would all surely be destroyed by a great punishment. (123)
Having heard the words of those bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas, Rāghava then immediately addressed Vibhīṣaṇa with these words.
O Vibhīṣaṇa, for as long as living beings shall endure, so long shall you exercise this great kingdom; you shall protect Laṅkā.
Rule this kingdom indeed; do not act otherwise than my word. Protect the subjects according to dharma; you ought not to speak further.
Having spoken thus, the descendant of Kakutstha then said to Hanumān: "O son of the Wind, may you live long; do not let your vow be in vain."
O bull among monkeys, as long as people shall speak of my story, so long must you sustain your life, fulfilling your vow.
Both Mainda and Dvivida have partaken of the nectar of immortality; as long as the worlds shall endure, so long shall these two endure.

"May the monkeys protect our sons and grandsons here in this world. Having spoken thus to all the monkeys, Rāghava, the descendant of Kakutstha, then said to them: "Come, let us depart together with me. (130)
When the night had turned to dawn, the broad-chested and mighty-armed Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, then spoke to the family priest.
Let the Agnihotra sacrifices go forth first, blazing in every direction; let the Vājapeya and Atirātra rites also proceed before me. (132)
Then the radiant Vasiṣṭha, having resolved everything in his mind, performed the ritual for the great departure according to the prescribed rules.
Then, wearing garments of linen and endowed with the vow of celibacy, he took up blades of kuśa grass in his hands and prepared for the Great Departure.
The lord of men uttered neither anything auspicious nor anything inauspicious, having departed from that city like the moon emerging from the ocean.
On Rāma’s left side Śrī, accompanied by Padmā, is seated; on his right is the large-eyed Hrī, and likewise Vyavasāya is in front.
Various kinds of weapons, including bows, bowstrings, and so forth, all followed the descendant of Kakutstha in human form. (137)
The Veda in the form of a Brāhmaṇa, Sāvitrī on the left and right, the syllable Om, and the syllable Vaṣaṭ—all these then went toward Rāma. || 138 ||
The high-souled sages and all the mountains likewise followed the descendant of Kakutstha as he approached the gateway to heaven. || 139 ||
Likewise, the women residing in the inner apartments followed the descendant of Kakutstha, including the elderly, children, female slaves, as well as the assembly and the door-keepers.
And Bharata, together with Śatrughna and the women of the inner apartments, went forth to meet Rāma as he was departing, all of them devotedly following the lineage of Raghu.
Then the high-souled Brahmins, accompanied by their sacred fires, followed the descendant of Kakutstha from all sides, together with their sons and wives.
The ministers, together with their servants, sons, and kinsmen—all of them, along with their followers, followed after Rāghava. || 143 ||
Then all the subjects, filled with joyful and well-fed people and delighted by his virtues, followed Raghava as he departed.
Likewise, all the subjects—along with their sons and all their kinsmen—became followers of Rāghava upon seeing him freed from all taint.
Having bathed, wearing white garments, and with minds fully composed, they all followed after Rāghava, making shouts of joy.
No one there was dejected, nor afraid, nor excessively distressed; everyone became exceedingly joyful, delighted, and filled with supreme wonder. || 147 ||

And the people of the kingdom, desiring to see the King’s nirvāṇa, arrived there as well; having seen the Wielder of the Wheel [the Buddha] on the path through the sky, they too reached that place. (148)
Bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas, as well as the people residing in the city, arrived and followed behind with supreme devotion. || 149 ||
Even those beings who had vanished within the city followed Rāghava as he approached the gateway to heaven. || 150 ||
Whatever beings, both stationary and moving, behold the descendant of Kakutstha, they too set their minds upon going to heaven. (151)
There was not even the slightest being in Ayodhyā who did not follow the descendant of Raghu as he stood at the gateway to heaven. 152.
Then, having traveled half a yojana, the joy of the Raghus went westward and beheld the Sarayū river of holy waters.

Then, at that very moment, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, surrounded by all the gods and high-souled sages, arrived there at the gateway to heaven where the descendant of Kakutstha was standing.
Surrounded on all sides by hundreds of millions of divine celestial chariots, he illuminated the entire sky as the unsurpassed embodiment of light.
And there, due to their own great self-radiant splendors resulting from meritorious deeds, pure, fragrant, and pleasant winds blew. || 156 ||
Accompanied by a rain of auspicious flowers and driven by a swift wind, the Sun took his place upon that chariot, which was attended by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Rāma touched the waters of the Śarayū with his feet; then Brahmā, accompanied by the gods, began to offer praise. 158.
For you are indeed the Lord of the World, O God; no one knows you. O large-eyed one, I am truly your former possession.
O you of great heroism, enter that form of your own which you desire for the welfare of the world—a great being, inconceivable, and imperishable.

At the word of his grandfather, he himself entered this very world; along with his younger brother, he entered that divine Vaiṣṇava splendor which is the cycle of transmigration. Then the gods, worshipping the best of deities, [honored] him who possessed the body of Viṣṇu.

The Maruts, together with Indra and led by Agni, were to be propitiated; as were the divine hosts of ṛṣis, the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the Suparṇas, Nāgas, Yakṣas, Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas. || 162 ||
All the gods, exceedingly thrilled and joyful, their desires fulfilled, exclaimed from their celestial abodes, "Excellent! Excellent! (163).
Then Viṣṇu, of great splendor, spoke to the Grandfather: "O you of noble vows, it behooves you to grant a world to these multitudes of people."
But all these men have come here out of love for me; they are devoted, full of devotion, and have surrendered themselves entirely.
Having heard that which was spoken by Viṣṇu, the Lord of all the worlds said: "Human beings shall indeed remain in the world named Santānika."
If one gives up one's life with devotion at this sacred ford, Svargadvāra, while meditating solely upon Rāma, one shall indeed obtain supreme progeny.

All [those born] from the continuum of existence are called "saṃtānika"; immediately after the Brahma-world, the monkeys return to their own womb, and the Rākṣasas likewise to their Rākṣasa womb. (168)
From her indeed issued forth those who were born from the bodies of gods and asuras, as well as Sugrīva, the son of the Sun, and the solar disc itself.
The sages, nāgas, and yakṣas shall each go to their own destination as the Lord of Gods speaks thus; meanwhile, Gopratāra has arrived.
That water then joined the full waters of the Sarayū; having plunged into the water, they all joyfully cast off their lives. || 171 ||
Having cast off their human bodies, they then ascended celestial chariots; and those who had been born in the animal realm entered the Sarayū at that time.
Having cast off their bodies there, they assumed divine forms; likewise, other beings as well—both stationary and moving—did the same. (173)

Having attained superior bodies, they indeed ascended to the world of the gods. When that [state] was reached there, the monkeys, bears, and rākṣasas all likewise entered [the divine realm], casting off their [former] bodies at that time.
Then, having all gone to heaven and remembering the omnipresent Teacher of the World, the high-minded Rāma, filled with joy, departed together with the gods.
Therefore, that sacred ford known as Gopratāra has attained renown; supreme liberation is found at Gopratāra, and does not exist in other sacred fords.
O Brahmin, if this yoga is obtained after hundreds of other births, then liberation is attained; but whether it is attained in a single birth or not, [depends on one's merit]. 177.
At Gopratāra, there is no doubt that even another person, being firmly established in devotion to Hari, attains both yoga and liberation in a single birth. (178)
Whatever learned man, being firm in resolve, bathes at Gopratāra, he enters the supreme abode that is difficult even for yogis to attain. (179)

On the full moon day of Kārttika, those who have conquered their senses should especially bathe; for in the month of Kārttika, O brahmin-sage, all the gods together with Indra come to bathe at Gopratāra in Ayodhyā, particularly on that occasion.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred ford equal to Gopratāra, where even the King of Prayāga comes to bathe during the month of Kārtika.
Free from sin and having cast off all impurity, with white limbs and a white garment, that best of sages, desiring righteousness for the sake of purification, went to Prayāga. (182)
O observer of noble vows, whatever sacred fords there are on earth, whether terrestrial or divine, they all truly reside at Gopratāra on the full moon day of Kārtika.
At Gopratāra, recitation, fire-offerings, bathing, and giving according to one's capacity—all these, as well as vows and observances performed with faith, attain imperishability. (184)
Having reached Kārttika, all those holy places (tīrthas) depart with the desire: "We shall go to Gopratāra in order to cast off our sin. (185)

A bath taken at Gopratāra destroys all sins. Having bathed at Gopratāra and beheld the omnipresent Lord Guptahari, a man shall be liberated from all sins; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (186)
Those endowed with faith and observant of their vows should perform the worship of Brahmins specifically for the sake of Viṣṇu, preceded by ritual bathing.

And a milch cow, adorned with ornaments according to one's ability, should be given by one who has restrained their self for the pleasure of Viṣṇu, to a Brāhmaṇa who is well-versed in the Vedas, devoted to observances and vows, and exceedingly pure. (168)
Various kinds of food, gold, and diverse garments should be given with supreme devotion for the sake of attaining Hari. (189)
Whatever merit is gained from the gift of a balance-scale at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse, or at the Narmadā during a lunar eclipse, that same merit is obtained here by the offering of a lamp.
O tiger among sages, for one whose lamp burns with ghee or even with sesame oil, what need is there for a horse sacrifice?
By him who has offered a lamp before Keśava during the month of Kārttika, all sacrifices have been performed and the bathing in sacred fords has been accomplished.
Various sacred fords that bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation do not equal even a sixteenth part of Gopratāra in this regard.
He who gives even a small amount of gold to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas attains an auspicious state and indeed shines like fire. || 194 ||
O twice-born one, by giving food according to the prescribed rite at the holy ford named Gopratāra, which is renowned throughout the three worlds, one is not born again.
The man who performs a bath there and gratifies the Brahmins obtains the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. || 196 ||
He who remains for a month there, restricted by his vows and taking but one meal a day, has the sins committed throughout his entire life instantly destroyed. (197)
O ascetic, those who enter the fire at Gopratāra according to the prescribed rite undoubtedly enter the abode of Viṣṇu. (198)
Those who, being firmly resolved through devotion to Viṣṇu, practice fasting unto death here, shall not return again even after hundreds of millions of kalpas.
The man who worships Govinda at Gopratāra indeed attains the merit proclaimed for Gopratāra, which is equal to ten gold pieces.
Incense offered to Govinda yields the fruit of the Agnihotra sacrifice; the fruit of offering fragrance is remembered as equal to the gift of land. (201)
O learned one, this place is proclaimed to be most wonderful; having bathed here especially on the full moon day of Kārttika, one who is pure in their vows [attains great merit].
Having bathed at Svargadvāra, a man obtains the fruit of ten gold pieces; and he who, endowed with faith, gives gold becomes a dweller in heaven. (203)

On an excellent festival day at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), which yields the fruit of ten pieces of gold, one should perform a vigil at night on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Having fasted, being pure and bathed, and intent upon the worship of Viṣṇu, one should diligently offer a lamp that bestows various fruits.
Meritorious deeds resound throughout heaven, the mortal world, and the netherworld only so long as one offers a lamp in the water before Keśava during the month of Kārttika.
On the full moon day, having bathed at dawn with a pure mind, one should worship Hari according to the prescribed rites and perform the śrāddha ceremony with devotion.
Having given food according to his ability and satisfied the Brāhmaṇas, he should then honor a Brāhmaṇa couple with garments and ornaments.
Having beheld the all-pervading Guptahari and having especially worshipped him, he, being pure and with his mind fixed upon Him, paid obeisance to that sacred ford.
And at midday, one should perform a ritual bath according to the rules at Svargadvāra; with one's self purified of all sins, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus, having performed the bath with great effort at Gopratāra according to the supreme injunctions, he whose form is the embodiment of celebrated merit, having cleansed all his sins and having worshipped Acyuta with devotion, attains stainless radiance and union with Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Svargadvāra-Gopratāra Tīrtha," in the Ayodhyā-Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Agastya said: I shall describe another sacred site known as Kṣīrodaka. It is situated to the northwest of Sītākuṇḍa, beautiful in its qualities, a place where a singular mass of merit resides, and a destroyer of all miseries. || 1 ||
In former times, King Daśaratha duly performed the sacrifice known by the name Putreṣṭi for the sake of obtaining sons, carrying it out with great devotion.
He joyfully completed the sacrifice accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees; at the conclusion of the rite, the Enjoyer of Sacrifices appeared there in embodied form.

Taking in his hand an unsurpassed golden vessel filled with sacrificial oblation (havis), in which the supreme Vaiṣṇava splendor was infused, the king divided that oblation into four parts and gave them to his wives.

The place where that attainment of milk occurred—which is exceedingly difficult to obtain—is known as Kṣīrodaka; it is a destroyer of sins, manifested by water, supreme, and bestowing excellent fruits. (5)
Having bathed there with devotion, a wise man who has conquered his senses attains all desires and sons who are deeply learned in the scriptures.

On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one who has mastered his vows, having bathed there according to the prescribed rite, should give a gift to a twice-born man according to his capacity.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rules, a man shall obtain all his desires; know that he shall likewise obtain sons and merits in accordance with the law.
Therefore, situated in the southwest direction from the place where the milk and water meet, there is the famous sacrificial pit of Bṛhaspati, adorned with lofty and fierce [flames].
It pacifies all sins and is rippled with the nectar of merit; it is there, indeed, that the Preceptor of the Gods himself established his residence.

And Bṛhaspati, of noble intellect, performed the sacrifice according to the prescribed rites; it was attended by various hosts of sages, delightful, and bestowing many fruits. That sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), endowed with the splendor of Garuḍa’s shadow, is difficult for sinners to attain.
Even the gods, beginning with Indra, having bathed there with great effort, attained their heart's desired fruits, becoming replete with beauty and magnanimity.
Whereby, through bathing and giving gifts, a person is liberated from sin.
A pilgrimage there on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada yields fruit; moreover, bathing on any other Thursday also bestows great merit.
Whoever performs the worship of Bṛhaspati and Viṣṇu there, being liberated from all sins, rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu. || 15 ||

If there should be affliction for anyone due to the piercing [of a planet] during its transit (gocara-vedha) by Jupiter, he should perform a ritual bath here according to the rules, preceded by a formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa), an image of the Guru fashioned from gold, dressed in yellow garments, should indeed be placed in water and given away.

Having bathed for the sake of removing affliction, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) there before a knower of the Vedas who is exceedingly pure, according to the rules for the recitation of the planetary mantras. || 18 ||
When this is done, there is no doubt that the affliction caused by the planets will perish. || 19 ||
To the south of that, O best of sages, is the excellent Rukmiṇī-kuṇḍa, which the goddess Rukmiṇī herself, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, created.
There, Viṣṇu himself then made his dwelling in the water; this was brought about by the granting of a boon and out of affection for his wife.
There, a self-restrained man should perform bathing, as well as giving gifts, the Vaiṣṇava fire-oblation, the worship of the twice-born, and the worship of Viṣṇu. (22)
There, the annual festival should be performed with great effort on the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, for the removal of all sins.
By performing this pilgrimage, even a barren woman gives birth to a son; of this there is no doubt. Whether by women or by men, the ritual bath must be performed with devotion. (24)
Having enjoyed all pleasures in their entirety, he rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu; therefore, one who desires prosperity should especially bathe there.
By bathing there, a person obtains all desires; and for the pleasure of Rukmiṇī and the Lord of Śrī, one should give according to one's ability. (26)
Worship according to the prescribed rites must be performed, especially for the Brāhmaṇas; there, the Lord of Lakṣmī, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace, is to be meditated upon.
Wearing yellow garments and adorned with garlands, he was praised by Nārada and others; seated upon Garuḍa, wearing a crown, and decorated like Mahendra and other gods.
Marked by the Kaustubha gem upon his chest for the attainment of all desired fruits, he is dark as an Atasī flower, with eyes as pure as lotuses.
When this is done, there is no doubt that one shall attain all desires; having enjoyed happiness in this world, one rejoices in the realm of Hari.
Henceforth, I shall describe another sacred site that destroys sins, which eradicates the defilements of the Kali age, and which is characterized by direct realization.
It is supremely pure, incomparable, and the bestower of the fulfillment of all desires and aims; it is renowned as Dhanayakṣa and produces supreme conviction.
The auspicious Rukmiṇī-kuṇḍa is remembered as being in the northwestern petal; there, the royal sage Hariścandra possessed great wealth.
For the sake of his protection, the Yakṣas guarded him most diligently; this was even before the sage Viśvāmitra defeated him.
He seized the entire kingdom, including its fourfold army, from King Hariścandra, who was supremely envious of his sovereignty.
Under his authority, that sage gave away all his excellent wealth; and for its protection, he diligently established a Yakṣa there.
It was known as Pramamthura, a temple of joy and bliss; he provided its protection with great effort in every respect.
On one occasion, that wise sage, who had conquered his senses, was gratified; filled with supreme affection, he spoke these sweet words.
Viśvāmitra said: "Choose a boon, O knower of dharma, quickly and without envy. O steadfast one, I am especially pleased by your supreme devotion. (39)

The Yakṣa said: "O best of Brahmins, if you grant me the boon I desire, then be gracious, O Lord of Sages, O Brahman-sage! My body has become exceedingly foul-smelling due to the curse of the king; please grant me the means to make it fragrant. (40)
Agastya said: When the Yakṣa had spoken thus, the sage, his eyes fixed in meditation, discerned him through this devotion and performed his consecration.
Having performed the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) with devotion according to the rules using water from a sacred ford (tīrtha), his body immediately became possessed of an exceedingly fragrant form.
Being thus situated, the wise one then stood before him with palms joined in reverence, bowing low in humility, and spoke sweetly. (43)
The Yakṣa said: "O wise one, by your grace I have become possessed of a fragrant body; O omniscient one, please act so that this place attains renown. (44)
O brahmin-sage, by your grace, please indeed exert such effort as is required.
Agastya said: Having been addressed thus, the sage meditated for a moment with steady eyes; then, with a gracious soul, he spoke to the Yakṣa in gentle words.
Viśvāmitra said: "O Yakṣa, this place shall attain incomparable renown; this holy site (tīrtha) shall become famous as 'Dhanayakṣa'."

It bestows beauty upon the body and is a supreme source of confidence; having bathed there according to the prescribed rite, one abandons foul odor in an instant. Therefore, those who desire merit should diligently perform their ablutions there. 48.
One should perform charity according to one's faith and capacity, and especially worship Lakṣmī; therein, through bathing and giving gifts, one especially pleases Lakṣmī. (49)
O observer of noble vows, by worshipping all nine treasures, one enjoys happiness in this world and rejoices in the next world.
Mahāpadma, Padma, Śaṅkha, Makara, Kacchapa, Mukunda, Kunda, Nīla, and Kharva are the nine treasures (nidhis). 51.
O sinless one, these [deities] shall also have their presence here in this sacrificial pit; moreover, their worship specifically bestows abundant fruit.
The worship of Nidhilakṣmī should be performed in the midst of water. || 53 ||
Various kinds of food and diverse garments should be given. || 54 ||
One should give gold and other gifts according to one's ability, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth; such secret giving should be performed with great effort and diligence. (55)
And golden fruits should especially be given as offerings. || 56 ||
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, bathing bestows abundant fruit; it should be performed with supreme faith, and indeed, with even greater faith. (57)
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, the annual pilgrimage takes place; there, one should especially perform ritual bathing and the libation for the ancestors.
Saying, "May the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, be satisfied," he should offer three handfuls of water according to the rule with his sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya).
O Yakṣa, a man who acts in this way is never deluded; one who bathes here goes to heaven, and one who bathes here shall become happy. (60)
O Yakṣa, after bathing here, you must first perform worship; by worshipping you according to the prescribed rites, the destruction of the sins of men shall occur.

"Obeisance to the King of the Pramathas"—this is declared to be the mantra for worship. Worship, the hearing [of the scripture], and so forth, should be performed in the midst of a sacred ford (tīrtha).
O Yakṣa, the worship of Nidhi and Lakṣmī is especially dear to you; the wise man who performs it in this manner shall obtain all his desires. || 63 ||
One who desires wealth obtains wealth; one who desires a son obtains a son; one who desires liberation obtains liberation—what, then, is not attained here? (64)
O Yakṣa, if any man indeed fails to perform his bath out of delusion, you shall seize all of his merit accumulated over the course of a year.
Having thus granted those boons to him, Viśvāmitra, the lord of sages and that foremost of ascetics, a treasure-house of austerity, then vanished from sight.
From that time forward, that place attained supreme renown; the entire ground of that sacred site was fashioned out of gold.
O wise one, he who thus constructs [this] temple, adorned on all sides and inlaid with a multitude of divine jewels, attains the supreme goal.
O twice-born one, situated in the northern direction from Dhanayakṣa is the renowned Vasiṣṭhakuṇḍa, which always destroys all sins.
The residence of Vasiṣṭha, that treasury of great austerity, was always there; Arundhatī, whose vows were stainless, was ever present with him. (70)
In this regard, the wise and diligent person who, being pure, performs a bath preceded by a śrāddha ceremony here especially, attains unsurpassed merit.
O sinless one, the presence of Vāmadeva exists in that very place; both Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva should be worshipped with great effort. (72)
The devoted wife and Arundhatī especially are to be honored; one should bathe according to the prescribed rite and give gifts according to one's capacity. (73)
The attainment of the fruits of all desires arises; there is no doubt in this matter. Whoever performs a ritual bath here shall become equal to Vasiṣṭha.
In the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight on the fifth lunar day, one who is firm in his vows should perform the annual festival according to the prescribed rites.
One should indeed perform the worship of Viṣṇu here with effort and faith; having one's self purified of all sins, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. || 76 ||
O best of Brahmins, to the west of Vasiṣṭhakuṇḍa is the famous Sāgarakuṇḍa, which grants the fulfillment of all desires and goals; by bathing and giving gifts there, one shall attain all desires.
Whatever merit a person may obtain by bathing in the ocean on the full moon day, that same imperishable merit a man shall obtain by bathing on this sacred festival day.
Therefore, one who desires a son should bathe here according to the prescribed rite; specifically, one should perform the bath on the full moon day of the month of Āśvina.
A wise man acting in this way is liberated from all sins; having bathed here and given according to his ability, a man shall go to heaven. (80)
To the southwest of the ocean is the excellent Yoginī-kuṇḍa, where sixty-four Yoginīs reside, stationed within the water.
They bestow the accomplishment of all goals upon men, and especially upon women; they all grant supreme success and yield the fruit of all desires.
Especially on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, men should bathe with great effort for the pleasure of the Yoginīs.
Here, bathing as well as giving gifts shall all attain fruitfulness; there is no doubt that the Yakṣiṇīs and other such beings become perfected ones (siddhas) here. || 84 ||
To the east of Yoginīkuṇḍa is the excellent Urvaśīkuṇḍa; O learned one, a man who bathes there shall attain the company of Urvaśī in heaven.
In ancient times, it is said, a wise sage named Raibhya, whose wealth was his asceticism, practiced penance on the slopes of the Himalayas, abstaining from food and having conquered his senses.
Having seen that extensive austerity, the Lord of the Gods was then terrified and, out of concern, earnestly dispatched Urvaśī to create an obstacle to his penance.
Then, sent by him, she who moved with the gait of an elephant arrived; she dwelt on the side of the Himavat, at the unsurpassed hermitage of Raibhya. (88)
In a bower of flowering forest creepers where birds warbled sweetly, the deer stood with limbs motionless at the playful songs of the kinnarīs.
It was made of *punnāga*, *kesara*, *aśoka*, and *chinna-kijalka* flowers, tawny in hue, fashioned like a second mountain of gold by the Creator himself.
She shone as the treasury of all the beauty of the flower-bowed god of love, an Urvaśī who was a river of the nectar of extraordinary loveliness.
