Adorned with white pearls against the golden luster of her limbs, she was graced by youth through the loveliness of her youth.
With the white luster of the waves from the corners of her clear eyes, she made her own lower lip appear like the hue of a fresh sprout.
With mango blossoms rich with bees humming against her ears, she was like a pārijāta creeper born from the very essence of nectar.
Slender-waisted with broad hips and breasts prominent with color, she was like the spear of the flower-bowed god, whetted on a grindstone. 95.
In that hermitage, the sage beheld the large-eyed woman, whose mind had been consumed by the fire of the eye of the God of Love.

She had assumed a female form solely for the purpose of deceiving the Three-eyed One; she was adorned with earrings fashioned from the flowers and creepers of the hermitage grove, and wore a girdle made of those same blossoms.
Beholding that large-eyed woman, the sage’s senses became agitated; he grew consumed by rage and, blazing with anger, uttered many curses.
Raibhya said: "O you who are proud of your beauty, quickly assume a hideous form, since you have come into my presence for the purpose of obstructing my ascetic penance. (99)
Agastya said: Having been thus cursed in anger by that sage, that woman of auspicious eyes, assuming the form of a female, spoke with reverence to the sage with her palms joined in salutation.
Urvaśī said: "O Blessed One, be gracious to me, for I am dependent on another; O you of firm vows, how shall there be liberation from your curse?"
Raibhya said: "In Ayodhyā there is a supreme and great purifying holy site (tīrtha). Perform your ablutions there today and attain supreme beauty. (102)
And by your name alone, that water will certainly attain renown. || 103 ||
Agastya said: Thus, at the word of the Brahmin, she performed everything with devotion; that Sundarī quickly became beautiful, and that place attained renown.
O best of sages, whatever person performs a ritual bath here according to the prescribed rules, supreme beauty shall be his; of this there is no doubt. (105)

On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, the annual festival (yātrā) shall take place; here Viṣṇu is to be worshipped by the people for the attainment of all desires and goals. (106)
Acting thus, a wise man shall dwell forever in the world of Viṣṇu; whether it be a man or a woman, they shall attain all their desires. (107)
O tiger among sages, to the south of the Urvaśī-kuṇḍa lies the supreme Ghoṣārka-kuṇḍa, which always destroys all sins.
By bathing and giving gifts here, one is glorified in the world of the Sun; there exists no other sacred site anywhere equal to this tīrtha. (109)
Even a man who is wounded, afflicted with leprosy, impoverished, or overcome by suffering, shall attain all his desires if he performs the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules. || 110 ||
On Sundays, especially on the sixth day of the bright fortnight in the months of Bhādrapada and Māgha, one should diligently perform the ritual bath with great reverence.
One should perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules with a desire for the world of the Sun; likewise, a bath on a Sunday in the month of Pauṣa is especially meritorious.
On the seventh lunar day conjoined with the Sun (Sunday), bathing yields abundant fruit. Formerly, there was a lord of men named Ghoṣa in the Solar dynasty. (113)
He alone protected the earth girdled by the ocean, whose fame indeed illuminates the spheres of the three worlds.
He who shines, throbbing with majesty like another sun, having shattered the circle of his enemies with his exceedingly fierce staff-like arms. (115)
Once, that protector of subjects, having entrusted the earth to his ministers, wandered about, addicted to hunting, in a forest of exceedingly dense trees. (116)
Due to the sins arising from his previous births, which were indicative of misfortune, that king—though handsome—had worms infesting his lotus-like hands and was stripped of his pride. || 117 ||
Once, while wandering in the forest during a hunt, there was a certain man who went here and there, slaying boars, lions, and deer. (118)
Overcome by thirst and with a withered body, the king saw a lake before him; there he beheld sages intent on their baths, twilight prayers, and other rites.
Then, having sipped water according to the prescribed rules, the lord of men performed his bath; thereupon he became possessed of a divine body, his mind pure with bliss.
Having recognized it as a sacred ford, the sages performed a beloved hymn of praise to the Sun.
The King said: O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, salutations to you, the conscious self; salutations to Savitṛ, to Sūrya, the bestower of joy upon the world. || 122 ||
Salutations to you, the radiant Lord, who has become the three Vedas; salutations to you, Vivasvat, the knower of yoga and the eternal Self.
Salutations always to you, the supreme lord, the dispeller of the darkness of the three worlds, the inconceivable one, whose splendor is like that of the sun. 124.
Constant salutations to the one who loves yoga, to Yoga, to the Knower of Yoga; to the one whose form is the syllable Om, whose form is the exclamation Vaṣaṭ, and whose form is knowledge.

Salutations to the sacrifice, to the sacrificer, to the oblation, and to the officiating priest; salutations to the destroyer of disease, to the one whose nature is the self, and to the bestower of joy upon Kamalā.
Salutations to the Lord of the gods, who is both exceedingly gentle and exceedingly fierce; salutations to you, the refuge of the sacrifice, the protector of devotees, whose nature is beloved.
O eternal illuminator of the worlds, who acts for the welfare of all beings, be gracious today to me, who am bowed before you and have personally offered devotion. (128)

Agastya said: As he was speaking thus, the Sun himself, being pleased, suddenly manifested before him out of a desire to do what was dear to his devotee. He spoke these sweet words to him, whose head was bowed in humility: 129. Ravi said: "Choose a boon, O Indra among kings; I am pleased before you. I shall grant you today that boon which is desired by your mind."
The king said: "O Blessed One, O Infinite Bhāskara, if you grant me a boon, then let your image, fashioned in my name, remain here forever, O All-pervading Lord. (131)
The Sun said: "So be it, O lord of men; your heart-captivating desire shall be fulfilled. Those human beings who shall recite this hymn spoken by you to me," (132)
O lord of men, being pleased with them, I shall grant all their desires; this place shall attain supreme fame on earth by your name.
One who performs a bath here attains all desires; O King, a bath must indeed always be performed here by my devotee.
Whatever desire one may wish for here, that very desire one shall obtain.
Agastya said: Having thus granted the boon, the radiant god of a thousand rays, filled with supreme compassion, then vanished from sight.
There the king installed the unsurpassed image of Ravi, which had arisen from the body of Bhāskara, and he himself performed its worship.
O King, that pool became famous by the name Ghoṣārka-kuṇḍa; by bathing there, a man shall dwell eternally in the world of the Sun.

Thus, having quickly worshipped the form of the Sun with pure and supreme devotion through beautiful rites and with great care, and having first performed his bath in that pool consisting of nectar, he of abundant and stainless fame shall dwell in the world of the Sun.
Agastya said: O brahmin-sage, situated on the western edge from the Ghoṣārka Tīrtha is the one renowned as Ratikuṇḍa, which always removes all sins.
In its western quarter is the place named Kusumāyudha, where by bathing and giving gifts one attains supreme splendor.

The well-known and incomparable Kuṇḍa exists for the fulfillment of all desires and goals; O Sage, by bathing and giving gifts there according to the prescribed rite, a man attains a form like that of Kandarpa—of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, O Brahmin, he who performs a bath with faith at Ratikuṇḍa and Kusumāyudhakuṇḍaka shall become supremely happy.
It is said that whatever couple performs a bath here in these two pools, they always become beautiful, renowned like Rati and Kāma.
Therefore, those who desire merit should bathe here according to the prescribed rite; and one should give gifts according to one's ability for the satisfaction of Rati and Kandarpa.
For him, Saṃtoṣa, Rati, and Ananga will certainly be pleased; for on the bright fifth day of the month of Māgha, bathing there bestows auspiciousness.
O Brahmin, on that day, a couple should diligently bathe first in the Ratikuṇḍa and afterwards in the Kandarpakuṇḍa.
A special worship of Rati and Kandarpa must be performed; the Brahmin couple should be honored with garments, ornaments, and other offerings.
One obtains all desires; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 10 ||
One should worship the Brahmin couple with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, saffron, and other such substances, as well as with various garments and flowers.
When this is done, there is no doubt that it leads to the satisfaction of Rati and Kandarpa; therefore, O Brahmin, Miśrūna shall attain equality with Rati and Kandarpa.
Situated to the west of Kusumāyudhakuṇḍa is that place known as Mantreśvara, which is difficult to attain on earth.
Having bathed at that sacred ford and beheld the omnipresent Lord Mantreśvara, those people shall not undergo rebirth even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
In former times, Rāma, the lord of men who performs pure deeds, having accomplished the work of the gods, entered into a consultation with Kāla.
At that very place where one who has conquered the senses bathes for the sake of journeying toward heaven, there stands a Liṅga known as Mantreśvara.
To the north of that is a beautiful lake adorned with white and blue lotuses; bathing there as well as giving gifts yields various supreme fruits.

The annual festival is traditionally held on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra. By bathing there, giving gifts, and honoring the Brāhmaṇas, one attains imperishable heaven; of this there is no doubt. 16.
O Brahmin, the greatness of Maṃtreśvara, who bestows the highest fruit, cannot be fully described by anyone; there has never been, nor will there ever be, a Liṅga equal to Maṃtreśvara.
He, who grants the fulfillment of all desires and aims, should be worshipped with effort using fragrant flowers, incense, and other blossoms, as well as unguents. || 20 ||
When this is done, there is no doubt that liberation stands within his grasp. O sinless one, Śītalā resides right there on the northern side.
Having worshipped her, a wise man is liberated from all sins. Her worship should always be performed with great effort by men for the sake of accomplishing all goals, especially on Mondays. (22)
When dangers such as eruptive boils and the like have arisen for men, worship should be performed properly; it destroys the fear of diseases and other afflictions. (23)
To the north of that, in that very place, is the goddess renowned as Vandī; by the mere remembrance of her, there is no fear of shackles or other such bonds.
Those who have been bound by an angry king with chains, fetters, and the like, shall indeed be liberated at that very moment upon the prisoner's recollection of the Goddess.
Men should endeavor with great effort to perform her pilgrimage, especially on an auspicious day, for she bestows the fulfillment of all desires and goals. (26)
O observer of noble vows, she should be worshipped with effort using perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and various kinds of food offerings.
O best of sages, for the pleasure of the captive, a meal for Brahmins should be provided; when this is done, there is no doubt that one shall obtain all desires. (28)
North of that, in that very place, Cūḍakī is celebrated on earth; she exists there as the embodiment of supreme accomplishment for men through mere remembrance. (29)
In matters that are highly doubtful and when danger has arisen, by the mere remembrance of her, all success is produced for men. (30)
At its head, men should always produce a sound with their thumbs; and those of self-restrained mind should diligently offer lamps.
The offering of lamps is praised as bestowing all desired objects upon men; on every fourteenth lunar day (Caturdaśī), a festival procession for it is established.
Thereafter, in the eastern direction, there exists an excellent holy site (tīrtha) renowned as Mahāratna, the most supreme among all holy sites. || 33 ||
Whereby, through bathing, giving gifts, and the worship of the twice-born, there shall be the accomplishment of all rites and goals; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (34)
The annual festival is prescribed for the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada; indeed, it is heard that his principal festival is known as Mahāratnā.
Therefore, that unsurpassed sacred ford is renowned as Mahāratna; there, one should perform acts of charity that bring satisfaction to the twice-born.

O brahmin-sage, even women should observe the festival of the vigil for the sake of constant endowment with virility, good fortune, and all happiness; therein, men should diligently perform their ablutions with faith. (37)
Then, in the southwestern direction, there exists the auspicious lake named Durbhara, as well as the Mahābhara lake, which is noble due to its meritorious deeds.
By bathing there, a person always attains the state of heaven; various kinds of wealth and diverse garments should be given as gifts. (39)
Having bathed in the two pools, men endowed with supreme devotion and various dispositions should perform the worship of Śiva. (40)
Maheśvara, the blue-throated one who is the enemy of Andhaka, should be worshipped with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; he is to be propitiated even by yogins.
Having thus meditated upon Śiva together with [Umā], the self-restrained man, freed from sin, shall quickly attain all desires and dwell forever in the world of Śiva. (42)
By doing this, O Brahmin, a man is liberated from all sins at the excellent Mahābhara Tīrtha as well as at the one known as Durbhara. (43)

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, he who, endowed with faith, performs the worship of Śiva according to the rules, and especially the worship of the twice-born (Brāhmaṇas), [attains the fruit].
The man who performs this with devotion shall dwell in the world of Śiva; acting thus, the wise man is never deluded. (45)
Viṣṇu and Rudra, the eternal ones, are exceedingly well-pleased with him; by the mere remembrance of them, one is liberated from all sins. (46)
Therefore, what is the use of much speaking? This unsurpassed pilgrimage site on the banks of the Vipāśā always pacifies the flood of all sins and fulfills every desire.
Hereafter, I shall describe another auspicious holy site (tīrtha), where neither pilgrimage nor charity can possibly occur without good fortune. (48)
In the northeast, from the place called Durbhara, there is the great [liṅga] named Mahāvidyā; by the sight of it, the supernatural powers (siddhis) of men shall be held in their very hands.
That man who, having bathed in the lake before it, beholds the Mahāvidyā with faith and devotion, attains the supreme goal.
Likewise, it is known as Siddhapīṭha, which produces perfect conviction; O twice-born one, worship should be performed there with supreme devotion. (51)
O Brahmin, whatever mantra—whether Śaiva, Śākta, Gāṇapatya, or Vaiṣṇava—one who is self-restrained recites there with faith; || 52 ||

O wise one, having propitiated [the deity] with a one-pointed mind, one should always cause [the mantra] to revolve; for such a person, O twice-born, there shall be constant success and wondrous power shall arise.
Therefore, those who are unwearied should perform the recitation of mantras and other rites here; and on the eighth and ninth days, there shall be a monthly procession.
Various kinds of food and many sorts of fruits should be offered; a bath with milk should be performed, and [the deity] should be worshipped with great care. (55)
Exorcisms and the like, as well as specifically those for deluding and so forth—by means of this particular place, even a wicked mantra attains success. (56)
In this place of the Siddhas, supreme liberation and the highest subjugation [of powers] are attained; likewise, recitation, fire-offerings, and charity—all shall become inexhaustible. (57)
O observer of noble vows, O Brahmin, by going there during the nine nights of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, a person is liberated from all sins. (58)
When the Lord of the Raghus, accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, had previously returned after completely conquering Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the world cry out.
Where the heroic and glorious Bharata, desiring Rāma, went on foot and stood with his followers, endowed with supreme splendor.
Thereupon, the celestial cow arrived and appeared with flowing udders; from her teats flowed milk of superior and manifold qualities.
Seeing the milk fallen upon that ground, the monkeys and rākṣasas were filled with supreme wonder; they moved about, observing everything moving and stationary.
"O Indra among kings, what is this? the scion of Raghu said to them; "Vasiṣṭha knows all of that, so let us question that sage."
Having been addressed thus, they all, standing with Vasiṣṭha at their head, placed the king at their front and questioned him with palms joined in reverence.
Vasiṣṭha, too, having meditated for a moment, addressed the unagitated Rāghava in the presence of everyone, awakening him to the truth.
Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O mighty-armed Rāma; this auspicious Kāmadhenu has arrived out of affection for you, milk flowing from her udder.
Rudra, having arisen from the midst of the milk, has come to see you—the one who has accomplished the task of the gods and who has utterly conquered the enemy.
Worship this quickly in the vicinity of this pool; you too should swiftly and with effort worship this auspicious Śiva, renowned as Dugdheshvara, the sacred one at Kṣīrakuṇḍa. 68.
Agastya said: Then the illustrious Lord of the Raghus, according to the procedure prescribed by Vasiṣṭha, worshipped that liṅga known as Dugdheśvara. (69)
Because that pool at the confluence of the Kṣīra was honored by Sītā, it thereafter attained the incomparable renown as "Sītākuṇḍa."
Having bathed in the Sītākuṇḍa and beheld the Lord Dugdheśvara, men are liberated from all sins; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Here, bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, and charity shall become inexhaustible; for by worshipping Sītā and Rāma along with Lakṣmaṇa at the Sītā-kuṇḍa, [one gains these rewards].
By worshipping Dugdheśvara, one shall attain all desires; the annual festival is prescribed for the fourteenth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Thus, he who is skilled in the dharma of compassion and performs this according to the rules goes to the supreme abode, having reached which he does not grieve.
There, in the eastern direction, there exists a great and auspicious holy site (tīrtha) established by Sugrīva in the vicinity of that treasury of asceticism.
Having bathed there, having given gifts, and having worshiped Rāma with diligence, one shall obtain all desires on that very day.
To the southwest of that is the place known as Hanumatkuṇḍa; to its west, O Brahmin, is the Vibhīṣaṇasara lake at a distance.

By bathing in those two, by giving gifts, and by worshipping Rāma according to the prescribed rites, one attains all desires right there. This is that supreme, pure Ayodhyā, remembered as the treasury of Dharma.

Having been addressed thus, they all, led by Vibhīṣaṇa, quickly questioned the sage Vasiṣṭha with respect and humility: "O mass of asceticism, tell us this story which is so very difficult to obtain. (79)
O Brahmin, quickly tell me all that which they describe as the supreme majesty of Ayodhyā; having heard this most excellent majesty, [I shall be satisfied]. (80)
O treasure of asceticism, having shown us compassion, please tell us how we shall undertake our journey in due order and according to the prescribed rites. (81)
Vasiṣṭha said: "Let all you sages hear the wonderful majesty of Ayodhyā; having heard it, one is liberated from all sins—of this there is no doubt. (82)
This most secret field, named Ayodhyā, is supreme; it is always the cause of liberation for all living beings.
In this place, perfected beings and gods, constantly established in the Vaiṣṇava vow, always bear various marks and long for the world of Viṣṇu. (84)
Having controlled their vital breaths and conquered their senses, they practice the supreme yoga in that place filled with various trees and inhabited by various birds.
Richly adorned with the beauty of lotuses and water-lilies, embellished by lakes, crowded with throngs of Apsarases, and always frequented by the auspicious; (86)
For residence here in this sacred field is always pleasing to Hari; all those who are devotees of Viṣṇu consider it so, having dedicated all their actions to Viṣṇu.

For just as liberation is attained here, it is not so anywhere else; therefore, this field is most excellent because it is the abode of Hari. Since it is the supreme great field, it is known by the name Ayodhyā.
Neither by bathing nor by frequenting Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, Gaṅgādvāra, or Puṣkara is liberation attained in such a manner.

Just as liberation is attained here, it is for that very reason distinguished; whether at Prayāga or here, liberation occurs through taking refuge in Hari. This alone is the great deed performed, surpassing all other foremost sacred sites.
Liberation, which is considered difficult to attain elsewhere, is obtained here by all the sages, perfected beings (siddhas), and great seers who possess unmanifest signs.
To them Hari grants the supreme yoga and sovereignty, as well as union with Himself and the desired, most excellent station.
Brahmā together with the divine sages, Śrī, Vāyu, Divākara, Śakra the king of the gods, and whatever other denizens of heaven there may be—|| 93 ||

Great-souled ones worship Hari with reverence everywhere; others as well—yogis, perfected beings, those of great vows who are the very embodiment of sacred fields—worship Hari at all times, having become single-minded in devotion.
Even a man whose mind is attached to sense objects and who has abandoned delight in dharma, if he dies in this sacred field, shall not become a transmigratory being again.
Furthermore, those who are dependent on the scriptures, established in truth, with senses subdued, observant of vows, and free from worldly undertakings—all of them are permeated by Hari.
Having brought about the dissolution of their bodies, those wise ones, free from all attachments, attained supreme liberation through the constant grace of Hari.
A yogi might not attain it even by practicing for thousands of other births; yet here, even through death, he attains that supreme liberation.
I shall speak briefly of this wonderful majesty of the sacred field (kṣetra). This alone is the supreme place; this alone is the supreme state. No other such place is seen anywhere else. 99.
O wise ones, having gone here, those who desire merit should perform the pilgrimage with effort, according to the prescribed rules, in due order, and endowed with faith. 100.
On the first day, those of self-restraint should observe a fast; thereafter, they should perform ritual bathing and give gifts according to their capacity.
But he who has turned away from sins and whose dwelling is with virtuous qualities—his is to be known as true fasting, being devoid of all worldly enjoyments. || 102 ||
Having observed a fast at Cakratīrtha, that virtuous man should bathe on the day of the fast and give gifts according to his capacity. (103)
Having duly honored the Brahmin, one should behold the all-pervading Lord Viṣṇu-Hari; likewise, a man who bathes at Svargadvāra and worships Viṣṇu with diligent effort [attains the same].
Then, at the one called Dharmā, the observer of the vow should have a shave; thereafter, he should bathe at Pāpamocanaka and then at Ṛṇamocanaka.
Having bathed in the Sahasradhārā and having diligently worshipped Śeṣa, one should then behold the god Candrahari and thereafter the omnipresent Dharmahari.

Then, having seen Cakrahari, a man should give gifts according to his capacity. Having bathed in the Brahma-kuṇḍa for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals, he should perform a vigil at night near Mahāvidyā.
Then, at the clear dawn, the observer of virtuous vows, having risen again, should diligently perform his bath according to the rules at Svargadvāra.

Having performed the śrāddha ceremony according to the rules and having given gifts according to his capacity, he should worship Viṣṇu according to the rules and the Brahmins as well, again and again. (109)
The couple should also be honored with effort using garments and other offerings; those endowed with supreme faith should bestow abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Having duly honored the Brahmins, the self-restrained man should eat.
Moreover, rising on another day, endowed with supreme faith, one should visit Rukmiṇī and the other [deities] as well as the sacred fords (tīrthas) there in their proper order.
Having bathed in each of those places and having given according to his ability, he should worship Viṣṇu with effort, being pure in mind, speech, and body. (113)
One who has restrained the self and maintains pure vows should properly complete the pilgrimage; wherever that steadfast one may die, he shall attain supreme liberation.
Agastya said: Having heard what was spoken by Vasiṣṭha and having performed it according to the prescribed rite, they, led by Vibhīṣaṇa, then became stainless.

Thus, having performed their pilgrimage according to many injunctions, those led by Sugrīva became filled with abundant merit; having cast off their impure bodies, they all came to possess a multitude of virtues multiplied through their efforts in the conduct of heaven.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sequence of the Pilgrimage to Ayodhyā, including the Mahāratna-tīrtha, Durbhara-mahābhara-tīrtha, Mahāvidyā-tīrtha, Siddhapīṭha, Kṣīreśvara, Sītākuṇḍa, Sugrīva-tīrtha, Hanumat-kuṇḍa, and Vibhīṣaṇa-saras," in the Ayodhyā-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Agastya said: To the southeast of Jaṭākuṇḍa, there is a great place known as Gayākūpa, which bestows the fruits of all desires.
Having bathed there and given gifts according to one's ability, a self-controlled and excellent twice-born man who performs a śrāddha ceremony attains all his desires.
Whosoever among the ancestors and grandfathers reside in hell, they indeed go to the world of Viṣṇu when that śrāddha has been performed.

O Brahmin, when that śrāddha has been performed, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors; the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should be made according to one's means, using barley and milk-rice (pāyasa).
A Śrāddha rite prescribed by the sages, performed with oil-cake or molasses at that sacred ford, is said to bring satisfaction to the ancestors.
In that regard, men endowed with faith should perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha); their ancestors will be satisfied, and all the deities shall be pleased.
When the ancestors are satisfied, one is born prosperous and likewise possessed of sons; for the ancestors, being gratified by the śrāddha, bestow many offspring.
Prosperity and abundant enjoyments [are granted] to those who perform the *śrāddha*; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, one should diligently perform it here according to the prescribed rule.
A śrāddha performed correctly by those endowed with faith and desiring their cherished fruits—especially one offered to the ancestors at Gayākūpa—is inexhaustible.
When the new moon day (Amāvāsyā) coincides with Monday, a Śrāddha performed for the ancestors on that occasion yields infinite fruit and becomes inexhaustible.
On another occasion, on a Monday, one should perform a Śrāddha there according to the prescribed rules; it always grants satisfaction to the ancestors, and what is given there becomes inexhaustible.
There, in the eastern direction, there exists a most excellent of all holy sites named Piśācamocana, which bestows its fruits.

Having bathed there and having given gifts, one is never born as a piśāca. Therefore, bathing, giving gifts, and especially the performance of śrāddha should be undertaken with great effort by men endowed with faith.
Especially on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should perform a ritual bath there for the sake of liberation from the state of being a piśāca.

In its eastern part, there is a sacred ford (tīrtha) by name Mānasa, the foremost abode of merit, where one should especially bathe; by bathing and giving gifts there, one shall attain all desires. || 15 ||
Furthermore, various kinds of sins, even those as vast as Mount Meru, go to destruction by bathing there; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Whatever sin exists—whether mental, physical, or likewise verbal—that sin shall go to dissolution through bathing.
O Brahmin, his festival procession should always be performed by meritorious men devoted to sacred rites, especially on the full moon day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada.
Therefore, in the southern direction lies the sole ground for meritorious deeds, the river named Tamasā, which destroys great sins.
Where bathing and likewise giving gifts always remove all sins, on whose delightful bank there is always the granting of fruits. (20)
There are various abodes of sages who have cultivated their souls; among them, the sin-destroying abode of the sage Māṇḍavya exists.
O best of sages, on its banks, everywhere most enchanting, was his delightful hermitage, beautiful with various kinds of trees.
From whatever place that river of waves arose through darkness, that forest is exceedingly meritorious, a purifying and supreme station.
By the sight of whom the destruction of all sins occurs for human beings. || 24 ||

It was beautified by various kinds of blossoming shrubs, lovely with its bowing under the spreading of creepers, and surrounded on all sides by *priyaṅgu* trees laden with grown flowers, as well as by *ketaka* trees that were fully bloomed and bristling with buds.

It was densely covered on all sides with fragrant tamāla thickets, along with karṇikāras and bakulas, as well as excellent aśoka and punnāga trees in full bloom, their clusters of flowers swarming with rows of bees.

In some places it resounded with birds adorned by the pollen of blooming lotuses and moving among beautiful fruits, as well as with cranes, ruddy geese, and other waterfowl, and with joyful flocks of intoxicated gallinules.

In some places it was made resonant by the cries of ruddy geese; in some places it was joined by flocks of water-fowl; in some places it was made to ring out with the calls of ducks; and in some places it was filled with swarms of intoxicated bees.

It was frequented from nearby by female bees excited by intoxication and possessed beautiful, fragrant flowers; in some places it had mango trees with creepers entwined around them, as well as tilaka trees.
Frequented by various kinds of joyful birds and made resonant by the cries of intoxicated hārītaka flocks, that great forest, shining brightly, possessed a beautiful appearance on every side.

It was dark with dense *nicula* thickets, delightful with blue-throated peacocks, and charming with the songs of flocks of birds intoxicated with passion; bees were clinging to the branches of flowering trees, it was graced by the beauty of fresh sprouts, and it was rich with excellent fruit. (31)

Thus, rich with many such beauties and enchanting in every direction, it was there indeed that the sage Māṇḍavya performed great penance; by its power, that great and purifying holy site (tīrtha) has always existed.
Before that was the great and purifying hermitage of the sage Gautama; before that, of the sage Cyavana; and this first of all, O best of sages, belonged to your father, that treasury of asceticism.
On its banks, on all sides, there exist various kinds of sacred fords (tīrthas) and hermitages belonging to ascetics.
That auspicious river should be known by the name Tamasā; it flows along, beautified on both sides in many places by sacrificial stakes that have been uprooted.
There, through bathing, giving gifts, and especially through the performance of *śrāddha*, there shall be the fulfillment of all desires and goals; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (36)
Especially on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, bathing always bestows the attainment of its fruit upon men.
Therefore, O best of sages, those with pure minds should diligently perform a bath here, which grants the fulfillment of all desires and aims. (38)
Hereafter, I shall describe the most auspicious Tamasā, renowned as Sītākuṇḍa, located in the vicinity of Śrī Dugdheśvara. (39)

On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, his festival procession brings auspiciousness; likewise, Vipreśvara should be worshipped for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. By the mere remembrance of him, there is the destruction of all obstacles. (40)
Therefore, in the southern quarter, there is one known by the name Bhairava; upon seeing him, one is liberated from all sins—of this there is no doubt. || 41 ||

Protected with care by Vāsudeva for the sake of guarding the sacred field (kṣetra), his worship should be performed with effort according to the prescribed rules; through constant devotion to Bhairava, one shall always obtain the fruits desired by the mind.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, that annual festival was established there for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
People should perform worship consisting of the offering of animals; the attainment of the fruits of all desires arises from this—of this there is no doubt. || 44 ||
Dwelling at the sacred site (tīrtha) occurs without obstacles through the grace of Bhairava; therefore, worship of him should be performed with diligent effort. || 45 ||
In this northern region is the delightful Bharatakuṇḍa; having bathed there, a person is liberated from sins—of this there is no doubt. || 46 ||
There, bathing as well as giving shall all become inexhaustible; various kinds of food and diverse garments should also be given. (47)
The deities should be worshipped with effort, adorned with garments and other offerings; formerly, Bharata, born of the Raghu dynasty, while dwelling in Nandigrāma, [acted thus].
Meditating on Rāmacandra in his heart, pure-souled and having conquered his senses, that beloved of the earth then remained there and protected all his subjects.
In that Cakra region, there was a great pool; there, a king named Bharata, having installed an image of Rāma, practiced his vows with his senses fully subdued.
That pool is exceedingly meritorious and endowed with various virtues; it is filled with water-lilies, blue lotuses, white lotuses, and red lotuses.
It was graced by birds such as swans, cranes, and ruddy geese; it was always spotless and beautifully shaded by the trees of its groves.

Bathing there is of great merit, pure with joy and bliss; for one who performs a bath and likewise a śrāddha ceremony there dedicated to the ancestors, his ancestors are gratified, and all the deities shall be pleased. (53)
Gold and food should be given to a twice-born according to the prescribed rite; this must be performed with faith by men who are self-restrained.
To the west of that is the unsurpassed Jaṭākuṇḍa, where Rāma and all the others cast off their own matted locks.
It is renowned as Jaṭākuṇḍa, the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas); by bathing and giving gifts there, one may attain all desires.

In the eastern ponds, Bharata, endowed with prosperity, is to be worshipped; in the Jaṭā-ponds, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, together with Sītā, are to be worshipped. On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, the annual festival shall take place.

Thus, having worshipped Rāma and Sītā with the supreme rites, and thereafter having worshipped Lakṣmaṇa in the Bharata-kuṇḍa, one who dwells there as an embodiment of merit resides in that world of Viṣṇu by bathing in pairs according to the rules in the Amṛta-kuṇḍa.
Agastya said: O Brahmin, whether a man remains without food or subsists on milk alone, if he worships Ajita, success rests in his very hand.
A great festival should be celebrated accompanied by song and instrumental music; the wise person who acts in this manner shall attain all desires.
Beyond this, O wise one of fixed vows, lies the abode of the intoxicated lordly elephant, which portends auspiciousness for the hero.
Having bathed in the lake in front of that [shrine], one should dwell there with firm resolve; one attains complete perfection, having attained which one does not grieve.
The heroic protector of Ayodhyā, who grants the fulfillment of all desires and aims, has an annual festival procession on the fifth day of the Navarātri.

He, who bestows the fulfillment of all desires and purposes, should be worshipped with diligence through the prescribed rites of perfumes, flowers, incense, food offerings, and so forth. Whatever desire one may wish for here, that very desire one shall attain.
To the south of this place, O Brahmin, dwells a Rākṣasī named Surasā, who is a devotee of Viṣṇu and always bestows success.
By worshipping her with devotion, a person shall obtain all their desires.
Brought here from the region of Laṅkā by Rāma of exalted deeds, she was established in Ayodhyā for its protection by those of fixed vows.

Having worshipped her according to the prescribed rites, one should behold her with reverence for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals; furthermore, a festival that bestows auspiciousness should be performed with great effort, accompanied by songs and instrumental music.

On the third day of the Navarātra, the annual procession shall take place; it bestows the ultimate goal and always leads to the attainment of happiness and progeny. It is enchanting with various songs, instrumental music, and dances.
When this is done, there is no doubt that he will be protected at all times.

O Sage, in this western direction resides the supreme one known as Piṇḍāraka, a hero of supreme prowess; he should be worshipped with effort by means of perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings. (13)
Since the accomplishments of men rest in the palm of their hands through the power of his worship, people should perform his worship according to the prescribed ritual.
Having bathed in the waters of the Sarayū, one should worship Piṇḍāraka, who always creates delusion for sinners and bestows wisdom upon the virtuous.
His procession should be performed during the nine nights of Navarātri, accompanied by flowers; one should indeed worship Vighneśa in the western direction of that [temple]. || 16 ||
Since no trace of obstacle is found for men through the sight of him, therefore Vighneśvara, the bestower of the fruits of all desires, is to be worshipped. || 17 ||
Therefore, by virtue of its location, the birth of Rāma takes place in the northeast; this is declared to be the birthplace that accomplishes fruits such as liberation. || 18 ||
The place of birth is traditionally remembered as being to the east of Vighneśvara, to the north of Vāsiṣṭha, and likewise to the west of Laumaśa.
Upon seeing which, a human being attains victory over dwelling in the womb, even without charity, without austerity, without sacred fords, and without sacrifices. (20)
When the ninth day arrives, the man who observes the vow is indeed liberated from the bondage of birth through the power of his ablutions and gifts.
Whoever gives thousands of tawny cows day after day obtains that same fruit simply by visiting one's place of birth. || 22 ||
For men dwelling in hermitages and for ascetics, the fruit is equal to thousands of Rājasūya sacrifices and to performing the Agnihotra sacrifice every year. (23)
Upon seeing a man established in religious observances, especially at his birthplace, or virtuous people who maintain devotion toward their mother, father, and teachers; ||| 24 ||
One obtains that fruit simply by visiting the place of birth. || 25 ||
Now follows the description of the Sarayū: there is inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors, and the fruit is even greater than that of a śrāddha performed at Gayā. (26)
Whatever fruit is obtained from residing in Kāśī for thousands of Manvantaras, that same fruit one attains when the sight of the Sarayū has been performed.
And those who, having performed the śrāddha at Gayā, perform the vision of Puruṣottama, the fruit of that is said to be obtained in the Kali age by visiting the city of the son of Daśaratha.
If a person dwells in Mathurā for one kalpa, he obtains that same fruit by beholding the Sarayū. || 29 ||
One obtains that same fruit by beholding the Sarayū as one does at Puṣkara, at Prayāga, or during the months of Māgha or Kārttika. || 30 ||
Indeed, whatever merit is obtained by residing in Avanti for thousands of millions of kalpas, that very fruit one attains when the sight of the Sarayū has been performed. || 31 ||
The fruit that results from bathing in the Bhāgīrathī for sixty thousand years is obtained in half a moment by visiting the city of the son of Daśaratha in the Kali age.
Whether for a moment or even half a moment, the contemplation of Rāma by living beings certainly becomes the destroyer of the ignorance that is the cause of saṃsāra. (33)
Whoever, staying wherever they may be, remembers Ayodhyā with their mind, shall not return again even after hundreds of other kalpas.
In the form of water, Brahmā himself is the Sarayū, who always bestows liberation; here there is no experience of the fruits of action, and a man becomes the very form of Rāma.
Even beasts, birds, wild animals, and others of sinful birth, they too go to heaven and are liberated, according to the word of Śrī Rāma. (36)
When the pot-born sage had ceased speaking after saying this, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa, whose wealth is austerity, spoke again.
The detailed discourse on all beings is difficult for all creatures to obtain in its proper sequence; likewise, the procedure for the pilgrimage of men who are arriving has been heard by me.
Now, O best of sages, O ascetic rich in penance, I wish to hear according to the rules about the sacred sites of the field and the proper sequence for the pilgrimage. (39)
O wise one, O best among the compassionate, if you have compassion for me, tell me in detail and in due order the fruit [of these practices], as I am asking you. (40)
O best among the all-knowing, O you of firm vows, act in such a way that, having heard [your instructions], I may undertake this journey by degrees through your grace.
Agastya said: Listen, I shall describe to you in truth, from the very beginning, the sequence of the pilgrimage to the seven holy fords of Ayodhyā, exactly and in their proper order. (42)

Having bathed in the mental holy places with a mind that is pure in thought, word, and deed, faultless within, and with senses conquered, he who performs the rite correctly indeed attains the fruit of the sacred fords.
Vyāsa said: O ascetic, tell me of those sacred sites that exist in the mind alone, by bathing in which men attain purification of the mind. (44)
Agastya said: Listen, O sinless one, as I speak of the mental holy places (tīrthas) within me, by bathing properly in which a man attains the supreme goal. (45)
Truth is a sacred ford, forgiveness is a sacred ford, restraint of the senses is a sacred ford, compassion toward all beings is a sacred ford; among all sacred fords, truthfulness is the supreme.
The seven sacred fords have been declared as the ford of knowledge and the ford of austerity; through the ford of compassion toward all beings, there arises purity of mind.

Bathing is not said to be for one whose body has merely been purified by water; that man alone is truly bathed whose mind is considered perfectly pure. Now hear the reason why even earthly pilgrimage sites possess sanctity.
Just as certain parts of the body are considered middling or superior, so too certain regions on earth are considered most meritorious. (49)
Therefore, one should dwell in both terrestrial and mental sacred fords; he who bathes in both attains the supreme goal.

Therefore, O best of Brahmins, you too should undertake this pilgrimage with a purified inner self; indeed, this pilgrimage has been enjoined by me. And I shall now describe to you, O best of Brahmins, the procedure for the pilgrimage to sacred sites in due order.
Aquatic creatures are born in the waters and die in the waters; yet, being impure-minded and defiled, they do not go to heaven.
Constant attachment to sense objects is called the impurity of the mind; indeed, by not becoming attached to those very objects, purity is proclaimed. (53)
A mind that is corrupt within is not purified by bathing at sacred fords; even if washed with water hundreds of times, a liquor jug remains impure.
Charity, sacrifice, austerity, purity, visiting sacred fords, and likewise sacred learning—all these are sacred fords if one is pure in disposition. (55)
Wherever a man dwells whose collection of senses is restrained, there for him is Kurukṣetra, as well as Naimiṣa and Puṣkara.
O Brahmin, this characteristic of the mental pilgrimage site has been told to you; by bathing in which, all rites of those who perform them become fruitful.
Having risen early in the morning, the wise man should perform his bath at the confluence; having beheld the omnipresent Viṣṇu, Hari, he should indeed bathe in the Brahmakuṇḍa.
Having bathed at Cakratīrtha and beheld the omnipresent Lord Cakrahari, and then having beheld Dharmahari, a person is liberated from all sins.
On every eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī), this pilgrimage brings auspiciousness; having risen early in the morning, the wise man should bathe in the waters of Svargadvāra.
Having performed his daily obligatory rites, he should gaze upon Ayodhyā; then, having seen the Sarayū, he should thereafter behold Mattagaja.
One should behold Baṇḍī, Śītalā, and Vaṭuka; having bathed in the lake in front of that, one should behold Mahāvidyā.
Then, having seen Piṇḍāraka, one sees Bhairava; this pilgrimage, performed on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, bestows its fruit.
On the fourth day of Aṅgāraka, one should also behold the previously mentioned deities, and thereafter Vighneśa, for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. (64)
Having risen early in the morning, the wise man, having bathed in the waters of Brahmakuṇḍa and beheld Viṣṇu, the Lord Hari, becomes pure in mind, speech, and body.
Then, having seen Maṃtreśvara, one should behold Mahāvidyā; and then, for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals, one should behold Ayodhyā.

Having bathed at Svargadvāra with his clothes on and with his senses subdued, a man's various kinds of sins committed over many lifetimes depart through that bathing with clothes; therefore, one should perform the bath with one's clothes on.
This auspicious pilgrimage, which removes all sins, has indeed been described.
For one who thus performs this pilgrimage, which constantly bestows auspicious fruits, there is no return to this world even after hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, you too should go to Ayodhyā without delay; having gone there, perform the pilgrimage in due order with your senses restrained.
Ayodhyā is the supreme place; Ayodhyā is the greatest of all. No city whatsoever is seen to be equal to Ayodhyā. (71)
Ayodhyā is the supreme place, established upon the discus of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O Brahmin, that which was asked by you has been told by me; O Sage, take refuge in her and grant me your permission to depart from here.
Sūta said: When the pitcher-born sage had finished speaking thus, Vyāsa, that treasure-house of austerities, addressed these sweet words to him.

Vyāsa said: "O Sage, I am blessed, I am favored, and I have accomplished my purpose. O Brahmin, truthfulness, purity, sacred learning, good character, forgiveness, and straightforwardness—all these are fruitless for one who has not come to Ayodhyā. (75)

"Since you, being well-pleased with me, have pronounced this definitive judgment on the Dharma, I shall now go to the stainless city of Ayodhyā. You too, O best of Brahmins, return to your own hermitage."
Sūta said: Having thus explained in due order this unsurpassed ritual for the pilgrimage, Agastya, the pitcher-born one and a mass of asceticism, departed.
The wise Vyāsa, a mass of splendor who had conquered his senses, returned to his own hermitage with eyes wide open in wonder. (78)
The brahmin arrived at Ayodhyā for the fulfillment of all desires and purposes; having arrived, he performed the pilgrimage according to this procedure and in the proper sequence. (79)
Having seen that most wonderful cause, that supreme sacred ford (tīrtha), the wise man, swelling with joy, duly performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) there.
Then that lord of brahmins, the sage, returned to his own hermitage; at that time, Vyāsa recounted this majesty to me in due order. (81)
Having heard its greatness and having performed the pilgrimage according to the prescribed rites, I have come to Kurukṣetra and related this before you. (82)
The man who, being self-restrained, recites this incomparable majesty, and he who listens to it with faith, attains the supreme goal. (83)
Therefore, this should always be listened to with diligence by people; the worship of the twice-born and the worship of Viṣṇu should be performed with great effort. (84)
Gold and other gifts should be given to a twice-born man according to one's capacity; one desiring a son obtains sons, and one desiring dharma attains dharma. (85)

That best of men who, endowed with the glory of Śrī, meditates here with supreme devotion upon this primordial and righteous majesty of the sacred field as described in its most extensive arrangements—he, having enjoyed all pleasures, proceeds perfectly to the abode of Hari.
He who, even on rare occasions, gives wealth according to his own capacity to a reciter—whether it be worthy vessels, beautiful garments, silver, gold, or cows—he shall be liberated.
Śaunaka said: O Sauti, for the welfare of living beings, you have described to us many means—dharma, knowledge, dispassion, yoga, and so forth. (1)
O one of great intelligence, we have all listened with reverence to those [teachings] whose meanings have been made perfectly clear by various kinds of historical narratives.
For all human beings, those [practices] are indeed difficult to perform; moreover, due to the abundance of obstacles, their accomplishment is also hard to attain. (3)
Even those things accomplished with great effort by men endowed with fortitude will succeed only after a long period of time.
Therefore, may you tell us, for the sake of the twice-born, the stages of life, and all others—including women and Śūdras—here on earth, the means that are easy to perform.
By whatever small deed performed by any embodied being whatsoever, there shall arise a great fruit indeed, unimpeded by obstacles. (6)
O one of great intelligence, having thoroughly investigated such a means for liberation, you ought to speak out of compassion for the benefit of all living beings. (7)
Through the grace of Baladeva, Vyāsa, and Janaka, you know everything; tell it to us who desire to know.
Sauti said: O Śaunaka, the great seer Sāvarṇi likewise, being humble, questioned Skanda, the son of Śaṅkara, once again.
Sāvarṇi said: "O Guha, various kinds of dharmas and manifold forms of Sāṅkhya knowledge have been heard by me, as well as the means such as Yoga and others spoken of by you."
I consider those deeds to be exceedingly difficult for people like us; indeed, even for other great beings, they would be accomplished only with great hardship over a long period of time.
Therefore, you should now tell me that most excellent means which brings about the highest good for those belonging to the castes and stages of life, and which is easy to perform.
Sauti said: Thus questioned by that lord of sages who was desirous of knowledge, Guha—that Kārttikeya—spoke while meditating upon Vāsudeva in his heart.
Skanda said: Listen, O Brahmin; I shall proclaim that which was heard by me from the mouth of my father—the means for attaining liberation that is easy to perform for all living beings. (14)
For those belonging to the various castes and stages of life who desire the attainment of their own cherished goals, there is no other means here equal to pleasing the deities. 15.
Even a very small virtuous deed performed through a connection with the gods yields its fruit without obstacle for men; indeed, that [connection] is truly great.

Rites for the gods, rites for the ancestors, one's own duty, and whatever action is performed for a specific desire—all these grant the immediate attainment of desired results through their connection with the deity. || 17 ||
Even that which was previously described as difficult—such as Sāṅkhya, Yoga, dispassion, and so forth—will indeed become easy through this alone, granting swift accomplishment.
Since one's desire is accomplished solely through the propitiation of the God, therefore He should be worshipped with affection by all human beings according to their capacity. 19.
Sāvarṇi said: "O Six-faced One, various kinds of gods were previously described by you to me, and the diverse methods for their propitiation have also been recounted. (20)
And all those fruits of action you have described individually—primarily the attainment of heaven and so forth—are indeed swallowed up by time. (21)

O Guha, for yogins whose nature is renunciation, the fruit of worshipping Brahmā is the attainment of the worlds beginning with Janaloka, which lasts until the end of two parārdhas and is subject to destruction.
If, after accomplishing difficult deeds here in this world with great hardship, the fruit obtained is subject to decay, then what is the purpose of acquiring them?
I do not approve of the worship of those gods whose bodies, status, strength, and so forth, perish with time. (24)
He who is himself fearless, the eternal remover of the fear of others, whose abode is perpetual, the bestower of imperishable fruit, and who is affectionate toward his devotees. || 25 ||
O Guha, tell me of that God by whose grace all the desires of everyone here may be fulfilled immediately and effortlessly.
Tell me fully, and especially with clarity, the method of propitiating Him which is easy to perform and approved by the learned; I desire to know this exactly as it is.
Sauti said: Thus questioned by that great seer, the blessed Guha, being highly pleased and honoring him, spoke these words with noble intellect.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Question of Sāvarṇi," in the *Śrī-Vāsudeva-Māhātmya*, within the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī-Skānda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Skanda said: "O sinless one, you ask here a great question, worthy of an expert in inquiry. Its answer cannot be stated through one's own reasoning even in hundreds of years, O Brahmin—even by the best of those possessing knowledge—without the grace of the God."
"By the grace of Vāsudeva, I have known it; I shall tell it to you. There is nothing that should not be told to you, O noble-minded one, who are steadfast in dharma."
In this very manner, when the Bhārata war had concluded, King Ajātaśatru questioned Bhīṣma, the foremost among those who know the dharma.
He lay upon a bed of arrows, having attained unwavering oneness with the Imperishable through meditation, and had reached the further shore of the Vedas and Agamas.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O dear one, among the four castes and even within the four stages of life, which deity should he worship who desires the accomplishment of the four aims of human existence?"

And what accomplishment can be attained without obstacles, and how might it be achieved in a short time? Furthermore, how may one of little merit reach the great state? O Grandfather, you are omniscient; please sever this doubt of mine.
Skanda said: O Sage, having been thus questioned by that righteous-souled one, the son of Śantanu smiled slightly upon beholding the lotus-face of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Urged by him with a glance, he spoke to his father that greatness of Śrī Vāsudeva which had been proclaimed by Nara and Nārāyaṇa and which he himself had heard.
Then, having heard this, Nārada went again to Kurukṣetra; returning to Kailāsa, he told that to my father, and he [my father] told it to me.
I shall explain that to you, who asks without guile, as it was determined without doubt by the best of sages in the great assembly.

Vāsudeva, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, is the Supreme Brahman; He is the God to be worshipped by men who are free from desires, as well as by those with desires, and even by those who are liberated.
By all means, through their respective duties and with devotion, this very [Lord] must be propitiated by the twice-born, those in the stages of life (āśramas), women, Śūdras, and others.

Therefore, all ritual action—whether pertaining to the gods or the ancestors—should always be performed for their pleasure alone, as prescribed by the Vedas and in accordance with what is appropriate.

Whatever auspicious action is performed here by men for the attainment of happiness, even if it is well-executed, if it is devoid of connection with Kṛṣṇa, then it should be known as perishable, yielding meager fruit, and consisting of the qualities (guṇas). || 14 ||

And that [practice] results in a deficiency of fruit due to association with an inauspicious place and so forth; it is full of obstacles for men and does not grant the attainment of what is desired. || 15 ||
If this very same action were performed for the sake of pleasing Śrī Kṛṣṇa, then by virtue of that connection, all of it would indeed become free from the guṇas. || 16 ||
It bestows an inexhaustible fruit even greater than one's own desire; nor does it suffer any deficiency due to association with an improper place or other such factors. (17)
O Brahman-sage, no obstacle whatsoever shall prevail against him anywhere by the power of the wielder of the discus; thus, it shall grant the attainment of his desired goals.
O Brahmin, although one's own merit may be small, it nevertheless becomes truly great through its direct connection with the Supreme Self.
Just as even a mere spark, through contact with a mass of wild wood, becomes an unstoppable forest fire, so too does this [evil] become so through association with Hari.
Therefore, whether the world is in a state of active engagement or of withdrawal, Vāsudeva should be worshipped by those men established in that Dharma who desire its perfect accomplishment.
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history, the conversation between Nārada and the sage Nārāyaṇa.
That Blessed Vāsudeva, who eternally resides in the city of Brahman, manifested through Dākṣāyaṇī for the sake of righteousness and the welfare of the world. (23)
O best of the twice-born, in the former Kṛta Yuga, during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, he appeared in two forms as Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
From Dharmāśrama, Nara and Nārāyaṇa went to Badaryāśrama on earth in order to perform austerities for the very welfare of men. (25)
There, those two original Lords of the World were emaciated and covered with visible veins; they blazed with their own splendor, being difficult even for the gods to behold.
Only he upon whom they bestow their grace is truly worthy to behold them; otherwise, it is not possible even for those who dwell in that very abode to see them.
Once, the yogi Nārada was longed to be seen by those two very persons, and he was also impelled within their hearts by virtue of being their inner self.
O Brahmin, from the peak of Meru, the great mountain, he immediately traveled by way of the sky to that place known as the hermitage of Badarī.
At the time for their daily rites, he arrived there quickly and saw them from a distance, intent upon the duties of their first stage of life.

Upon seeing that divine conduct of his, he was filled with wonder: "Aha! These two lords are worshiped by the entire world; they are the supreme Brahman for all embodied beings. What, then, is their daily ritual? (31)
These two high-minded ones are the parents of all beings and the deity of the deities; which deity, then, do they worship, or do they worship the ancestors?
Having thus reflected in his mind, that devotee of Nārāyaṇa approached him and stood with palms joined in reverence after bowing down. (33)
O sinless one, when the rites for the gods and the ancestors had been performed, he was beheld by those two and honored according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
Having seen that great wonder, an unprecedented and extensive ritual procedure, Nārada sat down nearby, well-pleased and filled with amazement. (35)
Having gazed upon Nārāyaṇa with a disciplined inner self and having paid homage to that god, he spoke these words: || 36 ||

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Meeting of Nārāyaṇa and Nārada," in the *Śrīvāsudevamāhātmya* of the second section (*Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa*) of the *Śrīskānda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, concerning the description of the means for attaining ultimate beatitude.

Nārada said: In the Vedas, along with the Purāṇas and their auxiliary branches (Aṅgas and Upāṅgas), you alone are sung as the eternal Creator, the Controller, the Immortal, and the Infallible. You are the Ordainer, and this entire universe is perpetually established within you.
For the four stages of life, O God, and all the social classes, through their respective duties, worship you day after day, as you abide in manifold forms.
The father and the mother are the eternal deity for everyone; yet we do not know which god or which father you yourself worship. (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "O Brahmin, although this secret concerning the Self should not be spoken, nevertheless, because you possess devotion toward me, I shall explain it to you exactly as it is."
He who is described in the Vedas as Brahman—truth, knowledge, and infinite—and who is the Puruṣa distinct from the three qualities (guṇas), possessing a divine form. || 5 ||
He who is called the Great Being (Mahāpuruṣa), the Lord Vāsudeva, the seer Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, and the Blessed One Kṛṣṇa—[he is that]. || 6 ||
"Know, O sir, that he alone is our god and our parents; for he is worshipped by us both in the rites ordained for the gods and for the ancestors. (7)
Therefore, O twice-born one, there is no father superior to him, nor even a god; for that Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the City of Brahman, is to be known as our very Self.
Therefore, O Brahmin, this world-sustaining boundary was established by him who desires the welfare of the world: that the rites for the gods and the ancestors must be performed.

Vedic action is twofold: that which leads to worldly involvement and that which leads to cessation; it is prescribed according to one's qualification for the attainment of the goals of human existence.

The acceptance of a wife appropriate to oneself according to the rites prescribed in the Tantras and Vedas, and the acquisition of wealth through righteous means—these are the material sacrifices performed with desire. (11)

Dwelling in villages and cities, as well as whatever works of public utility (pūrta) or sacrificial rites (iṣṭa) have been performed—all that which is characterized by worldly engagement (pravṛtta) is declared to be a cause of unrest.
The renunciation of women and wealth, as well as of lust, greed, and anger; dwelling in the forest, dispassion, austerity, forbearance, tranquility, and self-control. (13)

O Sage, the sacrifice of Veda-study, the sacrifice of yoga, the sacrifice of knowledge in all its forms, and the sacrifice of silent recitation—these are proclaimed as the karma of renunciation (nivṛtta).
O Sage, for those humans who practice the dharma of worldly activity, their destinies within the three worlds extend as far as the heavenly realm.
In the worlds of Indra, Candra, Agni, and others, they indeed enjoy various kinds of desired pleasures and sovereignty as the fruit of their respective merits. (16)
O gods, having enjoyed exactly as much as that merit allows, they then fall helplessly back to earth once their good deeds are exhausted.
For, O Sage, when their merit is exhausted, the destruction of enjoyments, sovereignty, and so forth occurs through the force of time, even against the will of those beings. (18)
Even for the gods who hold office, within a single day of Brahmā, there occurs the repeated destruction of their desired enjoyments and sovereign powers by the force of time. (19)
Those yogins and ascetics who are established in the dharma of cessation go to the three worlds beginning with Janaloka, yet they remain outside of the triple world.
They enjoy the sovereign powers and pleasures of their respective worlds as they desire; even during the daily dissolution, they remain at ease.
O Nārada, at the end of two parārdhas of Brahmā’s life, his enjoyments, sovereignty, and prosperity perish through the power of Time alone, as do those worlds of his.
Furthermore, O twice-born one, even though this twofold action consists of the qualities (guṇas), if it is performed while being connected with Viṣṇu, then it becomes devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Indeed, the fruit of that for men shall be inexhaustible and even greater than their own desires; through eight repetitions, those devotees go to the supreme abode of the Lord.
Therefore, those who possess discernment, being constantly endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu, perform all actions whatsoever—whether they be active or withdrawn.
Brahmā, Sthāṇu, Manu, Dakṣa, Bhṛgu, Dharma, as well as Yama; Marīci, Aṅgiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu. || 26 ||
O sage, Vaibhrāja, Vasiṣṭha, Vivasvat, Soma, Kaśyapa, Kardama, and others were the lords of progeny.
All the gods, all the sages, as well as all the social classes and stages of life, worship that very Lord, being established in the path of active worldly duty (pravṛttadharma).
Sana, Sanatsujāta, Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatkumāra, Kapila, Āruṇi, and Sanātana. || 29 ||
The Ṛbhus, Yatis, Haṃsas, and other sages who have taken lifelong vows worship that very Lord, being established in the dharma of renunciation.
Having contemplated the gods and the ancestors as being of the nature of Vāsudeva, they indeed worship them daily through the rite of non-violent (ahiṃsā) worship.

For according to their respective offices, these beings are appointed by him to that [task]; whether in the path of active engagement or of withdrawal from action, they uphold that dharma. Both of them likewise do not transgress the boundary established by that deity.
Among those four goals of life, whatever may be most desired by each individual, the Lord, the Master of all powers, surely fulfills that very thing for everyone.
The Blessed One, being pleased by even a small meritorious deed performed with devotion, surely grants its great, inexhaustible, and desired fruit.

Among those, however, there are some in this world who, through devotion to Him, have established themselves in single-mindedness toward Vāsudeva alone, with all their latent impressions completely extinguished.
At the end of their bodies, having attained His abode beyond darkness, they indeed serve Him with love by means of non-material bodies.

But other devotees, through the firmness of their worship over time, when the destruction of their latent impressions (vāsanā) has occurred, go to Him just like the exclusive devotees (ekāntika). || 37 ||
But whoever is connected with that [state] by whatever means whatsoever does not enter into the cycle of rebirth at all, unlike other living beings.
The perfect accomplishment of the yoga of action and the desired fulfillment of the yoga of knowledge come swiftly and without obstacle for men simply by taking refuge in Him. 39.
Therefore, that very Blessed One should be worshipped here with devotion according to the prescribed rites by all people for the sake of attaining their desired fruits. (40)
Even Brahmā, Śiva, and the others, though they have attained oneness with Brahman and are free from obstacles, practice devotion to Śrī Viṣṇu; such are His great qualities. (41)
Thus, O Nārada, this entire summary of the secret teachings has been proclaimed to you out of great affection, for you are constantly devoted to me with all your heart. (42)

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Worshipfulness of Śrī Vāsudeva by All," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Skanda said: Thus addressed by Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, he who is the best among the knowers of the Self, spoke these words to that Acyuta, the most venerable one in the worlds, whose dwelling is the welfare of the universe.

Nārada said: "O Lord, I have heard what you have spoken, which is consistent with your vast splendor concealed by the form of a sage. O Īśa, I know in my heart that all this is but the divine play (līlā) of you alone, the Lord of all. (2)
O Infinite One, by the mere sight of you, my heart's desire is fulfilled; nevertheless, O Lord, I wish to behold that former form of yours, for my curiosity is great.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: That true nature of Mine cannot be seen through gifts, sacrifices, yoga, Vedic study, or even austerity; rather, O Nārada, it is perceived through unswerving devotion by the best of devotees who are single-mindedly devoted.

Indeed, you possess unswerving devotion toward me, as well as knowledge joined with dispassion and your own duty; therefore, you shall attain that vision which is difficult even for the lords of the gods and others to obtain.
"Extremely pleased by your devotion, I now command you to go and behold him. Go to the White Island (Svetadvīpa); there, O best of brahmins, this desire of yours shall be fulfilled."
Skanda said: Having heard these words, the son of Parameṣṭhin, having likewise honored that ancient ṛṣi, soared into the sky endowed with supreme yoga and then suddenly alighted upon Mount Meru.
And having reached a secluded spot on a peak of that mountain, the sage remained there for a moment; looking toward the north-west, he beheld an exceedingly wonderful island.
To the north of the Ocean of Milk lies a vast island renowned by the name Śveta; it is eternally resplendent, being surrounded on all sides by an exceedingly extensive mass of light.

With many mango trees, *asana*, *aśoka*, *āmrātaka*, *nimba*, *kadamba*, and *nīpa* trees; with *bilva*, *madhūka*, and *suradāru* trees; and with *plakṣa*, *vaṭa*, *kiṃśuka*, and *candana* trees. || 10 ||

It was surrounded by *sarja*, *śāla*, *panasa*, and *tamāla* trees, by the trees of sages (*munidruma*), and by *ketaka*, *campaka*, *kunda*, jasmine (*jātī*), and fragrant *mallikā* trees, all bent low with flowers and fruit.

It was adorned with many groves of wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadruma), rows of golden plantains and betel-nut trees, numerous great and excellent gardens, rivers and lakes with blooming lotuses, flocks of sweet-sounding noble birds such as swans, and herds of beautiful, moving deer.
While observing that place where all living beings—both stationary and moving—are indeed liberated and dwell, he beheld the supreme devotees of the illustrious Puruṣottama.
Beyond the reach of the senses, free from all evil, lacking in [worldly] outflows, and fragrant; some have two arms, some four, some are white, and some have the luster of fresh clouds. (14)

With eyes like lotus petals, their limbs were symmetrical; they possessed beautiful, divine features and were of excellent substance. Their hair was always loose, they were eternally youthful, and they were endowed with all the auspicious marks.

With hands and feet marked by lotus lines, free from the six waves of worldly existence, possessing a splendor exceeding that of the sun, clad in white garments, devoted to meditation, and gentle—before them even Time is perpetually afraid.
Sāvarṇi said: Who are those men who are beyond the senses, free from affliction, without excrement, and fragrant? How were they born to be such, and what is their destination? (17)
Indeed, Śvetadvīpa exists upon the surface of the earth within the ocean of milk; how then was it stated by you that even its inhabitants possess supersensory faculties? (18)

Those who abide in the imperishable abode of Brahman, which consists of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, become liberated and composed of pure consciousness; others are certainly not so. || 19 ||
Cut through this doubt of mine, for my curiosity is great; indeed, you are an expert in all narratives, and therefore I have taken refuge in you. (20)

Skanda said: "By means of exclusive devotion alone to the Lord of Ramā in previous kalpas, those who have attained the state of Brahman have reached the condition of being undecaying and immortal. (21)
Those persons known as Akṣaras reside here in this abode, Śvetadvīpa, to serve that Vāsudeva, as they are beheld by the divine sage.
But when the time of dissolution arrives, they shall again abide in the abode of the Imperishable (akṣara-dhāman), independent and freed from the fear of Time and Māyā.
In this regard, those persons who are born of illusion are indeed perishable; yet they too are truly born as such through the means of the virtuous. || 24 ||
Through non-violence, austerity, one's own duty, and dispassion; through knowledge of the majesty of Vāsudeva, and indeed through steadfastness in the Self. || 25 ||
Through supreme devotion and constant association with great souls, even for those who have no desire for liberation, there is [attainment] through service to Hari. || 26 ||

O best of sages, those men who have no desire for any of the supernatural powers, such as *aṇimā* and the rest, and who instead mutually celebrate the births and deeds of Śrī Hari through their learning and fame, surely become like Him. (27)

Even when the creation of the world occurs, these [beings] do not arise at certain times due to the power of time; because of their independence, they do not perish like others during the dissolution.
In this regard, O Sage, I shall relate to you an ancient tale, concerning how even a man belonging to this very place attained such a state of being.
O Brahmin, this extensive narrative was heard by me in the presence of my father; that very same story must be told to you today, for it is remembered as the essence of all narratives.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberated Souls in Śvetadvīpa," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Skanda said: O Sage, in ancient times there was a king named Vasu, known as Uparicara; he was the son of King Āyu and was celebrated as Amāvasu. He was a friend of Indra and had attained devotion toward the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
He was righteous, devoted to his father, and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods; he was dedicated to virtuous conduct, skillful, patient, and free from malice.
Beneficial to all, tranquil, devoted to the holy life, and pure; free from anger, moderate in eating, gentle, free from vice—such is the sage.
Free from dualities, changeless, devoid of pride, steadfast, and a knower of the Self; free from deceit, honoring [the guru], a yogi, an ascetic, and one who has conquered the senses. || 4 ||
Detached from wealth, sons, wife, and kinsmen, that king daily chanted the mantra of Nārāyaṇa with devotion.
Then the blessed Lord Vāsudeva himself, being pleased with him, granted him sovereignty; yet he, remaining unattached to it, honored that [Lord] with devotion.
There, concentrated in the five periods of the day according to the prescribed rite, he worshipped the Lord of Gods, and with the remnants of that, he honored the deities and the ancestors.
Having shared those remains with the brahmins and his dependents, he ate the leftover food, being devoted to truth and non-violent toward all living beings.
The king perceived the fault in consuming the flesh of any living being whatsoever; he declared it to be a great sin (mahāpātaka), and his subjects spoke likewise.
With his whole being, he worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods, who is without beginning, middle, or end, the creator of the world, and the imperishable.
O King, he fixed his mind steadily upon the feet of Śrī Vāsudeva, and his ears were constantly engaged in hearing the narrations of the Blessed Lord.
That lord of the earth made his own eyes serve for the sight of Mukunda and His devotees, and he employed his speech for the singing of Hari’s qualities.
The king drew his life-breath from the fragrance of the Tulasī flowers touched by the feet of Nārāyaṇa, and never at any time from any other scent.
Upon touching garments and other items used by the Lord of Śrī, he made his own skin [his object of devotion], and regarding food offered to Nārāyaṇa, he made his tongue [his object]. (14)
The king likewise placed his two feet near the temple of the Blessed One’s field and his two hands in service to Hari.
He offered his head for the worship of Viṣṇu’s feet, and he formed a supreme friendship with the great devotees of the Lord.
Not even a single moment passed for that royal sage, who observed his vows, without devotion to the Lord of Ramā. (17)
With grand preparations, he celebrated the festival for Viṣṇu’s birthday, and for that purpose, he constructed gardens, temples, and groves.
O best of brahmins, while he was thus carrying devotion toward Nārāyaṇa, the King of the Gods himself granted him a single bed and seat.
Indra gave him the exceedingly beautiful Vaijayantī garland, made of unfading lotuses, as well as abundant jewels.
The self, the kingdom, wealth, the wife, the vehicles, and so forth—whatever that belongs to the Blessed One, all that was constantly observed by him as his own. (21)

Adopting the Sātvata ritual procedure with a concentrated mind, he performed all the supreme sacrificial rites—those performed for specific desires, those for occasional occasions, and those performed continuously.
In the house of that great-souled one, the foremost twice-born experts in the Pañcarātra ate the food provided by the Blessed One before him. (23)

While he, the slayer of enemies, was ruling the kingdom according to dharma, no untruthful word ever issued from his speech, nor did his mind become corrupt; nor did he commit even the slightest sin with his body.
Every day, the king listened to the *Pañcarātra*, the great tantra, from the mouths of the Lord’s devotees for the sake of nourishing his devotion to the Blessed One.
Establishing pure Dharma and delighting all his subjects, he protected the earth just as Ākhaṇḍala protects heaven. || 26 ||
Moreover, in his kingdom there was not even a single man who ate meat, nor anyone wearing the garb of a heretic, for seven generations.
