In his kingdom, there were no incurable women nor men who committed adultery; nor was anyone heard of who caused a confusion of dharma.
While he was ruling the kingdom, no one here even smelled the eleven kinds of intoxicating liquor or the three kinds of spirituous liquor. (29)
Possessing such virtues, he nevertheless fell from heaven due to the partiality of the gods and their false speech, and entered the surface of the earth.
And having entered beneath the earth, that constant lover of dharma, becoming devoted to Nārāyaṇa, steadfastly muttered His mantra.
And by his very grace, he rose up once again; having reached heaven, he experienced there the happiness desired by his heart.
Having again become the lord of Cedi on this earth due to his father’s curse, he devoted himself unweariedly to Hari according to the ritual prescribed in the Pañcarātra.
Then the king attained the heavenly world with a divine body, along with the hosts of supreme sages residing there who were performing worship.
Strengthening his faith, he dwelt there for some time with the Blessed One; then he attained the supreme, fearless state of Vāsudeva.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Virtues of Uparicara Vasu," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sāvarṇi said: That great king Vasu was indeed a devotee of the Blessed One; why did he speak falsely, by which he has gone from heaven to a hole in the earth?
By whom was he raised up again from the earth, and for what reason was he cursed by his ancestors? O Skanda, tell me how he was liberated from that state, O King.
Skanda said: Listen, O Brahmā, to this narrative of Vasu Vāsavaro-ciṣ, by the mere hearing of which there shall be an immediate destruction of all sins.
O Sage, formerly during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, the Indra named Viśvajit commenced a great sacrifice known as the Aśvamedha.
Bound animals, such as goats and others, were crying out there in great numbers; and all the hosts of gods, greedy for the essence [of the sacrifice], remained there at that time.
While wandering at will for the welfare of all the worlds, great sages, possessing the splendor of the sun, arrived there by chance.
Honored by the hosts of gods with water for the feet, offerings of respect, words of welcome, and other rites, those great sages beheld those sacrificial animals crying out.

And even those gods who were characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva), upon observing that extensive sacrifice of the gods—which was permeated with violence—were indeed struck with great wonder.
Then, seeing the transgression of Dharma, those best of the twice-born, whose minds were fixed on righteousness, spoke out of compassion to the gods headed by Mahendra.
The great seers said: O Mahendra, listen to our words together with the gods and the sages; for we shall declare the eternal essence of dharma exactly as it exists.
At the time of the creation of the world, you were indeed fashioned by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin out of the quality of goodness (sattva) as the upholders of the four-footed Dharma.
From rajas and tamas, he created the Manus and the lords of men, as well as the sovereigns of the Asuras who uphold dharma.
Then, for the welfare of you all, he created the Veda, which teaches the procedures for sacrifices and other rites, and bestows the fruits of all desired objects.
Non-violence alone is the supreme dharma; this is proclaimed therein in the Veda. The actual slaughter of animals in sacrifice is certainly not approved by the Veda.
For the Veda has its purpose solely in the preservation of the four-footed Dharma in every way; it certainly does not lie in its destruction through violence.

Nevertheless, due to the influence of the defects of *rajas* and *tamas*, those king-asuras, through the dullness of their intellect regarding such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with a pure goat," understood the meaning to be goats and the like, but they did not know it to be rice and the like.

But for you who are of a sattvic nature, the meaning of the Veda must be accepted exactly as it stands; it should never be understood otherwise, and such an [erroneous] practice would be improper. (17)
For whatever quality belongs to one's nature, such is that person; and according to one's own nature, there is engagement in action. (18)
For you who are of a sattvic nature, the Lord Viṣṇu, the husband of Ramā, is manifest; therefore, you have the right to perform the sacrifice of non-violence for his gratification.
O best of gods, that practice of performing a sacrifice by actually slaughtering an animal before one's eyes is indeed contrary to dharma for you.
Under the influence of the qualities of rajas and tamas, these priests of yours have indeed resorted to a demonic disposition, being ignorant of the Vedas. || 21 ||
It is certain that it is precisely due to association with him that a perversion of your minds has now arisen, and because of that, you have undertaken such an action. || 22 ||

For men who are characterized by passion (rājasa), darkness (tāmasa), or who are of demonic nature (āsura), there are deities such as Bhairava and others to be worshipped according to their respective qualities.
On this earth, for the sake of pleasing their own deities in accordance with their respective qualities, the performance of violent sacrifices is indeed appropriate for them alone. (24)
Even among those Daityas, Rakshasas, humans, and others who are devotees of Vishnu, a sacrifice involving violence is not appropriate; how much less so for you? (25)
For the remnant of the sacrifice belongs to all who perform the sacrificial rites; it is authorized for consumption by the Veda itself. (26)
We have never seen, nor have we ever heard from the mouths of the virtuous, that even among the sattvic deities there is anywhere the consumption of liquor or meat. (27)
Therefore, this sacrifice should be performed with rice, milk, clarified butter, and other pure food essences, and not by the slaughter of animals.
There too, one should sacrifice with seeds that have attained the state of being unborn, having remained for a period of three years, and which do not sprout again.
Absence of malice, absence of greed, self-control, compassion for all beings, austerity, celibacy, as well as truthfulness, lack of hypocrisy, forgiveness, and fortitude; || 30 ||
This is declared to be the form of the eternal Dharma; he who acts in transgression of it is a destroyer of Dharma and falls downward.

Skanda said: Although they were thus respectfully instructed with sound reasoning by the great sages who knew the secrets of the Vedas, they did not at all accept those words, for fear of violating their own vow; even though they were cognizant of its authority.
Then, due to their great transgression, pride, anger, intoxication, and other such vices—descendants of Unrighteousness who seek out vulnerabilities—entered into them. (33)
Then, while those disputants were saying, "The goat is unborn, not the seeds," and so forth, and while the best of sages were becoming dejected and attempting to enlighten them once more; || 34 ||
The illustrious King Uparicara, the supreme friend of Indra, arrived there by chance, illuminating the quarters with his splendor. (35)
Seeing Vasu approaching swiftly through the intermediate space, those twice-born ones said to the gods, "He will resolve this doubt."
Formerly, this lord of the earth performed thousands of great sacrifices according to the rules prescribed in the Sātvata-tantra and the Āraṇyaka.
In these [sacrifices], there was no slaughter of animals whatsoever, nor any substitute for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), nor any indirect worship of the gods with liquor.
Renowned everywhere for his non-violence and protection of dharma, that king was the foremost among the devotees of Viṣṇu, observing the great vow of having only one wife.
Such a supreme upholder of dharma, true to his word and knower of the Vedas—this great Vasu would never speak a word otherwise. (40)
Having thus reached an agreement, those wise ones and the sages, full of eagerness, approached King Vasu and questioned him immediately.
The divine sages said: "O King, with what should one sacrifice—with an animal or rather with medicinal herbs? Cut asunder this doubt of ours; you are considered by us to be the authority. (42)
Skanda said: Having joined his palms in reverence, Vasu indeed questioned them: "Whose side is favored by each of you? Speak the truth with composed minds. (43)
The great sages said: "O lord of men, our position is that one should sacrifice with grains; O King, the position of the gods is that an animal is the [proper] offering—state your own view. (44)
Skanda said: Having understood the opinion of the gods, Vasu, taking their side, then spoke these words: "The sacrifice should be performed with goats and other such animals. (45)
For thus, though he was a knower of dharma, that king took refuge in the side of the arrogant and spoke falsely, saying that the Veda is intent upon violence. (46)

At that very moment, due to the fault of his speech, the king suddenly fell from the sky and entered the earth. Having gone beneath the ground, the king encountered great calamity; yet, because he had taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa, mindfulness did not abandon him then.
Having released all the animals, those inhabitants of the third heaven then departed for the celestial realm, and the great seers returned to their own hermitages, fearing violence.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fall of Uparicara Vasu due to the Assertion that the Veda is Devoted to Violence," in the Śrī-Vāsudeva-Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Skānda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Skanda said: Then that king, situated in the midst of the earth, censuring his own deed and repenting intensely, while showing great honor to those great sages, constantly recited the three-syllabled mantra of the Lord within his mind.
There too, with supreme devotion and with his own mind, he worshipped Hari, the Lord of the Gods, within a cavity of the earth with great respect during the five periods of the day.
Then the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the Master of the Universe, was pleased with him as he worshipped Him according to the scriptures and at the proper time, even in times of adversity.
Then the Lord Viṣṇu, the bestower of boons, himself addressed Garuḍa of great speed, who was standing nearby, that most excellent of the twice-born.
The Blessed Lord said: "O most excellent of the twice-born, O highly fortunate one, go at my word. A sovereign king named Vasu, whose soul is devoted to dharma, has taken refuge in me."
Due to the fault of having transgressed against Brahmā, he has entered beneath the surface of the earth; therefore, show him honor by going to his presence today.
O Garuḍa, by my command, make this best of kings, who now moves below hidden in a crevice of the earth, a traveler of the sky; do not delay.
Skanda said: Then Garuḍa, possessing the speed of the wind, spread his wings and entered a hole in the earth where Vasu remained with his speech restrained.
Then, having lifted him up with its own beak, the son of Vinatā quickly soared into the sky and released him there.
At that very moment, King Uparicara was born again; having gone to heaven with his physical body, he attained supreme bliss.
Thus, O Brahman-sage, even that high-souled knower of dharma attained a state worthy of one who has not performed sacrifices, due to the fault of his speech and his contempt for the virtuous.
Merely by having served Hari, the Lord, that person quickly abandoned his sin and attained the heavenly world.
There he dwelt, enjoying various pleasures desired by his mind, like another Śakra, while his fame was being sung by the gods.
Once, Acchodā beheld him as he traveled by means of a celestial chariot that shone like the sun, accompanied by the Apsaras Adrikā.
For she was the mind-born daughter of the high-souled, formless Pitṛs known as the Agniṣvāttas, who abide in the realm of Soma. (15)
Because she was formless, that woman of pure smiles did not recognize her own ancestors; she regarded Vasu as her father, and he regarded her as his own daughter.
Then the ancestors, having observed such an attitude on the part of those two, said: "O maiden, you shall become the daughter of this king upon the earth. (17)
"O Vasu, having become human, you shall certainly procreate this daughter upon your own wife, this very Apsaras. (18)
Thus cursed by their fathers, the two of them then bowed down and entreated them for release from the curse; thereupon, those compassionate ones spoke to them. (19)
Since this was inevitably destined to happen, this curse that has been incurred by you both will result only in your own welfare. (20)
O Vasiṣṭha, in the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, you will become the son of the high-souled King Kṛtayajña on this earth.
And there too, just as now, you shall be endowed with all virtues, a traveler through the skies, and the foremost among the great devotees of the Lord.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu with devotion according to the ritual prescribed in the Pañcarātra, you, together with your progeny, shall worship us and the other gods with the remnants of that offering.
Then, with a divine body, you shall attain the heavenly world; having enjoyed divine pleasures there, you will indeed reach the station of Viṣṇu.
O Acchodā, you too shall become renowned on earth by the name Kālī; through a portion of yourself, you will be born from Adrikā, who possesses the body of a fish.
There, like a maiden, you shall obtain Hari as a son from Parāśara; by his very grace, you shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Skanda said: Thus cursed and yet blessed by his ancestors, that king was born here after performing sacrifices and became renowned for his virtues.
Just as in the past, Mahendra bestowed abundant wealth upon that friend of his, who was a devotee of Kṛṣṇa and an expert in the rites for the gods and ancestors.
That banner of victory which was formerly obtained from Vāsudeva on Śvetadvīpa by him for the sake of destroying his enemies—Indra gave that very banner to him as well.
The king, having traveled through the intermediate space and enjoyed earthly pleasures that are very difficult to obtain, finally attained the heavenly world with a divine body. || 30 ||
There, while enjoying various kinds of pleasures desired by his own mind as the fruit of the remainder of his former merit, he attained intense dispassion.
Then, on a solitary peak of Mount Meru, pure and having assumed a firm posture, he meditated upon his chosen deity, the Lord of Ramā, within the lotus of his own heart.

Then, having abandoned his divine body through the practice of yogic concentration, that sage reached the solar orb by means of his subtle body—that which they call the gateway to liberation for ascetic yogis.
With his subtle body consumed by that fire, he became exceedingly pure, consisting of existence and consciousness; that illustrious one had all his latent impressions completely extinguished.
Then, by the deities of the subtle body belonging to that maṇḍala, he was led to the wonderful abode of Viṣṇu known as Śvetadvīpa.
O Sage, although that island is situated on earth, it is extraordinary; for it is the abode of those devoted to Hari, reached through exclusive devotion.
O observer of noble vows, he is the gateway for those high-souled devotees who desire Goloka, Brahmapura, and Vaikuṇṭha. (37)
O Sage, those liberated souls of white complexion, possessing the characteristics previously described, lead the devotee to whichever abode he desires when he worships that [deity]. 38.
There, in that abode, he became possessed of a divine body like a liberated soul; then, having reached the realm of Goloka, he attained supreme bliss.
Those who propitiate Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, by means of this very exclusive dharma alone, become white-liberated (śvetāmukta). || 40 ||
O Sage, all this that you asked has been explained to you: the state of those who are exclusively devoted, and the characteristics of the White Abode.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of Upīracara Vasu," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sāvarṇi said: When the gods were restrained by the great ṛṣis and abandoned the sacrifice consisting of violence, how did such sacrifices again begin to be performed everywhere?
Among gods, sages, and kings—both ancient and modern—how has the eternal, pure Dharma fallen into perversion? (2)
O Six-faced One, a great doubt has arisen within me today; you, who know the truth of all scriptures, ought to dispel it.
Skanda said: "O Sage, Time is more powerful than the powerful; by it are the intellects of those possessed of desire, anger, the relish for sensory pleasures, greed, and pride shattered."
Through the transgression of great beings who speak according to truth and for the sake of welfare, the virtuous intellects of men are surely destroyed by the power of anger and pride.
Even at that time, though they were wise, they proceeded to perform even what should not be done; they then felt remorse and wandered about in the cycle of existence.
As for those Sātvatas who are free from desire and the like, and whose latent impressions have been exhausted—time is never able to cause a change in their intellect.
But no person at any time, if not relying upon the True Dharma, is ever liberated from cyclic existence; this word of mine is the truth.
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe to you the origin of the violent sacrifice and other such rites, exactly as it was heard by me previously from the mouth of my father.
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history (itihāsa), wherein the majesty of Nārāyaṇa and that of Lakṣmī are glorified.
O Sage, due to the fault of transgressing those great sages, there occurred a dissolution of Indra’s virtuous intellect, despite his being the conqueror of the universe.
Once, the ascetic sage Durvāsas, who was a portion of Śaṅkara, while wandering through the worlds at his own will, went to the river Puṣpabhadrā.
There he beheld the wife of the Vidyādhara Sumati, surrounded by her female companions, coming from heaven for the purpose of sporting in the water.
In her right hand she held a garland named Madakalā, strung with golden lotuses from the celestial Gaṅgā and possessing an exquisite fragrance.
Beholding her, the sage approached her and, like a madman, begged for that garland held by the Vidyādharī.
She too, immediately bowing to him and recognizing his greatness, placed that garland around his neck with the utmost reverence.
Then, proceeding with a joyful mind, singing like one intoxicated, the sage saw on the path Indra, the lord of the gods, approaching that great river.
He was mounted upon the lordly elephant, whose victory was being celebrated with sweet voices and rhythmic clapping by Apsarases and Gandharvas.
Delighted by the joy of hearing the sweet songs of Rambhā, his gaze was fixed upon her lotus-like face, and he was graced by the parasol and the chowries.
Seeing him disregarding himself, that son of Atri, laughing like a madman, threw the garland from his own neck at him.

Since Indra had already been possessed by unrighteousness, he then, under the sway of desire, placed it upon the two frontal globes of the elephant; the lordly elephant, his mind drawn by its fragrance, pulled it away with his trunk.
It fell from his trunk onto the ground, and as he was walking away, the elephant crushed it with his foot while that great seer, a treasury of ascetic powers, looked on.
Then, enraged, that Durvāsas, whose eyes were as tawny as the fire of universal destruction, said to Indra: "O intoxicated one of wicked soul, you have become arrogant, you lecherous wretch!"
"O fool, intoxicated with pride, you do not welcome with joy this garland, the abode of fortune, given by me out of affection; nor, O madman, do you even offer a salutation. (24)
You do not even look at me, your sole teacher who is intoxicated by you; now that you have become blind to the attainment of sovereignty over the three worlds, I shall instruct you thoroughly.
May that very Śrī, by whose grace you obtained the happiness of sovereignty over the three worlds, abandon you along with the three worlds and dissolve into the ocean.
Upon hearing those words, which were like a thunderbolt falling, Hari instantly leaped from his elephant, free from pride, and fell at his feet.
And trembling all over, he repeatedly prostrated before him and entreated: "O Compassionate One, you ought to show favor toward me, your servant. (28)
Then he said to him, "O Śakra, do not say that; I am indeed not the sage Gautama. Know me to be Durvāsas, whose entire essence consists of intolerance. (29)
Those other sages are wicked; they are merely your followers. But I, being free from desire, do not even count those like you as insects.
Who among those who commit evil deeds in the cosmic egg would not be terrified of me, with my mass of flaming matted hair and eyes curved in a frown?
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Curse of Devendra," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: O Sage, then, under the sway of the force of time during which the dharma of the future was being subverted, he said, "I will not endure this," and departed for Kailāsa.
Then, even the Goddess Śrī vanished from the three worlds into the ocean; leaving Indra, the Apsarases followed Śrī in every respect.
Austerity, purity, compassion, truth, the four feet of the True Dharma, the supernatural powers, the perfections, strength, and goodness followed Fortune from every side.
They cast down vehicles such as elephants, ornaments made of gold and other metals, jewels and gems, minerals, and various utensils.
Foodstuffs, medicinal herbs, and oils became scarce in a short time; even the milk of cows, buffaloes, and other such animals was no longer produced in their udders.
Even the nine treasures were lost from the palace of Kubera; Indra, along with the hosts of immortals, became like an ascetic.
All objects of enjoyment perished from the three worlds; gods, demons, and humans were all afflicted by poverty.
Deprived of its luster, the moon then turned into water in the great ocean; a massive drought ensued, causing the destruction of grain and seeds.
Crying out, "Where is food? Where is food?", emaciated by hunger and devoid of strength, they abandoned their villages and cities and dwelt in forests and on mountains.
Afflicted by hunger, they killed domestic and wild animals; some, having cooked them and others not, ate their flesh.
Furthermore, the learned ones and the sages who truly practice the true Dharma did not eat meat even when they were dying of hunger.
Then the aged sages, seeing them devoted to fasting, explained to them along with the Manus the dharma for times of distress as declared in the Vedas.

In that place, the sages, for the most part, their senses agitated by hunger, arrived at misconceptions regarding the meanings of the Vedas, which are intended to be understood through indirect expression.
They understood the primary meaning of words such as "goat" (aja) and so forth to be the animal itself; then they said, "O twice-born ones, perform sacrifices."
For that violence which is ordained by the Vedas is not violence that brings fault; therefore, slaughter auspicious animals for the sake of the gods and the ancestors. 15.
Eat the meat that has been consecrated with sprinkling and offered to the deities and the ancestors; do not slaughter animals for your own sake.
Then the celestial sages, kings, and men, enlightened by them, performed sacrifices according to their respective capacities, with the sole exception of those exclusively devoted to Hari.
They performed the Gomedha, Aśvamedha, and sacrifices beginning with the Naramedha, and they consumed the meat remaining from those sacrifices.
Some performed sacrifices for the sake of regaining lost prosperity; others did so for the sake of wives, sons, houses, and the like, while still others acted for their own livelihood.

Being unable to perform the great sacrifices, they slaughtered animals in abundance for the ancestral rites (śrāddhas) dedicated to the ancestors; thus they ate the meat themselves and likewise caused others to eat it.
Some people lived right on the banks of rivers and oceans; having caught fish with nets, they made that their food.
O Sage, having slaughtered only animals—headed by cows and goats—and offered them to the learned guests who had come to their own homes. || 22 ||

At that time, there was no rule regarding marriages within the same caste anywhere, due to the lack of confusion of religious duties and the absence of wealth, houses, and other such possessions. (23)

By the course of time, the Brāhmaṇas married women from the Kṣatriya and other castes, and the Kṣatriyas and others married the daughters of Brāhmaṇas, for the sake of the expansion of their respective lineages. (24)
Thus, in this great calamity, sacrifices consisting of violence were set in motion; dharma remained as a mere semblance, while prosperity itself followed after the Goddess of Fortune.
Adharma, along with its progeny, pervaded all three worlds on every side; in a short time it increased, becoming difficult to restrain even by the wise.
Then these sons of the poor ones were born in great numbers, and their extensive lineage increased greatly throughout the worlds.
Those who were born there as learned men considered that very dharma alone to be the primary one, and they composed treatises of a similar nature. || 28 ||
Those texts attained authority through tradition; for thus did the corruption of Dharma occur in the first Tretā Yuga. (29)
From that time forward, the slaughter of animals in sacrifices and other rites occurred in the worlds; however, in the Satya Yuga, the eternal Dharma prevailed.
After a long time, O sage, that lord of the gods, having propitiated the Lord Vāsudeva together with the deities, attained perfect prosperity.
Then, by the grace of Hari, the Lord of Śrī and abode of Dharma, the true Dharma was set in motion throughout the three worlds just as it was before.

Even there, some sages, kings, gods, and humans—whose true intellects have been impaired by the relish of desire, anger, and greed—still regard that dharma of distress as being preeminent even today. (33)

But those who were exclusively devoted to the Lord (Bhāgavatas), having conquered desire and the other [afflictions], did not accept it even in times of distress; how much less so at other times? (34)
Thus, O Brahmin, I have related to you how the performance of violent sacrifices occurred on earth during the primordial kalpa, under the influence of times of distress.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Causes for the Commencement of Sacrifices Involving Violence," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya, within the second section (Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sāvarṇi said: "O Skanda, how was the fortune that had gone to the ocean regained by Indra? Tell me this entire story concerning Nārāyaṇa."
Skanda said: "Deprived of his splendor, the lord of the gods was defeated by the Dānavas who were themselves bereft of splendor; he was stripped of his position and all his attendants were lost. (2)
Accompanied by Varuṇa and the other guardians of the directions, he wandered here and there through mountain caves, thickets, and forests.
Wearing garments of bark, skins, and cloth, and subsisting on the flesh of beasts and birds, the gods, Daityas, humans, and Nāgas were equal in their conduct and attire.
In the houses of all, the vessels were made of clay alone; and all the women were wretched, like female spirits (piśācīs). || 5 ||
In the beginning, there was a twelve-year drought upon the earth; thereafter, in some places there was a slight rain, and in others none at all.
In this manner, a hundred years passed for them in the misery of poverty; yet, because their commenced karma was so powerful, they did not die despite their extreme suffering.
Though they strove to attain prosperity through sacrifices and other rites, they did not obtain it; living as if dead, they were like denizens of hell within their own hells.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, all the gods, due to the curse of Durvāsas, went to Merau for refuge and sought counsel from Brahmā regarding Durvāsas.
Having bowed down to him, Vāsava and the other gods reported their own suffering; for he, being omniscient, already knew the distress of the gods from the very beginning.
Then Viriñca, together with Śaṅkara, having reproached Indra, desired to propitiate Viṣṇu in order to ward off that suffering.
Then, desiring to propitiate him who is fond of austerity through his own asceticism, he approached the Ocean of Milk accompanied by all the hosts of gods.
On its beautiful northern bank, they all, observing a vow of fasting, performed penance standing on one foot with their arms raised upward.
With their minds made one-pointed, they should place Keśava—the Lord of Lakṣmī, Vāsudeva, who destroys all afflictions—within their hearts.
Then, at the end of the hundred years, the Lord Viṣṇu himself, as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, showed compassion toward the gods who were in extreme distress and misery.
There, he whose form is invisible even to those who know the Self and to great ascetics appeared out of compassion, possessing a splendor like that of a million suns.
At the very beginning, all the gods suddenly beheld a great, white, incomparable, and dense orb of splendor that had burst forth. || 17 ||
In their midst, Brahmā and Śiva beheld the Lord of Ramā, dark as a rain cloud, four-armed, and bearing a mace, a lotus, and a discus.
Adorned with a crown, girdle, bracelets, earrings, and other ornaments, he wore yellow silken garments and possessed a divine and beautiful form. (19)
Overwhelmed with joy, the two Mānas prostrated themselves like a staff; then, by his will, the gods also saw him and bowed with delight.
They became exceedingly joyful, like the poor who have found a treasure; with palms joined in reverence, all the gods praised him with devotion.
The gods said: Oṃ! Salutations to you, the Blessed One; we meditate upon Vāsudeva. Salutations to Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and Saṃkarṣaṇa as well. || 22 ||

Salutation to Him whose form is the syllable Oṃ and the nature of Brahman, whose manifested forms are threefold, who is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the cosmic egg, and who is beyond all attributes.
Salutations to you, O Keśava, whose form brings joy to the eyes, who destroys the afflictions of those who bow before you, and who is the embodiment of the independent Lord.
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, who gladdens all his devotees, who deludes Time, Māyā, and the rest, who is eternal bliss, and who abides in the true Dharma. || 25 ||
Salutations to You, who are dark as a rain-cloud, whose form is beautiful to behold, and whose fame is capable of lifting up those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence. 26.
Salutations again and again to you, who bear the mace, lotus, conch, and discus with your long arms, and who are the protector of the gods, cows, brahmins, and the Dharma.
Salutations to You, the most excellent one who grants the desired boons to those who have sought refuge, who are known through the Nigamas and Āgamas, and whose womb is the Veda. || 28 ||
We bow to you, O Viṣṇu, who abide in the center of a circle of splendor, whose form is divinely beautiful, and who are higher than the highest. 29.
Salutations again and again to You, the Great One, whose majesty transcends speech and mind, who is of imperishable form, and who is the inner controller of all.
You alone are the source of happiness for those who depend upon you; therefore, we, afflicted by great calamities, have come to you for refuge. (31)
"O Durvāsas, because of our transgression against you, who are devoted to the God of gods, we have been deprived of our prosperity and have fallen into this miserable state. (32)

O Lord, even Dharma has abandoned us—who are destitute of clothing, food, drink, shelter, and the like—and has departed along with Prosperity; you alone are the Master capable of protecting them. (33)
Since we and the Dharma are renowned as being yours, it is therefore right for you alone to make us happy, just as before. (34)
Skanda said: Thus entreated by the gods, the Blessed One, that ocean of compassion, spoke, gladdening the deities with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Blessed Lord said: "O gods, all the suffering caused by your transgression is known to me. Employ this very means today which I shall declare for its cessation."
"Having cast all the medicinal herbs into the ocean, churn it together with the asuras, using Mount Mandara as the churning rod and the king of serpents as the rope. (37)
"First, having entered into an alliance with the Danujas, perform the churning of the ocean; I shall provide you assistance, so you need not feel any weariness in that regard. (38)
Having obtained the sight of Śrī and the nectar, the Daityas—possessing even greater vigor than before—will turn away from me and become partakers of suffering. (39)
Skanda said: Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the distress of his devotees, vanished. The gods, having bowed to him, began to carry out what he had commanded.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Grace of Śrī Vāsudeva," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: O Sage, having commanded Brahmā, Rudra, Mahendra, and the others to join with the Asuras, the gods went to their respective abodes and to the netherworld (rasātala).

Skilled in speech appropriate for the occasion, he enticed the Asuras with political wisdom and reasoning, and having won them over with a share of the fruit [of their labors], he made an alliance with them.
Then the hosts of gods and asuras assembled on the shore of the ocean; having brought many great medicinal herbs, they quickly deposited them there.
Then, having approached Mount Mandara, which was resplendent with various medicinal herbs, they all prepared to uproot it from its base in order to take it to the ocean.
Standing upon the earth at eleven thousand yojanas [in height], they were unable to lift it up; they then praised Hari.
Having understood this, the Blessed One [Viṣṇu] informed Saṃkarṣaṇa, the lord of the earth, in order to uproot that mountain which was firmly rooted.
With a single mere blast of breath, that Lord instantly cast him out from that place to a distance of two yojanas.
Beholding that great marvel, all the gods and asuras were delighted; they rushed toward him, running and raising a great clamor.
Though they were strong, possessed arms like iron bars, and exerted themselves with effort, they were unable to lift it up and carry it away; dejected and their labors fruitless, they desisted.
Having perceived that the hosts of gods were distressed, the Blessed One, the all-seeing, commanded Tārkṣya to swiftly lead them to that ocean.

The Lord, possessing the speed of thought, was able to hold even that cosmic egg along with its veil as if in play; having arrived there, he uprooted that mountain with his own beak alone, placed it on the shore of the ocean, and returned to Hari.
Then, with hearts full of joy, all the sons of Kaśyapa summoned Vāsuki under the promise of a share of the nectar.
He went there, and then they all prepared to churn the ocean; the Lord of Waters, appearing in person, approached them and spoke these words.
O gods and asuras, if you will grant me a portion of the nectar, then I shall endure the immense suffering caused by the whirling of Mount Mandara.
Having agreed, saying "So be it," and having cast medicinal herbs and creepers into the fire, they circumambulated the king of serpents on that golden mountain.
Then the gods remembered Hari in their hearts for the sake of accomplishing their task; as soon as he was remembered, the all-seeing Acyuta arrived there.
Beholding him, the hosts of gods were delighted; permitted by the Lord of Serpents, they stood taking their positions in front of him.
Manifesting his partiality toward the gods and acting as their lord, he took his stand wherever the gods were; consequently, the Daityas became enraged.
"Those who are senior by virtue of austerity, knowledge, or age [should occupy] the lower seat, which is inauspicious; how could we, who are not such fools, accept it? (19)
Then Viṣṇu himself, as if honoring them along with the gods, smiled and, having given them the front portion, seized the tail.
"The protection of the immortals from the burning heat of the hiss of the great serpent's venom—this is the conduct of the Lord of Śrī; thus do those Daityas not understand. (21)
Then those sons of Kaśyapa, having girded their loins with leather straps, lifted up Mount Mandara, which was as radiant as a mountain of gold and shimmering with its hosts of monkeys.
Crying out and exceedingly anxious, they placed that mountain, twenty-two thousand yojanas high, into the ocean.
Although being supported by them, the mountain, due to its extreme weight, lacked a foundation and immediately sank to the bottom; at that moment, they became utterly overwhelmed.
Then that Blessed One, who accomplishes the tasks of his devotees in every way, being praised by the immortals, assumed the form of a tortoise and lifted up the mountain.
Seeing him risen, they all quickly became joyful in heart and face; and he became steady upon the very broad back of the tortoise.
Then the gods and others, their faces panting with the exertion of their breath, mercilessly churned the ocean of waters with speed according to their strength.
Then, as the mountain was being whirled around, many trees fell from it; the fire produced by the friction of the upper trees burned the lions and other creatures dwelling there.
There, various aquatic creatures, crushed by the great mountain, met their destruction by the hundreds in the ocean of milk. (29)
There arose a great sound of churning, amplified by its own echoes, like the thundering of the massed clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
With their limbs exhausted from being excessively pulled by Vāsuki acting as the bowstring, the Daityas, their vital energy destroyed and utterly distressed, appeared like charred logs.
They repeatedly endure the unbearable fire of poison in many ways; a thousand heads of the serpent-king hang downwards.
Impelled by the Blessed One, the all-pervading Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, possessed of great splendor, suddenly sustained those [poisons], enduring the fire of the venom. || 33 ||
After a thousand years of churning the ocean of milk, the Hālāhala poison emerged, spreading its fumes toward the cardinal and intermediate directions.
As it is said: "That which is called Kālakūṭa burns all the worlds; with their limbs scorched by it, they fled. (35)
Then, O Sage, Brahmā, the lords of creatures, and all the gods, praising him with hymns, entreated the Lord of Umā for the purpose of drinking it.
Then the Blessed One said to him: "You are the first-born of the gods; therefore, O Śiva, accept this poison as the first-born of the ocean."
Seeing the fear of the gods and by the command of Hari, he, being compassionate, drew forth all the poison onto the palm of his hand by means of his yogic power.
He drank it into the middle of his throat and dried it up at that very moment; thus he became known as Nīlakaṇṭha and also received the name Śaṅkara.
As he was drinking, the drops that fell upon the ground from his hand were seized by serpents, scorpions, and others, as well as by certain medicinal herbs.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Arising of Poison during the Churning for Nectar," in the *Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya*, within the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 11.
Skanda said: Then the sons of Kaśyapa, being delighted, approached the place of churning and churned the ocean of milk once again for a thousand years.
Even by all of them together, nothing at all emerged from the ocean while it was being churned; nor did the churning-sticks become loosened, for their tips were fanned by the wind.
And the great serpent Vāsuki suffered a failure of breath, while even Mount Mandara did not maintain a steady position in one place during the time of churning.
Seeing them all devoid of energy, Pradyumna, with the permission of Viṣṇu, entered among the gods, asuras, and the king of serpents, and bestowed strength upon them.
Then Aniruddha, having likewise attacked that lord of mountains, stood with his thousand arms like another great mountain.
Then, having attained supreme vigor, those hosts of gods and asuras, filled with wonder and joy, swiftly churned the great ocean.
By the power of Nārāyaṇa, the gods and others did not experience fatigue; and that churning shone brightly due to the simultaneous pulling [of the rope].
As the great ocean was being churned, the resins of mighty trees and many juices of medicinal herbs then flowed forth in all directions.
From such an ocean there emerged the storehouse of digits (the moon), who is proclaimed as the presiding deity over all the medicinal herbs of splendor.
Then, the presiding deity of all cows, the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhuk), became the sacrificial cow (Havirdhānī), possessing a radiance like that of the moon. || 10 ||
The white horse was the presiding deity of horses; and Airāvata, the lord of elephants, possessed four tusks and the luster of the moon. || 11 ||
From that [tree] arose the divine Parijata, the king of trees; from that, the jewel-gem known as Kaustubha, a ruby, was produced. (12)
From that, there arose Apsarases, who were the very ground of beauty and charm; from that, the goddess Surā was born, the deity who intoxicates all.
Then there appeared the Śārṅga bow, the presiding deity of all weapons; thereafter, the Pāñcajanya conch became the presiding deity of musical instruments.
There, Candra, the Pārijāta tree, and likewise the host of Apsarases, took their stand at that very moment, having taken recourse to the path of the sun.
The lords of the Daityas quickly seized Vāruṇī and the king of horses; the king of the gods seized Airāvata with the permission of Hari.
The Kaustubha gem, the bow, and the conch shell all went to Viṣṇu alone; meanwhile, they all then gave the sacrificial fire-chamber (Havirdhānī) to the ascetics.
Furthermore, from the ocean being churned, Śrī herself appeared in person, gladdening the three worlds with her gaze, which eclipsed their own luster.
Indeed, all the gods, asuras, humans, and others desired to seize her; yet, due to her majesty, not one among them was able to approach her.
Then, recognizing her as Śrī by virtue of her lotus-hand, Vāsava attained supreme bliss, as did Brahmā and others who knew her.
Just then, the Ocean himself arrived there and, having seated her on a golden throne, said, "This girl is mine," and taking her onto his lap, he sat down.
Furthermore, although they were powerful and patient, and though they churned the ocean for the sake of nectar, no nectar at all emerged.
Then, O Sage, those descendants of Kaśyapa, their efforts slackened and their hopes for the production of the nectar gone, became dejected and their faces grew pale.
O Brahmin, seeing them in such a state, the Lord, the storehouse of compassion, the omnipresent one, smiling, himself became intent upon churning.
With the luster of yellow garments and a firm girdle of jewels fastened at his waist, he grasped the serpent by its middle with two pairs of arms on both sides.
The Daityas stood on one side with their mouths held by serpents, while all the gods stood on the other side holding its tail. 26.
And situated in their midst, the Blessed One sportively churned the ocean, bestowing delight upon the eyes with his shimmering arm-ornaments. (27)
Then Brahmā, stationed in the intermediate space together with the foremost of sages, showered him with flowers while raising shouts of "Victory! Victory! (jaya-jaya).
Then, from that ocean being churned, the male Dhanvantari was born, a fair-limbed portion of Viṣṇu, holding a jar of nectar in his hand.
Having taken that nectar—the supreme essence of all juices such as clarified butter and the rest—he approached the presence of Śrī.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Production of the Fourteen Jewels during the Churning for Nectar," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-Māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 12 ||
Skanda said: Then all those churners, while gazing at the one being born, beheld from afar Dhanvantari approaching, the very embodiment of Śrī.
O Brahmin, seeing that golden pitcher filled with nectar held in his hand, the Asuras suddenly leaped up and seized it.
There too, those who were strong seized [the others] and fled from there; the weak ones, pursued by them, restrained them with words of policy.
"Alas! This unrighteousness must not be committed by you who are devoted to dharma; having given [the Soma] to the gods who have exerted equal effort, it should be drunk, and not otherwise."
Disregarding those words, they departed for a great distance with great haste; even there, a massive mutual pulling by the hands occurred among them.
"I first, I first! Not you, not you—I shall drink! Thus disputing among themselves, they did not reach the moment for consuming it.
Then the gods, seeing the nectar seized by the Daityas, became dejected of face; being powerless to counteract it, they sought refuge in Acyuta.
Protect us, protect us, O Lord of the World! Our entire possession has been lost; all the nectar has been seized by the Daityas—what will our fate be? (8)
Even without drinking the nectar, these [demons] are fully capable of slaying us; but once the nectar has been drunk by them today, what shall we do? (9)

Skanda said: Having perceived the wretchedness of the gods, the Blessed One, who accomplishes the tasks of his devotees, said to the deities, "Do not fear," and desired to take the nectar from the Asura.
Assuming a wondrous female form that deludes all the worlds, she approached the presence of the Daitya and began playing with a ball.
But beholding her in that form, they were infatuated and overwhelmed by desire; abandoning their mutual struggle, they approached her and spoke these words: || 12 ||
"O blessed one, O lady of beautiful hips, take this jar of nectar and, having divided it among us, cause us all to drink; we are the sons of Kaśyapa. (13)
Having said this, they gave him to that woman even though she was unwilling; she replied, "I should not be trusted, for I am a wanton woman."
"Indeed, you have committed an improper act; I shall divide [the inheritance] according to my own will. Although addressed thus, those fools said, "Do as you please! (15)
Then, by his command, all the gods, the Daityas, and Vāsuki sat there in rows, each occupying their own respective circle.
While they were preparing to take their seats in rows, that Mohinī sat down from afar upon a golden throne directly facing the lines of gods.
Placing a jar of nectar near him, she stood for a moment with the playful gestures of a woman, looking here and there as if she were indifferent.
Then those leaders of the Dānava hosts, headed by Vipracitti, became doubtful in their minds regarding Mohinī while she stood in the presence of the gods.
Approaching slowly and deceiving his sight, those wicked men, being thirsty, went aside in secret and carried off the jar of nectar once again. (20)
Nara and Nārāyaṇa had also arrived there along with the sages; they both beheld those Dānavas carrying away the nectar.
Then, impelled by Nārāyaṇa, Nara suddenly struck them down; forcibly snatching that jar away, he quickly gave it to Mohinī.
Then the Dānavas, having taken up their weapons and desiring to kill Nara, rushed forward; indeed, there was a great dispersal of the ranks of the Asuras.
Then the powerful Lord Nara, being invincible and fearless even to gods, daityas, and men, fought alone against them all.
In the meantime, Viṣṇu, moving with swift strides, caused the gods standing in rows to drink the nectar by assuming the form of Mohinī.
Thereupon, the Dānava Rāhu, having entered between the sun and the moon, sat down unobserved within the row of the deities.
When Mohinī arrived there and was pouring nectar into his mouth, both the sun and the moon indicated him to her with their glances.
Then, with the wheel that had arrived through his mindfulness, the Lord instantly severed the head of that great illusory female form, which was still possessed of life.
Resembling a mountain peak, swallowing the worlds and roaring loudly, Hari established him in the state of a planet for the peace of the worlds.
Having caused the gods to drink the nectar, the Blessed One assumed his virile form; then the gods fought with the Dānavas.
On the shore of the ocean, there was a battle between the gods and the asuras; the gods, exceedingly powerful from drinking the nectar of immortality, were aided by Viṣṇu.
In that tumultuous battle, being struck down by Nara, Indra, and the others, those asuras fled and entered the subterranean realm (rasātala).
By that time the sun had set; then all the hosts of gods, for whom the sight of her was a great festival, approached Śrī.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Drinking of the Nectar of the Deities," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 13.
Skanda said: Brahmā, the lords of progeny, Śambhu, the Manus, and the great ṛṣis; the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, as well as the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas—(1).
The Sādhyas, the Maruts, the Viśvedevas, the lords of the quarters, the two Aśvins, Agni, the Moon, Dharma himself, and Prajāpati; || 2 ||
The Suparṇas, the Kinnaras, and other host-deities; the Vaiṣṇava Nāgas beginning with Śeṣa, and the wives of the gods from every quarter. || 3 ||
Sāvitrī, Pārvatī, Pṛthivī, Sarasvatī, Śacī, Gaurī, Śivā, Saṃjñā, Ṛddhi, Svāhā, Rohiṇī, Dhūmorṇā, Aditi, and the wives of Dharma—Mūrti, Dayā, and the others. || 4 ||
Arundhatī, Śāṇḍilī, and likewise Lopāmudrā, as well as Anasūyā and all other virtuous wives of sages.
The Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Revā, Yamunā, and likewise the Tapatī; the Candrabhāgā, Vipāśā, Śatadrū, and likewise the Devikā. || 6 ||
The Godāvarī, the Sarayū, the Kāverī, and likewise the Kauśikī; the Kṛṣṇā, the Veṇī, the Bhīmarathā, and the great river Tāmraparṇī.
The Kṛtamālā, Vitastā, Nirvindhyā, Surasā, Carmaṇvatī, Payoṣṇī, Viśvā, and other rivers arrived. || 8 ||
Rambhā, Ghṛtācī, Viśvācī, Menakā, Tilottamā, and Urvaśī—headed by these, all the Apsarases arrived there. || 9 ||
All the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha, as well as those of Goloka, and the foremost of Viṣṇu’s attendants, arrived there filled with great joy.
The eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*, the nine treasures such as Śaṅkha and Padma, and the personified treasures all came into the presence of Śrī.
Even the full autumn moon at that time brought delight to Śrī; it dispelled all the darkness of night, and the quarters of the sky became stainless.
Then, by the command of Brahmā, the Bull (Śiva) began her consecration; Tvaṣṭṛ immediately constructed an exceedingly beautiful pavilion.
It was adorned with long rows of thousands of jeweled pillars, with various multicolored canopies, and with plantain trees.
It was graced by rows of divine kalpa-trees bent with fragrant flowers, and it was beautiful to behold and captivating to the mind with its various features.
It was resplendent with rows of millions of jewel-lamps of pure radiance, and with arches adorned by hanging strings of pearls.
Having seated Śrī upon that jeweled throne to the accompaniment of song and instrumental music, the great sages performed her consecration.
Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka are the elephants of the quarters.
Performing these magnified rites, they consecrated him with auspicious waters drawn from golden jars and brought together from the four oceans.
There, the great rivers in embodied form offered waters, and the Vedas in personified form, together with the sages, uttered sacred mantras.
The Gandharvas with beautiful throats sang, the hosts of Apsaras danced, and other groups of gods then played musical instruments.
At that time, there was great joy for all embodied beings in the three worlds; the twice-born recited the Śrīsūkta and other hymns, and the women sang songs.
They played the gongs, cymbals, mṛdaṅgas, paṇavas, ānakas, and gomukhas; the clouds rained down, and the dundubhi drums resounded in the sky.
Then there was a rain of flowers accompanied by shouts of victory; and the wives of Dharma were present as Siddhis to attend upon him.
Then, to her who had been well-bathed, the Ocean gave two priceless garments of yellow silk and abundant ornaments made of jewels.
Indra brought forth for her a throne worthy of her sitting; Viśvakarman gave her bracelets and rings set with excellent jewels.
Her brother Sudhākara, however, gave her an excellent nose-ornament as well as hair-ornaments set with fine jewels.
The lotus-born Brahmā gave her a lotus, Sarasvatī a necklace of pearls, and the serpents, headed by Śeṣa, gave her two earrings made of the finest gems.
Durgā took collyrium and saffron, the marks of good fortune; Sāvitrī took a forehead mark, and Śacī took a betel-leaf box. (29)
Vasanta [offered] garlands of flowers; Śaṅkara, a necklace for the neck; Varuṇa, the Vaijayantī wreath; and Kubera, a jeweled mirror.
Agni gave her an invaluable bodice, and Yama gave a beautiful fan; others also gave her ornaments appropriate for that occasion.
Then the Ocean asked Brahmā, "To whom should I give this well-adorned daughter? Thereupon, the omniscient one replied.
"O Ocean, this maiden is yours; she is the mother of me, Śiva, and indeed of all the gods and of all the worlds. (33)
Except for Nārāyaṇa Vāsudeva, the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of all, the one Puruṣottama alone, she has no other husband.
Therefore, O Ocean, give [this] according to the prescribed rite to the Lord himself, the cause of happiness for the three worlds, who has arrived and is seated here.
Make your birth fruitful by purifying your own lineage; deliver us from the ocean of worldly existence by giving her to the Supreme Self.
Though you are one, you shall become renowned through seven forms according to the division of the seven continents; by performing this, you will attain great fame.
Thus addressed by Brahmā, the Ocean was delighted; with his hair standing on end from joy, he considered himself blessed and offered his daughter to Viṣṇu.
Then, having entreated that Lord together with the prescribed rites and having performed the formal betrothal and other ceremonies, he carried out the marriage ritual.
Dhanvantari, Candramas, Vāsava, and the other deities were on the side of the ocean at that wedding festival.
Indeed, they alone were preeminent in the giving of garments, ornaments, vehicles, and the like, in the act of providing food, and in the honoring of their kinsmen. (41)
In that auspicious rite for Lakṣmī, the women present were preeminent; there were the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, as well as the celestial nymphs beginning with Śacī.
Menā and the other wives of the mountain kings, the supernatural powers such as Aṇimā and the rest, as well as Kānti, the wife of the Moon, and all the Apsarases, O Sage. (43)
Then Brahmā, having reflected upon the principles of form and dharma, performed the marriage ceremony of the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa, thereby beautifying his parents.
This Dharma is the support of the world and is worthy of worship by all embodied beings; indeed, he is fit to be its father and is exceedingly affectionate toward it.
And this celebrated form, the birthplace of all excellent virtues, the daughter of Dakṣa and lawful wife of Dharma, ought to be my mother. (46)
Then, O Sage, these became the principal figures on the side of Dharma in the course of events; Śaṅkara was accompanied by Nandīśvara and Gaṇeśa.
The great sages beginning with Marīci, the lords of progeny, the sage Nārada, Vainateya, and the attendants beginning with Nanda and Śrīdāmā. || 48 ||
Durgā, Vedasū, and Vāṇī became the foremost among women; so too did the wives of the sages, such as Anasūyā and others, and all the wives devoted to righteousness.
Along with the Vedas and other scriptures, Brahmā was present on both sides, as were the Vedic Brahmins who were experts in the rules of marriage.
Then the Ocean, by the very grace of Śrī, immediately provided all the necessary materials, causing wonder among the gods.
Whatever he conceived in his heart was brought to him immediately; he saw it right before him, and thereupon he became exceedingly joyful.
In the center of the pavilion, however, he had a sacrificial altar for the installation of the fire constructed according to the rules by Brahmins who were learned in the Vedas.
He adorned that altar with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other such auspicious items, as well as with various beautiful colors, sprouts, and water-pots.
Then, having been bathed with mantras by the lords of sages amidst the sounds of great auspicious musical instruments, Viṣṇu donned priceless garments, jewel ornaments, and a divine crown.

Then, having approached that pavilion—which resounded with the noise of musical instruments and was beautified by the sweet songs of dancing celestial nymphs—he sat down upon a golden throne together with the gods who were offering him praise.

Then the Ocean, together with the Gaṅgā, washed his lotus feet with the excellent stream of water poured from a golden pitcher by his most beloved wife; and he, along with his lineage, bore that water upon his head.

Then, reciting auspicious hymns aloud, the Creator caused Śrī to be bestowed upon Acyuta by the Ocean; having kindled the fire according to the prescribed rite, he offered oblations together with the great sages.
Having bestowed his charming daughter upon him—her gaze fixed solely upon his lotus-feet—he gave many garments and jeweled ornaments to the Infinite One (Bhūman) along with his daughter.
Then Hari, together with Śrī, performed a circumambulation of that sacrificial fire which had been offered; he captivated the hearts of both the women and the men who beheld him.
Seated together on a single throne, those two—the parents of the universe, who were most charming—the hosts of gods along with their wives honored them with priceless garments and ornaments. (61)
And then Durgā and the other goddesses, including the daughter of Puloman, with their beautiful faces smiling, sang auspicious songs and praises describing the qualities of Viṣṇu and Śrī.
Having seated themselves in two groups facing one another, the throngs of celestial nymphs, eager to behold that couple, sang with an abundance of love.
Just as all the gods, the great sages, and even all the women, having heard that, beheld the Lord of Śrī shining within their own hearts along with Her, it was indeed like a marvel.

Having bowed with devotion and offered excellent unbroken rice and other gifts to them, the gods, filled with joy, praised those two individually with powerful words, standing humbly with palms joined in reverence.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Marriage Festival of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 14.

Brahmā said: Having repeatedly reflected upon the Vedas, I have arrived at this conclusion: when the devotion toward You, O delighter of Ramā, becomes exceedingly firm in embodied beings, then indeed their multitudes of enjoyments shall be free from decay, and the worlds shall truly become the ultimate goal, leading to the proximity of the Supreme Person.

Not knowing this, O Hari, people worship us gods—who are filled with the impurity of accumulated silver (or: who possess a body born of silver)—through various paths of penance and ritual service; they alone are called fools, for they never attain the imperishable bliss anywhere. Therefore, I indeed hold you, Keśava, within my own heart.

Śaṅkara said: O Lord, the three Vedas, Sāṃkhya, Vedānta, Yoga, as well as the Purāṇas and the Pañcarātra Dharmaśāstra, constantly sing with devotion through many modes of your own supreme majesty alone.

O Lord, from You alone did these scriptures arise in the primordial kalpa, having You as their sole refuge; I worship You, that primordial Vāsudeva, whose lotus feet are served by Ramā and who is the source of the scriptures.

Dharma said: Your story is the very nectar that releases beings from the bonds of worldly existence who are scorched by the threefold miseries; it removes the accumulation of sins from many lifetimes and swiftly expands devotion and wisdom toward you.

May that [name] called Ananta, emerging from Your very presence, always enter the cave of my heart through the path of my ears; may all other latent impressions (vāsanā) apart from Yours be removed. Salutations to You, the Lord, the ocean of compassion.

The Prajāpatis said: "Blessed are these Kalpa-trees, whose shade you have taken refuge in along with Śrī. Blessed is the maker of this pavilion for you; indeed, blessed is this earth where your throne stands, O Lord. (7)
"Truly, this ocean is blessed in the world, for he has personally given his daughter to you; and we too are blessed who behold you, for we bow down to you, the blessed Īśāna, the Lord of Śrī. (8)
The Mānavas said: O Mādhava, that devotion which is indeed faultless toward you, the ground of dharma, is truly the supreme dharma among all dharmas whatsoever.
O Blessed One, we praise you—the very soul of Dharma, the bearer of the yoke of Dharma, the protector of Dharma, for whom Dharma is most dear above all, and the source of Dharma’s manifestation.

The sages said: "One who is devoid of devotion and turned away from you, though seeking knowledge and striving again and again, does not attain success. How then, O great ocean of bliss, could one who is attached to rites for specific desires ever reach imperishable happiness?"

Therefore, out of devotion and endowed with faith through righteousness, austerity, the Vedas, and other means, we constantly meditate upon You alone—the one who transcends Māyā, the controller of time, the magnanimous, the beloved of Śrī, and the Supreme beyond the supreme.
Indra said: "O Blessed One, we are indeed deeply distressed by the offense against Durvāsas; for none of these, headed by Brahmā and Rudra, were able to protect us except for you."
Deprived of all wealth, lacking food, and reduced to the common state among the lowly on this earth, we have been instantly delivered from calamity by you alone; O Śrī Hari, salutations be unto you!

Agni said: "O Wise One, since food was indeed created by you alone for the sustenance of the gods, dānavas, humans, and others, the learned perform sacrifices to you with that very food; moreover, they present the remnants of what remains after you to the other denizens of heaven. (15)

Even those performers of sacrifices who are devoted to rites for desired fruits, having been swiftly liberated from the bondage of such actions, go to the state of Brahman; whereas others become mere thieves. I bow down to You, that Śrī Yajñapūruṣa. 16.

The Maruts said: "O Supreme Person, we are Your exclusive devotees; through our service at Your imperishable and supreme abode, we do not desire even residence, sovereignty, or the like, nor do we seek the singular liberation of *kaivalya*, which is a bliss surpassing all else. Yet, having taken refuge in the religion of exclusive devotion, we consider even birth in the family of a dog-eater to be superior if it is joined with You; indeed, we have approached You, the glorious Great Person, as our sole resort. (17)
The Siddhas said: We bow to You, the causeless cause of the creation and other processes of many universes; we bow to the Controller who abides within them and yet is distinct from them.
The Rudras said: Salutations to You, the Supreme Person, the deluder of Māyā who deludes all yet is free from delusion, and the time even of Mahākāla. || 19 ||
The Ādityas said: O Lord of Ramā, by whom we have been illumined so that we may illuminate the worlds, we bow down before you—him who is self-luminous, of vast radiance, and whose very form is light.

The Sādhyas said: You are the teacher of kings, of great serpents, of the lords of the Daityas, and of the lords of the gods; you indeed are [the teacher] of the Manus and the Prajāpatis. Homage be to you, the king of kings! (21)

The Vasus said: Whenever on this earth there occurs a great slaughter of those renowned for their eternal dharma and righteousness by the portions of asuras, then You Yourself descend; we bow to You, the protector of dharma.

The Cāraṇas said: O Lord who assumes many forms, your auspicious deeds are indeed sung by devotees through numerous compositions; for that [glory] instantly purifies both the listener and the speaker. We bow down to you, whose fame is meritorious.

The Gandharvas and Apsaras said: "O Lord, those people who, abandoning Your stories, recite or listen to other verses shall remain miserable, bound by the snares of saṃsāra; we bow down to You, our refuge. (24)

Samudra said: O Unconquered One, even if a person—be they small or great—performs service to you or to your people even once, with even a trifling amount of wealth, water, food, clothing, or any other such thing, that person attains the great path of the Great Ones; I bow down to that compassionate one.
The attendants said: "O Father, you are our kinsman; you are our desired preceptor, our friend, and the lord of our own selves. You alone are our supreme Lord; you are our entire wealth. (26)

Mūrtti said: I eternally worship you alone, the Lord of Goloka, by whose very association even women, Śūdras, Asuras, lowly beings, birds, animals, and even those of sinful nature attain the exalted state praised by the great; yet, deprived of whom, even the lords of the gods instantly become fallen when abandoned by their worship.

Sāvitrī said: At the time of creation, having perceived Prakṛti and Puruṣa and awakened them by your own power, you then, through that [Puruṣa], created the principles beginning with Mahat; and by means of those [principles] joined with the ego, you emanated many Virājs in manifold ways.

O Lord, having assumed the form of Vairāja and accepted the role of the creator of the world, you fashioned the gods, asuras, humans, serpents, and all that is stationary and moving; I take refuge in you, the primordial creator. (29)
Durga said: O All-pervading Lord, those on earth who contemplate You with supreme affection do not desire the bliss of Brahmā, nor the bliss of heaven, nor even the sovereignty over the entire earth.

Even though you were forcibly offered this incomparable pleasure by him, and even after having attained it there, you did not abandon it for even a moment; I bow to that leader of the Sātvatas, who acted with such power.

The rivers said: O Giver of Boons, we have today approached You, Nārāyaṇa, the friend of men, who protects even those who merely bow down or chant Your names—whether knowingly or unknowingly—from the fear of birth, death, and the cycle of existence.

The wives of the gods said: Your birth upon earth in a manifested form is auspicious; your conduct is wonderful and purifies the world. Yet everything about you is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), for you are the Supreme Brahman, which is beyond all qualities.

By taking refuge in you, even those people who are of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), passion (rājasa), or goodness (sāttvika) indeed become devoid of qualities (nirguṇa); therefore, we worship you as the one beyond all qualities.

The wives of the sages said: "O Infinite One, O God of gods, we have indeed come to you for refuge, knowing that the lotus feet of Viṣṇu alone are the sole pacifier of all calamities for those afflicted by great sins and the threefold miseries. (35)

The Earth said: I take refuge in Vāsudeva alone—whose face is like the full autumnal moon, whose long eyes are like the petals of an autumnal lotus, and who releases one from the manifold agonies of separation from Śrī. (36)

Sarasvatī said: O Acyuta, my two eyes have become like cakora birds fixed upon your exceedingly beautiful face, which is like the cool-rayed moon; since they do not turn elsewhere, let this very form alone remain eternally in my heart, and no other.
Skanda said: Thus praised by all the gods, he greeted them with a mere glance and said to Śrī, "O auspicious one, behold these gods and others."
Then, being gazed upon with affection by her with a sweet glance, all the inhabitants of the three worlds became prosperous once again, just as they were before.
Both those householders and those who had renounced the world enjoyed their respective prosperity; and Dharma and the other [Puruṣas] moved about joyfully, just as before.
The Blessed One gave his own chest as the abode for that Śrī; remaining there, she pervaded the three worlds by means of her nature as prosperity.
Then, through the power of Śrījani, Ratnākara truly became one whose name was meaningful, for he possessed jewels that were completely inexhaustible.
With four kinds of excellent foods possessing many flavors, which were like nectar, he respectfully gratified all those who had assembled there.
And with affection, he gave priceless garments, jeweled ornaments, and articles of use to all the gods and others, each one individually.
For the sake of pleasing his son-in-law, there was indeed nothing that could not be given by him to the bridegroom's party from the ocean; he was like a cloud raining down abundant wealth.
The Blessed One, having bestowed that dowry and much wealth upon the brahmins, vanished along with Śrī.
Greatly delighted by Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, the gods, headed by Indra, returned to heaven, while others went to their respective abodes.
And having regained their respective offices as before, they all became happy through the grace of the Lord of Kamalā.
And Tārkṣya, by the command of the Blessed One, brought Mount Mandara back to its own place and set it down with ease. 49.
Thus, O Brahman-sage, it was lost by Indra due to the curse of a Brāhmaṇa, but was recovered again through the grace of Nārāyaṇa. (50)
Whoever should hear this meritorious narrative of the Blessed Sage, or should recite it with a disciplined mind—both of them indeed attain prosperity. (51)

For householders there shall be the attainment of wealth, and for renunciants the fulfillment of their desires; indeed, through this [practice], the perfection of devotion, knowledge, detachment, and so forth, shall truly arise.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have told you how Indra attained prosperity and how that sage Nārada went to Śvetadvīpa; I shall explain all of that to you—listen with a single-minded heart.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: Having ascended the peak of Mount Meru, Nārada beheld Śvetadvīpa with his divine vision, seeing thousands of liberated souls residing there.
Fixing his gaze upon the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva at that very moment, the great yogi soared upward and immediately reached that abode.
Having reached the great white island, Nārada, with a joyful mind, beheld those very same devotees—white, auspicious, and possessing the luster of the moon.
He worshipped with his head and mind, and being worshipped by them, he remained intent on austerity, desiring to behold the supreme Brahman.
Having understood that he was a single-minded devotee of Viṣṇu, those Bhāgavatas, with delighted minds, spoke to him as he was chanting the twelve-syllabled mantra.
The White Pearls said: "O best of sages, since you are a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, why do you perform penance here, desiring that which is difficult even for the gods to behold?"
Nārada said: "O lords of devotees, I am eager to see the Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, the manifest Lord; O you who are dear to him, show him to me. (7)
Skanda said: Then one who had been released by Śveta, impelled in his heart by Kṛṣṇa, said, "Come, I will show you Kṛṣṇa," and appeared before him.
Delighted, the sage Nārada traveled with him through the path of the sky, and beholding the abodes of the gods, the muni proceeded further upward.
Having beheld the Seven Sages and Dhruva, and being unattached to anything whatsoever, O best of the twice-born, he passed beyond the worlds of Mahar, Jana, and Tapa.
Then, having seen the world of Brahmā, the sage Śvetamuktānuga reached the path even through the eight enclosures solely by the will of Kṛṣṇa.

Having traversed in succession the earth, water, fire, air, ether, ego, the Great Principle (Mahat), and Primordial Nature (Prakṛti)—each ten times greater than the preceding—he reached the wondrous Goloka.
For that abode, consisting of splendor, is to be attained by those who are single-mindedly devoted to Hari; while proceeding, he beheld the vast, unfathomable, and stainless river Virajā.
It possessed the fragrance of sandalwood washed by the bathing of the hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses, and was beautiful with white lotuses, red lotuses, and blue lotuses as well.
He reached its vast and enchanting shore, composed of crystal stones and resplendent with excellent gems of white, yellow, red, and green hues.
It was frequented by rows of wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa), adorned with sprouts of coral, and embellished by mines of gems such as the Syamantaka and sapphire.
It was beautiful with rows of steps inlaid with various kinds of precious gems, and it was frequented by sweetly warbling swans, kāraṇḍava ducks, and other such birds.
He passed by that place which was resplendent with herds of wish-fulfilling cows, lordly elephants, and horses, all of whom were drinking the pure water.
Then, by the will of the Lord, having crossed that divine river which had become the moat of that abode, he reached Śataśṛṅga in an instant.
It was made of gold, beautiful to behold, rising ten million yojanas high; in its breadth it was ten times ten million yojanas, captivating the mind.
It was filled with thousands of kalpa-trees and other trees such as the pārijāta, as well as with mallikā and yūthikā jasmine, and with creepers of cloves and cardamom.
It was graced by other trees such as the golden plantain, and by divine herds of deer, elephants, and birds with sweet warbling.
Upon the beautiful ridges of that very mountain which had been made difficult of access, he beheld many charming and expansive pavilions for the divine Rāsa dance.
They were beautifully adorned with four gates featuring door-panels studded with jewels, surrounded by rows of gardens fragrant with blooming flowers.
They were adorned with thousands of jeweled pillars featuring variegated archways, as well as plantain-tree columns, hanging pearl garlands, and canopies.
The courtyards were adorned with auspicious items such as dūrvā grass, parched grain, unbroken rice, and fruits, and were sprinkled with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron.
In those [forests], he beheld millions of herds of gopīs, made delightful by the sounds of various musical instruments that were most pleasant to hear.
They were adorned with priceless garments and ornaments, with bracelets of excellent gems and jewels, and beautified by waist-bands, anklets, armlets, and finger-rings.
Indeed, they were peerless in their youth, beauty, charm, and voices; they resembled Rādhā and Lakṣmī in appearance and were capable of evoking the sentiment of love. (29)
Amidst pavilions filled with various kinds of objects of enjoyment, they sport and sing charming songs of Kṛṣṇa.
Then, at the foot of that mountain, the sage Nārada beheld the great forest named Vṛndāvana during the Sāvarṇi Manvantara.
That place of their play was dear to Kṛṣṇa and Rādhikā; it was made beautiful by rows of wish-fulfilling trees and by lakes filled with lotuses.
With mangoes, hog-plums, nīpa trees, jujubes, and pomegranates; with date palms, betel-nut trees, oranges, coconuts, and sandalwood trees. || 33 ||
With rose-apples, citrons, jackfruits, akṣoda fruits, and deodar trees; with plantains, campaka flowers, grapes, and golden ketaka blossoms. || 34 ||
It was resplendent with various trees bent low under the weight of fruits and flowers, including mallikā, mādhavī, kunda, cloves, yūthikā, and others.
It was attended by a breeze that was gentle, cool, and fragrant, and it was moistened on all sides by waterfalls flowing from Mount Śataśṛṅga.
It was always rich with the splendor of spring, frequented by numerous groves adorned with rows of jewel-lamps and filled with erotic delights.

O Sage, the place resounded on all sides with the frequent chanting of Kṛṣṇa by the cowherds and cowherd girls, with the lowing of calves and the cries of birds, with the tinkling of various ornaments, and with the sounds of churning curd.
It was endowed with thirty-two other forests, beautiful and captivating to behold, adorned with various trees bending under the weight of blossoming flowers and fruits. (39)
Beholding that, he was filled with joy and reached the radiant city of Goloka, which was circular, possessed a fortress of jewels, and was adorned with royal highways.

It was likewise resplendent with tens of millions of celestial chariots belonging to the devotees of Kṛṣṇa, as well as with chariots inlaid with the finest gems and adorned with clusters of tinkling bells.
It was enchanting with millions of marvelous palaces arranged in rows, adorned with pillars of jewels and clusters of great, sovereign gems.
In the delightful pleasure-pavilions constructed from the finest jewels, it shone with multitudes of lamps made of the most excellent gems and with jeweled altars.
The courtyard was anointed with the liquid paste of saffron filaments, agallochum, musk, and saffron, and was beautified by curds, dūrvā grass, parched grain, betel nuts, and plantain trees.
The city was adorned with auspicious archways featuring golden jars filled with water, and its royal highways were paved with jewels and crowded with many moving elephants and horses.
It was thoroughly crowded with the leaders of many universes, such as Viriñci, Śaṅkara, and others, who had come for the sight of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and held offerings in their hands.
Seeing that great road, crowded with throngs of cowherds and cowherd-maidens who were traveling there to behold Kṛṣṇa, the sage rejoiced.
Then he reached Kṛṣṇa’s temple, which was full of all wonders and captivating, surrounded by rows of palatial mansions belonging to the cowherds, such as Nanda and Vṛṣabhānu.
