It was provided with four gates and sixteen fortresses surrounded by moats, each gate being well-guarded by ten million cowherds acting as gatekeepers.
On the jeweled pillars and door-panels situated at the front of the gates, he beheld the gatekeepers seated in their respective order.
Vīrabhānu, Candrabhānu, and Sūryabhānu as the third; then Vasubhānu, Devabhānu, and Śakrabhānu thereafter.
Ratnabhānu, Supārśva, Viśāla, Ṛṣabha, then Aṃśu, Bala, Subala, Devaprastha, and Varūthapa. || 52 ||
Having bowed down to Śrīdāmā, he entered within by his command; there, in the vast great quadrangle, he beheld a massive accumulation of light.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of Goloka," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 16.
Skanda said: O Sage, he beheld that great, divine, and exceedingly white splendor, which was like ten million times ten million suns arisen at a single moment. (1)

That which pervades all the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and that which extends above and below, is called the Imperishable Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.

Those perfected through yoga, by the grace of Vāsudeva, perceive both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, as well as all their effects in every respect, pervading the six cakras within themselves; having transcended these, they behold [the Supreme] in the crown of the head. || 3 ||
By whose light the sun, fire, the moon, and the stars are illuminated, so too does that self-luminous nectar illuminate the entire world.
That which the Sātvatas call the City of Brahman is the abode of the Blessed One, in whose vicinity millions of worshippers stand on all sides.
Indeed, multitudes of Brahmās and Śaṅkaras fall one above the other in great agitation, as do the hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses, with offerings in their hands, unto Him.
O Sage, he perceives that splendor in which the grace of Kṛṣṇa resides; others, however, see only the splendor itself and not Him.

There he beheld a wonderful, divine palace, composed of various supreme jewels and enchanting; it was beautiful with a thousand pillars radiant with gems, and as lovely to behold as a great assembly hall.
It was resplendent on all sides with numerous, brilliant palatial mansions belonging to its own devotees—both men and women adorned with various fine garments and precious jewels. (9)

There, the sage, filled with great joy, beheld a divine lion-throne fashioned from the finest essence of precious gems and the most excellent jewels, which caused wonder in the minds of those who gazed upon it. (10)
Then, he beheld there the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, established in his nature as Nārāyaṇa beyond all qualities—the omniscient Lord, the Supreme Person, whom the Sātvatas call Vāsudeva.

Some call him by the name Paramātman; some call him the Supreme Brahman and that which is higher than the highest; some call him Brahman, while others, his devotees, call him Bhagavān, Viṣṇu, and Parameśvara.

His limbs are as enchanting as a thousand gods of love; he is eternally youthful, a treasury of compassion, beautiful to behold with an exceedingly peaceful form, transcendent beyond both the perishable and the imperishable, and self-dependent.

He whose side-glances perform the play of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of many cosmic eggs; the great sovereign of countless millions of universes; the one uniquely adored by the entire world; appearing in the guise of the preeminent dancer. (14)

Clad in priceless, divine, and most excellent yellow garments, enriched with ornaments of many precious gems, possessing a complexion like that of a fresh rain-cloud, and wearing beautiful makara-shaped earrings shimmering upon his ears. (15)

He was described as white in complexion because he was enveloped by a vast mass of brilliant white light emanating from his own body; he wore a magnificent crown shining with the essence of excellent gems, and his beautiful eyes were like the petals of an autumn lotus.

His limbs were anointed with fragrant, pure sandalwood paste, and his chest was marked with the Śrīvatsa sign; holding the flute to his mouth with his two lotus-like beautiful arms, he made it resound sweetly.
He was being worshipped by Jayā, Suśīlā, Lalitā, and others, along with hosts of female companions and Rādhā; likewise, he was honored by Ramā, Bhāmā, Kalindajā, Jāmbavatī, and the rest.

He was attended by Dharma, all the Vedas, and the Bhagas, such as Jñāna and the rest, with their pairs of hands joined in reverence; and he was served by his many personal weapons, such as the Sudarśana discus, which had assumed embodied forms.

He was attended by his foremost personal associates, some with the color of emerald, ruby, and gold, and others white, led by Nanda and Sunanda, whose beautiful arms bore the discus, mace, lotus, and conch.

Then he was being attended by many two-armed cowherds, led by Śrīdāman, who were dressed in the attire of gopas and bowed low with devotion; and he was preceded by Garuḍa and the eight humbled manifestations of his own power.

He was served by physical form, tranquility, compassion, nourishment, contentment, and indeed by intelligence; likewise by faith, action, exaltations, friendliness, as well as by forbearance, mindfulness, and wisdom.

Beholding him of such exceedingly wonderful and divine form, with all his senses captivated by the beauty and fragrance of that form, his vision obstructed by tears of joy, his hair standing on end through love, he became filled with bliss. (23)
Having prostrated like a staff before Daṇḍavat, Nārada, overwhelmed with love, stood with his palms joined in reverence, gazing at His face.
Hari honored him, having respectfully inquired after his welfare; he was a singular devotee of his own, whom he himself desired to behold.
Having regained his self-recollection through tasting the nectar of the Blessed One’s words, and filled with the great bliss of seeing him, the sage praised him with devotion.
Nārada said: Victory to you, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O Blessed One, Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the universe! O Vāsudeva, abode of all, eternal beloved of the single-minded devotees! 27.
O You whose feet are to be worshipped even by Rādhikā, Kamalā, and others as a matter of wonder, You alone are the supreme goal for those who desire the ultimate good. 28.
O Hari, you are the eternal self of the eternal selves, the conscious one among the conscious, and you are the supreme Brahman, transcending both the perishable and the imperishable.
Just as purification and accomplishment are attained through supreme devotion to you, so they cannot be achieved by men through other means such as asceticism and the like.
O Lord of the Good, the singular divine moonlight of Your feet is able to instantly dispel the great darkness residing in the hearts of those seeking liberation. (31)
By all the Vedas you alone are to be worshipped, adored, and known; O Blessed One, you have been declared to be the cause of all causes.
In each and every pore of your body, there exists a white light that is peaceful and of the nature of bliss, surpassing the radiance of ten million moons. (33)
In this imperishable abode, which is devoid of qualities and designated as immortal—a mass of splendor—you, the Supreme Person, ever abide yourself, free from all attributes.
Through the power of worshiping you, your devotees indeed become liberated from Time, which strikes fear even into the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa), and from the great terror of Māyā.
I have come to you for refuge—you who are the Lord of the world, the soul of all, the all-pervading Brahman, the Great Person, and the Infallible One.
O Lord of Gods, you ought to grant such grace that my devotion to your lotus feet may always remain unwavering. (37)
Skanda said: Thus praised with devotion by the celestial sage, the Supreme Lord, gladdening him, addressed the muni with words comparable to nectar.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Vision of Śrī Vāsudeva," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 17.
The Blessed One said: "O great sage, that vision of me which has occurred for you is due to your eternal and exclusive devotion, your freedom from hypocrisy, and by my own will."
Non-violence and celibacy—these two are ever present in you, as well as your own duty, tranquility, dispassion, and self-knowledge.
Association with the virtuous, the eightfold yoga, complete restraint of the senses, subsistence on the food of sages, austerity, and freedom from all vices; || 3 ||
And because your devotion is exclusively directed toward me and is preceded by knowledge of my greatness, you indeed behold me here, O observer of noble vows.
O Brahmin, whatever other men may possess such characteristics as these, they too shall behold me, who am dear to those of single-minded devotion, in this very form.
O Brahman, here in this imperishable abode, I dwell eternally together with Rādhā and Lakṣmī, along with those who have taken refuge in me.
I am Vāsudeva in essence, the bestower of the fruits of all actions; I abide as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all embodied beings, being independent.
In that great abode called Vaikuṇṭha, I dwell with four arms together with Lakṣmī, along with my attendants headed by Nanda and Garuḍa.
In my divine abode of light, Śvetadvīpa, I grant my own vision five times daily on earth to those who are liberated while still alive.
Through my own forms known as Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Saṃkarṣaṇa, I perform the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of many millions of cosmic eggs.
At the beginning of creation, O Nārada, Brahmā was created by me from the lotus of my navel; he propitiated me through austerities and sacrifices.
Then, being pleased with him, I granted him his desired boons: "O Brahmin, you shall possess the power to create progeny."
By my boon, they shall all abide in your command alone; moreover, the eternal Vedas shall manifest within your intellect.
And knowledge of my true nature shall arise in you exactly as it is; furthermore, no one shall ever transgress the boundary established by you.
O Brahmā, you alone shall be the bestower of boons to the hosts of gods and asuras, and to the high-souled sages, whenever they desire a boon. 15.
O Creator, whenever you fall into delusion regarding any task that is impossible to accomplish, I shall manifest myself there; merely upon being remembered by you, I will act.

While you are creating the universe, I shall assume the form of a boar and, having slain the Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa who is arrogant in his strength, bring the lost earth back to its own place from the great ocean. (17)
At the end of the day, having become a fish, I shall support the earth along with its medicinal herbs like a boat, as well as Manu and the others, until the end of the night.

For the descendants of Kaśyapa, who were churning the ocean for nectar and were without support, I, in the form of a tortoise, shall bear the churning-stick upon my back, and I shall hold Mount Mandara.
"O Creator, having assumed the body of a man-lion, I shall slay Hiraṇyakaśipu, the son of Diti and destroyer of sacrifices, for the sake of the gods' mission. (20)
Virocana’s son will be the powerful and great asura Bali; he shall displace Śakra from his own sovereignty.
When the three worlds have been seized by him and the Lord of Śacī has turned his face away, I shall be born as the twelfth son of Kaśyapa from Aditi.

Then, O Creator, I shall restore the kingdom of heaven to the Lord of the Gods; I shall re-establish the deities in their own respective places, and I shall indeed pay tribute to Bali, who dwells in the depths of Pātāla.
Then, having been born as the one named Kapila from Kardama and Devahūtī, I shall, endowed with dispassion, propagate the Sāṃkhya system which has been lost over time.
O Creator, after Datta has been instructed by Anasūyā Bhūti in the science of Ānvīkṣikī, I shall then teach that knowledge to Prahlāda and to Yadu.
Having become my son Ṛṣabha on earth through Merudevī, the wife of Nābhi, I shall establish the eternal Dharma known as Pāramahaṃsya.
In the Tretā age, I shall become Rāma, the upholder of the Bhṛgu lineage; and I shall utterly destroy the Kṣatriyas who have broken the bridge and followed the path of the wicked.
When the junction between the Tretā and Dvāpara ages has arrived, I shall become Rāma, born of Kauśalyā from Daśaratha.
The daughter of Janaka, known as Sītā, shall be Lakṣmī incarnate; I shall marry her after breaking that great bow of Īśvara.
Then, in battle, I shall slay the terrible lord of the rākṣasas, who has committed offenses against the divine sages and who abducted Sītā, along with his younger brother.
But great sages such as Vālmīki and others shall then sing my deeds in many ways, by hearing which there shall be the destruction of sin. (31)

At the conclusion of the junction between the Dvāpara and Kali ages, for the sake of destroying the demons who are a burden to the earth and to protect righteousness and the righteous, I shall be born from Vasudeva in Devakī at the city of Mathurā.
"I shall be Kṛṣṇa, known as Vāsudeva, and likewise Saṃkarṣaṇa, Bala; Pradyumna and Aniruddha shall also appear in the lineage of Yadu. (33)
O Lotus-born One, Rādhā will be the daughter of Gopa Vṛṣabhānu; with her, I shall sport in Vṛndāvana.
And Lakṣmī herself, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka known as Rukmiṇī, shall become my wife; I shall marry her after defeating those kings in battle. (35)
Having slain the asuras who are enemies of Dharma, as well as the kings possessed by them, and thereby firmly establishing Dharma, I shall make the earth free from all burdens.
Whosoever’s mind shall be united with me by whatever disposition, I shall lead each and every one of them to the supreme state of Brahman.
Having established the Dharma on earth and brought about the destruction of the Yadu clan, I shall then vanish from this world while all the gods look on.
O Brahmin, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana and others shall indeed sing in many ways of my heroic deeds as Kṛṣṇa, which instantly remove all sins.
Becoming Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, the son of the sage Parāśara, I shall perform the division of the branches of the Veda, like that of a tree.
"Resorting to the Vedic injunctions, I shall become a Buddha and delude the asuras by means of deception—those who oppress the three worlds. (41)
Those Asuras whom I, Kṛṣṇa, together with Arjuna, have slain in battles will cause unrighteousness to prevail on earth when [the time comes].
Then, from the devoted Dharmadeva, I, the sage Nārāyaṇa, shall be born on earth in the land of Kośala as a twice-born chanter of the Sāman hymns.
O dear one, when the sages and Uddhava had thus fallen into falsehood due to the sage’s curse, I, the unborn one, protected them from the Asuras while establishing the true dharma.
At the end of the Kali age, having become Kalki, I shall wander upon a divine steed and slay the people on earth who are filled with Mlecchas and great sin.
And whenever the dharma declared in the Vedas is destroyed by the asuras, there shall be my manifestation for its protection at that very time.
"Therefore, casting aside all anxiety, create subjects just as before. Having granted these boons to him, I then vanished from sight.
O sage, just as those boons were granted to him, so indeed have I acted; I act now and shall continue to act immediately through my own powers.
O Brahmin, for me who am such as this, the Lord of all embodied beings, this vision has become difficult to attain; yet it has occurred solely through your exclusive devotion.
"Choose a boon from me, O best of sages, whatever you desire; I am greatly pleased with you, for my sight is never without fruit. (50)
Skanda said: Having heard these words of the Blessed One, Nārada, the best of sages, considering himself blessed, spoke to that Lord, O Sage. (51)
O Lord, by the mere sight of you, my heart's desire is fulfilled; for I consider this to be difficult to attain even for all embodied beings.
Therefore, for me, there is nothing else desired to be obtained beyond the direct vision of you two, of your followers, of this abode of yours, and of this nectar. (53)
O Acyuta, there is nothing else in this entire cosmic egg that is difficult to obtain for me, such that I would have you request it here from me. (54)
That happiness belonging to other worlds which is obtained through Vedic rites for the gods and the ancestors—even that is indeed perishable. (55)
O Lord, I do not desire any happiness from you beyond that; however, O bull among the bestowers of boons, I ask for one boon that is desired by you.
My intellect, ever increasing its affection for You, is intensely eager to sing of Your virtues and those of Your devotees at all times. (57)
Skanda said: Having promised "So be it," Kṛṣṇa, having been thus entreated by him, gave a great lute suitable for singing and spoke again.
The Blessed Lord said: "Go now from here, O divine sage, to Viśālā Badarī; there, O observer of noble vows, worship me with devotion as the son of Dharma."
For you are my exclusive devotee with a guileless heart; therefore, I hold you in higher regard than even Vidhi, your own father.
O Sage, my single-minded devotees know all of this about me: who I am, what my form is, and what my majesty is.
I alone am to be meditated upon in the hearts of those virtuous ones, and they are mine; for them there is nothing desired other than me, and for me there is nothing apart from them.
Just as chaste wives bring their virtuous husbands under their control by means of their own qualities, so too do my devotees bring even me under their control. 63.
I follow after them with my splendor, as if dependent upon them; for wherever they are, there indeed am I.

O celestial sage, for those on earth who desire liberation, the attainment of Me occurs only through association with the virtuous; it cannot be achieved by any other means—know this to be the truth. 65.
Whenever human beings take refuge in me alone, at that very moment they are liberated from the illusion that binds the living soul.
But a person who has taken refuge in me with whatever disposition may be, attains happiness as he desires, and does not undergo further worldly existence like others.
Skanda said: Having been addressed thus by the Blessed One and having obtained the desired favor, Nārada bowed down with tearful eyes and turned back.
Singing of that very same [being] upon his lute, he beheld a white, pearl-like form moving before him as it had done previously; the bull among the twice-born followed after it.
O Brahmin, having immediately reached the great white island and bowed down to those white beings, Nārada returned and swiftly arrived at Mount Meru.
Then he departed from Mount Meru for Mount Gandhamādana; and from the sky, he swiftly descended toward the vast Badarī.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Incarnation of Śrī Vāsudeva and Other Matters," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-Māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: Then he beheld those two ancient gods, the best of sages, performing a very great penance, established in the Self, and observing mighty vows.
They were even more radiant than the sun that illuminates all the worlds; they bore the Śrīvatsa mark, were worthy of worship, and wore circles of matted hair.
Their arms were marked with the sign of the lotus, and their feet bore the characteristic mark of the wheel; they had broad chests and long arms, and were clad in white, fine, and dense garments.
They had beautiful faces and broad foreheads, with lovely eyebrows and auspicious noses; endowed with auspicious marks, they possessed divine forms and a dense radiance.
Having approached them with humility and performed a circumambulation, she bowed with devotion using the eight limbs of her body and stood before them with palms joined in reverence.
Then those two sages, who were abodes of asceticism, fame, and splendor, having concluded their morning rites and released their silence, [spoke].
With joy and composure, the two of them honored Nārada with water for the feet and the guest-offering; then both he and Nārada sat upon seats made of kuśa grass.
When they had sat down there, that place shone brilliantly, like a sacrificial arena with fires whose great flames are fed by offerings of clarified butter.
Then Nārāyaṇa spoke these words there to Nārada, who was comfortably seated, rested, and had been well-honored with hospitality.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Brahmā, was that Blessed One, the eternal Supreme Soul and the ultimate cause of us both, seen by you in the abode of Brahmā?
Nārada said: O Blessed One, by your grace, I have beheld that Supreme Lord Vāsudeva, who resides in the imperishable abode (akṣaradhāman).
Having come here and been sent by him to serve you both, I shall remain constantly with you two, intent upon that [service].
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "Blessed are you, for you have been graced by the sight of the Lord himself; indeed, O Brahmā, neither any god nor any sage has ever beheld him."
Those who, through exclusive devotion to Him, have attained identity with the Imperishable—they alone, being devotees, behold Him as the cause of all. (14)
That Blessed One, the Supreme Person, possesses a divine form that is difficult to behold; O Nārada, this word which I have uttered is indeed the truth.
There is no one else in the world dearer to him than his devotee; therefore, O best of the twice-born, he himself revealed his own self to you.
With his limbs enveloped by a mass of splendor, possessing a wondrous form that transcends all qualities (guṇas), he is the embodiment of indivisible bliss; he is eternally pure and infallible.

Indeed, his physical form, complexion, and stage of life are not at all ordinary; for him, everything is divine, as are all his implements. He alone is the supreme goal for those devotees who are single-mindedly devoted. || 18 ||
Even by those who have attained the identity of the self with Brahman and from whom the qualities (guṇas) have ceased, devotion to Vāsudeva is performed; for such is his nature.
O great sage, who could possibly describe the majesty of this Supreme Self, the sovereign of inconceivable and infinite powers?
He is the self, the supreme self, and the imperishable self; he is as pure as space, perceivable by divine vision, pure existence alone, the Puruṣa born of Vasudeva.

He possesses all auspicious qualities yet is devoid of [material] attributes; he is the Lord of lords, the one to be known through supreme knowledge, the object of worship, and the sovereign master of those who know Brahman.
He who propitiates that Lord of divine form through exclusive austerity and through righteousness is called the most blessed.
Therefore, O celestial sage, you too, propitiating him through exclusive righteousness, perform austerities here for some time, my dear friend.

"Only through austerity will your soul become utterly purified, so that you shall understand the majesty of that Lord of the virtuous exactly as it is, in its entirety, as it is being told by me. (25)
Know, O Sage, that austerity is the means for accomplishing all goals; it is his heart. That Lord cannot be brought under control by one who has not performed abundant austerity.
Skanda said: Having been thus addressed by the Blessed One, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, that high-minded one was pleased and, desiring to perform penance, spoke to him.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Meeting of Nārada with Nara and Nārāyaṇa," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: O Blessed One, tell me that singular dharma approved by you, by which Vāsudeva, the Soul of the Universe, is always pleased.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "O Brahmin, you have asked well; indeed, your mind is pure. To you, who are affectionate and devoted to me, I shall speak even that which is secret."
This very eternal Dharma was proclaimed by me to Vivasvat at the beginning of the Kalpa; that same Dharma, O Sage, I shall declare to you.

That devotion which, together with knowledge of one's own duty and dispassion, is directed toward that Lord—who possesses all splendor—and is exclusive to Him alone, is indeed the religion of single-mindedness (ekāntika-dharma).
By that very act, the Lord of Goloka Himself becomes exceedingly pleased; and that devotee is born with all his desires completely fulfilled.
Nārada said: I desire to know the characteristics of one's own duty and the others individually; since you are the source of the scriptures, it behooves you to explain them to me.
O Lord of the virtuous, you alone are the root of all the scriptures of the Nigamas and Āgamas, in which the eternal Dharma resides. (7)
You alone are the Lord Vāsudeva in person, beyond the imperishable; as a treasury of compassion, you abide here for the welfare of all beings.

But others besides you—such as Brahmā and the rest—are dependent upon their own inherent natures and qualities; therefore, they do not understand the Dharma and other principles as they truly are. For this reason, please explain them.
Skanda said: Thus questioned by the divine sage, the Lord, the delighter of Dharma and knower of all things, explained his own duties and others in their proper sequence.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The good conduct of the social classes (varṇas) and the stages of life (āśramas) is both specific and general; that which is one's own duty (svadharma) is now being proclaimed.
First, hear the common duty for all men: non-violence is the supreme duty, and it is declared to be the very first among them. (12)

That which consists of not even mentally harming one's own primary duty or occupation, nor that of any living being whatsoever when another way is available—that is considered [the highest form of non-violence]. (13)
Speech should be truthful in such a way that it causes no injury to any living being; and austerity consists in the deliberate restriction of enjoyments prescribed by the scriptures. (14)
The practice of purification is twofold: external and internal. Not taking what belongs to another, whether in their absence or by means of deception, [is the external purification]. (15)
The conquest of lust, greed, and anger through appropriate celibacy; the joyful offering of wealth to a worthy recipient; and contentment with what is obtained from fate. (16)
At a sacred ford, in a holy field, at a sacrifice and the like, or for the attainment of the four aims of life—for oneself or for another—in every way, one must avoid causing harm.
The avoidance of those actions that cause loss of caste, as well as the restraint of the hands, feet, abdomen, genitals, and speech; (18)
The avoidance of all vices, the abstention from liquor and meat, the cessation of sexual misconduct, and the preservation of the noble family dharma; || 19 ||
The fasting of all Ekādaśīs together with the observance of restraints (yamas), and the straightforward performance of vows on the days of Hari’s birth.
Straightforwardness, service to the virtuous, sharing food and other provisions, and devotion to the Lord—these are the common duties for all human beings. (21)
The four castes are declared to be the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; O Sage, I shall describe to you their respective duties and specific characteristics.
Tranquility, self-restraint, forgiveness, purity, faith, devotion to the Lord, austerity, knowledge, and realized wisdom are the duties of the Brahmin, born of his own nature. (23)

Valor, fortitude, magnanimity, strength, splendor, and being a refuge; the protection of cows, Brahmins, and the virtuous, and the performance of sacrifices—these are proclaimed as the duties of the Kṣatriya. (24)

Furthermore, by means of political wisdom alone, these duties of the king consist of the protection of the subjects, the establishment of dharma on earth, and the infliction of punishment upon those deserving of punishment.

Faith in the existence of the afterlife, dedication to giving, service to virtuous Brahmins, lack of contentment with the accumulation of wealth, and industriousness—these indeed are the duties of a Vaiśya. (26)
O best of sages, the specific duty of a Śūdra has been declared as the sincere service of the twice-born, the gods, and cows.

Teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts from pure persons are declared to be the means of livelihood for a Brahmin; among these, the last is traditionally permitted only in times of distress.
For that best of the twice-born who perceives faults even in officiating at sacrifices or teaching, another fourfold means of livelihood has been prescribed.
Gathering grains, begging daily, farming with modest means, and agriculture—among these, O best of the twice-born, each preceding one should be known as superior to the following. (30)
O Nārada, in times of distress, a Brahmin may live by the occupation of a Vaiśya, or even by the occupation of a Kṣatriya, but never by the occupation of a dog.
The Kṣatriya should live by the sword, yet he must protect dharma in every way; if fallen into distress, he may indeed subsist by the occupation of a Vaiśya or act in the manner of a Brahmin.

The livelihood of the king, excluding the Brahmins, is said to consist of the collection of taxes and so forth, after he has gratified all his subjects in accordance with the requirements of place and time. (33)
Even in times of distress, for a Kṣatriya as for a Brāhmaṇa, service to the base is in every way censurable, as it causes the destruction of one's own splendor.

Agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and the fourth, living by lending at interest—these are declared to be the livelihoods of a Vaiśya; likewise, the occupation of a Śūdra is permitted for him in times of distress.
A Śūdra may live by means of wealth obtained through service to the twice-born; however, in times of distress, he may resort to the livelihood of a craftsman or other such occupations.
Once released from the calamity, everyone, having performed the appropriate expiation, should again engage in their respective primary occupations according to their own duties.
One belonging to any of the four castes should associate with the virtuous, but never with the wicked; for association with the virtuous bestows liberation, while evil association leads to hell. (38)
Those who have conquered lust, anger, the relish for flavors, pride, and envy, and who are free from deceit and devoted to Viṣṇu—they are considered by me to be the virtuous and the righteous. (39)

Attached to women and to what belongs to women, and to the tasting of flavors; greedy for wealth, violent, and full of deceitful pride—these are indeed wicked men who merely appear to be devotees. (40)

Having determined that the demonic nature (āsuri-sampat) exists among the wicked and the divine nature (daivi-sampat) among the virtuous as innate qualities, those who desire happiness should serve the holy ones. 41.
Whatever kind of scriptures or persons one associates with, one's intellect becomes like that; therefore, one should not associate with the wicked. (42)
For those men who take delight in serving the virtuous, there is indeed no exalted sovereignty whatsoever that cannot be attained through their own power.
But those men who, though established in their own duty, are hostile toward the virtuous, do not attain a good state by any means whatsoever through any action. 44.
Even if those devoted to Viṣṇu and intent on great worship should harbor malice toward the virtuous, He never becomes pleased with them at any time.
But those who betray their spiritual preceptor, at the end of the body, whatever womb they enter, there they are tormented by hunger and diseases until the end of their lives. (46)
Merely by transgressing against the virtuous, there shall be the immediate destruction of all merits, even those that are great, as well as of one's lifespan and all forms of prosperity. (47)
Therefore, service to the virtuous should be performed by all who desire happiness; sacred pilgrimage sites should be frequented, and Brahmins and cows should be honored. 48.
Those of evil intellect who revile sacred fords and images of the gods—those born of adultery—will certainly suffer the extinction of their lineage. (49)
When one Brahmin is satisfied with excellent food, sacrificial fees, and other offerings, the entire world becomes satisfied and Hari himself is pleased. (50)
If even a single Brāhmaṇa is harmed, the entire world would be harmed; therefore, Brāhmaṇas, who are the very form of Viṣṇu, should be worshipped according to one's ability.
All the hosts of gods reside within the limbs of cows; likewise, all sacred fords (tīrthas) always abide within them.
O Nārada, when one cow is worshipped, all the gods are worshipped; indeed, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) are also considered visited. (53)
If an offense is committed against even a single cow through negligence anywhere, all the deities and all the sacred fords (tīrthas) in their entirety would be offended.
Therefore, people of the four castes, established according to the prescribed rules, must strive with diligence and avoid what is forbidden. (55)

As for those who belong to castes other than the four [traditional] varṇas, their livelihood, provided it is appropriate to their family and entirely free from unrighteousness such as theft and violence, brings about their welfare.
O Sage, the duties of the social classes have been declared by me in brief; now I shall tell you the duties of the four stages of life.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Four Castes," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O best of sages, the student (brahmacārī), the householder (gṛhastha), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), and likewise the ascetic (yati)—these are declared to be the four stages of life (āśramas).
He who, purified by the sacraments and born of a pure womb, has attained the status of the twice-born—that person is indeed a *brahmacārī*; I shall now describe his duties from the beginning.
A student, dwelling in the teacher's house, pure, having conquered his senses and subdued his anger, humble and speaking the truth, should study the Veda.

Restrained, he should perform the fire-oblation in the evening and the morning, practice the wandering for alms, and likewise perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) at the three times of day as well as the daily worship of Viṣṇu.
By the command of the guru alone, one should eat measured food without agitation; one should be constantly devoted to the service of the guru and remain free from vices. || 5 ||
During bathing, eating, fire-offerings, and recitation, one should observe silence; one should not cut one's nails or hair, nor should one excessively scrub the teeth.
One should not run while wearing clothes and should be free from deceit toward the guru. When summoned, one should engage in study, and one should bow to him at the beginning and at the end.

He should not touch those who are untouchable, nor should he converse with those with whom one should not converse; he should never eat what is unfit for consumption, nor should he ever drink what is unfit for drinking.
He should carry a girdle, an antelope skin, a staff, and a water-pot; two white garments, a sacred thread, and a rosary for recitation.
With darbha grass in hand and wearing matted locks, he should avoid grooming his hair; he should also abstain from body ointments, flower garlands, and ornaments.
One should not perform an oil massage, nor apply collyrium or eye-salve; one should also diligently avoid contact with liquor and meat.
A student of sacred knowledge (varṇin) should avoid in every way looking at women, touching them, speaking with them, playing with them, and so forth; he should also avoid even gazing at a woman.
Furthermore, even toward a wooden statue or a painted image of a goddess, the wise man should not touch her, nor should he gaze upon her with the mind. (13)
He should never look at any living being engaged in sexual union; nor should he listen to the virtues or faults of women, nor speak of them.
One should salute even one's own teacher’s wife without touching her; moreover, one should never remain in a secluded place even with one's own mother.

Living with such conduct there, he should remain until he has completed his studies. Thereafter, being dispassionate, he may become a renunciant (nyāsī), or he may remain a lifelong celibate student (naiṣṭhika). It is declared that in the Kali age, those who observe the vow of lifelong studentship lack the necessary qualification [for renunciation].
It should be understood that the term "kali" is used here as a collective designation for sound; O Brahmin, it may mean a forest, or else it refers to a householder who is not dispassionate.

The student life (brahmacarya) is of four kinds: that pertaining to Prajāpati, that pertaining to Savitṛ, that pertaining to Brahmā, and the lifelong (naiṣṭhika); among these, one should adopt one according to one's capacity. || 18 ||

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of a Religious Student," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya, within the second section (Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: One who desires to become a householder should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru according to his own capacity, and by his permission alone, he should perform the rite of returning home (samāvartana).
Then, according to the prescribed rite, he should marry a woman who is suitable for his family, who is younger than himself, free from disease, devoid of masculine characteristics, and sinless.
Then, according to his own capacity, he should daily worship the gods, sages, ancestors, and elemental spirits with the prescribed rites for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa.

One should perform daily bathing, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), recitation (japa), fire-offerings (homa), self-study of scripture (svādhyāya), worship of Viṣṇu, libations (tarpaṇa), the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, and hospitality toward guests.

One should perform meritorious deeds according to one's capacity with wealth acquired through righteous means; being free from attachment, one should support those who depend on one and not oppress them.

One should not harbor enmity toward others regarding one's body or bodily possessions, as if they were cattle; rather, one should abandon the sense of "I" and "mine" with respect to the body and so forth.

One should untiringly seek the company of virtuous devotees of the Lord; one should not associate with those who are addicted to women, nor with those who are addicted to vices, nor with those who are greedy.
One should never look upon another’s wife with lustful intent; nor should one approach even one’s own wife on the occasion of a śrāddha, a festival, or while observing a vow.
Even a person who has attained full maturity in both Sāṃkhya and Yoga may become deluded in a secluded place through the influence of a daughter.
Therefore, a wise man should not sit in a secluded place even with his mother, sister, or daughter; how much less so with any other woman? (10)
Among all inauspicious things, a widow is indeed the most inauspicious; for seeing her or touching her steals away the merit of men. (11)
If, at the time of departure, a widow should appear directly in front [of one], then one must certainly not go; otherwise, death is certain.
The blessings of widowed women are equal to the hissing of black serpents; therefore, one should fear them as much as one would fear ogresses.
One should avoid from afar liquor, meat, intoxicants, gambling, and the like; one should never, even by word, commit an act of malice toward any living being whatsoever. (14)
A believer should listen daily to the accounts of Hari’s incarnations and deeds; he should perform all his actions for the sake of Vāsudeva.
In the months of Ūrja, Māgha, and Vaiśākha, during the Cāturmāsya period, in the intercalary month, and on other meritorious occasions, one should observe special vows.

In a meritorious place and at a meritorious time, a householder should give gifts according to his capacity to a worthy recipient in accordance with the prescribed rite; he should show compassion toward all living beings.
O sinless one, I shall describe to you in detail meritorious regions, meritorious times, and meritorious recipients, which cause the increase of dharma.
This region where I am established is indeed the most excellent on earth; for there, hosts of great sages observe their mighty vows while practicing austerities. (19)
Due to the greatness of this green rice (*haritadbhakta*), the regions possess sanctity; namely Gaṅgādvāra, Madhupurī, and Naimiṣāraṇya. (20)
Kurukṣetra, Ayodhyā, Prayāga, and Gayāśiras; the city of Vārāṇasī and the meritorious hermitage of Pulaha. || 21 ||
Kapilāśrama, Śrīraṅga, Prabhāsa, and Kuśasthalī; the sacred field known as Siddhapada and the great lake of Pauṣkara. || 22 ||
Mount Raivataka is the playground of the Blessed One together with Lakṣmī, as is the sacred Mount Govardhana and the forest of Vṛndāvana.
The seven principal mountain ranges, beginning with Mahendra and Malaya, as well as the highly meritorious Bhāgīrathī, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī. (24)
The Godāvarī, the Sarayū, the Kāverī, the Gomatī, and others—those meritorious great rivers and streams celebrated in the Purāṇas. || 25 ||
Wherever there may be worship of the Lord’s image with great festivals, and wherever there may be devotees who have no other [deity] than the Lord; 26.
Where the best of Brahmins would abide in their own duty, practicing non-violence, and where wild animals and beasts would roam about without fear. (27)
Wherever there are incarnations of Hari, or wherever He dwells—these regions on earth are especially most meritorious. (28)
Even a small act of dharma performed toward these [beings] becomes a thousandfold for men. Now listen, O Nārada, as I describe the times that increase merit. (29)
The two solstices, the equinox, the eclipses of the sun and moon, the day of loss (dinakṣaya), the vyatīpāta yoga, and all the śravaṇa constellations; || 30 ||
The twelfth and eleventh lunar days, the beginnings of the Manvantaras and the Yugas, all these auspicious lunar days, as well as the new moon and the Vaidhṛti yoga, are meritorious.
The four full-moon days conjoined with the lunar mansions of the months, as well as the eight Aṣṭakā days, one's own birth-star (nakṣatra), and the festival days of Hari's birth. || 32 ||
The consecration of oneself, one’s wife, and one’s children, as well as prosperity and the acquisition of worthy recipients—these are the most meritorious times. (33)
The worship of these—gods, ancestors, and the twice-born—according to one's ability, as well as bathing, giving gifts, recitation of mantras, and so forth, indeed yield infinite fruits. (34)
O Nārada, the worthy recipient is indeed the Blessed Lord himself; for just as water given to the root satisfies all the branches, that which is given to him brings satisfaction to everyone. (35)

Those twice-born ones who maintain non-violence, who find contentment through Vedic knowledge, who possess devotion to the true Dharma, and who place Viṣṇu within their hearts—they indeed are the worthy recipients.
Know that those who are single-minded devotees of the Blessed One and who liberate the bound are true worthy recipients (satpātra), for the Blessed One himself dwells within them. (37)
A wealthy person, moreover, should have firm temples built for Viṣṇu, and for the sake of ensuring the continuity of worship, he should also establish means of livelihood for those who perform it.
One should provide reservoirs of water and groves for the sake of Viṣṇu, and one should satisfy virtuous Brāhmaṇas with excellent and flavorful food. (39)
One should perform non-violent Vaiṣṇava sacrifices according to one's capacity and in accordance with the rules, as well as the vows and birth-festivals of Viṣṇu with abundant provisions.

On the new moon day of the dark fortnight of Prauṣṭhapada, on the anniversary of death, and on holy days or festivals, one should perform the Śrāddha for one's parents and their kinsmen according to one's ability.

In rites for the gods and rites for the ancestors, one should honor and feed devoted twice-born Brahmins who abide in their own dharma, regarding them with the thought that they are the Blessed Lord himself.
One should feed two Brahmins at the rite for the gods and three at the rite for the ancestors according to the rule; or one may feed only one at each, but one should never be prolix in the śrāddha.
The place, time, substance, recipient, and articles of worship—these must be extensive according to the scriptures; it is certain that otherwise they would not be so. (44)
A person should never offer meat at a śrāddha, nor should he eat it there; for the ancestors are greatly satisfied by forest foods, milk, and clarified butter.
That non-violence toward every living being through mind, speech, and body—by that alone do all the ancestors, who are exceedingly compassionate, become satisfied. (46)
Therefore, a person devoted to Vāsudeva should never offer meat at a śrāddha ceremony, having understood the true heart of the scriptures and avoided any evil company whatsoever. (47)
One should perform the vows of Viṣṇu together with the restraints such as celibacy and the like; being intent on that alone, one should perform no other task on that day.
One should observe the period of impurity for one's own relatives upon birth or death according to the scriptures, as well as during the eclipses of the sun and the moon.
In disputes concerning worldly affairs as well as in judicial decisions, those who have accepted a deposit and then abandoned it are neither fit for such tasks nor are they to be considered heirs.
O best of the twice-born, wherever these [obstacles] might exist, that task would never succeed; in such a case, there would be the loss of everything—this indeed is the settled conclusion. (51)
These duties of householders have been declared by me in brief; by the performance of which men shall attain their own desired, imperishable happiness. (52)

O Nārada, householders who are twice-born are proclaimed to be of four kinds according to the distinction of their livelihoods, such as that of the *śila* and others, each designated by its respective name.
Now, O best among the righteous, I shall proclaim the duties of women, by abiding in which all women attain their desired happiness. (54)
A husband must always be served and followed like a deity by married women, even if he is aged, diseased, or destitute. (55)
Her kinsmen should be attended to with appropriate service, and the household furnishings should be kept bright and well-ordered. (56)
The house should be kept clean day by day through sweeping, sprinkling, and other such means; one should speak what is pleasant and true, and always abide in purity.
Fickleness, excessive greed, anger, theft, and violence, as well as association with the unrighteous and with women, must be avoided by men. (58)
You must always be devoted to the duties of the Dharma; having abandoned arrogance, you should remain disciplined and have conquered your senses. (59)
Established in devotion to their husbands and in the dharma of the Lord of Ramā, they should practice devotion independently and must not be dependent on anyone else.
A widow, however, should always serve Viṣṇu with the same devotion she once had for her husband; she should neither listen to nor speak of matters related to sensual desire.
Except in times of distress, one should never touch or look upon those with whom one has a close relationship, nor any other persons, out of lustful desire.

There is no fault in a woman whose husband is away touching a child who nurses at the breast or an elderly man; nor is there any fault in speaking with them when some necessary business must be done. 63.
One should not engage in excessive dispute with men regarding worldly affairs; one may speak with them only when necessary, and even then, except in private.
One should never, even by thought, look upon a couple engaged in union, nor even at animals; one should renounce all sensual enjoyments and eat moderately only once a day.
He should not wear garments containing minute living organisms, nor should he wear ornaments; he should not sleep during the day, nor on a bedstead except in times of distress.
She should never consume betel-leaf, nor perform oil-massage or apply collyrium; she should always fear association with men as she would a black serpent.
There is no woman anywhere else who, upon seeing a man, would not fall into delusion, except for Lakṣmī alone. (68)
Therefore, a woman established in dharma who desires her own supreme welfare should not look at the form of a man, nor should she touch him intentionally. (69)
One should always perform vows such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa with devotion and without interruption, remaining ever intent upon the observances.
A young woman should not remain in private even with her father or sons, nor with a young man; she should avoid bad company in every respect. (71)

Whether she be a virtuous wife or a widow, a woman should never conceal the appearance of her own menses; rather, she should observe a fast for three nights and avoid touching humans and other beings.
On the first day she is a Caṇḍālī; on the second, a slayer of a Brahmin; on the third, she is called a washerwoman; on the fourth day, she becomes pure. (73)
Thus, I have described to you in brief the duties of women, by following which wives shall attain great happiness both in this world and the next. (74)

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of a Householder," in the *Śrī-Vāsudeva-Māhātmya*, within the second section (*Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī-Skānda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O sage, I shall now describe to you the rules for the forest-dweller (vānaprastha). The third stage of life is declared to be the third āśrama.
If his wife should be one who is compliant in service, detached from worldly pleasures, and fond of asceticism, then he should enter the forest together with her.
Otherwise, having entrusted her nourishment and protection to his sons and others, he, being detached, should enter the forest alone by himself.
Fearless and diligent, he should dwell there, delighting in austerity; he should build a hut for the sake of the sacred fire, but he himself should live outside it.

In summer he should practice the five-fire penance, in the cold season he should dwell in water, and during the rains he should remain in the open air; thus, having conquered anger and subdued his senses, he should live. || 5 ||
He should wear clothing made of grass, leaves, deerskin, or bark; he should eat the grains of the sages or wild food such as roots and fruits.
One may eat food cooked by fire, ripened by the sun, or even uncooked; however, in the absence of these, one may eat that which has been crushed with a stone or a mortar.
He himself should fetch food every day at the proper time; or he may accept what has been brought by another at the right time, but never at any other time.
Even when the crops are ready to be harvested in their season, he should not take them except in times of distress; rather, he should perform the fire-ritual as before using only wild grains.
He should carry a water-pot, a staff, and the implements for the Agnihotra sacrifice; he should maintain his hair, body hair, beard, and nails, and keep them clean.
He should bathe while massaging his limbs and sleep upon the ground; he should perform penance according to the requirements of place, time, strength, and condition.
The Phenapas, the Audumbaras, the Vālakhilyas, and likewise the Vaikhānasas—these are said to be the four types of forest-dwellers.
According to his capacity, he should dwell in the forest for twelve years, eight, or four; or even for two or one year, and thereafter he should take recourse to renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
If there should be intense dispassion, then renunciation is beneficial; otherwise, the twice-born man should dwell in the forest for as long as he lives.
Having performed renunciation according to the prescribed rules and entered the fourth stage of life (turīyāśrama), he should wear a loincloth for modesty and a single patched garment.
He should carry a staff, a water-pot, and a water-strainer; he should practice right conduct and go for alms at the proper time to the house of a twice-born man.
An ascetic should not go for alms at the house of only one person every day; he should never become greedy for flavors, and he should eat moderately.
A mendicant dwelling in the forest hermitage generally accepts alms; by means of that exceedingly pure food, his mind indeed becomes purified.
If one smells meat or liquor even with the nose, one should observe the Pārāka vow; one should remain purified through proper conduct and ritual cleanliness, and should not touch Śūdras and others.
One should perform the worship of Viṣṇu daily and eat what has been offered to Viṣṇu; one should also recite the twelve-syllable mantra of Viṣṇu or the eight-syllable mantra.
One should not engage in false speech, nor should one conduct discourse for the sake of a livelihood; one should not be attached to false scriptures, nor should one make one's living from them. (21)
He should study the true scripture which reveals bondage and liberation; he should not construct monasteries and the like, and he should abandon the notions of "I" and "mine."

Except during the four-month rainy season, he should not dwell in one place unless there is an emergency; and by means of knowledge, he should understand the true nature of his own self as being the form of Hari.

A practitioner of yoga should never indulge in lust, anger, fear, enmity, or the accumulation of wealth, grain, and the like; rather, he should observe the restraints (yamas) and the observances (niyamas).
Even if an ascetic is endowed with intense knowledge and detachment, he will certainly fall from his state through contact with women, wealth, ornaments, and fine garments. (25)
One who has renounced should avoid fragrant substances such as flowers, sandalwood paste, and oils; otherwise, he would indeed possess the notion that the body is the self.
To whatever extent one's food is, to that same extent desire for women will enter him; therefore, measured and flavorless food is beneficial for the renunciant. (27)
One who desires the attainment of liberation should not listen to vulgar talk; for by hearing such things, men's taste for the stories of Viṣṇu is instantly destroyed.
A renunciant should neither look at nor touch even a woman made of pictures; for merely by seeing the form of a woman, many ascetics have fallen from their state. (29)
The Kuṭīcaka, the Bahūdaka, the Haṃsa, and the Paramahaṃsaka—thus the ascetic is said to be of four kinds, according to the distinctions of dispassion.
Those virtuous ones who shall belong to me, clothed in saffron robes—even those established in the fourth stage of life—must perform for my sake the cooking of food and other such tasks. (31)
For those who are devotees of Śrī Vāsudeva and possess intense dispassion, their dharma is said to be service to Him, both by day and by night. (32)
And even a single moment of those who abound in wisdom and discernment would never be in vain without the ninefold devotion to Viṣṇu.
Even if one is endowed with all virtues, if he is averse to the Blessed One, the Vaiṣṇavas will surely abandon him, even if he be their own kinsman.
Every day, the devotees of Hari should eat the pleasing food of Lord Hari, which has been consecrated with the water from His feet and mixed with tulasī.
Those who contemplate Viṣṇu must absolutely avoid any association with women or those attached to women; otherwise, their meditation on Him will be lost.
Except for the Blessed Vāsudeva alone, there is no other man whatsoever who, upon seeing a woman, does not become infatuated. (37)

One who renounces should never dwell in a place where, by staying there, the hearing of women's voices and the sight of them would occur repeatedly; for by dwelling there, he would fall away from dharma.
Desire, greed, relishing flavors, attachment, pride, and likewise anger—these six defects that grant worldly existence must be abandoned with effort. (39)

Regarding these aforementioned duties, whatever transgression may occur for any person, an expiation for that must be performed according to one's ability and in accordance with the scriptures. || 40 ||
Thus, O Nārada, the duties of the four castes and the four stages of life, as well as those of the Vaiṣṇavas, have been declared by me to you in brief. (41)
The student and the ascetic, established in dharma, indeed attain the world of Brahmā; the forest-dweller attains the world of the Ṛṣis, and the householder shall obtain heaven.
Those people who perform these [rites] for Śrī Viṣṇu with devotion shall all, at the end of their bodies' existence, attain the world of Viṣṇu. || 43 ||

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of Forest-Dwellers and Ascetics," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-Māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Now I shall describe to you the nature of knowledge as determined by Sāṃkhya; for that by which the field (kṣetra) and so forth are known is indeed defined as knowledge. || 1 ||
Vāsudeva is the Supreme Brahman, the Great One in the abode of the Imperishable; in the beginning, He alone existed, without a second, devoid of qualities, and possessed of a divine form.
Then that primordial nature, which is the root of all effects and is endowed with time, became concealed within the imperishable splendor, like the night in the light of the sun.
When the desire to create the cosmic eggs arose within him, then, at the very beginning, that Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) manifested together with Time.
When Vāsudeva, taking up that power of time in his imperishable form, gazed upon it with the desire to create, then indeed she was agitated.
From her, O Sage, millions of primary beings (pradhāna) and individual spirits (puruṣa) were born; those spirits were then joined with the primary beings by the will of the Lord.
Men deposited embryos within them, and from those [embryos] were born countless cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas); among these, however, one is now being described in detail.
In the beginning, Mahat was born from that golden Puruṣa; from him arose Ahaṃkāra, and from that, the three qualities, Sattva and the others.
From Tamas, the five subtle elements (tanmātras) and the gross elements were born; from Rajas, the ten sense organs, along with the intellect (buddhi), and the great ego (mahat) arose.
From Sattva, the sense organs and the deities were born, as was the mind; these deities are generally proclaimed by the designation of "principles" (tattvas). || 10 ||
Impelled by Vāsudeva through their respective portions, they brought forth the divine body known as Virāṭ, which is the refuge of all moving and unmoving beings.
And because that Vairāja Puruṣa lay upon the waters he himself had created, he is called Nārāyaṇa by the Vedas and other scriptures.
From that navel-lotus Brahmā arose; then from the heart-lotus Viṣṇu was born, characterized by the quality of Sattva; and from the forehead Hara appeared, characterized by the quality of Tamas.

From these very places, three powers (śaktis) emerged; among them was Durgā, who was tāmasī, as well as Sāvitrī, who was rājasī, and Śrī, who was sāttvikī—all of them adorned with garments and ornaments. (14)
By the command of Vairāja, they approached the three beginning with Brahmā: Durgā approached Rudra, Sāvitrī approached Brahmā, and the last one [Lakṣmī] approached Viṣṇu. (15)

O Sage, Caṇḍikā and others were born by the thousand through a portion of Durgā; the powers headed by Trayī were born from a portion of Sāvitrī; and those headed by Dussahā were born from a portion of Śrī.
Therein, at the beginning, he who was Brahmā arose from the navel-lotus of Vairāja; situated upon that lotus in the single ocean, he did not perceive anything whatsoever.
Not yet having attained the awareness of his own emission, he did not recognize himself; reflecting "Who am I? From whence [did I come]? he desired to see that which is the support of the lotus.
Though he entered it and traveled downward, searching for its root, a hundred years passed for him, yet he did not find its end.
Having gone upward once more, he then sat down, exhausted; the Lord, whose form was invisible, said to him, "Perform austerity, perform austerity! (20)
Having heard that and not seeing its speaker anywhere, he performed penance for a thousand divine years, just as he had been instructed by his guru.
Then, to him who was performing penance in the lotus and whose soul was purified by austerity, Acyuta revealed his own abode, Vaikuṇṭha, while he was in meditative absorption.
In that place where even the three qualities of *pradhāna*, beginning with *rajas*, do not exist in the slightest degree, nor is there any fear of *kāla* or *māyā*.
In that splendor, radiant like ten thousand suns risen simultaneously, he beheld Vāsudeva, possessing a beautiful, divine, and dark form.
The omnipresent Lord has four arms, holding a mace, a lotus, a conch, and a discus; he wears yellow garments and is adorned with a crown of great jewels and other ornaments.
It was graced by Nanda, Tārkṣya, and other four-armed attendants (pārṣadas), as well as by the eight Siddhis and the six Bhagas, all with their palms joined in reverence.
Having prostrated before that Lord seated upon the lion-throne together with Śrī, Viriñca stood with palms joined in reverence, his mind filled with joy.
The Blessed One said to him, "O Brahmā, I am pleased with your austerity; choose from me a boon that you desire, for you are dear to me. (28)
Thus addressed by him, Brahmā—recognizing the Lord as the one who impels him toward austerity and himself as the creator of the universe—begged for his desired boon.
"O Lord, grant me the power to emit progeny; salutations to you! Furthermore, show such grace that I may not be bound even therein. (30)

Then the Blessed One said to him: "Your heart's desire shall be fulfilled. Having meditated upon oneness with me through the Vairāja-samādhi, create subjects; and whenever there is a task impossible for you to accomplish, remember me, the granter of wishes."
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu vanished; then Brahmā, through one-pointed concentration on the Vairāja state, beheld all the worlds that had previously been dissolved into himself.
Having attained the power of emission (visarga-śakti), he set his mind upon creation; at that moment, the Sun, consisting of the light of Brahman, appeared.
Having placed him within the egg, he then mentally created the four original sages, the Sanas, who were purified by austerity and devotion.
"Create progeny," he then said to them; but those foremost of lifelong celibates did not accept his word, and the Creator of the Universe became angry with them.
From the forehead of that enraged one, Rudra, consisting of darkness (tamas), emerged; then, restraining his fury with his mind, he created the lords of progeny (the Prajāpatis).
Marīci, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Bhṛgu, Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Kardama, Dakṣa, and likewise Aṅgiras; || 37 ||
Then he created Dharma from his heart and Adharma from his back; he produced Desire from his mind, Speech from his mouth, and Anger from his eyebrows. (38)
Then, from his four faces, he created these four pillars of dharma: purity, austerity, compassion, and truth. (39)
From his eastern mouth he created the Ṛgveda, from the southern the Yajurveda, from the western the Sāmaveda, and from the northern that known as the Atharvaveda.
From his mouth, he created the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the sacrifices, a hundred Brahmins, as well as the Vasus, Ādityas, Maruts, Viśvedevas, and Sādhyas.
From his two arms he created a hundred Kṣatriyas, from his two thighs a hundred Vaiśyas, and from his two feet a hundred Śūdras; he produced them together with their respective means of livelihood.

He created the stage of studentship (brahmacarya) from his heart, the householder’s life (gārhasthya) from his loins, the forest-dweller’s stage (vanāśrama) from his chest, and renunciation (saṃnyāsa) from his head. || 43 ||
From his chest he created the hosts of ancestors, from his hips the asuras, and from his anus he brought forth Death, Nirṛti, and the hells.
Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Siddhas, serpents, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas; mountains, clouds, and lightning, as well as oceans and rivers. || 45 ||
Brahmā, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, created from his own limbs all trees, animals, birds, and everything both stationary and moving.

When, even after beholding this creation, he was not entirely pleased, he then meditated upon Hari and, through austerity, knowledge, and meditative absorption, brought forth the sages beginning with Svāyambhuva, the Manus, and human beings as well.
Then, being pleased, he fashioned for the residence of all as was appropriate the worlds of Svarloka, Bhuvarloka, and Bhūrloka.
But for those whose past karma was of a certain kind, the Creator, having established them in corresponding places, ordained their respective modes of livelihood. (49)

He ordained nectar for the gods, food for men and sages, and medicinal herbs; he assigned wine and meat to the yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, tigers, serpents, and the like, and grass and such for the livelihood of cattle, deer, and other animals. (50)
He ordained the sacrificial offering for all the Viśvedevas, as well as the *kavya* (offering to ancestors) for the formless and the embodied Pitṛs.
And wine, meat, and other offerings were presented by Daityas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and others who were intent on the worship of those Śaktis born of the Durgās.
Likewise, by the worshippers of the Śaktis born of Sāvitrī, such as the Ṛṣis and others, sacrificial offerings were made at the sacrifice: the food of sages, grain, and medicinal herbs.
And by those devoted to the worship of the Śrījātā powers, milk-rice, clarified butter, sugar, and other offerings were presented by gods, asuras, and humans. (54)
Then that Lord of the Prajāpatis spoke to all the creatures: "The gods and the ancestors are to be worshipped with sacrifices consisting of *havya* and *kavya* offerings. (55)
For these will fulfill your cherished desires; indeed, those who do not worship them shall go to hell.
For this boundary was thus established by him, whose self is Nārāyaṇa; therefore, rites for the gods and the ancestors must always be performed by people according to the prescribed rules. (57)
Then Brahmā, for the protection of the bridge of dharma for all beings, established those who were the foremost among various classes as Manus.
O Sage, by the will of Vāsudeva alone, such manifold creation occurs from the Vairāja [Brahmā], who is of the nature of Brahman, in every single Kalpa.
Just as the designations, Vedas, scriptures, and rituals were in a previous kalpa, so too shall all those dharmas and their qualified practitioners be in another kalpa.
He who is called Viṣṇu is also of the nature of the Vairāja Puruṣa; he nourishes all the worlds while strictly maintaining the established boundaries.

When the embankments protected by Manu and others are breached by Asuras who can assume any form at will, then Vāsudeva himself, being entreated by Brahmā and the other gods, manifests upon the earth.
Those incarnations of the Blessed One that have occurred and those yet to be are such that their number cannot be calculated even by those most skilled in calculation. (63)
For the protection of the True Dharma, the gods, and the virtuous, for the death of those who harm them, and for the welfare of all beings, the manifestation of the Lord of Sages occurs. (64)
That Vāsudeva, the sovereign lord of all, abides both united with and separate from Prakṛti, Puruṣa, and their effects, within his own abode.
O Sage, just as Agni, Varuṇa, and the other gods remain in their respective worlds after pervading these worlds with their own portions, so does this Blessed One remain.
Just as He existed prior to creation—as pure Being-Consciousness-Bliss, singular, pure, and devoid of qualities—so too does He remain stainless even when associated [with the world].
Just as space, though pervading its respective effects within air, fire, water, and earth, remains untainted, so indeed does this [Self] remain as it was before.
He is proclaimed to be the one to be worshipped by all, the controller, and the all-pervading; furthermore, in ultimate dissolution, he remains exactly as he was before.
O Nārada, this Vairāja Puruṣa who is mentioned here is to be known as the one named Īśvara; he is independent, omniscient, and has brought Māyā under his control.
The three—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva—are indeed His own forms, endowed with the qualities of rajas and the others, performing actions in accordance with their respective qualities. (71)
Those gods, asuras, humans, and others who have arisen from Brahmā are indeed designated as "living beings" (jīva); they possess limited knowledge and are dependent upon another.

The bodies of both living beings and lords are designated as "fields" (kṣetra), consisting of the principles beginning with the Great One (mahat); however, those who know them are called "knowers of the field" (kṣetrajña).

The knowledge that consists of understanding the distinct characteristics of the fields, the knowers of the fields, the Pradhāna-puruṣa, Māyā, the power of Time (Kāla-śakti), the Imperishable (Akṣara), and the Supreme Self—that is called true knowledge. || 74 ||

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Knowledge," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O best of sages, I shall now describe to you the characteristic of detachment (vairāgya). It is defined as a complete lack of interest in all perishable objects. (1)
Indeed, all forms whatsoever that originate from the illusory person (māyāpuruṣa) are destroyed by the power of time belonging to the Blessed Lord, for they are subject to his control.
Through perception, inference, and verbal testimony, those possessed of discernment have determined the unreality of created things and the reality of the Self. (3)
This Time moves by means of constant dissolution, occasional dissolution, elemental dissolution, and absolute dissolution.
These embodied beings are constantly subject to decay and transformation; for it is observed there that childhood, youth, and old age follow one another in succession.
Because of its subtlety, it is not perceived, just like the movement of a lamp's flame or the gradual growth of fruit appearing on a tree.
In each and every state, great suffering is observed; indeed, suffering recurs again and again throughout the states of waking and the rest.
Abundant internal suffering is observed, as well as that arising from other beings; here too, there is indeed only suffering for embodied beings caused by divine forces.
"Alas, alas! My son has died; alas, my wife is dying! A tiger devoured my father, and my daughter-in-law was bitten by a snake. (9)
"Alas! My great mansion, along with its furnishings, has been consumed by fire today. How shall I nourish my own family, for Indra has not sent down rain? (10)
"Alas! My field, so rich with crops, has been burnt by the fire of frost; my cows are being carried off by thieves, and all my possessions have been plundered. (11)
"He has been severely punished by the king, and alas, he has been violently beaten by his enemy! What shall I do, and to whom shall I speak? My mother is unchaste. (12)
"I shall drink poison! Alas, alas! Today my wife has been seized by the enemy! Oh, my sister has been carried off by the Mlecchas! Alas, alas! The foe has struck at my vital organs!"
"O beloved, because of the extreme agony of fever, alas! these messengers of Yama!"—thus indeed are people seen everywhere crying out in lamentation. (14)
As the various states of the body undergo birth and death every moment through the passage of time, one experiences the suffering that is one's own *prārabdha* (commenced karma).
Indeed, at the end of one's prārabdha karma, there occurs the incomparable suffering of death; and even after dying, great misery is experienced in the form of the torments of Yama.
Then, having been born again and again among the womb-born, sprout-born, sweat-born, and egg-born classes of beings according to their karma, they die once more in a state of suffering.
Thus, O Sage, the eternal dissolution has been described to you through subtle vision; now I shall speak of the dissolution known as the occasional (naimittika).
That dissolution which occurs by taking the night as its cause belongs to the Creator of the Universe; it is called the occasional (naimittika) dissolution, and it is also the daily (dainandina) one.
O Sage, a thousand cycles of four yugas constitute a day of the Creator of the Universe, and his night is of equal duration; that pair is called a Kalpa.
O Brahmin, every single day there arise fourteen Manus who protect the bridge of dharma.
Among them, the first was Svāyambhuva Manu; after him were Svārociṣa, Auttami, Tāmasa, Raivata, and then Cākṣuṣa.
Śrāddhadeva, Sāvarṇi, Bhautya, and after that Raucya; then the one named Brahmasāvarṇi and Rudrasāvarṇi as well. (23)
Then there is the one named Merusāvarṇi, and Dakṣasāvarṇi is the last; these fourteen Manus are said to exist within a single day of Brahmā. (24)
The duration of each Manu is seventy-one cycles of the Yugas; and the time of one Yuga consists of twelve thousand divine years.
O best of sages, when the fourteenth Manu has reached his end, the evening twilight of the Creator arises.
At the end of the day, the Vairāja [Brahmā], established in his power, withdraws all energies; then Rudra, whose self is the Vairāja, strives to destroy the three worlds.
At first, there occurs an exceedingly fierce drought lasting for a hundred years; then, all living beings of little substance on earth perish entirely.
And the exceedingly fierce rays of the sun at the time of universal dissolution quickly drink up every bit of moisture on the earth, down even to the netherworld (pātāla).
Having dried up the water of the lakes, the rivers, and the oceans in every way, that sun brings all the worlds to destruction.
Then the earth becomes devoid of moisture, with all its stationary and moving beings destroyed; parched and severely shriveled, it resembles the back of a tortoise.
Then Kālāgnirudra emerges from the mouth of Śeṣa; he burns the seven nether worlds, as well as the realms of Bhuḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
Having consumed the ten worlds and being terrifying with its whirling flames, the Fire of Time (Kālāgni), which has driven the Maharloka to flight, revolves.
The thirty gods, whose authority on earth has ended and who dwell in heaven, go from Maharloka to Janaloka, severely afflicted by the flames of fire.
Furthermore, those sages who follow the dharma of renunciation and have attained the state of perfection likewise depart from the surface of the earth for the world of the ṛṣis.
Then, from that [place], terrible clouds of the dissolution arise in the sky—resembling herds of great elephants, flashing with lightning, and roaring loudly. (36)
Some were smoke-colored, some yellow, and some resembled the white water-lily; some were like the juice of lac, and others were like the feathers of a blue jay.

Having extinguished the great fire after raining for a hundred years day and night, those massive clouds, pouring down thick torrents and thundering, fill the interior of the cosmic egg as far as the pole star (dhruva).
In that single ocean of water, the Lord Vairāja-puruṣa, whose nature is Aniruddha, lies upon his bed of the king of serpents.

Then the gods and the sages, who were under the influence of the qualities of passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and darkness (tamas), and who were drawn by their own respective attributes along with Viriñca, entered his belly and lay there in a long sleep.
But those who, having realized the identity of Brahman and the Self, have brought the three qualities under control, worship Vāsudeva through the very dharma of renunciation. || 41 ||
Having made their abode in those four worlds beginning with Maharloka, they dwell there at ease, praising that Vairāja.
That Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, contemplating his own nature as the Supreme Self known as Vāsudeva, indeed lies in yogic sleep.
At the end of the night, all those who were his internal fires arise together with Brahmā, just as before, each according to their karma and their respective offices.
Thus, the incidental dissolution (naimittika), characterized by the destruction of the three worlds, has been described to you; now I shall proclaim the elemental dissolution (prākṛta).
Three hundred and sixty such kalpas as have been described constitute one year of Brahmā, the Creator.
Fifty of those constitute a *parārdha*; twice that is considered the lifespan of Brahmā. When the period known as *parā* is completed, the great dissolution (*mahā-saṃkṣaya*) occurs.
Having withdrawn his own Virāṭ body by means of the form of Saṃhāra-Rudra, Vairāja desires to go to his own supreme, attributeless (nirguṇa) nature.
Then there occurs a drought lasting for a hundred years as described before; and the Saṅkarṣaṇa fire of time burns the cosmic egg without exception.
Then, O Sage, the most terrifying clouds of dissolution rain down for a hundred years with torrents shaped like pestles.
Then, by the will of Vāsudeva, there occurs the complete dissolution of all modifications, beginning with the Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas. 51.
The waters indeed first swallow up the quality of the earth, which consists of smell; then, its smell having been taken away, the earth becomes fit for dissolution.
Fire, whose quality is heat, swallows taste; thereafter, that [taste] dissolves. Wind, whose quality is touch, swallows form; then that [form] dissolves. (53)
Then space swallows the quality of wind, which is touch; consequently, the wind becomes tranquil, while space remains unobstructed.
The source of the elements (bhūtādi) swallows its quality, sound, and the ether (kha) dissolves; thereafter, the sense organs dissolve into the ego (ahaṃkṛti) of the nature of light (taijasa).
In the sattvic ego, the mind dissolves into the deities; for whatever has arisen from something, that indeed dissolves back into it.
The threefold ego (ahaṃkāra) dissolves into the principle of the Great One (mahattattva); that [Great One] dissolves into Pradhāna, that into Puruṣa, and then that into Mūlaprakṛti.
