This is celebrated as the dissolution known as *prākṛtika*, wherein the individual souls (*jīva*) and lords (*īśa*) become latent within the unmanifest (*avyakta*) by the will of Hari.

And when Māyā and the two Puruṣas dissolve into the imperishable Radiance by His will, that one Lord alone remains; at that time, O Nārada, that dissolution should be known as the one called absolute (ātyantika).
Thus, by these four kinds of dissolutions through the temporal power of the Lord, having bound everything that is unreal therein, the resulting lack of attachment is called dispassion (vairāgya).

Knowing that all gods other than Vāsudeva are under the sway of time and illusion, and abandoning attachment to them while always maintaining it toward Him alone, that service performed with deep affection is called *bhakti*. (51)
Hearing [His name], chanting [His glories], remembering Him, serving His feet, worshiping Him, bowing down to Him, serving as His servant, befriending Him, and surrendering one's very self. (62)
He who serves with devotion by means of these nine dispositions, with an undistracted mind, is indeed called a devotee. (63)
O Sage, this devotion, when joined with the three qualities beginning with one's own duty (svadharma), is called "exclusive" (ekāntika) dharma, and it is that which is Bhāgavata.
Indeed, the exclusive dharma is attained by men through direct association with the Blessed One and with such devotees of his, and never otherwise. (65)
Indeed, for those seeking liberation, there is no other supreme means like this one, which brings about the highest good for men and destroys all that is inauspicious. (66)
O best of sages, for the sake of accomplishing the absolute Dharma, a person should be devoted to *kriyā-yoga*, by means of which action one attains freedom from all actions (*naiṣkarmya*).

O great sage, this supreme reality, the secret of the Vedas and Purāṇas which destroys the flood of sins, has been declared by me; you should grasp it in your heart with single-minded focus, a pure intellect, and true faith.
There is nothing more purifying than Vāsudeva; there is nothing more auspicious than Vāsudeva. There is no deity higher than Vāsudeva; there is no desired object greater than Vāsudeva. (69)

Even one who utters His name here but once, even without conscious intent, at the moment of the body's end—even if he be a Puṣkasa—is swiftly liberated from the stream of worldly existence; worship that Vāsudeva.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Dispassion and Devotion," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 25.
Skanda said: Having heard the exposition of the exclusive dharma (ekāntadharma) spoken by the Blessed One, Nārada, with a joyful mind, questioned him once again. || 1 ||
Nārada said: "O Lord, the exclusive dharma has been perfectly expounded by you. Having heard it, a great joy has arisen within my mind. (2)
O Blessed One, I wish to understand that Kriyāyoga which is taught by you for the sake of his accomplishment and which is approved by you. (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The ritual procedure for the worship of Vāsudeva, known as Kriyāyoga, is now proclaimed; it has indeed been described in many ways within the Vedas and the Tantras.
Due to the diversity of the inclinations of devotees and because of its manifold nature, that Vāsudeva is extensively manifested in many forms.
Indeed, there is no end to it when it is being told in its entirety; therefore, I shall speak to you in brief that which increases devotion.
Those of the four castes and the [four] stages of life who have indeed received the Vaiṣṇava initiation, as well as women of the four castes—these are declared to be the qualified candidates here.

O twice-born ones, initiated women should worship with mantras declared in the Vedas, Tantras, and Purāṇas, along with the root mantra; virtuous Śūdra women should worship using the root mantra alone. The root mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa should be known as the six-syllabled one (ṣaḍakṣara). || 8 ||
Vāsudeva should be worshipped with devotion and sincere hearts by all these people, as they each protect their own respective duty according to the prescribed rule.

At the outset, however, a person should receive Vaiṣṇava initiation from an excellent preceptor who is established in the ever-exclusive dharma, belongs to the Brahmin caste, and is a treasure-house of compassion. (10)
One who is endowed with both knowledge and devotion, yet devoid of his own duty (svadharma), or one whose soul is captivated by women, should never be made a guru. || 11 ||
Initiation, knowledge, and devotion obtained from a teacher who is dominated by women will never bear fruit, just as a young woman who consorts with a eunuch cannot produce offspring.
Therefore, having received initiation from a true guru, one should wear a garland of tulasī around the neck and apply vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the forehead and other parts with gopīcandana.
A devotee who delights in the worship of Viṣṇu, having thoroughly understood the procedure for worship as proclaimed in the scriptures by his guru, should then commence the worship.
Having risen during the final watch of the night, or at the Brahma-muhūrta, a devotee should meditate for half a muhūrta upon Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, within his heart.
Having recited its name and that of its constituent channels, one should then perform the rules of purification and proceed with the cleansing of the teeth.

Having first performed the bath for the purification of the limbs, one should bathe with the recitation of mantras; then, taking pure earth and other materials, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) that is an ancillary part of the bath.

Having put on two washed garments and seated oneself on a pure seat, and having applied the vertical *puṇḍra* mark, one should perform the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), the fire-oblation (*homa*), the recitation of mantras (*japa*), and so forth.
Then, one should bring all the offerings—clothing, sandalwood, flowers, and so forth—avoiding those that have come into contact with impure things such as meat or liquor. (19)
[These fruits] which have not been offered to the gods, the ancestors, or others; which have not been smelled by men; and which are free from hair, insects, and the like. (20)
Having arranged them on the right side, as well as the articles for worship, one should then light the lamp with clarified butter or with oil.
Then, one should sit upon a pure seat made of silk, wool, wood, or other materials, in the presence of an image of Vāsudeva.
O Sage, the image may be made of stone, metal, wood, or even painted, or it may be composed of jewels; it may be white, red, yellow, or black.
That [image] of Kṛṣṇa should be made with either two arms or four arms; in the case of the two-armed form, he should hold a flute in both hands.

Alternatively, she may hold a discus and a conch in her right hand, while in the other [left] hand she holds a lotus; or she may hold a lotus in her right hand and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in the left.
O best of sages, in the hands of the second [form], one should hold a mace, a lotus, a conch, and a discus, starting from the lower right hand in sequence.
One should place Śrī on the left side of both forms of Hari; however, on the left of the flute-holder, one should place Rādhā, the Queen of the Rāsa dance.
Moreover, this twofold form—indivisible, endowed with auspicious marks, and perfect in all its limbs—shall grant success to the worshiper. (28)
Lakṣmī, however, should be depicted with two arms in the presence of Vāsudeva, holding a lotus in her hand and adorned with garments and ornaments. (29)
Rādhikā, too, should be like Lakṣmī—two-armed and sweetly smiling—holding a lotus or a flower-garland in her lotus-like hands.
The image of Hari is of two kinds: immovable and movable. Regarding the former, there should be no performing of invocation (āvāhana) or dismissal (visarjana).

Furthermore, for the deities of its limbs, there is no requirement for invocation (āvāhana) and so forth; nor is there a fixed rule regarding the directions for their worship, though they should remain facing [the principal deity]. (32)

In the case of the Śālagrāma as well, it should be done exactly in this way, without the invocation (āvāhana) and other such rites; however, in other cases involving movable bases, those respective rites must be performed by the worshippers.
In that case as well, for a painting made on wood, the worshipper must not perform the touching with water or the anointing; rather, only the wiping clean should be performed.
Facing north, facing east, or facing the moving image, one should worship Hari with whatever offerings are available according to one's ability. (35)
The Soul of the Universe is pleased even with water offered with faith, sincerity, and devotion; how much more so, then, by every form of worship?
A man devoid of faith and other virtues does not joyfully accept gifts of ornaments such as gems and gold, nor the four kinds of food and so forth, even when they are offered.
Therefore, O Sage, for the sake of his own welfare, a man endowed with devotion should constantly perform the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who bestows all desired blessings. (38)

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Qualification for Kriyā-yoga and Other Matters," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 26 ||

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Once the surface of the earth has been purified by digging, sprinkling, smearing, and other means, one should place a four-legged pedestal that is beautifully adorned with various colors.
Facing east, the priest should cause the feet of the pedestal to be placed in the corners; upon those four, he should install the [deities] beginning with Dharma, in the form of lions.
One should place white Dharma in the southeast (Agni), red Jñāna in the southwest (Nairṛti), yellow Vairāgya in the northwest (Vāyu), and dark-blue Aiśvarya in the northeast (Aiśāna).
Then, one should sequentially place Manas, Dhī, Citta, and Ahaṃkāra—yellow, red, white, and black respectively—in the directions starting from the east upon the limbs of the pedestal.
O best of sages, the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas—red, white, and dark respectively—are to be established upon the three strips of the pedestal.
Then, one should install the Śaktis, beginning with Vimalā, two by two upon each of the four limbs that consist of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
One should place two fair-complexioned goddesses, Vimalā and Utkarṣiṇī, in the east; they play beautiful lutes, wear yellow garments, and are well-adorned.
One should place Jñāna and Kriyā in the south, dressed in yellow garments and possessing a reddish luster; one of them plays a cymbal (tāla) and the other likewise plays a drum (mṛdaṅga).
Thereafter, one should place the two Yogāpradhyās, both dark-complexioned and dressed in crimson garments, each playing a flute individually.
Then, one should place [the goddess] Satyeśānī, who is golden-colored, in the north; both of them are dressed in dark blue garments and are playing the parivādī lute.
One [deity] named Anugrahā should be placed on the fillet with palms joined in reverence; all of these, moreover, are to be made two-armed and well-adorned. || 11 ||
Upon the pedestal, one should fashion a white island with white cloth; in its center, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus with a radiant pericarp.
Having set aside one-twelfth [of the area] from the exterior of the lotus-field, one should divide its center into equal parts by means of three circles.

Among those, the first is the location of the pericarp (karṇikā), the middle is that of the filaments (kesara), the third is that of the petals (patra), and the tips of the petals (dalāgra) are on the outside. || 14 ||
And one should construct a city around it with four gates, using various colored materials such as turmeric, saffron, and the like. (15)
Or one should fashion beautiful lotuses and other designs there with rice grains; in the center, one should beautifully adorn the pericarp of the lotus with a golden color.
O Sage, the worshiper should place eight petals of crimson color, or of golden hue, all around that [lotus] in the eight directions.
The eastern gate should be red, and the southern one dark blue; the western one yellow, and likewise the northern one the color of crystal.
Having placed various flowers in the space between the city and the lotus, one should then place Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the center and Rādhikā to His left.
Then, one should place Saṃkarṣaṇa behind this Rādhākṛṣṇa; he has four arms, holds a parasol, has a fair complexion, and wears blue garments.
On the right, one should place Pradyumna of the Blessed One, clad in yellow garments, four-armed, dark as a rain-cloud, holding a chowrie and standing upon [a vehicle]. (21)
And on the left, one should place Aniruddha of Hari, dressed in crimson garments, dark as a sapphire gem, and standing while holding a chowrie.
All three of these, moreover, should be fashioned adorned with various ornaments, wearing crowns of priceless jewels, and captivating through their youth. (23)
Then, one should sequentially place the incarnations of Hari upon the eight filaments; two on each of the eight, thus making sixteen.
One should place the Buddha Vāmana on the eastern filament in front; for both of these are dark as a rain-cloud, compassionate, and celibate students (brahmacārins). || 25 ||
Wearing white garments, holding a full-blown lotus in their right hands and displaying the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) with their left hands, they are peaceful and wear sacred threads.
Then one should place Kalki and Paraśurāma in the south-eastern corner; there, Kalki has a sword in his hand, while the other likewise has an axe in his hand.

Both should be made fair-complexioned with copper-colored eyes, wearing matted hair and white garments; they should be depicted as wearing sacred threads, having abandoned anger and great violence. (28)
One should install Hayagrīva and Varāha on the southern filament; Hayagrīva has the face of a horse, a human body, and four arms. (29)
Holding a conch and other attributes, golden-hued, and wearing divine white garments, Varāha shall have the face of a boar, a human body, and four arms. (30)
Holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, and likewise wearing yellow garments, he should be depicted as honey-tawny in color, or else with two arms.
Then, one should place the Fish and the Tortoise on the filaments in the southwest; from the waist downwards they have those respective forms, but above that, they are human in shape.
Both should be depicted with dark and beautiful bodies, adorned with ornaments, and holding a conch in the left hand and a mace in the right hand.
One should place Dhanvantari and Nṛsiṃha on the western filament; Dhanvantari is clad in white garments, fair-limbed, and holds a jar of nectar.
Nṛsiṃha, however, has the face of a lion, a human body, and is endowed with a mane; he should be blue-lotus colored, two-armed, and bearing a mace and a discus. (35)
In the northwest (Vāyu), one should place both Haṃsa and Dattātreya, wearing matted hair, dressed as ascetics, white in color, and holding a staff and a water-pot in their hands.
Then one should place Vyāsa upon the northern filament, and thereafter Gaṇapati; there, Vyāsa is large-eyed, dark-complexioned, and dressed in white garments.
He should be depicted with two arms, holding the Vedas, wearing beautiful tawny matted hair, clad in a white sacred thread, and provided with a pavitra ring.
Gajāsya and Ekadanta, the red-hued Gaṇapati, shall be wearing red garments and possessing a serpent as his sacred thread. (39)
Pot-bellied and four-armed, he holds a noose, a goad, and a boon-granting gesture; and with one hand, he holds a beautiful pen for writing a manuscript.
Then the worshipper should place Kapila in the northeast on the filaments, and likewise the sage Sanatkumāra, who is a perpetual celibate student.
He should be depicted as tawny with white limbs, wearing beautiful white garments, holding a lotus and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in his two hands, and possessing a peaceful form.
The worshipper should represent the sage Sanatkumāra as a five-year-old child, naked, and wearing a few matted locks. (43)
Having thus established the deities upon the filaments of the lotus, the worshipper should place the attendants within the eight petals.
One should first install Viṣvaksena and Garuḍa there in the east; then, following the sequence from the right, one should install Prabala and Bala.
One should install Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Sunanda, and Nanda, as well as Śrutadeva, Jayanta, Vijaya, and Jaya. (46)
Then one should install Pracaṇḍa, Caṇḍa, Puṣpadanta, and Sātvata—two by two—in this manner, sequentially, in the eight locations.
All these [deities] should be made four-armed, holding a conch, a discus, a lotus, and a mace; they are crowned, dark-complexioned, dressed in yellow garments, and well-adorned.
One should place the eight Siddhis within the internal intervals; [surrounded] by those skilled in playing various auspicious musical instruments in due order. (49)
Aṇimā, laghimā, prāpti, prākāmya, mahimā, as well as īśitā, vaśitā, and the eighth, kāmāvasāyitā. || 50 ||
These [deities] should be depicted with a golden complexion, adorned with all ornaments, holding flutes, lutes, and other instruments in their hands, and dressed in variegated garments.
Then, one should place the Vedas and the Śāstras upon the eight tips of the petals; there, he should place the Vedas in the cardinal directions and the Śāstras in the intermediate directions.
In the east, one should place the Ṛgveda, white in color, holding a rosary, dwarfish, pot-bellied, gentle, with lotus-like eyes, and clad in white garments.
One should place the Yajurveda in the southern direction; its body is slender-waisted, with reddish-brown eyes and a thick neck, yellow in color and clad in beautiful red garments.
Holding a rosary of beads in his left hand and a vajra in his right, he bears the Sāmaveda on his back; he is tall and possesses the splendor of the sun.
One should place [the deity] holding a rosary in the right hand and a small drum (ḍamaru) in the left hand, wearing golden garments, possessing large eyes, and intent upon singing.

One should place Atharvan in the north, white-bodied and dressed in blue garments, holding a rosary in his left hand and a khaṭvāṅga staff in his right hand; he possesses the vigor of fire, has copper-colored eyes, and is likewise advanced in age.
In the southeast corner, one should place Dharmaśāstra upon a lotus seat, white in color, holding in his two arms a pearl necklace and likewise an incomparable [balance].
One should place Sāṃkhya, who has long hair and nails and is pot-bellied, in the southwest.
And he was white, holding a rosary and a staff in his two hands.
Then one should assign to the wind [the deity] Yoga, who is golden in color and thin-waisted, with both hands placed upon his thighs and his gaze fixed on the tip of his own nose.
Likewise, on the northeast (Īśāna), one should place the white Vanamālin for five nights, holding a rosary and a plow in his two hands.
The garments of these four should be white, fine, and thick; likewise, their eyes should be as broad as lotus petals.

In the intervals between the [deities] at the front, one should place the great sages together with their wives while reciting the Vedas, following the sequence starting from the east and the southeast.
He [beheld] Marīci joined with Kalā, Atri with Anasūyā, Aṅgiras together with Śraddhā, and Pulastya with Havirbhū.
One should place Pulaha together with Gati, Kratu together with Kriyā, Bhṛgu together with Khyāti, and Vasiṣṭha together with Arundhatī.
All of these should be depicted with two arms, possessing matted hair and beards, emaciated ascetics holding staffs and water-pots.
Outside the lotus, one should place the eight guardians of the quarters (dikpālas), headed by Indra, along with their vehicles, in the cardinal and intermediate directions as appropriate.
In the east, one should place the four-armed Indra, mounted upon Airāvata, resembling gold in color and holding a thunderbolt, a goad, a lotus, and a boon-granting gesture.
Clad in beautiful saffron-colored garments, adorned with various ornaments, with reddish outer corners of the eyes and large eyes, he was endowed with all the auspicious marks.
In the southeast corner, one should assign Agni, who is copper-colored and four-armed, holding in his hands a trident, a spear, a *sruk* ladle, and a *sruva* ladle.
Seated upon a golden chariot drawn by four parrots, with Vāyu as his charioteer, he has three eyes, wears smoky-colored garments, and possesses tawny beard, matted hair, and eyes.

One should place Yama to the south, dark-complexioned and clad in golden garments, four-armed, holding a staff, a sword, an axe, and a noose, mounted upon an intoxicated buffalo, and adorned with various ornaments. (72)
One should place Nairṛta, who has upright hair and deformed eyes, in the southwest; he holds a sword and a noose, possesses two arms, and has a man as his vehicle.
He had a tawny beard, was smoke-colored, and was draped in black garments; he was richly adorned with many ornaments of gold and struck fear into those who were not devotees of Viṣṇu.
Then, in the west, [he saw] Varuṇa, possessing the luster of a sapphire, wearing white garments, four-armed, and adorned with pearl necklaces.
One should install [the deity] mounted on a chariot drawn by seven swans, holding a noose with two arms and bearing a jewel-vessel and a conch shell with the other two.
In the northwest, one should place Vāyu, who is greenish-yellow in color, two-armed, clad in black garments, seated upon a spotted deer, with disheveled hair, a wide-open mouth, and bearing a banner.
In the north, one should place Kubera, who is golden-colored and four-armed, bearing a mace, a spear, a trident, and a vessel of jewels.
He was clad in blue garments, possessed a beard, and was seated upon a palanquin; he had tawny, small eyes, wore many ornaments, and was clad in armor.
Then, in the northeast, one should place Mūla-Rudra as Ardhanārīśvara; Pārvatī is to be fashioned in the left half, and Śaṅkara there in the right half.
On the half of the Lord (Śiva), a mass of matted hair adorned with the moon should be fashioned; on the half of Umā, a tilaka mark should be made, as well as a parting of the hair on the forehead.
One half is smeared with ashes and the other half is adorned with saffron; one half has a snake as a sacred thread and the other half is decorated with necklaces.
On the left half, a full breast covered by a bodice should be fashioned; on the waist, a golden girdle, and on the foot, a golden anklet.
He wears a saffron-colored garment, his two hands are adorned with bracelets, and he holds a trident and a rosary, both marked with jeweled rings.
On the right half [of the body], a snake should be made as a girdle; the garment is an elephant hide; and the two hands, adorned with serpent-bracelets, hold a mirror and a blue lotus.
In this manner, the worshipper should install Mahādeva, who has the bull as his vehicle; in this way, he should perform the installation of the lords of the eight directions.
Then, outside the city, the worshipper should establish the eight planets in their respective directions, situated upon their own respective vehicles and chariots.
There, in the eastern direction, one should place the Sun-god, clad in yellow garments, the color of vermilion, two-armed, holding a lotus in his hand, and seated upon a chariot.
This chariot of exceeding brilliance has a single wheel with twelve spokes; seven horses of greenish-gold hue are yoked on its left side. (89)
Then, in the southeast corner, Bhṛgu should be installed; he is white, dressed in white garments, two-armed, holding a staff and a water-pot, and of gentle appearance.
Seated upon a golden chariot drawn by ten horses of variegated colors, one should likewise place Bhauma (Mars) on the right, who is red and clad in red garments.
One should fashion a golden chariot for him, having four arms and holding a mace, a spear, a trident, and the gesture of granting boons, and it should be yoked to eight reddish-brown horses.
And Rāhu is in the south-western corner, blue-clad and four-armed; he has a terrifying face, is of the nature of darkness, and holds a shield, a sword, a spear, and a trident.
He should be placed upon a chariot drawn by eight horses with the color of bees; and Saturn, possessing a luster like a sapphire, should be stationed in the west.
Bearing a bow and a trident, two-armed, with downcast eyes and dressed in black garments, he stood upon a chariot made of black iron, yoked to eight brindled horses.
Then, in the northwest corner, one should place the Moon, clad in white garments, white in color, holding a mace in his hand, two-armed, and seated upon a chariot.
In his chariot, which consists of three wheels each with a hundred spokes and is made of water, there are ten horses, white as jasmine, yoked on both sides.

In the north, he should be depicted as two-armed, gentle, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and reddish-brown in color; he stands upon a golden chariot drawn by eight tawny horses and wears green garments.

And in the northeast, the Guru should be established, golden-hued and clad in white garments; he has two arms, lotus-like eyes, and holds a staff and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu); he is seated upon an excellent chariot made of gold, drawn by eight white horses. 99.
The worshipper should thus install all the deities of the limbs within the spaces from the pericarp to the edge of the city on the mountain, in their proper sequence.
One should install the Vaibhava forms of Vāsudeva and the Aṅgadevas; alternatively, one may install betel nuts, flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for Constructing the Worship Mandala," in the *Kriyāyoga* section of the *Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya*, within the second *Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 27.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having sipped water (ācamana) and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), he, with a composed mind, should offer salutations to his chosen deity and others, and then proclaim the place and time. || 1 ||

Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform the worship of Vāsudeva for the sake of accomplishing the exclusive Dharma," one should then carry out the ritual of ritual placement (nyāsa).
In the rite of Nyāsa, the mantras are to be known as the twelve-syllable Gāyatrī of Viṣṇu, the eight-syllable Nārāyaṇa, and the six-syllable [mantra] of Viṣṇu.

These [mantras] are prescribed for the twice-born; however, for others here, there are three: the eight-syllabled Vāsudeva, the five-syllabled Hari, and the six-syllabled Keśava—these are approved for ritual placement (nyāsa) and fire-offerings (homa).

Then, one should perform all the ritual depositions (nyāsas) upon the limbs of the image of Śrī Viṣṇu as if they were one's own limbs, using those respective mantras; thereafter, one should wipe the image with a cloth.
Having placed the water-pot on his own left side and invoked the sacred waters (tīrthas) therein, he should worship it with offerings such as perfumes and flowers.
Having sprinkled the materials for worship and oneself with that water, and having worshipped the conch and the bell, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having burned away the body of sinful nature with the internal fire and wind, one should remain steadfast and contemplate the identity of one's own pure self with Brahman.
Then, assuming the form of the imperishable Brahman, one should meditate with an undistracted mind upon the Lord Rādhākṛṣṇa within the heart while performing breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Visualizing the navel-lotus situated with its face downward like a plantain flower, one should bring the downward-moving breath (apāna) into union with the upward-moving breath (prāṇa). 10.

Having brought it [the bee] to the lotus stalk along with that [lotus], one should then draw that lotus upward; then, as it rises intensely, it reaches the heart. And there, within the space of the heart, it blossoms and shines forth.
There, amidst that mass of splendor, one should meditate upon the Lord of Śrī Rādhikā, who is most beautiful to behold and peaceful, possessing a radiance even greater than that.
One should meditate upon Him, whose form consists of divine consciousness, whether He is seated or standing, possessing the age of a youth and as beautiful as ten million Cupids.
He was characterized by divine limbs that were perfectly proportioned to his form; his body was as pure white as the autumnal moon, and he possessed two long and beautiful arms.
His lotus-feet possess toes that are beautiful with soft soles slightly reddened, while the moon is put to shame by the luster of his high, ruddy, and glossy nails.
Possessing the beauty of a pair of swan-like feet adorned with tinkling small bells and anklets, he has a pair of well-rounded calves and shanks that are beautiful with symmetrical knees and thighs.
The beauty of his waist was graced by yellow garments bound with a girdle of excellent gems; his belly was high, and within its center was a deep navel marked by three folds. (17)
His chest was broad and lofty, adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark; it was decorated with dangling clusters of flowers, half-clusters, and ornaments such as the *devacchanda*.
He wore garlands of various fragrant flowers and a golden sacred thread; his hands were adorned with bracelets that shone like full-blown red lotuses.
He wore a ring of many excellent gems that shone upon his fingers with subtle joints, and he was sounding a flute that was sweet and captivating to all.

He had broad shoulders, well-concealed collarbones, and great arms radiant with the luster of armlets; he wore a forest garland from which the humming of bees, greedy for its fragrance, was resonating.
His chest shone with a noble necklace and the Kaustubha gem, which were as radiant as conch shells; his jaw was beautiful, and his lower lip possessed the luster of a ripe bimba fruit.
His face resembles the full moon shining with a digit of white smiles; his beautiful nose has the appearance of a sesame flower. || 23 ||
He wore shimmering earrings in the shape of sea-monsters upon his symmetrical ears, and on top of his ears were ear-ornaments consisting of clusters of variegated flowers.
The beauty of his cheeks was illuminated by the moonlight of his even and fine teeth, and his eyes were lovely with slightly reddish corners, as broad as lotus petals.
With broad shoulders and a broad forehead, his eyebrows were like the bow of Kāma; his hair was curved, fine, black, glossy, and enchanting. (26)
Wearing a crown inlaid with various precious gems as a crest-ornament, he gazes upon his own [devotee] with love, gracious and with an affectionate glance.
Having thus meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, one should then contemplate Rādhā at his left side—two-armed, with limbs as fair as gold, and wearing pure garments dyed saffron.
Her ears were adorned with shimmering jewel-ornaments and fine cloth; she was a young maiden with eyes like those of a fawn and full, high, firm breasts. (29)
She has a slender waist and broad hips, adorned with a jeweled girdle; she wears many divine ornaments, and her face, like a full-blown lotus, bears a gentle smile.
Her hands were radiant with jeweled rings, armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments; her lotus-feet shone with tinkling anklets and girdles of swan-patterned bells.
Her forehead was adorned with a beautiful saffron tilaka upon her broad brow; she had lips like the bimba fruit and lovely cheeks, and a mālatī flower was woven into her braided hair.
Having thus meditated upon Rādhikā, who gazes at the Lord with love while holding a lotus in her hand, one should worship the Lord there together with her.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Meditation on the Forms of Śrī Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa," in the section on the Yoga of Action within the *Śrī Vāsudeva-Māhātmya*, in the second Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 28 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having worshipped Him with various kinds of mental offerings, the devotee, having invoked Him, should establish Him in the image by means of the *sthāpana-mudrā*.
Then, having invoked the deities of the limbs individually with their respective mantras, or by means of the name-mantras, he should well-establish them.
One should sound a bell or other musical instruments, or make the sound of clapping; then, as if he had just awakened from sleep, one should have him perform the cleansing of his teeth.

One should offer this water for the feet (pādya) to the Lord, consisting of *śyāmāka*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, *dūrvā*, and lotus flowers together with water; thereafter, one should offer the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*).
One should place sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, flowers, the tips of darbha grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, barley, and dūrvā grass into the arghya vessel filled with water.
One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) scented with nutmeg, clove, cardamom, kaṅkola, and uśīra; thereafter, one should bathe Hari.
First, one should perform an oil massage with fragrant flower oil; thereafter, one should perform an exfoliation with a paste of aromatic substances.
One should, with an undistracted mind, bathe Hari with milk, curds, clarified butter, honey, and sugar, each with its respective mantra.
Having caused him to bathe with fragrant, pure, and warm water, one should quickly worship him with perfumes and other offerings upon the bathing throne.

Then, having discarded the withered flowers and other offerings to the north, the twice-born should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with the *Rājana* and other *Sāman* chants, or with the *Mahāpuruṣavidyā*, the *Śrīsūkta*, and the *Viṣṇusūkta*. || 10 ||
Women and Śūdras who have been initiated should perform the consecration ceremony with the thousand names of Hari or with one hundred and eight names.
Then, having wiped him with a cloth, one should, out of great love, clothe him in priceless garments, as well as Rādhā and the others according to one's means.

One should offer a fine, white, and auspicious sacred thread (upavīta) to the Blessed One; and one should cause him, together with his attendants, to wear ornaments of jewels, gold, and other precious materials.
According to the season and the appropriate place, one should apply the proper tilaka and unguents with sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and other such substances as is fitting.
Having adorned Rādhikā with appropriate ornaments, he should apply a tilaka to both Rādhikā and Patralekhā using saffron and unbroken grains of rice.
Then, having shown him a mirror, one should worship him with flower garlands, crests, and the like, and with a thousand sprouts and leaves of tulasī.
Or else, with a Tulasī leaf or a flower, he should worship the Lord while reciting each Vaiṣṇava name, ending in the dative case and preceded by "namaḥ. || 17 ||
Then, having offered fragrant powders and auspicious substances, one should burn incense, such as the ten-ingredient *daśāṅga* or *amṛtā* and other varieties.
One should prepare a lamp with ghee, illuminated by two wicks; having prepared it according to one's capacity, one should offer pure, great food offerings (mahānaivedya).

One should place on a four-legged stand samyāva, milk-rice, cakes, śaṣkulī, khaṇḍalaḍḍuka, pūrikā, polikā, rice with mung beans, various side dishes, as well as curd, milk, ghee, and other such items. || 20 ||
Then, one should feed him with affection, offering water for drinking in the midst of the meal; and when half a muhūrta has passed, one should give water for washing the hands.
Having set aside the remnants of the Lord for the deities beginning with Viṣvaksena elsewhere, one should wipe that spot clean for one's own sake.

Then one should offer a mouth-perfume, a prepared roll of betel leaf (*tāmbūla-vīṭikā*), combined with areca nut powder (*pūga-cūrṇa*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), cardamom (*elā*), nutmeg (*jātīja*), and other such ingredients. (23)

Having offered fruits such as coconuts and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's capacity, one should perform the great lustration ceremony (mahānīrājana) preceded by song and instrumental music.
Then, having offered handfuls of flowers, he should praise Him with that very hymn; thereafter, he should perform the chanting of the Name, singing and dancing before Him.
Having performed this for a moment and having circumambulated [the deity], he should prostrate himself like a staff on the ground to the right of that [image].
A man should perform a prostration consisting of either eight limbs or five limbs; however, O best of sages, a woman should perform only the five-limbed prostration, and not otherwise.
With the two feet, the two hands, the two knees, the chest, the head, the eyes, the speech, and the mind—this is declared to be the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma).
With both arms, mind, head, speech, and sight—this is the five-limbed prostration; these two are the most excellent among forms of worship.
"O Lord, protect me who am afraid of saṃsāra and have sought refuge in you. Having thus prayed, one should perform the daily recitation of the Vedas according to one's ability. (30)

Having meditated and respectfully received with his head the remainder offered by Him, he should re-establish Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, who were previously invoked, within the lotus of his heart; then he should dismiss the secondary deities to their respective places.
Having laid down an image of Hari in a basket, on a bed, or in a temple, and having closed the door, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite.
Having distributed the pleasing food of Hari among his dependents and having eaten himself, he should pass the remainder of the day with the recitation of stories about Him and other such activities.
Whoever worships Viṣṇu daily with devotion by means of this prescribed rite of great worship shall become his attendant.
Having ascended a divine, radiant celestial chariot desired by the gods, the worshipper, with a divine body, goes to the abode of Hari known as Goloka.
Even he who worships him day after day with the intention of obtaining rewards shall attain his desired dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa. || 36 ||
Thus, one who is unable to perform the full ritual of worship together with Rādhā should worship Hari alone with whatever offerings are available, performed with devotion.
A twice-born man should worship Śrī Rādhākṛṣṇa with the twelve-syllable mantra, while others may do so with the name-mantra; in this matter, devotion alone is the giver of perfection.
On the eleventh day, especially during festivals such as the birth of Hari, a great worship (mahāpūjā) must be performed by all Vaiṣṇavas according to their own capacity. (39)
Even he who performs merely the consecration of a temple built by another shall indeed attain a universal sovereignty, with all his sins destroyed. (40)
A wealthy man who causes a beautiful and sturdy temple to be built for Hari shall indeed attain a kingdom over even the three worlds, free from all thorns.
That man who increases the continuity of worship by providing for its maintenance shall surely attain great happiness in the world of Viṣṇu. || 42 ||
He who causes these three—the consecration, the temple, and the worship—to be performed here certainly attains a sovereignty equal to that of Vāsudeva.
He who steals the property of Hari, whether it was acquired by himself or by another, shall indeed suffer the torments of Yama in hell for one kalpa.
The doer, the one who causes it to be done, the helper, and the one who approves—of these four, there is indeed a share in the fruit of both the well-done and its opposite. (45)
Thus, O Nārada, the rule for the yoga of action has been proclaimed by me; by means of this, the absolute dharma may be accomplished here for those whose souls are inclined toward it. 46.
If one contemplates sense objects in the mind while performing external worship of Hari, even with a great abundance of materials, one shall not obtain the fruit as it has been described.
Restraining his own mind from wandering here and there among vulgar pleasures, one who desires liberation should become diligent in the worship of Viṣṇu. (48)

Even those who observe the great vows, who are performers of abundant austerities, who have studied the Vedas, and who are possessed of intelligence—even they, though practicing Sāṃkhya and Yoga, do not attain perfection without the worship of Hari. (49)

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Worship of Śrī Vāsudeva," within the *Kriyāyoga* section of the *Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya*, in the second *Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 29 ||
Skanda said: Having thus heard the procedure for the worship of Vāsudeva, Nārada, being pleased, questioned again that supreme teacher of sages. (1)
Nārada said: "The Lord has correctly described the yoga of action, which yields great fruit; it must be performed with a single-minded focus by those desiring perfection. (2)
O true guru, even for the wise, the restraint of the mind there is difficult; how much more so, then, for men on earth whose nature is bound to karma? (3)
Without him, however, the worship of Hari does not bestow the desired fruit; therefore, you should also tell me the means for his subjugation.
Skanda said: Thus questioned by the sage, that lord of sages, Nārāyaṇa—the all-seeing friend of Nara—spoke to that Nārada.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O sage, you speak the truth; the mind possesses great power. Even when it is conquered, those lacking discernment do not place trust in it, as they would in an enemy.
For embodied beings, there is no enemy equal to the mind; indeed, through the practice of meditation on Viṣṇu, that [mind], being free from defect, becomes pacified.
This [mind], being difficult to restrain like an untamed horse, is therefore brought under control by men endowed with dispassion through excellent means. (8)
O noble-minded one, there are many means in this regard; yet among them, the practice of the eightfold yoga is the best, as it yields immediate results. (9)

O Brahmin, the restraints (yamas), the observances (niyamas), postures (āsanas), the excellent self-restraint (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna) as the seventh limb, and absorption (samādhi) is declared to be the eighth, according to the sequence of yoga.
In that regard, non-violence, celibacy, truthfulness, non-stealing, and non-possessiveness—these five are declared to be the restraints (yamās), which should be practiced with diligent effort. (11)
Purity, austerity, contentment, self-study, and the worship of Viṣṇu—these five are considered the observances (niyamas) as the second limb [of yoga]. (12)
O Sage, when one has abandoned the restlessness of the limbs and remains in a state of ease, that is called an *āsana*, such as the *svastika* and others, which conquers the affliction of dualities.
The retention of the vital breaths, which are flowing everywhere, in a single location according to the method taught by the Guru—that is called prāṇāyāma. (14)

When the breath moves, the mind moves; when it is steady, the mind is steady. Therefore, this [practice] should always be practiced in a suitable place through inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka). || 15 ||
The inward withdrawal of the functions of the mind and the senses from their respective objects is declared to be *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal). (16)
The fixing of the mind together with the vital breath upon the form of Vāsudeva in any one of the locations beginning with the navel is called *dhāraṇā*.
The contemplation of each individual limb of the Lord, such as His lotus feet and so forth, separately and individually, is proclaimed as *dhyāna*.
That cessation of both breath and mind through intense love for Hari is declared to be *samādhi*, which is desired by yogis. (19)
Indeed, when these eight limbs have been mastered under a perfected and true guru, yoga—characterized by the ripening of samādhi—is accomplished for men.
"Know this, O Nārada: for men who desire liberation, there is no other such perfect means for the restraint of the mind. (21)
For a yogi, there is never any fear whatsoever from Madana—the great enemy of ascetics who agitates even the cosmic egg.
Having determined the very time of his departure, the knower of yoga thus casts off his own body by means of samādhi through his own independent power.
Pressing the anus with the two heels and drawing up the air situated in the two feet very gradually, one leads that [air] to the seat of death.
Meditating on Keśava with the mind and reciting that six-syllabled mantra, he then leads this vital air (vāyu) to the abode of Prajāpati.
Then, the knower of yoga, devoted to Vāsudeva, leads the wind from the navel to the heart, the chest, and the throat, up to the *bhrukuṭi* (the space between the eyebrows).
In each of these six locations individually, the yogi practices the restraint and the release of his own vital breath, mind, and senses until he attains mastery over them. (27)
Leaving behind each stage as it is mastered, one proceeds to the next higher station; once the sixth station is attained, there is no further exertion required for its practice.
Then, having closed the seven apertures and having led the vital breath—conjoined with the senses and the mind—to the palate, that knower of yoga proceeds to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Therefore, having abandoned the latent impressions (vāsanā) of all things that are composed of illusion, he, with his mind fixed solely on Vāsudeva, casts off his own body.
Then, having approached the abode of the Blessed One Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which transcends darkness, he, possessing a divine body, rejoices while serving Him. || 31 ||
Thus, O Brahmin, this compendium of the Yogaśāstra has been told to you; having conquered your own mind by means of it, worship Him at all times. (32)

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Eightfold Yoga," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya of the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: Having heard all these righteous words of the Blessed One exactly as they were spoken, the sage, free from doubt, bowed with palms joined in reverence and spoke to him. (1)
Nārada said: O Blessed One, by your grace all my doubts have been destroyed; I have now clearly understood the majesty of Vāsudeva.
For some time here, performing penance together with you and constantly hearing the teachings on knowledge and other matters, I shall bring my own self to maturity.
Skanda said: Having spoken thus, Nārada was then commended by him; he remained there performing austerities for a thousand divine years.
And day by day, at the appropriate time, he listened from the mouth of Hari; thus, the king of yogis attained maturity therein through the knowledge of dharma and other means.
He attained supreme affection for Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the soul of all, and remained constantly devoted to singing His qualities as the foremost of the Bhāgavatas.
Then, pleased with that perfected yogi who had attained supreme devotion, the Blessed One, the benefactor of all embodied beings, spoke to him.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "O great sage, you have attained perfection today; go and act for the welfare of the world. You ought to propagate the religion of exclusive devotion everywhere."
Skanda said: Having accepted that command of the Teacher of the World upon his head, he departed; then, bowing down and standing with palms joined in reverence, he praised him.

Nārada said: Salutations, salutations to You, O Blessed One, Teacher of the World, Nārāyaṇa of divine and non-material form! You are the mine of infinite auspicious qualities; may You be exceedingly gracious toward me, Your servant. 10.

You are Vāsudeva, the abode of the universe; for the welfare of the world, you perform ascetic penance. O Lord of the lords of yoga, established in tranquility, you are the sovereign who delights in the Self, the true guru of the supreme *parahaṃsas*.

You are the all-pervading bull among sages, the imperishable Self; you are the controller of individual souls and lords alike. You are the witness, the Great Puruṣa, independent of any other self; even Time became great from the knitting of your brow.

O Lord, you perform the play of creation and so forth for the worlds through the nature of the Māyā-puruṣa; nevertheless, you are indeed a non-doer, for you are the attributeless, the Infinite, the Supreme Brahman, and higher than the highest.

You are the Truth, self-luminous, of inconceivable power; you are the embodiment of Brahman, whose form is contemplated by the wise; O Great Teacher of the vast vows, Lord of Great Sages, whose majesty destroys the pride of Kandarpa. 14.
Those who are well known as the enemies of ascetics—anger, passion, envy, greed, and the like—even they are never able to besiege this hermitage; for this is indeed your majesty.

Consisting of Vedic meters, consisting of knowledge, the path of immortality, the very soul of dharma, and the nourisher of the creation of dharma; you are the Great Soul who has uprooted the creation of adharma—indestructible, imperishable, and the kinsman of the unmanifest.

All your actions, O Lord, are indeed devoid of attributes, for you are of faultless form and yourself without attributes. You, the Sovereign, are to be worshipped by those desiring virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and by those seeking liberation, O Protector. You alone are capable of protecting us from the great fear of time, illusion, sin, and the cycle of worldly existence. Disregarding the offenses of your devotees, you are truly the Greatly Compassionate One, affectionate toward your devotees.

O Lord, whoever at the time of death remembers even the mere name or the form of You who have assumed an incarnation, is instantly liberated from the terrible mass of great sins and swiftly ascends to heaven.

But that man who, having abandoned you, becomes attached here to this body composed of the three elements, or to bodily things—such as wife, children, kinsmen, and wealth—is indeed a fool deceived by illusion. (20)
Only this human body is fit for devotion to you, which even those dwelling in heaven desire; indeed, I know that for one devoid of devotion to you, even the happiness of heaven is equal to hell. (21)

You perform penance for the happiness of the three worlds; even therein, Your grace toward the inhabitants of Bhārata is exceedingly great, since You shine forth, wandering about, having manifested an incarnation here.

Those who do not take you as their sole refuge here are considered ungrateful in the scriptures; therefore, let there be satisfaction for you in me, who resolutely and eternally take you alone as my refuge. (23)

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-Māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-Khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: Having thus praised that Lord Īśāna, O Brahmin, Nārada then departed from there for the hermitage of Vyāsa, known as Śamyāprāsa, which was located at the very beginning.
Honored by him with respect through rising from his seat, offering a seat, and other such gestures, he [the sage] taught the definitive Dharma to that seeker who desired to know it.
Then, having gone to the assembly of Brahmā while Brahmā was listening, the sage instructed the gods, the ancestors, and the great seers who were present there.
O Sage, while staying there, Bhāskara again heard this entire dharma from Nārada, which he had previously heard from Nārāyaṇa.
He spoke with reverence to the Vālakhilyas, who were his foremost followers: "They have subdued Indra and the other gods assembled on Mount Meru."
O best of the twice-born, having heard this dharma from them, the sage Asita went at one time to the world of the ancestors and recounted it to the Pitṛs.
Your ancestors, beginning with Aryaman, spoke thus to King Śantanu; he, in turn, related it exactly as it was to his son Bhīṣma.
At the conclusion of the Bharata war, he too, lying upon a bed of arrows, spoke to the inquiring Dharmarāja in the midst of a vast assembly.
Having heard that, O best of sages, Nārada also remained respectfully in the assembly; he spoke to Śaṅkara on Kailāsa, and he [Śaṅkara] spoke to me.
O Brahmin, I have told this to you because you asked as one who abides in dharma; for my father indeed said to me, "This must be given to a worthy recipient."
Wherever this majesty of the Lord of the Sātvatas was heard, each person there cultivated supreme devotion toward Him for the sake of their own liberation.
The royal sage Yudhiṣṭhira, having heard the majesty of the son of Devakī as proclaimed by Bhīṣma, rejoiced together with his brothers.
Having heard that his maternal cousin was the cause of all causes, the high-minded one sank into an ocean of wonder.
The king considered the entire array beginning with Vāsudeva, as well as the incarnations such as the Boar (Vārāha) and others, to belong to this very Lord of Ramā.
Thereupon, O best of the twice-born, the king, together with his younger brother, became exceedingly devoted to Kṛṣṇa, who possesses both divine and human forms.
Having heard this story, all the Brahmanas, kings, and celestial sages who were present there in the assembly were filled with wonder. || 16 ||
Having realized that Kṛṣṇa alone is the supreme Brahman in human form, they took refuge in devotion toward him, bowing down to him with reverence.
Such is his greatness; therefore, O one of noble mind, you too should worship that very Vāsudeva with devotion and with your whole being. (18)
This *Śrīvāsudevamāhātmya*, which pacifies evil tendencies and increases devotion to the Lord, has been narrated by me to you. (19)
O Brahmin, those narratives which I have previously recounted to you here in this Purāṇa—their essence has been extracted and brought forth by churning them.
O sinless one, this is indeed the essence of the Vedas and Upaniṣads, of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, of the entire Pañcarātra, and of the Dharmaśāstra.
This supreme auspiciousness, which bestows wealth, fame, and long life, was sung directly by the Blessed One; it destroys all that is inauspicious. (22)
Whoever hears this merit, whoever recites it, or whoever reads it, their intellect shall become unwavering and pure in Vāsudeva.
Those men who are his single-minded devotees become of the nature of Brahman; at the end, they go to the abode of Brahman, which is beyond darkness.
By this, one who seeks dharma obtains dharma, and one who desires pleasure obtains pleasure; one who seeks wealth attains wealth, and one who seeks liberation attains supreme liberation. || 25 ||
The seeker of knowledge shall obtain knowledge, and the sick person shall be freed from disease; by the mere hearing of this, there shall be the destruction of all sins. (26)
By hearing this, a Brahmin shall attain the splendor of Brahmā, a Kṣatriya shall obtain lordship over men, a Vaiśya shall gain wealth, and a Śūdra shall obtain happiness. (27)
Having heard this, a king going to battle shall obtain victory; a woman shall obtain good fortune, and a maiden her desired husband. (28)
From the mere hearing and glorification of this crest-jewel among all scriptural collections, whatever desire a person may long for, that very thing he shall obtain. (29)
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, always reciting this with devotion, you should worship Him who is kind to His devotees with your body, speech, and mind. (30)

Sauti said: Having drunk this nectar-like speech issuing from the lotus-face of Mahāsena, Sāvarṇi cultivated devotion toward the son of Vasudeva, who is Brahman in human form and the source of all auspiciousness.

And you all, who are knowers of the Nigamas and Agamas, remaining established in your own dharma, worship that one Lord Śrī Vāsudeva of noble fame, the God who is devoted to Brahman and worthy of adoration. || 32 ||
Salutations to Vāsudeva, the Lord of the realm of Goloka, whose form is a mass of light, and who increases the bliss of devotion. 33.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Tradition of the Text," in the Śrī Vāsudeva-māhātmya, within the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Thus ends the Vāsudevamāhātmya in the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. 9.
Thus ends the second section, the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. || 2 ||
